Compiled by the Śramaṇa Xifu of Jingshui Monastery, Volume One of the *Essential Compendium of the Profound Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra*.

Since the end of the Dahuang era, after I had ceased my lectures on the Vinaya, I have frequently traveled to the capital, where I have repeatedly attended the assemblies for the study of the Sūtras and Śāstras.
For many years, I have braved both frost and snow, undaunted by cold or heat. However, my mental faculties remained dim and clouded;

thus, as I toured the dharma-seats of various predecessors several times, I recorded whatever few well-spoken words I could grasp. I have compiled these into a single body of doctrine, hoping merely that they may be easily consulted.

Regarding this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, there have been sixteen translations throughout its history from beginning to end; if one includes both authentic and spurious versions, there are seventeen.

However, if we speak only of complete editions, there are six translations in total. Among these six translations that have been transmitted to the land of Han, three versions are currently in circulation:
the *Zhengfa* (Correct Dharma), the *Miaofa* (Sublime Dharma), and the *Tianpin* (Supplemented) *Fahua*. The version being expounded here now is the latter.

In the seventh year of the Hongshi era of the Qin dynasty, the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva translated the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (The Lotus Sutra) in either seven or eight fascicles, consisting of sixty thousand nine hundred and fifty-four words. Regarding the commentaries composed for it, there have been more than nineteen schools over time;
those that have been widely transmitted in the world are those of Tiantai, Jiguo, Jiexiang, and Cien. This is the Tiantai commentary.

The titles [of the commentaries] are: the *Mingwenju* (Explanations of Names and Phrases), the *Jiguomingzan* (Record of the Country’s Name and Praise), the *Jiaxiang Shumingyiji* (Jiaxiang’s Commentary on the Meaning of the Names), and the *Cien Shuxuanzan* (Cien’s Commentary on the Profound Praise).

The one used by lecturers today is the Cien commentary. In the Western Regions, there were a thousand masters of śāstras who composed treatises to explain the *Lotus Sūtra*, such as the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu.
In the land of Tang, there were a hundred masters of commentaries who composed commentaries to explain the *Lotus Sūtra*.
This refers to the Venerable Cien (Ci'en). Among the various masters of antiquity, there have been many who categorized and analyzed this sutra.

For now, let us consider how Master Dao’an categorized all the sutras into three parts. This was in implicit agreement with the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* by the Bodhisattva Bandhuprabha in India, which, when explaining this very sutra, divided it into three major sections:
the first chapter constitutes the introduction (*nidāna*). As for "introduction": ... [The remainder of the text follows] ... [End of excerpt]
It begins with Śāriputra; that is, the śrāvakas of the three capacities whose Mahāyāna nature has already matured.

The World-Honored One assembles followers of fifteen categories and first discourses on the *Anantārthasūtra*, which is the essence of the Lotus. Subsequently, he enters meditative concentration, rains flowers, and causes the earth to tremble;
he emits light to illuminate the realms, Maitreya poses questions, and Mañjuśrī provides the answers—all of which serve as the gradual preliminaries for expounding the true teaching.

The first part, from the beginning up to the "Expedient Means" chapter, is called the Introductory Section (*nidāna*). The second part, from the "Expedient Means" chapter through the "Bestowal of Prophecies upon Those Still Training and Those Beyond Training" chapter, constitutes the second section, the Main Body (*samyak-siddhānta*).

This refers to the period after the Buddha emerged from meditative absorption and, following the three requests, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma through parables and accounts of past causes and conditions to expound the Single Vehicle (*ekayāna*), causing the Śrāvakas to abandon the Lesser Vehicle and return to the Great, and bestowing upon them the prophecy of Bodhi to transform those two [vehicles].

Because it carries [beings] out of turbid waters, it is primarily for the sake of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha), while incidentally for the sake of bodhisattvas; this is called the "Section on the True Teaching" (*samyak-dharma-bhāga*).

The third section, consisting of nineteen chapters from the "Dharma Master Chapter" (*Dharmabhāṇaka-parivarta*) to the "Chapter on Samantabhadra’s Exhortation" (*Samantabhadra-utsāhana-parivarta*), is named the "Circulation Section" (*pariṇāmana-bhāga*).
This is that which reveals the transcription, veneration, giving to others, listening, and even the contemplation of this sutra.

The practice of the ten kinds of dharma-practice (dharmacaryā), as well as the merit obtained by persons or dharmas through the dissemination of this sutra, primarily benefits bodhisattvas and secondarily benefits śrāvakas;
this constitutes the third section, the Section on Dissemination (pariṇāmanā). Now, based on the first eight chapters, we establish the Section on the True Doctrine (śarīra).
Since the sutra to be explained is divided into three sections, the commentary that elucidates it is likewise divided into three.

It is likewise so. From "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) up to "having awakened to the provisional and the real" (*jue quan zhen yi xia*) constitutes the introductory section (*nidāna*) of the commentary.
"About to explain this sutra, I shall briefly analyze it through six gates" marks the beginning of the second section, the main body (*śarīra*).

"During my travels and discourse, I merely followed the transmission of Ling" and so forth constitutes the section on the dissemination (*pravartana*) of the commentary. These segments differ. Within the initial introduction, there are two parts; first, the explanation of the commentary.

Title. Next, the main text will be explained. First, let us interpret the title. As for the term "title" (*tìmù*): "title" refers to the scripture’s title, while "heading" (*mù*) refers to the headings of this commentary;
thus, it is called the "title. Now, the current version of the commentary mostly reads: *The Profound Praise of the Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma*, Scroll One.
"Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma" is its original name, while "Profound Praise" is the terminology used in the commentary. Since these [terms] already exist...
The original title shall now be briefly explained.
Regarding the phrase *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: the first four characters constitute the specific name (*viśeṣa-nāman*), as they apply exclusively to this sutra.
The character *sūtra* constitutes the general name (*sāmānya-nāman*), as it does not differ from other sutras. This is divided into two parts; first, the two characters *Miao Fa* (Wondrous Dharma).

This is the Dharma. The two characters "lotus" (*padma*) are a metaphor. The Wondrous Dharma is like a lotus flower; the lotus flower is the analogy (*upamāna*), and the Wondrous Dharma is the object of the analogy (*upameya*).

Therefore, one first explains the Wondrous Dharma and subsequently explains the lotus flower. First, there is the general explanation of the Wondrous Dharma; second, there is the specific explanation of the Wondrous Dharma.
What is the meaning of the general explanation of the Wondrous Dharma? The answer is: it is that which is profoundly deep and difficult to understand, subtle and marvelous.

It exists. Because it is unsurpassed and most excellent, it is called the "Sublime Dharma" (*saddharma*). As for this Sublime Dharma: within the heart of every sentient being’s mind, there is Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*);
this Buddha-nature is precisely what is named the Sublime Dharma. It has been present from the beginning within the deluded minds of sentient beings. How is this so?
It is like the nature of fire existing within wood, the nature of water within the earth, the nature of gold within a wall, and [the nature of an image] within a mirror.

Clarifying the nature: this is verifying that within the minds of sentient beings there is Buddha-nature. Although it is seen, it is indeed invisible; Buddha-nature fundamentally resides within each individual’s own mind.
Every person possesses Buddha-nature within their body. Buddha-nature is the wondrous Dharma. There are two aspects to the wondrous Dharma:

first, the wondrous Dharma of principle (*li*); second, the wondrous Dharma of practice (*xing*). The wondrous Dharma of principle is what is called *tathatā* (suchness). The wondrous Dharma of practice...
This is precisely Bodhi. Bodhi is the Perfect Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*). That which is called the "wondrous principle" is the Pure Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*).

This very Dharma Body is the essence of the title of this sutra, *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. To exhaustively reach the ultimate point of this wondrous Dharma is the Dharma and Reward Bodies within the minds of each individual.
Since it has been stated that these exist within the minds of sentient beings, there is a wondrous [Dharma] within each and every mind.
Regarding the Dharma: I have not yet discerned what specific contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) must be cultivated so that the sublime Dharma may arise within the mind.

It is like someone who desires gold from ore; when the ore is smelted, the gold manifests of itself. It is like someone who desires fire from wood; when the wood is drilled, the fire arises of itself.
It is like someone who desires clarity from a mirror; when the mirror is polished, the clarity emerges of itself. It is like someone who...
Regarding water at a vital site: when the earth is pierced, the water comes forth of its own accord. This must be because there is a sentient being with mind and consciousness present.

If every person desires the Buddha within their own mind, they should cultivate the wisdom of hearing, contemplation, and meditation to sever afflictions and hindrances; once these are exhausted, the Buddha will naturally arise within the mind.

For those who hear the teachings, contemplate them, and practice them, greed, anger, and delusion will diminish. Upon completing one, two, or three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, the fruits of the Dharma-body, Reward-body, and Transformation-body will become fully perfected.
If you wish to attain Buddhahood, simply cultivate the mind and cultivate purity; then the Buddha will arise from the mind. Good and evil arise from the mind; the mind is the master.
By cultivating the mind with determination, one will surely attain Bodhi. The Buddha has sent me to teach the cultivation of the mind—how could I dare not do so?
"If one does not practice, is there truly a sublime Dharma within the mind? Although the sublime Dharma resides in the mind, it is fundamentally invisible.

How can one cultivate the mind so that the sublime Dharma gives rise to the Buddha-way? Buddha-nature truly dwells within each individual's own mind; yet, though it is seen, it is fundamentally impossible to see.
This is simply because it is exceedingly profound and difficult to comprehend. To clarify this, I shall provide an analogy using the lotus flower: the nature of the lotus exists within the seed."
When the seed is opened, the flower is not seen; it is not that the flower is not seen at the time of opening. One says that the lotus flower has vanished within the lotus seed.
Likewise, when someone seeks the Buddha within the very heart of a sentient being's mind, they do not see him; it is not that the Buddha is not seen at the time of seeking.
One says that the Buddha-nature does not reside in the mind. Thus, for each and every sentient being, within their body of the five aggregates—
They are not distinct from the lotus pond; each possesses afflictions within their own heart, which is just like the mud within the pond.
Buddha-nature dwells precisely amidst these afflictions, resembling a lotus seed within the mud. While the conditions for the seed have not yet converged, it remains in the mud for a long time.
Yet, when the time comes for the convergence of conditions, the lotus flower emerges from within the seed.
Growing from within: we possess the Buddha-nature within our own minds. It must necessarily depend upon hearing the phrases of the sutras with the ears;

hearing these phrases serves as the causal condition that nourishes the seed of the Buddha within the mind. Gradually, one is able to awaken to and understand it within the mind, and thus the Buddha arises spontaneously within the mind itself.
For this reason, the wondrous Dharma is compared to the lotus flower: the lotus flower is like the wondrous Dharma, and the wondrous Dharma is precisely the One Vehicle.
The Vehicle. The One Vehicle is the treasure-store; the treasure-store is the wondrous Dharma; the wondrous Dharma is called Buddha-nature. Therefore, it is termed "wondrous Dharma.

Second, it is said that the two characters for "wondrous Dharma" belong to the Buddha-body. They both accord with principle and wisdom, and they pervade both cause and fruit. The principle of the cause and the principle of the fruit are both sublime;
the wisdom of the cause and the wisdom of the fruit are both profound and mysterious. The nature of the principle of cause and fruit is named the Dharmakāya. Cause and fruit...

The aspect of wisdom corresponds to the *dharmakāya* (reward-body) of the Buddha; it exhaustively penetrates the essence of the wondrous Dharma. This is the *dharmakāya* and *sambhogakāya* within each individual body, and is therefore called the "Wondrous Dharma.
The Wondrous Dharma is difficult to understand and difficult to clarify, whereas the lotus flower is easy to know and perceive.

One may fail to recognize the principle and wisdom within the mind, yet these resemble the lotus and its blossom in a pond. "Lotus" (*padma*) is used as a metaphor for the fruit, signifying the perfection of the fruit of the three bodies (*trikāya*). "Blossom" (*puṣpa*)...
This is the metaphor for the cause. It demonstrates that the causes of the myriad virtues are fulfilled.

Just as the lotus flower is unstained by the mud, the wondrous Dharma is not invaded by afflictions (*kleśa*). Since the lotus flower grows from within the mud, the wondrous Dharma likewise abides amidst afflictions.

Within afflictions there is Buddha-nature; within a pool of mud there is a lotus flower. When conditions meet, the lotus flower naturally blossoms; when the causes are perfected, the wondrous Dharma manifests.
They will certainly attain Buddhahood. [The Buddha] intends to cause every person to recognize their Buddha-nature; thus he brings forth the wondrous Dharma, and by extension, the Lotus Sūtra.
Third, it is said that the sūtra is also named "among" (the midst). Regarding the interpretations of these three masters:

the first takes only the practice and the fruit as the "Lotus," with practice being the flower and the fruit being the lotus. The second master takes only the teaching and the principle as the "Lotus," with the teaching being the flower and the principle being...
The Lotus. The third master [Nāgārjuna] explains that the teaching, principle, practice, and fruit are collectively termed the "Lotus Flower" (*padma*).
Both the teaching and the principle are flowers; both the principle and the fruit are lotuses. The teaching and practice both blossom, while the principle and fruit both emerge from the water.

As the Sūtra says, "The wisdom of all Buddhas is exceedingly profound and immeasurable"—this refers to the principle emerging from the water. "Entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision"—as the Sūtra says, "to fully practice all... [and so forth].
The Buddha’s immeasurable path-dharmas are expounded in the treatise to cause one to realize the stage of non-retrogression; this is the second turning of the ox-cart.

This vehicle, this precious vehicle, proceeds directly to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), which is the unfolding of practice. It reveals, shows, and awakens—these three—as well as the third turning of the jewel-treasury, which is the emergence of the fruit from the water.
The teaching possesses the merit of being able to unfold the subtle principle, and the principle possesses that which is unfolded and emerges.
The power of water lies in its function of proceeding from causes toward effects; for the fruit possesses the capacity to realize the seed and repay the cause.
(The first part generally clarifies the wondrous Dharma; the second part specifically clarifies the wondrous Dharma.)

First, one explains the "wondrous Dharma," and subsequently, the "Dharma. Regarding the "wondrous": first, according to the *Shu* (Commentary), it is explained through the five meanings within the Ten Mysterious Gates;
later, according to Master Zàn of Beijing, it is explained through ten meanings. These are: 1. the wondrousness of the root; 2. the wondrousness of the branches and ends; 3.

the wondrousness of subsuming the ends and returning to the root; 4. the wondrousness of transcending dependence; 5. the wondrousness of being without coarseness. First, regarding the wondrousness of the root:
This refers to the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka*, which clarifies the ultimate *dharmakāya* of the cause and fruit of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). It states:

"In order to cause sentient beings to give rise to joy, he is said to be born in a royal palace; in order to cause sentient beings to give rise to longing and veneration, he manifests extinction at the twin śāla trees.
The former is called the coarse [manifestation]. Furthermore, a sūtra says: "The Tathāgata truly neither appears in the world nor enters parinirvāṇa. Why is this?"
The Dharma-body is eternally abiding because it is identical to the Dharma-realm. This is also consistent with what this sutra says: "This Dharma abides in its own position;
the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding. Furthermore, the sutra states: "The Tathāgata knows and perceives the characteristics of the triple world as they truly are:

there is no birth-and-death, neither falling back nor emerging; there is neither one remaining in the world nor one who has entered parinirvāṇa; it is neither real nor unreal," and so forth. This is called the Root.

1. The excellence of the fundamental; 2. The excellence of the branches and their culmination. Within the One Buddha Vehicle, three are distinguished and taught. Of these three, two are designated as "coarse," while the Buddha Vehicle is supreme;
therefore, it is called the excellence of the branches and their culmination. 3. The excellence of subsuming the branches back into the fundamental:
the One Vehicle expounded in this sutra is ultimately perfect and complete, and is thus called "excellent. 4. The excellence of absolute transcendence: the three meanings mentioned above are all...

It is called "sublime" (miao) in contrast to the "coarse" (cu). This does not mean that its own essence is sublime prior to being contrasted with the coarse. Now, regarding this sublime essence, it is fundamentally beyond words;
yet we forcibly praise it as "sublime. What textual evidence is there for this? The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* answers: "One does not attain even a small portion of nirvāṇa [by such means]."
It is named Great Nirvāṇa. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The eighteen kinds of emptiness constitute emptiness through mutual dependence (*sāpekṣa-śūnyatā*).

Absolute emptiness (*kevala-śūnyatā*) is not emptiness through mutual dependence. Since there is both dependent and non-dependent emptiness, how could the Sublime (*miao*) lack both dependence and non-dependence?

Huiguan, a disciple of Kumārajīva, wrote the preface to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, stating: "It is called 'Sublime,' yet its essence transcends the refined and the coarse; it relies upon the flower to proclaim [the truth]."
The teaching transcends the realm of mystical phenomena; as it says below, "This Dharma cannot be shown; words and signs are quiescent. Kumārajīva sighed in admiration, saying:
"O son of good family, were one not to have deeply entered the treasury of the sūtras, one could not speak in such a way—transcending dependence on names and cutting off all conceptual extremes."
The fifth is the absence of the coarse and the sublime; this is the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land. Thus, the *Xiangji fo pin* (Chapter on the Buddha of Fragrant Accumulation) says:

"In my land, there is not even the name of śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha. This is the absence of the coarse. "There are only assemblies of pure great bodhisattvas. This is the sublime. The *Zhilun* (Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom) states:

"A world of the seven treasures consists purely of bodhisattvas," which is likewise the same as this [Pure Land teaching]. (The above constitutes the fundamental and the derivative, subsuming the derivative into the fundamental.)
This is the "Excellence of Being Fundamentally Unconditioned and Without Coarseness" (the fifth of the five excellences).

Next, according to Dharma Master Zàn, there are ten meanings of excellence: first, excellence in contrast; second, excellence in supplementary support; third, excellence in the place of teaching; fourth, excellence in duration; fifth, excellence in the abundance of dharmas; sixth, excellence in fixed names; seventh, excellence in the Middle Way;

eighth, excellence in majestic power; ninth, excellence in benefit; tenth, excellence in comparative evaluation. First: ... [text continues] ... (End of section) *Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment from a commentary on the Lotus Sutra (likely the *Fahua wenju* or similar), specifically concerning the "Ten Excellences" (*shiyi miao*) as interpreted by Dharma Master Zàn (Zhiyi).*

Regarding the exaltation of the sublime: while other sutras transform sentient beings through the teaching of a single Buddha-body in the present alone, this sutra is taught in common by all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
As for the "three periods": the World-Honored One Prabhūtaratna is a Buddha of the past;
as the sutra says, at that time a great sound issued from within the jeweled stupa, praising him, saying, "Excellent, excellent," and so forth. Śākyamuni Tathāgata is [the Buddha of the present].

The Buddhas of the present number eighty thousand; those of the future are likewise [innumerable]. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī is a Buddha of the past, the Compassionate Honored One (Maitreya) is a Buddha of the future, and our Original Teacher (Śākyamuni) is a Buddha of the present. Moreover, within the present, they pervade the ten directions. As a sutra says:
"At that time, in each and every direction, there were Buddhas, Tathāgatas, filling all the four million billion nayutas of lands."
At that time, each of the Buddhas was seated upon a lion throne beneath a precious tree.
They all dispatched messengers to inquire after Śākyamuni Buddha’s welfare, each carrying a handful of precious flowers and addressing them thus:
"Good son, go to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa to the place where Śākyamuni Buddha resides, and speak these words on my behalf: 'Are you free from illness and affliction? Are you physically strong and at ease?'"
[He asked] whether the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas were all at peace. Taking these precious flowers, he scattered them as an offering to the Buddha and spoke these words:
"That certain Buddha desires to open this jeweled stūpa. The dispatching of messengers by the various Buddhas was likewise so;
that is to say, the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time together transform sentient beings for a single assembly, which is not the case in other sūtras.
First is the excellence of the Buddha’s transformation; thus it is said that he "proclaims the sublime. Second is the excellence of the supportive retinue.

This consists of twenty-one assemblies in total. The first fifteen assemblies are as follows: First, the assembly of the pure and noble Śākyas; the sutra states, "Together with a great assembly of twelve thousand bhikṣus," and so forth.

Second, the assembly of those who have completed the path but are not yet fully perfected; the sutra states, "Furthermore, there were two thousand [monks], both those still in training and those beyond training."
Third, the assembly that entered the Way by receiving grace; the Sūtra calls them the Mahāprajāpatī Bhikṣuṇī. Fourth, the assembly with whom deep karmic bonds were formed;
the Sūtra calls them Rāhula’s mother, the Bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā. Fifth, the inconceivable holy assembly;
the Sūtra calls them eighty thousand Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, all [resolved] toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
6. Śakra, Lord of the Devas, presiding over the assembly of devas. The Sūtra says: "At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra was together with his retinue of twenty thousand sons of gods.
7. The assembly of those who protect and spread the radiance. The Sūtra says:

"Furthermore, there were the son of gods Moon, the son of gods Universal Fragrance, the son of gods Jewel Light, and the Four Great Heavenly Kings, together with their retinues of ten thousand sons of gods. 8. Minor... [text ends]
The assembly of Maheśvara. The Sūtra says: the Son of Heaven Maheśvara, together with his retinue of thirty thousand sons of heaven.
The assembly of the nine Vaśavartin deities. The Sūtra says: the Lord of the Sahā World, the Brahmā King.
Śikhin Mahābrahmā and others, together with their retinue of twelve thousand devaputras, filled the ten directions with a rain of water.
The sutra states there were eight nāga kings, such as Nanda Nāgarāja and Upananda Nāgarāja.
There was a group of eleven performing pure songs and elegant music; the sutra states there were four kiṃnara kings, such as Dharmakiṃnara and Sudharmakiṃnara.
The Nara kings and others constitute the twelfth assembly, the Victorious Fragrant and Fierce Music Devas;

the sutra mentions four gandharva kings, such as the Gandharva King Rati, the Gandharva King Rataghosa, and so forth. The thirteenth is the assembly of those who shake the mountains and surge the seas;
the sutra states there are four asura kings, such as the Asura King Bali and the Asura King Kharaskandha, and so forth.
14. The assembly that swallows dragons and devours poison. The sutra states there are four *garuḍa* kings:
the *garuḍa* king Mahātejas, the *garuḍa* king Mahākāya, and so forth. 15. The assembly of benevolent kings with sovereign power. The sutra states:
"The son of Vaidehī, King Ajātaśatru" (the fifteen assemblies above). As for the six subsequent assemblies: 1. The assembly of the jeweled stupa soaring through the air. The sutra states:
At that time, before the Buddha, there was a stupa made of the seven treasures, five hundred *yojanas* in height and exactly two hundred and fifty *yojanas* in length and breadth.
It surged forth from the earth and remained suspended in mid-air. Second, the various Buddhas who are emanations throughout the ten directions gathered from the eight directions;
they transformed the lands in three ways, and the eight directions were purified and adorned. Third, the ocean surged forth to support a lotus flower.
[The] Assembly. The Sūtra says: At that time, Mañjuśrī sat upon a thousand-petaled lotus flower as large as a chariot wheel.

The bodhisattvas who had come together likewise sat upon precious lotus flowers. The fourfold assembly, like stars scattered across the earth, heard the sound of the voice spoken by Śākyamuni Buddha and ascended from below; each and every bodhisattva was proclaimed by the great assembly.
The leaders of the guides each led retinues as numerous as the sands of sixty thousand Ganges Rivers. As the five kinds of phoenix songs resounded afar, the Sūtra says:
"At that time, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara vanished from that land and set out together with eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas.
As they passed through various lands, the earth shook in six ways, and it rained down seven-jeweled lotuses everywhere. (Sixth Section)

Regarding the multitudes from distant regions, the Sūtra states: "At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, by means of his sovereign supernormal powers, majestic virtue, and renown, arrived from the eastern direction accompanied by immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable great Bodhisattvas.

All the lands through which he passed were universally shaken," and so forth. Among these multitudes, there was not one who did not rush like clouds to Vulture Peak or gather like mist around the Sacred Mountain.
On the mountain, we all sigh that we were once situated within the two provisional teachings, yet we rejoice together now at hearing the one ultimate truth.

Even the multitudes who flocked to the Deer Park to seek the Way, or the followers who heard the sutras beneath the twin trees, could not surpass those who have come here. Thus it is said: "The assistance is wondrous;

the place of the threefold teaching is wondrous. Furthermore, the locations where various sutras were preached differ from one another; some were in the void, such as when the Buddha was in the air for the Śrīmālā-sūtra.

It appears within [the text]. Looking up with reverence to the Buddha, the World-Honored One, he manifests universally for the sake of all sentient beings. At times he dwells only on earth; at times he resides in defiled lands;

and at times he comes from pure realms. If this sutra were taught in all three places, first he would dwell in a defiled land to proclaim it, desiring to cause them to abandon provisional means and grow weary of the mundane;
next he would dwell in a pure realm to chant it, desiring to cause them to rejoice in the treasure-laden direction.
Subsequently, abiding in the midst of space, they ultimately return to true nature; therefore, it is called the "sublimity of abiding. Fourth is the sublimity of long duration.
To speak briefly of the temporal periods of various sutras, each is distinct. For instance, the past Buddha Dīpaṃkara expounded the teaching for humans for a full sixty minor kalpas.
As the sutra says: "The Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa, through the Bodhisattva Prabhāketu, expounded the Mahāyāna."
The sutra is titled *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and so forth. Furthermore, the Dharma Master Wonderful Light expounded it for others for eighty minor kalpas;
the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū did not cease or abandon it for eight thousand kalpas.

The sutra states that when the Buddha preached this sutra for eight thousand kalpas, the sixteen princes [expounded it] for eighty-four thousand kalpas, extensively propagating this sutra for the fourfold assembly.

In the introduction and main body of my current teaching as Śākyamuni Buddha, no specific time period is mentioned. However, within the "Emergence" chapter (*Samantabhadra-udgata-parivarta*), bodhisattvas offer praise for a full fifty minor kalpas;
furthermore, when describing the lifespan of the three bodies (*trikāya*), the duration of time is extremely long.

For these reasons, it is called "wondrous in its long duration. Regarding the five dharmas, they are many and wondrous. Thus, while the *Avataṃsaka* consists of one hundred thousand stanzas, the Great Brahma version contains thirty thousand verses. Now...
The version currently transmitted consists of barely seventy thousand verses; it does not compare to this sutra, which was spoken by the Tathāgata Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja in twenty quadrillion verses.
Since the period during which the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū taught the Dharma was so remote, its duration must also have been long.
As for the Lotus Sutra taught by the Tathāgata Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī, it consisted of six hundred and eighty quadrillion nayutas of verses.
Regarding these verses: because this Bodhisattva possesses numerous meanings, and wishing to manifest the breadth of their significance, it is said that "the dharmas are manifold and sublime.
Sixth is the "sublimity of concentration. Furthermore, the titles of various sutras are not fixed; for example, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, there are six [versions] of the Buddha Krakucchanda.
When ten thousand years had passed, [the Buddha] appeared; it was named the *Dharmādarśa-sūtra*. When forty thousand years had passed under Kanakamuni Buddha, [he] appeared;

it was named the *Amṛtadundubhi-sūtra*. When twenty thousand years had passed under Kāśyapa Buddha, [he] appeared; it was named the *Viviktatva-vibhaṅga-sūtra*. When one hundred years had passed under Śākyamuni Buddha, [he] appeared;
it was named the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*. These names are not fixed, but this sūtra is not like that. Under Dīpaṃkara Buddha... the Great [Sūtra].

The Buddhas Tongzhi (Universal Wisdom), Shengfo (Victorious Buddha), Weiyinwang (King of Awesome Sound), and Riyue Jingmingde (Sun-Moon Pure Brightness Virtue) all share the same title for their teaching:

the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (The Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma). This is designated as the "wonderful" in three senses: first, the wonderful of the definitive; second, the wonderful of the Middle Way. As it says below:

"In the worlds of the ten directions, there is only the One Vehicle; there is no second, nor is there a third. "No second" means there is no second vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle. "No third" means...
There is no third Śrāvaka vehicle; to reckon the two vehicles as ultimate is that which is subsumed under parikalpita (imagined nature), and this is emptiness.
That there is only the One Vehicle means that the One Vehicle consists of both principle and wisdom, which exist as the dependent and the perfected natures.
"Non-existence" refers to the meaning of emptiness; this is absent in the Two Vehicles. "Non-emptiness" refers to the meaning of existence; this exists in the One Vehicle.
Being neither empty nor existent, it is far removed from the two extremes; therefore, it is called the subtle Middle Way. Regarding the subtlety of the eightfold power:

for instance, when the Dragon Girl attained the Way in the ocean assembly of the Dragon Palace, it was through the superior power of the sutra, as recorded in the passage where Zhiji questions Mañjuśrī.

[The interlocutor] asked: "Virtuous One, as for the number of sentient beings you have converted while visiting the Dragon Palace, how many are there? Mañjuśrī replied: "Their number is immeasurable... [and so forth]. He further stated:
"Within the great ocean, I have always preached only the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and other such teachings. Moreover, the "Chapter on Never-Disparaging" says:
"I heard in full the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which was previously taught by the Buddha Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja, twenty million times over."
The excellence of the nine benefits (as explained in the "Benefit for This Life and Future Lives" section). Tenth, the excellence of comparative evaluation:
as in the twelve similes used for comparative evaluation in the "Chapter on the Original Acts of Medicine" (*Bhaiṣajyavastu*), which states:

"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, for example, among all streams, rivers, and great waters, the ocean is foremost," and so forth, as well as in the "Chapter on the Land of Coolness" (*Sukhāvatīvyūha*). Therefore, it is called the excellence of comparative evaluation. The above is the detailed explanation.

Exquisite. First, the exaltation; second, the assistance; third, the place of teaching; fourth, the duration of time; fifth, the abundance of dharmas; sixth, the determination of the name; seventh, the Middle Way;
eighth, the majestic power; ninth, the benefit; tenth, the comparative evaluation (the explanation of the fifteen meanings of "exquisite" is hereby complete).

Next, regarding the explanation of *dharma*: it may be understood as "that which can be upheld" (*dhāraṇīya*) and "that which can be followed" (*anuśāsana*). Indeed, whatever is called *dharma* must necessarily possess these two meanings.

For instance, both mundane and supramundane phenomena fully possess the meaning of being "upheld. Water has the nature of moisture, and fire has the nature of heat; this is the meaning of being "upheld.
When people hear the words "water" and "fire," they understand them as moisture and heat; this is the meaning of being "followed. Furthermore, as in the *Pramāṇavārttika*, the Buddha...
The disciple said to the master of phonology (śabdavādin): "Sound is a dharma-possessor (dharmin); this is the meaning of 'supporting. This is universally admitted through direct perception.

The Buddhist disciple takes 'impermanence' as the thesis (pakṣa) and forms the understanding of impermanence; this is the meaning of 'guidance. The non-Buddhist (tīrthika) takes 'permanence' as the thesis."
This constitutes the meaning of the "method" (nyāya). The thesis is: "The sound of the Buddha’s disciples is a subject that possesses the property of being impermanent.

The reason is: "Because it is produced. The similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is like a jar or a basin; the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is like space. Thus, [the reason] exists in the similar instances and does not exist in the dissimilar instances.
Furthermore, the purpose of providing an example is to establish the nature of being impermanent through distant application. A non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*) syllogism states: "Sound..."

This is an existent phenomenon (*dharma*). It is necessarily eternal because it is an object of cognition (*prameyatva*); this is the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*). The positive example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) is like space, while the negative example (*vipakṣadṛṣṭānta*) is like a jar or a basin.
[The reason] exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and does not exist in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), as explained at length in the *Nyāyapraveśa*.

Now, this phenomenon (*dharma*) pervades all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena, whether they be form (*rūpa*) or mind (*citta*), contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), and so forth. However, the "phenomenon" mentioned here refers only to...
One takes the fourfold categories of teaching, principle, practice, and fruit that correspond to the One Vehicle (ekayāna) and designates them as "Dharma.

Regarding the term "teaching" (śāsana), it refers to the expressive words that encompass the teachings of the three vehicles (triyāna). Within these teachings, there are both the fundamental [teachings] and the provisional (upāya) teachings. As for the provisional teachings:

The Sūtra says: "These ninefold teachings of mine are spoken in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings; they take entry into the Mahāyāna as their foundation, and for this reason I preach this sūtra.
The Śrīmālā-sūtra says: "The abiding of the True Dharma and the extinction of the True Dharma" refers to the fundamental teachings such as the Prātimokṣa.
The Sūtra says: "This gate of wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to enter," which refers to the principle-dharma (li-fa), namely the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha).

The principle of the emptiness of persons realized [by śrāvakas], and the principle of the twofold emptiness realized by bodhisattvas, are both included therein. As the Sūtra says: "This dharma abides in the station of dharmas;
the characteristics of the world are eternally constant. Having known this at the site of enlightenment, the Teacher spoke through skillful means.
The Śrīmālā-sūtra states: "Śrāvakas know the four noble truths with effort (*saṃskṛta*); the Buddha knows the four noble truths without effort (*asaṃskṛta*). (From the *Dharmapada-śāstra*).

It says: "As for 'contemplation and observation,' this refers to śrāvakas observing the selflessness of persons and so forth. As for 'practicing the Dharma,' this refers to the six perfections, the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), the seven stages, and the four bodhisattva practices—all of these are 'practice.
The sutra states: 'Riding upon this precious chariot, one proceeds directly to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).'"

Furthermore, the Śrīmālādevī-sūtra states: "The abiding of the True Dharma, the extinction of the True Dharma, the Prātimokṣa, the Vinaya, and the full ordination—these six points constitute the Mahāyāna.
Therefore, it is taught that the teaching is the basis upon which practice relies.

Consequently, the Lotus Sutra Commentary states that because Śrāvakas contemplate the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, they become weary of suffering, depart from suffering, and attain liberation; thus, these are the dharmas of the fruit.

This refers to the two bodies of Dharma and Reward (*dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya*). In the "Expedient Means" chapter, the first three types of knowledge and vision, as well as the ox-carts and the treasure place;

and in the "Life Span" chapter, it is all clarified that the three Buddhas appear in the world. Furthermore, it says: "This is the abiding of the Dharma in the station of the Dharma," which refers to the fruit-dharma.
Furthermore, that which the followers of the two vehicles have realized since antiquity is also subsumed herein. Thus, the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra* states: "The four wisdoms are not yet ultimate;

they are called 'proceeding toward the realm of nirvāṇa. Based on the scriptural authority, reasoning, practice, and fruition cited above, these fundamental means by which the virtues of a Buddha are accomplished are all designated as the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), for they all possess the functional capacity to transport beings [to liberation]. These four dharmas are all...
That which possesses the correct rules and maintains [the teachings] is collectively termed "Dharma. Because it corresponds with the One Vehicle, it is termed "Wondrous.

Upon the substance of these four dharmas, there exists this wondrous function corresponding to the One Vehicle; because the substance of the Dharma can maintain this wondrous function, it is called the "Wondrous Dharma" (Saddharma).

This is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound). Question: The sublime Dharma (*saddharma*) is the teaching, and the sūtra is also the teaching; why, then, is it called a "holder of its own function" (*karmadhāraya*)? Answer: The sūtra is the very sūtra that is spoken; this is the substance (*svabhāva*).

The sublime Dharma consists of phonemes (*śabda*), phrases (*pada*), and syllables (*vyañjana*). Names (*nāman*) express intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); phrases (*pada*) express distinctions (*viśeṣa*);

and syllables (*vyañjana*) are the letters (*akṣara*) which serve as the basis for these two. This [substance] constitutes the functional activity (*karman*) upon the sūtra; therefore, it is called a "holder of its own function. Question:

The "wonderful Dharma" (saddharma) is principle (*tattva*). What, then, is called the teaching (*śāsana*)? Answer: When one brings the principle into relation with the teaching, both may be termed "teaching.

That which expresses (*vācaka*) and that which is expressed (*vācya*) together may be termed "principle," and that which expresses and that which is expressed together may be termed "teaching. Principle serves as the cause for the arising of words. (First, the "Dharma" and the "Wonderful" were explained; subsequently, the "Dharma" was explained.

First, there was a general explanation of the "Wonderful Dharma," followed by a specific explanation of the "Wonderful Dharma. The explanation of the two characters "Wonderful Dharma" is now complete.)

Next, regarding the explanation of the lotus flower: what is the underlying intention? Is it that the lotus is used as a metaphor for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* (Lotus Sūtra)? Answer: The Buddha has sent forth the instruction to cultivate the mind;
how could one dare not to cultivate it? Does the Buddha-nature truly exist within the mind? Although the Buddha-nature resides in the mind, it is fundamentally invisible.
How can the Buddha-nature arise through the cultivation of the mind? The Buddha-nature truly dwells within one’s own mind; yet, upon seeing it, it is fundamentally impossible to see. It is simply...
It is said that this is profound and difficult to comprehend. The Blessed One employs a simile by way of the lotus: the nature of the lotus exists within the lotus seed;
yet when the seed is opened and broken, the flower is not seen. Consequently, one might say that the lotus seed has swallowed the lotus.

Similarly, some people do not see the Buddha within the mind of sentient beings, having never seen him before. However, it is not because they do not see him at that time that one can say the Buddha does not exist.
The nature does not abide within the mind. The five-aggregate bodies of each and every sentient being are no different from a lotus pond;
the afflictions within each respective body are identical to the mud within the pond. Buddha-nature abides precisely within these afflictions, just as a lotus flower exists within the mud.
When the conditions for the seed and the flower harmonize, it remains for a long time within the mud.
When the time for causes and conditions converges, the lotus flower grows spontaneously from within the lotus seed. Within the minds of sentient beings there is the Buddha-nature;

it must necessarily rely upon hearing the sutras with the ears. Hearing the phrases of the sutras with the ears serves as the causal condition that moistens the seeds of the Buddha-nature within the mind.
Gradually, the mind opens and one becomes able to realize and understand; thus, the Buddha arises spontaneously within the mind itself. Therefore, by means of this wondrous...

The Dharma is likened to the lotus flower; thus, the lotus is like the wondrous Dharma. The wondrous Dharma is fundamentally Buddha-nature, which resides solely within the deluded minds of sentient beings.
When the Buddhas of the three periods of time preach the sutras, every single Buddha speaks in this same way.
Desiring to cause people to understand Buddha-nature, they therefore use the wondrous Dharma as a metaphor for the lotus flower. Question: What is meant by "lotus flower"? What is a lotus flower?
The meaning is as follows: The answer states that "lotus" is a dharma possessing name and appearance (*nāma-rūpa*).

For the sake of sentient beings, it is taught by means of names and appearances, with the intention of causing sentient beings to realize the absence of names and appearances through these very names and appearances.

This is the underlying intent. Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "All sentient beings move within the realm of names and appearances; now, wishing to bring those names and appearances to rest, one borrows names [to express them]."

Regarding characteristics: one awakens to the fact that there are no names or characteristics. To speak of this in general terms, both the "Sublime Dharma" (*Saddharma*) and the "Lotus" (*Puṇḍarīka*) are its names.
As the Sūtra says: "I preach the Mahāyāna sūtra named the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. To speak of it specifically, the Sublime Dharma is the name of that which is nameless.

The lotus flower is formless yet possesses form; thus, the title of this sutra presents both the Dharma and its metaphor together. "Sublime Dharma" (Miaofa) refers to the Dharma, while "lotus flower" (Lianhua) is the metaphor;
hence they are presented together. Therefore, it is named the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* (The Lotus of the Sublime Dharma).
Furthermore, it is compared to a lotus flower for ten reasons. First, this flower grows from a seed; this metaphor signifies that this One Vehicle must necessarily have its seed. As the Sūtra says:
"The Buddhas, the Honored Ones among two-legged beings, know that all phenomena are eternally without intrinsic nature; the Buddha-seed arises from conditions."
For this reason, the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) is taught. Second, these flowers grow from the minute to the manifest; this is a metaphor for the Buddha-vehicle gradually increasing. As the Sūtra says:
"Gradually accumulating merit and fully possessing the mind of great compassion, they have all already attained the path of Buddhahood.
Third, when these flowers grow to fullness, they completely emerge from the turbid water; this is a metaphor for how there is no merit that is not perfected and no fruition that is not exhausted.
It has emerged from the turbid mud and water of birth and death. As the Sūtra says: "The Tathāgata has already left the burning house of the triple world.

Fourth, although this flower has emerged from the mud and water, it does not abandon the mud and water; this is a metaphor for how the Buddha, though he has emerged beyond the four floods (*catur-ogha*), does not abandon the midst of the triple world.
As the Sūtra says: "At that time, the master of the house was standing outside the gate and heard someone..."
He said, "O my sons, you previously entered this house while playing; being young and ignorant, you were joyfully attached to it.
Having heard this, the elder was startled and entered the burning house, thinking it necessary to rescue them.

Fifth, these flowers are subtle and wondrous, pure and pristine beyond compare, like the Buddha Vehicle, which is the most supreme among the five vehicles. As the sutra says: "This vehicle is subtle and wondrous."
First, it is supremely pure. Sixth, this flower is praised by both ordinary beings and sages;

the Buddha Vehicle is likewise praised, cherished, and so forth by ordinary beings and sages, both mundane and supramundane. As a sutra says: "That which the Buddha delights in and that which all sentient beings should praise.
Seventh, the petals and filaments of this flower are complete, serving as a metaphor for the myriad virtues of the Buddha Vehicle.
Perfectly complete. The Sūtra says: "The immeasurable billions of powers, liberations, meditative concentrations, wisdoms, and other Buddha-dharmas.
Eighth, just as these flowers serve as the seat upon which all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas sit, so too does the Mahāyāna serve as the dwelling wherein all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas abide.
The Sūtra says: "The Buddha himself abides in the Mahāyāna, according to the Dharma he has attained, by the power of his concentration and wisdom."

Adorned. By means of this, he delivers sentient beings. Ninth, these flowers open and close at specific times; this is a metaphor for how the Dharma of this One Vehicle is hidden or manifest at specific times.
As the Sūtra says: "The reason it has not been taught before is that the time for its teaching had not yet arrived.
Now is precisely that time; I shall definitively teach the Mahāyāna. Tenth, when this flower first formed at the beginning of the kalpa, the Great Brahmā King...
Seated upon it, he is the father of all sentient beings. As the Sūtra says: "For example, the Great Brahmā King is the father of all sentient beings;
this sūtra is likewise so—the father of all noble ones, both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), as well as those who have resolved to attain Bodhicitta.
Furthermore, the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-sūtra* states: "The Vaipulya sūtras are the eyes of all Buddhas and the cause of all Buddhas."
This is the attainment of the five eyes and birth from the Vaipulya sūtras. This is the Great Dharma Seal that seals the ocean of *nirvāṇa*.

Therefore, through the Vaipulya sūtras, the three bodies are produced. Regarding these three bodies: it is because of the Vaipulya sūtras that one awakens to the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) and severs all afflictions (*kleśa*).
Because the afflictions are severed, the *dharmakāya* manifests. Because the *dharmakāya* manifests, there is the *saṃbhogakāya*. The *saṃbhogakāya*...
Because [the Dharmakāya] exists, there is the Nirmāṇakāya. Because there are the three bodies (trikāya), the twelve divisions of the sūtras are taught.
Because the twelve divisions of the sūtras are taught, there is the Dharma-jewel. Because there are the Three Jewels, there are the three kinds of goodness—mundane and supramundane.

These three kinds of goodness consist of humans, devas, and those who have transcended the world. Therefore, one knows that the Lotus Sūtra is the root of both the mundane and the supramundane. Thus it is compared [to a tree].
It is the lotus flower.

The *Erya* states that it is called *fúqú* (mud-born) and also *fúróng* (lotus). Its general name is *liánhuá* (lotus flower). Regarding why the Buddha takes this as a metaphor, according to the masters of the fundamental treatise, the lotus has two meanings:
first, the meaning of emerging from water, which signifies emerging from the turbid mud-water of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).

Therefore, there are two meanings for "the blossoming of flowers": because the supreme teaching reveals the true principle (*tattva*). The former is the excellence of the teaching (*dharma*), and the latter is the excellence of the principle.
Since the treatise only explains the sixteenth name of the *Anantārtha-sūtra* as "Lotus Flower," it refers exclusively to these two types: teaching and principle.
According to the sub-commentary below, although the *Anantārtha-sūtra* explains the two meanings of the lotus flower, the fruit is preeminent over the cause.

The explanation does not deviate from the universal principle. That is to say, both the teaching and the practice possess the quality of blossoming; within the fruit of the principle, both are able to produce water.
Thus, they share the same essence as the four dharmas. This is not the same as the *Anantārthartha-sūtra*, yet it likewise does not contradict the two meanings of the lotus flower.
The intended meaning here is that regarding that lotus flower, there are two meanings: first, the lotus is...

The pedestal (*maṇḍala*) is the fruit. Second, the flower refers to the outer petals; this is the cause. Now, when speaking of the "lotus flower," both the meanings of cause and fruit are stated together.
Within this teaching, the means of expression (*vācaka*) is the cause, and that which is manifested (*vācya*) is the fruit.
Thus, it is said: "The trap lies in the fish; the words lie in the meaning. One thereby knows that the flower has not yet opened.
Yet the platform does not appear; the teaching does not speak, and the principle is not revealed. It is by the opening of the flower that the platform is seen;

through the proclamation of the teaching, one awakens to the essential meaning. Therefore, the sub-commentary states: "Just as a door is the means by which one enters a room, so the teaching is the locus where the principle is revealed.
As the scripture says: "Who enters a door that does not pass through the gate? For this reason, the teaching serves as the cause for the flower, and the principle is the lotus.
The fruit. Thus, the Treatise says: "Because the true principle is revealed through the words of the supreme teaching. The Sūtra says: "The wisdom of all Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable;
the gate of that wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to enter. This is the Lotus of Teaching and Principle. Second, conduct is the flower and the fruit is the lotus.
A lotus does not consist of a single leaf, nor can the fruit of Buddhahood be attained through a single practice alone.

Regarding the causes and conditions: just as many flower petals together nurture a single lotus pedestal, so too do the myriad practices reach perfection and together bring about the fruit of Buddhahood.
Consequently, "opening, showing, awakening, and entering" are taken as the fruit, while "entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision" is taken as the cause.

Synthesizing these two meanings, both the teaching and the practice are termed "flowers," as both possess the sense of blooming. Likewise, both the principle and the fruit are termed [the lotus pedestal].

The lotus all possesses the meaning of "emerging from water. This is especially evident when examining the four dharmas, as they all transcend the two vehicles and are thus collectively termed "emerging from water.
Now, the reason we speak specifically of the "emergence from water" regarding the fruit of principle (*li-guo*) is that the fruit of principle lacks the quality of "blooming";

therefore, it is singled out for the term "emergence. Conversely, the teaching and practice possess exclusively the meaning of "blooming," and for this reason, they are singled out for the term "blooming. If...
Regarding the statement that "the practice of the teaching has no emergence from water," does this mean that the practice of the teaching does not transcend the Two Vehicles?

Therefore, we know that this is merely a correlation based on a single sense. Thus, the sub-commentary below states: "Since the Dharma encompasses four meanings, the Flower likewise embraces the four virtues. As for the four meanings of the Dharma:

it accords with the subtle exegesis of the secret mysteries—this is the Teaching (*śāsana*); it harmonizes with the profound intent of the deep roots—this is the Principle (*tattva*). It excels upward... [text continues].
It is the profound practice of the Vehicle; it is the true essence of the fruit of perfect enlightenment. Its beauty is exhaustive; therefore, it is called "wondrous.
Regarding the four meanings of "flower": as the calyx unfolds, the lotus is revealed; likewise, through the exposition of the teachings, one awakens to the ultimate meaning.
The lotus emerges in splendor from the sacred pond; this metaphor illustrates how the principles repeatedly transcend the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).

Just as the flower opens and bears fruit, it is like the cause being solemn and the result being fulfilled. Designating the white flower as the root of color and manifesting Buddha-wisdom as the source of the vehicle—there is a profound reason for employing the analogy of the lotus.
Question: Is it not sufficient to simply name it the "Sublime Dharma" (*saddharma*)? Why is it necessary to establish the title by employing the metaphor of the lotus flower?
Answer: The sub-commentary states: "The Dharma relies on metaphors for clarity; the subtle is made manifest through attachment [to the concrete].

By means of the *utpala* flower and fruit, one illustrates the cause and fruit of the *saddharma*. Since the Dharma encompasses four meanings, the flower likewise embraces four virtues. Question: If, by means of the lotus...
Because flowers possess both the meanings of cause and effect, those who take them as a metaphor should find that all other flowers could likewise serve as metaphors for the Sublime Dharma; why?
Because they too possess flowers and fruits. The answer is: although various flowers possess both cause and effect, their significance is not fixed.
Consider, for example, the peach and plum trees: though their blossoms fill the branches, how many fruits can they actually bear? Why, then, do lotus flowers each invariably produce fruit?

Within the Dharma, when we speak of causes and effects, take those of the two vehicles with fixed natures as an example: by practicing the cause, they attain the fruit, which is like the ripening of fruit.
However, if those of the two vehicles with unfixed natures abandon the Small Vehicle and return to the Great, they all become part of the One Vehicle.
The path you are practicing is the bodhisattva way; it lacks the fruits of the two vehicles, which is like having flowers but no fruit.
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that there are cases where wholesome deeds with outflows (*sāsrava-kuśala*) lack their fruit, such as the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra.

As for those who have exhausted the karma of a Cakravartin king yet encounter evil results, such as King Ajātaśatru, who committed a heinous crime but ceased his karmic activity through repentance—in all these cases, there is the cause but no [resultant] fruit.

As for the fruit: this present One Vehicle, with its six perfections and myriad practices, will certainly result in Buddhahood; it is exactly like a lotus flower, each of which bears fruit, and thus it is taken as a metaphor.
Furthermore, while the various flowers on dry land possess both cause and fruit, they lack the function of emerging from the water.

Although there may be grass in the water, once it emerges from the water, it lacks the quality of blooming; although there may be flowers on land, even if they bloom, they lack the quality of emerging from the water.
Now, this One Vehicle (Ekayāna) first "emerges from the water," because it has emerged from the turbid waters of the Lesser Vehicles (Hīnayāna);
second, it is a "blooming flower," because it reveals the True Principle (tattva) and transforms sentient beings. Therefore, the Commentary states: "Flower."
It is both elegant and brilliant; it embodies all excellences and manifests the lotus. Body and practice are presented together, and dharma and metaphor are raised in tandem.
For this reason, the lotus flower is taken as a metaphor; there is indeed a basis for this. Furthermore, it is said that the flower and its petals correspond to the path of a bodhisattva.
A lotus seed is like the body of a Buddha; it requires many petals and leaves before a single lotus pedestal can grow and mature.
Likewise, one must cultivate the myriad practices in unison before finally attaining the fruit of Buddhahood. A single lotus seed falls into the pond.
A single lotus flower blooms upon the water; as they arise one after another, there is no end to their succession. Behold, the lotuses fill the pond;
when a single sentient being attains Buddhahood, they in turn preach the Lotus Sūtra for the sake of all others. Thus, these manifestations arise without end.
How is this different from lotuses blooming in a full pond? Master Zhang, the Registrar of Monks, said: "When the lotus buds open wide, their fragrance wafts richly near and far;
once the Buddha has transformed the mundane into the sacred, his majestic virtue and radiance pervade the ten directions."
If one touches a single lotus with the hand, its fragrance pervades the entire body and gives rise to joy. With a single thought of a virtuous mind, one draws near to the Buddha;
karmic obstacles are eliminated and merit arises. All other flowers are indeed flowers, yet compared to this lotus, they lack fragrance and purity.
Although Bodhisattvas and those of the Two Vehicles are holy, when compared to me, the Tathāgata, their holiness is not yet perfected. Within the mire of the pond...
Long lotuses grow; long do they attain the rich and fragrant scent of lotuses. From within afflictions emerges the Buddha-nature;
from it emerges the Buddha-body, the most honored of bodies. Once one knows that within the lotus seed there is a lotus, one then understands that within the mind there is Buddha-nature.

Desiring to cause every person to give rise to awakening and understanding, and to preserve the knowledge that Buddha-nature resides within the heart, one should skillfully practice through the wisdoms of hearing, contemplation, and cultivation.

Through the diligent observation of the trainings in morality, concentration, and wisdom, the Buddha’s compassionate intention established this analogy to point out to all practitioners that within each and every mind there is Buddha-nature.
To encourage sentient beings toward collective liberation, he compared the sublime Dharma to a lotus flower: whether the water is deep or shallow, the flower emerges.
Although the two obstacles differ in depth, True Suchness transcends them all.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of lotuses: first, the lotus within the mud, which is a metaphor for the wondrous Dharma within the bodies of ordinary beings.

Although the lotus seeds have not yet emerged from the mud, they will certainly grow into white lotuses; likewise, even if sentient beings have not yet understood how to practice, [the potential remains].
While ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) transmigrate through the cycle of existence, they now hear and study this sutra; it is like a lotus flower within the mud.

Afflictions (*kleśa*) are like that muddy silt, while the sublime Dharma is like the lotus seed. When an ordinary being hears the sutra and their mind does not regress, it is like a single lotus flower growing from within the mud.
Second is the lotus flower in turbid water, which serves as a metaphor for the sublime Dharma within the bodies of those of the Two Vehicles. The lotus flower emerges from it...
"In the mud": being born amidst turbid water. Although the *ātmagrāha* (self-clinging) of the *śrāvaka* has been eliminated, their *dharmagrāha* (clinging to phenomena) remains unsevered.
This *dharmagrāha* is like the turbid water, while the *ātmagrāha* is like the clear mud. Having removed the clear mud from within the turbid water, one beholds the lotus flower.
Third is the "lotus in clear water," which symbolizes the sublime Dharma within the body of a Bodhisattva. The lotus...
The lotus emerges from within the mud; it is born amidst turbid water, yet it rises out of that turbid water to grow within pure water.
This lotus of pure water surpasses the two previous kinds. How much more so the Bodhisattva, whose realization of principle becomes increasingly profound!
As for ordinary beings and those of lesser sanctity, the dual attachments to self and phenomena are both severed.
Like a lotus flower that is neither stained by muddy water nor by clear water, it emerges from the water and is viewed within the clear water; thus it blooms upon the surface of the water.

When the Bodhisattva’s cultivation is uninterrupted, why worry about not realizing Great Bodhi? Fourth is the "lotus emerging from the water," which is a metaphor for the wondrous Dharma within the Buddha-body.
A lotus flower blooms upon the surface of the water; originally from a lotus seed, it grows forth a sprout. So too do all Buddhas realize great Bodhi;
this is attained by ordinary beings through cultivation. (The first part is the Dharma, the latter is the simile; thus one understands the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.)

Regarding the term "sūtra" (*jing*), the sub-commentary below states: "It is for the sake of permanence and the Dharma; it is that which gathers and that which connects," citing the five meanings from the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*:
"garland," "plumb line," "source of birth," "manifestation," and "spring. It further states: "Sūtra means 'path' (*jìng*).
Just as when a person travels far to another land, one must know that there is a path; if one does not know the path, one's efforts will be in vain and one will pass through in empty toil."

Time passes; there will never be a day when it stops. It is the same for those who practice the Way: if one wishes to seek the realms of Śakra or Brahmā and transform others through the cultivation of the ten wholesome actions, one must do so.
If one wishes not to lose this human body, one must uphold the five precepts to attain it.
If one wishes to be reborn in Tuṣita, one must rely upon the eight precepts as adornment. If one wishes to see Amitābha Buddha early, [one must likewise cultivate the path].
The practice of the ten recitations must reach maturity. If one wishes to attain the Arhatship of the Hīnayāna, one must rely on the Four Noble Truths for bodily stability.

If one wishes to attain the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, one advances on the path by means of dependent origination. If one wishes to attain Buddhahood with this very body, [one must practice accordingly].
One must rely upon the sublime Dharma and practice with arduous effort. If one were to abandon these causes and conditions, one would forever lose the path to Bodhi and the way of the Buddha.
Therefore, using the character "徑" (jìng) to explain the term "經" (jīng), it is said that "經" means "徑. By hearing the sūtras, one will certainly attain the fruit of Bodhi;

there has never been one who heard the sūtras and failed to obtain the fruit, nor has there ever been one who obtained the fruit without relying on the sūtras. Thus, we know that the sūtra is the fruit.

The cause for the household: by means of this sutra, one will certainly attain the fruit of bodhi. Since both causes and conditions lead to the attainment of the fruit through this sutra, a person in life must study the Lotus Sutra (having mastered the interpretation of the sutra).

Regarding the title *Xuánzàn* (Profound Praise): Question: Why is it named *Xuánzàn*? Answer: There are two meanings. First, the sublime principle of *tathatā* (suchness) which is expounded is called "profound" (*xuán*).

The seven-fascicle *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and its ten-fascicle commentary are called "praise" (*zàn*). This is the praise of that which is profound; thus, it follows the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) analysis.
"Profound" (*xuán*) carries the meaning of being dark, remote, and deep. As the Sūtra says: "This Dharma-pitaka of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is deep, firm, obscure, and far-reaching."
"No one can overturn it. Furthermore, it is said: "The quiescent nature of all phenomena cannot be proclaimed in words. This is identical to the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Regarding the principle of the wondrous Dharma of True Suchness (*tathatā*) as elucidated by the teachings: it is realized only by fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).

Other forms of wisdom perceive only reflected images and do not directly apprehend it; therefore, it is termed "mysterious" (*xuan*). This interpretation is restricted solely to the principle of True Suchness and does not extend to the teachings or practices. Question:

What is meant by "assisting" (*zan*)? The answer is that "assisting" has the meaning of providing aid. For example, within a single commandery, there is an assistant official called a "dark gatekeeper" (*xuánfǔ*).

This official assists the chief magistrate in managing the affairs of the commandery through transformation and regulation; this is called "assisting. Since the principle of *tathatā* (suchness) is a dharma that transcends words and is devoid of marks, it is termed "dark" (*xuán*).
When one intends to employ this to teach and transform sentient beings, it is necessary to rely upon other dharmas as assistants.

Sentient beings have only now begun to assemble; therefore, within the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of the Tathāgata, names and signs are established upon dharmas that are devoid of names and signs, and the teaching is proclaimed.
Thus, the seven-fascicle *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* was spoken to assist the wordless teaching of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
The Sūtra states: "Furthermore, by means of other skillful expedients, one assists in manifesting the primary meaning. These "other skillful expedients" refer to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

When the Tathāgata preached the sūtras, he once explained the principle of *tathatā* (suchness); now, the Master of the Commentary has further composed this commentary to explain it based upon that foundation, so that the meaning may be clear and sentient beings may easily understand it.
This interpretation of the principle of *tathatā* is called "Mysterious" (*xuán*). [Volume Seven]

The text of the sutra consists of ten fascicles, and the title of the commentary is *Zàn* (Praise). Second, regarding the meaning: the four dharmas of teaching (*śāsana*), principle (*naya*), practice (*caryā*), and fruit (*phala*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* are termed "mysterious" (*xuán*).
This interpretation encompasses both the principles of the Way and the underlying logic. The ten-fascicle sub-commentary is titled *Zàn*. "Mysterious" (*xuán*) means profound and wondrous;

the four dharmas of teaching, principle, practice, and fruit are collectively designated as "mysterious. Regarding the principles of provisional and ultimate truth across the three assemblies, they have long been...
It is extremely clear. The Master of the Commentary further composed a sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) to explain it, making it easy for people to understand.
These ten fascicles of the commentary itself are simply called the *Zàn* (Praise/Commentary). This "Explanation of the Profundity" (*Xuánjiě*) is a sublime synonym for the Dharma;

"Praise" (*Zàn*) is an alternative term for "assistance. The Sūtra is the profundity, and the commentary is the praise; thus, it is a "praise of the profundity," analyzed according to the *tatpuruṣa* compound. This latter interpretation is particularly superior. Question:

Why is it that the latter meaning alone is predominant? Answer: If one takes the principle of *tathatā* (suchness) to be called "mysterious" (*xuan*), how could the teaching, principle, practice, and fruit not also be called mysterious?
Question: For what reason are the characters for "teaching," "principle," "practice," and "fruit" associated with the character for "mysterious"?
Answer: To synthesize the various texts now, "mysterious" (*xuan*) has two meanings. First, "mysterious" means "suspended," which carries the sense of "distant.
As a sutra says: "To encounter [the Buddha] suspended afar is difficult. Second, it has the meaning of "black," referring to the direction of the north, known as the "Mysterious Tiger.
The *Analects* says: "The lamb-skin robe and the black cap. This follows the first meaning. Furthermore, there are two other senses: first, that which is near is called "distant" (by contrast).

The intended meaning is as follows: that which is elucidated by this sutra is precisely the Buddha’s wisdom. This Buddha-wisdom is fivefold: first, the nature of wisdom, which is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*);
second, the aspect of wisdom, which is the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*); third, the object of wisdom, which is the principle of the ultimate and conventional truths.
Fourth, the companions of wisdom are the myriad virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Fifth, the causes of wisdom are what are called teaching and practice.

This sutra fully explains the two bodies—the Dharma-body and the Reward-body—along with their nature and characteristics. It requires three great kalpas of uninterrupted, long-term effort before one can realize perfection;
therefore, the fruit of Buddhahood is said to be "distant. It is like the Tripitaka Master of the Tang dynasty, who traveled back and forth between India for ten...
Seven years is indeed a long duration; thus, the time spent is great. How could this be the same as the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha), who realize [enlightenment] in three lifetimes?
That which is "mysterious" (*xuan*) is precisely the Sublime Dharma (*saddharma*); therefore, it is called "mysterious. This is explained in terms of the realization of the profound.

According to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-śāstra*, there are five kinds of profundity: first, profundity of meaning (*artha-gambhīrya*), which refers to the meaning of differentiation; second, profundity of essence (*svabhāva-gambhīrya*), because it is the nature of its own substance.

Third is the profundity of internal realization, because correct wisdom realizes suchness (*tathatā*). Fourth is the profundity of the basis, because the *dharmadhātu* and *dharmatā* are the fundamental source of all Buddhas.
Fifth is the unsurpassed profundity, because its essence is supreme. These are called the five profundities. Profundity is itself the sublime Dharma;
the sublime is precisely the profound. As the subsequent sutra says: "It is for the sake of expounding the Buddha’s wisdom that the Buddhas appear in the world. It further says:

Only after traveling five hundred *yojanas* does one reach the place of treasure; thus, "mysterious" (*xuan*) signifies "far. This "far" is termed "mysterious. Second, that which is profoundly remote is termed "far," just as the distance from *zhi* to a thousand *li*—where eight inches are called a *zhi*. The meaning here is that within the worlds of the ten directions, there is only the Single Vehicle Dharma (*ekayāna*). Although the Three Vehicles were previously taught, since the substance of the Three Vehicles does not exist, it is like [the following analogy]: [The text continues: "Suppose there were a man who, having traveled for many years, suddenly encountered a great mountain. He thought to himself: 'I have been traveling for a long time; I must now find a way to cross this mountain. He then saw a great elephant, a great horse, a great ox, and a great deer. Seeing them, he thought: 'These four can carry me across this mountain. Having thought this, he mounted the elephant and proceeded. After traveling for some time, he saw a great river. Seeing the river, he thought: 'I have already crossed the mountain, but I have not yet crossed the river. I must now find a way to cross this river. He then saw a raft, a boat, a bridge, and a ford. Seeing them, he thought: 'These four can carry me across this river. Having thought this, he boarded the raft and proceeded. After traveling for some time, he saw a great city. Seeing the city, he thought: 'I have already crossed the mountain and the river; I must now find a way to enter this city. He then saw a gate, a wall, a moat, and a bridge. Seeing them, he thought: 'These four can lead me into this city. Having thought this, he entered through the gate and proceeded. After traveling for some time, he saw a great palace. Seeing the palace, he thought: 'I have already entered the city; I must now find a way to enter this palace. He then saw a stairway, a ladder, a platform, and a dais. Seeing them, he thought: 'These four can lead me into this palace. Having thought this, he ascended the stairway and proceeded. After traveling for some time, he saw a great throne. Seeing the throne, he thought: 'I have already entered the palace; I must now find a way to ascend this throne. He then saw a cushion, a mat, a rug, and a seat. Seeing them, he thought: 'These four can support me upon this throne. Having thought this, he sat upon the cushion and proceeded. After traveling for some time, he saw a great king. Seeing the king, he thought: 'I have already ascended the throne; I must now find a way to meet this king. He then saw a crown, a robe, a scepter, and a seal. Seeing them, he thought: 'These four can establish my identity before this king. Having thought this, he donned the crown and proceeded. After traveling for some time, he saw a great minister. Seeing the minister, he thought: 'I have already met the king; I must now find a way to serve this minister. He then saw a staff, a tablet, a brush, and a document. Seeing them, he thought: 'These four can enable me to serve this minister. Having thought this, he took up the staff and proceeded. After traveling for some time, he saw a great army. Seeing the army, he thought: 'I have already served the minister; I must now find a way to command this army. He then saw a banner, a drum, a shield, and a sword. Seeing them, he thought: 'These four can enable me to command this army. Having thought this, he raised the banner and proceeded. After traveling for some time, he saw a great enemy. Seeing the enemy, he thought: 'I have already commanded the army; I must now find a way to defeat this enemy. He then saw a fortress, a trench, a rampart, and a watchtower. Seeing them, he thought: 'These four can enable me to defeat this enemy. Having thought this, he occupied the fortress and proceeded. After traveling for some time, he saw a great victory.
