Seeing the victory, he thought: 'I have already defeated the enemy; I must now find a way to celebrate this victory. He then saw a feast, a dance, a song, and a celebration. Seeing them, he thought: 'These four can enable me to celebrate this victory. Having thought this, he partook of the feast and proceeded. After traveling for some time, he saw a great peace. Seeing the peace, he thought: 'I have already celebrated the victory; I must now find a way to maintain this peace. He then saw a law, a decree, a covenant, and a peace treaty. Seeing them, he thought: 'These four can enable me to maintain this peace. Having thought this, he established the law and proceeded. After traveling for some time, he saw a great kingdom. Seeing the kingdom, he thought: 'I have already maintained the peace; I must now find a way to rule this kingdom. He then saw a ruler, a subject, a minister, and a commoner. Seeing them, he thought: 'These four can enable me to rule this kingdom. Having thought this, he governed the ruler and proceeded. After traveling for some time, he saw a great world. Seeing the world, he thought: 'I have already ruled the kingdom; I must now find a way to protect this world. He then saw a heaven, a hell, a human realm, and an animal realm. Seeing them, he thought: 'These four can enable me to protect this world. Having thought this, he protected the heaven and proceeded. After traveling for some time, he saw a great nirvana. Seeing nirvana, he thought: 'I have already protected the world; I must now find a way to enter this nirvana. He then saw a Buddha, a Dharma, a Sangha, and liberation. Seeing them, he thought: 'These four can enable me to enter this nirvana. Having thought this, he entered the Buddha and proceeded. After traveling for some time, he reached the ultimate destination. Having reached the ultimate destination, he thought: 'I have already entered nirvana; I must now find a way to realize the fruit. He then saw the path, the fruit, the extinction, and the cessation. Seeing them, he thought: 'These four can enable me to realize the fruit. Having thought this, he realized the path and proceeded. After traveling for some time, he attained the ultimate fruit. Having attained the ultimate fruit, he thought: 'I have already realized the fruit; I must now find a way to manifest this fruit. He then saw a body, a speech, a mind, and an activity. Seeing them, he thought: 'These four can enable me to manifest this fruit. Having thought this, he manifested the body and proceeded. After traveling for some time, he saw a great assembly. Seeing the assembly, he thought: 'I have already manifested the fruit; I must now find a way to teach this assembly. He then saw a teacher, a student, a listener, and a follower. Seeing them, he thought: 'These four can enable me to teach this assembly. Having thought this, he taught the teacher and proceeded. After traveling for some time, he saw a great teaching. Seeing the teaching, he thought: 'I have already taught the assembly; I must now find a way to uphold this teaching. He then saw a scripture, a commentary, a recitation, and a practice. Seeing them, he thought: 'These four can enable me to uphold this teaching. Having thought this, he upheld the scripture and proceeded. After traveling for some time, he saw a great lineage. Seeing the lineage, he thought: 'I have already upheld the teaching; I must now find a way to transmit this lineage. He then saw a patriarch, a successor, a disciple, and a dharma-heir. Seeing them, he thought: 'These four can enable me to transmit this lineage. Having thought this, he transmitted the patriarch and proceeded. After traveling for some time, he saw a great dharma-realm. Seeing the dharma-realm, he thought: 'I have already transmitted the lineage; I must now find a way to merge with this dharma-realm. He then saw emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and non-arising. Seeing them, he thought: 'These four can enable me to merge with this dharma-realm. Having thought this, he merged with emptiness and proceeded. After traveling for some time, he attained the ultimate merging. Having attained the ultimate merging, he thought: 'I have already merged with the dharma-realm; I must now find a way to perfect this merging. He then saw the ultimate, the profound, the subtle, and the wondrous. Seeing them, he thought: 'These four can enable me to perfect this merging. Having thought this, he perfected the ultimate and proceeded. After traveling for some time, he reached the final destination. Having reached the final destination, he thought: 'I have already perfected the merging; I must now find a way to rest in this destination. He then saw the stillness, the tranquility, the non-action, and the non-abiding. Seeing them, he thought: 'These four can enable me to rest in this destination. Having thought this, he rested in stillness and proceeded. After traveling for some time, he attained the ultimate rest. Having attained the ultimate rest, he thought
The elder said, "There are three carts; the sheep and deer carts exist only as provisional names. In reality, there is no substance to these two carts. The Two Vehicles exist only as designations;
ultimately, there is only the Dharma of the One Vehicle. The Dharma of the Two Vehicles does not exist.

Because those of the Two Vehicles do not fathom the intent behind the establishment of the teachings, they consequently cling to the notion that there are three vehicles. It is precisely because they do not fathom this that it is called 'Mysterious Praise' (Xuàn-zàn). As the Sūtra says:"
I say that these are skillful means to enable them to enter the Buddha-wisdom. Furthermore, it is said: "I merely use provisional names to guide sentient beings;

although I speak of various paths, their reality is the One Vehicle. These ninefold teachings of mine are spoken in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings, yet they take entry into the Mahāyāna as their foundation;
for this reason, I preach this sutra. This refers to the fact that those of the two vehicles do not know [this].
Regarding the name "Profound" (*gambhīra*) as applied to the gate of teaching, the *Śāstra* explains the five difficulties as follows:

"That gate of wisdom is difficult to see, difficult to awaken to, difficult to know, difficult to understand, and difficult to enter truly. Because the two vehicles do not know these five difficulties:

first, because the meaning realized is profound, the gate is difficult to see; second, because the essence of wisdom is profound, the gate is difficult to see and difficult to awaken to; third, because... [the text continues].
Because the wisdom that realizes it internally is profound, its gateway is difficult to know. Fourth, because the basis of that wisdom is profound, its gateway is difficult to understand.
Fifth, because that wisdom is unsurpassed and profound, its gateway is difficult to enter. The Master of the Commentary relies on this to describe it as "mysterious" (*xuán*).

This is based on the profundity of the *Catuṣ-āgama*. Regarding the first [meaning], "near" and "far" are explained: the initial sense is concluded as "far. Second is the meaning of "black. Furthermore, there is...
There are two meanings. First, because the Two Vehicles cannot fathom or know it, it is termed "black. Thus the Treatise says: "Second, it is difficult to comprehend;
it is that which all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are unable to know. Regarding the statement that it is "black" because it cannot be fathomed, it is as the *Daodejing* says:
"Vague and indistinct, yet within it there is something; profound and dark, yet within it there is an essence. This refers to the difficulty of [comprehending] the essence of the Way.

I understand. I shall now borrow that passage to clarify this meaning. This refers to the two kinds of profundity—the profundity of the teaching and the profundity of the principle—which the followers of the Two Vehicles cannot fathom.

As the sutra below states: "Even if the entire world were filled with beings like Śāriputra, and they were to exhaust their thoughts in collective deliberation, they could not fathom the Buddha’s wisdom.
This means that when one considers the two aforementioned types of profundity, neither can be measured; hence, it is called "mysterious" (*xuan*). This is identical to praising the Dharma.
The Master’s "Exquisite Commentary" consists of three sections and five parts; however, its realization of principle is not perfect, its merits are incomplete, and its exposition is not profound.
This constitutes the second level of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), for it is that which all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot know, being known only by the Buddha;
thus, it is called "mysterious" (*xuán*). Second, the commentator humbles himself, as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "When ordinary beings contemplate the Buddha-nature..."
The Two Vehicles view the Buddha-nature like those born blind. Bodhisattvas prior to the stages (bhūmi) see it like infants looking at the moon.
From the first stage to the seventh, they see it like a person with a diseased eye; as soon as they enter meditative observation they see it, but once they emerge from it, it is gone.
At the eighth and ninth stages, it is like seeing the moon through a thin silk gauze. Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage see only their own nature and do not see the Buddhas of others.
"Nature" (*xing*) means "darkness. The intention of the Commentary is that when one gazes afar at the Buddha’s wisdom, it is as obscure as wandering by night;

therefore, it is called "mysterious" (*xuan*). The interpretation provided here takes up both the sense of "distant" and the sense of "black. Although there were ancient explanations of the name, they did not extensively explain its formal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

Now, by explaining it through these two senses of profundity, the principle should be understood as universally applicable; thus, it is named "mysterious. "Praise" (*zan*) means "to assist. "Xian-zheng" [is a phonetic transcription].
They are called "Zan" (Aids). Thus, within a single commandery, the Commandery Magistrate is titled "Mingfu" (Illustrious Lord), while the various departments are titled "Zanfu" (Aiding Lords).

This is because the affairs of a commandery are so numerous that they must be simplified by establishing separate departmental categories, such as the Office of Merit (Gongcao) and the Office of Granaries (Cangcao).
However, these various departments do not exist apart from the jurisdiction of the county magistrate; the principle is the same.

The Sūtras are like the high official who governs all matters in general, while the commentaries (*śāstra*) are like the assistant officials who each handle specific categories. This is just as the *Abhidharmakośa* is divided into three sections and three cycles, and so forth.
The chapters on the One Vehicle, the Four Truths, and so forth are all auxiliary meanings. Furthermore, matters such as those concerning the *zàn-fǔ* (praise of the governor) require broad erudition;

one must be well-versed in antiquity and proficient in the present, taking the methods for governing people from the past and applying them according to the circumstances of the time to assist the magistrate.

Now, the author of this commentary relies fully upon the various teachings; first, he explains the scriptural text through the three turnings [of the Wheel of Dharma], thereby serving the Buddha’s intent.
Therefore, the sub-commentary below states: "With utmost care, we rely upon the holy teachings; with great vigilance, we gather the profound essence of the Mystery (Xuanzong).

Fearing that our intent might be erroneous or our words too sparse, how could we ever venture to cite [authorities] in a distorted manner? Although various offices each have their own jurisdiction, those they transform do not depart from the district (*xian*).
These are merely assistants who govern by division; now, by citing the single character "district," all are comprehensively encompassed. (Ten-Scroll Commentary)
Although the text is extensive, its principles do not depart from those within the sūtra; rather, it serves to clarify and analyze them, which is why it is called a "Commentary" (zàn).
Therefore, the sub-commentary (shù) refers to it as the *Miaofa lianhua jing xuàn zàn* (Profound Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra of the Wondrous Dharma).
"Volume" (*juan*) refers to the opening and closing, the rolling up and unfolding; thus it is called a "volume. "Number" (*di*) means sequence. "One" (*yi*) signifies the ultimate or the beginning.

This commentary consists of ten volumes, and as this stands at the very beginning, it is called the "First. Regarding the phrase "together with the preface" (*bing xu*): the term for one who composes a preface is *xiangxu*.
Mocheng says it is written on the margin. It is also called a "narrative" (*xu*). This character "narrative" (*xu*) has two meanings: first, it refers to the introductory headpiece.
Second is the sequential arrangement. As for the meaning of "head" (*tou*) in this context, its significance is similar to that of a "thread-end" (*xian*).

The "author" (*zuo-zhe*) is likewise the "thread" (*xu*) of the beginning. For example, when a household outside the city reels silk from a cocoon, they obtain what is called the "thread-head" (*xiu*).

A single fascicle of a commentary is like the head of the cocoon; a single sheet of the preface to the commentary is like the thread-head. If one wishes to reel out the silk, one must first obtain the thread-head; if one wishes to... [text ends].
I intend to compose a ten-fascicle commentary to explain this sutra. First, one must obtain the preface to the commentary. This is the sequence of order;
it is like the very first step when intending to travel a thousand li. When wishing to arrange the sequence and intending to compose a commentary, one must first have that initial sheet of paper.
The phrase "already below" refers to the sequential arrangement [of the commentary]. Between these two meanings, the sense of sequence is superior.
However, this differs from the character *xù* (序) used in the commentary. *Xù* means "orderly arrangement" (*xiángxù*). The *Liji* states that it refers to the national school;

the place where the sons of the state study is called the national school. Furthermore, schools located in cities, towns, villages, and marketplaces are all collectively termed *xiángxù*. Now, following...
The interpretation in the *Erlü* (爾疋) is most consistent with the commentary (*shū*). The *Erya* states: "The *xù* (序) refers to the eastern and western walls at the entrance;
it is the same as the *píngqiáng* (屏墻). This carries the meaning of "the beginning. Question: Why do the eastern and western walls carry the meaning of "the beginning"?

Answer: In this country, facing south is considered the position of honor. Official residences and private houses all face south. Upon entering an official residence, one first sees the eastern and western [walls]. Therefore, they signify the beginning.

The wall is the very beginning of seeing high officials and gentlemen. Upon entering the main gate of a residence and seeing the wooden screens and partitions, this is likewise the beginning of discerning whether the household will be auspicious or inauspicious.
Throughout these ten volumes of commentary, one sees this sequence at every turn;

this is the beginning of seeing the vastness of the Sūtra’s meaning and the profound depth of the Commentary’s meaning. Thus far has been the first sequence; next follows the sequence of propriety—the third sequence of meaning.
Regarding the sequence, being orderly is superior; between the two meanings, "orderly" (*xiángxù*) is the correct term.

As for the statement, "Composed by the Śramaṇa Ji of the Great Ci'en Monastery," this is a distinct designation established to honor both the excellence of the monastery and the venerability of the person.

As for "Great Ci'en Monastery": it is named "Ci'en" (Kindness and Gratitude) because it was established to repay the kindness of his compassionate mother; "Great" refers to the ten... [the ten directions].
This is the number of the Great Monasteries (*Mahāvihāra*). On the Left Street there are five monasteries: Anguo, Hoen, Jianfu, Cien, and Xingshan.
On the Right Street there are five monasteries: Zhuangyan (later changed to Shengshou), Yongtai, Ximing (later changed to Fushou), Xingfu (later changed to Feng'en), and Huadu.

On the twenty-second day of the sixth month in the twenty-third year of the Zhenguan era, while Emperor Gaozong was still in the position of Crown Prince, he was moved by the vastness of his great filial piety and stirred by his devotion to his noble mother;
thus, for his mother, Empress Wen-de, who had suddenly departed from the myriad realms, [he composed this inscription].
To repay the boundless grace of Heaven, he dispatched the Left Attendant-in-Ordinary to issue an edict to the relevant authorities:
to select within the city walls of the capital a former, abandoned monastery that must be located on a prominent and superior site, provided with flowing springs.

Consequently, they went out from the south of the palace toward Jinchang Li (formerly referred to as a "li" rather than a "fang"), facing the Qujiang Pond. There was a convent, the Jingjue Monastery, which had long been...
It was demolished and converted into a monastic residence named Daci'en Monastery. Its multi-storied pavilions and vast halls touched the clouds at dusk;
its tiered galleries and layered chambers gathered colored mists at dawn. At that time, the Crown Prince personally visited Cien Monastery.

Within the capital city, one thousand monks were ordained, and three hundred monks were requested from various temples to reside there. All necessary quarters and furnishings were ordered to be provided by the government; thus it was named.

It is named "Cien" (Great Compassion). Question: Since it is named "Great Cien," what is the meaning of the term *si* (temple)? Answer: "Si" is a name used here [in China]. In Sanskrit it is called *vihāra*;
in the language of Tang, it means "a place for wandering. It refers to a place where the assembly wanders; the characters were abbreviated for convenience.

Here in this land, the name *si* was substituted for it. The *Shiming* (Explanations of Names) states: "The name *si* means 'succession' (*si*), referring to the continuous succession of judicial officials."
"To succeed to and dwell [in a position] means that the former official has gone down and the new official has come up. Mo said: "In this country there are nine temples and nine ministries:

namely, the Minister of Light and Glory (Guanglu), the Ministry of Liquor and Meat (Jiurou), the Minister of Agriculture (Sionong), the Millers and Grinders (Nianmo), the Minister of Estates (Zhuangzhai), the Minister of the Imperial Guard (Weiwei), the Minister of Rites for Funerals (Xunyi), the Minister of the Grand Court of Sacrifices (Dachang) for Rites and Music, the Minister of Ancestral Temples (Zongzong), the Minister of Sons (Zongzi), the Minister of the Grand Treasury (Dafu), the Minister of Weights and Measures (Doucheng), the Minister of Great Chariots (Dahan), and the Minister of State Ceremonial (Honglu)."

The Ministry of Rites (Libu) was formerly called the "Guest Office" (Binkeshi), which is why it is now referred to as a "Temple" (Si). This institution was originally under the jurisdiction of the Court of State Ceremonial (Honglu).
It originated when Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna first arrived in the Han realm; they were treated like guests from foreign domains and were accommodated at the Court of State Ceremonial.

Monks were not permitted to reside together with those who had not yet received the precepts. Because Emperor Ming of the Han held them in such high esteem, separate quarters for monks were subsequently constructed within the Court of State Ceremonial.

He resided there and established the two monasteries of Baima and Xingsheng. From this point on, the single character "si" (monastery) began to be used for all monastic establishments throughout the world.
As for those who speak of the nature of a śramaṇa, its name is also called brāhmaṇa, and it is further termed the Brahma-wheel. Truly...
Because it is turned by Brahmā; "śramaṇa" here means "one who has stilled evil. The various untainted paths (anāsrava-mārga) constitute the nature of a śramaṇa;
one who harbors these paths is called a śramaṇa.

Regarding the phrase "compiled by Ji": "Ji" is the personal name of the commentator. At that time, during the early Tang dynasty, characters were not yet tabooed; it is now a character subject to national taboo.
Among the disciples of the Tripitaka Master of the Tang, many used their single-character names following the title "Mahāyāna," such as Mahāyāna Master Ji and Mahāyāna Master Guang.
There are also those who call him Huìjī (慧基) or Kuījī (窺基). Among these three names, "Ji" is the one...
He was most intimate with Kuiji. In the memorial submitted by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Tang dynasty when he was about to depart from the monastery, Kuiji’s name appears.
Furthermore, in the memorial requesting the Imperial Preface to the Sūtras, it states: "In the third year of the Longshuo era of the Great Tang, at Yuhua Palace."
He translated over six hundred fascicles of scriptures. On the twenty-third day of the eleventh month, he ordered his disciple Kuiji to submit a memorial to the throne.
The master’s name was Kuiji; his courtesy name was Hongdao; he was a native of Xiangzhou and surnamed Wei Chi.
In the twentieth year of the Zhenguan era, he removed his hairpin to enter the Way and was assigned to reside at Hongfu Monastery in Anding Ward—which is the present-day Xiude Ward.

The Yufu Temple has now been renamed Chongxian Temple. By imperial decree, five men of exceptional intelligence were selected to reside at the Great Ci’en Temple to serve the Tripiṭaka Master in person and study the Sanskrit language. Upon hearing a single correct exposition, they retained it without omission;

having surveyed the inner and outer scriptures with their own eyes, they transmitted them to their hearts, and having heard them but briefly, they could recite them from memory. Truly, they may be called sages.

A sage appeared from within the interval; a treasure of humanity emerged in full splendor. Unrivaled in excellence throughout a generation, a preeminent talent for a thousand years, he directed his thoughts within the literary arena and let his mind roam amidst the halls of calligraphy.
As his brush moved across the paper, words cascaded forth, fanning away the wind to discern the false and the deviant.
His mind was as clear as the autumn moon. He personally received the profound mysteries of the One Vehicle from former masters and revered the deep texts of the hundred [treatises] of Maitreya.
The *Xuanzan* (Profound Commentary) he composed exhausts all principles and is so wondrously transcendent that it is unprecedented throughout past and present.

At over twenty-five years of age, he responded to an imperial decree to translate scriptures and concurrently lecture on sutras and śāstras for more than thirty years, while also composing the *Fayuan Dacheng* (The Great Vehicle Garden of Dharma).
His commentaries on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and other works numbered over one hundred and were widely circulated in the world.

On the thirteenth day of the eleventh month of the second year of the Yongchun era (the year of Yiyou), he passed away in his small quarters beside the Sutra Translation Hall at the Great Ci’en Monastery at the age of fifty-one.
On the fourth day of the twelfth month of that same year, he was buried on the northern slope of Fanchuan. This is the third [entry] of the Tang dynasty.
The tomb of Master Zang is located at this site. Calculating from the year of his passing until the fourth year of the Qiánfú era, one hundred and ninety-eight years have elapsed.
Among the masters of the thousand treatises in the Western Regions was the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu; among the authors of the hundred commentaries in the Eastern Land was [Master Zang].
This refers to the Venerable Ci’en (Yijing). This ten-fascicle commentary (*śāstra*) is one of the hundred versions [of the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*].

As for the phrase "I have humbly heard" (*gǎiwén*), it is the commentator’s own expression of modesty. Regarding ancient commentaries, phrases such as "I have reverently heard" (*gōngwén gǎiwén*), "In detail," "I venture to say" (*qièyǐ*), and "Profoundly investigating" (*àotuī*) are all introductory phrases used to begin a discourse. If these are all introductory phrases, [why does this one specifically use "I have humbly heard"]?
Question: Why does he specifically begin with "I have heard"? Answer: The Master of the Commentary (Soshu) has placed "I have heard" here for a specific purpose;
it is not merely the opening of his discourse. What is that purpose? Answer: Mō says: It is the Master’s own expression of humility.
Hei (賀) says: "This establishes a phrase of doubt. [Question: How does this differ from the meaning of modesty (*kian-i*)? If one looks at the names alone, they appear distinct;

however, according to the underlying principle, the establishment of a phrase of doubt is itself the meaning of modesty. To intentionally express doubt despite knowing the truth is precisely what constitutes modesty.
The "three coverings" (*sangaē*) are merely an abbreviation. As for "establishing a phrase of doubt," it carries the sense of uncertainty. The intention of the Commentary (*Sō*) is as follows:
The principles of this sutra—whether provisional or ultimate—are such that even non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas remain confused; how then could ordinary beings attain understanding?
Now, I compose this commentary to explain the sutra, yet I do not dare claim it to be definitively aligned with the truth. Therefore, I say, "I have heard.

Since the meaning is not fixed, how can one compose a commentary to show it to later generations? Answer: Thus, when measuring the Sage by means of an ordinary person, heaven and earth are indeed [vast].
Because they differ, I shall now examine the principles of nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) by comparing and collating the preceding and following scriptural passages;

it is not necessarily the case that [the former] is entirely incorrect, nor is it necessarily fixed as such. Because this is not fixed, it is termed "doubt. Placing this here is intended to express the meaning of raising a doubt.
The *Śāstra* says: "Doubt has hesitation as its nature. One may ask: how can we know that the author of the commentary (*śūstrakāra*) did not dare to determine it definitively?
The response is as follows, according to the verses on the Burning House: first, half a verse illustrates greed, with the Sūtra stating, "owls, crows, vultures, and eagles";
one verse illustrates anger, with the Sūtra stating, "vipers, snakes, scorpions, and centipedes"; one verse illustrates delusion, with the Sūtra stating, "places reeking of excrement and urine";
one verse illustrates doubt, with the Sūtra stating, "foxes, wolves, and jackals"; and one and a half verses illustrate pride.
The Sūtra says, "By means of this, the pack of dogs, etc. Since the Sūtra text does not mention "combining" (*saṃyojana*) and so forth, how can one know that such an interpretation is made?

Answer: In the commentary below, it says: "To follow the ancients is thus for the time being; yet in principle, it is not necessarily so. Because the meaning accords with [the preceding], it is not necessarily the case that it is not so.

This means that since the house is used as a metaphor for the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), the various aggregates (*skandhas*) are the walls, the roof, and the like of that house. As for the five hundred people...
These are the designations for the five destinies (*pañca-gati*), the thirty sons, and the lineages of the three vehicles (*triyāna-gotra*).

Since it has been stated that there exist insects, spirits, and evil dharmas, this corresponds to the metaphorical representation of the ten afflictions (*daśa-kleśa*) as they manifest; thus it is said that "the meaning accords with [the teaching].
If one were to say that [these categories] are fixed, it would contradict the sutras, as it would not be the same as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. Alternatively, it may not be so, because these are not fixed.
This is a phrase used to express doubt. Question: How do we know that the character *gai* (蓋) is a term expressing doubt? Answer: The *Lunyu* says:

"The Master said, 'I have not yet seen one who loves virtue as much as they love beauty. Is it possible for someone seeking the mind for learning and practice to resemble the mind that seeks wealth and beauty?

Answer: If one were to say there is no such thing at all, then consider those who "suspended their heads" and "pierced their thighs," or who "bored through walls to steal light" in order to seek learning.
The mind of worldly ambition is of the same nature as the mind that seeks wealth and sensual pleasure.

If such a mind were ever present within the Way, it would merely be something heard with the ears, for one would not yet see it with the eyes. Therefore, the Master said: "It may indeed exist, but I have not yet seen it.

The word "perhaps" (*gai*) expresses doubt and is also a term of humility. Furthermore, the *Classic of Filial Piety* states that Zhongni recounted the five types of filial piety for the Son of Heaven... [text continues].

When discussing the practice of filial piety by the feudal lords, it is called "the filial piety of the feudal lords"; when discussing the filial piety of the high ministers, great officers, and scholars, it is all said to be "essentially the filial piety of the Son of Heaven.
Yet, when it comes to the practice of filial piety by the common people, one immediately says, "This is the filial piety of the common people.

The Master said, "I have never encountered the practice of filial piety by the Son of Heaven," for although the Master’s official rank reached that of Grand Master of Ceremonies, he never held a higher office. Not so.
In the past, I personally witnessed various feudal lords practicing filial piety; I did not dare to make a definitive judgment, and thus I said "it is likely" (*gai*).

When it came to the common people, I said, "This is the filial piety of the commoner. The Master said: "As for the matters of the commoners, I have personally experienced each and every one of them myself;
therefore, I do not say 'it is likely. [The questioner] asked: "When the Master established the rites and created the music, did he not know Heaven?"
"Does the son, the feudal lord, practice filial piety? He replied, "Master, you truly know; this is merely a hypothetical doubt. This very formulation of a doubt is itself a statement of humility.

As for the character *gài* (蓋), if it is interpreted in relation to the Master himself, then the "doubt" is a hypothetical construction, and the act of knowing yet asking anyway is a term of humility.
One who understands these two explanations will take the character *gài* as referring to the person of the commentator (*shuzhu*).

The preceding explanation also encompasses two meanings. If the commentator (*shuzhu*) is an emanation of a Bodhisattva, then the expression of doubt is a hypothetical device; furthermore, it may be termed "humility.

If the commentator is actually an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*), then the expression of doubt is a literal statement. The single character "gai" (蓋) applies only to the hypothetical expression of doubt and cannot be termed "humility.
Since the commentator is an ordinary being, separated by a vast distance from noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*), they have never personally realized [the truth].

I venture to offer this definitive judgment; therefore, I set aside further words. Mochizuki [Mō] said: "This also reveals that as the Dharma teachings flowed eastward, they gradually lost their true essence.

As the Tathāgata himself said, 'It is like leaves in one's hand. While the Three Piṭakas were compiled so that not a single word was lost, the Bodhisattvas composed treatises whose interpretations differ.
Translators did not transmit all the scriptures; as for the composition of commentaries (*śāstra*), they have become increasingly thin and numerous. Thus he described it himself.
Out of humility and reverence, I say "it is covered. During the lifetime of the Tathāgata, he transmitted it to Ānanda;

Ānanda transmitted it to a thousand great arhats. The arhats recorded it upon palm leaves (*tāla-patra*). When the Tripitaka was brought here and translated, it was like many people passing a handful of water from hand to hand;
gradually it was lost. Now that we are far removed from the Sage, those who compose commentaries to explain the teachings cannot fathom the Buddha’s intent.

I do not dare to establish a definitive standard; therefore, I have raised these doubts and used the term "perhaps" (*gài*). The "three obscurations" (*sāṃkleśika-dharma*) mentioned here is but a brief summary.

For instance, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* in six hundred fascicles extensively discusses the nature (*dhātu*). This corresponds to the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*) in this present sutra.
According to the biography of the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha, Nāgārjuna saw three versions of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the Great Sutra on the Inconceivable Liberation, within the ocean.
The original version consisted of verses numbering as many as the atoms in thirteen thousand great trichiliocosms and chapters numbering as many as the atoms in one four-continent world-system.
The intermediate version contained four hundred and ninety thousand verses and one thousand two hundred chapters. Both of these two versions are currently located within the Dragon Palace.

Even if one were to use Mount Sumeru as a brush and the waters of the four great oceans as ink to write out a single chapter of the *Sūtra* contemplated by the Bhikṣu Sāgaramegha, it could not be fully exhausted.
[End of] the original text. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda during the second year of the Xianqing era of the Great Tang.
However, this largely explains the characteristics [of phenomena], which is the "ox-cart" of this very sūtra; it awakens one to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Now, this one...
"Vehicle. Because both nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are explained together, the *Śāstra*’s commentary on the "Expedient Means" chapter states:

"From here below, the cause and fruit of the One Vehicle are revealed. The sub-commentary explains: "Because there are differences in essence, characteristics, and manifestations, these various sutras present this extensively;

this sutra is therefore called the abbreviated version, and thus it is said 'merely' (*kevalam*). However, according to this interpretation, the character 'merely' (*gai*) belongs to the sutra itself, and furthermore, it is not..."

This is the beginning of the spoken discourse; therefore, it does not rely [on further elaboration]. It merely adopts the first two interpretations: first, the expression of doubt; second, the sense of humility and reverence.
Regarding the word "to hear" (*wén*): the *Yùpiān* states that it means "to know sound. The *Qièyùn* states that "to hear" means "the ear knows. The emptiness of the ear constitutes...
Gate. It is only when one hears the object of sound that the character for "ear" is now placed within the gate. For the ear-faculty to hear sound, it must rely upon the condition of space (*ākāśa*).
If the ear-faculty is blocked, one does not hear sound; only when the ear is placed in a space can one hear sound. The "gate" is precisely this space.
If walls are built on all four sides and no gate is opened, there will be congestion and obstruction in the coming and going; therefore, one side must be opened.

This is the gateway of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). It is only when the gateway of emptiness is applied to the ear that it can be called "hearing. Ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) apprehends sound within the gateway of the ear-organ;

therefore, the character for "hearing" (*wen*, 聞) contains the character for "ear" (*er*, 耳). Among the six methods of writing (*liushu*), this is a "pictographic-synthetic" character (*huiyi zi*, 會意字).

The *Śāstra* states: "Eye-consciousness arises from nine conditions; ear-consciousness arises from only eight," and so forth. Question: Why does it not say that seeing, perceiving, and knowing are empty, while hearing is what is heard?

The answer is: These are merely the humble words of the Master of the Commentary (*śāstrakāra*). He employs the principles of inference based on what has been heard and reflected upon (*śruta-cintā*).

Such speech regarding "hearing" (*śruta*) indicates that this is not yet the direct realization (*pratyakṣa-sākṣātkāra*) of an Ārya; therefore, he does not speak of "seeing," "awakening," or "knowing. Having finished expressing his own humble intent, the commentary’s topical outline (*kośa*) labels this section as a "general exposition" (*sāmānya-nirdeśa*).
This means it applies universally to the three bodies (*trikāya*), and its teaching extends to other systems of instruction; hence, it is called a "general exposition."

Regarding the phrase "this school" (*cizong*), it refers exclusively to this particular school. Yongtai’s *Ke* (Outline) states: "To list exhaustively the ultimate teachings" refers to the two phrases "the ultimate awakening" and "expedient and true.
This praises the three bodies (*trikāya*) as being common to all sutras; thus, there is a sense in which the name is "common to the ultimate" (*tongzhi*).

Next, the two phrases beginning with "spiritual pivot" (*lingshu*) refer to the name being "common to the teaching" (*tongjiao*). Phrases such as "Zhenshan and Rongshan" specifically indicate the primary teaching. The *Lotus Sūtra* is the transformation [teaching].
The Buddha of the Body (*kāyabuddha*). In relation to those of the Two Vehicles and ordinary beings, he preaches the Dharma at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa; therefore, this is called the "Distinctive Teaching.

Furthermore, according to the outline by [Dao]mu, regarding the phrase "the manifestation of the body of Bodhi," it first provides a general praise of how the true body (*dharmakāya*) is able to manifest provisional bodies (*upāyakāya*).
The first phrase is a general praise of the *dharmakāya* (the body of reality), while the second phrase refers to the ability to manifest the *nirmāṇakāya* (the provisional body). Question:
What is meant by "the manifestation of the bodhi-body"? Answer: "Bodhi" refers to the *svasaṃbhogakāya* (body of self-enjoyment), which is the bodhi of the four wisdoms (*caturjñāna*).

It is called the "manifestation of the bodhi-body" because it possesses the capacity to manifest the *parasaṃbhogakāya* (body of enjoyment for others) and the various *nirmāṇakāyas* (emanated bodies). Regarding the statement "wisdom discerns in response to objects," next—

The commentary on the two lines generally praises the wisdom of reality (*dharmatā-jñāna*) as being able to manifest the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*). The first line generally praises the wisdom of reality;

the second line concerns the ability to manifest the wisdom of skillful means. This is the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhoga-kāya*), which possesses four and seven types of discerning functions for benefiting sentient beings;

these are termed "the discernment of wisdom that responds to objects. Regarding the phrase "becoming the wisdom of the superior body," the commentary on the latter two lines provides a general exposition of the provisional and the real.

Body and wisdom constitute the person who can preach the Dharma. The first phrase generally describes the provisional and real bodies; the second phrase generally describes the provisional and real wisdoms.

Combining these two phrases constitutes the person who can preach the Dharma. Shaking Mount Wuyue (Vibhūṣaṇa) to beautify the great trichiliocosm, this accomplishes the first and second phrases regarding the Buddha-body.
Surging forth from the vast ocean to provide access for the eighty thousand [dharmas], this accomplishes...

The third and fourth lines above refer to the Buddha-wisdom (*buddhajñāna*). Regarding the question of the manifestation of the *bodhi*-body: it is not yet clear which of the three bodies (*trikāya*) is manifested.

There are two interpretations: first, the interpretation based on essence (*svabhāva*); second, the interpretation based on characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Regarding the first, the Master of Essence says:
"The ultimate reality of the true nature is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); the ultimate function of that same reality is the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*). This is the essence.
Because they are inseparable, the one body is itself the three bodies. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "This body of mine is now the eternal body, the Dharma-body.
The *Yixing jie* (Explanation of the Single Nature) says: Within the state of Buddhahood, there are no conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).

One cannot, through cultivation over three great eons, seek a conditioned Buddha-body as a fruit. From the Path of Liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) onward, it is the Self-Enjoyment Body (*svasaṃbhoga-kāya*).

The four wisdoms of enlightenment are, in their entirety, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). Question: If this is so, how is it that the sacred teachings state that the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*) is a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*)?
Answer: The *Yichengzong hui* (Compendium of the One Vehicle School) explains: This is provisionally based on the stages from the seventeenth ground onward.

The body perceived by a bodhisattva is said to be conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). If there is a bodhisattva who has attained Buddhahood, other bodhisattvas of a similar class will accompany him as he proceeds to the seat of the Great Jewel Flower King (*mahāratnapadmarāja*).

At the moment he enters the vajra-untainted path (*vajrānantaryamārga*), his body still possesses limits; however, once he has entered the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), this Buddha-body becomes limitless. This is...

It is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). All the bodhisattvas who have come here see only the body of the path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*), and do not see the body of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

This is solely because they perceive the body of the path of uninterrupted realization as conditioned; they assume that the body belonging to one who has already entered the path of liberation is likewise conditioned.
Therefore, the masters of the Five-Nature School (*pañca-gotra*) speak within the holy teachings that even the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhoga-kāya*) is [conditioned].

This is the teaching of the Master of the Single-Nature School (Ekayāna). Having reckoned that [the stage of] the Vajra Uninterrupted Path (*anantarya-mārga*) is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and that from the Path of Liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) onward it is entirely unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), the second [explanation] is according to the interpretation of the School of Characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-vāda*).

Regarding the manifestation of Bodhi in the present body: if one analyzes phenomena (*dharma*) without confusion, the pure Dharma-realm (*viśuddha-dharmadhātu*) constitutes the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). That is to say—

This is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). The four wisdoms of bodhi constitute the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*), as well as the transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) of both the Great and Small Vehicles; these are the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Muzhou offers two interpretations. First, he says that when bodhi manifests its body, it universally manifests the bodies of the three Buddhas—Dharmakāya, Saṃbhogakāya, and Nirmāṇakāya.
Second, if one refers to the assembly on Vulture Peak, it was specifically for the sake of those with the three capacities.
Regarding the teaching that hearing the *Lotus Sūtra* refers only to the sixteen-foot transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), this is called the manifestation of the body of bodhi.

The *Pomuyi* (Exposition on the Meaning) states: "The initial [definition] is too broad and thus erroneous. The Dharma-body is formless and signless; the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*) is bodhi.
Now, when it says 'the manifestation of the body of bodhi,' one should take the body manifested by the family of bodhi; one should not take the other-enjoyment body (*parasaṃbhogakāya*)."

By means of the great and small transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*), bodhi is that which manifests, and the Buddha-body is that which is manifested; this is termed "the manifestation of the body of bodhi.

The latter interpretation is too narrow. Now, since it is stated that this serves as a general introduction for all sutras, there are also instances where it refers to the enjoyment body for others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*).
If one were to take only the small transformation body of sixteen feet as the "manifestation of the body of bodhi," it would then constitute a specific introduction.
This is not called the "General Preface. Now, relying on the straightforward principles of the Mahāyāna, I shall provide two interpretations myself.

First, regarding the meaning of "predominance," I interpret this as the manifestation of the body of Bodhi. Question: What is meant by "predominance"? Answer: Among the four wisdoms (*jñāna*), it refers to three of those wisdoms.

The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom manifests as the Bodhi of the Self-Enjoyment Body, excelling in manifesting the body while being subtle regarding the meaning of the Dharma. The Equality Wisdom manifests as the Bodhi of the Tenfold Other-Enjoyment Bodies, excelling in teaching the Dharma while being subtle regarding the body. The All-Accomplishing Wisdom manifests as the Bodhi of the various Great and Small Transformation Bodies, excelling in manifesting the body while being subtle regarding the meaning of the Dharma. The Wondrous Observational Wisdom... [excels] in teaching the Dharma while being subtle regarding the body.

Thus, the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom Bodhi manifests the Self-Enjoyment Body; the Equality Wisdom Bodhi manifests the ten grades of Other-Enjoyment Bodies; and the All-Accomplishing Wisdom Bodhi manifests the various Great and Small Transformation Bodies. The Wondrous Observational Wisdom... [excels] in... the Dharma.
The wisdom of bodhi teaches the Dharma in both pure and impure lands; this wisdom only teaches the Dharma and does not manifest its physical body.
Second, according to the principle of equality, the bodhi manifests its body; all four wisdoms are capable of manifesting the body and all are capable of teaching the Dharma.
This is called the manifestation of the body of Bodhi. The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom Bodhi can manifest the body and preach the Dharma;
the Wisdom of Equality Bodhi can manifest the body and preach the Dharma; the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done Bodhi can manifest the body and preach the Dharma;
the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation is likewise. If these four wisdoms were to manifest all three bodies simultaneously, it would not be possible. Furthermore, if they were to preach the Dharma alone—
One cannot manifest the body alone. If manifesting the body were insufficient for teaching the Dharma, then consider the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done).

Since this is the wisdom that manifests the body, how can the treatises state that it initiates transformations through the three types of action (*trikarma*) and provides the four kinds of answers (*catuḥpratisaraṇa*)?

If this wisdom is thus, so too are the others. Furthermore, within the state of Buddhahood, there would be no sense of mastery over its qualities; such would be the case for one who has attained unsurpassed enlightenment.
The supernormal powers are inconceivable; a dharma that lacks form or substance can manifest material images. Furthermore, there are two interpretations in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*. First:
the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) manifests the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*) manifests the Enjoyment-body (*saṃbhogakāya*);

the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) manifests bodies of various sizes; and the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) preaches the Dharma in both pure and impure lands. Second: [the wisdom of] purity...
The Dharma-realm manifests as the Dharma-body; the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom manifests as the self-enjoyment body;
the Wisdom of Equality manifests as the ten grades of the other-enjoyment body; the Wisdom of Accomplishing Tasks manifests as the great and small transformation bodies;

and the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation preaches the Dharma in both pure and impure lands. This latter interpretation is the correct meaning. According to the intent of the present commentary, *bodhi* (enlightenment) refers to the self-enjoyment [body].
Regarding the body: the body manifested by the family of the four wisdoms of bodhi is precisely the *parasaṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body for others) and the various *nirmāṇakāyas* (emanation bodies).

It is only when it manifests as a bodhisattva that the principle is correct. (The preceding section concludes the question-and-answer on the manifestation of the body of bodhi; below is a brief explanation of the three bodies, followed by a detailed commentary.)

The *Xianyang lun* (Exposition of the Manifestation), in its verse of homage, states: "The Sugata’s well-spoken and wondrous Three Bodies, The fearless and untainted realization and teaching, And the sons of the Muni of the Supreme Vehicle who realize the truth— To these I now offer praise and prostration with sincere devotion.

If one discusses the bodies of the Buddhas, fundamentally there are not two; yet, according to what sentient beings are fit to hear and see, they appear as three. First is the Dharmakāya, which is free from... [text fragment ends]

The reality that is free from defilement. Second is the *saṃbhogakāya* (Enjoyment Body), which is the actual wisdom that realizes suchness. Third is the *nirmāṇakāya* (Emanation Body), which is the provisional form that responds to sentient beings.

Thus, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "The self-nature body (*svābhāvikakāya*), the dharma body (*dharmakāya*), and the transformation body (*nairmāṇikakāya*) are distinguished as three bodies based on their different modes of manifestation.

Regarding the meaning of these three bodies, according to the treatise, there is a thirteenfold analysis: first, the explanation of names; second, the determination of essence; third... [and so forth].

1. The three constants and the three virtues; 2. Preaching the Dharma and not preaching the Dharma; 3. The distinction between the two benefits; 4. The difference between the views of ordinary beings and sages;
5. The distinctness of their respective merits; 6. The differentiation of their bases; 7. The identity and difference of their bodies and lands; 8. The causes and conditions for their establishment.

[The following] is subsumed within the *Dharmalakṣaṇa* (Characteristics of Phenomena) of the "Eleventh Five-Year Plan": 12. Distinguishing the quantity of characteristics; 13. Analysis through question and answer.

These cannot be explained in detail here; I shall briefly explain two gates: the explanation of names and the determination of essence (*svabhāva*). First, the explanation of names is divided into two parts. Initially, the explanation of the general name.

Regarding the general name: "Three" (*tri*) has the meaning of number. As for "body" (*kāya*), the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "The meanings of essence, basis, and collection. Taken together, it is called a [general] name.
The Body. Second, the section explaining the distinct names is divided into three parts: 1. The Pure Dharmakāya, Vairocana Buddha. The commentary states:

"Cutting off the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) is called 'pure' (*vi-*, *viśuddha*); cutting off the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is called 'clear' (*ru*, *loka*). 2. Another explanation states: "Cutting off the seeds of the two hindrances is called 'pure';

eliminating the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the two hindrances is called 'clear. 3. A third explanation states: "Subduing the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) of the hindrances is called 'pure'; cutting off the seeds and habitual tendencies of the hindrances is called 'clear. [This is] the supreme...
The *Sūtra of the Victorious King* states: "For example, when pure gold is melted and refined, once it has been smelted and beaten, there is no longer any dust or impurity;
this is because the nature of gold is fundamentally pure, and thus the essence of the gold is pure—it does not mean that the gold itself is non-existent.

In the same way, when the dharmakāya is freed from afflictions and the accumulation of suffering, no further habitual tendencies remain; this is because the buddha-nature is fundamentally pure—it does not mean [that the dharmakāya is non-existent]."
This means it is not non-existent. For example, when obscured by smoke, clouds, dust, or mist, the space-element remains;

it is not that space itself is non-existent once the obstructions have been cleared away. In the same way, because all sufferings have been completely exhausted within the Dharmakāya, it is described as "pure."
This does not mean that it lacks substance. "Dharma" (dharma) carries the meaning of "guiding and upholding. "Body" (kāya) carries the meaning of "substance" and the meaning of "basis.
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is the essential nature of reality; it lacks the meaning of "accumulation. Regarding *Vairocana*, this is translated as "Pervading All Places and Quiescent. Question:

Is the true reality possessed by ordinary beings, those of the two vehicles, and all bodhisattvas called the "Dharmakāya"? Answer: Because they do not yet possess the sense of being a "basis," it is not so named.

The Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Thus, the *Cheng weishi lun* (Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra) states: "The self-nature body (*svabhāvakāya*) refers to the true and pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) of all Tathāgatas.
It is the equal basis for the enjoyment (*saṃbhoga*) and transformation (*nirmāṇa*) bodies; it is free from characteristics, quiescent, and transcends all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
It possesses infinite, truly eternal merits and is the equal, ultimate nature of all phenomena. This very self-nature is also called the Dharma-body. Great.
Because it is the basis for the dharmas of merit, the "dharmas of great merit" refers precisely to the bodhi of the four wisdoms.
Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Thus, these categories of the four wisdoms completely encompass all conditioned merits of the Buddha and others.

Furthermore, the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra* says: "When enmeshed in defilements, it is called the Tathāgatagarbha; when free from enmeshment, it is called the Great Dharmakāya. The commentary explains: "As..."
The *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) has two aspects. First is the empty *tathāgatagarbha*. Because its afflictions are with-outflow (*sāsrava*), false, and unreal, it is called "empty.
Because it can conceal *tathatā* (suchness), it is called the *tathāgatagarbha*. Ci'en states that it is also called the "concealing storehouse";

it is named a "storehouse" (*garbha*) because it is like earth covering an object. Second is the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*. Because *tathatā* is without-outflow (*anāsrava*) and its essence is not false, it is called "non-empty."

That which is covered by afflictions is called the *tathāgatagarbha*. Ci'en says: it is also called "that which can manifest the revealed treasury," just as a gold ingot [is the source from which ornaments are made].
Question: True Suchness (*tathatā*) and Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) are that which is revealed; how can they instead be called "that which can manifest the revealed treasury"? Answer:

It is because True Suchness and Buddha-nature are the fundamental basis from which great meditative concentration, wisdom, compassion, and so forth flow forth, just as a gold ingot can produce [ornaments].
Regarding hairpins, bells, and bracelets: according to the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, there are also two kinds of *tathāgatagarbha*: first, the empty; second, the non-empty.

The eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) with outflows is called "empty" because its nature is false and illusory. It is called the *tathāgatagarbha* because it can contain the originally existing untainted seeds of the four wisdoms (*caturjñāna*).
Ci'en [Master Kuiji] says that it is named for its capacity to "contain and store," where "store" (garbha) is like a treasury or granary. [The four wisdoms are:]...
The seed-essence (*bīja*) is, in its nature, untainted (*anāsrava*) and not a false phenomenon; thus it is called "not empty" (*aśūnya*).

Because it can contain the future manifestation of the four wisdoms (*jñāna*), it is called the *tathāgatagarbha*. Ci'en says: "It is able to produce what is obtained as a 'store,' just like grain, wheat, and so forth.

Second, regarding the Perfectly Complete Reward Body (*pūrṇa-sambhoga-kāya*) Vairocana: the commentary states that "perfect" (*yuan*) means all-encompassing, and "complete" (*man*) means pervasive. As for "Vairocana," this—
Regarding the statement that "the light of radiance shines universally," there are two types: first, internal; second, external.

As for internal universal illumination, this refers to the *svasaṃbhoga-kāya* (self-enjoyment body), which, by means of untainted fundamental wisdom (*anāsrava-mūla-jñāna*), illuminates the darkness of the afflictive and cognitive obscurations within its own internal body. As for external universal illumination:
Next is the *sāmbhogika-kāya* (Enjoyment Body). It expounds the Dharma of the ten *pāramitās* and transforms Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

The beings thus transformed give rise to wisdom and sever their delusions; therefore, it is called "retribution" (*vipāka*). "Retribution" carries the sense of "requital. It is the body of fruition resulting from the influence of myriad practices;

because it requites past causal conduct, it is named "retribution. One should understand that this body possesses three meanings. There are two types of it: first, the *svasaṃbhogika-kāya* (Self-Enjoyment Body);...

Regarding the "Body" (*kāya*): The treatise states that it refers to the boundless, true merits arising from the immeasurable accumulations of merit and wisdom cultivated by all Tathāgatas over three incalculable eons, as well as their perfectly pure, eternal, and omnipresent form-body (*rūpakāya*), which remains in a state of continuous, profound stillness.
To the end of the future, he constantly enjoys the vast dharma-pleasure for himself; this is called the Body of Self-Enjoyment.
Second is the Body of Enjoyment for Others, which refers to the Tathāgatas manifesting subtle and pure bodies of merit through their wisdom of equality.

Dwelling in purely pure lands, they display great supernatural powers and turn the wheel of the true Dharma for the sake of the assembly of Bodhisattvas dwelling on the ten stages, resolving their doubts.
"Net. This causes them to enjoy the bliss of the Mahāyāna Dharma. When these two aspects are combined, it is called the *saṃbhogakāya* (Enjoyment Body). Question:

Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) have already transcended the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and are thus free from the net of doubts. How can the treatise state that [the Enjoyment Body] "resolves the nets of doubt for the assembly"?

Answer: There are two explanations by Cien (Yijing). First, he says: "If one considers doubt regarding the ultimate principle (*tattva*), it is eliminated upon entering the path of seeing. However, what is meant here is doubt regarding conventional phenomena (*vastu*); therefore, there is no contradiction."
It is permitted that there is [such a mind]. Second, it is said: This is a mind born of the maturation (*vipāka*) of the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*);

because it is indeterminate regarding its object and resembles doubt, it is designated by the name "doubt. The latter interpretation is superior. Regarding the phrase "three thousand billion transformation bodies of Śākyamuni Buddha":
the commentary states that "thousand billion" refers to the number. *Śākyamuni* means "Able to Pacify" (*neng ji*). There are two kinds of "able to pacify": first, the ability to pacify oneself...
"Śānta" (Quiescence) refers to the thirty-four moments of mind beneath the Bodhi tree, wherein the seeds and habitual tendencies of the afflictions (*kleśa*) were severed and extinguished.

The *Śata-śāstra-kārikā* states: "I prostrate at the Buddha’s feet; I take refuge in the World-Honored One, who for immeasurable eons bore manifold sufferings. His afflictions are exhausted and his habitual tendencies removed;
Brahmā, Śakra, nāgas, and devas feel deep reverence. "2. Ability to Quiesce Others" means causing those to be converted—the two vehicles (*yāna*) and bodhisattvas—to [attain] quiescence.

The term "Saṅgha" refers to those who have severed and extinguished the afflictions (*kleśa*). It is also said that Śākyamuni is his clan name; *Śākya* means "able," and *Muni* is his personal name, which is translated as "Benevolent.
The title "Able Benevolent One" (*Nengren*) is derived from this. The *Cheng weishi lun* (Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra) states: "Third is the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

This refers to all Tathāgatas who, by means of the wisdom of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), manifest immeasurable transformation bodies according to the various classes of beings, dwelling in the pure [lands]."

In this defiled land, for the sake of bodhisattvas who have not yet attained the stages (*bhūmi*), as well as followers of the two vehicles and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), he manifests supernatural powers and preaches the Dharma according to their respective capacities, causing each to obtain various benefits and joys.
The commentary states: "Transformation" (*nirmāṇa*) means that changing an old substance is called "transformation" (*pariṇāma*);

that which suddenly exists where there was none is called "manifestation" (*nirmita*). Therefore, it is called the "transformation body" (*nirmāṇakāya*). Question: Regarding the other two bodies, both are produced from the transformation of the five [aggregates].
Regarding the aggregates (*skandha*): how are the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) and *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) distinguished? Answer:

The *saṃbhogakāya* dwells in a purely pure land and manifests forms to teach the Dharma for the sake of the noble ones who have attained the stages (*bhūmi*). Therefore, it receives the name "enjoyment.

The *nirmāṇakāya* likewise dwells in impure lands and manifests as having wives, children, greed, anger, ignorance, and so forth, or [endures hardships such as] golden spikes or horse-barley, for the sake of transforming the assemblies of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) of small capacity.

It manifests various painful signs, such as back pain and so forth; therefore, it is called "transformation" (*nirmāṇa*). Furthermore, because the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) possesses subtle and exquisite physical characteristics, it receives the designation "body" (*kāya*);

because the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body) is coarse and manifest, it is termed "transformation. Finally, the conclusion is attributed to the six types of grammatical compounds (*ṣaṭ-vyākhyāna*). Cien (Ci'en) states:

"The three bodies are all exclusively *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compounds, such as 'the Dharma itself is the body' (*dharmas-tathatā-kāya*). Jianfu (Jianfu) states: "They also admit the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound."

The Dharma is ultimate truth (*tattva*). The essence of truth (*tattvātman*) is primary and serves as the basis for the *asaṃkhyeya* merits. The bodily functions are adventitious; this is the body of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
This is called a "dependent determinative compound" (*tatpuruṣa*) based on identity of substance. Furthermore, regarding the term "Dharmakāya" (Dharma-body):

the Dharma is ultimate truth, and "body" (*kāya*) has the meaning of a basis of reliance. By subsuming the function of reliance and returning it to the essence of ultimate truth, it is named the Dharmakāya.
"Dharma is itself the body" (dharmakāya) is an analysis based on the identity of the action and its agent (*karmadhāraya*). It is like saying "water is itself the waves.

This [interpretation] is still not fully understood, for how does it encompass the functional aspect that serves as the basis for taking refuge? One should say that both characters, "Dharma" and "Body," apply to both essence and function:

Dharma is itself the body, and the body is itself Dharma; only thus is the principle exhausted. It is like saying "discernment is itself the mind" (*manas*), or "the mind is itself discernment," and so forth. [This applies to] the *saṃbhogakāya*.
As for this: if explained in terms of the *svasaṃbhogakāya* (body of self-enjoyment), the "self-retribution" is the body itself; this is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound).

If discussed in terms of the *parasaṃbhogakāya* (body of enjoyment for others), it is the body that is the object of enjoyment for others; this is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound). Regarding the three bodies as the essence (*svabhāva*):

first, the *svābhāvikakāya* (essential body) takes true suchness (*tathatā*) among the one hundred dharmas as its essence. Question: Why does it not take the first five unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas as its essence?
Answer: The first five unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are provisional and not ultimate reality. Since the *dharmakāya* is itself suchness (*tathatā*), it is unconditioned;
it takes up the stainless suchness within the state of fruition (*phala-avasthā*), but does not take up the defiled suchness of the causal stage (*hetu-avasthā*).

Question: If the suchness within the causal stage possesses defilement, it should therefore not be pure. Answer: The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Although it may admit of being stained, its nature is fundamentally pure."
Like jade resting in mud, or a lotus flower in water. Question: If the true nature of suchness (*tathatā*) is not equal, then why are there two categories—the defiled and the undefiled?
Since suchness is an equal dharma, how can cause and effect be divided into two? Answer:

If we discuss suchness apart from verbal designations, its equal, ultimate reality is fundamentally non-dual. However, when approaching it through designations and according to stages, the gate of cause and effect is established.

The middle [category] is divided into two types. Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Suchness (*tathatā*) is the basis for both delusion and awakening. When it exists in the causal stage, it is the basis for delusion and cannot serve as the essence of the *dharmakāya*.
When it exists in the resultant stage, it is the basis for awakening and is capable of serving as the essence of the *dharmakāya*.

Second is the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*), which takes the actual untainted five aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*) as its essence; it is the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) and a portion of the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

It manifests as the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*). Thus, the *Cheng weishi lun* states: "The mental complex associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) is free from all conceptualization;
its objects and modes of activity are subtle and difficult to know. It is neither forgetful nor deluded regarding any objective phenomena, and its nature and characteristics are pure."

Free from all defilements, it is a pure and perfect excellence. As the support for both the manifest and the seeds, it can manifest and produce the reflections of bodies, lands, and wisdom, continuously and without interruption until the end of the future. It is like a great round mirror manifesting a variety of colors and forms. Commentary:

Regarding "free from all conceptualization," the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states that this refers to being free from the grasping at "mine" and all conceptualizations of the grasped object (*grāhya*) and the grasping subject (*grāhaka*).
Regarding the statement that "the conditions and aspects are subtle and difficult to know": both the objects and their aspects are generally difficult to fathom.
"Non-delusive" means they are constantly present before one; by virtue of this, the Tathāgata does not possess the quality of forgetfulness. "Non-ignorant" means he is not deluded or obscured.

For this reason, the Tathāgata is named the One of All-Knowledge (*sarvajña*) and the One of Knowledge of All Aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Regarding the phrase "whose nature and characteristics are pure and free from all defilements":

because outflows (*āsrava*) have been eternally extinguished, he is free from all impurities. Regarding the phrase "pure, perfect, and complete virtues": "pure" means being unmixed; this distinguishes him from the untainted (*anāsrava*) states that still belong to the causal stage.

"Pure" means being free from faults; it distinguishes [this quality] from all contaminated (*sāsrava*) virtues. "Perfect" has the meaning of fulfillment; it distinguishes it from the virtues of those in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) of the two vehicles.
Regarding "the support for both manifest and seeds": it is the support for manifest virtues and the seed that sustains the seeds of virtue.

Regarding that which can manifest and can produce the reflections of body, land, and wisdom: if one’s own form, mind, and so forth arise from seeds distinct from the eighth consciousness, they are called "that which can produce.
If the bodies of others, the various realms of existence (*gati*), and so forth lack distinct seeds and merely appear as reflections upon consciousness, they are called "that which can manifest.
Question: Within this realm of the Mirror-like Wisdom King, do these twenty-two factors undergo a common transformation (*sādhāraṇa-pariṇāma*)? Or is it only the self-experience...?

Regarding the body: does each [consciousness] transform it individually? Answer: It is real that this body is transformed by the mind-king (*citta-rāja*); that which is transformed by the mental factors (*caitta*) is merely a semblance.
If one were to say that the mental factors transform the body in the same way as the mind-king and that the body is real, one would commit the error of increasing the number of sentient beings.

If one were to claim that the mental factors do not transform it at all, then the conditions would be deficient. This is a counter-example to the principle of identity. Regarding the contaminated (*sāsrava*) cause and effect: the body transformed by the sovereign and its attendant mental factors of the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*). Mind...
The five objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the king-like [self-]aspect are conventional. Letting the real and the conventional intermingle, they together constitute a single body.

Regarding the third, the Body of Enjoyment for Others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*): it takes the transformation of the five aggregates as its essence; it is the objective aspect of the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*).

This objective aspect arises from the same seed as its subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*). Among these five aggregate-aspects, the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is a transformation-existence (*nirmāṇa-sattva*), resembling...
The function of form (*rūpa*) belongs to the other aggregates (*skandha*), which possess the function of mental apprehension (*ālambana*) similar to that of the mind.

Since this Buddha resides in an untainted pure land (*anāsrava-vyūha-kṣetra*), those he transforms are exclusively noble beings who have attained the stages (*bhūmi-praviṣṭa-ārya-saṃgha*); there are no devas, nāgas, or the eight classes of supernatural beings.

Among the mental factors (*caitta*), there are only the eleven universal (*sarvatraga*), object-specific (*viśeṣya*), and wholesome (*kuśala*) factors; there are no root-affiliated (*kleśa-mahābhūmika*) or indeterminate (*aniyata*) factors. 4.

The *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body) likewise takes the transformation of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as its essence; it is the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done).

The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "That which takes the transformation of the five aggregates as its essence does so by taking the sentient beings to be transformed as its substantial basis (*bimba*), like a tree outside a mirror.
The manifested Buddha-body is like the reflection of the tree within the mirror. Because the reflection resembles the basis, it is termed 'resembling' (*pratibimba*). This...

Among the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is a transformation-existence (*nirmāṇabhava*), possessing a function similar to that of physical matter. The remaining aggregates are mind-existences (*cittabhava*), possessing a function similar to that of cognitive engagement (*ālambana-manasikāra*).
(The following is the commentary from the *Xiaosushu*).

Regarding the phrase "the provisional is the true of ultimate awakening," there are three interpretations. The first states: "Ultimate awakening" is the general designation for the three bodies (*trikāya*).

It does not assign the name to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) alone; rather, it takes the two types of retributive bodies—those of self and others—along with the transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) of both the Great and Small Vehicles, collectively naming them "ultimate awakening.
The reason the Dharma-body is not included is that it lacks form and characteristics (*nimitta*); it is like space, which cannot be defiled by smoke or clouds, and like white jade.
Moistened yet not stained. Question: Regarding the three bodies—the *svasaṃbhogakāya*, *parasaṃbhogakāya*, and *nirmāṇakāya*—why are they collectively termed "Ultimate Enlightenment" (*zhìjué*)?

Answer: In Sanskrit, it is called *buddha*; here, it is translated as "the Awakened One. Because these three bodies constitute this totality, they are collectively termed "Ultimate Enlightenment. Question: What is meant by "expedient means" (*quán*)? Answer:

Expedient means refers to the *nirmāṇakāyas* of both the Mahayana and Hinayana which possess the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*). Those *nirmāṇakāyas* that manifest according to the various types of beings but do not possess these marks are collectively termed "expedient means."
The "True" refers to both the Body of Self-Enjoyment (*svasaṃbhogakāya*) and the Body of Enjoyment for Others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*); taken together, they are designated as "True. Question:

The Body of Self-Enjoyment has the five untainted aggregates (*anāsravaskandha*) as its essence and can thus be called "True. However, the Body of Enjoyment for Others does not consist of real qualities;

how can it also be called "True"? Answer: In relation to the Emanation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*), it is also called "True. Second, [another interpretation] states that the realization of awakening is the same as that of the aforementioned self and others.
The collective designation for the three bodies of transformation is "Ultimate Enlightenment" (Sambodhi). Question: What is meant by "provisional"? Answer:

The bodies of Great and Small Transformation that are received by others are called provisional. Question: What is meant by "real"? Answer: The Dharma-body and the Body of Self-Enjoyment are called real.

The Dharma-body is called "true" because it is free from delusion; the self-enjoyment body is called "true" because it is real. The third [master] says: that which reaches awakening is the reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*);

that which is provisional is the transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*); and that which is true is the Dharma-body. Muzhou says: regarding these two explanations, "that which reaches awakening" refers solely to the self [of the Buddha] and not to others;
it is exclusively the reality of the self-enjoyment body, and is thus named "reaching awakening. This distinguishes it from the merits of the other-enjoyment body.
The "Real" (shí) is subsumed within the character for "expedient means" (quán). Therefore, it is said that it is "only self and not other.
Second, the "Other-Enjoyment Body" (parasaṃbhogakāya) is also subsumed within "Ultimate Enlightenment" (zhìjué). Question: Why is the Other-Enjoyment Body called "Ultimate Enlightenment"? Answer:

Because it is able to teach and transform bodhisattvas of the highest stages; thus, the principal teacher, when discussed in relation to those being transformed, is also called "Ultimate Enlightenment. The character for "expedient means" (quán)...

There are also two explanations. The first is that both the *parasaṃbhogakāya* (body of communal enjoyment for others) and the various *nirmāṇakāyas* (emanation bodies) are collectively termed "expedient" (*upāya*).
Question: Why is the *parasaṃbhogakāya* termed "expedient"? Answer: It is the skillful application of wisdom upon the *samatājñāna* (wisdom of equality);

it is thus also termed "expedient. The second is that only the various *nirmāṇakāyas*, both great and small, are termed "expedient," thereby distinguishing them from the *parasaṃbhogakāya*, which is not expedient.

This is a summary. The single character "True" (zhen) corresponds exclusively to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). (The subsequent commentary on the passage beginning with "Ultimate Awakening" [zhì jué] below will explain the correlation with the three bodies.

"Ultimate" (*zhì*) means the limit, the exhaustion, and the boundary. "Awakening" (*jué*) is none other than the Buddha. It is both provisional (*upāya*) and ultimate reality (*tattva*). To state it concisely: it is the ultimate pinnacle.

"Ultimate" (*zhìjí*) is awakening; "ultimate awakening" (*zhìjí zhī jué*). These two interpretations—*dharmadhāraya* (attributive) and *tatpuruṣa* (possessive)—are applied. Question: How do these two interpretations apply? Answer:

In the preceding explanation of the two characters "ultimate awakening," it was shown that they encompass both the *dharmakāya* and the *saṃbhogakāya*; therefore, these two interpretations are employed. Question:
Within "the ultimate" (*zhì*), there is that which attains (*néng zhì*) and that which is attained (*suǒ zhì*). Which is that which attains, and which is that which is attained? Answer:
