Here, in praising the practice, we take only the perfection of the cause and not the perfection of the fruit. Furthermore, the seven stages are that which is supported, and the Bodhisattva is that which supports.

Now, we take only that which can be relied upon for practice, not the ground (bhūmi) upon which it relies. If one speaks of "seven grounds," it is broad, as it comprehensively includes those prior to the grounds;
thus it is termed a "cage" (*lóng*). If one speaks of "ten grounds," it is narrow, as it fails to include those prior to the grounds;
therefore, it is said to be "seven grounds. Regarding "solitary glory" (*gúróng*): "solitary" (*gú*) means alone; "glory" (*róng*) means flourishing and luxuriant growth. All bodhi...
The practices performed by the Bodhisattvas do not depart from these seven stages (*bhūmi*). Within these seven stages, all the bodhisattva practices are encompassed and exhausted within this sutra.
This One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) practice of the sutra possesses two functions: first, it can encompass the bodhisattva practices of the seven stages;
second, it isolates and surpasses the ninefold teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). Therefore, it is said to "encompass the seven stages and isolate the nine."

[Section] on the Divisions. Question: Regarding this praise of practice (*caryā*), why is it said that the ninefold teaching (*navāṅga-dharma*) is taught? Answer: This refers to the practice arising from beneath the ninefold teaching; it does not refer to the teaching itself.
This practice of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) flourishes uniquely amidst the practices arising from beneath the ninefold teaching of the Three Vehicles;

therefore, it is called "solitary flourishing" (*guyōng*). Question: Regarding the contemplation of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) in the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages (*bhūmi*).
[Question: It is identical to the practice of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*). This very bodhisattva practice is precisely the practice arising from the nine divisions (*navāṅga*).

How can it be said that [this practice] uniquely honors the nine divisions? [Answer: If one speaks in terms of the persons with whom [the bodhisattva] resembles them, it is identical to the practice of the two vehicles.

However, if one considers the Buddha-fruition (*buddhaphala*) which is to be attained, and discusses the practice cultivated therein, it is the bodhisattva practice. [Question: In what way does it uniquely honor [the nine divisions]?
Regarding the practice of the Mahāyāna, the commentary *Zhìyùn* answers: "There are two types of Mahāyāna practice: first, the common Mahāyāna practice; second, the exceptional Mahāyāna practice.
As for the practitioner of the common Mahāyāna practice, this refers to the practice of the three vehicles taught during the forty years [prior to the Lotus Sūtra].

Although it is practiced in common by those of the three vehicles, it is of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*) and is not called the exceptional practice; it is merely termed 'common practice,' like a house."
Internally, there is the proclamation of the three vehicles as being of one kind. Now, forty years later, at the assembly on Vulture Peak, he preaches the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*;
the śrāvakas turn their minds [toward enlightenment] and receive predictions of future buddhahood. This is the definitive Mahāyāna.

In contrast to the Mahāyāna practice of the forty years prior, it is called the "extraordinary practice" (*tokutatsu-gyō*). That is to say, after having already exited the gate, one sees only the ox-drawn carts.
This practice is particularly sublime; hence it is called "unique glory" (*guyōng*). As for the "nine divisions," these refer to the ninefold teachings of the Hīnayāna.
As the Sūtra says: "Either the *sūtra*, *geya*, and *itivṛttaka*; the *jātaka*, *adbhutadharma*, and also the *nidāna*;
the *avadāna* as well as the *geyya*; and the *upadeśa* sūtras. Zhiyi states: "Or perhaps they refer to the nine divisions of the Mahāyāna."
The classification is as explained in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. Those who protect the Mahāyāna uphold the ninefold division [of the scriptures].

However, among the twelve divisions of the Mahāyāna, the *upadeśa* (analytical exposition) is excluded; this is because Mahāyāna bodhisattvas do not require questions and answers, and thus the *upadeśa* is omitted.

Second, there is no transgression for bodhisattvas, as they do not require the commission of an offense to prompt the establishment of precepts; therefore, the *nidāna* (causal accounts) is excluded. Third, since bodhisattvas possess superior faculties...

There is no need for further explanation or illustration; therefore, the metaphors are set aside. This means that the commentary extols the teaching, principle, practice, and fruit as surpassing all other "traps" (expedient means) throughout the ages, even surpassing the Mahāyāna.
Why, then, does it speak only of the "solitary glory" of the ninefold divisions of the Hīnayāna?
This contradicts the commentary. Now, following the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, we take the ninefold division of the Mahāyāna as authoritative.
If one speaks of the ninefold division of the Hīnayāna, that is incorrect. (The first section is finished.)
The statement that "it crowns the five vehicles while remaining uniquely equal" praises the fruit [of enlightenment]. To "crown" means to place upon the head;
"head" refers to the top of the body, for nothing surpasses the head as the highest part of the person. A crown is placed above this head, signifying loftiness and superiority.

Thus it is called a *guàn* (pronounced *guǎn* in the ancient reading). At age twenty, one is said to reach the "crowning year. Here, however, we take the word in its original pronunciation (*guàn*). "Crown" (*guàn*) signifies covering or being supreme.
This sutra is the most supreme; it can overshadow the five vehicles, and is therefore called a "crown. As for the five vehicles:

the vehicle of humans and devas of fixed nature, the vehicle of śrāvakas of fixed nature, the vehicle of pratyekabuddhas of fixed nature, the vehicle of bodhisattvas of fixed nature, and the vehicle of those of indeterminate nature.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* transcends these five vehicles, and is therefore said to "pierce through" the five vehicles. It covers and surpasses them.

Regarding the "five vehicles" (*pañca-yāna*): as mentioned above, the title is like a cap or turban placed upon the heads of these five vehicles; hence it is said that it "caps the five vehicles. Question:

If the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* existed outside of the five vehicles, one could say it caps the five vehicles. However, since the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is itself included within the five vehicles—specifically subsumed under the "indeterminate vehicle" (*aniyata-yāna*)—if one excludes the indeterminate vehicle, it would only be appropriate to say it caps the four vehicles. Why, then, is it said to cap the five vehicles?

Answer: There are two interpretations. First, it is said that for forty years prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, there were the Mahāyāna of the teaching of emptiness and the Mahāyāna of the Middle Way;
these emerged from the Mahāyāna of the refutation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Thus, its name stands preeminent above the five vehicles (*pañca-yāna*).

Second, it is said that this sutra’s One Vehicle (*eka-yāna*) produces the fruits obtained by the other four vehicles. Furthermore, because the fruit-vehicle within the One Vehicle emerges from the causal vehicle, it is said to stand preeminent above the five.
[Question: If it is as you say, then all other Mahāyāna sūtras are likewise so; why is this sūtra alone singled out? [Answer:

It is merely to indicate that this sūtra emerged from among the five vehicles (*pañcayāna*), not to exclude other sūtras. If one were to follow the pattern of this sūtra, it would imply that what was previously non-existent has now come into being.

Discussing the former fruit as the latter cause clarifies the relinquishing of the provisional and the ripening of the real; such a supreme matter as the bestowing of predictions upon the śrāvakas is found in no other sūtra.
First, this is the Middle Way Mahāyāna, which crowns the so-called "characteristic" Mahāyāna. Second, it praises the fruition vehicle (phala-yāna) as crowning the causal vehicle (hetu-yāna).
Third, by bestowing predictions upon the śrāvakas, it elucidates the matters of the provisional and the real. Possessing these [qualities]...
"Much superior. "Solitary" (*du*) means "to crown. "Prominence" (*ying*) means "to emerge. The tip of a grain of rice is called *ying*.

When a single ear of grain emerges from among a patch of rice, rising above the rest of the stalks, it is named *ying*. The *Book of Documents* says, "The auspicious grain grew in different furrows yet shared the same ear.
Thus, *ying* carries the meaning of "emerging. Regarding "ten thousand ages" (*qian gu*), this is said in contrast to the "hundred patriarchs" (*bai zong*); the intent is to express this.
The Sūtra emerges from among the five vehicles, standing solitary and remote for a thousand ages. Its lifespan as the *svasaṃbhogakāya* is inexhaustible throughout kalpas as numerous as dust motes;

yet, speaking of its temporal limits, it is said to endure for a thousand ages. This refers precisely to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which emerges from the five vehicles, covers them all, and alone excels throughout the ages.
This is a praise of the fruit [of Buddhahood]. (Having separately praised the four dharmas above.)
The phrase "How great it is! serves as a general heading to praise the four dharmas. "How great it is! is a term of ultimate eulogy.
It is like when the Buddha Prabhūtaratna praised Śākyamuni Buddha, saying, "Excellent, excellent! You have skillfully preached this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*"; this is a term of supreme praise.
The Master of the Commentary [Zhiyi], because the essence of the sūtra is profound and remote and the purport of the treatise is subtle and penetrating, has stored and expounded [its meaning].
The words of this Phoenix propagate the wisdom of the Candle Dragon; they harmonize nature and characteristics within the single reality and consolidate the surging waves of the Nine Schools.
When the five metaphors are raised, the various philosophers know where to return; when the four dharmas are set forth, the hundred schools submit with joy.

I pray that you will explore the subtle within the ultimate perfection and point toward the comprehensive breadth contained within the scriptural chapters. Thus, one may say: "How great! How truly great! Why, then, is it distinguished [from other texts]?
Having finished the individual praises, does one offer a general praise? The answer is: because the preceding praises were not exhaustive.

For instance, when it is said, "The elegant prose surpasses all expressions," this only praises the teaching (*śāsana*), while the three aspects of principle (*tattva*), practice (*pratipatti*), and fruit (*phala*) are not praised therein.

When it is said, "Profoundly transcending the hundred schools," this only praises the principle, while the two aspects of practice and fruit are not praised therein. The same applies to practice and fruit. This is why there is this general [praise].
This is praise. For example, if one sees a gentleman today who is upright and handsome, one praises him by saying, "He is most upright;
he is a truly fine person. This may be understood as a general praise. Then one might say, "Your ears are magnificent; your nostrils are magnificent; your eyes are magnificent."
From dawn until dusk, although many words were spoken, the praise could never be exhausted. Now, the main intent of this commentary is merely to praise the four dharmas as being all-encompassing;
it does so by means of the three characters "Great indeed! (大矣哉), praising the entirety of this scripture’s doctrine, principle, practice, and fruition.
[This section] provides a general summary (the upper part indicates the heading, while the lower part explains it).

Regarding the statement, "Proclaiming the single reality and [attaining] equality," one may understand that this refers to the phrase "How great indeed! However, the specific meaning of "How great indeed!
remains unclear. The answer is given in the commentary: "Proclaiming the single reality," etc. "Proclaiming" (*yáng*) means to spread forth; "proclaiming" means to expound. One...
Reality is precisely the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). As a sutra says: "This alone is the one true reality; the other two are not real. Furthermore, a sutra states:

"The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world solely for the sake of the one great cause and condition. This "one great matter" refers to opening, showing, awakening, and entering into bodhi and nirvāṇa.
Although there are distinctions between principle and wisdom, they are all the single reality. "Encompassing" (*pao*) means to contain; it is to include them all.

This term "one" (or "this") is a comprehensive synthesis. The One Vehicle is vast and expansive; in principle, there is nothing it does not encompass, and in practice, there is nothing it does not include.

It speaks of both the real and the semblance. What is this "gate"? The answer is that it is very much like space. Space contains and accommodates all myriad phenomena—mountains, rivers, grasses, and trees are all included within it.
As for the "One Reality," whether in terms of phenomena or principle, whether provisional or ultimate, it is all contained therein.
There is nothing it does not encompass; thus, it is like the great void of space.

Regarding the phrase "shaking the two provisional means" (*liǎng quán*): "shaking" (*zhèn*) here means to raise up. Previously, in the case of "shaking Mount Rong," *zhèn* was interpreted as movement, meaning to cause displacement.
Now, this "shaking" is interpreted in the sense of raising up. As for "the two provisional means," these refer to the teachings of the Two Vehicles. (Mou)

It is said: To proclaim the one reality (*tattva*) above encompasses the entirety of the great void; in discussing reality, nothing is left unexhausted. To manifest the two provisional means (*upāya*) below sustains the myriad phenomena (*dharmas*);

in explaining the provisional, nothing is not fully encompassed. Thus, that the myriad phenomena do not pervade the great void signifies the narrowness and inferiority of the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*);
that the great void contains and accommodates the myriad phenomena signifies the ultimate consummation of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Within this sutra:
To raise two analogies: the functioning of these analogies is manifold. It is like the void, within which all myriad forms are sustained.
It is not that the void cannot contain the myriad forms; rather, the myriad forms rely upon the void.
Were it not for the void, it could not fully contain those myriad forms, and the myriad forms would not be able to rely upon any other dharma; they rely solely upon the void. The void is like this.

It is the One Reality. Without the One Reality, the two provisional means could not be contained. Other sutras speak of the two provisional means, yet their explanations of those other provisional practices are incomplete.
Within this sutra, the two provisional means are explained as being like the myriad phenomena within empty space;
just as the myriad phenomena cannot exist without relying upon empty space, so too the two provisional means do not rely upon the One Reality. Within the One Reality, they are contained.
The two characters "quan" (權) and "yi" (遺) are like the void containing the myriad phenomena within it. Regarding "yi," "yi" means to drop or omit;
this refers to the meaning below. The intent is that this sutra encompasses above the One Vehicle and its myriad practices, which is similar to the void;
below, it nets the practices of the Two Vehicles, which are like the myriad phenomena. Therefore, it is called "yi. Some write it as "wei" (維).
It means to maintain. It refers to the main cord of a net, and is also called "the great. Within this sutra, by exalting the one reality, all myriad practices are perfected.

Within this sutra, by presenting the two provisional means, all provisional practices are fully encompassed without exception. Question: To what is it comparable? Answer: It is like raising the main cord;
when the net is lifted, its myriad meshes unfold. It is like grasping the collar of a fur robe; when the collar is pulled, all the hairs are set in order.

"Thus, it is called 'weaving' (*vīta*), which means to encompass or weave together. As for 'the myriad phenomena' (*wanxiang*): in the Hīnayāna, the five aggregates (*skandha*), the three categories (*trivastu*), the conditioned and the unconditioned, whether form or mind—these are termed the myriad phenomena.

In the Mahāyāna, the myriad phenomena refer to the six perfections, the myriad practices, the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the three absences of nature (*tri-niḥsvabhāvatā*), and so forth; these are termed the myriad phenomena."
Regarding the phrase "How can one use the analogy of the vast ocean, etc.? this refutes the ancients.

Seeing the subsequent scriptural passage that uses mountains and oceans as metaphors, they proceeded to take these mountains and oceans to illustrate the teachings and principles of this sutra. Question: Who were these ancients? Answer: They were Master Jing of Jiguo Temple.
In Master Jing’s commentary (*shu*), he states: "Because [the depth] is identical to the vastness of the ocean, and [the height] is comparable to Mount Sumeru, its brilliance surpasses..."
The brilliance of the bright moon shatters the darkness with a power equal to that of the sun; this is used as a metaphor for this sutra. Therefore, the Commentary refutes [the objection], saying:
"How can one use the 'Ming' (溟) and 'Shu' (輸) as examples? How can one reproach the ancients by claiming both are incorrect? "Ming" refers to the names of the North Sea and the South Sea;
"Shu" is the place where nets are cast. "Profound meaning" refers to the principle (*li*). When the ancients saw the "Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta" chapter...
It is said that among all mountains, Mount Sumeru is the foremost; likewise, among all streams, rivers, and waters, the ocean is the foremost.
This is a partial analogy (a *pradeśopama*). Ancient scholars did not realize it was a partial analogy.
The mountain alone is used as a metaphor for the teachings of this sutra, and the ocean alone is used as an analogy for its principle; thus, the metaphor fully captures the meaning.
The Master of the Commentary (*Sūtra-vyākhyā*) says: "Though the vast ocean is deep, its depth of eighty thousand *yojanas* can still be known.
Yet the principle of the two kinds of emptiness in this sutra cannot be measured. How could the teachings of the *Lotus Sutra* be merely like the ocean? Though Mount Sumeru..."
Mount Sumeru is eighty-four thousand *yojanas* high and composed of the four precious substances; it can indeed be measured and known by its dimensions.

However, the teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) in this sutra is so profoundly deep that Mount Sumeru cannot serve as a metaphor for it. To do so would diminish the merit of the many sutras, which is why [the opponent] objects. How could they possibly be equal?
The ancients did not understand the subsequent passage; they took its partial metaphors and used the entirety of the mountains and seas to represent the doctrine and principles of this sutra.
Therefore, the commentary refutes this, saying: "How can it be? How can it be? "How can it be" means "it cannot. "Jùnzhú" (峻躅) refers to tracks or traces;
that is, the traces of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*’s teaching.

The phrase "First, it is called the 'Exquisite Dharma' and so forth" serves as the heading. "First" (shǒu) means the head; it carries the sense of the beginning. It refers to the opening of the scroll.

Regarding the phrase "Adorning the grand framework and so forth," this poses the question: what is the meaning of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*? The answer in the commentary states, "Adorning the grand framework and so forth.
Mǔ (Mó) says: "Adorning" (zǎo) refers to literary embellishment (*wénzǎo*). "Grand" (hóng) means great. "Framework" (gāng) refers to the large ropes on a net.
"Chord" (jō). "Ultimate Chant" (kyōshō) refers to the ultimate teaching. "Initial" (shisoku) means the very beginning; it is also the first of all.

The five characters of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* constitute the primary chant of this entire work. Regarding the discourse on the Dharma: what is meant by "Horizontal Beam" (kōkō), and what is meant by "Ultimate Chant"?
The answer is twofold. First, Mō states: Within the *Lotus Sūtra*, there are the seven parables, the three equalities, and the ten [qualities].
Above. This constitutes the grand framework of this treatise. The five titles of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* can serve as the grand framework for its literary ornamentation;
they can also serve as the grand framework for its primary and initial proclamations. When intending to expound the sutra, one must first proceed from the beginning.
By first placing the five characters "Myōhō-renge-kyō" at the beginning, it is therefore called the "initial proclamation. Initial.
"Chang" (to chant/sing) means the initial proclamation. Second, it is said: *The Lotus Sutra* is the great mainstay;
it is the adornment; it is the primary proclamation. The seven-fascicle *Lotus Sutra* is the mainstay. When a net is raised by its mainstay, the myriad meshes open wide;
when the mainstay is pulled, the meshes align correctly; when the collar is lifted, the hairs fall into place. Although there are many individual meshes upon the net, one raises the large [stays].

When the main framework is established, everything becomes visible. Although the textual passages and their meanings are extensive, one knows that this is the *Miao* (Wondrous) chapter simply by observing its title.
Therefore, it is said that this is the ultimate proclamation that adorns the grand framework.
Regarding the statement that the title serves as the banner for a single section of a scripture: Question: Why is it necessary to place a title at the beginning of a sutra? Answer:
A title acts as a banner (*dhvaja*) for a single section of a scripture; therefore, it is called a "banner. It is like seeing a white heron perched in a tree, which indicates the presence of water;

there is no scripture without a banner. This is similar to a military standard (*dhvaja-kiṅkiṇī*): when thousands or tens of thousands of soldiers are gathered in one place, it is by means of the banner that they can be distinguished.
One need only look at the banners to know that they belong to the Shen-ce (Divine Strategy), Wei-yuan (Majestic Reach), Jun-xiao-qi (Brave Cavalry), or Long-wu (Dragon Martial) armies;
the generals' flags are set up as markers to serve as the insignia for the three armies. Thus, "jiong" (旌) is defined as a "marker" (biao).

Although this scripture consists of seven fascicles and its prose and phrases are numerous, seeing the title "The Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma" (Miaofa Lianhua Jing), one immediately knows that the entirety of this single body of scripture is [the same].
By means of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, one immediately knows that it is not the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, nor the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, nor the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*;
each is distinct and does not become confused with the others. Therefore, the title is called a "banner" (*dhvaja*).

What is the difference in meaning between the title and the main body of the scripture? Answer: The title is the collective name for the entire work, while the body of the scripture consists of the individual texts within that single work.
This is the distinction. The teaching, the principle, the practice, and the fruit are all the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; they are distributed throughout the various chapters of this single scripture.
Now, since this title speaks of the "Sublime Dharma" (*Saddharma*), it serves as the comprehensive name for the sublime dharma found within the entire scripture.
Therefore, it is said that this signifies the collective title of the whole work.

Regarding the phrase "The First Chapter, the Introduction" (*nidāna-parivarta*): this is the citation. The two characters "Introduction Chapter" (*xu-pin*) are the designators (*vācaka*), while the scriptural text within this single chapter is the designated (*vācya*).
The designator designates that which is designated.

Regarding the meaning of the category of the "mirror": what is the meaning of the "Introductory Chapter" (Nidāna-parivarta)? The answer in the commentary states, "the meaning of the category of the mirror," and so forth.
Just as a mirror reflects objects—wherein the mirror is able to reflect the images of things, which appear clearly and distinctly within the mirror—so too, the teaching is the "expressor" (*vācaka*).

The expressor expresses the "expressed" principle (*vācya*), and that expressed principle appears distinctly within the scope of the teaching. Therefore, the teaching is metaphorically like a mirror. Question:

Why is it that the text of a single chapter is called the "signified" (*vācya*)? Answer: In the following section explaining how this chapter receives its name, it is the signifier (*vācaka*) that is actually the signified.
Here, however, the chapter itself is the signifier, while the textual content of the entire treatise is the signified.
Regarding the title of the sutra, it establishes that which is expounded. "Mirror" means to reflect. When a clear mirror is hung upon a stand, beauty and ugliness appear of themselves.
The two characters "Preface" (Nidāna) and "Chapter" (Varga) are like this mirror. As for "categories of meaning," these refer to the sevenfold accomplishment within the Preface Chapter;

they are the categories of meaning expounded by these sevenfold accomplishments. These are: the accomplishment of the preface, the accomplishment of the assembly, and the accomplishment of the arrival of the time for preaching the Dharma.

They are distinct. Although the seven categories of meaning expressed therein each differ from one another, because the two characters "Preface" (序品) are placed at the head, they illuminate that all seven categories within this single chapter belong collectively to the Preface.
Because these two characters are placed at the head as a mirror, one sees the beauty or ugliness of the face; thus, it reflects upon the mirror.
When illuminated, one immediately understands. Although the seven categories of meaning are numerous, by examining a single category, one understands them all;
this is entirely the sequence [of the method]. Question: What is meant by the term "grand signpost" (hóngbiāo)? Answer: The *Mao Shi* states: "Hóng means great.

That which is great is called hóng; that which is small is called yàn. Therefore, the character "hóng" is used to signify greatness. It is capable of serving as the title for the seven types of meaning categories, and when raised up, it reveals them.
The two characters of the "Preface Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*) constitute the general title for the category of the sevenfold accomplishment of meaning; thus, it is called the "Grand Signpost.

Regarding the statement that they are "distinct designations for the specific expressions," each of the seven accomplishments possesses both the expressive (the signifier) and the expressed (the signified). Question:

What is meant by "expressive" (*vyavahāra*), and what is meant by "specific designation" (*viśeṣa-nāman*)? Answer: Characters, words, and phrases are termed the "expressive. By means of these, the expressed...
The principles are distinct. Therefore, upon the expressive teachings, there are seven types of distinctions in wording and meaning; hence, they are called "different expressions" (*i-ch'üan*).
Placing a title upon these different expressions is called a "distinct heading for different expressions. A distinct heading refers to the "Introductory Chapter" (*hsü-p'in*).
Regarding the seven kinds of accomplishments, their titles differ from one another; this is termed "different expressions. Now, the two characters "Introductory Chapter" are placed at the beginning.

Furthermore, to provide distinct designations for these [sections], they are given different terms so that the seven kinds of accomplishment are collectively titled the "Introductory Chapter" (Xùpǐn).
These two characters, "Introductory Chapter," serve as a mirror for the seven types of accomplishment, acting both as a grand heading and as specific designations.
(The preceding provides a general explanation of the title of the scripture.)

Regarding the statement that "the term *dharma* contains the meanings of 'sustaining' (*dhāraṇa*) and 'normative standard' (*vidhi*)," this is an explanation of the word *dharma*. "Sustaining" means to maintain, that is, not to abandon one's own essence. "Normative standard" refers to a rule or model that causes beings to produce understanding;

therefore, it is called *dharma* because it contains the meanings of sustaining and normative standard. Question: Among the four dharmas—teaching (*śāsana*), principle (*yukti*), practice (*pratipatti*), and fruit (*phala*)—why are they called "sublime" (*praṇīta*)?

Answer: They are termed "sublime" because they encompass all auspiciousness (*maṅgala*). "Encompassing" (*praṇi*) has the meaning of "to gather" or "to include. "Auspiciousness" (*mala*) means "goodness. To encompass...
It encompasses all virtues; therefore, it is called "wondrous" (*miao*). Question: In what sense does it "bind and encompass" all meanings? Answer:

The teaching possesses the merit of being able to unfold the wondrous principle, while the principle possesses the power to emerge from the water [of the mundane]. Furthermore, it accords with the subtle and profound explanations of the secret mysteries.
It is the Teaching (*śāsana*). It penetrates the profound essence of the hidden roots; this is the Principle (*li*). It accomplishes the secret practices of the Supreme Vehicle;
this is the Practice (*xing*). It perfects the true doctrine of ultimate awakening; this is the Fruit (*guo*). Its excellence is exhaustive; therefore, it is called "wondrous" (*miao*). Question:
This sutra possesses four factors and is thus named "Wondrous. Other sutras also possess these four factors; for what reason do they not receive the name "Wondrous"? Answer: As for other sutras...
There are four dharmas. These four dharmas do not bind the multitude. This sutra possesses these four dharmas; it binds the multitude and brings them auspiciousness.
Therefore, it is called "Wondrous" (the first part specifically clarifies the Wondrous Dharma).
The phrase "the flower is both elegant and blooming" (*xiùfā*) is a specific interpretation of the *padma* (lotus). Question: What is meant by "elegant and blooming"? Answer: Mǔ says:

"Elegant" (*xiù*) has the meaning of emerging from the water; "blooming" (*fā*) has the meaning of opening and unfolding. If that were so, then all flowers on dry land would likewise be able to produce fruit.
If all these can bloom, should they be called "lotuses"? Answer: Those growing on land may only be called "flowers";

they cannot be called "lotus flowers" because they do not possess the full array of excellences. Although other flowers may be exquisite, they lack these manifold excellences and are therefore not lotuses.

These dharmas all contain the principles of maintenance (*dhāraṇa*), yet because they lack the multitude of auspicious signs, they are not "wondrous. Regarding this lotus, there are two meanings. First:

It possesses the meaning of forming fruit and the meaning of blossoming; thus, it is said to be "comprehensive. Furthermore, because it alone possesses all excellences, it is uniquely named the "lotus" (*padma*).

According to the commentary by Mu, if the previous explanations of "exquisite" (*xiù*) and "developed" (*fā*) were both applied to the flower itself, there would be no distinction among its various excellences, and the phrasing would be redundant.
This flower possesses both the meaning of blossoming and the meaning of forming fruit, and because it can contain all excellences, it is called the "lotus."
Flowers. The *Saddharma* (Sublime Dharma) surpasses all other dharmas; the lotus flower surpasses all other flowers. How much more so will this be for the Sublime Dharma that is yet to come?

The dharma and its metaphor are equal, without distinction. Even if one were to obtain peach, plum, and apricot blossoms in their thousands and tens of thousands, it would not be cause for boastful praise.
Yet, to offer a single lotus flower to the Buddha brings merit that is immeasurable and surpasses all other flowers. The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* says: "Compassion is the stem, and wisdom is..."

The petals are samādhi; the filaments are liberation; and the unfolding blossoms are the deliverances. The Bodhisattvas, like royal bees, gather its nectar; therefore, I prostrate before the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Question: Where is this lotus? It is where all excellences are gathered. Answer: When the buds open and unfold, the lotus is revealed;

likewise, when the teachings are proclaimed and exalted, the ultimate meaning is realized. Just as the lotus flower emerges in splendor from a sacred pond, so too does the principle manifest through its analogies.
It transcends the small lotus; by raising its flower, it attains the fruit. This is like how through the adornment of the cause, the result is fulfilled.

The fruit is designated as the basis for the formation of the flower, and the manifestation of Buddha-wisdom is revealed as the source of the vehicle. There is a profound reason for using the lotus as a metaphor.
These four lines are called "The Multitude of Beauties"; they represent the superior virtues of the lotus. Terrestrial flowers do not possess such virtues.
Regarding the phrase "the essence and function are both presented," this is a combined explanation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. "The essence and function are both presented" is the heading;

"the Dharma and the metaphor are raised together" is the explanation; and the two lines beginning with "half and full" are the conclusion. One interpretation states that "Dharma" is the essence and "wondrous" (*miau*) is the function.
Another interpretation states that its arising from the *Anantaparyāya-sūtra* is the essence, while its functional inclusion [of all teachings] within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is the function.

[The first view] takes [the Lotus Sūtra] as the function (*yòng*). The third says that the doctrine and principle (*jīlǐ*) are the essence (*tǐ*), while practice and fruit (*xíngguǒ*) are the function. The fourth says that the One Vehicle (*yīshèng*) is the essence, while the sublation of duality and the unification of the two vehicles are the function.

The fifth says that the Wondrous Dharma (*miàofǎ*) is the essence, while the lotus flower (*liánhuā*) is the function. Various commentaries selectively adopt [one of these views], asserting that "Dharma" is the essence and "Wondrous" is the function.

However, they only explain the essence and its activity (*tǐyè*) with respect to the Dharma itself, and do not explain the essence and its activity with respect to the metaphor. If this were the case...
In the debate over whether the name, essence, and function are all presented together, the present [text] takes "wondrous Dharma" as the essence and "lotus" as the function; thus, it is superior.

While some merely state that the wondrous Dharma is the essence and further add the lotus as the function—thereby presenting the name, essence, and function together—others merely state that the wondrous Dharma is the "Dharma" (the subject) and further add the lotus as the "analogy" (the illustration), thereby raising both the Dharma and the analogy together. Now, when it says "wondrous Dharma,"...

The "essence" (*tǐ*) refers to the teaching, principle, practice, and fruit. The "lotus flower" (*liánhuá*) is the function. One does not take the lotus flower as a visual object (*rūpa-dhātu*) perceived by the eye;

according to the subsequent "Gate of Explaining the Name," the Wondrous Dharma is like a lotus, which is also a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound. At present, there is no desire to analyze "lotus flower" separately.

Since the lotus flower is a material phenomenon (*rūpa-dharma*) and the Wondrous Dharma is a mental phenomenon (*citta-dharma*), a material phenomenon cannot constitute a *karmadhāraya*. Therefore, [the term] is taken here [in its conventional sense].
Within the essence of the Dharma—the teaching, principle, practice, and fruit—there is the functional capacity to bloom and emerge from the water.
This very capacity is precisely the meaning of "lotus. By subsuming this capacity within that essential nature of the Dharma, one speaks of both the essence and its function together.

This interpretation, first, accords with the commentary on the following verse, which presents both the Dharma and the metaphor simultaneously; second, it accords with the section below on the "Explanation of Names" (*nirukti*).
This is the traditional transmission.

Regarding the phrase "the paths of the Half and the Full are equal," these two lines are from the *Sūtra Commentary* (*Shu*). They conclude the preceding four characters, "Myōhō-renge" (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka).

In some versions of the *Sūtra Commentary*, the character is written as "tōro" (途路, path), while in others it is written as "tohai" (徒輩, followers); both are based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, which states that [the Buddha] acts for the sake of the śrāvakas.
Regarding "people": those who preach the teaching of the half-syllable are called śrāvakas; because they practice according to the teaching of the half-verse, they are termed the "half-disciples.

Bodhisattvas practice according to the teaching of the full-syllable; they are termed the "full-disciples. Regarding "dawn": when the sun is about to rise, the world becomes bright and clear, and all things are collectively called "dawn.
If the sky has not yet dawned, things cannot be seen. Before the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the śrāvakas had not yet...

The Dharma of the Two Vehicles practiced by the ignorant is the "half-teaching"; their own status as followers is that of the "half-disciples. Awakening to what is heard today is the "complete teaching";
practicing according to the Mahāyāna, one’s own status as a follower is that of a "complete disciple. The assembly at the Lotus Sutra is the place where this awakening occurs.

If one speaks of the "path," it is the path that penetrates the tracks and the principles; in contrast to the paths of selection and rejection followed by those below, one thereby knows the paths of the sheep and the deer.

One may abandon [the small carts]; the ox-cart may be taken. The conjured city may be abandoned; the place of jewels may be taken. One takes the place of jewels of the Single Vehicle and abandons the conjured city of the Two Vehicles;
one takes the single ox-cart and abandons the two sheep- and deer-carts. "Adhering" (*zhù*) means clarity; it is the understanding that corresponds to what was explained above.

Regarding the phrase "as for what is called 'sūtra' (*jing*)," it can be understood as referring to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. However, it is not yet clear what the meaning of the word "sūtra" is. The answer in the commentary states:
"As for what is called 'sūtra,' etc. This serves as the heading.

Regarding the statement, "To speak of 'permanence' (chang) is to equate it with the Way (dao)," the question is asked: What is the meaning of permanence? Is it the meaning of phenomena (dharma), the meaning of inclusion, or the meaning of penetration?

The commentary answers: "Permanence refers to the Way that guides the hundred kings," and so forth; this is the explanation. That which cannot be altered by the hundred kings is called "permanent. This permanence is precisely the Sūtra.
Because the Sūtra serves as the place for the hundred kings to travel upon, it is called the "Way" (dao). Furthermore, it serves as the unconditioned (wuwei) state for the hundred kings.
In the place of governance and transformation, one hangs the robe and faces south; therefore, it is called the Way (*Dao*). It provides a standard for a hundred kings and penetrates all rules;
therefore, it is called the Norm (*Gui*). First, it can serve as the Great Way for a hundred kings; second, it can serve as the penetrating standard for a hundred kings.
The succession of imperial dynasties cannot be altered; this is what is meant by "constancy" (*chang*). What is constant is the Sūtra. Question: Why is it called the "Dharma" (*fa*)? Answer:
The commentary states that the Dharma is the mold for the virtues of a thousand generations. This Sūtra’s Dharma serves as the source of virtue for a hundred kings; thus it is named "Virtue.
This Sūtra’s Dharma serves as the model and standard for a hundred kings; therefore, it is called "the Mold for the Virtues of a Thousand Leaves. One generation... one.
It serves as a single leaf for successive generations; it is the King of a thousand ages, unalterable (the preceding two points follow worldly convention).

Regarding the statement that "to encompass" means "to gather this," one asks: what is meant by "encompassing"? The answer is: "encompassing" means to gather this wondrous principle; it is to accord with the principle.

Question: What is meant by "penetration" (kan)? Answer: "Penetration" refers to guiding the common person to accord with their faculties; "teaching" refers to its ability to encompass principle, which is termed "collection" (shū).

As for "penetration," it means threading through without dispersal; as for "guiding" (go), it means restraining and controlling. In the Western Regions, one holds flowers to make offerings to the Buddha.

When encountered by the wind, they would be scattered; thus, all are strung together with thread so that they may not be lost. That sentient beings do not create evil karma is entirely due to being threaded together by the scriptural teachings.
Just as flowers, once secured by thread, remain unmoved even when encountering the wind, so too do sentient beings, having heard the sutras, remain unshaken when meeting with false views;

therefore, it is called "threading" (*guàn*). Furthermore, it governs those ordinary beings. "Ordinary" (*yōng*) carries the sense of being inferior or lowly; it refers to the common, ignorant, and dull-witted.
To lock those of inferior capacity is called treating ordinary people as ignorant and short-sighted. Their fundamental nature differs not at all from that of the Buddha;

yet they are unable to study the practice of renunciation and instead intend only for the cycle of rebirth in evil realms. Fearing their downfall, the World-Honored One therefore employs the sutras to restrain them.
One does not allow them to create evil karma or wander in saṃsāra, just as one uses a bit to restrain a horse. The Master said: "If one moves and acts without knowing what to pursue;
stands upright without knowing where to settle; chooses among things daily without knowing what is noble;
flows along with things without knowing where they lead—if such is the case, one may be called a common person of the vulgar stream."
Regarding the phrase "hoping to cause [them] to complete," it is asked: What is the Buddha’s intention in using the sutras and teachings to penetrate and sustain sentient beings?
The answer in the commentary states, "hoping to cause," etc., which praises the merit of the sutra. "Shu" (庶) carries three meanings: fortune (幸), universality (普), and exhaustiveness (盡).
"Bi" (畢) means ultimate completion (畢竟). Thus, the intent behind the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma is precisely to ensure that they ultimately transcend suffering.
Ferrying across (*jin*). The "ferry of suffering" refers to the two obstructions and the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Birth and death constitute this shore;
afflictions already arisen are the middle current; Great Parinirvāṇa is the other shore; and the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) are the boat.
To cross from this shore to the other shore is called "completely departing from the ferry of suffering. *Jin* (ferry) means the boundary.
Regarding the phrase "the shore of awakening" (*bodhy-anta*), it refers to *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*.
Regarding the statement that "the introduction" (*nidāna*) means "by means of" (*yī*), one asks: what is the meaning of "by means of" or "the beginning"?

The answer is that the commentary states, "The presentation of the teaching, its arising, and so forth," which is the explanation. In the "Expedient Means" chapter (*Upāya-paryāya*), the preaching of the One Vehicle is called the "arising of the teaching. This chapter [describes] the emission of light.
The raining of flowers and so forth serve as the causes for the arising of the teaching. Question: What is meant by "beginning"? Answer: "Beginning" refers to the initial point.

In the "Expedient Means" chapter, the preaching of the Dharma is called the "Arising of the Dharma. This introductory chapter’s emission of light, raining of flowers, and shaking of the earth serve as the gradual precursors to that arising of the Dharma.

Regarding the statement, "The 'Chapters' (*varga*) are categories," this is a heading. Question: What is meant by "chapter"? Answer: The commentary states, "To categorize the profound purport according to different types.

"Categorizing" (*qu*) means to divide. "Profound" (*xuan*) means deep. "Purport" (*zhi*) means intention or principle. It refers to dividing the principles being explained (*so-chuan li*) into twenty-eight sections;
therefore, they are called "different types. Question: What is meant by "distinct"? Answer: The commentary states, "To branch out the subtle explanations... [and so forth].

"Classified Collection" (*Huìbié*) refers to the teachings that can express [the truth]. "Branches" (*pài*) describes the appearance of water dividing into streams (pronounced *pǔbài*; it is also written with the sound *pà*).
It is like a single river being divided into several currents; the One Vehicle Dharma-gate is divided into twenty-eight chapters, which constitute the branches.

"Profound interpretation" refers to the teaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. This means that the chapters (*parivarta*) are able to distinguish its profound purport, establishing the meaning of its various categories through logical principles.
Although the doctrines within the seven fascicles are numerous, once they are categorized by these chapters, they constitute twenty-eight distinct classes.

Regarding the term "categorized" (*hui bie*): *wei* (class) refers to a category or type. The *Book of Changes* (*Zhou Yi*) says: "Pulling up the *mao* grass by its roots, they advance together in their classes. *Mao* is *mao* grass;
this plant grows in thousands and tens of thousands of stalks, all from a single root. If one grasps a single stalk, the entire root remains connected without interruption.
Similarly, the principle (*li*) elucidated in this sutra is one, yet the teachings (*jiao*) that express it consist of twenty-eight distinct chapters.
Although there are twenty-eight distinct chapters, each chapter equally elucidates the principle of the One Vehicle; thus, they are said to be "classified by category.
If one considers the Dharma of a single flavor, it would not logically consist of many different categories.
Fearing that sentient beings might find it difficult to understand, the categories were subsequently divided to make it easy to comprehend; this is what is meant by "classification by category."
Regarding the statement that the sutra consists of twenty-eight categories and sections, this summarizes the titles of the chapters within the entire collection of the sutra.
As for the phrase "Thus have I heard," Tianfeng says: because there is an explanation of the original text of the sutra based on the sixth gate, [this phrase is used].

This was a preliminary citation. Although previously I praised the introduction and so forth, I shall now briefly select a passage from a single scripture as a whole in order to explain its general meaning;
therefore, I first cite these four characters.
Regarding the statement "First, explaining the scriptural text," this is the heading (*mātra*). To provide a brief summary, I shall provisionally analyze it by way of six sections;

this is the introduction (*uddeśa*). Furthermore, some commentaries (*ṭīkā*) use the character "jiāng" (將) instead; "jiāng" signifies "intention" (*chanda*), "appropriateness" (*yukta*), or "should. Thus, "desiring to explain" means intending to provide an exposition. Prior to that unexplained portion:

This is briefly categorized and simplified by means of six sections. There are two senses of "brief" (*lue*): first, "abbreviated" (*shao-lue*), meaning that within this profound discourse, it is impossible to explain extensively, and even if explained extensively, one could not exhaust the subject;
thus, for the time being, it is briefly simplified using six sections. Second, "condensed" (*shu-lue*) or "comprehensive summary," which is why it is called "brief";
that is, the general purport of the three assemblies of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is summarized into these six sections.
It is called "abbreviated" because it exhaustively explains [the truth]. Yet this sutra contains both principle and wisdom within its essence; it manifests the provisional and reveals the ultimate.

Thus, the causes and conditions of the Great Matter bring the partial into the perfect; the purport of this profound scripture leads those following the paths of the sheep and the deer—stuck in the illusory city—to point toward the ox-cart, so they may return directly to the Treasure Place.
Only when non-outflow wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) gives rise to the eye of insight can the Wheel of Dharma be turned. Consciousness...
To discern what lies beyond the reach of measurement, I consult Mañjuśrī: though the virtues of Prabhūtaratna were perfected many kalpas ago, he still comes for the sake of the Dharma;
although Maitreya’s rank is but one birth away, he remains deluded regarding the Buddha’s affairs. These matters cannot be fully exhausted through the six gates of analysis;
therefore, at the beginning of this commentary, I have set forth a brief introduction. This concludes the opening statement.

Regarding the phrase "explaining the intent for the composition of the sūtra" and so forth, this is the formal enumeration of the six gates. These six gates are divided into five pairs: 1. The pair of the speaker and the spoken:
This explains the intent for the composition of the sūtra. One gate constitutes the speaker, while the remaining five gates constitute the spoken.

2. The pair of the signifier and the signified: This clarifies that the fundamental purport of the sūtra is the signified, while the understanding of the chapters and titles of the sūtra is the signifier.

The "expressive" (the means of expression) refers to the fact that the primary intent of the Sūtra is what is expressed by principle; the "named after its chapters" refers to the teaching itself as the expressive medium.

Third, the correspondence between the root and the branches: the Sūtra receiving its name is the root, spoken by the Buddha; the chapters receiving their names are the branches, compiled and arranged by Ānanda.

Furthermore, what was spoken by the Buddha is the root; what was spoken by the disciples is the branch. Fourth, the correspondence between the single and the multiple: this refers to the Sūtra itself.

This concerns the establishment and omission of chapters (*parivarta*). Regarding the establishment and omission of the sutra: the *Bhaiṣajyavarga* (Chapter on Medicinal Herbs) adds the analogy of the sun’s radiance, and there are the verses of the *Samantamukha-parivarta*.

These constitute the establishment and omission of the sutra; this refers to the single [chapter] titles. Question: What is meant by "repetition" (*chóng*)? Answer: To speak of the establishment and omission of the sutra in a single instance is called "single.

To further clarify the establishment and omission of the chapters is "repetition. This refers to the presence or absence of the *Devadatta-parivarta* and its placement before or after the *Anuparīndanā-parivarta*. This is the fifth point.

Next is the explanation of the text. Regarding "order," this refers to clarifying the sequence of the chapters. Regarding "explanation of the text," this refers to explaining the beginning and end of the sūtra text.

Question: Why are only six gates of explanation mentioned? Answer: It is said that when one is about to present the ultimate teaching (*tathāgata-śāsana*), there must be a source from which it proceeds.

Although the Sage is without [discursive] mind, he manifests in response to sentient beings; therefore, one first provides the "arousing of the intention" (*cittotpāda*) as the introduction to the verbal teaching.

Once established, there is necessarily that which is clarified; likewise, while great words have no fixed faction, they become manifest when confronted with the sense organs. Therefore, this follows the section on the Essential Principle (*zhǔngzī*).

Although the True Reality (*shíxiàng*) is prominent, conventional designations (*jiǎmíng*) still persist; thus, while the dark nature (*míngxìng*) is non-existent, it is provisionally established according to that darkness. Therefore, this follows the section on "Attaining Names.
Only then does one discuss their abolition and establishment, whereby both existence and non-existence are fully accounted for. As for the sequence of the discussion: [text continues].

Thus, the sequence of before and after is established. While transcending existence and non-existence, it is identical to existence and non-existence; while not being before and after, it remains before and after.

Since the profound portal has been opened, the ultimate teaching is now set forth. Therefore, following this, the text of the sūtra itself is explained, which is discussed hereafter. Thus says Master Lu.
Now, the teachings of the Tripiṭaka each have their own points of inquiry. Specifically, the Śāstras seek [truth] through both nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Therefore, the present Commentator, relying on this aforementioned principle, has divided the scriptural text into sections. First, he sets forth the purport of the sutra;

yet, although one may understand its underlying intent, if the school’s tenets and the practices to be cultivated are not opened up, there will be no point of return. Thus, secondly, he clarifies the fundamental tenets of the sutra. Although one is conversant with these tenets...
Having already clarified the destination to which one returns, if one does not understand the meaning signified by the chapter titles and the sūtra’s heading, there is therefore the third section:

the naming of the sūtra’s chapters. Although the chapter titles are explained, the criteria for their establishment or abolition are not yet opened up; because they are deficient due to confusion regarding these causes, there is the fourth section:

the establishment and abolition of the sūtra’s chapters. Although the establishment and abolition are made manifest, the sequence of the chapters must still be distinguished; therefore, there is the fifth section: the order of the chapters.
Having understood the sequence, one must recognize the original text; therefore, there is a sixth section consisting of the commentary on the scriptural text.
For this reason, the Master of the Subcommentary establishes six gates to explain this sutra (comprising both the general and the specific).
*Essential Collection of the Profound Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra*, Scroll One.
In the winter of the sixth year of the Qianfu era of the Tang dynasty, lectured at Kaiyuan Temple in Wenzhou by the Cien bhikṣu Hongju,
who transcribed and offered this copy for veneration.
This book came from the Great Tang; it was kept within the scriptural collection of Dharma Master Chishō and remained deeply secret, never being brought forth, so that only its name was heard.
Now, the monk Shinshō of Kōfuku-ji, together with his disciple Ajari Chishō, [have obtained it].

There was a friendship so deep that they would cut their own throats for one another. They requested [this work] from each other, first having it transcribed and later having it examined by the worthy.
This was during the Tianlu year, in the year of Gengwu.
On the twenty-third day of the seventh month in the first year of Kōjō (the Xin-you year),
the monk Shōzan of Hōryū-ji transcribed this entire work and deposited it in the Great Sutra Repository of his own temple, fearing that it might be lost due to the lack of other copies.
Copied again and completed.
At Hōryū Monastery of Learning:
*Jōō Hokekyō Genzan Yōshū*, Volume Two.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Xifu of Jingshui Temple.
Part One: Preface on the Intent of Composing the Scripture, etc. This refers back to what preceded. Now, the intent behind establishing a teaching each has its own specific purpose.
Lao Dan crossed the Flowing Sands to expound upon the *Daode* [Classic], while Confucius captured the Qilin to compose the *Chunqiu* [Spring and Autumn Annals].
Sunzi had his kneecaps removed, yet his Art of War flourished; Qu Yuan was exiled, yet the *Li Sao* was subsequently composed.
These are indeed matters of the mundane world and do not constitute discourse on that which lies beyond. As for our Master, however, he first manifested himself through great compassion.

This is intended to rescue those from the conflagration of the burning house and provide rest from the perils of the treacherous path; it drives the ox-cart upon the Eightfold Noble Path and reveals the Precious Abode within the two kinds of emptiness.
Thus, these words remain ever relevant to the times. Nevertheless, regarding the intent behind the emergence of this teaching, there is a distinction between its general and specific meanings.
What the former masters have set forth has only clarified the specific meaning; now, in discussing the general meaning, I shall briefly open two gates. First:
First, by emerging from the cage of birth-and-death; second, by reaching the other shore of bodhi.
Regarding the first intention, according to the *Tri-saraṇa Sūtra*, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "There are three things in the world that are not to be desired."
This is not radiant; this is not to be contemplated; this is not pleasing. What are these three? They are namely old age, sickness, and death.

If these three phenomena did not exist in the world, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, would not appear in the world to teach sentient beings the Dharma he has realized and the matters of discipline. Therefore, one should know that it is because these three phenomena exist that the Tathāgata [appears].
He appears in the world to preach the Dharma realized and the matters of discipline. Regarding the second intention, the subsequent sutra states:

"The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world solely for the sake of the one great causal matter," and it extensively explains the opening, revealing, awakening to, and entering into Bodhi and Nirvana.

This applies to all teachings and also encompasses this sutra in general; therefore, it is called the "General Intention" (the preceding being the general statement and the following being the specific intentions). [End of] the Commentary.

The character "之" (zhī) is not fixed. First, there is a version where the character "之" is absent from the phrase "序經起意" (xù jīng qǐ yì). Another version reads "起之意" (qǐ zhī yì), which implies that the sūtra itself is the "arising" (qǐ).
This would suggest that the sūtra comes first, while the "intention" (yì) follows. Third, in the reading "經之起意" (jīng zhī qǐ yì), the character "之" is placed above the character "起.
Following this interpretation, the Tathāgata is the agent who causes the arising, and the sūtra is that which arises. [This concludes] the two sections of the He-copy.

The arising of the interpretive understanding (*arthaviniścaya*). Regarding the three meanings of the intent of "arising," first, as for its initial occurrence, it encompasses both the subject and the object.
First, the subsequent wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) within the conventional person (*prajñapti-pudgala*) composed of the five aggregates of the Buddha is the subject that gives rise [to it];

thus, because it is the agent of arising, it is called "arising. Second, the teaching spoken by that wisdom is what is named "arising"; because it is the object of arising, it is called "arising" (the above two are the "arising of interpretive understanding"). Next are the three meanings of the intent [of the term].
First, the eight consciousnesses and the four wisdoms are collectively termed *manas*. It is called *manas* because it is capable of speaking;

this is understood as *manas* based on the principle of immediate succession (*samanantara-pratyaya*). Second, regarding that which is spoken, the entire *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is the Buddha’s *manas*, so it is named *manas* because it represents his intention and purpose.
Third, regarding the King Brahmā and Śāriputra’s hearts of thirsty longing, it is taken as *manas*. [End of] Section Ha.

The critique states: The first and last [interpretations] are likely incorrect; the second is correct. That is, taking the single section of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* that was expounded as the correct [basis].

Mou says: All three interpretations are generally incorrect. Furthermore, the first interpretation is too broad and commits a fault. The *Śāstra* states: "The wisdom of accomplished action manifests the body."
The *Pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna* (Wondrous Observational Wisdom) expounds the Dharma; it is solely a single consciousness and a single wisdom.
Now, if one were to take all eight consciousnesses collectively as the "intention" (*manas*), the definition would be too broad. The second interpretation commits the fault of contradicting the text.

If the exposition of this entire *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is taken as the "arising" (*utthāna*) by way of its thematic intent (*abhiprāya*), then according to this interpretation, the Sūtra itself is the "intention," and the "intention" is the "arising. This interpretation contradicts the commentary (*śāstra*). The [commentary on] the Sūtra...

"Rising of the intention" (*yi*) differs from "the sūtra" (*jing*). Regarding the third point, that the mind of yearning constitutes the "intention," this only encompasses one portion of the response to the request, while losing the six meanings within the response to the cause. Master Mu’s exposition of the correct principle states:

"There are two types of intention: first, the general; second, the specific. The general intention refers to the descent [from Tuṣita], birth, and attainment of enlightenment as the general intention for preaching the sūtra."

Just as when a Dharma Master ascends the seat, this is the intent behind preaching the Dharma; so too, when a Buddha appears in the world, his intent lies in preaching the Dharma. As the sutra below states:
"The Dharma King who shatters existence" up to "preaching various forms of the Dharma," and further says: "Because he preaches the wisdom of the Buddhas, the Buddhas appear in the world."
Second is the specific intention (*viśeṣābhiprāya*). Within the specific intention, there are two divisions: first, the distant intention; second, the proximate intention.

The sixteen princes and the twenty thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas [receiving predictions] specifically for the preaching of the sutra today constitute the distant intention. Second, the proximate intention refers to the preaching of the sutra and the conferring of predictions during the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Within the proximate intention, there are again two: first, the manifest; second, the secret. During the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the One Vehicle was taught manifestly.
The term "vehicle" (yāna) reveals the underlying intention. All that was done by me during the forty years prior [to teaching the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*] was always for the sake of a single purpose.
Furthermore, when I said, "The practice you all engage in is the bodhisattva path," I was secretly teaching the One Vehicle; this is called "intentional terminology" (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*).

Regarding the statement "briefly, by way of five meanings": Question: For what reason did the World-Honored One, forty years later, go to Vulture Peak near the royal city to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*?
What was the underlying significance in the arising of this sutra? Answer: The commentary states, "Briefly, by way of five meanings" (this is a summary).
This word "briefly" (*lue*) refers to a summary by way of grouping; when expanded, it constitutes a single gate, but when condensed, it comprises five meanings.

Regarding the statement "one [purpose] is to repay the request for the cause," etc., this enumerates five meanings in total. "Repaying the cause" refers to repaying oneself; "repaying the request" refers to repaying others.

Because the Buddha diligently practiced through three great eons during his causal stage and has now attained Buddhahood, he preaches this sutra to repay the practices performed during that causal stage;
this is called "repaying oneself. As for "repaying others": after the Buddha attained enlightenment, Brahmā King...
Regarding "repaying those who have invited [the Buddha] to preach the Dharma": this is called repaying an invitation. Second, regarding "for the purpose of destroying doubt and attachment":
destroying doubt causes faith to arise. For forty years prior, the Śrāvakas doubted that they themselves could become Buddhas;

today, by preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the Buddha declares that they shall become Buddhas. Thus, he destroys their doubts and causes them to give rise to faith. [This also serves to] destroy attachment.

To cause them to give rise to understanding: formerly, the śrāvakas clung to the minor fruit as the ultimate, saying that the three types of persons sit together upon the bed of liberation, and they stubbornly maintained that *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* was the reality.

Now, this sutra is preached to show that the deer and sheep carts are not true and the conjured city is not real, thereby removing their attachment to the minor [vehicle] and causing them to understand the one reality of the ox cart; this is called "breaking" [the delusion].

"Attachment" (*zhi*) means to cause them to give rise to understanding. Third, "to manifest the bestowal of the fruit upon the practitioner": this refers to the manifestation of the bestowal of the fruit of receiving [enlightenment].

Since the followers of the Two Vehicles have already eliminated the mind that clings to the Lesser Vehicle, the World-Honored One has individually conferred upon them the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of Bodhi-Buddhahood; hence it is called "receiving the fruit. To manifest the practice that leads to the cause:
although the predictions were conferred at Vulture Peak (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*), they all consisted of words concerning the future, each instructing [the practitioners] to cultivate one [of the paths].
The cause for mounting [the vehicle] is what is called "manifesting practice. Fourth, regarding "benefiting both the present and the future":

benefiting the present refers to the vision [of the Buddha], namely the fifteen classes of assemblies currently seated on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa who hear this sutra and all receive its benefits; this is termed "benefiting the present.
Benefiting the future refers to the subsequent [time], namely after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when those who uphold and recite this sutra all obtain blessings and merit.
This is called "conforming to the occasion. Fifth, regarding the manifestation according to the timing: this reveals that the timing is determined by the Dharma.

Specifically, before twelve years [had passed since his enlightenment], the great faculties were not yet mature, so he provisionally taught the teachings with phenomenal characteristics (*sāṃketika-dharma*). After twelve years, he predominantly taught the school of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vāda*), but had not yet taught this sutra.

It was only after forty years that the great faculties finally matured, at which point he taught this sutra. He did not teach it on previous days because the time for its teaching had not yet arrived.
[He] arrived. Because the *Lotus Sūtra* was preached at the assembly on Vulture Peak, the present moment is precisely that time;

thus, it is called "revealing the time" in reference to the Dharma. Regarding "revealing the faculties" in reference to persons: when the Buddha wished to preach this sūtra, he first examined their spiritual capacities (*indriya*).

If the faculties of a śrāvaka were mature, he would preach for them the Dharma-gate of the Four Noble Truths; for those of the pratyekabuddha vehicle, he would preach the Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination and so forth. Now...

Since it is known that those with the Mahāyāna capacity have matured faculties, this sūtra is preached for them; therefore, it is called "revealing the faculties" in reference to the persons [to whom it is addressed].
Thus, the Master of the Commentary (Sūshu) explains these five gates as the exposition of the intent behind the arising of the sūtra.

Regarding the statement that "the response to the request for causes has two parts," this refers to the previous section being further divided. Question: What is the meaning of "response" (*chou*)? Answer: "Response" means to repay or to reciprocate.
Now, there are three meanings of "response": first, repayment. Because [the Bodhisattvas] heard the *Lotus Sūtra* during the causal stage, they attained Buddhahood;
having now attained Buddhahood, they offer a reward. This refers to the *Lotus Sūtra* being proclaimed and praised from the mouth [of the Buddha] as described above.
Therefore, it is called "recompense. As the Sūtra says: "For this reason, he became a great king; through diligent seeking, he obtained this Dharma and subsequently attained Buddhahood.
Now, for your sake, I shall explain it. Second, the meaning of "response": the Sūtra says, "At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:
'Since you have already made three earnest requests, how could I now fail to speak? Listen attentively now, and reflect well upon it.'"
"I shall now analyze and explain this for you. Śāriputra and the other śrāvakas requested the realm; Mañjuśrī requested the practice; Maitreya requested the fruit.
The five chapters clarify the fruit of the One Vehicle. Regarding the meaning of the threefold offering, he exhorts the practice of this sutra and extensively encourages the making of vows, saying:
'The Sutra says that with a great voice, he universally addresses the fourfold assembly: "Who among you in this Sahā world...'"
On the earth, he extensively preached the Lotus Sūtra. "The Tathāgata shall soon enter parinirvāṇa; the Buddha wishes to entrust this wondrous Lotus Sūtra to those who shall uphold it.

The sūtra says: "Now, before the Buddha, he himself uttered a vow, whereby twenty thousand bodhisattvas requested that they uphold it in this world, while four classes of śrāvakas requested that they uphold it in other worlds. [There were] eighty trillion nayutas..."
Those other bodhisattvas both uphold it together; they travel back and forth through the lands of the ten directions, enabling sentient beings to copy and receive and uphold this sutra.
I do not cherish my own body or life, but only regret the lack of the unsurpassed Way.

All the great bodhisattvas offer their hearts of loyal sincerity toward this sutra; therefore, it is called "offering" (*xiàn*). What has been stated above is a repayment, repaying their past kindness.
To respond to those present before him, he offers gifts and exhorts them to practice. Among these three meanings, the sense of "recompense" (chūhō) is particularly predominant.
During his causal stage, the Tathāgata practiced for three great kalpas and attained Buddhahood through the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Having attained Buddhahood, he then preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; this is called "recompense. Question: He cultivated the cause of the One Vehicle during his causal stage, and now he has attained Buddhahood.

Question: When it is said that the sutra has been fully explained, how is this called "repaying the cause" (*chō-in*)? Answer: First, the causal practices of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) are fully contained within this sutra;

simply knowing that the sutra has been preached is itself the repayment of the cause. Second, the invitation by Brahmā and Śāriputra serves as the cause, while the Buddha’s preaching serves as the fruit; this is precisely what constitutes repaying the cause. Question:

Since the entirety is already the repayment of the cause, why is it necessary to speak of "repayment" (*chō*) separately? Answer: It is in contrast to the Buddha’s own person that [the repayment] is established. Repayment...
This is because the cause is distinct. If one were to address another person, the meaning of "repayment" (chou) and "invitation" (qing) would not be distinct.
Therefore, within the context of repaying a cause, one distinguishes the act of inviting; yet in reality, these two meanings are not different.

Regarding the statement that "the fruit of Buddhahood cannot be accomplished in vain," this is a response concerning the causal practice (*hetu-pratipatti*). It also serves as an exposition on the sequence of causes, as well as an establishment of those causes.
It may also be said to provide a brief clarification regarding increase and decrease. Question: Why does [the number of causes] not increase to seven or eight, nor decrease to four or five?
Furthermore, why are the cause of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-hetu*) not placed first with the cause of practice (*pratipatti-hetu*) as second, instead of placing practice first?

Yes. The commentary states: "The fruit of Buddhahood cannot be established in vain," and so forth. The author of the commentary [Yanshou] here performs two functions: first, he refutes the non-Buddhist (tīrthika) doctrine of spontaneity (*svabhāva*);
second, he also breaks the doctrine of the One-Nature School that "the mind itself is Buddha. This is because the fruit of Buddhahood cannot be established in vain;

it must arise through karmic practice, which is precisely what is meant by the Buddhist principle of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). Thus, he refutes the spontaneity of the non-Buddhists. Third, there is...

A Chan Master of the One-Nature School said: "The mind itself is the Buddha. It suffices merely to know and realize this; there is no need for further cultivation. The Way of the Buddha is not remote;
turning the mind is itself the Buddha within the heart. Why rely on seeking it externally? It is better to prostrate to the Buddha within one's own heart than to bow one's head.
It is better to recite the name of the Buddha within one's own heart than to let the voice go forth. There were many such Chan masters.
Having formed this realization, he also refuted the world in four ways. Furthermore, he loved the fruit but not the cause;

upon seeing that the Buddha possessed the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, he immediately desired to attain the Path, yet when it came to practice, he was unwilling. He felt attachment toward the prime minister.
When you are told to study, you are unwilling. There has never been one who attained the rank of Prime Minister without studying.
There has never been one who attained the fruit of Buddhahood without practicing. To claim that one attains the fruit of Buddhahood without practicing at all is called "attaining it in vain.

Furthermore, during the Buddha’s causal stage, if he had not practiced giving (*dāna*), how could he have pointed to empty space as a treasury or transformed the great earth into gold and silver? If he had not maintained [the precepts] during his causal stage...
How could one possibly attract the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages as their retinue through precepts alone? If one cannot practice patience, how can one obtain the thirty-two marks?
Within each mark, there are many subtle and beautiful qualities; if one does not cultivate the sixth perfection during the causal stage, [how could these be attained]?
How can one attain all-encompassing wisdom? Whenever one cultivates even a single act of goodness, it must be dedicated toward unsurpassed bodhi.

As the sutra says: "I have seen that Śākyamuni Tathāgata, throughout immeasurable kalpas, performed difficult practices and ascetic austerities, accumulating merit and virtue to seek the path of a bodhisattva;
only after this did he finally achieve the path of bodhi and complete his attainment of Buddhahood. Even a good deed as small as threading a needle [is thus dedicated]."

If even these are not neglected, how much more so should one practice while still on the causal stage? There has never been anyone who obtained the shade and coolness of peach and plum trees without first planting them;
likewise, grain and wheat cannot emerge of themselves, but must grow through plowing and cultivation. Thus, one must traverse the stages of practice over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*;
it is impossible to achieve perfect enlightenment immediately upon generating the bodhicitta.

Regarding the phrase "actions and speech do not arise in isolation," etc.: Question: Since the practice of emptiness naturally yields its fruit, why is it necessary to make aspirations? This constitutes the second point. Answer:
The commentary states that "actions and speech do not arise in isolation," etc., which concludes the discussion on the causal conditions for prior practice.

The necessity of relying upon aspiration refers to the generation of subsequent aspirational causes. "Isolation" (*gudu*) means being solitary; "assistance" (*zhuzi*) means support. When performing an action, one must obtain the assistance of aspiration so that it may be brought forth. [End of] Practice.
The two dharmas of practice and vow are like the two wheels of a chariot or the two wings of a bird; it is impossible for one to be lacking. Without two wheels, a chariot cannot travel far;
without two wings, a bird cannot soar to the heavens. Practice and vows supporting one another is likewise so.
If there is practice without a vow, the practice will surely be solitary; if there is a vow without practice, the vow will surely be empty. If practice possesses...

Vows ensure that practice is not solitary. If there are vows accompanied by practice, then those vows will not be in vain. Practice is like a precious jeweled chariot, while vows are like the driver of the chariot.
