Bodhisattvas retain their afflictions (*kleśa*) to moisten their rebirths, whereas those who have attained the fourth fruit of the noble ones (*ārya*) no longer undergo further existence.

Because the emanations (*nirmāṇakāya*) of Bodhisattvas are inexhaustible, these two cases are not the same. Question: Those who have ascended to the stages (*bhūmi*) and entered the state of the noble ones have severed the obstacles of affliction;

they are indeed the objects of refuge for sentient beings. Yet, as long as the afflictions prior to the stages (*pūrvabhūmi*) still remain, they are still ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*). Why, then, are they categorized within the first refuge? Answer: Upon ascending to the stages, one severs [the afflictions]. [The text continues: "Upon ascending to the stages... [and so forth].

Those who have realized the true principle serve as a reliance for Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*). Even those prior to the stages (*pṛthagjana*), who have partially subdued their afflictions (*kleśa*), may also serve as a reliance for those sentient beings.

As stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, a Bodhisattva at the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) can manifest the eight phases of enlightenment (*aṣṭākāra-abhisambodhi*) to transform and benefit sentient beings.
Since the benefit conferred is profound, there is no fault in relying upon them. It is asked: "How many Bodhisattvas of the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*) receive offerings? Twenty.

"Six Ganges-sands. I do not yet know how many [aeons] each relies upon. The answer in the *Shu* (Commentary) states: "The first reliance is on making offerings to five *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* [aeons], etc.";

this is according to the assignment by Paramārtha. Question: According to the sutra cited below, it says: "Ānanda, these people shall make offerings to as many Tathāgatas as there are atoms in fifty worlds.
Until the very end, they will simultaneously attain [enlightenment] in various lands throughout the ten directions. Each attains...

Question: All these Buddhas bear the same name, "Precious Mark" (Ratnalakṣaṇa). According to this, why is the number [of worlds] not the same as the twenty-six Ganges-sands? Answer: There are three interpretations. First, it is said that while he makes offerings to the Buddhas of his own land—twenty-six Ganges-sands—he simultaneously makes offerings to the Buddhas of other lands within fifty worlds. Second, it is said that through the power of his karma, he makes offerings to twenty-six Ganges-sands; if it were by means of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), [the number would be different]. Third, it is said that although the number of worlds is equal, the number of Buddhas differs because the lifespan of the Buddhas in those lands varies. Furthermore, it is said that the number of worlds is equal, but the number of Buddhas differs because the extent of their respective Buddha-lands varies. For example, in the *Sūtra on the Prophecy of the Five Hundred Disciples*, it is stated that the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni is five hundred yojanas in extent, whereas the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Amitāyus is immeasurable. Therefore, although the number of worlds is equal, the number of Buddhas is not necessarily the same. Furthermore, it is said that although the number of worlds is equal, the number of Buddhas differs because the number of kalpas until their parinirvāṇa varies. For instance, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni will attain parinirvāṇa after one hundred years, whereas the Tathāgata Amitāyus will remain for immeasurable kalpas. Therefore, although the number of worlds is equal, the number of Buddhas is not necessarily the same. Furthermore, it is said that although the number of worlds is equal, the number of Buddhas differs because the number of sentient beings to be converted varies. For example, the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni contains many sentient beings who are difficult to convert, whereas the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Amitāyus contains few such beings. Therefore, although the number of worlds is equal, the number of Buddhas is not necessarily the same. Furthermore, it is said that although the number of worlds is equal, the number of Buddhas differs because the number of bodhisattvas to be converted varies. For example, the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni contains many bodhisattvas who are difficult to convert, whereas the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Amitāyus contains few such bodhisattvas. Therefore, although the number of worlds is equal, the number of Buddhas is not necessarily the same. Furthermore, it is said that although the number of worlds is equal, the number of Buddhas differs because the number of śrāvakas to be converted varies. For example, the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni contains many śrāvakas who are difficult to convert, whereas the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Amitāyus contains few such śrāvakas. Therefore, although the number of worlds is equal, the number of Buddhas is not necessarily the same. Furthermore, it is said that although the number of worlds is equal, the number of Buddhas differs because the number of *pratyekabuddhas* to be converted varies. For example, the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni contains many *pratyekabuddhas* who are difficult to convert, whereas the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Amitāyus contains few such *pratyekabuddhas*. Therefore, although the number of worlds is equal, the number of Buddhas is not necessarily the same. Furthermore, it is said that although the number of worlds is equal, the number of Buddhas differs because the number of *cakravartin* kings to be converted varies. For example, the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni contains many *cakravartin* kings who are difficult to convert, whereas the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Amitāyus contains few such kings. Therefore, although the number of worlds is equal, the number of Buddhas is not necessarily the same. Furthermore, it is said that although the number of worlds is equal, the number of Buddhas differs because the number of gods and humans to be converted varies. For example, the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni contains many gods and humans who are difficult to convert, whereas the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Amitāyus contains few such gods and humans. Therefore, although the number of worlds is equal, the number of Buddhas is not necessarily the same. Furthermore, it is said that although the number of worlds is equal, the number of Buddhas differs because the number of those to be converted who have already entered the path varies. For example, the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni contains many who have already entered the path but are difficult to convert, whereas the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Amitāyus contains few such individuals. Therefore, although the number of worlds is equal, the number of Buddhas is not necessarily the same. Furthermore, it is said that although the number of worlds is equal, the number of Buddhas differs because the number of those to be converted who have already attained the fruit varies. For example, the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni contains many who have attained the fruit but are difficult to convert, whereas the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Amitāyus contains few such individuals. Therefore, although the number of worlds is equal, the number of Buddhas is not necessarily the same. Furthermore, it is said that although the number of worlds is equal, the number of Buddhas differs because the number of those to be converted who have already attained liberation varies. For example, the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni contains many who have attained liberation but are difficult to convert, whereas the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Amitāyus contains few such individuals. Therefore, although the number of worlds is equal, the number of Buddhas is not necessarily the same. Furthermore, it is said that although the number of worlds is equal, the number of Buddhas differs because the number of those to be converted who have already attained the ultimate goal varies. For example, the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni contains many who have attained the ultimate goal but are difficult to convert, whereas the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Amitāyus contains few such individuals. Therefore, although the number of worlds is equal, the number of Buddhas is not necessarily the same. Furthermore, it is said that although the number of worlds is equal, the number of Buddhas differs because the number of those to be converted who have already attained the stage of non-retrogression varies. For example, the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni contains many who have attained non-retrogression but are difficult to convert, whereas the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Amitāyus contains few such individuals. Therefore, although the number of worlds is equal, the number of Buddhas is not necessarily the same. Furthermore, it is said that although the number of worlds is equal, the number of Buddhas differs because the number of those to be converted who have already attained the stage of patience (*kṣānti*) varies. For example, the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni contains many who have attained patience but are difficult to convert, whereas the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Amitāyus contains few such individuals. Therefore, although the number of worlds is equal, the number of Buddhas is not necessarily the same. Furthermore, it is said that although the number of worlds is equal, the number of Buddhas differs because the number of those to be converted who have already attained the stage of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) varies. For example, the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni contains many who have attained the first fruit but are difficult to convert, whereas the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Amitāyus contains few such individuals. Therefore, although the number of worlds is equal, the number of Buddhas is not necessarily the same. Furthermore, it is said that although the number of worlds is equal, the number of Buddhas differs because the number of those to be converted who have already attained the stage of the second fruit (*sakṛdāgāmin*) varies. For example, the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni contains many who have attained the second fruit but are difficult to convert, whereas the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Amitāyus contains few such individuals. Therefore, although the number of worlds is equal, the number of Buddhas is not necessarily the same. Furthermore, it is said that although the number of worlds is equal, the number of Buddhas differs because the number of those to be converted who have already attained the stage of the third fruit (*anāgāmin*) varies. For example, the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni contains many who have attained the third fruit but are difficult to convert, whereas the Buddha-field
Regarding the offering of power: within the fifty worlds—whether according to the three or four reliances (*pratisaraṇa*)—there are the minds of entering, abiding, and emerging.
If discussed in terms of a single mind, it concerns twenty-six *asaṃkhyeya*-kalpas; if discussed in terms of the three minds, it concerns fifty worlds.

My own critical assessment states: the first two interpretations are excellent. If one follows the latter interpretation, taking the three minds collectively, the calculation reaches seventy-eight *asaṃkhyeya*-kalpas, corresponding to the five [aspects].
Ten worlds are also few. Furthermore, Rourou (糅) says: "If one offers the four requisites for the body as an act of worship, it covers twenty-six *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*;

if it is with a single flower or a single fruit, then it covers fifty worlds. Now, according to the scriptural text, honoring, praising, and protecting the treasury of the Dharma is done throughout one's entire life.
Lu (路) says: "Although it is said that when a Bodhisattva makes offerings according to the four reliances (*catur-yoni*), it covers twenty-six *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*."
It does not say that one attains Buddhahood merely by making offerings to this extent; rather, it allows for further offerings as well.

Regarding the phrase "meeting many [Buddhas]," etc., this is an explanation of a potential objection. It is also said to be "extracted from" [the text]. Question: Since this section discusses the causes for upholding [the Dharma], it would suffice to simply cite the scriptural passage on upholding the sutra.
Why is it necessary to discuss the quantity of offerings made to the Buddhas? Answer: The commentary states that the phrase "meeting many," etc., refers precisely to making offerings.

Since the Buddhas are numerous, the upholding [of their teachings] is also extensive. Furthermore, it is said that one encounters many virtuous friends; by making offerings to the Buddhas, one upholds [the teachings] for a long duration.
This summarizes the aforementioned upholding.

Regarding the phrase "Furthermore, Śākyamuni Tathāgata and others": Question: Since it is said that one must approach and make offerings to twenty-six *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas of Buddhas and uphold this sutra before attaining Buddhahood, this is indeed profoundly deep.
I wonder, World-Honored One, did you yourself, when you were a Bodhisattva following the four reliances (*catur-yoni*), ever uphold this sutra?
Furthermore, regarding the sutra now being preached, which is the fruition of past causes for upholding it—within those personal causes [of yours]...
Regarding the location of the passage on "upholding the sutra," the commentary (*shu*) answers: "Furthermore, Śākyamuni Tathāgata... The sutra states:

"At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta: 'In the distant past, beyond immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, a Buddha appeared in the world named Vairocana-rāja (King of Majestic Sound) Tathāgata. That Buddha Vairocana-rāja passed into extinction..."
After the passing [of the Buddha], once the True Dharma has ceased, during the period of the Semblance Dharma, there will be monks of overweening pride who possess great power.
At that time, there will be a monk named Constantly Not Disparaging (*Sadāparibhūta*) who attains great influence.
For what reason is he named Constantly Not Disparaging? This monk, whenever he sees any monks or others, bows down to them all (and so forth). This is...
In Śākyamuni’s causal stage, he maintained this sutra in the presence of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of twenty-six Ganges Rivers.
The commentary does not cite the preceding passage concerning being beaten and reviled; rather, it cites only the passage regarding receiving and maintaining a billion verses at the time of death.

This is because, during the period of the Semblance Dharma under Vipaśyin Buddha (Vīṇāpāda), he had previously maintained the sutra as a cause, and thus attained the power of *vīrya* (heroic vigor) at the time of his death.
The Buddha Ghoṣarāja bestowed his empowerment upon the voice from space, which taught twenty quadrillion verses; how could [the disciple] have been able to receive and uphold them all?
Furthermore, if he had never upheld them at all, and the Buddha had not seen him after his parinirvāṇa, for what reason would he have caused him to hear them?
Moreover, how could he have remembered twenty quadrillion verses? One might ask: the Lotus Sūtra consists of only seven fascicles; why is it now said to be twenty?
"Ten million billion verses—why is this so much? [The questioner asks. The answer is: "In the *Sūtra on the Lesser Transformation Land*, there are only seven fascicles;

the *Sūtra on the Greater Transformation Land* is extensive, and it is not at all preposterous for it to contain twenty million billion verses, such as the verses equal in number to the sands of the Ganges, numbering six hundred trillion *ya* (hundred billion)."
This is not at all excessive. Originally, the practice of upholding the sutra occurs at the end of the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*).

At the time of death, one is instructed by a voice from the void and hears twenty quadrillion verses; immediately, one attains the aforementioned purity of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*).

From this point on, one attains the aforementioned purity of the six sense faculties and enters the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*). The phrase "as mentioned above" refers to the merit of the Dharma Master.

Question: How do we know this refers to the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*)? Answer: The scriptural text states clearly: "Although he has not yet attained the bodhisattva's untainted (*anāsrava*) nose-faculty.
Based on this, it cannot be the first bhūmi. Furthermore, it speaks of the "pure physical eye born of one's parents."

The mention of "fleshly eyes" (māṃsa-cakṣus) indicates that these are not divine eyes (divya-cakṣus). For fleshly eyes to possess such superior function, it must necessarily be during the stage of equipment (sambhāra-avasthā), as they lack such capacity prior to this.
If one were to argue that the various sense faculties function interchangeably, that would require the first bhūmi;
since this does not exist prior to the bhūmis, it is indeed a matter of preparatory application (prayoga).

Regarding the statement, "one immediately attains the aforementioned six faculties, etc.": Question: By what cause does a bodhisattva increase their lifespan? Answer: They increase their lifespan through the power of the majesty (*dharmateja*) of the Dharma. Question:
The verse states that they augment their lifespan by means of the power of supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), yet it does not mention the power of the majesty of the Dharma.

Answer: There are two ways of increasing lifespan: first, through the power of the majesty of the Dharma; second, through the power of supernormal knowledges. [This is as explained] in the prose commentary.
Verse: [The two verses] each present only one side; in truth, it is superior to explain them as both. Question: How can supernormal powers (abhijñā) increase one’s lifespan? Answer:
As for the four bases of power (ṛddhipāda), remaining in the world for an eon is precisely what constitutes the extension of life.

Question: Originally, at what stage of practice and rank does this Bodhisattva stand? Even if he were to extend his lifespan excessively, would it not be like a worldly person merely reciting mantras?

[The Buddha] bestowed his empowerment [upon him]. It would cease in as little as ten or five years; even longer than that would not be the case. How much less so for a Bodhisattva who increases [his lifespan] by two hundred trillion nayutas of years?
Answer: An-guo says, "Because this Bodhisattva’s own life-span is naturally long while in the stage of application (prayoga-mārga), how much more so when he hears the power of the Dharma?
Question: How can there be the fourfold assembly within the stage of application? Answer: An-guo says:
This Bodhisattva is at the end of the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*). Therefore, there are four assemblies.

As he is about to enter the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*), there are four assemblies during the interval between the two [stages]. Question: Does "long life" refer specifically to the stage of application?

Since the four assemblies are mentioned, it is said that this refers to the mind at the end of the stage of equipment (this interpretation is incorrect). According to Lu, Vimalacitra Buddha (Vaiśvānara) is a Buddha of Enjoyment for Others (*parasaṃbhogakāya-buddha*) who resides therein.

Regarding the *vipākakṣetra* (retribution land): it is said that Bodhisattvas dwell therein with long lifespans, and that there are four assemblies; this implies that different things are seen in a single location within a *nirmāṇakṣetra* (transformation land).

This is also not the case. As for seeing different things in a single location, this refers to the Buddha speaking of Bodhisattvas; Bodhisattvas do not possess such a capacity [to manifest differences in a single place].

Now there is an interpretation which says: "The practice of receiving and upholding ten million billion verses increases one's lifespan; all of this belongs to the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*).
Question: How can there be the fourfold assembly [of disciples]? Answer: These are Bodhisattvas at the stage of preparatory application; it does not preclude the fourfold assembly from seeing them.

For instance, in the Western Regions, Vasubandhu and Asaṅga were at the stage of preparatory application and beyond, as well as being noble beings (*ārya*) on the first bhūmi; what prevents the fourfold assembly from seeing them?
It is seen.
As for the statement "constantly attaining the aforementioned [states]," this refers to entering the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*). Question: How is it known that this is the first stage? Answer:

Because there is the character "constant" (*chang*), it serves as proof of the principle of constancy. Therefore, one constantly attains the purification of the six sense faculties. Previously, when the principle had not yet been realized, such was not the case.

The character "Chang" (Constant). Question: What are the four stages of encountering the Buddha? Answer: First, during the period of the Semblance Dharma of the Buddha King Majestic Sound (Vaiśvānara-rāja), one practices the conduct of "Never Despising.

Until the very moment of death, one hears in full the Lotus Sūtra previously taught by the Buddha King Majestic Sound, consisting of twenty quadrillion verses, and is able to receive and uphold them all. Thereupon, one immediately attains the aforementioned purity of the faculty of the eye.

His eyes were purified; his ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind were purified. Having attained this purification of the six sense faculties, his lifespan was further increased by two hundred trillion nayutas of years.

He extensively preached this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for others, and even transformed thousands of millions of billions of beings, causing them to abide in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. This is the first stage. After his life came to an end...
Thereafter, he encountered two thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas, all named Candrasūryapradīpa (Sun-Moon-Lamp). Within their teachings, they preached this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.

This was the second stage. By these causes and conditions, he again encountered two thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas, all named Meghasvaraghoṣeśvararāja (Cloud-Sovereign-Lamp-King), who likewise preached this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* among the fourfold assembly with a mind free from fear. This was the third... [stage].
The third stage: From this point onward, they shall again encounter billions of buddhas and likewise preach this sutra within the teachings of all those buddhas.
Having accomplished these merits, they shall attain buddhahood; this is the fourth stage.
The mention of "Never-Disparaging" and others serves to reconcile the ancient and the modern. As the Sūtra says:
"If, in past lives, I had not received, upheld, read, recited, or explained the Lotus Sūtra to others, I would not have been able to quickly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi," and so forth.

Having attained great power, at that time the fourfold assembly of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, because they had treated me with contempt out of a mind of malice, for two hundred billion kalpas never encountered a Buddha, did not hear the Dharma, and did not see the Saṃgha.

For a thousand kalpas they underwent great suffering and affliction in the Avīci Hell. Once these karmic offenses were exhausted, they again encountered the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging, who taught and transformed them toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Bodhi," etc. Question: Why did the Bodhisattva not take hold of sentient beings, but instead prostrated to their teachers and endured being reviled for a thousand kalpas before entering hell?

Answer: It was because the faculties and natures of sentient beings were such that they required this. At that time, when the fourfold assembly struck the Bodhisattva, anger arose from within his mind and perfumed the seeds of the *darśana-bhāga* (perceptual portion). The karma thus created was karma for hell. At that moment, the Bodhisattva [reflected] from behind...

He was granted the prediction of attaining Buddhahood, and the sound of his preaching the Dharma entered the ears of "I," perfuming the seeds of its characteristics within the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
After passing through a thousand kalpas in hell, these seeds finally ripened;

emerging from hell, as the sutra says, "once these karmic retributions were finished," he again encountered the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging (*Sadāparibhūta*), who taught him toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. (Sutra evidence)
Regarding the phrase "therefore,

it was for the sake of the past," etc.: because he attained Buddhahood now by virtue of having upheld the sutra in the past, he now proclaims this teaching as a recompense for that past upholding of the sutra.

Regarding the exhortation to constantly receive and uphold [this sutra]: it is by virtue of having upheld this sutra in the past that one now attains Buddhahood. You, O Bodhisattva, must emulate my practice;

had you not upheld the wondrous Dharma in the past, you could not have so swiftly attained Bodhi. That you have now obtained the complete and perfect marks and signs is entirely due to the power of upholding this sutra.
Since you already aspire to the fruit of Buddhahood, you must necessarily receive and uphold this sutra. If you do so without interruption...
The mind that has severed [delusions] is such that its fulfillment of the fruit is no different from my own. First, it is to repay the past upholding of this sutra;
second, it is to exhort others to receive and study it. For these two reasons, I preach this sutra.

Regarding the phrase "the manifestation and the discourse are mutually causal": the manifested sign serves as the cause for the preaching of the sūtra, and the preaching of the sūtra is the response to the manifested sign (the subject and object being easily understood).

Question: The Buddha originally appeared in the world solely for the sake of benefiting sentient beings; he ought to have preached the sūtra immediately. Why was it necessary to manifest a sign? Answer:

The One Vehicle is profound and subtle, and its essential meaning is extremely difficult to grasp. It shatters the provisional teachings of the Two Vehicles to cause them to return to the single reality. It points back to the past non-existence [of duality] and speaks...

Now, there are those who discuss the preceding fruit as being the subsequent cause; fearing that doubts may arise and divergent views be produced, they manifest auspicious omens to dispel such skeptical sentiments.
Therefore, it is necessary to manifest signs. "Signs" (xiàng) refers to their specific characteristics. As for the single character *xiàng*, there have been many interpretations since antiquity.

1. The aspect of pacifying the nation and the ten kinds of understanding. This refers to the external praise of the true vehicle (*saddharma*), such as the preaching of the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*.

2. The internal aspect of examining the faculties of those present. This refers to entering the *Samādhi of the Station of Immeasurable Meanings*. 3. The aspect of gods and humans scattering flowers. This refers to the rain of the four kinds of flowers and so forth.
4. The aspect of the earth shaking and the subduing of Māra. This refers to the sixfold trembling of the earth. 5. The aspect of ordinary beings and sages rejoicing together. [The fourth...]
1. The assembly gazing up [at the Buddha], and so forth. 2. The light from the ūrṇā-kośa shining afar: "Emitting light from the ūrṇā" and below. 3. Manifesting the appearance of other lands:
"In this world, seeing those lands completely" and below. 4. The appearance of the adornments of this world:
"The Buddha emits a single ray of light" and below. 5. The appearance of Maitreya harboring doubt: "At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva had this thought" and below.
This is so. The ten [points] constitute the characteristics of Mañjuśrī’s response. From "Mañjuśrī said" onwards is this [section].

Among these, the seventh and eighth characteristics lack explicit clarification in the commentary; however, the intent is present within the passage concerning the arising of doubt after the assembly has seen this.
Doubt arises because they see the features of that land and the adornments of this realm. There are five paths: first, the external characteristic; second, ...

The internal signs: 1) the sign of the three heavens; 2) the sign of the four stages; 3) the sign of the radiance emitted from below the space between the eyebrows (this is the same as the fifth of the National Teacher Tong’an).
There are six interpretations of the "Golden City. The first four are identical to the [previous] path; the fifth and sixth are distinct. The fifth is the characteristic of others (*para-lakṣaṇa*):

emitting light that illuminates eight thousand worlds to the east. The sixth is the self-characteristic (*sva-lakṣaṇa*): seeing the various wonders and excellences of this realm. There are many such compilations and explanations;
however, the twelve characteristics compiled by Miyou are excessive, while the ten characteristics of Anshigao are too broad. [This is stated] in the Commentary.
Regarding the "existence and non-existence," the interpretation of the golden path as being either five or six [units] is too narrow; it is better to follow the six units of Zhangjing.
First, one explains and guides the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
"Forty years have already passed; will the Name-Body (Myōshō) preach this sutra? The answer is: first, it is possible for both [the Dharmakāya and the Nirmāṇakāya] to do so.
Second, it is highly reasonable to take the Nirmāṇakāya [as the speaker], because the manifestation of signs is the Nirmāṇakāya.

The phrase "previously for the sake of bodhisattvas, etc. describes the characteristics of the teachings and the objects [of those teachings]. Originally, this sutra was intended to be taught within the Land of Reward (*vipākabhūmi*);

however, it has now been brought forth to be taught here in the impure land of Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa. Because the faculties of those present are dull and the Dharma is profound and difficult to understand, there was fear that they might produce slander upon hearing it.

Consequently, he first taught the doctrine of existence (*astitva*) to lead them to realize the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), and subsequently spoke of the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) to refine and temper them.
Be careful. Now the father understands his son’s intent; he has gradually become enlightened and expansive, having accomplished his great aspiration and come to despise his former mind.
Consequently, at the assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, he widely summons those with whom he has a karmic connection, desiring to entrust his family wealth to the impoverished son.

He speaks of the fruits of his practice and the power of his integration, first acting as a Bodhisattva to discourse upon the emergence of the essence by preaching the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*.
Because one must know that the natures of medicines and illnesses are immeasurable, the dharmas are also immeasurable. Because the dharmas are immeasurable, their meanings are also immeasurable.
That which is immeasurable in meaning arises from a single dharma; this single dharma is what is called "signlessness" (animitta). Signlessness is the absence of signs.

This is called the "True Aspect" (bhūtalakṣaṇa). Its purpose is to cause those Śrāvakas who have struck the drum to turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna]; it intends for them to abandon the provisional and grasp the real.

Furthermore, because it is like a Bodhisattva who is about to sit upon a lotus flower, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Anantamukhanirhāra-dhāraṇī-sūtra* represent the fulfillment of the arrival of the time.
Regarding the statement "next, he enters the samādhi of immeasurable meanings," etc.: Question: Why is it necessary to enter meditative concentration? Answer:

If one does not enter concentration, how could one know that the Vulture Peak Son (Śāriputra) is of superior capacity and was given the teaching through direct discourse (*dharmadeśanā*), that the four persons were of middling capacity and were given the teaching through parables (*avadānadeśanā*), and that the five hundred, one thousand, and two hundred were of inferior capacity and were given the teaching through past-life causes and conditions (*pūrvayoga*)? If one does not enter concentration, there is no means by which to examine their capacities before subsequently expounding the teachings.
Because the Dharma is profound and subtle, it is thus; furthermore, it is to serve as a model for future generations.
For this reason, he entered the Samādhi of the Station of Immeasurable Meanings.
Regarding the statement that "the heavens rained four kinds of flowers," etc., this signifies the manifestation of auspicious omens by the two polarities of Heaven and Earth.

When an emperor spreads compassion to instruct the world, it moves the red phoenixes to soar and causes the Star of the Old Man (Kṛttikā) to appear; when benevolence and virtue nourish all things, sweet springs gush forth and auspicious grain grows.
Thus we know that when magnificent virtue is fully realized within, portents and blessings manifest without. Spreading the clouds of compassion across the *dharmadhātu*, they bring peace...
When the flames of the burning house reached their peak, he caused the sun of brilliant wisdom to shine across the great void and shattered the profound darkness of ignorance.
Having now finished preaching the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*, he immediately entered meditative absorption (*samādhi*). This matter is inconceivable;

it moved both heaven and earth, and the heavens rained down four kinds of flowers, signifying the deliverance of the four types of beings and the realization of the four nirvāṇas. He removed the stubborn and rigid attachment to the Lesser Vehicle and [proceeded with] his practice.

A great cause results in the attainment of a great fruit. That the earth shook in six ways signifies the startling and shaking of all Māras, the destruction of the afflictions of the six thieves, and the ensuring that the great assembly does not give rise to distracted thoughts while observing the place where I, the Tathāgata, preach the Dharma. Question:
Why did it not rain fruits, but rather rain flowers? Answer: If one were to obtain the fruit without having practiced the cause, then indeed it would have rained fruits.
Flowers do not rain [in ordinary times]. Now, because one must first practice the cause before subsequently attaining the fruit, flowers alone rain down.

Regarding the phrase "the fourfold assembly gazes up with longing" and so forth: the sentiments of the multitude all thirst for this auspicious sign. Question: Since flowers have rained down and the earth has trembled, what benefit is there? Answer:
The commentary states that the fourfold assembly and others likewise represent an auspicious sign shared by both the mundane and the sagely, through which they are able to hear the Dharma.
In the *Mātr̥kā-artha-sūtra*, it is further seen that when the Buddha enters the samādhi of quiescence, celestial flowers fall in profusion and the earth trembles and shakes;
thus, the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings all rejoice and gaze upon him with reverence.

Regarding the statement "emitting rays of light from his brow," this is a sign manifested to indicate [the event] from afar in other directions. As the World-Honored One was about to kindle the torch of wisdom, his bodily radiance shone forth;
thus he extended the jade-like luster from between his brows and displayed a rare wonder outside the city, causing the fourfold assembly to feel redoubled longing and veneration.
It was on this account that the Tathāgata preached this sūtra. The Great Dharma Master asked: "If it is said that the light shines upon the ten thousand [lands] of the eastern direction..."
As for the eight thousand worlds, why are they not recorded in the historical records of this land? Daolin replied: "When the Way harmonizes, there is a distant resonance across a thousand li;
when the world is discordant, even liver and gall are as far apart as Chu and Yue. The people of the Yin and Zhou eras were not suitable vessels for the Buddhist teaching.

Yan said: "Where there is affinity, one communicates across a thousand li; where there is no affinity, one is deaf even next door. A gentleman shares the same breeze at a distance of a thousand li, while a petty man remains separated by a mere path."
It differs from worldly conventions. If hearts are in accord, then those from Hu and Yue become brothers; if they are not in accord, then even liver and gall become enemies.
The Buddha originally emitted light to summon those with a karmic connection; if there was no such connection in this land, what prevented him from being seen at that time? Question:
For what reason were his descent into birth and entry into extinction made known to this land? Answer: His descent into birth and entry into extinction were intended to...

Regarding those who know in this land: they are made aware that a Buddha has appeared and that a Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa. He emits light fundamentally to summon those with whom he has a karmic affinity;

as for why he does not cause everyone to see [this], consider how on the assembly at Vulture Peak, he extended his tongue for fifty minor kalpas, yet in the scriptures it is only said that the Tathāgata entered parinirvāṇa at eighty minus one. Furthermore, he wishes to return to the Pure Land and transfer all [beings] there.

"O devas and humans! Let us set aside for a moment those who have been transferred to other lands. Even within this very assembly, there are those who can see [the light], yet there are also those who do not.
How does this failure to see the radiance from between the eyebrows in this land matter? It is like the sun and moon beautifying the sky, which are not seen by the blind;
or like the eight tones and six musical scales, which are not heard by the deaf. For this reason, in this region..."
The histories of the scriptures do not mention this.
As for the statement that "the assembly, having seen this, were all equal," this refers to the signs of the great assembly’s state of doubt.

Having heard the Buddha’s discourse on the Infinite Meanings conclude, they did not descend from their seats but instead entered into meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Then, the heavens rained down flowers, the earth shook, and the light from his brow-urṇā shone eastward across eighteen thousand worlds.

A thousand different manifestations appeared in the West; these seven matters were as clear as the light of day. Yet, amidst the assembly on Vulture Peak, none perceived the signs of the Great Sage, and each harbored doubts within their own minds.
Regarding the statement "Maitreya poses questions," etc., this refers to the mutual understanding between host and guest established from afar.
Maitreya, having attained the rank of the Regent (Upapadya), knew that the Buddha intended to preach this sutra out of compassion for all sentient beings;
thus, he manifested signs of doubt and, harboring both his own and others' concerns, addressed his questions to Mañjuśrī alone: "For what reason does the Guide today manifest these many [signs]?"
Regarding these auspicious signs of transformation: Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva is the patriarchal teacher of nine generations of Buddhas.

Seeing Maitreya posing questions by juxtaposing self and others, and wishing to know the auspicious signs of the manifested phenomena, he employed his knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*) to directly perceive the causal characteristics of the past.
He accomplished ten kinds of matters as if they were present before him. He replied to Maitreya, saying, "As it occurs to me... [The commentary] explains:
"Wait a moment while I reflect, deliberate, and measure the situation. The Buddha now intends to preach the Great Dharma; he intends to rain down the great rain of Dharma;
and even intends to expound the great meaning of the Dharma. In brief: Maitreya, beholding these current signs, asked this question.

Mañjuśrī answers by citing an ancient precedent. Since it is known that Śākyamuni was not a mere transformation body, this is verified by the meeting with Dīpaṃkara prior to the preaching of the Lotus Sūtra;
as the sūtra itself says: "I saw the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, from his original light and auspicious signs, until the Lotus Sūtra."
Regarding the statement "desiring to preach the Great Dharma," the *Śāstra* says: "Those who have doubts should have their doubts severed. Now, the Buddha wishes to preach [to Śāriputra and others].

Previously, while they were at the stage of ordinary beings (*bālapṛthagjana*), they had already received my transformation; regarding the Mahāyāna Dharma, they had planted the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*).
Yet, Śāriputra and the others did not know that such roots of liberation existed; they had not yet given rise to faith and understanding, and constantly harbored doubts.
"Net. Now, wishing to speak of the events of this sutra’s past in order to sever the net of doubt, it is said that "he wishes to preach the Great Dharma.

Regarding the phrase "raining down the great rain of Dharma," the *Śāstra* states: "For those who have already severed their doubts, it causes the sprouts of their wisdom to grow and reach full maturity.
Thus, the Buddha now intends to speak of the Dharma he turned during the forty years following his attainment of enlightenment and prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
It is like a wheel because it causes the sprouts of goodness to grow. Just as when seasonal rain falls, there is nothing it does not moisten and satisfy, so that all things accord with their wishes;
likewise, when the rain of the Dharma falls, those who have not yet resolved upon the Great Mind immediately resolve their minds, and the sprouts of goodness increase.
Regarding the phrase "blowing the great dharma conch," the *Śāstra* states that this is for the purpose of establishing names, phrases, and meanings.
Now, the Buddha wishes to declare that Śāriputra shall attain Buddhahood in the future, receiving the title Tathāgata Padmaprabha, and preach the Dharma of the Three Vehicles.

This is just as in the secular world, when a musical performance concludes, one blows a conch shell or similar instrument; the Buddha now acts in the same way, bestowing upon Śāriputra the prediction of his attainment of Buddhahood.
The event is called "the conclusion of the melody. To further explain it for others is called "blowing the Dharma conch.

As the Sūtra says, "The Tathāgata Flower-Light also [taught] by means of the three vehicles," and regarding the phrase "beating the great Dharma drum" and so forth, the Śāstra states: "This is the provisional and esoteric realm of the Śrāvakas; it is the secret word of the World-Honored One concerning the three [vehicles]."

When all people sit together upon the bed of liberation, it is called "mystery. Now, the Buddha wishes to preach the Dharma to awaken the followers of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas), causing them to abandon their attachment to the Lesser Vehicle;
this is called "beating the great Dharma drum. As the Sūtra says: "The other two are not the truth," thereby opening the way for those who previously followed the Śrāvaka vehicle.

This is for the sake of causing [beings] to abandon the provisional and secret realm; it reveals that what is now taught is the Bodhisattva Vehicle, which is for the sake of causing them to embrace the true realm.

As for the phrase "expounding the great Dharma-meaning" and so forth, this refers to Śāriputra attaining Buddhahood, as well as the granting of the prediction of Buddhahood to the Bodhisattva Kṣāntivardhana;
this is called "expounding the great Dharma-meaning."

Regarding the statement, "As for my [existence] in the past," the questioner asks, "How does Mañjuśrī know? The respondent answers with the commentary, "As for my [existence] in the past," etc., which cites the ancient.
Regarding the statement, "And so on, as extensively explained, 'the Tathāgata today,'" etc., this corroborates the present. Host and guest both clearly understand these signs.

Regarding the phrase "the Buddhas of the three periods," this distinguishes between existence and non-existence. Question: When intending to preach this sutra, does the manifestation of such auspicious signs occur only for Śākyamuni, or do all Buddhas likewise manifest them?
Answer: The commentary states, "The Buddhas of the three periods, etc. This indicates that it is by way of what is to come.
The Tathāgatas of the three periods, when they are about to preach this sutra, must first manifest various great signs. [End of excerpt]
Dīpaṃkara has passed away; Śākyamuni is present; Padmaprabha is yet to come. All of them first manifested signs and subsequently preached the sūtras.
Since these signs were not uniform, they are called "various."
Regarding the statement that "this is not the same as other sūtras," one asks: Since all scriptural teachings are spoken by the Buddha, why is this sūtra different from others?
The answer is: This teaching has never been heard before. If auspicious signs were not extensively manifested, how could those who are mired in attachment be awakened?
Desiring to preach this sūtra, he therefore manifested great signs. Master Mu said: "This sūtra opens the gate of expedient means and reveals the ultimate truth."

Regarding the marks: when [the Buddha] first taught that those of the two vehicles would attain Buddhahood, fearing they might not believe it, he manifested great marks to signify that this subtle and wondrous sutra was spoken without falsehood.
Question: What is called the "first great mark"? Answer: The *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* is the first great mark of this sutra. Question:

When the *Sūtra of the Bequeathed Teaching* is preached, it is preceded by the preaching of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. Since *Nirvāṇa* serves as the initial mark for the *Bequeathed Teaching*, this [mark] is precisely within this *Bequeathed Teaching*...
The teachings also have initial major characteristics; why should this sūtra alone be an exception? The answer has two interpretations. First, it is explained according to the sense of certainty:
prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Anantārthika-sūtra* must necessarily be preached, and once the *Anantārthika* is concluded, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* must necessarily be preached.

However, the *Śāsanāntima* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* are not so certain. For instance, in the case of the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa (Moon-Sun-Lamp Brightness), [the sequence was] Candrasūryavimalaprabha (Moon-Sun-Pure-Brightness).

The Buddha of Virtue, having finished preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, immediately proclaimed his passing into extinction; he did not further preach the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. As the sūtra says:
"I have already explained for you the meaning of the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) of all phenomena. This very night, at midnight, I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsa said: "You may prepare a seat; this very night I shall enter parinirvāṇa."
[The Master] also entrusted him with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and then immediately entered parinirvāṇa. Second, it is explained in terms of essence and function:

the *Anantamukha-parivarta-sūtra* (Wuliangyi jing) is the essence, while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is the function. The *Anantamukha-parivarta-sūtra* was taught for the sake of Bodhisattvas to reveal the emergence of the essence.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* discusses the function of subsuming [beings] through discourse for the sake of śrāvakas; the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Śāsanānuśāsana-sūtra* distinguish between essence and function.
Second, one does not take the *Anantārtha-sūtra*, but takes only the "Entering Samādhi" and "Emitting Light" as the primary great signs.

Regarding the question of the *Upapatti-parivarta-sūtra*: when preaching it, he emits golden light from his entire body; when preaching the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, he dwells in face-to-face mindfulness; and when preaching the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
From his face, he emits rays of light of various colors. Other sutras also describe emitting light while entering meditative absorption; how can you say they do not? Answer:
These three—entering absorption, raining flowers, and shaking the earth—are collectively termed the first great sign (*mahānimitta*).
This sutra possesses all six, whereas other sutras have only one or two, none of which are complete. Question: Among all the signs in the *Anantamukha-sūtra*, which is the very first?

Question: Why is the *Anantamukha-sūtra* not taken as the primary great sign? Answer: The *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* states that the *Anantamukha-sūtra* was taught primarily for Bodhisattvas and only incidentally for Śrāvakas.
One cannot take a sūtra heard by Bodhisattvas and equate it with a sūtra intended for the hearing of Śrāvakas as the primary great sign.
When the *Anantamukha-sūtra* was preached, the assembly had no doubts; therefore, [the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra*] records this.

This explains that [the first sign] is not taken [as the primary one]. If there were no contradiction, then among the seven accomplishments (*siddhi*), excluding the first two accomplishments—which were established by Ānanda—these would not be the "first signs.
However, the remaining five accomplishments are all considered the "first signs. Mǔ (Mou) said it is best to take them collectively. Question:

Since the emission of light and entry into meditative concentration (*samādhi*) occur later among the various signs, why are they called the "first signs"? Answer: This is in relation to the Correct [Dharma].
Prior to the main body [of the discourse], these are collectively termed the "initial signs. Question: For what reason does he manifest these initial great signs before preaching the sutra?
Answer: This sutra differs from other sutras. During the forty years prior [to this teaching], the World-Honored One censured the śrāvakas and praised the bodhisattvas.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: The Buddha addressed Kauśika, "If one enters the fixed course of correctness (*samyaktva-niyāma*) of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas..."
It should be known that such a person can no longer resolve their mind toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why is this?

Because they have established a barrier against birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Furthermore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* states: "A śrāvaka is like a rotten seed; even if one were to irrigate it," [it will not sprout].
Sprouts and stalks do not arise; it is just as lotuses do not grow upon high plateaus. The *Mahādruma-kinnara-sūtra* states:
"Śrāvakas have scorched and destroyed the seed; within the Mahāyāna, they are forever unfit vessels for the Dharma.
Only Bodhisattvas do not harbor such thoughts, saying, 'I and the Tathāgata share the same vehicle and the same seed,' yet they continue to practice with diligence—this is called the 'mud.'"
Lotus flowers may grow there. Those of the Two Vehicles then say, "I and the Tathāgata sit together upon the same bed of liberation.
Because they harbor such a fixed attachment, it is called a "high plateau. It is only within this sutra that it is taught that śrāvakas become Buddhas;

this matter is difficult to believe, for fear that doubt and strangeness might arise. Therefore, he first manifests a great sign: the entire assembly gathers on Vulture Peak. At the outset, the assembly...
The two returns become one; turning away from the Small Vehicle, they enter the Great Vehicle. Next, the three lands are transformed, and the eight directions are adorned and purified.
Guiding those with defiled minds to contemplate the Pure Land, once they have entered the Great Vehicle, there is no longer any Small Vehicle;

once they have contemplated the Pure Land, how could there remain any defiled realm? Then, the emanated Buddhas assemble and are universally present within the Pure Land, where they expound the meaning of the Eternal Body.
Other sutras do not possess this first great mark; indeed, the proofs thereof are numerous. Thus far, we have briefly categorized the various marks of the Introductory Section (*nidāna*).

The Exposition of the True Doctrine (*saddharma*) is taught precisely to respond to these. As for the Emission of Light and the Trembling of the Earth in the Subsequent Section on Dissemination (*parīndanā*), [these will be addressed later].

This is also explained in response through the *Saṃyukta Āgama*. In the following passage, the various Buddhas again emit light from their white tufts of hair to summon Gadgadasvara, while simultaneously extending the flesh protuberance on their crowns (*uṣṇīṣa*) to manifest it with earnestness.
They touch the heads of the assembly to reveal the truth of their sincerity; their tongues reach the First Dhyāna Heaven;
and the radiance from their pores, along with their clearing of throats and snapping of fingers, causes the earth to tremble once more—all because the entrustment was so profound. Again.
The manifestation of flying flowers also clarifies the greatness of their merit. Furthermore, celestial drums resound and heavenly robes descend;

jeweled canopies cover [the assembly] and precious necklaces hang down. These various manifestations are truly numerous and difficult to exhaust in detail; they all intend to circulate the ultimate teaching.
"To bequeath it to future descendants" does not refer to the orthodox lineage; it does not speak of recompensing them. A questioner asked:

"In the treatise, the fifth 'reliance' (niśraya) speaks of causes, while among the six causes, the 'mutual cause' (anyonya-hetu) is mentioned. Both are 'emitting light. What is the distinction between these two meanings? The answer is:

The "causes" spoken of in the treatise apply universally to the hearts of sentient beings who look up with longing. The "mutual cause" among the six causes refers exclusively to the Buddha’s activities and does not include [other matters].

Regarding the matter of the "provisional" (zishì): since it is said that the characteristics [of phenomena] are not eternal, one asks: "Does the World-Honored One not manifest characteristics in vain without teaching the Dharma? The commentary answers: "Since the characteristics are not eternal," and so forth;
this clearly indicates that he does indeed teach the Dharma. He teaches that it is extremely difficult for a śrāvaka to become a Buddha, and he intends to explain this.
At that time, he intentionally manifested extraordinary omens and originally displayed extraordinary signs; for their sake, he preached the Sutra of Impermanence.
Since the signs of impermanence have been made manifest, it was necessary to preach the Dharma of impermanence.
Regarding the statement, "He will now speak of these," it is asked: Does the World-Honored One respond by speaking of this sūtra, rather than other sūtras? The commentary replies:
"He will now speak of this sūtra" and so forth serves to clarify the purpose of the characteristics (lakṣaṇa). As for "seeing the characteristics," it refers to relying upon this sūtra.
The "Exposition of the Sūtra" relies upon its characteristics.
Regarding the phrase "the cause for responding and expounding," this restates the cause. Question: What is meant by "the cause for responding and expounding"? Answer:

The former exposition serves as the cause for the present exposition; thus, the present exposition responds to the former exposition. Consequently, the former exposition is that which is responded to (*pratipādya*), while the present exposition is that which responds (*pratipādaka*).

"Recompense" (*chou*) refers to the combined explanation of the subject (*neng*) and the object (*suo*); this is called the "cause of recompense-explanation. Within this cause of explanation, it is extremely difficult to grasp the intended meaning.

Since antiquity, various masters have proposed more than twenty interpretations, yet those that are precise are few. If one speaks of practicing the practices and making vows to seek upholding [the Dharma], it is subsumed under the first four causes.
If one speaks of the raining of flowers, the shaking of the earth, and the emitting of light, these are further subsumed under the fifth cause, the "cause of characteristics" (*xiang-yin*). Now...
This explains the cause (*hetu*). A phenomenon must have a cause before it can be designated as such; that which serves as the cause for an exposition is called the "cause of exposition.
There are those who take these ninefold teachings of mine as the basis for entering the Mahāyāna, and they serve as the cause for its exposition.

Thus, both the expounder and the one being expounded, as well as cause and effect, are all fully present therein. Furthermore, it is said that the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* serves as the cause, and sentient beings obtain [realization] upon hearing its sound.
The fruit is precisely what this sutra explains; explaining it is itself the cause. Therefore, it is extremely difficult to grasp its intended meaning.

First, regarding the *Śāstra-vyākhyāna-saṃgraha*, five interpretations are presented. The first three are the doctrines of the ancient masters, while the latter two are the author’s own explanations. As for the first three:

one says that during the forty years prior [to the preaching of this sutra], the ninefold teachings (*navāṅga-dharma*) served as the cause, and the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* was the recompense. The Sutra says: "I..."

These ninefold teachings take entry into the Mahāyāna as their foundation; that is, the ninefold teachings themselves are the "explanation" (*deśanā*). "Explanation" functions as a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound), meaning the explanation itself is the cause.

Alternatively, it may be understood as a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound). In this case, the word "explanation" belongs to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, while the word "cause" belongs to the ninefold teachings; thus, it is the cause for the one who explains (the *tatpuruṣa*: the cause belonging to the explainer).
Second, regarding the accomplishment of the cause for the teaching based on reliance: the sentient beings' heart of longing and aspiration serves as the cause for the teaching. Third.
It is said that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* which is taught is the cause; sentient beings who hear it and become attached to it attain the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñatā*) as the fruit.

Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* being taught is precisely the teaching of the cause. [The author] summarizes three ancient interpretations and then refutes them, before presenting two of his own interpretations.
The first says that becoming a Buddha and appearing in the world constitutes the cause for the teaching, which is the same as [the view of] Yuanzhao. This is why the commentary states: "Therefore..."
The Buddhas of the three periods of time, upon attaining ultimate enlightenment, must necessarily preach the One Vehicle.

Second, it refers to taking up the vows made during the causal stage, vowing that once Buddhahood is attained, one will preach the *Lotus Sūtra*. This very mind of vowing to preach the sūtra is what constitutes the cause; therefore, the Commentary states:
"All are expedient means sought and pursued during the causal stage," and further: "Thus, responding to past causes, he preaches this wondrous Dharma. Second, the Golden [Chapter].

There are three interpretations of the "City" (nagara). First, it is said that [the Buddha] taught the cause for beings who look up with longing and thirst. Second, it is said that he internally realized the profound mystery. Third, it is said that he externally manifested supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). Jin says that this third interpretation is the correct one. Furthermore, there are the extensive records of Master Heluo of Lu-fu (the *Mo-chao*) and others, which are so numerous they cannot be recounted in full. Now, taking the essential explanations, I shall set forth the interpretations of the ancient masters. Regarding "I" (aham): ... [text continues] ... In the commentary on the *Saṃyukta-āgama*, it is said: "The Tathāgata, having attained the supreme, perfect enlightenment, has fully realized the Dharma-realm; therefore, he is called 'I'. In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is said: "The Tathāgata’s body is the Dharma-body; because he has realized the Dharma, he is called 'I'. In the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, it is said: "The Tathāgata is free from the two extremes of existence and non-existence; because he has realized the Middle Way, he is called 'I'. In the *Śrīmālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, it is said: "The Tathāgata is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*); because he has realized the ultimate, he is called 'I'. In the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, it is said: "The Tathāgata is the self-nature of all dharmas; because he has realized the self-nature, he is called 'I'. In the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, it is said: "The Tathāgata is the great compassionate father of all sentient beings; because he has realized great compassion, he is called 'I'. In the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, it is said: "The Tathāgata is the treasury of all virtues; because he has realized all virtues, he is called 'I'. In the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, it is said: "The Tathāgata is the emptiness of all dharmas; because he has realized emptiness, he is called 'I'. In the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, it is said: "The Tathāgata is the signlessness of all dharmas; because he has realized signlessness, he is called 'I'. In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is said: "The Tathāgata is the wishlessness of all dharmas; because he has realized wishlessness, he is called 'I'. In the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, it is said: "The Tathāgata is the unconditioned nature of all dharmas; because he has realized the unconditioned, he is called 'I'. In the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*, it is said: "The Tathāgata is the ultimate truth of all dharmas; because he has realized the ultimate truth, he is called 'I'. In the *Amitābha-sūtra*, it is said: "The Tathāgata is the pure land of all dharmas; because he has realized the pure land, he is called 'I'. In the *Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha-rāja-sūtra*, it is said: "The Tathāgata is the medicine for all sentient beings; because he has realized the medicine, he is called 'I'. In the *Uṣṇīṣavijaya-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, it is said: "The Tathāgata is the power of all dharmas; because he has realized power, he is called 'I'. In the *Mahāmāyūrī-vidyārājñī-sūtra*, it is said: "The Tathāgata is the protection of all sentient beings; because he has realized protection, he is called 'I'. In the *Gaṇḍavyūha-sūtra*, it is said: "The Tathāgata is the path of all dharmas; because he has realized the path, he is called 'I'. In the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*, it is said: "The Tathāgata is the womb of all dharmas; because he has realized the womb, he is called 'I'. In the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, it is said: "The Tathāgata is the eternal, blissful, self, and pure; because he has realized the four virtues, he is called 'I'. In the *Lalitavistara-sūtra*, it is said: "The Tathāgata is the play of all dharmas; because he has realized the play, he is called 'I'. In the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*, it is said: "The Tathāgata is the mindfulness of all dharmas; because he has realized mindfulness, he is called 'I'. In the *Dharmacakra-pravartana-sūtra*, it is said: "The Tathāgata is the turning of the wheel of Dharma; because he has realized the turning, he is called 'I'. In the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*, it is said: "The Tathāgata is the ornament of all dharmas; because he has realized the ornament, he is called 'I'. In the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, it is said: "The Tathāgata is the storehouse of all dharmas; because he has realized the storehouse, he is called 'I'. In the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, it is said: "The Tathāgata is the ground of all dharmas; because he has realized the ground, he is called 'I'. In the *Madhyāntavibhāga-śāstra*, it is said: "The Tathāgata is the middle and the extreme; because he has realized the middle and the extreme, he is called 'I'. In the *Triṃśikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, it is said: "The Tathāgata is the transformation of consciousness; because he has realized the transformation, he is called 'I'. In the *Mahāyāna-abhisamaya-alaṃkāra-śāstra*, it is said: "The Tathāgata is the realization of all dharmas; because he has realized all dharmas, he is called 'I'. In the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, it is said: "The Tathāgata is the definitive determination of all dharmas; because he has realized the definitive determination, he is called 'I'. In the *Vinayavibhaṅga*, it is said: "The Tathāgata is the discipline of all dharmas; because he has realized the discipline, he is called 'I'. In the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, it is said: "The Tathāgata is the compendium of all dharmas; because he has realized the compendium, he is called 'I'. In the *Mahāvyutpatti*, it is said: "The Tathāgata is the etymological analysis of all dharmas; because he has realized the etymological analysis, he is called 'I'. In the *Pratītyasamutpādādivibhaṅganirdeśa-sūtra*, it is said: "The Tathāgata is the dependent origination of all dharmas; because he has realized dependent origination, he is called 'I'. In the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, it is said: "The Tathāgata is the ten stages of all dharmas; because he has realized the ten stages, he is called 'I'. In the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, it is said: "The Tathāgata is the stage of the bodhisattva; because he has realized the stage, he is called 'I'. In the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*, it is said: "The Tathāgata is the training of all dharmas; because he has realized the training, he is
These nine divisions [of the canon] are the very foundation. Furthermore, Master Daobao takes the Buddha’s attainment of Buddhahood and appearance in the world as the cause for this teaching.
Question: If he attained Buddhahood and appeared in the world, why is it only this sutra? Are not all sutras like this? Answer:

Although he preached various sutras, these were not the primary reason for his original appearance in the world. His fundamental purpose in appearing was solely to preach the Lotus Sutra; he did not do so for any other matter.
It is for the sake of expounding the Buddha’s wisdom that the Buddhas appear in the world; furthermore, it is said that they appear in the world solely for the sake of the one great matter.
It is like a man who has an only son: because he loves his son, the son studies for the civil service examinations and passes with honors.
Later, although the Minister of the Interior and his Assistant attained [realization], they originally did not yet accord with their true minds;
it was only after they later attained the position of Chancellor that they finally realized their original intent. It is the same in this case. Question:

If the original intention was to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, why did you not preach it immediately upon appearing in the world? Answer: The reason it has not been preached until now is that the time for its preaching had not yet arrived.
It cannot be explained by means of the sense-faculties; therefore, he spoke separately of the skillful means. During the twenty-one days, he contemplated these matters:
"The wisdom I have attained I intended to entrust [to others], yet sentient beings are unable to enter into it. He then contemplated further.

Suppose one were to explain the Mahāyāna *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* to them; the Bodhisattvas would awaken to and understand it, while the Śrāvakas would be like the deaf or the intoxicated, unable to enter it.
Therefore, one cannot avoid first teaching the provisional teachings (*upāya*) to fulfill their aspiration for Buddhahood and transcendence in this world.

Furthermore, this does not depend on the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* forty years later; by teaching [the provisional teachings] now, one already fulfills their aspiration for Buddhahood and transcendence in this world. Thus, throughout the three periods of time...
If the Buddha had preached the Mahāyāna to its conclusion but did not preach the entry into nirvāṇa according to the Hīnayāna, there would have been three Buddhas or five Buddhas;
if he had preached the Hīnayāna to its conclusion but did not preach the entry into nirvāṇa according to the Mahāyāna, there would have been none at all.
If the Buddha had not come into the world to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, for what reason would there have been the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsa and the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa?
Furthermore, having preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, he immediately entered *nirvāṇa* to signify that his worldly affairs were concluded and there was nothing further to be done.
Regarding the phrase "all Buddhas and Tathāgatas" and so forth, the "great matter" (*mahākārya*) refers precisely to the opening, revealing, awakening to, and entering into Bodhi and *nirvāṇa*.
As for the commentators taking the Buddha’s appearance in the world as the cause for preaching [the Dharma], one asks: what is it that can repay this?

[The question: What is the "recompense" (chou)? [The answer: In this commentary, the cited text states: "As it says below, 'It is solely for the sake of the one great cause and condition that he appears in the world.
This refers to the section on the "cause of the recompense" (*chou-shuo yin*), where the text brings forward the "capable recompense" (*neng-chou wen*).

Becoming a Buddha and appearing in the world is the "object of recompense" (*suo-chou*), while the *Lotus Sūtra* is the "capable recompense. The object of recompense is the cause; the capable recompense is...
This is the result. It is solely for the sake of explaining the one great cause and condition (*ekamahā-kāraṇa*) that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, appear in the world.
To explain the one great cause and condition is precisely to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; therefore, it is said that [the appearance of the Buddha] "is able to repay" [the debt]. Question:

Regarding the preceding five causes, which were explained individually and collectively as the texts to be repaid, the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is the result. Why, then, is it called "repayment"?
In the discussion concerning the causes, [the author] specifically cites the passages from the *Lotus Sūtra* that speak of the teaching of the Dharma as the response.

This does not hinder the fact that the methods employed by the author are manifold. Thus, taking the teaching of the *Lotus Sūtra*—the "great cause and condition" (*mahāntaṃ dharmaparyāyaṃ*) for the purpose of opening, showing, awakening, and entering—as the "enabling response," and taking the attainment of Buddhahood and appearing in the world as the "responded-to" object, does not contradict the interpretation of Master Daozhao.

Question: If it has been established up to this point that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world solely for the sake of the one great causal matter (*ekamahākaruṇāhetu*), then [the former] acts as the "agent" (*kartṛ*) and "attaining Buddhahood and appearing in the world" acts as the "object" (*karma*). Question:

The commentary cites the subsequent section of the sūtra, stating, "and so forth, as extensively explained," including the passage, "there are no śrāvaka disciples. Should this not be rendered useless? It is highly inconsistent [with the preceding].

It is indeed so. The answer is clear: it must be so. Now, the Buddha’s appearance in the world is fundamentally for the purpose of preaching the Lotus Sūtra—the great matter of the causes and conditions of Bodhi and Nirvāṇa—and not for preaching the minor matters of the Śrāvakas.

This is why this section of the sūtra distinguishes his appearance in the world as being for more than the Small Vehicle. The Buddha’s original intention in descending to Jambudvīpa was precisely this.
He preaches the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for the sake of the great causal conditions; he does not preach for the sake of the minor matters of the śrāvakas.
Thus, his attaining Buddhahood and appearing in the world is for the purpose of preaching these causes, which is precisely what he has come to repay. As it says below:

"The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, appear in the world solely for the sake of one great causal condition. This is to manifest that until the very end, he teaches only the bodhisattvas. There is no [other teaching].

Regarding the statement that there are no śrāvaka disciples: from the point where the prose section begins with "having long desired to penetrate [the truth]" until the end, these are all the textual passages capable of responding within the context of explaining the causes.
Question: The Sūtra states that there are no śrāvaka disciples; yet, those currently being taught possess the three faculties (trividha-indriya). Who are they? Answer:

Although they are śrāvakas who are being taught the three faculties, they were originally śrāvakas but later become bodhisattvas. Therefore, for forty years prior [to their enlightenment], they acted as [śrāvakas].
Regarding the śrāvakas who turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle and become bodhisattvas, they ultimately attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).

Although there have been many interpretations above, the first—taking the ninefold canon (navāṅga-dharma) as the basis—is consistent with the scriptural text; the second—taking the attainment of Buddhahood and appearance in the world as the primary meaning—is the correct one.

First, it accords with the scriptural passage cited; second, it accords with the concluding text below. Zhangjing says: "This is in accordance with the elder’s original intention to give the ox-carts to all.
Because the children did not wish to come out during the causal stage, he provisionally proclaimed the sheep and deer carts.

The Master’s (the Buddha’s) original intention was to have them reach the place of treasure; because the merchants were unwilling to proceed further along the way, he then provisionally established the transformation [vehicles]."

The city was established to cause them to stay; the proclamation of the sheep and deer carts served as a gradual preparation for the ox cart. The establishment of the conjured city was the foundation for proceeding to the place of treasure.
Thus we know that the former preaching of the ninefold canon of the Hīnayāna was the cause for entering the Mahāyāna, and today this sutra is preached.
This then fulfills what was previously stated. This interpretation accords with the core tenet of the sūtra: that which was provisional in the past is now realized as the ultimate truth. Hoen states:

From the "Expedient Means" chapter, beginning with the praise of the two kinds of profundity and extending up to, but not including, the formal exposition of the Great Matter, all is termed the "Exposition of Causes.
Within this section, the three requests are excluded; these belong to the subsequent "Response to Requests. Now, taking the three instances of refusal, we shall resolve [the matter].

The cause for the concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*) extends from the granting of the prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*) up until the point where [the assembly] has expressed their aspiration to hear it; this serves as the cause for the discourse in response.
Furthermore, one should take the passage following the second cessation (*śamatha*), not the first, because the Buddha’s original resolve was to definitively preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
This is established from the section following the second cessation. As the treatise states: "The Buddha’s mind already possessed the determination regarding that which was to be accomplished."
A person. From this, there subsequently follows the section on "Cessation" (*nirodha*) and the "Exposition.
Regarding the phrase "therefore, the destinations (*gati*), etc.," it serves as a general conclusion for the six causes. Question:

If this is indeed the text concluding the six causes, why does the Master [of the Commentary] further state that "the preceding categories of scriptural passages are very numerous"? If one points to and describes them, then they constitute the conclusion of the six...
Regarding the passage on "causes" (*hetu*): How can it be said that "all are expedient means sought within the causes"? This concludes the four preceding causes.

The phrase "though cultivation and study are complete," etc., concludes the two causes by way of their characteristics. Therefore, "tending toward past causes," etc., collectively concludes the six causes. Thus, one knows that An-guo’s interpretation is likely not correct.
Consequently, as explained by Mou, this is the textual passage concluding the exposition of the causes. Question: Regarding the exposition of the causes...
This is stated in terms of the fruit. Why, then, is it said that all are sought through skillful means within the cause?

For this reason, in the concluding summary of the passage on the cause, there is reference to others and reference to oneself. The commentary states, "Therefore, the Buddhas of the three periods of time," which refers to others.

The commentary states, "Although their cultivation and study are complete," which refers to oneself. The commentary states, "Therefore, responding to past causes," which collectively concludes both self and others. Question:
Question: Since the term "Buddhas of the three periods" does not appear in the preceding heading, why does it appear in the concluding summary?
Answer: Because the preceding commentary contains the phrase "and so forth, as extensively explained," this wording is broad and inclusive;

therefore, it is permissible to include it in the conclusion. Question: What is the intention of An-guo in stating that the six causes are summarized within the context of the "cause"? Answer: The six causes.

Regarding the explanation of the general designation as "causes for exposition" (*ākhyāna-hetu*): these are collectively termed the causes for exposition. However, within this category, six specific causes are established according to their predominant characteristics.

Because the excellence of practice is paramount, the cause of practice (*caryā-hetu*) is established; because the excellence of making vows is paramount, the cause of vows (*praṇidhāna-hetu*) is established;

because the excellence of seeking the Dharma is paramount, the cause of seeking (*paryeṣaṇā-hetu*) is established; because the excellence of upholding [the teachings] is paramount, the cause of upholding (*dhāraṇā-hetu*) is established, and so forth. Question: Regarding the six causes in relation to exposition...
