For those who attain sudden enlightenment prior to the [first] stage (*bhūmi*), it consists of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) and the two attachments (*grāha*).

For those who attain gradual enlightenment prior to the stage, it consists of one obstacle and one attachment. Because of horizontal conceptualization, one thinks that the fruit is difficult to attain;

thus, this is an attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*). Its specific nature is characterized by indolence (*kausīdya*). The three refinements (*pariśodhana*) are the remedies, while the three forms of despondency (*parikheda*) are what are to be overcome.

Regarding the antidotes and that which is to be remedied: the first consists of heedlessness, the second of indolence, and the third of ignorance. The former one pertains to awakening (*bodhi*), while the latter one pertains to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
Among these, there is regression from the fruit and regression from the cause; the latter refers to the difficulty of cultivating the myriad practices.
Third, regarding the analysis of the modes of practice (*ākāra*), this is explained as a general exposition. Citing the treatise, it says:
"In immeasurable worlds, for immeasurable sentient beings, to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment in every single moment—this is the first training of the mind.
By means of this intention, one is able to practice the perfections (*pāramitā*) such as generosity. As I have attained [this]...
This is the intention: "By means of this, I shall attain the fulfillment of the perfections, such as generosity, by expending little effort.

This is called the second refinement of the mind. If one who has accomplished virtuous deeds that are subject to obstacles is reborn at the time of death with a desirable and complete physical form, I possess such sublime virtue.
This obstructs the wholesome; how then could one attain all perfections at that time? This is called the third refinement of the mind.

Because bodhisattvas, upon hearing that unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is most supreme, profound, vast, and difficult to realize, their minds become discouraged and retreat; as an antidote to this, they cultivate the first refinement of the mind.
Furthermore, when bodhisattvas hear that the perfections practiced through hearing are most excellent, profound, vast, and difficult to realize, their minds may become discouraged.
To counteract this, they practice the second refinement of the mind.
Moreover, when bodhisattvas are contemplating, deliberating, and thoroughly investigating the profound and vast teachings, and their skill in these increases and develops, they reflect as follows:
Unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is difficult to realize; thus, the mind may become discouraged. To counteract this, one cultivates the third refinement of the mind.
First, regarding the discouragement caused by the vastness of supreme enlightenment, one refines the mind by using others as a point of comparison for oneself.

As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only), Chapter Nine, states: "First, upon hearing that unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is vast and profound, the mind becomes discouraged. This...
They immediately realize that they have retreated from the supreme Buddha-knowledge and vision. It is "vast" because it extends boundlessly throughout the ten directions;

it is "great" because it is unsurpassed and transcends the three realms; it is "deep" because it is difficult to fathom, such that even Bodhisattvas at the stage of Equal Enlightenment cannot measure or know it;
it is "distant" because its duration is long, as it spans the vast expanse of three incalculable eons. This refers to all sentient beings in immeasurable worlds.

In every single moment of thought, all are able to give rise to the resolve for awakening and realize the fruit of Bodhi. Since I am the same as they, why do I not give rise to the resolve and strive toward it?
By using others to illustrate my own case, I shall realize great Bodhi, refine my own mind, and proceed with courageous vigor without retreating. As the *Nirākāra-stotra* says:
"All sentient beings in the worlds of the ten directions swiftly realize the fruit of the Sugata in every moment of thought; since they are already such great men, so am I."
It is likewise so. One should not disparage oneself and thus succumb to despondency. "Despondency" (*hāni*) refers to retreating; "succumbing" (*nīca*) refers to being cowed.

The precious mountain of Bodhi and Nirvāṇa is both high and vast; it is vast and moreover steep. Upon hearing of this, the followers of the Two Vehicles and ordinary worldlings do not dare to undertake its cultivation, and their minds immediately become despondent.
They instead pursue the Two Vehicles for three births, sixty-four births, or one hundred kalpas, seeking only [their respective goals].

The fruit of the vehicle. Second, when one feels discouraged because the twenty thousand practices are difficult to cultivate, one reflects upon oneself and increases one's cultivation and refinement. As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

"Second, when one hears that the perfections such as giving are extremely difficult to practice, the mind becomes disheartened and retreats. One then reflects upon one’s own disposition and realizes that one is indeed capable of practicing giving and the other perfections."
Cultivate and refine your own mind with courage and without retreating. Form this thought: "For immeasurable eons, I have fallen into hell in vain.
Yet, even when merely hearing the voice of the Bodhisattva of Great Compassion as he ceaselessly rescues beings from suffering, I am now able to attain the fruit of Buddhahood through my practice;
why then should I not cultivate it? You must examine and reproach yourself: since immeasurable eons past, you have endured all manner of..."
It is distressing. The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states: "In the hells, sentient beings are boiled and stewed; their stench assails one, causing everyone to flee to the margins of the ground.
Throughout many kalpas and for a long duration, you have endured these various sufferings—what benefit has there been in this?"
If one were to practice this [path], it would not equal even a hundred-thousand-millionth part of the suffering experienced by those [in the lower realms].
How can you feel discouraged, thinking that practicing so little will yield the fruit of Buddhahood? Therefore, that verse says: "You have already wandered through the evil realms for many kalpas."

Without benefit, one exerts effort in hardship; those of superior capacity can proceed toward it. By practicing sublime conduct even slightly, one attains Bodhi. One should not give rise to despondency regarding such great benefit.
When the three turnings of the basis are difficult to realize, one may feel discouraged. To counter this, one employs "coarse comparison" to refine the mind. As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

"Hearing that the perfect transformation of the basis of all Buddhas is extremely difficult to realize, the mind becomes despondent. One then cites the coarse virtues of others to compare with one's own sublime causes, thereby exercising refinement."
One’s own mind must be courageous and never retreat. For instance, even if one merely desires to attain the bodies of gods or humans, one must still practice the five or eight precepts and so forth;
how could the wondrous fruit of unsurpassed *bodhi* be obtained without cultivation? A verse says:

"Even ordinary beings on the stage of the 'thin' (*tanutva*) who have first resolved their minds intend to advance toward the fruit of *bodhi*; you, having already practiced for many eons, [should not regress]."
One should not succumb to despondency or sink into stagnation; this refers to the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*).
To give rise to despondency therein is a fault. Fourth, regarding the correlation with the stages: Question: In which stage do these three forms of "tempering" (*pariṣodhana*) reside? Answer:

According to the intent of the *Śū* commentary, these three all reside within the three stages of the Path of Provisions (*sambhāramārga*). Question: How is it known that they reside in the Path of Provisions? Answer: The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: [text follows].

In the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), which consists of the forty mental states (*citta*) prior to entering the stage of application (*prayoga*), one should properly cultivate this. Therefore, the treatise states:
"Although the two obstacles have not yet been suppressed or eliminated in this stage, when cultivating the sublime practices, there are three points of retreat;

yet, by means of the three ways of refining the mind, one remains courageous and does not retreat from this realization and cultivation. Based on this, it is situated within the stage of equipment. Question:
If one practices the refinement of the provisions during the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), how is it that it was previously stated:

"I possess within all ten stages the well-accumulated provisions of merit and wisdom"? Answer: This is discussed from the perspective of the beginning; since one practices without falling back and will certainly attain [the goal], there is no contradiction in meaning.
Question: How are the three refinements (*parikarman*) and the four obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) related? Answer:
These three refinements serve as antidotes to the three types of despondency (*laya*), but they do not serve as antidotes to the four obstacles. Question:

Since both the three types of despondency and the four obstacles are hindrances, why do the three refinements not sever the four obstacles, but instead only act as antidotes to the three types of despondency?
"Defeated. The answer is: because one has cultivated oneself through the three types of regression (*parihāṇi*) that are to be remedied;

or, because the first two obstacles arise from the three types of regression, one cultivates the mind so as to sever those two obstacles. The statement that "the four obstacles are severed" follows from the force of the textual context.

Regarding the statement "eliminating the obstructions of the four bases": a question is asked as to what is meant by the "four bases. The answer is that in the contemplative practice of a bodhisattva, there are four which are called the four bases.
"Base" (sthāna) refers to a locus; it refers to the four loci of obstruction. These arise from the four defiled factors, namely: the intention to convert those of the two vehicles, and so forth.

This is an obstruction. It obstructs the four types of contemplative practice (*catur-vidha-bhāvanā*) of other bodhisattvas; it is an obstruction to these four bases (*catvāri sthānāni*). This is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) compound.

Second, according to the treatise, there is no word for "obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*); it simply mentions the "four bases. If the word "obstruction" were absent, then [the obstructions would refer to] the mental attention (*manasikāra*) of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*), and so forth.

This refers to the four bases (*catvāri sthānāni*). The four bases are themselves the obstructions; this is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound). They are called "abandoned" because they have been suppressed.

Mūla says: Question: Who is the agent that abandons? Answer: It is due to the four contemplations; namely, the signless (*animitta*) and the three types of wisdom (*jñāna*) act as the agents of abandonment. Question: What is named the obstruction? Answer:
The first two are obstructions that hinder the practice of wearying of the small [vehicle] and aspiring toward the great. The latter two are obstructions that hinder the relinquishing [of the small].
Because it acts as an obstacle to the practice of realizing truth, it receives the name "hindrance.

Regarding the statement that it takes the meaning of the Dharma as its object: this refers to the teaching that expresses [the meaning] (the *vācaka*). "Meaning" (*artha*) refers to the expressed content (*vācya*).

"Taking as an object" refers to the cognizing minds of all sentient beings and bodhisattvas. It takes as its basis the subsequently attained *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (all-accomplishing wisdom) of the Tathāgata.

Regarding the meaning within the *Zhìshèlùn* (Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness): since the conditions do not actually attach [to external objects], one instead gives rise to images that take those [objects] as conditions.

One can only say that these resemble phenomena (*dharma*) and resemble meanings (*artha*), but they are not real; therefore, it is said that one takes phenomena and meanings as objects by means of these resemblances.

As for "resembling words" and "resembling meanings," the commentary explains that they manifest as if they were external forms, yet in reality they exist only internally. They take existence as non-existence and the internal as external, just as a cow’s horn resembles a rabbit’s horn.
It is like cow hair being like tortoise hair; this is the meaning of Dharmapāla’s interpretation.

As for Sthiramati, he maintains that non-existence appears as existence and the external appears as internal, like a performer appearing as a real person. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* explains: "In this stage, the Bodhisattva contemplates those phenomena."
It is merely mental discourse (*manojalpa*). Having set aside its objective aspect (*grāhyāṃśa*), this mental discourse also lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Having set aside its subjective aspect (*grāhakāṃśa*), it is said to take the meaning of the Dharma as its object. Due to the power of prior cultivation through extensive hearing (*bahuśruta-vāsanā*), from that point onward, when one attends to things correctly (*yoniśo-manasikāra*), images within the mind arise that resemble their original substrates; these appearances of the Dharma and its meaning arise from provisional designation and are termed [conceptual images].

This constitutes their "resemblance. This clarifies the meaning of phenomena arising through transformation upon the mental consciousness; they are called "resembling phenomena" and "resembling objects. This is because the internal resembles the external;

in reality, they do not exist externally, as they are solely internal consciousness. This cognizing mind, by means of vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought), observes vitarka and vicāra, which are termed the "objects of vitarka and vicāra.
Their self-nature and distinctions exist only nominally and lack substantial reality. Thus, the names and the objects are distinct from one another. Therefore...
One does not seek two separate characteristics; because the two characteristics are identical, they are combined in contemplation. The former two refer to name (*nāman*) and object (*artha*);
the latter two refer to intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and distinction (*viśeṣa*). This reveals that upon the two phenomena of name and object, there exist intrinsic nature and distinction.

Thus, in this treatise, the phenomena and their meanings are first indicated, and subsequently four types are opened up—whether opened or combined, there is no contradiction in principle. Question: Regarding cultivation...

Regarding the stage at which this contemplation occurs: the answer is that, as stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, one is able to cultivate this contemplation during the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśalamūla*) within the stage of application (*prayoga*).

Specifically, during the two stages of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and "Summit" (*mūrdhan*), one performs the four investigations (*catasraḥ paryeṣaṇāḥ*); in the stages of "Patience" (*kṣānti*) and "Supreme Worldly Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*), one practices the four types of knowledge of reality (*catasro yathābhūtaparijñāḥ*).
Therefore, the treatise states: "The four dharmas, beginning with Heat, rely upon the four investigations and the four knowledges of reality, [occurring] in the initial and final stages."

Established upon the *ālokalabdha-samādhi*, one gives rise to inferior grades of investigation (*vitarka*) and analysis (*vicāra*) that perceive no objective referent (*anupalambha*); this is established as the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*).

Relying upon the *vṛddhāloka-samādhi*, one gives rise to superior grades of investigation and analysis that perceive no objective referent; this is given the name of the stage of "Summits" (*mūrdhan*).

In this stage, one repeatedly contemplates that the so-called "names" and other phenomena are all transformations of one's own mind. Relying upon the *anulomiki-samādhi*, one gives rise to inferior grades of knowledge in accordance with reality regarding the objective referent.
There is no definitive sealing or maintaining; within the absence of a grasper (*grāhaka*), there is likewise compliance with joyful patience (*kṣānti*).

Since there is no real object, apart from the grasper-consciousness (*grāhakavijñāna*), one speaks of a "real consciousness" that is apart from the grasped object (*grāhyaviṣaya*). Because the grasped and the grasper are established in mutual dependence, the terms "sealing," "compliance," and "patience" are collectively designated as *kṣānti*.

"Sealing" refers to what precedes, and "compliance" to what follows; thus the names "sealing" and "compliance" are established. Patience regarding the emptiness of both object and consciousness is collectively termed [the stage of] patience.

Patience (*kṣānti*). Relying on the uninterrupted concentration (*ānantarya-samādhi*), one gives rise to the seal of superior suchness-knowledge (*yathābhūta-jñāna-mudrā*). The duality of grasping is determined to be empty; this is called the "Supreme Worldly Dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*).

This means that while the preceding stage of "superior patience" sealed the subject (*grāhaka*), this present stage seals both. Immediately following this, one will necessarily enter the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) within the truly arising dharmas.

Because this is the most supreme among them, it is named the "Supreme Worldly Dharma. In the two stages of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and "Summit" (*mūrdhan*), one relies on the contemplation of the subject.

The apprehended object does not exist. When the lower stage of patience (*kṣānti*) arises, one seals the emptiness of the apprehended object. At the stage when the middle stage of patience arises, one observes that the apprehending consciousness is empty just like its object, and thus joyfully accepts this.
When the upper stage of patience arises, one seals the emptiness of the apprehending subject. With the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*), one seals the emptiness of both;
yet, because reality has not yet been realized, it is said that for the Bodhisattva’s various higher stages, [this realization] is established through direct manifestation.

A slight object. The verse says: "To posit a slight object before one, claiming it to be the nature of consciousness-only—because there is something apprehended, one does not truly abide in consciousness-only.
Therefore, it is said that one takes the meaning of the dharma as the objective condition.

Regarding the "mental orientation of the two vehicles" (*dvayayāna-manasikāra*): first, there is the beginner bodhisattva who, weary of the suffering of *saṃsāra* and longing for the bliss of *nirvāṇa*, obstructs other bodhisattvas from practicing the dual benefit of self and others.

Since a bodhisattva dwells neither in *saṃsāra* nor in *nirvāṇa*, the perception of a distinction between *saṃsāra* and *nirvāṇa* constitutes the mental orientation of the two vehicles; this is termed the "mental orientation of the two vehicles."

Obstruction. Because it obstructs great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*). Second, those who have attained the fruit of arhatship cling to their own fruit as ultimate and are unwilling to turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle;

this is called the mental engagement of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna-manasikāra*). Third, those who have attained the three preceding fruits are unwilling to turn their minds to cultivate Mahāyāna practices and instead aspire toward the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*) of their own vehicle; this is also called the mental engagement of the two vehicles. Fourth, the seven...

Those of expedient means who are unwilling to turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle and instead delight in pursuing the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*) of their own vehicle are termed those with the mental engagement (*manasikāra*) of the Two Vehicles.

Fifth, those of a nature prone to alarm and fear regarding manifold affairs, whose practice is extensive and long-lasting, yet who wish to regress and enter the Two Vehicles, are termed those with the mental engagement of the Two Vehicles.
Among these five, if one speaks of the primary cases, it refers to those of manifold affairs and alarm, as well as small-bodhisattvas who are weary of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Those who aspire to *nirvāṇa*—these two categories are the essential points; they are precisely subsumed within the mental orientations (*manasikāra*) of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*).
The other three types of orientation serve as the requirements for these [two]. According to the *Śāstra-vyākhyā*, there are five interpretations divided into two groups:

first, the aspiration and longing of the mental orientations of the two vehicles; second, the disregard and contempt of the mental orientations of the two vehicles. These apply to those first cultivating the bodhisattva path, as well as to those with the seven stages of the *aśaikṣa*.

"Ordinary people. The four classes of people are called "those who admire," because they admire the Two Vehicles. The fifth type, the "one of understanding," refers to the Bodhisattva of Sudden Enlightenment.
Those who abide in the Two Vehicles cannot become Buddhas; this is termed "contemptuous neglect."
Regarding the phrase "the various doubts, etc.": first, since the doubts are not singular, they are termed "various doubts. That which can sever these doubts is termed "freedom from doubt.
Second, the Śrāvakas are termed "those with various doubts," while the Bodhisattvas of sudden enlightenment are "free from doubt. These are stated together.
Third, prior to the sixth stage, bodhisattvas of indeterminate lineage doubt whether they will attain the fruit of Buddhahood and enlightenment or not;
this is called "possessing doubts. Even if they subsequently regress and enter the two vehicles, once their minds achieve certainty, it is called "being free from doubt.

Fourth, regarding the esoteric teachings of the three vehicles, one may harbor doubts and then cling to one as the sole truth while dismissing the others as false; this is called "being free from doubt. Among these four interpretations:
Regarding the correct apprehension of the Three Vehicles of Dharma, one may give rise to doubt and attachment, holding that one alone is correct and thereby repudiating the others as incorrect.
Now, it is held that all such doubts constitute obstacles; being free from doubt is what constitutes the correct state.

Regarding the phrase "among the dharmas heard and contemplated," this refers to the teachings heard during the stage of hearing (*śruta*) and the meanings heard during the wisdom of contemplation (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).

Within these dharmas heard and contemplated, one fails to understand that they are merely conventionally existent and lack substantial reality, instead clinging to them as having an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

This directly obstructs the wisdom-contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-jñāna-vipaśyanā*) within the gateway to the first bhūmi. To enter the objective characteristic (*lakṣya*), it is necessary to first sever this [clinging].

Regarding the statement "the four [factors] in the skeleton chain, and so forth," this contemplation has two aspects: first, within the Hīnayāna, one performs the meditation on white bones (*asthi-śaṅkalā*) to subdue sensual desire;

second, Bodhisattvas of the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages perform this contemplative practice to subdue and transform those of the Two Vehicles, causing Bodhisattvas prior to these stages to train in this meditation.
This is the obstacle of conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa-āvaraṇa*); there is a general [summary].

There is a distinction. In general, this refers to all conceptualized phenomena; specifically, it refers only to the wisdom capable of observation belonging to this single stage of patience (*kṣānti*).

This wisdom is termed "conceptualization" (*vikalpa*), and the obstruction to this very conceptualization is called "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*) when it is extinguished upon entering the first stage (*bhūmi*).

Question: Why must this conceptualizing wisdom of the stage of patience be abandoned? Answer: Because through this preparatory application (*prayoga*), although one is free from the [subjective] capacity...
The conceptualization of what is grasped (*grāhya-vikalpa*) itself possesses subtle conceptualizations that obstruct the non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) of the first stage;
therefore, it must be abandoned. The *Śāstra* states: "Such objects are established as manifest before one. However, there are two types. First is the defiled object (*kliṣṭa-viṣaya*).

There are two kinds of defiled objects: first, objects induced by karma, such as mountains, rivers, and the great earth; second, objects of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), namely the [meditation on] bones.

The "contemplation of the skeleton" (*asthi-saṃjñā*) and so forth are objects induced by meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Third is the pure object (*viśuddha-viṣaya*). There are two types of pure objects:
first, the provisional object of pure phenomena (*dharma-prajñapti-viṣaya*), which is the conventional body of the Buddhas consisting of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*);

second, the real object of pure phenomena (*dharma-dravya-viṣaya*), which refers to the dharmas of *bodhi*, *nirvāṇa*, and the *pāramitās*. Regarding these objects, one is able to permanently abandon all grasping and conceptual discrimination. This clarifies...
"Detached from the pure object, it is distinct and clear. According to reality, even regarding the upward-directed chain of bones, there is attachment and conceptualization;

regarding the upward-directed category of bodhi, there is likewise attachment and conceptualization. This is why it is said that "the mind extends to both places. Question: What dharma does each of these four places obstruct? Answer:
The mental application (*manasikāra*) of the two vehicles, their various doubts, and their departure from doubt—these directly obstruct the practice of the Mahāyāna. Regarding...
Within the teachings heard and contemplated, the thought "I am able to do so" constitutes a direct obstacle to the Mahāyāna contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

Fourth, the conceptualization of the chain of bones (*asthi-śaṅkalikā*) constitutes a direct obstacle to the non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) of the Mahāyāna. Question: At what stage are these four obstacles severed? Answer:

They are severed at the stage of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā-bhūmi*) by those who apply the mental attention (*manasikāra*) of the Two Vehicles (*dvi-yāna*), because they have abandoned the mind of the Lesser Vehicle. Second, as for the separation from doubt (*kāṅkṣā-vigama*), it occurs in...
The tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*) is abandoned during the stage of practice (*caryābhūmi*), because one practices correctly within the Mahāyāna and becomes free from delusion.

Third, regarding the thought "I am capable" concerning the teachings heard and reflected upon, this is abandoned from the stage of the ten dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*) up to the stage of patience (*kṣānti*).

Fourth, from the visualization of the skeleton (*asthisaṃkalā*) up to conceptualization (*vikalpa*), these are abandoned at the stage of the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*). Question: Why are the three refinements (*paricaya*) each opened into three, while there are four locations?

Question: Why are the obstacles combined into one? Answer: The three refinements serve as antidotes to the three types of despondency; because these remedial practices are real, they are separately distinguished as three.
Regarding the abandonment of the obstacles at the four stages: although there are four points of regression, the capacity for abandonment is not different, and thus they are combined into one.

Question: Upon abandoning the four stages, what kind of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is attained? Answer: Although the four stages are abandoned, analytical cessation has not yet been attained; it is merely...

That which lies dormant and does not arise is termed "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*). Question: How many factors must be present to enter the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*)? Answer: One enters the Path of Seeing by means of eight factors:

three types of refinement (*parikarman*), four bases (*sthāna*), taking the meaning of the Dharma as the object (*ālambana*), long-term cultivation of calm abiding and insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*), earnest application (*prayoga*), and freedom from negligence (*apramāda*). The commentary cites the first five of these.
Regarding the phrase "the mental orientations (*manasikāra*) of the two vehicles" and so forth: this refutes the attachment of the *śrāvakas*.

Persons of the two vehicles perceive saṃsāra and nirvāṇa with feelings of aversion and longing; they single-mindedly abandon saṃsāra and long for nirvāṇa. Because of these mental orientations, they obstruct the two benefits of the Mahāyāna.
Thus, the mental orientation itself is the obstruction.
The phrase "gradual enlighteners (anupūrva-abhisamaya) clinging to the Buddha and so forth" refers to the clinging of gradual enlighteners.
The phrase "furthermore, sudden enlighteners (sakṛt-abhisamaya) and various small bodhisattvas clinging and so forth" clarifies the clinging of sudden enlighteners.
The statement "now refuting this attachment" refers to refuting the attachment of those small bodhisattvas who realize awakening instantaneously (*tongwu*).
The statement "revealing that the two vehicles are not ultimate" refers to refuting the attachment of those small bodhisattvas who realize awakening gradually (*jianwu*).

The statement that those abiding in the two vehicles can also become Buddhas refutes the attachment of those who hold to sudden enlightenment, for such followers of the two vehicles cannot become Buddhas.
The phrase "therefore he preaches this sutra" means that he preaches the sutra in order to refute the attachments of both Bodhisattvas of sudden and gradual enlightenment.
Regarding the phrase "by this, [the treatises such as] the *Saṃgraha*," etc., it is a further classification of the textual arguments.

"By this" means that because there are two types of people—those who grasp [the teachings] all at once (*yugapat*) and those who do so gradually (*anupūrveṇa*)—the Bodhisattva composed the treatise to refute their attachments. This is what Sthiramati means by the word "by this."
Regarding the statement "the four bases" (*catvāri āyatanāni*), various commentaries state as follows. First, Jin says: "The first section of the commentary states:

'Those of the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*) form mental engagements (*manasikāra*) by clinging to the two fruits as ultimate. The second section concerns the gradually enlightened Bodhisattvas, who cling to the notion that Buddhahood and Bodhisattvahood are not their portion.
The third section concerns those such as the small Bodhisattvas of sudden enlightenment; this [passage] first cites from the preceding [text]."
The three provisional explanations are concluded. Next, the three sections of the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* are used to sequentially correlate with the three sections of the commentary:
namely, first, the mental application of the two vehicles; second, the removal of doubts regarding various uncertainties; and third, the claim, "I am able to do this, whereas others cannot."
The fourth skeletal outline is not what is required here. The *Sheshi ke* (Outline of Exegesis) states:

"One takes the 'two-vehicle persons' from the first section of the commentary, as well as the 'gradually enlightened bodhisattvas' from the second section; these two types of persons are collectively included within the 'attention of the two vehicles.
The treatise says: "The attention of the two vehicles"—this single phrase from the treatise concludes the preceding two sections. This follows the sequence of the commentary.
This concludes the first section. Now we proceed to the second section, "All Doubts Depart," which we shall not cite for now;
we take directly from the third section, where it says, "I am able to do so, while others cannot"—this summarizes the preceding discussion on sudden enlightenment.

Regarding the phrase "these two kinds": those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) and the bodhisattvas of gradual enlightenment (*anupūrva-abhisamaya*) constitute one kind, while the bodhisattvas of sudden enlightenment (*tadaṅga-abhisamaya*) constitute the second kind.
Regarding the phrase "those whose doubts have been dispelled" (*sarvakāṅkṣā-vigata*), one asks: why is this not correlated with the second line, "those whose doubts have been dispelled"?
Answering various doubts and being free from doubt is a matter belonging to the section on "Breaking Doubtful Attachments" (*pō-yízhí-mén*); it is not what is required here.

This was already indicated in the preceding section on "Breaking Doubts" (*pō-yí-mén*), specifically in the passage where the doubts of the bodhisattvas were resolved. Question: Why are four types mentioned in the initial listing, yet only two kinds are stated in the concluding text? Answer:

The passage concerning the "chain of bones" (*gūsù*) does not need to be strictly correlated [with the categories]. It is included here for the sake of textual convenience. All [doubts] are [thus resolved].

"Doubt is severed from doubt" refers to what is subsumed under the section on "Breaking through Doubtful Attachments. Therefore, it concludes by stating, "This is the same as the previous [section]" (having finished breaking through doubtful attachments).

Regarding the statement that there are two types of "manifesting the records and practices," the question that arises concerns the "arising of the intent. "Intent" refers to the underlying purpose or significance. It is asked: "I do not yet understand;
what further intent does the Buddha have in preaching this sutra? The answer is: There are five kinds of intents for preaching the sutra; we shall now address the first.
Third, the manifestation of the prediction of practice (*karmavācanā*). When the Tathāgata preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, "manifestation" (*chāng*) carries the meaning of making clear;
"prediction" (*jì*) means to distinguish and explain. Although he had preached other sūtras for forty years, he had not yet manifested the prediction of enlightenment for the śrāvakas.

Now, he clearly and manifestly grants predictions to the śrāvakas; therefore, this is truly the manifestation of the prediction. Question: Regarding the Tathāgata’s granting of predictions to the śrāvakas, there is...
"What was the intention? [The Buddha] replied: "Forty years ago, as a śrāvaka, I doubted that I would attain bodhi.
Seeing the Buddha amidst the great assembly, his fame filling the ten directions and extensively benefiting sentient beings, I thought to myself that I had lost this benefit.
Day and night, I constantly contemplated this matter, wishing to ask the World-Honored One whether I had lost it or not. Furthermore, I always said..."
Having seen the World-Honored One and heard his praise of the bodhisattvas, these four individuals of middling capacity spent their days and nights contemplating this matter.
Even as they were about to receive their prediction of enlightenment, they said: "It is as if we had come from a land of famine and suddenly encountered the meal of a great king;
our minds still harbor doubt and fear, so we do not yet dare to eat. This is why the World-Honored One spoke of the fruit of Buddhahood in the future.
[The Buddha] points out that while his internal virtues are perfected and his external adornments established, his preaching of the Dharma is identical to that of today;

only the name of the kalpa differs. He further says: "That is none other than your own body; you should rejoice in this. Since you already know that you yourself shall become a Buddha, you must practice the various deeds.
If you doubt that you can attain Buddhahood, your practice will lack determination. Now, he bestows upon you the prediction of enlightenment.
This causes them to resolve upon practicing the single vehicle (*ekayāna*). For this reason, the Tathāgata manifests and bestows predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) regarding their practice. Question:

World-Honored One, if one wishes to receive a prediction for a *śrāvaka*, would it not suffice to simply grant that prediction? Why is it necessary to grant it through the teaching of this sutra? Answer:
All the dharmas of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for all bodhisattvas emerge from this sutra. This includes the fruit of Buddhahood and the three bodies (*trikāya*).

The merits and the ten thousand practices of a bodhisattva are all contained within this sutra. If one intends to bestow a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), it is necessary to preach the sutra.

When preaching the sutra, one is simultaneously preaching cause and fruit: specifically, in the first week, the three stages of opening, showing, and awakening constitute the fruit, while entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision constitutes the cause.
In the second week, the ox-carts are the cause; in the third week, the treasure place is the fruit.

Furthermore, the "Chapter on Peaceful Practices" (Anrakugyō-hon) and the "Chapter on the Emergence from the Earth" (Yūshutsu-hon) clarify the practice of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), while the "Chapter on the Lifespan" (Juryō-hon) clarifies its fruit.

It was for the purpose of manifesting these recorded practices that the sutra was preached. Question: What is the distinction between this "that which manifests" (*nōshō*) and "that which is manifested" (*shōshō*)?
Answer: That which manifests is the teaching (*kyō*); that which is manifested is the practice (*gyō*). Therefore, they are distinct.

Regarding the phrase "The Buddha himself attained the Way," etc., this indicates the intent of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). Within this intent, there are two parts: first, the intent regarding the period before the prediction was bestowed forty years prior;
second, the intent regarding the bestowal of the prediction at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* assembly. Taken together, these are termed the "indication of the intent of the prediction.

In the subsequent sections where the scriptural text is cited, both points are likewise verified. This refers to the Buddha’s intent—since his own attainment of the Way—to either bestow or not bestow predictions upon the śrāvakas.

This refers to the intent behind bestowing a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). It is asked: On the seventh day after the Buddha attained the Way, he immediately bestowed predictions upon Trapusa and Bhallika and five hundred merchants.
Among these five hundred people, could there not have been even one who possessed the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) of a śrāvaka?
If there were even one person with the lineage of a śrāvaka, that would constitute bestowing a prediction upon a śrāvaka. As [it is said]:...

Why is it said that there are none? The answer is that while the words refer to the group as a whole, the meaning refers to the individuals. In the words, he generally announces the prediction for five hundred people;
in the meaning, he specifically bestows the prediction upon Trapusa alone, saying, "You shall become a Buddha. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "I have never before spoken of you all [in this way]."

"One shall attain the Buddha-way. [The interlocutor] asks: Is this prediction granted with reference to those who possess the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), or is it granted with reference to those who lack the spiritual lineage?

If it were granted with reference to those who lack the spiritual lineage, then the statement that they will all universally attain Buddhahood would mean that the World-Honored One has spoken falsely.

If it were granted with reference to sentient beings who possess the spiritual lineage, then since their attainment of Buddhahood is already determined, why is it necessary to grant them a prediction?

Regarding the bestowal of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*): First, for those of indeterminate nature who practice the Great Vehicle and experience both progress and regression, the prediction is given in order to cause them to give rise to a mind of certainty.
Second, regarding the prediction given to Śrāvakas: it is intended to inspire in the other members of the assembly a longing for the Bodhicitta of the Buddha-fruit.
Thus the Sūtra says: "O Śāriputra of great wisdom, you have now received the prediction of the Honored One. I...
The same applies to others as well; they will certainly attain Buddhahood. Furthermore, the *Mūla-śāstra* states:

"When the Buddha arose from meditative absorption, he addressed Śāriputra alone and did not address the bodhisattvas, in order to cause other people to contemplate [the matter] with skillful mindfulness" (the meaning of the preceding note).
Regarding the phrase "therefore, as stated below in the sutra, 'I have established... and so forth: this cites seven and a half verses from the "Expedient Means" (Upāya-kauśalya) chapter.

These are divided into four parts: first, the introduction; second, the explanation; third, the reconciliation; and fourth, the exhortation to abide [in the teaching]. This is the initial section, comprising both the introduction and the explanatory text.
"I have established these expedients to enable them to enter the Buddha-wisdom, until they attain the path of Buddhahood"—this is the introduction. Now...

"This is precisely the time," etc., is the explanation. "I have established these skillful means to enable them to enter the Buddha-wisdom. To testify to this, he now bestows the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
At the assembly on Vulture Peak, their faculties and the Dharma accorded; thus, he directly abandons the skillful means and speaks only of the Unsurpassed Way.
I have never said to you, "You shall attain the Buddha-way. The reason I have not said so is that the time for such a declaration had not yet arrived;

my intention was not to grant you a prediction [of enlightenment] at that time. I said that forty years ago your faculties were not yet mature, and thus I provisionally established skillful means to lead you to seek the lesser fruits.
Now is precisely the right time; I am definitively proclaiming the Mahāyāna and, having realized this, I now grant you the prediction. This is...

Therefore, this sutra was preached. Regarding the question that the sutra says "never before preached": for instance, in the past, when the sixteen princes heard a single verse of the Lotus Sutra being preached, it was clear that they would all attain Buddhahood;
why then does it say they had not been granted a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*)? Answer:

Since their own subsequent entry into the stage of the śrāvaka, they have not been granted a prediction. Furthermore, what was previously preached to them has already been forgotten. Therefore, the sutra says:
In the past, I taught you to set your aspirations on the path to Buddhahood, yet you have now completely forgotten this and instead claim that you have already attained nirvāṇa.
Because I now wish to cause you to remember your original vows and the path you were to practice, I am preaching this Mahāyāna sūtra and others for the sake of the śrāvakas.
[The interlocutor asks: What was there to be withheld in the past that you did not preach to the śrāvakas? Why is it only today?
"Is he then immediately given a prediction [of enlightenment]? Answer: The Buddha does not grant such a prediction because there would be many faults. As the sutra says:

"Those of dull faculties who delight in inferior teachings, who are greedily attached to birth and death, who do not practice the profound and wondrous path under the countless Buddhas, and who are distressed and distracted by manifold sufferings—for these he speaks of nirvana.
The reason it is spoken now is due to five virtues. As the subsequent sutra states: "There are..."
The sons of the Buddha have pure minds, are gentle and pliant, and possess sharp faculties; they have practiced the profound and wondrous Way under immeasurable Buddhas.
For these sons of the Buddha, I preach this Mahāyāna sūtra. For this reason, I did not speak of it until now; it is only today that I finally speak it.
(The above is the passage concerning those of superior faculties.)

Regarding the phrase "Furthermore, Kāśyapa says," etc.: [Question] Why is the scriptural passage for those of inferior capacity (*hīnendriya*) not cited? [Answer] The text concerning those of inferior capacity is subsumed under the middle and superior capacities;
this is to cite the superior to encompass the inferior. The passage cited here is from the "Chapter on Resolute Belief" (*Adhimukty-adhikāra*), which recounts the acceptance [of the teaching].

Therein, the four types of people’s acceptance are categorized according to the dharma, the parable, and their combination. First, it reveals that they previously did not aspire [to the Mahāyāna]; subsequently, it manifests...
"Now it has been attained" clarifies that it has now been attained. Regarding what was not previously sought, there is first a brief statement and later an extensive explanation.

Within the extensive explanation, the first part recounts past events, while the latter explains the reasons for them. This section contains two points: first, "My path is fulfilled; my mind is at peace as suffering has ceased. As the Sūtra says:
"The World-Honored One has caused us to emerge from the three realms and attain the realization of Nirvāṇa. Second, "I am already aged and decrepit; my teeth have fallen out."

They become disheartened regarding the Mahāyāna and give rise to a mind that considers themselves beyond its scope; like one who, having attained the rank of a minor king, deems it sufficient and no longer aspires to the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin).
As the Sūtra says, they do not produce even a single thought of longing for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This is the text concerning those who have not yet received a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). (The above citation refers to the passage on those not yet predicted.)
Regarding the statement, "Or it is said that the Sūtras, etc.," this refers to texts where the prophecy has not yet been recorded; this treatise, however, clarifies those that have been recorded.

These should also be explained together. The three types of śrāvakas who receive prophecies are mentioned in the sūtras, which also include the *svayambhū* (self-proclaimed) and *vaipulya* (extensive) categories; these are included here for the sake of convenience.

If this refers to the manifestation of practice, it merely explains that practice; subsequently, it also discusses the five kinds of *prajñā*, which is the intended meaning of the commentary (*śāstra*).

Regarding the six verses in the "Expedient Means" chapter, the first four and a half verses describe [the subject], while the section beginning with "Why is this so? constitutes the explanatory text (*vyākhyāna*).
This text is divided into two parts: one verse on "innumerable expedient means," and two verses on "various causes, conditions, parables, and also words."
The prose and verse state: "The thoughts in the minds of sentient beings, and the various paths they travel"—this one and a half verses expound upon all dharmas.

The verse continues: "Or he speaks of the *sūtras*, *gāthās*, *itivṛttakas*, and so forth. The commentary cites this passage. Regarding *sūtra*: it refers to the *sūtras* (scriptural discourses) of the Hīnayāna.
Because they accord with both principle (*li*) and the faculties (*gen*) of sentient beings, they are collectively termed *sūtras*. *Gāthā*...

*Geya* (Verses) refers to those passages that praise and extol virtues through exquisite diction. *Itivṛttaka* (Thus-it-was-said) refers to the proclamation of past events concerning the noble disciples;
thus it is called *itivṛttaka*. *Jātaka* (Birth Stories) refers to the proclamation of the past lives of the Blessed One; thus it is called *jātaka*.
*Adbhutadharma* (Marvels) refers to the proclamation of all the extraordinary and astonishing deeds of the eight classes of noble disciples; thus it is called *adbhutadharma*.
There are three types of causes and conditions [for the Buddha’s teaching]: first, speaking at the request of others; second, establishing precepts due to an offense;

and third, preaching the Dharma in response to specific events. Regarding the *Avadāna* (Pariyāya): this refers to the parables taught within the Sūtras and Vinaya, which are spoken as metaphors to clarify the original meaning.

Regarding *Geya* (Ge-yi): this is translated as "Verses in Response" (*Saṃgīti*). There are two purposes: first, to benefit future generations; and second, to elucidate what was not fully understood previously.

*Artha* (meaning) and *upadeśa* (instruction)—the latter being translated here as "discourse on meaning"—involve refining and investigating the nature and characteristics (*dharmatā-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena.

These were taught solely for the sake of the *śrāvakas* in the ninefold canon (*navāṅga-buddhavacana*), where prophetic declarations (*vyākaraṇa*) were not spoken. However, if one considers the specific explanations (*vyākaraṇa*) regarding the profound and secret meaning, such [prophetic declarations] are also taught.

The Vaipulya (Extensive) is not [the subject] here. "Va" means correct principle; "pulya" means vast and inclusive. It refers to the Vaipulya that extensively expounds the true Dharma, rather than being merely the absence of such exposition.

Regarding the "Unasked Spontaneous Discourse": this refers to instances within formal requests where the speaker does not explicitly reveal the requester, yet speaks without being asked in order to ensure that the true Dharma remains for a long time in the future.
The second and third inquiries both concern the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). This is from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* assembly.

[Question: Above, you recorded the *śrāvakas*. What constitutes the text concerning those who have not yet received a prediction (*avyākṛta*)? [Answer: It is when it has never been said, "You shall attain the Buddha-way";

this is what is meant by not having been granted a prediction. There is no need for the specific word "prediction" [to appear]. (The three preceding sections are all texts concerning those who have not yet received a prediction.)
The phrase "therefore, prior to this" and so forth refers to the period before the assembly at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. It concludes what was previously unrecorded.

The phrase "now, for the sake of bestowing a prediction" refers to the occasion of the assembly at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Because predictions had not been bestowed since the past, they are now bestowed;
thus, it concludes the previous predictions and explains that this very scripture is being taught (the above demonstrates that the predictions are complete).
Regarding the phrase "manifesting conduct later": "manifesting" (*zhāng*) means to clarify (*míng*). "Conduct" (*xíng*) refers to the four bodhisattva practices of the seventh stage.

The preceding section manifested the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), which is the exposition of the fruit (*phala*). Since the fruit has already been identified, one must know the causal practice; therefore, there is the manifestation of conduct.
Regarding the statement, "The practitioner of the One Vehicle of the Bodhisattva," it now explains the practice of the Bodhisattva’s One Vehicle.

It reveals the practice by means of the person, because the One Vehicle is precisely the Bodhisattva's practice; it reveals the person by means of the practice. Question: For what reason must the practice of the One Vehicle be established?
Answer: Because the One Vehicle is precisely the Bodhisattva's practice. The Bodhisattva's practice does not exceed the seven stages (*bhūmi*).
The four bodhisattva practices are all gathered together and unified, not exceeding the practice of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

Since this practice of the One Vehicle is contained within this sutra, and in order to manifest the bodhisattva practices, this sutra is taught. Question: Why are other sutras not taught to manifest the bodhisattva practices? Answer:

If one were to teach various other sutras, they would not exhaustively describe the practices of other bodhisattvas. Question: Is it because the bodhisattvas have not yet [attained] them in their entirety?
"One practices the path of the One Vehicle. Does this mean that although the World-Honored One has already practiced the path, he must still rely on the preaching of the sutras to manifest it?
Or does it mean that even though one has already practiced the path, one still requires the World-Honored One’s preaching of the sutras to manifest that practice?

If it is argued that for those who have not yet practiced, the path must be manifested through teaching, then why would a Bodhisattva of sudden enlightenment—who has already cultivated the practice of the One Vehicle—require the World-Honored One to manifest that practice? Answer: Although one may have already practiced the path of the One Vehicle, if it is not manifested...
[The Buddha] said: "The bodhisattva’s practice does not attain vastness. [I] desire to cause the bodhisattva’s practice to become a vast practice.

There are two intentions for manifesting the practice for the sake of the śrāvakas: first, regarding the two-vehicle practices cultivated during the forty years prior, they did not know these were practices of the One Vehicle;
therefore, they regretted their cultivation. Today, by manifesting the practice, the intention is to cause them to understand. Second, [it is] to question the śrāvakas."
Previously, it was taught that Bodhisattvas practice vast deeds (*udāra-caryā*) so that those of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) might see their excellence and aspire to emulate them.
Furthermore, although these were practiced in the past, they were not clearly explained to others at that time; now, they are explained clearly so that others may understand.

Therefore, these practices are made manifest. Question: Regarding the "practice of subduing" (*vinaya-caryā*), how does the practice of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) differ from that within this present section?

What is the distinction regarding the clarification of the practices of the Two Vehicles? Answer: Before this sutra was preached, the practices of the Two Vehicles were merely causes for Arhatship and could only bring about the fruit of Arhatship.
However, once the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is preached, the practices of the Two Vehicles are clearly revealed as being the cause for the Bodhi of Buddhahood;
they can then bring about the fruit of Buddhahood. This is like a single grain of cinnabar that, when applied to iron, transforms it into gold.
This is always the practice of a bodhisattva. It is because those of the two vehicles did not know this in the past but now come to know it that their practice is made manifest.
As the Sūtra says: "The path you all practice is the bodhisattva way."

Regarding the phrase "therefore," the subsequent sutra states, "There is a son of the Buddha. This is manifested among the assembly through his conduct. The entire scriptural text consists of three sections.

The first section comprises seven and a half stanzas from the verses of the *Upāya-kauśalya-parivarta* (Expedient Means Chapter), which describe the prose narrative and exhort [the bodhisattvas] to abide [in the path]. This is divided into four parts; the first is the heading.

There are four parts: (1) the two explanations, (2) the three assemblies, (3) the exhortation to remain, and (4) what is cited here in the commentary. This citation belongs to the third assembly, which is divided into three sections.

The first verse demonstrates that dharmas are not real; it is presented as the fundamental text, beginning with: "These ninefold teachings of mine are spoken in accordance with sentient beings," and so forth.
The first one and a half verses reveal the excellence and sublimity of the Great Dharma, which is taught for superior persons: "There are sons of the Buddha whose minds are pure," and so forth.
The second verse concludes its sublimity: "I prophesy that such a person shall attain the path of Buddhahood in a future life, by recollecting the Buddha with a profound mind."
Because of practicing pure precepts. The second section further states: "Whether śrāvakas or bodhisattvas," etc.; this is the verse that establishes the subject.
The fourth section is the prose text that exhorts one to abide [in that state]. The third section further states:
"Śāriputra, all Buddhas and Tathāgatas teach and transform only bodhisattvas," etc. Within this, there is both a thesis and an explanation; what follows is the explanation.
Wenjin Qie. The second verse and a half reveals the supreme excellence of the Great Dharma, which is taught for superior persons. Question:
Why is it necessary here to cite the five qualities of a son of the Buddha as evidence to manifest this practice? Answer:
Because the single line of scripture stating, "One practices the profound and wondrous path based on conditions," is identical to what is presented here; therefore, it is cited.
Regarding the term "sons of the Buddha": these are Bodhisattvas who have attained awakening through either the sudden or gradual approaches. Regarding the five virtues:
first is purity of mind, which consists of seeking exclusively the Mahāyāna wisdom of the Buddha without delighting in inferior states, because one has eliminated the two obstacles.

Second is gentleness, which means gathering the mind through meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and remaining free from a distracted mind; thus, being gentle, one can benefit others, endure toil and fatigue, and accomplish great undertakings with diligence.
Fourth, because they are diligent and never ceasing. Fifth, those with sharp faculties are sagacious and wise; by nature they strive to uproot suffering and are able to bestow happiness upon others.
They treat all equally, enter the Dharma swiftly upon hearing it, have long encountered excellent conditions in the presence of immeasurable Buddhas, and have constantly polished themselves.
Sixth, they practice the profound and subtle path, cultivating both merit and wisdom in equal measure to conform to the Truth. If there is a son of the Buddha who possesses [these qualities]...
These five qualities may be explained as the Mahāyāna to inspire them toward its practice. Question: Do the śrāvakas possess those five qualities?
Answer: They do possess the five qualities. First, the severing of afflictions is called "purity of mind. Second, because they see the heavens raining four kinds of flowers, they are "supple."
Third, they possess sharp faculties because they enter [the path] swiftly upon hearing the Dharma; for example, Śāriputra understood it immediately upon hearing it once.
Fourth, they have already been transformed by the Buddhas in immeasurable places—specifically, throughout hundreds, thousands, millions, and billions of lifetimes.

Fifth, regarding those who "practice the profound and wondrous path," this refers to the stage up until the sixth *vihāra* (abode), which is subsumed under the practice of the profound and wondrous path. Question: If there was no prior practice, how is it so now?

To speak of causing [others] to practice is what is called manifesting practice; there are indeed sons of the Buddha. As for "the purity of mind" and so forth, these are practices already performed previously.

How then can one say that speaking of the sutras now constitutes manifesting practice? Answer: One must cite great practices that were previously performed so that later practitioners of lesser capacity may also admire those lofty traces.

By citing the superior to lead the inferior, it is intended that those of the Two Vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) will see the worthy and strive to emulate them. The commentary cites this as "merely speaking of the sutras to manifest [practice]."

Regarding the composition: regardless of whether [the command] has been carried out or not, the preceding section clarifies that the Great Dharma is supreme and wondrous, and is taught for the sake of superior persons.
This does not intend to subsume difficult cases as being merely secondary; rather, one should apply a fourfold analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*).

First, there are those who are virtuous but not gentle, such as the conceited Vinaya Master. Second, there are those who are gentle but not virtuous, namely all officials and the like. Third, there are those who are both gentle and virtuous... [etc.]
These refer to such passages as "There are sons of the Buddha whose minds are pure," and so forth. It is like speaking of a fine horse, which is matched with a gentleman;
or that the highest goodness is like water, conforming to the square or roundness of its vessel. Those who possess the four unwholesome states and lack suppleness are the icchantikas.
Regarding the phrase "for these sons of the Buddhas," this summarizes the aforementioned five virtues; by means of these five virtues, one's practice is truly manifested.
Regarding the phrase "furthermore, whether śrāvakas or bodhisattvas," etc., this is the second section of the sutra. Question: What is meant by hearing even a single verse of the sutra?

This is the teaching. How does one manifest this practice? Answer: Although it is said that hearing even a single verse constitutes the teaching, the mind that is able to hear that single verse is itself the practice;
this is precisely one of the ten dharma-practices. Furthermore, it is said that one takes the practice discussed below as being subordinate to the teaching of a single verse.
Of these two interpretations, the former is superior.
Regarding the statement, "Furthermore, Śāriputra, all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, etc.," the phrase "etc. refers to the third section of the sutra text. Question: This sutra teaches and transforms śrāvakas;
why then does it speak only of teaching and transforming bodhisattvas? Answer: Although they were previously śrāvakas, they later become bodhisattvas.
Thus, by turning their minds toward the Mahāyāna, they are in every respect bodhisattvas. It is revealed that while practicing the paths of the two vehicles, they are in truth the One Vehicle.
[This is] practice. [Question: Why does the Commentary selectively cite these three passages, neither adding nor omitting anything? [Answer:

The first passage cites the "sons of the Buddha endowed with five virtues" who "practice the profound and wondrous Way"; this is precisely the One Vehicle practice cultivated by both Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas.
The second passage exhorts those of both the sudden and gradual types to abide in the Mahāyāna. The third... the Great [Vehicle].
Riding upon this correctness is the practice of a bodhisattva. The third section of the sutra text teaches only the bodhisattvas, manifesting both sudden and gradual bodhisattva practices.
"Whatever one does" refers to the practices of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
"Always doing one thing" refers to the fruit of Buddhahood, *bodhi*, which is termed "one thing. Thus, the preceding two sections are the cause, while the third section is the fruit. From cause to—
"Result. This means that the significance is nearly complete (clarifying the "conduct").
Regarding the statement that it "necessarily depends on cultivating merit, wisdom, and so forth," the question is: by what specific practices does one practice to become a Buddha?

The answer in the Commentary states: "Necessarily depends on cultivation, etc. Mǔ says: "This is stated extensively according to principle. The Chapter says: "These six phrases of the Commentary text conclude the preceding [section]."
This is a three-part passage. Since the character "hence" (故) is placed here, one knows that the text originates from what precedes it.
Were it otherwise, these six lines of commentary would appear to be an isolated interpolation; therefore, establishing this section in this manner is appropriate.

The first two lines—“By cultivating merit and wisdom, they illuminate both existence and emptiness”—conclude the previous section on the pure mind of the Buddha’s sons, leading up to the phrase “practicing the profound and wondrous path,” which constitutes the five virtues.

O Son of the Buddha: the practice of cultivation does not transcend merit, wisdom, emptiness, and existence. Second, by investigating the teachings through which they are expressed, one exhaustively studies the profound principle.
This concludes the preceding section on śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and so forth. Third, when true understanding arises, one awakens to the One Vehicle.

This concludes the preceding passage from "The Buddhas and Tathāgatas teach and transform only bodhisattvas" down to the point of "one matter. When true understanding arises, one enters the Path. This concludes the preceding section from "only teaching and transforming bodhisattvas" onwards.
Whatever is performed is always for the sake of a single purpose. Thus, one knows that this interpretation accords with the *Śāstra* (commentary).

If one were to elaborate extensively on the underlying principles, the *Śāstra* text would comprehensively resolve all these meanings, which are identical to those of Mou [Zongshun]. This encompasses four interpretations: first, it is said that one must rely upon the cultivation of merit and wisdom:
the *prajñā* of retinue illuminates existence and emptiness; the *prajñā* of the objective realm seeks out the meaning of the teachings; and the *prajñā* of words consists of the written characters.
Investigating the profound principle gives rise to the *prajñā* of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*), while the sixth [stage] gives rise to the *prajñā* of contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā*).
The first five serve as the cause, and the sixth realizes the fruit of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Second, it is said that one must rely on the cultivation of merit and wisdom;

during the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), one practices the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) in a somewhat disordered manner, primarily relying on external means to cultivate the bodhisattva path. Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Chapter 9) states: "The Bodhisattva, for this reason, within the stage of equipment..."

Regarding the two types of coarse active manifestations (*paryavasthāna*): although there may be those that have been suppressed, as for the subtle ones and the two latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), the power of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* is weak and has not yet been able to suppress or eliminate them.

Since it is stated "regarding *śamatha*," this clarifies that one has also attained meditative concentration (*samādhi*). One illuminates existence and emptiness, seeks out the meanings of the teachings, and investigates the profound principles while in the stage of application (*prayoga-mārga*).
Relying on the internal gate, one cultivates the bodhisattva practices; therefore, within this stage, when one intends to illuminate...

There is emptiness. One must investigate the teachings to interpret them. Contemplating what appears to be the literal text and the literal meaning is called "investigating the interpretation of the teachings.

Based on these very teachings, one contemplates that the self-nature and so forth are conventionally existent but ultimately non-existent; this is called "investigating the profound principle. By attaining entry into the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), one realizes the principle of the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*).

The arising of the two wisdoms—the wondrous and the equanimous—is called "the true awakening of origination. Realizing the universally pervasive *tathatā* (suchness) is called "awakening to the One Vehicle.

The third [point] concerns the understanding of the subject that observes and the object observed. This necessarily depends on the first five perfections as merit (*puṇya*), while the sixth is wisdom (*prajñā*).

When practicing wisdom, one must observe the objects of emptiness and existence; since emptiness and existence encompass everything without exception, it is said that one "illuminates both existence and emptiness."
Having already known that there is emptiness, one may not yet know how to practice; what is the sequence? Therefore, it is necessary to seek the meaning expressed in the teachings.

Once the teachings have been sought, by relying on them one will surely be able to awaken to the principle. Therefore, in investigating the profound principle, by relying on that principle one will surely be able to initiate practice.

Therefore, when true understanding arises, by relying on that practice one will surely be able to realize the fruit. Therefore, one awakens to the One Vehicle. This is the essential point. (Section Four)
By means of cultivating merit and wisdom, those who have first begun their practice are unable to forget conceptual signs (*nimitta*) and thus cultivate merit and wisdom.

Only after practicing for a long time can they contemplate emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and penetrate existence (*bhava*). To understand the profound principle of emptiness and existence, one must seek out the teachings;

only then can one reach a definitive resolution. Thoroughly investigating the sublime purport of the Tripiṭaka is called "examining the profound principle. Through these four preceding matters, right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) arises; this is termed [the stage of]...
True understanding arises. It is through the preceding five [factors] that one realizes the principle being expounded; this is called "awakening to the One Vehicle. Question:

Since the fundamental [teaching] manifests through practice (*caryā*), why do you speak of that principle and its fruit? Answer: Although it is said to concern practice, it necessarily depends upon the teaching and the principle.

If not by means of the expression (*abhilāpa*), from where would practice arise? If one does not know the principle and its fruit, what would there be to aspire toward? Therefore, there is no fault in speaking thus. If...

Regarding the assignment to the five stages (*pañca-avasthā*): although this encompasses long-term practice, it does not include the initial cultivation, such as the three faculties (*trīṇi indriyāṇi*) and so forth.

Furthermore, one who awakens to and understands the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) and receives the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of future Buddhahood has not yet reached the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*). Within what stage, then, is the beginner’s mind included? [The previous systems] do not provide an answer for these cases. Now, regarding the alternative explanation:
"one who practices through merit and wisdom" refers to the cultivation of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). The first five are called merit (*puṇya*), and the sixth is called wisdom (*prajñā*).

Although one practices giving and the other perfections, one must understand that the substance of these three matters is empty. Because the Bodhisattva clings to the idea that sentient beings can be saved and that enlightenment can be sought, they perceive both emptiness and existence.
Although they perceive both emptiness and existence, if they do not rely on the teachings, they may find themselves without a basis;

therefore, they seek the expressions of the teachings, which ultimately provide a point of return. Thus, they investigate the profound principle. Since this principle is not perceived in isolation, it must necessarily rely upon the mirror of wisdom; hence, true understanding arises.
[The text] begins: "If it is thus, it is called awakening to the One Vehicle (Ekayāna). Huìyuǎn says: "One must rely on the cultivation of merit and wisdom;

wisdom is the companion. Wisdom illuminates the objective realm of emptiness and existence; wisdom seeks the cause as expressed by the teachings; wisdom investigates the profound principle of the nature [of reality];
and true understanding gives rise to the characteristic of wisdom. Only through these five aspects does one awaken to the One Vehicle. Hè Pòjīn says: "If these are correlated with the five..."

"Wisdom" thus lacks the practice of merit. Mou [Zong] says: "Nor is it that merit is lacking. Why? Because both [the first two and the latter four] of the six perfections encompass both the two kinds of merit and wisdom.
The *Treatise* states: "The general characteristic of the six types of pāramitās is that they all comprise both [merit and wisdom]. It further states that these are assigned to the five stages.

Those who have not yet mastered the initial stage of practice belong to families with differing aspirations. This is because the Master of the Commentary first established the vehicle of causal practice;
that is, as the Sūtra says, "riding this precious vehicle" directly to the site of enlightenment, even down to the ox-cart of the first bhūmi, whereby one enters the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Therefore, he assigns the five stages to merit, wisdom, and so forth. For those who awaken to the One Vehicle, realization constitutes [the goal].
It is said: "Those of the three capacities who awaken to the One Vehicle—this awakening is an awakening of understanding that is not subsumed under these [categories].
Each is a distinct realization; why must it necessarily be excluded?"

Regarding the statement that the One Vehicle has both cause and fruit: this is a general heading that includes the fruit, because it clarifies that practice is not in vain, as its fruit will necessarily be realized.
By manifesting the practice, it includes the fruit; this is the profound intention of the Master of the Commentary (*śāstrakāra*).

If one practices this path, one will certainly obtain this fruit; therefore, by citing the fruit, he demonstrates that the practice is not in vain. Now, if one wishes to realize the fruit, one must...

One must practice the cause; if the cause is not cultivated, from what could the fruit arise? A sutra states: "Even children playing, gathering sand to make Buddha-stupas, have all already attained the path of Buddhahood.
It further says: "If there are those who hear the Dharma, there is not one who does not possess the cause for becoming a Buddha.
For these reasons, it is also called the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).

Regarding the statement that the "causes" refer to the four bodhisattvas of the seven stages (*bhūmi*), this precisely clarifies their causes. The seven stages are analyzed through five gates: first, listing the names; second, identifying their essence (*svabhāva*);

third, correlating them with the stages; fourth, discerning their characteristics; and fifth, assigning them to the sūtras. First, as for listing the names, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 59, states:

(1) the stage of the nature of the lineage (*gotra-bhūmi*); (2) the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*); (3) the stage of pure superior intention (*śuddhādhyāśaya-bhūmi*); (4) [the stage of practicing through superior intention]...
The Stage of Correct Practice; the Fifth, the Stage of Certainty; the Sixth, the Stage of Certain Practice; and the Seventh, the Stage of Ultimate Attainment.
Regarding the second point, the determination of its essential nature, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Thus, it collectively subsumes all conditioned virtues as its intrinsic nature.

This category of mind is conditioned wisdom (*jñāna*), while the unconditioned is principle (*tattva*). As for the seven stages, they consist of the seeds of both contaminated and uncontaminated wisdom within the causal state, which manifest...
The stage of abiding in the spiritual lineage (*gotra-vihāra*) has as its essence solely the seeds of both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

The stage of abiding in practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-vihāra*) has as its essence the functioning of the three types of contaminated wisdom (*prajñā*), the innate uncontaminated seeds, and the faculty of resolute belief (*adhimokṣa*) among the five object-specific mental factors (*viśeṣa-viṣaya*).

From the stage of pure superior intention (*śuddhādhyāśaya-bhūmi*) up to the stage of practicing correct conduct (*caryāpratipatti-bhūmi*), it has as its essence the seeds of both contaminated and uncontaminated knowledge.

The first [three] stages have as their essence the manifestation [of wisdom]. The latter three stages have as their essence both the seeds and the manifestations of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*). In its ultimate reality, it has only discernment (*prajñā*) as its essence.
If including its associated factors, it has the twenty-two mental states and mental concomitants as its essence. Including its retinue, it has the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as its essence.

Third, regarding the correspondence with the stages (*bhūmi*): first, the stage of the lineage (*gotrabhūmi*). It is also called the "abiding in the lineage" (*gotrastha*) or the "abiding prior to the arousal of the mind" (*anutpāditacittastha*).

This refers to the naturally abiding lineage (*prakṛtistha-gotra*). One has not yet entered the *saṃkhyāta* (the stage of the multitude); possessing this lineage, one is still an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
Therefore, it is called the "Stage of the Seed-lineage" (*gotrabhūmi*). "Upper" refers to the essence (*svabhāva*); "lower" refers to the category (*jāti*), which is the untainted (*anāsrava*) class.

The "seeds" are the untainted seeds that have, from time immemorial, been dependent upon the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*). They have never been cultivated or caused to increase through perfuming;
rather, they abide as their original substance. These seeds of bodhi differ in their lineage (*gotra-jāti-viśeṣa*), and this is not something produced by present conditions.

Second is the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), which corresponds to the third dwelling of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-vihāra*). This begins from the point where faith has been generated and extends up to the end of the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*).
