The treatise states: "In this stage, one has not yet realized the suchness of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātratā-tathatā*); relying on the power of resolute belief, one cultivates various forms of resolute belief."

It should be understood that this is also subsumed under the stage of practice through realization (*adhigama-caryā-bhūmi*). That is to say, the excellence of the wholesome factors of the stage of discernment (*nirvedha-bhāgīya*) arising from resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) is called the stage of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-bhūmi*).

This extends from the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) up to the stage of application (*prayoga*). This refers to the mental factor of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) among the five object-specific mental factors (*viṣaya-niyata*), which repeatedly gives rise to superior resolve and understanding.
1. The stage of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), which consists of definitively grasping [the teachings], is also called the "dwelling of joy" (*pramuditā-vihāra*);

it is located in the first stage (*bhūmi*). 4. The stage of practicing correct conduct (*samyak-pratipatti-bhūmi*), which is also called the "dwelling of superior ethical discipline" (*adhiśīla-vihāra*), begins from the point when the mind has emerged from the first stage onward.

Upon reaching the fulfillment of the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), there is the fifth stage, the Stage of Certainty (*niyata-bhūmi*), which is also called the Abiding in Effortlessness and Non-application (*anābhoga-anābhoga-vihāra*).
The eighth stage is the sixth, the Stage of Certain Practice (*niyata-caryā-bhūmi*), which is also called the Abiding in Unimpeded Understanding (*pratisaṃvid-vihāra*).

Being in the ninth stage is the seventh, the Stage of Reaching the Ultimate (*niṣṭhā-gamana-bhūmi*), which is also called the Abiding of the Most Perfectly Accomplished Bodhisattva (*parama-pariniṣpanna-bodhisattva-vihāra*) and the Abiding of the Tathāgata (*tathāgata-vihāra*). This occurs in the tenth stage and in Buddhahood.

The Grounds: The tenth ground is the culmination of the cause; the Buddha-ground is the culmination of the fruit. It is the full possession of the three bodies (*trikāya*) and the perfect clarity of the four wisdoms (*caturjñāna*).

Regarding the characteristics of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*): first is the stage of the lineage (*gotrabhūmi*), which is the naturally abiding lineage (*prakṛtistha-gotra*) prior to entering the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.

That is to say, within the stage of ordinary beings prior to the ten levels of faith, the untainted seeds have existed since beginningless time, naturally inherent and dependent upon the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
They are not produced by perfuming. Abiding in this stage of the lineage, it is called the "stage of the lineage" (*gotrabhūmi*).

Because of the existence of this lineage, one's nature is inherently benevolent and virtuous, and one's nature is inherently matured; thus, the bodhisattva’s merits arise without the occurrence of the highest-grade afflictions.

[This refers to those who] are bound by the *paryavasthānas*, commit the deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*), do not sever their roots of virtue (*kuśala-mūla*), and so forth. Second, the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*) refers to the position prior to the [first] ground.

That is to say, the cultivation of the wholesome factors conducive to liberation and the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedha-bhāgīya-kuśala*) is called the stage of practice through resolute belief; it corresponds to the mental factor of resolute belief (*adhimukti*) among the specific objects of cognition (*viṣaya-viśeṣa*).
This means "to seal and uphold. There are three types of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*): first, because one seals and upholds all causes and effects pertaining to *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*;

second, because one definitively seals and upholds the objects of the profound and subtle principles; and third, because one definitively seals and upholds the hearing, reflection, and cultivation regarding the noble Dharma.
Collectively, these are called the Stage of Practice through Resolute Conviction (*adhimukticaryā-bhūmi*). [This is from] Master Xu’s *Commentary on the Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that from the initial generation of the bodhicitta up until the first bhūmi, this stage has not yet realized the suchness (*tathatā*) of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).

Because one cultivates various forms of resolute conviction through the power of superior resolve (*adhimukti*), it is called the Stage of Practice through Resolute Conviction (*adhimukticaryā-bhūmi*).

Regarding the "Third Pure Stage of Superior Intention" (*śuddhādhyāśaya-bhūmi*), it is also called the "Abode of Supreme Joy" (*pramuditā-vihāra*). It resides in the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) of the first bhūmi; that is to say, this Path of Seeing realizes the hundred [dharmas].

The Dharma-Illumination Gate (*dharmāloka-mukha*). Because one severs the two obstacles of conceptual discrimination, realizes the principle of the two kinds of emptiness, and gives rise to great joy, there are three types of joy.

First is the joy of illumination like the sun: by severing afflictions of conceptual discrimination and realizing the suchness of the two kinds of emptiness—just as the light of the sun destroys the darkness of the world—one realizes the Dharma-Illumination Gate of the hundred dharmas, attains the ten kinds of equality, and gains birth into the Buddha-family; therefore, it is great joy. Second...

"Abandoning what is difficult to realize and delighting in what is easy": this refers to the dharmas of superior resolve (adhimukti) cultivated prior to the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), which constitute difficult practice;

and the realization of the easy-to-realize dharmas, which is the joy of the sudden realization of the gateways of clarity—namely, entering the Path of Seeing, the "Gateway of Clarity of the Hundred Dharmas," and the wondrous principle of the two voids (*dvaya-śūnyatā*)."

All of these are sudden realizations (*sadyo-bodha*). Because of these three joys, it is called the "Abode of Supreme Joy" (*pramuditā-vihāra*). Furthermore, the understanding that severs conceptual afflictions is called "Pure Transcendence.

That which precedes the stages is called "Victorious," characterized by mastery according to one's vows and the realization of the "Gate of Illumination of a Hundred Dharmas" (*śata-dharma-prabheda-mukha*), which is termed "Intentional Resolve" (*āśaya*).

Regarding the four practices of the stage of correct practice, Lü (Lü Cai) states: from the initial dwelling of the mind in the first stage (*bhūmi*) up until the final moment of mind in the seventh stage.

This is called the Stage of Correct Practice (*samyakpratipattibhūmi*). It comprises the dwelling of higher morality (*adhiśīla-vihāra*) within the first stage; the dwelling of higher mind (*adhicitta-vihāra*) in the second, the Stainless Stage (*vimalā-bhūmi*);

and the dwelling of higher wisdom associated with the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣyādhiprajñā-vihāra*) in the third, the Luminous Stage (*prabhākārī-bhūmi*). The fourth is the Blazing Wisdom Stage (*arciṣmatī-bhūmi*).
The dwelling in higher wisdom associated with the truths is the fifth stage, the Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjaya*).

The dwelling in higher wisdom associated with the cessation of the flow of dependent origination is the sixth stage, the Manifest (*abhimukhī*). The dwelling in signlessness with effort is the seventh stage, the Far-Reaching (*dūraṅgamā*).
These six stages taken together are called the stages of practicing correct conduct; that is to say, in the second stage, one cultivates pure observance free from transgressions.
The three types of action (karma) receive the designation "preeminent. There are three kinds: first, the subtle ethical discipline (*śīla*) of mental action.

Because the Bodhisattva does not give rise to the appearance of transgressing the precepts, all movements of the mind and physical actions are entirely superior ethical discipline; thus, in this stage, the Bodhisattva is able to remain free from the defilements of subtle ethical discipline.
Second, the ethical discipline of abiding in the factors of form (*rūpa-skandha*). In this stage, the Bodhisattva guards against what is improper and ceases evil, attaining [the state of] non-...

Because it manifests ethical discipline (*śīla*), there are three aspects to the abiding in the rules of conduct (*ācāra*). When a bodhisattva on this stage practices and maintains them, they do not violate these rules;

if one violates the rules, that constitutes a transgression of ethical discipline. For these three reasons, it is called the "Abiding in Higher Ethical Discipline" (*adhiśīla*) and the "Abiding in Higher Mind" (*adhicitta*).

Because the third stage is able to abide in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there are three further meanings: first, abiding in the eight characteristics; second, being able to remain free from the regression of concentration; and third...

It can give rise to the three types of wisdom. That is to say, by attaining superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one can produce the light of wisdom; because the light of wisdom is able to destroy darkness.

In the fourth stage (*bhūmi*), one is able to practice the contemplation of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*). In the fifth stage, the Bodhisattva is able to practice the contemplation of the two truths—the ultimate and the conventional—and the four noble truths.
In the sixth stage, the Bodhisattva is able to practice the contemplation of the twelvefold dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). In the seventh stage, the Bodhisattva...
[Sa]. One is able to perform the contemplation of emptiness through the deconstruction of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), yet there still remains preparatory application (*prayoga*).

The fifth stage, the Stage of Certainty (*niyata-bhūmi*), is also called the Abiding Without Preparatory Application and Without Effort (*anābhoga-anābhoga-sthiti*). This occurs in the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*) and possesses three certainties:

first, certainty of lineage (*gotra-niyama*); second, certainty of the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda-niyama*); and third, certainty of non-futile practice (*avandhya-caryā-niyama*). This means that for a Bodhisattva in the eighth stage, effortful application (*prayoga*) has for the first time been severed.
Abiding in the principle of signlessness (*animitta*), all the myriad practices (*sarva-caryā*) progress spontaneously. Moment by moment, there is no passing in vain;
this is called "non-empty practice. The sixth stage is the Stage of Definitive Practice (*niyata-caryā-bhūmi*), also known as the Stage of Unimpeded Understanding (*pratisaṃvid-avasthā*).
Regarding the ninth stage, it means that the Bodhisattvas of this stage realize *dhāraṇī* and unimpeded eloquence (*asaṅga-pratibhāna*), explaining the meanings of the Dharma to benefit others.
Practice. It can pervade the ten directions. In this stage, sentient beings of immeasurable worlds each pose difficult questions to the Bodhisattva using different phrasing and different meanings;
yet the Bodhisattva, by expounding the Dharma in a single word, is able to sever all their doubts.
The eighth stage is called only the "Stage of Certainty" (*niyata-bhūmi*), not the "Stage of Certain Practice. Reaching the ultimate point of the seventh stage is precisely this.
The supreme fulfillment of the Bodhisattva abodes and the Tathāgata abode occurs in the tenth stage and the Buddha stage. In the tenth stage, the cause is perfected;
in the state of Buddhahood, the fruit is perfected. Now, in explaining the bodhisattva practice, we take only the perfection of the cause and not the perfection of the fruit.
When the practice of the tenth stage is fulfilled, the flourishing fruit blossoms, and one arrives at the Buddha stage.
One exhausts the nature of ultimate reality and reaches the source of the *dharmadhātu*. Delusions and karma are both extinguished, and one realizes the boundless fruit.

The treatise states that each of the physical marks and secondary characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) is produced by being drawn forth from infinite and limitless roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). Regarding the four types of bodhisattva practice:

first is the practice of the perfections (*pāramitā*), which refers to the six paramitas; second is the practice of maturing sentient beings, which refers to the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) and the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).
These are the practices of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*). The four bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*) are the six supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*).
Among these, the first two are the practices of the Bodhisattva’s own vehicle (*svayāna*), while the latter two are practices for subduing others.

Regarding the practices of one's own vehicle, there are two: first, practicing the six perfections (*pāramitā*) and so forth to accomplish the practice of self-benefit; second, [the practice of benefiting others].

This refers to accomplishing the practice of benefiting others by cultivating the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*). There are also two types of subduing practices: first, the practice of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).

This is the practice for subduing those of the two vehicles. Śrāvakas cultivate the dharmas such as the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*), bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), and factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) as their own personal practice. Since a Bodhisattva is already the teacher of the five destinies and acts within the three realms...
Lord, there is not a single dharma that he does not know; therefore, he subdues those of the two vehicles.
If one does not cultivate those practices of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma), the śrāvakas will say, "The Bodhisattva does not know the practice of our factors of enlightenment."

Only the six perfections, the four means of integration, and so forth, constitute the practice of a bodhisattva; I do not know [of any other]. If one lacks either this or that, the practice should be equalized.
For this reason, one cultivates those practices to subdue the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), for such is not the practice performed by a bodhisattva.
Second is the practice of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) to subdue non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Most non-Buddhists rely extensively upon supernatural powers.
He acts for the sake of virtue; while in the world, he transforms sentient beings, and many worldly fools take refuge in him.

This commentary relies on that Bodhisattva’s possession of both types of practice to transform all sentient beings, causing them to turn away from the heterodox and enter the orthodox. It is also, among the eighteen kinds of opposition, included within the category of "restraining the supernatural powers of others."
Regarding the phrase "according to what is appropriate" and so forth: Question: It would suffice merely to clarify the four bodhisattva practices of the seventh stage;

why is it necessary to correlate them with the subsequent scriptural text? Answer: It is for the purpose of manifesting the practices. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* was preached for this reason; the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

The One Vehicle (Ekayāna) encompasses both cause and fruit. If these were not correlated with the subsequent scriptural passages, the Master of the Commentary feared that people might doubt whether the seven stages and four bodhisattvas—stated to be the causes of the One Vehicle—actually exist within the *Lotus Sūtra* (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*) or not.
Therefore, he now correlates them with the subsequent scriptural passages to demonstrate that this sūtra exhaustively encompasses both the causes and the fruits; yet, this correlation is not fixed.
Regarding their status, they are assigned according to their correspondence with the meaning. As for those of the "One-Kind Nature" (ekajātīya-bhūmi), the *Vṛṣṭyupama-sūtra* states:
"Just as all trees, whether large or small, receive [rain] according to their superior, middling, or inferior [capacity], yet each is called 'unsurpassed' in its seed.

Furthermore, in the "Chapter on the Dharma Master," it is said that the eight classes of beings received their predictions; such individuals as these all heard even a single phrase of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* before the Buddha.

One verse: the generation of the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is called the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra-bhūmi*). Second, the stage of practice through resolute conviction (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*) consists of the provisions (*saṃbhāra*) and the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
As the Sūtra says: "Furthermore, there were sentient beings as numerous as the atoms in eight worlds who generated the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;

this refers to the stage of provisions (*saṃbhāra-avasthā*). And as the Sūtra says: "Furthermore, there were Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in four sets of four-continent worlds. (The fourth [stage]...)
"Shall attain equality in this life" refers to the stage of application (*prayoga*). The *Bukōhon* (Chapter on Not Despising) states:

"Even upon seeing the fourfold assembly, he would intentionally go to pay them homage and say: 'I do not dare to despise you. The Master of the Treatise assigns this to the stage of equipment (*sambhāra*).
At the time of his death, he fully heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in twenty thousand [stanzas] as preached before the Buddha Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja.

He is able to receive and uphold ten trillion verses. He immediately attains the aforementioned purity of the six sense faculties and further increases his lifespan by two hundred trillion nayutas of years.
This stage of applied practice (*prayoga-avasthā*), combined with the preceding two stages, constitutes the entire Stage of Practice through Superior Conviction (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*).
Third, regarding the Stage of Pure Superior Intention (*śuddhādhyāśaya-bhūmi*): the Sūtra says that when the long duration of the Tathāgata’s lifespan was being proclaimed, the six...
One hundred and eighty trillion nayutas of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

This is the realization of the four unshakeable faiths at the first stage; it is called the Stage of Supreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). They were born into the family of the Tathāgata and dwelt in the Stage of Supreme Joy.

At this time, one is called a true son of the Buddha. If these refer to the three stages of the worthy ones prior to the [first] bhūmi, they are the thirty individuals of the noble embryo (*āryagarbha*) within the stage of subduing patience (*vinirdhāvana-kṣānti*), who are as if still in the womb and have not yet been born.

Regarding those on the four practices and the stage of correct practice, from the initial stage of abiding in the mind and emerging from the mind up until the completion of the seventh bhūmi, the Sūtra says: "Furthermore, there are a thousandfold more bodhisattva-mahāsattvas."
One attains the dhāraṇī-door of hearing and retaining. This initial attainment occurs in the third bhūmi; its continuity occurs in the ninth bhūmi;
and its perfection occurs in the Buddha-bhūmi. Although the first three bhūmis share the same mundane correct practice, the scriptural text mentions only those below the third bhūmi.
The Sūtra speaks of "various marks" (*lakṣaṇa*). Since these marks pervade the ten stages (*bhūmi*), they may thus be understood to extend through the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages as well.
The Sūtra further states: "There were also bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as numerous as the atoms in a world-system, who attained hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *āvartana-dhāraṇī* gates.

This refers to the seventh stage, where one attains correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*) at times; therein, one slightly attains the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and correctly contemplates emptiness.

At that time, one slightly attains the contemplation of existence (*bhāva*) and revolves within the cycle of emptiness and existence; this is called the *Svādhiṣṭhāna-dhāraṇī*. Regarding the "five stages of certainty," the Sūtra states:
"Furthermore, there were Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, as numerous as the atoms in three thousand great thousandfold world systems, who were able to turn the non-retrogressive wheel of Dharma.

The Commentary states: "Possessing the four types of non-retrogression, this corresponds to the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*). As for the previous mention of "attaining the dharma of non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma*), [it refers to this stage].

Regarding patience (*kṣānti*): from the first through the fifth stages (*bhūmi*), there is much contemplation with signs (*sanimitta-bhāvanā*) and little contemplation without signs (*animitta-bhāvanā*).

In the sixth stage, contemplation without signs is still slight. In the seventh stage, it is purely contemplation without signs; yet, although it is signless, it is characterized by effortful activity (*sābhoga-pracāra*).

Upon reaching the eighth stage, one enters the state of signlessness without effort (*animitta-anābhoga-avasthā*), which is called "unfailing practice" (*amogha-caryā*), because one proceeds spontaneously within the swift current of the Dharma. Thus, one attains mastery over form (*rūpa-vaśitā*). That is to say—

The co-nascent, unconditioned, and mentally produced body manifests forms according to the various types of beings, and so forth. Regarding the sixth stage, the Stage of Definite Practice (*niyata-caryā-bhūmi*):
this refers to the ninth stage, known as the Great Dharma Preacher (*mahā-dharmabhāṇaka*). As the Sūtra says:

"Furthermore, there were Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, as numerous as the atoms in a world-system, who had attained the unhindered eloquence of joyful speech (*pratibhāna*), the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the seven analytical knowledges, and the preaching of the Dharma. These Bodhisattvas have attained...

They possess mastery over the mind and preach the Dharma without hindrance. Regarding the seventh, those who have reached the stage of ultimate perfection: first is the perfection of cause. As the Sūtra says:
"Furthermore, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in two thousand intermediate lands, who were able to turn the pure wheel of the Dharma."

The Master of the Commentary (*śāstrakāra*) explains that being unstained and free from hindrances constitutes the essence of purity; this corresponds to the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), the culmination of the two fruits.
As stated in the *Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta* and the *Tri-kāya-sūtra*, this represents the culmination of the fruit. When correlated with the practices of the four types of bodhisattvas:

first, the practitioner of the perfections (*pāramitā*). The Sūtra says: "There are those who practice giving gold, silver, coral, and so forth. Second, the practitioner who brings sentient beings to maturity.
Regarding "practice": the sutra states that this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is the excellent medicine for the illnesses of Jambudvīpa. Regarding "the practice of the factors of *sambodhi*":
the sutra states that [the Bodhisattva] holds a vessel for removing filth in his right hand. *Bodhi* is the fruit; "factors" (*aṅga*) has the meaning of cause.

Regarding the four bases of spiritual power (*ṛddhipāda*), the falling of the four kinds of flowers from heaven, the shaking of the earth, the emission of light, the flowing forth of water, and so on, it is said:

"These should correspond to the *pādas* (practices), yet they are specifically assigned to the *bhūmis* (stages). The *bhūmi* serves as the basis, while the *pāda* is that which is cultivated. By citing the *bhūmi*, the *pāda* is revealed;
thus the meaning of the *pāda* is established. (End of section on causes).

Regarding the statement that "the fruit" refers to the stage of Buddhahood, namely *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*: Question: Since the original [treatise] already clarifies the practices (*caryā*), why is it necessary to speak of the fruit?

Answer: Although the practices are discussed, if the fruit were not made clear, toward what would one aspire and proceed? Therefore, the fruit is explained next so that there may be a destination toward which one can turn.

There are four types of *bodhi*, which are those obtained through transformation and those obtained through arising. As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "First is the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*)."

The corresponding mental state (*citta-pakṣa*) refers to this state of mind which is free from all conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Its objects of perception (*ālambana*) and modes of activity (*ākāra*) are subtle and difficult to discern.

It is non-forgetful and non-deluded; its essence and nature are further purified, being free from all obstructive defilements. It is a pure, perfect excellence that serves as the support for both the manifest and the seeds.
It is capable of manifesting and generating the reflections of bodies, lands, and wisdom, continuing without interval or interruption until the end of the future. As it is said:
The Great Perfect Mirror manifests all manner of forms and images; it is named according to this metaphor. Second is the mental state associated with the Wisdom of Equality.
This means that this mental state contemplates all phenomena and all sentient beings—self and others—as entirely equal.

It is constantly associated with great compassion and other such qualities, manifesting various images of enjoyment-bodies (*saṃbhogakāya*) and their lands according to the inclinations of sentient beings.
Distinct. It is the uncommon basis of the wondrous wisdom of observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*), established by non-abiding nirvāṇa.
It is a single-flavored continuity that extends to the end of the future. Regarding the mental states associated with this wondrous wisdom of observation:

these mental states skillfully observe the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena, functioning without obstruction. They encompass and observe immeasurable doors of dhāraṇī and meditative concentration (*samādhi*), as well as their...
It gives rise to the jewels of merit and virtue. Within the great assemblies, it manifests an infinite variety of activities with complete mastery.
It rains down the great rain of Dharma, cuts through all doubts, and causes all sentient beings to obtain benefit and happiness. Named according to its cause, this is the fourth:
the mental state associated with the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*). That is to say, this mental state desires to bring benefit and happiness to all beings.
Out of compassion, they universally manifest various transformations of the three karmas throughout the ten directions to accomplish the deeds required by their original vow-power.

These names are established based on their respective causes. Question: At what stage do these four wisdoms first arise? Answer: The two wisdoms of wondrous sameness (*miao-ting*) first arise at the first stage (*bhūmi*).

The remaining two categories of wisdom arise only at the stage of fruition (*phala*). Question: Which seeds—original or new—give rise to them? Answer: The two wisdoms of wondrous sameness... [arise from both].
Regarding the two knowledges: in the first moment, there is only the original [knowledge]; in the second moment, both the original and the newly arisen arise together.
The same applies to the other two knowledges. As for the four types of *nirvāṇa*, these refer to that which is manifested among those attained through transformation.

First is the *nirvāṇa* of the originally pure intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-viśuddha-nirvāṇa*), which refers to the principle of *tathatā* (suchness) as it corresponds to all phenomena; although it is susceptible to defilement, it remains...
It is pure by nature, endowed with immeasurable and subtle merits, without arising or ceasing, and as serene as empty space.
It is equally shared by all sentient beings and is neither identical to nor different from all phenomena. It is free from all marks and all conceptualization;
the paths of investigation and analysis are cut off, and the way of names and words is severed. It is realized only within the self-awareness of true noble ones.

Its nature is fundamentally quiescent; therefore, it is called *nirvāṇa*. Second is *nirvāṇa with remainder*. This refers to true suchness (*tathatā*) from which the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) have been eliminated.
Although there remains a subtle suffering because its basis has not yet been extinguished, its shadow is eternally stilled; thus, it is called *nirvāṇa*.

This is explained in reference to the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). Alternatively, regarding the physical and mental qualities of the Tathāgata’s Buddha-body, their untainted basis (*anāsrava-āśraya*) is [the state where] the tainted [basis] has ceased.
...the remainder. Although there is no actual basis, it appears as if there were; therefore, it is so called. Third is *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder).

This refers to the emergence from the suffering of birth and death within true suchness (*tathatā*). Once the afflictions (*kleśa*) have been exhausted, the remaining basis (*upadhi*) is also extinguished, and all sufferings are eternally stilled;

hence it is named "nirvana. This is also discussed in relation to the two vehicles (*yāna*). At the time when the Buddha’s path of liberation arises, all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and out-flowing (*āsrava*) wholesome [states]...

The habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and the inferior outflow-free states (*anāsrava*) are both permanently abandoned; this is called "nirvana without remainder" (*nirupadhiśeṣa*). Because of these two types, the meanings of parinirvāṇa differ.

Thus, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* says: "Abandoning impermanent form is precisely 'without remainder. It is because of this distinction that [the nirvana of a Buddha] differs from the nirvana with and without remainder attained by those of the Two Vehicles.
Fourth is "non-abiding nirvana" (*apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa*), which refers to True Suchness (*tathatā*) emerging from...

Knowing the obstacles, they are constantly assisted by great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). Because of this, they do not abide in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa, but benefit sentient beings until the end of the future.
While active, they are eternally quiescent; therefore, it is called "nirvāṇa. Because of great compassion, they do not abide in nirvāṇa;
because of great wisdom, they do not abide in saṃsāra. This is called "non-abiding nirvāṇa" (*apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa*). All sentient beings...
All possess the first [of these four]. Those of the two vehicles who have attained the stage of no-more-learning may possess the first three; only I, the Tathāgata, can be said to possess all four.

Alternatively, "nirvāṇa" refers to that which is accomplished by the three matters, such as the Great Parinirvāṇa. Regarding its presence within the three bodies: the first is the *svābhāvikakāya* (self-nature body).
This refers to the pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Second, the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) has two aspects.

First is the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*), which refers to the infinite, true, and eternal merits attained by all Tathāgatas through the cultivation of merit and wisdom over three incalculable eons; its mind is identical to the dharma-realm.
Its magnitude is equal to empty space; its physical form is perfectly round and likewise limitless. Until the end of the future, it constantly experiences the bliss of the Dharma.

Second is the Body of Enjoyment for Others (*para-sambhogakāya*), which refers to the various Tathāgatas manifesting ten grades of bodies for the enjoyment of others according to the needs of Bodhisattvas on the ten stages.
They turn the wheel of the sublime Dharma, enabling others to enjoy the bliss of the Mahāyāna; thus it is called the Body of Enjoyment for Others.

The union of these [two], self and other, is called the *saṃbhogakāya* (Enjoyment Body). Third is the *nirmāṇakāya* (Transformation Body), which refers to the manifestation of supernatural powers and the preaching of the Dharma by all Tathāgatas in accordance with the various classes of beings—such as those on the stages, the two vehicles, and ordinary worldlings—and is thus named the Transformation Body. Question:

What is meant by "abiding within" among the three bodies? Answer: That which was previously termed *nirvāṇa* is the *svābhāvikakāya* (Essential Body); that which was previously termed *bodhi* (Awakening) is the *svasaṃbhogakāya* (Self-Enjoyment Body).
Regarding the [three] bodies: the remaining two bodies are merely manifestations of the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*) and are not real.
If one discusses the Dharma-body as the nirvāṇa of the three matters, it is of one kind, namely the essential body (*svabhāvakāya*). Great Prajñā is the self-enjoyment body.
Liberation is common to all three bodies.

Regarding the statement that "all these are fully subsumed," there are various excerpts that explain this in the same manner as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only) concerning the five dharmas and the subsumption of the three bodies (*trikāya*).

Specifically, it states that the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) and the Pure Dharma Realm (*dharmadhātu*) subsume the Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*), while the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*) subsumes the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*).

The interpretation that the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) subsumes both the great and small transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) is incorrect. The correct meaning states: the pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) subsumes the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*);

the great perfect mirror wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) subsumes the self-enjoyment reward body (*svasaṃbhoga-kāya*); the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*) subsumes the other-enjoyment body (*parasaṃbhoga-kāya*);

the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done subsumes the great and small transformation bodies; and the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) is taught in relation to both the pure and impure lands.
Fazheng: This meaning refers to the bodhi, nirvāṇa, and the three bodies within the sutra. The sutra states that all bodhisattvas' anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi belongs to this sutra;
that is to say, it is the opening, revealing, and awakening of the three [bodies] within the "Expedient Means" chapter of this sutra.
The "Chapter on Lifespan" (Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta) subsumes the three types of *bodhi* taught in all the scriptures, as well as *nirvāṇa* and the three bodies (*trikāya*).
Therefore, it is said that these are all fully encompassed therein.

Regarding the phrase "again, three cycles" (*san-zhōu*): "cycle" (*zhōu*) signifies being complete and perfect. As the World-Honored One taught the Dharma, Śāriputra attained realization, the Tathāgata confirmed his attainment and bestowed a prophecy;
only when these necessary tasks were fulfilled could the cycle be considered complete. The first twelve chapters clarify the realm (*viṣaya*) of the One Vehicle.

From the "Expedient Means" chapter (*upāya-paṭala*) to the "Encouragement to Maintain" chapter (*dhāraṇī-paṭala*), the subsequent two chapters clarify the practice (*caryā*) of the One Vehicle. Peace... [text ends]

The "Chapter on Joy" explains the practice of the One Vehicle; the "Chapter on the Emergence" identifies the practitioners capable of that practice. Both the practitioner and the practice are entirely the practice of the One Vehicle.
The five chapters from "Life Span" onward clarify the fruit of the One Vehicle. The "Life Span" chapter clarifies the fruit of ultimate purity, perfection, and luminosity;
continuing through to the "Chapter on Never-Despising," it cites those who have already realized this fruit.

Regarding the phrase "clarifying the object and so forth": Question: Why is it necessary to speak of the three—object (*viṣaya*), practice (*caryā*), and fruit (*phala*)? Answer: The commentary states that clarifying the object causes one to give rise to the mind of a śrāvaka and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "thereby one anticipates [the goal]": "anticipates" (*qi*) means to expect or aim for. It means that by practicing the bodhisattva path, one subsequently expects to attain Buddhahood.
This refers to the merit of the fruit.
The statement "to manifest for the sake of the Bodhisattvas" is the concluding summary.

*Fahua jing xuanyan yaoji*, Scroll Four.

Regarding the phrase "benefiting the present and the future": this refers to the present and the future in terms of both the current and the subsequent. That which is taken up here is the assembly on Vulture Peak, where the World-Honored One...
At the time of preaching this sutra, all sentient beings in the single assembly who hear the sutra and obtain benefit—whether in terms of causes or fruits—all derive benefit for the present.

From the time after the dispersal of the assembly until the Tathāgata’s thirty-fifth year and his parinirvāṇa, continuing until the future time when the human lifespan reaches sixty thousand years, all those who hear the sutra and obtain benefit during that interval derive benefit for the future. Thus the Tathāgata perceives...

Present-day sentient beings possess great benefit. Seeing that future sentient beings will hear this sutra and obtain immeasurable benefit, the Tathāgata, for the sake of benefiting those of the future, preached this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. Master Zhao says: "It is also fitting that there was benefit for the past;

when the Constantly Non-Disparaging Bodhisattva previously conferred predictions upon the fourfold assembly, that was precisely the benefit for the past. Although one knows this to be so, it does not arise solely from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
This refers to the benefit (*hita*).

Regarding the phrase "the single assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*," this precisely identifies the temporal occasion. The phrase "the single assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*" explains the character "now" (*jin*);
the two phrases "it is appropriate to hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and thereby obtain benefit" explain the character "benefit" (*li*). Furthermore, it says "the *Dharma*..."

Regarding those who gather for this single assembly: as for the ordinary and holy beings who obtain benefit, and the individuals who gain profit—namely, those whose faculties are such that they are fit to hear the *Lotus Sūtra* and thereby attain benefit—this precisely clarifies the attainment of benefit. Furthermore, it is also the teaching that brings about such benefit.
It is because the World-Honored One perceives that such benefit exists that he preaches this sūtra.

The phrase "there are two such types" refers to those who obtained benefit from hearing the sutra mentioned previously; that is, within this single assembly of the *Lotus Sutra*, there were these two types of people who gained benefit from hearing the sutra.

Regarding the phrase "the fruit, the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), the benefit (*hita*), and so forth": "fruit" refers to the qualities within the fruit; the fruit itself is the fruit of Buddhahood (*buddhatva*). "Prediction" means detailed explanation;

it is the prediction of that fruit, thus following the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound. Alternatively, "prediction" is identical to "benefit," following the *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound. As for "presently realized benefit":

The merits within the causal stage are realized in the present; "realization in the present" (a *tatpuruṣa* compound) or "present realization" (meaning benefit)—both interpretations are acceptable—and this refers precisely to the merits within the causal stage.
Question: Within this section, why is it said that the benefits of the fruit are recorded?

How does this differ from the previous "Record of Manifestation" (Zhāngjì)? The answer, as cited in the *Shè* (Compendium), states: The former provides a general discourse on the bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*), while the latter section specifically explains the benefits;

therefore, they are divided into two sections. Furthermore, it is explained that the former section concerns the Dharma, whereas this section concerns persons; thus, a distinction is established. Question:

Having heard the sūtra and attained the prediction of the fruit, one must still pass through three great eons before finally attaining the fruit of Buddhahood. Why, then, is this not called "attaining benefit"?
Regarding "subsequent benefit": the answer is that since it is obtained from the present, it is likewise categorized as a benefit received in the present.

However, within this category of benefits received in the present, there are two meanings in the text: the merits attained within the fruit are called "attainment of the fruit" (phala-prāpti), while the merits within the cause are called "benefit of present realization" (pratyakṣa-lābha).
Regarding the phrase "it constitutes the three capacities," a question is asked: *Where is the locus of the merit and benefit of attaining the fruit?* The answer states:
The commentary says, "it constitutes the three capacities," meaning that the three cycles (*tri-parivarta*) are precisely the locus where benefit is obtained.

The World-Honored One preached the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) in three cycles, thereby reconciling and subverting duality. Second, this refers to reconciling the teaching, principle, practice, and fruit. To first reconcile the teaching: "In this [teaching] of mine... [and so forth].
The ninefold teachings were expounded in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings; that they take entry into the Mahāyāna as their foundation is the convergence of the teachings (*jiao*).

"What you have attained is not extinction" refers to the Buddha’s omniscience; this is the convergence of the principle (*li*). "The path you practice is the bodhisattva way" is the convergence of the practice (*xing*).
The convergence of the practices cultivated by those of the two vehicles as being the cause of the Mahāyāna is called the second [convergence]. [The metaphors of] the sheep and the deer...

The "Vehicle" (yāna) refers to the realization of the fruit. "Breaking the two" means breaking through their attachment to the Two Vehicles as being ultimate and lacking true nature, causing them to return to the Great Vehicle;

this is called "breaking the two. Regarding the three cycles of teaching, all of them break [the duality]: the first cycle says, "In the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the One Vehicle Dharma;
there is neither a second nor a third, except for the Buddha’s skillful means. The second cycle says, "Furthermore, there is no..."
Regarding the other vehicles, setting aside the skillful means taught by the Tathāgatas, the third cycle states: "Because they are places of rest, two [vehicles] are spoken of. It further states:

"In the world, there are no two vehicles that attain extinction (*nirvāṇa*). This "convergence" refers to converging upon the essence of the Dharma; it does not destroy the essence of the Dharma, but merely destroys that grasping mind.

Regarding the phrase "the lower part of the 'Expedient Means' chapter" and so forth: this refers to the scope of the first cycle (*prathama-parivarta*). "Cycle" (*parivarta*) carries the meaning of being complete and fully perfected. It consists of four textual sections:

the formal teaching, the comprehension, the corroboration, and the bestowal of prophecy. This is termed a "cycle" because the task of establishing that the Śrāvakas shall attain Buddhahood is completed.
Within this section, there is not only the bestowal of prophecy, but it also concurrently analyzes the profound and esoteric meanings. Thus concludes the topical outline for the first cycle.
It consists of four parts. The first two are profound and were proclaimed first to awaken the minds of the assembly in the secret district.

These have two sections. The first, the prose section, is divided into two: first, praising the excellence of the Dharma taught; second, praising the excellence of the Tathāgata’s body as the teacher capable of teaching the Dharma.

This latter part has two sub-sections. First, indicating the excellence, which is divided into two: first, manifesting mastery by arising from meditative concentration; second, addressing Śāriputra to formally present what is to be said.
The Sūtra says: "At that time, the World-Honored One arose serenely from samādhi and proceeded to that which cannot be known. Next, it explains this supreme excellence.

The Sūtra asks: "For what reason? It refers to the eight passages on profound depth, stating that the Buddha had personally attended upon hundreds of thousands of millions of [Buddhas], and that the Dharma he realized and preached was sublime.
Finally, it praises the Tathāgata as the Teacher who is capable of both realizing and preaching the Dharma.
Excellently marvelous. The Sūtra says: "Śāriputra, since my attainment of Buddhahood, through various causes and conditions...
and so forth. Second, the fourfold assembly was struck with wonder and doubt; this gave rise to the request of Śāriputra. The Sūtra says:

"At that time, within the great assembly, there were śrāvakas and arhats whose outflows were exhausted," up to "the Unsurpassed Honored One among Two-legged Beings" (the excellent sūtra does not end here, as in the original). Third, the cycle.

This reveals the true reality (*dharmatā*). The initial prose section has two parts: first, it clarifies the two types of prediction (*vyākaraṇa*); second, from the passage on the "five turbidities" (*pañca-kāṣāya*) onwards, it properly refutes the four doubts.

Regarding the first two predictions: the first consists of granting a prediction, giving permission, and providing acceptance. As the Sūtra says: "Since you have already made your earnest request three times, how could I not speak?
The latter two constitute the actual bestowal of the prediction. This proper explanation has six points; the first is to cause those who have not yet heard [the teaching] to...
Upon hearing this, he marveled at the rarity of the Dharma. The Sūtra states: "Such a wondrous Dharma as this is preached by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, only from time to time.
Second, it is stated that the intent behind the Buddhas' preaching of the Dharma according to what is appropriate is difficult to understand. Third, regarding the meaning upon which it relies:

first, as for the heading, the Sūtra says, "The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do so solely for the sake of the one great cause and condition," and so forth; second, as for the subsequent explanation, the Sūtra...

It says: "Śāriputra, what is meant by 'the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones'? From the passage beginning 'solely for the sake of one great causal matter' [downward], the fourth point, 'causing them to abide,' encourages them to come and abide within the One Vehicle. The Sūtra says:
'Śāriputra, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma to sentient beings solely by means of the Buddha Vehicle; there is no other vehicle, whether two or three. [End of section]
Regarding the five points based on the Dharma: the Sūtra says, "Śāriputra, all the teachings of the Buddhas of the ten directions are likewise," and so forth.
Regarding the sixth, the negation: it negates and dispels both types of grasping and both types of reality.

The Sūtra says, "Śāriputra, within the worlds of the ten directions, there is not even the Two Vehicles, let alone [the Three Vehicles]," and so forth. (The preceding six sections clarify the two records. Following this, from "the five turbidities" onwards, the four [graspings] are directly refuted.
Doubts. The first doubt asks: At what time did the Buddha appear? [The answer is: "All Buddhas appear in the world of the five turbidities. The second asks:

How is one to know of those with overweening pride? [The answer is: "If my disciples claim for themselves to be Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and so forth... The third asks: How can one be fit to preach? Regarding the initial presentation of the answers:

The initial heading states: "(Except after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when there is no present Buddha...). The commentary explains: "Why is this so? Because after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, [those who] uphold such sutras as these...

The fourth section asks: "How does one not become a person who speaks falsely? The sutra says: "You all should with single-mindedness believe, understand, and uphold the Buddha’s words... The six preceding sections collectively clarify this true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
From here, the fourth [section] encourages the arousal of a joyful mind. The sutra says: "Since you already know the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones..."

The first section is "The Teacher’s Instruction" (from "At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra" downward). The second is "Śāriputra’s Comprehension and Understanding" (from "At that time, Śāriputra leaped for joy" downward).

The third is "The Buddha’s Reiteration and Confirmation" (from "At that time, the Buddha told Śāriputra: 'I now, among devas, humans, śramaṇas,' etc., downward). The fourth is "Providing the Basis for Him" (from "Śāriputra, in a future age, after immeasurable [eons]...
downward), continuing until "At that time, the fourfold assembly... downward. All of these constitute the first cycle of teaching.

Regarding the statement in the "Parable Chapter" that "The Tathāgata is likewise," and so forth: first is the formal presentation of the parable (the section beginning with "Just as in a kingdom, city, or village");

second is the demonstration that [the Buddha's power] is not limited; third is the contemplation of how to deliver [beings]; and fourth is the formal teaching of the three vehicles (which may be understood without citing further scriptures).

Regarding the phrase "in the *Adhimukty-adhikāra*," there are three parts. First is the narration of the joy and reverence of the four individuals, beginning from "At that time, the Venerable Subhūti...
and so forth. Second is the summary and exposition by the four individuals (the subsequent sections may be understood accordingly).
Regarding the account of the bestowal of the prophecy upon Mahākāśyapa: at that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, he addressed the great assembly, proclaiming these words:
"This disciple of mine, Mahākāśyapa, shall in a future age behold three hundred trillion Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and eventually attain Buddhahood as the Tathāgata named Prabhāsa."
...and so forth. Subhūti shall be named Mingxiang (Name-Aspect). Kātyāyana shall attain Buddhahood and be named Yaṃbūdīpakanakaprabha Tathāgata.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana shall attain Buddhahood and be named Tamālapatracandanagandha Tathāgata.
The middle-capacity [beings] are recorded as having attained realization.

Regarding the statement that the third cycle consists of the "Parable of the City of Illusion" chapter and others, it is divided into four parts. First, within the main section using the parable to transform [the disciples], there are two sub-sections.

First, he explains their past causes, causing them to remember their regression from the Great Vehicle and their inclination toward the Small Vehicle. Second, he reveals their present fruits, causing them to abandon their provisional [attainments].
Taking up the main text, the first section is divided into two parts. First, the narration of past connections that relate to the Buddha’s own life story;

second, the narration of past connections that relate to the disciples’ lives. The first of these is further divided into two: first, one prose passage and one verse stating how long ago the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū lived;
second, from the words "He addressed the bhikṣus," the actual account of those events, which is divided into four parts. The first...
The Buddha’s lifespan since attaining enlightenment; the second turning of the wheel of the True Dharma; the three sons successively transmitting the lamp;

and the fourth assembly becoming the present Buddha—these four distinct sections precisely clarify those events. First, it clarifies the duration of time from the Great Penetrating Wisdom Buddha until the present; subsequently, it precisely clarifies those events.

In total, this first part explains the past causes, intending to cause [beings] who have regressed from the Great Vehicle to turn toward the Small Vehicle, and later reveals the present fruit, intending to...

One should know that this involves relinquishing the provisional to grasp the real, transforming the illustrative into the factual, and employing the discourse of the Dharma, the discourse of parables, and the combined discourse; in sum, these use parables to correctly transform and guide.

Next, the "Chapter on the Bestowal of Prophecies upon the Five Hundred Disciples" is divided into three parts: the disciples' realization and understanding, the Buddha’s confirmation and completion, and the bestowal of the prophecies.
There are four types of realization: first, realizing the preaching of the Dharma; second, realizing the bestowal of predictions; third, realizing past causes and conditions;
and fourth, realizing supernatural powers. Next is the description of confirmation: asking the assembly whether they see [the Buddha], praising his present virtues, and praising his past virtues.
Regarding the statement that he immediately conferred [predictions] upon the five hundred disciples and others:

Pūrṇa shall attain Buddhahood after the passage of immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, and his name shall be Dharmaprabhāsa. Next, the one thousand two hundred arhats such as Cunda and others shall be named Samantaprabhāsa.

Furthermore, the "Chapter on the Prediction for Learners and Non-learners" states: Ānanda shall be named Sāgarabuddhi-vaiśvāsika-abhijñārāja (King of Ocean-like Wisdom and Sovereign Supernatural Powers). Rā... [text fragment]
Ghoṣila was named Tādacintyavajrapadmarāja Tathāgata; two thousand others shared the name Ratnākara.
This refers to the present assembly. The meaning is that the scope of what has been expounded throughout the three previous turnings of the wheel was precisely for the sake of the śrāvakas.
Regarding the statement, "Although it is known that the six bases (ṣaḍāyatana) are manifested," this refers to the inclusion [of these matters] within the six types of prediction (vyākaraṇa).
The World-Honored One’s threefold exposition of the One Vehicle was entirely for the purpose of bestowing predictions upon the śrāvakas. As the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu also states:

those of superior and middling faculties each receive their predictions individually, whereas those of inferior faculties—the five hundred, the one thousand, and the two hundred—receive their predictions in a single location; yet in none of these cases is a formal prediction established.
Regarding the title: it is actually the Master of the Commentary (*śāstrakāra*) who has established these six names for the records (*ṭīkā*).

Although the single character "though" (*sui*) contains both the meanings of gain and loss, when a written text carries this character, it implies two possibilities. Within the headings of the text, listing the names of the six records constitutes a gain;

however, in the present case, only five records are taken up while the name of the remaining one record is not taken up—this constitutes a loss. Second, [the phrase] "although" (*suiran*) generally...

There are six types of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*). Among them, some obtain a prediction through hearing the sutras, while others obtain a prediction without hearing the sutras. A third [source] states:
although it is known that there are six types of predictions in total, among them, some are for those who are currently [spiritually] sharp, while others are not for those who are currently sharp.

This is precisely the prediction based on causes (*hetu-vyākaraṇa*). The following two points provide the explanation. However, according to the flow of the text, once the two headings have been established in succession, one should proceed directly to the discourse.
Yet, because the fifth prediction concerns the intensity of craving, the sixth prediction is separated by the intervening text.
This very word "thus" (*ran*) also arises from the preceding word "although" (*sui*), and by placing this word "thus" here, it becomes non-definitive. Thus...

The text contains two interpretive perspectives. First, although it is known that the bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) consists of six sections in total, the first five are predictions of the fruit, while the sixth is a prediction concerning the possession of causes;
it is a prediction regarding the causes. Second, although there are six sections in the prediction...

However, the first five types of prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) pertain to the present, while the sixth, which possesses the causes, concerns past events. This also serves as a general response to the objection.

Regarding the inquiry into the "sharpness" (*tīkṣṇatva*) of the present, the "prediction of fruit" (*phala-vyākaraṇa*) is explained; specifically, within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-śāstra*, there are six kinds of predictions.

How many of these belong to this section on the "prediction of fruit"? The answer, as stated in the commentary (*ṭīkā*), is that although it is known and so forth, they are not fixed; the meaning is inclusive.
Regarding "taking and discarding, gain and loss" as a "manifestation": this means to clearly instruct and reveal.

While the intent is consistent with the *Fahua lun* (Treatise on the Lotus Sutra), which speaks of "manifestations and bestowals of prediction in six ways," the first five predictions are included here as the fruit-prediction for those who have gathered the benefits;
the sixth, however, possesses the causes and is not subsumed within this. Therefore, taking the first five predictions and discarding the sixth, it says, "although it mentions... and so forth.
The first five predictions of Buddhahood are termed "attainment" (*prāpti*), while the sixth prediction of Bodhisattvahood is termed "distinct" (*viśeṣa*).

Alternatively, the first three and the fifth are termed "attainment" because they receive the prediction through hearing the sūtras; the fourth and the sixth are termed "distinct" because they do not receive the prediction through hearing the sūtras.
This concludes the response to the introductory text, which also states that the six predictions are explained by way of subsumption.
The term "one" refers to the individual prediction (*vyākaraṇa*); this is the heading. "Śāriputra and others" identifies those who have received the prediction.

"Known by all" expresses the meaning of receiving an individual prediction; because kings, princes, ministers, commoners, and even the Brahmā kings recognize them, they are known for their physical form, yet do not know their virtues, or they may know their virtues but... [do not know their future destiny].
They do not recognize his form. There are those who recognize his form and also know his virtue; for this reason, the *Śūtra* says he is "known by all.

There are two distinct meanings for why he is recorded separately: first, because he is known by all, he is recorded separately; second, because his name and title are different, he is recorded separately.
For example, Śāriputra’s title is Huaguang (Flower Light), while Kāśyapa’s name is Guangming (Radiant Light), and Subhūti’s...
Their titles were designated as follows: Kātyāyana was named Jambūdvīpa-suvarṇaprabhāsa; Mahāmaudgalyāyana was titled Tamālapatracandanagandha.
Because their names were distinct, they were each given separate records. Thus, there is a distinction in name, a distinction in scope, and a distinction in faculties.
The three meanings are distinct.
Regarding the statement "the two are recorded together," this is the heading. As for "Pūrṇa and others," this identifies those who are recorded together;
there are two interpretations of this. First, it is said that the five hundred are distinct from the twelve hundred. Second, it is said that the five hundred are identical to the twelve hundred.
It is correct that they are included among the "one hundred. Question: How is this known? Answer: Because the scriptural text is thus.

As for those five hundred arhats, they were successively granted the prediction (vyākaraṇa) of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; the remaining śrāvakas are subsumed within the "seven hundred" who share the same name, which expresses the meaning of receiving the prediction together.
There is an interpretation which says: "Zhou" means the same root and the same name; "Gao" means the name is lofty.
Regarding these groups: first, the distinct; second, the identical. Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra is titled Dharmaprabha, which is called "the distinct.

Kauṇḍinya, along with the five hundred, one thousand, and two hundred [disciples], are all equally titled Samantaprabha, which is called "the two identical. This is not like the group of those with lofty names, where there is one identical and two distinct.

Two thousand people share the same name, "Ratnalakṣaṇa" (Precious Mark), so their names are identical. Ānanda is titled "Ocean-Mountain Wisdom," and Rāhula is titled "Treading upon Seven-Jeweled Flowers," so their names are distinct.
Question: If this principle is followed, why is the case where there is one shared prediction with distinct individuals not included among the distinct?

And why is the case where there is one shared prediction with identical individuals not subsumed under the identical? Regarding the case where there is one shared prediction with distinct individuals, [the person] named Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra...
Question: The name "Dharma" (法) is distinct from the names of the five hundred thousand and two hundred people; why then is it not included among those recorded as having different names? Answer:

Although the specific instances differ, they are alike in clarifying the name; therefore, it is also called a "record of identical names. Objection: If that were so, then Śāriputra received a prediction with the title "Flower Radiance" (華光), while Mahākāśyapa was titled "Light" (光明);

since these differ in their specific characters yet share the common element "light" (光), they should also be classified as a "record of identical names. Answer: Regarding the discussion of this matter...
The same applies to the record [of the disciples]. The matters must be identical in terms of their scope (*paryanta*), category (*nikāya*), faculty (*indriya*), and name (*nāman*).

In the case of Śāriputra and the four others, although they were identical in scope, faculty, and name, because the three meanings [of their names] differed, they were recorded separately by name alone. Question: In the subsequent record, there is one instance of identity; why is it not subsumed under the section on "identical" [disciples]?

Furthermore, two thousand people shared the same name, "Ratnalakṣaṇa" (寶相); why were they not included within the record of those who are "identical"? Answer: They were not well-known to the general assembly.
Furthermore, regarding those of dull faculties, a prediction given at a later time is called a "subsequent prediction" (*paścādvyañjana*), not a "simultaneous prediction" (*sahavyañjana*). Question:
Ānanda and Rāhula were also well-known to the assembly; why was a subsequent prediction given to them? Answer:

Because Ānanda was still a learner (*śaikṣa*), he is included among those for whom a subsequent prediction is made, rather than being categorized among those for whom a simultaneous prediction is made. Question: Rāhula was also...
Regarding those who have no more to learn (*aśaikṣa*): why are they also included within the subsequent predictions (*paścāt-vyākaraṇa*)? Answer:

In reality, Pūrṇa, Ānanda, and Rāhula are collectively included within the individual predictions (*pratyeka-vyākaraṇa*). This is because they are all transformed *śrāvakas*, intended to lead those of inferior faculties among the actual *śrāvakas*.
For this reason, they are not included in the common prediction (*sādhāraṇa-vyākaraṇa*), but are subsumed within the subsequent predictions. If it were otherwise, [the case of] Pūrṇa...
The Buddha himself praised him, saying: "No one can exhaust the eloquence of the Tathāgata’s discourse; Ānanda’s stage of practice is reckoned to be that of a Bodhisattva of the Ninth Ground.
Furthermore, Ānanda and the World-Honored One simultaneously resolved their minds toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi under the Buddha Śūnyarāja.
Moreover, Rāhula is the Buddha’s son, and in the future, he shall serve as the eldest son of all Buddhas.
Thus we know this was a transformation [of beings]. Five hundred thousand and two hundred people were easy to transform;
only Pūrṇa alone remained. Two thousand people were difficult to transform; therefore, Ānanda and Rāhula together transformed them. Question:
The five hundred thousand and two hundred may be said to share the same name, but how can one person, Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, constitute a "shared prediction" (sādhāraṇavyākaraṇa)? Answer:

Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra was a transformational manifestation; he was not the primary [recipient]. Although the Master of the Treatise (the author) mentions him, his underlying intent is to include the five hundred, the thousand, and the twelve hundred who were the actual primary objects of the teaching, which is termed the "Fivefold Common Record" (*pañca-sādhāraṇa-vyākaraṇa*). This does not refer to Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra. Had the treatise been intended for Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, it would have provided a separate record for him.
This is the profound foresight of the Master of the Treatise. Zhi Miao failed to understand this and consequently made a hasty generalization, stating that although Fa Pu... [text truncated]

They are different. Although the names "Ming" (Brightness) and "Xian" (Manifestation) are the same, it is therefore called a "record of identical names. Question: The name of Subhūti is "Name-Aspect" (Mingxiang), while the two thousand learners and non-learners are named "Jewel-Aspect" (Baoxiang).

Since the aspects of their names are identical, they should constitute a "record of identical records. Answer: The chapters of the sutra are different, and their faculties and natures are also distinct;
thus, this cannot be raised as an objection.
Regarding the phrase "the three [categories] are recorded later," this is the heading. "Learners and non-learners, etc. identifies those who will provide the subsequent records.
"Not well-known to the public, etc. explains the meaning of recording them later. Question: What is the reason they are called "subsequently recorded"? Answer:
The commentary states, "not known to the public," and so forth. First, they are not well-known to the public; second, they share a common name; third, they are [recorded] at a later time.
Commentary: For these three reasons, it is called the "Later Record" (Houji). Question: Ānanda served as an attendant for a long time; Rāhula was the beloved son of the Buddha;
their names ranked among the Ten Holy Ones, and their reputations resounded throughout the Five Regions. Yet you say that such men were not known to the masses.
This is like the light of the sun and moon or the roar of thunder being unable to reach those who are blind or deaf. Answer: To cite many [examples]...

Regarding the inclusion of the minor [categories]: what contradiction is there in the later commentary? Since the faculties (*indriya*), natures (*gotra*), and grades (*pakṣa*) are all identical, they are included within the later commentary.
The treatise does not rely on sequential order; rather, those whose meaning is the same are collected in one place, without excluding what appears later from being subsumed earlier.
Second, regarding the four types of "unanimous" predictions (*avyākṛta*): according to the commentary’s interpretation of the sūtra, with respect to Devadatta, the Tathāgata...
Because there is no enmity or ill will. A sutra says that he addressed the fourfold assembly:
"Devadatta, after the passing of immeasurable kalpas, shall attain Buddhahood and be named Tathāgata Devendra. Liang said: "The seer spoke of 'favorable conditions' as a virtuous friend;

Devadatta’s harming of the Buddha was a 'contrary condition,' yet both are virtuous friends. Although they differ as favorable and contrary, both are virtuous friends because they are without enmity. [Question: What about this?

"Being free from enmity" is what is recorded by the eyes; it refers to a person whose eyes are capable of such recording. The answer to this treatise is based on the Buddha, demonstrating that the Tathāgata is free from enmity and malice;
thus, the eyes are able to record the person. Yuanquan states: "This demonstrates that Devadatta harbored no heart of enmity or malice toward the Buddha."

Because he wished to manifest the merits of the Tathāgata, it was not an evil person who was given this prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). Furthermore, along with his previous excellent understanding, he was included among those for whom the prediction was intended.
The *Śāstra* states: "Devadatta was entirely a bodhisattva of great power, a bodhisattva in the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*).
[Objection: If Devadatta was constantly a great adversary to the Bodhisattva throughout five hundred lifetimes, how is this so?
Furthermore, it was said: "The Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta replied, 'Devadatta is not an enemy of the Bodhisattva. Why is this?
If he were an enemy of the Buddha, how could Devadatta—who constantly commits all manner of evils—be able to encounter the Bodhisattva, who cultivates goodness, in every successive lifetime?
For this reason, Devadatta is not an enemy of the Bodhisattva. It is like two people walking together; one person heads toward [the north],'" and so forth.
To the east, one person moves westward; with every step they grow further apart, always turning away from one another. How could they ever meet?
If Devadatta were truly an enemy, the Buddha would have various faults: first, he would not be an omniscient person, for he was unaware when the mountain was crushed down upon him;
second, he would lack supernatural power, as he could not restrain the mace-wielding assailant who sought to harm him.
Third, the Buddha has the fault of ignorance: seeing an enemy approach to cause harm, he does not avoid him. Fourth, the fault of not protecting sentient beings:
although Devadatta committed the five heinous crimes, he was not rescued. Fifth, the Buddha does not possess a vajra-body;
even a Cakravartin King, due to his meager merit, is free from such harm, so how much more so would the Tathāgata be wounded by a stone until blood flowed?

Because he emerged [from the womb], one should know that his body was not made of vajra. Sixth, there is the fault of residual karma not yet exhausted: being struck by others is entirely summoned by karma.

Thus, one knows that the Tathāgata had residual karma not yet exhausted; however, this was merely a manifestation of performing karma and falling into the great hells, intended to demonstrate clearly that karmic retribution cannot be destroyed.
Furthermore, it was for the sake of sentient beings who have fallen into hell so that they might take refuge in the Tathāgata.

It is for the sake of providing protection and rescue; furthermore, it is so that sentient beings of future generations who enter the Buddha-dharma and encounter injury or destruction may form this thought:
"If even the body of the Tathāgata was subjected to such harm and injury, how much more so for us ordinary persons," [as in the case of] Devadatta.
This is the Bodhisattva Mahāpiṅgala. In order to prevent sentient beings from committing the crime of parricide, he fell into hell.
It is like a fragrant elephant contending in strength; it is not something a donkey can endure. If he were not a transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), why would he enter hell?
The World-Honored One had Ānanda inquire whether his suffering was bearable. He replied, "I am experiencing the bliss of the third dhyāna; however—"
Through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), they subdue sentient beings by manifesting the commission of two heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) and falling into the Avīci Hell.
The previous statement regarding whether one is an enemy or not an enemy shows that these all pertain to the individuals being prophesied.

When the sutra speaks of those who act as Māras, these are mostly Bodhisattvas dwelling in the inconceivable liberation (*acintya-vimokṣa*) who, through the power of their skillful means, go to test them so as to cause their resolve to become firm.
Gu asked: "How do you reconcile these two treatises? He replied: "Jin says: 'The other five records all refer to the persons being recorded. Why is there such a contradiction?

It is simply that since Devadatta harbored no enmity toward the Buddha, the Tathāgata likewise harbored no enmity toward him. Each of the two treatises relies on one side of the matter. [The interlocutor] asks:

'If Devadatta harmed the Buddha and the Buddha nonetheless gave him a prediction, why did Shanhuang not also receive a prediction when he did the same? He replied: 'Devadatta..."* (text fragmentary). *Note: The provided source text ends abruptly with "He replied: 'Devadatta...". The translation reflects the available text.*

Śāriputra had previously served as a teacher; because he understood that matter, he was granted a prediction of enlightenment. However, Shanhuang was not a teacher of Śākyamuni, and therefore he is not granted a prediction within this assembly.

Regarding the phrase "the prediction of the fivefold practice," this is the designation of the name; it refers to the prediction that one who practices the bodhisattva path will attain buddhahood, hence it is called the "prediction of the practice.
Regarding the phrase "revealing women, householders, and so forth," this clarifies the persons to whom the prediction is given. This scriptural passage is found in the "Dharma Master" chapter.
This is the first [section].
Regarding the statement that those who cultivate the bodhisattva practices all realize the fruit of Buddhahood: this sets forth the reasons for receiving the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).

Therefore, he grants predictions to the bhikṣuṇīs and the celestial maidens, thereby concluding the section on the prediction of universal practice (*sāmānya-pratipatti-vyākaraṇa*). Now, concerning those who have received the prediction, it is asked: why is it called "universal practice"?
The Hīnayāna permits women to attain the fruits of sainthood; however, in the Mahāyāna, it is not permitted for women to enter the Path of Seeing, much less achieve Buddhahood.
Answer: This was the case before they had heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Once they have heard this sutra, even a dragon girl can attain Buddhahood, let alone others. Now, here we do not distinguish between the fourfold assembly or the eight classes of beings.

This applies throughout this sutra regarding the cultivation of practice and the attainment of the fruit. As for why the World-Honored One bestowed predictions upon the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings—namely, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and goddesses—one might ask:
"Which of these is the goddess? Throughout the upper and lower sections of this single scripture, there is no passage where a goddess receives a prediction.
To this, some reply: "The prediction was given to Yaśodharā; Yaśas is a goddess. This...
This interpretation is incorrect. Furthermore, Yaśodharā was not a celestial maiden (*devakanyā*). Even if she were a celestial maiden, she would have already entered the order of nuns;

how then could she still be called a celestial maiden? Thus, we know she was not one. Moreover, another interpretation holds that "heaven" refers to the heavenly beings (*devaputra*); it means that heavenly beings came to listen.
They must necessarily be accompanied by women; therefore, they are called "celestial maidens" (*devī*). Wherever there is a celestial realm, there are women who accompany [the gods].
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that "celestial" refers to female celestials. Since "celestial beings" (*deva*) comprises the fourfold assembly, these [women] are among them as *upāsikās*.

Within the two destinies of humans and celestials, the first is mentioned to include the latter; thus they are named "celestial maidens. This interpretation is superior. That is to say, they are called "human... [and so forth].

Regarding the female [receptivity], as previously prophesied, it had not yet been established as occurring across all five destinies; it was restricted to the human realm, specifically to those with both sexual organs and to the male body.

Now, however, it is extended to include the celestial realm and is made to apply to females as well. This demonstrates that the prophecy applies universally. By speaking of "celestial females," the treatise skillfully employs its terminology.

Regarding the mention of "gods and goddesses," there may be no room for doubt. As explained extensively above, according to the *Dharmabhāṇaka-parivarta*, it is stated that when the eight classes of beings and the fourfold assembly hear this sutra, they all receive predictions of enlightenment;
since this passage is broad in scope, it follows that goddesses may also receive such predictions.
The statement "these five [types of] predictions above" is the conclusion; collectively, they are termed "predictions for the present.

The statement "six causes of prediction" indicates the presence of the causal factors. Question: Regarding these predictions for the present, why is it necessary to cite the predictions concerning the presence of causal factors?
Those pertain to matters of the past and do not provide benefit for the present time. Answer: Within these predictions for the present, the specific causes are explained separately.
The "prediction" (vyākaraṇa) is the same as the "subsequent prediction. All those who possess the Mahāyāna nature are said to receive the prediction of a bodhisattva;

it does not refer exclusively to those with the [Mahāyāna] nature, for among them there are also those without the nature. This intention is to clarify the distinction between the prediction bestowed upon a bodhisattva and that of a Tathāgata;
