therefore, it cites the "prediction based on possessing the cause. "Possessing" (samanvāgata) means having. "Cause" (hetu) has the sense of a seed. The meaning is that [this seed] exists within the body.
To possess the seed of bodhi is called the prediction based on possessing the cause (*hetu-vyākaraṇa*). Second, regarding the two causes from the perspective of production (*utpāda*):

the seed of bodhi is the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*), and the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) of nirvāṇa is the revealing cause (*vyañjaka-hetu*). To possess these two meanings is called the prediction based on possessing the cause.
Regarding the two explanations of "transformative deliverance" (*parinirvāṇa*): one says that all sentient beings fully possess the cause of Buddha-nature; this is termed "possessing the cause."

The second [type of] "endowment" refers to sentient beings. Because it pertains to the causal stage of a bodhisattva, it speaks of how the Buddha-nature is inherently present within the fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) of those sentient beings;
this is termed "endowment with the cause. This is an *avyayībhāva* (adverbial) compound.
As the Sūtra says: "I do not pass by you all; you shall all become Buddhas. This is cited to demonstrate that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature. Thus, it is quoted.
This is the explanation of the causes for the prediction. The phrase "the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging" refers to the person who bestows the prediction.
The phrase "prostrating, praising, and so forth" sets forth the meaning of the complete causes.
Regarding the phrase "manifesting to sentient beings" and so forth: Question: One observes only the fourfold assembly prostrating and praising, all saying, "He shall become a Buddha.
What is the underlying meaning? Answer: The commentary states that "manifesting to sentient beings" means to clearly demonstrate.
The intention is to manifest and clearly show that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; therefore, they prostrate and praise, saying, "He shall [become a Buddha]."

Regarding the statement "becoming a Buddha" and the phrase "this kind of bodhisattva and so forth," the intended meaning is that this prediction is a prediction for a bodhisattva, not a prediction for a Tathāgata.
It describes the benefits from past times rather than discussing the assembly at hand; it is a prediction based on the fulfillment of causes.
Regarding the phrase "the first three," etc., this is an analytical summary of the six types of records (*ji*).

The "first three" refer to the Separate Record (*bie ji*), the Common Record (*tong ji*), and the Subsequent Record (*hou ji*), as well as the fifth, which is the Universal Record (*tongxing ji*). These four categories were all present at Vulture Peak (*Lingshan*), where they heard this Dharma and received its spiritual benefits.
Regarding the phrase "the other two types" and so forth: this refers to the fourth type of prediction, the "prediction of enmity-free [karma]," which benefits the present life.
This does not derive benefit from hearing the sutra; rather, at the time the sutra was being preached, Devadatta was in hell and was not present in the assembly.

If one considers that it does not benefit the present life, it is categorized solely as the sixth type of prediction, which possesses both causes. Question: Since Devadatta was not present in the assembly, how can it be called [a prediction]?
"Benefiting the present. Answer: Obtaining a prediction (vyākaraṇa) within this assembly is also called "benefiting the present.

Regarding the statement, "Furthermore, the first five predictions," Mochizuki [Mō] says: If one considers obtaining a prediction through hearing the sutra, one takes only the first three and the fifth;
however, if one argues from the perspective of benefiting the present, all five preceding predictions are included herein. Those who obtain predictions in this assembly...
"Renown and profit in the present and the future. Alternatively, this may be the heading from the text within the *Sūtrālaṃkāra-bhāṣya*.

Although the treatise states that there are six types of manifestations of prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*), the first five prophecies all concern "renown and profit in the present," which refers precisely to the prophecy regarding benefit (*hitavyākaraṇa*).

Question: The prophecy regarding the possession of causes (*hetu-vyākaraṇa*) is also spoken within the assembly of this sūtra; why does it not receive the designation "renown and profit in the present"? Answer: Although it is indeed spoken within the assembly of this sūtra...
What has been stated is not a Tathāgata’s prediction concerning past events; therefore, it is not included within the present or the intermediate [time], because the present is not the past.
As for the statement, "Thus, regarding the predictions for the śrāvakas," one asks: since those who are śrāvakas have forever exhausted future existence (*punarbhava*), how [is this so]?
It is possible to realize unsurpassed *bodhi*. Answer: This is based on the *parināmika-kāya* (transformation body), not the *vipākaja-kāya* (body born of karmic fruition);
thus, there is no contradiction. Question: Why must one specifically point to the meaning of the transformation body? Answer: It is because some say that the bodies of *śrāvakas* are limited;
after receiving their prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), they must pass through three great eons (*kalpa*) before attaining *bodhi*. How could a limited body [accomplish this]?
This refers to the ability to endure for a long duration. Therefore, it is necessary to point to the gateway of the meaning of *parināmika-śarīra* (the body of transformation). The intent is this:

although the Śrāvakas have a fixed limit, after receiving their prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), they undergo the body of transformation and pass through three great eons (*mahākalpa*) before attaining the realization of Bodhi.

Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "As some treatises say, if the Śrāvaka who is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) has forever exhausted future existence (*punarbhava*), how can he realize unsurpassed Bodhi?"

[The Buddha] said: "It is based on the *pariṇāmika-kāya* (transformation body) that one realizes the unsurpassed fruit; it is not the *karmaphala-kāya* (body born of karmic fruition). Therefore, there is no contradiction with reason.
Regarding this interpretation of the prophecy, the treatise states: "There are two kinds of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*): first, *paricchinnaka-saṃsāra* (segmented birth-and-death);

second, *pariṇāmika-saṃsāra* (transformative birth-and-death). This transformative birth-and-death has three names in total: first, the *pariṇāmika-kāya*; second, the *manomaya-kāya* (mind-made body); third, the *anāsrava-kāya* (untainted body).
This is a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). However, regarding the death and rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāmikī cyuti*), there is no separate karma that summons it;

it is simply the residual karma from previous lives within the body of segmented birth (*prātibhāvikī cyuti*). This karma exists upon the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), and the functional capacity for continuity also exists there.

Therefore, when the [present] karma is exhausted, the functional capacity for continuity also ceases. Consequently, when the task is complete, one must obtain a body based on the original [karma]. In its fundamental state...

Therefore, while the physical constituents resulting from past karma are coarse, they are now assisted by the power of meditative vows (*samādhi-praṇidhāna*), which possesses a superior capacity to yield results continuously over a long period.
This transformation-death (*pariṇāma-cyuti*) must necessarily have uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) yet discriminative karma as its cause.
"Uncontaminated" (*anāsrava*) excludes the contaminated; "discriminative" (*vikalpa*) excludes the non-discriminative. Taking the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) as the condition:
while the cognitive obstacle is the failure to fully comprehend all phenomena, here we take the grasping that enlightenment is to be sought and sentient beings are to be saved.
This serves to assist those who have previously practiced, providing repeated support for their fixed vows, and thereby transforming and removing prior evils.
After being reborn, it becomes increasingly subtle and refined until one attains unsurpassed bodhi.

If one does not grasp at the bodhi to be sought or the sentient beings to be saved, there would be no way to give rise to intense compassion and vows; this is called "transformative birth" (nirmāṇa-janman).

Regarding the "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*): this refers to the segmented bodies of humans, devas, and those of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), which, according to their desires, undergo this transformational body that is radiant and sovereign;

this is called the characteristic of transformation. Regarding the "essence" (*tattva*): it is the eighth consciousness, the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), which serves as the essence of transformational birth and death (*pariṇāmikī-jarāmaraṇa*).
As the treatise states: "This consciousness is sufficient to serve as the essence of the realms, destinies, and births. This transformation...
The body within the three realms is also called the "body of transformed maturation" (*nirmāṇa-vipākaja*). Regarding its nature as having the *ālayavijñāna* as its essence:
it takes uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) differentiated karma as its cause and the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) as its condition.

It transforms the coarse into the subtle and the short into the long, and is finally relinquished only at the stage of Buddhahood during the Path of Liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). This is the meaning of "transformation. Question 2.

Regarding the transformation of the mind (*cittavivartana*): after which realm does it induce the arising of outflows (*āsrava*)? Answer: There are two interpretations regarding consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*). The first master says:

For all followers of the Two Vehicles, whether in training (*śaikṣa*) or beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), when they generate the resolve for enlightenment in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), they necessarily do so after [residing in] the desire realm, as they induce the arising of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state while maintaining their bodies through the power of their vows (*praṇidhāna-bala*) solely within the desire realm.
This is because there are no such noble beings who transform their minds in the higher realms, nor is there [such a process] in the lower realms.

Regarding the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*): after death, one is born in the higher realms while leaving behind a physical body; thus, following the desire realm, one induces the production of the untainted (*anāsrava*).

The two masters state that there are also śrāvakas in the form realm who arouse the mind directed toward the Mahāyāna, and they allow that even Buddhas go there, as do Bodhisattvas, in order to transform those beings.

Furthermore, there are also noble ones of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna-ārya*) in the form realm; following the tainted (*sāsrava*) eighth consciousness of the form realm, [the untainted arises]. No [untainted state] exists prior to it.

The outflows manifest, because there are śrāvakas who, having developed the resolve [for awakening], remain in that body. This excludes those in the first two fruits and the pratyekabuddhas, as they do not develop such a resolve there;
furthermore, in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), there are certainly no who turn their minds toward the Mahāyāna.
There are only five types of abodes where no one at all develops the resolve, for the sūtras do not state that they develop the Great [Vehicle].

Because of the mind. The two sūtras permit both the arousal of the thought [of awakening] and the mind of faith and inclination, as well as the mind that does not yet set out toward it. This is because the five Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa) are inhabited only by those of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*).

Question: Śāriputra was one who had attained the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); he immediately underwent the transformation of the body (*pariṇāmika-kāya*) upon turning his mind [toward the Mahāyāna].
Why, then, did his disciple Gavāmpati say, "When my preceptor Śāriputra has passed into parinirvāṇa, I too shall follow him"? From this, one knows that he had realized the state of no-learning.

Question: Regarding the fruit of learning, one who has not yet undergone the transformation of the body (*pariṇāmanakāya*) and is destined to receive a future existence—does this refer to manifesting *nirvāṇa*? Answer: No. Question:
If an Arhat turns their mind toward the Great Vehicle and undergoes the transformation of the body, how can a female body attain realization of the first stage (*bhūmi*)? Answer:

Through the assistance of untainted concentration and vows, at the time when the old causes are supported, the female form is transformed into a male, and one attains entry into the first stage. Question: When a sage turns [their mind]...

The mind immediately undergoes transformation; or does it not? The answer is that their intentions differ. If one has a profound sense of revulsion toward the *pariccheda* (segmented existence), they turn their minds and immediately undergo transformation.

If one lacks such profound revulsion, they may remain in the *pariccheda* state for the full lifespan of Jambudvīpa, or even for many eons, employing skillful means until they eventually undergo transformation.

Regarding the phrase "the benefit of manifest realization" (*pratyakṣa-lābha*) and so forth: "manifest" (*pratyakṣa*) means being present before one's eyes; "realization" (*sākṣāt-karaṇa*) means attaining; and "benefit" (*hita*) means welfare.

Because they will hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* within the assembly and thereby obtain benefits in the present life, it is called the "benefit of manifest realization. Furthermore, there are many kinds [of such benefits].

Furthermore, it is due to perfuming (*vāsanā*). Among the benefits of the previously mentioned prophetic records, there were many types of benefit; likewise, among the benefits of this present realization, there are also many kinds of benefit.
Therefore, it is said to be "of many kinds. This refers to those who obtain benefit through the twenty-five categories mentioned below.
This refers to various types of individuals.
Regarding the mention of "such as Devadatta and others," the text cites passages from eight chapters of the sutra to demonstrate twenty-five categories of those who derive benefit.
These eight chapters of sutra text are divided into eight sections; the first section cited is the "Devadatta Chapter."

Regarding the phrase "though they emerged from the dragon palace," this serves to distinguish those who do not receive benefit. This refers to those who hear the *Lotus Sūtra* within the assembly and obtain immediate benefit;

hence, it is called "benefit realized in the present" (*pratyakṣa-lābha*). Although immeasurable bodhisattvas emerged from the dragon palace and attained the Way, they were all [previously] taught by Mañjuśrī in the lower regions and had already obtained realization there; it was not through hearing the Dharma at Vulture Peak that they attained this benefit.
Because they derive benefit, the *Devadatta-parivarta* speaks only of four kinds of benefits realized through direct perception (*pratyakṣa-lābha*), and does not mention those who "emerge.

The immeasurable bodhisattvas and nāga girls are likewise included within the benefits realized through direct perception; therefore, it is said that they are omitted and not mentioned. The Sūtra states:
"Their number is immeasurable, beyond calculation, not to be proclaimed by mouth, and not to be fathomed by mind. Wait but a moment."

There shall surely be witnesses to this. Before he had finished speaking, countless bodhisattvas emerged from the sea, seated upon precious lotus flowers, and proceeded to Vulture Peak Mountain, where they remained suspended in mid-air. These bodhisattvas were all those whom Mañjuśrī had transformed and guided;
they were fully endowed with the practices of a bodhisattva and were collectively discussing the six *pāramitās*. Those who were originally *śrāvakas* were [also] in the void...
In the air, he preached the practices of the śrāvakas; now they all practice the Mahāyāna meaning of emptiness and so forth, and the dragon girl has attained the Way.
These are not benefits for Vulture Peak, nor are they benefits for the present. The benefit of manifest realization here is even more restricted than the benefit of the prediction of future fruit.
Regarding the benefit of the prediction of the fruit (*phala-vyākaraṇa*), it is already admitted that one will only obtain the fruit in the future.

However, the benefit realized in the present—namely, the benefit obtained by hearing the Dharma during the interval before the assembly has dispersed, even though the Tathāgata is still preaching the Dharma—is included within this category. As for the benefit after the assembly has dispersed:
[the text asks] since the holy teachings state that it is not permitted for those in animal bodies to enter the noble path (*āryamārga*), how can these two...?
[Question: "If they are like humans, how can they obtain such great benefit? [Answer: In reality, this is not permitted; however, in terms of transformation (*nirmāṇa*), it does not pose an obstacle.

There are two intentions behind the transformation: first, to lead real nāgas to develop faith; second, to lead the actual śrāvakas of Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa who have turned their minds [toward the Mahāyāna].
Those who were originally śrāvakas were in the void expounding the practices of śrāvakas; these are actually nāga assemblies who have manifested as śrāvakas to lead the real ones.
"Śrāvaka. This was brought forth by Zhiji (Jñānakuṭi) during his debate; he was originally Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, who preached the *Lotus Sūtra* to transform and benefit others.
Although they benefited from hearing the sūtra, this does not refer to benefiting those present here. Question:

When the World-Honored One preached the sūtra on Vulture Peak, he shattered the doubts and attachments of the "turning-of-the-heart" śrāvakas and bestowed predictions upon them through his preaching, causing them to give rise to a mind of certainty.

Those who have come to this ocean-like assembly are still Śrāvakas who have turned their minds [toward enlightenment]. Why has the World-Honored One not bestowed predictions of their future enlightenment upon them?
If he were to bestow such predictions, there would be no explicit textual evidence for it in the sūtras. If he does not bestow such predictions, then he is neither attracting nor sustaining them.
One might raise the doubt that this [bodhisattva] would harbor a mind of attachment and consequently regress to the level of a śrāvaka. The answer is that there are three reasons.
First, when this bodhisattva arrived at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, he saw the World-Honored One dispelling the doubts of the śrāvakas of the three capacities by declaring:

"In the buddha-fields of the ten directions, there is only the Single Vehicle Dharma. This class of bodhisattvas does not give rise to such doubts themselves; therefore, it is unnecessary to bestow a prediction of enlightenment upon them.
Second, these are emanations and not real; the intention is merely to testify that on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, the śrāvakas truly turned their minds [toward enlightenment] with certainty.

Since they are emanations and not real, there was no need for them to receive a prediction (vyākaraṇa). Third, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva brought them forth; the intention is to testify to the vastness of the power of this sutra and the swiftness of its power.
Originally, they were not eligible for a prediction. At the beginning of the Introductory Chapter (Nidāna-parivarta), he distinguishes [them] from Mañjuśrī.

The Bodhisattva was seated [in the assembly]. Why do you now say that he has emerged from the sea? He replied: "The spiritual transformations (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*) of the Sage’s responsive resonance are inconceivable.
According to those to be transformed, he manifests traces without fixed location; he comes from nowhere and goes nowhere.

He cannot be sought through marks (*lakṣaṇa*), nor can he be grasped through phenomena (*dharma*). Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: 'In each of the ten directions, there is a great Bodhisattva who, together with...'"
Each was accompanied by a retinue of bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-worlds, namely Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Bhadramukha Bodhisattva, and others.
These are indeed the bodies of bodhisattvas that pervade the entire dharma-realm to benefit all sentient beings; how could they be restricted merely to the dragon palace?
According to another account, after the "Introduction Chapter" concludes with Maitreya’s inquiry, [the Buddha] immediately enters the dragon palace to transform all sentient beings.
Upon reaching the "Chapter on Devadatta," there is a passage stating that [the assembly] emerges from the ocean (one may choose between the two explanations to distinguish the incorrect).
It says that there are only dragon girls and so forth; this section divides the assembly into six parts, and this text attains benefit. This combines the benefits of four positions.
If one follows the flow of the text, it is all-inclusive, with its progression and regression being indeterminate. Excluding the section on Maitreya Buddha’s descent to be born in the world.
It is certain that [the former] has attained it, while others certainly have not. Even the Master of the Commentary (*śāstrakāra*) did not dare to make a definitive judgment.
From the passage "Only the dragon girl attains the Way" down to "all pay respectful salutations from afar," the benefits are divided into four stages.

In the commentary’s statement, "Innumerable sentient beings hear the Dharma and attain realization," this refers to the benefit of the first stage: those who would have regressed now do not. "Innumerable sentient beings receive the prediction of enlightenment" refers to the second stage.
The benefit for two individuals: descending six times to the Stainless World (*vimalā-loka*). The benefit for three individuals:
three thousand sentient beings generating the bodhicitta. The benefit for four individuals: from after the six descents to the Stainless World and so forth. The benefit for two individuals.
It is certain that these benefits are included within the present [aeon] of this world-system. As for the two preceding stages, they are benefits for either this world-system or another world-system;
thus, the *Aniyata-sūtra* states: "Immeasurable sentient beings, upon hearing the Dharma, attain realization and reach the stage of non-retrogression;

immeasurable sentient beings receive the prediction of attaining the Way. Regarding these two categories, some may raise the doubt: "Are these [beings] from the stainless world (*vimala-loka*)? or "Not so?"

[The Buddha] measured the sentient beings: immeasurable sentient beings heard the Dharma, attained realization, and reached the stage of non-retrogression; immeasurable sentient beings received the prediction of their attainment of the Way.

Furthermore, were these immeasurable sentient beings who heard the Dharma, attained realization, reached the stage of non-retrogression, and received the prediction of their attainment of the Way from this Sahā world?
If it is certain that this benefit belongs to this region, the Master of the Commentary [Vasubandhu] will explain the original text below.

In the section on the text, it is categorized as the benefit for the Immaculate World (*vimala-loka*). If the meditative path were the benefit for that [Immaculate] region alone, the Master of the Commentary (*śāstrakāra*) would have categorized it here as being included within the "benefit for this world.
Answer: First, if one follows the passage where the Dragon Girl attained enlightenment and preached the Dharma, it refers to the Sahā world.
If one takes the term "Sahā world" and reads it upward in connection with what precedes it, it directly [indicates the present].

From the time immeasurable sentient beings heard the Dharma, attained realization, and reached the stage of non-retrogression, until immeasurable sentient beings received their predictions and were established on the Path—this constitutes the benefit for two realms. The phrasing suggests this belongs to the benefit within the Sahā world.
In the second section, it begins again from the moment the Dragon Girl alone attained enlightenment and preached the Dharma, continuing down to "all [beings] paid distant homage."
The two benefits. Reading separately until the phrase "the world of Vimalā shook six times," the textual momentum seems to belong to the benefit of the world of Vimalā.
The *Shè* (Summary) states that the sutra contains both tendencies; this is why the Master of the Commentary divided it according to its progression and regression.

Here, it belongs to the benefit [of sentient beings] and is included within the middle section. In the main text, it belongs to the benefit of the world of Vimalā. Master He said: "The previous two positions..."
It is further [the benefit]. It definitely belongs to the benefit of the Stainless World (Amala-loka). Why? Because the answer refers to the latter two stages.
Since there is the word "Sahā-world" to distinguish it, we know that the latter two stages definitely belong to this direction (this world-system).
Since the former two stages lack the word "Sahā-world" for distinction, we know they definitely belong to the benefit of the Stainless World. Question: Why does [the text] not follow from "only"?
After the dragon girl had attained the Way, she sent down a written memorial; when it reached Xi, he paid his respects from afar.

There were also characters for "Saha World" that were very distinct. He replied by saying, "Having already paid my respects from afar," and although the characters for "Saha World" appeared before this, [the text remains as such].
As for the devas, nāgas, the eight classes of beings, humans, non-humans, and so forth—these constitute the number of three thousand within the final two positions.
Each of these final two positions has three thousand individuals; they are no different from the devas, nāgas, the eight classes of beings, humans, and non-humans mentioned in the preceding text.
Although the term "sentient beings of the Sahā world" appears here, they all belong to the final two [positions].

The phrase "included within the benefit of the assembly" has two interpretations. The first says that, according to actual fact, the persons of the preceding two assemblies were physically present in the world of Vimalā beneath the assembly of the Dragon Girl, where they heard the Dharma from her side; they did not hear the sutra at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.

Nevertheless, if one discusses their benefit, it is subsumed under the benefit of the assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa. How is this known? It is because the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* was preached at the assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.

Only then did the dragon girl attain Buddhahood, preach the Dharma, and bring benefit to others. Attributing this merit to its source, it was indeed the benefit conferred at the assembly on Vulture Peak.
Subsequently, the two individuals were seated beneath Śākyamuni Buddha at the assembly on Vulture Peak;
from afar, they saw the world of Vimalā shake six times, and that three thousand sentient beings in the Sahā world had attained the stage of non-retrogression. Furthermore...
Three thousand sentient beings resolved their minds on Bodhi and received a prediction of Buddhahood from the Dragon Girl.

Thus, the benefits of the four stages are subsumed by the Master of the Commentary (Sūzhǔ) entirely within "benefiting the present. Question: How do we know that the Master of the Commentary has categorized [the text] as benefiting the present exclusively? Answer:
It is simply because this commentary states, "The benefits of the four stages are combined," which contains the phrase "four stages. Furthermore, it is evident from the concluding text below.

These twenty-five instances of benefit are collectively termed "benefit in the present. Furthermore, among the various categories [of benefits], this specifically excludes those that are not relevant;
it excludes only the case of the Dragon Girl who emerged from the Dragon Palace and attained the Way, but does not exclude the listeners who obtained benefit when the Dragon Girl preached the Dharma.
Therefore, a fourfold classification is established: first, there are those who obtain benefit by hearing the sutra while their bodies are not present at the assembly. This is not...

1. Those who have already received the benefit are now gathered here; these are the Bodhisattvas of the Ocean-like Assembly. 2. Those who did not receive the benefit because they did not hear the sutra, yet whose bodies are present in the assembly;
this benefit is now being received; these are the latter two classes [of Śrāvakas]. 3. Those who received the benefit because they heard the sutra, and whose bodies are also present in the assembly;

this benefit is now being received; these are the Śrāvakas of the three faculties. 4. Those whose bodies were in that other realm when they heard the sutra and received the benefit, but whose bodies are not present in the assembly; this [benefit]...
The benefit is now gathered. The first two stages constitute the second intention. According to the force of the scriptural passage, it says:

"The bodhisattvas of the Sahā world all see from afar that dragon girl Buddha. During the first two stages, while their bodies remain in the Sahā world, they see from afar the dragon girl attaining the Buddha-way and hear from afar her preaching of the Dharma;
through joy, prostration, and receiving benefit, they proceed. During the latter two stages, they see from afar..."
The Vimalā world shook six times, and he received a prophecy from the Buddha Nāgarāja. Regarding the four classes of people, their bodies are all located in this region.

Question: Since the Master [Yixing] has already included these four classes within the benefits of this region, why does he record the "Vimalā World" in the central section and also mention the Sahā World? Answer: If one were to record them all under the Sahā World...
The character "jie" (界). Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the persons of the four stages arouse the aspiration for enlightenment within the *Amala-loka* (Stainless World).

In response, the term "Stainless World" is written in its entirety. Moreover, fearing that people might suspect that the persons of all four stages reside collectively within the Stainless World, both worlds are mentioned together to distinguish them.
Question: If these four [stages] generally belong to this region of benefit, what is their distinction?

Answer: Those in the first two positions heard the sūtra with joy at the assembly where the Dragon Girl attained the Way and preached the Dharma, and thereupon received their prediction from the Buddha.
Those in the latter two positions received their prediction upon seeing the world *Vimalā* shake. As the *She wèn* (Inquiry on the Śrīmālā) states:
"Among the four positions, the second and fourth receive their predictions. This is because the texts concerning "this Buddha" and "that Buddha" do not differ.

Question: What is the distinction between the two pairs of stages regarding the attainment of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*)? Answer: Regarding the first two stages, attaining the prediction of the path refers to the meaning of "cause" (*hetu*);

it is a prediction based on the cause. Regarding the latter two stages, the initial arousal of the bodhicitta and the first thought of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) are likewise predictions based on the cause.

The second interpretation states: The first two stages involve attaining the prediction of the path; the latter two stages involve arousing the mind and thereby receiving the prediction. Since it says...

The prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*) is precisely the prediction regarding the fruit. Question: Since it is a prediction regarding the fruit, why is it not included within the benefit of the prediction regarding the fruit?
For what reason is it included within the benefit of direct realization? Answer: Because the prediction given to the Dragon Girl is not a matter concerning the person of Śākyamuni Buddha himself;

therefore, it is not included within the benefit of the prediction regarding the fruit. There is an interpretation that this is because the conditions for clearly describing the [future] land were not met.
Regarding the mention of the name of a land (*kṣetra-nāman*): it does not qualify as being included within the benefit of the prediction to the fruit (*phala-vyākaraṇa-lābha*).

If that were the case, even a prediction regarding universal practice (*samudācāra-vyākaraṇa*) would not be a clear statement of the name of a land; how then could it be included in the benefit of the prediction to the fruit?

Therefore, one should know that it is not simply because Śākyamuni Buddha did not grant the prediction that it is excluded from the benefit of the prediction to the fruit; rather, it is precisely for that reason that it is so. Question: Regarding the persons of the latter two stages, how can they [be predicted] from afar?

Regarding the statement that one hears the voice of the prediction for the śrāvakas in the world *Amala* (Stainless), if it were the case that the sutra combines two directions for the sake of benefit, then saying "one awakens through understanding upon hearing the Dharma" would imply that the assembly in the *Amala* world hears the Dharma without doubt, whereas hearing this sutra in this world would contradict correct principle.

How could the fifteen assemblies on Vulture Peak and the others possibly take the sound-objects of that world as their cognitive domain? The answer is that this expresses the inconceivable. If this is accepted...

Seeing that he has attained Buddhahood and is preaching the Dharma, how could one have any doubt upon hearing this? [The opponent] argues: "The preaching of the Dharma in the world of Vimala is a real phenomenon;

it is merely perceived here in this place and time because it corresponds to its own object. [The proponent's] thesis is as stated. The reason is: "Because it is a cognition through contact with an external object (*bahir-viṣaya-jñāna*).

The similar example is: "Just like the visual consciousness here in this place. This visual consciousness here in this place is a cognition through contact with an external object; this visual consciousness here in this place is capable of...
Because of that, the ear-consciousness here in this direction cognizes objects at a distance, just as the eye-consciousness there is able to perceive those dharmas.
It is said that one hears the sutras and teachings spoken by the Buddhas; it is said that one sees the Buddha’s light depart from here, and hears the sound of the Dharma coming from there.

This is precisely the mark of the Brahma-voice of the Dragon Girl attaining Buddhahood: its pure and penetrating resonance is heard afar, causing it to be heard here in this direction, just as with Maudgalyāyana.
Whether in the wilderness or throughout the world, hearing the sound of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* being preached on Vulture Peak is no different from being present in the assembly below it.
This is also the same as when Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, while in the land of the Buddha Ratnatejobhyudgatarāja, heard from afar this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* being preached in this Sahā world.

Regarding the question of what the five consciousnesses take as their objects: they must necessarily rely upon the eighth consciousness; only then can the eye and ear consciousnesses perceive their respective objects.

Regarding those forms and sounds, it is not yet certain whether they take as their object what is transformed by one’s own eighth consciousness or what is transformed by another’s eighth consciousness.

If they take what is transformed by another as their object, then the doctrine of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) is not established. If they take what is transformed by one’s own consciousness as their object, then since that [other person] does not belong to this realm, it would be as if there were a separation between realms.

How is this realm perceived as an object? The answer is: it is perceived by means of itself. Regarding the three [aspects] transformed by its own eight [consciousnesses], the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only), fascicle 2, states:

"Apart from the transformation of maturation (*vipākavipariṇāma*), these appear as such. One interpretation holds that, as the sūtras state, they are produced collectively through the sovereign power of the karma of all sentient beings.
Another interpretation holds that they belong to those currently dwelling in or about to be born in that [realm]; these are their maturation-consciousnesses (*vipākavijñāna*).
It transforms into this realm. Third, it is said that even if one is born in another region within one’s own level (*svabhūmi*), that consciousness can likewise transform into this land.

This is the correct doctrine of Dharmapāla alone: that in another region, within one’s own level, both parties mutually transform this realm. For sentient beings, when viewed from the perspective of that [other region], this [present] realm is also their own level;
therefore, it can serve as the objective basis (*ālambana-pratibimba*) for those five consciousnesses. If this is so, as stated above...

One with the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) belonging to a higher realm sees the three lower calamities; while the body resides in a higher realm, one uses the divine eye to see the forms (*rūpa*) and so forth of the lower stages.

But would it not follow that the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is also permitted to take the forms of lower stages as its object? No, for it is not permitted, because the eighth consciousness undergoes transformation (*pariṇāma*) by crossing over realms.

If it does not transform into those [lower objects], how can the five consciousnesses necessarily have an objective basis (*ālambana-pratyaya*)? Answer: The five consciousnesses must necessarily have a remote objective condition (*viprakṛṣṭa-ālambana-pratyaya*). With respect to...

This is explained in terms of those belonging to one's own stage (*svabhūmi*) and those closely adjacent to it. As for those belonging to different stages who are separated by great distance, this does not necessarily apply to all of them.

The Master of the Commentary (*ṭīkākāra*), in his explanation of the eighth [cognition], the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), states: Question: Since sentient beings have originally not yet ascended to the [spiritual] stages (*bhūmi*), how can they be said to possess "realization" (*avabodha*)?
Answer: To understand through faith in the Dharma is also called realization; to understand through hearing and reflection (*śruta-mayī* and *cintā-mayī*) is also called realization.
Regarding the phrase "attaining non-retrogression," this refers to non-retrogression in faith among the four types of non-retrogression.
Regarding the phrase "abiding on the stage of non-retrogression," this refers to non-retrogression in realization and practice.
Regarding the statement that three thousand sentient beings have resolved their minds toward enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), this is assigned to the stage of superior conviction (*adhimukti*).
Regarding the statement that these four stages are combined, this refers to the comprehensive inclusion of both [the former and the latter].

Regarding the passage on the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merits" and so forth: when bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges emerged from the earth, Maitreya and others were filled with doubt and requested the Buddha to explain.

The Buddha said, "All these bodhisattvas have been transformed by me. When the assembly saw them emerge, they wondered whether these were not transformations, given that the father was young while the son was old, and thus doubted that they were created by Śākyamuni. Consequently, [the Buddha] spoke of the lifespan of the three bodies to resolve their doubts.

The preceding section addresses doubts. It clarifies that since the Buddha attained the Way long ago, those he has transformed must certainly be numerous. Because the Buddha’s virtue is profound and subtle, many hear and believe it;

as his benefit is vast, his merit is even more manifold. Consequently, there are eleven stages of those who have attained realization and one stage of those who have resolved their minds, totaling twelve stages for those who currently realize and obtain benefit.
For this reason, the Master of the Commentary includes them within the benefits of current realization. Thus far...
The Master of the Commentary explains: There are five types of merit based on the power of the Dharma; herein, there are three. First, realization, which refers to the eleven stages.
Second, faith, such as the generation of the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by sentient beings numbering as many as the atoms in eight worlds. Third, making offerings.

The heavens rained down flowers and so forth. Furthermore, among the eleven stages, the first six are based on the stages themselves, while the [remaining] five are based on birth, realization, and attainment.

As for the statement that "the Buddha said these are like the Tathāgatas," it refers to sand as fine as flour covering a square area of forty *li*, which constitutes one *Gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (a Ganges-sand).
Question: How many Ganges sands are there? Answer: There are *nayuta* Ganges sands. *Nayuta* is a Sanskrit term;
here it is called "hài" (a myriad). Question: How many *nayutas* are there? Answer: In total, there are six hundred and eighty million billion *nayutas* of Ganges sands.

Regarding the "patience of non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*): its initial attainment occurs in the first stage (*bhūmi*); its continuity occurs in the eighth stage; and its perfection occurs in the Buddha-stage.
Non-arising phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma*) are precisely suchness (*tathatā*). Non-arising phenomena are the object.

When a bodhisattva enters the first stage, they verify the principle of non-arising through fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), and they verify the teaching of non-arising through subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*). Both mind and object—
It is non-arising. All phenomena are originally quiescent; having arisen, they do not abide. Since abiding is unattainable, arising is likewise unattainable;
therefore, it is called non-arising. There are three kinds of non-arising: first, non-arising as the fundamental nature.

It is also called the non-arising of characteristics (*lakṣaṇānutpāda*). It exists in the realm of mental construction but is non-existent in reality; this is the *parikalpita* (imagined nature). Second is the non-arising of spontaneity (*svabhāvānutpāda*).

It is provisionally existent but substantially non-existent; this is the *paratantra* (dependent nature). Third is the non-arising of afflictions and suffering (*kleśaduḥkhānutpāda*). It is substantially existent but provisionally non-existent;

this is the *pariniṣpanna* (perfected nature). Regarding the non-arising of the fundamental essence: that which was originally non-existent now comes into being is the *paratantra-svabhāva*, which is precisely "that which was originally non-existent now comes into being."
The suffering of delusion is non-arising; it exists as it has always existed and exists as it is now.

Its fundamental substance is without arising, just like mistaking a rope for a snake, mistaking a utility pole for a ghost, or [perceiving] flowers in the sky, a second moon, tortoise hair, or rabbit horns. In the darkness, one falsely takes a rope to be a snake;
this is to speak of existence where there is none. When clarity arrives, that which was "existent" becomes non-existent. Thus, through the realization of false sentiments, [the delusion] is ended.
It is simply non-existent; it is entirely the objective aspect (*viṣayāṃśa*) of the mind that gives rise to an "image-only" object (*pratibimba-viṣaya*), such as the perception of a snake.
It is likewise with sentient beings who falsely cling to a self (*ātman*) upon the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).

That which is "naturally unarisen" means that which was originally non-existent but now exists—just as a rope was originally hemp and only later becomes a rope. Furthermore, whatever is a conditioned phenomenon (*rūpa-dharma*) arises from two conditions.

The causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) are as follows: hemp is the causal condition; when human effort is applied to it to form a rope, that effort is the dominant condition.

Thus, the hemp itself is the proximate condition, while human effort and so forth are the remote conditions. Similarly, the seeds of rice, wheat, and so on, are the causal conditions, while water and soil are the dominant conditions.
In the same way, this very body takes the seeds of names and phrases within the *ālaya-vijñāna* as its causal condition, [and the father...]

The mother’s union and karma act as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the arising of these five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). The preceding mental states and so forth arise from four conditions;

how could this be the same as the non-Buddhists’ doctrine of spontaneous origination (*svabhāva*)? The seed of visual consciousness acts as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), while the sense faculty (*indriya*) that can produce consciousness acts as the dominant condition.

The cessation of the preceding moment and the arising of the succeeding moment is called the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). The preceding object is the... [object-condition].
Regarding the condition of objects (*ālambana-pratyaya*): as for the non-arising of delusion and suffering, it is like sesame seeds which exist now just as they did originally;

this is not the same as a rope. When delusion and suffering are removed, the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*) manifests spontaneously. The principle of True Suchness is primordially pure and has never possessed delusion or suffering.
Now that one has realized this, how could suffering arise? This is called "non-arising" (*anutpāda*). One can only say it is "manifested," but it cannot be [said to be produced].

Regarding the term "arising," "patience" (kṣānti) refers to the endurance of suffering; it is the mind that recognizes and confirms [the truth]. When a Bodhisattva is still on the stages prior to the grounds (bhūmi-pūrvamgama), although they have heard [the teachings] in the past, they have not yet been able to realize them through wisdom.
Once a great eon is fulfilled, they suddenly abide in the Ground of Supreme Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi) and are born into the family of the Tathāgata.

Compared to what was previously merely heard, they now attain realization of the principle; this confirmation within the mind is called "patience. Patience is the meaning of "seal" (mudrā). It is the patience of the seal.

This also relies on the Master. Huapudu asked: "In the 'Chapter on Differentiation,' eleven stages are mentioned regarding the attainment of benefits. Upon which specific stage does each rely? Answer:
"The first six stages are called the 'Stages of Increasing the Path' (*vṛddhimārga*), because they consist of the noble path (*āryamārga*) of those Bodhisattvas.

The next five stages are each 'Stages of Diminishing Birth. 'Diminishing' (*kṣaya*) refers to the reduction of all evils; 'birth' (*janman*) refers to the production of all roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). The final stage is called..."
Regarding the stage of generating the resolve (*cittotpāda*):
since at the very beginning all have generated the supreme resolve, the statement "ten billion bodhisattvas and so forth" has two interpretations.

One says that it takes the aforementioned six hundred and eighty million *koṭi-nayuta* Ganges-sands of sentient beings as the standard; from one, it becomes two; from two, it becomes four; from four... [it continues].
Twice eight. In this manner, it continues up to a thousandfold. The second [explanation] says: from one to two; from two, doubled, four;

thus, doubled a thousand times. Regarding "retaining what is heard" (*śruta-dhara*): upon hearing, one is immediately able to retain it. Following the *dhāraṇī*, it takes mindfulness and wisdom as its essence.
When a bodhisattva attains this mindfulness and wisdom, they retain the teachings they have heard without forgetting them; this is called "retaining what is heard. As for ordinary people who hear...
One forgets what has been understood; one hears but cannot retain it. When a Bodhisattva attains this *dhāraṇī*, it constitutes total retention (*saṃdhāraṇa*).

It comprises three aspects: the dharma, the meaning, and the mantra. Its initial attainment occurs on the third stage (*bhūmi*); its continuity on the ninth stage; and its perfection on the Buddha stage. Muzhou said:
"The number of people who have realized these [attainments] is such that even a single transformed Buddha-land could not contain them. Thus says the treatise.

This refers to the Land of Reward (*vipākakṣetra*). Although it is Mount Gṛdhrakū�ța, there is a difference in the manner of perception. "A thousandfold" means a thousand times more than the previous number of sands of the Ganges.
By departing from the two obstacles of desire for fame and profit and envy of others, one attains the *dhāraṇī* gate of hearing and retaining.

Regarding the phrase "furthermore, one world, etc.," this refers to a single trichiliocosm being pulverized into atoms. As for "eloquence" (*pratibhāna*), it is first attained at the fifth stage (*bhūmi*).
When a Bodhisattva enters this stage, they understand the five sciences (*pañca-vidyā-sthāna*); the Bodhisattva of this stage preaches the Dharma.
It is spoken as it must be spoken, for there is no stammering. When this is discussed in terms of the mind, it is called the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*);

when it pertains to the mouth, it is the unimpeded eloquence of speech. This exists in the ninth stage (*bhūmi*) and continues through the tenth stage, reaching full perfection at the level of Buddhahood.
Regarding the phrase "equal to the atoms of a world," the *Śāstra* states that "immeasurable" refers to number. Question: How many such immeasurables are there? Answer: Ten trillion.
"Immeasurable. Question: "How many billions? Answer: "A hundred thousand billions. Regarding the *amitā-bhramana-dhāraṇī*: "Bhramana" (旋) means "object" (*viṣaya*).
It refers to revolving and observing the objects within the realm of emptiness and existence, as well as the mental activities of sentient beings;

because it can comprehend and know these with instantaneous swiftness, it is called "revolving" (*bhramana*). Question: "How many objects within the realm of emptiness and existence are there? Answer: "Hundreds of thousands of millions."
There are immeasurable billions of objects consisting of both emptiness and existence. A bodhisattva gives rise to a single cognition;
in a single kṣaṇa, they are able to take as their object all such objects of emptiness and existence. Prior to the fifth bhūmi, when contemplating emptiness, one has not yet reached existence;
when reaching existence, one has not yet contemplated emptiness. Upon reaching this bhūmi, the wisdom that is itself emptiness is able to reach existence. First.
In a single instant, when contemplating emptiness, one is able to penetrate existence; when penetrating existence, one is able to contemplate emptiness.
This Bodhisattva of the Wisdom of Skillful Means regarding Emptiness initiates sublime practices within existence and swiftly observes this realm of both emptiness and existence;
thus, it is established with the name "Revolution. From the fifth bhūmi onward, the ultimate and the conventional are in opposition; regarding this opposing realm, [the Bodhisattva] is able to...

He observes them like an old owl circling in the air, intending to seize its prey. The Bodhisattva, within the emptiness of the *dharmatā*, simply contemplates the capacities and natures of sentient beings;

though the natures of water and fire are utterly opposed, the mirror can reflect them both at once within their opposing conditions. This is also like that.
This is so. Not being obstructed by emptiness or existence is called "revolving. When contemplating emptiness, one immediately realizes ultimate truth;

when contemplating existence, one immediately penetrates the distinctions of the conventional. Contemplating emptiness is original wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*); contemplating existence is subsequent wisdom (*prṣṭha-labdha-jñāna*). This is according to their full accomplishment.
This occurs in the tenth stage (*bhūmi*).
Regarding the mention of the "trichiliocosm" and so forth, this refers to the eighth stage. Here, one possesses the four types of non-retrogression.
In the eighth stage, there is signlessness and effortlessness; because one turns [the wheel] spontaneously within the swift current of the Dharma, it is called the "Wheel of Non-Retrogression."
Regarding the phrase "two thousand lands" and so forth: this refers to the tenth stage (*bhūmi*). As for the "pure wheel of Dharma" (*dharmacakra*): the wheel of Dharma is fundamentally pure.
When it is transformed by the tainted minds (*sāsrava-citta*) of sentient beings, it is tainted, being identical to the transforming consciousness (*pariṇāma-vijñāna*).

When it is transformed by untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*), it is untainted, being identical to the transforming consciousness. Just as [the stages] prior to the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrva*) are tainted, [so too is the seventh stage].

Because there is a mixed cultivation of both outflowing (*sāsrava*) and non-outflowing (*anāsrava*) states; because from the eighth stage upward it is purely non-outflowing (the aforementioned six [stages] are realized based on their respective positions).

Regarding the phrase "a small thousandfold world system" and so forth: these five subsequent stages are realized based on rebirth. This refers to the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*) prior to the [first] stage.

Consequently, one may enter the Path of Seeing after one, or even up to eight, lifetimes, thereby attaining the rank of a Bodhisattva of the First Ground (*prathamabhūmi*).
If it is asked: "How can this be called the benefit of 'present realization' (*sākṣāt-pratyakṣa-lābha*), when the fruit is only attained after three or four future lifetimes? [The answer follows:]...

Regarding the phrase "four sets of four world-systems," this refers to sixteen bodhisattvas, numbering as many as the atoms in Jambudvīpa, who after passing through four births attain entry into the first stage (bhūmi).
This is based on the varying degrees of nearness and distance in the bodhisattvas' cultivation; it is for this reason that the number of births differs, being more or less.
The five kinds of bodhi: this refers to the bodhi of the enlightened mind (the first stage, based on birth, realization, and attainment).
As for the statement "furthermore, there are eight worlds and so forth," this refers to ordinary beings who have resolved their minds toward bodhi;

Regarding the statement "as explained in the *Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta* and other chapters": *dhāraṇī* is precisely mindfulness and wisdom (*smṛti-prajñā*).

This concludes the third section.

"Samādhi" refers to meditative concentration; it is capable of manifesting all form-bodies (*rūpa-kāya*). The name is established based on the capacity to manifest [the bodies]. This is called the first.
This is the Samādhi of the Body of All Colors (*sarva-rūpa-kāya-samādhi*). It refers to the eighteen types of bodies.
Regarding the statement that forty-two thousand devaputras attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), [Mi-xing] says there are three kinds of non-arising:

first, the non-arising of the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*), which is the absence of the two attachments to self and dharmas, through the realization of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) as having no intrinsic nature (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*); second, the natural... Non-arising: one realizes that upon the *paratantra* (dependent) nature there is no inherent nature of spontaneous arising; thus, the afflictions and suffering of the three delusions do not arise.

Regarding the statement that the Bodhisattva Flower Virtue (Huade) attained the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and so forth: "samādhi" refers to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the principle of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
Arising from the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) of the fourth dhyāna, one realizes the principle of the One Vehicle; this is called the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.
There is yet another significant point here which the commentators failed to cite, thereby omitting it. The Sūtra states: "When he had spoken this 'Chapter on the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara'..."
At that time, the eighty-four thousand people who had come together with the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara attained the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Forms.
This is what is described in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* regarding the eighth stage; it explains the fifth stage, the Stage of Certainty (the fourth section is concluded).

Regarding the statement that there are eighty thousand [versions] of the "Chapter on the Contemplation of Avalokiteśvara" and so forth: this refers to the arousal of the mind of the four great vows, the seeking of the bodhicitta.

The answer is: neither worldly nor two-vehicle minds can equal that unequaled mind.

Therefore, it is called "equal to the equal" (*samasama*). This primarily refers to the initial stage of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*). Second, it is said that the Tathāgata is a person without equal;

because there is nothing superior to him in either the mundane or supramundane realms, he is called "without equal. A Bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind (*prathama-cittotpāda*) is equal in merit to the Buddha.
Furthermore, when sentient beings also resolve to seek *bodhicitta*, they become equal to those Tathāgatas. Thus, the *bodhicitta* of sentient beings...

Because the mind and so forth attain the peerless, it is called "equal to the unequaled" (*asamasama*). Because the bodhi of sentient beings equally attains the peerless merits within the human body, it is called "equal to the unequaled.
This is precisely the non-duality of the initial resolve and the ultimate [attainment];
thus, between these two states of mind, the initial resolve is difficult to achieve. (The fifth section concludes.)
Regarding the mention of the "Dhāraṇī Chapter" and so forth, the "patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) has already been explained [in the sixth section].

Regarding the mention of "Exquisite Adornment" and so forth, An-guo states that there are two explanations in the Mahāyāna: first, the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) severs the seeds and manifestations of afflictions, which is termed "distant from dust";

this is called "dust-free. In the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), one severs the seeds of delusion; this is called "free from impurity. Regarding the "Dharma-eye": "Dharma" is suchness (*tathatā*), the ultimate principle, hence it is called "Dharma.
"Eye" is untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) that realizes this principle, hence it is called "pure. This is precisely what is meant by "eye, wisdom, clarity, and awakening."
The sub-commentary states: "Because one has attained the first fruit; this is not the Mahāyāna path of vision" (the eighth section concludes).
Regarding the mention of the *Samantabhadra-utsāha-parivarta* and other such texts: "Universal" (*samanta*) means all-pervading; "Worthy" (*bhadra*) means virtuous and excellent.
Thus, it is the principle of universal excellence that is named Samantabhadra. Now, practicing the causal conduct of Samantabhadra is called being "Samantabhadra."
The Path is that which can realize wisdom; it is called the Path of Samantabhadra.

Regarding the statement "the five types of predictions": these refer to the benefits of the prediction of the fruit. Among the six types of predictions, excluding the prediction of the possession of causes, the remaining five predictions record the future attainment of Buddhahood.

Regarding the statement "these twenty-five categories," etc.: the "Chapter on Manifest Realization" (Pratyutpanna-samādhi) comprises one category; the "Chapter on Devadatta" (Devadatta-parivarta) comprises four categories; the "Chapter on Discrimination" (Vibhaṅga-parivarta) comprises twelve categories;

the "Chapter on Bhaiṣajyarāja" (Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta) comprises one category; the "Chapter on Gadgadasvara" (Gadgadasvara-parivarta) comprises three categories; the "Chapter on Avalokiteśvara" (Avalokiteśvara-parivarta) comprises one category;

"Categories. These twenty-five stages are "realized and received as benefits.
