Regarding the phrase "as it has been taught": since the expression "as it has been taught" is present, it is clearly understood that this refers to the sūtra that provides the scriptural proof.
The sūtra says: "At that time, from within the jeweled stūpa, a great voice issued forth, praising: 'Excellent, excellent!
Śākyamuni World-Honored One, you are able, with your impartial great wisdom, to teach the Dharma for bodhisattvas, which is protected by the Buddhas. It is marvelous...
The Lotus Sūtra was preached for the great assembly. "It is so, it is so," said Śākyamuni, the World-Honored One;

"all that has been spoken is the absolute truth. Furthermore, he said: "If, after I have attained Buddhahood and entered parinirvāṇa, there is a place in the lands of the ten directions where the Lotus Sūtra is being preached, my stūpa shall manifest before them for the sake of hearing this sūtra, and shall act as their protector."
Verification. [The Buddha] praised him, saying, "Excellent. Originally, Jñānakośa accompanied Prabhūtaratna Buddha to come and verify this sutra.

Therefore, when the Bodhisattva saw that Prabhūtaratna Buddha had finished verifying the sutra, he thought there was nothing further to do and requested to return. He questioned Prabhūtaratna, who did not say he would go;
why then did Jñānakośa say he would go? The answer is: those below cannot fathom the mind of those above. What is known below is not the same as what is known above.
He requested to return because he wished for the Many Treasures Stūpa to descend to listen to the remainder of the sutra; this is why he did not say "depart.

It is known that the eight chapters constitute the main body (*śarīra*). Master Lu said: "The Master of the Commentary (*shuzhu*) cites this scriptural passage as if to prove that the ten and a half chapters of the sutra text constitute the main body.
If it were not so, why would three more chapters of the sutra text be preached after the main body before [the conclusion]?"

Zhijí spoke of his return. [The Buddha] replied, "This is also not so. When the Buddha Prabhūtaratna was in his own land, he heard that the eight chapters of the true teaching were completed and immediately came here;

even until his arrival at this place, once the 'Dharmabhāṇaka-parivarta' had concluded, the stupa surged forth to testify to the scripture, and then Zhijí requested his return. The sequence of events is arranged in this manner."

Regarding the statement "if one does not speak of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) and so forth," this refers to the established position of former masters, namely Master Jing of Jiguo Monastery; however, all who obtain benefit therein belong to the True Teaching (*saddharma*).

Regarding the phrase "in the *Samantabhadra-parivarta* and so forth," this cites examples to demonstrate that [the teaching] is not [the finality]. It is only upon reaching the *Samantabhadra-parivarta* that [the One Vehicle] is not spoken of.

If all who obtain benefit [from the teaching] of the One Vehicle are considered to accord with the true doctrine, the ancient masters replied: "From the beginning until the *Samantabhadra* chapter, all constitute obtaining benefit;
what fault could there be in this?"

If one says that, according to the ancients such as Master Zunliao, even if it were granted that [the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*] is not [the primary teaching], the intention is that whatever brings benefit is all part of the orthodox tradition;
this would be identical to the interpretation of the ancient Master Zunliao, who explained its benefits across twenty-seven chapters.
Regarding the phrase "Furthermore, since the matter is not yet concluded," etc., this is a citation of the text used to provide a further refutation. It refutes Master Jing:
if the nineteen chapters constitute the main body of the teaching (*śāstramūla*), then the main body has not yet been fully expounded.

Furthermore, according to the ancient Master Zun, from the "Expedient Means" chapter (*upāyakauśalya-parivarta*) downward through twenty-seven chapters, the benefits are elucidated; since those benefits are not yet concluded, how could Zhiji have requested to return midway? Therefore...
It is known that the eight chapters constitute the main body of the text and are virtuous.

Regarding the statement "or including the Dharma Master and others," the commentator (the author of the sub-commentary) further establishes a second section, which additionally incorporates the passage from the *Dharmabhāṇaka-parivarta* concerning the initial bestowal of predictions upon the eight classes of beings:
those seeking the path of the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, and the Buddha-way, and so forth.

"Whoever, in the presence of the Buddha, hears even a single verse or a single phrase of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and rejoices in it for even a single thought-moment—I shall bestow upon them all the prediction that they shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. This passage from the scripture is also part of the main body (*samyag-artham*).
Furthermore, it says: 'To prevent external objections. An objection is raised: 'If every place where there is a prediction constitutes the main body, then [the section on] the Dharma..."
In the beginning of the "Chapter on the Teacher" (*Śāstṛ-parivarta*), there is also a prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*). Why is it not judged to be the "True Doctrine" (*saddharma*)?

The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows: Thesis (*pakṣa*): The "Chapter on the Dharma Master" (*Dharmabhāṇaka-parivarta*) is also entitled to be called the True Doctrine. Reason (*hetu*): Because it contains a prophecy. Similar Example (*sapakṣa*): Just like the preceding eight chapters.
Among the eight chapters, there is the bestowal of a prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*); thus it may be designated as the section of the "True Doctrine" (*saddharma*).

Yet, although there is a prophecy within the "Dharma Master" chapter (*dharmabhāṇaka-parivarta*), why is it not included within the "True Doctrine"? Although there is a prophecy in the "Dharma Master" chapter, it cannot be called a section of the "True Doctrine.
Since there is a prophecy among the [other] eight chapters, it likewise is not included within the "True Doctrine. The *Commentary* (*shu*) answers: "Alternatively, including the Dharma..."
The Master and others say that although the "Chapter on Encouraging Retention" (Kanji-hon) is granted to those present in the assembly and so forth, the Commentary asks:

"If the 'Exposition of the One Vehicle' (Ichijō-setsu) and the 'Bestowal of Predictions' (Juki-sho) constitute the primary teaching (shōjū), then since predictions are also bestowed upon two classes of nuns within the 'Chapter on Encouraging Retention,' why is this not considered a segment of the primary teaching?"

The commentary on the response states: Although the "Chapter on Upholding" (Dhāraṇī-parivarta) is equal [to the others], there are three reasons why it does not constitute the section of the main teaching (saddharma):

first, because the Buddha bestows a prediction (vyākaraṇa) upon those who request the upholding of the sutra; second, because it further states that he has already bestowed a general prediction previously; and third, because it does not record the One Vehicle (ekayāna).
Therefore, it is not the primary teaching. The *Vyākaraṇa-sūtra* states: "Kauṭamī, I have previously declared in general that all śrāvakas have already received their predictions.
Now, if you wish to know your own prediction, in a future age you shall become a Buddha named Sarvasattvapriyadarśana Tathāgata.
The Buddha then told Yaśodharā: "In a future age, for hundreds of thousands of millions..."
Within the teachings of billions of Buddhas, he shall cultivate the bodhisattva practices and serve as a great Dharma teacher.
Gradually perfecting the path to Buddhahood, he will attain enlightenment in the land of *Sukhāvatī*, where he shall become a Buddha named *Sahasrakoṭiraśmilakṣaṇaparipūrṇa Tathāgata*.
Regarding the request to uphold the sutra: the sutra states, "O World-Honored One, O Guide, who brings peace and security to devas and humans;

having heard this prediction, our minds are fully at ease. After the bhikṣuṇīs had spoken these verses, they addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, we too shall widely proclaim this sutra in other lands.
[The Buddha] then asked them in return, "Has the World-Honored One already bestowed predictions upon you?"
Then he maintains the sutra. This means that first there is the bestowal of the prediction (vyākaraṇa), and subsequently the request to maintain the sutra.

How can it be said that the prediction comes only after the request to maintain the sutra? The answer is: from the perspective of the Buddha’s original intention, he rewards him for maintaining the sutra; thus, the resolve to maintain the sutra is what precedes.
The bestowal of the prediction (vyākaraṇa) occurs later. Originally, she intended to uphold the sutra; the nun also harbored a look of sorrow in her heart.

However, the request to uphold the sutra served as the cause for the prediction, which was subsequently bestowed as the result; therefore, it is said that she "requested [the prediction] by means of the cause. Furthermore, it says:

Because the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja had previously requested that he uphold this sutra, and because the Buddha intended to have two classes of nuns likewise request its upholding, He first bestowed the prediction of enlightenment upon him.

Regarding the statement that the remaining nineteen chapters constitute a collective title, Master Lu says that they should actually be called "eighteen and a half chapters. The answer is that this is merely a general designation.

This is the section on characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Regarding the phrases "praise, testimony, reception, and entrustment," there are five types of circulation [of the teaching]: first, praise and veneration;

this refers to the beginning of the "Dharma Master" chapter, which praises the virtues of the Dharma master to inspire reverence. Second, testimony and faith; this refers to the "Jeweled Stupa" and "Heavenly Bestowal" chapters.

1. The Jeweled Stupa: the realization of others; 2. Devadatta: the self-realization; 3. Receiving the Mandate: from the Chapter on Upholding (*Dhāraṇī-parivarta*) to the Chapter on Never-Despising (*Sadāparibhūta*), which constitutes the Chapter on Upholding;
this is the correct reception of the mandate to uphold the sutra, while the remaining chapters arise sequentially from it;

4. Entrustment: the Chapter on Supernatural Power and the Chapter on Exhortation (*Anuparindanā-parivarta*); 5. Distribution: the distribution and circulation [of the teaching], from the Chapter on Bhaiṣajyarāja to the Chapter on Samantabhadra. Bhaiṣajyarāja...

The Bodhisattva [Samantabhadra] personally practices asceticism to circulate [the teaching]. The Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound (Ghoṣadatta) teaches and transforms sentient beings through the practice of asceticism;

therefore, he is named "Causing Practice" (Li-xing). According to the Master of the Commentary’s topical outline, the first four chapters constitute the "Circulation by Way of Praising and Valuing," wherein both the Dharma and the person are praised as worthy of honor and esteem;
this is the praise for realization within the traces. The subsequent seven chapters constitute the "Circulation by Way of Learning and Practice," concerning the study of propagation...

This sutra consists of the primary practice and its auxiliary practices, which ensure that [the teaching] remains unimpaired; this corresponds to the "Receiving the Mandate" (*śāsana*) section within the commentary.
The final eight chapters constitute the entrustment for circulation, wherein the signs of entrustment are shown and the mandate is received for practice.
This is because it represents the entrustment of the mandate for practice within the assembly (the second major division of the commentary’s eight-and-a-half chapters on the "True Teaching").

Regarding the phrase "or the initial introductory section, etc.," this is the topical outline (*pīṭhikā*) provided by Master Jing. It refers to the "Introductory Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*), which clarifies the reasons for the arising [of the teaching].

Regarding the phrase "from the 'Expedient Means' chapter down to... and so forth, this records the nineteen chapters designated as the "True Doctrine" (*saddharma*) by Master Jigu. From here on, it relies upon...

Yoga consists of three sections: the object (*ālambana*), the practice (*prayoga*), and the fruit (*phala*). Question: If this is so, how should one reconcile the fact that Zhiji requested to return midway through the nineteen chapters of the main teaching (*saddharma*)?
Answer: It is as explained in the *She dasheng lun shi* (Commentary on the Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra). Those of inferior faculties cannot fathom the activities of superior wisdom;
they assume that the exposition of the main teaching has concluded, and for this reason they request to return. This is why Prabhūtaratna did not depart.
Regarding the phrase "to make known the realm of verbal expression," this is the meaning explained below. Question: Why is it necessary to speak of the realm? Answer: The commentary states:

"To make known the realm of verbal expression, etc. Forty years ago, when the Tathāgata taught the provisional [teachings], people did not recognize them as provisional, but instead clung to them as ultimate.
When the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* was preached at the assembly, they did not know it was the truth; moreover, they were startled and filled with doubt and wonder.

Why did the Tathāgata preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, preaching the provisional to cause them to relinquish it, and preaching the real to cause them to grasp it? To relinquish the sheep- and deer-carts and ascend the ox-cart; to abandon the conjured city and return to the treasure place.
This very distinction between the provisional and the real, when confronted by Śāriputra’s cognitive mind, is immediately termed the "object" (*viṣaya*). Sound...
Upon hearing this, he immediately received his prediction [of enlightenment]. The Sūtra says: "That is your very self; you should rejoice. It further states:

"The twelve hundred arhats shall all likewise become Buddhas. From the "Expedient Means" chapter (Upāya-paṛivarta) to the "Entrustment" chapter (Parīndanā-paṛivarta), these twelve chapters together clarify the realm of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
Within this realm, there are both the provisional and the real. These are designated as the objects of the cognitive mind of the śrāvakas.

This refers to the objective realm (*viṣaya*). It is said that through the practice of discourse, one causes [others] to know the causes and so forth. Question: Why is it necessary to speak of practice? Answer:

Regarding the objective realms mentioned previously, Śāriputra already knew that the provisional could be abandoned and the real could be grasped; however, he did not yet recognize the practice of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Therefore, the practice has been explained here to cause him to know the causes.
To distinguish between right and wrong, one causes them to recognize that the four practices of peace and happiness are right, while the ten kinds of evil conditions are wrong.

One encourages them to study what is right and eliminate what is wrong. As the Sūtra says: "Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates all phenomena as empty, according to their true mark (*yathābhūtalakṣaṇa*), non-perverted, unmoving, non-retrogressive, and unchanging; this is the study of what is right. The Sūtra further says: "One does not associate with [evil] nations..."
Kings, princes, ministers, and high officials do not associate with various non-Buddhist practitioners, such as brahmins or Nirgranthas;
this is the exclusion [of such persons]. While the Tathāgata was thus correctly teaching the sequence of practices, Bodhisattvas from the lower regions surged forth from the earth.

Regarding the matter of responding to stimuli, this is precisely the practice of the four practices of peaceful dwelling (*catur-āśvāsa-caryā*). Those who uphold the sutra obtain the first grade of peace and bliss. This clarifies the practices to be performed.
The "Emerged Bodhisattvas" (*utsada-bodhisattva*) are all practitioners capable of such conduct; these two grades are collectively termed "practice. Question:
How can those who are capable practitioners also be called "practice"? Answer: A person is formed by gathering together the dharmas. It is that which a person...
It is accomplished; it is also called "practice.

Regarding the statement that "through the fruit of discourse, one causes [others] to know the true and transformational aspects of the body," the question is: for what reason is the fruit of discourse taught? The answer is:

through the fruit of various discourses, one causes [others] to know the conditions of the true and transformational bodies. Having previously abandoned the provisional to grasp the real, the śrāvakas now practice the path of the One Vehicle and attain [it].
The fruit of the One Vehicle. [Sentient beings] mistakenly believe that the sixteen-foot body is the true Buddha;
thus, wishing to seek the Buddha-body of Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, Maitreya requests the fruit. The Tathāgata then teaches the fruit of the three bodies and the lifespan.

Within this section on the fruit, the commentators divide the five chapters of the sutra from the "Tathāgata’s Lifespan" chapter to the "Never-Despising" chapter as the fruit of the One Vehicle. This constitutes the "Lifespan."

The fruit of the ultimate purity and perfect luminosity; the fruit of the analytical merits; the fruit of the partial realization of the noble ones; the chapter on the merit of sympathetic joy; the fruit of supernatural powers and supreme excellence;
the merits of the Dharma Master; the inconceivable fruit of the power of the sutra; and the Chapter of the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging.

This introduces those who have already realized the fruit. The first two chapters clarify the fulfilled fruit (*paripūrṇa-phala*), while the latter three chapters clarify the unfulfilled fruit (*aparipūrṇa-phala*).
According to the common interpretation, the "Chapter on the Lifespan of the Tathāgata" and the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merits" are called the fulfilled fruit.

However, it is not appropriate to call the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merits" the fulfilled fruit; rather, because one hears of the merits that are already fulfilled, it is also termed "fulfilled."
Regarding the fruit: here, this chapter on the "Life Span" (*āyus-pramāṇa*) is called the "Fruit of Full Completion. The remaining four chapters are called the "Fruits of Non-Completion.

Although this present chapter explains the fruit, it is a fruit within the context of the cause. Among the four chapters [of the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*], the first division of these four is called the "Fruit of Non-Completion";
although this present chapter explains the fruit, it is a fruit within the context of the cause. This is stated among the four chapters in their initial division.
The Chapter on Distinct Qualities (*Pṛthagguṇa-varga*). The fruit of the untainted (*anāsrava*). The last three chapters concern the fruit of the tainted (*sāsrava*).

Within the fruit of the tainted, one chapter concerns the ancillary practice (*pārśvagamana*), and two chapters concern the primary practice (*mukhyagamana*). Furthermore, one chapter concerns the dharma that is practiced, and one chapter concerns the person who practices it. It is also said:

the Chapter on Lifespan (*Āyus-pramāṇa-varga*) concerns the fruit within the stage of culmination (*niṣṭhāgata-bhūmi*); the Chapter on Distinguishing Qualities (*Guṇavibhāga-varga*) concerns the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).

The fruit of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is found in the "Chapter on the Merit of the Dharma Master. The fruit within the stage of application (*prayogamārga*) is found in the "Chapter on the Merit of Rejoicing.

The fruit within the stage of equipment (*sambhāramārga*) is [found in the "Chapter on the Prediction"]. Question: Why is the "Chapter on Never-Disparaging" not mentioned? Answer: That chapter concerns the person who is capable of practicing the conduct.

This refers to the realization of the four preceding stages; it cites what has already been realized. By stating "the fruit" (the result), he causes [beings] to know the true and the manifested aspects of the body.

Having first established the fulfillment of the fruit with the initial three phrases, the question is asked: what is the intention behind stating the fruit? The answer is: by stating the fruit, one causes [beings] to know the true and the manifested aspects of the body.

The character "true" (zhen) refers to the *dharmakāya* and the *saṃbhogakāya*. The character "manifested" (hua) refers to the *nirmāṇakāya*, which even manifests ten kinds [of manifestations] for Bodhisattvas up to the tenth stage.

The bodies and so forth are all transformations. The transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the body of communal enjoyment for others (*sambhogakāya* for others) are like the reflection of the moon in water; the Dharma body (*dharmakāya*) is like space;
and the body of self-enjoyment (*svasaṃbhogakāya*) is like the moon in the heavens. Since one merely realizes the fruition of the Dharma, why worry about not obtaining the transformation body?

Regarding the phrase "the fruit and cause of realization" (*zheng*): the character *zheng* (realization) pertains to the Buddha; the fruit of Buddhahood is called "realization. As for "fruit and cause," Lu says:

it is the fruit of the cause of realization, hence "the fruit of realization"; the character "cause" (*yin*) serves as a syntactic particle. Alternatively, it may mean "attaining the fruit" or "attaining the cause."

The phrase "the cause and fruit of the realization of the name" (with the upper heading indicating the fulfillment of the fruit) refers to the transformation body that encourages consciousness and so forth; these two lines explain the fulfillment of the fruit. This encourages consciousness regarding the six-foot transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

To know that the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) is provisional is to seek realization in the true; the *dharmakāya* and *sambhogakāya* (dharma and enjoyment bodies) are termed "the true. (The above clarifies the fulfillment of the ultimate fruit.)

Regarding the phrase "gradually attaining cause and fruit," this explains the fruit that is not yet fulfilled. The character for "cause" (yin) refers to the fruit that is not yet fulfilled, namely the paths of accumulation (*sambhāra-mārga*), preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), seeing (*darśana-mārga*), and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
The character for "fruit" (guo) refers exclusively to the cause; it is the fruit of the paths of seeing and cultivation.

This refers to the fruit that is not yet fulfilled; therefore, it is called "gradually attaining cause and fruit. The combination of these merits of cause and fruit is termed "the superior virtues of the two stages.
As for the statement, "The Bodhisattva, knowing this, then [attains] equality," these two phrases reveal the person who attains them, namely, the attainment of the eleven stages.

This is correct. Regarding the statement "fully manifesting the fruit, the cause, and so forth," these two phrases together explain the five categories. "Cause" refers to the fruit that is not yet fulfilled;
"fruit" refers to the fruit that is already fulfilled. Because the cause and fruit are explained collectively, it is called "fully manifesting."

Regarding the "supreme virtues accomplished through speech," these are the merits of the three bodies; they constitute the Buddha-fruit attained by those who previously resided in the stage of incomplete fruition.
(The nineteenth chapter of the Main Doctrine concludes here.)

Regarding the phrase "The Chapter on Supernatural Powers (Ṛddhi-paṭala), Part II," etc.: the remaining eight chapters are titled the "Circulation" (Pravartana). There are three types of circulation: first, the circulation by demonstration of signs (*liṅga-pravartana*), which is the Chapter on Supernatural Powers;

this involves demonstrating signs by extending the tongue and emitting light. Second, the circulation by entrustment (*parindanā-pravartana*), which is the Chapter on Entrustment (*Parīndanā-paṭala*).
The third, "Receiving the Mandate and Circulating [the Text]," covers from the "Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta" until the end of the sūtra.
When it says, "All such origins are equal," this refers back to the preceding section to judge the three parts beginning with the "Introduction Chapter.
Such origins will all be extensively analyzed in the commentary on the main text below. Mou says: "Above..."

The explanation concludes with this structural analysis (*ko-p'an*), which establishes the three divisions as definitive. This corresponds to the Venerable Dao’an of the Jin dynasty, who categorized all sutras into three parts;
it is appropriate to harmonize this with the Western master Vasubandhu’s *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, which likewise divides all sutras into three parts.
Question: What does the World-Honored One intend to signify by now teaching these three divisions? Answer:
Yet, when the Great Sage appeared in the world, his sole concern was to benefit all beings. His compassionate teaching was invariably suited to the capacities of those who received it.

Thus, forty years later, he gathered at Vulture Peak to open the wondrous gate. Saints and ordinary beings assembled like clouds; the Sage remained within his cave of meditative concentration, while the radiance of his *ūrṇā* mark coalesced into a brilliant glow.
The earth shook, awakening those of narrow minds, and celestial flowers rained down, startling the great multitude. Then, suddenly—

The ears and eyes serve as the causes for the correct exposition. The ritual preceding the preaching of the Dharma is called the *nidāna* (introductory section). What is termed the *samyak-siddhānta* (main body)?

Since the introduction has already been established, it is appropriate to expound the main body. Therefore, [the Buddha] arose from meditative concentration with a composed and serene air and issued a command so that the principles and phenomena might be clearly understood according to the faculties of the listeners.

He distinguished both the Dharma and its analogies, thereby moistening and refreshing the assembly and benefiting the three faculties. This present condition is what is called the "correct" [section].
[The Buddha] spoke. Why? The propagation [of the teaching] relies solely upon the Tathāgata’s dissemination of the Dharma; it does not refer to mutual benefit.
At that time, wishing to speak of this sutra from afar so that its benefits might reach the distant future, he transformed the pure land three times and commanded four [beings] to uphold the sutra.

Whether by gazing into their hearts to entrust it, or by stroking them with his hand to exhort them, there were those of great resolve and lofty conduct who responded to the command to propagate and proclaim it, or who protected it.
The Dharma-Charioteer [the Buddha] caused some to burn their bodies or sear their arms to hear and uphold the benefits of the *dhāraṇīs*. Such people exceeded the number of motes of dust;
the benefits for all beings in a single lifetime surpassed the sands of the Ganges. This is indeed a vast benefit without limit, a transmission that flows without end, reaching into distant ages;
therefore, it is called "circulation. This is a brief explanation of the scope of the sutra.

The statement that "the *Sūtrālaṃkāra*, Chapter One, has seven [sections]" indicates the general title. The term "accomplishment" (*siddhi*) explains this general title.
Question: What is the meaning of "accomplishment"? Answer: There are two meanings: first, the sense of being complete; second, the sense of being perfect. As for "complete":
The seven meanings are not few; thus, it is called "complete. Within these seven meanings, each and every one is termed a "perfect" meaning. Question:

What is the distinction between "complete" (*pūrṇa*) and "perfect" (*paripūrṇa*)? Answer: "Complete" is a term of direct affirmation (*paryudāsa*), indicating that this sūtra alone possesses the seven meanings.

"Perfect" is a term of negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), signifying that other sūtras do not possess the seven meanings and therefore cannot be considered perfect. This is why [the commentary] states...
Question: Since these [features] are not found in other sūtras, why are they restricted to this sūtra alone?
Answer: It is not that other sūtras lack them; however, if a sūtra possesses the sevenfold perfection as in this one, it is not [necessary to mention them elsewhere].
(This concludes the general heading.)

Regarding the statement, "To first describe the general causes," this explains the initial specific title. Question: What is meant by "introduction" (*nidāna*)? Answer: The commentary states, "To first describe the general causes.

This interpretation takes "introduction" (*nidāna*) as "the beginning" (*ādi*). It refers to the initial general narration which serves as the cause for the sevenfold accomplishment (*saptavidha-samudāgama*), and also serves as the general cause for all sūtras.
If one were to speak only of the "accomplishment of mountain cities" (*śaila-nagara-samudāgama*), it would fail to encompass the time when the Buddha was present. If one were to say... [text ends]

The Buddha’s accomplishment [is established]. Within this, the section on the Mountain City (Śrāvastī) establishes the introductory portion (nidāna) by means of the general statement of non-attachment;

therefore, it is called the "Universal Introduction" (sāmānyanidāna). Question: Regarding the seven accomplishments, all are introductions when contrasted with the main body (śarīra). Why, then, is only the "Accomplishment of the Introduction" specifically named "Introduction"?

The answer has two meanings. First, it uses a general term for others to designate a specific name. For example, when one says "that which is seen by the eye among the eleven types of form," that alone is called "eye-form.

Or as when one speaks of a "malignant disease," all diseases are collectively termed "real" (actual), yet the introductory section alone is called the "Introduction" once the introduction is established.
Furthermore, it is like the ring finger: while the other fingers all have names, this finger is "nameless."
As for the "name" (nāman): it takes that which is nameless and makes it a name. The remaining six accomplishments (*siddhi*) also have distinct names and distinct meanings.
This accomplishment of the introductory section (*nidāna*) contains many dharmas; since no other specific name can be established, the introductory section itself serves as its name.
This is because it is said to be "endowed with perfection," etc., being complete in its mountain-like fortress and circularity.
The *Pūrṇa* alone receives the title of "Introduction" (*nidāna*) because it excels all others; that is to say, it is superior to other sūtras. There are two senses in which it is called "superior":
first, in contrast to the six subsequent chapters on accomplishment, it is called "superior to the others"; second, in contrast to other sūtras, it is called "superior to the others.
Possessing these meanings, it alone receives the title of "Introduction. In reality, all seven [chapters] are introductions. [Question: Regarding Rājagṛha and Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain... all [the monks].
All sūtras contain [references to] mountains and cities; why then is this sūtra alone said to be "perfectly complete"? The answer is twofold:

First, it does not deny that other sūtras have mountains and cities; it merely excludes a specific class of sūtras—those not spoken at royal cities or Vulture Peak. This exclusion pertains to their absence, not to their presence.
Second, while other sūtras mention mountains and cities, they do so without symbolic significance. This sūtra, however, uses the city as a metaphor for the teaching, and...
The mountain, moreover, represents principle (li). Thus the commentary states: "Either the teaching is as wondrous as a city because it contains wondrous principles;

or the principle is as lofty as a mountain because it transcends the two vehicles. Therefore, the fact that the Sūtra is located in the royal city yet dwells upon Vulture Peak has a symbolic significance.

Consequently, it is said that the accomplishment of the introduction (nidāna) possesses this unique function alone. Thus, everything from "Thus have I heard" up to "in the mountains" constitutes the introduction.
This constitutes the fulfillment [of the assembly].
Regarding the statement that the fulfillment of the two assemblies is equal to that of the Great [Vehicle], there are two sections in the treatise (*śāstra*).

First, number: this refers to the fact that the great assembly is innumerable; thus, it is spoken of collectively as "innumerable. As the Sūtra says: "Twelve thousand people, etc. Second, practice: the treatise states, "the śrāvakas..."
The practitioner of the Hīnayāna cultivates the practices of the Lesser Vehicle; the Bodhisattva cultivates the practices of the Mahāyāna. Question: The sūtra does not mention "practices" (caryā);
how can the masters of the śāstras speak of them? Answer: There are two interpretations. First, when the śāstra mentions [the name] but the sūtra does not, they are mutually implied by ellipsis.
Second, the very names within the sūtra constitute the practices themselves; for both Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas, the name is derived from their practice.
Regarding the term "bhikṣu," this is translated as "mendicant" (*kṣānti*). Seeking alms is his practice. Regarding the name "Bodhisattva," it means one who seeks *bodhi*.

Delivering sentient beings is his practice. The *Tri-saṃgraha-guṇa-śāstra* states that these are all sixteen phrases concerning the great *arhats*, which manifest the accomplishment of the qualities of the *śrāvakas*. All [of them] [aspire] toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Non-retrogression. The thirteen phrases manifest the accomplishment of the merits of bodhi. Regarding the four modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*), the *Dharmasthitinirdeśasūtra* states:
"At that time, the World-Honored One and the fourfold assembly reached [the point of] praise. There is an interpretation that these modes of deportment pertain to the audience.

"Abiding according to the Dharma belongs to the Buddha. When the Buddha abides within these modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*) in accordance with the Dharma, it is called "abiding in deportment according to the Dharma.
Regarding the phrase "because it is complete and excels other sūtras," this single sentence explains only the four meanings among the [six] characteristics of the assembly's accomplishment.
The perfection of number, the perfection of practice, and the perfection of merit—these three aspects are fully realized and function throughout the aforementioned three stages. Question:
Since all other [sūtras] possess these accomplishments, why is it said that this one excels other sūtras? Answer: Other sūtras do not fully possess these four meanings.
It is not called "perfect.
Regarding the statement that the three Tathāgatas wish to preach the Dharma (up to) "accomplishment," etc., the Sūtra says:

"For the sake of all Bodhisattvas, he preached a Mahāyāna sūtra named *Ananta-artha* (Infinite Meanings), which possesses seventeen names; it is superior to others. If he did not preach infinite meanings..."

Regarding the sūtra: when the time to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* has not yet arrived, one merely preaches the *Anantamukhanirhāra-dhāraṇī* (or *Anantārtha-sūtra*) until that time for preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* arrives.
As for the phrase "the four bases upon which the preaching and so forth depend," this refers to the deportment of the Tathāgata’s preaching, which is in accordance with his own mode of conduct.
Furthermore, if the Tathāgata intends to preach the Dharma, but the heavens do not rain flowers and the earth does not tremble, it is not called "conformity.
When the Tathāgata intends to preach the Dharma, the heavens rain four kinds of flowers and the earth shakes in six ways; this is called "conforming to the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma.

Here, the majestic deportment (īryāpatha) is that which conforms, and the preaching of the Dharma is that which is conformed to. The Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma is that which abides, and the majestic deportment...
"Ritual propriety (*īryāpatha*) is that which is dwelt in. It should be said that it is the accomplishment of dwelling in accordance with the basis of the teaching of the Dharma.

If one follows the text of the treatise, the order is reversed. Question: What is the difference between this "intermediate" ritual propriety and the ritual propriety within the "accomplishment of the assembly"?

Answer: Because of the distinction between the speaker and the listener. This [intermediate propriety] refers solely to the Buddha, while that [propriety of the assembly] refers to the audience; thus, both are distinct.
Regarding the statement "the five bases for preaching," etc.: the thirsting and yearning mind of sentient beings serves as the cause for the teaching.
The Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma is the "supporter" (āśraya), while the thirsting and yearning mind of sentient beings is the "supported" (āśrita).

Since this thirsting and yearning mind acts as the cause for the preaching of the Dharma, what need is there for the emission of light? Answer: To obtain the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma, it is necessary that those sentient beings possess such thirsting and yearning.
The "aspiring mind" (*āśaya-citta*). There is nothing that surpasses the emission of light to illuminate the objective realm in order to attain the aspiring minds of sentient beings.

By emitting light to illuminate the objective realm, one can generate the aspiring minds of sentient beings. If discussed in general terms, both the emission of light and the aspiring minds of sentient beings are collectively termed the "causes for teaching.
However, if discussed according to their essential nature, it refers specifically to the aspiring mind itself. This is not found in other sutras.

This [sūtra] alone possesses this emission of light; within that light are seven matters, and sentient beings look up to it with longing hearts. If one were to discuss them, each is fully present here, whereas they are not found in other sūtras.
Regarding the phrase "the six great assemblies and others": at that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva thought, "Since I do not know the way, whom should I ask?
Who is able to answer? The sentient beings harbor doubts; whom should they ask? He intended to manifest the appearance of harboring doubt. At that moment, Maitreya Bodhisattva had this thought:
"Now the World-Honored One has manifested these signs of supernatural power; by what causes and conditions have they come to be?"
Regarding this auspicious omen, the minds of the two groups of people were truly perplexed. As the Sūtra says: "At that time, the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs [asked], 'Until now, we have always asked whom?
" Thirdly, Maitreya extended both intentions to pose a question concerning the prior cause. At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva, wishing to resolve his own doubts, asked:
"By what causes and conditions has this auspicious omen appeared? Although he questioned only one person, many wished to hear the answer.
A sense of rare wonder arose. There are two types of people who ask questions: first, those who are capable of asking; second, those who are asked.

The one from whom [Mañjuśrī] heard was Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva himself, which constitutes the seventh accomplishment. Now, taking the one who is capable of asking, that is Maitreya, which constitutes the sixth accomplishment.
The assembly in the hall harbored doubts; with one mind and a single purpose, they desired to obtain [the answer] from Maitreya alone, rather than from many.
A person raised a question. Although the question was addressed to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva alone, those present in the assembly were many.

These many people, with one mind and a single intent, desired to grasp the meaning of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva’s answer so as to understand the causes and conditions of the Dharma teaching and resolve the nets of doubt within their hearts;
thus it is said that "many people desire to hear" and give rise to a heart of rare longing. Why do you not ask?
Whether there are ten people or five, one asks only a single person. If that person can answer the doubts, then thousands or tens of thousands of people are resolved.

If one person can resolve the points of doubt for many, and even sever the doubts of many, it is still just that one person who can sever them. This is why many people are not questioned. [As stated in] other sutras...
Regarding "without cause": if one discusses Maitreya’s questions and Mañjuśrī’s answers, this is not found in other sūtras.

As for the statement "Mañjuśrī and the others [numbering] seven," it means that through his knowledge of past lives (*pūrvajātismṛti-jñāna*), Mañjuśrī knew that in a past life he had been the Dharma Master *Prabhāsa*.
He saw that Maitreya was a Bodhisattva seeking fame; thus, by directly perceiving the characteristics of past causes and effects, he accomplished the ten [powers].

Regarding the various matters, they appear as they do in the present. Therefore, the answer states: "as they appear in the present," which indicates that this is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) rather than inference (*anumāna*), thereby encompassing the capacity for knowledge.
The *Śāstra* says: "As for the causal characteristics (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*), Mañjuśrī himself saw his own body practicing various deeds in various Buddha-lands;
these serve as the causes for the present time. The *Commentary* says: "Because it refers to the causal practices of a Bodhisattva, it is precisely [this]."

This is due to the Buddha Joyful-Treasury-Maṇi-Jewel-Accumulation as its cause. As for what is called the "characteristic of the fruit," it refers to the very self-substance upon which one relied in the past;

that is, the Body of Sublime Radiance (*Prabhāsa*). In relation to the causes of the five precepts and ten wholesome deeds from previous lives, the attainment of this Body of Sublime Radiance constitutes the characteristic of the fruit.
When the Body of Sublime Radiance ascends the seat and preaches the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for twenty billion bodhisattvas...
“Sa” (薩) is the causal characteristic (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*). It serves as the cause for the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrīprabha to attain Buddhahood in the future;
thus it is called the causal characteristic. Regarding the ten kinds of matters: first, the cause of the presently perceived great meaning, which refers to the eight great meanings;

second, the cause of the presently perceived profound intent of the worldly chapters; and so on, up to tenth, the cause of the presently perceived events experienced by oneself. As the Sūtra says: “Wondrous Light.”

The Dharma Master was none other than my own self. When he came to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he manifested ten kinds of signs of cause and effect that do not appear in any other sutras. (End of the preceding topical outline.)

Regarding the statement "dividing the seven into two," the commentator (the *shuzhu*) classifies the sevenfold accomplishment (*saptavidha-sampad*) into two parts: first, the general introduction (*sāmānyamukha-nidāna*); second, the specific introduction (*viśeṣamukha-nidāna*).
While the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-śāstra* divides [the nidāna] into seven, various sūtras combine them into two. These two types of introductions further constitute five pairs:
first, the pair of the "testimony of faith" (*śraddhā-prasāda*) and the "initiation" (*utthāna*). The testimony of faith applies to all sūtras, whereas the initiation applies only to specific ones.

Regarding the sūtra: because it initiates the main body of the teaching, there are two parts—the sequence after the sūtra and the sequence before the sūtra. The four characters "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) were placed at the conclusion after the preaching of the sūtra, upon entering parinirvāṇa;
this is called the "Postscript to the Sūtra. From the words "At one time" (*ekasmin samaye*) onwards, the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* was preached;

the rain of flowers on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, the earth being planted [with them], and the emission of light that illuminated the realm and summoned the fourfold assembly—this is called the "Preface to the Sūtra."

1. The correspondence between Ānanda and the Tathāgata: "Thus have I heard" is the introduction by Ānanda; from "at one time" onwards is the introduction by the Tathāgata. 2. The correspondence between the future and the present:
"Thus have I heard" refers to the future; from "at one time" onwards refers to the present. 3. The correspondence between the general and the specific:
From "Thus have I heard" down to the "accomplishment of the assembly" is the general introduction (*sūtra-piṭaka*). [The section on] the teaching of non-existence... [is the specific introduction].

From the *Mānavadharmaśāstra-sūtra* onwards is the specific introduction (*pratyuddeśa*). Now, this commentary contains a structural outline (*ko-p'an*), which comprises both the general and specific introductions.
"General" refers to all sūtras; "specific" refers to this particular teaching.

To say that the general introduction (*sādhāraṇa-nidāna*) has five parts is to explain the general introduction. However, the classification of the general introduction varies across the various teachings.
First, according to the *Prajñā-piṭaka* by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha, it is divided into seven parts: first, "Thus" (*evam*), which indicates the Dharma heard; second, "I" (*aham*).

1. "The one who was able to hear" (the person capable of hearing). 2. "The three types of hearing": this refers to personally receiving the words and intent [of the Buddha]. 3. "At one time" (*ekasmin samaye*):

this reveals that the Dharma heard is perfectly suited to the faculties and needs [of the listeners]. 4. "The Buddha": this clarifies the master who preached the Dharma. 5. "The dwelling place": this reveals that there is a specific location.

6. "Together with a great assembly of bhikṣus": this reveals that it was not heard alone. The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra* categorizes these into five parts: first, the general indication of what has been heard, which points to the entire treatise as a whole.

Because it is the Sublime Dharma, it is said to be "comprehensively revealed. Because it was heard directly from [the Buddha], it is said that "[I] have already heard it. Question: Why is it called "at one time"? Answer:
Because the speaker and the listener encountered one another, and there was no distinction in the temporal interval, the Sūtra establishes the phrase "at one time.
Question: Sūtras are spoken by five types of persons: Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, seers, transformed beings, and disciples. It is not yet clear whether this particular Sūtra belongs to...
Who said it? The answer is: It was spoken by the Honored Master, the Victorious One who embodies the Dharma; it was not spoken by anyone else. Therefore, it is the Buddha’s teaching.
Regarding the word "Buddha" mentioned in the sutra, one might ask: The teachings of external paths claim they descended from heaven, or that a vermilion bird brought them here;

yet they have no source at all. I do not know whether this sutra states that there is a specific place of origin. The answer is: The sutra says it was "staying in the city of Rājagṛha, on Vulture Peak Mountain."

This refers to the place of teaching. [The Buddha] asked Ānanda, saying, "Thus have I heard. It is not yet clear whether Śāriputra alone heard it, or if there were others who heard it together with him.
The word *sārdham* (with) carries the meaning of combining, joining, and being together. He was "together with a great assembly of twelve thousand bhikṣus";
thus, there was an assembly that heard it together. For this reason, these five sections appear within the general introduction (*nidāna*).
The first section generally reveals the equality [of the teachings]. In the Master’s commentary on the Sūtra, the "General Introduction" (*sūtrāvatāra*) subsumes these five.

In the Master’s topical outline (*śāstravyavasthāna*) of the treatise, the "Introduction" (*nidāna*) subsumes four; the fifth section, concerning the "audience for whom it is intended," is included within the "Accomplishment of Entering the Assembly.

Thus, both the Introduction and the Accomplishment consist of four sections each. Now, we shall first explain the "Introduction" and the "Accomplishment. Within these, there are four sections, each of which, according to the actual facts, is listed as follows:

The first recitation: Fearing that the scriptural text would become fragmented, the Master of the Commentary combined these four sections into a single recitation. Within this recitation, the commentary states:
"Thus have I heard" constitutes the first [section]. This is where the scripture was lost.

Regarding the statement that the *Śāstra* (treatise) is the basis for discussion and speaks only of the introductory section (*nidāna*) and so forth: this refers to the intention of the *Śāstra*-author’s own topical outline (*vyavasthāna*).

The Master of the Commentary (*ṭīkākāra*) outlines four parts within the accomplishment of the introductory section. However, within the Master of the Treatise’s (*śāstrakāra*) own outline of the accomplishment of the introductory section, he praises only the Mountain City (*Śrāvastī*) and does not mention the other three.
Question: If that is so, then the *Śāstra*-author’s accomplishment of the introductory section fails to encompass the Dharma exhaustively.

Answer: The Master of the Treatise (Śāstrin) bases his praise on the preeminent location, extolling the City of Śrāvastī (Śrāvastī-nagara). Although the other three locations are not praised, they are nonetheless included within the introductory section (nidāna).
Because the City of Śrāvastī possesses a specific symbolic significance, it is distinguished from other sūtras; this is why it is mentioned specifically.

As for the other three, since they do not differ from other sūtras, the treatise does not mention them. Question: Since the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* mentions both the city of Rājagṛha and Vulture Peak (Gṛdhrakūṭa), how can you say [this]?
[Question: Is it not so? [Answer: Although it appears in other sūtras, it does not manifest the specific character of this sūtra. The Treatise says:
"The accomplishment of the introductory section (nidāna) is because two kinds of meanings are manifested within this dharma-gate: first, the manifestation of the excellence of all dharma-gates;
second, the manifestation of the accomplishment of sovereign merit. It is like the city of Rājagṛha, which excels all other cities."
Therefore, because Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain is superior to other mountains, this Dharma-gate is revealed as the most excellent. As it is said in the sūtra:
"The Buddha was dwelling at Rājagṛha on Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain."

Regarding the phrase "the reasons for the single recitation" and so forth: the question asks about the reasons for the recitation and the grounds for its establishment; what is the intended distinction between them?
As for the statement that the sūtra begins with "Thus have I heard," what is the source of this? "By" (yī) refers to the cause or reason. The answer is:
when the Tathāgata entered nirvāṇa, he left behind Ānanda to establish [the teachings]; this is the reason for the recitation. Second, as for the grounds for its establishment: the Buddha...
The term "jiao" (交) is established as "zhù" (著). What is the reason for this? It is because of its usage (*yòng*). For what purpose is it used? The answer is: to cause the arising of faith.

Regarding the meaning of "causing the arising of faith," there are ten interpretations. Furthermore, it is said that "that which is the source" (*suǒyóu*) refers to sound, while "the reason why" (*suǒyǐ*) refers to the function of sound; thus, there is a distinction between them.
Regarding the statement that "the source of discourse is like the *Mahāmāyā* and so forth": this refers to the *Mahāmāyā Sūtra* (*Mahā* meaning "Great" and *Māyā* meaning "Artifice").
This is Lady Māyā, the Holy Mother of the Buddha, whose name was Mahāmāyā. She ascended to heaven for a three-month retreat (*an-gu*), during which she preached the sūtra for ninety days;
thus it is called the *Mahāmāyā Sūtra*. According to a careful examination of that sūtra: when the Buddha had first attained enlightenment, in order to repay [his debt]...

Regarding the "Gratitude to the Mother": this sutra was spoken [by the Buddha]. Thus have I heard: when the Buddha was about to enter *parinirvāṇa*, he established [this teaching] for the sake of his mother.
Since a great deal of time has elapsed [between that event and the present], how can it be called the *Mahāmāyūrī-vidyārājñī-sūtra*? Answer: It is discussed from beginning to end.

From the initial attainment of enlightenment until the golden coffin was opened again, the teachings he preached for his mother are collectively termed the *Mahāmāyūrī-sūtra*. The word "etc. includes the *Jhāpana-sūtra* (the Sutra on the Cremation).
The *Vinayapiṭaka*, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-saṃgraha*, and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* recount the original circumstances:

when the World-Honored One lay with his head toward the north on the banks of the Hiranyavati River in Kuśinagara, the birthplace of the Mallas, about to enter parinirvāṇa, Ānanda— his beloved younger cousin—
beheld the signs of the Tathāgata’s final passing and sank into an ocean of grief, unable to restrain himself.
However, not long after the Buddha had attained enlightenment, the celestial Mara Pāpīyān requested for the first time that the Buddha enter parinirvāṇa.
The Buddha said, "Go for now; my original purpose in leaving the household life was solely to deliver sentient beings. Since I attained enlightenment, I have not yet brought benefit to all.
I shall wait until I have delivered my wise disciples before entering parinirvāṇa. Not much time passed before there appeared a householder...
"Ānanda, the bhikṣu Aśvajit, who was a teacher of the brahmins, entered the city to beg for alms.

Śāriputra encountered him and, seeing that his deportment was serene and elegant and his appearance was dignified, asked: 'Under whom does your teacher study? Aśvajit answered Śāriputra by expounding the Dharma of the Three Truths.

At the conclusion of those words, [Śāriputra] attained the realization of the first fruit [of the path]. Later, he returned to take refuge in the Buddha. The Buddha said, 'Welcome,' and so forth; thus he attained [the state of a Stream-enterer]."
Regarding the fruits of his training, he was foremost in wisdom among the ten great disciples.
As soon as he had converted the disciple foremost in wisdom, for a second time Māra, the Lord of Heaven, came to request that the Buddha enter parinirvāṇa. The World-Honored One said, "Go for now;
although I have converted the disciple foremost in wisdom, I do not yet have a disciple with supernormal powers. Later, Maudgalyāyana saw Śāriputra, and Śāriputra [acted] for him...
He preached the Dharma of the Three Truths to Aśvajit; at the conclusion of the words, [Aśvajit] attained the first fruit. Later, he joined the Buddha and left the household life.
When the World-Honored One called out, "Welcome," etc., at the conclusion of those words, he attained the first fruit. He became foremost in supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).

When the celestial Māra saw this, for the third time he requested the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa. The World-Honored One replied, "Wait for a while; although I have wisdom and supernatural powers, I do not yet have a disciple [who possesses them]."
Among the disciples who possessed great learning and the power of dhāraṇī, there was later Ānanda.

When twenty years had passed, the World-Honored One spoke for Ānanda concerning the sūtras and teachings he had expounded during those preceding twenty years, briefly indicating their general direction and summarizing them in verse, as the sūtra says:
"The World-Honored One is most rare and extraordinary; he causes me to recollect the immeasurable teachings of the Buddhas of the past, just as they are now."
"What I have heard today, I now have no further doubt about; I shall abide securely in the Buddha-way and serve as an attendant through skillful means, upholding all the Buddhas' teachings.
As soon as Ānanda finished speaking, they all attained realization and understanding. For the third time, the celestial Māra spoke again:
"Since you have already delivered so many disciples who are deeply learned, why do you not enter parinirvāṇa? At that moment, Ānanda was standing by the Buddha’s side. The world...
The World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying: "The celestial Māra has invited me to enter parinirvāṇa.
Now, one who has well cultivated the four bases of psychic power can remain for an eon, or even less than an eon. I have well cultivated the dharmas of the four bases of psychic power;

what is your intention—do you wish for me to remain, or to enter parinirvāṇa? Although the World-Honored One asked this three times, Ānanda’s ears were blocked by Māra, and he did not hear a single word of the Buddha's voice.
Māra remained silent and did not answer. Māra said, "Even the Buddha’s own disciples do not wish for this; how much less so can we?

Then the World-Honored One addressed Māra, saying, "I accept your request. I shall wait until those sentient beings with whom I have a karmic connection who have not yet been delivered are delivered, and until those who have not yet heard the teachings of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* are made to hear them. Once the fourfold assembly has gathered, I will personally entrust [the teaching] to them."

The teachings of the Three Vehicles have been transmitted for the benefit of future generations; having dispelled darkness and eliminated doubt, the task is now complete. In three months’ time, I shall enter nirvana with you.
If I do not wait these three months, my transformative mission will not be fully exhausted; if I wait these three months, my transformative mission will then be concluded.
Having heard these words, Pāpīyān returned to his palace in joy. Fearing that Ānanda would fall into grief or regret, the World-Honored One then spoke.
"Ānanda, you should sit quietly beneath a tree in the rear garden and cultivate meditative practice to contemplate the cessation of the root of suffering.
Observe from where this body of yours has come. Following these instructions, Ānanda went to the foot of the tree;

as he was about to enter meditative absorption but before his contemplation was fully accomplished, his mind became drowsy, and he suddenly had a dream in which he saw a great tree rising above a multitude of groves.
Reaching upward as far as the Heaven of the Peak of Existence and extending laterally across the realms of the three states of existence, the tree bore flowers and fruits.
All sentient beings gathered its flowers and ate its fruits, dwelling in reliance upon the tree; they all said, "I rely on this tree to sustain my life."
After he had been searching for a long time, suddenly a fierce Vairambha wind arose and blew this tree down.
It was crushed into fine dust amidst the Śāla grove at the birthplace of the Malla warriors. Ānanda woke up in a state of great terror, realizing that his dream was inauspicious.
Filled with grief and distress, he went to the Buddha and requested that the reason for this be explained. The Buddha told Ānanda, "The great tree was my own body.
That it had flowers and fruit represents the teachings of the Three Vehicles.
The arrival of the violent wind and the toppling of the great tree represent Māra coming to invite me to enter parinirvāṇa. Within the thicket of the forest, I have now vanished."
The ground was the site of the Śāla grove, the birthplace of the Mallas, where [the Buddha] entered parinirvāṇa.
Upon hearing this report, Ānanda wept and wailed aloud. The World-Honored One said to Ānanda: "I have already asked you three times, yet you remained silent.
What is the use of lamenting and wailing? Carrying a medicine bag behind a funeral carriage is of no avail; drawing a bow after the thieves have fled—this is the case now, Ānanda."
It was difficult. He was filled with grief, sorrow, and suffering; his mind was deranged and disordered like that of one heavily intoxicated, such that he had no awareness at all.

He did not see the fourfold assembly, nor did he know whether the Tathāgata had already entered parinirvāṇa or had not yet entered it. Ānanda wept with such intensity that he could not restrain himself.
The Buddha said to Ānanda: "Suppose there were a person who provided the four kinds of offerings, making such offerings for a full three thousand [worlds]..."
The world is filled with Arhats as numerous as rice, hemp, bamboo, and reeds; yet none are equal to a single person who offers incense and flowers in worship to the Buddha.
Although you have served me personally for twenty-five years and attained the first fruit through immeasurable merit, why must you weep in sorrow?
During every peaceful night and auspicious hour, I have taught Ānanda the Dharma he had not heard before for twenty years.
He said, "I first delivered the five men at the Deer Park; next, I delivered fifty people at Yaśas;
next, I delivered five hundred people from Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, and two hundred from Gayā-Kāśyapa. Having heard this, Ānanda—
His grief and lamentation redoubled: "It is because I served as his attendant that he left behind his fetters and did not realize the ultimate fruit.

Indeed, one who serves as an attendant does not take up the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), for fear of negligence; yet he does not take up the ultimate fruit, lest he become identical with the Buddha’s state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
He remains at the first fruit alone. The Buddha said: "It is like the countless fish in the great ocean who, wishing to reach the shore, must swallow the hook."
"The bait has already been swallowed; you have taken the hook and shall now enter the cycle of birth and death.

When Ānanda heard these words as if he had realized the fruit of Arhatship, he wept bitterly and fainted upon the ground. Aniruddha sprinkled cold water on Ānanda’s face and comforted him with kind words:
"The Tathāgata wishes to enter parinirvāṇa; no one among gods or humans is able to detain him."
Aniruddha said to Ānanda, "All conditioned things are impermanent and subject to decay and dissolution. He further spoke these words: "The world is empty and void;
the Unsurpassed Dharma King is about to pass away. The profound great river is about to run dry; the lamp of the Great Dharma will soon be extinguished.
The mountain of Dharma is about to collapse; the ship of Dharma is about to sink; the bridge of Dharma is about to fall apart; and the Good Friend..."
I wish to depart. The fear of fire is about to arrive; the banner of Dharma is about to fall; the tree of Dharma is about to break; the sun of the Buddha is about to set.

Do not be distressed like an ordinary person. Furthermore, the Great Teacher, the Buddha, has personally entrusted to you the treasure of Dharma accumulated through difficult and ascetic practices over three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
If you become despondent, you will forget the true nectar-like flavor of the Tathāgata for all sentient beings.
We are adrift and drowning in the torrential current of birth and death; within this ocean of suffering, by what means can we find liberation?
You should consult the Great Muni regarding the affairs of future lives. What is the use of mere lamentation?

Once we have departed from the Unsurpassed World-Honored One, if doubts arise, whom shall we ask again? Ānanda said, "I am filled with grief and distress; I do not know what I should ask. The Venerable One—

[The Buddha] entered parinirvāṇa. He addressed Ānanda, saying: "Why did you not ask about the Dharma of the four matters? Furthermore, why did you not entreat the Tathāgata to remain in the world and not enter parinirvāṇa?

Why did you not inquire about the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*? [It is said that] Aniruddha prompted Ānanda to ask [these questions], while the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that Upāli prompted Ānanda to ask.
Why do these two accounts differ? The answer is: both individuals were present at the assembly and prompted [Ānanda] at the same time.

If he were still in the world, the assembly of sages would adorn him, like stars constantly surrounding the moon on all four sides.
The World-Honored One said to Ānanda: "Where there is meeting, there must be parting; where there is birth, there is inevitably extinction. I have already accepted the invitation of Pāpīyas."
One will certainly enter *nirvāṇa*. If you have doubts, ask them quickly.
Regarding the statement that the Buddha’s teaching says "I shall attain extinction" (*parinirvāṇa*) and so forth—this answers the first question. *Prātimokṣa* is a Sanskrit term;
it refers to this separate liberation precept (*prātimokṣa-śīla*). Liberation is the fruit of *nirvāṇa*. It separately prevents various transgressions, whereby one attains [liberation].
This fruit of nirvāṇa is called "analytical liberation" (prātimokṣa). Question: Since ethical discipline (śīla) is a gateway to merit, how can one attain this nirvāṇic liberation through it?

Answer: It cannot be attained by the direct cause alone; rather, by relying upon its favorable conditions, one is able to give rise to meditative concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (prajñā), and thereby attains liberation.

Thus, there is a verse that says: "If ethical discipline (śīla) is not pure, meditative concentration (samādhi) will not manifest. If meditative concentration does not manifest, the Noble Path cannot arise.
Nuo said: "If one's bodily conduct avoids killing and stealing, and does not fall into the three miserable realms, this is itself liberation."
Why must one necessarily seek nirvana and liberation?
Regarding the statement "take [the precepts] as your great teacher" and so forth: while the Buddha was in the world, take the Buddha as your teacher;
after the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, take the precepts as your teacher. Therefore, the *Śāsanānuśāsana Sūtra* (The Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching) says: "The prātimokṣa..."
"Know that this is your Great Teacher.

Regarding the statement "relying upon the four foundations of mindfulness," etc., this answers the second question: "Upon what do the bhikṣus rely for their dwelling? There are two meanings of "dwelling":

first, dwelling of the body; second, dwelling of the mind. A monastery is the place where the body dwells; the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness is [the place where] the mind dwells.

This is the locus where the mind abides. Regarding the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*), body, sensation, mind, and phenomena are the four objects upon which one abides.

"Mindfulness" (*smṛti*) is so named because it is proximate to wisdom (*prajñā*). While the two dharmas of mindfulness and wisdom act as the agents of abiding, fixing the mind within these four bases is called "abiding in the four foundations of mindfulness.
First, one contemplates the impurity of the body to eliminate the inversion of perceiving it as pure.

First, by contemplating suffering, one causes the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) to be known. Second, by contemplating the suffering inherent in sensation, one removes the misconception of pleasure and causes the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*) to be abandoned.

Third, by contemplating the impermanence of the mind, one removes the misconception of permanence and causes the cessation (*nirodha*) to be realized. Fourth, by contemplating the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*), one removes the misconception of a self and causes the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*) to be cultivated.
Furthermore, regarding the contemplation of the impurity of the body: since beginningless time, all sentient beings have given rise to craving and attachment toward their own bodies.
Regarding those in the world with red lips and white teeth whom one wishes to eliminate and sever [attachment to], a beginner must first practice the contemplation of their own impurity.
According to the *Secret Essentials of Dhyāna Sūtra*, one should first contemplate from the tips of the toes, observing a small area of cracked skin;

because of this, blood appears, which then forms blisters and sores, and pus and blood flow out, gradually extending to cover one foot and eventually the entire body—all of which are thus [contemplated].

Impurity. Just as it is with one's own body, so it is with the bodies of others; by not giving rise to thoughts of desire toward them, and by applying this contemplation to all things, craving and attachment will naturally subside. First, regarding the contemplation of the body’s impurity, there are five aspects.
First is impurity of the seed: just as the peony flower is fragrant because it arises from a fragrant peony root, and the *eranda* tree arises from an *eranda* seed.
One further contemplates [the impurity of] the fruits of the three vehicles, which arise from precepts, patience, and so forth, and are thus pure.
Ordinary beings, however, are summoned by the seeds of ignorance, craving, and afflictions; therefore, it is called the "impurity of the seed.
Some say that this practice of impurity-contemplation in the Lesser Vehicle concerns only the physical body inherited from one's parents as being impure. Thus, Nāgārjuna’s verse says: "This body..."
It is of an impure nature, not some other exquisite jewel; it does not arise from purity, but emerges only from a foul passage.

Regarding the second point, the impurity of its dwelling place: it is within the mother’s womb, situated between the stomach (the organ of raw food) and the large intestine (the organ of digested food), in a place of putrid filth.
While dwelling here, when the mother eats hot food, it is as if she were in the Hell of Boiling Cauldrons; when she eats cold food, it is as if she were in the Hell of Ice Blocks.
When the mother is hungry, it is as if she were in the Hell of Hanging Upside Down; when she is full, it is as if she were in the Hell of Narrow Rocks.
Therefore, it is called "abiding. Because its location is impure, a verse in the treatise says: "This body is foul and filthy;

it does not arise from the blooming of a flower, nor from the *campaka*, nor from a mountain of jewels. Regarding the third point, the impurity of its own substance: it consists of earth, water, fire, and wind.

Through the provisional combination and continuous maintenance of skin, flesh, sinews, bones, and the thirty-six impure substances, the body is formed; this is called the impurity of its own substance.
Thus, a verse in the treatise says: "The elements of earth, water, fire, and wind can transform into impurity; even if one were to empty the ocean to wash this body,"

It cannot be made fragrant or clean. Fourth, regarding the impurity of external characteristics: it is also said that its own characteristics consist of the nine apertures constantly discharging filth, stench, and impurity;
there are wounds, pus, blood, sweat, tears, mucus, and saliva—thus its characteristics are impure. Therefore, a verse in the treatise says:
"Various kinds of impure things fill the interior of the body, flowing out incessantly, like a leaking sack containing objects. (5)

Regarding ultimate impurity: for those who are born, after death, illness, and the cessation of breath, the body becomes bloated, putrid, and decays, turning into ash and dust—all of which are impure.
This, in turn, invites future bodies, causing one to sink into the six realms of existence and be unable to escape.
Thus, a verse says: "Examine this body with discernment; it ultimately returns to the place of death. It is difficult to restrain and does not turn back; it betrays its benefactor like..."
The child (having first contemplated the body): second, he contemplates that feeling is suffering. Feeling refers to the three types of feeling—painful, pleasant, and neutral.

That which causes one to experience these throughout the duration of a single lifetime is called "feeling" (*vedanā*). Because it is tormented by the eight types of suffering, feeling is said to be suffering. "Suffering" (*duḥkha*) has the meaning of oppression.
Ordinary worldlings do not realize this is suffering; they falsely reckon it to be pleasure. Now that he contemplates it, he sees that there is no pleasure, only suffering. First.
One contemplates painful feeling as the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*). If one speaks of painful feeling in general terms, it is already "suffering" (*duḥkha*);

furthermore, upon this suffering, one adds the sufferings of birth, aging, sickness, death, and association with the disliked. These five sufferings follow along; this suffering upon suffering is called the suffering of suffering.
Second, one contemplates pleasant feeling as the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*). Pleasant feeling, in its very essence, is a contaminated phenomenon (*sāsrava-dharma*); it is already...

Beyond the suffering of physical pain, it is further pursued by the sufferings of separation from the beloved and the failure to obtain what one seeks; this is called the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*).
The gathering together of worldly wealth, fame, profit, and kinsmen may seem pleasant for a time, but when that pleasure changes and decays, [it turns into suffering].

That which can give rise to sorrow and affliction is called the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*). Third, one contemplates equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) as the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*).

Although equanimity is superior [to other feelings], it is subject to the flux of the four characteristics—arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing. This constant flux and lack of stability is called the suffering of conditioned formations. Ordinary beings do not perceive this as suffering, but for Bodhisattvas, it is a source of great terror.

Thus, when Bodhisattvas contemplate the aggregates (*skandha*) of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), they regard them as being like the Avīci Hell. Therefore, there is a verse:
It is said: Just as when a single eyelash is placed in the palm of the hand, it is not noticed, yet if it is placed upon the eye, it causes extreme suffering and unrest;

so it is with ordinary beings, who are like the palm of the hand and do not perceive the eyelash of the suffering inherent in conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), whereas the wise are like the eye and give rise to intense revulsion toward its conditions.
One contemplates the mind as impermanent: every mental state and mental factor is momentarily impermanent, ceasing as one arises, just like [the eyelash].
The monkey never dwells for even a moment. There is permanence within impermanence, yet there is no change in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

There is no impermanence within that which is not permanent, nor is it like the horns of a rabbit. It lacks those two characteristics of permanence—both existence and non-existence—and is thus designated as "impermanence.

Therefore, a verse in the Sūtra says: "Form is like a mass of foam; it cannot be grasped. Feeling is like a floating bubble; it cannot endure long. Perception is like a mirage, arising from thirst..."
Craving arises. Formations are like the plantain tree; they have no core within. Consciousness is like a magical illusion, produced by perversion.

Fourth, regarding the contemplation of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*): one contemplates that within these phenomena—the three categories and five aggregates—there is absolutely no self.
To cling to the existence of a self is erroneous. To cling to the existence of a sovereign controller is termed the "self of persons" (*pudgalātmagraha*). If one clings to [the existence of...]
The *pradhāna* (Primal Nature) is what is termed the "self of phenomena" (*dharmātman*). When the Tathāgata observes all phenomena, he sees that there is absolutely no self within them.
Yet ordinary beings, through deluded attachment, insistently grasp at a self where there is no self; it is like seeing a snake where there is actually no snake upon a rope.

Whether one conceives of a self as being identical with the aggregates (*skandha*) or as distinct from the aggregates, among the phenomena of the three categories (*triskandha*), there are only things arising from conditions; there is absolutely no self. Furthermore...

By practicing these four contemplations, one eliminates the six types of vitarka and gives rise to the nine types of bhāvanā. Regarding the six vitarkas: they are those of sensual desire, ill will, harm, relatives, country, and immortality.
Regarding the nine bhāvanās, the Abhidharma states: first, the cultivation of desire, which eliminates non-attention; second, the cultivation of diligence.
1. Cultivation through removal of laziness. 2. Cultivation through elevation to remove dullness and torpor. 3. Cultivation through exertion to remove self-contempt. 4.

Cultivation through vigor to remove lack of food and clothing, for the sake of seeking to leave the household life. 5. Cultivation without regression, because of gradual and superior progress. 6. Cultivation of right mindfulness, to remove loss of mindfulness. 7.
Cultivation of wisdom, to remove improper spheres of activity by being careful not to enter them, and to distance oneself from evil preceptors. And...

Because of [the absence of] wrong thoughts and so forth, one practices the ninth cultivation of not abandoning the yoke of virtue (*akuśala-yoga*). Even after attaining the fruits [of the path], one remains ever heedful.

Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* (Chapter 35) speaks of four kinds of foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) as one's own domain, and five kinds of exquisite sensual desires (*pañca kāmaguṇāḥ*) as the domain of others.
Just as the *rāva* bird dwells within its own domain and is not thrown by others, this refers to repentance and shame (*kaukṛtya-vyapatrāpya*). *Rāva*.
As for the bird, it is the *alaṃtāya*; it dwells within its own territory, which is its own domain. If it were to dwell in the void, it would be in another’s domain.
As the verse says: "The flying bird comes from the sky; Rāva dwells in his own realm. Though he may exert his heroic power, take care that his body is not harmed.
