Because they reckon the fifteen elements (*dhātu*) of the Tathāgata to be entirely with outflows (*sāsrava*), the Buddha, in order to eliminate this perverted understanding, provisionally designates as "permanent, blissful, self, and pure" that dharma of nirvāṇa which transcends all verbal expression.
Purity. As the verses of the *Śataśāstra* state: "The Buddhas sometimes speak of permanence, and at other times speak of non-self.

Within the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, there is neither self nor non-self. The first line eliminates the distortions of the two vehicles; the second line eliminates the distortions of ordinary beings; and the final two lines reveal the ultimate meaning.
Furthermore, it speaks of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) to eliminate the distortions of ordinary beings. When the two vehicles cultivate these, by means of...

Regarding the fruit of the Path: at the time of the correct realization of the principle, there is not a single thing; yet later, upon emerging from meditative equipoise and reflecting back, one perceives that within that equipoise there was nothing at all.
Consequently, one sees the emptiness, impermanence, and so forth within the preceding path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), and takes this to be the ultimate fruit.

[The Buddha taught] that the Tathāgata sits with me upon the same bed of liberation, yet [such practitioners] cling to the notion that the Buddha also possesses meanings such as impermanence. [This teaching is given] to eliminate [this error].

This is an inversion. Upon the dharmakāya, the meanings of permanence, bliss, and so forth are provisionally established; because these four are unattainable, they are termed "provisional establishments."
Regarding the phrase "pervasive throughout the three times" (*tri-kāla-prasṛta*): "pervasive" (*prasṛta*) means to circulate; "throughout" (*prati*) means to be universal.

It refers to what is commonly transmitted and reckoned by the world, such as [the names] Devadatta or Buddhadāsa. This "self" (*ātman*) here is likewise; because it conforms to worldly convention, it is also called "self. The treatise states:
"The various characteristics of the self" refers to sentient beings, living beings, stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*), once-returners (*sakṛdāgāmin*), and so forth. Question:

Regarding "the worldly convention of 'self'": among the two types of grasping, under which is it subsumed? Answer: It is subsumed under the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*). Because it does not obstruct the Path;
because names such as those of the noble ones (*ārya*) are all worldly conventions; because when one calls out a name, there is something designated and a sense of a governing subject;
therefore, when the name is invoked, its meaning is equivalent to that of a "self. Thus, it is subsumed under the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Regarding the statement that "Devadatta and others are commonly transmitted [as names]": *Deva* here means "Heaven" (*deva*), and *datta* here means "Bestowed" (*datta*).

Because he was requested from the gods and they bestowed him upon him, he was given this name accordingly. Question: Since it is commonly circulated in the world that I am called Devadatta, [how is this so?]
"How is it, Ānanda, that you conform to worldly convention by simply saying 'I'? He replied: "There are two kinds: the general and the specific.
The general refers to calling oneself 'I'; the specific refers to stating one's name. Ānanda merely conforms to the general worldly designation; therefore, he says, 'Thus have I heard.'"
Regarding the statement that this is not the same as the previous two types, the *She* (攝) commentary says: It is not the same as the first [type] because it is not a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*) view;

it is not the same as the second because the "self" (*ātman*) provisionally established there is not the ultimate fruit, and because it is called the "Great Self" (*mahātman*) of non-self (*anātman*) due to the absence of self-clinging (*ātmagrāha), yet possessing the quality of sovereignty—referring here to Ānanda. This is like the worldly saying: "one who does not cut down his own tree."
Its merit is even greater. Because one realizes non-self (*anātman*), mastery increases further; therefore, it is called the "Great Self" (*mahātman*).
Regarding the statement that "the dharmas of all Buddhas are equal," it is said: this question has two intentions. The first asks why [the Buddha] does not refer to [himself] as "non-self."

Regarding the second question as to why names are not mentioned, and the statement "one word," "speech," and so forth: He (賀) says that if one were to say "I heard" in reference to a conventional person (*pudgala*), it would be easily understood by others;

furthermore, it would be easy to distinguish [the speaker]. Therefore, he says "no-self" (*anātman*), which applies universally to all phenomena such as the aggregates (*skandha*). [The questioner] now asks: "In relation to whom does one know [this 'self']?"

Regarding the term "self," it refers only to the conventional person (*pudgala*) based upon the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), and thus it is easily understood. However, if one speaks of "non-self" (*anātman*), it applies universally to the three categories [of aggregates, bases, and elements], making it difficult to distinguish between self and other.
It is also used as a vocative address; for instance, when one says, "Who do you know this to be? The questioner asks: "Does 'non-self' apply to the aggregates and so forth?"
If one says there is no "I" who hears, then when it is said that one knows, of whom is it said? Of whom is the "I" who hears spoken of here?
The answer is: the meaning of "no-self" (anātman) pervades the aggregates (skandhas) and so forth; these aggregates apply to both one's own body and the bodies of others.

Therefore, it is said, "I heard. Now, regarding the meaning of this "I": although it pervades all aggregates within one's own body and the bodies of others, when the term "I" is employed, there is an immediate distinction.
As it is said here: "Because it is traditionally used as a self-designation," just as a woman of the world might say, "Whose thing is this?"

Answer: This person understands that these are the belongings of that woman. Although all are called "persons" (pudgala), and everyone is indeed a person, one simply says "this person" to refer to this specific individual.
As for "belongings," all things possess a self (ātman). Knowing that the teaching of "I" refers to this very self, one hears it thus.

Regarding the two ways of conforming to the world, He says: first, conforming to worldly dharmas. This refers to when the followers of the Two Vehicles practice the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā) and consequently fear the annihilation of the self;

therefore, [the Buddha] speaks of dharmas such as the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu) so that he may cause the followers of the Two Vehicles to rejoice. Second, the "summit" (mūrdhan).
Regarding the world of sentient beings, because ordinary people take delight [in worldly things], I know that light is free from attachment; thus, I am not like those of the mundane world.
Whether great or small, all are able to address me as "I. Even in the West, when a subject addresses a sovereign, they likewise use the term "I."

Regarding the statement "fear of selflessness throughout the three time periods," Nyang says: first, it causes one to generate the resolve for enlightenment; second, it causes one to engage in cultivation and study.

If one were not taught that there is a "self," for whose sake would one cultivate and study? Thus, the Holy Teaching states: "It is better to cling to the view of existence as large as Mount Sumeru than to cling to emptiness."

It is seen as being like a mustard seed. Due to the grasping at a self, one subsequently attains non-self. For example, when a person who has attained the first fruit enters meditative observation (*vipaśyanā*), they sever the coarse, conceptualized self;
however, the remaining innate, subtle self remains and is not perceived during that observation. This refers to the coarse, conceptualized self.

One must not say: "Now, where does this 'I' exist? To speak of the existence of self, other, defilement, and so forth, is to designate one's own name as "self" and the names of others as "other. This applies to all ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).

Sentient beings of the five destinies are collectively termed the "defiled self. Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas possess both the defiled and the pure [self]. The Tathāgata possesses only the pure self. That which is defiled arises from the worldly self;
that which is pure arises from the noble self. To perform wholesome karma and receive the pleasant fruits of humans and devas is called the "wholesome cause-and-effect self.
To perform unwholesome karma and receive the suffering fruits of the three miserable realms is called the "defiled cause-and-effect self."

The "self" of monastics and nuns takes the practice of the Way through renunciation as their vocation; the "self" among the laity takes the vocations of scholar, farmer, artisan, or merchant as theirs.
Within these contexts, if one were to speak of "non-self," there would be no distinction; therefore, one speaks of "self."
Regarding the statement, "To say 'I heard' does not contradict worldly convention," He [He Yan] says: This truly does not contradict worldly convention.

While the truth is revealed within the main body of the teaching (*siddhānta*), it is shown not to contradict worldly convention within the introductory section (*nidāna*); therefore, it is said, "I heard."

Regarding the phrase "although the principle is manifest and subtle," etc.: although the principle being expounded is the teaching of selflessness (*anātman*), the expressive teaching provisionally states "I heard.
Regarding the phrase "desiring to manifest the ultimate truth," etc.: [this addresses] the question that the statement of selflessness does not contradict conventional reality, nor is it coarse.

[Question: What does this intend to clarify? [Answer: The commentary states, "It intends to clarify," and so forth. Within the *Prakṛta* (the main body of the teaching), the teaching of non-self (*anātman*) clarifies the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Within the *Nidāna* (the introductory section), the teaching of self (*ātman*) does not contradict conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Among the principles being explained (*lakṣya*), the principle of non-self is the sublime Dharma;

among the teachings that explain them (*lakṣaṇa*), the mention of "self" does not contradict coarse and superficial matters. Within the context of non-self, [the term "self"] is used as a provisional designation...

Regarding the phrase "pointing to me": this is intended to reveal that the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is not separate from the conventional (*saṃvṛti*). Question: Why is it not in conflict with the conventional? Answer: There are two explanations.

First, while the primary focus is on the ultimate, the conventional is introduced as its sequence. Second, the principle is subtle, yet the expression is coarse. This is because, according to Indian custom, regardless of one's status—whether noble or lowly—everyone may refer to themselves as "I.

Thus, here the true and the false, as well as the conventional, are made manifest. Furthermore, these two are also phenomena that exist in mutual dependence upon one another. [The passage] is about to...
The conventional reveals the ultimate, and the ultimate reveals the conventional. If there were no conventional truth, where could the ultimate be established?

If there were no ultimate truth, where could the conventional be established? As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-kārikā* states: "Therefore, this [the perfected nature] and the dependent nature are neither different nor non-different.
This is precisely the meaning of the non-separation of the ultimate and the conventional. Fools perceive saṃsāra and nirvāṇa as being utterly distinct, like water and its waves.
The wise understand this: their essence is one, just as water and ice are one in essence.
In the summer months, ice melts into water; in winter, when it freezes, water becomes ice. It is the same with the ultimate and the conventional:

that which is "with self" is precisely "without self," and that which is "without self" is precisely "with self. If one speaks of "having a self," then the parikalpita (imagined nature) is non-existent. If...
Regarding the statement "there is no self": it exists precisely within the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
This is the meaning of the non-separation of the ultimate and the conventional, just as there is hemp within a rope, fire within wood, warmth within water, and emptiness within form.
Regarding the statement "two selves," it means that within the second sense, there is in fact only one person whose names differ according to their respective virtues.
Ancient teachings asserted that there were actually three persons; it is in contrast to these ancient views that this statement is made. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
Śāriputra asked the goddess, "Among the Three Vehicles, which do you seek to pursue? The goddess replied, "If one transforms others through the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths..."
Regarding sentient beings: if I transform sentient beings through the dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination, I am a *śrāvaka*;
if I transform them through the Mahāyāna dharma, I am a *bodhisattva*. Now, because the *śrāvaka* is the most inferior, he is simply called "Ānanda" (Joyful).

The Pratyekabuddha was next most excellent, named Nanda-bhadra; the Bodhisattva was the most excellent, further named Nanda-sāgara. These three names were established according to their respective virtues and transformations.
As for the term "Nanda" (Greeting Joy), it marks the beginning of his aspiration; he was born on the night he attained the Way, and his face was like—
His face was like the full moon, and his eyes were like blue lotuses; he could delight the spirits of those who beheld him and also bring joy to the Great King.
Therefore, he was named "Joyous" (Pūrṇābhirāma). This name marked the beginning of the arising of his vows. That is to say, in the past, he was a potter.
Second, it is said that when the World-Honored One first attained the Way, the celestial Māra informed King Śuddhodana: "Great King, Prince Siddhārtha, Sarvārthasiddha, last night..."
Half of them had already died. When King Śuddhodana suddenly heard this, he was overcome with grief and distress; the entire palace wept aloud in mourning. Shortly thereafter, another report arrived:
"Great King, Prince Siddhārtha, Sarvārthasiddha, has attained Perfect Enlightenment this past night at the appearance of the morning star."
The King asked, "Who was it that first announced his death? And who was it that later announced his attainment of the Way?

The voice from the sky replied, "Great King, the one who first announced his death was the Heavenly Māra; the one who later announced his attainment of the Way was I, namely Queen Māyā—or, according to some, the deity of the Bodhi tree.
At dawn, the dukes, marquises, and various kings congratulated the Great King on his joy.
King Droṇodana further reported, saying: "Last night, your majesty, a son was born to me. Your majesty, please grant him the name 'Ānanda' (Joy). The Venerable One replied:
"The *Saṃyuktāgama* states that there are three distinct Piṭakas. Since Pratyekabuddhas have no separate classification, they are subsumed within the Śrāvaka Piṭaka.
This is for the sake of those who seek the state of a Śrāvaka and so forth."
Regarding the term "Ocean of Joy" (*Sukhasāgara*): Question: Why is it called the Ocean of Joy? Answer: Śrāvakas are like small puddles of water; pratyekabuddhas are like medium rivers;
and bodhisattvas are like the great ocean. Therefore, it is called an "ocean."

Regarding the statement that names are distinguished according to qualities: it is like how one person in the world is called a "son" in relation to his father, an "uncle by marriage" in relation to his maternal uncle, and an "uncle" in relation to his nephew;
though it is but one person, he receives these various names according to the three vehicles transmitted by the Sages.
It is not that their essence is different.

Regarding the phrase "Ānanda, by this much and so forth": "much learning" (*bahuśruta*) refers to the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). "Hearing and retaining" refers to the wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).

The accumulation of what has been heard constitutes the wisdom derived from cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Because one can listen to and receive immeasurable sūtras that are well-balanced in their beginning, middle, and end, it is called 'much learning.
Because one can remember and maintain all meanings as they were heard, ensuring they are not forgotten, it is called 'hearing and retaining. [This] is repeatedly accumulated..."

The meaning of the text is to cause one to abide firmly; therefore, it is called the "accumulation of what has been heard" (*śruta-saṃbhāra*). When there is the wisdom of hearing (*śruta-prajñā*) in the Hīnayāna, there is no wisdom of reflection (*cintā*) or cultivation (*bhāvanā*);

when there is the wisdom of reflection, there is no wisdom of hearing or cultivation. Thus, the three types of wisdom do not arise simultaneously. In the Mahāyāna Yoga, all three types of wisdom take [the teachings] as their object simultaneously.
This distinction between the teaching and the principle (*naya*) and that of the Hīnayāna is the difference.

Regarding the statement "if one mentions names and so forth": although this accords with the principle of the selflessness of others, it also accords with the worldly principles of the Five Constants.
It does not, however, possess the meaning of attaining mastery over all phenomena (*dharmas*). The teachings of the Tripiṭaka are what are called "all phenomena.

If one were to say merely, "Thus did Ānanda hear," one would assume that this explains the emptiness of the Śrāvaka Piṭaka, but not the emptiness of the other two Piṭakas. This is directed toward the Śrāvakas.
[The Buddha] has attained mastery; the other two collections [of the Tripiṭaka] do not possess such mastery.

If one were to say, "I have heard," regarding all three collections collectively, the expression would be overly cumbersome if the three names were used as a collective designation. For this reason, simply saying "I have heard" avoids the aforementioned fault.
The single character "I" (aham) permeates all three names; as a collective "I," it encompasses every meaning without exception. If one were to say...
Regarding the alternative name: because it lacks the other two meanings, it is not referred to by that name.
As for the "three selves," the meaning of "intimate" (*qin*) is as follows: when people in the world say, "I see" or "I hear," this refers to the intimate sense.
If one were to say "Ānanda hears," it would be distant. If one identifies Ānanda with the lower consciousnesses, one knows that the true Ānanda is upon the high seat. If...
As for those who say, "Ānanda was not present in the assembly," if one claims that Ānanda heard [the teaching] from below the assembly, there would then be another person of the same name, Ānanda.
People of the time would ask: "Is this Ānanda from Vaiśālī, or is it Ānanda from Rājagṛha?
Or they might say, "Ānanda heard it," while the assembly doubted whether he had heard it directly or had received it through others. This is the question regarding the commentary.
Question: What is the difference between "not hearing directly" and "receiving from another"? Answer: "Not hearing directly" means one suspects that it was not heard from the Buddha himself;
"receiving from another" means one suspects that it was heard from someone else.
Regarding the statement "to cause Ānanda and others to hear," it is explained in the *Jiejing* (Decisive Commentary): Question:

Twenty years after the Tathāgata attained enlightenment, Ānanda only then left the household life to become his attendant. How is it that for teachings he did not hear during those twenty years, the beginning of every sutra says, "Thus have I heard"?
Answer: After Ānanda had left the household life, the Buddha spoke them again for him. These were spoken based on what had been previously taught.

The sūtras may likewise be prefaced with "Thus have I heard. Now, considering that Ānanda was able to recollect the entire treasury of the Buddhas' Dharma he had maintained since receiving his prediction of enlightenment, how much more so could he not maintain the sūtra teachings of the twenty years [following the Buddha's passing]?

To say now that he personally heard what was spoken refers specifically to the passage from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, in the chapter on the Entrustment of the Teaching, which was spoken forty years later. Ānanda...
It is difficult to stand before the Buddha and personally hear the bestowal of the prediction of enlightenment, as well as the adornments of the buddha-field, with all one's aspirations fulfilled;
yet, at that very moment, one recollects the dharma-treasuries of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of past Buddhas and attains unimpeded penetration.
Thus, it is said: "I have heard"—hearing the sublime proclamation of reality and attaining the profound discourse of ultimate truth, fully comprehending tens of millions.
How much more so for those who lived twenty years prior! Therefore, to summarize "I have heard" (*evaṃ mayā śrutam*) is certainly not contrary to reason.
When all the texts are taken together, they can be explained through seven interpretations: first, by the power of original vows; second, by successive hearing;

third, by the power of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*); fourth, because the Buddha spoke in brief; fifth, by the power of the three [auxiliary] supports; sixth, by the power of hearing from you; and seventh...

"By the power of the prophecy," it is said that "hearing refers to the ear-faculty and so forth. This is an explanation that subsumes the specific under the general. Furthermore, regarding the external commentary, there are differing interpretations by three masters of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna schools.
First, the master Śabdika (Sound-Heaven) maintains that the faculty hears while consciousness does not; it is consciousness that is capable of discernment.

Others cannot hear; hearing sound requires the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*). Second, Paramārtha establishes that consciousness hears while the faculty does not, because the faculty is material (*rūpa*) and thus cannot apprehend an object;
the faculty is like a rolled-up painting. Third, Guṇamitra establishes that both the faculty and consciousness hear.
Question: How does this third master differ from the Mahāyāna? Answer: It differs precisely because of the disagreement regarding the fuel. In the Mahāyāna...

Hearing occurs only when the three—sense faculty, object, and consciousness—are in conjunction. In the Hīnayāna, it is held that the object exists separately outside of consciousness and that the object and consciousness are distinct.

In the Mahāyāna, this is not so; the object is not separate from the mind, as it is a transformation of the mind. In actual fact, all three factors—the sense faculty, consciousness, and sound—must be present.
Within this context, "hearing" refers to the ear-faculty reaching toward and uniting with its object; only then is it designated as "hearing. This is the commentary.

The primary meaning of "hearing" (*śruta*) is as follows: "Hearing" refers exclusively to the apprehension of the ear-faculty (*śrotrendriya*). It gives rise to the ear-consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*), which apprehends sound.

The object of sound is apprehended solely through direct sensory contact. Question: Why is it that only the apprehension of the ear-faculty, which gives rise to the ear-consciousness, is called "hearing"?

Answer: This is explained in terms of the fundamental basis and in terms of the initial moment. Because that ear-faculty serves as the clear support (*āśraya*) for the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), if the ears were blocked, [the hearing would cease].
Thus, one does not hear [with the ear-faculty alone]. It is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that hears the teaching. However, this requires the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*) as its gateway;

therefore, from the perspective of the primary basis, it is said that "the ear hears. Furthermore, sound is the object apprehended by the ear-faculty. Moreover, sound serves as the support for the apprehension of names (*nāma*), phrases (*pada*), and syllables (*vyañjana*).

These names, phrases, and syllables serve as the objects of perception (*ālambana*) for the mental consciousness. Furthermore, they are the objects of perception for the mental consciousness, which apprehends the names and so forth.
Because it relies [on the ear], only hearing by the ear is mentioned; hearing by the mind is not mentioned. This is the intention of the Master of the Commentary’s first interpretation.

Question: What is meant by "hearing"? Answer: The Commentary states that "hearing" refers to the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*) and so forth; that is, relying on the ear-faculty, the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) arises to hear the object, which is sound.

Regarding the statement, "Now, setting aside the ear and its particulars," etc.: Question: When perceiving an object, since it is the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*) that gives rise to ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) to hear the object of sound, why is it not said that "the ear hears," but rather that "I hear"? Answer: The commentary states: "Now, setting aside the ear and its particulars.
The ear is one among the six faculties; when specifically praising the ear, it subsumes all six faculties, and thus one cannot say "I. "I" refers instead to the five [aggregates].
The term "aggregate" (skandha) is a general designation; therefore, the specific [term] is set aside. This is spoken with reference to the ear from the perspective of the self.

Regarding the statement, "Although it is based on the Mahāyāna, [it concerns] the ear and so forth": Question: According to the doctrine of the Mahāyāna alone, the conjunction of the three—organ, object, and consciousness—is called "hearing.
Why, then, is "hearing" explained here solely in relation to the ear, rather than being explained in terms of consciousness and the object? Answer: The Commentary states: Although...

According to the Mahāyāna, however, the faculties (indriya) are superior to consciousness (vijñāna) and so forth in five respects. These five aspects are: first, superiority of the basis (*āśraya-viśeṣa*).

Consciousness depends upon the faculties, whereas the faculties do not depend upon consciousness. It may well be that where there is a faculty, there is no consciousness; yet it is never the case that where there is consciousness, there is no faculty.
The faculties serve as the direct basis for the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*), whereas although objects (*viṣaya*) can induce their arising...
Regarding the mind: because it is not the basis for that which is non-affinal, (1) when a superior consciousness arises, it depends on many conditions and is thus inferior;
when a root arises, it depends on few conditions and is thus superior. From the seed of form, the manifest form arises; once the root exists, the supported consciousness can then exist.
Consciousness necessarily arises dependent upon the root; the root does not arise dependent upon consciousness. (3) The continuity.

Victorious! The five sense-faculties (*pañcendriya*) are the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of the eighth consciousness. Where there is the eighth consciousness, there are the five sense-faculties.
The eighth consciousness is constantly continuous; the five sense-faculties are likewise continuous. From birth until death, they continue without exhaustion.

While the various parts such as the eyes are intermittent and their three natures (*tridharmasvabhāva*) are easily displaced, these five sense-faculties are of a single class of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); therefore, they are called "continuous. This is the fourth mastery.
"Superior," because it can act as the sovereign. Among the three—faculty, consciousness, and object—it is these two [the faculty and consciousness] that act as the sovereign;
thus, in relation to the arising of mind and mental factors, they receive the name "sovereign. Regarding the five adornments, they cause the body to be upright, handsome, and magnificent.

Since mind and mental factors are devoid of physical form and lack such excellence, they must first rely upon the pure material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*) as their support; therefore, there exist the auxiliary material faculties, such as the ear-faculty.

Adornment (*vyūha*). It causes the body to be upright, dignified, and beautiful. Since the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) have no formal characteristics (*nimitta*) and possess no such adornment, these five meanings [are established] according to the *Abhidharma-śāstra*.
Question: Why are the names not established in accordance with their objects? Answer: The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states:
The name is established according to the faculties (*indriya*), because they possess five meanings: namely, (1) depending upon the faculty; (2) being produced by the two [the faculty and the object];
(3) belonging to the faculty; (4) assisting the faculty; and (5) being similar to the five [sensory] faculties. First, consciousness arises in dependence upon the eye-faculty.

Consciousness does not arise determinately from the presence of form alone; for example, in a person whose sense organs are impaired, consciousness does not arise even when confronted with an object of form.

It is the second organ [the mind] that can give rise to consciousness. If the organ undergoes transformation, consciousness necessarily undergoes transformation—just as those suffering from the disease kāmalā see all blue and other colors as yellow because their eyes are damaged. It is not the case that consciousness is called "impaired" at the time the object's color is impaired.
Third, "belonging": the consciousness that belongs to the eye arises by following after the sense organ (indriya) through the seed of consciousness;

therefore, it is called "belonging. Fourth, "assisting": the portion that assists the eye; because the sense organ conjoins with consciousness, there is what is experienced, which causes benefit or harm to the sense organ, as when observing the sun and moon.
Fifth, "likeness": the likeness between the sense organs and their respective consciousnesses; both the sense organ and the consciousness are present together.

Because it belongs to the category of sentient beings, it is called "suchness" (*tathatā*). The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* establishes its name based solely on the sense faculties (*indriya*) and not from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*);
therefore, the Sūtra does not adopt that [definition]. Furthermore, following the treatise of the Abhidharmakośa, it is explained according to the ultimate. Question:

What constitutes the essence of the five faculties, such as the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*)? Answer: The Chancellor stated that there are eleven schools with distinct interpretations regarding the meaning of the faculties. Among them, the Mahāsāṃghika school establishes...

1. The five material faculties (*rūpīndriya*): their essence consists of internal cohesion (*saṃghāta*). 2. The Sarvāstivādins: apart from the mind, they still possess substantial reality (*dravyasat*). 3. The Sāṃmitīyas (the Master Si Cao says):
due to the four objects—color, odor, taste, and touch—and the predominant derived great elements (*bhūta*), these are impermanent phenomena;
herein, the great elements collectively constitute the essence of the faculties. 4. The Sautrāntikas: although the five faculties... [text incomplete]

All [of these] are conventional (*prajñapti*). However, they are composed of real atoms (*paramāṇu*). The five schools that assert the conventional: for them, the sense faculties (*indriya*) are both conventional and real;

within the framework of the five aggregates (*skandha*), they are real, while within the frameworks of the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*), they are conventional. The sixth, the Lokāyata (Worldly Heretics), takes the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) themselves as the substance of the eye and other sense faculties.

7. The Ekavyāvahārikas maintain that there is only the name of the faculties, but no substantial entity of the faculties at all. 8. The Saṃkhyas calculate that the eye-faculty is identical to the object;
the ear-faculty is identical to space; the nose-faculty is identical to earth; the tongue-faculty is identical to water; and the body-faculty is identical to wind. 9.

Master Nanda views the seeds of the discerning portion as being named the five faculties, such as the eye and so forth. 10. Bodhisattva Sthiramati [maintains] that by means of the parikalpita-svabhāva...
The arising aspect is divided into the substance of the five faculties (*indriya*), because they arise as the false construction of the grasper and the grasped.

Regarding the eleven [factors] that protect the Dharma, the sense-faculties and consciousnesses each arise from seeds; therein there are two views: first, that they exist only as manifest; second, that they pertain to both seeds and manifestations.
Therefore, it is said that the ear-faculty possesses five meanings, etc. (The preceding [section] subsumes the specific within the general).

Regarding the statement, "If one merely hears sounds, etc.," this compares the direct and the indirect. Question: The ear-faculty hears only sound; it does not hear the entities of names, phrases, and syllables.
For these phenomena to actually exist, the four factors of sound, name, phrase, and syllable must be fully present. Why, then, is it said...?

[Question: When one speaks of the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*), does one not also speak of the sixth consciousness (*ṣaṣṭha-vijñāna*)? [Commentary] The Sub-commentary (*Śū*) answers: "If it were merely [the case that]... and so forth.

If it were merely taking the actual sound as its object, that would pertain solely to the ear-faculty; the ear-faculty does not take names, phrases, or phonemes (*nāma-pada-vyañjana*) as its objects. However, when the conventional and the real are spoken of together, the process necessarily involves the sixth consciousness as well, for only then can it be called "hearing.

"Name" refers to names, phrases, and phonemes; "meaning" (*artha*) refers to the principle (*tattva*) that is expressed. [Question: ... *Note: The final "Question" (*wèn*) indicates the end of this section of the commentary.*

The sixth consciousness takes names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and phonemes (*vyañjana*) as its objects, and it also takes sound (*śabda*) as its object. Why, then, is it said that it takes "name" and "meaning" (*artha*) as its objects, rather than saying it takes "sound" as its object?
Answer: Sound is common to both the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) and the sixth consciousness; however, when manifesting the perception of an object, the sixth consciousness is predominant.

To single out the sixth consciousness from this context, one excludes the portion of the ear-faculty (*śrotrendriya*) that perceives the empty sound itself. Thus, it is said that [the sixth consciousness] takes [the meaning] as its object.
Regarding the term "name-meaning" (*nāma-artha*), it does not refer to the sound of the conditions (*pratyaya*).
As for the phrase "such as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*," this cites the treatises to establish the proof. Question:

Since various sacred teachings state that names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and phonemes (*vyañjana*) are conventional dharmas (*prajñapti-dharma*), how can they be called "phonemes"? Answer: The commentary states that the *Yogācāra* [treatises] consider those names, phrases, and phonemes to be...
It is a conceptual construct (*prajñapti*). When the sixth consciousness takes it as its object, it is termed inference (*anumāna*). Furthermore, it was asked:

"When the sixth consciousness perceives an object, since it encompasses all three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), why does the *Yogācārabhūmi* speak only of inference? The answer is: within the treatise, it specifically refers to the conceptual construction (*prajñapti*) as the object.

It does not refer exclusively to the conditions of reality (*vastu*). It refers specifically to the conditions of names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and syllables (*vyañjana*), but not to the conditions of sound (*śabda*).

It refers specifically to the distracted state, but not to the concentrated state; hearing with a concentrated mind is subsumed under direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). There are four types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): first, direct perception; second, inference (*anumāna*);

third, non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*); and fourth, authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*). For example, seeing colors such as blue or yellow with the eye is direct perception. Second, for example, seeing distant smoke with the eye [is inference].
"There must be fire" is an inference (*anumāna*). The three cases of sky-flowers, tortoise-hair, and rabbit-horns are non-valid cognitions (*apramāṇa*).

If [the sixth consciousness] takes the five sensory objects as its domain in the same manner as the first five [consciousnesses], it is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). This is said with reference to the state of dispersion (*vyutthāna*). If within the state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the sixth [consciousness] is exclusively direct perception.

Regarding the statement "the ear is called 'hearing' (*śravaṇa*)," etc.: Question: Since the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that the sixth consciousness is what hears, why does it not say "the mind hears" (*mano-śravaṇa*), but instead says "the ear hears"?
Answer: The commentary states that the ear is called "hearing" because there are two senses in which it hears: First, the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*) directly hears sounds;
these sounds serve as the basis for names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and syllables (*vyañjana*). Second, [the ear serves as the basis for the consciousness that cognizes them].

The mind serves as the gateway; for the ear-faculty and the mental consciousness, it serves as the gateway of clarity. Because it possesses this superior function, the ear is specifically mentioned here.
Now, although the mind is capable of discrimination, it is only through the ear serving as the gateway for the mind that the mental consciousness is able to discriminate;
thus, it is the mind that hears. If the ear alone were to hear, it could not discriminate; it is because the mind is able to discriminate [that hearing occurs].

This is because it is the meaning of the Dharma. It is said that [the ear] again serves as a gateway for the ear. Now, regarding the case where the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises simultaneously with the five sensory consciousnesses:

in that instance, it is treated as a question [concerning the ear]. If, however, it arises independently (*svatantra*), it is not treated as such a question. This is provided that it is based on a direct condition (*pratyaya*) regarding sound.
This refers to the eighth consciousness. Why is it that the name "hearing" cannot be apprehended by the eighth consciousness? The answer is:
because the eighth consciousness cannot perfuse seeds; this is what has already been excluded.
Regarding the statement "taking two as the gate," etc.: the ear and the body constitute one gate; the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) constitutes the second gate.

Ear-consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*) and mental consciousness serve as gates for the perfuming (*vāsanā*). The seeds thus perfumed fall within the eighth consciousness and are termed "perfuming in the aggregate" (*saṃgraha*).
This "aggregate" has two meanings: first, the eighth consciousness is called the aggregate; second, the five-aggregate body (*pañcaskandhaka-ātmabhāva*) is also called the aggregate.

Regarding the statement "due to hearing the accomplished [wisdom]" (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) and so forth, this establishes the meaning of "hearing-perfuming" (*śruta-vāsanā*). It refers to the seeds of names and words (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-bīja*) that arise from what is accomplished through hearing;

these are collectively termed "hearing. What was previously discussed—wherein hearing was established as inference (*anumāna*)—served to prove that the sixth consciousness is named "hearing"; here, it is the ear itself that is named "hearing."
The realization of ear-consciousness is termed "hearing. Taking these two as the gateways, the perfuming occurs in the aggregate.

The realization that the eighth consciousness is able to maintain seeds and is itself that which is perfumed—when it is said that "the distinctions of the ear, mind, and so forth are set aside," the question is: why does Ānanda not say that it is heard by the ear? The commentary answers: [it is] set aside...

Regarding "separately" and so forth: the ear is distinct within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), while consciousness is a mental factor distinct within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).

If one were to speak of "form" and "consciousness" alone, one would obtain only two types [of aggregates] and lose the remaining three; therefore, setting aside the particulars to take the whole, it is said, "I heard."
Regarding the statement "seeing, awakening, and so forth": A question is raised: At that time, Ānanda saw the Buddha speak, heard the Buddha speak, and awakened to the Buddha speaking.

Why is it that these four modes are all expressed simply as "I have heard," and placed at the beginning of the sūtra? As for the other three meanings—seeing, reading, and knowing—why are they not designated?
The Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) explains: what is seen by the eye and heard by the ear is known by the mind; the three faculties of nose, tongue, and body are termed "reading" (or "text").

[The text] says: "Seeing. If one follows the Mahāyāna, the three [faculties] of nose, tongue, and body are called "cognition" (*jñāna*), while the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is called "seeing through words" (*vyañjana-darśana*). Question:

Regarding the apprehension of objects by the sixth consciousness, which consciousnesses apprehending objects are designated as "seeing," "hearing," and so forth? Answer: Apprehending an object by the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) is called "seeing"; the auditory [consciousness] is called "hearing."

The three faculties of nose, tongue, and body are called "cognition" (*jñāna*), because cognition occurs through contact. The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is called "textual vision" (*vyañjana-dṛṣṭi*).

Question: Ānanda, for what reason did he not speak of "vision" and so forth? Answer: There are three reasons. As for these three reasons: first, for those who wish to realize the profound principle...

Conditioned by sound, there arise names, phrases, and syllables, through which their meanings are realized. Specifically, names express intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); phrases express distinctions (*viśeṣa*); and syllables are the basis for both.
Within syllables there are names; within names there are meanings. These meanings consist of the two categories of cultivation and abandonment.
To inquire about these two meanings—delight and aversion—one must first hear the vocal teaching of the Tathāgata. For the sake of sentient beings, the Buddha...
In the teaching of the Dharma, there are names and so forth upon sounds that can express meaning and principle; when listeners awaken to this, they gradually realize the profound truth.

For this reason, the beginning of this sutra states the measure of "I have heard. If one were to say "I saw forms" and so forth—where "and so forth" includes the three [objects] of smell, taste, and touch—one would not yet have awakened to the Dharma, because upon forms and the other objects, there are no names to serve as proof or to express their meaning. Therefore, at the outset, it does not say "I saw or heard."

Regarding the phrase "these two realms [are distinguished] by sound, etc.": Question: Why is it that for this realm, seeing forms and smelling fragrances are not mentioned, while only hearing sounds is specified?
Answer: It is simply because in this land, the Buddha’s work is performed through sound; it is sound that serves as the means of expression (*abhidhāna*).

Names and so forth take sound as their basis; this realm does not perform the Buddha-work by means of visible form, odor, flavor, or tangibility, because names and so forth do not depend upon visible form and the other [sensory objects].

Regarding the statement that "sound is the basis for the [name-group, etc.]," this refers to the three—names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and phonemes (*vyañjana*)—which are established based upon sound and take sound as their support;
thus, names and so forth are the supported (*āśrita*). Question: For what reason is it not accepted that names and so forth depend upon form (*rūpa*)?

Answer: Because in this realm, the Buddha’s activity is carried out by means of vocal sound. Question: Just as when a person waves their hand and another understands the intention, is it not the case that names and phrases depend upon form?

Regarding the term *vyañjana* (phoneme/syllable): the answer is that it is spoken according to the majority of cases. Thus, the treatise says: "However, based on the distinctions among the various states of vocal sound, one conventionally establishes names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and phonemes (*vyañjana*)."

Regarding the statement, "The three aspirations for realizing *bodhi*, etc.," He-hsiu says: If one seeks with joy to realize *bodhi*, it must take the perfuming of extensive learning (*bahuśruta-vāsanā*) as its cause before one can reach the supramundane.
The Mahāyāna states that the seed of the supramundane mind is the perfuming of extensive learning;
it does not become supramundane through the perfuming of [right] view. It further states that there is no external perfuming, nor is it internal...
It should be understood that it is illogical for the seeds of hearing and so forth to produce fruit without being perfumed; therefore, "I saw" is not stated.
Regarding the phrase "by virtue of this, at the beginning of the sūtra," Yongyun states: "Because of these three meanings, 'I heard' is said, rather than 'I saw' and so forth."

Regarding the statement "to rely on the facts at that time": It is asked, when the layman Vimalakīrti remained silent in Vaiśālī and Mañjuśrī attained awakening to non-duality upon seeing this, was it not the case that form and other phenomena were able to express the principle?
It is answered: Initially, the shallow principle was discussed; subsequently, one arrives at the profound and subtle.

Discursive speech is severed and the pathways of the mind vanish; thus, one reveals the ultimate truth through wordlessness. Speaking from the perspective of the fundamental source, this also arises from diligent hearing.
Furthermore, having seen that which is not form, one awakens to non-duality.
Regarding the phrase "the foremost among all other Buddha-lands," does this light consist of form (*rūpa*) and so forth?

Since it possesses fragrance, flavor, and tangibility, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* states that when Maitreya enters the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, he emits a great radiance; within that radiance, various kinds of written characters appear.
This is the realization of the Way through the perception of form. It is like the story of two fellow students from the past who were traveling to the provincial capital.

When he was about to depart, he took leave of the Master. The Master, with his shoulders bare in the secluded stillness, raised his head toward him; the disciple responded with a "Nuo" (an affirmative chant) and set out on the road.
Little Di asked the Master, "Just now, when you raised your head toward the Master, for what reason did you chant 'Nuo'? Zu said: [The text provided ends here.]
"You do not know my intention; see that these two of us have come, and the Master has instructed you to exert yourself.

Furthermore, it is said: "In the world of Gandhavatī, all the bodhisattvas sit beneath fragrant trees; upon smelling this wondrous fragrance, they immediately attain the Samādhi of the Treasury of All Virtues.
This is awakening to the Way by means of fragrance. It also says: "At that time, those among the great assembly who eat this food... This refers to...

One attains awakening by tasting its flavor. Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that when the youth Sudhana sought out spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), he went before the daughter of an elder to seek the Dharma.
The woman said, "Virtuous one, take my hand, and I shall cause you to attain a Dharma never before experienced.
The youth replied, "I will not violate my pure conduct (*brahmacarya*. The woman said, "Great Being, one who practices the bodhisattva path does not depend upon the body."
"Command me! How much more so would I not refuse to take your hand? The youth then immediately took his hand.
Having taken his hand, he saw within the mirror the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the past performing difficult and painful practices.

He also saw within the curtain immeasurable hundreds of thousands of subtle and wondrous Buddha-lands. Furthermore, he saw within the wall immeasurable Buddhas, each preaching inconceivable [teachings].
Discourse on the Dharma. This refers to awakening to the Way through contact (*sparśa*). Question:

Since all the great Bodhisattvas are fully endowed with *dhāraṇī*, why is it that Ānanda alone maintains the treasury of the Dharma (*dharmakośa*)? Answer: The fortieth fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"Although there are immeasurable and boundless Bodhisattvas who possess great compassion, each of them is preoccupied with disciplining their retinues and adorning their own persons; for this reason..."
"Because of this cause and condition, after my parinirvāṇa, he will be unable to proclaim the twelve divisions of the sūtras;
or even if he should manage to proclaim them, people will not believe or accept them. The Buddha told Mañjuśrī, "The bhikṣu Ānanda was my younger brother.
From beginning to end, he has served me for more than twenty years. Whatever Dharma he has heard, he has fully received and upheld, just as if one were pouring it from one vessel into another."
There are eight kinds of inconceivable qualities. First, since he began serving me, he has never accepted an invitation for a separate meal.
Second, since he began serving me, he has never accepted my own personal robes. Third, since he began serving me, whenever he comes to my presence, he never eats at an improper time.
Fourth, since he began serving me, although he possesses afflictions, he follows me in entering and leaving all [monasteries].
Fifth, although he was a Kṣatriya king of noble and eminent lineage, upon seeing women or the daughters of devas and nāgas, he did not give rise to thoughts of desire.
Sixth, since he began attending upon me, he has upheld the twelve divisions of the sūtras I have taught;

once they have passed through his ears, he has never asked about them again, with the single exception of one question concerning the samādhi of emptiness. Seventh, since he began attending upon me, although he has not yet attained the knowledge of others' minds...

With his mental faculty, he constantly knows the Tathāgata’s entry into and emergence from all meditative absorptions. Seventh, since coming into my service, he has been able to fully comprehend all matters regarding which he had not yet attained the knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*).
Thus, these sentient beings have distinguished the Tathāgata’s present manifestations and have all attained the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
There are those who have attained human bodies or celestial bodies. Eighth, since they first attended upon me, they have been able to fully comprehend all the secret teachings of the Tathāgata;
it is because of this that they have exclusively transmitted the Dharma-treasury.
Regarding the phrase "arising from this meaning," etc., it is explained by means of the very words of the question itself.
If one says that the Dharma was not taught, the *Udānavarga* states: "The Dharma I have taught is like the leaves in my hand; the Dharma I have not yet taught is like the leaves in the forest.
If one says that the Dharma was taught, how can one say "I heard" [it], given that the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "I [received it] from Prabhāsa"?
It culminates in nirvāṇa. Throughout this interval, not a single word is spoken. How, then, can there be speech? Regarding the two interpretations of the response:
Mǔ states that there are four schools of tenets whose teachings differ. Concerning this analogy of the substance and its shadow, one should apply a fourfold analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*):
first, those who maintain only the substance exists and no shadow, such as the Mahāsāṃghika and others; second, those who maintain only the shadow...

1. No objective support (anālambana): Bhadanta Dharmatrāta and others. 2. Both objective support and reflection exist (sālambana-sapratibhāsa): Bandhuśrī and others. 3. Both objective support and reflection exist (sālambana-sapratibimba): Yaśomitra and others. 4. Neither objective support nor reflection exists (anālambana-apratibhāsa): Bhāviveka and others;
according to them, in ultimate truth (paramārthasatya), both mind and objects are empty.
Regarding the statement "Nāgārjuna and others": this bodhisattva subdued rival schools just as a dragon king can destroy all enemies;
because he possessed great majesty and ferocity, he was called Nāgasena (Dragon Army).

Seven hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there was a master of śāstras named Nāgārjuna in South India who composed the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* and commented upon the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. Thus it is said.

Regarding the term "and so forth": the disciple Deva composed the *Śataśāstra* and other works, extensively elucidating the teaching of emptiness to shatter the minds of those who cling to [false views].

The Dharma taught by the Buddha is the primary substance (*mūla*), while that heard by sentient beings is the shadow-teaching (*chāyā-dharma*). These are now the two interpretations of these two schools.

These include masters such as Nāgasena and Prabhāmitra. According to the view of this first master, in the resultant stage (*phala-avasthā*) of the Tathāgata, the first fifteen elements (*dhātu*)—namely, the five sense organs, the five consciousnesses, and the five objects—are absent.
Since these first fifteen elements do not exist, the sound element (*śabda-dhātu*) is likewise absent.

Because the sound element is missing, there are no names, phrases, or syllables; therefore, the Buddha does not preach the Dharma. Question: Why are the first fifteen elements absent? Answer: The Tathāgata...

The merits of the body and the land are profoundly deep and subtle; they are neither existent nor non-existent, free from all conceptual discrimination, and cut off from all frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*).

They are not dharmas such as the elements (*dhātu*) or bases (*āyatana*). Regarding the question of what is included [in the categories]: among the first fifteen elements (*dhātu*), only those pertaining to sentient beings are included, as they do not extend to the state of fruition.

This is for two reasons: first, within the stage of the Buddha’s fruition, there are no contaminated faculties (*sāsrava-indriya*); second, it is taught in the treatises that the Buddha’s mind is always in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and thus the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) do not function.
Because their nature is distracted, there are only the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*), and the mental-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*).

Regarding the statement that the Buddha possesses only three [great qualities]: among these three dharmas, the first two are for one's own benefit (*svārtha*), and the third is for the benefit of others (*parārtha*).

Great meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is the Buddha’s virtue of self-benefit; great wisdom (*prajñā*) is the fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*); and great meditative concentration is the basis upon which the other two wisdoms rely. The fourth...

Within dhyāna, there is the ninth stage of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is the Buddha’s virtue of benefiting others; it is the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), because it transforms all beings.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of great concentration: first, the extremely subtle concentration, which the Tathāgata is able to attain.

Although those in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are able to attain meditative concentration, they do not enter the subtle concentration. Second is the all-pervading concentration (*sarvatraga-samādhi*): the Tathāgata, throughout the ten stages, is able to enter all concentrations;
yet because [the bodhisattvas'] realization is not yet vast, only the Tathāgata, being vastly expansive, attains Great Wisdom.

This has three aspects: first, the nature of the wisdom of the perfected characteristics of the essence (*dharmatā*), which is the characteristic of True Suchness (*tathatā*) and corresponds to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Regarding this, the Tathāgata—

The two minds of the ultimate and the conventional are universally able to realize and enter into a state of perfect fusion, clarity, and penetration; therefore, it is called the "Wisdom of Perfectly Illuminating Characteristics and Nature.
Second is the "Wisdom of Miraculous Functionality Extending to the Margins. This wisdom of the Tathāgata is able to perform great deeds; because it is utterly vast, it is without limit or measure.

Its functioning is unrestricted, and thus it constitutes "miraculous functionality. Third is the "Wisdom of Skillfully Comprehending the Suitability of Faculties. This wisdom of the Tathāgata is able to...

Knowing the faculties and capacities of the three vehicles among the sentient beings of the triple world—whether they are mature or immature—and so forth, there are three kinds of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*):
First, the compassion that universally uproots all suffering. This compassion of the Tathāgata is able to uproot the three sufferings and eight sufferings within the triple world.

Second, the compassion of impartial liberation. As this sutra says: "He bestows ox-carts equally," meaning his love is without partiality or favoritism. Third, the compassion of universal writing... [text truncated]
Compassion for all sufferings. This refers to the fact that even the Three Vehicles of the present day eliminate various attachments, defilements, and so forth (the above explains the tenet).

To say that one has long been free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and has never been otherwise is also logical. For indeed, all discourse regarding the Dharma is itself conceptual proliferation.
Since there is no conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), for what reason would one preach the Dharma? There are three types of conceptual proliferation:

first, that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) is called conceptual proliferation, while that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*) is called non-proliferation; second, discrimination (*vikalpa*) is called conceptual proliferation, while non-discrimination is called non-proliferation;
third, preaching the Dharma is called conceptual proliferation, while not preaching the Dharma is called non-proliferation. The body, land, and merits of the Tathāgata are profoundly deep and subtle.

It is neither existent nor non-existent; it is free from all conceptual discrimination and bestows an end to all frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*). Since it is not subsumed within the categories of the elements (*dhātu*), the sense bases (*āyatana*), or other such dharma-gates, he does not speak of it.

The phrase "by the Buddha’s compassion, etc. is an explanation of a difficulty. Question: If one who is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) does not speak in accordance with conventional dharmas, why did the Venerable Ānanda say, "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*)? Answer: The commentary states, "By the Buddha’s compassion, etc.
This means that throughout immeasurable kalpas during his causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*), the Buddha constantly made this vow: "When I attain Buddhahood, may all sentient beings see my body."
Those who have resolved their minds on Bodhi and heard my name shall sever evil and cultivate goodness; therefore, I have now attained the Way.

When sentient beings see the Buddha, understanding arises within their own minds, as if the Buddha were preaching the Dharma for them. Furthermore, they themselves make vows, thinking: "Just like us sentient beings..."
Throughout immeasurable lifetimes, he has made this vow: "May I always see the Buddha and hear the Dharma. First, there is the power of the sentient being’s own aspiration;

second, because their roots of goodness have matured; and third, by taking the original vow of the Tathāgata as the power of conditions, the aspects of words and meanings arise within the consciousness of the sentient being.
For followers of the Hīnayāna, these are the words and meanings of the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination.

They arise in mutual correspondence. In the Mahāyāna, the words and meanings of the six pāramitās for sentient beings arise in mutual correspondence. It is like sound being transmitted through an empty valley or practice being heard in a vacant hall.
Just as the World-Honored One today has no teaching that he does not proclaim, so too do the scriptures and teachings exist inherently within the various consciousnesses.

The characteristics of words and meanings appear; from this, sentient beings who possess the necessary conditions perceive the arising of signs of meaning such as the sūtras and teachings within their own minds.
In reality, however, the Tathāgata has never preached the Dharma.
Regarding the statement that "the words, meanings, and characteristics are identical," a question is raised:

if these words and meanings arise upon consciousness through the power of the sentient beings' own roots of goodness, why is it said that "the Buddha preached such-and-such a sutra" and so forth? The commentary answers: "The words, meanings, and characteristics are identical. The intended meaning is as follows:

Although sentient beings themselves possess the power of roots of goodness that arise [within them], they rely upon the Buddha as a powerful external condition for the cessation of evil; this is what is called "the Buddha's teaching.
It is just as when, after one's parents have passed away, sons and daughters see them in their dreams giving instructions and guidance, which perfectly illuminates their minds.
As for those who see [the Buddha] from above: their own mind of attachment transforms into an image. If one discusses the original source of the initial examination, it has never come from anywhere;
today, when the World-Honored One preaches the Dharma, it is likewise so. This is because during his causal stage, the World-Honored One made this vow:

"After I have attained Buddhahood, may those sentient beings who see me perceive the arising of words and meanings within the consciousness-mind, whereby their afflictions shall be extinguished," and so forth.

Regarding the name "Recollection" (nianming): all attain awakening to the Way and so forth. If one says it relies on the power of one's own roots of goodness, this is not merely a discourse on the name "shadow";
the body is also called a shadow. For instance, the dimensions of the bodies seen by those prior to the stages (bhūmi), those on the stages, and even those up to the tenth stage differ;
therefore, we know they are only shadows. If one discusses the true body, it is realized only through direct testimony (sākṣātkāra); how then could ordinary beings and others perceive it?

Regarding the phrase "the absence of intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāva*) and so forth: this is cited as scriptural evidence that the aspects of words and meanings arise within the consciousness of sentient beings.
"Absence of intrinsic nature" refers to Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*, distinguishing it from Maitreya’s *Saṃgraha*. As for the "eight times" (*aṣṭakāla*):

according to the translation by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Tang dynasty, *aṣṭakāla* means "eight times," which refers to the temporal periods experienced by the listener. One interpretation states they are the "eight case-endings" (*aṣṭavibhakti*), such as the agent (*kartṛ*), the object (*karman*), and so forth.
(The interpretation as "the correct" [reading] follows from the explanation). Second, it is said: "The *Avataṃsaka* assembly has eight periods (*aṣṭakāla*).

There is also a tradition which states that for each of the four directions, there are four periods of day and four periods of night, thus making eight periods (one theory). Tripitaka Master Yijing stated: *iṣṭaka*; this is translated as "the period of desire.
Among the eight periods, this refers specifically to the time when the listeners desire to hear the Dharma. (An-guo).

Question: These two Tripiṭaka masters both visited the Jetavana and personally consulted the sacred commentary. For what reason do their translations differ regarding a single meaning? Answer: It follows the Sanskrit original.

Since *aṣṭa* and *eka* can both be translated [as "eight"], there is no error. The Tripiṭaka Master from Tang (Xuanzang) referred to the time experienced by the listeners, and thus spoke of "eight periods.
The Tripiṭaka Master Jing (Yijing) referred to the time the listeners heard the Dharma; although it is general, [the distinction lies therein].
This is the interpretation of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*; the preceding and following [explanations] differ. Mou says: "Taking the time of desire is superior.

Among the eight times, it is because that desire belongs to the listener that it is established upon the consciousness of the listener. If one relies on the eight times as the times of the eight grammatical cases (*vibhakti*), then that is superior."
Regarding the statement "direct speech is not equal [to indirect speech]," this encompasses three interpretations: First, prose is called "direct," while verse is called "not direct.

Second, according to the specific characteristics within the twelve divisions of the teaching (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*), the single division of *sūtra* is called "direct exposition," while the remaining eleven divisions are called "indirect exposition.

Third, names (*nāman*) that express intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) are called "direct exposition," while phrases (*pada*) that express distinctions (*viśeṣa*) are called "indirect exposition. As it is said:

To speak of "great" is to refer to its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), which is called "direct. If one speaks of the grass, chaff, or magnitude [of the path], these are distinctions and are not direct.

For example, among the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is direct as an intrinsic nature, whereas [attributes such as] permanence or impermanence are not direct.

Regarding the phrase "the manifestation of an accumulation of words," the followers of the Hīnayāna ask: "In our school, the three time periods are substantially existent and their continuity is uninterrupted;

thus, they can constitute the substance of the teaching. In your Mahāyāna school, however, a single dharma-moment of the present has utility only for a brief duration, and upon flowing into the past, it ceases to exist.

Since the Mahāyāna maintains that the past and future lack substantial existence, how can they constitute the substance of the teaching? The answer, as stated by Ān-guó, is as follows: [The passage continues: "It emerges..."

The substance [of the teaching] is twofold: first, that which takes the seven mental states as its substance, arising through continuous connection; second, that which takes the twelve mental states as its substance, arising anew at every moment.
All such substances of the teaching are, in essence, the immediate seeking and the definitive outflow of defilement and purity.

This constitutes five moments of mind. Regarding the possession of seven moments of mind: as when pronouncing various syllables, there are two moments of mind—namely, the sudden (*ābhoga*) and the seeking (*paryeṣaka*).
When hearing the syllable *ha*, there is only one moment of mind, which is the determining (*niścaya*). When hearing the syllable *na*, there is one moment of seeking.
When hearing the syllable *chāng* (常), there arise three minds—namely, the determinative, the defiled, and the outflowing mind; these are called the seven minds. Regarding the twelve minds:
upon hearing the various syllables, there are two minds—the sudden and the investigative; upon hearing the syllable *xíng* (行), there are three minds—the sudden, the investigative, and the decisive;
upon hearing the syllable *wú* (無), there are two minds—the sudden and the investigative; and upon hearing the syllable *chāng* (常), five minds manifest simultaneously. These are called the twelve.
It is the mind (*citta*). Fayuan states: "By recollecting the preceding syllables, they undergo successive perfuming (*vāsanā*) such that subsequent syllables arise;

it is only at the final moment that one is able to understand the meaning. Although there is no limit [to the number of syllables], the essence of the teaching nonetheless forms a complete composition. This is what is meant by 'manifesting as a collection.

The intent clarifies that the sound of the preceding thought-moment, having already ceased, perfumes the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) to form the nature of a seed (*bīja*); subsequently, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)..."
In the present moment, although the essence of sound has already ceased, it appears as a reflection through the power of its seeds;
even until many moments have accumulated and arisen together, they function as a signifier. This is called "manifestation through accumulation."

Regarding the phrase "He himself raises the objection, etc.," this refers to a question and answer. In this treatise, the order of the citations is reversed; it would properly correspond to what was stated previously.

That treatise begins by stating that for the sake of manifesting the greatness of the essence and the greatness of the function of the Mahāyāna, the Bodhisattva who has already well entered the Mahāyāna expounds the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-pariccheda*.
Next, the intent of the treatise is cited: the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-śāstra* is [the work of] the West... [text truncated].
It was composed by the Bodhisattva [Asaṅga]. The *Jianyao* states: "He explained the Western *Abhidharma-sūtra*. This sūtra consists of seven hundred fascicles, but it did not come to this land;
only one chapter remains, titled the 'Chapter on the Compendium of the Mahāyāna' (*Mahāyānasaṃgraha*). This chapter has a particular affinity with sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva subsequently composed the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-śāstra*, which specifically explains this single chapter. Question: Was it further [composed] by the Tathāgata?
The Abhidharma-sūtra is taught in reality. The Bodhisattva composes treatises to explain and realize it.

Regarding the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma, does it not arise as the appearance of the textual meaning of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* within the self-cognition of that Bodhisattva, thereby realizing that the Tathāgata did not [explicitly] teach it?

If the Buddha-Dharma must necessarily be taught by the Bodhisattva, yet the Buddha did not teach it, the Bodhisattva would not teach it either. Answer: One view holds that the Bodhisattva is indeed able to teach it.

This is the Dharma. In the preceding establishment of the principle, it was stated that the Buddha has long since transcended conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and thus does not preach the Dharma.

While Bodhisattvas, while still on the path of causes, possess conceptual proliferation, what prevents them from preaching the Dharma? The Buddha, abiding in the state of fruition, is without conceptual proliferation and therefore does not preach the Dharma.
If this is so, then the very fact that Bodhisattvas compose treatises and preach the Dharma serves as a counter-proof that the Tathāgata does not preach the Dharma. Second:

The sūtras are that which is to be explained, and the Bodhisattvas compose treatises as the means of explaining them. Even including the sūtras that are to be explained, the Buddha did not speak them;
rather, the Bodhisattvas see that these sūtras likewise arise from the patterns of words and meanings within their own consciousness as Mahāyāna Abhidharma.
Therefore, the commentary itself answers this by stating: "According to the intended meaning of the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā* and other [sūtras], the Buddha did not teach the Dharma."
Within the Bodhisattva’s own consciousness, the characteristics of the words and meanings of the Mahāyāna Abhidharma arise.
These characteristics of words and meanings also rely upon the Buddha’s power of altruistic vows as their dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Because these characteristics appear within the Bodhisattva’s own consciousness, they are designated as "the Buddha’s teaching" by virtue of this predominant condition.
Regarding the phrase "for example, as with the gods" and so forth: it is like a person who requests from the gods the permission to study treatises, mantras, and the like.
At night, they dream that a celestial deity bestows upon them a treatise or a mantra. Within the dream, auditory consciousness does not function, and thus there is no opening for sound;

nor does the deity speak. Rather, the celestial deity acts as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), and the appearance of the treatise, mantra, and so forth manifests within the person's own mental consciousness.
Therefore, one should know that in this person’s dream, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is unable to discern the essential nature [of objects].

This is because the treatise, citing the conditions for incantations (*mantra*), states that there is no auditory consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*). However, the incantations seen therein are merely manifestations appearing to one's own mind; this case is likewise so. Question:

Since the six consciousnesses are not functioning during sleep, how can there be a sudden auditory consciousness (*tadānīntana-śrotravijñāna*) occurring simultaneously with a mental consciousness? How is this possible?
One hears [the teaching] and subsequently retains it in memory. The answer is that there are two types of sleep: first, that with mental activity (*sacittaka*);
second, that without mental activity (*acittaka*). This state with mental activity involves dreams; the state without mental activity, when it is extremely profound, is dreamless.

Now, the sixth consciousness independently gives rise to two kinds of "solitary-image" objects (*svapratibhāsa-viṣaya*). These two are also not real. When deities such as those of the heavens are about to bestow spells upon one, it is solely due to the power of those deities increasing [one's capacity].

Due to the power of the superior [state], the treatises and mantras appear clearly within the mental consciousness; therefore, they are cited as metaphors to prove that there is only one's own consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*). Question:

Since the Buddha is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and has transcended all names and expressions, whereas Bodhisattvas have not yet eliminated [conceptualization], how can they be said to be identical to the state of no-explanation?

Answer: It is not that Bodhisattvas of non-nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) do not speak; rather, their speaking is like obtaining treatises and mantras within a dream. Thus, by directly realizing the nature of reality, they skillfully enter the Mahāyāna, even amidst conceptual proliferation.
It is also lost.
As for the statement that the "ancient sutra" also speaks of the "beginning" and so forth—these sixteen characters are likewise the Buddha acting as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Upon the consciousness of sentient beings themselves, these sixteen characters appear as images. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* says: The Buddha addressed Subhūti... [text continues].
"Ananda, I have not uttered a single word here, nor have you heard anything; what, then, is there to be understood? Why is this?
Because the profound Prajñā is utterly free from verbal expression."
Regarding the statement "like the teeth of a mother," the *Biographies of Former Worthies of Runan* says: Zhou Chang was a native of Ancheng. He was compassionate and filial;
when his mother fell ill and he was away in the countryside, she desired to see her son. She bit her finger, and he arrived immediately. His mother did not even call out to him.
The son also did not hear it; yet the son was born from the mother and is called "understanding. When He asked, "If you truly do not speak, how can the Sūtra say:

'The Dharma I have taught is like the leaves in my hand'? The answer is: for the sake of acting as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) to cause others to obtain benefit, it is called "teaching," just like the leaves in one's hand.
This is the intention of the master Asvabhāva regarding the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma; now, [the commentary] explains it.

Regarding the partial discussion of that which is not spoken of: this is the intended meaning of the *Śāstra*. Since it is stated that no dharma is taught, one asks: what constitutes the essence (*tattva*) of the Buddha’s teaching? The answer is:

its essence consists in the appearance of words and meanings (*nāma-artha-nimitta*) upon the consciousness of sentient beings. To prove this, the *Nirākāra-vijñapti-mātratā* (the naturelessness of phenomena) is cited as evidence.

The intent of the *Nirākāra* position is that the essence [of the teaching] consists in the appearance of words and meanings within the consciousness of sentient beings; for two reasons: first, because of the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only); and second, because of the cause...

Because of these conditions, it is as when one speaks of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). The syllables and sounds of the past do not exist; the syllables reside in the future within twelve moments of mind.
