Of these, the first eleven moments have already fallen away into the past, yet their images and characteristics are all cognized by the mind.

When the seeing [aspect] arises through the connection with the perceived [aspect], because the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) and the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) arise from the same seed, they constitute the immediate causal condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). Furthermore, regarding the consciousness of the speaker, the words and meanings are transmitted in succession.

It is transmitted as the essence of the teaching (*śāsana*). It does not take the sound, name, or phrase that can hear or speak as its essence. Question: Why is it "without intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāva*)? The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:
"This was spoken in order to manifest the greatness of the essence of the Mahāyāna for those bodhisattvas who have already well entered [the path].

Thus, the words and phrases themselves constitute the essence. Answer: That *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* was spoken with the intention of acting as a dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*); therefore, it makes this statement. It is like the case of the gods and so forth.

Regarding "hearing by power": it is not hearing with the ears. It is not that the celestial beings (devas) speak in words; rather, they cause treatises, mantras, and so forth to appear within the mind.

With the celestial beings and spirits acting as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), they apprehend for the seeker those phenomena—treatises, mantras, and the like—which are transformations of the pacified mind.
Thus, these serve as the essence [of the teaching], and one does not take the treatises or mantras of the celestial beings themselves as the essence.
Regarding the mention of "the two," "Bandhuprabha" (親光) refers to [Sthiramati]. Regarding the word "and so forth" (等), it includes Bodhisattva Dharmapāla.

The Buddha-body possesses the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), and so on. Furthermore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (成唯識論), fascicle 9, states: "The merit, body, and lands of the Tathāgata are, as appropriate, subsumed within the aggregates, bases, and elements.
Moreover, it is stated in various places that one attains [mastery] over impermanent form (*rūpa*). Huìhuà (化度) says: "Among the five aggregates, sound..."
This is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), which is subsumed within the eleven types of form. Names, phrases, and phonemes are subsumed within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).

Among the twelve bases (*āyatana*), sound is the base of sound; names, phrases, and phonemes are the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). Among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), sound is the element of sound; names, phrases, and phonemes are the element of phenomena.
Since there are eighteen elements, and since there exist sounds, names, phrases, and phonemes, how can it be said that [the Buddha] did not teach the Dharma? This clarifies [the point].
The scholar Fazang, in his *Commentary on the Profound Meaning of the Awakening of Faith*, states:

"It is known that the Tathāgata’s five faculties (indriya) are certainly not non-existent, because they are subsumed under one or another of the six faculties, just like the mind-faculty (manas-indriya). Secondly, it is said:

"The Tathāgata’s five objects (viṣaya) are certainly not non-existent, because they are subsumed under one or another of the six elements (dhātu), just like the dharma-element (dharma-dhātu). Thirdly, it is said: "The Tathāgata’s five consciousnesses (vijñāna), up to and including the mental consciousness (mano-vijñāna)..."
(Refuting what is known through valid cognition: Since the eighteen *dhātus* have already been established, it is known that [the Buddha] taught the Dharma.

Regarding the statement "by being free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and so forth," the former masters such as Nāgārjuna and others claimed: "He has long since transcended conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and has never taught the Dharma.

To be "free from conceptual construction" means to be without conceptual proliferation. As for the claim that he "has never taught the Dharma"—does this not mean that he did teach the Dharma? It is called [such] because...

Is it free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*)? Within the state of Buddhahood, speech is uttered spontaneously; thus, the teaching of the Dharma is distinct from conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).
Conceptual discrimination belongs to the mind of preparatory application (*prayoga*), whereas in the state of Buddhahood there is no such application.

Furthermore, according to the school that maintains that Buddhas do not speak through vitarka and vicāra, they hold that the designation "teaching the Dharma" is merely conceptual proliferation. Consequently, [the Buddha] does not speak in the state of Buddhahood.

The Dharma does not involve the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) of whether the Buddha’s state exists or not; it is simply taught as being free from marks (*lakṣaṇa*), abiding nowhere within the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*).

It is merely that the Buddha teaches without giving rise to a discriminating mind. Question: How can he teach the Dharma without a discriminating mind? Answer: The Buddha’s teaching is like a single rain.
The rain from heaven is one, yet the nature of the roots of grasses and trees differs; they receive the moisture in various ways. It is not...
Rain comes in two or three kinds, yet when the Buddha preaches the Dharma, he speaks only of the single flavor of the Dharma.

Because there are three types of sentient beings according to their faculties, there appear to be three vehicles (triyāna), and five vehicles (pañcayāna). Yet the Buddha makes no such distinctions; it is simply that he manifests as three or five vehicles to accord with those who understand this.
When I preach the Four Noble Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and so forth to you, you should know that the Buddha has nothing he does not [accommodate].

Because [the Buddha] is free from conceptual discrimination, a sutra says: "The Tathāgata speaks with equality regarding a single utterance. Furthermore, another sutra says: "The Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice.

This means that the Buddha speaks with a mind devoid of conceptual discrimination; this is what is called "being without discursive proliferation" (*niṣprapañca*). It does not mean that he does not teach the Dharma; rather, it is called being without discursive proliferation because he speaks without a discriminating mind.
The phrase "those who hear directly" and so forth serves to explain the meaning. "Those who hear directly" refers to sentient beings of the three vehicles and five natures.
Regarding the roots of goodness and original vows, there are two types. The first is that which sentient beings have previously made since beginningless time.

"May I see the Buddha, hear the Dharma, and encounter spiritual friends. By means of these roots of goodness, may the appearance of the marks of words and meanings arise upon the consciousness of the Tathāgata.
Second, these marks of words and meanings upon the consciousness of the Buddha arise from the Tathāgata’s roots of goodness for the benefit of others;

therefore, they are called 'the Buddha's teaching. This refers directly to the person who teaches the Dharma. Previously, the reason the school did not speak of the Dharma was because of the Buddha..."
In the causal stage, the arousal of a vow serves as the condition for the arising of the marks of words and meanings upon the consciousness of sentient beings.

Now, within this school of the teaching of the Dharma, by virtue of the vow made by sentient beings acting as a condition, the marks of words and meanings arise upon the consciousness of the Tathāgata.

The essential nature and characteristics are the reverse of this. The commentary contains two points: first, [the case] from the perspective of those who hear directly, based on the conditions of their roots of goodness and original vows.

[The section on] "Power. The portion above belongs to sentient beings; the following passage, "the marks and meanings of the text arise upon the consciousness of the Tathāgata," etc., belongs to the Tathāgata.

The second section states: "That which is called 'direct,' etc., refers to the roots of goodness," which belongs to sentient beings. From "by the power of the conditions of the original vow" up to "spoken by the Buddha" belongs to the Tathāgata.
Within the context of the Buddha’s benefit for others, it is because of these words that these marks and meanings of the text [are established].
Having made the vow to benefit others, one aspires to attain Buddhahood. One initiates the transformation of sentient beings through the three karmas [of body, speech, and mind].

By the power of the conditions of that original vow, mental images of words and meanings arise upon the Buddha-consciousness. For those seeking the vehicle of the Śrāvaka, the mental images of the words and meanings of the Four Noble Truths appear.
These arise from the roots of goodness of the Buddha’s altruistic activity; this is the wooden-text teaching, which is called "Buddha."
It is said:

"That which is heard, such as the mental image upon consciousness," refers to the teaching of the reflected image (*pratibimba*). The Buddha relies upon the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) of sentient beings, while sentient beings rely upon the Buddha’s vows for the benefit of others made throughout three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) as their own roots of goodness;
thus, there is a distinction between the substantial basis (*bimba*) and the reflection (*pratibimba*). Question: Regarding the Tathāgata’s teaching...

[Question: Sound is indeed untainted (*anāsrava*), whereas the mental consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*) of sentient beings is tainted (*sāsrava*). Since the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) cannot directly apprehend the essence of the untainted teaching, how can it now be said that "I have heard"?
[Answer: The *Śū* (Commentary) states: "As for 'hearing,' it refers to [the transformation] upon the consciousness and so forth.

Just as a mirror reflects an object such that it resembles it, this is called the 'transformative condition' (*pratibimba-pratyaya*) of the illuminating agent. Because it resembles that [untainted essence], it is termed 'I'."

The Master Wenxiang said: "The Dharma taught by the Buddha has the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) as its essential substance (*bhāva*). When a listener’s mind undergoes transformation, it takes this as an object through the medium of outflows (*sāsrava*).

Since the image and the substance differ, it is said that one does not directly apprehend [the teaching]. The characteristics of the words and meanings transformed by the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of the eighth stage and above—which is outflow-free—are also outflow-free teachings in their substantial reality (*dravya*), even when appearing within the [subjective] vision (*darśana*). Prior to the seventh stage, they are common to both the outflow-free and the outflow-possessing."

It is untainted (*anāsrava*). Those below the stages [of the path] and the small sages (*śrāvaka*) possess only that which is tainted. Although the followers of the two vehicles possess a portion of untainted subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), they cannot take phenomena as their object;
they can only take suchness (*tathatā*) as their object. Now, Ānanda, you should understand this according to what is appropriate.
Regarding the phrase "Vasubandhu says... and so forth, this cites the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* as proof.

Vasubandhu states that it is because [the Buddha's body] is distinct from the consciousnesses within other continuums (*saṃtāna*). This refers to the Buddha-body. As for the term "others," it refers to the Tathāgatas who are the teachers of the Dharma.
Sentient beings are those who can hear the Dharma; they are called "others" because they are the remainder of those who can hear.
"Continuity" (saṃtati) has the meaning of "ear," which refers to the conventional designation of the Buddha’s body as the five aggregates.

"Distinction" (viśeṣa) refers to the teachings as the untainted objective essence upon the Buddha’s consciousness, wherein the various aspects of both words and meanings differ; this is what is meant by the "distinction of consciousness. Taking this as a condition...
It causes other continuities to give rise to differentiated consciousness. "Causing others" refers specifically to sentient beings.
Since the Buddha is the speaker and sentient beings are the listeners, they are called "others" because they are distinct from the speaker. "Continuity" (saṃtati) means the body.
As for "differentiated," it refers to the various different forms of teaching reflected upon the consciousness of sentient beings themselves; this is termed "differentiation."
Regarding the arising of consciousness:

as for the statement that "this and that are mutually [causes]," the Buddha’s roots of goodness for the benefit of others act as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for sentient beings to hear [the teaching];

the roots of goodness of sentient beings act as the dominant condition for the Buddha to be moved to speak. This is what is meant by being "mutually [causes]. Although the Buddha has attained [enlightenment]...
The Way. If there were no sentient beings, for whom would one wish to preach? Therefore, we know that sentient beings also serve as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the Buddha.

Thus, the moon in the sky is like the Buddha’s fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*); through its power as a condition, the moon in the water arises as the appearance of words and meanings within the consciousness of sentient beings.
Question: If the Buddha truly speaks and sentient beings truly hear, how can the mind of consciousness be established as having the meaning of "not being separate from consciousness"?
The answer states: Through the power of successive reinforcement, the two consciousnesses achieve the definitive power to benefit others.

Not being separate from the Buddha’s consciousness-mind, and the roots of goodness of sentient beings not being separate from the consciousness of sentient beings—this is called the meaning of "not being separate."
Regarding the statement, "By this sūtra, what I have taught, etc.," this is a citation of scripture. As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi*, fascicle 64, the *Śiṃśapāvanasūtra* says:
"In the language of India, it is called Śiṃśapā; in the language of Tang, it is called 'Walnut Grove' (*huáotáo lín*).
It is also called 'Forest of Separation from the Mind' (*líxīn*), 'Forest of Sinu' (*shēnnù lín*), and also 'Forest of Shenyun' (*shēnyún lín*)."
Regarding the statement "like a maṇi jewel" and so forth: this serves as proof that the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma without conceptual discrimination.
A maṇi is a gem that, being devoid of conceptual discrimination, can fulfill the wishes of sentient beings. The celestial drum is the drum within the palace of Śakra; it is struck by no one.
It can fulfill the wishes of the devas by producing four kinds of sounds—such as those concerning enemies coming or going, or the arising of weariness toward worldly pleasures (as may be understood).

Mouzi said: "The celestial drum is used as an analogy for the Buddha’s body, and the drum itself as an analogy for the preaching of the Dharma. Furthermore, although the jewel has no thought, it rains down various treasures which sentient beings truly obtain and enjoy;
likewise, although the Buddha has no thought, he preaches, and Ānanda truly hears and receives it. The celestial drum has no thought..."
A sound issues forth. Śakra is indeed able to understand it. The jewel and the drum do not exceed two purposes: first, the benefit of manifesting transformation bodies, like a wish-fulfilling jewel;
second, the benefit of preaching the Dharma, like the celestial drum.
Regarding the statement, "In this context, the two interpretations follow those [masters]," it refers to the two schools of thought concerning whether the Buddha taught the Dharma or not.

The master Nāgārjuna cites a sūtra to prove that the Buddha did not teach the Dharma, while the master Bandhuprabha (Vasubandhu) cites a sūtra to prove that he did; these are the two textual passages. As for the "mutual discrepancy," Nāgārjuna maintains that the Buddha did not speak;
rather, on the consciousness of sentient beings, there naturally arise the appearances of words and meanings. In other instances, it is said that he did teach the Dharma.
This refers to his superior birth; therefore, he speaks thus. Bandhuprabha (Kin-kwang) states that the Buddha truly taught the Dharma.

Nāgārjuna (Lung-chün), citing scriptural passages, proves that no Dharma was taught. [Bandhuprabha] refutes Nāgārjuna’s citation as being a teaching of the Dharma, while [Nāgārjuna] refutes Bandhuprabha’s interpretation to establish that no Dharma was taught. Thus, it is called "following those two texts," and so forth. Kin...
Regarding the scriptural passage cited by Master Longjun, which states that "the Buddha did not speak a single word of Dharma and you did not hear it," there are ten meanings.

First, with respect to the *dharmatā-svabhāva-kāya* (the body of the intrinsic nature of phenomena), it is said that he did not speak. As the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "The Tathāgata has nothing to teach.
Second, with respect to the *prathama-sambhogakāya* (the first enjoyment body), it is said that he did not speak; for only a Buddha and a Buddha can truly know [this].

Third, with respect to the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) of others, it is said that he does not preach. As the treatise states: "The emanated body is not the true Buddha, nor is it the preacher of the Dharma.
Fourth, with respect to what is preached by all Buddhas, it is not a result; because it is not a result, it is called "not preaching. As it says below:
All the World-Honored Ones preach the single vehicle path; they transmit it without creating it anew. Fifth, they do not speak of dharmas that fall into the realm of words and letters.

As the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra says: "The nature of words and letters is detached from them; there are no words and letters. Sixth, because there is nothing that the Buddhas do not realize and know.

Therefore, it is not spoken. (1) Because the Buddha has personally realized both principle and phenomena (*dharmatā* and *dharma*). (2) Regarding the perfect nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), there is no verbal expression; thus it is said to be "not spoken.
(3) Regarding the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), phenomena produced by conditions are illusory and unreal.

(4) Regarding the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), they are conceptual constructions of deluded sentiment; though existent in sentiment, they are non-existent in reality, and are therefore called "not spoken. (5) Regarding...
The Dharma taught by the Buddha is not "taught" because it is not an object of direct perception for the listener; therefore, it is said that he does not teach it.

Since the listener must necessarily undergo a transformation of the mental image (*pratibimba*), the verse concludes: "The three bodies are non-different, yet one falls into words; without realizing the three natures, one is distant from the object of perception.
The holy teachings rely upon this principle; therefore, Nāgārjuna did not say that the Buddha teaches the Dharma. Question: We see the Buddha proclaiming all dharmas.

Why is it said that not a single word was spoken? The answer is: based on the fundamental non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) that realizes the Dharma, there is no verbal expression whatsoever;
therefore, it is said that not a single word was spoken. Herein, the essence of the teaching (*deśanā-śarīra*) is briefly analyzed through ten gates.

First, the gate of subsuming characteristics back into their nature: the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states, "All dharmas are suchness (*tathatā*). The *She-lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha) of the Liang dynasty states, "From the most supreme... [text continues].
From the pure ocean flows forth correct gnosis (*samyag-jñāna*). From correct gnosis flows forth subsequently attained gnosis (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

From subsequently attained gnosis flow forth the twelvefold teaching (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*). This brings the branches back to the root, for the textual expressions are not one. Second is the gate of discarding objects to discuss consciousness.
The *Avataṃsaka* says: "O Son of the Buddha, the three realms are false and illusory; they arise solely from consciousness. Everything revolves from the mind. If a person understands it thus..."

One is called a true son of the Buddha. Third is the gate of subsuming the provisional back into the real: all dharmas take sound as their substance because names, phrases, and so forth are merely provisional.
Apart from sound, there are no separate names or the like. The Abhidharma states: "Sound that is produced by formation serves as the basis for all teachings.
These names and so forth are provisional; this is explained here according to the conventions of this land. In other buddha-fields, they likewise use light [to convey meaning].
1. The Gate of Abandoning the Real to Discourse on the Conventional (*prajñapti-mukha*): This takes the vocal modulations upon sound as its essence. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

"Although these three [types of speech] have no separate essence apart from sound, because the conventional and the real differ, they are nonetheless sound. 2. The Gate of Discourse on the Conventional Alone (*kevala-prajñapti-mukha*):
This takes the four dharmas as its essence. The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states: "There are some buddha-fields that take sounds and language..."
[They] perform the Buddha-work through words and letters. The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Both speaker and listener attain completion only by means of two things:
first, excellent sound; second, excellent letters. Regarding the six gates of the tainted and untainted, [this refers to] the person who speaks.

Regarding the hearing of the untainted (anāsrava) teachings, they may be understood by applying the same principles through reflection. 7. The Gate of the Expressive and the Expressed: This takes both the letter (vyañjana) and the meaning (artha) as its essence.
As the *Aṣṭadaśa-bhūmi-śāstra* states: "The essence of the sūtra is briefly of two kinds: first, the letter; second, the meaning. The letter is the expressive;

the meaning is that which is expressed. 8. The Gate of the Five Dharmas and Their Clarification: There are two [aspects]. First, the five dharmas beginning with mind (citta); second, names (nāman) and so forth.
Because there are distinctions among the five dharmas: first, those subsumed under mind and mental factors take the provisional as following from the real, with sound as their substance;

those subsumed under form take the object as following from the mind, with the mind as their substance; consciousness abandons the real to follow the provisional, taking non-associated formations as its substance; and the inclusion of characteristics within nature.

The first [consciousness] has the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as its essence. The second subsumes objects within the mind; it takes non-conceptual correct wisdom (*nirvikalpa-samyagjñāna*) as its essence.

The third is based on both the existence of substance and its nature, corresponding respectively to the two gates of the ninefold reality and the shadow-image. The fourth is the discrimination [of four cases]:

first, there is only the substance without the shadow, as held by the Saṃmitīya school and also included among the Sarvāstivādins; they maintain that prior to the Buddha’s [enlightenment], there was...
The five elements (dhātus) are with outflows (sāsrava); therefore, there is this censure. Devadatta is incomparable. Women give rise to craving for existence;

[the Vaibhāṣikas] take the Buddha’s words with outflows as the very essence of the teaching. [The Sautrāntikas] maintain that both [the body and speech] are merely shadows and lack intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva).

The treatise calculates that while the Buddha manifests his body and preaches the Dharma, one does not take the Buddha’s physical substance as the teaching, fearing that one might grasp at phenomena external to the mind. If it were according to the school of Nāgārjuna, he would neither manifest a body nor preach.

Regarding the Dharma, both [masters] do not take it as a substantial entity; they are alike in entering this category of "all three being present. Regarding the presence of all three, Dharmapāla and Yaśomitra state in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*:

"By the superior power of the roots of goodness of the listener, the aspects of the text and meaning—which possess both contaminated and uncontaminated seeds—are projected upon the consciousness of the listener.
Furthermore, the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Through the successive superior power [of these factors], the two consciousnesses become determinate."
Thus, the wisdom of sentient beings is determined, and the compassion of the Buddha is determined; therefore, it is said that "the two meanings establish determination.

Dharmapāla states: Although the aspects of the words and meanings manifested upon the consciousness of the speaker are external dharmas to the consciousness-mind of the noble listener, from the perspective of [the listener's] own [consciousness], this does not contradict the meaning of *vijñaptimātra* (mind-only). Fifteenth: The Section on the Manifestation of the Collection of Minds. The Sautrāntika school.

The objection states: "I maintain that the three times exist because their continuity can be apprehended; thus, the Mahāyāna is established. Since the past and future do not exist [as substantial entities], how can they constitute the body of the teaching?
They function through mutual connection, such that a collective understanding arises upon the consciousness of the listener. Therefore, Asvabhāva says:
Because it pierces through and stitches together [the teachings], it is called a *sūtra*.
Regarding the statement that one avoids "addition" (*āgama*) and "subtraction" (*apagama*): adding the Buddha’s words is called "addition"; omitting the Buddha’s words is called "subtraction.

For example, when the Tathāgata taught three cycles [of instruction] and Ānanda spoke of only two, this is called "subtraction. Furthermore, when the Tathāgata taught that the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is non-existent, and Ānanda... [omitted].
To say "it exists" when it is not is called adding to the Buddha’s words; therefore, this is termed "adding or subtracting.

To reverse the order of words—taking what came first as the condition and what came later as the precedent—wherein matter and mind differ and principle and phenomena contradict one another, is collectively termed "divergent division" (*vibhāga*). "Divergent" (*vi*) means distinct; "division" (*bhāga*) means differentiation.
For example, when the Tathāgata speaks of emptiness, Ānanda changes it to "existence"; this is called altering the Buddha’s words, and is thus termed "divergent division. (In response to a question)
"Reversal" refers to the sense of cause; it means that faults are caused by such things as "I" and so forth.
The statement "such dharmas as these" is intended to inspire faith, so that one may believe the words of Ānanda and not those spoken by others.
This is not a hearsay transmitted through successive intermediaries. The character *tā* (他) is read separately from *krama* (展轉), indicating the listener.
The term "capable" (*kṣama*) refers to being endowed with the necessary capacity; it is called "capable" because it is free from the faults of exaggeration, depreciation, or deviation.
This first phrase establishes faith in Ānanda’s person—that all he has heard is trustworthy—and faith in the Dharma taught by Ānanda.
It is said that they are not like the foolish and so forth. Mou (Mouzi) says: "As for the five matters of Mahādeva, others are led astray by ignorance, and so on (*etc.*).
This interpretation need not necessarily refer to Mahādeva; it simply refers to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
It is not as if, when hearing the Dharma, all [foolish ones] are unable to free themselves from such faults; this is called being "incapable. Whatever one hears may, or may not...

To be free from exaggeration, depreciation, and heterogeneity, those who transmit the Buddha’s teachings when compiling the Dharma rely on the Tathāgata’s instruction and utter these words at the outset:
"Such a Dharma as this, I have personally heard from the Buddha. Thus, both the phrasing and the meaning are definitive, free from heterogeneity, and without any deficiency or reduction.

Regarding the phrase "Therefore, [it is said] 'Thus have I heard,'" these three lines of the commentary correspond to the three types of wisdom: hearing, reflection, and cultivation. Cheng Tai states:
"The reason the Buddha’s original teaching places the words 'Thus have I heard' at the beginning is to manifest that what is being transmitted is free from the faults of omission or distortion."
In order to cause all sentient beings to give rise to faith and compliance, they should, upon hearing this Dharma, diligently practice and study it.
*The Essential Compendium of the Profound Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra*, Fascicle Seven.
*Fahua jing xuanzan yaoji*, Scroll Eight.
Recorded by the Mirror-Water Śramaṇa Xifu.
Regarding the phrase "The Dharma King inaugurates his transformation," etc.: according to the essentials within the sutra, there are only these two instances of "at that time."

There is no separate time; it is distinguished by reference to the Dharma. First, regarding the sequence from "Thus have I heard" up to "having paid homage, they practiced accordingly," the exposition is delivered in a dispersed manner over one year or half a year. By this time, the Buddha has finished preaching the Dharma, and sentient beings have finished hearing the Dharma.

Within this, the arising and ceasing described in the *Mahāvaipulya* sūtras are excluded by way of distinction and are not taken up. When those sentient beings hear the sūtra, the entire sequence of events reaches its conclusion;

this is collectively termed "one time. The "Initiator of Transformation" (*kai-ka*) refers to the one who transforms. The "Dharma King" refers to the Buddha; when the Buddha initiates transformation, he is the Buddha who opens the way to transformation, personally opening the Dharma to teach and transform sentient beings.
This includes both his own emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and other emanation bodies. By analogy with this exclusion, the *dharmakāya* and the *svasaṃbhogakāya* are not included.
[This refers to] the body. Question: How is it known that [the Buddha] also takes up the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*)? Answer: It is stated below, "The royal city, Vulture Peak, and so forth.
This serves as proof, proving that he takes up the Enjoyment Body.

Regarding the phrase "vessels and so forth," these refer to those who are to be transformed. As for "faculties and vessels," it means that the root-natures of the assemblies of the three vehicles are all perfected;
this is termed "gathering together. The Buddha is the speaker, and the three faculties are the listeners. This describes the event of speaking and listening within a single assembly.

The general name for this is "one time. Mouzi says: the ripening of the faculties of sentient beings constitutes the "capacity to evoke," while the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma and his transformative teaching constitute the "capacity to respond.

Regarding the mention of "the two—preaching and listening"—this refers to the ripening of the faculties of the assembly such that they desire to hear the Dharma; it is the Tathāgata’s skillful means for benefiting others.

The faculties are the basis for teaching. Speaking and listening occur simultaneously, without priority or sequence; this is precisely when the faculties of the assembly have matured, and it is thus the time for the Tathāgata to preach the Dharma.

It is like a hen incubating her eggs: the pecking of the chick and the brooding of the mother occur at the same moment. If one were to preach the Dharma before the faculties have matured, [it would be ineffective].

He immediately cried out in grievance, shouting, "I have not offended you; why are you seizing me? If my faculties had already matured, the Buddha would have failed in his duty to benefit sentient beings by missing the opportune moment to preach the Dharma.
Thirty years ago, my faculties were not yet mature, and it was not the time for the Tathāgata to preach the Dharma.
Now, at the assembly on Vulture Peak, my Mahāyāna faculties have matured; this is precisely the time for the Tathāgata to preach the Dharma. Thus it is said in the Sūtra.
[The Master] said: "Because the time for speaking had not yet arrived; now is precisely that time. I shall definitively expound the Mahāyāna. [The interlocutor] asked:

"The assembly of those with the capacity [to understand] has gathered and met together. What is the distinction between these two occasions? [The Master] replied: "Regarding the first occasion, it was based on the time of speaking and listening and the purpose served therein."

The completion of an action necessarily requires many kṣaṇas; these are collectively termed "one moment" (ekakāla). Later, based on the simultaneity of the teaching and the listening, and their mutual resonance, it is designated as "one moment," which constitutes this distinction.
Regarding the phrase "the occasion, resonance, response, transformation, etc.," these two lines of the commentary explain the second meaning:

that at the moment of simultaneous encounter—like a chick pecking from within and a parent tapping from without—there is no distinction in the timing. Second, it further clarifies this by distinguishing it from the previous two meanings:

[the first] being the meaning of the Dharma King initiating transformation while the faculties and capacities gather through resonance; and [the second] being the meaning of the timing of their mutual encounter occurring through the vehicle. The upper line provides the analysis.

The first phrase refers to the primary meaning (*paramārtha*), and the subsequent phrase refers to the secondary meaning (*anvaya-artha*). This is because the Master of the Commentary (*śāstrakāra*) cites the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, stating that it is the "textual marker.

Since the second meaning previously explained the matter of the simultaneous occurrence of the faculties (*indriya*) and their objects, he has already cited the scriptural authority (*sūtra*) for that as well;

therefore, he does not provide further explanation below. The following section provides a comprehensive re-explanation of the first meaning, which consists of two parts: first, the time of logical principle (*yukti-kāla*); second, [the time of conventional designation].
At the stage of Consciousness-Only, arising and ceasing are identical. Within this, the essence and characteristics of phenomena are divided into two types;
the reason for this distinction will be explained below through a twofold interpretation of the Path.

Regarding the initial discussion of moments (*kṣaṇa*) and their characteristics: when first explaining the aforementioned meaning of "moment," it refers to the cessation of the preceding moment and the arising of the succeeding moment.
Within a single thought-instant (*ekacitta*), there are nine hundred births and cessations. Time has no separate substance; it is established in dependence upon phenomena.

In relation to the long, it is long; in relation to the short, it is short; in its intermediate state, it is neither long nor short. This is the "time" within the category of the non-concurrent (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
This is a provisional phenomenon (*prajñapti-dharma*). Provisional phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*tathatā*), because they do not arise from causes and conditions.

Rather, they are designated as "one moment" through the continuous reading of characteristics moment by moment. These three stages are provisionally established upon [the continuum]; they do not arise from seeds. (From the *Śata-dharmaka-śāstra*)
It is said: "Because of the distinctions among the three stages.
Regarding the statement that "one [time] is established by way of principle, time, and so forth," in the Mahāyāna, the past and future lack intrinsic substance (*svabhāva*).

Rather, based solely upon a single momentary phenomenon (*dharma*) in the present, the three times are provisionally established in relation to what precedes and follows it: the past is designated as "prior," and the future as "subsequent," while the present is... [the current moment].

Regarding the nature of phenomena (*dharma*), there is a response to what precedes that induces what follows; thus, the three time periods are established. If the phenomenon of the preceding moment has not ceased, the subsequent moment will not arise.
It is necessary for the phenomenon of the preceding moment to cease, thereby vacating space and providing an opening for guidance, so that the subsequent phenomenon may then arise.
Thus, the single moment of the present phenomenon is established as the inducer (*ākṣepaka*), and the future phenomenon as the induced (*ākṣipta*). Taking this inducer...
The name "future" is established based on what is to be drawn forth. Past phenomena have already ceased, and present phenomena arise as a response to past phenomena;
thus, the present phenomenon is the "respondent" (*pratidāna*) and the past phenomenon is the "responded-to.

The name "past" is established by referring to the respondent with respect to the responded-to. That is, the "past" is provisionally established based on that which is responded-to. It is precisely based on that...

By way of inference, the future is provisionally established; in contrast to that past and future, it is called the present. It is precisely upon this single momentary dharma of the present that the principle of the three times is provisionally established;
this is what is termed "time by way of principle" (*yukti-kāla*).

Regarding the phrase "the two groups of speakers and listeners," Mou says: This refers to the present phenomena of a single lifetime, and based on the principle of momentary arising and ceasing, it discusses the matters of responding to and inducing [karmic results] across the three periods of time.

Regarding the statement, "In this very present life, there is a retribution for what preceded it," Zhe says: Among the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharmas arise from preceding seeds;
thus they may be said to "recompense" the past. However, since they are indeterminate, they cannot perfume seeds. How, then, can they have the capacity to project future [results]?
For example, within the six consciousnesses, those that are weakly indeterminate by way of maturation (*vipākaja*)—such as the eighth and the first five [consciousnesses]—[cannot project].

[This view] cannot account for the projection of future [existence]; therefore, it does not fully accord with reason. If it were the case that once wholesome or unwholesome seeds have produced their manifest activities (*pravṛtti*), they could subsequently plant further seeds, this would lead to another absurdity:
even the manifest dharmas of the Tathāgata’s fruition stage would not perfume seeds, because a Buddha possesses no further perfuming.
Now, one should provide the correct explanation: the three time periods are established based upon seeds; thus, there is both the repayment of what preceded and the projection of what follows.

The meaning [of this] is that because it arises from the preceding moment, it is the repayment of the former and the production of the latter seed; thus, it is the "inducing of the latter. Mo says: "Not so.

In the *Śāstra*, it is clearly stated that the manifest phenomena (*pravṛtti-dharma*) are metaphorically designated as seeds. The explanation of 'repayment' and 'induction' refers to the analogy of a woodworm:
having been born from the wood, it returns to eat the very wood. The intent of the *Śāstra* is to speak of those five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) in their manifest momentary state."

Regarding arising and ceasing: if the preceding thought and the succeeding thought ultimately do not arise [in succession], then one speaks of the preceding thought being able to induce the succeeding thought.

Who is it that acts as the seed? Only this can be called "inducing" (ākṣepa) and "recompensing" (vipāka). This does not contradict the three meanings of the seed; thus, it establishes the main intent of the Commentary. There are four types in total.
First, because it serves as the basis for the arising and ceasing of those [phenomena]: the conditioned formations of the five aggregates arise and cease moment by moment.
Second, because it distinguishes arising and ceasing based on present phenomena: that is, this present phenomenon possesses the sense of "recompensing" what preceded and "inducing" what follows.

Third, because it distinguishes recompense and induction based on the phenomena of arising and ceasing: that which is recompensed is conventionally designated as the "past," while the future is that which is capable of recompensing.

The present is that which is being repaid; therefore, in relation to the subsequent future, it is conventionally designated as "past. Regarding the four bases for the repayment and induction of dharmas, the treatise explains the three times as follows:
that which is induced is conventionally designated as "future," while the past is the inducer and the present is the induced.
In relation to that past, it is conventionally designated as "future"; yet, within the past itself, it is further called "present."

Regarding the statement "in contrast to these two kinds," it means that [the term] "capable of repaying" (nirvartaka) is established in contrast to the past, while "capable of projecting" (ākṣepaka) is designated in contrast to the future.
These two kinds both exist only in the present; the two time periods of the past and future are both conventionally designated upon present phenomena.
In the Mahāyāna, all things of the past are merely conventional designations.
Regarding the statement "all phenomena of the five aggregates": now, both speaker and listener are addressed. From a general perspective, there are five aggregates;
yet at this very single moment of the present, that which has already fallen away belongs to the past.

Regarding the statement "not [referring to] a single arising and ceasing, etc.": Question: When the sutra says "at one time," does it not simply take this moment of arising and ceasing within the three periods of time?
Answer: It does not. If one were to rely on a single assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, there are sixty-five kṣaṇas in the duration of a finger-snap.

Within a single kṣaṇa, there are nine hundred cycles of arising and ceasing. The "time" mentioned in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* does not take these [subtle moments], but takes only the [conventional] event.
The entirety of the sequence, from beginning to end, is collectively termed "one moment"; it does not refer to the single moment of arising and ceasing.

As for the statement that "the two are the time of consciousness-only," this merely excludes external objects to distinguish [this system] from the Hinayana; "consciousness" indicates the internal mind.
The Bodhisattva Prabhākaramitra refutes the internal referent (*antar-artha*), asserting that there is no such thing.

He maintains that although past, future, and present, as well as long and short durations, differ in terms of activity and understanding, in the Mahāyāna, the past has already ceased and thus lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); the future has not yet arisen and is likewise without intrinsic nature.
It is only upon phenomena that possess substantiality in the present that past, future, and present appearances arise through transformation.

Upon hearing the names of the Buddhas Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū and Candrasūryapradīpa at the assembly on Vulture Peak, one immediately produces a conceptualization of a long duration in the past within the consciousness.
Likewise, if it is said that the Greatly Wise Śāriputra shall become a Buddha in the future, named Puṣpārāma, [one likewise produces a conceptualization of the future].

One then forms a conception of "long duration" regarding the future. If one hears that a dragon girl has attained Buddhahood, one then forms a conception of "short duration" regarding the present form and mind.
These conceptions of long and short duration—whether past, future, or present—are all provisionally established upon a single momentary instance of present form and mind.
When considering the time of principle (*tattva*) and the time of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), both are of the same nature as the present.

Regarding the three periods established by Dharmottara, what is their distinction? The answer is: the period of *yukti* (reasoning) is spoken of in terms of the fundamental essence (*svabhāva*) of the dharma-body;

the period of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only) is spoken of in terms of the manifestation of the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*). Question: Is it not the case that the long and short durations manifested upon the consciousness itself are precisely what is meant by "at one time" at the beginning of the sūtras?
Answer: No, that is not accepted. When the sūtras say, "Thus have I heard at one time," [it does not refer to the duration of the manifestation].
Taking that conscious mind, one gathers together infinite long and short durations of time spent hearing the sutras until the task is fully completed;
this is collectively termed "one period."
The statement, "like what is seen in a dream, one says it exists," etc., is an illustration used to establish the point. As the *Tattvārthā-śāstra* (Wúxìng Shèlùn) states:
"In a dream one may think many years have passed, yet upon waking it is but a brief moment; thus, although time is immeasurable, it is subsumed within a single kṣaṇa.
Furthermore, the *Record of the Western Regions* (*Xīyùjì*) states: "Traveling five or six li east from the Deer Park (*Mṛgadāva*), there is a stūpa. Beside it is a dried-up pond."

It measures over eighty paces in circumference. According to the records of former scholars, several hundred years ago, there was a recluse who built a hut by the side of this pond and lived there in seclusion.
He was extensively learned in the arts and sciences and had reached the ultimate depths of spiritual principles; he was even able to transform tiles and rubble into precious gems.

Humans and animals may exchange their forms, yet they have not yet been able to ride upon the wind and clouds to accompany the celestial chariots. Examining diagrams and ancient records, one seeks further the arts of the immortals.
The method for this is as follows: The state of being an immortal is the art of longevity. If one wishes to study it, one must first establish one's resolve.
When constructing the altar for the ritual, one must command a valiant hero to stand at a corner of the altar holding a long sword, remaining silent and breathless from dusk until dawn.
The seeker of the immortal shall sit within the altar, hand upon the long sword, reciting the divine mantra while withdrawing the senses and turning inward to listen;
thus, by daybreak, one ascends to immortality. Having obtained this method of attaining the immortal, the person then sought out a valiant hero to assist in the endeavor.
For many years, he had not been able to fulfill his heart’s wish. Later, he obtained a man of heroic spirit who had previously worked as a hired laborer for others for four or five years of hardship.
One day, having lost his way from his master, he was subsequently beaten and humiliated, receiving nothing in return. Weeping bitterly, he wandered along the road.
A hermit saw him and repeatedly bestowed generous gifts upon him, secretly practicing virtuous deeds that moved the hero's heart. The hero then repeatedly sought to offer his services.

He issued the command. To repay his kindness, the hermit said, "I have awaited your arrival for many years; it is fortunate that we have finally met, as your extraordinary appearance accords with the ancient charts.
There is no other reason for my request than this: I wish only for one night of silence. The knight replied, "I would not even decline death itself, so how could I fail to comply with your request?
Thereupon, he received the methods of the immortals at the ritual altar and performed the rites according to the prescribed rules. At the onset of dusk—
Later, while waiting for a lapse in the people's activities, the hermit recited incantations and the knight pressed his sharp blade against him.
As dawn was about to break, a voice suddenly broke out with a loud cry of "Kū! Kū! At that moment, fire, smoke, and clouds rushed forth from the sky.
The hermit quickly led this man into a pond to take refuge. Afterward, he asked him: "I warned you not to make a sound; why did you cry out so alarmingly? The knight replied: "I received..."
After his life had ended, when the night was deep, he fell into a state of dazed confusion as if in a dream. He saw his former master coming personally to his side;
moved by the depth of that kindness, he could not bear to speak with him. The man became enraged and subsequently killed him. He then underwent another intermediate state existence (*antarābhava*).
He was then reborn into the family of a great Brahmin in South India. From his conception until birth, he underwent all manner of hardships and calamities;

yet, out of gratitude for their kindness, he endured them in silence. As he grew up, pursued his studies, was married, sought a bride, and fathered children, he constantly recalled his former debt of gratitude and remained silent.
His entire family and relatives all regarded him with wonder and suspicion. When he reached the age of sixty...
He had an only son. His wife said to him, "You must speak! If you do not speak, I shall kill your son.
At that time, I recalled that many lifetimes had already passed; looking upon my own old age and this lone infant, how could I bear to slaughter him?
Therefore, I restrained my wife and resolved not to cause such harm, and it was for this reason that I uttered those words. The hermit said, "This was my fault."
"This is merely the harassment of Māra. As a man of integrity, I am grateful for his kindness, yet my purpose shall not be thwarted.
In a fit of indignation, he declared: "Both dreams and waking states—ten thousand objects are all the mind. Thus, by citing the time of dreaming, one clarifies the state of awakening.

It is like two people in prison: one whose release is set for the next day finds the night long; the other, who is to die and undergo punishment the next day, likewise finds the night short. Therefore, we know that time [is relative]."
There is no distinction between them; it is merely the consciousness-mind itself that transforms and manifests as long and short.
Regarding the statement that "the listener’s mind transforms [the sound] and so forth," Wu said: "In a dreamer's vision, many things appear to arise, but in reality, there is only the mind."

There are no objects produced by many births; it is the listener who transforms the three periods of time. In reality, there is only mind; in reality, there are no objects of the three periods of time. Question:
Since both the speaker and the listener are transformations of the mind, why is it said that only the listener [transforms]? Answer: Master Lu says:

Because the speaker has realized that objects do not exist, the commentary does not state that the speaker is like a dream. Question: What is the difference between this principle and the doctrine of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only)?

Answer: From the perspective of the principle regarding the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), it is thus unalterable; for example, the distinctions between spring, autumn, winter, and summer, or cold and warmth.
Consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) merely follows its own mind, transforming into long or short [durations], and forming the past and future.

If one is a listener who thirsts for and yearns after the Dharma, they will not perceive the cold or warmth while listening and receiving instruction in a single sitting. As the saying goes: "The man of resolve regrets the brevity of the day; the sorrowful person knows the length of the night."

Regarding the statement "it is perceived solely by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)," this refers to the period [of perception] during the analysis of the dissociated factors (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*). However, these five [faculties] and the eighth [consciousness] are exclusively direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);

they perceive the real and do not perceive the conventional (*prajñapti*). The second type of person directs their attention inwardly because they take the eighth [consciousness] as their object. Now, when we speak of "time," it is as follows:

It is perceived solely by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and does not extend to other forms of consciousness. Among the one hundred dharmas, it is subsumed under the category of non-associated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*).

Within the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), it is included in the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*). Among the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*), it is subsumed within the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). Among the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), it is included within the base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
If one considers the factors subsumed under the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) and the constituent of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), there are eighty-one factors:

namely, fifty-one mental concomitants (*caitta*), twenty-four dissociated factors (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), and six unconditioned factors (*asaṃskṛta*). Thus, there are eighty-one factors in total. The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) comprises seventy-three of these factors.
Time is one among the eighty-one dharmas; therefore, it is perceived solely by the mind (*manas*). This is because the mind is universally capable of perceiving those eighteen realms (*dhātu*).
Question: Among the three types of objects, under which category is time subsumed when the mind perceives it? Answer:

If the mind perceives time alone without also perceiving the objective image (*nimitta-bhāga*)—which is a transformation of the real dharma that serves as its basis—then it is an object consisting of a solitary reflection (*kevala-pratibimba*) that is of the same nature as the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*).

[Included in] the "Shou" [category]. If it also includes actual conditions (*vastu-pratyaya*), the aspect (*nimitta*) follows its basis; thus, if the aspect and the substance (*dravya*) are of the same kind, it is subsumed under the "aspect-with-substance" (*sābhāsa-vastu*) object.
The *Shuyao* states: "The objective realm of nature (*svabhāva-viṣaya*) does not follow the mind; the 'solitary shadow' (*kevala-chāyā*) follows only the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*);

the 'aspect-with-substance' is common to both the mental and the objective; the fundamental nature, seeds (*bīja*), etc., follow as appropriate. Master Xiangguo stated: "In total, there are three kinds that encompass all objects: first, the objective realm of nature (*svabhāva-viṣaya*), which consists of all real..."

The objective realm of phenomena (*dharmālambana*) is termed the "objective sphere" (*svabhāvaviṣaya*). Matter is actual matter; mind is actual mind. Because these objects each possess their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), there are three aspects that do not conform to the mind.

First, non-conformity of nature (*svabhāva-ananuvartana*): as with the five real sense-objects (*pañca viṣayāḥ*), they possess only the nature of arising (*utpatti-svabhāva*) and do not conform to the five consciousnesses (*pañca vijñānāni*) which serve as their cognitive supports (*ālambaka*), for those [consciousnesses] can be of all three moral natures (*tri-prakāra*).
Second, non-conformity of realm-bondage (*dhātu-bandhana-ananuvartana*): as with the eighth consciousness (*aṣṭama-vijñāna*), it is of one [nature].

Regarding the bondage by realm (*dhātu-bandhana*): the seeds of the objects of perception (*ālambana*) pertain to all three realms. Alternatively, when the body is in a higher stage, the visual and auditory consciousnesses may take objects of the desire realm;

in this case, the consciousness is bound to the higher stage while the object is bound to the lower stage. From the second dhyāna upward, the visual, auditory, and tactile consciousnesses take objects of their own stage;

here, the consciousness is bound to the first dhyāna while the object is bound to its own stage. In these two cases, the seeds do not follow [the status of the consciousness or the object], because they are seeds of the perceived characteristics (*nimitta*).

First, because their respective substances are distinct. Second, the "solitary-reflection" object (*ekacchāyā-viṣaya*). This refers to objects that arise solely from seeds of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and whose nature and category of bondage (*dhātu-bandhana*) are necessarily identical.
For example, when the sixth consciousness perceives empty flowers (*ākāśa-puṣpa*) and the like, these are all merely following the mind; they have no separate substance or function.
Because they are subsumed under that [mental] object, they are called "solitary-reflection objects. That is to say, there is only the solitary reflection, while its original [substance] is absent.
Substance. Third, the realm of the "substantiated" (*pratibimba*). This means that this reflected image possesses a real substance, just as a primary object (*mūla-bimba*) serves as a cause.

Regarding the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) transformed by the seventh consciousness: insofar as it proceeds from the primary object, it is non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*); yet, insofar as it proceeds from the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*), it is subsumed under the obscured [indeterminate].
It may also be said to arise from the seeds of the primary object, and it may also be said to arise from the seeds of the subjective aspect; the meaning is not [contradictory].

The term "determined" refers to the categories [of objects] such as seeds and so forth. The phrase "according to circumstances" implies that the cause is not fixed; this meaning reveals three types of objects.

These arise in dependence upon a collection of mental states (*citta-saṃghāta*), wherein there may be only one object, or two, or three, as they are not fixed. Regarding those that are singular, this has already been explained previously.

Regarding those that are dual, it is like the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) taking both self and other as its dispersed objects; here, the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) takes a "nature-object" (*xing-jing*) as its perceived object.

Because they possess practical utility. If the five categories of mental factors (caitta) are included within the category of "images-only" (pratibimba-ālambana), it is because, like seeds, they do not produce manifest results.

Furthermore, when the five consciousnesses (pañca-vijñāna) take the five objects of their own level as their domain, these are "original-nature objects" (mūla-svabhāva-ālambana); yet they may also be called "objects with substance" (sadravya-ālambana), because they perceive by means of transformed images.
Moreover, when the sixth consciousness takes the five aggregates (skandha) of the past or future as its object, these are "images-only objects," and they may likewise be so designated.
This is called the "object with substance" (*sadravya-viṣaya*), because it perfumes seeds that give rise to the primary object (*mūla-dravya*). There are three types of objects that arise together:

for example, when the eighth consciousness within the causal state (*hetu-bhūmi*) takes conditioned fruit-form (*niṣyanda-rūpa*) as its object; mental states and their concomitants take "solely projected images" (*pratibimba-mātra*) as their objects; and the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) takes "objects with substance" (*dravya-viṣaya*) as its objects.

Because it is real, it may also be called an "object possessing a substantial basis" (*saviṣaya*), since the color-form that is the result of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*) transformed by the sixth consciousness serves as its substantial basis.

Question: Since dimensions such as length are subsumed under the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*), and time is established based on the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), why is time not also subsumed under the real dharmas (*dravyadharma*) of the five aggregates?

Answer: Length depends upon real color-form; therefore, as a provisional construct following its basis, it is subsumed under the sense-base of form. Time, however, is established based upon a plurality of phenomena (*dharmas*). Thus, while length is a provisional designation applied to a single real entity (color-form), time is a designation applied to a collection of many factors. Therefore, they differ in their mode of establishment.

Because they are provisional, they cannot [be classified as real entities]. However, since the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are comprised of real dharmas, these [factors] are therefore subsumed within the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*).
They are: 1. acquisition (*prāpti*); 2. the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*); 3. the homogeneous character of the group (*nikāya-sabhāgatā*); 4. the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*); 5.

the attainment of non-ideation (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*); 6. the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*); 7. non-informative matter (*avijñapti*); 8. names (*nāman*); 9. phrases (*pada*); 10. syllables (*vyañjana*); 11. birth (*jāti*); 12. aging (*jarā*); 13. duration (*sthiti*); 14. impermanence (*anityatā*).
15. Constant succession; 16. Specific difference; 17. Correspondence of perception; 18. Velocity; 19. Sequence;
20. Time; 21. Space; 22. Number; 23. The nature of combination; 24.
The nature of non-combination.
Regarding the statement "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*) and so forth: this refers to the initial specific [objection] among the general refutations. The question asks:

when it says "at one time," does "one" refer to (1) a single *kṣaṇa* being called "one time"? Or (2) a continuous succession being called "one time"? Or (3) the four seasons—spring, summer, autumn, and winter—being called "one time"?
Or (4) practicing the path during the six periods of the day being called "one time"? Or (5) the hours of the tiger (*yīn*) and the hare (*mǎo*)...?

The twelve periods [of time] are collectively called "one period. Regarding the four [periods], is it not the case that they are designated as "one period" based on the seven months or one year and six months following his attainment of enlightenment?
The Commentary answers: This term "one period" is not fixed; it may refer to a single *kṣaṇa* (instant) and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "merely those who listen," etc.: Question: At what time is this taken? Answer: The commentary states, "merely those who listen," etc.
Regarding the statement that it is not restricted to a single *kṣaṇa* (moment), etc.: Within a single utterance, the Tathāgata expounds an ocean of boundless sūtras.
At the time of this exposition, the time spent by sentient beings listening is many *kṣaṇas*; it takes immeasurable *kṣaṇas* [to complete].
This is the explanation. Some say that when the teaching is long, the hearing is superior, and the superiority of the hearing is also long;

this refers to those among the three grades of *śrāvakas* with inferior faculties (*mṛdv-indriya*), numbering five hundred thousand and two hundred. Furthermore, the Tathāgata preached three times for those of inferior faculties, and only at the third repetition did they understand.
This means both the time of the explanation and the time of listening were long, as in the saying: "A yellow silk scarf, a young woman, an external grandson, and pickled vegetables."

Jiù. This was the servant girl of Cao É who reported it above. When Cáo Cão opened the script and read the explanation, there were two instances where he understood it immediately and one instance where he only realized its meaning after traveling thirty li.
Regarding the statement that "speech is also not fixed with respect to the continuum (*saṃtāna*) and so forth": "continuum" means the body. It refers to the persons who speak and listen;
from beginningless time, they have possessed this body in a continuous succession. Question: Is it not the case that speech is spoken in reference to the body within the continuum?
Answer: Within a single sound of the Buddha, all sounds are manifested; within a single moment, all syllables are manifested. This is in terms of their arising. If...
Regarding the listener: this bodhisattva has attained dhāraṇī, or possesses the mutual functioning of the sense faculties. When hearing a single syllable, they penetrate immeasurable syllables.
Alternatively, for those of dull faculties, they prolong a brief moment of thought into many kalpas, so that understanding occurs only after many kalpas;

for those of sharp faculties, they condense many kalpas into a brief moment of thought, so that understanding occurs within that brief moment. Therefore, one cannot define [the duration] based on a continuous body.
