The six periods for performing prostrations and repentance (*li-chàn*) are: the early morning (*yín-zhāo*), noon (*wǔ-shí*), dusk (*huáng-hūn*), the first watch of the night (*chū-yè*), the middle watch (*zhōng-yè*), and the last watch (*hòu-yè*).

As for the eight periods, these refer to the times of the eight case-inflections (*bā-zhuǎn-shēng*): namely, the agent (*tǐ*), the object (*yè*), the instrument (*jù*), as well as the ablative (*shuō*), the dative (*shǔ*), the locative (*yī*), and the vocative (*hū*).
The twelve periods are: dawn at *yín*, sunrise at *mǎo*, the time for eating at *chén*, and so forth.
Regarding the statement, "The sun and moon shine for one day," etc.: Question: Why are the various times mentioned previously not taken up? Answer:
The commentary states, "The sun and moon shine for four [periods] during one day. He (賀) says: In this region (Jambudvīpa), when the sun moves northward, the days lengthen;

in Uttarakuru, when the sun moves northward, the days shorten. Conversely, in Uttarakuru, when the sun moves southward, the days lengthen; in Jambudvīpa, when the sun moves southward, the days shorten. Question: Why is this so?
It is thus. The answer is that when the sun approaches the mountains from both the southern and northern continents, its path across the front of the mountains is long;

when it moves far from the mountains, the path is short. Therefore, on the southern continent the days are long and the nights are short, while on the northern continent the days are short and the nights are long.
If one understands the course of the sun’s movement according to this principle, there are both southern and northern paths. This...
The world narrows toward the south and widens toward the north; thus, the treatise states: "Jambudvīpa in the south is like a chariot.
In the summer months, as the sun travels along the northern path, the days are long; in the winter months, as it travels along the southern narrow path, the days are short.

Regarding the instability of heat and cold: when the sun in Jambudvīpa moves toward the southern path, its light strikes the waters of the southern ocean, and the resulting vapors [cause the climate to change].
It becomes cold. When the sun in the northern continent (Uttarakuru) travels southward, it illuminates the Seven Golden Mountains (Saptakāñcanaparvata), which then become hot.
When the sun in the southern continent (Jambudvīpa) travels northward on its path, it illuminates the Seven Golden Mountains, and the heat from the gold causes them to become hot.

When the sun in the northern continent travels northward, it illuminates the vapors of the northern ocean waters, which then become cold. Regarding the uncertainty of near and far: when the sun in the southern continent travels southward, it moves away from the mountains.

When the sun moves southward from the northern continent (Uttarakuru), it is close to the southern continent (Jambudvīpa). When the sun moves northward toward the southern continent, it is close [to the northern continent];

when the sun moves northward from the northern continent, it is distant. Regarding the variability of day and night: when it is midday in the southern continent, it is midnight in the northern continent;
when it is sunset in the eastern continent (Pūrvavideha), it is sunrise in the western continent (Aparagodānīya). These various directions refer to the four continents under heaven.

Regarding the statement "the two continents of Jambudvīpa and Aparagoyānī are simultaneous," when it is midday in Jambudvīpa (the southern continent), it is sunrise in Aparagoyānī (the western continent);

these two continents function simultaneously. When it is midnight in Uttarakuru (the northern continent), it is sunset in Pūrvavideha (the eastern continent); these two continents likewise function simultaneously.
Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "The sun and moon are at the midpoint of Mount Meru; Fifty-one [yojanas] and fifty [yojanas] [respectively]. At midnight, sunset, midday, and sunrise..."

Regarding the four continents and so forth, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the sun is composed of fire-crystal (*sūryakānta-sphaṭika*) and the moon is composed of water-crystal (*candrakānta-sphaṭika*).
As for the phrase "furthermore, excluding... and below, the term "below" refers to the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājika-deva*), which is the region illuminated by the sun and moon.
Consequently, there would be occurrences such as long and short days, heat and cold, and so forth; it would then be identical to the four continents.
As for the statement regarding the various heavens above, it means that where the sun and moon do not reach with their light, there are no seasonal changes of heat and cold.

Regarding the statement that the sutra is modeled after the Vaipulya [Mahāyāna] scriptures, one asks: why is it necessary to state that the various heavens above lack the four seasons and the eight periods?
Yes. The commentary states: "The Sūtra refers to the higher realms, etc. If one says that the four seasons do not circulate universally, it is because the various heavens above lack the four seasons;
however, with the exception of Uttarakuru, they circulate throughout the other three continents. Question:

Just as this continent’s place where the sun rises is the east, I wonder whether the directions of the four continents are the same. Answer: On the other continents, the place where the sun rises is not [necessarily] the east.
Question: Since the Dharma is not practiced in the other three continents, why is it said that [this teaching] circulates in all directions?
Answer: Because this sutra is also transmitted in both the eastern and western continents.

Regarding the statement that the "sitting" [under the Bodhi tree] is also not fixed in relation to the attainment of enlightenment and so forth: when it is said, "Thus have I heard," at the time of the attainment of enlightenment, one does not yet obtain the Buddha-body.

Within a single assembly, there are differences in what is perceived regarding the universal manifestation and transformation; furthermore, there are differences in perceiving the Buddha of retribution (*vipākabuddha*) and the distance of his attainment of enlightenment, as in the passage beginning, "Since I attained Buddhahood.

For ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), the perception of the Buddha of transformation (*nirmāṇabuddha*) attaining enlightenment appears proximate, as in the passage beginning, "He emerged from the Śākya clan."
The palace of the [former] clan was not far from the city of Gaya.

Regarding the statement that the sūtras are modeled after the three vehicles and so forth: it is asked, why are long and short durations not established in accordance with what is perceived by those being transformed?

The answer in the commentary states: "The sūtra is intended for the three vehicles, etc. If considered according to the chronological periods, it applies only to ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles, and does not extend to great bodhisattvas;
it merely establishes a single period in general.
Regarding the statement that some sūtras speak of "continuity" (*saṃtāna*) and so forth:
it is asked, why does this sūtra not state at its beginning, "Thus have I heard, during sixty minor kalpas"? The answer is: for the indolent, it truly lasts for sixty minor kalpas;
for the diligent, it is said to be like the time it takes to eat a meal. Therefore, one knows that this is not based on a continuous duration of time.

Regarding the statement that there are teachings concerning the four seasons and so forth: according to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it is at the end of the fifteenth day of the second month; however, this is also not fixed. In the heavens above, there is no exhaustion.

Among humans, across the four continents, the exhaustion [of the kalpa] is also indeterminate. On the Southern Continent (Jambudvīpa), it is summer; on the Western Continent (Aparagoyānī), it is autumn;

on the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru), it is winter; and on the Eastern Continent (Pūrvavideha), it is spring. These cycles revolve indeterminately. Even speaking only of this [Southern] region, it is not fixed.
It is not fixed. For instance, prior to the Zhou dynasty, the eleventh month was regarded as the first month of the year; now, the twelfth month is regarded as the first.

This corresponds to what was the second month in those former times; thus, we know it is not fixed. If one speaks of the time for chewing the *yángzhī* (willow twig), that refers to the hour of Yín (the third watch).

The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "When the meal was finished and the feet had been washed, he spread out his seat and sat down. This refers to the time when the sun is at its zenith, which concludes the first twelve hours of the day.
Regarding the phrase "The *Ūrdhva-janma-sūtra* says, etc.," these are all included within the first six periods.
Regarding the phrase "Some say that after attaining enlightenment, etc.," the question is: [Is it] said that [the teaching] exists within twelve years, or after twelve years?
Regarding the teaching of the three periods, such as emptiness and so forth, the middle period is said to teach that which is neither empty nor existent.
If one takes the second week after his attainment of enlightenment as the time when he taught the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, then the third period teaching is not fixed.
Regarding the phrase "although there is this teaching," Jin says: This refers to the teachings of four periods, eight periods, or six periods, which follow the inhabitants of a particular region.
The teachings of two weeks or forty years follow the sentient beings of the transformed land (*nirmāṇakāya-kṣetra*). These are spoken thus because direct perceptions differ;
they are merely provisional explanations.
Regarding the statement, "It is still not the initial 'total' [time]," this merely refers to the time mentioned within the sutra, rather than the "one time" at the very beginning of the sutra.

Regarding the statement, "In the place of questioning, there is purity, etc.," it says: To pose a question. The intent of the question is as follows: The Buddha resides on Vulture Peak, which is a defiled place;
the emanation-buddhas arrive and transform the defilement into purity. Since the places of purity and defilement are fixed, why is the time not fixed? Why not...?
The intention of this question is to explain that long and short durations are spoken of in accordance with ordinary beings and sages.
Regarding the statement that the "place of the answer" indicates [the location] and so forth: if it is pure, it is truly pure; if it is defiled, it is truly defiled.
Purity and defilement are definitive: what is not defiled is pure, and what is not pure is defiled. Apart from these, there is no other distinct location. Therefore...
Regarding the determination of purity and defilement, there are three temporal periods. First, the distinction between sharp and dull faculties:
for those of sharp faculties, understanding occurs immediately upon hearing, and thus the duration is brief; for those of dull faculties, realization is slow, and thus the duration is long.
Second, the distinction between the noble and the ordinary: for the noble ones, the duration is long; for ordinary persons, the duration is brief. Third, the distinction in intentionality (*āśaya*).
There may be cases where the duration of pleasure is brief; in such instances, what is long is shortened. There may be cases where the duration of pleasure is long;
in such instances, what is brief is extended. Because the duration is not fixed, it is not explained separately; "time" is mentioned only in general terms.
Regarding the third point, concerning the teacher who expounded the scripture: the sutra says "Buddha. Now, it is asked whether the term "sutra" applies to the teachings of five types of speakers:
first, the Buddha; second, his disciples; third, devas; fourth, ṛṣis; and fifth, those manifested through transformation. It is not yet clear who spoke this particular sutra.
The answer is that it is indicated to be none other than [the Buddha], for the sutra says "Buddha."

Regarding the term "Buddha" (梵云 *buddha*): it should be spoken in its full form as "Buddha. Within the Sanskrit language, because the meaning arises from the production of goodness (*kuśala*), it is abbreviated as "Fo" (佛).
This is an abbreviation within the Sanskrit language itself; it is not an abbreviation made in the Tang [Chinese] language. When it comes to the commentary (*śāstra*), [it is explained as follows].
This is based on a complete understanding of the Sanskrit language. Furthermore, the ancient translations state: "Buddha" means "Lord of Wisdom.
This has two meanings. First, Bodhisattvas of the ten stages are called "possessors of wisdom," and since the Buddha is the sovereign among those who possess wisdom, he is named the "Lord of Wisdom.
Second, the four wisdoms within this very body of the Buddha are themselves called "wisdom."

The Buddha. The "Lord" (prabhu) is the designation for the body of the conventional person (pudgala) consisting of the five untainted aggregates (anāsrava-skandha). This is the Lord of Evil. In ancient translations, this was called the "Lord of Wisdom" (jñāna-prabhu);

although the meaning is the same, it is not as precise as saying "the Awakened One" (buddha). In the new translation, it is rendered as "the Awakened One. Wisdom is itself awakening; "Lord" refers to the "one who possesses.
Thus, it is one who possesses awakening, and is therefore called "the Awakened One. This "one" is the conventional person consisting of the five aggregates; it is the body of the conventional person.

Because there is wisdom within it, it is called "the Awakened One" (*buddha*). Question: Since all sentient beings collectively possess the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), one should logically refer to them as "beings.

Why then do you speak of "emptiness"? Answer: By speaking of emptiness, one attains that which cannot be described as "beings. As for ordinary people (*pṛthagjana*), they should be said to be "non-existent.

Question: What is the meaning of "awakening" (*bodhi*)? Answer: Awakening means to discern and examine. It is to discern and examine afflictions (*kleśa*) and delusive thoughts (*vikalpa*), just as a person fears the entry of a thief.
Come. First, you must observe: ordinary beings possess one hundred and twenty-eight afflictions that enter the house of the five aggregates and descend into ignorance.
Throughout the long night of birth and death, they remain unaware and unknowing. Second, there is awakening and knowledge: within the body there are two kinds of Buddha-nature.
If one wishes to attain Buddhahood, it is necessary to awaken to and know this nature. [Question: What is the difference between wisdom and...

What is the distinction between wisdom (*jñāna*) and insight (*prajñā*)? The answer is: if it refers to the awakening that realizes the unconditioned principle (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), it is called insight; if it refers to the severing of conditioned afflictions (*saṃskṛta-kleśa*), it is called wisdom.
As for the statement "one awakens by oneself," it means awakening to the fact that within one's own continuum there exist these two distinct natures: *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*.
Generally, those who do not possess self-awareness are called "unenlightened," whereas the Buddha is "self-awakened. By being able to sever the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), one attains Buddhahood.

Ordinary beings do not fear the bitter fruits they will undergo in future lives; thus they act with negligence in this life. Such negligence leads to birth and death, and various transgressions that are difficult to enumerate exhaustively—this is termed "lack of self-awareness.
The Buddha, however, is fully self-aware of each and every thing, having realized the wisdom of unconditioned *tathatā* (suchness), wherein not a single thing exists.
Yet they do not know this.
Regarding the statement "the two types of awakening others," it means causing others to realize that within their own bodies there exists this nature of *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*. Question:

The followers of the Two Vehicles realize the emptiness of sentient beings (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and know that birth and death are illusory; they personally realize the emptiness of self (*ātma-śūnyatā*) within their own bodies and do not create [further karma]. Why is this?

[Objection: One who possesses such karma should be called a Buddha. [Response: This is not so. Although one has attained self-awakening, if one awakens only to one’s own single body and does not awaken to and examine all sentient beings, one cannot be called a Buddha.
A Buddha is one who has awakened to himself and furthermore examines all sentient beings, causing them all to sever delusions and realize the Truth;
therefore, he is called a Buddha. The followers of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas) remain stalled in *nirvāṇa* precisely because they do not awaken others.

Regarding the phrase "the perfection of the three types of awakening and practice," it means that the two types of awakening of a bodhisattva are not yet fulfilled, as they remain partially obstructed by both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
Question: What is meant by the two types of awakening being unfulfilled? Answer: First, self-benefit is unfulfilled.

Fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) realizes the principle and eliminates delusions, while subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) manifests images to take the *tathatā* (suchness) as its object. Because fundamental wisdom’s realization of the principle is not yet complete, the obstructions have not been entirely eliminated. In total...

This is called the non-fulfillment of self-benefit. Question: What is meant by the non-fulfillment of benefiting others? Answer: The subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) that takes phenomena as its object is called benefiting others.

A Bodhisattva on the first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*) transforms sentient beings within three thousandfold world systems; beyond this, they are unable to transform them. Therefore, it is said to be unfulfilled.
In the Tathāgata, both awakening and practice are perfected; his awakening and practice consist of the conduct performed throughout the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
It is full. If explained in terms of complete fulfillment, awakening (*bodhi*) is also full, and practice (*caryā*) is also full.
Regarding the statement in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* that "it possesses all [dharmas]," one asks: what is meant by "all"? The answer is:

"All" refers to all phenomena (*sarvadharma*), because they include the mundane and supramundane, the contaminated and uncontaminated, and the sentient and non-sentient; thus they are called "all dharmas. True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the principle.
One Dharma. This One Dharma pervades all phenomena, both conditioned and unconditioned;
there is nothing whatsoever that does not rely upon *tathatā* (suchness). This *tathatā* alone acts as the agent and the object for all phenomena.
When *tathatā* receives all names, it causes those other names to be taken as its own possessives (*sadhana*). If this is so, then the Truth is named "All. This is Fundamental Wisdom.
It realizes all principles. Because the wisdom that can realize them arises from these principles, it is named "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñā*). Second, the name is established according to its function:
"all" refers to the afflictions; because this wisdom eradicates all these afflictions, it is named "all-knowledge. This refers to the elimination of the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Regarding the term "omniscience" (*sarvākārajñatā*): all categories of both form and mind are called "all aspects.

Subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) knows these all categories both collectively and individually—namely, ultimate truth and conventional truth, the contaminated and the uncontaminated, the conditioned and the unconditioned, sentient beings and non-sentient things, as well as the various kinds of minds of such living beings. Thus, subsequently attained wisdom knows them all.

Explanation: It is called "knowledge of all modes" (*sarvākārajñatā*) because it exhausts all categories [of phenomena] and is named after its object; it refers to the severance of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "capable of awakening oneself," this refers to the wisdom of self-benefit. "Awakening" (*kai*) carries the meaning of giving birth to, manifesting, and realizing.

Arising from one's own fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*), it exhausts afflictions and deluded conceptualizations, and realizes the principle of one's own *tathatā* (suchness); thus, it is termed the "wisdom of self-awakening."

To say that one is "able to awaken all" refers to both self-benefit and the benefit of others. Having completed the three great eons and following the vajra-mind (*vajracitta*), one realizes primordial wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) within the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Being fully endowed with the three bodies (*trikāya*) and possessing the four wisdoms (*caturjñāna*) in their perfect clarity, this is called being able to awaken oneself.

Subsequently, arising from the subsequently-attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), one gives rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) to benefit sentient beings; this is likewise called being able to awaken others.

The Tathāgata is able to know all sentient beings, whether their minds or their objects. Now, as sentient beings sever evil and cultivate goodness, they give rise to wisdom and sever afflictions, thereby being able to awaken all other sentient beings.

If the followers of the Two Vehicles possess only fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and lack subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), they possess only the bodies of sheep and deer, but lack the chariot (the preceding four points constitute the explanation of the Dharma).
The phrase "like awakening from a dream" is a metaphor for understanding; it refers to the wisdom of self-benefit (*svārtha-jñāna*).

Just as when one is dreaming while asleep and knows [the dream] upon waking, yet others do not know it, so too the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) realizes the principle (*tattva*); it is known only by itself and does not extend to being known by others. Question:

Is the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), which takes the transformation of images as its object, not a form of knowing? Answer: It is precisely this transformation of images that constitutes it.
"It is not known. Because it cannot be directly perceived by others. To further explain: this [passage] simply means that one knows for oneself, while others do not know;

this interpretation is excellent. If one says that after waking from sleep, one subsequently observes the events of the dream, and that this subsequent observation refers to the transformation toward the Dharma, then this would indeed be the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). However, at the very moment the sleeping person is actually asleep, they do not know that [the dream] is occurring.
A dream: only upon waking does one look back and realize it was a dream; this is like the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

Now, we consider the ordinary person prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), whose afflictions are not yet severed and whose sleep has not yet awakened; they have not attained true awakening and remain constantly within a dream.

Within the gateway of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), one realizes the two wisdoms of wondrous [equality] and [subsequently attained] equality; this is also called "awakening from a dream. This is termed partial awakening (*vibuddha*) at the level of Buddhahood, which brings about the wisdom of awakening.

As for the statement "like the blooming of a lotus flower" and so forth, this refers to the wisdom that benefits others. When one subsequently attains superior benefit and answers the merits of sentient beings, it is called the "blooming of the lotus.
If the lotus does not bloom, that is all; but once it blooms, those who see it perceive its fragrance. Thus it is known by the Buddha.
If one encounters [this teaching], that is sufficient; upon encountering it, sentient beings will receive benefit. It is further said: "If the lotus flower opens, its stamen must be seen;

when the subsequent wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) preaches the Dharma, one will certainly be able to realize the principle. Therefore, it is named "Buddha" (the Awakened). [The section on] "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*) and so forth concludes the treatise.

Because the preceding exposition by the master of the treatise did not fully exhaust the subject of knowledge, the commentator (*śāstrakāra*), relying on his commentary, reclassifies it. (Note: The above text concludes the first part based on the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* and its commentaries, clarifying the six types of wisdom.)

In both the fundamental and subsequent [wisdoms], there are six types of wisdom. Regarding what is called "the wisdom that contemplates emptiness," there are two meanings: first, the principle of *tathatā* (suchness) is the nature of true emptiness;

knowing and realizing this principle is termed the wisdom that contemplates emptiness. Second, upon the ultimate truth, the absence of the two attachments to self and phenomena is termed the wisdom of emptiness;
realizing this principle is termed the wisdom of emptiness. This is contrasted with subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
This exists; it is the establishment of the name "wisdom of emptiness.
Regarding the term "wisdom of principle" (*li-zhi*): this name is established in contrast to the subsequently attained wisdom that takes phenomena as its object.

Regarding the term "true wisdom" (*zhen-zhi*): this wisdom realizes *tathatā* (suchness); the name "true wisdom" is established in contrast to the subsequently attained wisdom that perceives delusion.
Regarding the term "non-conceptual wisdom" (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), there are two meanings. First, that which is free from the characteristics of the grasper and the grasped is called non-conceptual.
Second, the principle of *tathatā* (suchness) is itself non-conceptual wisdom; realizing this principle is termed non-conceptual wisdom. At the time of its initial realization—
One does not perceive that which realizes nor that which is realized. Like a mani jewel or a celestial drum, they accomplish their own tasks without volition and without conceptual discrimination;
thus, the various deeds of a Buddha are accomplished. The path of language is cut off, and the sphere of mental activity is extinguished.

Mind merges with its object, and principle unites with spirit. The object is like wisdom, and wisdom is like the object; this is called *tathatā* (suchness) and is termed non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*). Muzhou asked: "Non-conceptual..."
When non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) directly realizes suchness, is it a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the object itself, or does it perceive a transformation of its image?

If it is a direct perception, then the mind would be apprehending an external object, and the doctrine of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*) would not be established. If it perceives a transformed image, what difference would there be from subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*)?

Answer: One must first determine whether the two parts [the grasped and the grasper] exist or not; only then can this be reconciled. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that there are three masters who have explained this. The first says: "This..."

1. It is said that both the wisdom (*jñāna*) and the vision (*darśana*) lack the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*), because it is taught that there is no apprehended object (*grāhya*). 2. A second [view] says: Both this wisdom and vision possess the objective aspect;

they arise bearing that aspect, and are thus called "simultaneously perceiving that. 3. A third [view] says: This wisdom and vision possess the aspect but lack [the apprehended object], because it is taught that there is no apprehended object.

Because it does not grasp at signs (*nimitta*), although it possesses a seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), it is without conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and is therefore said not to be a grasper (*grāhaka*). This does not mean that grasping is rendered non-existent;

rather, as Ci'en (Kuiji) takes the third explanation, this wisdom is based on the fact that it does not undergo transformation into images (*nimittapariṇāma*) and takes true suchness (*tathatā*) as its object, distinguishing it from subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
Question: What are called the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*)? They are composed of four parts. Since this [wisdom] lacks these signs, how can it be so? Answer: Indeed.

This is the true principle. Because it cognizes the actual nature [of objects], although it directly conditions them, the object is not separate from the mind. This does not negate *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only).

It is not the case that something is not *vijñaptimātra* simply because it does not directly condition an object; for even if it does not transform into a mental image (*nimitta-bimba*), it still apprehends that object and possesses a direct objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*).
Thus, it is not that it is not composed of the four parts (*catuṣkoṭi*). Therefore, there is a distinction between what is direct and what is remote. This is how it is analyzed.

"Carrying the image of what has already been perceived" (*sanimittatā*). "Carrying" refers to the mind; it belongs to the subjective perceiver (*ālambaka*). "Already perceived" refers to the object (*ālambana*); it belongs to the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*).
This means that when the subjective perceiving mind takes up the objective aspect as its object, it carries along with it the image of the entity of the object;

this is called "carrying the image of what has already been perceived. Based on this, the teachers of the Hīnayāna refute the Mahāyāna, saying: "Non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) does not carry the image of *tathatā* (suchness) as something already perceived."

Regarding "characteristic" (*nimitta*): True Suchness (*tathatā*) and noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) should not be object-conditions (*ālambanapratyaya*). The Tripitaka Master of the Tang dynasty said: "You followers of the Hīnayāna do not understand the meaning of my Mahāyāna.
There are two ways in which [consciousness] 'bears' [the object]: first, 'narrowly bearing,' which means the cognizing mind directly adheres to the substance of the object while cognizing it;
second, 'transformatively bearing,' which means the cognizing mind transforms and gives rise to a phenomenal portion (*nimittabhāga*) while cognizing it. Regarding "characteristic":
This also has two kinds: first, the characteristic of essence (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*); second, the characteristic of appearance (*ākāra*). Characteristic refers to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

When non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) takes suchness (*tathatā*) as its object, it takes it by encompassing the characteristic of essence; this is the "object-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

When contaminated minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), as well as uncontaminated subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), take an object, they do so by transforming and encompassing the characteristic of appearance.

Object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). This refers to the object-condition. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, in the chapter on the "Excellence of Wisdom," states: "It is called non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*) by virtue of being free from five kinds of characteristics.

First, it is free from the characteristic of non-attention (*amanasikāra*), thereby distinguishing [non-conceptual wisdom] from states such as sleep and intoxication. Second, it is free from vitarka and vicāra, thereby distinguishing it from the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and those above them.

Third, it is free from the characteristic of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedita-nirodha*), thereby distinguishing it from the two mindless states (*acittaka*). Fourth, it is free from form (*rūpa*)."
Its specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) is distinguished from derived matter (upādāyarūpa). It is fivefold in its separation from the outflow-free (anāsrava), conceptual mind.
Only when separated from these five characteristics is it the non-conceptual wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna) herein referred to.

Regarding the phrase "as it is" (*yathāvad*), it encompasses three interpretations: First, "as it is" (*yathā*) is a term used for direct designation. It refers to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena within the two truths—the ultimate and the conventional.
This nature of phenomena is called "as it is. Furthermore, because these natures of phenomena are known, the object is raised to manifest the wisdom;
thus, it is called "that which exists" (*tathā*). Second, it is said that suchness (*tathatā*) is as it is. All the aforementioned wisdoms are entirely situated upon this suchness.
"Existing as it is" (yathāvad-bhāvikatā) refers to the suchness of all things. Third, [Sthiramati] says: "All defiled and pure phenomena are called the true nature of phenomena as they exist;
this is precisely the wisdom of suchness (*tathatā-jñāna*). To be able to know the nature of suchness within these existing phenomena is called 'existing as it is'.
[Vinītadeva] says: "The first two [types of wisdom] explain 'the good' (*kuśala*). [Buddhasimha] says: "These seven types of wisdom above must all realize suchness before they can be so named."

This knowledge is like the knowledge of what exists within a house; it is called "knowledge of things as they are" (*yathābhūtajñāna*). Furthermore, true suchness (*tathatā*) is that which possesses, and wisdom is that which is possessed.
This is also consistent with the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, which states: "All phenomena are established based on the root of non-abiding.
To speak in terms of their essential nature, such wisdom of true suchness arises from this [root]; thus it is called "as-it-is" (*yathāvat*). True suchness and all myriad phenomena—
It serves as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). If, with respect to the *tathatā* (suchness) that gives rise [to wisdom], *tathatā* is taken as the producer and wisdom as the produced;
*tathatā* as the possessor and wisdom as the possessed—this is called "as-it-is-ness" (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*).

Regarding the statement "in terms of general characteristics" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Cheng weishi lun), fascicle 1, states: "By severing the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) that cause rebirth, one realizes true liberation;
by severing the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that cause discursive thought, one attains great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*). This is what is meant by "general characteristics."

This is not yet an explanation of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). According to reality, the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) do not merely obstruct emptiness and nirvāṇa; they also obstruct bodhi.
The cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) do not merely obstruct bodhi; they also obstruct the emptiness of nirvāṇa.

Regarding the statement "severing the afflictive hindrances," this is spoken from one perspective based on their predominance; therefore, it is called the "general characteristic" (as understood by the aforementioned *mūla-jñāna*).
Regarding the term "knowledge of all aspects" (*sarvākārajñatā*), it refers to the ability to know all categories of phenomena that constitute the knowledge of all aspects.
Regarding the phrase "awakening sentient beings": this refers to the aforementioned ability to awaken all sentient beings and to bring them to birth through transformation (*nirmāṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "like a lotus blooming," Huapudu (Huadu) said: "If a lotus has not yet bloomed, it possesses no fragrance. If the flower..."

Once it was opened, the fragrance wafted far, perceived by all who heard and saw it. This is a metaphor for the Buddha’s knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*): his preaching of the Dharma transforms and gives birth to beings, and his fame resounds afar.
To speak of "observing that which exists" (*sat*) refers to the fundamental wisdom that contemplates emptiness; this is termed "existence."
Regarding "knowledge of phenomena" (*vastu-jñāna*): in contrast to principle (*tattva*), it is called "phenomena.
Regarding "conventional knowledge" (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*): in contrast to the ultimate (*paramārtha*), it is called "conventional.

Regarding "subsequently attained knowledge" (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*): this distinguishes it from non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*); because it is attained at a subsequent time, it is named "subsequently attained knowledge. That is to say...

Because the realization of the conventional arises from the realization of the ultimate, it is called "subsequently attained wisdom" (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). It possesses two characteristics: first, it comprehends the distinctions of the conventional; second, it takes the transformation of images as its object of cognition rather than directly realizing [the ultimate] itself. Question:

From the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) downward, when a Bodhisattva’s fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) realizes the ultimate, subsequently attained wisdom arises one moment later to comprehend the conventional and benefit sentient beings; this may be termed "subsequently attained. However, for a Bodhisattva of the eighth stage and above, since fundamental and subsequently attained wisdoms occur simultaneously, how can they be the same? [Answer: They are indeed the same. Although the fundamental wisdom realizes the ultimate and the subsequently attained wisdom comprehends the conventional, their objects are not distinct. This is because the ultimate is the very nature of the conventional, and the conventional is the manifestation of the ultimate. Therefore, when the fundamental wisdom realizes the ultimate, it simultaneously realizes the conventional; likewise, when the subsequently attained wisdom comprehends the conventional, it simultaneously comprehends the ultimate. Consequently, even though they appear to function at different times, their essence is identical. Thus, they are said to be simultaneous. Furthermore, because the Bodhisattva of the eighth stage has attained mastery over the non-conceptual state, the two wisdoms arise together without obstruction. Hence, they are said to be the same.
In a single kṣaṇa, there is neither before nor after; movement does not obstruct stillness, for stillness is itself movement. How can one speak of "subsequently attained"? Answer:
Although they occur simultaneously, when considered in relation to preceding stages—just as the eighth bhūmi is considered subsequent to what precedes it—it is called "subsequently attained.
This is not contradictory. Furthermore, within the state of Buddhahood, it is accepted that both the fundamental [wisdom] and the subsequently attained wisdom arise simultaneously.

Regarding the phrase "exhausting all that exists" (*yāvadbhāvikatā*), it encompasses two explanations. The first states: This refers to the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) which universally takes both the ultimate (*paramārtha*) and the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) as its objects, exhausting all that exists.
When it is said to "universally take all that exists," this points to the term "phenomena" (*dharma*). This wisdom of the differentiation of phenomena is able to fully know the objects presented;

because it reveals wisdom through these objects, it is called "exhausting all that exists. The second states: Because it fully encompasses both existence and non-existence, it is called "exhausting all that exists."
There is that which wisdom can fully know; this is called "the extent of existence" (*yāvadbhāvikatā*).

Regarding the statement that it "comprehensively cuts off what is to be known," this refers exclusively to subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). As for the statement that it "cuts off the cognitive obscuration" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*):

the object of knowledge is not itself the obscuration, nor is the obscuration itself the object of knowledge. Because the obscuration obstructs the object of knowledge, it is termed "cognitive obscuration."

Obstruction. It obstructs the objects of knowledge, causing wisdom not to be clear. Subsequently-acquired wisdom takes phenomena as its object; for this reason, it is specifically said that one attains the abandonment of the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

Fundamental wisdom realizes the truth; for this reason, it is specifically said that one attains the abandonment of the afflictive obstruction (*kleśāvaraṇa*). In reality, however, these two are mutually interpenetrating.
Regarding the statement that this accords with various sūtras and is [the term] "Brahmā" and so forth: whether ordinary or noble, all in the Western lands transmit this name.
Among all names, this is the most supreme; it is fitting that the Buddha places it at the beginning of the sūtras. Question: The Buddha has ten titles.
Why is it that only this single title is established, rather than all the various names? The answer is: because this one word encompasses all virtues.
As a verse in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Sovereignty, brilliance, and magnificence;
renown, auspiciousness, and nobility—one should know that these six meanings together constitute the general name 'Bhagavat'. *Bhaga* refers to sound.
"Brahmā" signifies "possessing virtue. If one is designated by this title "Bhagavān," they are able to personally conquer the four māras and must necessarily possess six virtues:
first, the virtue of mastery, because they are forever unbound by any afflictions; second, the virtue of brilliance, because they have been refined by the blazing fire of wisdom;
third, the virtue of physical majesty, being adorned with the thirty-two marks and a golden complexion.
1. The thirty-two marks and so forth. 2. The virtue of renown: because there is nothing that the Buddha’s supreme fame does not reach, his reputation fills the ten directions and so forth.
3. The virtue of auspiciousness: because he constantly employs skillful means to benefit sentient beings, performing acts of auspiciousness.

4. The virtue of nobility: because he is revered by all in both the mundane and supramundane realms; as it is said, "In the heavens above and the earth below, none is equal to the Buddha. If one recites...

Regarding other titles: [the Buddha] lacks the six qualities [of the common epithet]. Question: Non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) also refer to their own founders as *Bhagavat* (World-Honored One) and *Buddha*.
Disciples of the Buddha also refer to their Master as *Bhagavat*. I do not yet understand what distinguishes them. Answer: This is to distinguish him from the non-Buddhists.
Furthermore, regarding the character for "Buddha" (佛): this refers to what was translated as "Buddha Bhagavān" by Paramārtha in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*. Question:

Since the Buddha’s teachings establish [the title] as "Buddha Bhagavān," why is only the character for "Buddha" used here? Answer: The Master of the State (Kuo) says there are three reasons for using only the name "Buddha":
first, because the people of Qin prefer brevity; second, to generate wholesome roots according to local conditions; and third, because it accords with the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*).

First, regarding those who prefer brevity: the term *Bhagavān* is more extensive, while the term *Buddha* is abbreviated by two syllables. Second, regarding what gives rise to goodness according to the region:
within this region, the word "Buddha" most effectively engenders goodness. Third, regarding superiority in meaning: within the sense of superiority, there are ten meanings.

First, the excellence of awakening surpasses that of the celestial drum. The drum possesses four qualities: first, it can perceive the arrival of an enemy and announce, "An enemy has come"; when he departs, [it announces his departure].

It is said that when enmity departs, the name of the Buddha is likewise. It can awaken sentient beings to whether the afflictions of the three poisons have arisen or ceased, and it proclaims their cessation.
Second, it can protect the devas and defeat the asuras; the name of the Buddha is likewise, for it can rescue [beings] from the three sufferings and destroy the four māras.
Third, the celestial drum enables the devas to experience the pleasures of the five desires; the name of the Buddha is likewise, for it can cause the multitude...

Those born [in the heavens] experience supramundane bliss. While the drums of the Four Heavenly Kings can cause the devas to give rise to a mind of craving and attachment, the Buddha’s name can cause sentient beings to give rise to a supramundane mind.
These four superior qualities mentioned above are all functions of the drum; collectively, they are called the "Awakening Drum Superior to the Heavenly Drums."
Second, awakening not through another, because of the teacherless wisdom (*aśaikṣajñāna*) that realizes all phenomena. Third, severing the two types of ignorance;
"ignorance" here refers to the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Fourth, having transcended sleep and dreams;

ordinary beings who have not yet attained true awakening constantly dwell within a dream, whereas the Tathāgata neither sleeps nor dreams, and is thus said to have "transcended. Fifth, like a lotus flower blooming.

Touched by the light of the sun of wisdom, the lotus immediately opens; the practices of the ten stages are perfected, and the Buddha-wisdom spontaneously arises. The six natures are pure and undefiled.

Although afflictions exist within the *tathatā* (suchness) of the causal stage, it remains unstained for five reasons: first, because it is signless (*animitta*), like space which cannot be defiled by smoke or mist;
second, because it is not an object of antidotes (*pratipakṣa*), like a red-hot iron that does not harbor mosquitoes or gadflies; third... [text continues]
1. Because it is not a locus [for defilement]; for example, a great stone cannot remain suspended in the air. 2. Because it is devoid of transformation;
for example, white silk remains unstained even when dyed black. 3. Because falsehood cannot defile the Truth; for example, a lead blade cannot cut through stone. 4.

Because even while the cause contains delusion, it cannot yet stain [the nature]; how much less so when delusion is exhausted within the fruit? 5. Because it is fully endowed with the three meanings; these three meanings are...

1. The three bodies (*trikāya*). 2. The possession of the eightfold perfection of the three virtues, namely: wisdom (*jñāna*), abandonment (*prahāṇa*), and beneficence (*anugraha*). 3. The possession of the nature of the Three Jewels;

that is, the Three Jewels of identical essence (*sāmbhogika-triratna*). 4. Self-knowledge and causing others to know: by the power of wisdom, one realizes the realm of *tathatā* (suchness); this is called "self-knowledge.

Furthermore, by the power of compassion, one proclaims the twelvefold teaching (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*) to cause others to know. Because it possesses these ten meanings, [the Buddha] is singled out for mention.
The name of the Buddha refers to his specific title;
other appellations are not mentioned here. Regarding the statement, "Among these three bodies, which one does [the phrase] 'Thus have I heard, at one time, the Buddha' subsume?

the commentary answers: "The answer is determined by the context and so forth. According to the Hīnayāna school, there are two types: first, the birth-body (*janma-kāya*), which was born in a royal palace.

The first is the birth-body (*janma-kāya*). The second is the dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*), which is the fivefold dharma-body consisting of the perfumes of precept, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.

The third is the transformation-body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*), such as those of monkeys, deer, horses, and so forth. Question: Among the three bodies—the dharma, enjoyment, and transformation bodies—according to the Mahāyāna school, which body preaches the Dharma?

Answer: It is definitively the enjoyment and transformation bodies that preach. However, if one follows the specific location or the specific faculties [of the audience], it may be the śrāvaka [body].
As for the transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇa-buddha*), the location is Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in the city of Rājagṛha; this is the criterion for the location.
The faculties refer to those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*). Since the two vehicles and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are the primary audience, the Buddha is a minor transformation body.

If one judges by the location and the faculties, it is certainly a transformation body in an impure land (*saṃkliṣṭa-kṣetra*) preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. If, however, one judges by the text and the capacity [of the audience], [it is a pure land].

That which manifests in response to bodhisattvas is the *saṃbhogakāya*. According to the scriptural text, it constantly dwells on Vulture Peak (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*) and other various abodes, until it is said:
"In this land of mine there is peace and security; devas and humans are always abundant. Regarding the analogy of the vessel:

in the *Parīndanā-parivarta* (Distribution) section of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, for the sake of the bodhisattvas, Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra are present in the assembly; this is precisely the *saṃbhogakāya* and the *saṃbhogakṣetra*.
Regarding the statement that "the causes and conditions differ because their faculties and capacities are different," this refers to the distinction between the two types: Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas.

Because it manifests in accordance with [their needs], it is said to "communicate through transformation. The Buddha-body is fundamentally non-dual; it is merely that what is manifested differs according to the recipient.

To Bodhisattvas, the Reward Body (Sambhogakāya) is manifested; to Śrāvakas, the Transformation Body (Nirmāṇakāya) is manifested. It is like five people seeing the moon differently—the four [others]... [are not the same].
Whether one goes east, west, south, or north, it seems as though the moon follows the person. Yet, when a single person sits without moving, they see that the moon likewise does not move.
The substance of the moon is one; it is fundamentally unmoving.
The mention of Rājagṛha, Vulture Peak, and so forth explains the underlying reason [for the location].

As for the question, "Why does it not mention being swept away by the waters at the end of a kalpa or swept away by the winds, but instead speaks of the calamity of fire? the answer is: because among the three calamities, the calamity of fire occurs first; therefore, it is singled out for mention.
Regarding the statement that "my land is peaceful and secure": although the Buddha’s body resides in a single location, what is perceived differs according to the faculties [of sentient beings].
Question: How can there be only one Buddha-land? For what reason is there both burning and non-burning? Answer:

For a single person at the first stage (*bhūmi*), the *paranirmita-vashavartin* (other-dependent) enjoyment land serves as the basis. Upon this basis, for every hundred people, there is a trichiliocosm (*trisāhasra-mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu*). One...
The world of the hundred-fold [sahasra-lokadhātu] is entirely consumed by fire, but the *parabhogakṣetra* (land of enjoyment for others) is not burned. Question:

How is it known that this is the *parabhogakṣetra*? Answer: The Sūtra says, "He always dwells on Vulture Peak Mountain," and so forth. Śāriputra hearing the Sūtra refers to the *nirmāṇabuddha* (emanation Buddha).
Mañjuśrī being present therein refers to the *saṃbhogabuddha* (enjoyment Buddha).

Regarding the statement, "The response-body and transformation-bodies are not the true Buddha," the intent of the *Shu* (Commentary) is as follows: Since the Buddha encompasses both the retribution-body (*vipākakāya*) and the transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), he must also possess those bodies.
Where there is the manifestation of function, there must be the substance; where there is the retribution-land (*vipākabhūmi*), there must be the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

Since the Dharma-body exists, it logically follows that the Dharma-body is capable of preaching the Dharma. Therefore, [the author] cites Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* to prove the existence of the Dharma-body. This is so.

Regarding the statement, "The one who can truly preach the Dharma," the treatise (śāstra) merely proves that the *nirmāṇakāya* (response-body) is not the true Buddha and not the true preacher of the Dharma;
it does not prove that another, the *dharmakāya*, is the preacher of the Dharma. Why, then, did the commentator add: "Attributing the merit to its source, it is the *dharmakāya* that preaches"?
Answer: The commentator has skillfully grasped the intent of the treatise. The meaning of the treatise is simply to establish the conclusion through a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*).
The Dharma-body is the true speaker of the Dharma; therefore, it is specifically the Reward-body and Transformation-body that are said to be non-genuine and lacking reality.

These [latter bodies] consist of the five aggregates that lack reality, as well as minds and mental factors that lack reality—like fire in a mirror, or like a phantom person preaching the Dharma to another phantom person.
If the Dharma-body were not the true speaker of the Dharma, then in relation to whom would the Transformation-body be designated as "non-genuine"? Therefore, [the text] below cites...
"Realization. This refers to the explanation of the Dharmakāya abiding in the *dharmadhātugarbha*.

Regarding the phrase "abiding in the *dharmadhātugarbha*" and so forth, the interpretation of "garbha" (matrix/storehouse) here differs from the interpretations found previously in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* and the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*.
Because those [beings] have their true name-treasury covered by afflictions, the *dharmatā* and *tathatā* within this realm is called the *dharmadhātu*.
It contains all unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; the *dharmakāya* abides therein, and thus it is called "abiding in the *dharmadhātugarbha*.

Question: How can there be a sense of differentiation upon that which is of a single essence? Answer: The treatise states: "Although the essence of these bodies and lands is without differentiation, they nevertheless belong to..."
Because the nature (*dharmatā*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the Buddha-dharma are distinct: the characteristics correspond to the Buddha, while the nature corresponds to the Dharma.

The "Buddha" here refers to the Dharmakāya Buddha, who serves as the support and the essence for the dharmas of great merit. The characteristics are termed the "body" (*kāya*), and because this body sustains its own essence, it is called the "land" (*kṣetra*).

The earth is itself the treasury; it is the *dharmatā*-land (*dharmatā-kṣetra*). Question: What is meant by "expounding the Dharma" (*dharma-deśanā*)? Answer: There are two meanings for the term "expounding the Dharma.

First, that the twelvefold teaching (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*) flows forth from the *dharmakāya* is called expounding the Dharma. Second, that which causes wisdom to arise and reach understanding is called expounding the Dharma.
Question: Who listens to the Dharma? Answer: Sixty-six persons constitute the assembly of listeners. The Great Perfect Mirror...

Regarding the three fundamental wisdoms—Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, Equality Wisdom, and Wondrous Observation Wisdom—at the time they realize *tathatā* (suchness), each is associated with twenty-two mental states and mental factors, totaling sixty-six.
Question: What dharma do they teach? Answer: When fundamental wisdom realizes *tathatā*, it gives rise to a single-flavored (*ekarasa*) pure aspect;
this is called the "Dharmakāya preaching the Dharma. If one says that the single-flavored purity [is the teaching], it is already not so.
This is the teaching on the Dharma. At the time of the correct realization of truth, there is no conceptualizing mind; it is simply a single-flavored, pure aspect.

Regarding the mention of the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* and so forth concerning the "abodes" (*vihāra*) and so on, this refers to the realization of the preaching of the Dharma by the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*).

This is the land where the Body of Enjoyment for Others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*) resides, manifesting supernatural powers and preaching the Dharma for the sake of all Bodhisattvas. Its seat possesses ten characteristics, and its land possesses ten [features].
Regarding the eighth perfection, the *Daśabhūmika-bhāṣya* (Commentary on the Ten Stages), chapter ten, states: "The Great Jewel Lotus King Throne has ten characteristics.
First is the characteristic of the lord: as the sutra says, when this samādhi manifests before one, a great jewel lotus immediately appears.
Second is the characteristic of measure: as the sutra says, it is like ten hundred-thousand asaṃkhyeyas of trichiliocosms."
3. The characteristic of excellence: as the sūtra says, "because it is adorned and embellished with all kinds of jewels.

4. The characteristic of the stage: the sūtra says, "because it transcends all worldly spheres. 5. The characteristic of the cause: as the sūtra says, "because it is produced by supramundane roots of goodness.
6. The characteristic of accomplishment: as the sūtra says, "because it is accomplished through the sphere of the illusory nature of all phenomena. 7. The ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
9. The characteristic marks (*lakṣaṇa*). As the sūtra says: "The light universally illuminates the entire dharma-realm. 10. The eightfold meritorious characteristics (*aṣṭāṅga-guṇa-lakṣaṇa*).
As the sūtra says: "Because it transcends all the realms of the various devas. 11. The essential characteristic (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*). As the sūtra says:
"It has a stem made of great lapis lazuli maṇi jewels, a pedestal of immeasurable sandalwood, filaments of great agate, and petals of Jambūnada gold. 12. [The tenth...]
It is fully adorned with the marks [of perfection]. As the sutra says: "The body upon the flower-seat possesses immeasurable radiance;
it is interspersed within with every kind of jewel, and immeasurable jeweled nets completely cover it from above."
Regarding the phrase "the eighteen perfections" and so forth, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: first, perfection of color (*varṇa-saṃpad*), as in all boundless worlds;
second, perfection of shape (*saṃsthāna-saṃpad*), as in the immeasurable locations being exquisitely adorned and arranged;
third, perfection of dimension (*pramāṇa-saṃpad*), as in the palaces being perfectly circular and limitless, their dimensions difficult to measure; fourth, perfection of location (*deśa-saṃpad*).
1. Perfection of the cause (*hetu-saṃpad*), as the sūtra says: "It transcends the sphere of activity of the three realms. 2. Perfection of the fruit (*phala-saṃpad*), as the sūtra says:

"It gives rise to supramundane roots of goodness that are supreme. 3. Perfection of the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa-saṃpad*), as the sūtra says: "Its characteristic is the most supremely sovereign pure consciousness (*viśuddha-vijñāna*). 4. Perfection of the location (*sthāna-saṃpad*), as the sūtra says:
"It is the capital city where the Tathāgatas reside. 5. Perfection of the retinue (*parivāra-saṃpad*), as the sūtra says: "It is surrounded by a cloud-like assembly of great bodhisattvas."

1. Perfection of assembly: as the sūtra says, he is constantly attended by immeasurable devas, nāgas, humans, and others. 2. Perfection of retinue: as the sūtra says, his retinue is complete. 3. Perfection of sustenance:
as the sūtra says, he is sustained by the joy and bliss of the flavor of the vast Mahāyāna Dharma. 4. Perfection of activity.
As the sūtra says, [the first is] the perfection of benefit for all sentient beings, which brings about all meaningful advantages;

as the sūtra says, [the second is] the perfection of the twelve types of assistance, which completely eliminates all afflictions, calamities, entanglements, and impurities; as the sūtra says, [the third is] the perfection of fearlessness, which remains far removed from all Māras;
as the sūtra says, [the fourth is] the perfection of the dwelling place, which is the locus that relies upon all various adornments; as the sūtra says, [the fifth is] the perfection of the path...

Taking the practice of great mindfulness and wisdom as the path for travel. As for "Golden Cloud," mindfulness refers to the wisdom of hearing; wisdom is reflection; and the practice of reflection is the wisdom of cultivation.
These three types of wisdom serve as the path for travel for Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Regarding the perfection of the sixteen vehicles, it is as the sutra says:
taking the great, correct, and wondrous contemplation as the vehicle. Regarding the perfection of the seventeen gates, it is as the sutra says: the perfection of the great emptiness.

The gates of entry are the liberations of signlessness and wishlessness. It is the eighteenfold perfection of the support (*āśraya*) that is taught in this sūtra within a great palace established upon a king of great jewel-flowers, adorned by an immeasurable multitude of merits;
therefore, it is called the "Perfection of the Eighteen. This is the teaching of the *saṃbhogakāya*.
Regarding the statement "this king of sutras, the city, and so forth," it refers to the text of the sutra itself. This concerns the word "Buddha" at the beginning of the sutra;
since the sutra states that he was dwelling in the city of Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain, this refers to the manifested body of the Buddha.

Regarding the statement that [the Buddha] manifests bodies in accordance with sentient beings: in response to the Wisdom of the Correct Essence (*samyaktva-jñāna*), he manifests the Pure Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*);

in response to the enjoyment of the bliss of the Dharma, he manifests the Body of Self-enjoyment (*svasaṃbhogakāya*); in response to Bodhisattvas of the ten stages, he manifests the ten grades of the Body of Enjoyment for Others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*);

and in response to those of the two vehicles and the two types of ordinary beings, he manifests the minor Emanation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). This is because it is said that all of these preach the Dharma.

Regarding the statement that the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says "and so forth," this serves as proof that the three bodies (*trikāya*) preach the Dharma. It may be understood that the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) and the transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) preach the Dharma;

however, how does the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*) preach the Dharma? If one considers the self-enjoyment body, its sense faculties and marks of excellence (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) each pervade all things.
How, then, can it be said that it divides itself into lands and subsequently preaches the Dharma? Answer: This refers to the retribution-enjoyment (*vipākasaṃbhoga*).

The meaning is called the "body" (*kāya*); the meaning of that which is supported is called the "land" (*kṣetra*). This has two interpretations. First, it is said that its substance is all-pervasive, and thus Buddhas do not see one another—whether as self or other.
If they were to delight in seeing one another, the sense of being all-pervasive would not be established. Second, it is said that its substance is all-pervasive, and thus Buddhas see one another.
If they did not see one another, there would be no sense of sovereign mastery. This refers to the body and land of the *svasaṃbhogakāya* (self-enjoyment body).

Furthermore, the *svasaṃbhogakāya* (self-enjoyment body) preaches the Dharma. There are two meanings to this preaching of the Dharma by the body: first, Buddhas perceive one another and engage in mutual consultation, which is termed "preaching the Dharma.
Second, the *mūlajñāna* (fundamental wisdom) and the *prsthalabdha-jñāna* (subsequently attained wisdom) preach the Dharma.

Within the three [aspects of] fundamental wisdom, all the sands-of-the-Ganges-like merits realized therein are entirely the preaching of the Dharma through non-words; they shatter the attachments to the reflected images transformed by subsequently attained wisdom.
Although one does not personally attain them, it is said that each and every one is brought forth [to one].

Subsequently, within the wisdom of subsequent attainment (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), names and signs are established and taught upon phenomena that are themselves devoid of names and signs; this is the teaching of the *svasaṃbhogakāya*.
The ten levels of the *parasaṃbhogakāya* and the various *nirmāṇakāyas* are those who listen to the Dharma from the side of the *svasaṃbhogakāya*. Jin says: "Three."
The body preaches the Dharma. This should be analyzed through four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). Regarding "one preaches and two do not preach":

the first [preaching] refers to the *svasaṃbhoga-kāya* (self-enjoyment body), which is called "one preaching" because it experiences the bliss of the Dharma for itself. The "two who do not preach" are as stated in the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
"The response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is not the true Buddha, nor is it the preacher of the Dharma. This is called "two not preaching. Second, "two preach and one does not preach": the second...

Regarding "those who teach": as in the case of the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*), there are sentient beings to be converted; this is called "the two who teach. First, regarding "those who do not teach":

the Self-Enjoyment Body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*) has no sentient beings to be converted; this is called "the one who does not teach. Third, all three bodies teach the Dharma together, as stated in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*:
"The Dharma-body teaches the Dharma so that wisdom may arise and understand; the Self-enjoyment body teaches the Dharma... [Self-enjoyment...]
The "Dharma-pleasure" refers to the teaching of the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body). "Teaching" refers to those sentient beings who are to be transformed.
Fourth, there is the position that none of the three bodies teach the Dharma; this is the school of Nāgārjuna.
The phrase "by means of this Kauśika and others" explains the intention behind the differences in physical manifestations and methods of teaching the Dharma.
The *Jingyin* (Sound of the Sūtras) states: Kauśika is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as the Layman Wondrous Sound (*Ghoṣila*). He resided in the city of Rājagṛha and was three feet tall.
Feeling ashamed of his short stature, he was embarrassed to appear before the Tathāgata and thought to himself: "The Tathāgata possesses a body sixteen feet tall."
His body was the color of purple-polished gold, and he constantly yearned to behold and worship him; yet, how could he overcome his physical limitations?

The Tathāgata, knowing that his faculties were now mature, manifested a body identical to his own and went to the gate to beg for alms. When the elder saw him from within the door, a sense of rare wonder arose in him, and he made extensive offerings.
He preached the essentials of the Dharma for them, and upon hearing these words, they immediately attained the first fruit of the path.

As for the five hundred brahmins who sought liberation by smearing their bodies with blue ash, the Tathāgata, wishing to transform such a class of people, manifested a body smeared with ash once again. When those brahmins saw him, their minds...

He gave rise to joy. "Gautama, you have now studied my path of the sages. The Tathāgata preached the essentials of the Dharma for him, and at the conclusion of those words, he realized the first fruit [of the path].
Regarding the so-called Bodhisattva Anantagātra and others: there was a bodhisattva who came from the eastern direction. I heard that in the Sahā world...
In this world there is the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, whose body is sixteen feet tall. Since I possess this boundless body, I should contemplate that Buddha’s mark of the invisible crown of the head;
thus, I measured it with a bamboo staff sixteen feet long, yet the Tathāgata’s manifested form exceeded sixteen feet.
Continuing in this manner upward as far as the buddha-field of King of Radiance, it always exceeded sixteen feet, until finally—
Unable to see the Tathāgata’s mark of the uṣṇīṣa on his crown, the Bodhisattva took up his bamboo staff and spoke this verse:
“Space has no boundaries, and the Buddha’s merit is likewise. Even if there were one capable of measuring it, one could not exhaust it even through the end of kalpas.

Transcending the realm of space and across immeasurable buddha-fields, one beholds the body of the Lion of the Śākyas, exactly as it was before, without any difference. Question: Since it is said that [it] does not exist...
The Bodhisattva Boundless Body possesses a physical dimension that is boundless, pervading the entire dharma-realm. How can it be said that he comes from the eastern direction?
Answer: If one discusses his physical dimension, it is indeed boundless. However, when one contemplates the mark of the Buddha’s crown (*uṣṇīṣa*), it is another body that arrives.

The intention behind citing this Bodhisattva is to demonstrate that within the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) there exists the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*), and that within the reward body there likewise exists [the dharma-body].
The manifestation body (nirmāṇakāya) cannot be fixed with certainty.
As for the statement regarding "ordinary beings who abide as lesser sages" and so forth: "lesser sages" refers to the lesser śrāvakas;
"ordinary beings of the three vehicles" refers to all ordinary beings prior to the four types of bodhi. Regarding the observation of the sixteen-foot [body] without end, there are two [points].
