Whoever is able to protect this Dharma of the sutra thereby makes offerings to me and to Prabhūtaratna.
By this standard, it is known that practicing according to the Dharma is itself an act of making offerings and showing reverence to the Buddha’s body. As the saying goes:

“To establish oneself in the Way and bring one's name to fame in future generations, thereby bringing glory to one's parents—this is the ultimate fulfillment of filial piety. Now, the Arhats have already practiced in accordance with the teachings of the Dharma.

To practice offerings is what ought to be done; this is precisely the practice of the Dharma-offering (*dharmapūjā*). Regarding the character "practice" (*xing*), which is pronounced with both the level and departing tones:

"correct practice" (*samyakpratipatti*) is itself the Dharma-offering. This refers to the ten Dharma-practices (*daśadharmacaryā*) and so forth, as they are subsumed under the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
Since the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is already perfected, one has personally completed the offering through the Path.

Regarding the statement "the six [factors] are fully grasped and perfected," Mou says: This refers to the ability to fulfill the stage of training (*śaikṣa-bhūmi*), which is the stage of no-more-training (*aśaikṣa*).

Since those in training have not yet exhausted their afflictions (*kleśa*), and because analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is non-different [from that state], this is described as reaching the stage of no-more-training based on a single characteristic;
why would it not be complete? Yong says: The Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) is the task accomplished by an Arhat; it is through the realization of cessation [that this is so].

Truth. It is the fulfillment of what was to be accomplished; it is the completion of the stage of training (*śaikṣa-bhūmi*). Question: How are the perfected qualities (*paripūrṇa-guṇa*) subsumed? Answer:
That which is realized by an Arhat—namely, *nirvāṇa-with-remainder* (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*)—is called the perfected quality.

Since *nirvāṇa-with-remainder* is that which was to be accomplished and has now been accomplished, it is called the perfected quality. This is precisely the fulfillment of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).

Regarding the phrase "the seven excellences that transcend attachment" (*atikrānta-rāga*), the character *guò* (transcend) is pronounced only with the departing tone (*qù yīn*), not the level tone (*píng shēng*).
As for the first phrase, "transcending attachment," the Sūtra says: "Having cast off all heavy burdens. The causes and effects of birth and death are called "heavy burdens";
since these originally arise from craving and attachment (*tṛṣṇā*), casting them off now is termed "transcending attachment. The subsequent Sūtra states: "The cause of all sufferings..."
Craving is the root. Ordinary worldlings are unable to cast off the heavy burden of birth and death because they possess craving and attachment.
Now, the Arhat has no craving; therefore, he is able to cast off the heavy burden of birth and death, having transcended craving.
Regarding the phrase "transcending wrong livelihood and so forth," the Sūtra states:
"Having attained one's own benefit, the Arhat realizes the *nirvāṇa* with remainder as his own personal benefit; he does not rely on worldly food and clothing for his livelihood.
All ordinary beings who have not yet realized *nirvāṇa* are characterized by wrong livelihood; now, by distancing oneself from these, it is called 'transcending.'"
Regarding the phrase "transcending the upper and lower realms" in the subsequent clause: the Sūtra states that one has "exhausted all fetters of existence.

Since the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) are by nature stages of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmi*), they are combined into a single designation and thus called the "upper realm" (*ūrdhvadhātu*). The desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is the "lower" stage of distraction (*vikṣepabhūmi*), and is therefore separately designated as the "lower realm" (*adharadhātu*).
The nine fetters (*nava-saṃyojana*) and afflictions are the causes for these upper and lower realms; since these have now all been severed, it is said that one has "transcended" them.

Furthermore, according to the Hīnayāna, there are five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*): first, sensual desire; second, ill-will; third, the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*);

fourth, attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*); and fifth, doubt (*vicikitsā*). A person who has attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) has not yet completely severed the latter three fetters and thus does not transcend the desire realm.

One who has attained the fruit of *anāgāmin* (non-returner) has completely severed all five lower fetters; because they have transcended these lower fetters, they are said to have "transcended the desire realm. As for the five upper fetters (*pañca ūrdhva-bhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*): [they are:]...

They are: first, greed for the realm of form (*rūparāga*); second, greed for the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*); third, restlessness (*auddhatya*); fourth, pride (*māna*); and fifth, ignorance (*avidyā*).

When a person beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) has completely severed these five fetters (*saṃyojana*), they are said to have "transcended the fetters of the higher and lower realms. Question: Since the essence of greed pervades all three realms, why is it divided into three when categorized among the fetters?
Ignorance (*avidyā*) pervades the three realms; why then is it established as only one? Answer: For the noble ones (*ārya*), there still remains the moisture [of craving] that gives rise to birth;

because these are categorized separately, they are divided into three. Ignorance has no further arising; because it is subsumed [under craving], it is established as only one. Question: The karma that produces birth for the noble ones is manifest; even so, it may be included within the "moisture.

However, since discrimination has ceased among the fetters (*saṃyojana*), how can there be "moisture" for karma? Answer: The noble ones possess karma from previous lives which still brings about [birth]. It is this that is moistened.
There is craving for future existence. From the arising of craving, there is continuous rebirth; through this, there is the presence of moisture.
Question: How does an Arhat transcend merit? Answer: Because he has cast off all heavy burdens. An Arhat has not yet attained the casting off of burdens; an Arhat does not transcend craving.
Since the Arhat has already abandoned the burden of birth and death, he transcends craving; therefore, it is called "transcending merit."

Question: How does one exceed improper livelihood (*mithyājīva*)? Answer: Because they have already attained their own benefit, Arhats do not seek *nirvāṇa* [as a goal for themselves] and further pursue wrong occupations to sustain their lives.
Having realized *nirvāṇa*, the deathless dharma, why would they need to seek wealth and profit to support their lives?
Question: How does one transcend the upper and lower realms? Answer: By exhausting all fetters of existence (*bhava-saṃyojana*). If [one exhausts them] within the nine [realms] of the three worlds...
If one abides in a particular stage (*bhūmi*), there remains the fetter of craving for that stage; thus, one cannot be said to have transcended its qualities.

An Arhat, however, has exhausted all nine fetters of the three realms and is therefore said to have transcended those qualities. Those in the first and third fruits have not yet exhausted their fetters.

Although one in the second fruit has severed six grades of the desire realm, and one in the third fruit has already transcended the fetters of the desire realm, because they still possess the fetters of the two higher realms, they cannot collectively be so designated.
It surpasses merit. Now, this state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) completely exhausts the three realms;
therefore, it attains merit that transcends the three realms, which is called "surpassing merit. Thus, all three phrases are termed "surpassing merit."

Regarding the statement that "the eight [liberations] encompass the supreme and superlative virtues," Yuan Yong says: The first fruit (*srotāpanna*) is superior to ordinary beings; those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are superior to those still in training (*śaikṣa*);

and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is superior to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Therefore, they receive the name "supreme and superlative. These are exclusively the true unconditioned state of liberation.
In the section on the "Gate of Arising in the Ultimate" (*uttarottara-utpatti-mukha*) presented above, the third phrase explains the fourteenth phrase.
The fourteenth phrase refers to "liberation through right knowledge" (*samyagjñāna-vimukti*). Right knowledge is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); liberation is realized by means of right knowledge.
This liberation is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) nirvāṇa. Thus, it is the distinction between the conditioned and the unconditioned. Second interpretation: by means of the fourteenth phrase...

This explains the sixteenth phrase: "well-attained liberation of mind. The inclusion of the word "mind" (*citta*) indicates that "mind" here refers to the wisdom within meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
By attaining the various merits of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), this reveals the Arhat who is liberated in both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*). Third, regarding the general explanation:

within the section on specific characteristics, it says "liberation through right knowledge" (*samyagjñāna-vimukti*). When one speaks only of "right knowledge" without the word "mind," it refers to liberation through right knowledge alone. This is the general [explanation].

This is supernormal power (*abhijñā*). Because one is deluded and obscured by afflictions (*kleśa*) regarding the principle of suchness (*tathatā*), one attains liberation from neither [affliction] nor [principle].

Through the arising of wisdom (*prajñā*), one severs the afflictions; thus, both principle and wisdom attain liberation. It is precisely this wisdom of liberation that can give rise to supernormal powers;
therefore, correct wisdom and liberation are termed "supernormal power. This is the fourth interpretation. Now, within the section on the gate of encompassing phenomena:

Regarding the phrase "liberation of the mind through right knowledge" (*samyagjñāna-citta-vimukti*): although the word "mind" (*citta*) is added, it is understood collectively as the unconditioned fruit (*asaṃskṛta-phala*).
Question: Why are there four different explanations in the commentary (*śāstra*)? Answer: Because the Sūtra and the Śāstra differ. The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says, "right knowledge and liberation.
The *Treatise by Vasubandhu* says, "right knowledge and liberation of the mind. Each of the Sūtra and the Śāstra relies on a single meaning. If the Master of the Commentary follows...
To follow the sutra would contradict the śāstra; to rely on the śāstra would contradict the sutra. Therefore, this [text] contains both perspectives.

The Master of the Commentary (Sūzhǔ) may interpret the śāstra by means of the sutra, or interpret the sutra by means of the śāstra; since the two texts differ in their presentation, there is no further fault. Question:

Which among the merits in the sutra are the "supreme-of-the-supreme" (uttarottara-guṇa)? Answer: The commentary states: they are the mind-liberation through right knowledge (samyagjñāna-ceto-vimukti). Right knowledge is that which realizes [liberation].
Wisdom and liberation are the nirvāṇa that is realized. The merit of nirvāṇa in this sūtra is called the "supreme supreme merit.
Question: In what sense are wisdom and liberation the nirvāṇa that is realized? Answer: The commentary states: "Liberation is so called because it is an unconditioned fruit (*asaṃskṛta-phala*)."
Since this liberation is an unconditioned fruit, it is precisely *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. Question:
How is it known that the liberation and nirvāṇa realized therein are called the "supreme and unsurpassed merit"? Answer: The commentary states that because they are the most supreme among all merits.

Regarding the statement "the nine types of grasping that should be practiced": previously, in the section on the "Successive Arising Gate," fifteen phrases were explained individually, stating that "because one reaches the wisdom of the path of seeing and the path of cultivation, all afflictions are exhausted, and one reaches mastery over the mind. This is according to the interpretation of wisdom.

Second, regarding the gate of general and specific characteristics, one should arrive at the qualities of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). That is to say, this mastery over the mind realizes non-existence.

For this reason, regarding the understanding through realization, it is the third section on the gate of grasping the objective; regarding the understanding through supernormal powers, it is because one attains mastery over the mind by giving rise to the attainment of supernormal powers.

Regarding the "practice of gathering and benefiting," there are two interpretations: first, because one attains mastery over the mind through the arising of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), it is called the practice of benefiting sentient beings;
second, because one’s own person is free from afflictions (*kleśa*) and is thus capable of serving as a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), this too is the practice of benefiting sentient beings.
These two types of practice are fully present within the body; the practice of gathering and benefiting does not exceed these.
There are two kinds: first, the practice of one’s own vehicle; second, the practice of subduing others.

What is now referred to as "attaining supernatural powers" (abhijñā) is the realization of the practice of subduing non-Buddhists, because it is free from fetters. This is precisely the perfection of self-benefit within the practice of self-benefit.
Since all those present today are great śrāvakas who have turned their minds [toward the Mahāyāna], this interpretation is made according to the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the phrase "the ten that are foremost in their inclusion," the *Sūtra* says, "The first is ultimate. The term *pāramitā* refers to the Śrāvaka, according to the *Śāstra*.

The commentary by the Master of the Sub-commentary (*Ṭīkākāra*) explains that it is "capable of reaching the other shore. First, "attainment" means eternal attainment; this is called "ultimate" (*niṣṭhā*). This is the principle.

The two types of wisdom are both called "attainment" (*pāramitā*), and thus they are termed "reaching the other shore. Question: What is the distinction between the two dharmas, "the supreme" (*uttara*) and "the foremost" (*agrya*)? Answer:
"The supreme" refers exclusively to principle (*tattva*), whereas "the foremost" encompasses both principle and wisdom (*jñāna*); this is the distinction between the two. Question:

The Master of the Commentary previously explained in his sub-commentary that, according to their respective applications, among the ten kinds of merit, the second, seventh, eighth, and tenth comprehensively include conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).

Regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*): why is it that now, upon explaining the eighth [category], one immediately states that "the highest of the high" (*uttarottara*) refers exclusively to principle (*li*)? Answer: Previously, this was based on the definition of its essential nature (*svabhāva*), where both wisdom (*jñāna*) and principle were equally applicable.
Now, however, this is based on the explanation of its name; since the conditioned cannot be called "the highest of the high," it is stated here that it refers exclusively to principle. Mou says:

"Supreme of the supreme" refers to the fruit; since both principle and wisdom are supreme of the supreme, this refers to the dharmas. "Foremost of the supreme" refers to the Śrāvakas who have reached the other shore;
this refers to persons. Question: Is the nirvāṇa of the two vehicles the emptiness of dharmas? If so, it may be called the first and ultimate inclusion.
If the nirvāṇa of the two vehicles is not the emptiness of dharmas, how can it be named the first? Answer: Taking those of the two vehicles...

Regarding the emptiness of persons and nirvāṇa within the Mahāyāna, these are not the foremost; however, since this discussion is based on the ultimate fruit of one's own vehicle, they are also called "foremost.
As for the statement that the first two are "comprehension," this refers to the two phrases within the "merit of comprehension" of the foremost [stage], namely:
All outflows are exhausted; there are no further afflictions.
Regarding the statement that "the next three [qualities] encompass all virtues," this refers to the inclusion of all meritorious qualities in three phrases:
namely, having attained true mastery, being well-liberated in mind, and being well-liberated through wisdom.
Regarding the phrase "conformity, excellence, action, and fulfillment": "Conformity" refers to the third quality, non-contradiction, which means being like a fine horse.
"Excellence" refers to the fourth quality, superiority, which is also like a great dragon.
"Action" refers to the fifth quality, the excellence of undertaking what ought to be done, meaning having completed what was to be done. "Fulfillment" refers to the sixth [quality].

This refers to the fulfillment of the qualities of attainment, meaning that what was to be accomplished has already been accomplished. Thus, the commentary states that these are to be assigned respectively to the four phrases.

As for the statement that "the three phrases are called the inclusion of faults," this refers to the seventh fault, which is the quality of merit consisting in having cast off all heavy burdens (*bhāra*).

This encompasses three phrases: attaining one's own benefit, exhausting all fetters of existence, and transcending the lower and upper realms. The first phrase transcends craving; the second phrase transcends wrong livelihood;
and the third phrase transcends the lower and upper realms.
Regarding the phrase "the supreme among the supreme, the benefit, the foremost, and so forth," the commentary states:
"The supreme among the supreme" refers to the eighth [perfection], which comprises the supreme merit of right knowledge and liberation.

"Benefit" refers to the ninth [perfection], which comprises the merit of performing what is beneficial for sentient beings, namely, mastery over the mind. "Foremost" refers to the tenth [perfection], which comprises the foremost merit.
Virtue. Regarding the statement that this sutra comprises six phrases: "All outflows are exhausted and there are no further afflictions"—these two phrases encompass the first virtue.
"Having attained one's own benefit and exhausted all fetters of existence"—these two phrases encompass the seventh virtue.
Virtue. "Mastery over the mind through the ultimate state" refers to attaining mastery over the mind; this subsumes the ninth merit of benefiting sentient beings.
The single phrase "Arhat" is the general term and is not included here; only the following fifteen phrases are taken to subsume the merits.
When these fifteen phrases are condensed into one place, they constitute the single meaning of an Arhat as one who is worthy. If they are expanded, they are divided [into specific categories].
There are fifteen [sections].
Regarding the explanation of the three meanings within the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*: the Arhat is subsumed under the first three gates. Question:

Do these three meanings in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* exhaustively encompass the contents of this gate? Answer: Briefly stated, it is the "Gate of Successive Arising" (*uttarottara-pravṛtti-dvāra*).

The inclusion [of this teaching] should be understood as permanently destroying the thieves of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and ensuring that one no longer undergoes further birth in the realm of segmented existence (*prātibhajika-jāti*).

Regarding the inclusion through the gate of specific and general characteristics, it should be understood as receiving sublime offerings. Question: Among the three meanings of the "gate of the objects of inclusion," which meaning does this inclusion correspond to? Answer:

The Master of the Commentary’s gate of the objects of inclusion does not correspond to those three types of inclusion; none of the three meanings are included therein. That [former system] is broad while this [present system] is narrow.

Regarding the statement that those three refer only to the definitive sense: in that treatise, six types of arhats are discussed in terms of their general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), without distinguishing between those of sharp or dull faculties;
all of them possess these three meanings. However, this present section on the "gathering of matters" speaks specifically of the arhat who is liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*).
Therefore, since it is stated within this section on the gathering of matters that it "gathers superior qualities," we know that this refers to the one liberated both ways.
This refers to a person of liberation.
Regarding the statement "furthermore, the gate of ascending to the highest," the commentary correlates the three meanings found in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* with these three gates:

the gate of ascending to the highest corresponds to the permanent destruction of the thieves of affliction (*kleśa*), and the gate of the general and specific characteristics corresponds to being worthy of receiving sublime offerings.
Regarding the statement that "the categories of grasping (*parigraha*) are assigned to birth without segmentation," and so forth:
these are assigned merely according to their coarse characteristics; they do not yet constitute a detailed analysis of the minute particulars.

This assignment of the meaning of the school’s tenets (*siddhānta*) across the three major sections is not the primary intent of this treatise, nor is it the actual reality according to logical principle. Such is the case in this treatise.

This differs from the tenets of the Sūtra school. Mouzi states: "As for the tenets of our school, since there is no further existence (punarbhava) for Arhats, it is irrelevant whether [the path] consists of both [concentration and wisdom] or of wisdom alone;
therefore, this [Sūtra] does not correspond [to our view]. According to the *Dharmapada-śāstra*, such is the principle;
however, the underlying intent is to take that which possesses both."

Regarding the statement that the "newly translated scriptures" say [this], it means that what was previously omitted is now provided. In the sūtras and śāstras translated during the Great Tang, Ānanda is invariably excluded;
this scripture likewise lacks the three preceding sections praising his virtues. This is because Nandika (Ānanda) was still at the stage of a learner (*śaikṣa*), and thus he was set aside.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: "For what reason was Ānanda still at the stage of a learner (*śaikṣa*)? It answers:
"In the previous praise of the arhats, Ānanda was not included in their number. Why? Because he remained at the stage of a learner and had not yet abandoned desire. It further asks:

"The Venerable Ānanda, having extensively realized nirvāṇa, has for immeasurable kalpas constantly attended upon the Buddha, upheld the treasury of the Dharma, and possessed sharp faculties and wisdom."
“Wisdom! Why have you not yet abandoned desire and remained a person in training (śaikṣa)? Answer: “My original vow was thus: ‘Among those of great learning, I am the foremost.
If I were to attain the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya), I would be far removed from the Buddha and unable to provide him with service and offerings.
Therefore, I remain on the stage of training. This passage is omitted in the version translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Tang dynasty.
"Sūtra" is the general title for a new scripture.
Regarding the listing of titles: sixteen phrases extensively praise its efficacy; since its virtue is most honorable, its name should be prominent.
It shall indeed increase one's merit, and truly, one should joyfully desire to hear it. Twenty-one persons are designated to form four invocations. This is the plan.

It is said: Although the great assembly numbered twelve thousand people, the fact that only twenty-one individuals are specifically designated is merely the intention of the compilers to exercise brevity;
it carries no other special significance. Nevertheless, within the listing of names, the structural divisions (*ko-wen*) appear to be interrupted. To discuss the general intent of these divisions:
In total there are four types of structural divisions (*kośa*): first, division according to distinct categories; second, division according to the mutual following of thematic classes;
third, division of the text according to its meaning; and fourth, division of the meaning according to the text. For these reasons, when dividing the text, there may occasionally be interruptions.
Briefly stated, there are twenty-one persons, divided into nine pairs: first, the initial pair of two who abandon the heterodox and depart from defilement—Caitra abandoning suffering and pleasure.
[The first] group of three is named for their abandonment of error; Kāśyapa was so called because he was free from defilement.
The second group of three consists of those paired with dragons, elephants, mountains, and rivers: Uruvilvā was named after the dragon [there], Gayā after the mountain, and Nadī after the river.

The third group of two consists of those paired with supreme wisdom and wondrous supernormal powers: Śāriputra possessed supreme wisdom, and Mahāmaudgalyāyana possessed wondrous supernormal powers. The fourth group of three...
Regarding the pairings of those with eloquent speech and vast vision: Mahākatyāyana possessed eloquent speech, while Aniruddha possessed vast vision;
Kapphiṇa was capable of both. In the fifth instance, two individuals achieved their pairings through the fruition of past habitual tendencies:

Gavāmpati’s was due to past habituation, while Revata’s was due to what was accomplished in the present, being a matter of this very life. In the sixth instance, two individuals were hindered by residual habits and adverse conditions.
"Correct. Pilindavatsa is named 'Residual Habit. Bakula is named 'Adverse Conditions'; adverse conditions refers to his stepmother.
This constitutes the third instance of three people reversing their delusion and severing attachment. Mahākauṣṭhila and Nanda constitute the second instance of two people reversing their delusion.
Sundarananda severed his attachment; these eight pairs were matched by two individuals who transformed existence and discoursed on emptiness:
Pūrṇa transformed existence, while Subhūti discoursed on emptiness. The ninth pair consisted of those who understood the profound and practiced the secret:

Ānanda understood the profound, while Rāhula practiced the secret. These nine pairs were distinct. Now follows the first: abandoning error and departing from defilement—the Dragon, the Elephant, the Mountain, and the Water.
These are combined into a single recitation.
Regarding the statement "among these twenty-one persons, there are two types": first, a general summary of the sequence; second, the detailed analysis of five individuals.

The initial section has three parts: first, renunciation; second, virtues; third, the differentiation of alternative names. These are categorized according to the chronological order of their renunciation.
First, the five individuals beginning with Ājñātakauṇḍinya are listed.
As for the statement "such as the *Baoen jing* (Sūtra on Requiting Kindness)," the seven subsequent classes of persons all refer to the sequence of those who left the household life.
The total of one thousand two hundred and fifty people is cited as a general figure. Among the names recorded in the summary, only six are actually enumerated.
As for the categories, the first five groups were not included; thus, there are one thousand two hundred and fifty [monks].
Although the bhikṣus numbered twelve thousand, only twenty-one individuals are listed because the compilers intended to be concise, and there is no other underlying meaning.
Regarding the statement that "the practice and virtue may be greater, lesser, or equal": first, he converted the five bhikṣus; next, he converted Mahākāśyapa;
and next, he converted the three Kāśyapas. If one follows the chronological order of their renunciation, Mahākāśyapa was ordained after the three Kāśyapas, and Śāriputra was ordained after Kātyāyana.
Since these two individuals are listed here first, [it is because their virtues were greater].
It should be understood that the names are not listed according to the sequence of their renunciation, but rather according to the magnitude of their virtues.
Regarding the statement "the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*," the question is whether this sequence of virtues is based solely on this sutra, or if it applies to other sutras as well.
The answer in the commentary states: "The *Vimalakīrti* and others are arranged in order according to their virtuous conduct. Thus, it says: "This excludes others."
This is the teaching.
Regarding the statement "twelve [categories] according to the *Sūtra* and so forth," one asks:

The previously cited *Sūtra on Repaying Kindness through Cause and Effect* states that after the Buddha attained enlightenment, he went to the Deer Park after twenty-one days, first ordaining five people, and subsequently ordaining Nanda and others. Why, then, [does this differ from] the ten...?
Second, due to differences among the sūtras. The *Dapian* (Great Commentary) states: "Twelve [differences] arise from the sūtras and so forth.

This refers to the discrepancies in what was recited by the Venerable Elders (*sthavira*) within the cave, those outside the hall, and the Great Assembly (*mahāsāṃghika*), and so on. (The above constitutes the general sequence of conditions.)

Regarding the mention of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* and others: next, below, the five persons are formally identified. "Original Limit" (*mūlānta*) refers to the principle of the Four Noble Truths. "One who has realized" (*vijñātṛ*) means one who understands the meaning.
Because he was formerly deluded and now understands, he is so named. Yong says: Suffering (*duḥkha*) and its Accumulation (*samudaya*) constitute the original limit of saṃsāra;

Cessation (*nirodha*) and the Path (*mārga*) constitute the original limit of world-transcendence. He is called "One who has Realized the Original Limit" because he understood the principle of the Four Noble Truths, namely, Aśvajit.
"Root" (*mūla*) refers to True Suchness (*tathatā*); it is the root of all phenomena. "Understanding" (*vidyā*) is a designation applied to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

"Limit" (*koṭi*) is a designation applied to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Thus, it is called the "Ultimate Limit of the Root" (*mūlakoṭi*). Mouzi said: "Non-Buddhists also have an 'ultimate limit' (*koṭi*).

This refers to the first chapter of the *Śata-śāstra*, which refutes thirteen types of great non-Buddhist schools; therein, the "ultimate limit" is also discussed. The treatise states: "Others falsely conceptualize that there is one..."

"O Mahābrahmā, [the notions of] time, direction, the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*), spontaneous emptiness, and our own eternal, substantially existent selves—which possess all functional capacities and give rise to all phenomena—are all refuted in the same manner. This refers to the Āndhaka heretics;

they reckon that originally there were no sun, moon, stars, planets, empty space, or heaven and earth, but only a great mass of water. At that time, the Āndhaka was born from it like a golden egg, encircled by a golden hue."
At that time, the matured [egg] broke into two parts: one part became heaven, and one part became earth.
In the space between them, a Great Brahmā King was born, acting as the progenitor of all sentient beings and the lord of all things animate and inanimate.
Therefore, the non-Buddhist teacher Āṇḍa spoke of the "Great Āṇḍa," which he claimed was born from Brahmā; he held that Brahmā is eternally one and is the cause of nirvāṇa.
Such a primordial limit is not the meaning intended here.
Regarding the statement that "in Sanskrit it is called Ajñāta" and so forth, this indicates that this Venerable One was male.
If one says "Gautamī," the sound "mī" indicates she is female; in the Western Regions (India), these two sounds distinguish between male and female. "Ajñāta" is the name.
Regarding "understanding the meaning" (*ajñāta-kaundinya*): because he was the first to attain awakening and understanding, the name "Understanding" (*Ajñāta*) was established.
First, he is the foremost among those liberated by Śākyamuni; second, he is the first of the five [monks]. Therefore, he is called "the first. Lü [Cheng] says: Kauṇḍinya is a Brahmin surname.
According to the general custom of the Western regions (India), one takes fire-vessels as a clan name. *Kaundinya* means "fire-vessel" in this language. His ancestor...
He served the sacrificial fire, and from this he derived his clan name. Based on the single name Kauṇḍinya, the three characters "Ajñāta" are added.
"Ajñāta" is also said to mean "without knowledge. Because he has already realized the principle of non-self and thereby generated wisdom, he is named Ajñāta.
"Ajñāta" carries the sense of awakening and understanding. Thus, when one says "Ājñātakauṇḍinya," it refers to both his personal and family names.
Both terms are raised together. This name was established because the Śuddhāvāsa devas saw his initial awakening, thereby distinguishing him from other noble ones (*ārya*).
As for the term *Inga-kyo* (Sutra of Cause and Effect), it refers to the extensive exposition of the teachings.
Regarding those spoken of as "inner and outer relatives": there are three from the father’s lineage—first, Aśvaka; second, Aniruddha;
and third, Mahānāman—and two from the maternal uncle’s lineage—Kauṇḍinya and Daśabalakāśyapa. The father’s lineage is called "inner," while the mother’s side is called "outer."
Those of the same surname are called "relatives" (*jñāti*); those of different surnames are called "clansmen" (*gotra*).
These are the relatives among all kinsmen. As for the statement regarding the five men who disputed: there were three paternal uncles who calculated that asceticism was the Way;
seeing the Prince eating hemp and wheat, they abandoned him and departed. There were two maternal uncles who calculated that austerity was the Way; seeing the Prince eat... [text ends].
He abandoned the milk-rice and departed. The five men gathered together at Rṣipatana Deer Park and discussed the matter of the Prince’s success or failure.

Regarding their statement that the Prince had tested himself by following the various non-Buddhist practitioners, [the commentary] says: "Question: For six years he practiced only asceticism; how was this?"

When asked, "Is it pleasure? he replied: "Under Udraka Rāmaputra, I studied the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). The concentration of mind was serene and joyful; this was the bliss of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
In contrast to his six years of asceticism, this is called 'blissful practice'. Zao says: "Because it accords with both body and mind, it is called 'bliss'."

Mou said: "It is certainly of a wholesome nature (*kuśala*). Among the mental factors associated with the wholesome, there is the bliss of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), which is also termed 'bliss' (*sukha*). This is included within the category of the wholesome.
As for the statement that it 'surpasses those practitioners,' since those non-Buddhists consume only one sesame seed and one grain of barley per day, it is said to surpass them. [End of] Excerpt.
There are two explanations: first, the meaning of "guarding" (wei), which refers to the path; second, the meaning of "method" (shu), which refers to skillful arts.
Regarding the statement that the Venerable One renounced the milk-rice porridge, the fifth chapter on Cause and Effect states: after the Prince had practiced austerities for six years...
He thought to himself, "I cannot attain perfect enlightenment with this emaciated body. He then went to the Nairañjanā River to bathe.
After he had bathed, a deity pressed down upon a tree branch so that the Prince could grasp it and emerge from the water. By the riverbank was a cowherd girl named Nandabalā;
the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven exhorted her to prepare and offer milk-rice as an offering. Upon hearing this, the girl was greatly delighted.
From within the earth, a thousand-petaled lotus flower emerged, upon which was milk-rice porridge.

When the woman saw this, she felt a sense of wonder and immediately offered it to the Prince for him to eat. After he had eaten, he recited a prayer of aspiration and then proceeded toward the Bodhi tree.
On the way, he encountered the elder Śubhavyūha, who offered him grass to sit upon. This elder was an emanation of Śakra; having sat upon the grass, he attained perfect enlightenment.

Having attained awakening and realized perfect enlightenment, he reflected upon those who should be delivered. He thought that only Udraka Rāmaputra had realized the meditative attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and was capable of receiving the sublime Dharma.
A voice from the sky announced: "Since his death, seven days have already passed. The Tathāgata sighed, saying: "How is it that he did not meet [me]?
Furthermore, he observed again and saw that Ārāḍa Kālāma was sitting in the meditative concentration of the sphere of nothingness and was fit to receive [the teaching].

Regarding the ultimate truth, the devas replied: "It has been five days since his death. The Tathāgata sighed again, pitying their meager merit, and after observing once more that only these five individuals remained, he proceeded to the Deer Park to deliver these five men and first turn the Wheel of Dharma.
The Buddha asked whether they had understood. Among the five men, Ājñāta-Kauṇḍinya was the first to report, saying, "I have understood the Dharma.

In this manner, it was successively reported by the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven and others that they too had understood. Thus, he was given the name based on the meaning of "understanding" (Ājñāta).
Regarding the statement "that is a masculine sound" and so forth: in the Western [tradition] of explaining phenomena (*dharma*), there are eight case-inflections (*vibhakti*).

These consist of the nominative (*kartṛ*), accusative (*karman*), instrumental (*karaṇa*), ablative (*apādāna*), locative (*adhikaraṇa*), and vocative (*saṃbodhana*). Since all phenomena are expressed through these eight cases, the term "masculine sound" refers to that which is expressed within the category of the "virile and weighty" (*puṃliṅga*) sounds.
If one pronounces it with a light and clear tone, it is called by a feminine sound, which likewise corresponds to the four tones of this region.
As for the name Mahākāśyapa, it is translated here as "Great Kūrma" (Great Turtle).

His ancestors practiced the Way and moved a numinous tortoise to carry forth a divine chart as an auspicious omen; from this he derived his name and was thus called Kūrma. His alternative name is Pilātong.
He was named "Son" (*Putta*) because he was born beneath a *piyāla* tree.
He served as the elder of the five mountains and acted as the chief elder (*sthavira*) among the monks of Jambudvīpa, practicing the twelve *dhūta* austerities. Kāśyapa was foremost among them.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that when the devas requested the compilation of the scriptures (*saṃgīti*), they praised him, saying: "In his old age, desire, anger, and pride have already been eliminated."
His form was like a pillar of purple-gold, majestic from top to bottom and incomparably sublime. His eyes were pure and clear like lotus flowers.
As for the reason he is called Kāśyapa, "Kāśyapa" is the clan name of the Brahmins.
Regarding the statement that "in ancient times there were sages whose bodies [possessed light]," the question is asked: "By what cause is his clan name Kāśyapa?
The answer, as stated in the commentary, is: "In ancient times there were sages whose bodies possessed radiance that eclipsed the light of the sun and moon;
Kāśyapa belongs to their lineage, and for this reason his clan name is Kāśyapa (Drinking-Light). Furthermore, he himself also..."

His radiance was such that it could drink in and eclipse the light of the sun and moon; therefore, his clan name was Kāśyapa (Drinking Light), and he took this clan name as his personal name, being called Kāśyapa.
Question: By what cause did he possess bodily radiance? Answer: The *Dharmatrāta-dharmadāna-saṃgraha* (Fu fǎ chuán) states:
Ninety-one kalpas ago, a Buddha appeared in the world named Vipaśyin Buddha. After he entered nirvana, his fourfold assembly of disciples erected a stūpa made of the seven precious gems.
At that time, within that stūpa there was an image of the Buddha, yet its face lacked a golden hue.

There was a poor woman who, while wandering about begging for food, picked up a single gold bead. Desiring to use this bead to restore the Buddha’s face, she went at once to a goldsmith to consult him.
Upon seeing her, the goldsmith said, "If you can give up the bead, I can give up my craft. Thus they made an agreement together.

He made a vow: "May we always be husband and wife; may our bodies be golden in color; may we possess bodies that experience supreme happiness; and may we constantly practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
From that time forth, for ninety-one *kalpas*, his body was of true golden color, and he experienced supreme and wondrous bliss among gods and humans.
In his final birth, he was born in the Heaven of Limited Purity (*Parittaśubha*) within the seventh Brahma-world, where he enjoyed various forms of happiness. At that time, in Magadha...
In the kingdom of Tā, there was a brahmin named Kulida. His family was immensely wealthy, surpassing King Bimbisāra by a thousandfold.
In his house, even the lowest quality of white cotton cloth was worth one hundred thousand pieces of gold.
He possessed sixty granaries of golden grain, with each granary containing three hundred and thirty *hu*. Although his family was so wealthy, they had no offspring. At that time, the heavens...
He made offerings at shrines and temples, seeking [blessings] without fail, yet for many years there was no sign. Later, beside his house, there was a sacred tree.
The husband and wife would often go there to pray; they vowed together that if there were no response within seven days, they would surely cut it down and burn it.
The tree spirit became distressed and fearful, and reported this to the Four Heavenly Kings. The Four Heavenly Kings reported it to Śakra. Śakra immediately—

He went to the Brahmā King and related the aforementioned matters in detail. The Brahmā King then saw that among the Śuddhāvāsa-devas of the seventh heaven, a master goldsmith, having exhausted his celestial retribution, was about to descend for rebirth. He then exhorted him to be born into the family of Kūṭadanta.

Once he had been conceived, ten months were fulfilled, and then a divine form was born, peerless in its upright beauty; his body was like the color of gold, with golden light radiating from its sides.
It illuminated more than forty *li*. An astrologer divined and said, "This child possesses the blessings of past lives; he will certainly leave the household life.
When his parents heard this, they were all filled with sorrow and distress. They deliberated together, saying, "That which the world craves most is beautiful form.
If we betroth him a wife, he will surely feel attachment and longing. When he was only fifteen years old, they arranged his marriage. Kāśyapa then spoke to his parents, saying:

"My aspiration is for purity; I do not desire a wife. For the sake of his welfare, he devised a plan and said to his parents, "If you can obtain for me a golden-hued maiden of incomparable beauty, I shall then take her as my wife. His parents immediately summoned a brahmin.
They searched everywhere for such a person. Then, several Brahmins cast a golden deity with a handsome and upright countenance.
They traveled through various kingdoms, towns, villages, and hamlets by means of a carriage, proclaiming in a loud voice:

"If there is any woman who beholds this golden deity and pays it homage, she shall surely obtain a fine husband when the time comes for her to marry. Hearing this, women vied with one another to come out and pay their respects.
Then he saw a woman whose body was like gold, her features extraordinary and unlike those of ordinary people.

This woman had been a poor girl who, in the past, had offered a golden pearl to the city. Subsequently, several Brahmins had conspired together and married her to the son of Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana as his wife.
Once the marriage was completed, the husband and wife each made a supreme vow. Although they were...
The husband and wife had no thoughts of sensual desire; each occupied a separate room, and together they practiced meditative contemplation, their pure conduct being identical.
When their parents heard this, they thought to themselves in secret: "I married them off for fear they would renounce the world. Now, observing their demeanor, both wish to leave the household.
Thereupon, they demolished the two rooms and made them into a single chamber, providing them with a single bed. Later, they further established a formal agreement.
"When I am asleep, you shall practice the Way; when you are lying down, I shall practice the Way. Later, as his wife fell fast asleep, she placed her hand upon the bedside table.
A venomous snake entered the room, intending to sting her hand. Upon seeing this, Kāśyapa wrapped his own robe around her hand and lifted it onto the bed.
His wife then woke up and rebuked him, saying: "You made a vow with me that we would not..."
[The husband] drew near. He asked again, "For what purpose do you raise your hand? Kāśyapa replied, "A snake has entered; fearing it might harm your hand, I am merely lifting it up.
Thereupon, his wife answered him with a verse: "Better that my own body be consumed by the venomous snake, than that you should ever violate your vow by touching it.
Snake venom may cause a single life to perish, but the poison of defilement leads to an endless sinking into ruin."
The father replied, "To thrust a sharp blade into fire is indeed difficult, but practicing the path before you is more difficult than this.

The pond where the dragon resided was also called the Mucilinda Pond. If the name is established based on the dragon, it is spoken according to the root;
if the name of the forest is established, it is spoken according to the branches and leaves. Now, the swelling that has arisen upon his chest is derived from [the dragon].

Mountain. To the southeast of the mountain is a stūpa; this was the village of Kāśyapa’s former birthplace.

Answer: Regarding the explanation of the summary: in the western regions, a year consists of three seasons. First is the hot season, lasting four months;

"I shall now go there to deliver them. Having reflected thus, he set out from the city of Vārāṇasī for the kingdom of Magadha.

"This is contradictory. All the other rooms are already occupied by disciples; only this stone chamber is extremely quiet and could accommodate you.

"Although there is a malevolent dragon, it has already been granted [to you]. Kāśyapa spoke again, saying, “If you can remain here, you may do as you please.
The Buddha said, “Excellent,” and at that very moment, he entered the stone chamber, sat down cross-legged, and entered into samādhi.

At that time, the evil dragon’s poisonous mind grew even more intense, and smoke issued from its entire body. The World-Honored One immediately entered the *tejo-dhātu-samādhi* (fire-element samādhi).
When the dragon saw this, its flames surged toward heaven, burning the stone cave. Seeing this fire, Kāśyapa’s disciples returned to their teacher;
seeing that the young śramaṇa was now being harmed by the fire-dragon, they were deeply grieved and immediately urged their fellow disciples [to intervene].

They tried to extinguish it with water, but the fire could not be put out; instead, it blazed even more fiercely until the entire stone chamber was filled with flame. At that time, the World-Honored One remained unmoving in body and mind, his countenance serene.

When dawn had broken, Kāśyapa and his disciples went together to the Buddha’s dwelling. [There they saw] the young śramaṇa and the dragon...
"The fire is fierce; will you be harmed by it? The Buddha said, "My interior is pure;

When Kāśyapa and his disciples saw that the śramaṇa remained unburned amidst the fire and had subdued the evil dragon, placing it within his alms-bowl, they marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.

"It is because he has come to hear the Dharma that this light appears; it is merely his radiance.

When the third night arrived, Śakra descended to listen to the Dharma, emitting a great radiance like the rising sun. On the fourth night, Mahābrahmā descended.
While listening to the Dharma, [the Buddha] emitted a great radiance like the sun at its zenith. Having seen this, Kāśyapa thought to himself:

The Tathāgata then ignited the fire himself. Once the offerings were completed and he intended to extinguish it, the fire refused to go out.

He related the preceding events in detail. The Buddha said, "Go away quickly. Immediately, the fire extinguished itself.
Kāśyapa thought to himself, "Although this young śramaṇa possesses supernatural powers, they are not equal to the true path of my own.
At that time, Kāśyapa sent his disciples out at dawn to split wood, but their axes could not be lifted. They then sought the World-Honored One; once he had lifted them, they again refused to work.
He descended and reported this to the World-Honored One. The World-Honored One said, "Go back quickly; you must let the axe fall.

"Pūrvavideha. This fruit in my alms bowl is from there; tomorrow, when it is time to eat, you must act accordingly.
Again, he went to Pūrvavideha and took an āmra fruit to show to Kāśyapa. On the following day, he went to Aparagoyānī and took a harītakī.

Māgandiya said: "Young śramaṇa, although your supernatural powers are swift, they are ultimately not equal to the true and correct path of mine.

Regarding Śāriputra: the old translation was "Sheli," which is a corruption and abbreviation of "Shenzi" (Son of Śarī). Śāriputra is named after his mother.
As for the claim that "Śarī" refers to the *śārika* bird, it is not contradictory in the Western Regions to call the thrush the *śārika*; however, here [in China], the *śārika* is...

Regarding the statement that [the name] is due to the mother’s eloquence: the character for "son" (*zi*) belongs to the Venerable One, while the character for "śuka" (*tǐu*) belongs to the mother. Thus, the mother's name was Śukī.

His father was of lofty talent and vast learning, possessing profound insight into the subtle and the refined; there were no scriptures he had not thoroughly studied. His wife was moved by a dream and related it in detail to her husband, saying:

Suddenly she became pregnant. Her mother suddenly became wise and eloquent; her discourse was profound and her speech flowed without impediment.

The Three Truths. This correctly elucidates the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). Question: Why is the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) not mentioned? Answer: Śāriputra possesses sharp faculties;

by briefly stating that which is realized, it is certain that he knows there must be that which realizes it. At that time, having heard this teaching, Śāriputra immediately realized the first fruit (*srotāpatti-phala*) upon hearing the words.

Regarding the phrase "not only now, but also [in the past]," the Sūtra says: In a past life, Śāriputra was a potter who encountered a Buddha appearing in the world, also named Śākyamuni, and he had a disciple also named Śāriputra. He then made this vow:
"I vow that in a future life I shall meet Śākyamuni Buddha and become his wise disciple, also named Śāriputra.
As for the statement that he was "also named Upatiṣya," this translates as "one who discusses the meaning" (a debater). He was named after his father;

since his father was able to discuss the meaning [of the Dharma], those in the Western Regions who explain the meaning of treatises are collectively called Upadeśaka. Thus, it is appropriate to name him after his father. Because...

The father was inferior and the mother was superior; thus, the name was established based on the superior one. At first glance, reading the commentary, it seems as though Śāriputra himself explained the meaning of the treatise and thereby acquired this name for himself.
However, according to the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, the name was derived from his father.

Regarding the statement that he is called "Great Collector of Beans" (Mahā-mudgalaputra): this is taking the mother’s surname as his name. "Beans" (*mudga*) is the general term for all varieties of legumes.
In ancient times, the ancestors of the Sage lived in a secluded mountain retreat and constantly gathered green and yellow beans to eat; it was from this that their clan name was established.
The Venerable One’s mother belonged to that lineage, and thus he took her family name. Maudgalyāyana and Śāriputra were both possessed of brilliant wisdom and insight.

They were different [in appearance], yet the Venerable One’s refined discernment surpassed all others, and their wisdom and talent were equal. Having been close friends since youth, they were always together in every movement and action.
They formed a pact to travel for study and, sharing a mutual distaste for worldly life, both left the household life to become monks.
Regarding the phrase "attaining great supernormal powers" (*mahābhijñā*): this distinguishes him from others who merely gather beans, and thus he receives the title "Great" (*Mahā*).

He returned to the great city, where Śāriputra met Aśvajit and attained the first fruit of the path (*srotāpatti-phala*). Maudgalyāyana then recounted this to Śāriputra, who thereby attained realization and understanding.

Having attained the first fruit under Śāriputra, he and his followers went together to the place where the World-Honored One was. From afar, the World-Honored One pointed toward them and addressed them.
He said, "The one who has come here is a disciple of my supernormal powers. The World-Honored One said, "Welcome, Bhikṣu!
His beard and hair fell away naturally, and the saffron robe was donned upon his body. After seven days had passed, he attained the fruit of Arhatship.

At one time, while the Buddha was at the Lake of No-Heat (Anavatapta), in the course of preaching the Dharma, the eight classes of beings and the fourfold assembly had all gathered. The Buddha said, "Observe those within the assembly."
[Fragmentary] "Śāriputra, for what reason have you not come? Therefore, I have sent Maudgalyāyana to summon you.
He encountered Śāriputra while he was mending his robes in the mountains. [Śāriputra said: "Wait a moment until I have finished mending my robes. Maudgalyāyana said:
"If you do not go quickly, I shall move this mountain along with you to the great assembly. Śāriputra then placed his robe and belt upon the ground and said to Maudgalyāyana: "If..."
When he lifted this belt, the mountain also moved. Maudgalyāyana exerted all his supernatural powers, yet he could not lift it; the earth shook because of it.
He withdrew his distant supernatural power and returned, only to see Śāriputra sitting in the assembly. Maudgalyāyana looked up and sighed, saying:
"Today I have finally realized that supernatural power is not as superior as wisdom (the supreme, wondrous, and penetrating understanding)."
Regarding the statement that "in Sanskrit it is Mahākātyāyana": this is the fourth term, meaning "one of lofty views and broad perspective.

*Mahākātyāyana* is a clan name (*gotra*). *Naḥ* is the masculine form; this translates as "one of the shearing/clipping lineage" (*kṣauraka-vamśa*), which is a Brahmin clan, taking "shearing" as their family name.
Regarding the phrase "may all the sages grant their vows," there is also a variant manuscript that reads "may they obtain. The sages' prayer for blessing says, "May you attain the Way of the Buddha";
thus it is said, "may all the sages grant their vows for [his] attainment. It is on this basis that the name was established.
Regarding the statement that the Venerable’s body is male, there are two interpretations. First, it is called "Great" (Mahā) to distinguish him from other men of low birth.

Second, it is said that because the Buddha constantly praised him, saying, "Among my disciples, he is the foremost among those who preach the Dharma," he is called "Great" on account of receiving the Buddha's praise.
Regarding what is called the "rope-fan": in the Western Regions, where the heat is great, people place fans at the entrances of their homes.
Later, some ignorant person gradually began to carry them away; consequently, they tied them with ropes.
Once, when Kātyāyanī’s mother was raising Kātyāyana alone after her husband had passed away, she went out accompanied by her son and saw a rope-fan at the entrance of a house being carried along.
The fan fluttered in the wind but did not fall to the ground. The mother asked her son, "Why does the fan not fall?

The son replied, "It is because it is tied with a cord. The mother said, "My not remarrying is also due to you; therefore, let us call you Cord-Fan (Śaṅkhapāla). This name was derived from the metaphor."
Regarding the statement that "Cintāmaṇi" means "Superior through Reflection": there was a ṛṣi who, by virtue of possessing [the wisdom of] hearing and reflection, was superior to other persons;
because the Venerable One belongs to that lineage of ṛṣis, he is called "Superior through Reflection. This is not correct.

Regarding the term *Aniruddha* in the Sanskrit language: he was the son of King Amṛtodana, the nephew of King Śuddhodana, the cousin of the World-Honored One (*Bhagavān*), the elder brother of Ānanda, and the uncle of Rāhula.
In the past, during the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, he was the son of an elder named Mahādatta; by means of offering lamps from a hundred *droṇas*, he constantly...
He attained preeminence in the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). The *Upamā-sūtra* states: "Innumerable kalpas ago, Aniruddha was once a bandit.

During the night, encountering wind and rain, he entered a Buddhist shrine to take shelter. While resting there, he saw that a lamp was about to go out; he used the tip of an arrow to poke the flame back up.
Seeing the Buddha’s radiance, the hairs on his body stood on end, and he thought: 'How noble are these people who can practice such generosity!'"

"What have I stolen? he thought, and thus he abandoned that deed. Because he continued this root of goodness through illumination, for ninety-one *kalpas* he constantly possessed the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
Since his root of goodness was never extinguished, he is named Aniruddha ("Unextinguished"). Furthermore, in the past, he once offered a single meal to a *pratyekabuddha*.
For fifty *kalpas*, he experienced superior blessings and happiness among gods and humans. Subsequently, he attained the fruit of *aśaikṣa* (Arhatship) and remained constant.
He attained his wish and was no longer poor. When the Tathāgata preached the Dharma, Aniruddha would fall asleep; this occurred in every assembly.
The Buddha rebuked him before the multitude: "Alas! Why do you sleep? You are like a snail, a clam, or a bivalve shell, remaining thus for hundreds or thousands of years, revolving without end.
Having heard this, Aniruddha felt ashamed before the assembly and immediately took a bamboo twig...

He plucked out his eyes and did not sleep for many days, whereupon he lost his sight. He summoned the physician Jīvaka, who said, "Because you have not slept for a long time, your visual faculty has been starved to death;
it cannot be cured. The Buddha taught that one should cultivate the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). Among the noble disciples (*ārya-śrāvaka*), [it was cultivated thus].
He was foremost in the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). Lufu said: "He could see the affairs of the trichiliocosm; people of the time called him 'Half-Head Divine Eye.
When one possesses [the divine eye] fully, it is called 'Full-Head'; having lost the fleshly eye while possessing only the divine eye, he is named 'Half-Head.
The Tathāgata would cite the pure matter (*rūpa*) of the Form Realm as 'Full-Head,' while Aniruddha, by virtue of his partial attainment, is named 'Half-Head. These two interpretations are correct."
Regarding the statement that the character "應" (yīng) should be written with the radical "而" (ér): this is because one does not know from which [radical] the character "菟" (tù) is derived.
Regarding this constellation of Bharaṇī: Kapphiṇa was capable of two things. When this bhikṣu first left the household life and sought to see the Buddha, he set out toward the Buddha’s dwelling.
Encountering rain, he took up lodging at the house of a potter and used grass as his seat. Another bhikṣu then arrived seeking lodging;
[Kapphiṇa] immediately pushed aside the grass seat to yield it to him and sat upon the ground. Later, they questioned one another regarding where he intended to go.

"Where are you going? he asked. He replied, "I am going to see the Buddha. Later, the bhikṣu preached the Dharma for him, and he suddenly attained the Way. This later bhikṣu was none other than the Buddha himself.
As for what is called the "Housing Star" (Fángxīng), it appears at dusk in the *chén* position in the fourth month, and it is seen at dusk in the *yǐ* position in the fifth month. Thus, these two...

The eighteen lunar mansions revolve clockwise according to their ascending and descending nodes, while the sun, moon, and five planets move counter-clockwise. However, the lunar mansion *Mṛgaśiras* (the Deer Head) appears monthly;
this Venerable One was born when this mansion appeared, and thus it is said he was born when *Mṛgaśiras* appeared.
As for the statement that "in Sanskrit it is called *gupta-pati*," this refers to the fifth [stage], present habitual tendencies; the sixth, present residual karmic conditions of evil;
and the seventh, returning delusion. These are combined into a single recitation.
Regarding the statement that in the past he plucked a stalk of rice: in former times, the Venerable One was once an ox tied to the threshing floor of a certain house.
Later at night, a bandit came to steal grain from the floor; the ox then bellowed to warn him, not allowing him to take the grain.

The bandit stepped forward, intending to seize him, but was again rebuffed by the ox's bellowing. Realizing it was an ox, the bandit asked for the reason behind this, and [the ox] recounted in detail the events of his previous life, including the matter of the harvested grain.
The bandit then departed in shame. Question: Since its appearance is like that of an ox, it must be a being whose physical form is close to that of an animal;
how, then, could it have attained sainthood? Answer: It manifested these signs provisionally; they were not actually so.

Regarding the term "ox-chewer" (*gomaya*) bhikṣu: "chew" (*ma*) refers to chewing or rumination; "chewer" (*go*) refers to the food regurgitated by an ox. An-guo (An Shigao) states that the *Pinfen Gongde Lun* (Treatise on the Analysis of Merit) says:

Fearing that people might slander him and thereby incur transgression, the Buddha ordered [the bhikṣu] to cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) in the Śirīṣa grove within the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
The term "Śirīṣa" refers here to the *he-zang* tree (Acacia suma). When the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa...
After the parinirvāṇa, when the Dharma was being compiled, Mahākāśyapa dispatched a junior monk named Tissa, instructing him:
"Go and summon [Kauṇḍinya], for there is now a great matter of the Saṃgha that requires his presence; he should come quickly. Kauṇḍinya asked the messenger who had come: "What is it?"
"Has the Buddha entered *nirvāṇa*? He replied, "The Buddha has passed into extinction. Again he asked, "Is my preceptor Śāriputra still present?

He replied, "He has already entered extinction. Having heard this, Pāṭaliputra fainted for a long time; upon regaining consciousness, he sighed and said, "The Tathāgata has entered *nirvāṇa*, and now the Great Master, my preceptor, has also passed away.
The world is empty and void; I can no longer remain here. He then ignited fire to cremate his own body and immediately entered *nirvāṇa*.
First, he manifested four streams of water flowing down to the place of the council in Jambudvīpa. Within the water, he spoke this verse:
"Kauṇḍinya bows his head in homage To the Great Virtuous Saṃgha, supreme among the wondrous assembly. Hearing that the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, I too shall pass away."
Just as when a great elephant departs, its calf follows;
as for the statement that this refers to the constellation Śravaṇā, it is the constellation of the northern quarter. Alternatively, it is called a comet, which is a malevolent star.
Because he was born when this star appeared, he was named accordingly. The passage beginning with "This is sometimes called... and following is an interpolation in the commentary (*śū*).
One should examine various editions, as their presence or absence is not fixed.
Regarding the two ghosts mentioned in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*: the treatise states that one ghost devours [the person], signifying that birth must inevitably lead to death;

the other ghost revives them, signifying that death must inevitably lead to birth. These occur simultaneously. At that time, Revata was sent on a distant journey and stayed alone overnight in an empty dwelling.
In an empty house during the night, there was one ghost carrying a dead person. Another ghost followed behind, angrily reviling the first ghost, saying:
"This dead person is my property! How can you claim it? You previously said it was your property!"
"I brought this myself. Later, the other ghost also said, "It is truly my property; I brought it myself.
Thus, the two ghosts each held a dead person, their hands contending with one another. The first ghost said, "There is someone in this house;
ask him and you will know. The second ghost then questioned him. The man was terrified and spoke thus:
He thought to himself, "Everyone, whether tall or short, must die. Since I am now dead, I must not speak falsely. He then spoke according to the truth. "Alas!
This dead man was brought here by a ghost from the front; he was taken by a ghost from behind. When the latter ghost heard this, he became greatly enraged and seized the man's two hands and two feet.
"Uprooting" means to depart after separating [the limbs]. Having eaten one of this person's thighs, the ghost departed. The man felt ashamed and reflected upon its virtue;
he took the hands and feet of another dead person, joined them together, and restored him to life.

The man then contemplated: "The body my parents gave me has been devoured by the ghost until it is gone. Now, this entire body consists of another's flesh. Does this body of mine truly exist, or does it not?"
If one says it exists, it is entirely another's body; if one says it does not exist, this present body is here.
Reflecting thus, his mind and body became confused. A traveler seeking a path entered a temple and saw a monk there, asking him:
"Does my body exist, or does it not? The bhikṣus asked in return: "Who are you? He replied: "I am also..."
They did not know whether he was a human or a non-human. He related the aforementioned matters in detail. The bhikṣus said, "This person knows for himself that there is no self;
he is easy to teach and transform. They then spoke to him, saying, "From the very beginning, your body has always been without a self.

It is merely due to the temporary conjunction of the four great elements that it is called a 'conventional combination. " At that moment, he attained realization and severed all afflictions, attaining the fruit of arhatship.

Regarding the phrase "nominal conventional designation" (*prajñapti-saṃvṛti*), the *Cheng weishi lun shuji* (Commentary on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*) poses a question: "A corpse is insentient; how can it serve as a limb for a sentient being? The answer provides two interpretations: first, it is through the power of spirits and deities;

second, in reality this is not so—it is merely a demonstration of appearance. This is done to refute the attachment to a real self among sentient beings by revealing that what is conventionally designated lacks a self. Regarding the author's own objection: The *Cheng weishi lun shuji* raises a difficulty: if the corpse is merely a nominal designation, how can it be a limb of a sentient being? The response is that there are two explanations. One says it is due to the power of ghosts and spirits. The other says that in actual fact this is not the case; rather, it is a display of appearances.
This is intended to destroy the grasping at a truly existent self among sentient beings by demonstrating that these appearances are devoid of self. Thus, the *Shuji* itself presents the objection.

[The opponent] says: "The previous interpretation contradicts the principles of Vijñaptimātra. Once the various ripening consciousnesses (*vipākavijñāna*) have abandoned this body, they cause [the continuum] to take up another body;
there is no principle for it to be born again. How, then, could it be reconnected after having been severed? Mǔ replies: "This can also be explained by the power of ghosts and spirits."

The statement that [the consciousness] departs from and relies upon another body is spoken in reference to the power of karma. As for what is said to contradict reason, it contradicts the power of karma.
Furthermore, it is said that the power of meditative concentration and supernormal penetration is not fixed (it is merely the maturation of past habitual tendencies in the present).

Regarding the statement that "residual habits (vāsanā) still remain": Question: How can an Arhat possess residual habits? Within the praises of their virtues, it is stated that they have "well attained liberation of mind" because they have severed the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Now, to speak of "residual habits" seems quite contradictory. Answer: There are two kinds of habituation. First, afflictions themselves are habituation, as they arise from [past] cognition.
Second, the wisdom of Nirvana possesses a portion of the scent of delusion which is termed "habituation," like [the scent remaining in] a cloth that has been wrapped with incense.
Paper: Arhats are not without faults; this arises from the habituation of anger.
Regarding the statement "as if scolding the River Goddess": the goddess of the Ganges was, in a previous life, a maidservant in the household of Viśvāmitra.
She was later reborn as the river goddess. Once, while crossing the Ganges, Piṅgala [the Elder] addressed the goddess, who was a woman, as follows:
Piliṅga spoke: "Hey! You slave-girl, do not let the water flow. I wish to go away for a moment.

The goddess was filled with shame and quickly went to inform the Buddha, requesting that he cause him to repent and apologize for his transgression. She then joined her palms and said: "O slave-girl, do not be angry.
Had I known your name was 'slave-girl,' I would not have called you 'slave-girl. It was because I did not know your name that I called you 'slave-girl.'"
The son acted as a maidservant. This was the fault of calling him "maidservant" regarding what he previously possessed. "I pray that you, maidservant, may give with joy.
The maidservant opened her eyes wide and bared her beak in anger; the great assembly laughed all at once. The Buddha said, "Such are the residual habits; it is not a malicious intent.
It is like a śrāvaka breaking into dance, a pratyekabuddha putting on makeup, or Śāriputra seeing a gandharva playing the lute."

He then rose to dance. That he alone perceived the *yan-zhi* (a type of pigment) applied to his mouth and that his eyebrows were completely filled with ink—all these are residual habits (*vāsanā*). (The above concerns the exhaustion of residual habits.
As for the statement "holding one *harītakī*," the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* says: "There is one kind of *harītakī*."
It is endowed with six tastes and can eliminate all diseases; it is the king among medicines that require no dietary restrictions. The *Piyu jing* (Sutra of Similes) states:
"When Jīvaka died, the medicinal herbs of the world wept simultaneously, each saying: 'Only Jīvaka was able to know our respective potencies.
Now that Jīvaka is gone, who will be able to know these potencies of ours? We may be used incorrectly, or [the dosage] may be increased."
Sometimes [the medicine] was deficient, causing the illness not to be cured. The people of the world thought it was ineffective; only the harītakī fruit laughed out loud, "Ha ha!
and stood apart on one side, saying to itself, "I alone can cure all diseases; there is no need for compounding. For this reason, it neither wept nor laughed.
This arhat was once a drunkard in a past life who lay down at the entrance of a monastery. When the monks saw him, they placed him within the monastery.
In the middle of the night, while the monks were paying homage to the Buddha, there was one monk suffering from a headache. He was given a single harītakī fruit as an offering;
having consumed it, he was immediately cured. From that time forward, for ninety-one kalpas, he experienced supreme blessings and happiness among gods and humans.
Now, in this life, he has been born into a brahmin family.
Regarding the mention of his mother and others, there is another sutra which says: During the time of Vipaśyin Buddha, he was born as a slave.
From the Saṃgha, he received only the precept against killing; he said, "Because of my lowly status, I am unable to receive the other four precepts. By virtue of this causal condition...
He survived five times without dying. The former [cases] were due to the condition of being free from illness; the latter was due to the condition of not dying.
Regarding the two hundred and fifty precepts and the eight precepts for one day and one night, the matter requires that they be received and maintained in their entirety.

As for the five precepts, if one receives and maintains them, then it is considered complete. His father went far away, and subsequently his stepmother killed him; he survived five times without dying. First.

First, he could not die when boiled in a cauldron. Second, he was not scorched when fried on two griddles. Third, he did not perish when drowned in water. Fourth, he did not rot when swallowed by a fish.
Fifth, he was not wounded when cut with a blade.
Regarding the statement that "the eyes do not look upon women," a worldly proverb says: "A falcon that has been wounded by a bowstring is wary even when seeing a curved branch;
one who has once been bitten by a snake fears seeing a broken cord; one who has once been startled by a tiger is timid upon seeing a plow.
This Venerable One was once cruelly oppressed by his stepmother, and thus he is fearful of seeing women.

Regarding the King Aśoka: this arhat was one who, during his lifetime, had few desires and was content with little. Later, when King Aśoka offered him only a single coin, the arhat did not accept it as the stūpa rose up. The Master [Dao]xuan asked: "If this arhat attained the Mahāyāna at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and his body underwent the transformation of the 'changeable' (*pariṇāmika*), why is there now the matter of his physical remains and the building of a stūpa to make offerings to them? He replied: [The answer follows: "This is because he had previously made a vow to benefit sentient beings. Furthermore, although he had already attained the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*) and would never again undergo birth and death, he manifested the appearance of passing away for the sake of those to be converted, so that they might plant roots of goodness. It is like the Elder Śāriputra, who, though having long since realized the fruit of Arhatship, manifested the appearance of entering parinirvāṇa for the sake of the Licchavi youth. Thus, while he had indeed attained the Mahāyāna, he manifested the appearance of being a Hīnayāna arhat to guide those of inferior faculties. This is why he appeared to pass away and left behind relics. It is also like the Elder Subhūti, who, though having long since realized the fruit of Arhatship, manifested the appearance of entering parinirvāṇa for the sake of the Elder Śāriputra. Therefore, although he had long since attained the Mahāyāna, he manifested the appearance of being a Hīnayāna arhat to guide those of inferior faculties. This is why he appeared to pass away and left behind relics. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Whenever one undergoes the transformation of change (*pariṇāmika-śarīra*), one must first separately manifest a portion of a body subject to temporal limits (*paricchinna-kāya*) and enter parinirvāṇa, in order to demonstrate this to the non-Buddhists and ordinary worldlings. If it were not so, those non-Buddhists would harbor doubts, thinking:

'This is merely a dragon or a ghost, not a human being,' for there would be no corpse or spirit at all. Therefore, it is necessary to manifest death. At that time, there was also a stupa, which [would otherwise] not exist."
This is contradictory.
Regarding the statement that the Sanskrit term is *mahākūṣmāṇḍa*, the Master of the Commentary (Suzhou) followed ancient tradition and provisionally offered this explanation.
The Sanskrit is *mahākūṣmāṇḍīra*; this is translated as "Great-Bellied Upholder. *Mahā* means "great," and *kūṣmāṇḍī*... [text fragment] ...*ra*.
The three characters mean "belly-holder. Rāhula held the Tripitaka and the four classes of scriptures entirely within his abdomen;
because he memorized them without forgetting, he was called "Holder" (Dhara). This is a corruption of Kūṭila.
Regarding the mention of Śāriputra’s maternal uncle, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that he was of the same clan as Śāriputra.

However, the sister and her brother would regularly debate points of doctrine; initially, when the sister was pregnant, she could not match her brother. But after she had become pregnant, the brother frequently suffered defeat.
The brother thought to himself, "The ability of this child in the womb is already difficult to withstand; once born, how could it possibly be rivaled? Thereupon, he abandoned [the debate].

He attended to domestic duties and entered the mountains to study extensively for fifteen years. During this time, he did not shave his hair; as his nails and hair grew somewhat long, he became known as the Brahmacārin Dīrghanakha (Long-Nail).
