On the day of his return, he carried a fire bowl upon his head and wrapped his abdomen in iron leaves, wandering among the people.

He returned home by stages. Pitying those in the world who dwell in darkness, he thought it fitting to illuminate them with the light of fire. Having studied extensively yet remaining narrow-minded, he wrapped his belly with iron plates.
Upon arriving home, he asked his sister, "Is your son still there? His sister replied to her brother, "He was born eight years ago.
He has read all the scriptures; at the age of sixteen, he excelled all others in debate. Now, having resolved his mind, he follows the Buddha."
He left the household life. His elder brother then became angry and resentful, saying, "I intended to instruct him myself so that his fame might overshadow the whole world;
what kind of śramaṇa dares to seduce and train him? He then went to the Buddha's location to seek a debate, thinking, "If I am victorious..."
"Return my nephew to me; if I am defeated, I shall serve you with respect. At that time, Śāriputra had been ordained for only half a month and was standing in attendance by the Buddha's side.
The Buddha said, "State your own proposition. This heretic, being arrogant, established his thesis, saying, "Non-acceptance of all dharmas is my thesis.
His intention was that if the Buddha were to raise an objection, he would not accept it at all, thereby conforming to his own doctrine. The Tathāgata, for [the sake of...]"
To refute this evil view, he challenges him, saying: "Do you yourself accept [this position]? If you accept it, you contradict your own tenet;
if you say you do not, then since everyone has seen and heard it with their own eyes and ears, your established thesis must not be subsumed under "all phenomena.

If you say you do not accept it, then you have no tenet at all. The former challenge reveals a contradiction in your own words (*svavacanavirodha*); the latter challenge reveals a deficiency in your fundamental tenet (*pratijñāhāni*). The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows: You...

The view is a functional entity (*dharma*). It should not be the case that it is not apprehended. The reason (*hetu*) is: "Because you admit its arising from both self and other. The concordant example (*sapakṣa*) is: "Like other views.
Other views are admitted by both oneself and others to arise; other views are not non-apprehended. Your view is admitted by both yourself and others to arise; your view is not non-apprehended.
Since both [the reason and the example] are unestablished (*asiddha*), one should know that defeat is incurred. This is like being struck down by a fire-bowl being hurled at one.

He cast off his iron leaf-garment and requested to return to the Buddha to enter the monastic life. At that time, Śāriputra, having received the precepts for only half a month, was standing by the Buddha’s side;
upon hearing a discourse on the Dharma, he subsequently realized the fruit of Arhatship (the stage of No-more-learning).
The Brahmin Dīrghanakha was Śāriputra’s maternal uncle, and Śāriputra was the son of his sister.

Regarding the statement that "Nanda" in Sanskrit refers to this: hereafter, the seventh [chapter] is "Severing Attachment," the eighth is "Transforming Existence and Discoursing on Emptiness," and the ninth is "Understanding the Profound and Practicing the Esoteric. These six persons constitute one chant.
To say that this is translated as "joy" (喜) means *pramuditā* (rejoicing).

To say that the "root" refers to the cowherd: the *Upamāna-sūtra* states that King Bimbisāra of Magadha invited the Buddha to spend the three-month summer retreat (*varṣā*), and together with five hundred disciples, he provided offerings of fresh milk, ghee, and curds for the Buddha.
He also provided for the community of bhikṣus. He commanded the cowherd to live near the city and provide milk and curds daily.
When the three months of offerings were completed, the king went to see the Buddha and immediately thought to himself: "The Buddha is an omniscient person;

he clearly understands the Vedas and scriptures, as well as the sixty-four kinds of worldly arts and crafts. Yet, he does not even know my cows. The Tripitaka Master said: [The Buddha] did not fail to understand them clearly. However, he simply did not know *my* cows.
"If I know the matters concerning cattle, I shall take refuge. He asked the Buddha, "How many methods for tending cattle are there so that the herd may prosper?
The Buddha replied, "There are eleven matters: first, knowing color; by knowing the color of the hair, one distinguishes between one's own cattle and those of others.

This represents the bhikṣu’s practice, which requires discerning between the heterodox and the orthodox, and between internal and external paths. As the Sūtra says: 'It is like the various bhikṣus who know the four assemblies.'"

Form. Second is the characteristic of cognition, namely the characteristics of fatness and leanness. A bhikṣu practicing cultivation must know these two characteristics of good and evil, which manifest the cultivation of merit and wisdom.
As the Sūtra says: "O bhikṣus, you should know the characteristic of delusion; the karmic action of ink is called the characteristic of delusion."
White karma is the mark of wisdom. Third is knowing how to scrub and brush away filth and impure soil; this represents a bhikṣu’s practice of frequent confession. As the Sūtra says:

"It is like those bhikṣus who, although greed and anger may arise, are able to restrain and distance themselves from them, and by frequently expelling evil views, they do not conceal their transgressions.
Fourth is knowing the wound; on a wound, one must apply medicinal ointment and remove parasites with honey. This represents...
The bhikṣu guards the gates of the six sense faculties and does not become attached to their objects. Fifth, "knowing when to emit smoke" means driving away mosquitoes;
this symbolizes the bhikṣu’s diligent practice in severing unwholesome dharmas. As the Sūtra says:

"From time to time one emits smoke," which is a metaphor for what the bhikṣu has studied, heard, and realized, as explained at length. Sixth, "knowing where to go" means recognizing the path so as not to harm the ox.
Furthermore, it signifies that the bhikṣu practices and understands the Three Vehicles; he should practice the Eightfold Noble Path and must not enter brothels, wine shops, or gambling dens at will.
Seventh, it signifies knowing the destination and whether the ox is at ease or not. This represents the bhikṣu’s departure from unwholesome factors.
As the Sūtra says: "Knowing the beloved ox" is a metaphor for when a bhikṣu hears the Dharma being preached, listening with a sincere heart and leaping with joy.
8. Knowing the crossing of the water: If one crosses the water without reaching the shore, there is fear that the ox will be blown back by the wind.
This symbolizes the bhikṣu’s practice: knowing the Four Truths, he ferries all sentient beings across the ocean of birth and death to reach the shore of Nirvāṇa.
9. Knowing the limits of food and drink: If the water and grass exceed their proper measure, they will harm the ox. This symbolizes the bhikṣu’s practice of [the matter of]... (text fragment)

One must have few desires. As the Sūtra says: "It is like the four foundations of mindfulness (catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni) for the bhikṣus. The four foundations of mindfulness refer to the four applications of mindfulness (catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni).

Just as this ox directs its mind toward water and grass, the bhikṣu directs his mind toward the four foundations of mindfulness. Furthermore, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* (Sutra on the Bequeathed Teaching) says:
10. Knowing the measure of food and drink. Tenth, knowing when to leave behind milk. When milking a cow, it is necessary to leave some milk behind; if one does not, one starves the calf.

This represents the bhikṣu’s contentment. As the Sūtra says: "Knowing the remnants left after milking" is a metaphor for how a bhikṣu, though the offerings may be many, knows his own sufficiency and must not accept them all.
11. Knowing the cow and the owner of the cow. That is, within the herd...
The "special ox" is able to lead all other oxen without them being lost. The *Zhongshan jing* (Sūtra on the Assembly of Goodness) states:
"Distinguishing between the good and bad oxen and knowing those who can be raised" is a metaphor for a bhikṣu showing respect to his elders. Master Lu says: Furthermore, there are eleven matters:

first, not being on a high mountain; second, not dwelling in a deep abyss; third, the grass being free of hardness and roughness; fourth, the water possessing three qualities—being neither cold nor hot.
1. [The milk] must not be salty. 2. The five places of dwelling must be level. 3. The head must not be scrubbed with a brush. 4. One must walk slowly toward the water.
5. One may drink three times a day. 6. One must rest three times for each lead. 7. One’s entry and exit must be clear; that is, one must keep the light hanging down. 8.

The master must always follow and attend to the cow. Afterward, when Nanda heard this, he realized that the Buddha possessed all-knowing wisdom, yet he had previously thought that the World-Honored One did not know.

Regarding the matter of oxen: the World-Honored One has the most excellent hands among oxen; there is none superior to him. Later, he followed the Buddha and left the household life, becoming fully endowed with the marks of a Brahmā and capable of performing the Brahma-sound.
The term "Sundara" (in Sanskrit, pronounced with a retroflex *ṣ* as in *suṇḍara*) means "exquisite beauty.
Regarding the statement that he was a disciple of the Buddha: he was the son of King Śuddhodana who, in a former life, had seen a stūpa of the Buddha and erected a *kīla* pillar there.
Furthermore, because he had established the hanging dew-dish, by these causes and conditions, he was now born into the palace of the Śākyas. His body was one *zhang*, five *chi*, and two *cun* tall;
he was handsome, noble, and dignified. To summarize: he was born on the ninth day of the fourth month; he was four fingers shorter than the Buddha;

his appearance was exceptionally distinguished and far superior to that of ordinary people. If he entered a great assembly and those present did not yet recognize the Buddha, they would mistakenly call him Śākyamuni.
This refers to the Muni Buddha.

Regarding the statement that the Buddha returned to his native city for two days: after attaining enlightenment, twelve years passed before he returned to his native city and preached the Dharma for two days.
Later, the *Fadu yinyi* (Explanations of Buddhist Terms) states that the *Benxing jing* (Sutra of Past Deeds) says: "At that time, the World-Honored One taught..."
The Buddha transformed the youth Nanda, extensively expounding upon the merits of leaving the household life.
He repeatedly explained the causes and conditions for renunciation and further praised those causes and conditions, exhorting him to leave the household life.

Nanda said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, I would rather provide the Tathāgata and the community of bhikṣus with the four requisites, making offerings to them until the end of my life; I will never leave the household life."
At that time, the World-Honored One, having finished his meal, took a single attendant and went to Nanda’s gate.
He saw Nanda together with Sundarī, sitting leisurely upon a high pavilion. Seeing from afar that the World-Honored One was approaching, Nanda quickly rose and descended from the pavilion;
he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, from where have you come so far?”
"May you enter my hall and ascend the seat. After the World-Honored One had entered, he sat in silence.
Nanda addressed him, saying, "I pray that you will accept my offering of food and drink. The Buddha said, "The meal is finished; there is no need to prepare anything further.
Nanda spoke again, "There is honeyed syrup here now; may it be drunk outside of the proper time? The Buddha told Nanda, "I shall follow your wish. Thereupon, Nanda took hold of it.
He took the Buddha’s bowl, filled it with non-timely juice, and offered it to the World-Honored One. At that time, the World-Honored One did not accept it and gave it to his attendant;
the attendant likewise did not accept it. The Buddha rose from his seat and wished to return to his original place.
Then the Śākya youth also took that honey-juice from the upper story and desired to follow the Buddha. At that moment, Sundarī saw the Śākya Nanda holding [the bowl].
Nanda followed the Buddha. While he was still combing his hair, he called out in a loud voice, "Nanda, the Holy Son, where do you wish to go?
At that time, Nanda pointed to the bowl and said, "I wish to deliver this to the Tathāgata and return immediately.
He replied, "Come back quickly; do not stay there long. If you stay there for too long, I shall go to the monastery for a short while and call for you. Do not say [otherwise]."
[The Buddha] did not speak. At that time, the World-Honored One went to the Kalandaka grove and called for a bhikṣu to prepare honey syrup.

Nanda took leave of the Buddha, but the Buddha said, "Do not go; you should renounce the householder's life. Nanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "I do not wish to renounce the householder's life now."
"I would rather provide the four requisites for the Buddha and the Saṃgha. The Buddha then spoke to him of the merits of renunciation and the faults and afflictions of all sensual desires.
Nevertheless, Nanda’s mind still had no desire to renounce the world; yet, out of respect for the Buddha, he humbly submitted, saying, "I shall go forth.
At that time, the World-Honored One said, "Summon a barber to come," and immediately summoned the assembly.
Among them was one barber who stood before Nanda, holding a razor in his hand, intending to shave Nanda’s hair and beard.
Nanda seized the barber and said to him, "By what power do you dare to shave my head? The World-Honored One then spoke.
"Come, bhikṣu, enter my Dharma and practice the holy life (brahmacarya) for the sake of ending all suffering. Thus he became a renunciant and received full ordination (upasampadā).
Now Nanda was handsome and pleasing, a sight for all people to behold, and possessed the thirty-two marks of a great man.
His feet were complete and without deficiency; his body was golden in color, yet he was four finger-widths shorter than the Tathāgata.

The *kāṣāya* robes he wore were identical to the Buddha’s garments, with no difference between them. When the bhikṣus saw him from afar, they all suspected he was the Buddha and wished to rise to greet him.
When he realized his error, he simply returned to his original seat. Having understood this, the World-Honored One established the rule for equal proportions.

Furthermore, when Nanda polished his robes until they were glossy, applied seductive ointments to his eyes, adorned his body, wore straw sandals on his feet, held a parasol in his right hand, and carried an alms bowl in his left, the Buddha prohibited all of these.
Moreover, one should remember Sundarī; because of her deception, he did not practice the holy life.
Desiring to renounce the precepts and return to his home, for this reason he would constantly take pieces of pottery or wooden boards and paint the image of the Śākya maiden Sundarī;
thus he passed his days gazing upon it. The bhikṣus became suspicious of him and informed the Buddha.
The Buddha then established a precept, forbidding the taking of forms from a woman’s body that could give rise to lustful thoughts. Furthermore, on another occasion...
At that time, the bhikṣu Nanda arrived in turn for his duty of guarding the monastery quarters.
He thought to himself, "When the Buddha enters the village, at that time I shall be able to return home.

The World-Honored One, knowing this, said, "Nanda, if you wish to go, you must first close all the doors of the rooms and then depart. Having spoken, he immediately went into the village. Nanda desired—
He returned and saw that the World-Honored One’s room door was not closed. He thought to himself, "I shall close this door before I go back.
He then closed the Buddha’s door, but he saw that the doors of Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Kāśyapa, and the others were all open.
As he closed them one after another in succession, they opened again. Fearing that the World-Honored One would arrive soon, and having formed this thought, he departed from the Nyagrodha [Grove].
When he was about to depart from within the Laṭṭhika grove, the World-Honored One, having seen him with his divine eye, vanished from the city and appeared there.
Upon seeing the Buddha, Nanda immediately took refuge beneath a nyagrodha tree and sat down, concealing his body.
The Buddha, by means of his supernormal powers, lifted that great tree and placed it in the air. Seeing Nanda sitting there with his body concealed, he asked, "Nanda, where do you wish to go?
Nanda related his situation in full. The Buddha preached the Dharma for him. Furthermore, there was an elder...
He invited the Buddha to partake of a meal. At that time, Nanda was next in charge of guarding the monastery, yet he thought only of returning home.

The Buddha, knowing this, addressed him, saying: "Nanda, you must know the proper time to sweep the grounds of the monastery; ensure that all the basins for washing are filled with water. Having given these instructions, the Buddha departed for the invitation.

Nanda first began to sweep the ground; when he swept from west to east, the wind blew it back toward the west; when he swept from east to west, the wind blew it back toward the east. [This occurred] four times.
As he was sweeping, a whirlwind blew up; the water jar turned over, and as the water poured out, it made a splashing sound.
Nanda thought to himself, "What use have I for sweeping the ground and refilling the jar? The Tathāgata will soon return. I shall now go quickly home."
With his divine eye, the Blessed One saw that Nanda had departed from there and was heading toward home. He immediately manifested a separate body before Nanda;
as Nanda saw him from afar, the Buddha vanished into a mountain cleft and sat down with his body crouched.
By means of his supernormal power, the Buddha made the ground level like the palm of a hand. Seeing him sitting there, he addressed Nanda: "You are here now; what do you intend to do?"
[Regarding] this matter, Nanda said to the Buddha: "I have already promised to let Sundarī return home; for this reason, I have uttered much false speech.
The Buddha told Nanda: "Why must you see Sundarī now? Her body is like this:
it is composed of thirty-six impure substances, foul and filthy. Why do you not feel revulsion for it? At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of these circumstances, spoke a verse:
He said: "Desiring to leave the dense forest, you have already left it; having escaped from the forest, you enter it again.

You, O puggala (person), observe these who, having attained liberation from bondage, return once more to bondage. At that time, the World-Honored One instructed Nanda to practice the pure brahmacariya in order to extinguish all suffering.
Although Nanda was thus exhorted, he still did not take pleasure in practicing it.
Regarding his pure brahmacarya, the World-Honored One, having understood this, reflected: "Now, Nanda’s afflictions are so intense;
how could a mere slight instruction break through them? I must now employ an expedient means to cause him to resolve his mind.
It is like the worldly analogy of using fire to extinguish fire, or using poison to treat poison. Thinking thus, he took Nanda by the hand and, by means of his supernormal power, concealed [himself].
His body vanished, and suddenly he was upon Mount Gandhamādana. At that time, on that mountain, the wind blew and the rain fell;

the trees rubbed against one another, and fire immediately broke out. A column of smoke and flames reached the heavens as it consumed the mountain. There were many monkeys on the mountain, numbering five hundred;
their fur was scorched by the fire, and they all crouched on the ground, rubbing themselves to extinguish the flames. Among them was a female, blind monkey.
Within that troop, he extinguished the fire on his body. The Buddha said to Nanda, "Do you see this now? He replied, "I have seen it.
[The Buddha asked,] "Between your Sundarī, who is lovely and beautiful, and this monkey, which of the two is superior? Nanda then addressed the Buddha.
With his brows furrowed and his face contorted, he remained silent and spoke not.

The World-Honored One took Nanda by the hand and vanished from Mount Gandhamādana, arriving at the Heaven of the Thirty-three, manifesting beneath a Pārijātaka tree. At that time, Śakra entered the garden to sport.
Five hundred court ladies surrounded him on all sides. The Buddha said to Nanda, "Do you see this now? He replied, "I have seen it.
The Buddha asked, "Are these five hundred court ladies more beautiful, or is Sundarī more beautiful? Nanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
It would be a hundred thousand million times more impossible to compare a blind monkey to Sundarī.
The Buddha asked, "Nanda, do you wish to enjoy yourself with this woman?
Nanda leaped for joy and said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, according to my own wishes, I truly desire to enjoy myself with those five hundred court ladies. The Buddha spoke.
"Nanda, you cannot now enjoy yourself with them in this ordinary body. If you wish to attain this, you must, with a joyful heart, practice the holy life (brahmacarya) within my Dharma;

I shall grant it to you. If you can now comply with this teaching and practice pure conduct, at the end of your life you will certainly be born in this place to enjoy yourself with the celestial maidens."—The World-Honored One.
Again, the Blessed One took Nanda by the hand and vanished from that heaven, returning to his original location.

At that time, for the sake of seeking a celestial maiden, Nanda exerted all the strength of his body throughout the first and last watches of the night to practice the holy life and other such disciplines. Then the Blessed One—
Seeing Nanda practicing the holy life among the palace maidens, he then took Nanda by the hand and departed from the Nyagrodha Grove.
They vanished from sight and entered into the depths of hell, where he saw a copper cauldron with a fierce fire burning beneath it, surging and boiling.
There was no one present who was undergoing punishment. Nanda asked the warder, "For whom is this cauldron being heated? The warder replied, "The Buddha has a nephew born of his maternal aunt;

he is the Buddha’s younger brother, Nanda. Having practiced the holy life (*brahmacarya*) for the sake of seeking five hundred celestial maidens, when his heavenly merit is exhausted, he shall be reborn here to undergo this retribution of suffering. Upon hearing this, Nanda was terrified, and the hair on his body stood on end.
The youth resolved his mind to repent and practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*) in order to seek the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*).
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "Among my śrāvaka disciples, the bhikṣu Nanda is foremost in the taming of the sense faculties.
It was only after two days had passed since he arrived at his native city that he was permitted to receive ordination; it was not because of a period of two days spent in instruction.
Truly taming the faculties; the number of days was not many (the above clarifies the reversal of the seven delusions and the severing of attachment).
As for the statement that "Pūrṇa" is his name: Pūrṇa is the name of the Venerable One. "Maitrī" is the nature of a mother. Mǔ says:
If one considers "mother-nature," it is the surname of that benevolence. If one speaks of mother-nature as benevolence, it is the nature of the mind.
This venerable one is the son born of that daughter of benevolence; thus he is named Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra.
Regarding the statement "Pūrṇa together with Maitrī," this is the second interpretation. For a long time she had no son;
she prayed to the gods, and in a dream, she saw a precious jar filled with treasures suddenly enter her womb. Consequently, she became pregnant and gave birth to the Venerable One.
Thus Pūrṇa fulfilled the wish of her compassionate mother and was named Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra. He was originally from a village in the kingdom of Kośala. [He departed...]
Not far from the city of Kapilavastu, there was a brahmin who served as the royal preceptor for King Śuddhodana.
His family was immensely wealthy, and he had an only son named Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, who was born at the same time as Prince Siddhārtha.
By nature, he was weary of the world and resolved to seek liberation. After the Tathāgata had attained enlightenment, he sought [to become his disciple].
He requested ordination and, through diligent practice, attained the state of Arhat before long.
As for why he is called "Sudatta" (Good Appearance), at the time of his birth, auspicious signs appeared within his household; therefore, he was named Sudatta.
Regarding the statement that he was formerly called Subhūti: on the day of his birth, all the storehouses within the household became empty.
His parents were afraid and consulted a physiognomist. The physiognomist said, "This is only good; it is auspicious. Thus, he was named Shanji (Subhūti). Such is the nature of Shanji.

He was also called Kūṇika (Empty-born). At the time of his birth, all the storehouses were completely empty; this signified that he would be foremost in the realization of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), hence the name Empty-born.
The Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of the An-guo Monastery stated regarding Prajñāpāramitā: "Subhūti is the manifestation of the Buddha Śikhin from the world-system of the East.
The *Xiyu ji* states: "The Tathāgata returned from the celestial palace to the Jambudvīpa continent."
One day, while Subhūti was seated in quietude within his stone chamber, he reflected to himself: "Today the Tathāgata has descended upon Jambudvīpa and the multitude has gone out to welcome him.

As for me now, what need is there for me to go? He had often heard the Buddha teach that one who understands the emptiness of all dharmas and knows the nature of all dharmas may, by means of the eye of wisdom, behold the Dharma-body. At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā—

Desiring to see the Buddha for the first time, he manifested as a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin), accompanied by the seven treasures and a thousand sons leading and following him, with the four continents providing guard.

Upon arriving at the place of the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata said to him: "It is not for the first time that you have seen my body. He who truly sees well is said to have seen my Dharma-body for the first time."
Regarding the name "Ānanda," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: On the night the Tathāgata attained the Way, he was born.

When the Tathāgata achieved enlightenment, the Māra Pāpīyas led eight thousand *koṭis* of beings to harass and disturb the World-Honored One. The World-Honored One entered the *maitrī-samādhi*, and the demonic army retreated and dispersed.
The Demon King said, "Since I have been unable to afflict and harm Gautama, I shall go instead to King Śuddhodana. There, in the void...
From the sky, a voice cried out: "Prince Siddhārtha died last night!
Upon hearing these words, the King fell from his bed in a state of shock, writhing upon the ground like a fish on hot sand, unable to regain consciousness.
After a long while, the deity of the Bodhi tree, holding *mandārava* flowers, reported to King Śuddhodana: "Prince Siddhārtha, last night, under the morning star..."

When [the Buddha] emerged and attained perfect enlightenment, the King heard these words. Having previously been told that he was already dead, and now being told that he had attained the Way, he wondered which was right and which was wrong.
The tree deity replied, "The one who came earlier was Māra; the one who came later is the Bodhi-tree deity.

Having personally witnessed the World-Honored One’s attainment of enlightenment, I have come to inform you. King Śuddhodana was filled with great joy and leaped for gladness, and he informed all the Śākyas.
At the time of the grand morning audience, when all the subjects and citizens within the kingdom universally proclaimed "Ten-thousand years!
and were making music in joy, King Śuklodana entered. Having heard that a son had been born to his humble concubine the night before, he was filled with even greater joy.
Because he was born at the very moment of the Great King’s celebration, he was named Nanda (Joy).
Regarding the term "seizing the sun" (*sūryagraha*), there are two interpretations. First, it refers to the Asura King seizing the sun with his hand;
because he was born at the time of a solar eclipse, he is said to seize the sun. Second, it is explained that the Buddha is likened to the sun, and "seizing" (*graha*) has the meaning of obstructing.

Rāhu remained in the womb for six years, obstructing the Prince so that he could not attain enlightenment; thus, he obstructed the Buddha-sun, and for this reason, he is called the "seizer of the sun."
Question: How is it that Rāhula remained in the womb for six years? Answer: Long ago, there was a king who fathered two sons;
the elder was named Sūryarāja (Sun King) and the younger was named Candrarāja (Moon King). After the father-king passed away, Sūryarāja grew weary of his position and sought to renounce the world.
He entrusted the kingdom to his younger brother, left the household life to practice the Way, and then made this vow: "May this body of mine, from this day forward..."

Thereafter, regarding property belonging to an owner, he did not take what was not given. Later, on one occasion, having forgotten his vow, he traveled at night and, being thirsty, mistakenly drank water from a lotus pond.
Having drunk it, he realized his error and thought, "Today I have become a thief. He went to the presence of King Candra.
"I have committed an offense. I pray that Your Majesty will punish me. The King said, "This is naturally occurring water. What crime has the ṛṣi committed? The ṛṣi refused to accept this.

The King then ordered him to be sent out to the rear garden. King Candra subsequently forgot about him. After six days had passed, on account of a general amnesty for the empire where prisoners were released from their crimes, he suddenly remembered the ṛṣi;
having risen from his hunger strike, the ṛṣi had collapsed. The King repented and reproached himself with his own hands.
[He] fed [him] rice. The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "The rishi of that time was my own self in this present life.
The Moon King of that time was Rāhula. Because of the rishi, he underwent immeasurable suffering; due to the remaining karma from that, he remained in the womb for six years.
Question: Why did Yaśodharā carry Rāhula in her womb for six years? Answer: Furthermore, in the distant past, a herd of cattle was grazing in a field. They were released...
The cowherd’s wife took a daughter with her and went to the herd of cattle to fetch milk and curds.
She carried two vessels; both were filled to the brim. She sent her daughter to carry the larger vessel while she herself held the smaller one.
As they traveled along the road, she said to her as follows: "Walk quickly! This path here is treacherous and feared by people. She spoke thus a second and a third time. The girl—
She thought to herself, "She sent me to carry this large vessel," and as she was further urged on, she became angry and said to her mother, "Let me carry the largest vessel and go ahead;
you follow behind. The daughter then walked slowly and deliberately, causing her mother to carry the heavy load for six *krośas*.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus, "That daughter was Yaśodharā. He sent her...
The mother bore this heavy burden and endured immeasurable suffering; as for the remaining karma from her final existence, she carried the fetus for six years.
Furthermore, because Rāhula had once blocked a rat hole for six days in a previous life, when the Prince desired to leave the household, King Śuddhodana would not permit it.
"I shall allow you to leave the household life once you have borne a son who can succeed to the throne. The Prince leaped over the city wall and departed;
he then pointed his finger at Yaśodharā’s womb, and she subsequently became pregnant. When six years had been fulfilled, King Śuddhodana said:
"The Prince has been gone since he leaped over the city wall for six years, yet Yaśodharā has not protected my honor nor brought shame upon my kin. If this were only fifteen months..."

Regarding the child born posthumously, the sovereign immediately assembled his ministers, each of whom proposed a harsh punishment. One minister petitioned, saying, "One should shave its hair and strike it with a staff;
once struck, its face shall be marked. Another minister said, "One should cut off its ears," meaning to excise both its ears and nose.
Some said to cast it into a great pit; some said to saw it apart; others said to divide it limb from limb.
Section Eight. The World-Honored One knew that Yaśodharā and her son were in the midst of mortal peril; he looked around to his left and right.
King Vaiśravaṇa, perceiving the Buddha’s intention, plucked a leaf from a *pātra* tree and brought it forth. The World-Honored One composed a letter for his father, stating:
"Rāhula is truly the child conceived by me. When the Buddha returned to his native city, the Father King invited the Buddha to receive offerings. Next—
Mahāprajāpatī invited the Buddha for a meal offering. Next, Yaśodharā announced, “I invite the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus to a meal offering.
Yaśodharā took a branch of *modaka* cakes and placed it in Rāhula’s hand, saying, “Go find your father and offer this to him.
At that time, Rāhula was six years old; he went among the bhikṣus and approached them one by one.
Standing before the World-Honored One, he prostrated himself and spoke in verse: "So it is, so it is! Śramaṇa, śramaṇa! Sālaṃ sālaṃ!
How wonderful, how wonderful! At that time, the World-Honored One said to the King, his father: "Do not doubt; Yaśodharā’s Rāhula is truly my son.
When the meal was finished and the assembly had dispersed, Rāhula ran and hid himself inside the Buddha’s robe.
As he stood there, the bhikṣus wished to prevent him from entering. The Buddha said, "Let him enter; he shall come within my robes. Rāhula followed the Buddha out through the palace gate.
The Buddha extended his hand and gave him his sandals, instructing him to hold them as firmly as one might tether a horse with a rope, so that they were never parted.
They proceeded to the Nyagrodha Grove, where the World-Honored One asked, "Have you already followed me into the homeless life? He replied:
[The Buddha] consented. He appointed Śāriputra as his preceptor (*upādhyāya*). From this time forth, there were śrāmaṇeras for the first time.

Later, when the father-king did not see Rāhula, he searched throughout the household for food and drink but could not find him. Hearing that the World-Honored One had taken him away and he had already completed his renunciation, the king fainted;
after a long while, he regained consciousness. He went to the side of the World-Honored One and engaged in various reasoned discourses. At that time, the Tathāgata...
Therefore, it was established: "If one's parents do not give permission, one may not go forth [into the homeless life]. (The names listed above are concluded.
Regarding the commentary on the title, it is said that those whose names are high [in rank] are referred to as "those such as these" (*evam-ādi*) in the Sūtra.

The term "such as these" is a word used for specific designation; it points to twenty-one individuals, and thus says "such as these. These Arhats are [honored] by the assembly of both ordinary beings and sages.
Those who are known to all are all great Arhats. As the Sūtra says regarding those "known to all":
it means that one knows they possess mindfulness and recognizes their appearance. A fool in a distant place neither knows of their virtue nor recognizes their appearance;
a wise person in a distant place does not recognize their appearance but knows they possess virtue; and a fool in a nearby place recognizes their appearance but does not know [their virtue].
Regarding those who possess virtue: they draw near to the wise and, moreover, recognize their character to know that they possess virtue.
As for the phrase "the sutra says" and so forth, there are two meanings: first, internal equality; second, external equality. Within internal equality, there are two further points.
The first lists twenty-one individuals and applies the term "equal" (*samāna*) to them; internally, it refers only to these twenty-one individuals. The second... [text continues]
Regarding "the internal" and so forth: those who are Arhats, etc., are not non-Arhats; the one who is a non-Arhat is Ānanda alone. As the Sūtra says:
"Only Ānanda alone dwells on the stage of a learner (*śaikṣa*). The second interpretation takes "external" and so forth to refer to twenty-one individuals specifically, while "etc.
includes the twelve thousand [monks] (this concludes the commentary on the Sūtra).
Regarding the statement "first explaining [the distinction between] noble and base," etc.: A question arises concerning the explanation of the term *yan* (言) in the preceding treatise.
Since it says that Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of superior wisdom all "know" (*shiki*, 識) [it], why does the commentary’s explanation instead narrow [the scope]?

Why is it that for the assembly of the noble and the base, one speaks of "knowing" (*chi*, 知) but not "knowing-cognizing" (*shiki*), whereas for Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one speaks of "knowing-cognizing" but not "knowing"? Answer: When Buddhas and Bodhisattvas speak of "knowing-cognizing," they inherently know [it].
Regarding the statement "knowing at the time," this refers fundamentally to consciousness; both [meanings] are applicable.
As for the phrase "Vimalakīrti and others," it cites the text to provide dual proof. "Known by the assembly of sages" concludes the preceding discussion on "knowledge.

The second [meaning], namely the assembly of the noble and the lowly, as well as the ordinary and the sage, encompasses these two senses and thus constitutes "knowledge. The former interpretation emphasizes "goodness."
Regarding the statement "citing twenty-one examples to represent the 'equal'": this means citing other individuals; these "other individuals" refer to the two thousand people.

Regarding the statement "all are called 'Great' and so forth": this is a concise summary of the great significance. The term "Great" (mahā) is explained according to the great significance of their virtues.
Regarding the statement "those such as the Arhats," this explains the meaning of the term "etc. Question: Previously, twenty-one individuals were listed individually;
since Ānanda is already included among the number of Arhats, why is it necessary to further state that they are "not those beyond training" (aśaikṣa)? Answer: Those listed in the sūtra...

Regarding the time of the First Council, they had already attained arhatship. The commentary’s use of the term "and so forth" (等) includes those in the initial stage who have not yet attained the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*);
thus, there is no contradiction in speaking of two [categories].
Regarding the phrase "the assembly of great virtuous ones who are nameless," the Sūtra states: "Furthermore, there were two thousand [monks], both those in training and those beyond training.
Some say that these are all collectively "beyond training" (aśaikṣa) because they have already accomplished what was to be learned; thus they are called "beyond training.

This refers to those not widely known to the public, as distinct from those previously listed individually. Jiguō says: "These are those in the three fruits and four stages of the path, who are still in training" (śaikṣa).
Those who are learners (śaikṣa) study that which is beyond learning (aśaikṣa), yet because they have not yet accomplished it, they are called "learners and those beyond learning.

Although the two categories of those beyond learning are distinct and the two types of persons differ from one another, their designation as "those beyond learning" is one and the same; therefore, they constitute a single assembly.

Regarding the statement that the three—precept (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*)—are precisely what constitutes "training" (*śikṣā*) and so forth: these take only the three untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas as their essence.

Within the category of precepts, both tainted and untainted types exist; here, only the untainted is taken. In the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), the concentration-concomitant precept (*samādhisamvara-śīla*) encompasses both the tainted and the untainted, whereas the path-concomitant precept (*mārgasamvara-śīla*) is exclusively untainted.

As for the concentration-concomitant, it takes the four dhyānas, the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), and the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) as its basis, distinguishing them as untainted concentrations.

It takes as its essence [the three trainings]. Third, it refers exclusively to the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) of the paths of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning. Mochizuki states: "That which is learned is exclusively untainted;

tainted phenomena cannot be learned. These [trainings of] morality, concentration, and wisdom constitute the essence of the learner (*śaikṣa*) when they exist within the paths of seeing and cultivation, and the essence of the one beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*) when they exist within the path of no-more-learning. (The above explains the terminology of the learner.)

Regarding the phrase "the perfection of progress and so forth," this explains the designation of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). Question: One who is liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*) may be said to be perfected;

however, for one liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*), the training in meditative concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*) is not yet complete and the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*) is not yet fulfilled. Why, then, is such a person called "one beyond training"? Answer:

They are designated as "one beyond training" based on the fulfillment of their own stage. If it were otherwise, even those who have turned their minds toward the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*)—though they may be liberated both ways—would likewise [not be so designated].
"Not yet full" (the first part explains the assembly of monks).
Regarding the statement "respecting the community of bhikṣuṇīs and so forth," Mǔ says: The Great Victorious Jīvandhara was the Tathāgata’s maternal aunt;

she nurtured the World-Honored One with kindness equal to that of a mother. Her retinue of six thousand came together to this Dharma assembly to hear the teaching of the One Vehicle; therefore, [she is mentioned].
The bestowal of the prophecy is called "veneration.

Regarding the statement that there are three types of Buddha-mothers: these are the three mothers of the Buddha. First is the Great Artisan (Mahāmāyā), who is the mother who gives birth to the Buddha.

Second is the Great Victorious Birth-Mistress (Mahāprajāpatī), who is the mother who nurtures the Buddha. Third is the one who neither gives birth nor nurtures. In the sutras, [the first] is most frequently mentioned.
It is not listed. Question: Since she is not a Buddha who nourishes life, why is she called a "mother"? Answer: The wife of one's father is the mother.
Since there are three such mothers, it can be inferred that the ancient Son of Heaven had one hundred and twenty chambers, rotating every fifteen days.
The Empress alone knows him for one night; the three Consorts together know him for one night; the twenty-seven Senior Ladies-in-waiting together know him for three nights;

nine persons know him for one night; and the eighty-one Palace Attendants together know him for nine nights—nine persons knowing him for one night, continuing in this manner until eighty-one persons. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "He departed from Kapilavastu..."
Not far from that city was another city. In that city lived an elder named Śikṣita. This elder had eight daughters.
King Śuddhodana and his three brothers each took two of them as wives. The eldest was Queen Māyā;
the most excellent was Mahāmāyā, the mistress of the world. The remaining six daughters were married to the other three kings.

Regarding the statement that "Mahāgovinda was born seven days after the Buddha," [the interlocutor] asks: If it is the case that merely taking refuge in and paying homage to the Buddhas brings about the increase of one's lifespan and longevity, why is it that the physical form of the Tathāgata’s own birth, on the contrary, resulted in a short life? The answer is: The Tathāgata’s establishment of transformation (teachings) does not follow a single path;
his every movement and action is not without purpose. [The interlocutor] says: When the Buddha was in the Tuṣita Heaven, he was about to descend to be born.
At that time, he first contemplated four matters: first, he contemplated being born in a central land; second, he contemplated that his parents must be of the Brahmin or Kṣatriya caste;
third, he contemplated that the faculties of sentient beings must be matured; and fourth, he contemplated that his mother’s life span must end seven days after his birth.
Thus, the *Mahā-upāya-kauśalya Sūtra* states: "When about to descend [into the womb], he observed Lady Māyā; furthermore, her karmic lifespan was exhausted, and ten months had been fulfilled."

It is sufficient. There remain seven days; because a woman’s virtue is slight and her defilements heavy, she cannot endure the ritual courtesy due to a Bodhisattva’s minister or son, and for this reason she passed away.
Mou said: "This interpretation is superficial. If a person of great capacity cannot endure the ritual courtesy of a minister or son," [then what of it?]
He passed away on the seventh day. Since King Śuddhodana was one whom [the Queen] revered so much, why did he not die for such a long time?

Furthermore, the *Pūrva-caryā-sūtra* provides three explanations in total. First: when seven days had just passed since the Prince’s birth, the Lady passed away because she could no longer sustain the power of the devas;
this was because the Bodhisattva was in her womb and the devas were protecting him. Second, it says: because of the Bodhi... [text truncated]
When Sākyamuni left home to become a monk at a young age, his mother’s heart shattered upon seeing this, and she immediately passed away.

According to another account, when the mother saw her son’s body full, robust, and dignified, her entire being leaped with joy; unable to contain her happiness, she then passed away. According to Mūlasarvāstivāda tradition: [the text continues as above].

The third interpretation seems unlikely to be correct. If it is said that she did not obtain the protective power of the devas or the guardian of the womb, and that the devas did not protect her before she descended into the womb, then she ought to have died long ago.
Furthermore, as for those who see their sons renounce the world and have their hearts shattered by grief—

All the various schools state that he left the household life at twenty-nine and shaved his hair in the forest; how then could he have seen [the Buddha] and left the household life after only seven days?
Furthermore, regarding the statement that he was overcome by joy because his lifespan was ending: if that were so, then upon his initial birth, his joyful mind would have been even more intense.
"How is it that he passed away only after seven days? This is merely the compiler of the sūtra recording what others had already said; it is not the correct interpretation. Mǔ says:

"The end of life occurs when the retribution of a single lifetime is exhausted"—this is somewhat close [to the truth]. Furthermore, he says: "By the power of his merit, he ought to have been reborn in the higher realms"—this is the orthodox view.
Regarding the mention of "the sisters of Mahāmāyā" and so forth, these were simply her biological sisters.
Originally they were her paternal aunts, and as she became their mother-in-law, they were thus called *mātulānī* (maternal aunts); it was not that they were designated as such by title alone.
Regarding the term "Mahāsaṃmatī" (Great Victorious Birth-Mistress) and so forth: this was originally the name of a Brahmā King, Mahāsaṃmata. This nun obtained [the name] by begging it from him;
thus, based on her request for the name, she was named Mahāsaṃmatī. It is also said: those born from Brahmā who obtain the four continents are called "Great Beings" (Mahājana);
those born from Brahmā who obtain various [other] beings are called "Victorious Beings" (Saṃmata). These two categories combined constitute the name.

He is named Mahāsaṃbhava (Great Arising). Thirdly, it is said: "Buddha" means *mahat* (great). "Arising" (*saṃbhava*) refers to the name given to all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who have attained the stages prior to the path of seeing;
thus, he is the arising of the great, and is called Mahāsaṃbhava. If one has arisen as a noble disciple (*ārya-śrāvaka*) of the Three Vehicles, he is called a superior arising (*viśiṣṭasaṃbhava*);
Buddha is therefore named Mahāsaṃbhava. This Niyaṅ Buddha is named Mahāsaṃbhava. As for his original name as a Brahmā King, [it was] Brahmā King...
He is the father of all sentient beings; therefore, he is called "Great" (*mahā*). His capacity to give birth is called "Victorious" (*jaya*).
Being the master of that which gives birth, he is named the "Great Victorious Lord of Birth" (*Mahājaya-janēśvara*).
This aunt obtained [the child] from that Brahmā deity; she is named after what was requested. Second, the Buddha is called "Great. He gave birth to all ordinary beings...
Now, all ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) are the birth of the great; thus they are called "great births" (*mahājāti*). Furthermore, the Buddha is also called "victorious" (*jina*).

The noble disciples (*ārya-śrāvaka*) of the three vehicles who are born [from him] are the birth of the victorious; thus they are called "victorious births" (*jinajāti*). The term "birth" (*jāti*) refers to all sentient beings and the noble assemblies of the three vehicles.
Since the Buddha is both great and victorious, he is called the "Great Victorious Birth" (*mahājinajāti*). This nun, who nurtures the Buddha, is therefore called "Great" (*Mahā*).

"Jaya-sambhava" (Victorious Birth). It belongs to the Buddha; the character "master" (主) belongs to the aunt. According to the interpretation in the Lu-fu [commentary], the first explanation in the *Shu* states:
the Buddha’s full name is Mahā-jaya-sambhava, which belongs to the master. This nun raised the Buddha; she is named after the place where she raised him, indicating possession (*saviśeṣa*).
The phrase "although obtained by begging from them" and so forth concludes the two preceding meanings; it establishes the name based on the object begged for.
It is also a name established according to its meaning.
Regarding the statement that "the circumstances for this transition are as in the Vinaya," the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: At that time, the World-Honored One was in the kingdom of Nyagrodha.

Then Mahāprajāpatī, together with five hundred Śākya women, went to where the World-Honored One was and said to him, "World-Honored One, we pray that you will permit women to leave the household life and study the Path within the Buddha-dharma. The Buddha said, "Stop, Gautamī."
"Do not speak thus! Do not allow women to leave the household life to study the Path, lest my True Dharma be diminished by five hundred years and fail to endure for long.
Later, at one time, while the Buddha was staying at the Jetavana Monastery, Mahāprajāpatī and her followers all shaved their heads and donned the saffron robes.
They stood by the gate of the Jetavana with dust covering their bodies and tears streaming down their faces.
They wept and each requested to leave the household life and seek to receive full ordination. At that time, Ānanda, having heard this, related the aforementioned matters in detail.
The first [disciple] directly requested that the Buddha grant him ordination. The Buddha said, "Stop! This will ruin my True Dharma.
It is like a householder’s family where the men are few and the women many; that family will surely decline. It is like a fertile field where the grain is nearly ripe, yet a calamity strikes."
The wind causes the grain to spoil again, just as when many thorns are sown in a good field; the fertile field will surely be ruined. Thus the Buddha told them.
Ānanda, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, if laypeople each take precious vessels filled with exquisite food and drink and wait by the roadside to invite bhikṣus for a meal,
yet still fail to obtain their invitation, they may further spread fine robes upon the road.

He had the bhikṣus tread upon it with their feet. Furthermore, he spread out his hair to brush the dust from the bhikṣus' feet. Because of these acts of serving women, these matters were all concluded.
Second, Ānanda spoke of the kindness of her nurturing him, saying to the World-Honored One: "Mahāprajāpatī..."
The World-Honored One has rendered great kindness and virtue [to me]. Seven days after my birth, my noble mother passed away, and my maternal aunt raised me.
I have not repaid the debt of her nursing and upbringing. The Buddha said: "I have already fulfilled my repayment of that kindness.

It was because of me that she heard the names of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha; thus, I have rendered great kindness and virtue to my maternal aunt. Third, Ānanda cited the cause and its corresponding result.
Therefore, he requested, saying: "World-Honored One, does the World-Honored One permit women to leave the household life and attain the fruits of holiness?
The Buddha replied: "I permit it; they may attain them. He asked again: "Did the Buddhas of the past deliver their parents? The Buddha replied: "I permitted it; they were delivered. Ānanda said:
"World-Honored One, for what reason do you not permit women to leave the household life? The Buddha said: "Because by permitting women to enter my Dharma, it will diminish my [teaching]."
"The True Dharma shall endure for five hundred years. It is for this reason that she was not permitted [to ordain].

However, if she can practice the Eight Respectful Rules (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*) for as long as her life lasts, she may also be permitted to leave the household life and receive full ordination (*upasampadā*). Having heard this, Ānanda related these matters in detail.
At that moment, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī and the five hundred Śākya women immediately received the precepts upon hearing these words; they were filled with joy and leaped for gladness.
Having paid his respects, he departed. Later, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī, unable to bear witnessing the Buddha’s entry into parinirvāṇa, entered nirvāṇa first.
Together with five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, she rubbed the Buddha’s feet with her hands, circumambulated him three times, prostrated herself, and then rose.
She performed the eighteen transformations and emitted great radiance before entering nirvāṇa. The Buddha said to Ānanda: "You must take [the relics]..."
“Śāriputra, place these relics in my bowl and bring them here. The Buddha received them with his hands and placed them upon his head;
holding them in his palms, he showed them to the assembly, saying, “These relics are those of my maternal aunt.

Because she nurtured my body, all sentient beings may hear the Dharma, leave suffering behind, and attain liberation. At that time, Ānanda and Rāhula each intended to request the Buddha’s mother’s [relics].
[The relatives] offered a grand供养 (offering). The Buddha forbade it. When parents raise a child, they feel a sense of indebtedness for the benefit they have provided.
Having nurtured and nourished me, I must now provide for them in return to repay their kindness. On the day his father, the King, passed away, the Tathāgata personally carried the coffin.

Now that his maternal aunt is entering nirvana, he does not permit others to prepare the offerings. The mothers of the Buddhas of the three periods—past, future, and present—all pass into extinction first. All...
This is for one's own offering, with the desire to cause all sentient beings to be filial and obedient toward their parents.
Regarding the "four inner retinues of bhikṣuṇīs," Mǔ says: Yaśodharā, the mother of Rāhula, who managed the domestic affairs and was wedded to a man of high station;
once the Tathāgata had attained the Way, she too left the household life and heard the Dharma. Since she is called "inner," [she is included among them].
The *kuan* (female relatives) also arrived at Mount Ling. Therefore, the sutra begins with "the Buddha’s household," referring to the female monastics who were his kin.
Regarding the statement that their appearance was beautiful and so forth, there were two causes and conditions by which they gained renown: first, the beauty of their physical form.
Second, regarding the birth of Rāhula, the phrase "as explained in the traditional commentaries" serves to resolve potential objections.

While various sacred teachings state that Yaśodharā was a *gandharva* maiden and must therefore have been a celestial nymph (*yù nǚ*), the three sections of this commentary prove she was not a celestial nymph: first, she became the wife of the Buddha.
"She is not a jade maiden. This is a passage from the commentary (*śāstra*).
As for the statement "if she is called a jade maiden," etc., she is not a jade maiden because she has two sons; a jade maiden has no children.
Regarding the statement "after the Buddha had left the household life": his parents brought him back home.

According to the custom of the Western lands (India), when a daughter serves another family and has no son within three years, her original parents do not welcome her back. Now, because she was pregnant, her parents brought her back; therefore, she was not a "Jade Maiden" (an unmarried woman).
Regarding the mention of the *Adbhuta-dharma* and other such scriptures, these synthesize various teachings. Various sūtras state that Rāhula was the son of Gopī;
this is said with reference to his biological mother. Gopī, however, was actually a noble lady (*yù nǚ*). The Buddha had three principal wives, and Gopī was the senior wife.
Regarding the statement "that sutra says 'from these [persons]...": Question: If one follows the sutras, Rāhula was born of Yaśodharā;
why then does the *Adbhutadharma-paryāya-sūtra* state that he was born of Gopī? Answer: Gopī was a jade-like woman (a celestial maiden) who originally did not give birth to children.
Among those who did give birth, Yaśodharā was the eldest. If one considers seniority by age, Gopī is the elder; however, according to the actual facts [of paternity], [Yaśodharā is the mother].
He was simply the son of Yaśodharā. As for the statement in that sutra that he was born of Gopī, this is merely a name derived from his maternal grandmother.
Regarding the claim that there is a sutra stating the Buddha had three sons: the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that Sunakṣatra was the son of the Bodhisattva while he was still a householder.
If this is so, how is it that when the Crown Prince first intended to renounce the world, his parents and the King would not permit it?
"Wait until you have a son, then you may go. Later, he pointed to Yaśodharā’s womb; it was only then that Rāhula was born. Did he not say that there was a son named Sunakṣatra?
The answer is that because Sunakṣatra was born of Mṛgī, he was unfit to succeed to the throne; therefore, on that day, it was said that there was no son. [The interlocutor asks:
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that Sunakṣatra was the eldest son; how can the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* state that Rāhula was [the eldest]?
Regarding the "eldest son": he is called the eldest because he was born from the Deer Lady (*Mṛgajā*), as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

The *Lotus Sūtra* refers to him as the eldest in reference to his being the son born of the Senior Queen (*Mahādevī*), who succeeded to the throne as the legitimate heir; thus he is called the eldest. Question: There is also a tradition stating that Yaśodharā was the Senior Queen.
It does not state how Gopī [was designated]. The answer is twofold: first, after Gopī died, Yaśodharā became the principal consort;
second, because she was the mother of a son who was noble and capable of succeeding to the throne, the mother attained the title of "Principal Consort."

Regarding the statement that "those with whom one has a connection all arrive," this means that the *saṃyojana* (fetters) also come together with their retinue. Question: Why do they not come on their own? Answer:
Because those with whom one has a connection all arrive; for this reason, they come accompanied by their retinue.
From here below begins the commentary on the second fascicle of the *Xuánzàn*.

Regarding the phrase "the assembly whose holy virtue is inconceivable": these are eighty thousand bodhisattvas from the third eon who have attained *dhāraṇī* and realized *avaivartika* [non-retrogression].

They temporarily reside in this defiled land, manifesting their traces as fellow listeners; thus their holy virtue is inconceivable. Although the Sūtra designates them as a single assembly, they are also...

Question: After listing the assembly of *śrāvakas* following the phrase "the great assembly of divine merit," what is the purpose of further enumerating the assembly of Bodhisattvas? Answer: There are two meanings.

First, it is intended to authenticate Ānanda. If Ānanda had heard the Mahāyāna teachings together with only those of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), then as a *śrāvaka* whose spiritual capacity and measure are narrow and inferior, he would not be fully trustworthy.
Now, by hearing them together with eighty thousand great Bodhisattvas, [his credibility is established].

Because it is the Great Dharma, the sutra is trustworthy. Second, it is to manifest the Buddha’s virtues. Even if there were śrāvakas present, they would not manifest the Buddha’s noble and majestic virtue.
The Buddha is a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa) because he is supported by greatness; thus his virtue is supreme.

If only a few people were surrounding the Buddha, his virtue would appear slight. Therefore, the term "Great Man" is designated to exalt the Buddha’s virtue, and thus the bodhisattvas are listed. As...

When it is said that "the king comes," it necessarily implies he is accompanied by his ministers and retinue. When one asks about the six meanings of *vaibhāṣika*, one should teach and transform the assembly.

Within the fifteen meanings concerning the assembly, one should lead the great multitude through teaching and transformation. What is the difference between the modes of practice for the two types of benefit—great and small? Answer:

When those of the Two Vehicles perform acts of benefiting others from within a mind focused on their own self-benefit, it is like a person in the world who practices giving merely out of a desire for fame. Therefore, the Bodhisattva...
Such a person, with a mind intent on benefiting others, performs acts for their own benefit. This is like a teacher of music who first practices the melodies themselves in order to benefit others.
A question is raised: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that a Bodhisattva, if remaining at home, does not transgress the status of an upāsaka or upāsikā;
if they leave the home life, they do not transgress the status of a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī. Since it is sufficient to mention these four assemblies [of the Sangha], why is it necessary to further...

To the question of whether those listed are bodhisattvas, the answer is not fixed. While a bodhisattva must necessarily belong to one of the fourfold assembly, those in the fourfold assembly are not necessarily bodhisattvas.

For instance, those śrāvakas of fixed nature, those without the spiritual lineage (agotra), and those who have never resolved upon the Mahāyāna mind—these members of the fourfold assembly are not bodhisattvas.
Regarding the term *bodhisattva-mahāsattva*, the Chinese translation is abbreviated; it is shortened to *pú-sà* (菩薩).

This is because the *mahā* (摩訶) of *mahāsattva* is dropped, and the *ti* (提) of *sattva* is dropped, hence it is called *pú-sà*. It is also translated as "sentient being" (*yǒuqíng*). The name *pú-sà* applies generally to all three vehicles:

those seeking the state of a *śrāvaka* are called *śrāvaka-bodhisattvas*, and those seeking the state of a *pratyekabuddha* are called *pratyekabuddha-bodhisattvas*; these are collectively termed *pú-sà*. Now, [the text] distinguishes [them].
Because the three vehicles (*triyāna*) are excluded, the term "mahāsattva" is added.
Regarding the statement that "the practice of the bodhisattva is, in brief, equal," there are four distinct interpretations of the two characters *bodhisattva*.

The first and third are from the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā-vṛtti-śāstra* (Wu xing lun); the second is from the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra*; and the final interpretation is that of the Master of the Commentary (*śāstrakāra*).
Yongtai said: "The Dharma taught by the Buddha consists of four aspects: namely, doctrine, principle, practice, and fruition.

The names established for the Three Vehicles are also based on these four. The Śrāvaka is named according to the doctrine, for they attain their fruition by hearing the voice of the Buddha's teaching.
The Pratyekabuddha is named according to principle, for they contemplate the principle of the twelve links of dependent origination. The Bodhisattva is named according to practice..."
He establishes its designation. [The Tathāgata] is able to cultivate practices for the benefit of self and others; the Tathāgata establishes his title based on the fruit [of these practices].
Now, it is shown that a Bodhisattva establishes [their name] based on practice. Therefore, it is said that the cultivation of a Bodhisattva briefly consists of two kinds.
Regarding the statement "Great Wisdom is foremost": Question: Why is it that, having asked this question, the explanation now speaks of practice? Answer:

The name "Bodhisattva" is established based on the two types of beneficial conduct. Although there are ten thousand practices cultivated by a Bodhisattva, when summarized, they do not exceed two kinds.

The first is self-benefit, for which Great Wisdom is foremost. The word "foremost" (shou) serves to distinguish this from other forms of self-benefit; though many such practices exist, [none surpass this].
The measurement of phenomena (*pramāṇa-dharma*) is, in general, for one's own benefit. Now, we take only "great wisdom" (*mahājñāna*) as the foremost among these self-benefiting practices.
That which is cultivated by Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*)—namely, the attainment of the two kinds of *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*—is called great wisdom.

Although the fruit is not yet perfected, because they gradually eliminate the attachment to phenomena (*dharman-grāha*) through the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā-jñāna*), sever the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), and realize the principle of the emptiness of phenomena, it is so named.

Great wisdom (*mahāprajñā*) and the function of great wisdom personally and intimately realize the principle and spontaneously experience the bliss of the Dharma; therefore, it is called "benefiting oneself.

Only when one primarily takes the fundamental [wisdom] as the basis can it be considered great wisdom. Subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), which takes conventional reality as its object, benefits oneself only slightly.
Regarding the phrase "the two benefits for others, preceded by great compassion" (*mahākaruṇā-pūrvaka*), the word "preceded" (*pūrva*) also serves to distinguish this from other dharmas.
Although practices such as the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) are indeed beneficial to others and essential for saving living beings, they are "preceded by great compassion.

Because there is great compassion, one does not abide in *nirvāṇa*, remaining identical with the class of worldly phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) to rescue [beings] from the two types of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). Because there is great wisdom (*mahājñāna*), one does not abide in *saṃsāra*, merging in secret harmony [with reality].
The truth is the eternal dharma-joy. It does not cling to the ultimate or the conventional, nor does it depart from the ultimate or the conventional.

One diligently cultivates the two benefits to seek awakening. Question: How is wisdom self-benefit? Answer: A bodhisattva’s fundamental wisdom is exclusively self-benefit, because it realizes only suchness (*tathatā*) and does not externally perceive other phenomena;
thus, it lacks the sense of benefiting others. A bodhisattva’s subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) encompasses both self-benefit and benefit for others.
Benefiting others. The subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) that takes principles as its object is exclusively for one’s own benefit.

Within the subsequently attained wisdom that takes phenomena as its object, taking as objects one's own five faculties (*indriya*), five powers (*bala*), the six perfections (*pāramitā*) for one's own benefit, and the mind seeking enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), is also for one's own benefit.

If, within subsequently attained wisdom, one cultivates the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), or performs teaching and conversion for others, this is called benefiting others. If one cultivates the ten perfections, [this is also for one's own benefit].

For the most part, these involve self-benefit and only a small portion of benefiting others. When a Bodhisattva of the first stage (*bhūmi*) teaches the "Gate of Illumination of a Hundred Dharmas" (*śatadharmavidyāmukha*), or a Bodhisattva of the second stage teaches the "Dharmas of a Thousand" and so forth to transform sentient beings, this is called benefiting others.

Now, we take only the cultivation for self-benefit based on fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*) and subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdhajñāna*), seeking the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*); this is called self-benefit. Furthermore, with great wisdom as the primary focus—
This is the gateway of wisdom. Second, regarding "having great compassion as the priority for the benefit of others":

during eons of famine, he transforms into fish, rice, and so forth, to provide relief and benefit to sentient beings. During eons of disease, he manifests as medicinal trees to cure the ailments of the multitude.
Amidst perilous paths, he can manifest bridges and the like, as well as preach hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates to benefit sentient beings; all these are termed "Great [Compassion]."
Compassion (*karuṇā*). It refers exclusively to a portion of subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) that benefits sentient beings; this is termed the "Gate of Great Compassion.
Regarding the phrase "bodhi-awakening," etc., this is the translation by the Tang Tripiṭaka Master. The ancient translation states: "Bodhi is called the Way (*mārga*); *sattva* means sentient beings.
Because they are sentient beings with the mind of the Great Way, they are called Bodhisattvas. This is an erroneous and mistaken interpretation. *Bodhi* means awakening.
"Meaning" (*artha*) refers to the *bodhi* of the Buddha-fruit; it is not the great wisdom within the provisional body of the bodhisattva.
The great wisdom within the provisional body of the bodhisattva serves as the seeker, while this *bodhi* of the Buddha-fruit is that which is sought.

"Sattva" means "sentient being"; it refers to the sentient beings to be delivered by compassion. Great compassion within the provisional body of the bodhisattva serves as the deliverer. There are... [text continues].

Sentient beings (*sattva*) are those who are to be delivered. Because one is named a *bodhisattva* based on both that which is sought and that which is to be delivered—being named "Bodhi" (*bodhi*) after what is sought and "Sattva" (*sattva*) after those to be delivered—one takes the body that is capable of seeking and capable of delivering and designates it by the names of that which is sought and that which is to be delivered;
thus, it is called a *bodhisattva*. That which is sought and that which is to be delivered are the objects of focus (*ālambana-viṣaya*). The capacity to seek and...

"Deliverance" (*tāraṇa*) refers to that which is capable of being the object-condition (*ālambana*). Question: What is the difference between awakening (*bodhi*) and wisdom (*jñāna*)? Answer: The former is the cause and the latter is the fruit.

This means that within the gateway of wisdom (*jñāna-mukha*), it is the fruit sought; it is not the sentient beings delivered within the gateway of compassion (*karuṇā-mukha*). Furthermore, it is said:

"The preceding stages constitute causal wisdom (*hetu-jñāna*), while the succeeding stages constitute resultant wisdom (*phala-jñāna*); they differ according to each stage (*bhūmi*) and each category (*prakāra*)."
Therefore, it is said that this is the fruit sought by wisdom.

Regarding the phrase "relying on the words of the great vows," this refers to the *Mahāyānasamgraha* (Compendium of the Great Vehicle). That is, one establishes the name "Bodhisattva" based on the words of the great vows.
Specifically, among the Four Great Vows, these are: "I vow to deliver boundless sentient beings" and "I vow to realize the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood. This [distinction] is made...
Ordinary beings and śrāvakas of fixed nature, although they may take the two objects as their focus, do not make the Buddha’s great vow;
because they are unwilling to resolve to seek bodhi and deliver sentient beings, they are not called bodhisattvas. "Now, relying on the great vow" refers to the four great vows:
"Sentient beings are boundless; I vow to deliver them," which corresponds to benefiting others and is preceded by great compassion; the remaining three vows correspond to the former [self-benefit].
Regarding self-benefit, great wisdom is primary. Furthermore, it is said that among the Four Great Vows, three vows are named *pu* (bodhi) and the first vow is named *sa* (sattva);
thus one is called a Bodhisattva. The vow to achieve the unsurpassed Buddha-way is named *pu*; the vow to deliver boundless sentient beings is named *sa*.
Therefore, it is said that [the name] is based on the words of these great vows.
Regarding the statement "taking the two as objects," etc., this refers to the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*. Enlightenment (*bodhi*) is the object sought by the great wisdom of a bodhisattva;
sentient beings are the objects to be delivered by the great compassion of a bodhisattva. Here, we do not rely on that which initiates the vow, but rather on the vow itself that is initiated.
We do not rely on the wisdom and compassion that act as the subjective conditions, but rather on the two objects themselves that are the objective conditions. As for enlightenment...
Because these two factors—sentiment (*citta*) and suchness (*tathatā*)—are present, one is called a *bodhisattva*. This is an *adhikaraṇa-sarvadhātuka* (possessive) compound.
*Bodhi* and *sattva* are the "wealth" (*sattva*) belonging to the house of the Bodhisattva’s compassion and wisdom; they encompass both that which is sought and that which is to be delivered.

The term *sattva* (sentient being) is applied to the person of the Bodhisattva based on the attainment of *bodhi*, and thus he is named a *bodhisattva*. Since this name depends upon another [factor], it is termed a possessive compound.
Regarding the statement that "enlightenment (*bodhi*) is that which is sought," etc., this is the second interpretation.

It is the same as the previous interpretation, except that *sattva* is attributed to the person who practices as a bodhisattva; one simply calls such a person a *sattva*. The meaning of *sattva* is "sentient being" (*sattvārtha*).

Regarding the phrase "seeking *sambodhi*": [Question] All sentient beings, individually and collectively, are termed "sentient beings" (*sattva*). I do not yet know which kind of sentient being this refers to.
[Answer] It refers to the sentient being who seeks *sambodhi*. As for *sambodhi*, it may be the *bodhi* of a *śrāvaka*, the *bodhi* of a *pratyekabuddha*, or the *bodhi* of the fruit of Buddhahood.
Lù says: Or it may be the *bodhi* of the three Buddhas; it is only the Great [Bodhi].
It is a vehicle (*yāna*). It is the bodhi of the Dharma, Sambhoga, and Nirmāṇa bodies; or it is the bodhi of Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and Equal Enlightenment (*samatā-bodhi*).

Furthermore, regarding the bodhi of Perfect Enlightenment, according to the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, one who seeks the bodhi of the three vehicles is generally termed a Bodhisattva, but is not specifically termed a Mahāsattva.

Question: Since the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is not wisdom (*jñāna*), how can one speak of the three bodies and the three types of bodhi? Answer: The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "The five... [The text continues from here.]

The Dharma encompasses the three bodies (*trikāya*). Regarding this, there are two masters’ explanations. According to the first two [masters], the pure *dharmadhātu* and the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) subsume the *svābhāvikakāya*.
This is because the Sūtras state that True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the *dharmakāya*, and the Śāstra says: "By transforming and eliminating the *ālayavijñāna*, one attains the *svābhāvikakāya*;
it is realized through the category of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom by transforming and eliminating the *ālayavijñāna*. The middle two [wisdoms] subsume the transformational categories.
The Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*). The latter category subsumes the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*). A second interpretation states:

There is a view that the first [category] subsumes the Essential Body (*svābhāvikakāya*), which consists of the true merits within the category of the four wisdoms (*caturjñāna*) and the eternal, pervasive form-body (*rūpakāya*) arising from the Mirror-like Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*);

this is the Self-Enjoyment Body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*), which fully subsumes all four wisdoms. The Buddha-body manifested within the category of the Equality Wisdom (*samatājñāna*) subsumes the Other-Enjoyment Body (*parasambhogakāya*). The All-Accomplishing Wisdom (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*)... [subsumes the Transformation Body].

The various bodily forms manifested according to the categories [of beings] within the chapters are subsumed under the *nirmāṇakāya*. Now, regarding the statement that "enlightenment consists of the three bodies," this follows the second master’s view;
it takes only the *saṃbhogakāya* (for oneself and others) and the *nirmāṇakāya*, but does not take the *svābhāvikakāya*.
