Once, having been sent by the Buddha as an emissary to the outskirts of the Vārāṇasī forest to subdue Māra, he was praised by the assembled multitude; then, he was dispatched to the city of Vaiśālī to inquire after his illness.
At other times, he taught the dragon girl at sea, causing her to swiftly awaken to the One Vehicle; or he testified to the sutras on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
When this Bodhisattva sat during the time of the eight sons of Dīpaṃkara, the lands of various jewels shook all at once.
When he came and when he went, he came without the appearance of coming; he went without the appearance of going.

When he manifested transformations and appeared, he turned the great earth into mountains of gold and churned the long rivers into ghee and curd. In times of compassion and pity, he regarded all enemies as...
Like an infant, they possess all samādhis; like the great ocean, they abide in the bodhisattva precepts; like Mount Sumeru, their mind of patience is like a diamond;
their vigorous diligence is like a swift wind; in subduing all non-Buddhists, they are like lions; they can purify all views, like falling rain;
and they cause the sprouts of goodness to grow, like the moisture of spring. Adorned...
The Bodhisattva is like a garland of flowers; he is like a thunderbolt that shatters the enemies of affliction; he is like a bright mirror that reveals good and evil deeds;
he is like a precious vase that relieves all who are destitute; he is the sun for those in darkness, the companion for those who have lost their way, and the ladder for those ascending to heaven;
he is the bridge to the land of Nirvana and the great ship for crossing over birth and death; he is the parasol for those tormented by feverish distress—for all sentient beings.
The unsurpassed field of merit, the foremost minister of all Buddhas of the three periods of time. Question:

Since Bodhisattvas transform beings throughout all six realms of existence, for what reason do you reside exclusively within Mount Qingliang? Answer: There are two reasons. First, to subdue the venomous dragons;

that is to say, there are many venomous dragons on that mountain who afflict and harm sentient beings, and for this reason, the World-Honored One dispatched you to come and act as a guardian. Second, due to [the karmic] conditions...
The sentient beings of this realm delight in the Mahāyāna. Here, he secretly transforms the fourfold assembly and constantly preaches the Mahāyāna.

In truth, he attained Buddhahood long ago, yet manifests as a bodhisattva to serve as a supporting condition for the propagation of the Buddha-dharma. Formerly the Teacher of Gods and Humans, he is now a Prince of the Dharma.
Since two honored ones do not manifest their transformations simultaneously, he appears in the form of a bodhisattva.
Regarding the phrase "observing the three karmas," it means that by observing the three karmas of sentient beings, one attains mastery.

If a sentient being performs prostration through the karma of the body, the Bodhisattva observes it with the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). If they offer praise through the karma of speech, the Bodhisattva hears it with the supernormal power of the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*).

If they contemplate with the mind, the Bodhisattva observes it with the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others (*paracittajñāna*) through their own mental karma. Thus, one rides upon these three karmas and...
To rescue and deliver them. If one says "Avalokiteśvara," it fully encompasses the three karmas of sentient beings;
if one says "Avalokitasvara," one only attains the karma of speech and loses the other two karmas. This Bodhisattva concentrates his spirit in the Pure Land while manifesting his traces in Sahā.

He displays the six supernormal powers within his light; he does not merely pay homage to names within various lands. Standing upon the crown of a Buddha’s head, he manifests the salvation from suffering.

Like sands of the Ganges, these [practices] can cause the wheel of the seven calamities to vanish and fulfill the two types of aspirations. When urged by the lofty [teaching], even when facing the blade, it is severed;
renowned monks reach death without being harmed. With a long-drawn-out single chant, the wind turns back; upon hearing and reciting the name, the fire is extinguished.

The various secret records are complete; they may be summarized as follows (the preceding was established by name according to practice). Furthermore, regarding the establishment of the name according to vows, as stated in the *Vīramatī-sāgarabuddhi-sūtra*:
"Why is it that Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva has a particular affinity for this land? The answer is:
"In the past, in Jambudvīpa, there was a king named Viśeṣamati who had five hundred princes. The eldest among them was named Sudhana."
Guang encountered the Buddha Avalokiteśvara, King of Emptiness, and made ten great vows: first, to know all dharmas; second, to board the ship of Prajñā;
third, to encounter the wind of wisdom; fourth, to obtain skillful means; fifth, to deliver all people;
sixth, to cross over the sea of suffering; seventh, to attain the maintenance of the precepts; eighth, to ascend the mountain of Nirvāṇa.
Ninth, he vowed to realize the robe of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Tenth, he vowed to share in the body of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā-kāya*). Furthermore, he made this vow:

"In future lives, may I also be named Avalokiteśvara. If there are those suffering from the ailments of sentient beings who invoke my name three times, and I do not go to rescue them, I vow never to attain a sublime physical body. This is why he has a special affinity with this land.
Regarding the statement that Amitābha Buddha enters parinirvāṇa: if one asks, according to what is set forth in the sūtras, this is his *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body);

how could there be parinirvāṇa for such a body? The answer is: it refers to the *paranirmita-saṃbhogakāya* (body of enjoyment for others). This body of enjoyment appears in response to bodhisattvas from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) downward who have an abundance of compassion.
There may be parinirvāṇa, yet [the Buddha] eternally accords with those he transforms by assuming a body of segmented existence (*bhavāgra-śarīra*), because it is subject to birth and death.

Therefore, it is said that Amitābha’s father is named Candracchattra and his mother is named Viśeṣacārumukhī. However, when contrasted with those of increased wisdom—those from the eighth bhūmi upward—in the *paranirmita-vaiśvarya* [body], there is no birth or death.

Regarding the phrase "attaining great power" (*mahāsthāmaprāpta*) and so forth: if, while walking, one can cause everything from the adamantine wheel below up to the Buddha-field of King of Radiance above to tremble simultaneously, possessing such great majestic power, one is therefore named Mahāsthāmaprāpta.

Regarding the statement that there are "two capacities": it possesses Mañjuśrī’s capacity to bestow bliss as described in the preceding text, and it also possesses Avalokiteśvara’s capacity to extract one from suffering; therefore, they are called the "two capacities.

Regarding the statement that these two [capacities] constitute self-benefit and so forth: although the practices for self-benefit and benefiting others—whether wisdom-increasing or compassion-increasing—have ten thousand gateways, they do not...

Two matters emerge: exerting oneself without ceasing, and bestowing gifts impartially according to the needs of others. Reverently, the Sage always maintains this intention and constantly refines his own benefit.
If one eliminates and halts evil as if extinguishing a fire on one's head, and if one seeks Bodhi without regard for time or place, never resting—this is the benefit of others.
Because sentient beings are inexhaustible, one constantly rescues them from suffering; this is stated from one perspective.

It can be said that within this, both [self-benefit and benefiting others] are encompassed without obstruction. When a bodhisattva practices for self-benefit, it is fundamentally for the sake of sentient beings.
It is like a person who, though studying diligently, applies the results to their own benefit; yet because they originally intended to explain it to others, it is subsumed under benefiting others.
The bodhisattva is likewise.
Regarding the phrase "relieving poverty and saving those who are ill," this subsumes three individuals: Ratnapāṇi (Precious Hand), Bhaiṣajyarāja (Medicine King), and Śūradatta (Valiant Bestower).

Regarding Ratnapāṇi relieving poverty and so forth, it refers to Vaiḍūrya jewels, sphaṭika crystals, coral, amber, jade, white jade, conch shells, ghaṇṭā-kośa, indranīla, and mahānīla gems. When there is currently visible suffering from poverty, [he causes these] to emerge from his hand.
[The questioner asks: "Why do you not save them? [The Buddha] answers, as stated in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*: "These sentient beings are merely moved by their own karma. It says:

"If Bodhisattvas are fully endowed with all inexhaustible treasures and have perfected great compassion, for what reason are there currently sentient beings in the world who are poor, suffering, and destitute?
The Buddha replied: "Good son, these sentient beings are [the result of] their own karma."
This has passed by. If it were not so, the Bodhisattva would always harbor a mind intent on benefiting others and would always be fully possessed of inexhaustible wealth and treasures.
It is like a hungry ghost who sees the great ocean as a raging fire; this is not the fault of the great ocean, but the fault of the hungry ghost’s own karma.
Thus, there is a verse that says: "Like a mother's milk, all shall become wealthy and noble; from their hands, treasures shall emerge. This is the meaning.
It is established. There are currently people in the world who suffer from poverty. The Bodhisattva’s reputation for being a "Jewel-Palm" (Ratnapāṇi) is empty and of no benefit.
If the river flows eastward with its waters surging, yet jewels emerge from within it, how could those of evil karma possibly enjoy them? One might ask:

the Bodhisattva’s compassionate heart is universal, and his bestowal of jewels should cause all to share equally. Yet, the poor and the wealthy in the world differ by ten thousand degrees; the Bodhisattva treats enemies and kin unequally.

[Question: Even though Mencius was poor all his life, he still craved beauty and pursued fame; how much more so would one who is moderately well-off and wealthy refuse to walk with measured steps and circumscribed decorum?
If the wealth and poverty of sentient beings are already determined by their own karma, how can a Bodhisattva provide for them through charity?

[Answer: It is appropriate that they receive [benefits]. Although they are equal in terms of the general conditions, there are distinctions based on specific causes, just as when people of the world receive their respective stipends. It is not otherwise.
It is possible to obtain it; yet even if obtained, it would eventually turn back into rubble.

Just as when one's understanding of a single object becomes distorted, the Bodhisattva observes that sentient beings become heedless when they possess wealth and property, thereby extensively creating evil karma; however, when oppressed by suffering, they are immediately able to resolve their minds toward awakening.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva knows that such treasures are of no benefit, and for this reason, he does not rain them down.
Regarding the "great medicinal trees" and so forth, the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states:

Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja made various vows, vowing that during the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa, he would make offerings to each one at the time they first attained Buddhahood, and he would erect stupas for each upon their entry into parinirvāṇa.
I shall protect and deliver all sentient beings suffering at the end of the kalpa. Amidst the kalpas of warfare and pestilence, I shall act as a Great King of Physicians.
During the kalpa of pestilence, the Bodhisattva’s great compassion manifests as a King of Medicine Trees; those who consume its roots, stems, branches, and leaves have their illnesses cured.
Furthermore, upon seeing its form, hearing its sound, smelling its fragrance, tasting its flavor, or feeling its touch, all shall find their illnesses cured. Thereafter, he shall act...
The Buddha is none other than Rāhula-tathāgata. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"There was a king of trees named Aṅgada. A venomous snake pursued a frog; the frog fled to a medicinal tree and felt peace and comfort in its heart.
The snake went seven paces away from the tree, where it encountered the medicinal vapor lingering on the ground; it writhed in agony and died. Good son, the Bodhisattva..."
It is also like this. The medicinal tree represents the bodhisattva; the frog represents sentient beings; and the venomous snake represents the celestial Māra Pāpīyān.
As for the mention of "Vīradatta" and others, it refers to the Great Being who, having realized emptiness—because of ultimate emptiness—sacrifices body, life, and wealth without any fear.
It is weak, yet it can also relieve poverty and later save one from illness.

It is said that it guides the enlightened and destroys darkness; these three are Ratnacandra (Jewel Moon), Candracandra (Moon Light), and Pūrṇacandra (Full Moon). Question: Why is he named Ratnacandra? Answer:
The eyes of sentient beings see objects during the day, but at night they cannot see objects; they must rely on the guidance of moonlight before they can see.

Just as the eye perceives objects, so it is with the Bodhisattva. Uncontaminated wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) is like the sun; it can dispel the darkness of ignorance within the bodies of sentient beings and induce wisdom within them.
Therefore, it is called "Guiding Light" (*nayanaprabha*). The Bodhisattva’s wisdom is accomplished through the uncontaminated and its essence is composed of jewels;
because sentient beings hold it in high esteem, it is called "Jewel Moon" (*ratnacandra*). Mǔ says: "The essence of wisdom is termed 'light,' while the deluded mind..."
This is darkness. Within the aperture lies the gate of human death; there are no ghosts gazing upon their kin. It is like a torch illuminating a room, like a boat unmooring its moorings.

It guides sentient beings to leave behind the burden of suffering. Question: What is meant by "Moonlight"? Answer: Because it can discern both the ultimate and the conventional truths, and because it illuminates the roots of all things, it is called Moonlight;
it is capable of destroying darkness. As for the "High Full Moon," its merits are complete and perfect, just like—
The moon is full; its virtue is nowhere incomplete, and its illumination is nowhere not universal. It can lead toward clarity and also shatter the darkness of ignorance.

Regarding the statement that supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) are small or great, Master Mu said: "Supernatural powers arise based on wisdom. Even by exerting such divine power, one purifies this long night, causing the world to sway and the lands of the Central Kingdom and the Barbarians to tremble.
Sentient beings thus arouse the aspiration for enlightenment, and the turbid age is left far behind."

Regarding the phrase "Great Power" (*mahābala*) and so forth, the commentary states: Explained according to principle, afflictions (*kleśa*) are able to cause the three realms to be in turmoil and cause those of the two vehicles to be deluded;
thus, their power is the greatest. Because Bodhisattvas are able to destroy these great evil dharmas, they are called "Great Power."
Regarding the term "immeasurable power" (*anantabala*): some say it refers to the power of signlessness (*animitta*), and that it is not named as power because it possesses a measurable limit.

Huìhuàdù says: "By means of performing supernatural transformations (*ṛddhi*), one awakens and examines those with whom there is a karmic connection, causing them all to resolve their minds [for enlightenment].
This is because by shaking the earth, sentient beings are startled into awareness, knowing that all worlds are entirely impermanent. Why is this? Although the world is vast, it undergoes movement."
How much more so my own body, which can never endure for long? Thus, I shall briefly discuss the lands according to the facts. First, at the first stage (*bhūmi*), one shakes a hundred Buddha-worlds;
this is called "Great Power. At the second stage, one shakes a thousand worlds; at the third stage, a hundred thousand worlds; at the fourth stage, ten billion; at the fifth stage, a hundred billion;
at the sixth stage, a hundred thousand billion worlds; and at the seventh stage, one shakes...

In a single kṣaṇa, a bodhisattva of the tenth stage can cause to tremble hundreds of thousands of koṭi-nayuta worlds; eight stages of earth tremble as many worlds as there are atoms in a hundred thousand million great trichiliocosms;
the ninth stage causes to tremble as many worlds as there are atoms in ten asaṃkhyeya hundreds of thousands of buddha-fields;
and a bodhisattva of the tenth stage can, in a single instant, cause to tremble ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayuta atoms of worlds.
The world-system is named "Immeasurable Power.
Regarding the statement that these two are free from defilement (*vītarāga*) and so forth: this includes two types of persons. Transcending the three realms is "freedom from defilement";
defilement is precisely the saṃsāra of the three realms. To be well able to leave the three realms is "excellent progress," as in the case of Bhadrapāla.

Regarding the phrase "transcending the three realms," Lü says: Suppose there is a man who has three people as his close friends—a son of the Kāśyapa clan, a son of a high minister, and the crown prince of a king—and they have made a pact together, saying, "If we obtain flavors, we shall share them equally;
if we encounter suffering, we shall suffer it in each other's stead. At that time, that man was imprisoned for some reason. The son of the Kāśyapa clan, however, was only able to...

They were provided with food and clothing, yet there was no means by which they could escape their shackles and fetters. The minister’s son was able to entreat the prison official to remove their chains and collars.
The Prince possessed great strength; he pushed down the prison wall, enabling those criminals to emerge openly.
The same applies to practicing generosity, maintaining ethical discipline, and cultivating wisdom. Sentient beings are imprisoned within the fortress of the three realms.
Even if one practices generosity, such that they lack nothing in terms of clothing or food within the three realms, they are still unable to escape from the various sufferings.
One who upholds the precepts, though able to escape the retribution of the three evil realms, is still unable to transcend the triple world.
One who cultivates wisdom can sever the afflictions and swiftly transcend the triple world.
This is like that prince who pushed down the prison wall, causing those confined within to emerge naturally; it clarifies how this bodhisattva, regarding generosity, morality, and cultivation—
He has perfected [his practice], transcended the three realms, and ascended purely to the other shore; therefore, he is named the Bodhisattva Who Has Transcended the Three Realms.
As for the name "Bhadrapāla," he is one who rivals the Great Sage, thus he is called "Worthy" (Bhadra); his virtuous conduct is fully preserved, thus he is called "Guardian" (Pāla).
Regarding the terms "mundane" (*laukika*) and "supramundane" (*lokottara*), there are three [texts] concerning this: the *Maitreya*, the *Ratnakūṭa*, and the *Śāstṛ*. Question:

What is meant by "mundane" and "supramundane"? Answer: That which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) is called mundane; that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*) is called supramundane. It is like ascending a high platform, or like falling into a dark chamber.
It is the fundamental means for delivering sentient beings and the method for attaining Buddhahood. Among the eighteen [treatises], it is categorized as the first.

7. Regarding the statement that "Maitreya’s *śīla* (surname) is 'Compassion' (*maitrī*)": in many versions of the commentary, the character for "surname" (*xìng*) is used; there are also instances where it is written as "lineage" (*xìngshì*) or "nature" (*xìng*).
The term "nature" (*xìng*) or "mental nature" (*xìngxīn*) is the correct Sanskrit form, which should be *Maitreya*. This is translated as "Compassion" (*mèi*). The ancients referred to it as "Mi."
"Dili" or "Mile" are both corruptions. The *Xiányújīng* (Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish), fascicle ten, states:
He was born in the village of Kapilavastu in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī as the son of a high minister. At the moment of his birth, he possessed the thirty-two marks and a purple-golden complexion.
His parents then summoned a physiognomist to examine him. The physiognomist said: "At the time of his descent [into the womb], what were the omens?"...
The divination was auspicious. His father replied, "His mother’s nature was originally unbalanced, but since she conceived him, her character has become largely benevolent and compassionate.
The physiognomist said, "This is the virtue of the child. Consequently, he was given a name; he was named Maitreya. There are three reasons for which this name was bestowed.
First is maternal compassion (*maitrī*); this refers to the mother’s clan name (*gotra*). Second is the compassionate nature of the mother’s mind;
this Bodhisattva takes the mother’s mind as his very nature. Third, the name is established based on a vow. As stated in the *Sarvajñāprabha-ṛṣi-sūtra*: [text continues].
In the past, Maitreya was the Rishi Sarvajñāprabha (All-Wisdom Light). He encountered the Buddha Maitreya, who taught him the Samādhi of Compassionate Mind.
As stated in the sutra: "I vow that when I attain Buddhahood in the future, I shall also be named Maitreya. This is explained in detail as set forth in the *Sarvajñāprabha-rishi-sūtra*.
There was a Brahmin who requested the Buddha to explain the causes and conditions regarding Maitreya. The Buddha said: "In the past... [The text continues from this point.]
At a time immeasurable asincalpya kalpas ago, there was a world named Śrīpuṣpāvatī. The Buddha told Maitreya:
"Always with a mind of loving-kindness, teach and transform all sentient beings through the Dharma of the Immeasurable. This sutra is titled *Maitrīcittasamādhi-mahākaruṇāsāgaramegha*.
Those who hear it will surely transcend the sins of ten billion kalpas and attain Buddhahood without doubt. There was a great brāhmaṇa..."
His gate was named All-Wisdom Light. He possessed sixty-four capacities and was profoundly wise and erudite.
Upon hearing the Buddha preach that sutra, he immediately conceived faith and made this vow: "I wish to uphold that sutra and, in a future life, attain Buddhahood under the name Maitreya."

He immediately left his home and entered the mountains, where he practiced the holy life for eighty years. He lived on alms and recited the sūtras. At that time, a famine occurred and he was unable to obtain food;
he remained there for seven days without eating. At that moment, there were five hundred white rabbits in the forest, among whom was a rabbit king.
Seeing that the seer had not eaten for many days because of his devotion to the Dharma, he spoke these words: "The seer, for the sake of the Dharma, has not eaten for many days."

"The Dharma is about to perish; the ocean of Dharma is about to dry up. I shall now sacrifice my life for the sake of the Dharma. He then addressed the rabbits: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent.

Sentient beings have received these bodies, yet they have never acted for the sake of the Dharma. I wish to sacrifice this body as an offering to the Dharma Master, so that the Dharma may endure for a long time.
The rabbit king and his offspring circumambulated the seer seven times and said to him: "Great Master, we now offer ourselves as an offering to Your Honor for the sake of the Dharma."
The seer said, "You are a beast; this resolve is difficult to fulfill. The hare spoke to its offspring, saying, "You may seek water and grass as you please.
Hearing his mother's words, the offspring replied to her, "I too wish to follow you.
He then threw himself into the fire, and his mother followed after him. At that moment, the great earth shook, and the devas scattered flowers.
He took it and used it as an offering. After the meat was cooked, the various deities said to the seer, "The meat is now cooked;
you may eat it. Upon hearing the words of the deities, the seer was overcome with grief and spoke this verse:

"Better to burn one's own body or have one's eyes and ears destroyed, than to bear to commit killing and eat a living being. Having spoken these words, he threw himself into the fire to end his life, together with the rabbit.
At that time, he died. The Buddha told the brahmin: "The hare-king was my own self; the rabbit was Rāhula;
and the seer who recited the sūtras is now Maitreya. He is not called 'Maitreya' (the Benevolent One) merely because he received that name from his compassionate mother;

rather, it is because he has long cultivated a mind of loving-kindness throughout his very being, thus naming himself Maitreya. From his stage as a causal practitioner until his attainment of Buddhahood, he has always been so."
He is named Maitreya. Some say his clan name is Bharadvāja and his personal name is Ajita, which means "Unconquered.
Regarding the phrase "Baoji (Treasure-accumulation) leads to Bodhi," etc.: "Treasurer" (*bao*) signifies that which is worthy of respect; "accumulation" (*ji*) signifies piling up layer upon layer.

The essence of the four wisdoms of enlightenment (*bodhi*) is untainted (*anāsrava*); because it is worthy of veneration, it is called a "treasure. This refers to the fact that the substance of the four wisdoms is...
Conditioned phenomena differ in their categories; their varying heights and depths are what is meant by "accumulation.

As for the term "Great Guide," it refers to one who leads sentient beings through the gates of the Dharma, possessing exquisite mastery over what is correct and what is deviant, just as a guide across the sea skillfully and eternally levels the treacherous and the perilous.
It is asked: Zhuang Zhou said that the Divine Man has no merit and the Sage has no name; yet here we speak of the Dharmakāya Bodhisattva.
It cannot be measured by forms; it cannot be known by wisdom. For what reason, then, is a name established? The answer is given in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:
"It is like the *ren-po* insect, which in reality does not eat oil, yet is forcibly called an 'oil-eater. Nirvāṇa is also like this: within that which is without names or marks."

This is an explanation established through the forceful application of names and characteristics. Nirvāṇa is a dharma that possesses an essential substance; since it currently lacks a name, one has forcefully assigned a name to it.
As for the statement that "these three are distinct," the intended meaning is that the Jewel Accumulation (Ratnakūṭa) leads one to Bodhi, while the Guide leads one to Nirvāṇa.
Maitreya has extracted himself from the suffering heard in the world; thus, these three are distinct.
As for the phrase "such as these" mentioned in the Sūtra, these eighteen bodhisattvas are the specific names.
Generally, there are sixteen: first, Bodhisattva-sattva; second, Mahāsattva; third, Siddhabuddhi; fourth, Parama-jaya.
1. Illuminator; 2. Most Excellent Son; 3. Most Excellent Sustainer; 4. Most Excellent Subduer;
5. Most Excellent Sprout; 6. Ninth, the Valiant; 7. Tenth, the Preceptor; 8. Eleventh, the Great Caravan Leader.
12. Great Renown; 13. Most Supreme Compassion; 14. Great Field of Merit;
15. Sovereign Wealth; 16. Great Dharma Teacher.

Regarding the statement that these are all the "unborn body" (*anutpattika-kāya*) of the Bodhisattva: it is not called "unborn" because it does not arise; rather, there is nowhere it does not arise, and thus it is called "unborn.
This is like saying that *prajñā* is "without knowledge," yet because there is nothing it does not know, it is called "without knowledge.
The Bodhisattva is likewise: manifesting in the six destinies according to form, he appears in eighteen or nineteen types of bodies; there is nowhere he does not arise.
Therefore it is called "unborn" (*anutpāda*). This refers to the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body), not the *dharmakāya* (true body).
As for the statement "blocking the gates of the three realms," the intended meaning is that there is no place where this unborn body does not arise; thus it is called "unborn."
The Chancellor said: "Being moved by the karma of the three realms constitutes the gateway; that which can give rise to the three realms is called 'entering the house.
Now, this Bodhisattva’s delusions and karma are exhausted, and thus he does not give rise to the three realms; this is called 'blocking the gateways of the three realms.
Question: What are the gateways of the three realms? Answer: There are two factors called the gateways of the three realms: first, karma; second, afflictions. For this reason..."
With delusion and karma as causes, one brings about the fruit of birth and death—the body composed of the five aggregates within the three realms.

Because the presence of delusion and karma allows one to enter the three realms without obstruction, they are called the "gates of the three realms. Now, this Bodhisattva has severed and exhausted all karma, afflictions, and the like, such that the birth and death of the three realms can no longer find entry;
thus, it is called "blocking the gates of the three realms. The gates of the realms do not admit the birth and death of this Bodhisattva.

Therefore, it is called "blocking. Furthermore, it is said that when a Bodhisattva enters the body of transformation (*pariṇāmika-kāya*), they do not receive the body of分段生死 (*bheda-maraṇa*)—this is called "non-arising" (*anutpāda*).

Because there is no arising, they block the gates of the triple world (*tridhātu*). Unlike ordinary sentient beings who do not exit the triple world, blocking the gates of the triple world is precisely what constitutes not exiting the triple world.

Regarding the statement "there is nowhere he is not born": because he is free from afflictions and karma, he is able to manifest transformation bodies (nirmāṇakāya) everywhere to teach and transform sentient beings by manifesting birth;
therefore, it is called "there is nowhere he is not born."

Regarding the statement that "he manifests forms throughout the six realms," the *Xiangyun* (Cloud of Characteristics) says: "He transforms the beings of the six realms and four modes of birth until they are all completely exhausted, thereby fulfilling his original vow.
Thus, the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states: "It is like the waters of Lake Anavatapta, which flow forth as four rivers;
they cannot be exhausted, filling Jambudvīpa and continuing to increase until they fill the great ocean. In the same way, O Son of the Buddha, from the bodhisattva-mind..."
It flows forth the waters of the great vows of the roots of goodness, filling sentient beings through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) without end;
it increases further and further until it fills all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñā*) and omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Regarding the statement, "The above clarifies internal protection (*adhyātma-rakṣā*) and so forth," it is asked: what is meant by "internal protection"? The answer is as Mochizuki states: "Virtue is hidden from the multitude;

one moves alone with a concealed form. One polishes the power of wisdom to its utmost and extends shelter like a medicinal tree. Such that the myriad dharmas do not fall away and the four modes of birth are attended to—sustaining these through one's own power is called 'internal protection.'"

Regarding the phrase "clarifying external protection (*bāhyarakṣā*) and so forth" under the words [of the verse]: Question: What is meant by "external protection"? Answer: Mochizuki states: Celestial precipices are difficult to ascend; who speaks of travel on such paths?
Terrestrial precipices consist of hills and mounds, which become fortified because of people. Kings and dukes provide defense against calamities, while sages and philosophers distribute their gifts.

That which is sustained by the power of vows (*praṇidhāna-bala*) is called external protection. As for the "ten assemblies" (*daśa-parṣad*): 1. Śakra approaches the assembly of devas. 2. Kuṇāla extends [the teaching].

1. The Assembly of Radiant Multitudes; 2. The Assembly of Mastery over the Small and the Great; 3. The Assembly that Oversteps and Grasps the Sahā World; 4. The Assembly that Obscures the Void and Contains the Rain;

5. The Assembly of Pure Song and Elegant Music; 6. The Assembly of Ascending Fragrance and Arrayed Music; 7. The Assembly that Moves Mountains and Surges Seas; 8. The Assembly that Swallows Dragons and Devours Poison.
Regarding the ten sovereigns of the benevolent kings, it is said that among them, humans and non-humans constitute two categories. King Ajātaśatru, the son of Vaidehī, is human;
the others are non-humans. This interpretation of "non-human" differs from the common usage where yakṣas are called non-humans; however, [this specific context] does not refer to them.
This is the general name for "non-humans" (amanuṣya). First the non-humans are listed, followed by humans.
Regarding the statement that among non-humans there are "neither-gods-nor-non-gods" (asura), this refers to those other than the gods of the desire and form realms; the rest are called "non-gods.
They are termed "non-gods" simply because they are not gods; it is not necessarily the case that one must call the asuras "non-gods."
Regarding the mention of "desire and form realms among the heavens," this refers to the sequence of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) within the heavens.
The Sūtra says: "At that time" means at that specific moment; it is called "at that time. Question: At the assembly on Vulture Peak, ordinary beings and sages dwell together in a mixed fashion.

Since the Brahmā King of the Form Realm is the sovereign of the world, for what reason does he provide external protection for the tenfold assembly by first citing Śakra? If one proceeds from the bottom up...

Regarding the upward progression: why are the Four Heavenly Kings not listed first? The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that after attaining the first fruit [of the path], one attains the third fruit.

The *Pañcaviṃśati-sāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states that after attaining the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, twenty-four kalpas beyond the Bhadrakalpa, one shall become a Buddha named the World-Honored One Without Attachment (Aśoka). For these reasons, they are listed first.
Regarding the statement that "Śākya" refers to a clan name (*gotra*): some say that the character for "clan" (*xing*) should be understood as the "nature of the mind" (*cittaprakṛti*).

However, upon careful examination of the subsequent scripture which states, "departing from the palace of the Śākya clan," it is clear that this refers to a family surname. Even if one possesses benevolence and compassion, one must still be identified by their clan name, just as in the case of Maitreya (the Compassionate One).
Regarding the statement that "the names are both corrupted and inverted": in the correct Sanskrit, it should be *Śakradevānām-indra*, consisting of seven syllables.
By omitting three syllables, it is now referred to by the four-syllable name *Śakro-devānām-indra*; thus, it is a corruption and an abbreviation.

If one follows the Sanskrit original, the family name precedes the given name; however, when translated into the language of Tang (Chinese), it is customary to place the family name first and the given name last. Thus, it should be called "Nengtian" (Capable Heavenly One).

If one were to say "Tiandi Shí" (Heavenly Lord Śakra) as is currently done, this would be correct according to the Sanskrit order, but it would be an inversion of the Chinese linguistic convention. Therefore, it is referred to as "Tiandi Shí."
The name comes first, followed by the clan name; furthermore, the title "Śakra" is also a Sanskrit term that correctly translates as "Capable.
If one says "Śakra Devendra," this is a name established by combining the Chinese and Sanskrit terms.
Regarding the statement that this is located on the summit of Mount Sumeru: Question: To what rank does this Śakra belong? Answer:
The commentary states, "This is located on [Mount] Sumeru," and so forth. Question: How wide is the circumference of the summit of Mount Sumeru? Answer: There are two explanations. One says:
its circumference on all four sides is eighty thousand *yojanas*, meaning that each of the four sides is twenty thousand *yojanas* long.
The second [interpretation] says: One side is eighty thousand *yojanas*; all four sides together total three hundred and twenty thousand *yojanas*.

For now, we speak of one side; therefore, it is said that "Sumeru is eighty thousand. Regarding the interpretation of the path: taking one side as being eighty thousand *yojanas* is taken as the correct [view]. Question:
On what teaching and basis is it established that there are eighty thousand *yojanas*? Answer: A verse in the *Abhidharmakośa* states:
The summit of Sumeru is eighty thousand [yojanas] high; there dwell the Trāyastriṃśa gods. At its four corners are four peaks where Vajrapāṇi resides.
In the center is the palace named Sudarśana, ten thousand yojanas in circumference and five thousand high, with golden walls and a ground adorned with various jewels and soft to the touch.
Within it is the Palace of Excellence (*Vaijayanta*), measuring one thousand *yojanas* in circumference. It is adorned on the outside by four gardens: Saṃcāra, Caitraratha, Miśra, and Nandana.

These are situated at the four corners upon a wondrous ground, each separated from its neighbor by twenty [yojanas]. To the northeast stands the Pārijātaka tree; to the southwest is the Sudharmā Hall.
Question: Where do the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three (Trāyastriṃśa) dwell? Answer: The verse says, "Sudharmā, etc. The prose commentary explains:

The gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three dwell on Mount Meru. Each of its four sides at the summit measures eighty thousand [yojanas], and this dimension is no different from its four sides at the base.
That is to say, it rises eighty thousand yojanas above the earth. At each of the four corners of the mountain summit, there is a peak. Within...
It stands firmly. Copper fangs and iron claws guard its outer perimeter, protecting Śakra and the various devas.

In the center of the mountain summit, the ground is soft and supple, adorned with various jewels; when one places a foot upon it, it sinks to the knee, and when the foot is lifted, it returns to levelness.

In the center of the summit is a palace named Sudarśana (Good View), measuring two thousand five hundred yojanas on each side and ten thousand yojanas in circumference. Its golden city wall is high in measure.
It measures one and a half *yojanas*. The ground is level and composed of pure gold, adorned solely with celestial silks and various jewels.
Its surface is as soft to the touch as *tūla* cotton; when stepped upon, it yields and rises according to the movement of the feet.
This is the city where Śakra, Lord of Devas, resides. Within the city is a preeminent palace, fully adorned with all kinds of exquisite jewels, surpassing [all others].
The various palaces are thus called "Excellently Superior" (*viśeṣa*). Each side measures two hundred and fifty *yojanas*, and the circumference is one thousand *yojanas*.
These are the delightful things within the city. In total, including both the center and the periphery, there are thirty-three heavens. As for these thirty-three heavens:

According to the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, there are: first, the gods dwelling in the Hall of Dharma; second, the gods dwelling on the peaks; third, the gods dwelling on mountain summits; fourth, the gods of the City of Good Manifestation (*Sudarśana*);
fifth, the gods of the *Pārśva* ground; sixth, the gods dwelling in the *Kūṭa* [palaces]; seventh, the gods of the Variegated Palaces (*Citraprāsāda*);
eighth, the gods dwelling in the Joyful Garden (*Nandana-vana*); ninth, the gods of the Luminous Heaven (*Ābhāsvara*); tenth, the gods of the *Pārijāta* tree garden; eleventh, the gods dwelling in...
12. The Heaven of the Precipitous Shore; 13. The Heaven of Mixed Precipitous Shores; 14. The Heaven of the Maṇi Treasury; 15.
The Heaven of the Ground of Bestowing Gifts; 16. The Heaven of the Golden Palace; 17. The Heaven of the Garlanded Abode; 18. The Heaven Dwelling on the Soft Ground.
18. The Heaven of Various Adornments; 19. The Heaven of the Wish-Fulfilling Ground; 20. The Heaven of Subtle Conduct; 21.
The Heaven of Joyful Sound of the Twenty-One Classes; 22. The Heaven of Majestic Virtue Wheels; 23. The Heaven of Shared Practice;
24. The Heaven of Jambū-bhara; 25. The Heaven of Swift Movement; 26. The Heaven of Foreknowledge; 2. [End of section].
Seventeen: the Heaven of Wisdom-Conduct; eighteen: the Heaven of Joyful Portions; nineteen: the Heaven Abiding on Wheels; twenty:
the Heaven of Majestic Virtue and Countenance; twenty-one: the Heaven of Majestic Virtue and Flaming Wheels; twenty-two: the Heaven of Reflected Radiance;

twenty-three: the Heaven of Purity. These are called the Thirty-three Heavens. On the four sides outside the city, there are four gardens adorned with splendor. First: [The Garden of Fragrant Waters].
1. To the east is the Caitraratha Grove; within this grove are golden wheels and other such objects. 2. To the south is the Pāruṣyaka Grove;
here are the battle banners, armor, and cavalry used when fighting the asuras. 3. To the west is the Miśrakāvana (Nandana) Grove;

when the gods have previously experienced strife, anger, and resentment, they enter this grove and find delight. 4. To the north is the Miśraka Grove; the trees of this grove are of various colors, like brocade.
It is exquisitely distinct; while the gods differ in beauty, stature, and appearance, once they enter this grove, they all become identical.
Thus, the exterior serves as its ornament. On each of the four sides of the grove, there is a wondrous ground extending twenty *yojana*s from the grove;
these are the places where those gods sport. To the northeast of the city stands a tree named the *Pārijāta*, also called the *Pāri*.
There is also the *Citrā* tree. Its root-stump is five *yojana*s in depth and breadth;
its trunk rises upward, and its branches spread out to the sides, such that their height and width are equal at five *yojana*s. It stands preeminent and bears flowers that emit a wondrous fragrance;
with the wind, its scent perfumes an area of one hundred *yojana*s, and even against the wind, it extends beyond fifty *yojana*s. To the west of the city...
At the southern corner is the Sudharmā Hall, where the devas assemble from time to time to deliberate in detail upon matters that are in accordance with the Dharma and those that are not.
Thus, a verse in the Abhidharmakośa says: "On the summit of Sumeru, eighty thousand [yojanas] high, dwell the Trāyastriṃśa gods. At its four corners are four peaks, the abodes of Vajrapāṇi.
In the center is the palace named Sudarśana, ten thousand yojanas in circumference; half as high, it has golden walls adorned with various ornaments."
In the region of *Yauṣmāka*, there is a magnificent palace measuring one thousand *yojanas* in circumference, adorned on the outside by the four gardens: Caitraratha, Pāruṣyaka, Miśraka, and Nandana.
As for the mention of the name "Kauśika" and so forth in the past, this explains the name of the country; it was his name during a former period of low status.
Regarding the term "Magadha" and so forth: this is translated as "The Land Without Poisonous Harm. It is named after its people;
"Without Poisonous Harm" is its honorific name from ancient times. In the past, Śakra ruled here as king, transforming the people through his compassionate virtue and refraining from inflicting harm.
Even when people violated the law, he did not impose punishments, but merely expelled them from the borders to let their transgressions take effect elsewhere. This is why...
Because his past causes involved little harm or malice, he is said to be "without poison or harm. Ji Guo’s commentary states:

"In the three instances of verification, there was no one who had committed a crime, nor was anyone subjected to flogging or torture. First, they were weighed on a scale. The judge recited this mantra:

'If there is no offense, the object shall weigh more and the person less; if there is an offense, the object shall weigh less and the person more. If the results remained inconclusive, it was necessary to verify by means of water."
A person who has committed an offense is like a stone; they are both submerged together in the river. He then recites a mantra, saying:
"If you have committed no offense, let the person float and the stone sink. If there is an offense, let the person sink and the stone float. If this does not succeed, then burn iron and stones."
He was told to touch it with his hand. The judge recited a mantra, saying: "If you are innocent, though you touch it, you shall suffer no harm;

if you are guilty, touching it will immediately injure you. Having thus ascertained the truth, he imposed no further punishment, but merely banished him from the country, leaving him to survive on his own.

Therefore, they are free from poisonous harm. Judging by this interpretation, although poisonous harm is more prevalent, those who, due to the roots of goodness from past causes, transform others through kindness and compassion, are mostly free from poisonous harm; thus, they are superior.
Regarding the statement that the former name of that country was "Placing Ambrosia" (Amṛta), the *Śāsanodbhāvana-cakra* states:
In ancient times, the various devas and asuras were heavily attached to sensual desires and were harmed by poison; consequently, their lifespans were short.

Brahmā, mindful of this, used a dragon as a rope and a mountain as a drill to churn the Milk Ocean. First, he obtained poisonous medicine and gave it to Lakuṭīkara, Mahodara, and others to eat. Subsequently—
He obtained wine and gave it to the Asuras; he obtained the shape of a half-moon and gave it to Maheśvara; on his forehead he obtained a jade maiden and gave her to Viṣṇu;
before the moon he obtained a cow and gave it to Brahmā; he rode upon a white horse and became a Cakravartin King of the Northern Continent;
he obtained ambrosia and distributed it for the people to consume, extensively eliminating poison and harm. At that time, by the power of the merit of sentient beings, the ocean was established.
It turned into milk, which further became nectar (*amṛta*). It was placed in this location; by consuming it, one attains longevity and is freed from all toxic harms.
Thus it received its name. These accounts are all as described in the secular classics of the Western Regions, similar to what is said in the secular traditions of this land [China]:
that the sky was deficient in the southwest, and Nüwa smelted stones of five colors to repair it. Bian states: This was introduced due to the narration of the country’s name; it is not [the case].
This is the essential point.
Regarding the statement that "in the past, Śakra had thirty-two companions," this refers to the stage of practicing the causal conditions.
At the beginning of the kalpa, Śakra was named *Kṣullaka* (the Little One); he was a lowly servant. Later, when his master fell into poverty, he was subsequently hired [as a laborer].
Jian'er was appointed as a jailer. By nature, Jian'er was benevolent and compassionate; he always administered justice with impartiality and integrity.

He was skilled at instructing and admonishing the prisoners, causing their minds to find peace. The prisoners were grateful for his kindness and compassion; whenever one person was released from prison, they would leave behind their upper garments as a gift.
Before long, his wealth and possessions had become abundant. The master of the house recognized the value of his ability.

The matter was thus resolved, and he was released to live as a free man; furthermore, a donkey was granted to him. Before his release, whenever the master arrived at seasonal festivals or the winter solstice, he would allow him to go out and roam.
Consequently, he formed a fellowship with thirty-two companions of similar status, who said to one another:
"We were planted in this life as thieves and prisoners, reduced to servitude; how could we fail to reform upon encountering our faults, and embrace goodness as soon as we see it?"
They moved on. From that time forward, whenever they encountered dangerous roads along which people traveled back and forth, they would labor together to repair them.
Following their advice, within a few days, all the perilous paths were leveled. Later, a celestial messenger came to inspect the borders of the kingdom.
Seeing that this road was level and smooth, they wished to attribute the merit to the magistrate. The common people said, "This was not done by the magistrate.
Within our borders there were previously thirty-two men who, though formerly lowly servants, all revered the service of the Buddha and repaired the dangerous roads.

Your Majesty’s envoy values the magistrate and allows him to receive heavenly emolument in vain. They prepared a formal report and submitted it to the throne. The Son of Heaven praised their meritorious deeds.
Gong was subsequently commanded to govern this county. Once he had assumed his office, wealth and honor were his;
pride and luxury filled his heart. He then took a wife named Shanfa (Dharmā). Later, as their amorous pleasures increased, he took three more wives:
namely, Lady Huankxi (Nandā), Lady Yuansheng (Pūrṇamāsī), and Lady Sheshi (Śrīmatī). Furthermore, using his stipend, he ransomed thirty-two people out of bondage. Because of this—
He said to them, "I shall now build the Hall of the True Dharma together with you; will you follow my words? The people, grateful for his benevolence, all replied that they would comply.
The magistrate had made an agreement: "If this hall is built, no offerings from women shall be accepted.
Having heard this, Sādhudharma spoke privately to the craftsmen, saying, "Can you create a precious vase for me? He did not obey the command clearly.
The Prefect understood. On the day of the *Daichōdō* (Hall of Waiting for Celebration), he finally reported that [the hall] was ready for installation.

Later, when the rear hall was completed, the celebration (*keisan*) was held. He asked those nearby, "What more is lacking? They replied directly, "All the work is finished; only the precious vase (*hōbyō*) remains.

The Prefect said, "It seems the time has come; how shall we procure it? The artisan replied, "The Lady of the Dharma (*Zennō Fujin*) previously fashioned a precious vase; let it be installed in the Dharma [hall]."
The hall must necessarily be commensurate with its contents. The Magistrate said, "Since that is so, let it be installed for now; the price shall be paid later.

Once the precious vase had been installed, the Lady remarked, "Of all the beauties of this hall, the precious vase is the foremost. It should now be titled 'Hall of the Good Dharma' before the assembly.
When the Lady of Joy saw this, she harbored feelings of jealousy and subsequently relinquished her wealth and gave up the hall.
She purchased gardens on all four sides and planted flowers and fruits everywhere to provide for her offerings; because of this, she was given the name "Joy" (Huanxi).
The Lady [Mādrī] planted many fruit trees along the wilderness roads to provide food for sentient beings and to offer them shade;
thus she was named "Garden-Born Tree" (Yuanshengshu). As for the fourth, Śrīmatī, although she saw the three ladies performing such deeds, in her cultivation...
She had no inclination toward merit at all, but occupied herself solely with adornment. The three ladies said, "Why do you not cultivate merit?
She replied, "You have been treated with contempt by your husband; if you wish to seek his love and respect so that I may gain even more favor, what use have I for merit?
Later, when the Magistrate’s term of office expired, thirty-two of the ladies' donkeys died one after another, as did their cocoons.
The boy’s life came to an end, and he was reborn atop Mount Sumeru in the Supreme Palace (Vaijayanta), where he became Śakra.
His three wives were also reborn in the heavens: the first wife was reborn in the Hall of Good Dharma (Sudharmā); the second wife was reborn in the Garden of Joy (Nandana);
and the third wife was reborn in the Forest Grove of Blessings (Pāruṣyaka). These thirty-three beings were reborn on the four sides, dwelling in the eight palaces.

He became a minister of Śakra. After the donkey’s life ended, he was reborn to the north of the Snowy Mountains and south of the Fragrant Mountain as a white elephant, eating nothing but the roots of lotuses from the pond.
Once Śakra had been reborn there, he saw only his three consorts and thirty-two attendants;
then, using his divine eye, he observed where the consort Śeṣavatī and the donkey she had ridden had been reborn, and he saw them.
After Lady Śakuntalā had died, she was reborn as a water-fowl by the side of the Elephant Pond, where she subsisted solely on frogs and other aquatic creatures.
When Śakra saw her, he felt deep compassion and likewise transformed himself into a water-fowl, flying before her.
He approached him with skillful means and asked, "Do you know me? He then exerted his supernatural power to cause [the man] to remember his past lives.
[The man] realized that in a former time, their feelings as husband and wife had been deep.
Śakra then restored his original form, took this water-bird on his arm, and ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. There, upon the Victorious Palace, he placed it upon a rack. All three queens...
Let us look at them. Each one plucks at its beak; some pull at its tail, while others rub against its head.
Each speaks a verse. The first, Lady Dharmā, says: "In former days I was your mistress, My lips stained with vermilion rouge;
Yet because of the forms of self and other, I now endure this ugliness. The second lady says: "To speak of cultivating merit, One speaks of being old..."
At that time, Xiū thrust his head into a hair-sack; the multitude together roamed about at night, taking Āmǎng’s wicked beak and fitting it onto Liú Qiūdiāo’s mouth.
The third lady, Huānxǐ, said: "His hands and feet are too long; his snout is like a black wolf."
"I shall abandon this coarse face-milk and learn from you to ascend to heaven. My tail is like a wooden stake, my head is of high-quality ginger, and even water-crows do not submit to me.
Yet she replied: 'Before long, you shall receive this body; being slighted, it will be difficult to save.
If you should succeed in ascending to heaven, come back and seize my husband. If you happen to meet me again, you shall be my third husband.'"
Bā. Having been entirely replaced by water-crazed birds, his body and mind were filled with shame and remorse;
he truly found no joy. He then said to Śakra: "Release me so that I may go back to my original place. At that time, Śakra conferred upon him the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts.

When the Three Refuges were completed, he next explained the characteristics of the precepts, saying: "From this time forth, for as long as you live, you shall not kill living beings. This is the precept of the water-crazed bird."
"Will you accept it? He asked this five times, and each time the answer was the same. "I shall henceforth refrain from killing living beings; I will eat only that which dies of its own accord.
Having returned to his original pond, he saw a frog on the surface of the water, moving with the current as it flowed forward.
Desiring to eat the frog, the bird suddenly flipped over and turned away; though he pursued it for an entire day, he could not catch it to eat. On the following day, he saw another dead fish.
He intended to eat her, but she returned to life again. In this way, for six or seven days he was unable to eat and consequently died of starvation.
Although he had received the five precepts, because of his original jealousy, after death he was reborn in the palace of Vemacitrin as an asura woman.
Among the asuras, sons born are ugly, but daughters are beautiful; she was exceptionally handsome and possessed a most extraordinary beauty, even surpassing that of Śakra’s palace.
There are four kinds of *sodā* flavors—blue, yellow, red, and white—that can be consumed, yet there are no women in the palaces of the asuras.
Although there are women in the palaces of the asuras, they lack the four kinds of *sodā* flavors. For this reason, they contend with one another over beauty and flavor.
They raised arms and took up weapons in competition. At that time, his son was about sixteen or seventeen years old.
The asura Vemacitra said, "I wish to give my daughter in marriage; we must assemble the people of the four continents to select a bridegroom for her.

He then spoke to his daughter, saying, "Whoever captures your heart, I shall immediately give you to him. Having finished these deliberations, he issued a broad summons to the gentlemen of the four continents.
In the future, Śakra will hide his form and first go to the palace to speak privately and grant permission for their meeting.
I shall transform myself into an ugly brahmin and lead the way at the very front. If you see me, give me the flowers; then I shall become your husband.
At that time, Śreṇika immediately understood her meaning. On the day of the selection, he first encountered the brahmin and...
As he passed by Puṣpa and the brahmin, Śakra then restored his original form. Upon seeing this, the asura immediately gave rise to resentment, saying, "You were previously an enemy to me;
I cannot give my daughter to you. Thereupon, Śakra took Śacī and returned to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
From that time on, Śakra would occasionally compete with the asuras in the display of their splendor.
[They] quarrel over the flavor of the *soma* juice, constantly contending and never ceasing.

Regarding the statement that the three luminaries are [included within] the Four Great Kings and so forth: Question: How are the devas of the three luminaries subsumed within the Heaven of the Four Great Kings?

Why are the heavens of the three luminaries not established separately? Answer: Because among the heavens of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), there is no separate heaven of the three luminaries; therefore...
They are also subsumed within the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*). An ancient said: "The deities of the Three Luminaries (*Trayo-loka-prabhā*) have separate residences.
The intention of the *Śū* (Commentary) is that since the deities of the Three Luminaries dwell in space, they should be categorized under the Heaven of Those Who Dwell in Space (*Ākāśavāsin*).

However, because they actually reside within the Heaven of the Four Great Kings—specifically, their celestial palaces are situated at the summit of Mount Sumeru—they are subsumed under the terrestrial heavens (*Bhauma-deva*) and have no other location. Furthermore, it is said: "They exist only..."
"In the sky, the *saṃjñin* devas dwell scattered about"—this statement is incorrect.

As for the mention of the *Sūtra on Avalokiteśvara* and others, this is merely identifying the titles; such citations have been made since ancient times, yet it remains uncertain which specific sūtra is meant. The name of Avalokiteśvara is *Ratnamati*; he acts as the Sun Deity (*Āditya-rāja*). This is precisely what is called *Ratnaprabha* in this very sūtra.

"Treasure" (*ratna*) carries the meaning of being worthy of reverence, while "light" (*prabha*)— [Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragmentary commentary or critical note regarding Buddhist cosmology and scriptural citations, specifically concerning the identity of the deity Avalokiteśvara and his appearance in various sūtras.]
This refers to the meaning of "dispelling darkness. Mahāsthāmaprāpta is named Ratnaśrī;

he acts as the Moon Deity (*Candradeva*), able to remove feverish affliction and create coolness, bringing auspicious matters to humanity. Ākāśagarbha Bodhisattva acts as the Star Deity, named Samantagandha.
His fragrance pervades all lands and universally permeates the moon throughout the myriad things. "Myriad things" are termed "fragrance," for fragrance depends upon substance.

There are [beings] who possess fragrance but lack substance; for example, the heavens are like the substance and the stars are like the fragrance. "Universal" (*pūrṇa*) has the meaning of being uninterrupted;

because their fragrance is uninterrupted, they are called "Universal Fragrance. Question: Why are the Four Heavenly Kings listed first and the Three Luminaries listed later, rather than after Śakra? Answer:

Because they constitute the vanguard of Śakra, the Lord of Devas, and furthermore, because they occupy the lowest position, they are listed first. As for the six heavens of the Desire Realm, they are situated upon the earth.
There are two types of dwellings: those of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings and those of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

Although the three luminaries move in constant circulation and are scattered throughout space, they are classified as "earth-dwellers" because they are subsumed under the Heaven of the Four Great Kings. Furthermore, as they do not exceed the mountain peaks, they are earth-dwellers. (The definition of the names is thus clarified.)

Regarding the statement that the "Sun Palace" is made of the essence of fire (*tejas*), this distinguishes its essential nature and magnitude. The "Sun" (*sūrya*) signifies reality; its radiance constitutes reality, and it is capable of producing and bringing all things to completion.
The "Moon" (*candra*) signifies deficiency; "deficiency" (*candra*) is precisely "lack. Because it possesses both fullness and lack, it is called the moon. The "Star" (*tārakā*) signifies essence;
the vital essence of the myriad things transforms into stars, serving as the masters of the vital essences of the myriad things in the heavens.
It is held and maintained; only when it reaches the grasses and trees below do they first attain sweetness. If there were no vital essence (*ojas*) to sustain them, all would be tasteless.
The "star" (*tārakā*) is the fragrance of all things; since fragrance is itself vital essence, the star is called "Universal Fragrance."
According to the text cited in the Commentary, they follow the sequence as they do today; this is the general rule for reading the text. However, the Sūtra itself does not follow this sequence:

it first mentions *Nāmacandra*, who is the Moon Deva-son (*candradevaputra*); next it names *Samantagandha*, who is the Star Deva-son (*tārakadevaputra*); and finally it names *Ratnaprabhā*, who is the Sun Deva-son (*sūryadevaputra*).
Why is the sequence different between the Sūtra and the Commentary? The answer is that the Sūtra follows their relative physical dimensions.
A small portion [is as follows]: the sequence is moon, sun, and stars; however, this sūtra differs in its distinctions and does not follow that sequence, listing them as moon, stars, and sun.
The commentator has arranged them by aligning this sūtra with that sequence, thus providing this correlation:
the solar palace is composed of fire-crystal (sphaṭika) and is fifty-one yojanas in diameter; the lunar orb is composed of water-crystal and is fifty yojanas in diameter.
A *yojana* is measured by a single path and not by a square or circular dimension. The largest stars are eighteen *krośas*, which is thirty-six *li*;
the medium-sized are ten *krośas*; and the smallest are four *krośas* and eight [hundred paces]. The old term was *youxun* (由旬), while the new term is *yuzhenana* (瑜繕那).
According to ancient tradition, when a single army of a sage-king marched, it covered forty *li*. This is the traditional account.
According to the local custom of India, one *yojana* is thirty *li*; however, as recorded in the Noble Teachings, it is sixteen *li*.

One *yojana* consists of eight *krośas*. A *krośa* refers to the maximum distance at which the bellowing of a large bull can be heard, which is slightly more than two *li*, measured as five hundred *dhanus* (bows).
It is said that the sun, moon, and stars all revolve through the air around the four continents (*caturdvīpa*). As for the four continents: first is Pūrvavideha (East Victory Body Continent).
Because the bodies of its inhabitants are superior to those of the southern continent, it is called "Victory Body. In Sanskrit it is called *Videha*, which here means "Victory Body.
The southern continent, Jambudvīpa, is named after a tree; to the south of Mount Sumeru in this world-system, there is a tree named Jambu.
Regarding Jambudvīpa: it is named after gold. There is gold beneath the *jambu* tree, and as it is the most excellent world among those of gold, it is named Jambudvīpa after that gold.
Aparagoyānī is the western continent; this is translated as "Cow-Property.
It is said that there is a golden ox there, from which people all shave off the gold to use as currency. Uttarakuru is the northern continent; this is translated as "Superior Above."

The *pṛthivīkṣetra* (field of merit) excels the other three continents; thus it is called "Supremely Victorious" (*uttara-vijayā*). When one voids excrement or urine, the ground cracks and then closes back together.
Their lifespan is fixed at one thousand years. Question: For what reason is the solar disk always full, while the moon undergoes waning and waxing?

Answer: The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "When [the moon] is near the sun, it is obscured by its own shadow; therefore, the lunar disk appears deficient. If it is far from the sun, the moon is full. When it is near the sun..."
It is thus deficient. From the first day of the month until the fourteenth day, [the moon] gradually moves further away, and the moon gradually becomes full.
On the fifteenth day, the sun and moon are directly opposite each other; therefore, it is completely bright. From the sixteenth day until the twenty-ninth day, [they gradually move closer].
Gradually, as it approaches the sun, the moon appears to be eclipsed. When the moon is in the west and the sun is in the east, it is obscured by the sun;
when the sun is in the west and the moon is in the east, it is likewise obscured. When the sunlight is at its peak, the full moonlight is eclipsed.
If the sun is in the west and the moon is in the east, the sun in the west casts its glare so that the moonlight’s shadow falls toward the east; those on the western side cannot see it.

One sees the western half [of the moon] obscured; it is as if the moon’s own shadow covers the western half of the moonlight. Therefore, it is said that "as it approaches the sun, its own shadow covers it.
Second, according to the Sautrāntika school, the paths of waxing and waning are distinct: when the moon travels upon the path of waxing, it appears full;
by this standard, during the first fifteen days it travels on the path of waxing, and during the latter fifteen days it travels on the path of waning. Great.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "It is clear that there is a moon with both its correct and obverse sides. It resembles the appearance of a single-sided mirror;
it seems as though there is light on the face of the moon and no light on its back. When facing a person, it has light; when turned away from a person, it has no light.
On the day of the new moon, it is like a mirror: facing upward and with its back downward, one sees no light. From the first day of the moon, it gradually turns over until—"
On the fifteenth day, it is like the surface of a mirror; looking downward, the moonlight is perfectly round. From the sixteenth day onward, it gradually turns upward again;

as the light becomes partial, when viewed from the side, there is a visible deficiency. As stated in external (non-Buddhist) texts: the sun is composed of fire-essence, thus it is dark within and bright without;
the moon is composed of water-essence, thus it is bright within and dark without, such that its outer surface is entirely devoid of light. Why is this so?
Regarding the waxing and waning [of the moon]: the lunar phenomenon must receive the illumination of the sun’s rays before the moonlight can emerge.

It is like a person's eye which, though possessing its own light, cannot see objects in the dark; it requires the guidance of a lamp’s light. Likewise, the lunar light requires the guidance of the solar light.
On the fifteenth day, as the moon approaches the sun, the solar illumination is distinct and clear, and thus it appears full. From the sixteenth day onwards...
Gradually the days grow longer; gradually it wanes. On the first day of the month, it gradually approaches the sun, and gradually it becomes full.
All the explanations mentioned above are not that it was originally deficient. Question: If it is composed of the essence of fire (*tejas*), why is it hot in summer and cold in winter?
Answer: The *Lokadhātunirdeśa-sūtra* (Qishi jing) states: "If, during the summer season, the sun travels the northern path, it shines upon the seven [mountains]..."
The Golden Mountain (Sumeru) consequently becomes very hot. When winter arrives, the sun travels along the southern path and illuminates the ocean waters, causing them to become cold.

It is due to this difference that, according to the historical records of this region, the first day of the fifth month marks the arising of the first *yin* (and thus it is cold), while the first day of the eleventh month marks the arising of the first *yang* (and thus it is hot).
Having established these positions for the cold and heat of the four seasons, one may ask: what is the nature of the "mutual eclipsing" (*paryupāsana*) of the sun and moon?
Answer: The body of Śakra resides upon the summit of that mountain, while the abode of the asuras is situated within the ocean.
They contend with one another over beauty and sensory flavors, vying in the raising of weapons more often than not during the new and full moons.

However, when Śakra’s vanguard, the Sun and Moon Devas, radiate their majestic light and strike the eyes of the asuras, the asuras shield the sun with their hands; thus, an eclipse is perceived. Furthermore, externally...

The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "The sun eclipses because it should conjoin but does not; the moon eclipses because it should meet but does not. As for the terms "conjunction" and "meeting," they refer to being on the same path.
When the sun comes from the east and the moon goes from the west, if their paths do not intersect, they do not shadow one another, and thus there is no eclipse.
If the Yin and Yang lose their proper timing, such that they should conjoin but do not, or if their upper and lower positions are offset, they will reflect upon one another [causing an eclipse].
When it is eclipsed, there is an obscuration. A question was asked: "By what cause does the hare in the moon exist? The answer is given in the *Adbhutadharmaparyāya Sūtra*:
To the west of the Heroic Pond (*Vīrapuṣkariṇī*) in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there is a stūpa containing three animals—a fox, a monkey, and a hare.
This was the place where the Tathāgata practiced as a bodhisattva; at that time, he took the form of a hare and offered his own body by burning it. Śakra, taking [the remains]...
The skeleton is placed within the moon to demonstrate it to the people of the world. When asked how there can be the shadow of a tree, he replied:
"The *Āgama* Sūtras state that as the sun and moon travel in their orbits, there is a great golden mountain on the northern shore of this very continent called Jambū."
Within it there is a tree, extremely large and forty *yojana*s in height. Its fruit is like ten *shi* measures; its juice is like milk and sweet in taste.
Since the tree is so tall and great, the lunar disc shines upon it, and because of this lunar disc, the shadow of the tree appears. At that time, people called it the *sāla* tree. [Question:
What kind of phenomenon is the black portion within the moon? [Answer: It is the reflection of fish and turtles from the ocean entering into the moon.
Question: Why do the reflections of all mountains, rivers, and the great earth not enter into the midst of space, while the reflections of fish and turtles do?
Answer: It is because things of similar nature resonate with one another. The moon is the essence of water, and fish are insects that dwell within water.

Question: All physical forms have something upon which they depend. Upon what do the movements of the three luminaries depend for their abiding? Answer: The sutras state that these belong to the *vāyu-loka* (the realm of wind).

Because it abides in space, it rests upon the wind. The *Lokadhātu-prajñapti* (*Qishi jing*) states that there are five kinds of winds that blow and move: first, the supporting wind; second, the stabilizing wind;

third, the conforming wind; fourth, the sustaining wind; and fifth, the propelling wind. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that [the sun] circles Mount Sumeru once every day and night, for the sake of adorning the kalpa.
The treatise says: "It is by the predominant power of the karma of all sentient beings, acting in concert..."
Because they draw forth the winds that arise, they circulate around Mount Sumeru, swirling through the air to transport and sustain the sun and other celestial bodies so that they do not fall.
Stars have both general and specific [classifications]. For example, the North Star belongs only to this continent (Jambudvīpa), whereas others belong to all three continents.

Furthermore, there are differences between them, such as the comet and the planet Mars, because their respective natures differ. According to the *Sūtra on the Three Luminaries* (Trimaṇḍala-devaputra-sūtra), all three luminaries are bodhisattvas.
The Bodhisattva manifests transformations for the benefit of sentient beings: he acts as a lamp of illumination in worlds shrouded in blindness;
in lands of famine, he assumes the body of a great fish; in worlds of false views, he establishes the Right Path. He serves as a boat, as a raft, as medicine, and as a tree.
Yet, because their own karma differs, they encounter such diverse darknesses. This also signifies that when things flourish, they must inevitably decline. So it is said:
Because fullness is followed by deficiency, the *Yījīng* says: "When the sun is full, it wanes; when the moon is full, it declines.

The waxing and waning of heaven and earth correspond to the rhythms of time; how much more so for human beings? Therefore, those who ascend to the heavens possess superior wholesome karma, and thus their bodies emit radiance that does not depend on the sun or moon.
Question: How do they know day and night? Answer: By the opening and closing of flowers and the chirping of birds.
Silence. [This is] to distinguish day from night. In the hells, there is only evil karma and only darkness. Among humans, there is both good and evil, and there are days and nights.
If there were only the sun and no moon, although there would be illumination, there would be no coolness; all things would wither and parch.
If there were only the moon and no sun, although there would be coolness, there would be no illumination. Therefore, both must exist.
As for the mention of the Four Kings and so forth, this is a listing of their names. In the east is Dhṛtarāṣṭra, here translated as "Holder of the Nation" (Chíguó).
He dwells on the White Silver Mountain and governs the *gandharvas*, *piśācas*, and other spirits and deities, protecting the eastern continent of Pūrvavideha and preventing it from being invaded.
[He] prevents damage. On the highest first tier of the south is the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa, here translated as "Increase" (Zēngzhǎng), for he increases virtuous matters.
He dwells on Mount Vaiḍūrya and leads the Kumbhāṇḍas and Pretas to protect the southern continent of Jambudvīpa, preventing it from being harmed or damaged.
On the highest tier of the west is the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka; in Sanskrit he is called Virūḍhaka, here translated as "Ugly Eyes" (Qiūmù), for his eyes...

Because he is the most hideous, he dwells on the Golden Mountain (*Huangjin shan*), where he governs all the *nāgas* and *piśācas*, protecting the western continent of Aparagodānīya and preventing it from being harmed or damaged.
Regarding the first and highest tier of the north: in Sanskrit he is called Vaiśravaṇa Deva-rāja;
in this language, he is called "Much-Hearing" (*Duowen*). Jiaxiang says that he constantly guards the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) with the Buddha, because he has heard much of the Dharma.

Therefore, it is said that there are many gates. He dwells on Mount Vaidūrya (Water-Crystal Mountain) and leads hosts of yakṣas, rākṣasas, and other spirits to protect the continent of Uttarakuru, preventing them from being harmed or plundered.
Each of the Four Heavenly Kings resides on the mid-slopes of Mount Sumeru; for instance, regarding Mount Sumeru:
It emerges from the water for eighty thousand *yojanas*. From the midpoint of its belly downward, there are four tiers.

According to the Hīnayāna, Mount Sumeru has four terraces, each separated by ten thousand *yojanas*. They extend outward for sixteen thousand, eight thousand, four thousand, and two thousand *yojanas* respectively.
The Devas Dṛḍhapāṇi, Mālādharas, Sadāmattas, and Mahārājikas dwell on these four terraces in order. They also reside on the other seven golden mountains. Thus says the *Lù* (Record).
Mount Sumeru rises eighty thousand *yojana*s above the waters and has four terraces.
The first terrace is ten thousand *yojana*s from this [base], extending sixteen *yojana*s outward; the deity Dṛḍhamati resides there. This deity has copper fangs and iron claws.
The second terrace is twenty thousand *yojana*s from this, extending eight thousand *yojana*s outward; the deity Mālādhara resides there. This deity is constant...
Adorned with flower garlands, the third tier is thirty thousand yojanas from this [second tier] and extends four thousand yojanas outward;
the *Nitya-kauḍa* deities dwell there. Because their minds are filled with pride, the karmic retribution of these deities is superior to that of others.
The fourth tier is forty thousand yojanas from this [third tier] and extends two thousand yojanas outward; the Four Great Heavenly Kings dwell there, each governing various spirits and ghosts.

One obtains the name "Heavenly King. The Four Heavenly Kings reside at the midpoint of the mountain's belly. From this point upward, the body of the mountain rises as solitary peaks for forty thousand yojanas;
