its summit is named Trāyastriṃśa (the Heaven of the Thirty-three). Question: To which category of birth do the Four Heavenly Kings belong? Answer: [They belong to the category of] birth from transformation (*upapāduka*).

These are comprised within the category of miraculous birth (*upapāduka*). The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle five, states: "Among all the devas of the desire realm, there are none who are born from a mother’s womb.
The deities of the Four Great Kings are suddenly miraculously born upon the shoulders or in the laps of their parents, appearing like children of five years of age.
Those of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven appear like children of six years, and so on up to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, where they appear like children of ten years of age."
Regarding the statement that they also dwell upon the peaks of the seven golden mountains: first is Gandhamādana, which means "Holding the Pair.
Because there are twin tracks like those of a chariot on its summit, it is named "Holding the Pair. Second is Īṣādhāra;
in Sanskrit, this means "Axle-Holding Mountain," as the shape of the mountain resembles a chariot axle. Third is Kailāsa; in Sanskrit, this means "Forest-Bearing Mountain. It possesses...
The forest trees were suitable for making carrying poles. This refers to humans at the beginning of the eon, whose bodies were extremely large;
they used these logs as poles to carry small mountain rocks and move them to secluded places, hence it is named Mount Dhanvana (Carrying Forest).
Fourth is Mount Sudarśana, which translates as "Well-Appearing" or "Good-to-See"; because this mountain is so excellent, those who see it experience joy. Fifth is Mount Aśvakarṇa...
1. Makara: this is translated as "Horse Ear," for the shape of the mountain resembles a horse's ear. 2. Vinataka:
this is translated as "Elephant Trunk," for its upper portion is thick and its lower portion is thin, like an elephant's trunk. 3. Nimindhara: this is translated as "Fish Snout";
it is the place where the Four Heavenly Kings reside separately.

Regarding the mention of the "three lights" and the "four kings," this refers to their relative proximity and distance. Question: How far from this earthly plane are these three lights and four kings located? Answer: The three lights, the four kings, and so forth— [The text continues: ...are situated at varying distances from here. Specifically, the three lights are one hundred yojanas above the earth; the four great kings reside at two hundred yojanas; the Suyama Heaven is at four hundred yojanas; the Tuṣita Heaven is at eight hundred yojanas; the Nirmāṇarati Heaven is at sixteen hundred yojanas; and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven is at thirty-two hundred yojanas. Beyond these heavens, there are the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, Mahābrahmā, Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, Ābhāsvara, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Śubhakṛtsna, Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, Bṛhatphala, Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and finally the Akaniṣṭha Heavens, each doubling the height of the preceding. Furthermore, the Cāturmahārājika Heaven is two hundred yojanas from the earth; the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven is four hundred yojanas; the Yāma Heaven is eight hundred yojanas; the Tuṣita Heaven is sixteen hundred yojanas; the Nirmāṇarati Heaven is thirty-two hundred yojanas; and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven is sixty-four hundred yojanas. From there, the realms of the first dhyāna, second dhyāna, third dhyāna, and fourth dhyāna increase in height by doubling successively, reaching up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven. Thus, the three lights, the four kings, and the rest are situated at these respective distances from the surface of the earth.
Regarding the mention of "life span, physical dimensions, and so forth," this refers to the meaning of other categories. The treatise states:
Among the six heavens of the desire realm, the physical dimension of those in the lowest heaven is one-quarter of a *krośa*, which is half a *li* or nine hundred *chi*.
Thus, for each successive heaven, the dimensions increase by one unit until the sixth heaven, where the body measures one and a half *krośas*, which is three *li*. As for the life span...
The verse says: "Fifty years among humans / Is one day and night in the lower heaven; / Based on this, their lifespan is five hundred years;
/ For each higher level, it doubles fivefold. That is, fifty human years constitute one day and night for the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*).
Calculating thirty such days as one month and twelve such months as one year, their lifespan is five hundred years. As for the second heaven...

One hundred years among humans constitute one day and night for the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven. One should understand that this duration doubles progressively for each higher realm. As the Sūtra says:

"The Īśvara devaputras and the Maheśvara devaputras" refers to the Yāma and Tuṣita heavens, which are sky-dwelling deities. In relation to the lower Trāyastriṃśa and Cāturmahārājika heavens, they are called Īśvara devaputras.
[In the heavens above,] they transform themselves and others through the power of others' emanations and the power of their own emanations.
Regarding the instruments of pleasure, they are superior to those of the two lower heavens and are called "Great Sovereignty" (Maheśvara).

As for the statement "attaining the fruit of maturation" (*vipāka-phala*) and so forth: it is asked whether that which is experienced as the internal body may be termed maturation, while that which is experienced as external fruits [cannot].

Regarding the question of why food and drink are called "ripening" (*vipāka*), Jin replies that there are two explanations. First, from the perspective of the reduction of karma, they are collectively termed "ripening.
Second, it is said that the food and drink of these two types of devas do not depend on water to be obtained; rather, they arrive simply through the power of thought.
Because they arise from the ripening of celestial [merit], they are called "ripening," though they are not true *vipāka*.
Regarding the phrase "according to what is thought in the mind" and so forth: it is asked, what is the distinction among the fruits of the six heavens of the desire realm?

The answer is: in the first two heavens, one obtains things by seeking them under trees; in the next two heavens, they are obtained immediately upon thought. All of these are induced by prior karma, and their forms and categories are fixed.
However, they manifest only when there is a need for enjoyment and do not appear when there is no need. Thus, the two highest heavens lack such inferior fruits.

By means of supernormal powers acquired at birth, whether for oneself or others, they manifest new transformations moment by moment; since their objects are not uniform, this is called "Great Sovereignty" (Maheśvara).
Regarding the statement that the two lower heavens rely on trees and so forth: there are ten kinds of trees. First, food trees; second, drink trees, which produce various...
There are trees for medicinal decoctions; trees of the three robes, where various devas and humans obtain whatever robes they desire simply by wishing for them;
trees of the four vehicles, which refers to mounts such as dragons and domestic animals; and trees of adornments, which provide celestial crowns, earrings, and other ornaments for the body.
Sixth are the fragrant trees (*gandhavṛkṣa*). When gods and humans desire to perfume their garments, they obtain them from these trees. Seventh are the great assembly trees (*mahāsaṃnipātavṛkṣa*).

Gods and humans gather beneath these trees for assemblies. Eighth are the joyous trees (*hasitavṛkṣa*). When gods and humans are unable to find joy or laughter, musical instruments such as the *vīṇā* (harp) and other objects emerge from these trees.
Ninth are the sustenance trees (*upakaraṇavṛkṣa*). They provide all the implements and utensils necessary for domestic life. Tenth are the throne trees (*āsanavṛkṣa*).

Regarding the tree: originally, only nine kinds of things emerge from the tree. Some people, regarding the ninth category—requisites for life (*upakaraṇa*)—separate out beds and seats, thereby making ten.
Thus, the Four Great Kings Heaven and the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven must seek their necessary objects of enjoyment from the trees;
they arrive there through the mental intention of those two higher heavens, while the two lower heavens rely on the trees to obtain them.
It is attained, yet it is not called "mastery.
As for the statement that "attaining [what one] desires now is called 'equality' (sama)," this explains why the Yāma and Tuṣita heavens are named the Heaven of Mastery (Īśvaradeva).
That is to say, although they arrive through mere thought, even though they attain things according to their desire, it is still due to prior karma. Question: Is it further...?
[Question: Does one arrive only when there is already a thought of longing (*abhilāṣa*), or does one arrive even when there is originally no such thought?
[Answer: All [beings] newly come into existence. [Question: If that were so, it would contradict other *yogācāra* texts. The *Yoga* states:

"The various devas from Tuṣita downward are called 'those currently dwelling in the generation of sensual desires'. Now you say they arrive through "thought of longing"; will this not conflict with those texts? [Answer: The *Śāstravyākhyāna* (*She-shi lun*) says: "If we consider..."
Regarding the enjoyment of requisites: it is not that the requisites themselves prevent other thoughts from arising.
If one refers to the palaces being enjoyed, these were already existing and currently inhabited; [the claim] that one desires to sit within one newly produced is incorrect.

If one says that the palace was already existing, then even the palaces as far as those of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven were established at the time of the formation eon (*vivartakalpa*), and thus they too would be pre-existing.
This refers to the material requisites they enjoy; whenever they desire them, they are obtained and never again perish.

The enjoyment of these celestial bodies is called "arising from dwelling in present sensual objects" (*vartamāna-kāmaviṣaya-ja*), which distinguishes it from the two higher heavens. In those two higher heavens, [the objects] arise anew and anew through transformation.
Regarding the statement "not delighting in maturation (*vipāka*) and so forth," this explains that the two heavens of Paranirmita-vaśavartin and Nirmāṇarati are called Maheśvara.
Question: As for the four lower heavens—Yāma, Tuṣita, and the two lowest heavens—their attainment depends upon trees;
these are all the result of the karma of observing the precepts in previous lives. Furthermore, both the Nirmāṇarati and Paranirmita-vaśavartin heavens are [the result of] past wholesome [karma].
That which is induced by karma is collectively termed the "ripened fruit" (vipākaphala). How is it that the two highest heavens are said not to delight in ripened fruit? Answer:

If one speaks of ripened fruit in general, it exists throughout all the upper and lower heavens. However, in the two highest heavens, that which is produced through one's own transformation (*svapariṇāma*) or the transformation of others (*parapariṇāma*) is superior.
Now, with respect to this excellence, they feel aversion toward the two lower heavens; therefore, it is said that they do not delight in ripened fruit. Furthermore...
The Paranirmita-vaśavartin and Nirmāṇarati heavens are called "Masters" (*vaśavartin*) because they are superior to those preceding them; thus, they receive the name "Great Mastery. Question:
What is the distinction between the transformations (*nirmāṇa*) of these two upper heavens and the mental creations (*manasikāra*) of the lower Yāma and Tuṣita heavens? Answer:

Mental creation refers to that which occurs spontaneously (*anābhoga*), whereas transformation refers to that which results from deliberate application (*prayoga*); this is the distinction between the two. Question: Should not the two lower heavens be superior to the two upper ones?
"Is it the gods? Answer: "Even if the lower two classes of gods were to apply effort and practice, they still could not transform the depths of others;

therefore, it should not be considered a perversion. Question: "Could this not be supernormal power (*abhijñā*)? Answer: "In the Desire Realm there is no fruit of supernormal power; this is merely a supernormal power of karma.

Because that [higher realm] possesses the fruit of supernormal power, while this is the power of karma, it is also called 'supernormal power acquired at birth. As for the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (*Nirmāṇarati*), they require objects..."
Regarding enjoyment: [the objects] arise anew and anew; they are enjoyed through one's own transformation alone.

As for the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*), powerful devas cause inferior devas to transform [objects]. If the power of both parties is equal, they transform [objects] for one another. Regarding "mental conception" (*saṃkalpa*):
the six heavens of the desire realm are collectively termed "mental conception. Thus, in the two lowest heavens, [objects] are obtained by relying on trees. The highest...
In the two higher heavens, new things arise anew. This is why the two intermediate heavens engage in distinct contemplations.

The two heavens of Nirmāṇarati (Delighting in Emanation) and Paranirmita-vaśavartin (Mastery over Others' Emanations) grow weary of the old objects of the two lower heavens and desire that new things arise anew.

Therefore, the Commentary states: "They do not delight in the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*); they do not delight in enjoying old objects; thus, the contemplations of the two intermediate heavens are said to be attained."

The object is called the *vipākaphala* (maturation fruit). Question: Even if it arises through transformation (*nirmāṇa*), it must be admitted as a remote cause. Within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), what kind of transformations exist? Answer:
It should be called that which is manifested by maturation-karma (*vipākakarman*). It resembles that which is transformed by the power of supernatural faculties (*abhijñā*);

its arising is termed "attaining transformation," and the object thus transformed is called the "transformed object. All of these arise from one's own mind; they are experienced by one's own mind as if they were transformations produced by another. Answer: As you have permitted.

The transformation of the *āśraya* (the physical body) is for one's own enjoyment; it does not transform the sense organs to be enjoyed by others, and thus it is accepted that they are transformed for others.

The transformation of objects of pleasure follows the same principle. This is an analogy based on the primary substance (*bhūta-rūpa*). If, however, we consider the reflected image (*pratibimba*), everything is an object transformed for enjoyment, which does not contradict the principle of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*).

Regarding the statement "furthermore, according to the interpretation of others, the Lord of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*) and so forth," this recounts an ancient interpretation.

According to this interpretation, among the four classes of gods dwelling in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), only those from the single heaven of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations come; the remaining heavens—Yāma, Tuṣita, and Nirmāṇarati—do not come at all.
Regarding the statement that Maheśvara is the Lord (Indra) and so forth: he is the General of the Army and one of the Four Heavenly Kings.
Maheśvara is the teacher of Śakra; he is Maheśvara Mahādeva, the Brahmā King of the Fourth Dhyāna.
According to this latter interpretation, none of the deities of the Four Formless Heavens (Ārūpyadhātu) come at all. Question: What fault is there in their not coming? Answer: If...
This is the teacher of Śakra; why do the four lords of the divine realms not proclaim a single point of clarity toward the rear?
If they were subjects of Śakra, they ought to have been questioned by the Four Heavenly Kings as being included in a single category. Therefore, there is an error. This is why the commentary states:
According to the latter two interpretations, there are no gods of the four *ākāśāyatana* heavens residing in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Regarding the statement that this [world] is called "Endurance" (*Sahā*) and so forth, this explains the name of the world-system. This name is established based on its presiding deity.

The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* calls it the "Land of Endurance. Paramārtha states: "Endurance" refers to the Brahmā King; because he is able to endure the superior achievements of others, he does not give rise to jealousy.
Therefore, it is called "Endurance" (Sahā). First, this Brahmā King is the lord of the world; named after his lord, it is called the Sahā World.
Second, it is named after its environment: within this realm, there are the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals, with the suffering of boiling cauldrons and burning coals.
Because all sentient beings therein endure immeasurable and boundless great suffering, it is named the Sahā World. Third, from...
This is the name of a practice. One hundred kalpas of cultivation in the world of Kāṣāyadhvaja do not equal one day in the land of Amitābha Buddha.
One hundred kalpas of cultivation in the land of Amitābha Buddha do not equal one day in the Sahā world.
If one practices giving, it can be practiced throughout all the pure lands. If one practices patience, it must be practiced within this world. Gold.
It must be tested by fire. This world is a place for practicing patience (*kṣānti*).

Because the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to endure great toil and suffering, it is called "Endurance" (*Sahā*). If a bodhisattva acts as a king within this realm to transform others, he must be able to endure;
only then can he dwell in and transform beings within this trichiliocosm. Therefore, it is named "Endurance."
Regarding the statement that "Saha" is a corruption: formerly it was called *Saha*, which means "a place of mixed evil. The name is established based on the things [the beings] therein endure.
While the Pure Land consists purely of bliss and the hells consist purely of suffering, this world is both pleasant and painful, and contains both good and evil;
therefore, it is called "mixed. Furthermore, because beings there create mixed karma, it is called "mixed. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "All bodhisattvas... [and so forth].

Sadāprarudita said: "It is truly marvelous! The World-Honored One, Śākyamuni Buddha, conceals his immeasurable power of mastery and instead delivers sentient beings through the Dharma that the poor delight in.
These bodhisattvas, too, are able to exercise such toil and humility, giving rise to this buddha-field out of immeasurable great compassion.
They are just like the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging, who was struck with sticks, wood, tiles, and stones."
He throws it down.
Regarding the statement that the dimensions of the first dhyāna are equal [to those of the desire realm], this explains the measurement of the world-systems.

To begin with, the measurement of the first dhyāna is similar to the measurement of one set of four continents within the desire realm; thus they are said to be "equal. Below the second dhyāna, there are one thousand Mount Sumerus, suns, and moons each.
Because one thousand first dhyānas are equal to one second dhyāna, it is like arranging one thousand coins and covering them all with a single plate.
Below the third dhyāna, there are one million and one thousand Sumerus, suns, and moons each; because two dhyānas are equal to three dhyānas.
One thousand is a single thousand. Ten thousands are ten thousand. A hundred thousands are one hundred thousand. A thousand thousands are one million.

If one were to take the previous thousand and arrange coins upon the ground, covering them all with a single counting-board (piṇḍa), then beneath these four types [of calculations], Mount Sumeru, the sun, and the moon each have ten thousand.
One hundred million and ten thousand. One thousand sets of the third dhyāna are equal to one set of the fourth dhyāna;
thus, this constitutes one million. Ten million is ten lakhs (koṭi). One hundred million is ten million (ayuta). One thousand million is one hundred million (niyuta).
It is as if, having previously given one thousand coins, one now places a large tray upon the ground and spreads a cloth over it. Furthermore...
A single great disk covers it. Thus, they all share the same formation and destruction. As the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states:
"The four continents, the sun and moon, Mount Sumeru, the desire heavens, and the Brahma worlds—each one thousand of these is called a small chiliocosm.
A thousand times this small chiliocosm is called a medium chiliocosm. A thousand times this is a trichiliocosm; all of these share the same formation and destruction, and are thus termed 'Great'."

The Thousandfold World System. Question: What is the time of initial destruction? Answer: The verse says: Destruction begins from the non-arising [of beings] in hell, until the external receptacle world is entirely exhausted.
Formation begins from the arising of the wind, until the first birth in hell. What are the characteristics of formation and destruction, and how do they occur?
The verse says: "In establishing the receptacle world, the wind-circle dwells at the very bottom. Furthermore, when the world is destroyed, there are briefly two kinds:
first, the world of sentient beings; second, the receptacle world. When the kalpa is about to be destroyed, among the humans, a certain sentient being—
The second dhyāna, which is attained through the natural course of things (*dharmatā*), is learned by all sentient beings therein one after another;
from that point onward, they are reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven. When the two types of the physical world (*bhājana-loka*) are destroyed, there are again three kinds of destruction:

first, destruction by fire; second, destruction by water; and third, destruction by wind. Regarding destruction by fire, the *Lokadhātunirdeśa-sūtra* states that the wind blows the foam of the ocean [to form clouds].
The Sun Deity, having fully completed seven sets of fire palaces, dissolves the world until it is entirely destroyed.
Regarding the second destruction by the calamity of water: the Sūtra says that great clouds spread everywhere until they fill the light-sound heavens (*ābhāsvara*).
From this point downward, boiling ash-water rains down, dissolving all the palaces belonging to the light-sound heavens, and so on, up to Mount Sumeru. As it is said:
Water dissolves salt; all things are transformed and utterly destroyed. Regarding the destruction by the three wind-disasters, the *Samādhi Sūtra* states:

from between the Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*), a great wind arises, blowing through the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, and blowing across the various continents, Mount Sumeru, and the three-thousandfold world system.

It is like blowing away dust and soil, until all is completely dispersed. These three thousand great chiliocosms, with their thousands of millions of billions of Mount Sumerus, four great continents, suns, moons, and so forth, all belong to a single great transformation-body (mahā-nirmāṇakāya) of the Tathāgata.

Therefore, these hundreds of millions of minor transformation-bodies are all contained within a single flower upon one of the thousand petals; they collectively belong to that one great transformation-body. One great transformation-body...
The realm over which the body reigns is said, in its entirety, to belong to the Tathāgata’s single transformative enjoyment (*ekapariṇāmanā-bhoga*).

According to reality, however, the fire calamity reaches only as far as the first dhyāna; the water calamity reaches the second dhyāna; and the wind calamity reaches the third dhyāna, but does not reach the fourth dhyāna.

As for what is now called the "summit" (*mūrdhan*), there are two kinds: first, the inward-facing summit; second, the outward-facing summit. For example, the summit of a preceptor is called the [inward-facing] summit.
The inner crown. The term "crown" (*ding*) refers to the outward-facing crown of the *kapiśa* (cap).
Regarding the phrase "the lord of the Sahā world," there are two interpretations of the word "lord" (*zhu*). The first interpretation states: Question:
Who is the lord of the Sahā world? Answer: The lord of the fourth dhyāna is the lord of the Sahā world, the trichiliocosm.
He is the Lord of the World. Śikhin [attained] the fourth dhyāna; Prabhāsa [attained] the second dhyāna; "etc. includes the first and third dhyānas.
Regarding the term *brahmā*, the word "equal" (*sam*) explains the meaning of *brahman*. *Brahmā* is the complete Sanskrit form;
here it means "tranquil," because he does not commit unwholesome karma. "Pure" (*śuci*) means he is free from hatred. "Clean" (*viśuddha*) means his body possesses radiance.
Question: The bodies of the gods of the six desire heavens also possess radiance; why then do you not say they are "pure and clean"? Answer: Because they are subject to the five signs of decay.
If one says *brahma*, this is exclusively a term from the Sanskrit (Fan) language. If one says "quiescent," "pure," or "clean and clean," these are exclusively terms from the Chinese (Tang) language.
If one says *brahma-śuddha* (梵潔), it combines both the Sanskrit and the Chinese. Now, using only the word *brahma*, it is simply according to the Sanskrit language.
The character for "Māra" is omitted; hence it is called "abbreviated.
Regarding the statement that "Śikhin is the summit of the fire calamity," the second interpretation states:
the Brahmā King, Lord of the Sahā World, and the Great Brahmā Śikhin are subsumed as one. This refers to taking the Lord of the Sahā World, who is the Brahmā King of the First Dhyāna.
This is because the First Dhyāna is the summit of the calamity of fire; thus it is called *Śikhin*. *Śikhin* means "topknot.
Therefore, the Brahmā King of the First Dhyāna is taken as the lord of the Sahā world. "Radiance" refers to the Second Dhyāna; within the Second Dhyāna, all are designated by the name "radiance.
Within the word "etcetera," the Third and Fourth Dhyanas are included. This is from the Commentary (*śūtra*).
The Master adopts the second interpretation. There are a thousand gates and ten thousand doors; the explanations of the meaning differ.
When it says, "Furthermore, the *Pañcaśatikā-prajñāpāramitā*," etc., he is reconciling the scriptural text. Regarding the Master’s second interpretation:
if Śikhin Brahmā were the Brahmā of the First Dhyāna and the lord of a small chiliocosm, how could one reconcile this with the *Prajñāpāramitā*?
Regarding the scriptural passage: *Śikhin* means "topknot. This refers to the Brahmā King Śikhin, who is the lord of this Sahā world.

Based on the flow of the text, it appears to refer to the Brahmā King of the Fourth Dhyāna. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* answers that *Śikhin* is a Sanskrit term, while "Holder of the Topknot" (*Śikhi-dhara*) is the Chinese translation;
because that Brahmā King of the Conch-topknot in the Fourth Dhyāna bears a fleshly topknot upon his head, he is called the "Holder."
Regarding the *uṣṇīṣa*: only the Brahmā King of the Fourth Dhyāna possesses this mark alone; thus, the *uṣṇīṣa* is simply another name for the Brahmā King of the First Dhyāna.
Therefore, the first interpretation takes the Brahmā King of the Fourth Dhyāna as the Lord of the Sahā World.

The second interpretation follows the Master of the Commentary (*śūstrakāra*), who, based on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, states that "Śikhin" is a Sanskrit term, which, when translated into the language of Tang, means [the one with] a topknot.
It is also called *Cūḍā* (Topknot) and also called *Dhara-cūḍā* (Holder of the Topknot). This refers to the Brahmā King of the First Dhyāna, who is the summit of the dust of this fire-disaster kalpa;
it carries this same meaning. It is also consistent with what is stated in the *Dīrgha Āgama*: "Śikhin" refers to the body of the First Dhyāna.
Therefore, the Master of the Commentary offers the second interpretation: the Lord of the Sahā World is the Brahmā King of the First Dhyāna, named Śikhin, whose [epithet] is "Topknot."
Śikhin belongs to the fourth dhyāna, whereas the Brahmā King of the first dhyāna—if one speaks of the Brahmā King, he encompasses all four dhyānas;
if one speaks of Śikhin, it refers specifically to the first dhyāna of the fourth dhyāna. "Śikhin" is a Sanskrit term translated here as "Uṣṇīṣadhara" (Holder of the Topknot);
this is a specific name for the Brahmā King of the fourth dhyāna, who bears a fleshy uṣṇīṣa upon his head. It is also a specific name for the Brahmā King Śaṅkhakuṭa (Conch-Topknot).
Thus he is called "Holding the Topknot" (Cūḍā). If one says "Śikhin," this is a Sanskrit term translated here as "Topknot.
It is also an alternative name for the Brahmā King of the First Dhyāna. Furthermore, the "dust-peak" at the summit during the calamity of fire is also referred to as the "Topknot."
Regarding the statement that "light" refers to the others and so forth: this refers to the lord of the second dhyāna. As for the word "etc. in the sutra, it includes the third dhyāna;
according to the *Dīrgha Āgama*, this refers to the first two [dhyānas] while including the third and fourth by means of the term "etc. (paryāya).

Regarding the term "the assembly of nāgas," there are two [categories], the second being the tenth: the assembly of those who obscure the void and contain the spray. Within this assembly of nāgas, the golden division is further divided into four pairs:
first, the pair of Nandana and Bhadanta (Nanda Nāgarāja and Upananda Nāgarāja); second, the pair of the eight-headed and nine-headed dragons (Sāgara and Vāsuki);
third, the pair of the many-thousand-headed and few-affliction dragons (Takṣaka Nāgarāja and Anavatapta); and fourth, the pair of those who rely on mind and those who rely on form.

[The dragon] Manasvin, [who has a mind like an *utpala* flower and hair like its down]. Question: Since dragons belong to the realm of animals (*tiryagyoni*), for what reason are they placed after the assembly of devas and before the assembly of Śakra-rājas?
Question: Why is it called "Fierce"? Answer: There are generally four meanings. First, because its power is the greatest; among the five kinds of inconceivable powers, the dragon occupies one:
first, the inconceivable power of karma; second, the inconceivable power of the world; third, the supernatural power of dragons;
fourth, the power of meditative concentration; and fifth, the power of the Buddha. Second, because it assists the devas in battle. As stated in the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*: [text continues].
Evil dragons assist the asuras in battle; virtuous dragons assist the devas in battle. Since this is a virtuous dragon, it therefore assists the devas.

Third, because it harmonizes yin and yang, it bestows grace upon humanity; thus, it ranks next after the devas. Fourth, because it protects the Dharma-treasury of the Buddhas of the thousand eons, it ranks next after the former heroes.
Question: Since dragons are able to harmonize yin and yang, why does there still occur drought? Answer: It is due to five reasons.

Therefore, there is drought in heaven. First, the fire element increases excessively, causing the clouds to scatter in all directions. Second, the wind element increases excessively, blowing the clouds away in all directions.
Third, the asuras gather the clouds and return them to the great ocean. Fourth, the cloud-masters and rain-masters are often negligent. Fifth, sentient beings are stingy, greedy, and jealous;
because they have summoned many evil karmas, [the rains do not fall]. Furthermore, among the species of mythical creatures, the dragon is their leader.
Their virtue matches that of the Five Spirits. They can become large or small; they can be hidden or manifest. In spring they ascend to heaven; in winter they enter the springs.
Their transformations occur in an instant and cannot be fully described. The *Guangya* states: "Those with scales and shells are *jiaolong*;
those with wings are *yinglong*; those with horns are *qiulong*; those without horns are *chilong*. Within the *Zhuangjiao*, there is mention of the egg-born.
The four modes of birth—oviparous, viviparous, moisture-born, and transformation-born—are those of the nāgas.
Regarding the phrase "these two brothers and so forth," An-guo states: "These are the nāgas of Rājagṛha; they reside in the vicinity of the city."
The rains fall in their proper seasons, and there is constant abundance of harvests; for this reason, the Buddha frequently brought his disciples to stay in this city.
As for the phrase "the wind does not rustle the branches" and so forth: whatever deeds are performed accord well with the hearts of people, and all who see them rejoice;
therefore, it is called "Joy."

Regarding the statement, "The first can cause joy, etc.": A question is asked as to why the first two *nāgas* are named "Joy" (*prīti*) and the latter is named "Worthy" (*sat*). The commentary answers:
"Because the first can cause people to rejoice, it is therefore named 'Joy'."
Regarding the statement "his nature is virtuous and his name is Joyful": this dragon is by nature gentle and good, bringing joy to others.
Regarding the term "Sāgara": this dragon dwells outside the world in the eighth salt sea; it is the Sāgara Dragon Palace mentioned in the *Devadatta-parivarta*.
It is named after its supporting sea. The *Lokotpatti-sūtra* states that at the bottom of the great ocean there is...
The palace of the Sāgara Dragon King is exactly eighty thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth—note that the two pronunciations "Ga" and "Ke" are similar.
The Jiǔ (紏) country states: this was originally the name of a kingdom; a seer (*ṛṣi*) lived near this land, and by means of his incantations, he transformed the entire kingdom into an ocean.
This dragon dwells therein, hence it is named after him.
As for the term "Aśvakarṇa" (Horse-Ear), it refers to the nine-headed dragon.
Regarding the phrase "intending to bind [the mountain]," there are two interpretations: first, he wished to bind the mountain so as to sever it and seize Śakra; [the second interpretation follows...]
[The Buddha] ate. Śakra, having assembled the hosts of devas in the Sudharmā Hall, recollected the Prajñāpāramitā;
the dragon’s majesty subsided of its own accord. Second, this dragon was protecting the devas and enjoying this mountain, and therefore [the Buddha] bound him with a cord.
Both interpretations are excellent, for the eight great nāga kings are mostly meritorious and virtuous dragons. As for this class of dragons...
The number is not one; it refers to that entire class, hence the term "of this kind. These nine-headed dragons belong to the Dragon King of the Country of Birds.
It was because the Śākyas first pursued him that he manifested as an elephant to carry the Śākyas away.
Regarding the term "loquacious" (*bahujalpa*): it is called "loquacious" because one possesses many tongues; alternatively, it is called "loquacious" because one utters many words.

As for the phrase "or due to a fondness for speech," one is called "fond of speech" because of the profusion of their talk. This is like people saying of someone who is very busy, "This person has seven hands and eight feet"—it is not that such things actually exist.

Regarding the statement that this is called "Free from Affliction" (Anavatapta): "Free from affliction" is the opposite of having few afflictions. The old translation as "Lake Anavatapta" is entirely erroneous.
This dragon derives its name from the lake upon which it relies. That lake lies north of Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and south of Mount Gandhamādana;
it is eight hundred *li* in circumference, and the dragon’s palace is situated within it.

Regarding the phrase "free from the three kinds of burning affliction," the *Loutan jing* (Ratnakūṭa-sūtra) and the *Qishi jing* (Lokasthāna-sūtra) state that the dragons in this pond are free from these three types of burning affliction:

first, they are not scorched by hot sands; for when the dragons sport, they frequently transform themselves into human beings, and if they were suddenly struck by hot sand or gravel, they would immediately revert to their original form.
Second, they are not stripped of their clothing by the wind to expose their bodies; when the dragons transform into humans...
He could not change his tail; the wind blew his robe away, exposing his body. When he saw his own form, his mind was filled with burning distress.
Thirdly, there were those who were eaten by garuḍas. The *Anavatapta-hrada-upaniṣad-sūtra* states: When the Buddha wished to go to that lake, he transformed himself into various nāgas to depart.
He first dispatched Maudgalyāyana to startle and awaken those beings. At that time, Maudgalyāyana transformed into a garuḍa, flapping his wings and striking with his beak. All...
The dragon princes and their attendants were filled with extreme alarm and fear; they went before the king and spoke thus: "Hitherto such a thing has never occurred; why has it suddenly happened now?
Therefore, it is said that the dragons of this lake are not eaten by the garuḍas. The Golden City [Sūtra] states there are three further reasons:
fourth, when they eat fragrant food, it transforms into frogs; fifth, their bodies have upward-pointing scales, through which sand and stones enter.
Internally, if one acts with defilement, it is exposed like a coiled snake.
Regarding the statement in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* concerning "the great earth" and so forth, a commentary states: "Even Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage are without afflictions (*kleśa*)."
Since the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) corresponds to the third *kalpa*, it is called the "Great Stage" (*mahābhūmi*).

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that because one traverses the three *kalpas* through ten kinds of superior practices, their designations differ: the first *kalpa* is simply called a *pāramitā*; the second *kalpa* is called a "near-*pāramitā*" (*upapāramitā*);
and the third *kalpa* is called a "great-*pāramitā*" (*mahāpāramitā*). Therefore, it is named the Great Stage. Question: Regarding these various nāgas...
Question: Are those who appear later always emanations of Bodhisattvas, or are they actual [beings]? Answer: They fall into both categories.

If they are actual [beings], most of these dragons have broken the precepts and fallen into the state of dragons. Question: How is this known? Answer: The *Sāgaranāgarājaparipṛcchā-sūtra*, fascicle three, states:
The Dragon King addressed the Buddha, saying, "Since the time of Krakucchanda Buddha, I have been born among the dragons. Regarding all these dragons...
"Their wives, children, and retinues are all few; why is it that the assembly of nāgas is so vast now? The Buddha told the Nāga King:
"During the time of Krakucchanda Buddha, there were ninety-eight billion people who broke the precepts who were reborn among the nāgas.
During the time of Kanakamuni Buddha, there were eight billion people. During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there were sixty-four billion people—both householders and those who had left the home life."

Those who break the precepts are born among the nāgas. Within my Dharma, nine hundred and ninety billion people—both householders and renunciants—who have violated the prohibitions and precepts are all born among the nāgas. For this reason, their wives, children, and retinues are beyond calculation.
Because of this, those transformed within the nāga realm are truly of two kinds; if they are those of actual retribution, they are mostly those who broke the precepts.
Regarding the phrase "the dharma-gate of departing from suffering" and so forth: Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage are able to transform sentient beings so that they depart from suffering.
Thus, they can cause water to flow from within the scales of nāgas and kinnaras to provide relief for the beings of Jambudvīpa, liberating them from the suffering of hunger and thirst.
That which is called "the mind of loving-kindness" (maitrī-citta) is also referred to as "relying on the mind. With respect to sentient beings, there are times when rain is not desired;

therefore, clouds first gather for seven days, and thus it is termed "the mind of loving-kindness. That which is contrary to this is not loving-kindness. It is like a person whose house has caught fire: one cannot simply wait for clouds to gather first.
Regarding the term *utpala*, this is translated as "relying on color" (*yise*). Lü [Cheng] says it refers to flowers of four colors; he states that *utpala* is the blue lotus.
The Master of the Commentary [Yuan Ce] says it is the red lotus, but this is an error. This is also not the case. The two characters *you* and *po* differ entirely in their semantic basis:
*utpala* is blue, while *utpala* (with the prefix *u-*) is red. It is not an error. This is like how in the Chinese language, adding the character "not" (*bu*) changes the meaning.

It has no meaning. If the character "also" (亦) were added, it would have meaning. One cannot claim that because *palāśa* is the same [in name], there is consequently no distinction between blue and red;
it does not preclude the existence of distinct meanings. This [term] is likewise named after its location in a pond.
Regarding the term *kiṃnara* in Sanskrit: this refers to the eleventh class of beings, the assembly of those who perform refined songs and elegant music.

As for the term "song-deity" (*gāndharva*), it carries the meaning of one who chants and extols sublime virtue. It does not mean that by means of the Four Truths, Dependent Origination, or the Six Perfections, one simply composes songs in the melodic modes of the Western Regions (Liangzhou) as if they were mere entertainment;
rather, it is like the case of Gao Yao of the Shangshu, whose compositions were recorded in the *Soubei* and whose songs celebrated the virtues of the sovereign.
How enlightened! How excellent are his ministers! How peaceful are all affairs! Or how might it be? Regarding Brahmā and others, the text below states: "Singing hymns to praise his virtues.

The matter is explained in the commentary. The sutra says: "He has the body of a beast and the face of a human, yet possesses a single horn. Formerly, he was called the "Mysterious Immortal" (Yíshénxiān).
Everyone views them with suspicion, wondering whether they are human or non-human. It is further said that they have the head of a horse and the body of a human and are capable of speech.
When asked to which realm (*gati*) they belong, the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* states: "They are included among animals. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 12, states:

"They are included among the devas; because they are slightly inferior, like worldly servants who are employed by humans, these beings are instead employed by devas, and thus are categorized within the human realm."

Thus, it is known that this belongs to the celestial realm (*devagati*) and is situated among the Ten Jewel Mountains (*daśaratnaparvata*). The *gandharva* and *mārgaṇa* deities provide music for the various gods, taking turns moving between the upper and lower levels.
According to the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*, there is a separate mountain in the Northern Continent called Mount Wish-Fulfilling (*cintāmaṇi-parvata*).

Because the pleasures, clothing, food, and other enjoyments received there are identical to those of the heavens, it is also called Mount Sorrowless (*aśoka-parvata*). Upon entering this [mountain]...
As for the mountain, because it is entirely blissful, four celestial musicians (gandharvas) each dwell in one of its corners. Their appearances also differ:
one corner is like the color of golden-yellow, one side is like the color of white silver, one side is red, and one corner is purple.
Regarding the statement that "the first song [sings] of the Four Noble Truths and so forth": Question:

How is it that the first song of the Four Noble Truths is assigned to the *Dharma-kinnara*, while the subsequent song of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is assigned to the *Saddharma-kinnara* and others? Answer: That which is called "Dharma" consists merely of names, phrases, and syllables.

Yet, they lack substantial reality and are merely designated as "dharmas. Because the faculties of the śrāvakas are inferior, for them the Four Truths alone constitute the Dharma. Next, regarding the verse on dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*):
it excels the preceding Four Truths and thus receives the name "Sublime Dharma" (*saddharma*). Next, regarding the verse on the Six Perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*):

because it encompasses the vast and great, it is called the "Great Dharma" (*mahādharma*). It is called the Great Dharma for three reasons: first, the Four Truths, dependent origination, and the Six Perfections are all collectively the objects of focus (*ālambana*).
Regarding the "object" (*viṣaya*): among the three kinds of objects, this is the greatest; therefore, it is called the "Great Dharma. Second, regarding its inclusion and comprehensive subsumption:
the myriad things are the myriad practices, and since their essence is great, it is called the "Great Dharma. Third, because it can induce a great fruit, it is called the "Great Dharma."

Later, it praises the One Vehicle (ekayāna), and is therefore called "Upholding the Dharma" (*dharmadhara*). Because it can sustain that which is neither empty nor existent, it is called "Upholding the Dharma.
Question: What is the difference between this and the One Vehicle? Answer: The Six Perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) are the sudden teaching of the Mahāyāna within the Three Vehicles.
The One Vehicle is the gradual teaching of the Mahāyāna taught after forty years. Because they meet at different points, each has its own distinct sustaining power. The Śrāvakas do not...

[The previous position] is set aside; it is then designated as "upholding the Dharma. Furthermore, it is taught that the Six Perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) are the provisional Mahāyāna within the Three Vehicles prior to the forty years [of the Buddha’s teaching].
This present One Vehicle (ekayāna), however, is the definitive Mahāyāna subsequent to those forty years.
Alternatively, the One Vehicle encompasses both the exoteric teachings and so forth, whereas the four dharmas and the six perfections are merely practices, as they constitute distinct categories.
Regarding the statement "or the first three kinds of songs and so forth": the first song concerns the teachings and practices of the Śrāvakas, which is called the Dharma;

the next song concerns the teachings and practices of the Pratyekabuddhas, which is called the Sublime Dharma; the next song concerns the teachings and practices of the Six Pāramitās, which is called the Great Dharma; and the final song concerns the principle and fruit of the One Vehicle.
He is called a "Holder of the Dharma" because he can sustain the principle and fruit of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), which is neither existent nor empty. Question:
Why are the first three songs dedicated to the teachings, practices, and fruits of the Three Vehicles (Triyāna), while the last one concerns only the principle and fruit of the One Vehicle? Answer:

This accords with the essential intent of the Sūtra. It causes those who hear the teachings of the Three Vehicles to awaken to the principle of the One Vehicle, practice the causes of the Three Vehicles, and proceed toward the One Vehicle.

...the fruit. Therefore, the first three songs concern the teachings and practices of the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*), while the final song concerns the principle and fruit of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
As for the statement that "some songs [concern] the teaching and principle of the One Vehicle," singing the teaching of the One Vehicle is called the *Dharma*;

singing the principle of the One Vehicle is called the *Saddharma* (Sublime Dharma); singing the practice of the One Vehicle is called the *Mahādharma* (Great Dharma); and singing the fruit of the One Vehicle—

It is named "Upholder of the Dharma" (*dharmadhara*). There are three interpretations in the commentary: the first interpretation holds that it upholds the four dharmas of the One Vehicle—teaching, principle, practice, and fruit;

the second holds that it upholds only principle and fruit; and the third holds that it upholds only the fruit. All of these establish the name based on what is upheld (*upātta*), with the intent of causing those of the Two Vehicles to turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle.
Regarding the phrase "in accordance with what the Buddha has taught in a single assembly," Muo says: This summarizes the virtues being extolled.

Whatever Dharma was taught by the Buddha in a single assembly was intended to accommodate the various faculties [of sentient beings]. Therefore, this deity praises these matters through concrete phenomena;
it does not merely chant the *Lotus Sūtra* in the air, nor chant the Dharma-gate of Non-duality under the *Vimalakīrti* assembly, nor chant the Buddha-nature under the *Nirvāṇa* assembly.
Regarding the phrase "like the sounds of worldly music," this refers to works such as the *Qin Wang Po Zhen Yue* (The Emperor of Qin’s Music of the Broken Array).

As for the *sūtra*s' mention of "gandharvas" and so forth, they are the hosts who perform soaring and fragrant, intense music. In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, they are called *t'ung-lung-mo*; this translates as "tree.
They dwell upon the mountains of ten treasures on the earth. Their names are fully detailed in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
Regarding the phrase "the sound of music" (*yue-yin*, with the character *yue* pronounced as *wu-xiao-fan*), the character *yue* is called out [as a phonetic].
Regarding the statement "in Sanskrit it is called *manu*," *manu* means "mind. If one says "it may be," *sāvara* is the name for sound.
If one follows the sequence of the Sanskrit language, the name is *manojña-śabda* (agreeable sound). This corresponds to the Chinese term *kě-yì-yīn* (agreeable sound).
It is called "agreeable" because it is a sound that people find pleasant and desire to hear; thus, it is "joyful. It is also termed *yì-rú-yì-yīn* (sound according to one's wish).

The translators of the scriptures intended to be concise, and therefore simply said "joyful" (*lè*). The Master of the Commentary explains the character "joyful" (*lè*) with a single phrase, and its meaning is thereby fully exhausted.
"Rāga" (pleasure/delight) means that which causes people to love and delight in something. This is not a literal translation; rather, it is established according to its meaning.

"To the heart's content" (*kāma*) and "according to one's wish" (*yathāmanas*) both carry the sense of "pleasure. The two kings, Rāga-gandharva-rāja and Manojña-gandharva-rāja, do not contain the character for "sound" (*śabda*) in the sūtra;
they correspond in meaning to *manuṣya* (human). If one speaks of "the sound of pleasure," [it refers to the Gandharvas].
Regarding the two kings, Bāvarī and the Gandharva Surūpa: in the sutra, the character "yīn" (音) corresponds to the meaning of *śabda* in the Sanskrit language.
Regarding the statement in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* that "soft" (*mṛdu*) refers to the absence of sound and syllables, this refers to the Gandharva King *Ratipriya* mentioned in this sutra.
Regarding the statement that "harmonious sound" (*saṃgīti*) refers to the presence of sound and syllables, this refers to the Gandharva King *Ghoṣavat* mentioned in this sutra. The above...

Their voices are as they wish, harmonious, and pleasing to the mind; all of them are such that people delight in hearing them. To explain this according to the characters of the *Yuelu* (Record of Music):
when Śakra and the various devas desire to produce music, a strange phenomenon occurs; they immediately fly up into the sky and take turns ascending and descending with the kiṃnaras.
Those who have horns on their heads are called kiṃnaras; those without horns are called gandharvas.

"Bhā," he asked, "to which realm does this belong? He replied: "Some say it belongs to the realm of hungry ghosts (preta), others say it belongs to the realm of asuras; in truth, it belongs to the realm of devas.
It is comprised among the inferior devas because they provide music and song for entertainment and protect the various devas."

Regarding the statement that the Sanskrit term *gandharva* and so forth refers to musicians in the Western Regions: there, musicians are called *gandharva*, which in the language of Tang (Chinese) means "those who travel seeking fragrance.
This is because these musical deities do not engage in worldly occupations, but constantly perform music and discourse upon the Way.

Whether it be when high officials change their positions or when a household experiences a celebratory occasion, they seek out fragrances; thus, in the Western Regions, they are called "musicians" (*yue*).
The person is called "Fragrance-Seeker" (*gandharva*). Because they act by listening to and gathering [fragrances], it is called "Fragrance-Seeking Conduct.

Alternatively, because they provide music for others, or perhaps move about seeking the fragrance of wine and food, it is called "Fragrance-Seeking Conduct. This deity of pleasure (*nandana*) is metaphorically compared to those musicians who disperse [the fragrance].
Thus, the name *gandharva* is derived from the meaning of "Fragrance-Seeking Conduct" in this context. There are three types in total. First:

[This refers to] the fundamental gandharva, who feeds on subtle fragrance like the body of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Second, they provide music for the various devas. Third, there is the mirage over the ocean.
These are the two meanings of the "dispersed" (or "scattered") gandharva. As for the question regarding the "fundamental," it is named after that [first type].

However, within the category of the "seeking fragrance" (*gandha-āhāra*), there is a slight distinction: the fundamental one specifically feeds on subtle fragrance, just as in the case of the dispersed musicians in the West.
"Gandharva" (尋香) refers to making music; it is so named because they seek the fragrance of the banquet hall, which is the same as the previous definition.
As for the "Gandharva City" (乾闥婆城), which is a mirage on the sea, it is named after the *gandharvas* who create false cities and such things through their magical arts.
Regarding the statement that "one [type of sound] is not from strings or bamboo, such as drums," the musical instruments employed do not exceed the eight sounds (*aṣṭa-tūrya*). A book states:

"When the eight sounds are harmoniously blended, it is called music. First is metal (*tāla*), referring to bells and the like; second is stone (*śilā*), referring to the *qing* chime which produces sound when struck upon its stand.
Three are of silk: the strings of the *zheng*, *qin*, and *se* lutes. Four are of bamboo: referring to the *xiao*, *di*, and other such instruments. Five are of gourd: namely the *sheng*;
its handle resembles a sauce ladle, and it is held in the mouth. Six are of earth: the *xuan* and *chi* flutes, shaped like yellow gourds, which are blown. Seven refers to leather:
that which has hair is called "skin" (*pi*), while that without hair is called "leather" (*ge*); this refers to drum-skins. Eight is wood; within wood there is...
Two: First is the *jī* (one-mechanism), which consists of a wooden barrel fitted with a tongue that is shaken; all the instruments move simultaneously.
Second is the *què* (the missing/notch), which is a board carved into the shape of a tiger, with the body of the tiger hollowed out and twenty-four teeth mounted on its back.
When the music nears its conclusion, one takes a bamboo broom and brushes it to produce a sound, whereupon all the instruments stop playing at once.
This is also termed "discordance.
As for the statement that they are not among those below the lute and flute players: these four gandharva kings are fully subsumed within those two aforementioned categories.
He [He] says: "If one relies on the various musical instruments, all five notes are complete; each is a distinct tradition, and there is no superiority or inferiority among them.
It is merely due to the superiority or inferiority of the performer that they are divided into 'upper' and 'lower' categories. This interpretation is incorrect.

The commentary further states that within music there are two types, which does not refer to the performer. Thus, He’s statement is not appropriate. Furthermore, among the music of the eight sounds, some is licentious and some is...

It is correct. That which is performed today at the great state rituals are all *yaya* (elegant) music. All the various sections of the Han, Zhen, and Hu traditions currently in use are the music of Zheng and Wei.
Therefore, the stringed and wind instruments, as well as those that are not stringed or wind instruments, are distinguished by their relative superiority or inferiority.

Thus, the Preface to the *Shijing* says: "Emotion issues forth in sound; sound is formed into patterns, which are called 'yinsheng' (melodic sounds). These possess the notes gong, shang, jue, and zhi."
Wings. When these form patterns, they become the notes *gong* and *shang*. When the high and low pitches correspond to one another, it is called "tone" (*yin*).

Thus, there is music for a well-governed age whose tones are upright and harmonious; the music of a chaotic age is resentful and angry because its tones are discordant. The music of a state on the verge of ruin is sorrowful and plaintive because its people are in distress.
The *Analects* says, "I detest the sounds of Zheng, for they disturb the refined music (*yale*). From this, we know that music has both the licentious and the correct.

There are two distinctions. The "upper" and "lower" mentioned here refer to what are called *mañju-ghoṣa* (exquisite sounds); thus, they are named according to the quality of the sound itself. This refers specifically to the music being performed.
For instance, when one speaks of *gandharva* or *sugandharva*, the name is derived from the performer—the one who plays the music or the one who makes it beautiful—rather than from the music itself.
The commentary on the sutra states: "First, there is music without sound," as in the case of [the following] performance.
Regarding the *huántuó* dance and others: the inferior are called the *gandharva* kings of music, while the superior are called the beautiful *gandharva* kings.
Second, there is music with sound, such as the *xiāo* and *dí* flutes; the inferior are called musical sounds, while the superior are called beautiful sounds.

Regarding the phrase "or this is the same as before" and so forth: it is just like the case of the *kiṃnara*s and others. First, they produce a melodic composition (*gīta*) on the Four Truths, which is called "music" (*gīta*).

Next, they produce a melodic composition on Dependent Origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), which is called "musical sound" (*gītisvara*). Next, they produce a melodic composition on the Six Perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), which is called "beauty" (*śobhā*).

Finally, they produce a melodic composition on the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), which is called "beautiful sound" (*śobhanasvara*). Alternatively, they may produce a melodic composition on the teachings and practices of the Śrāvaka vehicle, which is called "music. Or they may produce...
The melodic strains of the teachings and practices of the Pratyekabuddhas are called "Music. Next, the melodic strains of the teachings and practices of the Six Perfections are called "Beautiful.

Finally, the melodic strains of the principle and fruition of the One Vehicle are called "Beautiful Sound. Once, there was a person who could recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* from memory while playing the *konghou* lute.
It is also like the case of the Jade Gourd (Jingke) piercing the King of Qin; the King invited a beautiful woman to perform a single piece of music on the zither for him to hear.
The account of the beautiful woman within the lute who instructed the King to pull back his sleeves and leap over the screen is of this same category.
As for the statement that the sutra mentions "the four asura kings" and so forth, these are not members of the deva hosts. They are also called the "thirteenth group:
those who shake the mountains and surge the seas. This refers to the asuras who dwell beneath the great ocean; when they desire to wage war against Śakra, they emerge from [the depths].

The Sea-god dispatches his troops; he exhales his breath, which strikes the waters of the ocean, causing them to boil and surge, shaking Mount Sumeru. This is called "the mountain moving and the sea surging.

Regarding the mention of Brahmā, Asura, and so forth, this is an explanation of their collective designation. Question: Why is it called a collective designation? Answer: The commentary states that in the Sanskrit language...
Asura. This is translated as "Non-God" (fei-tian). To call them *asura* is a corruption.

According to the Master of the Commentary’s interpretation, *sura* is a synonym for "God," and they are all subsumed within the realm of gods (*deva-gati*). Question: Since these are still gods, why are they called "Non-Gods"?
Answer: They are gods who lack the conduct of gods; they are termed "Non-Gods" by way of censure. Although they lack divine conduct, they are fundamentally gods.
Regarding the statement "because of much flattery and deceit," it is asked: Why are they not called *asura* (non-gods)? Sōrakuten (Svarloka) asks:

From the heavens above up to the Brahma-world, there is flattery and deceit everywhere; why are they not called *asura*? He answers: Because of their excessive flattery and deceit, they practice flattery exclusively.

If one simplifies the categories of the heavens, [the asuras] are inferior; or they exist only temporarily, unlike the devas. Therefore, it is said that among the heavens, those are called "upright and honest.
What was mentioned above regarding the arrival of the asuras is included within the category of the heavens.
Regarding the statement, "As with a person who is unrighteous, they are also called [something else]": it is like a person who does not practice human conduct;

though they are originally a human being, they are censured and called 'non-human. The intended meaning is that because this person's bodily conduct is unrighteous, they are said to be 'non-devas' (asura).
It does not mean they are non-animal. Since asuras are included within the category of devas, yet lack deva-like conduct, they are called 'non-devas.'

Regarding the mention of the *Yogācārabhūmi* and other such texts, the Master of the Commentary (*Sūzhǔ*) provisionally cites various teachings; while these generally fall under the category of the "Universal Vehicle" (*pūtuyōng*), they are not definitively subsumed within the "Three Vehicles" (*sānqù*). They are indeterminate.
As for the statement regarding Rāhu, the asura, and others: consider, for instance, the Vātsīputrīyas and the Kaurukullakas, or King Bandhumat;
would these not also be categorized as belonging to the realm of animals?

Regarding the statement, "Now, relying on the Mahāyāna Yoga [Śāstra] and so forth," the commentator (Sūzhǔ) concludes: "Now, relying on the Mahāyāna Yoga as the correct [authority] is what is intended.
Regarding the phrase, "The first, the extremely weak, resides among humans," it is said that even now, in the West (India), there are still seen to exist caves of the asuras. That is to say—

This is also the dwelling place of the Bodhisattva Bhāviveka. The *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) states that not far to the south of the city of Dhānakaṭaka, there is a great mountain cliff where the Bodhisattva Bhāvaviveka—translated into Chinese as the Master of Treatises Bhāviveka—resides in the palace of the Asuras.
He awaits the time when Maitreya Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood and descends to be born, at which point he will emerge. This master of treatises heard...
In the kingdom of Magadha, the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla proclaimed the teachings of the Dharma; his disciples numbered in the thousands.

There was a teacher who disrupted the exposition of the doctrine, so [Dharmapāla] set out with staff and mendicant’s bowl. Upon reaching the city of Pāṭaliputra, he learned that the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla was at the Bodhi tree.
The master of the treatise then commanded his disciples, saying: "Go to the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla at the Bodhi tree and speak these words on my behalf:"
The Bodhisattva has proclaimed the Bequeathed Teachings and guided those who were lost; they have looked up to his virtue with a humble mind for many days.

Yet, because his original vow has not yet been fulfilled, he has not yet succeeded in paying his respects. As for the Bodhi tree, he has vowed that it shall not be seen in vain; when he sees it, there shall surely be realization.

He was titled the Teacher of Gods and Humans (*Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām*). The Bodhisattva Dharmapāla said to his messenger, "Human existence is like an illusion; life and body are as fleeting as a bubble.

Though I am parched with thirst for the truth, I have not yet found the leisure for it. People believe what they hear in discussion, but after our back-and-forth exchange, we did not reach a consensus.

Let us go see the Master of Treatises (*Śāstrin*), and then return to our own land. There he reflected in stillness, "If not when Maitreya attains Buddhahood, who will resolve my doubts? [Thus he sought] Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva...
Before the image of the Buddha, he recited the *Sui-xin* (Heart-according-to-desire) *dhāraṇī* while abstaining from grain and subsisting only on water for three years.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara manifested a body of wondrous color. The Master of Treatises said, "I pray that you remain here with this body until I may behold Maitreya.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva said, "Human life is precarious and fragile; the world is fleeting and illusory. You should cultivate supreme goodness and aspire to be born in Tuṣita."
"O Celestial One, if you pay homage here, you shall surely succeed in seeing him. The Master of Treatises said, "One's resolve must not be old-fashioned; one's mind must not be divided.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva said, "If that is so, you should go to the mountain cliff south of the city of Dhānakaṭaka to the abode of the Vajrapāṇi deity.
If you recite and maintain the Vajrapāṇi Dhāraṇī with sincere devotion, you shall achieve this."
The Master of Shastras went there and recited [the scriptures]. After three years, the deity said to him, "What is your aspiration for which you have exerted yourself here so diligently?
The Master replied, "I wish to remain in this body until I may behold Maitreya. Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva sent me here to request [this favor];
let all my wishes be fulfilled. The deity pointed and said, "Within this rock lies an Asura..."
At the palace in Luoyang, he made a formal request according to the Dharma. The stone wall was said to open; as soon as it opened, he entered within and waited for a vision.
The Master of Śāstras said, "I dwell in seclusion and see nothing; how could I know that a Buddha has appeared? The spirit said, "When Maitreya appears, I shall manifest a sign for you.

Having received this command, the Master devoted himself single-mindedly to recitation and retention. Another three years passed, yet no extraordinary signs occurred. He then took mustard seeds and struck [the wall] with them.
The stone cavern was wide and opened like a grotto. At that time, hundreds of thousands of people watched it, so entranced that they forgot to leave.

The Master of Treatises (Lunshi) summoned them again and again, yet everyone who saw him was struck with fear; only six people entered together. Once they had entered, the walls closed shut. This is one such instance.
As for the others, they dwell beneath the great ocean—some say they live in water, while others say they live in caves on Mount Sumeru.

Regarding the phrase "within the northern caverns," it refers to the four categories mentioned below. As for the statement that the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* speaks of the two "wonders" (*prātihārya*) and so forth:

these four successive categories are each twenty-one thousand *yojanas*, totaling eighty-four thousand *yojanas*. According to the underlying principle, this reaches through into the Golden Wheel (*kāñcanamaṇḍala*).
Regarding the statement "from this point downward, eighty-four thousand [yojanas]," etc., a question arises:

since the base of Mount Sumeru rests upon the Golden Wheel (kāñcanacakravāḍa), it would follow that its depth exceeds the height of Mount Sumeru itself, which entails the error of it penetrating through the Golden Wheel. How should this be interpreted? Answer:
There are three explanations from the Lu Prefecture (Lufu). First, the measurements of size differ; originally, it was simply eighty thousand yojanas, but it was measured using a smaller scale.

[The depth] increases by four thousand *yojanas*. A second [view] states that this is brought about by the power of karma (*karmabala*); however, this too suffers from the same fault as the latter [position], such as [the claim that] there are sentient beings within stones, within iron, or within fire.

The Golden Wheel (*kāñcanacakravāḍa*) cannot be penetrated; it is the power of karma that makes it so. If it were indeed to penetrate the Golden Wheel, it would likewise have to be due to the power of karma.
A third [view] states that according to reality, the seawater is also eighty-four thousand [yojanas deep]; this merely cites its...
The total number is actually eighty-four thousand, yet it is simply stated as eighty thousand. As the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* says: "The Muni taught eighty thousand aggregates of Dharma.
According to the actual count, however, there are eighty-four thousand. (The above explains the superiority of the power of karma.)
Regarding the claim that this contradicts the *Lokadhātu-vibhāga-sūtra* (Qishi jing) and so forth: first, there is a difference in the directions; second, there is a difference regarding the waters.

In that [sūtra], the statement "To the east of Mount Sumeru" constitutes one phrase, while "a thousand [yojanas] to the west" constitutes another phrase; thus, the underlying principle becomes clearly evident.
Regarding the statement "these are separate villages and so forth": one thousand *yojanas* to the west of the mountain where there is a palace constitutes a separate village;
this does not preclude their being scattered as the other seven golden mountains and so on, just as people in the present day reside in separate houses and dwellings.
Furthermore, what is lost [by this]?
As for the statement that "Rāhu" here means "equal" (or "same"), it explains a specific name. Now, in this commentary, the sequence is determined according to the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*.
First, Rāhu, the King of the Asuras, is listed; yet according to the underlying principle, he should also have been listed first, as his dwelling is at the very summit.
Furthermore, because he was the vanguard of the army, he should have been listed first. It is merely a matter of the translator’s arrangement that he is placed later.
In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the Asura King Bhañji is listed first, and the Asura King Rāhu is listed last;

this does not depend on their relative size. Now, the Master of the Commentary does not follow the sequence in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, but rather follows the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, listing Rāhu first.
*Hou*. In Sanskrit, it is called *Rāhu*; here it means "the Seizer," signifying the sense of obstruction.
When the Asura King Rāhu fought with the devas, the Sun and Moon Devaputras emitted intense radiance that struck Rāhu’s eyes.

Furthermore, as Rāhu was the vanguard of the Asuras against the gods, he used his hands to shield the sun, causing it to temporarily vanish; thus he is called the "Seizer of the Sun. This is as described in the case of Yaśodharā.

The son's name is Rāhu; because he obstructs the sun of the Buddha, he is called "the Seizer of the Sun. This refers merely to his blocking it with his hand; it does not mean that his hand actually commits an offense against the sun.
As for the term Bāli, the ancient [Chinese] translation was "the Bound One"; this is the interpretation of the ancients.
Regarding the terms "round" (*tuán*) and so forth, they carry the meaning of "perfection. Because his physical form is full and substantial, he is called "perfectly complete" (*yuánmǎn*).

Because he possesses great power and is victorious over his adversaries in battle, he is called "supremely victorious" (*zuìshèng*). Because he possesses courage and decisiveness in combat, he is called "valiant and robust" (*yǒngjiàn*). In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he is called "supremely victorious";
the meaning here is similar to that of "valiant and robust."
Regarding the statement that "the meaning of *baddha* and so forth" refers to *Bali* and *Bālika*: these five characters differ in their breadth and brevity.
In the main section, it is correctly translated as "round" (*tuányuán*). If it were translated as "bound" (*pèifù*), it would be an error.

Regarding the phrase "Kha-ra-khyen" and so forth: the two characters *kha* and *khyen* are both pronounced with the departing tone (4th tone). The character *da* is pronounced with the level tone (1st tone);
its sound is identical to *tha*.
Regarding the phrase "broad shoulders," it means the shoulders are wide and thick.
The phrase "to illustrate one's person" means to paint one's body. Even now, this custom exists among the tribes of Jingman.
In ancient times, King Tai of Zhou had three elder sons: the eldest was named Taibo, the second Zhongyong, and the youngest Ji-li.
Ji-li was virtuous and moreover fathered a sage son. The father-king said, "Taibo wishes to occupy the throne himself; I fear [the succession will be lost]."
His rank was insufficient. King Wen said, "Therefore, I shall yield the empire to Ji Li and cut off my hair myself;
I shall tattoo my body and alter my appearance as ornaments, and go to the Jing and Man tribes."
It is said that this is the greatest, meaning that its physical form is vast. The Āgama Sūtra states:

When the world was first formed, a Devaputra from the Ābhāsvara Heaven of the Form Realm descended from the heavens and entered the ocean to bathe. His vital essence flowed into the water and transformed into a single eggshell.
After eight thousand years had passed, it opened and gave birth to a female asura whose body was like Mount Sumeru and who possessed one fewer than a thousand heads.
Later, water touched the woman’s body; because of this, she became pregnant and subsequently gave birth to a son named Vemacitra.
His body was four times larger than his mother’s; he had nine heads, eight feet, and one fewer than a thousand hands.

Later, he took as his wife the Gandharva maiden from Mount Gandhamādana, who bore him Queen Śacī—the very father of Śakra. [The Buddha] asked: "Among the various heavens of the desire realm, there is still none—"

Regarding "semen and impurity": how can there be semen among the gods of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*)? The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Only the gods of the six desire realms (*kāmadhātu*) experience the objects of exquisite desire.
The first two [heavens] dwell upon the earth; their forms transform into passion no differently than that of humans, yet they discharge it as wind."
The torment of heat is thereby removed. It is not as it is in the human realm, where there remains some impurity. Among the hosts of the Yāma Heaven, desire is fulfilled by merely embracing;
among those of Tuṣita Heaven, by holding hands; among those of Nirmāṇarati Heaven, by smiling; and among those of Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, by gazing at one another.

How can it be said that semen flows in the heavens of form? Sthiramati answers: This is a description of the doctrines of non-Buddhists within the Sautrāntika school; therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore—
The palaces of the asuras are only eighty thousand yojanas in height. Now, the body of Mātṛceṭa is four times larger than that;
since her body’s dimensions already equal those of Mount Sumeru, how could she possibly dwell within those palaces? Therefore, it is known that this is the doctrine of the non-Buddhists.
The Sanskrit term is *garuḍa*, which here means "Wondrous-Winged Bird" (*miaochi niao*). It is also called "Dragon-Swallower" (*tunlong*) and "Consumer of Poisonous Multitudes.
Regarding the statement that it is not only gold: this refutes the ancient masters who claimed that the color of the *garuḍa*’s wings and feathers is wondrous because they are not exclusively golden.
Regarding the statement, "O Bhikṣus, you should know that as for egg-born birds and the like," the *Loutan jing* (Lokasthāna-sūtra), fascicle 4, states:
To the south of Mount Sumeru and to the north of the great ocean, there is a great iron tree named *Kulisaṃ* (pronounced *xián*).
Its trunk and stem are two hundred and eighty *li* in circumference and four thousand *li* in height; its branches and leaves extend over two thousand *li*. On the eastern side of the tree...
There are egg-born birds and egg-born nāgas on the southern side; on the western side are womb-born birds and womb-born nāgas;
and on the northern side are transformation-born birds and transformation-born nāgas.
When an egg-born bird wishes to eat an egg-born nāga, it flies toward a branch on the eastern side and looks down at the ocean water.
They flap their two wings to part the waters and seize the egg-born *nāgas* to devour them; however, they cannot devour those born from the womb, from moisture, or by transformation.

When a womb-born bird wishes to devour an egg-born or womb-born *nāga*, it flies up onto the southern branch and flaps its wings to part the waters, seizing the egg-born or womb-born *nāga* to devour it.
This continues until, when a transformation-born bird wishes to devour a transformation-born *nāga*, it ascends the northern branch and flaps its wings.
He caused them to open [their mouths]. [The king] took the first four born dragons and ate them.

Each of these birds has its own palace, twenty-four thousand *li* in circumference, with sevenfold city walls made entirely of the seven treasures, sevenfold railings, trees, groves, and gardens, where small birds warble in harmony.
Furthermore, the *Upamāna-sūtra* states that to the northwest of the kingdom of Magadha, there are nine Black Mountains (*Kṛṣṇa-parvata*).
Beyond the mountains lies Mount Gandhamādana. Within Mount Gandhamādana is the tree called Mālāmālī, which in this language is known as the "Iron Fork Tree.
This tree is immense in height and as hard as iron. Various garuḍas constantly dwell upon this tree;
these birds are so large that the distance between their two wings spans three million three hundred and sixty thousand li, yet when they perch upon the tree, the tree does not move.
