Regarding the realm over which he reigns, it is therefore called the "trichiliocosm" (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*). Thirdly, these four continents alone are the domain of the Great Transformation Body (*mahānirmāṇakāya*), which governs the trichiliocosm;
since this refers to the total number under his jurisdiction, it is said that he "dwells in the city of Chang'an.
This does not mean that he physically occupies the entire city of Chang'an, but rather that his residence is located within the city of Chang'an.

Regarding the statement "this refers to the place of movement": the preceding explanation—that the Buddha’s emitted light illuminates eighteen thousand worlds and causes the earth to tremble—applies only to the Sahā world.
Regarding the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the subsequent verse, one might ask: how does the commentator know that only the Sahā world trembled and the others did not?

Regarding the "world-system" (*dhātu*): the answer concerns the essence of the self as explained by the Master of the Commentary. This accords with the intent of the Sūtra in the following verse. The Sūtra states:
"And this world-system shook in six ways. Therefore, we know that it was only the world-system ruled by Śākyamuni that shook, not the eighteen thousand world-systems.
Regarding the statement, "Or this 'universal shaking' is equal [to the emission of light]," one asks: Why does the Master of the Commentary (Shuzhu) provide this second interpretation? Answer:

The Master of the Commentary provides this second interpretation because he takes the underlying intent of the subsequent passage of the Sūtra into consideration. The Sūtra states: "At that moment, all Buddha-lands shook violently.
Since it says "all," the Master of the Commentary establishes the second interpretation, stating that the emission of light and the shaking of the earth are equivalent. Thus it is established.
The principle says it is not so. The emission of light is broad, whereas the shaking of the earth is narrow.

Regarding the statement that the subsequent passage refers to what is proximate and so forth: Question: Since it is said that the emission of light and the shaking of the realm are equal, why does it say, "this world shakes in six ways"?
Answer: The commentary states that the subsequent passage refers to what is equal. The subsequent passage refers to what is proximate and does not mention [the emission of light].
[The Buddha] is distant. He manifests in this world because there are those who abandon the provisional to attain the real.

When it says below, "in this world," this is said provisionally based on those in this realm who abandon the provisional to attain the real; it is intended specifically to awaken the śrāvakas and is spoken with reference to a limited, proximate location.
In reality, however, the entire universe trembles.
Regarding the phrase "if one relies on the first interpretation," etc., this serves to reaffirm the meaning presented immediately prior. Question:

Since there are both provisional and ultimate worlds within the light, why does [the world] not move? Answer: There are two reasons why other-worldly realms do not move: first, because their faculties (*indriya*) are not yet matured;

second, even if their faculties were matured, those realms already possess their own Buddhas who provide transformation and guidance, such that they do not open up [space for] the Buddha of this realm.
Regarding the matter: it is for this reason that it is said to be "unmoving" (understanding the universal Buddha-world).
As for what is called "trembling," the Sūtra speaks of six kinds of trembling. First is the characteristic of movement; second is the cause of movement. Now, regarding the characteristic of movement:
first, the shaking of the earth is a sign of instability, indicating that the Two Vehicles are provisional, and it strikes down the attachment to the teachings of the Two Vehicles.
Those with stubborn minds cling to the two vehicles as ultimate and refuse to turn their hearts toward the Great Vehicle.

Now, the World-Honored One causes the world to tremble to signify that the two vehicles are not the final goal. As for the twice-shaking of the earth, it is a rare and marvelous sign that signifies a longing thirst to hear the Dharma.

Regarding the statement that the *Dīrgha Āgama* speaks of the six periods and so forth: among the movements during these six periods, the "turning of the wheel of Dharma" does not refer exclusively to the occasion at the Deer Park;
rather, every instance of preaching the Dharma is collectively termed the "turning of the wheel of Dharma."

Regarding the statement "the two [directions] and the six directions shake greatly," etc.: suddenly the eastern end rises while the western end sinks, like grain being overturned on a winnowing basket;

this is called "rising in the east and sinking in the west. The western end rises while the eastern end sinks; this is called "rising in the west and sinking in the east. "Surging" (yǒng) means to rise up.

The same applies to the north and south. Regarding "the center surges while the periphery subsides": this refers to the central area rising while the four directions sink; it is like the upper and lower surfaces of a griddle.
If the center subsides while the periphery surges, it is like ripples struck by a stone dropped into a pool;

the movement spreading toward the four directions is called the "periphery. Regarding "the center subsides": it is like pouring oil into a mold, where the four sides and the center all sink. Furthermore, there are three [types] categorized according to people.
Regarding the statement that "the west surges while the east submerges": when Samantabhadra of Wondrous Sound comes from the east, it is called "the east submerging.
Upon arriving at the assembly on Vulture Peak, it is called "the west surging. When he has finished hearing the sutra here and returns, it is called "the west submerging.

Upon reaching the east, it is called "the east surging. Regarding "the south surges while the north submerges": after Mañjuśrī and Maitreya have finished their dialogue, [Samantabhadra] departs from here for Sāgara.

To go to the Dragon Palace is called "sinking in the north. Upon arriving there, it is called "surfacing in the south. When the dragon girl departs from the sea, it is called "sinking in the south. Upon arriving here, it is called "surfacing in the center.
Having finished the affairs here, she departs; this is called "sinking in the center. Regarding "surfacing in the center and sinking at the periphery":
when the emanations from the ten directions come from their original lands, it is called "sinking at the periphery. Upon arriving here, it is called "surfacing in the center. This...
When an interval of affairs has been concluded, it is called "disappearance within" (*madhyāntar-hāni*). Upon reaching that place, it is called "disappearance at the limit" (*paryanta-hāni*).
As for the statement, "Perhaps this is that," the intended meaning is that when this Buddha wished to preach this sutra, the earth shook in six ways;
or perhaps, within this *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the shaking of the six directions is what is termed the "sixfold movement."
Regarding the phrase "the movement of the three six-fold characteristics," this indicates the six characteristics.
Regarding the phrase "wavering and unsettled," etc., this explains the six characteristics. "Wavering" (*yáng*) refers to clouds being blown by the wind and flying away.

"Scale-like ridges" (*línlǒng*): "scale" (*lín*) refers to fish scales; "ridge" (*lǒng*) refers to newly plowed furrows. The term "scale-ridge" signifies that the undulations within the furrows resemble fish scales. "Undulation" (*āo'cù*) refers to these uneven elevations and depressions.
This refers to the appearance of being uneven, with elevations and depressions.
Regarding the phrase "or the six directions, etc.," it is asked: what is meant by "surging"? The answer is: the emergence and submergence in the six directions constitutes "surging";
these are the aforementioned Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Regarding the phrase "there is a rumbling sound": Question: What is meant by "vibrating" (zhèn)? Answer: It refers to having a rumbling sound, like the rising of thunder.
It carries the sense of awe-inspiring dread. For example, when spring begins, thunder sounds from beneath the earth; people themselves do not know of it, but the wild pheasant knows.
Upon hearing it, it immediately becomes alert and makes a sound.
Regarding the statement that the old [commentary] says "from below, etc.," it is asked: what is meant by "striking" (*ki*)? The answer is the ancient interpretation:

to strike from below upward to form a single mound of earth is the "bone-ground" (*kotsuchi*) produced on level ground. The current [interpretation] states: that which involves knocking or striking is called "striking.
The sound of the knock is similar to striking an object; thus, they are called "similar."

Regarding the phrase "resounding with thunderous crashes," it is asked: what is meant by "roaring"? It is answered: "thunderous crashes" and so forth. The sound *pēng* (pronounced as in *pǔgēng*) and the sound *kè* (pronounced as in *kǒuwèn*) both refer to the sound of thunder and are also termed "sound."

Regarding the statement that the old translation says "to cause awakening to arise": Question: What is meant by "explosion" (*pāṭa*)? Answer: The old translation says it means "to cause awakening to arise.
Seeing the earth outside tremble, one realizes that the body is impermanent. The current [translation] says that to produce a sound of startling wonder is an "explosion";
because it suddenly strikes like a thunderclap, they are similar. Question: What is the distinction between the six characteristics? Answer: "Trembling" refers to the state of tranquility.

Regarding the characteristics: "surging" refers to the characteristic of rising and falling; "vibrating" refers to a sound that is faint and prolonged; "striking" refers to a sound that is faint and abrupt;
"roaring" refers to a sound that is loud and prolonged; and "bursting" refers to a sound that is loud and abrupt—these are the distinctions.
Regarding the statement that even a slight movement is called "movement" and so forth: Question: How is it designated as "movement"? Answer: The first instance of movement is simply called "movement.
Subsequent movements of the great earth are called "equal movement," "extreme movement," "surging," "extreme surging," "trembling," "quaking," "extreme trembling," and "shaking."
"Striking, striking again, and striking intensely; roaring, roaring again, and roaring intensely; the sound of bursting is greater than the former, and the sound of intense bursting is greatest.
By mentioning the first [term] to include the subsequent ones, it is said that the remaining five characteristics should all be understood accordingly.

Regarding the statement, "Now, this citation refers to the general [categories]," etc.: Question: Since there are eighteen modes of movement (*iṅgita*), why does the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* speak of only six modes of movement?
Answer: The commentary states, "Now, this citation refers to the general [categories]," etc. Mǔ (Mǔ-zhì) says:

Within the two characters "six movements" (*liù-dòng*) in the sūtra, there are two types of general meanings: first, they generally subsume the three preceding sets of six modes; second, they generally subsume all eighteen modes.
The statement "only among the eighteen transformations" refers specifically to the first of the eighteen transformations, namely, "trembling.

Regarding the phrase "the Brahmā-deva of Superior Reflection (*Abhyudgata-cintī*) and others," this refers to the cause of the trembling. Question: For what reason does the World-Honored One initiate these six kinds of tremblings? Answer:

The commentary states that the *Sūtra on the Brahmā-deva of Superior Reflection* (*Abhyudgata-cintī-brahma-paripṛcchā-sūtra*) and its treatise (*śāstra*) constitute the textual reading [for this passage]. A Bodhisattva composed the treatise.
The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* (Jiesheng siming fandan jing) is one with its commentary (*śāstra*) in this context; if read separately, it would be among other treatises.
Because it possesses seven causes, it causes the world to tremble. This sūtra consists of four fascicles.

Regarding the phrase "first, to cause alarm and fear," it means to make [beings] aware that the Buddha has appeared and is preaching the Dharma, so that they may be struck with awe and dread, and thus not be harmed by violating the Buddha.
Regarding the phrase "third, to cause negligence," it means that even the external great earth itself undergoes shaking; how much more so this body? How could it possibly remain unmoved?

Can one attain permanence? If one is negligent regarding the realm of sensory objects, one will surely sink into discursive thought. Only by being able to give rise to the mind of awakening can one extinguish all bonds of suffering.

Thus, there is a verse that says: "It would be better to remain destitute of wealth and status in the present life than to allow riches and nobility to disturb the faculties, thereby causing one to experience the vessels of various sufferings in the future."

Regarding the statement that "the four [types of earthquakes] cause one to contemplate the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*)," An Guo says: "One contemplates this shaking so as to cause sentient beings to reflect:
'What dharma will the World-Honored One now preach? Jin says: "After causing all sentient beings to see the earth shake, they form this thought:
'All phenomena are subject to change and decay; if even the great earth is thus, how much more so other things? This causes them to contemplate suffering, emptiness, and impermanence."
Regarding the statement "five reasons for observing the place of teaching," the *Shōshaku* (Explanatory Commentary) says: "Two [mean] 'teaching' and two mean 'place. 'Place' refers to the Dharma;
seeing the earth tremble now, one knows that the Buddhas wish to teach other dharmas. It further states: "'Place' means location; having seen the earth tremble..."

Regarding the recollection of where the Tathāgata preached the Dharma, the latter interpretation is correct. If one follows the former interpretation, it would not differ from the recollection of the characteristics of the Dharma (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
As for the "sixfold accomplishment," the *Vyākhyā* states: "Like the śrāvakas, those whose faculties have matured over three lifetimes [attain it] through seeing and hearing."
The earth shook, and they immediately attained the first fruit and other forms of liberation.

Regarding the statement that "seven things accord with the correct meaning of the questions," it is as follows: the Tathāgata’s intention within his mind to expound the One Vehicle is the "conformed-to" (the object);
Maitreya’s questioning and the fourfold assembly’s questioning are the "conformers" (the subject). As for "questioning the correct meaning," this refers to the present Buddha-world.

The Venerable One wishes to expound what Dharma? Because he asks about the ultimate truth, it is like grass bending before the wind; for the transformed person follows his own master. Muzhe (Maudgalyāyana) said:
"The Tathāgata intends to expound the One Vehicle from within his heart, and therefore manifests this auspicious sign. Subsequently, Maitreya asked and Mañjuśrī answered accordingly.
This is called "conformity.
When it says "these sentient beings of the world," it does not refer to the number of individuals; rather, it takes up the heart of thirsty longing within the bodies of sentient beings.
Regarding the statement "Upa, ka, and so forth": the three characters *upa-ka* are the same for both male and female [names]. However, the characters *sa* and *si* differ;
*sa* is a deep, heavy (masculine) sound, while *si* is a light, clear (feminine) sound. Thus, male and female are distinguished.

Regarding the phrase "all men and women," it is asked: what qualities and capacities do these two groups of lay followers possess, and for what reason are they called *upāsaka* (laymen) and *upāsikā* (laywomen)?
The answer, as stated in the commentary (*śū*), is that "all men and women" refers precisely to those who observe the five precepts (*pañca-śīla*).

There are transcribed notes which correlate this with the accomplishment of the five precepts: a man who has accomplished the five precepts is fit to draw near to the bhikṣus; one who has accomplished the five precepts [is likewise a laywoman].
"Daughter, you are fit to associate with bhikṣuṇīs; do not make such a pairing. If one has not accomplished the five precepts, then it is not permitted.
Since one has already accomplished the five precepts, what harm is there in both communities being mutually accessible? Question:

"Since there are bodhisattvas present at this assembly of the sutra, why are they not mentioned? Answer: "Because bodhisattvas manifest their bodies to teach and transform sentient beings, they do not depart from the four [noble truths]."
Regarding the phrase "the assembly," it includes bodhisattvas; thus, they must necessarily be among the fourfold assembly. However, the fourfold assembly does not necessarily consist of bodhisattvas;

therefore, bodhisattvas are not explicitly mentioned [as a separate category]. As the Sūtra says: "As for devas and nāgas, there are those who interpret 'nāga' as the name for a celestial being. This interpretation is incorrect."
The devas and nāgas are distinct. The assemblies of devas and nāgas have been explained previously.
As for the yakṣas: their bodies are red in color; although they lack wings or feathers, they are able to fly through the air. They possess great supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) and produce great sounds;
therefore, they are called "Valiant" (*vīryavanta*). They are also translated as "Celestial Messengers," because they act as messengers for all the devas. Thus it is recorded.

In Chinese, this is translated as the "Light-Quick Ghost" (qīngjié guǐ). It is also called the "Celestial Dog" (tiān gǒu). The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states: "The nature of yakṣas is to crave warm blood.
Whenever they ascend Mount Sumeru, they gaze about for where there might be a battle; if they do not find food in the interim, they sigh deeply and longingly.
Their breath ascends to heaven and becomes the Broom Star (fèoxīng), also called the Comet (huìxīng), and also called the Chénqīng Star. [Heaven]...
If there are stars above, there will certainly be matters concerning weapons and armor. They dwell on the third tier of Mount Sumeru.
Regarding the statement that they "govern the terrestrial species": *rākṣasas* are terrestrial species; however, in the present scripture, only *yakṣas* are mentioned and *rākṣasas* are not.
*Rākṣasas* are subsumed within the category of *yakṣas*. While *yakṣas* travel through the air, *rākṣasas* travel upon the earth; thus, they are included among the *yakṣas*.
This is included within the [category of] *śakti* (forks). A question was asked: "By cultivating what karma is one born among the *rākṣasas*? The answer is found in the *Dharmolkā-dhāraṇī-sūtra*:

"One who rebels against the teacher’s instructions is born among the *yakṣas*. One who speaks with the mouth but does not act accordingly, and who envies the fame and profit of others, is born among the *rākṣasas*.
Because they belong to the same class, the *rākṣasa* is thus subsumed.
Regarding the statement that "all those are corruptions": it means that the names *yakṣa* and *rākṣasa*, as spoken [in those texts], are all corrupt.
Regarding the mention of the "great python," "field," and "mosquito": the character for "python" (*mǎng*, pronounced with the initial *yú* and *lǎng*) refers to a snake.

The *Erya* states: "The python is the king of snakes. The character for "mosquito" (*wén*, pronounced *qiè* and *wú*) refers to a large frog. Question: Since mosquitoes have legs, why are they said to "crawl on their bellies"? Answer: They do indeed have legs.
Those that move by resting their bellies on the ground are collectively called "belly-crawlers" (*udvartaka*).
Regarding the phrase "the rest is as previously explained": here, "humans" refers to the fourfold assembly, while "non-humans" refers to the eight classes of beings (*aṣṭau devanikāyāḥ*).

Since many of these eight classes transform themselves into human form to come and listen to the Dharma, they are termed "non-humans. This refers back to the previous explanation; there is nothing further to be said in this regard.
It is said, "therefore it is as stated before.

Regarding the statement that there are four types of *cakravartin* (wheel-turning sage-kings), this explains the two kinds of kings. The sutra says: "as well as various minor kings and *cakravartin*s.
"Minor kings" refers to the *kṣudraka-rāja*s (scattered minor kings). "Kṣudra" is a metaphor for smallness; "scattered" means numerous. This refers to the number of minor kings.
"Much. This is like scattering millet (as explained previously in the section on the assembled multitude). Next is the Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*). There are four types of wheel-turning kings.

The *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra) clarifies the Dharma-gate of the Five Patiences (*pañca-kṣānti*) in two lines of verse. The first line of verse clarifies the "Patience of Expedient Means," which is adjacent to the stage of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*).

The subsequent verse clarifies the "Patience of Subjugation" (*vinaya-kṣānti*), which resides in the stage of the Three Worthies (*tri-satpuruṣa*). The verse says: "The Bodhisattva of the Ten Wholesome Paths arouses the Great Mind, forever parting from the three realms."
Regarding the "ocean of the wheel of suffering," this explains the first two lines of a verse from the first chapter of the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*:

"The Bodhisattvas of the Ten Wholesome Paths, having resolved upon the Great Mind, forever part from the ocean of the wheel of suffering of the triple world. As for "resolving upon the Great Mind," it refers to the mind of the Four Great Vows:
first, the vow to sever the boundless afflictions, because that which is to be severed is vast; second, the vow to deliver the boundless sentient beings.
Because that which is to be saved is great, one vows to study the inexhaustible Dharma-gates. Because that which is to be studied is great, one vows to accomplish the unsurpassed Buddha-way.

Because that which is to be accomplished is great, it is called "Great. Since both that which is sought and that which is to be saved are termed "great," the mind capable of seeking and saving is therefore called the "Arousing of the Great Mind" (*mahācittotpāda*).
[This concerns] the cycle of birth and death within the three realms and the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) for all sentient beings.

"Birth" is named the wheel (*cakra*). "Drowning" in the sense of being adrift is named the ocean (*sāgara*). If a Bodhisattva who awakens through gradual realization (*anupūrva-abhisambodha*) reaches this stage, it is called "long-term separation.

If a Bodhisattva who awakens through sudden realization (*sakṛd-abhisambodha*) reaches this stage, they are about to depart from their initial resolve; therefore, it is called "separation" (*pratyeka*).
(The preceding two phrases are thus explained.)

Regarding the phrase "middling and inferior grades of wholesome *kṣullaka* [sovereigns]," this explains the next two lines of the sūtra. Within this stage, the bodhisattva practices the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*), which consist of three grades.
One who possesses the superior grade of the ten wholesome paths becomes an Iron-Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) over Jambudvīpa.
He causes an iron wheel with two hundred and fifty spokes to appear atop his head; when subjects within his domain do not submit, he leads his troops [to subdue them].

In fierce battles, they achieve victory without further inflicting harm; having brought others into submission, they lead them to practice the ten wholesome deeds, such that no one dares to give rise to an evil mind again.
From the time when the human lifespan was one hundred years up until it reached a thousand years, there were kings of this kind.

These are the kings who experience the retribution of middling and lower-grade wholesome karma—so-called "minor kings. Within these middling and lower grades of the ten wholesome deeds, [there are ten...]
The six great kings and this King of Tang are the result of the middling grade of the ten wholesome actions.
As for the kings of the Uyghurs and the Tibetans, they are the result of the lower grade of the ten wholesome actions. (First line)

Regarding the statement "the seeds of practice, the copper-wheel kings, and the two heavens," etc.: in that *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*, the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*) are subsumed within the ten abodes (*bhūmi*);

the four stages of preparatory application (*prayoga*) are subsumed within the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*). There are only the ten abodes, ten practices, and ten dedications; these preceding thirty mental states are called the "patience of subduing" (*kṣānti*).

The second, the "patience of faith" (*śraddhākṣānti*), resides in the first, second, and third grounds; the third, the "patience of conformity" (*anulomikakṣānti*), resides in the fourth, fifth, and sixth grounds.

The four *anutpattika-dharmakṣānti* (patiences regarding the non-arising of phenomena) pertain to the seventh, eighth, and ninth stages. The fifth is *śānti* (quiescence). Of these, the first four each have three grades, while the fifth has only two.
The lower grade belongs to Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage and those in the position of *samyak-saṃbodhi*; the upper grade is the stage of Buddhahood.

As for the verse stating, "The *śikṣā-bīja* (seed of training) [is like] a copper wheel over two continents," the *Jin* commentary says: this means that a Bodhisattva of the ten *vihāras* acts as a copper-wheel-turning king (*tāmra-cakra-vartin*).

The King rules over the eastern continent and the southern continent. This stage-bodhisattva cultivates the lower grade of patience (*kṣānti*), gradually subduing the afflictions of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
Abiding in the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*), he obtains a copper wheel with five hundred spokes that rests upon the crown of his head.

Regarding those in the eastern and southern continents who do not submit, once they have been subdued, they no longer give rise to rebellious thoughts; he exhorts them to practice the ten wholesome paths (*daśakuśala-karma-patha*) for more than a thousand years.

When the human lifespan reached forty thousand years, this king appeared. As for the verse stating that the silver wheel-turning king belongs to the three heavens and the lineage of the *gotra*, it refers to the stage of the ten practices (*daśabhūmi-pratipatti*), wherein one gradually subdues the afflictions of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivates the medium degree of patience in subduing (*madhyama-kṣānti-vinaya*), thereby becoming a silver wheel-turning king.
The king of the three regions—east, south, and west—attained seven hundred and fifty silver wheels, which rested upon the crown of his head.

Should there be any among the people of these three regions who did not submit, he would dispatch an envoy with a message, and they would immediately surrender; thereafter, they would never again give rise to evil intent.
From ten thousand years ago until the time of sixty thousand years, this king appeared, possessing the nature of the lineage.

The Bodhisattva of Nature becomes a silver wheel-turning king (*rājā cakravartin*). A verse states: "The wheel-turning king of firm virtue in the stage of the lineage of the path (*mārgajñatā*). Question: What is meant by the "lineage of the path" (*mārgajñatā-gotra*)?
Answer: It refers to the untainted noble path (*anāsrava-āryamārga*). Question: In what stage does this lineage of the path reside? Answer:

This resides in the stage of the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*). Because it is proximate to and primarily concerns the noble path, and because it is the cause that brings about the noble path, it is called the "lineage of the path. [He] becomes a golden...

The Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) rules over the four continents under heaven. He receives a golden wheel, composed entirely of pure gold and possessing a thousand spokes, which rests upon the crown of his head.
Throughout the four continents and their eight-four thousand minor kingdoms, all submit to his influence at the mere sight of him;
there are none who do not come to pay homage. Each kingdom brings precious offerings and requests the King to travel to their respective lands to transform them with his teaching.
From the time when the human lifespan was sixty thousand years until it reached eighty thousand years, this king appeared; his noble virtue was firm and steadfast, and thus he was named Drḍhadatta.
According to the holy teachings, only a Cakravartin King possesses the primary and secondary marks of physical excellence, while others do not.

Regarding the phrase "the seven treasures, golden light, and so forth," Lu says: according to the exposition in that sutra, only a Golden Wheel-turning King (Cakravartin) possesses the seven treasures;
the other three [types of kings] do not. The first is the Woman Treasure (Strī-ratna). From within the body of the king’s consort, the fragrance of priceless sandalwood constantly emanates;
from her mouth, the fragrance of the *utpala* lotus constantly issues forth; and her bodily touch is as soft and delicate as that of the *kalaviṅka* bird. If...
Those who touch this bird are freed from fatigue, hunger, thirst, sorrow, and affliction. It is the same for the wife of that wheel-turning monarch;
whether they see her or touch her, all experience happiness. In cold weather, her body is warm; in heat, it is cool.
All men who behold this woman perceive her with a discerning mind as a mother or a sister. Furthermore, she possesses five kinds of qualities.
She is endowed with virtues: first, she accords with her husband’s wishes; second, she gives birth mostly to sons;
third, her lineage is not inferior, and she delights in excellence while harboring no jealousy; fourth, when her husband enjoys himself with other women, she does not give rise to envy;
fifth, the sons she bears are all brave and robust, foremost among men, capable of defeating enemy armies, and of the lineage of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*).
Regarding the characteristics of its lineage: the question is asked, "By what karma is this summoned? The answer is: "It is produced by the power of wholesome karma that is free from anger.
Second is the jewel, which possesses eight virtues: (1) It performs good works in the darkness of night, its radiance filling a hundred *yojanas*;
if it is during the day when the sun is scorching, it can emit cool light and so forth. (2) If one travels through a wilderness, it can cause many signs of the eight flavors to appear.
1. It is pure water that removes all thirst. 2. If the Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin) calls it to mind, it flows forth according to his will.
3. It possesses eight facets; on each facet there are rays of light—blue, yellow, red, white, purple, crystal, and so forth. 4.
It can cause all people within five hundred *yojanas* to be free from illness and affliction, and to have upright thoughts and conduct. 5. It can cause evil... [text continues]
The dragons do not send down calamitous rain. Seventh, in the wilderness, they can cause the earth, trees, springs, ponds, lotuses, blue lilies, and soft grasses to flourish.
Eighth, they can ensure that humans do not suffer untimely deaths and that their lifespans are not cut short;

they can also cause animals not to devour one another and not to harbor mutual hatred or jealousy. (The eight types of jewels). As for the three precious wheels, they possess five virtues. First, they are complete.
The thousand-spoked wheel is made entirely of Jāmbūnada gold; it is five hundred yojanas in breadth and resembles a second sun.
Second, its two movements are unimpeded as it travels through the air; in a single day, it can travel a hundred thousand yojanas.
Third, it follows the king’s thoughts, traveling to various places not merely by way of the sky. Fourth, if there are those who are disobedient, it is able to subdue them.
There are five things with which he cannot be rivaled; when kings or those like them see him, they immediately take refuge in his heart.

As for the four marks of the elephant-treasure, it is foremost in its docility and its limbs touch the ground—namely, its four feet, tail, trunk, tusks, and so forth. If one possesses these seven characteristics in their entirety:
It possesses a strength one thousand times greater than other weak beings and is capable of fighting in three places: on water, on land, and in the air.
In a single day, it can travel three times around Jambudvīpa. By nature it is gentle and compliant;

with a single thread tied around its neck, it can be led wherever the Wheel-Turning King wishes to go, arriving there at will. Children who see it feel no fear. When engaged in battle, it is exceedingly powerful.
The brave and fierce horse-treasure is white in color like a swan; its entire body is adorned with celestial swirls and other marks.
In a single day, it can travel three times around Jambudvīpa without its body becoming fatigued.
The sixth is the minister-treasure of the military commander, who acts in accordance with the king’s thoughts, understands his intentions, and is able to accomplish all that he undertakes.
He benefits all sentient beings in the world, just like a father and mother. As for the seventh treasure, the Minister-Treasurer,
he is a great and wealthy elder who is able to fill all pits,
ravines, deep mountains, secluded valleys, and uneven places with gold, jewels, indranīla-blue gems, and various other kinds of treasures.
Without waiting for the King’s command, the jewels are never exhausted; how much more so for gold, silver, and the like.

One should know that because the Wheel-Turning Sage King possesses these seven jewels for use, they are all the result of his cultivation of the first of the ten wholesome paths: the abstention from anger.
Furthermore, there are seven similar jewels: first, the sword jewel; second, the skin jewel; third, the bed jewel; fifth, the palace jewel.
Sixth is the treasure of garments; seventh is the treasure of sandals. Regarding the possession of the sword-treasure:

if there is a kingdom that gives rise to a rebellious or resistant mind, this sword-treasure will swiftly go there; it does not harm people, but upon being seen, they are subdued. Second is the treasure of skins.
It emerged from the midst of the ocean and was obtained by a man who presented it to the Wheel. It is five yojanas wide and ten yojanas long;
it is the hide of the Naga King of the Ocean. In the rain it does not rot, the wind cannot move it, and fire cannot burn it; in cold weather, it provides warmth.
In times of heat, it can provide coolness. Following wherever the king’s army travels, it can serve as dwellings capable of accommodating the king and his entire host.
Each member of the retinue has their own separate quarters, yet their wives are not separated from them; they do not see one another. Its color is bright white.
It is like the light of the sun. As for the three precious couches, they are soft, fine, and smooth; when one sits upon them, they sink, and when one rises, they return to levelness.
If one sits on those couches, even if thoughts of desire arise in the mind, one is immediately able to become free from desire.

Even women who have conceived the utmost lustful thoughts toward the king, upon seeing these precious couches, find their minds free from defilement. As for the four precious groves, if the king remembers to go there for recreation...
In that grove, flowers and fruits grow; there are *sāragha* birds and flowing lotus ponds. At the river crossings, celestial musicians and apsaras also gather.

As for the five palaces made of jewels, when the king lies down at night within a palace and wishes to see the stars and moon, the stars and moon appear therein. Having seen them, his eyes rejoice; they are thus [made] of pearls.
His eyes sleep in peace; having slept, he has auspicious dreams and beholds wondrous and joyful things. In cold weather, he is fanned by warm breezes;
in hot weather, he experiences the pleasure of cool and refreshing sensations. As for his six garments of jewels, they are woven with fine threads, supremely soft, and unstained by impurities.
When the King wears them, he is free from cold and heat, hunger and thirst, and they eliminate exhaustion and extreme fatigue. Fire does not [burn him].
It can burn, yet a sword cannot cut it. The seventh treasure is the divine sandals (*pādukā*).

When the king wears them, he can travel a hundred *yojanas* as if walking on land while moving through water, without his majestic deportment being impaired and without his body becoming exhausted. Thus is the Wheel-Turning King endowed with the seven treasures.
Furthermore, there are such similar seven treasures that may be enjoyed according to one's heart's desire. By what karma are they summoned? The answer is:
they are the result summoned by wholesome karma free from anger.
Regarding the statement that this [text] differs from other sūtras in its threefold nature: other sūtras do not possess the three natures; they have only two natures.
One should therefore say that the three natures of this sūtra are distinct from those of other sūtras. The *Ratnarāśi* (Renwang) has three natures, whereas other sūtras establish two natures.
These "other sūtras" refer to the *Śīlasamvara-sūtra* (Shanjie jing), as well as the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the *Yogācārabhūmi*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, and so forth.

This is a treatise. The *Śīlasamvara-sūtra*, fascicle one, states: "There are two types of bodhisattvas: first, those of innate nature (*prakṛti-gotra*); second, those of adventitious nature (*āgantuka-gotra*).

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-śāstra* all speak of "the lineage abiding in its original nature" (*prakṛtistha-gotra*) and "the lineage accomplished through cultivation" (*samudānīta-gotra*).

These differ from the *Ratnaketuparipṛcchā-sūtra* (Renwang jing). Question: Why is this so? Answer: The *Śīlasamvara-sūtra* and other such texts rely upon the naturally existing untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*).
My son, later, through the cultivation and increase [of virtue], as well as the seeds newly perfumed, it is also called the "cultivated lineage" (*śikṣā-gotra*).
This means that the "nature lineage" (*prakṛti-gotra*) comes first, while the "cultivated nature" (*śikṣā-prakṛti-gotra*) follows.

In the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*, it does not speak of the original nature lineage, but rather speaks of the new perfuming and the progressive advancement of practice: the initial cultivation is called "cultivation," and once cultivated without falling back, it is called the "nature lineage."

The lineage further increases and becomes superior, and is thus called the "nature of the path-seeds" (*mārga-gotra*). This means that the "cultivated seeds" (*śikṣā-gotra*) come first, while the "innate nature seeds" (*prakṛti-gotra*) follow.

As for the statement that it is "also consistent with the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* and others," this merely refers to a difference in the assignment of stages; within the *Renwang jing*, there are ten [stages].

The Four Kings: those prior to the stages of the *bhūmis* are the four *cakravartin* kings; the Bodhisattvas of the ten *bhūmis* are the six heavenly kings of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the kings of the four dhyānas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). These are assigned in order from the bottom upward, each serving as a single king.

In the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, the Bodhisattvas of the ten *bhūmis* are treated as *cakravartins* who have come forth, being named "Golden Wheel" (*suvarṇa-cakra*); this is because their status is distinct. This is based on the *Ratnarāśi-sūtra* (Renwang jing).
Regarding their assignments: Bodhisattvas of the first stage become kings of the Four Heavenly Kings; Bodhisattvas of the second stage become kings of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;

Bodhisattvas of the third stage become kings of the Yāma Heaven; Bodhisattvas of the fourth stage become kings of the Tuṣita Heaven; Bodhisattvas of the fifth stage become kings of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven;
Bodhisattvas of the sixth stage become kings of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage become kings of the First Dhyāna; and Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage...
One becomes a king of the second dhyāna. A bodhisattva of the ninth stage becomes a king of the third dhyāna.

A bodhisattva of the tenth stage becomes a king of the fourth dhyāna (the two kings above are thus assigned). According to the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, a bodhisattva of the first stage is a king of Jambudvīpa; that is, an iron-wheel-turning king (*cakravartin*).
A Bodhisattva of the second bhūmi is a Cakravartin King of the Golden Wheel; a Bodhisattva of the third bhūmi is a King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
a Bodhisattva of the fourth bhūmi is a King of the Yāma Heaven; a Bodhisattva of the fifth bhūmi is a King of the Tuṣita Heaven; a Bodhisattva of the sixth bhūmi is a King of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven;

a Bodhisattva of the seventh bhūmi is a King of the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven; a Bodhisattva of the eighth bhūmi is a King of the First Dhyāna; a Bodhisattva of the ninth bhūmi is a King of the Second Dhyāna; [and so on] up to a Bodhisattva of the tenth bhūmi...

The Bodhisattva is the king of the four *dhyānas*. This is assigned according to the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*. Regarding why he does not become the king of the eastern or western continents, Master Lu says it is because those regions are peripheral.
Furthermore, there is another explanation: it is due to the difference in the power of their vows. The vow-power of a Bodhisattva on the first stage (*bhūmi*) is inferior;
thus, they may become kings of other continents such as the east or west, but cannot become kings of the southern continent alone. This continues until the Bodhisattva reaches the second stage.
His power was superior; he did not belong to either the East or West provinces, but became the king of the North province. It is like one who has just completed his ordination:

although the master-monks have not yet authorized him to serve as a *dianzhi* (administrative official), he temporarily serves as the *weina*. After three or five years of performing his duties, having recognized the relative ranks of others, he does not act as an administrative official but becomes an *upādhyāya* (senior elder).
If it is said that this is partial, it is spoken only with reference to this region; if it were in the Western [countries],...

The east is considered superior; the south and north are likewise peripheral. [The wheel-turning king] does not become a Cāturmahārājika deity because the gods there serve as ministers and lack a sovereign;

he does not become a ruler of the Third Dhyāna heaven because its bliss is so transcendent. Question: Why do the two sūtras differ in their classification? Answer: There are two types of wheel-turning kings:
first, ordinary beings (pṛthagjana), and second, noble ones (ārya). The *Ratnarāja-sūtra* applies this to those within the stage of the ordinary person (pṛthagjana), making them wheel-turning kings.

This is because the King [of the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*] corresponds to the stage of the forty minds (*cittotpāda*). The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* speaks solely in terms of the noble wheel-turning king (*cakravartin*), and thus it assigns [the title] to Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
Alternatively, while the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* encompasses both karmic retribution and aspiration, the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* refers specifically to the power of vows. Question:

Since a Bodhisattva seeks the wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), they must further humble themselves and benefit others. How can one serve as a wheel-turning king for many eons, thereby increasing one's own pride (*māna*)?

Answer: It is provisionally taught that they are born into superior stations in order to attract other wise ones and cause them to resolve their minds [on enlightenment]. Since the benefit is thus great, there is no fault.
Regarding the statement "it should be explained through reconciliation," this means that a single phrase applies universally across the three distinct types of spiritual lineages mentioned above.
Regarding the phrase "beholding the rare divine transformations," Lu says: "Beholding celestial flowers that delight the eyes, and perceiving the trembling of the earth that startles the heart—
combining these two kinds of majestic manifestations, they are collectively termed 'beholding the rare and marvelous divine transformations, such as never before experienced.'"
Regarding the phrase "giving rise to the superior mind" (*śreṣṭha-citta*) and so forth, Muzhou said: "The root-dharma is supported, like the joining of two palms.

Regarding the phrase "clarifying the emotions and becoming tranquil," this signifies the absence of other thoughts and the lack of further divergent objects; it is called "single-mindedness" (*ekāgra*).

Regarding the phrase "I hope to bring forth golden words" (*jì fā jīnyán*): "hope" (*jì*) means aspiration. "Golden words" (*jīnyán*) refers to the teachings issued from the golden mouth of the Tathāgata;
thus they are called golden words. Alternatively, the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) is as precious as gold, and thus it is called golden.

Regarding the statement that the fifth [point] concerns the teaching on causes and so forth: the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma is the support (āśraya), while the minds of sentient beings are the supported (āśrita).
The Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma is the fruit (phala), and the minds of sentient beings characterized by longing and aspiration are the cause (hetu).

Regarding the two interpretations of the statement [that "speech has two explanations"]: it is asked, "By what dharma does one take as the cause for speaking? The answer is that there are two interpretations of the treatise (*śāstra*).

First, taking the sentient beings' hearts of longing and aspiration as the cause for speaking; second, taking the emission of light as the cause for speaking. This is the master of the commentary (*ṭīkākāra*) selecting and indicating the intent of the treatise.
According to the meaning of the *śāstra*, there should be two interpretations combined; this is not the actual text of the *śāstra* itself.
Regarding the statement "as for 'those various great assemblies,'" this is the Master of the Treatise explaining the reason.
Those "great assemblies" in the treatise refer to the fifteen types of assemblies present at the assembly on Vulture Peak.

Regarding the statement that "the manifestation of distinct signs cannot be equated [with ordinary phenomena]," this refers to the rain of flowers, the shaking of the earth, and the emission of light illuminating the realm;
what is perceived as these combined distinct signs constitutes an inconceivable event. This very thing is precisely what gives rise to a mind of yearning and reverence (*utkaṇṭhā-citta*).

Question: What is meant by a "mind of yearning and reverence"? Answer: Once such auspicious signs have manifested, one subsequently forms the thought: "The Tathāgata should surely preach the Dharma for my sake."
"What dharma do you thirstily desire to hear?"—this gives rise to a mind of rare longing (*āścarya-citta*).

By specifically taking up this thirsty and longing mind, [the Buddha] explains the cause, saying, "Therefore, he emits great rays of light," and so forth; this is the Master of the Treatise’s own summary of its distinct characteristics.
"Various matters" refers precisely to the seven matters within the light.
Regarding the statement "the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma, etc.," this is the Master of the Commentary’s primary interpretation of the treatise’s intent.
That which is the result of what is taught is called the "arousing of a mind of longing and thirst"; this is termed the "cause of teaching," meaning the cause for teaching the Dharma.
The statement, "This clarifies the cause upon which the teaching of the Dharma relies," serves as a general conclusion.

The Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma is the supported (the effect), while the longing and yearning of sentient beings for the light is the support (the cause). The longing and yearning of sentient beings serve as the cause, and the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma serves as the result.
(In the aforementioned commentary, the Master explains this as the cause.)
Regarding the phrase "emitting light that shines afar," "emitting light that shines afar" restates the previous illumination of the object.
The two characters "distinctive marks" (xiàng) restate the seven things previously seen. These seven things serve as the cause for the hearts of sentient beings' thirsty longing.
Regarding the statement that "the great assembly beheld the light," this refers to the seven matters seen by the sentient beings on Mount Ling within the light of the eighteen thousand worlds.
As for "thereupon giving rise to right mindfulness," this refers to [the thought]: "What Dharma is the Tathāgata preaching for us?"
Regarding the statement, "Therefore, the emission of light can produce [the result]," etc., this is the first interpretation of the Master of the Commentary (Sūzhǔ).
Regarding the second point, "First, he manifests," etc.: the commentary states that "etc. refers to the rain of flowers; these are combined to designate the cause of the teaching.
"Manifesting" is designated as "first" because it precedes the main body of the text concerning external phenomena. Question: Why does the second interpretation apply to what precedes?

The earth shook and flowers rained down. The answer is given according to the previous interpretation in the treatise: it takes only the ability to generate a heart of reverent devotion in sentient beings as the cause.

Now, this second interpretation takes both the raining of flowers and the shaking of the earth as the causes for the teaching, as these are both externally manifested miraculous transformations (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*).
Therefore, within the phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*), the entry into meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is not included; entering concentration is not an external matter.
Regarding the phrase "the subsequent manifestation" and so forth, Jin says: "The Dharma-gate is precisely the emission of light;

this Dharma-gate is so named because it first causes the earth to tremble and subsequently emits divine light. Since it follows the preceding earthquake, the emission of light constitutes this Dharma-gate. This explanation is incorrect.

Rather, one should take the section from the "Expedient Means" chapter (*upāya-paṭala*) downward, specifically the place where the One Vehicle is correctly taught through the stages of opening, showing, awakening, and entering, and name that [the Dharma-gate].
It serves as a gateway to the Dharma because it encompasses both internal realization and external exposition; thus, the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* contains the term "middle" (*madhya*).

As for the statement that it concerns the profound and secret Dharma of internal realization, this refers to the Buddha’s own internal realization and accomplishment, through which he attained the two dharmas of *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*.
It is also called the *Vyākaraṇa-sūtra* (Sutra of Prophecy).

Regarding the statement that the supernatural external matters are manifested first, this is the commentary by the Master [of the Subcommentary]. This treatise’s Dharma is the teaching of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), which arises from internal realization;
thus, this is an explanation proceeding from the external toward the internal. Question: Why are supernatural external matters first manifested?
What is the intention? The answer is: he intends to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* for the sake of sentient beings externally. Question:
For what reason does he intend to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* for sentient beings? Answer: It is precisely because of his internal realization of the profound and secret [Dharma].

Regarding the statement, "Furthermore, it is because of internal realization of the profound," etc., this is the second interpretation. It is an explanation that proceeds from the internal toward the external.
Thus, the spiritual transformations manifested internally are directed outwardly. Question: What is the purpose of manifesting spiritual transformations externally? Answer:

It is intended for the sake of sentient beings, in order to preach the Dharma that is to be taught. The Dharma to be preached is precisely the One Vehicle of the Lotus Sūtra. (The foregoing constitutes the general presentation of external matters.)
Regarding the statement, "Although it was previously said that flowers rained down and the earth shook," etc.: next, the specific reason for emitting light also serves to resolve the objection.

Previously, we proceeded from the outside toward the inside, where the external factors included both the raining of flowers and the shaking of the earth. From this point on, the Master of the Commentary (*śāstrakāra*) specifically re-examines the matter and selects only the emission of light.

Question: Why did the Master previously include all factors, yet here he again excludes them? Answer: [The previous inclusion was for the sake of the general context; here, the selection is made for the sake of the specific analysis.]

The commentary’s main intent is as follows: If one considers the Master [Nāgārjuna] having attained the hearts of sentient beings’ yearning and reverence such that flowers rained down and the earth shook, he certainly possessed all these capacities.
However, if we take this as the fifth reason for the accomplishment of the teaching, the emission of light is particularly preeminent. Regarding the phrase "extraordinary wonders" and so forth:
This is even more extraordinary than the previous rain of flowers that shook the earth. Although they were both single events, this emission of light reached as far as eighteen thousand other lands.
What was seen in those seven matters was witnessed here in this assembly one by one; this is truly a marvel.
Regarding the phrase "emitting a single ray of light," Master Jing states: "About to kindle the torch of wisdom, he causes his body to radiate brilliance;
the jade-like luster spread from between his eyebrows manifests a rare wonder beyond the city walls. Sentient beings behold it and look up with longing;

for this reason, the Tathāgata preaches the sutra, thus taking the emission of light as the cause for the teaching. There are two meanings to the emission of light: first, the extension of the hair-tuft between the eyebrows.
The hair is manifest; its name is "Emanation. From the two tufts of hair on his head, light issues forth, spontaneously pervading the three thousandfold world system.

When withdrawn, it is the constant light extending one fathom; when extended, it fills the entire dharma-realm. Its name is "Emanation" (*fang*); "emanation" carries the meaning of unfolding or extension.

The Tathāgata’s great compassion constantly maintains self-mastery over his body, illuminating each of the four directions for one fathom. The circular halo behind his neck and back surpasses a hundred thousand suns.
"Eyebrows" refers to that which brings grace to the face and head. When the Sūtra speaks of "between the eyebrows," it refers to the space between the two eyebrows.
Since neither brow-surface exists as a substantial entity, they are neither existent nor empty; this space between them is the Middle Way. "Between" (間) signifies the Middle Path.

The eyebrows are the head of the face. Among all features upon the face, none is more preeminent than the eyebrows. "Eyebrows" (mei) signify "charm" (mei). At the top of the face, they are indispensable;
together with the head and the face, they constitute beauty and grace. There is one instance regarding food and seven instances regarding clothing.
She applied makeup and drew her eyebrows with coquettish charm. At that time, Zhang Chang, the Governor of Jingzhao, drew his wife's eyebrows for her;
when the Ministry of Justice reported this, he replied: "I have a wife for whom I paint her eyebrows; this is indeed the fruit of having a country.

Furthermore, if there were no eyebrows on a person's face, it would be like a leprous child—Lu Shaolun was a scholar who did not believe in the Buddha-dharma and treated Buddhist scriptures as mere toilet paper.
Soil. Later, his eyebrows and hair fell out. Suffering from leprosy, he composed a poem which says: "The leprosy departs! The leprosy departs!
This is most excellent. My eyebrows have all fallen away; where can my grief now rest? Furthermore, there is a section of the Lotus Sutra that resembles the face of a beautiful woman.

At the head of this section are five characters, using the phrase "beautiful eyebrows" (mei mei). A beautiful woman is naturally upright and graceful; how much more so when her face is further adorned with painted brows!
With a pair of eyebrows, one can achieve the power to "make a city fall at a single glance" or "buy a smile for a thousand pieces of gold.

The twenty-eight chapters of the sutra text are already inconceivable; yet, by adding the five characters "Myōhō Renge Kyō" (The Lotus Sutra) to each and every chapter, the entire Lotus Sutra is made to possess a fullness of grace, just like painting a pair of eyebrows upon a woman's face. Forty years ago, the Śrāvakas did not...
He turned his mind [toward the Buddha]. The World-Honored One’s brow remained furrowed and did not relax.

How could he have known that his father had been constantly thinking of his son for over fifty years since their separation, yet had never mentioned such a matter to anyone, but only brooded over it in solitude with a heart full of regret?
Today, on this assembly at Vulture Peak, those who were śrāvakas have turned their minds [toward enlightenment]. They are children born from the Buddha’s own mouth;

they are children born through transformation by the Dharma. From this moment, the World-Honored One spreads his eyebrows, and from the tip of his white tuft of hair, he emits white light—this is precisely the time for preaching the Lotus Sutra.
As the sutra says: "Now is the very time; I shall definitively preach the Mahayana."

Regarding the statement "the term *háo* refers to long hair and so forth": long hair is made into a *háo*. If one takes the word *háo* as distinct from "hair" (*máo*), it is also understood as the most excellent among all hairs.
A *háo* is a superior hair; according to the *Huainanzi*, one whose wisdom exceeds ten thousand people is called a *háo*.
Both characters are acceptable.

Regarding the statement that both the internal and external are empty: the internal emptiness is like a tube of lapis lazuli; seeing the external through the interior is called external emptiness, and seeing the interior through the exterior is called internal emptiness.
Thus, it is said that both the internal and external are empty. Internally and externally, they do not obstruct one another.
Regarding the statement "releasing it in a circular coil," after releasing it, one draws it back up to coil it upon the forehead;
its shape is like the full autumn moon, and its color is as brilliant and pure as the full autumn moon.

Regarding the statement "the circumference is like three [units]," the commentary (shūbon) clarifies that if the character for "round" (en) is used, it refers to a hair-tip being three inches in circumference.

(If the character is "round," then the hair-tip—with its square and round diameter—is three inches both horizontally and vertically. Thus there are three [dimensions]. If the character for "round" is used, the diameter at the tip is three inches both horizontally and vertically;

this refers to the square and round diameter at the point where it is coiled. It is one inch [in thickness] and three inches [in circumference]; it does not refer to the squareness of the hair-tip itself.
It is one inch in diameter; all of these are irregularities.
As for the statement that it inspires pure faith: since there is light externally, there must be superior virtue within, and thus it is called a "superior person."
Regarding the statement that "the two can destroy darkness": once the sunlight has emerged, the darkness of the world is entirely dispelled;

when the light from the [Buddha’s] brow is extended, it signifies the simultaneous eradication of the ignorance within the bodies of sentient beings. As the Sūtra says: "Wherever the majestic radiance of the sun and moon does not reach, all becomes brilliantly illuminated," because the realms of delusion and confusion are thereby made intelligible.
As for "darkness and gloom," this does not necessarily mean the transformation of evening; rather, it refers to the breaking of the vessel [of ignorance].
Regarding the phrase "dispelling the darkness and folly of the world": it means to shatter the darkness of the world of sentient beings.
As for the statement "the three can lead to illumination," although sentient beings possess the faculty of sight, they see objects during the day but not at night;
this requires the illumination of the sun and moon to direct the eyes outward, so that light may perceive objects. Sentient beings...
When one gives birth, there is within the body the radiance of wisdom; this must necessarily be drawn forth by the light of the Tathāgata’s body before it can arise.
Thus, when it is said that the light of wisdom is emitted from within the four boundaries, it is because there is the light of the body externally.
Regarding the statement that "the five [powers] can alleviate all sufferings" and so forth, this indicates that the Buddha emits light to extinguish the suffering of the hells. As a sutra says:

"While dwelling in the forest, he emits light to relieve the suffering of those in hell. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The Buddha emitted the radiance of the Moon-Love Samādhi (*candravimala-samādhi*), whereby King Ajātaśatru’s bodily sores were subsequently eliminated."

Regarding the phrase "awakening the sentiments of the multitude," it means that by observing the light, all who have a connection with it arrive. It is like a secular lecturer who, when about to preach, summons people from various places;
likewise, when the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma, he first emits light to summon them, causing them to become aware and come forth to the site of enlightenment (the *bodhimaṇḍa*).

Question: The commentary states that "all those with whom there is a karmic connection arrive. Does this refer to this world-system (*dhātu*) or to other world-systems? Answer: It refers exclusively to this world-system.

Examining the subsequent text, one does not see it mentioned that they seek out light in other directions. Question: Below it says, "Furthermore, the wheel-turning sage-kings (*cakravartin*) from ten thousand *koṭis* of lands arrive.

How can the path be described as such? [The answer is: Because within the three-thousandfold world-system (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*), there are likewise ten thousand *koṭis* of wheel-turning kings who arrive. If...
The passage below from Huaiwen states: "Those equal in number to the atoms of a thousand worlds, as well as Miaoyin and others, also come from other directions.
This interpretation is excellent. Hege refutes this, saying: "According to the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*, one flower covers ten billion lands;

since there are ten billion lands, the wheel-turning kings (cakravartin) must likewise be ten billion. How could there be ten trillion wheel-turning kings within a trichiliocosm? Mocheng says: "This refutation is irrational."
The *Commentary on the Bodhisattva Precepts* states: "The new and old translations differ. [In the old system,] one hundred thousand is a *koṭi*, which is ten billion;
one million is a *koṭi*, which is ten billion. As stated in the calculations of the *Abhidharmakośa*, one hundred thousand is a *lakṣa*; ten lakṣas [is a *prayuta*]."
A *lakṣa* is ten million; a hundred *lakṣas* are one *koṭi*. A *koṭi* is one billion (or, according to the system where ten thousand is a "hundred million," it is ten times that).

For example, beneath the third dhyāna there are said to be a hundred billion suns and moons. If we rely on this system of a hundred billion, then ten million is one hundred million (*koṭi*), and a hundred million is one billion (*arbuda*);
thus, it is a hundred billion. This is identical to the calculation of the *ruta* [system], and therefore [the former claim] is refuted.
That is not correct. However, Lu says that [the claim] "from the trichiliocosm" is incorrect.
According to the commentary below, it explains that in ten thousand billion places where Buddhas appear in this land, there are no wheel-turning kings (*cakravartin*). The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states:
"Each sits beneath a bodhi tree and simultaneously attains the Buddha-way. How could there be a Buddha and yet still another wheel-turning king?

Regarding the statement "the seven [qualities] cause one to feel revulsion for form (*rūpa*) and so forth," Mochizuki states: The Tathāgata’s divine radiance possesses a brilliance of color that is peerless, transcending the objects of the five sensory dusts (*pañca-viṣaya*) of the world;
therefore, it causes one to develop revulsion toward the world. Thus, beautiful forms are not equal to the Buddha’s light. This can be understood through two analogies:
like a man who, having first married an ugly wife, later takes a beautiful consort. The meaning of these two metaphors is clear.

Regarding the statement "thereupon [they] become weary of birth and death, etc.": it means that once sentient beings have seen the Buddha’s untainted (anāsrava) light from between his eyebrows, they come to know that their own tainted (sāsrava) form is coarse, evil, and a thing to be loathed; therefore, it is said that they "thereupon become weary."
Regarding the statement that there are four colors of *nirvāṇa*, that sutra speaks of "various colored lights" but does not explicitly mention four kinds.
Nevertheless, these do not exceed the four primary colors as their basis. The term "face-gate" (*mukha-dvāra*) refers to the mouth. These four colors symbolize the four virtues of *nirvāṇa*.
Even if there were categories such as red, green, purple, blue, or black, they would all, by analogy, be subsumed within the four colors of blue, yellow, red, and white.

Regarding the phrase "raising [the hand] to signify ascending birth" (*ūrdhva-janma-saṃsūcana*): "raising" (*saṃsūcana*) means pervasiveness. It signifies that Maitreya’s compassion is universal and impartial.
As for the statement "each has its own symbolic meaning": *nirvāṇa* symbolizes the four virtues—permanence (*nitya*), bliss (*sukha*), self (*ātman*), and purity (*śubha*).

"Ascending birth" symbolizes the fulfillment of Maitreya’s fruition; thus, he raises his body to emit light and entrusts all Buddha-activities to Maitreya. The light is like the color of gold, manifesting [this truth].
Because it is worthy of reverence, the light of his entire body is raised to signify the meaning of perfection. The Sūtra says:

"At that time, during the first watch of the night, the World-Honored One emitted golden light from his entire body; this light circled the Jeta Grove seven times and illuminated the house of Sudatta, making it likewise golden," and so forth.
The *Bodhisattva-upāya-sūtra* states: "When he wishes to preach the Dharma for the śrāvakas, he immediately emits [light] from his..."
If he wishes to preach the Dharma of the *pratyekabuddha*, he emits light from his mouth; if he wishes to preach the Dharma of the *bodhisattva*, he emits light from the crown of his head.

Regarding the phrase "the supernormal power of knowledge of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhividhi-jñānābhijñā*) and so forth," this refers to their inclusion within the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). There are eighteen transformations belonging to the supernormal power of knowledge of the bases of psychic power.

The "divine" (*deva*) refers to meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Because the functioning of this concentration is unfathomable, it is called "divine. That which is transformed by concentration is called the "object" (*viṣaya*). "Knowledge" (*jñāna*) refers to the Tathāgata’s subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*);

therefore, it is termed the "supernormal power of knowledge regarding the divine objects" (*ṛddhiviṣayajñānābhijñā*). Within this supernormal power of knowledge, there are two aspects: first, the ability to transform (*pariṇāma*), and second, the ability to emanate (*nirmāṇa*).
Emanation means that what was non-existent suddenly comes into being; transformation means the conversion of an existing substance. This refers to the eighteen transformations. First.
1. Trembling: such as the sixfold trembling of this world-system. 2. Blazing: water issuing from the upper part of the body and fire issuing from the lower part of the body. 3. Pervading:
that is, emitting rays of light from the hair-tufts to illuminate afar other lands and so forth. 4. Manifestation:
that is, opening the Stūpa of Prabhūtaratna to show it to the assembled multitude, so that within this world they see that land in its entirety. 5. Transformation: as, for example—
He transforms the Sahā world into a pure land; the dragon girl transforms her body into that of a male, and so forth. Regarding the "six times coming and going":
as described in the text, after Mañjuśrī has finished his dialogue with Maitreya here, he conceals his form and proceeds to the palace of the Sāgara Dragon King, from which he emerges once more.

"Coming from the Dragon Palace" means that, in relation to the other [place], it is called "going," while in relation to this [place], it is called "coming. 1. "The Seven Rolls" refers to the retraction of the tongue-mark and other such signs. 2.
"The Eight Extensions" refers to, for example, the manifestation of the broad and long tongue-mark. 3. "Various Images Entering the Body": "Images" (xiàng) refers to manifest forms;
"entering" (rù) has the sense of coming. This is because, as in a single mirror, there are many images. 4. "A Hair Swallows the Vast Sea" and "A Mustard Seed Contains Mount Sumeru."

*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 35, states: "It refers to the Buddha or Bodhisattva, by virtue of mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi*), being able to withdraw the assembly present before them, as well as all villages, towns, hamlets, grasses, trees, forests, thickets, mountains, the great earth, and all such forms, and place them within their own body, causing the various classes of devas to each know for themselves that they have entered within his body; this is called 'the multitude'."

1. Entering the body (*kāyapraveśa*). 2. Approaching those of the same class (*sabhāgatopasaṃkrānti*), as in the sūtra where [the Buddha] taught the Dharma by assuming the bodies of an elder, a boy, or a girl.
3. Concealment (*saṃvṛti*), such as when mountains do not appear during the transformation of the earth, or as when the Buddha enters parinirvāṇa.
4. Manifestation (*vivṛti*), such as the accomplishment of the eightfold path (*aṣṭalakṣaṇābhisambodhi*), or emerging from the earth. 5. What is performed (*kṛtya*).
1. The Sovereign One transforms the great earth into gold and silver, and further casts the world into other realms. 2. Fourteen:
He subdues the supernatural powers of others, such as the celestial Māra Pāpīyan, rendering them devoid of such powers.
3. Fifteen: He can bestow eloquence, just as he empowered Subhūti to preach the Prajñāpāramitā. 4. Sixteen: He can bestow mindfulness, such as causing Ānanda to recollect [the teachings].

The Dharma-treasuries of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddhas of the past; furthermore, like the daughter of Vasiṣṭha, who upon seeing the World-Honored One conceived the thought that he was her own son and thereby regained her original mind;

seventeenth, the ability to bestow peace and happiness, as when five hundred bands of robbers had their eyes gouged out by King Prasenajit and, unable to endure the suffering, were led to practice mindfulness of the Buddha’s giving through the Tathāgata’s supernatural power.
The fragrance from Mount Cūḍāmaṇi fills the eye sockets; all obtain eyes, and their manifold sufferings are immediately eliminated.
This is called "Bestowing Peace and Bliss. Eighteenth, he emits great rays of light. These emitted rays are like those [described] for the space between the eyebrows and so forth.

Question: What is the difference between this emission of light and its "pervasive diffusion"? Answer: If the light is simply emitted and shines from afar, it is merely called "emission of light" and not "pervasive diffusion. If...

The emission of light extends upward, downward, and in all directions; this is termed "pervasive diffusion. Question: These eighteen transformations are subsumed within the supernormal power of the base (ṛddhividhi-jñāna) among the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

It is not yet known what must first be accomplished for them to be achieved. Answer: This is because one forms the mental image of lightness and levity. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 31, states:
"Forming the mental image of lightness and levity means that by means of this mental image, one gives rise to the resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding the body's lightness and levity."
Having generated such a resolute conviction (*adhimukti*)—that [the body] is like tūla-cotton or resembles a wind-wheel—one causes one's body and so forth to drift and turn here and there.

Regarding the statement "raining down the four flowers" and so on, it refers to what is appropriate to the context. Question: Previously, flowers rained down, the earth shook, light was emitted, and the six realms of existence were seen. What is the significance of this?

Within which of the eighteen transformations are these subsumed? The Commentary answers: "The raining of the four flowers" is the transformation of mastery (*vaśitā-vaikṛta*), specifically the thirteenth, the transformation of mastery over what is produced (*nirmāṇa-vaśitā*).
"The sixfold shaking" is subsumed under the first, the transformation of vibration (*prakampana-vaikṛta*).

"The emission of light" is the transformation of diffusion (*prasaraṇa-vaikṛta*), specifically the third, the transformation of diffusion. "Seeing the six realms of existence" is the fourth, the transformation of manifestation (*darśana-vaikṛta*).
The Manifestation is the Subsumption (the upper part is able to illuminate).
*Fahua jing xuanzan yaoji*, Scroll 11; *Fahua jing xuanzan yaoji*, Scroll 12.
"Mirror-Water Śramaṇa Xifu recorded these words to illuminate the objects [of perception].
Regarding the phrase "the objects illuminated," it refers to the objects that are illuminated. As the Sūtra says, "Illuminating eighteen thousand [worlds] in the eastern direction," Jiguō states:
"The reason it mentions only the eastern direction is to indicate the beginning by way of the end; this is because the text is abbreviated. In reality, however, it applies universally."
"Shining upon the ten directions. The ancient masters mistakenly cited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, saying: "It shines universally upon eighteen thousand lands in the eastern direction;
its light is great and brilliant, illuminating all those lands without exception. Even the sūtras and dharmas preached by the Buddhas of the ten directions are heard everywhere therein.
The intention of the commentary follows this [interpretation], yet it refers only to the ten [directions] within the worlds of the eastern direction that are illuminated.
This is not that the Buddha’s light does not directly illuminate the ten directions. Kai Zhong says: "The eastern direction is the head of all directions;

this symbolizes that the One Vehicle is the beginning of the Three Vehicles. Jia Xiang says: "That it illuminates only one direction and not the other nine symbolizes that there is only the One Vehicle and no other vehicles.
That which was previously taught as three from the perspective of the One symbolizes [the truth of] today."
This means to subsume the two into one.

Regarding the phrase "one world" and so forth, this explains the world-system. Within world-systems there are large and small; the "world" mentioned here refers specifically to a single trichiliocosm.
Within each such world-system, there are the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). As [it is said]:

This illuminates eighteen thousand Buddha-worlds. Regarding the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) of the World-Honored One mentioned previously, there is the mark of always facing [beings] and never turning one's back.
Because during the causal stage he did not turn his back on any sentient being, in the resultant stage each person sees the World-Honored One before them;
there is no one who does not see the face of the World-Honored One. Suddenly, if a person were sitting to the west, they would likewise see him.
The World-Honored One sat facing west. It would follow that he must first have gone from east to west.

However, since the Sūtra states that "he illuminated only the eastern direction," it is impossible that the World-Honored One, while facing west, emitted light that reached the western boundary and then returned toward the east to illuminate it. To this, there are two explanations.
First interpretation: Since the sutra has already circulated in the East, it states that at that time the World-Honored One emitted light illuminating the East;
had it circulated in the South, it would have stated that at that time the World-Honored One emitted light illuminating the South. This applies to all other directions as well.

According to this first explanation, light illuminates all ten directions, yet the scriptural text varies according to the specific direction. Second interpretation: This is the unique quality (*āveṇika-dharma*) of the Buddha.

Regarding this merit and the inconceivable power of the Tathāgata: although all sentient beings see the World-Honored One facing toward their own original direction while sitting and emitting light, it does not hinder the fact that he has originally been shining toward the east.

Regarding the statement "only illuminating the eastern direction" and so forth: the east is the foundation of all directions, signifying that the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) is the source of the Three Vehicles (Triyāna).
