Furthermore, it is said that while other masters [such as Zhiyi] rely on the fact that the capacity to cover [the teachings] is unique, the Master of the Commentary (Suzhou) reveals the excellence of the faculties of those being covered.
These two perspectives mutually reflect and illuminate one another, such that the meaning is complete and sufficient.

Regarding the statement that "east of the Western Regions" signifies the "supreme among the superior": it indicates that among the five vehicles, those with the *gotra* (disposition) of the Mahāyāna are supreme.
It reveals that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* specifically favors those with the Mahāyāna *gotra*. As explained previously concerning Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa:

the summit of that mountain is long from east to west and narrow from south to north. On its western slope, bordering the cliff, there is a brick vihāra; its height and breadth are such that its door opens toward the east.
Regarding the orientation of doors: observing the customs of this Western Region (India), they regard the east as superior, taking the place where the sun rises as the direction of honor.

Even kings face east to signify that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is supreme and does not illuminate the other three directions. In this region (China), however, the south-facing direction is held to be honorable.

The Son of Heaven faces south. All private residences have their gates opening toward the south. The south presides over Yang (the masculine principle), while the north presides over Yin (the feminine principle).
Yin is inferior and Yang is superior. Furthermore, according to the local gazetteers, this region was the fiefdom of Xuan-yuan and is governed by the Four Kings.
Extending from south of the Snow Mountains to the Southern Ocean, it is named Elephant-Master. The terrain is exclusively hot and humid, being particularly suited for [elephants].

The Elephant [Kingdom]: The ruler dwells with an elephant army and brings peace to his country. From the midst of the Snowy Mountains to the Western Sea, he is known as the King of the Jewel-Royal Kingdom.
Its territory borders the Western Sea and abounds in rare and extraordinary treasures; its people honor etiquette lightly but value wealth highly.
North of the Snowy Mountains to the Northern Sea, the land is cold and well-suited for horses; he is enfeoffed as the Lord of Horses. The customs of that region are fierce and violent.
The land where the body hair stands on end consists of the kingdoms of the Turks and others. From the Snow Mountains to the east as far as the Eastern Sea is called the Land of the Human Ruler;
this is the kingdom of China, which in antiquity was called Zhendan. Here, Luoyang is pointed out as the very center of the realm.

This is the territory conferred by Xuanyuan. If one follows this principle, the East is considered superior. In the East are Jia and Yi, representing Wood; it presides over Spring, when all things are brought to life.
Among the four seasons, the East is held to be superior. In the South are Bing and Ding, representing Fire, which presides over Summer.

In the West are Geng and Xin, representing Metal, which presides over Autumn. In the North are Ren and Gui, representing Water, which presides over Winter. In the Center are Wu and Ji, representing Earth; Earth is fundamentally the primary element.
The forms correspond to the Kings of the Four Seasons. The East represents bodhisattvas of the fixed nature in the Mahāyāna;

the South represents śrāvakas of the fixed nature; the West represents pratyekabuddhas of the fixed nature; the North represents those of no spiritual lineage (agotra); and the Center represents sentient beings of the indeterminate nature.
Within the bodies of these beings of indeterminate nature, there exist the natures of the four vehicles. If they give rise to the bodhicitta, [they may attain enlightenment].

Those who belong to the category of Bodhisattvas fixed in their nature are gathered in one place in the East; those who give rise to the mind of a Śrāvaka are gathered in one place in the South among those fixed in the nature of Śrāvakas;
and those who give rise to the mind of a Pratyekabuddha are gathered in one place in the West among those fixed in the nature of Pratyekabuddhas.

If one were to develop the aspiration for the vehicle of humans and devas of fixed nature, they would be subsumed under the North, which is the single location for those of fixed nature among humans and devas.

However, this person is a bodhisattva of indeterminate nature within the Hīnayāna; if they develop the bodhicitta, they are subsumed under the East, which is the location for bodhisattvas of fixed nature.
Therefore, the emission of light shines only upon the East.
The phrase "for example, etc. introduces a simile.

Regarding the phrase "in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*," the commentator (the Master of the Sub-commentary) refutes the erroneous citation by Ji-guo, who quotes the passage from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* stating that [the light] "illuminates the ten directions.
He refutes it by saying: "In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it also illuminates the eastern direction; there is absolutely no mention of it illuminating those other [directions]."
Regarding the phrase "ten thousand" in the text:

it explains the eighteen thousand [lines]. The commentary states: "The limit of conditions reaches this point; it corresponds precisely to the eighteen thousand, and there is no further connection with the past or the sutra.
Jiaxiang says: "Ten thousand represents the fulfillment of the vehicle of fruition (phala-yāna), while eight thousand..."

This indicates that there is a deficiency in the causal vehicle (*hetuyāna*). Thus, the relationship between response and stimulus is such that since the stimuli of sentient beings do not pervade all directions, the Buddha’s responsive manifestations (*nirmāṇa*) are likewise not universal.

Regarding the statement that "this explains the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) and so forth": the emission of light illuminates whether the numbers are complete or incomplete; the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* clarifies the reality and the provisional aspects of the One Vehicle.

Regarding the statement that "furthermore, ten thousand represents *nirvāṇa*": the ten thousand represent the ten thousand virtues of *nirvāṇa*, and the eight thousand represent the eight [thousand] virtues of *bodhi*.
"Correct.
Regarding the statement "about to expound this sūtra," etc., this concludes the meaning. This sūtra is about to expound nirvāṇa and bodhi;
this sūtra can lead to nirvāṇa and bodhi; those who hear this sūtra will fully accomplish and realize nirvāṇa and bodhi.

The phrase "therefore, it illuminates only you" serves as a double conclusion for the two interpretations. By virtue of these three meanings, the illumination of eighteen thousand [beings] is thereby indicated.
"Shining upon those below" signifies that all who suffer are uprooted; this is the function of illuminating the lower realms.

"Reaching upward to the heavens" means exhorting those who enjoy pleasure to seek the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), causing them to realize the nature of the pleasures of the five desires and to seek supramundane bliss;

this is the illumination of the upper realms. [Objection: While it may be appropriate to exhort those in the Form Heavens (*rūpadeva*) and Desire Heavens (*kāmadeva*) to renounce their pleasures, within the Fourth Dhyāna there is only...

Regarding the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), how can it be said that there is "equanimity and bliss"? The answer is twofold: first, some say that within the fourth dhyāna there is no actual bliss;

however, because it possesses the quality of being agreeable to body and mind, it resembles bliss. Second, others say that there is an agreeable and beneficial feeling of equanimity, which is also close to bliss.
Regarding "compassion" (*karuṇā*): it explains what was previously mentioned as "above and below.
Regarding "universal and vast": it is called "universal" because both suffering and joy are moistened by it; it is called "vast" because it illuminates everything above and below.

Regarding the statement, "As for the beings in the hells," this serves as a general rebuttal to an objection. Question: If those with a karmic connection are all illuminated, and the various devas of the upper realms emit light that shines upon them such that those with a connection all come, then why must light be emitted for the sake of sentient beings in hell who lack such a connection and do not arrive at the assembly? Answer: The commentary states, "As for the sentient beings in hell," and so forth. This means that although these beings do not come to the assembly, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, out of great compassion, universally illuminate all places where there are sentient beings; it is not that they only illuminate those who have arrived. Furthermore, even though these beings do not come to the assembly, they can still see the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas from afar because the light illuminates them. Moreover, even if they do not see the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas directly, they will certainly experience a transformation of their mental state through the power of that light, thereby attaining liberation. Therefore, the emission of light is not in vain. This is what is meant by the phrase "even though they do not come to the assembly. It is like the case of the hungry ghosts in the *Sūtra on the Past Deeds of King Śubhavyūha*, who, though not coming to the assembly, were nonetheless able to see the Buddha from afar due to the power of the light. Thus, the emission of light is indeed purposeful. This is the meaning of the passage. To speak of this as "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*) is an explanation of the Avīci Hell. There are five kinds of uninterruptedness:

first, uninterruptedness of retribution, wherein one who has created and acquired this karma receives its fruit solely in the very next life; upon death, one is immediately reborn there, with no other intervening births or realms.

Therefore, it is called "uninterrupted retribution. "Interrupted" (*antara*) means "separated. Second, there is the uninterruptedness of lifespan: their life span is one intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*), and there are none who die prematurely;
therefore, it is called "uninterrupted. Third, there is the uninterruptedness of physical form: those who enter the hells have bodies that are vast and pervasive, equal [in size];
therefore, it is called "uninterrupted. Fourth, there is the uninterruptedness of suffering: while those in other minor hells experience the suffering of heat, there is...
In the intervals between the cool winds, this hell is purely suffering; there is no further interval. It is "uninterrupted" (ānantarya) in five respects:
it has no intervals, and its locations are not separated by other distinct places.
Regarding the statement that the lowest among the eight hells is [Avīci], this is based on the primary teaching. The *Mahā-śāstra* states:
"Thirty-two thousand yojanas below this is the Saṃjīva hell; four thousand yojanas below Saṃjīva are the remaining seven hells."
Because [the light] spreads out to all sides. Question: Why does the text not say that the light illuminates the seven hells above and below, but only says it illuminates the Avīci hell below?
Answer: The fact that the sūtra specifically mentions the illumination of Avīci indicates that the seven upper hells are also illuminated.

Regarding the phrase "the suffering endured without ceasing," among these five [types of suffering], this specifically cites the one aspect of suffering to demonstrate that all four remaining types are likewise endowed with suffering.
Regarding the term "instrument of suffering," it refers to the vessel or implement for those who undergo punishment.
Regarding the phrase "located in various places": since the fundamental hells are situated beneath the earth, they are named after their primary location.

As for the other solitary hells, they exist both upon the earth and among humans; therefore, they are called "various places. Furthermore, the term translated as "hell" (*dīyù*) is not a direct transcription from Sanskrit, but was established based on its meaning.
The character for "hell" (*yù*) is pronounced with the initial *yu* (as in "fish") and the final *yù* (as in "desire"). It originated from [the name of] Gao Yao...
It is so constructed.
As for the term "Akaniṣṭha": *ni* (pronounced as in "nü jǐ") + *ḍha* (pronounced as in "dǎ hǔ") + *taṭa* (pronounced as in "rèn xià").
Regarding the term "Akaniṣṭha" (the Ultimate Form), it is understood to mean that the light illuminates that realm. Question:

Why does the Buddha’s emission of light reach only as far as the Akaniṣṭha Heaven? Answer: The commentary states that the Akaniṣṭha Heaven is the pinnacle of all material forms; it is the furthest extent to which light can reach.

Regarding the statement that "light does not illuminate the formless [realms] (*ārūpya*) and so forth": Question: Since it is admitted that there is "form produced by meditative concentration" (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*) in the formless realms, why does light not illuminate them?
Answer: It is because such form does not exist at all times or in all places; therefore, it does not illuminate. Furthermore, there is no "form that is the fruit of karma" (*karmaphala-rūpa*) there.

Although there is form produced by meditative concentration, it is not present everywhere in its entirety and thus cannot be illuminated selectively. Moreover, since there is no objective support (*ālambana*), how could it possibly be illuminated?

The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "In the formless realm, there is no location; it is through birth that there are four types [of beings]. Relying upon the homogeneous character (*nikāyasabhāga*) and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), they cause the mind and its concomitants to continue in succession."
Regarding the statement that [the light] encompasses the five destinies: the question asks whether each of the eighteen thousand worlds is individually illuminated. The answer is:

since it is stated that they are all seen, it is clear that they are universally illuminated. The meaning is that within each individual world, the five destinies are all illuminated; therefore, it is said that there is nothing to which it does not pervade.
The statement, "As for the claim that vibration occurs only in this [realm]," explains the intent behind the objection. Question: Why does vibration occur only in this realm? Answer:

It specifically alerts those with whom it has a karmic connection (*sālambana*); other realms lack such a connection, and the earth itself does not move. Question: Why, then, does the emission of light illuminate [everything]?
"Other realms. Answer: The emission of light subsequently reaches eighteen thousand [realms]. This is because it manifests the relinquishing of the provisional and the embracing of the real.

The commentary on this section appears to be confused; in the preceding discussion regarding the emission of light and the shaking of realms, it was stated that the emitted light illuminates eighteen thousand [realms].
The shaking of the earth occurs only in this realm (*dhātu*), because in this realm one abandons the provisional (*upāya*) and proceeds toward the real (*bhūta*).

Now, in this context, the teaching is turned back to explain the abandonment of the provisional and the proceeding toward the real in terms of the upward direction of light. Previously, the shaking of the earth occurred only in this realm;

when discussing the abandonment of the provisional and the proceeding toward the real, it was explained in terms of the faculties (*indriya*) directed upward. Now, in this context, regarding the emission of light and the discussion of abandoning the provisional and proceeding toward the real, it is explained in terms of the capacity [to perceive].

This is taught above. The teaching encompasses both the provisional and the real. The previous emission of light illuminating ten thousand [worlds] symbolizes that the number of those of the One Vehicle is complete;
the eight thousand [worlds] symbolize that the number of those of the Two Vehicles is insufficient. This serves as a metaphor for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as the teaching that expresses:

it expresses the reality of the One Vehicle and the provisionality of the Two Vehicles. "Completeness" illustrates the reality of the One Vehicle, while "insufficiency" illustrates the provisionality of the Two Vehicles. What is expressed...

Having attained this principle, it is expressed by way of reference to the higher [realms]. Although both the provisional and the real are explained in general, there is no hindrance to abandoning the provisional and adhering to the real;
this occurs solely within this realm.

The statement "speech is also like light illuminating" serves as an illustrative example to establish the point. It is a metaphor for the Buddha emitting light that illuminates the eastern direction and preaching the Dharma of relinquishing the provisional to realize the ultimate.

Regarding the phrase "the conditions for hearing and so forth having assembled," the question is: if the emitted light illuminates the six realms of existence, why speak only of four? The answer is: the light illuminates all six realms.
All of them receive [the teaching] by virtue of the convergence of conditions to hear the sutra; this occurs only within the five destinies, excluding the hells.
If the asuras are categorized under the heavens, or alternatively under the hungry ghosts or animals, there is no contradiction with the statement in the commentary that there are four [destinies].
Regarding the statement that "these seven parts are of three grades," the *Śāstra* (Explanatory Commentary) raises a question:

If those of the Two Vehicles naturally perceive a small thousand-world system (*sāhasra-cūḍika-lokadhātu*), and those of the highest grade of perception see a medium thousand-world system (*dvisāhasra-madhyama-lokadhātu*), while Aniruddha sees a great thousand-world system (*trisāhasra-mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu*), it would still not be possible for them to see eighteen thousand worlds;
how then can ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) see eighteen thousand worlds? The answer is: all such cases are due to the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgata.

To cause them to see. Question: What is the intent behind causing them to see [these events] in alternation? Answer: Seeing the alternation of birth-and-death and its sinking into delusion causes one to give rise to revulsion;

seeing the appearance of the Triple Gem causes one to give rise to joy. Seeing the alternation of the Buddha entering parinirvāṇa causes both joy and revulsion, thereby inducing the arousal of the aspiration for enlightenment.
For if even the Buddha enters parinirvāṇa, how much more so can we expect to remain firm and enduring? This is intended to cause revulsion and to cause [the arousal of the aspiration].

"Joy. This refers to the mind that rejoices in hearing the Dharma, thinking: "Even though the Buddha within the light has already entered parinirvāṇa, we should quickly go before the Buddha to hear the Dharma.
Will our original teacher, Śākyamuni, not likewise enter parinirvāṇa like the Buddha in the light?
Furthermore, Śāriputra saw the bodhisattvas below the stages and the bodhisattvas on the stages within the light practicing the bodhisattva path, and thus gave rise to a heart of joyful admiration.
It gives rise to the aspiration to see the worthy and strive for equality with them; thus, the Buddha’s emission of light is his primary intention.
Regarding the phrase "sinking and revolving in this cycle of birth and death," the Sūtra states, "In this world," and so forth.
At the assembly on Vulture Peak, whether they were ordinary beings or sages, all saw eighteen thousand worlds within the light; in each of these worlds, from the hells at the bottom...

Reaching upward as far as the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), within the radiance of each and every world, he saw sentient beings in the hells being subjected to boiling cauldrons and glowing embers, copper dogs and iron snakes, the Sword-Tree and the Blade-Mountain, and the fierce flames of fiery furnaces; day and night, they die ten thousand times and are reborn ten thousand times.

They undergo immeasurable suffering. Furthermore, he sees those in the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*), with flaming hair and mouths like torches, whose throats are as narrow as needles so that not even a drop of water can pass through;
they suffer from hunger and thirst. When they encounter food and wish to eat, it turns into fierce flames; when they approach a river wishing to drink, it transforms into molten copper.
He also sees those in the realm of animals (*tiryagyoni*), covered in fur and bearing horns, who are subjected to beatings with staves and whips, yet are unable to speak.

They experience various sufferings and afflictions. Furthermore, they see among human beings the suffering of birth, old age, sickness, and death; the suffering of separation from the beloved; the suffering of encountering the hated; and the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.

They also see the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), and the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). These are the sufferings of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) above.

Furthermore, they see that in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) there are wild beasts, venomous insects, and the like. They also see the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Moreover, they see that for all hungry ghosts (*preta*), fire blazes upon their heads.

Regarding the phrase "six," this is the name for the number; it explains the word *ṣaṭ* (six). Regarding "destinations" (*gati*), this is the word *gati*; these six locations are the places where sentient beings go toward and take refuge, hence they are called "destinations.
This clarifies that the term is derived from the essential nature of the realms, destinies, and births. Question: Is it not the case that the celestial palaces are [the destinations]?
The eight precepts are the destination to which one goes. Hell is the destination to which those who commit transgressions go. Answer:

This interpretation refers merely to the instruments of the destination, not the essence of the destination itself. It is not like taking up a body that receives the fruits of retribution within the six destinies in the future;
rather, it is the hell-body itself that constitutes the destination. Sentient beings who have committed evil karma in their present life are the agents who go [to that destination]. In the future...
The hellish body is the destination for sentient beings who have committed evil in this life;

the future hungry ghost body is the destination, and the karma of stinginess is the means by which they go there. The future hungry ghost body is the place of refuge for sentient beings who have practiced stinginess in this life.
The future animal body—covered in fur and bearing horns—is the destination; it is for those who have been shameless and... in this life.

Those sentient beings who possess shamelessness and lack of remorse for evil karma are the ones who will take rebirth as animals in the future; this is the destination to which such shameless and unremorseful beings of the present life go.

Those who in this life take the five precepts are the ones who will take rebirth as humans with round heads and square feet in the future; this is the destination to which they go. Those who in this life...
[receive the five precepts] are the ones who will take rebirth as radiant and sovereign devas in the future; this is the destination to which they go. In this life... [receive the five precepts].
Taking up the eight precepts constitutes the body that is capable of proceeding.
Regarding the statement that the five aggregates are "provisional" and that afflictions and so forth arise: afflictions and karma are what constitute the capacity to proceed.
When afflictions and karma have not yet arisen, one does not yet know the destination to which one will return. Once afflictions and karma arise, [one enters] the six realms of existence.
The "middle" is the place where sentient beings take refuge. Just as wholesome formations, preceded by ignorance, accumulate the seeds of the five fruits;

these are bound together in one place, moistened by craving, and transformed in essence into *bhava* (becoming). Because *bhava* brings about the fruit of future birth, it is called the "place of refuge.
Question: What are called afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma? Answer: Afflictions refer to ignorance (*avidyā*) among the twelve links of dependent origination.

Craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) constitute the afflictions (*kleśa*). Karma consists of the link of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and a portion of the link of existence (*bhava*), which is termed "karma.
It creates and acquires the seeds for the five fruits within the six destinies, causing one to be born in the various locations of the six realms in the future.

Therefore, the afflictions and karma are the "agents of going," while the six realms are the "destinations. Mǔ (Mokṣala) says: "Ignorance (*avidyā*) is like a hostess; the link of volitional formations is like a messenger."
The sons are like the five [factors] beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*); craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) resemble the *karmadāna* (the monk who distributes food);

recording names resembles the link of existence (*bhava*); entering the door of a house where one does not eat resembles the link of birth (*jāti*); and having finished eating resembles the link of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).

Furthermore, among the ten afflictions (*kleśa*), conceptual ignorance (*parikalpita-avidyā*) is that which truly initiates karma, while the others assist in its initiation; within innate [afflictions], greed (*rāga*) truly moistens [the seeds of rebirth], while the others assist in moistening them. Moreover, regarding conceptual [ignorance]:
Among the innate [afflictions], hatred only brings about non-moistening; among the innate, the two views of self-identity and extremes only assist in moistening but do not bring them forth.

As for those that assist the discriminative [afflictions], they all assist in bringing them forth; as for those that are innate, they all assist in moistening. It is through this moistening and bringing forth that [the afflictions arise].
This invites rebirth in the miserable realms (*durgati*). There are three types of karma. First, non-meritorious karma (*apuṇya-karma*) has three grades:
the superior grade invites rebirth in hell; the middling grade invites rebirth as an animal; and the inferior grade invites rebirth as a hungry ghost (*preta*).

These three types of karma are produced by superior-grade ignorance (*avidyā*). Second, meritorious karma (*puṇya-karma*) also has three grades: the inferior grade results in birth in Jambudvīpa and the two eastern and western continents.
The medium grade [of non-concentrated karma] leads to rebirth in the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru); the superior grade leads to rebirth among the gods of the six desire realms (*ṣaḍ-kāmadhātu*).

These three are all produced by medium-grade ignorance (*avidyā*). There are three grades of the three types of immovable karma (*āniñjya-karma*): the inferior grade leads to rebirth in the lower three dhyānas; the medium grade leads to rebirth in the fourth dhyāna;

and the superior grade leads to rebirth in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). These three types of karma are all produced by inferior-grade ignorance. Question: Regarding the distinctions in the moistening of rebirth (*upapatti-parigraha*), what is the general [principle]?

Question: What is meant by "saint" (*ārya*)? Answer: The *Mahā-śāstra* states: First, those who continue the process of rebirth through both manifest fetters (*paryavasthāna*) and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), namely ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Second, those who continue the process of rebirth solely through latent tendencies, namely those who have seen the tracks of the truths (*dṛṣṭasatya*).

If this is so, consider one who, relying on the *anāgamya* concentration, suppresses the nine grades of afflictions of the lower realm and then passes away; since such a person is still an ordinary worldling, how can they be "moistened" by manifest fetters?

Because the lower [stages] have already been subdued, the higher ones have not yet been attained. Since the fundamental meditative absorptions (*mauladhyāna*) do not arise until one has transcended the lower stages, the *anāgamya* (preliminary) concentration subdues the afflictions (*kleśa*).
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "When the body is in a lower stage and one has not yet abandoned the defilements of that lower stage, the afflictions of the higher stages do not manifest.
For those afflictions of a higher stage to potentially manifest before one, it is necessary to have attained the fundamental absorption of that higher stage. It further states: "Attaining..."

Once that concentration has been attained, the various afflictions (*kleśa*)—both those arising through discrimination (*vikalpa-ja*) and those arising simultaneously with birth (*sahaja*)—are all capable of manifesting. There are two interpretations of the answer:
First, it is said that a person in this state certainly does not pass away. One can only pass away after attaining a fundamental dhyāna (*mauladhyāna*), or after falling away from that concentration.

Therefore, the fetters (*paryavasthāna*) and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) act as the moisture for rebirth. Second, it is said that the seeds of the higher stages moisten those of the lower stages.

Regarding seeds that have already been subdued and lack manifest power, although it is said that the fetters (*paryavasthāna*) and latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) provide moisture, this is not necessarily the case for all of them.
For example, regarding the statement on the "track of seeing the truths" (*dṛṣṭasatya*), it is said that moisture occurs solely through the seeds;

yet, this does not preclude that those in the first and second fruits (*phala*) may also possess manifest moisture. Although there is this explanation, the former interpretation is superior. (The above explains that the six destinies are collectively termed "understood").
Regarding the phrase "as stated in the *Bhūmivastu*," etc., this explains below the specific names for the six destinies (*ṣadgati*). Question: What is meant by "heaven" (*deva*)?

Once born there, all requisites for sustaining the body are fully provided; the objects one enjoys are obtained spontaneously and are not like those in the human realm, which must be sought and may not be found.
If it is as stated in the *Bhūmivastu-śāstra*, Chapter Three, that these arise continuously through transformation based on the recollection of trees...
First, the Heaven of Natural Reception (*Arūpyadhātu*); second, the Heaven of Radiant Sovereignty (*Rūpadhātu*); third, the Heaven of Spiritual Function (*Ārūpyadhātu*).

Because there is no form (*arūpa*), it is not called "radiant. What is termed "spiritual function" appears to be the power of karma rather than supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); thus it is named "spiritual function."

Regarding the statement, "The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says... and so forth: Question: What is meant by a "human" (*puruṣa*)? Answer: A human is explained through three meanings. In Sanskrit, it is called *manu*; this is translated here as "human.
First, they are called humans because they possess much thought (*manas*). Among the various realms of existence, the human realm possesses the strongest capacity for deliberation.

Those in the hells are so oppressed by suffering that they have no leisure for reflection. Animals merely think of water and grass. Hungry ghosts (preta) are consumed by hunger; because they endure the pangs of hunger and thirst, they lack [the capacity for thought]. Thus, [these other realms] do not [qualify as humans].

Regarding the term "human" (*puruṣa*): Second, the *Sheyun* (攝云) states that it is because of the abundance of kindness; among humans, there is much kindness and virtue. This interpretation is incorrect.
If one discusses kindness and virtue, even animals that raise their offspring possess such kindness. Third, the *Zhengyi* (正義) states: "Because the mind is tranquil, one is called a human. Question:
When comparing humans to devas, the devas are even more tranquil; why then does the text speak of "humans"? Answer: Regarding humans, [it refers to] the three... [triple realms].
Regarding the "evil destinies" (*durgati*): this refers to those who do not aspire to heaven. The *Śāstra* (the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*) states: "Quiescence" (*śānti*) is the principle of *nirvāṇa*.
To realize this principle through the mind is called "mental quiescence" (*citta-śānti*). Secondly, it means not being distracted by extreme suffering or pleasure.

The mental state of those in the three miserable realms (*trāya*) is not quiescent due to their afflictions; the minds of the gods are not quiescent because they experience nothing but pleasure. [These states] do not compare [to true quiescence].
This refers to a human being; it does not refer to one who is not human. One must not use the characters "benevolent" (ren) or "virtuous" (de).

Regarding the statement that the *Yazaxin lun* (Treatise on Miscellaneous Minds) says "following [others]," etc., this explains the meaning of the hungry ghosts (*preta*). They constantly seek from others, yet after seeking for a long time, they do not obtain anything.
They constantly suffer from hunger and emptiness; these are the nine types of *preta* (hungry ghosts), which one should examine.
Regarding the statement in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* that they are "horizontal" (*tiryak*) and so forth, it is also called "animal birth" (*tiryagyoni*). The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"Because their form is horizontal and their movement is likewise horizontal, they are called 'horizontal beings' (*tiryag-yoni*). My analysis is as follows: having the head above and the feet below is termed "horizontal"; [alternatively,] having the head in front and the tail behind—
"Later" refers to what is called "horizontal" (*tiryak*). The new [translation] states that "animals" (*tiryagyoni*) encompass all sentient classes because their movement is horizontal.

Although human movement is also horizontal, because the head is positioned above, humans are not called "horizontal-beings. The term "horizontal-beings" is broad and pervasive. The ancient translations provide four interpretations of "animal" (*tiryak*):

first, "to accumulate" (*chù*), which refers to the human character of scheming (the character is pronounced *móu*, with the second tone); it carries the meaning of accumulation. Second, it is said to mean "to store" (*chù*).

1. *Sheng* (pronounced with the *qu* tone). Third, "domestic animals" (*chùshēng*). This refers to those bound by ropes. 2. *Chù* (pronounced with the *yù* tone). Fourth, "domestic animals. This carries the meaning of being raised or nurtured.

When reading commentaries, one should follow this pronunciation; other pronunciations are incorrect. Question: It may be so for species such as oxen and donkeys, but as for species such as tigers, foxes, and wolves, who would raise them?
Answer: For the most part, they are designated as "domestic animals" because they are raised. Second interpretation: They are simply... [text ends]
If people do not nurture others, there is no one who cannot be nurtured. For example, Master Chou raised tigers;
originally, oxen and horses are also wild creatures, yet once they submit to the Way, they are driven to plow the fields and immediately become docile.
Regarding the phrase "predominantly loathsome," etc., this refers to what is predominantly loathsome and unpleasant; this is the explanation from the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*.

Regarding the statement on the "substantial essence" (svabhāva), the phrase "all six destinies (*gati*) consist of... correctly identifies the essence of the destinies. This is stated according to their predominant characteristics;

in reality, however, they possess all three categories (*skandha*, *dhātu*, *āyatana*) as their essence. There are three types of maturation (*vipāka*): first, that which matures at a different time, where the cause and fruit are distinct; this is called... [text fragment ends].

First, maturation as the ripening that recompenses the cause; this is called "maturation" (*vipāka*). Second, maturation through transformation; because the cause undergoes transformation, it is called "transformation," and since the fruit only then matures, it is called "maturation.
Third, maturation as a different category; a virtuous or non-virtuous cause produces a neutral fruit, such that the cause and the fruit are of different types.

It is called "differentiation" (*visabhāga*). When the fruit ripens to repay the cause, it is called "ripening" (*vipāka*). Question: Why is only the eighth consciousness, the *vipākavijñāna*, taken as the substantial entity of the destinies (*gati*) and births (*upapatti*)?
Answer: Because it possesses four characteristics, it is designated as the substance of the destinies and births. First, the characteristic of being real (*dravya-sat*):

This excludes the Sarvāstivādins, who hold that the destinies and births have as their substance the conventional phenomena of the homogeneous character (*nikāyasabhāga*) and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). Now, the eighth consciousness is real; therefore, it constitutes the substance of the destinies. Question:
The eighth [category] already possesses the meaning of reality (*tattvārtha*). The eighth, which is the maturation (*vipāka*), is named the "substance of the destinies" (*gati-bhāva*).

The five material sense-faculties (*indriya*) and the five consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) are also real sense-faculties; they are named the "substance of birth in the destinies. For this reason, the second [category] possesses the meaning of pervasiveness (*vyāpti*), and is thus called the substance of the destinies.

This distinguishes them from the five material sense-faculties and the five consciousnesses, because these do not pervade the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). The five faculties and five consciousnesses are not...

The entity that constitutes the "destiny" (*gati*) is the eighth consciousness alone, because it pervades all three realms; therefore, it is the entity that constitutes the destiny of rebirth. Question:

Since the eighth consciousness pervades the three realms, the eighth consciousness is named the entity of the destiny. Yet the sixth consciousness also pervades the three realms; why is the sixth consciousness not named the entity of the destiny? Answer:

Because this third [consciousness] possesses the quality of constancy (*nitya*), it is named the entity of the destiny. The sixth consciousness, however, enters states such as the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

At times, it is interrupted and does not function; therefore, it is not the essence of a *gati* (destiny). Question: Because the eighth consciousness possesses reality, pervasiveness, and constancy, the eighth is designated as the essence of a *gati*.
Since the seventh consciousness also possesses reality, pervasiveness, and constancy, the seventh consciousness is likewise named the essence of a *gati*.

Answer: This fourth [characteristic] possesses the meaning of being unmixed; therefore, it is called the essence of the destinies (*gati*). The seventh consciousness is of an obscured nature and is thus interspersed with other factors, so it is not the essence of the destinies.
Only the eighth consciousness is non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*); because its realm is unmixed, it possesses these four meanings.

The eighth consciousness is called the "substantial entity of the destination" (*gati*). Question: Even if the eighth consciousness were not exclusively non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), could it still be called the substantial entity of the destination?

Answer: No. If the eighth consciousness were of other natures [such as wholesome or defiled], then both the cause and fruit of transmigration (*pravṛtti*) and cessation (*nivṛtti*) would be impossible to establish.

Only when it is exclusively non-obscured neutral can it be designated as the substantial entity of the destination. As the treatise says: "If the maturation (*vipāka*) were of a wholesome or defiled nature, then transmigration..."
[The process of] cessation and extinction would not be possible.

Regarding the statement "Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says... and so forth: [Question] What scriptural authority states that the eighth consciousness is named the "substance of the destinies" (*gati*)?

[Answer] The commentary states: "Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*," and so forth. "Realms" (*dhātu*) refers to the three realms; "destinies" (*gati*) refers to the five destinies; and "births" (*yoni*) refers to the four modes of birth. These constitute its substance.

This principle must be based on reality. The eighth fascicle of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* states: "The term 'constant' (*nitya*) refers to this consciousness which, from beginningless time, has continued as a single homogeneous stream, always uninterrupted.
It is the fundamental basis for the designation of realms (*dhātu*), destinies (*gati*), and births (*jāti*). By nature, it firmly maintains the seeds."
It is so that [the continuity] may not be lost. This commentary explains that [the ālayavijñāna] constantly revolves like a torrential stream: "The ādānavijñāna is profound and subtle;
all seeds are like a torrential stream. I do not reveal this to the foolish and the ignorant, for fear they might conceptually grasp it as a self."

Question: Regarding these three categories, how do their scopes compare in breadth? Answer: The meaning of "realm" (*dhātu*) is the broadest; it encompasses both sentient and insentient beings, as well as the subject that proceeds and the object toward which one proceeds.

Next, the meaning of "nature" (*gotra*) is broader; although it consists solely of nature, it extends to both the subject and the object of progression. Finally, the meaning of "lineage" (*vamsa*) is the narrowest, as it refers exclusively to the object of progression.

Regarding the statement, "Furthermore, this consciousness is sufficient to serve as the *dhātu* [constituent], etc.," this refers to the first section of this treatise where the author refutes the Hīnayāna attachment to the existence of a real life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) that is neither form (*rūpa*) nor mind (*citta*).

The master refutes it by saying: "Moreover, since it has already been established that form is not separate from consciousness, there should likewise be no distinct life-faculty apart from consciousness.
The life-faculty is simply 'vitality' (*āyus*) among the three factors, while form is simply 'warmth' (*uṣman*) among those same three factors."
Universally, among these three factors, vitality (āyus) subsumes matter (rūpa). Apart from consciousness (vijñāna), the substance of matter lacks the life-faculty (jīvitendriya).

If the three factors were to exclude matter, they would necessarily become merely nominal. Furthermore, it is refuted as follows: If the life-faculty were a distinct entity from consciousness that exists substantially, then—just like vitality and so forth—it would not be a substantial life-faculty.

Universally, vitality and so forth exist apart from consciousness, yet vitality and so forth are not the life-faculty. If the life-faculty existed apart from consciousness, it ought to be the same [as those cases].

Regarding "life-span" (*āyus*) and so forth: having extensively refuted [the opposing views] previously, it was stated that this consciousness alone suffices as the basis for the realms (*dhātu*), destinies (*gati*), and births (*upapatti*).

Since its essence is the pervasive, constant, and continuous fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*), there is no need for the laborious postulation of a separate, real life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). This [consciousness] possesses three meanings: first, "pervasive," which distinguishes it from the five sensory consciousnesses.
The five consciousnesses do not pervade all realms (*dhātu*) or stages (*bhūmi*). The three—eye, ear, and body—pertain to two realms and two stages;
the nose and tongue consciousnesses pertain to one realm and one stage. "Two are constantly continuous" excludes the sixth consciousness, because it is interrupted during five states.

"Three are maturation fruits (*vipāka-phala*)" excludes the seventh consciousness, because the essence of that consciousness is neither a maturation fruit nor a cause of maturation; furthermore, because it is neither virtuous nor non-virtuous, it is not a cause. This is because...

Because it is obscured by afflictions, it is not a fruit. To state the correct principle: however, based on the seeds that directly produce this consciousness, which are drawn forth by karma and possess distinct functional capacities with a determined duration of abiding, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is conventionally established.

Regarding the statement "furthermore, sentient beings transmigrate," etc., it is stated in the third proof concerning the substance of the realms, destinies, and births within the *Triṃśikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*:
"Furthermore, a sūtra says that sentient beings transmigrate through the five destinies and four modes of birth. If this consciousness did not exist..."

Because the entity of those destinies and births should not exist [as such]. That is to say, only if there were a truly existent, permanent, pervasive, and unmixed dharma could one establish a "truly real" destiny or birth;

this must possess four characteristics: (1) it is truly existent, which excludes non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) and conventional phenomena (*prajñapti-dharma*); (2) it is eternally continuous, which excludes the sixth [consciousness] which is intermittent;

(3) it pervades the five consciousnesses and the matter of maturation (*vipāka-rūpa*), yet does not pervade all realms (*dhātu*) or stages (*bhūmi*), and thus (4) it is unmixed, which distinguishes one destiny from another.

Because it gives rise to other dharmas. For example, when a body born in the desire realm produces the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) of the form realm and so forth, these are collectively termed "mixed" (*miśra*);
this refers to the arising of dharmas belonging to other destinies (*gati*). The birth in various destinies is not like this, for there would be the fault of two destinies arising simultaneously.

Therefore, the treatise states that it is not a ripening dharma (*vipāka-dharma*). If destinies were mixed, one would arise in this [present] destiny while giving rise to the dharmas of other destinies.
Regarding the term "vipāka" (maturation): it is called vipāka because it matures as something of a different category.

It refers to the eighth consciousness, which is of an unobscured-neutral nature (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), receiving the fruit of karma created by the preceding six types of wholesome and unwholesome minds and mental factors.

Because the cause comprises both the wholesome and the unwholesome while the fruit is exclusively neutral, the difference in nature between cause and effect constitutes "maturation" (*vipāka*). Furthermore, it is called vipāka because it matures at a different time; having been performed in the past...

Karma: when the fruit is experienced in the present, the cause and effect occur at different times; this is termed "maturation" (*vipāka*). Its substance is the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).

Regarding the terms "opening" and "closing": because the sutras contain the term "six destinies" (*ṣadgati*), while various sacred teachings speak of "five destinies," the Master of the Commentary (*ṭīkākāra*) discusses these here in terms of opening and closing.
This is why the Master extensively brings forth various dharmas, arranging them in sequence to clarify their distinctions.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that the six destinies (*ṣadgati*) are collectively categorized as one class: when all sentient beings within the three realms (*tridhātu*) transition into the aggregates (*skandha*), it is called "birth into the aggregates";
if they perish and cease, it is called "death. Question: Why is it not said "death and birth," but rather just "death"? Answer: Because births are more numerous.
Death is few; birth is many. If one considers that all things undergo birth, there are many varieties. Death, however, is of only one kind.
Birth varies according to the different modes of womb, egg, moisture, and transformation; because birth is manifold, it is listed first. Because death is uniform, it is listed last.
In the course of this discussion, it is further divided into two: namely, the "wholesome" (kuśala). All humans and devas are called the "wholesome realms" (sugati).

The three miserable states (apāya) are called the "unwholesome realms" (durgati). The two realms of humans and devas are termed "wholesome realms" because they are summoned and experienced as the result of wholesome karma (*kuśala-karma*).

The three miserable states are termed "unwholesome realms" because they are summoned and experienced as the result of unwholesome karma (*akuśala-karma*). Their essential nature, however, is neither wholesome nor unwholesome, because the resultant form and mind (*vipāka-rūpa-citta*) are all indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Only...
The *Vijñānakāya* states: That which is beneficial and conducive in both this life and future lives is called "wholesome" (*kuśala*).

Although the pleasant fruits of humans and devas are beneficial in this life, they are not so in future lives; therefore, they are not called wholesome, for they involve decline in subsequent existences and thus do not benefit both periods.
That which is detrimental and obstructive in both periods is called "unwholesome. [This applies to] the five destinies (*pañca-gati*).
As for the fruit of suffering: although it can cause harm and opposition in this life, because it does not do so in other lives, it is not called "wholesome.

Regarding the phrase "segmented birth and death" (*paricchinna-jarā-maraṇa*) and so forth, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Furthermore, the continuity of birth and death arises from internal causes and conditions."

It does not depend on external conditions; therefore, there is only consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*). Because it is based upon and conditioned by contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) karma that it directly brings about birth and death (*saṃsāra*), it is called the "cause.

As for "conditions," these refer to the two obstacles—the afflictive obstacle (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)—which assist in bringing about birth and death, and are therefore called "conditions."
Therefore, it is said that there are two types of birth and death. First, regarding the "segmented" (fen-duan):

as for the explanation of its name, this refers to the coarse, heterogeneous maturation fruits (*vipāka-phala*) of the three realms, which are produced by various contaminated (*sāsrava*) wholesome and unwholesome karmas through the auxiliary power of the affliction-obscuration (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Because the duration of the body and life has fixed limits according to the force of causes and conditions, it is called "segmented. "Segment" (*fen*) means a fixed limit; that is to say—

The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). "Segment" (*bhāga*) refers to differentiation; it is of the nature of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). Because this body of the five aggregates has limits, it is called "segmented" (*pratibhāga*);

this is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive) compound. Furthermore, it is said: "This 'segmented' [life] is exclusively the life-faculty; according to its causes and conditions, it possesses a fixed limit."

It is both "divided" (*bhāga*) and "segmented" (*khanda*). It is a *karmadhāraya* compound. It is acquired through the creation of prior karma. It has fixed limits of one year or one hundred years, and the physical form is long;
this applies even to the various devas. This is called "segmented birth-and-death" (*paricchinna-bhava*). Regarding the statement on its essential nature: it refers to segmented birth-and-death.
It takes exclusively the eighth *vipākavijñāna* (retributive consciousness) and the other *vipākavijñānas* as its substance, consisting of four aggregates (*skandha*) or five aggregates.
In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), it consists of five aggregates; in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), it consists of four aggregates. Question:

Since there is "meditative-resultant matter" (*samāpattiphala-rūpa*) in the formless realm, may it not be said that [the retributive consciousness] consists of five aggregates? Answer: No. The "segmental body" (*prādeśika-kāya*) is spoken of only in reference to the body resulting from karma.

It does not take the form of matter produced by meditative concentration (*samādhija-rūpa*) as its essence; rather, its essence consists of the four aggregates (*catur-skandha*). The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that its essence is the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), coarse (*audārika*), and maturational (*vipāka*) fruit of the three realms.

Question: What is meant by "coarse maturational fruit"? Answer: There are four explanations. First, it is called "coarse" because it is easily visible. Second, because it has fixed limits. Third, because it is easy to discern.
Fourth, because it is commonly known by both those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). Thus, it is termed "coarse maturational fruit."
The matured [state] has the five aggregates as its substance. Regarding the statement that it clarifies the causes capable of inducing [rebirth]:

"segmented" refers to the seeds of the five factors—such as consciousness—which are perfumed by names and phrases, acting as the direct cause. The three types of karma—meritorious, non-meritorious, and immovable—act as the conditions that induce [the result].
All afflictions act as the conditions for initiating karma and moistening rebirth. Because birth is obtained through their conjunction, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* asks:

Just as with grasping (*upādāna*) as a condition, tainted karma (*sāsrava-karman*) acts as the cause for the arising of the three realms of existence (*tri-bhava*), which is termed "segmented" (*paricchinna*).
Why is it contradictory that [the sūtras] do not state that consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the other four [aggregates] are the direct seeds (*pratyakṣa-bīja*)? Answer:

Those sūtras and śāstras conceal those direct seeds and instead cite only the external conditions, the predominant factors, and the causal conditions; therefore, there is no fault. The *Mahāśāstra* and others explain that wholesome and unwholesome karma...

The primary cause for the actualization [of rebirth] is the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), which act as the conditions that assist in the actualization of the desirable and undesirable matured fruits (*vipākaphala*) within the three realms.

That which is actualized by the twelve links consists of: ignorance (*avidyā*) as the primary factor in initiating karma; and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*)—which arise simultaneously with it—as the primary factors in moistening rebirth.

Thus, from beginningless time, the cycle of transmigration continues without interruption. Furthermore, the link of formative action (*saṃskāra*) is the primary cause for actualization, while the three links of ignorance, craving, and grasping [act as its conditions].

They serve as conditions and aids. The five links beginning with consciousness constitute the seeds of *paricchinna-utpāda* (segmented birth and death). The links of birth and old age/death constitute the fruit of *paricchinna-utpāda*.
Regarding the four categories of persons: Question: What kind of person undergoes *paricchinna-utpāda*? Answer: All ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) possess *paricchinna-utpāda*.
Furthermore, those who have attained the first three fruits of the path and have not yet turned their minds toward awakening likewise experience only *paricchinna-utpāda*. As for the fourth fruit...

When a person has not entered *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and has not turned their mind [toward the Mahāyāna], yet the body that serves as the basis for suffering still remains, this is collectively termed "segmented" (*paricchinna*) birth-and-death. Question:

When an Arhat discards his robes and bowl and performs the method for prolonging life so that the body remains for a long time, what is this called in terms of birth-and-death? Answer: It is also called segmented birth-and-death.
This is because all members of the same class of noble ones perceive it as such; it is like taking an elixir of immortality to cause the body to remain for a long time. Collectively...

This is called "segmented" (bheda). Furthermore, for Bodhisattvas prior to the stages [of the ten bhūmis] who have attained sudden enlightenment, from the seven stages of expedient means (*upāya*) until they have not yet entered the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), as well as for those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*) who have turned their minds [toward Mahāyāna], all such states prior to the stages are collectively termed "segmented.

Moreover, even for those whose compassion and wisdom are equal, there is still "segmented" existence during the first three stages, so long as they have not entered the "transformation" (*parināma*) birth. If it is only Bodhisattvas in whom compassion predominates who do not fear birth and death, then [the seventh stage...]
The stages prior to the eighth ground are also called "segmented birth and death" (*paricchinna-jarāmaraṇa*). There are none who, from the eighth ground upward, receive a segmented body;
they have all entered into "transformative birth and death" (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*).

To speak of "transformative birth and death" is an explanation of its name: "transformation" (*pariṇāma*) has the meaning of alteration, and "change" (*pariṇati*) has the meaning of transition; it refers to the alteration and transition of the old.
Because one transforms coarse and inferior birth-and-death into this subtle, wondrous, and superior birth-and-death, it is called "transformation" (*pariṇāma*).

Furthermore, because one alters the limited body of a previous sentient being into an unlimited body, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "By the power of compassion and vows, one transforms and sustains life;
because there is no fixed limit, it is called transformation birth-and-death. Question: Since there is no fixed limit for the body and life, [how is it so?]
For a long duration. What is meant by "birth and death"? Answer: That which is sustained and increased is called "birth"; when its momentum is about to be exhausted, it is called "death.

This refers to a Bodhisattva who possesses the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*). Knowing that his body is about to pass away, he employs meditative concentration and vows to sustain the life-span of his body for a certain number of kalpas; this is called "birth.

When his vow is fulfilled and the limit of his concentrated body is reached, it is figuratively termed "death," whereupon he enters the untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*). Furthermore, it is also "sustenance" (*āhāra*).

Second, regarding the essential nature (*ātman*): Question: What dharma constitutes the essence of the *pariṇāma-vipariṇāma-jarāmaraṇa* (transformation-death)? Answer: Primarily, it takes the eighth consciousness, the *vipākavijñāna*, as its essence;

concurrently, it also encompasses the other consciousnesses, taking the five *skandhas* of maturation (*vipāka*) as its essence. The *Lun-chao* (Commentary on the Treatise) states: "It refers to the subtle, neutral (*avyākṛta*), and matured [states] within the desire and form realms. Question:
Why is it not said that the four *skandhas* constitute its essence, but rather that the five *skandhas* constitute its essence? Answer: Because there is no... [text ends].
Form has no segmentation, because the form-body undergoes transformation. It does not exist in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), because it enters into transformation (*pariṇāma*).

It does not have the four aggregates as its essence. Regarding the statement that it is "the cause capable of inducing transformation," one asks: what dharma serves as the inducing cause for the death-rebirth of transformation? The answer is:

the seeds of the five resultant members, beginning with grasping (*upādāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), serve as the direct cause. [This includes] the meritorious karma of the desire realm and the form...

Regarding the immovable karma of the realms: with the exception of the karma of the non-percipient beings and the Pure Abodes, the immovable karma of other gods and so forth serves as the proximate superior condition.

The meditative absorption and vows associated with compassion and wisdom—attained subsequent to the realization of the uncontaminated state and based upon the four dhyānas while taking phenomena as objects—serve as the remote superior condition.

Furthermore, by means of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), one perceives Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and sentient beings as truly existent, thereby giving rise to compassion and vows; this also constitutes [a condition].
Because this [body] must be severed in order to remain for a long duration, the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) can serve as its condition. Question:
The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states that the untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*) is the cause and the cognitive obstructions are the condition for the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*).

Why, then, is it said here that the seeds of verbal designations (*nāma-vikalpa-bīja*) are the cause and immovable karma (*āniñjya-karma*) etc. are the proximate conditions? Answer: The Sūtra conceals that which is supported (the cause) and mentions only that which supports (the condition).

Because there are both proximate and remote conditions, there is no fault. Question: Since there is already a direct cause and the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), why is it necessary to further employ uncontaminated karma (*anāsrava-karman*) as a cause?
Answer: If there were no uncontaminated [karma], there would be no condition capable of inducing the transformation of birth-and-death (*pariṇāmi-jāti-maraṇa*).

Therefore, one must rely on these resources; thus, it is necessary to have uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) karma as a remote cause (*viprakṛṣṭa-hetu*) for the induction of the transformation birth (*nairmāṇika-jāti*).

Now, the explanation is as follows: Question: What dharma serves as the direct cause (*hetu-pratyaya*)? Answer: It is said that the uncontaminated "subsequent existence" (*pṛṣṭha-labdha*) and discriminating karma (*savikalpa-karma*) act as the cause, while the object of cognition (*ālambana*) acts as the assisting condition (*pratyaya*) to induce the transformation birth. Question: How is the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) taken as a condition?
With untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*) as the cause, one experiences a transformational birth (*pariṇāmi-jāti*). The answer is:

the Bodhisattva does not realize that bodhi is not something to be sought, nor that sentient beings are like illusions and not something to be delivered. Consequently, they grasp at bodhi as truly something to be sought and sentient beings as truly deliverable;

this is the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) consisting of attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*). Thereupon, they give rise to compassionate vows, intending to seek bodhi above and deliver sentient beings below. Its...
When a Bodhisattva’s own body, consisting of a single period of segmented existence (*kalala-ātmabhāva*), is about to end, they fear the severance of the physical form.

Furthermore, because there is no longer the affliction of initiating new karma (*karmābhisamskāra-kleśa*), they fear that without a body they would be unable to seek enlightenment or deliver sentient beings. Consequently, they enter a superior meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and give rise to uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) karma involving conceptual discrimination (*savikalpa-karma*).

By utilizing this to support their prior karma, they cause the body to endure for a long time so as to seek enlightenment and deliver sentient beings; upon emerging from concentration, they obtain [the result].

Because it is the subtle body of transformation (*pariṇāma-kāya*), we know that it necessarily takes the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) as its condition and uncontaminated karma (*anāsrava-karma*) as its cause to bring about birth-and-death through transformation.

Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Since one has not yet fully realized signless great compassion, and does not grasp at awakening or sentient beings as being substantially real, one lacks the capacity to give rise to intense compassionate vows; therefore, one provisionally takes the cognitive obstructions as a condition for uncontaminated [karma]."

Karma is the cause that brings about the birth-and-death of transformation (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*). Fourth, regarding persons: the question is, within the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, what kind of person enters into the birth-and-death of transformation?

The answer has two interpretations: first, sudden enlightenment (*tad-ekavāra-abhisambodhi*); second, gradual enlightenment (*anupūrva-abhisambodhi*). Regarding sudden enlightenment, there are three types.
First, those for whom wisdom increases enter at the first stage (*bhūmi*). Second, those for whom compassion alone increases enter at the beginning of the eighth stage.

Regarding those for whom compassion and wisdom are equal, there are two types: if they fear the afflictions (*kleśa*), they enter at the first stage; if they do not fear the afflictions, they enter from the second or third stage.

As for those who attain gradual awakening, it is permitted that all five fruits may turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna]; those who turn their minds from the first fruit require eighty thousand *kalpas* to reach the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*).

Regarding the initial stage: eighty thousand kalpas constitute the beginning, at which point one enters the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya). The same applies to those in the second, third, and fourth fruits; it is permitted that all may enter. Question:
When those in the first fruit turn their minds toward enlightenment, do they immediately enter the transformation body? Answer: It is not necessarily so; this depends on conditions.
Furthermore, there is the body of segmented existence (*prādeśika-kāya*) consisting of seven births, wherein one wanders back and forth seven times among humans and devas.

For those who fear the afflictions (*kleśa*), they may enter [the path] immediately upon first turning their minds toward awakening; or, having already turned their minds, they may enter after passing through one or two births, up to six births.

It is also possible to enter even while still in the seventh birth of segmented existence. However, it is impossible to enter the state of transformation (*pariṇāma*) after the seventh birth has passed. This is because...

Because there is no eighth birth in the *paricchinna-bhava* (segmented existence), those who first turn their minds [toward enlightenment] upon attaining the second fruit may also enter *parināmita-śarīra* (transformed existence).
If, after having turned their minds, they undergo one more birth in *paricchinna-bhava*, they may also enter *parināmita-śarīra* during that second birth.

This is because for those in the second fruit who have the nature of coming and going between the human and celestial realms, there is no case where they turn their minds and then enter [the transformed state] during a third or fourth birth.
Regarding those who undergo transformation (*parivṛtti*): it can also be attained by one who has first turned their mind [toward the Mahāyāna] upon reaching the third fruit;

or, being weary of the body in the desire realm, after dying from that body in the desire realm, they receive a body in the form realm and enter [the path] while in that body in the form realm. This also applies to arhats.
It must be that one enters the transformation body (*pariṇāmika-deha*) while still in the physical body.
There is no Arhat who, having already abandoned the body of suffering, subsequently enters the transformation body, because they no longer possess the conditions for rebirth. Question:

If it is granted that those in the first three fruits who turn their minds toward enlightenment enter the transformation body, as well as Bodhisattvas of sudden awakening prior to the seventh stage who enter the transformation body, why do the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* and other texts state that the Arhat...?
The three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*)—those of Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and sovereign Bodhisattvas—are not said to extend to others.

The answer is that this sutra is based on a general classification; it speaks according to the ultimate [state], and thus there is no error. (The above explains the names, the essential nature, the causes capable of producing them, and the persons [who possess them]).
Regarding the statement that these may be expanded into four types, they are: womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born.

Regarding "existence at birth" (*upapatti-bhava*): from the initial entry into the mother's womb, through the five stages within the womb, until the first emergence from the mother's womb, all are termed existence at birth.
Regarding "fundamental existence" (*mūla-bhava*): existence itself is the fundamental; the existence brought about by past karma is called fundamental existence.
The "prior existence" (*pūrvakālabhava*) refers to the period from after birth from the womb until one reaches sixty or seventy years of age, up until the end of life;

all of this is termed prior existence. Regarding the "existence at death" (*maraṇabhava*): at the very moment of relinquishing life, when the eyes roll upward and froth issues from the mouth, it is called existence at death;
that is, the final momentary aggregate of death immediately following the prior existence is termed existence at death. Fourth is the "intermediate existence" (*antarābhava*), which is...

The existence of death (*cyuty-bhava*) follows after, and the existence of birth (*upapatti-bhava*) precedes; because the aggregates (*skandha*) arise in the interval between them, it is called the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*).
Regarding the statement "the four kinds of birth and death," An-guo says: according to the *Anuttara-śraya-sūtra*, [the first] is the birth and death of segmented form (*paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa*).

There are four types of higher [difficulties], illustrated by the metaphor of transformation. They likewise establish four types of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Regarding the four difficulties of the *pariccheda* (segmented) [birth and death]:

first, the difficulty of afflictions (*kleśa*), namely ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*); second, the difficulty of karma (*karman*), namely the entire member of formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and a portion of the member of existence (*bhava*);

third, the difficulty of retribution (*vipāka*), namely the seeds of the five fruits of consciousness (*vijñāna*) as well as birth, old age, death, and a portion of the member of existence; fourth, the difficulty of faults (*doṣa*).

Difficult [to understand]. This refers to birth, abiding, change, and cessation, as well as sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction. Now, upon the body of transformation (*pariṇāma-kāya*), these are used in sequence as metaphors for the four kinds of birth and death established for the *paricchinna-bhava* (segmented existence).

First, "birth and death of expedient means" (*upāya-jāti-maraṇa*) refers to the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), the attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), and so forth, which serve as the expedient means.

Second, "birth and death of causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya-jāti-maraṇa*) refers to the fundamental wisdom that takes as its object the non-outflow (*anāsrava*) karma accompanied by conceptual differentiation.

That which is called "non-conceptual activity" refers to the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) taking names as its object; this is called "conceptual activity. It is called the "condition of causes" (*hetu-pratyaya*). Regarding the third point, "existence within existence" (*bhava-bhava*):
this refers to the body of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) in the context of the transformation-death (*pariṇāmi-cyuti*).

This constitutes one layer of existence. Above this, there are further the three characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing; furthermore, this [transformation-death] constitutes a lower layer of existence. That which exists above this layer of existence is called "existence within existence. Fourth.
Regarding "there is no birth-and-death": there is no further coarse result of suffering as a subsequent fruit; therefore, it is called "no birth-and-death.
As for the statement "or opening five [realms]," this excludes the realm of asuras.
Regarding the statement that "some open [the list] to six," this includes the asuras.

Regarding the statement in the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* that they are "neither devas and so forth," the question is: "To which realm (*gati*) are the asuras subsumed? The answer is: "The *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* and other [texts]."

Regarding the statement, "Now, based on Mahāyāna sūtras and so forth": Question: Among the five types of sacred teachings, which should be taken as authoritative? Answer: The commentary states, "Now, based on Mahāyāna sūtras and so forth.
Regarding the term "six destinies" (*ṣadgati*): this refers to the separate opening of the *asura* destiny within the realm of the heavenly destinies.

Regarding the phrase "their speech and conduct are mostly unreal," one asks: what is the reason for this? Within the realm of celestial beings (*deva-gati*), why is the asura category established separately?

The answer is that the commentary states their speech and conduct are mostly unreal. If a sutra says there are five [realms] and they are included within the celestial realm, it is clearly understood that their conduct does not resemble that of the devas;
thus they are called "non-devas" (*asura*). To say they are ghosts or animals is incorrect. One asks: for what reason do various sutras and treatises state...

As for the *piśāca*: it is categorized as a ghost (*preta*) because it possesses the power of transformation; it is categorized as an animal (*tiryagyoni*) because, according to ancient tradition, it was born from a lion cub;
and it is categorized as a deva by the *Ābhāsvara* devas. Categorization as a deva is correct.

Regarding the statement "as with a person who is not benevolent": the meaning of benevolence (*ren*) and worthiness is compassion, patience, and non-harming; extending one's own self to others is called benevolence.
Since asuras currently lack such benevolent virtue, they are said to be non-benevolent. Because the conduct of asuras is not the conduct of devas, they are subsumed under the category of devas.
The statement that it is "neither a ghost nor the like" refutes divergent views. If it were included among ghosts or animals, why would it not have been stated as "neither a ghost nor an animal"?
Since it is now stated to be "not a deva," it must therefore be included among the devas.

Regarding the statement that [the realms] may be expanded to seven existences (*bhava*): Lu says that the five destinies (*gati*) are the "destinations" (the objects of transition), while the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) is the "means of transition" (the agent of transition).
Because these—the agent and the object—are spoken of together, there are only seven. Question: How is it that karma and the intermediate existence are the "means of transition"? Answer:

Karma has the capacity to produce [existence], and the intermediate existence has the capacity to continue the production [of birth]. The five destinies are the states of abiding in production; thus, the former two serve as the means of transition, while the five [destinies] are the destinations.

"Destinations" (*gati*) are that which is gone toward. Question: Afflictions (*kleśa*) are also capable of being the "goer," for there is no going toward a fruit without being caused by delusion (*moha*).
Why is this not mentioned? Answer: This is stated based on the immediate cause; the remote cause is omitted and thus not mentioned. Question:

Regarding the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) as the "goer," it is not yet clear whether there is an intermediate state for those born into the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Answer: The Mahāsāṃghikas and other schools maintain that there is subtle matter (*rūpa*) [in the formless realm].
They definitively maintain that there is no intermediate state (*antarābhava*) for those born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) according to the Mahāyāna and the Sarvāstivāda.

However, in the desire and form realms, as well as among humans in the three continents, one who has previously cultivated and attained a formless concentration does not leave their original location;

rather, while remaining at a single infinitesimal particle (*paramāṇu*) of earth, they relinquish their retribution-body and receive a body in the formless realm. Furthermore, they do not abandon the human body, but instead transform into various types of beings.

Furthermore, there is no intermediate state (*antarābhava*) according to the Mahāsāṃghika school’s calculation. Those who fall into the Avīci Hell have their birth-bodies sink directly into it; all lack an intermediate state.
For example, when the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra fell into the Avīci Hell, once he was burned and killed, he did not leave his original location but immediately received that hellish body.

The Sarvāstivāda school and the Mahāyāna do not hold this view; rather, they maintain that one sinks from the place of birth because of the extreme rapidity [of the transition], and thus it is so described.

It is non-existent. At the time of being burned and killed and falling [into hell], there is definitely an intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Furthermore, it is said that when reborn in the Western Pure Land, there is likewise no intermediate state.
