Question: The intermediate state is at its longest forty-nine days; yet, there are those who perform the Great Unobstructed Assembly (*maha-amogha-pūjā*), by the power of which extraordinary merit—
After the end of life, one is destined to become a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*). Yet, during the period when the eon is in decline (*kalpa-kṣaya*), there is no place for rebirth.

How is this so? The answer is that only the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states: "For those who have committed the acts of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karman*), after the end of life, it takes half an eon (*ardha-kalpa*) before they reach the Avīci Hell.
Based on this, it is clear that they remain for a long time; thus, an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) must exist. Since it specifies "half an eon," it is evident that this refers to the Mahāyāna.

There is no restriction regarding the duration of time; why then limit it to forty-nine days? Consider, for example, the case of a universal monarch (cakravartin) who may remain in the intermediate state (antarābhava) for as long as one kalpa before finally taking birth.
Regarding the statement that "delusion is expanded into nine types," this refers to adding two further categories to the previously mentioned seven stations of consciousness (*vijñāna-sthiti*).

As for a "station of consciousness," it is a state where, while not yet dwelling, one desires to dwell; and once having dwelt, one does not wish to depart from the characteristics of that station of consciousness.
The seven stations of consciousness consist of: (1) diversity of body and diversity of perception, which refers to the humans and devas of the desire realm who experience both joy and sorrow.

They differ. Their physical forms are also distinct. In the three continents of the south, the sizes of their bodies are unequal; this is called "difference of body" (*kāya-nānātva*). Their thoughts and perceptions are not uniform;

this is called "difference of perception" (*saṃjñā-nānātva*). Among the gods of the six heavens of the desire realm, there are differences in the size of their forms; this is called "difference of body.
When elder-born devas perceive the five signs of decline, they experience sorrow and suffering, whereas newly born devas experience joy; this is called "difference of perception."
Furthermore, the second type is "different bodies but a single perception. This refers to the first Brahmā King of the First Dhyāna at the beginning of the kalpa’s formation.

He dwelt alone for ten kalpas, then thought of the gods of the Brahma-purohitas and the Brahma-pārṣadyas, who subsequently came to be born there. The Brahmā King thought, "I was able to bring them into existence.

Later, those newly born gods developed the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*) and knew that the Brahmā King had had this thought; they also said, "We were born from the Brahmā King."

In this [first dhyāna], the perception is the same and the designation is the same. The body of the Brahmā King is superior, while other bodies are inferior; since superiority and inferiority differ, the designations of the bodies are distinct.

In the third [dhyāna], the body is the same but the perception is different; that is to say, in the second dhyāna, the size of the physical bodies is of one kind, so the designation of the bodies is the same.

When a newly born deva sees the fire descending from below, he is struck with fear; however, a deva who has been born there for a long time knows that it will not come to him. Therefore, this is called "diversity of perception" (*saṃjñā-nānātva*).

In the fourth [dhyāna], there is "unity of body and unity of perception" (*eka-kāya eka-saṃjñā*); that is, because all share the same perception of bliss in the third dhyāna, it is called "unity of perception," and because their physical forms are of one kind, it is called "unity of body.
Adding the three heavens of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, and the sphere of nothingness, these constitute the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñāna-sthiti*).

[The consciousness] dwells there. Question: What is it that causes the consciousness not to delight in dwelling? Answer: Within the three miserable realms (trāya), suffering is abundant and joy is meager;
this is detrimental to the consciousness, so the consciousness does not delight in dwelling there. In the fourth dhyāna, both ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) and noble ones (ārya) are born together.

When ordinary beings are born into the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva-deva), that heaven is mostly inhabited by non-Buddhists (tīrthika). Furthermore, when noble ones extinguish their mental conceptions, they are born into the fifth... [heaven].
As for the Śuddhāvāsa deities: those gods are mostly *anāgāmins* of fixed nature who have turned their backs on birth and death (*saṃsāra*) and seek to realize *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*;

therefore, they are not established as stations of consciousness (*vijñāna-sthiti*). Furthermore, some say that because the fourth dhyāna possesses pure equanimity (*upekṣā-pariśuddhi*) and lacks a mind that dwells in pleasure (*sukha*), it is not established as a station of consciousness.

Upon the aforementioned seven stations of consciousness, one additionally designates the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*) and the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) of the upper realm.
The Heaven of Non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva*) constitutes the ninth abode of sentient beings. Question: Why are these two heavens further established as "abodes"? Answer:

Because the minds of the gods in the Heaven of Non-perception are subtle and weak, and because they lack the mind of joy (*nirāmiṣa*), they are established as an abode. Because the minds of the gods in the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) are dull and weak, they are likewise established as an abode despite lacking joy.
Thus, the verse in the *Abhidharmakośa* says: [The verse follows: "Because their minds are subtle and weak, and because they lack joy, these two are established as abodes."

There are those with different bodies and different perceptions; those with different bodies and identical perception; the opposite of these, with identical body and perception; and the lower three formless realms.

Thus, there are seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*). The others are not [stations] because they involve impairment. One should know that this includes the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*).
These are the nine abodes of sentient beings; others are not places where one dwells with delight.

As for the statement that they may be expanded into twenty-five and so forth: the four continents, the four evil destinies, the Brahmā kings, the six heavens of the desire realm, the non-percipient beings, the Pure Abodes, the four formless attainments, and the four dhyānas—these are called the twenty-five types of sentient beings. The Brahmā king is the divine sovereign.

Because they are distinct, the Brahma King is mentioned separately within the First Dhyāna; likewise, the Heaven of Non-conceptualization is where non-Buddhist practitioners dwell, while the Pure Abodes are where noble sages reside.

This is why the doctrine of the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*) is specifically taught, as explained at length in the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" chapter (the meaning of the preceding text is thus clarified).

The phrase "the remaining gates are as explained below" refers to the meaning of the other gates. Among the six gates of explanation regarding the meaning of the six destinies (*ṣadgati*), three gates have already been interpreted above;
the locations of the remaining gates and their lifespans, causes, and effects are indicated for explanation in the sixth section of the commentary.
Therefore, it says "as will be explained below. The subsequent commentary indicates the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other such works.
The statement, "This explains the eighteen thousand [worlds] and so forth," is the formal commentary on the scriptural text. Its meaning is as follows:
The World-Honored One emitted light that illuminated the sentient beings of the six destinies within eighteen thousand worlds in the eastern direction. The scripture says: "In this world..."
In this Sahā world, one sees the sentient beings of the six destinies in eighteen thousand worlds to the east [sinking and transmigrating through birth and death].

As for the mention of "one Buddha," the Sūtra says: "Furthermore, one sees the various Buddhas currently residing in those lands. If this refers to the *parabhogika* (enjoyment for others) body, it is as follows.

The ground is of lapis lazuli; golden cords are laid out, with seven rows of trees and seven layers of jeweled nets. Within this, the Buddha further perceives other Buddhas of Enjoyment for Others (*parabhogika-buddha*).
Their eyes are like the waters of the four great oceans, and their *ūrṇā-kośa* (hair-treasure) is like the five Mount Sumerus.

Furthermore, they possess eighty-four thousand marks and signs of excellence (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*). All Buddhas from the third stage (*bhūmi*) onward perceive these collectively. Question: How is this known? Answer: [As stated in the scriptures.]
The jeweled stupa is lofty and sublime, measuring five thousand yojanas; thus we know it belongs to the stages prior to the third bhūmi.

If it were a stupa of the third bhūmi or above, its dimensions would have to be immeasurable. Furthermore, if this world were a great transformation pure land, there would be a Great Transformation Buddha one thousand *zhang* tall.
Moreover, if this world were a transformed impure land, it would be uneven with heights and depths, consisting of earth, stone, and various other elements.
Mountains filled with filth and impurity; the four great continents, the sun and moon, the seven mountain ranges, and the eight seas.
Furthermore, the Buddha is a minor transformation body, possessing the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs. To see the Buddha above is the Jewel of the Buddha.
Regarding the "two dharmas": they are the sūtras and the various sūtra-teachings spoken by the Buddhas; these are the Dharma-Jewel.
For those seeking the state of a śrāvaka, [the Buddha] teaches the Dharma corresponding to the Four Noble Truths and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "these śrāvakas and others," the Sūtra says: "And see those bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs who are intent on practice:
the five contemplations for settling the mind (*pañca-vastuka-vipaśyanā*), the contemplation of specific mindfulness, and the contemplation of general mindfulness.

Question: Why are the upāsakas and upāsikās categorized and extracted here within the section on the Saṃgha? Answer: The commentary states: "The term 'Saṃgha' has the meaning of 'harmony' (*saṃghāta*); it is a single principle."

Harmony. There are two kinds of harmony. Since it is permitted for laypeople to attain the first two fruits [of the path], it is clear that they possess harmony in principle and may also be called *saṃgha*.
Furthermore, some say that the inferior follows the superior; in this case, laymen and women are inferior, while those who have left the household life are superior.

Regarding the statement "cultivation, etc.," there are two interpretations. First: those who have not yet attained [the fruit] are called ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), while those who have attained the fruit are called noble ones (*ārya*).
Second: both ordinary persons and those in the four stages of approach (*pratipannaka*) are called "not yet having attained" because they are each supporting their own respective fruits;
those who abide in the stage of fruition are called "those who have attained the path."
Regarding the statement that "the cause is observed through the eyes" and so forth, Zhen asked: "It may be that the Buddha is seen because his radiant light shines afar;
however, since light does not illuminate sound, how can one hear the Dharma? He replied: "When seeing the Buddha, the light departs from here; when hearing the Dharma, the sound comes from there.
It is for this reason that one is able to hear the Dharma from a distance."
Regarding the phrase "this bodhisattva," one does not perceive a bodhisattva. As the Sūtra says: "Furthermore, one perceives various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Here, according to the school of the *Śāstra*, this is categorized among the seven sections as the fourth: the perception of the fourfold assembly (*catur-parṣad*).

The Master of the Commentary (*Sūtra-vyākhyā*) categorizes it under three [sections], within the appearance of the Triple Gem (*triratna*), specifically under the Sangha, and within that, under the bodhisattvas.
Question: For what purpose does one practice the bodhisattva path? Answer: One practices the bodhisattva path for various causes and conditions.

It is for the sake of seeking the causes and conditions for transcending birth and death; thus, the bodhisattva practices the path for the sake of swiftly realizing the fruit of Buddhahood through these causes and conditions.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva practices the Way for the sake of the causes and conditions for the liberation of sentient beings; it is for this reason that he practices the Bodhisattva path.

Furthermore, due to these various causes and conditions, he practices the Bodhisattva path, whereby he attains entry into the stage of faith and understanding prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*) and the stage of the characteristics of the grounds above.
It is through the preceding cultivation that he subsequently attains these two stages. (The scripture has been explained.)
Regarding the meaning of the term "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*): it does not mean practicing the bodhisattva path through a single cause and condition;
rather, it means practicing the bodhisattva path through various causes and conditions.
Regarding the statement, "seeking to transcend birth and death, etc.": Question: For what reason does a bodhisattva practice the bodhisattva path?

Answer: It is because they perform the three sublime contemplations; this is why they practice the bodhisattva path. Question: What are called the three sublime contemplations? Answer: The commentary states:

"Seeking to transcend birth and death" refers to the mind of weary detachment from the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). This involves upholding the *saṃvara-śīla* (the morality of restraint) and vowing to sever all evil.
One shall attain the Dharma-body. For this cause and condition, one practices the Bodhisattva path.

Regarding the statement "swiftly realizing [enlightenment]," it means upholding the precept of gathering wholesome dharmas and vowing to cultivate all virtues; this is the mind that seeks bodhi. One shall attain the Reward-body (Sambhogakāya).
For this cause and condition, one practices the Bodhisattva path. Regarding the statement "delivering sentient beings," it means upholding the precept of benefiting others.

The precepts for sentient beings consist of the vow to deliver all living beings and the deep mindfulness of the minds of sentient beings; these shall induce the manifestation of transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Regarding the phrase "for this cause and condition," these two lines conclude the three preceding types of sublime contemplation.
With these three kinds of causes and conditions, the path of the Bodhisattva is termed "various."

Regarding the phrase "or for the sake of adornment and purification," etc., these refer to the four types of bodhisattva practice and understanding. The first is the adornment and purification of buddha-fields, which consists of practicing the *pāramitās*.
There are six such practices: first, generosity (*dāna*) to counteract stinginess and greed; second, ethical discipline (*śīla*) to counteract the violation of precepts;

third, patience (*kṣānti*) to counteract anger and resentment; fourth, diligence (*vīrya*) to counteract indolence; fifth, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) to counteract distraction; and sixth, wisdom (*prajñā*).
It remedies ignorance. It is for the sake of the causes and conditions for adorning the Buddha-field that one practices the bodhisattva path.
As for what is called "accomplishing sentient beings," this refers to the practice of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārthacaryā*).

To speak of "cultivating the factors of enlightenment" (bodhipākṣika-dharma) refers to the practice of these factors of enlightenment; it is exclusively the practice of the supernormal powers (abhijñā).

To speak of "practicing for the sake of the four means of attraction" (saṃgrahavastu) and so forth: the four means of attraction are for the benefit of others, while the six perfections (pāramitā) are for one's own benefit.
One practices the bodhisattva path for the sake of establishing the causes and conditions for these two benefits.
The phrase "various such as these" serves to conclude what precedes and introduce what follows.

Its intended meaning is that by means of the various causes and conditions mentioned previously as expedients, one is able to enter the subsequent stage of the characteristics of the state of faith and understanding (*adhimukti*).
Regarding the term "resolute belief" (*adhimukti*): it is asked, how do we know that resolute belief belongs to the stage prior to the [first] bhūmi? It is answered:
as for "resolute belief," since the sūtras do not speak of "realized understanding" (*pratyakṣa-adhigama*) but only of "resolute belief," it is clearly known to be the stage prior to the bhūmis.

Regarding the phrase "believing and understanding," the *Treatise* states: "In this stage, because the Bodhisattva relies upon the four superior powers—the power of the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), the power of mental attention (*manasikāra*), and the power of the provisions (*saṃbhāra*)—he possesses deep faith and understanding in the principle of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*). Nevertheless, he has not yet fully realized the emptiness of the grasper and the grasped;
for the most part, he dwells in the 'external gate' while practicing the Bodhisattva path."

Regarding the phrase "the characteristics of the three karmas and so forth": when practicing on the ground, one should speak of two karmas, because that mental karma (*manas-karman*) lacks physical form.
Mochizuki states: "If it is perceived by the eye or heard by the ear, mental karma is not a formal characteristic (*nimitta*);

however, from the perspective of its objective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*), it is termed a formal characteristic. The two karmas of body and speech are induced by mental karma; such is the practice of the Bodhisattva path."

Regarding the establishment of "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) by taking the general forms and rituals of the three types of action (*trikarma*): this also applies to their specific essential natures (*svabhāva*). It is discussed that the two actions of body and speech possess such forms and rituals. Question:

How is it known that these characteristics belong to those on the stages (*bhūmi*)? Answer: The Master of the Commentary (*ṭīkākāra*) previously revealed that faith and understanding (*adhimukti*) pertain to the stage prior to the stages (*prathamabhūmi-pūrva*).
Since these are characteristics of the stage prior to the stages, they must necessarily correspond to those of the actual stages.
Regarding "speech, appearance, and deportment" (*yan-mao-yi*): [the character for] "appearance" (*mao*) is not read as *jiao* or *fan*.

One must take this specific form of the character as the standard. As for the claim that other forms of the character for appearance are all incorrect: among the various styles of characters, there are correct, variant, and erroneous forms. This particular form is a variant; that other form is erroneous.
To exclude those who are common [to other vehicles], it is said that "none of them are [the true ones].
Regarding the statement "dwelling in the ten stages," a question is asked: "In what position do these bodhisattvas abide while practicing various characteristics?
The answer states in the commentary: "Dwelling in the stages," etc., refers to the six perfections of the bodhisattvas of the ten stages, followed by their subsequent training, and so forth.

Regarding those who have "already attained the fruit of the Way": this refers only to having attained the causal principle and wisdom (*prajñā*) of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*); it does not mean they have already attained the fruit of Buddhahood itself.
As for the phrase "due to various reasons" and so forth, this concludes the first section. [The text] asks: regarding the various causes and conditions mentioned previously...
Regarding the practice of the bodhisattva path through various types of faith-understanding (*adhimukti*) and various characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), what is the resulting fruit?
The commentary answers: "Because one practices the bodhisattva path by means of these various causes and conditions, one enters the two stages.

These are the stages prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*) and those upon the grounds; they are precisely the faith-understandings and characteristics. "Various" (*nānāvidha*) has the meaning of "many kinds. That is to say, throughout...
During the forty stages of mental distraction, one cultivates the six perfections; this is called "various.
Within the stage of signs (*nimitta*), one serves twenty-six *gaṅgā*-sands of Buddhas and subsequently cultivates the myriad practices of the six perfections; this is called "various."

Regarding the phrase "furthermore, by means of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) and so forth," this refers to the second section below, which explains exclusively the characteristics of the resolute belief (*adhimukti*) based on causes and conditions, rather than the practice of the bodhisattva path.
The characteristics of this causal resolute belief are explained individually. As for "causes and conditions": externally, one encounters a virtuous condition;
this "condition" (*pratyaya*) refers specifically to the Buddhas encountered prior to the stages (*bhūmi*). Question: For what reason is a Buddha called a "virtuous condition"?
The commentary quotes a sutra, saying: "A spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) is a great causal condition (hetu-pratyaya). Question:

What is the difference between the "causal condition" in the previous explanation and this "causal condition"? Answer: There is a difference. The "causal condition" in the former case has the sense of "reason" (so-yi), whereas the "causal condition" in the latter case—
This refers to associating with virtuous friends. There is a distinction between these two aspects.

Regarding the phrase "the characteristics of faith and understanding" (*śraddhā-adhimukti-nimitta*): Question: What are called the characteristics of faith and understanding? Answer: Within internal practice, the mental activity (*manas-karman*) is called faith and understanding;
externally, the praise of the Buddha through body and speech is called the characteristics. Thus, the three activities (*tri-karman*) of the bodhisattva are practiced in unison.

Regarding the statement "the mind contemplates the subtle principle," this is the second interpretation. "The mind contemplating the subtle principle" is termed *śraddhā-adhimukti* (faith-understanding).

The practice of giving away one's head, eyes, and so forth, throughout the stages from the first ground (*bhūmi*) up to before the tenth ground, is termed the "manifestation" (*nimitta*). This refers to the cultivation of the path (*bhāvanāmārga*) within the ten grounds. The latter two interpretations do not [apply here].
This distinguishes the stages; it merely implies that [the stage of] "dark penetration" (*andong*) refers to the stages prior to the first bhūmi.

If one speaks in terms of general characteristics, the practice of a Bodhisattva on the ten bhūmis consists of both faith-understanding (*śraddhā-adhimukti*) and marks (*nimitta*), and the practice of a Bodhisattva prior to the bhūmis likewise consists of both faith-understanding and marks.

The *Śū* (Commentary) explains based on the manifest state: those prior to the bhūmis are called "faith-understanding," while those on the ten bhūmis are called "marks. Thus far, this section has taken up the Bodhi...

The three characters "Bodhisattva Path" (薩道) are explained in one place together with the various causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). Their characteristics of faith and understanding (*adhimukti*) differ from one another.
In the second section, there is only an explanation of the characteristics of faith and understanding regarding causes and conditions, without explaining the practice of the Bodhisattva path.
The preceding two sections are both the explanations of the Master of the Commentary (*śāstrakāra*).
Regarding the statement "discourse relies upon the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) and so forth," there are three successive interpretations by the commentator.

These interpret only the practice of the bodhisattva path and do not explain the remaining phrases. The two previous interpretations were merely general explanations of practicing the bodhisattva path; they were not yet explicit.
Now, each [phrase] will be explained individually as the practice of the bodhisattva path. Question: By what gate of practice does a bodhisattva rely when cultivating the bodhisattva path?

[The text] proceeds. The *Vyākhyā* (Commentary) answers the *Śāstra* (Treatise), stating: "By means of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), the bodhisattva takes these four methods as skillful means to gather in sentient beings.

Regarding the phrase "the characteristics of faith and understanding" (*śraddhādhimukti-nimitta*), [the questioner] asks: "The bodhisattva’s practice does not transcend the conduct of the two benefits [for self and others]. I do not yet understand..."
Under which category of practice are the characteristics of prior *adhimukti* (resolute belief) subsumed? Under which practice is the cultivation of the bodhisattva path included?

The answer, as stated in the commentary (*śāstra*), is: "The characteristics of *adhimukti*, etc. The intention of the commentator (*śāstrakāra*) within this treatise is that since the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) are bodhisattva practices, the characteristics of *adhimukti* are likewise the practices of bodhisattvas both before and after the stages (*bhūmi*). The characteristics of *adhimukti* constitute practices for one's own benefit (*svārtha*). Practice...

The Bodhisattva path is the practice of benefiting others. This refers to the extensive practice of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) characterized by faith and understanding, undertaken for the sake of seeking supreme enlightenment.

Therefore, the six perfections from the stage prior to the [first] bhūmi are called "perfection practices" (*pāramitā-caryā*). From the first bhūmi through the seventh, the six perfections are called "near-perfection practices.
On the eighth, ninth, and tenth bhumis, one does not practice only the six perfections, but cultivates all ten perfections; these are called "great perfections."
The practice of honey is such a practice: it is the single-minded pursuit of enlightenment for one's own benefit, which benefits the path to enlightenment.

Cultivating the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) is called the practice for the benefit of others, because one gathers in sentient beings through these four methods. For those who are impoverished, one gathers them through generosity;

for those who have broken the precepts and so forth, one gathers them through pure ethical discipline. In the bodhisattva’s cultivation, there is no transgressing of self-benefit and the benefit of others.

The gates of practice do not transcend the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) and the six perfections (*pāramitā*). Even if one cultivates the myriad practices, they are all fully subsumed within these four means of integration and six perfections.

Regarding the "four means of integration," this is the initial general designation. "Integration" (*saṃgraha*) means to gather and sustain; it refers to gathering sentient beings by means of four types of methods. Or...

"Comprehension" (*saṃgraha*) means to gather and benefit. One gathers and benefits sentient beings through giving (*dāna*), causing them to achieve accomplishment. Second, the specific explanation of the names: first, regarding "giving" (*dāna*):
the universal extension of the mind is called "spreading" (*dā*); the withholding of oneself to bestow upon others is called "giving" (*na*). This is thus a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.

Regarding "loving speech" (*priyavāditā*): it is called "speech" because it is expressed through vocal sounds; it is called "loving" because those who hear it find joy in their hearts. Here, "love" is the subjective faculty (*ālambaka*) and "speech" is the objective object (*ālambana*);

thus, it is the speech of love. Regarding "beneficial conduct" (*arthacaryā*): "benefit" (*artha*) is a name for the result, and "conduct" (*caryā*) is a name for the cause. Conduct is the cause of benefit, and one receives the fruit of that benefit;

thus, it is the conduct of benefit, following the *tatpuruṣa* compound. Regarding "common purpose" (*samānārthatā*): "common" (*samāna*) has the sense of equality, and "purpose" (*artha*) refers to the task.

This refers to the meaning of "activity" (*karma*). It means that one shares the same activities and conduct as sentient beings; since the action itself is shared, it is a "term expressing both the activity and its possessor" (*dharmadharmivācaka*).
Regarding the phrase "generosity and so forth," the third section explains the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) according to the treatise, which is divided into four parts.

As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 43, and so on, each [means] possesses nine gateways: (1) the essential nature of agreeable speech (*priyavāditā*), (2) all [aspects], (3)... [text fragment].
Difficult practice; (4) all gates; (5) virtuous deeds; (6) all modes; (7) fulfillment of wishes; (8) the three times; and (9) purity.
Furthermore, each of the four means of attraction—generosity, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation—is endowed with these nine gates.

What is cited here in this commentary is entirely incomplete and lacks portions. Regarding the first gate, that of generosity, it is entirely absent from this [text]; it is pointed out in the *Xiang* [commentary].
In the subsequent verses explaining the section on the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), there are thirty-one lines of the bodhisattva path:
the first verse concerns various causes and conditions; seventeen verses concern various characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); and thirteen verses concern various types of resolute belief (*adhimukti*).

Regarding kind speech (*priyavāda*), there are only five gates: the first four and the seventh gate, making five in total. Regarding beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*), there are six, of which the first three...
Seven, eight, nine. Regarding "one [type of] commonality," this refers to the objective basis (*vastu*).

As for the two types of "loving speech" (*priyavāditā*): first, that which is always pleasant to hear, which is to say, being free from harsh and abusive speech; second, that which is truthful, which is to say, being free from false and deceptive speech;

third, that which is in accordance with the Dharma, which is to say, being free from divisive speech; and fourth, that which is meaningful speech—here, "meaning" (*artha*) refers to the ultimate purpose or benefit.
Beneficial speech. There is no frivolous chatter; this is also called not being separated from the avoidance of harsh speech.
Regarding the phrase "being free from frowning and so forth," there are three types of all-encompassing kind speech (*priyavāditā*): first, consoling speech.

When a Bodhisattva sees someone, he first smiles and remains free from a frowning expression; toward those superior to himself, he approaches and inquires after their well-being, and toward those inferior to himself...
This means that life is peaceful.
As for the statement regarding those who proclaim "prosperity" (*śrī*) and so forth, these are two kinds of joyful speech. "Prosperity" (*śrī*) refers to flourishing wealth and nobility.
For one who is content, this is known as wealth and nobility; for one who is discontented, it is not known as such. What was explained above is intended to make this known.
Regarding "speaking without self-awareness": this refers to not knowing that one’s present wealth and nobility were brought about by the practice of giving (*dāna*) in a previous life.

Speaking in order to make others aware of this and to cause them to cultivate giving is called "increasing the wholesome dharma through awakening. Furthermore, "awakening" has the sense of seeing and knowing.

Seeing others practicing giving and maintaining the precepts (*śīla*), one rejoices (*anumodana*) in their future rebirths, praising them to make them joyful; thus, one knows that the former person possesses [the capacity for] hearing [the Dharma].
The sequence proceeds by way of exhortation toward the higher [stages], which is called the "increase of wholesome dharmas.

Regarding the phrase "speaking the Buddha’s teachings and the Dharma," this refers to the three types of speech that bring supreme benefit. Speaking the Buddha’s teachings and the Dharma always serves to bring supreme benefit to sentient beings.
Of the two preceding types [of speech], one follows worldly conventions; based on the latter type, which brings supreme benefit, one accords with the correct teaching of the Dharma.
Regarding the phrase "toward one's own enemies and so forth," this refers to the third type of difficult-to-practice loving speech (*priyavāditā*). Within this, there are three aspects.
First, regarding one's own enemies—those who have come to repay [one's wrongs]—the repayment owed by parents is incomparable to heaven and earth;

the repayment owed by siblings is incomparable to the sun and moon. Toward such persons, one gives rise to a pure intention (*viśuddhacitta*) and does not harbor thoughts of resentment; this is called "purity."
Regarding the phrase "extreme delusion and so forth," this refers to the second intention. At first glance, the commentary (*śāstra*) appears to be removing the doubts of others;
however, this is actually the Bodhisattva removing his own doubts. If he encounters an extremely deluded sentient being, the Bodhisattva reflects:
"I am teaching and transforming him—will I succeed or not? This very thought constitutes a doubt, which is also an obstacle for the Bodhisattva.
When a bodhisattva does not form such thoughts, they have severed doubt. They develop a resolute mind toward all sentient beings and make a vow not to harbor hesitation;
this is called "vowing to eliminate doubt and confusion."

Regarding the phrase "in the true field of merit," etc., this is the third intention. A "true field of merit" refers to making offerings to the Triple Gem and being filial and obedient toward one's parents;
these are called the true field of merit. Now, failing to show respect to the Buddha and failing to be filial toward one's parents is termed deceitful and evil conduct.
Toward such persons, the Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion and preaches the essentials of the Dharma for them, never [failing to do so].
To give rise to resentment, to utter harsh and evil words, and to revile with a single shout—these three types of difficult conduct are therefore called "difficult-to-practice loving speech.

As for the phrase "or removing hindrances and coverings," this refers to the fourth type, "loving speech through all doors. "Hindrances" (āvaraṇa) refers to the two hindrances; "coverings" (nīvaraṇa) [refers to the five hindrances].
This refers to the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*). When a Bodhisattva wishes to instruct sentient beings to eliminate these hindrances, what should be done first? The answer is twofold:

first, one explains the joyful fruits of humans and devas, and causes them to uphold the five precepts and the ten wholesome courses of action; this is called "preliminary practice. This refers to the discussion of what has been accomplished.
The intent is that since such wholesome karma exists, one has obtained this human body; thus, cause and effect are clearly manifest. As it is said: [The text continues with a citation].
Why not remove the hindrances and coverings? Second, for those who wish to remove the hindrances and coverings, one explains the preliminary practice (*pūrvakṛta*).

The initial cultivation of the five contemplations for settling the mind (*pañca-vastu-sthāpana-citta*) is called "preliminary. In relation to the subsequent noble practices of the three vehicles, it is termed "preliminary."
Regarding those whose minds are well-tamed and virtuous, one teaches them the Dharma of the Truths— that is, the True Dharma corresponding to the Four Noble Truths.

Regarding those who are largely heedless— specifically the three types of householders who are heedless— one employs the skillful means of admonition and instruction to cause them to transcend heedlessness and practice non-heedlessness.

Regarding the mention of "those who have doubts": for those who have many doubts concerning various phenomena, he provides discourses on definitive discernment (*viniścaya*) to cause them to be free from doubt.

This concludes the fourth [section], *Affectionate Speech through All Gates*. Next is the fifth, *Affectionate Speech of a Noble Being*, and the sixth, *Affectionate Speech of Every Kind*, which are not cited here in brief.
Regarding the phrase "based on the four pure modes of speech," etc., the seventh is agreeable speech that fulfills requests. The four pure modes of speech are: first, abstaining from false speech;
second, abstaining from harsh speech; third, abstaining from divisive speech; and fourth, abstaining from frivolous speech.

The eight noble modes of speech consist of speaking truthfully regarding what has been seen, heard, sensed, and known, while not claiming to have seen, heard, sensed, or known what was not actually experienced; these are called the eight noble [modes of speech].
Regarding speech: "Noble" means correct meaning. The seventh is the completion of seeking loving speech; the eighth is the loving speech of the two worlds;
the ninth is pure loving speech. These are omitted in the commentary for brevity. Loving speech is thus fully encompassed.
Regarding the statement "the three are beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*) and so forth," this clarifies the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of beneficial conduct.

Regarding the statement "by means of pleasant speech (*priyavāditā*), one first demonstrates the correct principle," a question is raised: what is the difference between the essential nature of beneficial conduct in this context and the essential nature of pleasant speech in the preceding section?
The answer is that they differ in their scope: the aforementioned pleasant speech refers to the teaching (*śāsana*), the principle (*nyāya*), and the practice (*pratipatti*) in a general sense.
Regarding the resultant dharmas: here, in this context of beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*), one causes those of the three vehicles to engage with their respective faculties through cultivation.
Thus, one first uses kind speech (*priyavāditā*) to proclaim the correct principles, causing them to engage in practice and cultivate the paths of the three vehicles.

Furthermore, it is said that one may also seek benefit in accordance with [the recipient's needs] and lead them by means of arts and skills; the former is induction through speech, while this is induction through action.
Regarding the phrase "in accordance with what has been studied" and so forth: (2) it causes one to abandon the mind of seeking fame and profit.
Regarding the phrase "exhorting and subduing": (3) it refers to the joint cultivation of the three trainings and the establishment of the correct practice of the two vehicles.
Regarding the phrase "that which enables one to obtain," etc., this refers to the third category, "all practices. First, concerning that which enables obtaining:

the *Śāstra* states that a bodhisattva bestows three things upon sentient beings—first, dharmas; second, actions (*karman*); and third, qualities (*guṇa*)—thereby causing them to obtain great wealth and high status in the present life. First, regarding "dharmas":
these are magical arts (*vidyā*), such as those for burning gold, silver, and precious gems to produce great benefit. Second, regarding "actions": [this refers to] ritual activities.

As for these, the four classes—officials, farmers, artisans, and merchants—each pursue their respective vocations; by following the path of learning of each person, they cause them to obtain great wealth.

As for the three virtues, one bestows virtue and artistry upon sentient beings; by becoming scholars who have mastered the classics, one causes them to attain the positions of prime minister or regional commander, thereby enabling sentient beings to obtain great wealth and status.

Regarding the statement "benefiting others by encouraging their renunciation": one should use various means to exhort them toward the Path, leading them to renounce the world, abandon wealth and status, and go forth in purity.
Having received the practice of alms-gathering to sustain one's life, this enables them to definitely attain [the goal] and abide in peace;
yet in the present life, it is not fixed.

Regarding the term "benefit for both" (*ubhayārtha*): it refers to various forms of exhortation that lead one to practice the renunciation of desire and attain meditative concentration of the higher stages, whereby body and mind experience joy;
this is called "present benefit. Furthermore, being reborn in the five Pure Abodes (*pañca śuddhāvāsāḥ*) and subsequently attaining liberation is called "benefit for both."
Regarding the statement "associating with evil friends," there are three types of difficult practices for this third [category]. First is associating with evil friends and spiritual mentors.
This class of person does not slander the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Sangha; they simply associate with evil friends and are unwilling to cultivate goodness.
This is called the first difficulty.

Regarding the phrase "being attached to great wealth, status, and so forth": it refers to those who are deeply addicted to their present great wealth and high status, such that they do not move their roots of goodness.
That a bodhisattva is able to practice for their benefit is called the second difficult practice.

Regarding the phrase "the heterodox and their perverse attachments," this refers to those who have left the household life as heterodox practitioners. Because they are deluded and dogmatically attached to their own tenets, these heterodox followers cling to a self;
they follow the practices of deviant views of other paths and, being attached to their own opinions, they harbor hatred toward and turn their backs on the True Dharma.
This is the third difficult practice.

Regarding the statement "constantly giving rise to the eight *paryavasthānas*," there are three types of conduct for seeking gain in the fourth [stage]. First, constantly giving rise to the eight *paryavasthānas*.
The eight *paryavasthānas* are: first, torpor (*styāna*); second, drowsiness (*middha*); third, restlessness (*auddhatya*); fourth, regret (*kaukṛtya*); fifth, envy (*īrṣyā*);

sixth, stinginess (*mātsarya*); seventh, lack of shame (*āhrīkya*); and eighth, lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*). The ten *paryavasthānas* are formed by adding anger (*krodha*) and concealment (*mrakṣa*) to these. When a Bodhisattva sees sentient beings...
When the mind is prone to shamelessness, one should apply skillful means to cause it to be freed from the fetter of non-shame; the same applies to the other seven [fetters].
Regarding the ten unwholesome actions—three of the body, four of speech, and three of the mind—the mind is the root.
By relying on the purity of the three types of action, a bodhisattva is able to exhort and transform all such evil persons, causing them to abandon the ten unwholesome actions.
Regarding the phrase "arousing the mind of great compassion" and so forth: there are five aspects of the fifth [category], the pure beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*).

First, as for "arousing the mind of great compassion": the bodhisattva arouses vast compassion toward all sentient beings; with such an intention manifest before them, they engage in beneficial conduct.
The phrase "although undergoing great suffering and so forth" refers to the second section.

Regarding the beneficial deeds performed by a bodhisattva for all sentient beings, although he undergoes every kind of great suffering and toil, his mind never grows weary; rather, he gives rise to deep joy as he carries out acts of benefit.
The phrase "though dwelling in wealth and status" refers to the third section.

Although the Bodhisattva is foremost among those with wealth and foremost in status, for the sake of transforming sentient beings, he is able to humble himself, acting like a slave, a servant, or even a caṇḍāla.
This is called "Austere Fervor. They shake bells and carry bamboo poles as identifying marks; thus, in the Western Regions, they are considered people of low and evil character.

The meaning is that for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings, Bodhisattvas are able to perform such low and evil deeds, even including acts such as filial piety, acting without pride or self-clinging while carrying out beneficial conduct.

Regarding the phrase "unstained and without hypocrisy," etc., this is the fourth section. It means that toward all sentient beings, the bodhisattva’s mind is free from attachment and devoid of hypocrisy;
with genuine compassion for sentient beings, they carry out beneficial conduct.
Regarding the phrase "the mind of loving-kindness and compassion" and so forth, this is the fifth section.

It means that the Bodhisattva gives rise toward all sentient beings to a mind of compassion that is ultimately and eternally non-retrogressive, constantly acting to rescue and deliver them. (This is the ninth practice of benefit.)

Regarding the statement "the four [means of attraction], such as samānārthatā (common purpose)," among the nine categories of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, there is only the single category of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and not the latter eight categories.
This refers to the aforementioned practice of performing the same actions as all sentient beings.
For instance, if a bodhisattva intends to transform those who drink alcohol, he drinks alcohol; if he intends to transform those who eat meat, he eats meat.
Regarding the phrase "having been taught and having known," the character *yi* (已) is used because its pronunciation is identical [to that of *ji* (既)].
Regarding the phrase "causing them to form this thought," it is because they understand it themselves; therefore, I instruct them to act, for if one does not act oneself, [one cannot lead others].
He then says: "Since he himself does not understand, how can he teach us? This implies that you should first learn from others.
To refute this objection, the Bodhisattva practices it himself. The commentary concludes: "Therefore, one must practice it oneself."

Regarding the statement that "the bodhisattva’s practice of benefiting others is equal," the question is: why is it that among the practices of a bodhisattva, only the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) are clarified?
The answer, as stated in the Commentary (*śāstra*), is: "The bodhisattva’s benefiting of others is equal... [and so forth].
Regarding the term *yuánjì* (圓寂): formerly it was called *nirvāṇa*; in the new [translation], it is called *parinirvāṇa*.

*Pari* has the meaning of "perfect" (*yuán*), and *nirvāṇa* has the meaning of "quiescence" (*jì*). There are three ways to explain *yuánjì*: first, being endowed with the four virtues is called "perfect.

These are the four virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity; being fully possessed of these is called "perfect. "Quiescence" means cessation. To extinguish the defilements of the two obstacles is called "quiescence."

It is called "quiescent" (*śānta*) because it is free from clamor and bustle; that is, since sentient beings are otherwise disturbed by the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), being now free from these two is termed "quiescent.

It is called "perfect" (*paripūrṇa*) because it possesses all virtues; it is so named because it is endowed with the three virtues: the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇaguṇa*), the virtue of knowledge (*jñānaguṇa*), and the virtue of benefit (*anugrahaguṇa*).
Because these three virtues are accomplished based upon *tathatā* (Suchness), it is called "perfect" (*yuan*). Because it is free from the two types of death, it is called "quiescent" (*ji*).

Sentient beings, being conditioned by objects, are deluded by the two deaths; therefore, they are not said to be quiescent. At the stage of fruition, one is free from the two kinds of birth-and-death, and thus it is called quiescent.

It is both perfect and quiescent; this is a *dharmadhāraya* compound (a term that denotes its own function). "Perfect" excludes the ultimate specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), for since specific characteristics are limited, they are not perfect. Question: Why?
This is called "specific characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*). Answer: Water has moisture as its intrinsic nature; fire has heat as its intrinsic nature.

The characteristic of heat does not pervade within the characteristic of moisture, and the characteristic of moisture does not pervade within the characteristic of heat. These, such as water and fire, are phenomena of specific characteristics.

The limited [nature] is attached to its own specific substance; therefore, it is called "partial" and not "perfect. Now, the essence of True Suchness (tathatā) pervades all phenomena because it is their very self-nature (svabhāva).

It is quiescent (śānta) in its distinction from those common characteristics (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa), such as space, suffering, emptiness, and impermanence. Although these qualities pervade all phenomena, they are perfect yet not quiescent;
therefore, it is called "Perfect Quiescence" (yuan-ji).

Regarding the statement "the essence of these four": the question asks what constitutes the essence of the four nirvāṇas. The answer, as stated in the sub-commentary (*śū*), says: "The essence of these four," etc.
Having thoroughly understood the four kinds of nirvāṇa, the author of the sub-commentary then states: "The essence of these four is precisely the Great Nirvāṇa (*mahāparinirvāṇa*)."

If one explains the general name, "nirvāṇa" has the meaning of perfect stillness (*parinirvāṇa*). If one explains the specific names according to their distinct stages, there are four types of nirvāṇa, all of which are generally termed "stillness.

First is *prakṛti-viśuddhi-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa of natural purity), which is stillness by its very nature. Second is *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder), wherein the afflictions are eternally stilled.
Third is *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa without remainder), wherein all sufferings are eternally stilled. Fourth is *apratisthita-nirvāṇa* (non-abiding nirvāṇa).
While functioning, it is eternally quiescent. Furthermore, if explained in terms of its function, it refers to the distinctions among the four types of nirvāṇa;
if explained in terms of its essence, it is simply the single Great Nirvāṇa. The essence of Great Parinirvāṇa is precisely True Suchness (tathatā).

Regarding the statement that "the substance of the one and the four is entirely one": the Master of the Commentary intends to proceed below to explain the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, and thus first discusses True Suchness (*tathatā*).
His intention is to say that the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* is also established upon True Suchness; they are both the single True Suchness.
It is only when True Suchness possesses the three [aspects] that it is designated as *Mahāparinirvāṇa*. That is to say, upon this single True Suchness, [the term] "Mā" is established...

Regarding the statement that the *prajñāpāramitā*, liberation, and the *dharmakāya* can give rise to *pariniṣpanna-bodhi*: Question: Since *tathatā* is a single, unitary reality (*ekalakṣaṇadharma*), how can it possess these three meanings when viewed from the higher perspective?
Answer: The sub-commentary states: "First, it can give rise to *pariniṣpanna-bodhi," etc. This explains the *tathatā* that gives rise [to phenomena] by way of what is produced.

The verbal expression "the essence of *tathatā* (suchness) is principle" means that because it possesses the capacity to give rise to *pariniṣpanna-bodhi* (perfect enlightenment), it is also called "perfect enlightenment.

Question: How can an unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) principle give rise to a conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) wisdom? Answer: This statement regarding "arising" does not refer to the arising of a manifest state (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) from a seed;
rather, it refers to "arising" within the context of the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). There are two senses in which it can "give rise": first, [the sense of being a cause].

The meaning of "basis" (*āśraya*) is explained as "that which gives rise to the limit" (*pratyanta-janaka*). Just as the earth can give rise to all grasses and trees—though the grasses and trees possess their own seeds—it is because they rely upon the earth that the earth receives the name "giver of birth.
Second, it is that which, by serving as an object (*viṣaya*), can draw forth and produce [cognition]. Untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) is also called "that which gives rise to.
The mind does not arise in isolation; it arises only by depending upon an object. Since the arising of wisdom must necessarily depend on being drawn forth by an object, [it is so designated].
For this reason, it is also called Mahāprajñā (Great Wisdom).
Regarding the phrase "the essence is the nature of awakening": Question: True Suchness can only give rise to the wisdom of perfect awakening (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*).

Since the essence of that wisdom is not itself the wisdom of perfect awakening, how can it be named *prajñā*? Answer: The commentary states, "Because its essence is the nature of awakening. This means that while the essence is not itself the act of awakening, it is the nature of awakening.
Because it is the nature of this [wisdom], it is also called Mahāprajñā. It is named Mahāprajñā because it is, first, the nature of awakening, and second, that which can produce awakening.

Regarding the statement "it exists in the stages of the two vehicles," one might ask: does not true suchness also exist within the bodies of those of the two vehicles, and is it not also capable of producing awakening?
"Why is it not called *mahāprajñā* (Great Wisdom)? The commentary answers: "Regarding the stage of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) and so forth:

although the *tathatā* (Suchness) in the stage of the two vehicles has emerged from the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), because it is still covered by the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), this *tathatā* produces only partial awakening (*pratyekabuddha-jñāna*).

It cannot produce perfect awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Since it does not produce perfect awakening, it is not termed 'awakened nature' (*bodhita*). Since it is not termed 'awakened nature,' it is also not termed..."

Regarding the Dharma-body: because the True Suchness (*tathatā*) produced by the two vehicles is not called Mahāprajñā, the True Suchness within the bodies of those of the two vehicles is a conditioned phenomenon (*bhāva*).

It should be produced, whereas the nature of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha-svabhāva*) is real. The thesis (*pakṣa*) and reason (*hetu*) are as follows: "Because they are identical in being unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

The analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like the Perfect Enlightenment within the Buddha-body; the Perfect Enlightenment within the Buddha-body is unconditioned, and that which is unconditioned is designated as "Perfect."

Enlightenment (*bodhi*). Within the bodies of those of the Two Vehicles, this is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); identical to that Buddha-body, it is Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). The refutation by means of the two measures (*pramāṇa*) states:

You admit that the *tathatā* within the bodies of those of the Two Vehicles is a real entity (*dharmin*), yet it certainly cannot give rise to Perfect Enlightenment; this is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is as follows:
Because those obstacles exist, it serves as a common analogy: it is like the *tathatā* within the body of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).

Since the *tathatā* within the body of an ordinary person possesses those two types of obstacles—afflictive (*kleśa*) and cognitive (*jñeya*)—it cannot give rise to the perfect [enlightenment]. This is the same as seeing that the bodies of the Two Vehicles possess those cognitive obstacles;
like those ordinary persons, they lack *pariniṣpanna-bodhi*.

Regarding the phrase "the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra and so forth," it is asked: Prajñā is wisdom (*jñāna*); wisdom is a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) that serves as the means of realization.

How, then, can the *tathatā* (suchness) which is realized be also called "Prajñā"? The answer is provided by the commentator in his sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*), who explains three points regarding the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and other texts.
Following the discussion on *nirvāṇa*, he refers to *tathatā* as "Mahāprajñā. Fearing that people might harbor doubts about this, he cites the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

This is also corroborated by the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. The treatise states: "The teaching is wisdom; it is for the purpose of realizing wisdom. Wisdom abides in the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*);
this principle is the locus upon which wisdom relies. This 'locus' is also called Prajñā. How could this not contradict the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, which takes the principle as wisdom?
Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The intrinsically pure mind is also called unlearned wisdom (*asaikṣa-jñāna*). Mind has two aspects.

It is taught that there are two [kinds of] mind: first, the truly real mind; second, the mind of objective conceptualization (*ālambana-citta*). This refers to the truly real mind which takes *tathatā* (suchness) as its principle.

Because *tathatā* constitutes the nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena, it is called "self-nature" (*svabhāva*). Thus, because *tathatā* is free from the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), it is called "pure.
Since *tathatā* is the nature of the mind, it is called "mind. Therefore, *tathatā* is termed the "intrinsically pure mind" (*prakṛti-viśuddha-citta*). In Sanskrit, it is called *kṣiti*.
*Ṛtaccitta*. This is translated as "the true mind. Just as the heartwood of a worldly tree is the most authentic part, it is the unconditioned mind;
that is, the intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara-citta*). When *citta* alone is used, it means "accumulation"; it is called "mind" because of its accumulation [of seeds].
This refers to the eighth fundamental consciousness, which is the conditioned mind (*saṃskṛta-citta*).
Regarding the statement that it is also called "unlearned wisdom" (*aśaikṣajñāna*): because this wisdom does not arise from external conditions, it is termed "unlearned wisdom.

Furthermore, because it is the very nature of wisdom, wisdom is identified as *tathatā* (suchness). Since it is not produced by a productive cause (*janaka-hetu*) but is attained through a revealing cause (*vyañjaka-hetu*), it is termed "unlearned wisdom."
What prevents this question? The nature of wisdom is called *mahāprajñā*.

Regarding the phrase "exiting the objects of knowledge" (*jñeya*) and so forth: the question asks, upon what principle is the name "Dharmakāya" established above True Suchness (*tathatā*)? The answer, as stated in the Commentary, is twofold:
first, exiting the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), and second, [the two meanings]. First, if there were cognitive obstructions present within True Suchness, it would not be so named.

Regarding the *dharmakāya*: first, because it has not yet abandoned the bonds of affliction (*kleśa-āvaraṇa*); second, because it cannot serve as the basis for the myriad virtues, it is not called the *dharmakāya*.

Now, the ultimate truth within the state of fruition (the result) is called the *dharmakāya* because, first, it has emerged from the cognitive obscurations (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*), and second, it serves as the basis for the myriad virtues.

Question: How does the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only) explain that one realizes the *dharmakāya* by abandoning the afflictive obscurations, and abandons the cognitive obscurations [to realize the *svabhāvakāya*]?
One attains the *saṃbhogakāya*. Now, as for the statement that emerging from the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is called the *dharmakāya*, does this not constitute a contradiction? Answer:
This is stated according to one aspect of the meaning, speaking in terms of what is predominant. If speaking in terms of the ultimate, it is necessary to be completely free from both obstructions.

Regarding the passage beginning with "The Śrīmālādevī-sūtra says," etc.: Question: For what reason must one be separated from the two obstacles (*dvividhāvaraṇa*) before it can be called the *dharmakāya*?

Answer: The Commentary states, "The Śrīmālādevī-sūtra says," etc. Question: True Suchness (*tathatā*) within the fruit [of Buddhahood] emerges from the obstacle to the known (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and is thus named the *dharmakāya*.

However, the truth of a Bodhisattva on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) also emerges from the obstacle to the known; should this not likewise be named the *dharmakāya*? Answer: [This is because] for a Bodhisattva on the ten stages, there remains the obstacle of limited birth (*paricchinna-janman*).

Regarding the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*): although the innate cognitive obstacles associated with the lower stages and the *tathatā* (suchness) are both distinguished as cognitive obstacles, they are not yet called the "Dharmakāya" because the subtle, innate cognitive obstacles of the higher stages have not been completely severed.
It is only when the *tathatā* within the fruition state is entirely freed from the entanglements of the cognitive obstacles that it is named the Dharmakāya.
Regarding the phrase "as for those in the Two Vehicles (*dvayāyānika*) and so forth": Question: Bodhisattvas on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are still within the causal state;

they have not yet attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), nor have they emerged from the bonds of affliction (*saṃyojana*). The *tathatā* (suchness) they realize is therefore not the *dharmakāya*. However, the no-more-learners of the Two Vehicles have eternally severed all afflictions and, having fully realized *tathatā*, have likewise emerged from the bonds.
They ought to be called *dharmakāya*. Answer: The commentary states, "As for those in the Two Vehicles and so forth. The intended meaning is as follows: regarding the Two Vehicles...

Although they have emerged from the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), they lack the ten thousand virtues; therefore, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) they have realized does not serve as the basis for those ten thousand virtues and is thus not called the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Furthermore, because the followers of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayānika*) have not at all severed the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), it is not called the Dharma-body.
It is merely called the "body of liberation," but it is not the "dharma-body. As the subsequent sutra states: "In reality, they have not attained all-encompassing liberation;
the Buddha says that such persons have not yet truly entered parinirvāṇa, because they have not yet attained the unsurpassed path. It is merely termed 'nirvana.'"
This, however, is not the Great Parinirvāṇa.

Regarding the statement that "the three categories of suffering are entirely exhausted" and so forth: Question: How is it that True Suchness (*tathatā*) is also called liberation (*vimukti*)? Answer: The Commentary states:

"The 'three categories of suffering' and so forth refer to the two types of birth and death—namely, the *pariṇāmika* (transformative) and the *aupapāduka* (segmentary)—which are termed 'the three categories of suffering. To be free from these two forms of death [is liberation]."

Therefore, it is called "complete exhaustion. To be free from the two obstacles and the two types of death is called "liberation. Question: Since Bodhisattvas of the ten stages also sever both obstacles, they should likewise attain this liberation. Answer:
Although those in the ten stages have realized a portion of True Suchness (*tathatā*), they have not yet transcended the *pariṇāmika* (transformation) birth-and-death;
thus, they are not called "liberated. Now, at the stage of fruition, one is free from the two deaths and the two obstacles, and is therefore called "liberated."

Regarding the phrase "as taught for the two vehicles, etc.": Question: For those of the two vehicles who have attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), all remaining bases of suffering have been exhausted;

should this not be called "liberation"? Answer: The Commentary states: "As taught for the two vehicles, [the exhaustion of] 'segmented existence' (*paricchinna-bhava*) and so forth" refers to the exhaustion of both the "associated bonds" (*saṃprayukta-bandhana*) and the "object-bound bonds" (*ālambana-bandhana*).

These constitute the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*). As for "associated," it refers to the twenty-two factors consisting of the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and its mental concomitants (*caitta*).
This is not inherently a bond; it is a pure, indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) phenomenon. It arises in association with the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion.

The afflictions themselves constitute the bond. Because this phenomenon is associated with that mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*), it prevents the associated mind and mental factors from attaining liberation;
thus, it is called "association" (*saṃprayoga*). This association itself is the bond, and is therefore termed "the bond of association" (*saṃprayoga-bandhana*). (2)

Regarding "object-binding" (*ālambana-bandhana*), there are two meanings. First, the binding of the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*): the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) takes the object as its condition, yet it is bound by that very object-condition;
because the objective realm strongly binds the subjective mind, preventing its liberation, this is called "object-binding.

Second, due to the subjective mind being associated with afflictions such as greed and hatred, it clings to objects such as forms and mental phenomena; thus, the subjective mind of greed becomes fettered.
The object of cognition is bound; one who cannot attain liberation from that which binds the cognizing subject is called "bound by the object" (*ālambana-bandhana*).
Regarding the phrase "likewise, the two vehicles, etc.," it is asked: The holy teachings state that the Blessed One said, "Three types of persons sit together upon the bed of liberation."

[Question: "Since both I and you have already attained the great liberation and *nirvāṇa* of a Buddha, why is it that the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) do not likewise attain the great liberation and *nirvāṇa*?
[Answer: The commentary states: "However, those of the two vehicles also attain this [liberation] subtly. There is also a commentary which states: "They attain this gradually."

Regarding the statement that "the three vehicles sit together upon the bed of liberation," this refers, for the time being, to the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*). It is said that they have attained half-liberation;
it is not that the ultimate truth of perfect liberation serves as their basis. Therefore, it is called a "bed. Because they realize it through wisdom, it is termed "sitting together."

Regarding the statement, "For this reason, the two vehicles are also said to have attained it": Question: The *tathatā* (suchness) realized by those in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) within the two vehicles is designated as *nirvāṇa*.
Why is it not called *mahāparinirvāṇa*? Answer: The commentary states: "For this reason, the two vehicles are also said to have attained *nirvāṇa*."
However, it is not the Great Parinirvāṇa.
Regarding the statement that its meaning is incomplete: Question: Why is it not called "Great Parinirvāṇa"? Answer: The commentary states: Because its meaning is incomplete;
it has not yet attained perfect liberation, and furthermore, it lacks the basis for the ten thousand virtues. Therefore, it is said that its meaning is incomplete.
Regarding the statement "also based on the second fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*," both the Dharma and a metaphor are presented together. The question asks:
according to what teaching is it said that the three matters must be complete to be called *Mahāparinirvāṇa*? The answer in the commentary states: "Also based on the *Nirvāṇa* and so forth.

*Mahāprajñā* is the wisdom of the two emptinesses; the *Dharmakāya* is the principle of *tathatā*. Because this wisdom realizes this principle, at the point where the two obstacles are exhausted, within the principle of the *Dharmakāya*...
Above, the designation "liberation" is established. When these three factors are complete, it is called Great Nirvāṇa; if even one is lacking, it is not termed Great Parinirvāṇa. Question:
Is liberation established upon the basis of wisdom, or is it established upon the basis of principle? Answer:
Since all six unconditioned phenomena are established based upon True Suchness (Tathatā), it is correct to establish liberation upon the basis of principle.
Regarding the statement that "Prajñā can realize the two kinds of emptiness," etc., it is asked: what is the essence of Prajñā? What is the essence of the Dharmakāya?
And what is the essence of Vimukti? The Commentary answers: "The essence of Prajñā is realized as the provisional analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
That is to say, these three things—the means of realization—must be the wisdom of the two kinds of emptiness, while the objects of realization must be the two kinds of emptiness."
The suchness of this [reality]—liberation must consist in being free from the two obstructions and the two deaths; only then is liberation termed Great Parinirvāṇa.

If there were only the wisdom of the emptiness of persons, or only the realization of the principle of the emptiness of persons, it would merely be the liberation from the bondage of a portion of the death of the aggregates by way of abandoning only the afflictive obstructions.
Although these involve three factors, they are not called Great Parinirvāṇa.
Regarding the statement that "liberation is identical [to the others]," Zhe says: The sunlight is used as an analogy for the wisdom (*prajñā*) that realizes [reality];
the emptiness of space (*ākāśa*) is a metaphor for the principle of the *dharmakāya*; and the point where the signs of darkness have completely vanished serves as an analogy for liberation.

This is because when the sunlight has not yet arisen, the signs of darkness merge with space; once the sunlight emerges, at the very point where the signs of darkness have been exhausted, the sunlight [shines forth].
When the sun merges with space, it is precisely at the moment when the aspect of darkness exists; this is precisely the moment when sunlight merges with space.
When sunlight merges with space, it is precisely when the aspect of darkness is exhausted. This is precisely when Mahāprajñā wisdom arises;
this is precisely when obstructions are exhausted. This is precisely when Mahāprajñā wisdom realizes the Dharmakāya; this is liberation.
Because it occurs at the time of liberation, "liberation" is provisionally established upon the principle of the *dharmakāya*.

Regarding the statement that the essence of *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (analytical cessation) is provisional, Mǔ states: "Among the six unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), the first five have both names and essences that are provisional;

since the unconditioned phenomenon of *tathatā* (suchness) has a provisional name but a real essence, *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* is said to be provisional. This is because it is produced by the power of analysis.

The attainment of cessation is termed "cessation through deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). How much more so when, based upon the principle of wisdom, suffering does not arise; this is metaphorically designated as "liberation.

Its essence is non-existent, hence it is called a "provisional cessation through deliberation. In reality, it is the nature of True Reality (*tattva*) that has the capacity to extinguish [suffering]. Because its essence is not non-existent, it is therefore named "provisional cessation through deliberation."
Regarding the statement "like the three dots of the letter *i*," this is an analogy cited in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Just as the worldly letter *i* and the Sanskrit letter *i* have two dots above and one dot below— resembling the inverted writing of the worldly character *pin* (品)—
if one asks whether this contradicts the subsequent scriptural passage [which describes] the three eyes on the face of Maheśvara, those three eyes and...
The letter *i* illustrates all three matters. In the two texts concerning *nirvāṇa*, the forms differ: in one, a single dot is above; in the other, a single dot is below.
In one, three eyes are above and two eyes are below; in the other, it is the reverse. Since these metaphors are not fixed, how can the Dharma be transformed?
"Transformation" (turning) means penetration. Master Zhe replied: "One need only take up the meaning of the three dharmas being neither vertical, nor horizontal, nor distinct.
Why insist on demanding that their numerical positions above and below be identical? Those who possess wisdom should not find fault with metaphors. Another interpretation states:
"This does not even hinder the three eyes of Maheśvara, much less the relationship between the realization and that which is realized. Mahāprajñāpāramitā is..."
The wisdom that is capable of realization is like the single eye above; the *dharmakāya* of liberation, which is the principle to be realized, is like the two eyes below.
If this is the letter *i*, it is understood as the relationship between the supported and the support.

The two dots above represent *prajñā* and liberation as the supported, while the single dot below represents the *dharmakāya* as the support (the preceding explanation serves as the heading for the text).
Regarding the phrase "individually they are not established," etc., this is a detailed explanation. It is like the three dots of the letter *i*: individually, they do not constitute it.
If one were to take the three dots of the letter *i* and place them separately, scattered and far apart, could they form the letter *i*? Answer: Individually, they do not constitute the letter *i*.

Furthermore, if one arranges three dots vertically, one above the other, does it resemble the character *ī* (伊) formed by water flowing through them? Answer: Even arranged vertically, it does not form it.
Question: If one were to arrange the three dots horizontally, like a firebrand moved across the day of the Tai-sui star, would it form the character *ī* when laid horizontally?

Answer: Even arranged horizontally, it does not form it. The Sarvāstivāda school of the Hīnayāna asserts that the wisdom which realizes [the truth] is distinct, and the principle realized is also distinct.
Regarding the distinction between liberation (*vimukti*) and [nirvāṇa]: these three matters are distinct in their respective entities and do not constitute nirvāṇa.

The statement "it is admitted that they are attained at different times," etc., serves as a conclusion. For example, when one realizes cessation through the liberation that abandons the afflictions (*kleśa*) without interruption, the subsequent body and wisdom are non-spatial;

this manifestation of the state without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*) is called liberation, which is precisely what is meant by "attainment at a different time. This is from the perspective of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
When realizing the principle through wisdom, liberation—the non-arising of suffering—is also neither prior nor subsequent.

According to the actual principle, when one has exhausted the afflictions through the uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the three vehicles and attained untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*), one does not yet possess complete liberation.

Only when the body that serves as the basis for future suffering is exhausted—when the physical form is reduced to ashes and consciousness is extinguished—one is finally freed from all bonds; this is termed "liberation. These are the three matters.
Transversely and sequentially, it is called "attainment at another time," but it is not called the Great Nirvāṇa.

Regarding the statement that the three matters—Nirvāṇa—are neither different nor identical, there are three interpretations. Prajñā is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), while principle (*tattva*) is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
because the conditioned and the unconditioned are distinct, they are said to be "not identical. When wisdom realizes principle, they merge into a single locus in profound stillness.

The names are not different. Second, it is said: the *dharmakāya* is real, while liberation (*vimukti*) is provisional; since the provisional and the real are distinct, they are not identical in name.

By subsuming the provisional into the real, the names are not different. Mo says: according to the Dharma-character school (*Faxiang zong*), as when speaking of the *prajñāpāramitā* in relation to the *dharmakāya*.
Wisdom and principle are distinct in essence and differ in their natures—imperfect and perfect—thus they are not one. Wisdom merges with principle like the sun shining upon the sky;
within this, no distinctions or differences can be discerned, thus they are not different. Furthermore, when wisdom and principle are contrasted with liberation:

the former possess an essence capable of extinguishing the nature of extinction, and because they are substantially existent, while liberation is merely nominal, they are not one. This is like the sunlight and [the sky].
When emptiness and form unite, there is no obstruction in between; this is conventionally termed "liberation. Furthermore, it cannot be conceptually differentiated because they are not distinct.
