First, regarding what is seen within the light: it is difficult to apply [the teaching] because there is no basis for following what is seen; one must immediately ask why the treatise possesses a sequence of prior and subsequent stages.
Second, Bodhisattvas of the ten stages cultivate [the perfections] in succession, and thus they first cultivate giving (*dāna*).

Furthermore, Bodhisattvas prior to the stages cultivate the six perfections in a non-sequential manner, and thus when they first resolve their minds to practice, they first cultivate diligence (*vīrya*).
Regarding the statement, "Faith is the basis for aspiration," etc.: Question: How is it that diligence (*vīrya*) is practiced first among the six perfections?
Answer: The commentary states, "Faith is the basis for aspiration," etc. First, one gives rise to faith; subsequently, based on faith, aspiration arises.

With aspiration as the cause, diligence then exists as the result. Therefore, diligence is cultivated at the very beginning. Question: Since diligence has already been established, what was the preceding stage of faith and aspiration? [End of excerpt]

Is it that within the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), faith and aspiration are established as the means of crossing over? Answer: Within the six perfections, only the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā) is established;
faith and aspiration are not established as separate crossings. Once one has faith in the Triple Gem and gives rise to aspiration, that which follows aspiration is precisely vigor.
Therefore, vigor is mentioned first. Only the perfection of vigor is established, and not a "perfection of faith," because vigor is universally applicable to all wholesome qualities.

Because they govern and control all activities and sustain them, the six perfections (ṣaḍpāramitā) encompass faith (*śraddhā*). Although the mind may be purified, it is not called a "perfection" because it does not universally govern and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "therefore, this is merely [faith] etc.," the intended meaning is that, according to the actual reality, faith and aspiration (*chanda*) should properly come first; they are not themselves the six perfections.
Therefore, one first applies diligence.

Regarding the statement that faith comes before the others, it means that within the stage of the ten minds of faith, the first is the mind of faith, the second is the mind of mindfulness, and the third is the mind of diligence;
hence, it is said that diligence follows [faith].

Regarding the phrase "the precepts of a single verse," the Sūtra says: "Furthermore, one sees those who possess the precepts. Jingzhi (貞) says: "Possessing the precepts of fundamental gravity is called 'possessing the precepts' (*śīlavat*);

having no deficiency in dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*) refers to the precept for avoiding worldly censure. Furthermore, regarding "one who possesses the precepts," this designates a person who maintains the precepts;
"having no deficiency in dignified deportment" means that they do not violate even minor matters, let alone other grave ones. Jiguō (紀國) says: [The same].
Furthermore, one sees those who possess the precepts—persons who uphold the discipline, whose deportment is flawless, and whose marks of upholding the precepts are as pure as exquisite jewels;

this manifests the virtue of the precepts. One sees those who seek the path to Buddhahood; this manifests the fruit of the precepts. Moreover, one sees those who possess the precepts; this reveals their own essential nature.

Regarding "one whose dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*) is without deficiency," this refers to the application of effort. Regarding "pure as a precious jewel," this refers to the perfection and luminosity of the precepts. These are sought for the sake of the Buddha-way and result in the attainment of the corresponding fruit.

As for the phrase "the three karmas, dignified deportment, and so forth," a question is raised: what constitutes the fullness of dignified deportment? The answer, as stated in the commentary, is: the three karmas.
Because his deportment (*īryāpatha*) is always without deficiency or diminution, it is called "deportment without defect.

Regarding the statement, "Do not underestimate even minor offenses," etc., the question is: by what cause does a bodhisattva attain such flawless deportment? The answer, as stated in the Commentary, is:
"Do not underestimate even minor offenses," etc. This explains the reason for guarding against subtle transgressions.
The phrase "pure like a precious gem" is an illustration. That which is round is called a *maṇi* (gem); that which is square is a *jī* (pearl). Here, the round variety is taken.
A gem is pure by virtue of being free from obscurations and blemishes; alternatively, it is pure by virtue of being without deficiency or decay.
Furthermore, there are three aspects: first, its purity is like that of a gem; second, its perfection is like that of a gem; and third, its worthiness of esteem is like that of a gem.
Regarding the statement "being flawless internally and externally": natural precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*) are called "internal," while prohibitive precepts (*pratikṣepaṇa-śīla*) are called "external.

If one commits the four *pārājika* offenses, it is like having a flaw within a gem; as for the remaining prohibitive precepts, it is like having a flaw in the gem. Not committing [offenses] through mental action is called being "flawless internally";

not committing [offenses] through bodily or verbal action is called being "flawless externally. Maintaining the natural precepts is called being "flawless internally," and maintaining the prohibitive precepts is called being "flawless externally."
It is said that externally there are no flaws.

Regarding the statement that the two types of preceptual virtue are perfect and complete: the two hundred and fifty precepts and the five hundred precepts are called the perfection of majestic virtue;
the three thousand modes of deportment are all likewise perfected.

Regarding the phrase "the three majestic radiances, such as the radiance of the sun," the Chancellor (Xiangguo) said: There is a sutra which states that those who firmly uphold the precepts constantly have light emanating from all the pores of their bodies.
Devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits all see this; they constantly scatter fragrant flowers from afar upon such a person and circumambulate them in worship.
Wherever they travel, ghosts and spirits clear the way for them. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka* says: "If one upholds purity..."
Precepts. They accord perfectly with the principles of the teachings and are praised by all Buddhas and noble sages. Thus, a verse says: "The precepts are the foundation of unsurpassed Bodhi;
one should fully maintain the pure precepts. The pearl's substance possesses radiance, which serves as a metaphor for the light of the precepts.
Its ability to illuminate dark paths is called "radiant splendor" (guāngyào).
Regarding what is said about being beloved by the fourfold assembly: spirits and deities look up to and revere such a person. For example, Vinaya Master Xuán was attended by a son of Vaiśravaṇa.
If one breaks the precepts, spirits and deities constantly seek an opportunity to take advantage of them. The Bodhisattva Precepts state:

"Five hundred great spirits sweep away the footprints of [the transgressor]. It further states: "The head of a person who maintains the precepts is radiant with light, extending one zhang and five chi."
A person who breaks the precepts has a blood-red light upon their head, one zhang and five chi in length; even flying birds are terrified by it.
As for the statement "because of this, the goose swallowed the pearl," etc., this is the judgment of the commentator (the *shuzhu*).

Among these four phrases, the first three concern the conditions for upholding the precepts, while the fourth concerns the conditions for breaking them. Question: In the third phrase, the wild geese follow the *zhishi* (administrative officer); is this not breaking [the precepts]?
Regarding the precepts: why is this also considered "maintaining the precepts"? It is because by maintaining the precepts, one consumes pure meat;

thus, it becomes a condition for the response of an emanation body to fall. This is a condition for maintaining the precepts. Some say it is a condition for breaking the precepts, but that is incorrect.

Formerly, there was a bhikṣu who went to a pearl merchant’s house while begging for food. The owner said, "This is a pearl from the king's state elephant. He took the food and gave it to the śramaṇa, whose robes...
The red [light] reflected off the color of that jewel, making it appear like a lump of flesh. A goose, thinking it was meat, swallowed it down into its belly.
When the bhikṣu realized this, fearing he might harm the life of the goose, he endured the pain in silence. Blood flowed from his body as he was beaten.
Seeing the blood on the ground, the goose came to lick it; as it drank, its life ended. Seeing that the goose had died, the bhikṣu then informed the owner of the jewel, saying, "The jewel is here."

"The Goose's Belly": It was obtained by opening the belly [of a goose]. There is also a tradition which says that when a bhikṣu entered the royal palace, a pearl atop the palace pavilion was swallowed by a goose.
Regarding the account of the monk who gave up his body by binding himself with grass: There was a bhikṣu practicing the Way in the mountains. A band of five hundred thieves plundered his three robes.
Not knowing that the bhikṣu maintained the precepts, and fearing he might be pursued later, the thieves immediately bound the bhikṣu’s body with grass.
Fearing that the grass might be damaged or that living things within it might be harmed, the bhikṣu lay there and did not dare to move. At that time, the King of Kāśī was traveling abroad.
Having seen this, he asked in verse: "Behold this young man, in the prime of his years and possessed of great strength;
why does he lie here among the grass, silent and unmoving? The bhikṣu replied in verse: "Great King, you should now know: this grass is exceedingly fragile and brittle.
When I move or turn upon it, I fear I might violate the precepts of the Tathāgata. The king then ordered him to be released and departed.

Regarding the statement that "the geese followed the knowledge of the administrator": In the Western lands (India), there were monasteries where it was permitted to consume pure meat for the first time.
For several days, the administrator was unable to provide meat as an offering to the monks. The monastics then mocked the administrator.
Suddenly, the administrator saw a flock of geese flying across the sky. He thought to himself, "How is it that these *sattvas* do not know the proper time? They have already betrayed me."
The assembly of monks in the hall reviled the administrator for his misconduct. At that moment, the wild geese followed the sound.

The administrator then managed the affairs and made offerings to the community of monks. The senior monk (upādhyāya) was astonished and questioned him. The administrator recounted the preceding events in detail.
The senior monk said, "This is a bodhisattva; these are not actual geese. I do not dare to eat them. He then collected their bones, erected a stūpa, and made offerings to them. [The Geese]...

The matter of the stūpa arose because of this. Because of this establishment of the precepts, there was praise that said: "The eminent and noble Dharma companions dwell in solemn seclusion, cut off from all offerings.
The solemn guest-birds cast their bodies to manifest their loyalty. They vow to follow their teacher and savor the flavor [of the Dharma], willingly submitting even to falling into extinction.

When the water itched [for meat] (the 'yang' tone for 'hu'), they called out to the funeral mound (the 'fen' tone for 'lin'). Thus, following the auspicious precedent, they immediately ceased eating meat."
Regarding the statement that a dragon was born from an *eranda* tree: during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was a bhikṣu who sat in meditation and practiced the Way beneath an *eranda* tree.
When the tree brushed against his body, he immediately gave rise to anger and snapped off one of its branches.
After his life came to an end, he was reborn as a great dragon, known as the Dragon King *Ibbara*, with an *eranda* tree growing upon his head, its roots coiled and its branches interlaced.
Its branches and leaves are innumerable. Whenever a great wind arises, the tree shakes, causing the dragon’s head to split open; pus and blood flow forth, and its suffering is beyond measure.
If even a single branch causes such distress, how much more so when many are destroyed? This is the karmic condition for violating the precepts.
Regarding the phrase "the jar according to one's desire" and so forth, this refers generally to the conditions for maintaining or breaking the precepts.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* state that there exists a "jar of merit" (*guṇa-kumbha*) which can, according to one’s wishes, flow forth with precious jewels, food, drink, medicinal elixirs, and the like;

once these have been enjoyed, they return and flow back into the jar. Formerly, there was a husband and wife who constantly made offerings at a celestial shrine. Later, they were moved by divine grace... [text continues].
A celestial shrine (devakula) possesses a precious vase; from within this precious vase emerge all manner of things—money, wealth, food and drink, gardens, and dwellings—all of which are sufficient.

The virtue of ethical discipline (*śīla*) is likewise: if one possesses the virtue of ethical discipline in its entirety, one will constantly be reborn among humans and devas, enjoying wealth, nobility, and happiness, until even the attainment of Buddhahood.
If the virtue of ethical discipline is broken, nothing at all will be accomplished. Thus, a verse in the Sūtra says: "If..."
If one does not maintain the precepts in body, it is like a bow without a string; when a thief arrives, there is nothing to pull back against him—how could one dare to advance? As the Sūtra says:
"By relying on and depending upon this precept, one attains birth in the First Dhyāna, as well as the wisdom that extinguishes suffering.

Regarding the aforementioned cases of the goose and the pearl being struck (from the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*), the grass-tethering and the renunciation of the body (from the *Vyūha-śāstra*), and the wild geese following the ritual master (from the *Record of the Western Regions*): [Note: The text provided appears to be a fragmentary commentary or summary of various Jātaka and historical narratives concerning the power of the precepts.]
The *Śikṣāsamuccaya* states that from a dragon is born the *eranda* tree;

the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and other texts (such as the *Vinayaviniścaya*) state that this one and a half verses concerning "enduring resentment" and so forth are spoken in the Sūtra: "Furthermore, one sees sons of the Buddha who abide in the power of patience."
These two lines express the characteristic of transcending [the world]. "When people of overweening pride revile or strike one" clarifies the object of patience (*kṣānti*).
"Being able to endure all of this in order to seek the Buddha-way" clarifies the purpose of patience. Jiguo says: furthermore, "seeing a son of the Buddha" [is as follows].
One who dwells in patience; one who is dedicated to the power of forbearance; one on the stage of patient endurance (*kṣānti-bhūmi*);

one who is able to endure all things when encountering objects of patience, even when reviled or struck by those of overweening pride (*adhimāna*); one who manifests the power of patience in order to seek the path of the Buddha; one who seeks the fruit of patience;
furthermore, one who sees a son of the Buddha is one who practices patience, dwells in the power of forbearance, and cultivates the practice of patience—such is the person of overweening pride.
When encountering conditions that provoke patience—such as those who revile or strike one—one who is able to exercise patience in all such instances achieves the perfection of patience.
For one who seeks the path of the Buddha, the *Ekottarika Āgama* states that there are six kinds of power:
first, the power of a small child is crying; whenever they desire something, they must first cry. Second, the power of a woman is anger. Whenever she desires...
Because when one has a need, one must first overcome anger. Third, the kings possess power through pride and arrogance; fourth, the arhats possess power through diligence;
fifth, the Buddhas possess power through compassion; sixth, the bhikṣus possess power through patience.
This present case refers to the sixth power. As the sutra says: "Because the Buddha’s son and the bhikṣu do not conflict with one another, patience is like a great ship. It may be used.

This is for the sake of crossing over difficulties. Mochizuki says: "The patience practiced previously is of a kind similar to that of a Bodhisattva, because one does not disparage the practice cultivated in the past.
As a verse says: "The strength to strike a thousand people is not called true might; the strength to turn one's head away when spat upon is immeasurably greater.
This is the patience of enduring enmity and harm. Practicing patience toward those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*) is likewise peace.
"Enduring suffering" refers to the causes for being beaten, such as claiming to have gained much when one has gained little, and so forth. The four fruits of śrāmaṇya are superior dharmas;
yet, by regarding the attainment of the four dhyānas as these four fruits of śrāmaṇya, one treats those superior dharmas with contempt. Therefore, it is so named.
Overweening pride (*adhimāna*). Furthermore, having attained the four dhyānas, one considers what is obtained as little to be the attainment of the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, yet claims it to be much;
this is called overweening pride. The treatise says [at length]: What is pride? It is to rely on oneself and to look down upon others. Its essential nature is haughtiness, and it acts as an obstacle.
It is not pride (*māna*). Its function is to give rise to suffering.
Regarding the phrase "relying on one's lineage and so forth," a question is asked: what is meant by "pride"? The answer states:
the commentary says it is "relying on one's lineage and so forth," such as the Cui of Boling, the Lu of Fanyang, the Liu of Hedong, the Li of Longxi, the Zi, and others.
Regarding the phrase "physical beauty, strength, and so forth": "physical beauty" refers to one's appearance, such as that of Fan Anren, whose pomegranates filled his carriage when he threw them;
or He Yan, whom people suspected of applying face powder; or those whose intelligence was such that they could read a stone monument from behind or solve a game of Go with their backs turned.

"Wealth" refers to those like Zou Luotuo, Shi Chong, and Lin Lukzi. "Fame" refers to those like An Yuan and Ci'en. One gives rise to a sense of superiority and excellence toward oneself based on these qualities.
Thus, one proceeds with striking and scolding as a means of transformation.

It is said that a bodhisattva employs five kinds of contemplations and so forth; this clarifies the capacity for practice. Therefore, a bodhisattva practices patience through five kinds of contemplative exercises.
First, when a bodhisattva is struck, they contemplate all enemies as having the character of relatives, just as one views one’s parents.
When my brother strikes me, how can I not endure it? Second, I contemplate only the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*); I do not see one who can strike.

It is merely the three categories and five aggregates (*triskandha-pañcaskandha*). It is like an aggregate of form striking an aggregate of form, or like space acting upon space—what concern is this of mine?

That which is reviled belongs to the sphere of sound (*śabdadhātu*), and that which hears is the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*). Sound as an object reviles the ear; the ear-faculty apprehends the object of sound—this is its natural function. There is no [self here].
There is a presiding master; there is only the perception of dharmas. One should maintain three recollections, including the perception of suffering. The Bodhisattva reflects:
"If he were not suffering, I would have to repay him by making him suffer in turn. He already possesses the five kinds of suffering, which are inherently within his own person;
why must I further requite him? I must simply endure it. Furthermore, if one is suddenly in a mountain forest and flying sand and rolling stones strike them, what need is there to respond further?
[The Buddha] replied: "Go and answer Ānanda. Furthermore, regarding the path of a Bodhisattva: 'I have come originally to uproot the suffering of sentient beings;

if I were now to undergo suffering myself while transforming others, how could that be logical? This body of mine is painful even if not struck; therefore, one must be able to endure suffering when it is encountered.'"
Fourth is the perception of impermanence. The Bodhisattva contemplates that this body which strikes him is subject to the four marks [of birth, aging, sickness, and death] throughout day and night;

it does not abide for even a single moment of thought. Why, then, should he retaliate? It arises and perishes in an instant, and its life will ultimately come to an end. As for those who struck me before—[they too are likewise impermanent].

They have long since fallen away; they are themselves subject to impermanence, so why should one further harm them? Having already formed the perception of impermanence, one is thus able to endure [such thoughts].

Regarding the fifth, the perception of gathering in (*saṃgraha-saṃjñā*): the Bodhisattva reflects, "I am now gathering in all sentient beings, originally intending to deliver them and lead them to the fruit of Buddhahood.
If I were now to harm others, it would constitute abandonment and could not be called 'deliverance. Because [of this]..."

5. Endurance. If one does not endure such things as malicious abuse, one should not take those types of sentient beings under one's care—just as a monastic community might not accept a novice or a young attendant who has faults or engages in disputes.

However, a preceptor (upādhyāya) uses skillful means to observe and guide them, thereby being able to take them under his care. For this reason, a bodhisattva possesses the perception of inclusion and is thus able to endure them. 5.

Among the various perceptions, both the subject and the object are included; however, impermanence pertains only to the subject and serves as its antidote, thus falling under the category of another’s inquiry.

Why, then, is it said that one should contemplate the "harm-doer"? There are two explanations: first, that harm applies to both subject and object; second, that this is stated from the perspective of the majority.

Regarding the term *chui* (捶), "striking" (*da*) is precisely what is meant by *chui*. [The former explains the act of striking; the latter explains that one can endure all such things. Confucius said: "If the Son of Heaven endures it, he achieves [his goal]."
If one can endure great things, the feudal lords will tolerate them, and the state will suffer no harm. If officials and commoners can endure them, their positions will advance.

If brothers can endure them, the family will be wealthy and noble. If husband and wife can endure them, the way of the household will flourish. If friends can endure them, one’s reputation will manifest of itself. If one can endure within oneself, [all blessings follow].

Having finished discussing calamities and harms, he asked, "What is 'intolerance' (*arati*)? He replied, "O Son of Heaven, when the state and its cities are empty, there is intolerance. When the feudal lords lose their territories, there is intolerance.

When officials and commoners face punishments and executions, there is intolerance. When brothers are separated and live apart, there is intolerance. When husband and wife [are estranged], there is intolerance."
To leave one's son orphaned is something one cannot bear oneself; when both suffering and harm coexist, even friends cannot bear it, and thus they become estranged.

Regarding the two verses on meditative concentration (*samādhi*), Ji Guo states: "The first verse describes the characteristics of being free from distraction, while the latter verse manifests the characteristics of concentration."

The Sūtra says: "Furthermore, seeing bodhisattvas who cause distracted people to leave behind all frivolous laughter is [the perfection of] leaving behind distracted activities; who leave behind foolish retinues is [the perfection of] leaving behind the causes of distraction;

who associate with the wise is [the perfection of] becoming intimate with stable conditions; who single-mindedly eliminate distraction and withdraw their thoughts in mountain forests is [the perfection of] manifesting the signs of meditative concentration;
who spend billions of years is [the perfection of] accumulating the power of concentration; and who seek the path of the Buddha is [the perfection of] seeking the fruit of concentration."
Regarding the statement that there are four things to be abandoned, when a bodhisattva practices meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there are four things to be abandoned.

First is the abandonment of frivolous play (*vikṣepa*), which refers to conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Question: What is meant by "conceptual proliferation"? Answer: The Commentary provides two interpretations.

That which is with conceptualization is called conceptual proliferation; that which is without conceptualization is called non-proliferation. Question: At this stage, by what cause does the bodhisattva attain non-conceptualization?

A separate wisdom. Answer: Bodhisattvas prior to the stages [of the path] abandon the mind that discriminates between the grasper and the grasped; this awakening to such abandonment is called "abandonment by name.
Second, that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) is called "conceptual proliferation" (*prapañca*), while that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*) is called "non-proliferation."

Regarding "speaking and laughing" as referring to frivolous jesting: the *Śrī-mālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* says, "Frivolous jesting, laughter, and arrogance. Such talk and jesting constitute the distraction (with the "xuan" [虗] and "yue" [約] rhymes).

Regarding the "four abandonments of evil associates," these are also conditions for distraction, because they involve seeking out those who are separated from one's kin. There are four kinds of such seeking:

first, seeking after relatives (*jñāti-vitarka*), which involves weighing the circumstances of one's kin and associates, such as their poverty or wealth; second, seeking after countries (*janapada-vitarka*).

Regarding matters such as military combat, there are three types of *vyāpāda-vitarka* (ill-will thoughts); this refers to anger. Fourth is *vihiṃsā-vitarka* (harmful thoughts), which involves plotting to kill or harm sentient beings;

the present case refers to the first of these thoughts, namely the evil associates known as *jñāti-vitarka* (thoughts concerning kinsmen). Furthermore, it describes *kāma-vitarka* (thoughts concerning sensual desires) regarding what was previously experienced and what has been traversed.

Regarding the phrase "not departing from speech has two reversals, the fourth, etc.," the sutra says, "approaching the wise," which is the reversal of the fourth [point], namely, avoiding evil associates. Regarding the phrase "two:
one-pointedness of mind and removing distraction, etc.," the sutra says, "one-pointedness of mind and removing distraction," which is the reversal of the preceding three types. First:

Discriminative conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Second, one abandons laughter, idle talk, and jesting. Third, one abandons one's own ignorance; thus it is called "single-mindedly removing distraction.

Regarding the statement, "Therefore, the *Śāstrāṃśa-śikṣāpada-sūtra* (The Sutra on the Bequeathed Teaching) says," etc.: the Truth of Suffering is named "suffering" (*duḥkha*), and the Truth of Origination is named "the root" (*mūla*); "root" refers to the cause (*hetu*).
To sever its fruit, one must first sever its cause; this reflects the contemplation of extinguishing the root of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
Regarding the phrase "other food and drink" and so forth: it may refer to seeing Bodhisattvas within the light offering meals and food.
The character *xi* (希) means to act alone, to eat, or to consume.
Regarding the phrase "the category of vegetables and the like": vegetables are the things eaten and consumed; one must not take the person who consumes them.
*Xi* (希) means "many" or "abundance. The vegetables that are eaten are called *xi*. It is also said that the "fruit of the bean" refers to the green bean pod;
when small bean pods come forth and are made into vegetables, they are named *xi*. (The above explains *xi-cai*).
Regarding the statement that "shàn (膳) refers to prepared food," the Master of the Commentary explains: what we nowadays call "delicious things" are also termed "zhēnshàn (珍膳, precious delicacies).
Furthermore, while there is a character [zhāi (齋)] meaning "vegetables," the character *shàn* is a name for fine and delicious food and drink.
Regarding the statement that "in the vulgar interpretation, 'yáo-shèn' refers to meat," this is precisely how the character *xī* is explained within the *Guoyu*:
it applies both to vegetables and to meat. If one explains it according to secular texts, it refers to meat. Jiaxiang says: "*Xī* means to mince meat finely."
He then explains: Prior to the assembly at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the World-Honored One had not yet prohibited meat;

he still permitted his disciples to eat the "threefold pure" meat, provided it was not seen to have been killed for oneself, not heard to have been killed for oneself, and not suspected in one's mind to have been killed for oneself.
The author of the sub-commentary does not permit this. Jiaxiang’s interpretation is that such was the local custom within that Western land, and it was not necessarily [a universal rule].
Regarding the phrase "offering meat within the light" and the statement "it is not so now," if both characters are applied toward the side of "food" (食), both are incorrect.
If both characters are applied toward the side of "ancient meat" (古肉), both are also incorrect. The character 希 (xī) is used alone; the character 膳 (shàn) is formed from "ancient meat."

This is correct. In secular usage, the character for "food" (食) is formed with the radical for "meat" (肉) on its side; its substance is good, and its form and sound are appropriate. The character for "fine food" (膳) means "good.

When these characters were first created, the meaning was not yet fully developed, so it did not preclude calling meat alone "fine food" (shàn). Since later times, however, this has referred to all types of food and drink.
This is the general term for "food" (shàn). Question: Since "shàn" is a general term for food and drink, why is it written with the "grass" radical (艹) rather than the "meat" radical (肉)?

Answer: This interpretation is not correct. The character "bodhi" (菩提) is not a simplified form of "grass"; it is not composed from below the "grass" radical. Furthermore, the character "shàn" is not "meat."
What prevents the character from being derived from the ancient form with the "flesh" (肉) radical?
To say that sandalwood (*candana*) and the like are also included within the category of bedding. Question: Why does the Master of the Commentary explain *candana* here in this manner? Answer:
Because the sutra contains the word *candana*, the intention is to convey that all *candana* found in this world does not exceed three types. As for "red," it refers to...

Regarding "ox-head" and so forth, the intent is that these merely resemble the local *candana* (red sandalwood) and white sandalwood; they do not directly refer to the types of sandalwood found here [in this land].
(The three preceding lines concern the completion of the offering.)

Regarding the phrase "among superior and exquisite gifts," this explains what constitutes a superior and exquisite gift. Question: For what reason are the previous four matters not called superior and exquisite? Answer:
Because the preceding scriptural passage does not mention purity, they are not called superior and exquisite. Now it says: "a pure grove."
When flowers and fruits flourish and there are flowing springs and bathing pools, to bestow these upon the Buddha and the Sangha is truly the most sublime offering. [The interlocutor] asks:

The scriptural passage on the most sublime offerings mentions only giving to the Buddha and the Sangha; it does not mention one's parents, the sick, Dharma masters, or Bodhisattvas in their final birth.

The phrase "approaching" (*jang-gip*) refers to the Buddha’s body and simultaneously encompasses one's parents. The phrase "approaching" also refers to the Saṅgha, simultaneously encompassing the Dharma-preacher as well as Bodhisattvas in their final birth.

As a verse says: "Parents, the sick, a Dharma-preacher, and a Bodhisattva in his final birth— even if they have not realized the state of an Arya, the fruit of giving to them is immeasurable. [These are: first, the father; second, the mother; third, the sick person; fourth...

Regarding the "Dharma Master" and the "Bodhisattva in his final existence": according to the interpretation of the Hīnayāna, Prince Siddhārtha, born in the royal palace, was prior to his attainment of Buddhahood;
while his body still possessed outflows (*sāsrava*), he was called a Bodhisattva in his final existence. If one follows the Mahāyāna, this is merely a manifestation.
Regarding the statement, "Even if one is not a realized noble being," it asks how a Bodhisattva in their final body of the Hīnayāna can also accomplish supreme and wondrous giving.
The commentary answers: "Even if one is not a realized noble being," and so forth.

Regarding the statement, "Furthermore, it is said that if one possesses the feet of precepts, etc.," [the question is asked]: How can ordinary bhikṣus and those who have violated the dharma of the precepts also accomplish supreme and wondrous giving?
The answer is given in the commentary: "If one possesses the feet of precepts, etc. The Buddha stated that there are two types of right practice.
One will swiftly attain rebirth in heaven. First, by making offerings to one's parents; second, by performing various kinds of wholesome deeds for one's parents.
According to the *Kusha-śāstra*, even those who merely provide offerings [to the sick] obtain visible retribution in this life, let alone those who personally attend to the sick.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Precepts state that among the eight fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), the field of merit of nursing the sick is the foremost. Regarding this verse:
What is the distinction between the former and the latter *dharma-bhāṇakas*? Answer: There is no distinction regarding their ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Regarding the phrase "the six kinds of intentionality in giving," etc., according to the treatise, there are six kinds of intentionality in the joy of giving (*dāna-āśaya*).

First is the "vast intentionality" (*udāra-āśaya*). Question: Do the four types of giving mentioned by the preceding Sūtra author, as well as the "exquisite giving," fulfill this intentionality? These two...

Explanation: First, regarding the vastness of the substance of the gift: it consists of offering kingdoms, cities, wives, children, and gold, silver, and so forth, filling all of Jambudvīpa—this is the fourfold material offering.
Second, regarding the mind of the donor, it refers to the vast intention (*āśaya*):

because one can practice giving without discriminating between enemies and kin, or those known and unknown, it is called "vast. Third, regarding tireless giving: as the sutra says, "tireless" (*atṛpta*). Third.

Giving with joy is not associated with a mind of anger. Giving out of the four debts of gratitude involves feeling shame before the Buddha and regarding all sentient beings as having been kind to me, because by receiving my gifts they enable me to attain *bodhi*. There are two aspects to "unstained" giving:
first, being without regret during the three periods [of time] is called unstained; sixth is "excellent giving," which is dedicated toward [the goal of] a bodhisattva.
Regarding the statement that there are three types within this [category], these are found in this very sutra; according to the scriptural text, there are three kinds.

Now, we shall correlate these three types from the sutra with the six types in the treatise (*śāstra*). The scriptural text mentions "generosity with joy," "insatiable generosity," and "excellent generosity.
These three correspond to the three types in the treatise, as their names are identical. What the sutra calls "joy" is precisely what the treatise refers to...
"Giving with joy" corresponds to what the two sūtras call "insatiability," which is the "insatiable giving" (an-alaṃ-dāna) of the treatise.

"Seeking the unsurpassed path" corresponds to what the sūtras call "excellent giving" (praṇīta-dāna), which is the "excellent giving" of the treatise. Since these three types in this sūtra correspond to the three designations in the treatise, the three names from the sūtra are used to subsume the three categories of the treatise.

Regarding the statement that "the first four matters are equivalent," from the perspective of this treatise (*śāstra*), there are three further names: namely, "vastness" (*audārya*), "benefit" (*anugraha*), and "absence of defilement" (*nirāmiṣatva*).
These exist in the treatise but are not present in the sūtra. Thus, the three meanings found in the sūtra subsume these three names of the treatise.
In the preceding sūtra, the four matters constitute the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*); in the treatise, this is termed "vast giving. In the sūtra... [text fragment ends].

When a bodhisattva practices giving, they bear the debt of gratitude toward the recipient who accepts their gift; because that person receives their gift, it enables the bodhisattva to fulfill the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).

This is what the treatise refers to as "generosity characterized by the virtue of benefiting others. Furthermore, when a bodhisattva gives according to the Sūtras, there is no regret regarding the preparatory, fundamental, or subsequent stages of the act;
this is what the treatise calls "untainted generosity" (*asaṃkliṣṭadāna*).
Regarding the statement "giving food, drink, and so forth," there are two meanings herein: first, the fulfillment of worldly fruits;
for by giving food, drink, and so forth, one does not fall into kalpas of famine—this refers to worldly fruits. Second, supramundane fruits. This refers to worldly fruits.
Regarding the statement that by giving medicine one shall obtain [certain results]: the supramundane result is the absence of all diseases;
the mundane result is as stated regarding the giving of bedding and so forth. "And so forth" refers to the mundane.

Regarding the phrase "entering the empty and quiescent abode" and so forth, these refer to supramundane fruits. Furthermore, regarding each of the four types of giving mentioned previously, there are both causal and resultant fruits consisting of two aspects:

the sublime mental disposition (*āśaya*) and the actual result. Here, the explanation is based solely on the causal aspect. The "Dharma-food" is termed the causal aspect; "not falling into famine" is termed the resultant aspect.
"Obtaining the Dharma-medicine" is termed the causal aspect; "being free from all illnesses" is termed the resultant aspect. "The seven-jeweled robes" are termed the resultant aspect.

Possessing a sense of shame and remorse is termed "principle" (*li*); possessing the necessary provisions and conditions is termed "phenomenon" (*shi*). Entering the dwelling of empty tranquility is termed "principle.

However, the joy of the Dharma and the delight of dhyāna are called "food," because they nourish, develop, and sustain the body of wisdom. The Dharma is called "medicine" because it counteracts and heals unwholesome conduct.
Gentleness and patience are analogous to "clothing," for they shield the physical form from the encroachments of external objects. Possessing a sense of shame...
As for "shame" (*hrī*), it is so called because it conceals evil from manifestation, just as a garment covers [the body]; thus both are termed "garments.
Because the Bodhisattva abides in the mind within the sphere of ultimate emptiness and compassion, it is named "dwelling" (*śaya*).

Regarding the statement "giving gardens and groves, etc.": it is endowed with all merits, just like a garden park. The various untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas grow and flourish within it, and thus it is called a "grove.
The seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) are the cause; because the cause is able to evoke the fruit, they are likened to flowers.
The former garden refers to the essence (*tattva*), while this garden refers to its function (*vṛtti*); thus, they are distinguished.

Regarding the statement that by giving fruit one attains the four fruits of the noble ones (*āryaphala*): Question: How is it that a great bodhisattva, when practicing generosity, does not take up the fruit of Buddhahood, but instead takes up the four fruits of the noble ones?
Answer: The four fruits of the noble ones are precisely the arhat. The arhat is common to the three vehicles (*triyāna*). There are also...

This is called an Arhat. Furthermore, there is another explanation: these are merely general terms for the four fruits of sainthood; it does not necessarily mean that each individual has actually attained all four fruits of sainthood.

As for the statement regarding the gift of bathing pools and so forth: in the Hīnayāna, this refers to the elimination of desire for the realm of form (*rūpa-rāga*); in the Mahāyāna, it refers to the elimination of the obstructions to transformation (*nirmāṇa-āvaraṇa*) and so on.
Regarding the statement "the wisdom first attained and subsequently acquired," the Sūtra says: "There may be bodhisattvas who preach the dharma of quiescence (śānti-dharma).

Here, *nirvāṇa* in its essential nature is called the dharma of quiescence. In the case of *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, one attains quiescence by pacifying the hindrances; in the case of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, one attains quiescence by pacifying suffering.

Furthermore, it is said: "The two dharmas of a Bodhisattva are both the dharma of quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirvāṇa*). If one relies on this latter interpretation, although it accords with the literal text of the sutra, it contradicts the intended meaning of the recited teaching.

If one refers to this recitation, the sutra text speaks of the dharma of quiescent extinction as *tathatā* (suchness), because it is taught within the context of the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) that realizes fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). Thus, it is called the "dharma of quiescent extinction. The sutra says: "Various instructions... [and so forth]. No [contradiction].
This refers to the faculties possessed by various sentient beings. As the Sūtra says: "Or one may see a Bodhisattva contemplating the nature of all dharmas," etc.

This single line refers to fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the nature of all dharmas. Regarding the phrase "there are no two characteristics": it means that there is no duality of subject and object.
To be free from the signs of conceptual attachment and free from the signs of the grasper and the grasped is called the "non-dual sign.
Within this nature, neither a sign can be found, nor can a signless state be found; therefore, it is said that there are no two signs.
Alternatively, it is said that being free from the two signs of existence and non-existence is called the "non-dual sign. Question: What is the non-dual sign like? Answer: It is just like space.

Emptiness. The Sūtra says: "Furthermore, one sees the sons of the Buddha whose minds are unattached. By means of this wondrous, wondrous wisdom—'wisdom' here meaning *jñāna*—they seek the two paths through the wisdom of application (*prayoga-jñāna*):

the path of true seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of semblance seeing (*nimitta-darśana-mārga*). Those who seek the unsurpassed path [seek] the fruit of Buddhahood, which is bodhi and nirvāṇa. (The preceding section concludes the Sūtra.)
Regarding the statement "because the gift of Dharma is inexhaustible": the first line clarifies the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

This single sentence from the commentary itself serves as an explanation for the one line of the sutra concerning the dharma of quiescence (*śānta-dharma*). It is simply because the teaching of the dharma differs;

when speaking of the dharma of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*), there is that which can be exhausted. As the sutra says: "From kalpas of long ago, [the Buddha] has praised and revealed the dharma of nirvāṇa. [The cycle of] birth and death...
Regarding the phrase "the eternal extinction of suffering,

etc.," the mention of the *Kāśyapa Sūtra* serves as proof that the teaching of the inexhaustibility of the Dharma surpasses even the offering of material wealth; such material offerings do not equal even a single instance of the gift of Dharma.

Regarding the statement "giving that is not in accordance with the Dharma" and so forth: this does not refer to giving the Dharma; rather, it refers to making offerings of precious jewels under the name of "Dharma-giving.
It is because the Tathāgata does not give the Dharma to sentient beings in such a manner as to cause them to attain Buddhahood.
Regarding the statement that "one realizes the signless through right wisdom," the Sūtra says: "There are no two signs;

what are called the two signs refer to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). The Master of the Commentary explains this as being free from conceptual construction, which consists of the signs of the grasper and the grasped.
Alternatively, it is said that there are no two signs of existence and emptiness; thus, it is called the absence of these two signs.
The phrase "the absence of dual characteristics" refers collectively to other sutras.
Regarding the statement, "As it is said in those three categories," what is meant by the "Dharma-gate of Non-duality"?

The answer is that the Master of the Commentary [Wŏnhyo], following those three categories, explains the meaning of non-duality. According to the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, thirty-three sages clarify the meaning of non-duality, which is divided into three parts.
Regarding the categories: the first category consists of thirty-one individuals, such as Ratnamudrāhasta and others;
taking the mind of discriminative grasping as "two," the principle of non-discrimination is called "non-dual wisdom" (*advayajñāna*). To realize this principle is called "entering non-duality.
This uses words to dispel conceptual marks, yet it still retains words. The second category: Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva takes those verbal expressions themselves and names them "two."
The ineffable true nature is called "non-duality. When wisdom realizes this principle, it is called "entering non-duality.

This is the third category: using words to dispel words is termed "non-duality. For Vimalakīrti, both provisional wisdom and verbal expression are termed "duality," while the dharmatā-tathatā is termed "non-duality.
Realizing the principle of tathatā through correct wisdom is called "entering non-duality. This is achieved through silence.
"Sending away words" is called the "gate of non-dual dharmas. This refers to the simultaneous relinquishing of both words and cognition.

Regarding the statement that those before the stages (*bhūmi*) train in the "manifestation of signs" (*sanimitta*) and so forth: Question: How do Bodhisattvas prior to the [first] stage attain fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and realize the principle of signlessness (*animitta*)?

Answer: The Master of the Commentary states that those prior to the stage train in the manifestation of signs. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only), fascicle nine, says: "In this stage, the Bodhisattva..."

The Bodhisattva observes both the established truths (*vyavasthāpita-satya*) and the non-established truth (*avyavasthāpita-satya*) simultaneously during training, in order to induce the two types of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) in the future and to suppress the two types of conceptual obstacles (*parikalpita-āvaraṇa*). This [observation] is of two kinds: first, the eight truths of the upper and lower realms;

second, the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*). These are all termed the observation of the established truths. Second, there is also the non-established truth, which likewise has two [aspects].
The seedless True Suchness (tathatā) is called the non-established truth (apratiṣṭhita-satya) because it is free from all marks (lakṣaṇa).

The two emptinesses (śūnyatā), which are the objects of observation for the path of insight consisting of the three or two mental moments, are called "non-established" because they are not established through the differentiation of the four truths as they are. Question:
Why is it necessary to perform these two types of contemplation prior to the [first] stage (bhūmi)? Answer: First, in order to induce the future establishment and the non-establishment.

Second, because it is the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*). Second, because it serves to suppress and eliminate the two obstacles—the afflictive (*kleśa-āvaraṇa*) and the cognitive (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*)—which are conceptually constructed.

The Chancellor (Xiangguo) said: "Prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), actual wisdom consists only of preparatory application (*prayoga*); since it is now said that one 'practices' [it], it encompasses both types of wisdom.

In reality, the presence or absence of these two aspects within this stage depends on one's own subjective perception. As that treatise states: "Those two aspects of emptiness and existence have not yet been eliminated; they still carry [the traces of conceptualization]."
Indeed, in this stage, the two characteristics of existence and non-existence arise from one's own subjective perceptions. As that treatise states:
"Those two characteristics of emptiness and existence have not yet reached the limit; they are accompanied by signs because the observing mind still apprehends something."

Regarding the statement "subsequently, through one application (*prayoga*), one seeks the correct and equal [enlightenment]," this refers to seeking the true path. This explains the meaning of *prayoga*:

by applying effort and practice, one seeks the path that was previously absent. First, through the wisdom of application (*prayogajñāna*), one eliminates [obstructions] and gives rise to the two types of right paths;

these are the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) consisting of the Path of Reality (*abhisamayamārga*) and the Path of Subsequent Realization (*anvayajñānamārga*). Based on these three fundamental wisdoms, the subsequent wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) correctly realizes and discriminates them through application.

Because they arise from seeking, and because the three types of knowledge are established. As a verse says: "Like a mute person seeking to experience an object; like a mute person correctly experiencing an object;
like one who is not mute experiencing an object."
To speak of "illumination" means that illumination arises from clarity.

To say that the foolish are obscured regarding accomplished matters means that fools are obscured regarding matters already completed; the wise, however, penetrate them before they have even sprouted, foreseeing events beforehand.

Fools are obscured regarding accomplished matters; only when the matter is finished and they have already consumed its consequences do they realize their transgressions. This is solely because of their darkness.

This is clarity. To "accomplish the matter" means that the matter has been completed. It is precisely because of obscurity and a lack of discernment that one becomes attached to things and commits transgressions.
To speak to others so that they may understand and repent is called an "edict" (zhào). An edict arises from clarity.
Regarding the statement that the oral teaching contains no level (even) tones: in ancient times, characters were insufficient, so they now employ cross-phonetic readings (*jiaoyin*).
As for the statement that the sixth section contains seven verses praising the construction of stupas and so forth, it is only because the entry into *parinirvāṇa* is not praised;

thus, while there are seven lines in the prose (*chángxíng*) of the sūtra, there are only six in the verse (*gāthā*). The sūtra says: "Mañjuśrī, furthermore, when the Buddha has entered *parinirvāṇa*, there are bodhisattvas..."

Regarding the subsequent passage on making offerings to the *śarīra*, the Great Upādhyāya’s commentary states: "The seven verses describe seeing the Buddha enter *parinirvāṇa* and erecting a stūpa for worship.
This first verse specifically describes his entry into *parinirvāṇa*; how then can it be said that he does not describe the entry into *parinirvāṇa*?
The remaining six lines of verse describe the erection of the stūpa after his passing. The initial scriptural text was poorly translated; it should properly have read 'Mañjuśrī'."
Furthermore, one observes that the various Buddhas manifest parinirvāṇa and distribute their relics;

those who are able to reform [their conduct] obtain immeasurable merit, and even if they do not reform, they likewise obtain immeasurable merit. Moreover, the Sūtra states: "After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, making offerings to his relics [yields great reward]."

This verse indeed describes the entry into *parinirvāṇa*. According to the master of the commentary’s structural analysis (*pīṭhikā*), seven lines describe the construction of stupas and the offering of relics after the passing, but do not describe the sixth section, the entry into *parinirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, while there are seven verses in the prose (*gadya*), the text contains only six.
Now, according to the master of the present commentary, he analyzes it twice. In the first analysis, the first line concerns the Buddha’s *parinirvāṇa*.

The subsequent verses on making offerings to the *śarīra* (relics) and the final six verses concerning the construction of stūpas for worship constitute a general summary of the prose section regarding the erection of stūpas after the [Buddha’s] parinirvāṇa.
If that were the case, there would be a redundancy. If these six verses were intended as a general summary of the prose section on building stūpas, then the Sūtra says:
"O sons of the Buddha, in order to make offerings to the *śarīra*, they adorned the stūpas and temples," continuing until the passage on the flowers.

The two lines of verse have been expanded; they do not exist at all within the prose commentary. How is it that these six verses collectively describe the construction of stupas after the [Buddha’s] parinirvāṇa, as found in the prose?
Because this classification of the meaning is incomplete, the Master of the Commentary has further provided a second round of classification.

Regarding the statement that "the seven verses are further divided into two parts," this is the second major section. The first five verses describe the construction of the stūpa as set forth in the prose commentary;

the final two verses conclude with the excellence of constructing the stūpa. If one were to categorize these as the conclusion on the excellence of the stūpa, then the entire section would be exhausted.
Regarding the phrase "this first," it refers to the initial line among the seven verses, which describes the Bodhisattva’s offering of relics;
this is precisely what should be chanted from the sūtra text. This single verse clarifies only the offering of relics and does not mention the construction of stūpas.

Within these offerings, there are instances where Bodhisattvas burn their bodies or cauterize their arms to present incense and flowers as offerings. Since the Master of the Commentary [has already] addressed this within his current verse...
There was another offering of the śarīra, for which a stupa made of the seven precious substances was erected; this is the long account of the śarīra. There are three kinds of śarīra:
first, hair-śarīra; second, flesh-śarīra; and third, bone-śarīra. Within the white [bone-śarīra], there are two types: first, grain-like śarīra.
The two sacred tusks—these three types of relics—if one makes offerings to them, one will be reborn in the heavens a thousand times.

Finally, the Dragon King of the Sea collected them and took them into the ocean to worship them within his palace. After the passage of a kalpa, they transformed into wish-fulfilling jewels. (The above concludes the account of making offerings to the bodily relics.)

Regarding the statement that three verses concern the construction of stupas and one verse concerns counting, the Sūtra says: "Furthermore, one sees sons of the Buddha constructing various stupas and temples.
A *stūpa* is a place where relics (*śarīra*) are present; a place where no relics are present is also called a "sacred temple" (*ling-miao*), which resembles the Buddhist halls of today.
Regarding the measure of a single verse, the Sūtra says: "The precious and wondrous [stūpas] are five thousand yojanas [in height]," and so forth.
Regarding the adornment of a single verse, the Sūtra says: "Each stūpa and temple has one thousand banners and pennants," and so forth.
Zhen says: "Each stūpa and temple has five types of adornments; atop each stūpa there are one thousand banners, planted in the ground and extending everywhere."
1. Each stūpa is one thousand *krośas* in height; banners are suspended from the *yaṣṭi*, fluttering in the wind at every point.
2. On each stūpa there are one thousand pearls; when the pearls intersect, they form a jeweled net that covers [the structure] completely. 3.

On each stūpa there are one thousand canopies of dew-pearls (*amala-ka*), intricately woven and mounted upon the upper part. 4. On each stūpa there are one thousand precious bells, hung from the corners by cords. The jewels...
"The bells chime in harmony. "Harmony" means being in accord; "chiming" refers to sound.

When the Tathāgata originally appeared in the world, it was because the faculties and dispositions of those of middling capacity had matured, and the conditions for those to be converted had already reached their limit. He taught that he could not remain in the world.

To cause those people at the great assembly on Mount Ling to desire to hear the nectar-like Dharma, he manifested birth and death like an ordinary being, concealing his eternal body and entering *nirvāṇa*.

This was so that they might instead make offerings to the Buddha’s true body, constructing stupas of supreme height and breadth, with banners, streamers, and jeweled canopies numbering in the millions, while celestial music resounded with subtle and wondrous tones. [Question: What is meant by "transcendence" (*zòng*)?
[Guang] answers: There are two interpretations of this. One says: The jeweled stupa is five thousand *yojana* in height; this is its vertical measurement.

It is two thousand *yojana* in horizontal width; this is its lateral measurement. Thus, "vertical" (*zong*) refers to the height, which is five thousand *yojana*, and "horizontal" (*guang*) refers to the width, which is two thousand *yojana*.
If this is so, how is it that the sutra speaks of it as being "exactly [in length and breadth]"?
[Question: "Etc. [Answer: Previously, it was stated that the length is five thousand *yojana*s. From this, subtract two thousand;
take the remaining two thousand as the width, and divide the other two thousand equally between the top and bottom. Thus, there are two thousand *yojana*s from the center to the top or bottom.

Aside from this, the measurements of one inch or one foot are not equal. [Question: How many *li* is the breadth? [Answer: Taking two thousand [units] from the top to the bottom is exactly equal to the breadth; this is called "length" (*āyāma*).
"Extensive and equal. Question: The sutra states that the precious stupa is five thousand *yojanas* high and exquisite.
Since "height" refers to the vertical dimension, one would expect the "width" to be explained separately. Why, then, are height and width mentioned together in this single passage? Answer:

This provides a second interpretation based on conventional worldly explanations. In common usage, north-south is called "length" (*āyāma*) and east-west is called "width" (*vistāra*). [In this case,] the north-south dimension is two thousand *yojanas*.

It is ten *yojana*s [in height]. It is two thousand *yojana*s from east to west; therefore, it is said that its length and breadth are exactly equal. Regarding this meaning, there are two explanations.
According to the first master, one side is taken as two thousand *yojana*s, and all four sides together are calculated as eight thousand *yojana*s.

"Length" refers to north to south; it is two thousand *yojana*s in length. On the western edge of the western side of the stūpa, the measurement from north to south is two thousand *yojana*s. To the east of the stūpa...

From west to east it is a ridge; from south to north, its measurement is two thousand [yojanas]. When the two sides of this longitudinal axis are combined, they total four thousand yojanas; this is called "length.
Furthermore, as for the "width," the measurement from west to east on the northern side is two thousand, and the measurement from west to east on the southern side is also two thousand.
When the two sides of this transverse axis are combined, they are said to total four thousand yojanas. The scriptural text, however, speaks according to only one side of the longitudinal axis.
Taking one side, and taking one side across the middle, it is said that the length and width are each exactly two thousand *yojanas*.
According to the second master’s interpretation, one side of the stupa is only one thousand *yojanas* wide; thus, the four sides together amount to four thousand *yojanas*.

For example, if taken as the longitudinal center, the eastern edge of the east face is likewise so; when both are combined, the length is said to be two thousand. If taken transversely, it is the same.
The east-west measurement of both sides is one thousand [yojanas]. The north side’s east-west measurement is also one thousand. Taken together for both sides, there are two thousand across;
therefore, it is said that its length and breadth are exactly equal at two thousand yojanas each. Between these two interpretations, the former is correct. As the Sūtra says:
"Its length and breadth are exactly equal, each being two thousand yojanas. (The first part [above] explains the Sūtra; the second part [below] clarifies the *yojana*.)
The phrase "as stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*" clarifies the number of stupas to be constructed and so forth.
The phrase "one shall obtain immeasurable [merit]" clarifies the fruit of constructing stupas. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"The merit of one person in Jambudvīpa is equal to that of one Cakravartin king; the merit of the king and the people of Jambudvīpa together is equal to the merit of one person in Aparagoyānī."

The merit of the people of the four directions is not equal to the merit of a single deva of the six heavens of the desire realm (*ṣaḍ-kāmadhātu*). Likewise, the merit of the devas of the six heavens of the desire realm is not equal to the merit of a single Brahmā-rāja.
When a bhikṣu asked the Buddha how much merit constitutes the "Brahma-merit," the Buddha replied that it is immeasurable and boundless.
The *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra* states: "For example, it is as if water were poured down until it reached the Golden Wheel (*kāñcanamaṇḍala*) below, filling all the way up to the Brahma-world."

The interior is entirely water. Suppose there were a person who took a single cow-hair, divided it into three parts, and used one part to drop into the waters of the great earth until they were exhausted;
yet the merit of Brahmā would not be exhausted. Someone might ask: "If one constructs a stūpa with a distracted mind, how can one obtain the merit of Brahmā?
The merit of Brahmā must surely be produced by determinate karma. The answer is: if we distinguish according to their characteristics, first, regarding the construction of a stūpa...

Through making offerings and hearing the Dharma, one gives rise to the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). Once the wisdom derived from hearing has arisen, from that point onward one is able to be born in the higher realms.
This is the second interpretation: it is not necessary to be born in those heavens to receive the fruit;

rather, because the excellence of receiving the fruit within the four continents of the desire realm resembles the merit of Brahmā (*brahma-puṇya*), it is also established as Brahmā-merit. Furthermore, it serves as the requisite for the fruit of Buddhahood. This is so.
The outflow-free Brahma-merit serves as the cause for the outflow-free Brahma-merit; the Buddha is this outflow-free Brahma-merit.
Regarding the term *yojana* (translated as "Brahma" in the Chinese text), it explains the meaning of a *yojana*. In the world-system of the Mahāyāna, [the world] is a transformation of consciousness;
in the world-system of the Hīnayāna, it is composed of atoms (*paramāṇu*).
Regarding the statement in the *Abhidharmakośakārikā*, "The atom, the minute particle, gold, water, and so forth," this is the formal exposition.

First is the *paramāṇu* (extreme atom). Seven of these *paramāṇus* constitute one *aṇu* (minute particle). Seven *aṇus* constitute one *trasareṇu* (gold-dust mote). Seven *trasareṇus* constitute one *vātāyanacchidrarajaḥ* (water-dust mote).
Seven *vātāyanacchidrarajas* constitute one *śaśarajaḥ* (hare-hair dust mote). Seven... [of hare-hair dust motes constitute one sheep-hair dust mote].
Seven rabbit-hair dust particles form one sheep-hair dust particle. Seven sheep-hair dust particles form one cow-hair dust particle.
Seven cow-hair dust particles form one crevice-dust particle. Seven crevice-dust particles form one nit.
Seven nits form one louse. Seven lice form one barley grain. Seven barley grains form one finger-breadth.
Section. Twenty-four finger-widths laid side-by-side constitute one *hasta* (cubit), measuring one chi and eight cun. Four *hasta* make one *dhanus* (bow-length), measuring seven chi and two cun.

Five hundred *dhanus* measure one *krośa*, which is equivalent to two *li*, calculated as seven hundred and twenty paces, or three thousand six hundred chi. Eight *krośa* amount to sixteen *li*. This constitutes [the first section].
One yojana. Regarding the phrase "if based on other sūtras and so forth," this is because the travel distance for kings in those Western countries is sixteen *li*;
therefore, [the text] takes the larger figure. For commoners, the travel distance is not fixed at thirty or forty *li*. (The above explains that the precious stūpa is five thousand yojanas high.)

Regarding the phrase "lengthwise, sound, etc.": this explains that the length and breadth are exactly equal at two thousand *yojanas*. In ancient times, the character for "length" (*zòng*) was incomplete;

the character "zòng" is pronounced with the "róng" (容) radical reversed, meaning "to extend from a source. In modern times, the character is standardized with the "biān" (邊) radical added. In the *Qieyun*, there are three instances of "zòng":
it means "long," it means "track," and it refers to the "tracks of a carriage wheel" (*chēcè*). The term "cōngrán" (樅然) is also commonly pronounced with the "zòng" (縱) sound.
In some commentaries, the character "cong" (from) is used; "guang" (broad) refers to the horizontal. Question: What is meant by "vertical and broad"? Answer:
One cannot discuss verticality and breadth in terms of above and below. The previous statement that the jeweled stupa was five thousand *yojanas* high already described its vertical measurement.

Now, we shall simply calculate the dimensions based on the ground surface, according to the cardinal directions of east, west, south, and north. The *Han shi wai zhuan* states: "That which runs north-south is called 'length' (*zòng*);

that which runs east-west is called 'width' (*guǎng*). This refers to fixed spatial locations. However, the intent of the Commentary (*Shū*) is not to rely on fixed locations, but rather to define length and width in relation to the human body.
For instance, if one stands facing east or west, and a person looking toward the west observes the stupa, then [the orientation] is east-west.

Regarding the longitudinal and transverse dimensions of the stūpa: if one stands on the southern side and looks toward the stūpa, then the north-south axis is the longitudinal dimension and the east-west axis is the transverse dimension.
Regarding the statement that "exposed" (*lu*) means "not covered" (*bu fu*) and so forth, this clarifies the meaning of a canopy or covering (*man fu*). The Sūtra says:

"At each stūpa and temple, there were a thousand banners and streamers, with canopies of interlaced pearls and exposed lattices. Here, what is placed over something is called a "covering," while what is not placed over it is called "exposed."
Regarding the statement that this clarifies the jeweled stupas and so forth of the land of recompense: the dimensions of these stupas are vast and their number is great;
these are what is seen by bodhisattvas of the highest stage. A single stupa measures five thousand *yojanas*, let alone those that are even beyond measure.
Thus, one knows that these are the stupas within the land of recompense.
As for the statement, "It is not so; in this continent, etc.," it means that [the stūpa] transforms into a stūpa within the *vipākabhūmi* (retribution land).
It is not the case that a single stūpa is placed in Jambudvīpa, this southern continent; how much less so could many stūpas be established here? Question:
This interpretation concerns the jeweled stūpa in the eastern world-system. How can one take this as proof that a stūpa cannot be established in this continent? Answer: In this direction...
In the Jambudvīpa of this defiled land, it is not permitted to install [the stūpa]. Within the manifest light, the Jambudvīpa of the defiled land is likewise not permitted to install it.
Not even two may be installed per continent; this is already a restriction. Even if there were four continents, it would still not be permitted to install many stūpas.

Therefore, we know that these are stūpas within the *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense land). It is only said here that stūpas are to be installed in this direction’s *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation land), and this does not apply to the former.

Regarding the understanding of the worlds of the East: it is impossible to establish lands within the transformation [bodies]. Although the transformation and reward Buddha-lands of the East and West differ, the Buddha-lands of the Reward and Transformation Buddhas are identical for each Buddha.
If one takes this realm of transformation as an example, it cannot accommodate many; it is clear that only the Reward Land can accommodate them.

Regarding the statement "there are those called curtains and canopies," this refers to the silk and brocade coverings placed above; these may also be termed "curtains" (*mañca*) or "canopies" (*vitāna*).

Regarding the statement "exposed" (*lū*), which refers to being covered and exposed, this is an explanation of the character *lū*. Previously, when first explaining the place where the covering is attached, it was termed a "curtain" (*mañca*); here, the curtain covers [the space].
Generally, that which is not covered is called "exposed" (*lù*). Later, when explaining the places where the canopy is attached, those very places where it is attached are also called "exposed.

Question: How can the places where [the canopy] is attached be called "exposed"? Answer: It is like a wooden barrel exposed to the dew. Because the canopy is attached there, those places cannot be called "exposed";
rather, they are formed by the interlacing of pearl cords at the ends to ward off fierce winds. This is the same as the "interlaced pearls and dew" mentioned in various sutras.
"Covering" (*gai*) is equivalent to "concluding" (*zhong*).
It is said that where some write the character *man* (縵), it should instead be written as *man* (幔); there is no scriptural authority for writing it as *man*.
Regarding the statement that "constructing stupas, victory banners," and so forth, Maitreya Bodhisattva asked Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva: "For what reason, among all..."
The sons of the Buddha and others make offerings to the śarīra and adorn the stūpas and temples. Originally, the construction of stūpas was solely for the purpose of making offerings;

even after the stūpas are completed, the realm naturally becomes magnificent and beautiful. Just as planting trees is fundamentally for the sake of bearing fruit, and once the flowers bloom, the trees themselves become dignified and majestic, so too the construction of stūpas is fundamentally for the purpose of making offerings to the True Body (dharmakāya). Once those stūpas are completed, the realm naturally becomes magnificent.

"Good. You ask: 'Because of the construction of stupas, the national borders become magnificent and beautiful. Since this originally stems from adorning the state, why does it open up [the possibility] for making offerings to the true body?

The commentary states: 'The excellence of constructing stupas,' etc. The meaning is that while flowers originally bloom in order to produce fruit, this does not prevent the tree itself from being adorned.
Likewise, while the primary intent of constructing stupas is to make offerings to the entire body (śarīra), what prevents the national borders from becoming magnificent and pure?"
"Profound" (*daojie*) means "distant.
Regarding the statement that the second section contains eight verses on the invitation (*qing*) and so forth: the question is, what is the origin of the word "invitation"? The answer is:

within the topical outline (*kewen*) of the subsequent scripture, there are instances of "inviting an answer by inferring the time" and "inviting an answer by inferring the matter"; it is for this reason that the word "invitation" is placed here at the beginning of the inquiry.
Regarding the phrase "this is the first": the Sūtra says, "The Buddha emits a single ray of light; this is the light of this world-system.
I and the assembly see the various wonders and excellences of this land. Furthermore, it says, "The Buddha emits a single ray of light; this is the light of this world-system.
In the phrase "I and [the assembly]," "I" refers to one's own person, while "the assembly" refers to others. They see this Sahā world-system.
The world is manifold and wondrously sublime; "wondrous" (*kī*) means extraordinary, which refers to the emission of light.

Regarding the subsequent verse that restates the vision of the distant wonders, the Sūtra says: "By the supernatural power (*ṛddhibala*) of all Buddhas," and so forth. "Supernatural power" refers to the emission of light.
Because the light of wisdom is rare and marvelous, the pure radiance illuminates immeasurable lands for eighteen thousand eons.

The realms are distant and marvelous. A questioner asks: Śākyamuni, as a single Buddha, alone emits divine light; for what reason, then, does Maitreya’s inquiry refer to the "spiritual power of all Buddhas"? Answer:
According to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, regarding the commonality and distinctness of those to be converted (*vineya*), it states: "Among those to be converted, there are those who are common.

Those who are common are those who, in the same place and at the same time, are transformed by various Buddhas individually—whether as bodies or as lands—with similar forms and characteristics. It does not [state that they are transformed by a single Buddha].

They mutually obstruct one another and are intermingled with one another, acting as dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) that cause the consciousnesses of those to be transformed to manifest [the Buddhas].
Thus, it is said that in a single land there is a single Buddha-body who manifests supernatural powers and preaches the Dharma for the benefit [of beings]; therefore, they may be called "many.
From the perspective of sentient beings, one speaks of "one Buddha," or, based on the non-duality of their spiritual power, one speaks of "many."

Regarding the statement that the first verse sets forth the two views of self and other: the Sūtra says, "We have seen these," where the word "we" (我) refers to oneself, and the word "these" (等) refers to others.
The *Shouji* (攝取) commentary states that this includes the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings; thus, they are called the two views of self and other.
The Buddha’s son Mañjuśrī wishes to resolve the doubts of the multitude. Mañjuśrī speaks to Maitreya: "The great assembly has seen the emission of light."
"Why is it that you alone have put forth your head to speak of such troubling matters? Why do you not ask the others? Maitreya replied, "It is not that I alone wish to question the Great Being;
I, too, am not my own master. He cited the Sūtra: "The fourfold assembly looks up to you with joy, as does I.
This was intended to address the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of supernatural beings. By saying "I look up to you," he meant that he desired the Great Being himself.
This is the answer. [The text] says, "He looked at me and wished to receive from me the question," which is why no other person is mentioned; I, likewise, did not ask anyone else.
When it asks, "World-Honored One, for what reason did you emit this radiance? it combines both the perspectives of self and other, as found in the prose section (*chángxíng*).
Here, the self-view and the view of others are treated as a single unit, while "this" and "that" looking constitute two distinct matters.

These are two matters. Question: Why is it that the emission of light is specifically discussed here? Answer: The intention is to indicate that the emission of light is precisely the cause for the teaching.
Regarding the phrase "this is the beginning," one verse infers the time and requests an answer; it is also Mañjuśrī’s response to the emission of light.

The Sūtra says: "The Son of the Buddha answers at the proper time, resolving doubts and causing joy," and so forth. "Evolve" (*yan*) refers to the manner in which water flows continuously; it means light extending from this place to that. Thus, it is called "evolve. Now, this single verse dedicates the timing for requesting an answer.
