"How can one wait until the World-Honored One emerges from samādhi? For instance, when the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū entered samādhi for eighty-four thousand kalpas, how could Śākyamuni Tathāgata have waited so long if it were like this?
Maitreya said to Mañjuśrī, "The Son of the Buddha answers at the proper time.

He is called the "Son of the Buddha who answers at the proper time" because he alone succeeds to the rank of the Dharma King. Within the phrase "at the proper time," there are two meanings. First, [the meaning of]...
The Bodhisattva knows the proper time to give an answer. One who well knows the proper time is called a Great Dharma Master. Second, regarding "time":

it is precisely the time when sentient beings thirst and look up in longing; it is further the time for the Bodhisattva to provide an answer. When sentient beings are currently looking up in thirsty longing, it is precisely the time for the Bodhisattva to answer.
It is like the moment an egg makes a sound; that is precisely the moment the mother hen pecks it open. Precisely...
This is the time when the great assembly harbors doubts; it is precisely this moment when Mañjuśrī provides the answer. The Sūtra says:

"The Son of the Buddha answers at the proper time, resolving doubts and causing joy. When the people have doubts, their hearts are filled with displeasure; only when their doubts are severed do they finally rejoice.
To attain such joy, one must necessarily sever doubt. What benefit does this bring? He manifests this radiance (the explanation of the Sūtra is complete).
Regarding the phrase "the fourfold assembly longing and thirsting," this refers to their aspiration and desire to hear [the teaching]. It means resolving their doubts and causing them joy.
The intent is that if the fourfold assembly did not look up to [the teaching] with longing, they would be incapable of hearing the Mahāyāna;
only once they have given rise to such longing can the supreme path be expounded for them—this is what is meant by "expounding the sūtra."

Regarding the phrase "it is precisely the right time": this refers to the time when the fourfold assembly is capable of hearing the Dharma; it is precisely at this moment that the Bodhisattva provides his response.

Regarding the statement "one who preaches the Dharma must always adapt": *dòu* means to detain or to cause to remain; it carries the sense of causing [the listener] to abide and settle within the Dharma within their own being.

The intended meaning is that when preaching the Dharma, one must necessarily cause them to abide and settle in the Dharma. Since the members of the present assembly desire to hear it, one must preach for them; this is called [adapting].
This is to accommodate the capacities of sentient beings. One must truly possess a heart of longing and yearning before preaching the Dharma.
Regarding the statement that the first verse refers to two matters: the Sūtra says, "The wondrous Dharma attained by the Buddha while sitting at the site of enlightenment," and so forth.
Maitreya said to Mañjuśrī: "Do not constrain me; when I examine myself, I have attained eight or nine out of ten [of the Dharma]. Today..."
Flowers rained down and the earth shook; these events did not exceed two paths: first, the desire to expound the Dharma realized within liberation;
second, the bestowing of predictions upon the śrāvakas. As the Sūtra says: "The wondrous Dharma attained by the Buddha while seated at the site of enlightenment is the fruit of the One Vehicle."
This is intended to explain this; it is intended to bestow a prediction (vyākaraṇa) regarding the cause of the One Vehicle (ekayāna).

Furthermore, it is said that by sitting at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), one manifests the One and thereby bestows a prediction that shatters the duality [of the two vehicles]. Mañjuśrī said to Maitreya: "If you have attained realization, simply speak of it yourself;
why must you ask me? Maitreya replied: "I could indeed speak of it all at once; however, if one definitively and universally explains the Dharma and bestows predictions, then it is..."
"I cannot. My usual worldly affairs I can settle and decide; but today is a matter of the utmost gravity.
This matter requires a response from a Great Being (Mahāsattva); no other answer will suffice."
Regarding the statement that the subsequent verse clarifies that the matter is "extremely great" and so forth: Question: How is it known that this is a great matter? Answer: The Sūtra says:

"He reveals the Buddha-lands, adorned and purified with various jewels, and one beholds the Buddhas; this is no small cause. If one were to speak of the fruits of humans and devas or the fruits of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha), these would be called minor causes and conditions.
The sphere of activity for those of the two vehicles is not vast, and thus it is not called a "great matter. Now, however, this is...
There are eighteen thousand lands of retribution and transformation. Because they are the result of extremely great causes and conditions, it is said that "this is no small matter. A verse states:
"Furthermore, one sees various Buddha-lands adorned with myriad jewels, possessing the colors of lapis lazuli and crystal; this is due to the illumination of the Buddha’s light.
If one sees the land of retribution where lapis lazuli forms the ground, with golden cords and sevenfold railings, and sevenfold nets..."

Lattices, water-birds, and groves of trees; mindfulness of the Buddha and mindfulness of the Dharma. If one sees the Buddha, this is the *saṃbhogakāya*. The Buddha’s eyes are like the waters of the four great oceans. If one sees a minor transformation land (*nirmāṇakṣetra*), which is the place where all sentient beings undergo the retribution of birth and death through their karma, this refers to the four great continents, the sun and moon, and so forth. Question: Upon what kind of land do these Buddha-bodies rely? Answer: The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Cheng weishi lun), fascicle 10, states: "Furthermore, there are two kinds of pure lands: first, the pure land of the *saṃbhogakāya*, which is adorned with immeasurable and boundless merits; second, the pure land of the *nirmāṇakāya*, which is adorned with various kinds of wondrous things. The *saṃbhogakāya* relies upon the pure land of the *saṃbhogakāya*, while the *nirmāṇakāya* relies upon the pure land of the *nirmāṇakāya*. The *saṃbhogakāya* is not subject to transformation, whereas the *nirmāṇakāya* manifests according to the capacities of sentient beings. Thus it is said. Furthermore, the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* (She dasheng lun), fascicle 9, states: "The *saṃbhogakāya* is the body of enjoyment, which is the fruit of the practice of the Mahāyāna; it is the body that enjoys the Dharma. It is adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics, and its light shines throughout the ten directions. It is the body that eternally dwells in the pure land, enjoying the sublime Dharma together with bodhisattvas of equal rank. The *nirmāṇakāya* is the body of transformation, which is the fruit of the practice of the Mahāyāna; it is the body that manifests in various forms to transform sentient beings. It may manifest as a Buddha, a śrāvaka, a pratyekabuddha, or even as a bird, a beast, or a tree. It appears in accordance with the inclinations of sentient beings to lead them to liberation. Thus it is said. Therefore, the *saṃbhogakāya* relies upon the pure land of the *saṃbhogakāya*, while the *nirmāṇakāya* relies upon the pure land of the *nirmāṇakāya*. The former is the realm of ultimate reality, while the latter is the realm of expedient manifestation. One should know that these two bodies and their respective lands are distinct and not confused. This is the definitive teaching of the Great Vehicle. Thus it is said. Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Yuqie shidi lun), fascicle 86, states: "The *saṃbhogakāya* is the body of enjoyment, which is the fruit of the practice of the Mahāyāna; it is the body that enjoys the Dharma. The *svābhāvikakāya* (Self-Nature Body) is based upon the *dharmatā-dhātu* (Dharma-Nature Realm). Nevertheless, according to its phenomenal characteristics, its magnitude is boundless, like space pervading all things.
Although there is no distinction in essence between this body and its realm, they are designated differently in terms of their attributes:

that which pertains to the Buddha is called "body" (*kāya*), while that which pertains to the Dharma is called "realm" (*dhātu*). That which pertains to the Buddha is a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and is therefore termed "body"; that which pertains to the Dharma is the essential nature (*dharmatā*).
This is why it is called "land. The Enjoyment Body likewise relies upon its own land, which is circular and boundless, adorned with various jewels.

The Self-Enjoyment Body constantly dwells in reliance upon this land. The Other-Enjoyment Body also relies upon its own land, transforming it into a pure land according to what is appropriate for Bodhisattvas of the ten stages.
It may be small or large, inferior or superior, changing and shifting from one state to another. Thus is the Other-Enjoyment Body.
The *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) dwells in reliance upon this. If it is a *nirmāṇakāya*, it dwells in reliance upon a *nirmāṇabhūmi* (emanation land).

According to what is appropriate for sentient beings who have not yet ascended to the [bodhisattva] stages (*bhūmi*), it manifests as a buddha-land—whether pure or impure, small or large—and changes and transforms from one state to another.
The Buddha’s *nirmāṇakāya* dwells in reliance upon this. Question: For what reason does the preceding verse say, "The light from between the eyebrows illuminates the eastern direction"?

The eighteen thousand lands are all like the color of gold. This [description] indicates that the various Buddha-lands here are adorned and purified by various jewels. The answer is that this refers to their essential nature;

in their essential nature, they are adorned and purified by various jewels. That description [of them being like gold] refers to the illumination of the Buddhas' light, whereby they all appear like the color of gold.
This demonstrates the purity of the Buddha-land.

Regarding the phrase "formally requesting [an answer] from him," the Sūtra says: "Mañjuśrī, you should know that the fourfold assembly, along with the nāgas and devas, are looking toward you, O Benevolent One;
what will you preach? Why is it that previously it was said they were looking toward both the Benevolent One and me, whereas here it is said only that they are looking toward the Benevolent One?
Answer: As previously stated, [the assembly] gazes upon me and rejoices at my inquiry. Why do the multitude gaze upon me?

Now that I have finished asking, they gaze solely upon you, hoping that you will answer and decisively sever the net of doubt for the assembly. "Doubt" refers to hesitation between two ends, whether advancing or retreating;
it is likened to a net, which ensnares sentient beings. [The question was: Why did Śākyamuni emit light? Maitreya asked, and Mañjuśrī replied.
Answer: This statement is intended to clarify that the Buddhas of the three periods—past, future, and present—are all together on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa to reveal the Mahāyāna.
Śākyamuni is the Buddha of the present and is thus able to emit light; Maitreya is the Buddha of the future and is thus able to pose the question.
Mañjuśrī is a Buddha of the past; therefore, he is able to provide the answer.

Regarding the statement in the *Yulanpen jing* (Ullambana Sūtra) that "Mañjuśrī, by means of his knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsa*), etc.," this first section briefly indicates the purport of Mañjuśrī’s response according to the treatise.
"Past" (*su*) refers to former lives; the object resides in the past, and the Bodhisattva’s wisdom abides within those former lives. Thus, [the wisdom] is singular.

To observe this once: the wisdom that is able to take this as its object is called the "knowledge of past lives" (pūrvanivāsajñāna). "Directly seeing" means seeing with clarity; seeing through direct perception (pratyakṣa) is what is meant by "directly seeing.
As for the "characteristics of cause and effect," these refer specifically to the characteristics of the cause. This refers to such cause and effect.

This is established based on the single body of Wondrous Light (Prabhāsa). That is to say, the body of Wondrous Light is considered an effect in relation to what precedes it, yet it is considered a cause in relation to what follows it, extending through to the bodies of Mañjuśrī and the Bodhisattva Ajita. The body of Wondrous Light prior [to this stage] is the cause within the causes;
the body of Wondrous Light subsequent [to this stage] is the effect within the causes; and the Buddha’s *bodhi* is the effect within the effects.

Regarding the statement "accomplishing ten kinds of matters" and so forth: it is asked, since eight of the ten matters concern events from the assembly on Vulture Peak, how can they also be called "past"?
The answer is: these very eight great meanings were also witnessed by Mañjuśrī in the past.

Therefore, what is pointed out today is also called the past. When Mañjuśrī was with the twenty thousand Lamp-Light Buddha of the past, he personally realized ten matters under the Dharma Master Wonderful Light.
Today, within his concentrated mind, he perceives each one clearly; seeing these ten matters as if they were present before him, he is thus able to answer the question regarding the Great [Vehicle].
Regarding the meaning of "riding" [upon them]: since the past and future lack substantiality, how can the ten kinds of objects appear as if they were present?
Answer: Mañjuśrī has long ago attained unsurpassed enlightenment; his spiritual power is inconceivable.

Although these phenomena are formless, he is able to manifest them and, within a state of meditative concentration, can transform and bring them forth so that they appear clearly and distinctly. Therefore, they are called "manifestly perceived. The ten kinds of objects are thus as if present.
It was present before; therefore, he was able to answer.

Regarding the statement "it is not an inference, nor is it a fabrication," the Master of the Commentary explains that "not an inference" means it is not a non-perceptual [cognition], and "not a fabrication" means it is not a false construction.

"Not a measure" (non-cognition) clearly indicates that the mind of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). The question is: using the present to verify the past, and using the past to verify the present. Furthermore, the Sūtra...
He said: "In the past, I have seen this omen among the Buddhas of the past; whenever this light appeared, they immediately preached the Great Dharma.

Therefore, you should know that the present Buddha’s manifestation of light is likewise so. He further said: "I saw that when the Buddha Dīpaṃkara manifested such a sign of his original light, I thereby knew that the present Buddha intends to preach the Lotus Sūtra.
How can you say this is not direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)? [The answer is: It is because the Bodhisattva’s mind is concentrated in meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
This is solely direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Now, by citing a past Buddha, one speaks by means of inference (*anumāna*) regarding present events.

The "causal basis for arising" refers to the source from which something originates; such a matter must cite the past to provide corroboration for the present. From this point, he speaks to answer the great assembly.
Upon hearing this, the doubts of the assembly are severed, and they regard this locus of speech as being indeed based on direct perception. Question: Since it is...
[Question: Regarding direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), how can it be said that "it is as I have conceived"? [Answer: It is because he indicates the appearance (*nimitta*).

This indicates that it is not [the ultimate] reality. These are words of the Bodhisattva’s humility; they conform to worldly convention, so he speaks of "conceiving" rather than "inferring. The Master of the Commentary concludes:
"Therefore, this is not a response constructed from emptiness, for the mind in meditative concentration (*samāhita-citta*) taking an object is direct perception. [Question: As with Śāriputra...

The *Jì* (Commentary) states: "White forehead" (*bái è*) and "born" (*shēng*) refer to the white tail-tip; thus we know that when small sages (*xiǎo shèng*) prior to the stages (*dì qián*) and those of the two vehicles (*èr shèng*) take objects as their conditions within meditative concentration (*dìng*), it is not necessarily the case that these are all direct perception (*xiàn liàng*). This is because there are also states of meditative mind that are not direct perception. Answer:

It is simply that states of meditative mind have both coarse and subtle aspects, yet they are not non-valid cognition (*fēi shì liàng*). For example, when the eye perceives form (*sè*), it knows it as a general aggregate; how could this be [non-perception]?

He then says: "This is not a non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*); therefore, it is distinct from inference (*anumāna*). Because one expresses a thesis through self-attesting understanding, and because this speech is the cause for the arising [of that understanding], the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra* states:

'In order to clarify one's own words, one should know that these are exclusively direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Mañjuśrī established a formal argument (*prayoga*) for the sake of sentient beings, saying:
'The present Buddha Śākyamuni is the subject (*dharmin*); he intends to preach the Great Dharma'—this is the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*)."
It says: "Because he manifests great signs, it is analogous. Just as the Buddha Dīpaṃkara manifested great signs and Dīpaṃkara preached the Lotus Sūtra, so too does Śākyamuni manifest great signs;
he is identical to Dīpaṃkara in preaching the Lotus Sūtra."
Regarding the statement "as for the characteristics of the cause," the passage beginning with "Mañjuśrī himself saw" and so forth cites the treatise to explain the characteristics of the cause.

Since the Buddha-fields are not uniform, they are termed "this and that" (*tattat*). This refers to hearing the Dharma and practicing it across five *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (Ganges-sand) numbers of Buddha-fields throughout three great *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*;
this is termed "this and that. Furthermore, hearing the Dharma and practicing it within the lands enjoyed during the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) is likewise termed [the characteristics of the cause].
"In those buddha-fields he cultivates the bodhisattva practice. Second, it says: "In those various buddha-fields" refers to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva himself seeing his own person;
having personally attended upon and made offerings to twenty thousand Buddhas under the assemblies of the Lamp-Light (Dīpaṃkara) Buddha in the past, the buddha-fields were not uniform.
Therefore, they are called "this and that.

Regarding the statement, "The practice is the present time, etc.": the Bodhisattva perceives that his own practice of the Bodhisattva path at that time was the cause for the present Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva;
it was precisely because he practiced the Bodhisattva path at that time that he brought forth the present-day Mañjuśrī as a result.

Body. Therefore, it is called the cause at the present time. Question: Since he serves as the cause for Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, why does the Master of the Commentary explain it below by saying, "Because it is the causal practice for bodhi"?
Answer: It is explained that Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva attained Buddhahood long ago and manifests as a bodhisattva;
thus, he serves as the cause for the Mañjuśrī of the present day. This is precisely what constitutes the causal practice of a bodhisattva. Therefore, there is...

The verse states: "In the past, he was the teacher of Śākyamuni; now, he is a disciple of the Buddha. Since two Honored Ones do not appear simultaneously to transform beings, I am therefore a bodhisattva.
There are three interpretations in total: first, the interpretation of the three periods of time;

second, that Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva has come after the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa and, prior to the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, is collectively designated as belonging to the past; and third, that which will be accomplished in the future.
To universally behold the Buddha-body is called the future. From the assembly of the Lotus Sūtra onwards, until the time when one has not yet attained Buddhahood in the future, is called the present.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva personally beheld his own body in various Buddha-lands of the past.
Cultivating the practices of a bodhisattva constitutes the causal practice for Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva as he exists today;

it is the causal practice for the bodhisattva within the body of a bodhisattva. Second, it is said that the causal practices cultivated in the past serve as the cause for the body of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva today, and likewise serve as the causal practice within the body of the Tathāgata Samantamukha in the future.
It is as if one cause produces two effects. Third, it says: Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva himself saw his own body in past lives practicing the bodhisattva path;
for whom did he serve as a cause? The answer is: this was the causal practice for Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva’s attainment of Buddhahood.
This interpretation generally constitutes the causal practice for Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva’s attainment of Buddhahood, viewed collectively.
This is the explanation of the fruit-stage of the Tathāgata’s Buddhahood (the first section: the gate of explaining the characteristics of the cause).
Regarding the statement, "As for 'fruit,' it refers to that which was relied upon in the past," this explains the characteristics of the fruit.

That which was relied upon in the past—the physical body, the six perfections, the myriad practices, and the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*—constitutes the "relying subject" (*āśrayin*). The three categories of phenomena (*triskandha-dharma*) constitute the "relied-upon object" (*āśraya*). This [body] itself is...
This refers to the body of the Dharma Master Sunlight (Prabhāsa).
Regarding the statement in the discourse that "Mañjuśrī saw his own body," this is the Master of the Treatise’s explanation.
It means that in the past, he was once the Dharma Master Sunlight and heard this Dharma-gate from various Buddhas; specifically, he heard it in the presence of the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* was turned and preached for the sake of sentient beings; this refers to what the sūtra says: "For eighty minor kalpas, he expounded it for the sake of humans" (this is the *Śāstra*’s explanation of the characteristics of the fruit).
Regarding the statement, "This refers to former lives, the past, and so forth," the Master of the Commentary explains the characteristic of the fruit (*phala-lakṣaṇa*). He asks:
Of what, and in relation to whom, is this body of the Dharma Master Miaoguang the fruit? Answer: It is the five precepts and ten wholesome actions of former lives that serve as the cause.
In relation to these five precepts and ten wholesome actions, the body of Miaoguang is the fruit. Answer: The practice performed in former lives is itself the cause for the fruit of Buddhahood.
Furthermore, his present birth with this body of wondrous light is the fruit of having observed the five precepts and left the household life in previous lives.

The commentary states that this is not merely the fruit of a cause as it appears; rather, the Dharma Master Wondrous Light heard the *Lotus Sūtra* from twenty thousand past Buddhas named Dīpaṃkara and subsequently preached it to others.
This is what is termed "that which was heard and seen. Based on these causes of hearing and seeing...

Regarding "experiencing the fruit": this refers to the present-life body of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva. Fearing that people might mistakenly identify the fruit of the five precepts and ten wholesome actions as the fruit of what is seen and heard, he has therefore made this distinction.
Regarding the phrase "those causes," the Sub-commentator (*Sūshǔ*) divides them into two categories to distinguish between cause and effect.

Those "causes" are precisely the causes for the present Buddha-fruit—the fruit of the five precepts and the ten wholesome paths of action. Question: Why must Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva perceive the characteristics of past causes and effects?
Is there a specific reason for this? Answer: The body of Dharma Master Miaoguang was the result of what he had accumulated over many lifetimes; only then did he manifest [this realization].
The body of Wonderful Light (Prabhāpāla) was the very body in which he first heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.

At that time, because Wonderful Light upheld the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he attained the state of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva. These characteristics of cause and effect are both established by the power of the sutra, manifesting the inconceivability of this scripture;
therefore, the characteristics of the fruit are specifically explained.
Regarding the term "that fruit": it refers to the body of Sublime Light (Prabhāsa), which unifies cause and fruit.
Both that Sublime Light and its fruit were all causes for the present Buddha, Joy-Treasury (Nandagarbha); what is now his attainment of Buddhahood is entirely the fruit.

Regarding the statement, "This refers to the first [section]," it means that the initial title serves as a general announcement. The Sūtra says: "At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the 'good sons' (kulaputra) and so forth.
One is designated a "good son" only when endowed with eleven kinds of virtues: (1) being fully possessed of compassion;
(2) having no faults in one's two-fold karma (body and speech); (3) drawing near to virtuous friends; (4) not manifesting one's own virtues; and (5) conforming to the assembly.
1. The human mind. 2. Not speaking of the faults of others. 3. Not seeking fame or profit. 4. Delighting only in the Way and its virtue. 5. One’s own karma being pure. 6.
The mind valuing the true mark (*dharmatā*). 7. Regarding defiled phenomena with lightness.

Regarding the statement, "However, according to the root treatise, this answer [is given] therein," first, the ten causes are assigned. Question: From which scriptural passage do these ten causes arise? Answer:

They arise from the passage in this sutra beginning with, "Now the Buddha, the World-Honored One, wishing to preach the Great Dharma and rain down the Great Dharma Rain," and ending with, "Having emitted this light, he immediately preached the Great Dharma. Question: How is this known? Answer: It is known from Vasubandhu.

The commentary states: Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, by means of his knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*), perceives the ten kinds of phenomena regarding the characteristics of causes and effects from the past as if they were present before him.
For this reason, he is able to provide the answer. If he did not perceive these ten kinds of phenomena, how could he possibly provide the answer?

Regarding the phrase "the causes for manifesting the great meaning" (*pratyakṣa-mahārtha-hetu*), according to the main treatise (*śāstra*), the word "maturation" (*paripāka*) appears within each of the ten causes;
the commentary (*ṭīkā*) has omitted this text. "Manifestly seeing" (*pratyakṣa*) means clearly perceiving those eight kinds of great meanings; it is now capable of providing the answer.
"Manifestly seeing the great meaning" is a *karmadhāraya* compound (where the qualifier and the qualified refer to the same object; the same applies to subsequent instances).

Regarding the statement, "The visible worldly letters, phrases, and so forth," it is asked: Since these are established upon the Tathāgata’s untainted (*anāsrava*) voice, why are they called "worldly" (*laukika*) letters?
"Worldly" carries the sense of being subject to destruction. The answer is that there are three reasons:

first, because they serve as an antidote for the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*), they are termed "worldly letters"; second, with respect to the Buddha's essential teaching, it is untainted; [the third point follows this].

Now, based on the teaching of reflected images (*pratibimba*), the transformation of contaminated consciousness (*sāsrava-vijñāna*) is termed "mundane" (*laukika*). Because these three borrow from the mundane, they are called "mundane.
As for "words" (*akṣara*), they belong to the mundane world of others; because one uses the words of that other mundane world to manifest meaning, they are called "mundane words.

The above three interpretations contradict the *Śāstra* (the commentary), which states of its own accord: "Conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is termed 'mundane'"; first, it possesses discrimination (*vikalpa*).
Conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). That which is non-conceptual is called non-proliferation. Both [types of] verbal expression are conceptual proliferation;
collectively, they are termed "worldly letters. Question: What is the profound meaning of the term "worldly letters"? Answer: Worldly letters are fundamentally not profound.
It is arranged and set forth according to the intention of the Tathāgata; even those of the Two Vehicles cannot fathom it.

One kind is merely the literal text, unable to compose poetry or arrange it in such a way, and thus they do not attain its profound depth. Once it is arranged by someone who understands how to compose poetry, it becomes profoundly deep.
"Intentionality" (saṃcetanā) is termed "profound"; this explains the reason for the teaching.

As for the phrase "manifesting rare causes," it refers to the time of praise: praising the name of the Buddha as rare after a long period of time, praising the Dharma as supreme and wondrous, and praising the arising of benefit and response as rare.

Regarding what is called the "manifestly visible supreme and wondrous causes": the names are identical in their excellence, being named *Sūryapradīpa* (Sun-Lamp-Light). The clans are identical in their excellence, being of the *Bhāradvāja* clan.
The titles are identical in their excellence, being fully endowed with the ten epithets. The Dharma is identical in its excellence, being excellent in the beginning, middle, and end.
Regarding the "visible cause for the enjoyment [of results]": this refers to householders enjoying the pleasures of the five senses, and renunciants enjoying the joy of the Dharma (*dharmasukha*).
Regarding the "visible cause for the appropriation of the Buddhas' turning of the wheel of Dharma": [the question is] after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, who [will turn] the wheel of Dharma?
"Is it included? He replied: "The Bodhisattva Wonderful Light includes [them]; this refers to the meaning of inclusion, reception, and acceptance. It is like a lecturer who receives his students.
Regarding the statement, "He directly beheld the Tathāgata Good Firmness and others," it means that Wonderful Light taught the eight princes and caused them—
Firmly established in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. "Firm and solid" means the sense of non-retrogression; regarding the *tathāgata*'s wheel of Dharma, there is no further retrogression upward.
As for the statement "presently seeing the cause capable of entering," this refers to the eight princes of the Lamp-Light (*Dīpamkara*), who were great *bodhisattvas* named...
"Entering" (*praveśa*) means advancing toward attainment; "entering" (*avatāra*) means realizing and entering [the truth]. This refers to the eight princes, all of whom attained Buddhahood.

Regarding the phrase "the cause of present recollection" (*pratyakṣasmṛtihetu*): the question is, since all ten causes are in fact the recollections of Mañjuśrī, why is only the ninth cause specifically given this name?
There are three reasons for this: first, Mañjuśrī’s recollection was directed toward Maitreya for the sake of seeking [enlightenment]; second... [text fragmentary].
Regarding the name of the Bodhisattva: second, by recollecting the voice of the eight sons after his attainment of Buddhahood, he was named Dīpaṃkara (The Lamp-Lighter).
Dīpaṃkara was the predecessor of Śākyamuni. Third, by recollecting himself as the occasion for the Dharma Master Varaprabha, among the preceding eight causes—
The eight sons had not yet been given names. Now, because he attains Buddhahood within this causal stage, he is named "Recollection of Characteristics" (Smṛtilakṣaṇa).

Regarding the statement that he "manifestly perceives the events experienced by his own body": this refers to Mañjuśrī himself experiencing supreme and wondrous bliss, which is precisely the account of his own experience with the Dharma Master Wondrous Light (Sudarśana).
Regarding the statement "the meaning of 'cause' (*hetu*) is that which serves as the reason," this explains that "cause" refers to the causal basis.
By means of these ten causes, the general purpose for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is established.
Regarding the statement "or these ten matters," this refers to a small portion belonging to the present.
Among the ten causes, seven in their entirety and two in part belong to the past; one cause in its entirety and two causes in part belong to the present.
The first cause, the cause of the great meaning directly perceived, exists entirely at Vulture Peak; the second and tenth causes exist in part at Vulture Peak.
The second sutra states: "In the past, regarding the various Buddhas, I have seen this omen: immediately after emitting light, they preached the Great Dharma. This refers to the past.
Therefore, one should know that the present Buddha’s manifestation of light is likewise so.
This refers to the present at Vulture Peak. In the tenth [chapter], it says: "At that time, who was the Bodhisattva Wonderful Light? Was he anyone else in former ages?"
It is so. My own body is it; this is the present. Seeking-Fame Bodhisattva was it; this was the past; you yourself are it; this is the present.
Regarding the statement that these ten causes are collectively categorized into five pairs, this distinguishes five pairs: first, the pair of meaning and teaching, which refers to the eight... [etc.]
"Great meaning" refers to the signified sense. "Teaching" refers to the worldly words and phrases; it is the cause for the profound intent. Second is the pair of "rare" and "excellent":
"rare" means marvelous, and "excellent" means sublime. Third is the pair of "turning" and "succession": "turning" refers to turning the wheel of Dharma.
At that time, the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa preached a Mahāyāna sūtra titled *The Teaching of Immeasurable Meanings*, which instructs bodhisattvas and is protected by the Buddhas.
The "successor" refers to the Bodhisattva Prabhāpāla, who, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, upheld the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and expounded it for eighty minor kalpas for the sake of others;
because he thus sustained the turning of the Dharma wheel, he was the successor. Second:
The eight princes remained in the secular world, each ruling over the four continents as a Cakravartin King. Their reigns were not simultaneous;
rather, they succeeded one another in succession, which is why it is called "transmission" (zhuan). It also carries the sense of "successive transition" (zhuan).
Once the eight sons had left the household life and attained Buddhahood, the first prince bestowed a prediction of enlightenment upon the second prince, and the second prince...
The prophecy for the third prince (and so forth). There is also a tradition stating that each successor shall govern the four continents in succession.

This interpretation contradicts the headings and titles of the treatise’s structural outline. [The fourth pair is] "Firmness" (*dhṛti*) and "Exertion" (*vīrya*). "Firmness" refers to wholesome firmness and solidity, which is the cause of the Tathāgata’s Wheel of Dharma.
"Exertion" refers to the ability to enter into that cause. [The fifth pair is] "Other" (*para*) and "Self" (*ātman*), which refers to the cause of mindfulness (*smṛti*).
"Regarding others" refers to those other than oneself; "regarding oneself" refers to one's own experience. "Others" refers to Maitreya, and "oneself" refers to Mañjuśrī.

As for the statement that this section is divided into four parts, the commentator [the *Sūtra-ṭīkā* author] has condensed the ten causal factors from the treatise into the four responses found in the sūtra.
First, the response consisting of indicating characteristics and deliberating: although Mañjuśrī truly knows, he deliberates and measures out [his reply].
Answer (following the section on "the cause for manifesting the great meaning"):
Regarding the statement that "citing the past establishes the present," this means citing the former Dīpaṃkara as the establisher and the present Śākyamuni as the established.
This refers to the profound underlying cause observed in the worldly words, phrases, and sentences.
Regarding the "answer that points to specific matters": this refers to the matter of the lamp’s light, wherein each individual point specifically presents the inclusion of the seven causes.
Regarding the "answer that identifies the ancient with the present": this refers to the causes of events experienced by one's own person in the present;

taking the whole from the perspective of the ancient, the present Mañjuśrī is identical to the former Prabhāsa; taking the ancient from the perspective of the present, the former Seeker of Fame (Yaśaskāma) is identical to the present Maitreya.
Regarding the phrase "now this indicates the signs and so forth," the Sūtra says: "As I reflect, etc. "Reflect" (惟忖) means to contemplate and deliberate.
When I try to reflect and deliberate upon these auspicious signs, it is clear that the Buddha now certainly intends to preach the Great Dharma;
he wishes to rain down the great rain of Dharma, to blow the great conch of Dharma, to beat the great drum of Dharma, and to expound the great meaning of the Dharma.
Regarding the phrase "The discourse is named 'Manifesting the Causes of the Great Meaning,'" Jin says: This clearly explains the intent behind Mañjuśrī attaining the eight great meanings;
how much more so regarding the reasons for its arrival.

Regarding the statement that "the sūtra has five phrases," etc.: the treatise cites the Sanskrit original as having eight phrases, whereas here, Kumārajīva’s Chinese translation of the sūtra contains only five.
Now, the Master of the Commentary (Sūzhǔ) explains the basis [of the sūtra] cited within the treatise, but he does not explain this local [Chinese] sūtra.
Because this local sūtra is deficient and incomplete, he does not explain it. He relies on the treatise to explain the eight great meanings, as quoted in the commentary.
The distinction is easy to understand.

Regarding the statement that the Master of the Treatise (Śāstrakāra) explains "non-interruption" and so forth as the seventh point, this differs from the sequence of the eight great meanings in the Master of the Commentary’s (Ṭīkākāra) interpretation.
While the Master of the Treatise explains the seventh [point] as the "uninterrupted great Dharma-drum," the Master of the Commentary has modified it.

Regarding its placement as the fourth: the final rain among the eight great meanings is the object of the mind. Now, this [meaning] is a resultant dharma (*phala-dharma*), while the preceding six are causal dharmas (*hetu*).
If the Master had placed it within the seventh [category], it would have been situated alongside the eighth resultant dharma, thereby conflating cause and effect.
Therefore, it was moved to the fourth position to accord with the sequence of cause and effect and the "hook-and-chain" (*kīla-śṛṅkhalā*) logic.
This is the sequential order. The above is based on the Master of the Commentary’s distinct arrangement of the sequence of transformations.

As for the phrase "now, by inferring through the meaning," this establishes a logical principle: although the *Śāstra* only speaks of the non-interruption of the Great Dharma Drum in the seventh chapter, by inferring through the meaning, it is spoken of in the fourth chapter; thus, there is no contradiction.

Regarding the phrase "proceeding from the initial transformation," "chang" (昌) refers to "transformation" (biàn), and it is pronounced with a level tone (as explained in the *Commentary on the Sūtra of the Eight Great Meanings* regarding existence and non-existence).

As for the statement in the discourse, "because doubt is severed by means of discussion," according to the commentary’s explanation of the text, the eight great meanings arise through a succession of links like hooks and chains.
The ancients interpreted the first two meanings as referring to the period prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* assembly. Regarding the first meaning:

from the time after the sixteen princes under the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū until just before Śākyamuni attained Buddhahood in his present life, this entire interval is collectively termed "the period when the Great Dharma was about to be preached.
As for the three grades of śrāvakas, they were formerly at the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). How does one reconcile this with the treatise? It says:
"Those who doubt" refers to those whose doubts are severed. The answer is that there were originally thousands of millions of kinds of people who all gave rise to doubt;
when the sixteenth prince taught and inspired them to resolve their minds toward enlightenment, this was precisely "severing the doubts of those who doubt. Question:

If the doubts have already been broken, why does the commentary say "wishing to break"? Answer: That Śāriputra, while practicing, had reached the stage prior to the sixth abode (*vihāra*), where his mind of doubt—
Based on what precedes, it arises again. Because he intends to preach the Dharma hereafter to sever doubts, it is said that he "wishes to break [them]. Regarding the second meaning:
from after the Deer Park until before the assembly at the Lotus Sutra, this is called "raining down the great Dharma rain.

It refers to entering from the outer ordinary beings (bāla-pṛthagjana) into the inner ordinary beings (śaikṣa), and from the inner ordinary beings into the noble ones (ārya). The two meanings provided by the ancients above are thus assigned to the period prior to the assembly at the Lotus Sutra.

Furthermore, the third is the striking of the great Dharma drum; the fourth is the non-interruption of the great Dharma drum—these two are assigned to the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, precisely for when the śrāvakas relinquish the provisional to grasp the real.
The fifth is the erecting of the great Dharma banner; the sixth is the kindling of the great Dharma torch.
This would cause Śāriputra to attain Buddhahood, named Huaguang (Flower Radiance). The seventh [blowing] would be the blowing of the great Dharma conch;

the eighth would be the expounding of the great Dharma meaning, returning to have Huaguang preach the Dharma and transform the Bodhisattva Jianman. These two interpretations from the ancients both contradict the *Śāstra* and the *Vyākhyā*.

Next is the Master of the *Śāstra’s* explanation, which is the correct interpretation: the eight great meanings are entirely matters pertaining to the assembly at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* assembly.
Among the eight meanings, the first six cause Śāriputra himself to become a Buddha, while the latter two transform others so that they may attain Buddhahood.

Within the six statements, the first four pertain to the causal stage and the latter two pertain to the resultant stage; alternatively, the fifth may be understood as encompassing both cause and result.
The ox-cart likewise encompasses both cause and result. The *Śāstra* states: "The doubter has their doubt severed. The doubter is precisely Śāriputra. The fourth... [text ends].
There was a long-standing doubt regarding the ten years; upon hearing the proclamation of the two kinds of profound [teachings], the śrāvakas of the three capacities all had their doubts severed.

Therefore, they are called "those whose doubts are severed. Question: What is meant by "severing doubts"? Answer: When the śrāvakas of the three capacities hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, this is precisely the severing of their doubts.
Regarding the eight great meanings, they specifically refer to the section following the formal exposition in the "Expedient Means" chapter (as explained in the preceding commentary on the treatise).
Regarding the phrase "desiring to preach the Great Dharma," the Master of the Commentary (*shuzhu*) cites the scriptural text from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which is titled the "Great Dharma.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva announced the news, saying, "He desires to preach the Great Dharma," and therefore first rained down flowers.

Regarding the phrase "intending to break prior doubts, etc.," this is the commentary of the Master of the Sub-commentary (*Sū*). Question: On the occasion of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* assembly, this refers to the present meaning; how, then, can it constitute "prior doubt"? Answer: In contrast to that which has not yet been broken, everything prior to its being broken is collectively termed "prior doubt. Question: Since persons of the Two Vehicles have already attained the nature of the noble ones (*ārya*), why are they called "external ordinary beings" (*bāhyapṛthagjana*)? Answer: There are two interpretations for the term "external": first, it refers to those prior to the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*). Second, it refers to those who have not yet entered the stages of the Bodhisattva. This is the meaning here. It is not that they are external to the Buddha-nature; rather, it means they are external to the stage of the Bodhisattva. Furthermore, this is a provisional teaching; ultimately, there is no distinction between the Two Vehicles and the One Vehicle. Thus, the term "external" is used to indicate their relative position. Finally, it is because they have not yet severed the afflictions of the desire realm. Therefore, they are called "external ordinary beings. This is the meaning. Those prior to the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) are called "external"; those from the ten stages of faith onward are called "internal. Another interpretation states that those from the ten abodes (*vihāra*) onward are internal ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), while the ten stages of faith are external ordinary beings.

According to the intent of the commentary (*śāstra*), the three types of śrāvakas with their respective faculties are categorized as follows: those prior to the ten stages of faith are taken as "external," and those from the ten stages of faith onward are taken as "internal.
Since these śrāvakas are still far removed from the stage of the ten stages of faith, they are collectively designated as external ordinary beings.

Regarding the statement, "Having already severed doubt, [the qualities] such as increase [arise]," the wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*) is precisely the originally existing seeds. "Pure" (*śuddha*) carries the meaning of being singular and unadulterated.
This refers to the intention that after turning the mind [toward enlightenment], one enters the stage of the inner ordinary person (*prthagjana*).

When the six perfections are practiced in a seemingly disordered manner, yet wisdom becomes thoroughly matured, this is identical to the dedication toward the Great [Vehicle]; it is then termed the "provisional emergence of meaning. However, the actual emergence of utility occurs at the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Regarding the statement "it rains the great Dharma rain," Mañjuśrī replies to Maitreya: "The Tathāgata emits light because he intends to subsequently rain the great Dharma rain.

This refers to those who have severed their doubts; that is, from the stage of the outer ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*) entering the stage of the inner ordinary person (*adhyātmapṛthagjana*), prior to the [first] bhūmi.

Regarding the phrase "having extensively heard and contemplated over great kalpas" and so forth: this refers to the fact that one perfumes the seeds inherently present within the body, causing them to reach full maturity;

this is the commentary of the Master of the Sub-commentary (Sūshǔ). This phrasing is inverted; it should rather say, "First being free from doubt, one dwells in the stage of an Inner Worldling (ābhyantarapṛthagjana).
If we discuss the assembly at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, those who hear the *Lotus Sūtra* have not yet reached the stage of an Inner Worldling.

The sprouts of goodness have not yet begun to grow; one has not yet entered the stage of a sage (*ārya*). This discourse on the Buddha’s words is intended ultimately to cause entry [into that stage], rather than indicating that one has already actually entered it, because one will certainly enter it in the future.
It is as Śāriputra said: "Abiding in true wisdom, I shall certainly become a Buddha," because he will certainly become one.

Question: At the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, those who heard the *Lotus Sūtra* had not yet fully entered the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), nor had the sprouts of goodness begun to grow.
How is it that the Lotus Sūtra is called "the rain of the great Dharma"? Answer: It is because by hearing the Lotus Sūtra, one severs doubt;

thereafter, one turns the mind [toward awakening], enters the stage of the ordinary person (pṛthagjana), and causes the sprouts [of the roots of goodness] to grow. Attributing this merit to its source, it is due to hearing the Lotus Sūtra.
Therefore, this sutra is named "The Rain of Dharma. This samādhi was attained by hearing the sutra at the assembly on Vulture Peak and receiving its benefits.

Although the time spent practicing—having heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* at Vulture Peak for five hundred or a thousand kalpas—is indeed long, it is still called "the benefit of the Vulture Peak assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Even though one subsequently increases the sprouts of wisdom for a hundred or a thousand kalpas, [it remains so].
It prevents [the rain] from being called the "Dharma Rain" that adorns Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa. The two stages of *prabhākārī* (Radiant) and *arciṣmatī* (Blazing) cause one to enter the stage of the sages;
this "stage of the sages" refers to the first bhūmi (*pramuditā*). Because it seeks to increase wholesome qualities, it constitutes the gradual entry into the first bhūmi.

Regarding the statement, "The meaning of this root treatise is as follows, from beginning to end," etc.: the commentator (the *shuzhu*) concludes the preceding two phrases, intending to convey that all subsequent phrases—such as those previously explained concerning the arising of the teaching of the Dharma—are stated in their proper sequence.
Regarding the phrase "the faculties of speech are matured" (*vāgindriya-paripakva*), this represents the commentator’s intended interpretation of the general meaning of the third and fourth lines.

Due to the extensive hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintā*) mentioned previously, the innate seeds (*bīja*) are nourished, and one gradually enters the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*); this is termed "maturity of the faculties. Question:

The Master of the Commentary clearly states that the "hook and chain" (*kīla-śṛṅkhalā*) are linked together; does this not correspond to the very first teaching given at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, where the faculties were already matured?
Question: By hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, one severs doubt, abandons the provisional for the real, and only then enters the stage of the "inner ordinary person" (*ābhyantarapṛthagjana*).

Why, then, do you first speak of the inner ordinary person and only later say that the faculties have matured? Answer: From a superficial perspective, this sequence seems to be inconsistent with the "hook-and-chain" (*gōraku*) method of progression.

However, when the underlying principles are properly arranged, it is indeed the hook-and-chain method. Question: For what reason does one sever doubt and turn the mind [toward the Mahāyāna], thereby being able to enter the inner ordinary person?

Answer: This is simply because those with the foremost Mahāyāna faculties have first matured; they are then able to abandon the provisional and grasp the real, severing doubts and practicing until they reach the stage of the inner ordinary person (ārya-pudgala). The realms of the Śrāvaka and the realms of the Bodhisattva are called the "two secrets.

Because the matters of the provisional and the real established by the Tathāgata are difficult to comprehend, they are termed "secret" (guhya). In relation to the cognizing mind, they are termed "objects" (viṣaya). Question: Why?
This is called the "two secret realms. The answer is given in three parts: first, the provisional secret realm of the śrāvakas and the real secret realm of the bodhisattvas;
these are called the two families. Second, regarding the provisional secret realm, this refers to the ordinary śrāvakas, while for the bodhisattvas, there are two [realms].

Therefore, these are called the two secrets. In comparison with the Śrāvakas, there is a provisional secret; for Bodhisattvas, there is a provisional secret—these are termed the "realms of the two secrets.

Question: What is meant by the provisional secret of the Bodhisattvas? Answer: Because Bodhisattvas who attain awakening gradually might fear falling back into the Two Vehicles, [the Buddha] teaches them that there is neither two nor three vehicles.
Therefore, this is called the provisional [teaching] for Bodhisattvas. Question: What is meant by the provisional secret of the Śrāvakas?

The answer is that this was spoken in response to śrāvakas of indeterminate nature who had heard of the Way but did not yet know of the two vehicles; therefore, the śrāvaka stage is provisional and esoteric.

Third, it is said that although they previously acted as śrāvakas, they later became bodhisattvas; thus, this was addressed to the śrāvakas before they had turned their minds [toward the Mahāyāna] at the assembly.

This is called the provisional-secret realm. From the point when one has turned the mind [toward enlightenment] onwards, it is called the true-secret realm of the Bodhisattvas (as indicated by these two meanings within the Commentary;
so states the Treatise).

Regarding the statement "immediately striking the great Dharma drum" and so forth, this is a correlation with the sutra. In the Sanskrit version of the sutra cited by the *Śāstra*, the passage on "not ceasing the great Dharma drum" stands as the seventh [section].
The Master of the Commentary (*Sūtra-vyākhyāna*) has moved it to the fourth position. There are two reasons for this: first, because the "great Dharma conch" expounds the meaning of the Great Dharma;
these two results are intermediate [in sequence], and if the text regarding "not ceasing the great Dharma drum" were separated [from them], the underlying intent would be interrupted.

Therefore, the second [interpretation] states: "Regarding the intention to place [the teaching] in the fourth [period], striking the Great Dharma Drum based on the third [period] represents the disclosure of the provisional (upāya), while not ceasing the Great Dharma Drum represents the manifestation of the ultimate (paramārtha).
Because of this textual structure, it is placed in the fourth. Question: What is meant by "striking the Great Dharma Drum"? Answer:
Some say that the tongue-faculty (*jihvendriya*) of the Tathāgata is called the drumstick, and the teaching that discloses the provisional and manifests the ultimate is called the drum.

The drum: it produces vocal sounds and preaches the Dharma; this is called "the drum emitting sound. Second, it is said: the provisional and real teachings of the *Lotus Sūtra* constitute the Great Dharma Drum.
Within the preaching of the two vehicles, which is like striking the drum, the provisional is called "emitting sound. Striking this Great Dharma Drum is the opening of the provisional (*kaikwan*).

Not interrupting the Great Dharma Drum is the manifestation of the real (*kenshi*). Furthermore, striking the Great Dharma Drum signifies that the provisional has already been relinquished and fully understood.
Furthermore, one no longer cultivates expedient means. It is like striking the Dharma drum: once the task for a single period is completed with a single strike, it is not struck again.

Yet, one does not cease the Great Dharma Drum; by practicing according to the Mahāyāna, one attains Buddhahood, and the benefit and joy [bestowed] are inexhaustible. Therefore, it is named "Uninterrupted."

Question: Since you have explained that the Two Vehicles are provisional, how can this be called "beating the great Dharma drum"? It would logically follow that it is merely a small drum. Answer: It may also be called the great Dharma drum.
Those of the Small Vehicle are unwilling to admit that the Small Vehicle is provisional; however, it is simply within the Great Vehicle that the Small Vehicle is taught as provisional.
This very teaching of the provisional and the real is itself the Great Vehicle, and is thus named the great Dharma drum. (The preceding concludes the exegesis of the scripture.)
Regarding the phrase "because it is heard from afar," this is the Master of the Treatise’s (Śāstrin) explanation. The term "heard from afar" precisely explains the meaning of the drum.
When a drum is struck, it is heard both near and far. Likewise, when the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma, his Brahma-voice is heard throughout the worlds of the ten directions;
this is called being "heard from afar."
Regarding the statement that they are "assigned in sequence," this is the interpretation of the Master of the Commentary (*Sū*).

Some say that the words of Yuanwen do not constitute an explanation of the eight great meanings, but rather serve as a detailed analysis that brings forth the principles of the seventh and fourth [meanings].

It is precisely because of Yuanwen’s [explanation] that they are assigned in sequence. The third [meaning] is "beating the great Dharma-drum" to reveal the provisional (*upāya*); the fourth is "not severing the... [great compassion].
The Dharma Drum reveals the truth; it is provisional first and true later—such is the sequence. From this point forward, one cultivates the wisdom of the two emptinesses;
when attaining Buddhahood in the future, because it will never be exhausted until the very limit of saṃsāra, it is called "far-reaching renown.
Because it possesses the capacity for far-reaching renown that is continuous and enduring, it is placed fourth.
The phrase "that which is spoken immediately clarifies the present" and so forth is the commentary of the Master of the Sub-commentary (*Sūshǔ*).

Opening up the past Śrāvaka vehicle as the provisional and secret realm signifies that the Śrāvaka is provisional. Explaining the striking of the great Dharma drum signifies that the Bodhisattva vehicle currently taught is the real and secret realm;
this reveals the reality. Explaining the non-interruption of the great Dharma drum [is the response]. Question: How is the Śrāvaka vehicle named?
"Secret. The answer is that the Two Vehicles are provisional; because they themselves do not know they are provisional, it is called "secret.

For those of indeterminate nature, it negates the absence of the Two Vehicles and asserts that there is only the One Vehicle, which only Buddhas and Buddhas can fully know. The Bodhisattva Vehicle, in contrast to the Two Vehicles, is called the "Second Secret.
Regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, the teaching that expresses these meanings has two functions: first, to express the provisional; second, to express [the ultimate].
In truth, for forty years prior, the Buddha taught the Three Vehicles. Because the followers of the Two Vehicles could not fathom the Buddha’s intention, this was termed "esoteric.

Today, at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the profound *Āgamas*—that is, the teachings that previously expounded the three vehicles—are revealed to be the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* itself.

Yet, it is said that those teachings from forty years ago were provisional; this is because the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* reveals that very provisionality. Thus, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is able to...
The place where the three teachings are explained as provisional is called the "provisional-and-secret realm. This is precisely the striking of the great Dharma drum;

the texts of the *Hīnayāna* (the sheep and deer vehicles) serve as evidence for the provisional. This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which explains the teaching that reveals the real, manifests the present Bodhisattva vehicle.
It constitutes the realm of the true secret. This is precisely the uninterrupted Great Dharma Drum.

Regarding the statement that "the ox-cart realizes the truth" and "causes the faculties to ripen," one asks: What is the intention behind the Buddha’s teaching of these provisional and real secrets of the Śrāvakas? The answer is:
The phrase "causing the faculties to ripen" means causing [disciples] such as Śāriputra to abandon the provisional and take up the real.
Regarding the statement "entering the realm of the Secret [Mantra]," wisdom (*jñāna*) is that which enters, and the realm is that which is entered. *Mu* (the commentary) states:
This means knowing that the Two Vehicles are provisional (*upāya*) and knowing that the Bodhisattvas are real.

Seeing that the Tathāgata, in former times, taught the provisional by speaking of three [vehicles] while the reality was one, and realizing this intent, is called "entry. This continues until the attainment of the fruit.
These are collectively termed "entering the realm of the secret.

Regarding the statement "causing them to advance toward the highest-of-the-high [rank]," this refers to the four wisdoms of bodhi within the fruition, which are untainted (*anāsrava*). They are called "high" because they transcend the untainted states of the causal stage;

they are called "highest-of-the-high" because they surpass the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*); and they are called "pure" because they are free from all hindrances. Now, let [the practitioner]...
The practice of Śāriputra and others involves advancing toward the Buddha-fruit, the four wisdoms of enlightenment (*catur-jñāna-bodhi*), which are supremely pure.

The statement "thereupon erecting the great Dharma-banner" (*mahā-dharma-dhvaja*) serves as a commentary on the sutra. Question: Regarding the aforementioned meaning of supreme purity, what dharma constitutes this meaning of supreme purity?
Answer: The sub-commentary states: "erecting the great Dharma-banner."
Regarding the phrase "establishing the sublime wisdom of bodhi," this is the commentary of the Master of the Sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*).

It means that Śāriputra and others shall attain bodhi, being as lofty and prominent as a banner. As the Sūtra says: "They shall become Buddhas, named Padmaprabha. This refers to the ox-cart being high and broad.
Regarding the statement "by knowing the provisional and the real, etc.": from the first bhūmi upward, it is termed "establishment and cultivation.

Because one has attained a state of high prominence from the outset, and further scriptures state that after a great asaṃkhyeya-kalpa, one establishes transcendence beyond the three realms, it is called "highly elevated.

Because the two realms are termed "manifest," it is said to be "extremely high and manifest. Because one is free from the two obstacles, it is termed "free from obstacles. Because it is untainted (anāsrava), it is pure.
Regarding "purity," "discourse on progress toward the supreme purity," and so forth: that which is untainted (*anāsrava*) is called "supreme" because it transcends [the world].

That which is the "supreme purity" of the two vehicles is precisely the absence of defilement. Mañjuśrī answered Maitreya, saying: "As for the Tathāgata emitting light, it is the kindling of the Great..."

The Dharma-torch has departed. The treatise states that "progressive attainment" refers to the meaning of cultivation. "Omniscience" refers to the fundamental wisdom that directly realizes and perceives *tathatā* (suchness).
Regarding the phrase "immediately kindling the great Dharma-torch," this corresponds to the scriptural text; it refers both to the *nirvāṇa* that is realized and the wisdom that realizes it.

There are two meanings to "kindling a torch": first, to destroy darkness, because it eliminates the afflictions (*kleśa*); second, to reveal objects, because it illuminates the ultimate truth (*tattva*).
This causes the śrāvakas and others to realize *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, the subsequent scripture says: "The place of jewels is near, like a torch that dispels [darkness]."
Regarding "darkness" and so forth:
as for the statement "having already attained true wisdom," the question is: how does one kindle the great Dharma-torch? This is the principle of the Dharmakāya. The answer in the commentary states:
"As for 'having already attained true wisdom' and so forth, it is like various treasures originally existing within a hall that cannot be seen because of the darkness."

When the door is opened and the lamp is brought forth, all the various jewels are seen in their entirety. Human beings all possess the True Principle, yet it is not seen because it is shrouded by the veils of entanglement.
When the True Fruit emerges from within these obstructions, the perfectly luminous Dharmakāya and its myriad virtues are all fully perceived.

The statement "like a torch illuminating objects" is a metaphor. "Illuminating" (zhào) has the meaning of direct perception. Fundamental wisdom takes suchness as its object and directly attains its essence;
this is called "illumination," which is precisely the realization of nirvana.
Regarding the statement, "one who takes up all-knowledge and perceives it directly," this refers to the seventh phrase. As for "blowing the great dharma-conch," Mañjuśrī says:

"The Tathāgata emits light, desiring to blow the great dharma-conch. The phrase "taking up all-knowledge and perceiving it directly" reiterates the previously mentioned "kindling the great dharma-torch," which is the wisdom of bodhi.
That which is called "all phenomena" is precisely suchness (*tathatā*).
That which is called "establishing names and so forth" refers to the realization through fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) regarding the ineffable Dharma.

The establishment of names, phrases, and expressions through subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) is precisely the teaching of the Dharma by means of that subsequent wisdom. It refers to the preaching of the twelvefold scriptural teachings (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*) exactly as they were realized;
therefore, it is called "establishment" (*vyavasthāpana*).

The statement that "once the true object is attained, it must necessarily be equal" means that at the time of realizing the principle, both the subject that realizes and the object realized are realized within the principle itself.
Once the Buddhas have attained Buddhahood, they must necessarily preach the Dharma to teach and transform sentient beings.
This indicates that once the three types of *śrāvakas* have completed their attainment of the fruit, they must establish names for that fruit; it is like when worldly music has concluded.
He blew the great conch and let out a roar; thus, Flower-Light Buddha received his prediction. He likewise taught and transformed sentient beings through the three vehicles.

As for the phrase "the song ended and the position was fulfilled," this is a metaphorical illustration. Just as when a musical piece concludes and the position is fulfilled, one blows the conch to signal the time;

so too, the completion of the song represents the attainment of Buddhahood, while blowing the conch is a metaphor for preaching the Dharma. Previously, he erected the great Dharma-banner and lit the great...

The "Dharma Torch" refers to Śāriputra’s future attainment of Buddhahood. "Blowing the Great Dharma Conch" signifies Śāriputra’s subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) preaching the Dharma of the Three Vehicles and transforming the Bodhisattva Jianman.
"Kindling the Great Dharma Torch" signifies his fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) realizing the ultimate principle.
Regarding the statement "establishing names and so forth," this refers to the teaching of the Three Vehicles.

Regarding the statement "causing them to enter the ineffable," this means causing the bodhisattvas and others who are to be converted to enter from the first bhūmi onward and realize the all-pervading *tathatā* (suchness);
this is called "unrealizable wisdom" (*apratiṣedhya-jñāna*), which is none other than the two fundamental wisdoms: the wondrous and the equanimous. It is [a state of] profound stillness...
In accordance with principle and timing, this very right gnosis is called "ineffable. Fundamental gnosis realizes the teaching of non-dharma;
subsequently attained gnosis explains it for the sake of sentient beings—this is called "turning the wheel of Dharma."

Regarding the phrase "to expound the great Dharma-meaning": "expound" means to flow forth and spread. For those śrāvakas of indeterminate nature who have turned their minds toward the Great Vehicle, one preaches the Mahāyāna;
this is called "expounding the great Dharma-meaning."

Regarding the phrase "discourse on the teaching," etc., this is an explanation from the *Śāstra*. It refers to those who were to be saved by the Buddha Padmaprabha; that is to say, the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhavīrya.
He causes the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhavīrya to enter into realized wisdom and realize *tathatā*, thereby accomplishing the turning of the wheel of Dharma and crushing the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Now, when a Buddha preaches the Dharma, it is intended to bring benefit to living beings: first, to enable them to personally attain the fruit, as mentioned previously.
There are six meanings. Two of them cause others to attain Buddhahood; these are the latter two meanings. The Sūtra says: "He is called the Pure Body;

he shall deliver immeasurable multitudes. This speaks only of the turning of the wheel of Dharma after one has attained sainthood. Among the first six, the first four are causes, while the fifth and sixth are results.
Alternatively, the fifth may be understood as encompassing both cause and result, meaning that by means of this precious vehicle, one reaches the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
Regarding the term "equal" (or "etc. [in the phrase "the above resolves the knots and gives rise to the marks"]:
these eight phrases are grouped into four pairs. First is the pair of destroying evil and advancing toward good.

To preach the Great Dharma is called "destroying evil. To rain down the great Dharma rain is called "advancing toward goodness. Second, regarding the opening of the provisional to reveal the real: striking the great Dharma drum is the opening of the provisional;

not ceasing the sounding of the great Dharma drum is the revealing of the real. Third, regarding attaining wisdom and realizing the truth: erecting the great Dharma banner is the attainment of wisdom;
lighting the great Dharma torch is the realization of the truth. Fourth, regarding preaching the Dharma to benefit sentient beings: blowing the great Dharma... [conch shell].

The conch shell is the preaching of the Dharma; expounding the great principles of the Dharma is the benefiting of sentient beings. When these words circulate in this manner, it is called the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*).
Having personally attained the fruit [of enlightenment], he is Flower Light (*Puṣpārāma*); desiring to cause sentient beings to realize the holy, true wisdom, he is Firm and Full (*Dṛḍhavati*).
Since this treatise analyzes the sūtras through a systematic chain of reasoning, it is here contrasted with "mutual multiplication" (*xiāngchéng*).

Regarding the phrase "capable of being opened and understood," Mǔ says: "One may open and examine the principles and meanings that have preceded it, thereby comprehending and interpreting its intent."
This is one's own awakening. Those who come after may peruse this commentary to know that I have understood the meaning of this sutra;

by investigating the origins of its exposition, they will likewise awaken to the truth for others. This means that by investigating the origins of the eight great principles, and moreover by examining them in detail, one may unravel the intended meaning.
To unravel this is to understand the intent behind the transmission. By seeking these underlying principles, one ensures that the Wheel of Dharma remains uninterrupted.
Regarding the origin of this [passage]: (The "jie" in "qián jiè" is pronounced xié; the "jiè" in "shàng kuàng jiè" is pronounced jiē).
To speak of "destroying evil and advancing goodness" means that one wishes to expound the Great Dharma to destroy evil, and wishes to rain down the great Dharma-rain to advance goodness.

To speak of "preaching the Dharma to benefit sentient beings" means to blow the great Dharma-conch, to preach the Dharma and expound the great meaning of the Dharma, and to strike the great Dharma-drum to benefit sentient beings.
The drum is expedient means (*upāya*).

As for the phrase "furthermore, manifesting the real" and so forth: it means not ceasing the great Dharma-drum, truly erecting the great Dharma-banner, attaining wisdom, and lighting the great Dharma-torch—these signify the realization of truth (*satya*).
Essential Compendium of the Profound Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra,
Scroll Thirteen Essential Compendium of the Profound Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra,
Scroll Fourteen Compiled by the Mirror-Water Śramaṇa Xifu (Qifu)
Regarding the phrase "worldly letters and so forth": Question: What are called worldly letters, phrases, and sentences? Answer:
If one considers them in relation to the Tathāgata’s untainted (anāsrava) teaching, sounds would not be termed worldly letters, phrases, and sentences. However, there are two kinds of "worldly."
First, that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) is called "the worldly" (*loka*). Second, it is called "the worldly" because it involves verbal expression.
Now, the Bodhisattva Āryadeva states that "worldly letters" are spoken within the marks of the Tathāgata’s Brahma-voice.

If one is detached from worldly phenomena, that is the realization of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*); if one follows worldly phenomena, that is verbal expression. It merely establishes names, phrases, and letters.
"Worldly" refers to the profound meaning, which is the intended purport; that is, the principles of the provisional and the real as they are expounded.
Because the followers of the Two Vehicles cannot fathom it, it is called "profound."

Regarding the statement that "the verbal teachings are worldly conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and so forth," this is the commentary of the Master of the Sub-commentary (*ṭīkākāra*). There are two types of conceptual proliferation:

first, that which is characterized by discrimination is called conceptual proliferation; second, that which consists of verbal expression is called conceptual proliferation. Whatever constitutes conceptual proliferation is termed "worldly.
Some say that this refers to the "dharma-worldly," meaning the teaching itself, and not the mundane world.

Regarding the phrase "the meaning of the intention": as for "the intention, the implication," and so forth, it refers to the words, phrases, and chapters of the Mahāyāna teachings spoken by the Buddhas of the past and present.
These are brought into accord with reality and are ultimately profound; therefore, they are difficult for the world to believe. Thus, he manifests auspicious signs before speaking.
The reason for teaching in this manner is precisely the meaning of "the intention and the implication."
The phrase "the beginning" refers to the past. Mañjuśrī said to Maitreya, "You ask me about the emission of light. You have indeed asked the right person.

As for this emission of light, it was intended by Śākyamuni Tathāgata to preach the sūtra, to cause Śāriputra to attain Buddhahood, and to transform the Bodhisattva Kṣemadatta so that he would attain Buddhahood.
This is seen as the exposition of the eight great meanings. Do not, in questioning, engage in arbitrary matching, measuring, or constructing empty fabrications.
"Harmony. Is it like seeing a white heron perched in a tree, which indicates that water is not absent?
Or is it like seeing smoke on a distant mountain, from which one knows there is fire, knowing it through inference? Or is it because the eye has seen it before? He answered Mañjuśrī, saying:
"In the past, I had seen each of these individually before I was able to answer. It is like the eight great meanings I have just now answered."
The following section explains the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as the cause and basis for this event. The Sūtra says:
"O son of good family, in the past, I have witnessed such an auspicious omen from various Buddhas. This cites the ancient deeds of the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa;
having emitted this light, he preached the Great Dharma, which establishes the present deeds of Śākyamuni. Mañjuśrī states: "I have seen that when the Buddhas of the past emitted this light..."
He then expounded the Great Dharma. Vasubandhu Bodhisattva explained that the "Great Dharma" refers to the profound meaning within the words and phrases of the mundane world.
For this reason, the Master of the Treatise categorized it as the "Cause of Names."
Regarding this explanation of its intent, as for the purpose of emitting light: those who hope to ascend the hall must necessarily have the doors and windows opened for them;

those who wish to mount the elegant carriage must necessarily follow a distinguished track. Thus we know that while the orchid blooms in spring and the chrysanthemum in autumn, each is fragrant in its own season.
For what reason did Śākyamuni emulate that Lamp-Lighter by emitting light before preaching the Dharma? That an auspicious omen manifests now must surely have its underlying cause.
Let us cite the scriptural passage. I hope you will explain the "Emission of Light. What is its meaning? Answer: The scripture says:
"In order to cause all sentient beings to hear and know the Dharma that is difficult for all the world to believe, he manifests this auspicious sign; therefore, he emits light. Question:

What is called the "Dharma difficult to believe"? Answer: That which was previously termed the "Ultimate" (the fruit of no-more-learning) forty years ago is now, when it is realized as a future retribution, called the "Difficult-to-Believe Dharma."
"Shen" (身) means "newly ultimate. It is not only difficult to have faith regarding the teachings; it is also difficult to attain understanding regarding the principles.
"Zhi" (旨) refers to intention, beauty, resolve, and expression.
Regarding the statement that "the time of a single praise is long and rare," the intended meaning is as follows:
