praising the name of the Buddha, praising the excellence of the sublime Dharma, and praising the benefit of birth [in this world]—such matters cannot be encountered even in immeasurable time; therefore, they are called "rare.
It is not merely a matter of speaking of kalpas; since these matters depend upon kalpas, the four rarities are thus described.
Regarding the statement "inconceivable," and so forth: each of these three phrases refers to *asaṃkhyeya*.
The commentator cites the Sanskrit original of the sutra, which lacks the meaning of "boundless" (*ananta*), and thus adds "inexpressible.
Furthermore, when the commentary speaks of "immeasurable," this corresponds to "measureless" (*apramāṇa*) in the sutra. As for the commentary's statement "unattainable," it means "invisible."

The mind wishes to take it as an object, yet deliberation ceases; thus, it transcends the sphere of intellectual calculation. Because the mind’s objects of perception cannot reach it, it is called "inconceivable" (*acintya*).
The mouth wishes to speak of it, yet words fail; because it transcends the sphere of verbal discussion, the explanations of language cannot reach it, and it is called "inexpressible" (*anabhilāpya*).
The path of mind and speech is cut off; it is called "immeasurable. Therefore, it is termed an *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "an immeasurable time cannot be grasped," there are two intentions. First, it means that the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa attained Buddhahood after an immeasurable period of time.
The second [master] says: When Mañjuśrī manifested the signs and called to mind that King Candrasūryapradīpa, he could not find him even after an immeasurable period of time;
therefore, it is said to be "inconceivable."
Regarding the term *asaṃkhyeya* and so forth: *khye* means "to look toward" or "to expect. The translators merely adopted the phonetic equivalent;

there is no further distinct meaning. This is translated as "incalculable" (*wúshù*). Although it is "incalculable," it is still a form of calculation; it is treated as being beyond number because it cannot be calculated.
Regarding the mention of the *Abhidharmakośa* and so forth: Question: Since it is said that they are "ultimate" (*parama*), why are they called "innumerable" (*asaṃkhyeya*)? Answer:
Although the fifty-second number is indeed a countable number, because it reaches the limit of what can be counted, it is called "innumerable.
Originally there were sixty numbers, but here this *asaṃkhyeya* corresponds to the fifty-second number; there remain eight more numbers thereafter. [The sequence begins] from one... the fifty-second.
Reaching ten, ten tens make a hundred; ten hundreds make a thousand; ten thousands make ten thousand; ten thousand makes a lakṣa.
Following this sequence up to the fifty-second numerical position is called asaṃkhyeya, which here is translated as "incalculable."

Regarding the statement that "the original number was sixty plus eight," etc., the question is asked: "Who transmitted this error? The answer is: some say it was an error made by Vasubandhu when he composed the treatise;
some say it was forgotten during Ānanda’s compilation of the canon; others say it was forgotten during the translation by the Tripiṭaka masters.

According to these accounts of what was forgotten, it was not Ānanda who forgot it. If that were not so, how could it be called "Thus have I heard"? It is merely the case of an ordinary person outside the cave [of the Saṃgha].
Generally, when the assembly was compiling [the canon], there were omissions and errors in the transmission.
Regarding the statement that the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says so forth: if one follows the Mahāyāna *Avataṃsaka*, "one hundred and twenty" corresponds to the number one hundred and twelve;

"asaṃkhyeya" corresponds to the number one hundred and twelve; "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) corresponds to the number one hundred and seven; and "boundless" (*ananta*) corresponds to the number one hundred and nine.
The number "incalculable" (*asaṃkhyeya*) corresponds to the one hundred and fifteenth number. The "inconceivable" (*acintya*) corresponds to the one hundred and seventeenth number.
Since *asaṃkhyeya* is the one hundred and twelfth number, counting from this up to the "immeasurable" (*aprameya*) is called the "immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya*" (*apramāṇāsaṃkhyeya*).
Counting from this up to the "boundless" (*ananta*) is called the "boundless *asaṃkhyeya*" (*anantāsaṃkhyeya*). Counting from this up to the "inexpressible" (*anabhilāpya*)...

"Countable" (*saṃkhyeya*) refers to the number of *asaṃkhyeya* that cannot be counted; when one counts these until they reach the inconceivable, it is called "inconceivable *asaṃkhyeya*" (*acintya-asaṃkhyeya*).
Regarding the term "kalpa" and so forth, this is translated as "time-period" (*kāla-bhāga*). The pronunciation is *fu* with the *wen* tone; it carries the meaning of a distinct portion or division.

Regarding the phrase "inconceivable" (*acintya*) and so forth, this is a brief explanation based on the heading. Master Lü (Lùfǔ) says: it is an object that cannot be surpassed by the sphere of perception;

it is an object that cannot be deliberated upon by the sphere of conceptual calculation. This is the general meaning within the commentary. "Ineffable" (*anabhilāpya*) means that it transcends the sphere of speech and deliberation;
even the establishment of words and discourse cannot be found there, nor can the formulation of linguistic arguments be found.
Regarding the phrase "immeasurable" (*aprameya*) and so forth: it cannot be obtained by taking other objects to compare with it; it cannot be obtained by using objects or analogies;
nor can it be obtained through calculation. Therefore, it is said that it "exceeds the scope of analogy and calculation" (as stated in the aforementioned treatise).

Regarding the statement in the present sutra that [the Buddha’s lifespan] is "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) and so forth: there is no object that can serve as a metaphor by which its quantity might be known, nor can it be calculated.
Regarding the statement that it is "boundless" (*ananta*) and so forth: every single temporal division possesses its own limit.
Regarding the statement that "it is identical to the *prajñā* [wisdom] and so forth," the verse from Vasubandhu’s commentary states: "In terms of number, power, and incomparability, it is supreme;

the incomparable cause is likewise so. Among all worldly phenomena, none can serve as a metaphor. It further says: "In number, it surpasses calculation by a factor of ten million (*koṭi*). As the Sūtra says:
A hundredth part, a thousandth part—even a ten-million-billionth part—cannot equal it.

If a person were to offer the seven treasures of the three-thousandfold world system as a gift, it would not be equal to the merit of someone who upholds even a single four-line verse (*gāthā*), which is truly immeasurable;
therefore, it is said to "exceed all numerical divisions. Second is "exceeding the division of power," where "power" refers to time.
Furthermore, the power of the Dharma exceeds the power of giving; this refers to the division of time. Within the realm of form, the smallest unit does not exceed an atom (*paramāṇu*).
Within the realm of time, the briefest duration does not exceed the moment of taking birth; this is called one *kalā*.

If a person were to offer their body and life as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges during the first division of the day, and likewise offer their body and life as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges during the middle division of the day...

Regarding the section on the superiority of the three incomparable [merits], the "Exceeding the Time" portion: On subsequent days, one might give away as many lives as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, practicing such giving at the three times of day for immeasurable periods.
This does not equal the merit of someone who, for even a single *kalā* moment, upholds a single four-line verse (*catuspāda-gāthā*) of this sutra.
Because it exceeds that time period, it is said that its power is superior. (End of the Western Section)
The elder Kṣemadatta was wealthy, noble, and possessed of merit comparable to King Aśoka; yet there is nothing in the world that can serve as a metaphor for King Aśoka.
Likewise, the merit of upholding this sutra cannot be illustrated by any thing whatsoever. Therefore, it is said to be "beyond calculation and beyond metaphor.
Fourth is the stage of the excellence of causes, which refers to the stage where the excellence of cause and effect surpasses all conceptual estimations. In the world...

The fruits resulting from occasional generosity and the observance of precepts are the tainted (sāsrava) results of human and celestial rebirth. The merit of upholding this sutra brings about the untainted (anāsrava) fruit of Buddhahood;

thus, there is a distinction between superior and inferior causes. Therefore, within the *Vajracchedikā*, there are four textual divisions. The "Numerous Victories" (*Saṃkhyā-viśeṣa*) section of that sutra is identical to the "Immeasurable Calculations" (*Apramāṇa-gaṇanā*) section of this sutra.
The "Powerful Victory" (*Bala-viśeṣa*) section of that sutra is identical to the "Boundless" (*Ananta*) section of this one.
This refers to the "transcendence of temporal divisions. That sutra is superior because it is identical to this sutra’s inconceivable transcendence of conceptual calculations regarding time.

As for the statement that the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* explains kalpas and so forth, this clarifies their categories. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "First, a single heavenly robe brushes away a stone."
In a kalpa, there is a great stone forty *li* square. A long-lived celestial being comes once every hundred years and brushes it with a fine, soft cloth until it is completely worn away;
only then is it called one kalpa. It is also said that there is a great city forty *li* in size, filled to the brim with mustard seeds.
There are long-lived devas; if one were to take a single mustard seed every hundred years until all the mustard seeds were exhausted, that duration is called a *mahākalpa*.
These are all ancient translations. The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states: "There are two kinds of kalpas:

first, those measured by days, nights, and years—where one day constitutes one kalpa, one night constitutes one kalpa, or three or ten years constitute one kalpa; or [second,] where one night constitutes one kalpa."
"Three years" or "ten years" refers to the calculation of years.
As for the expression "two asaṃkhyeyas," according to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* of the Hīnayāna tradition, it explains that from one to ten, ten constitutes a hundred.
Ten hundreds make one thousand. In this manner, by multiplying ten times ten, up to the fifty-second number, it is called one *asaṃkhyeya*.
According to the Mahāyāna *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, from one to ten, counting up to the one hundred and twelfth number, it is called one *asaṃkhyeya*.
Furthermore, when referring to the *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas at the time of attaining Buddhahood, they are distinct; that is, three times reaching the point of being uncountable.
These are called the three great *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
Regarding the statement that the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* further explains [them], this refers to the minor calamities (*antara-kalpa*) within the *mahā-kalpa* of abiding.
During each period of decrease, the three calamities arise. Mǔ (Mokṣala) says: "This means that from a human lifespan of eighty thousand years, it decreases by one year every hundred years."

It decreases until the human lifespan reaches thirty years; this is the age of famine (*durbhikṣa-kalpa*). Then, for another hundred years, it decreases by one year each year until it reaches twenty years;

at that point, the age of disease (*roga-kalpa*) arises. Again, for another hundred years, it decreases by one year each year until it reaches ten years; then, the age of weapons (*śastra-kalpa*) arises.

From this ten-year lifespan, children come to trust their fathers, and the lifespan increases back up to eighty thousand years; this is called one kalpa of increase and decrease (*vivarta-saṃvarta-kalpa*).
(From the section on the hells below: the period from ten years increasing to eighty thousand years is called one intermediate kalpa. Master An states:

"Twenty such cycles of increase and decrease are named 'Kalpa of the Water-drawing Wheel' (*gargarī-kalpa*) after their metaphorical analogy. Question: Among the twenty *kalpas* of increase and decrease in the Lesser Vehicle system, eighteen intermediate *kalpas* involve both increase and decrease;
the first one involves only decrease and no increase, while the last one involves only increase and no decrease. How is this so?
This constitutes twenty aeons of increase and decrease (*vivarta-kalpa* and *saṃvarta-kalpa*). To answer: during the initial period of decrease, when merit is supreme, the decrease is extremely slow.
At the end, when human merit is inferior, the increase is extremely slow. At the beginning, when human merit is supreme, it gradually decreases;

as it moves toward evil, the decrease is extremely slow. This also equals one aeon of increase and decrease. At the end, when human merit is inferior, it gradually increases; as it moves toward goodness, the increase is extremely slow. This also...

This constitutes one period of increase and decrease; therefore, there are also twenty such periods of increase and decrease. Question: Within the *sthiti-kalpa* (abiding eon), it is permissible that there are increases and decreases to constitute twenty eons.
However, for the remaining three—the *saṃvarta*, *vivarta*, and *śūnya* kalpas—there are no increases or decreases.

How, then, can they constitute twenty eons? Answer: The treatise states: "However, by virtue of their temporal duration being equal to that of the *sthiti-kalpa*, they are reckoned according to the *sthiti-kalpa*."
Each kalpa consists of twenty intermediate kalpas. Question: At what time do the three calamities, such as famine, appear? Answer:
According to the second fascicle of the Mahāyāna *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, within a *sthiti-kalpa* (abiding kalpa), there are twenty cycles of increase and decrease. During each period of decrease:
All [world systems] possess the three calamities; this refers to the minor calamities occurring during the kalpas of increase and decrease. These are famine, disease, and warfare.
Specifically, from the time when the human lifespan is eighty thousand years, as it decreases by one hundred years per century until the human lifespan reaches thirty years, famine arises.
The devas and nāgas become enraged and do not send down sweet rain. After a long period has passed, plants and trees wither and die, and the springs and wells...
They were also parched with thirst. For seven years, seven months, and seven days and nights, they initially sustained their lives by eating tree bark and grass roots.
Once these were exhausted, they gathered grain roots or boiled them to extract the juice in order to preserve their lives.
Driven by famine, there arose the signs of hoarding and the piling up of white bones, each having two characteristics. Regarding the two characteristics of hoarding, it is said that there was one...
First, like those driven by hunger who all head toward a spring or well, they arrive and cannot turn back, gathering together to die of starvation.
Second, ten, fifteen, or twenty people find grains, wheat, sesame, or beans; they take them as seeds and store them within chests and baskets like *maṇi* jewels.
Gathering them in one place and guarding them in rows is called "accumulation" (*caya*). Regarding the two signs of "shifting the tally" (*gaṇanā-cālana*): shifting...
This refers to the turning of tally-sticks (*śalākā*). It means gathering grains, roots, or boiling them to extract their juice, or pounding them into flour.

All members of the household sit together and share a single tally; only when it reaches one person does that individual receive a mouthful of food. Those who do not hold a tally are given a contract.
Second, at the site of the old threshing floor or mill, tallies are used to distribute the old grains—millet, wheat, and beans—from the field.
They boil it into a broth, which they place in a vessel. Returning, they cast a tally-stick (*śalākā*) into the presence of one person and drop the stick into the broth;

having sucked it once, they pass on. Regarding the two signs of the white bones (*asthi-śvetaka*): for a long time they have been starved until their flesh and marrow have withered away, and the skin has torn away so that the white bones are exposed.
Second, they take the white bones of the dead, pile them up, and sustain their lives by boiling them in broth. As it is said:
It was only after seven years, seven months, seven days, and seven nights that they were finally able to pass through.

Once the kalpa had ended, a seer possessing the five supernatural powers (pañcābhijñā) came from the mountains and informed them, saying: "Because you committed the evil karma of stinginess and greed, you now undergo this suffering;
I urge you to cultivate goodness. Consequently, they gave rise to a sense of renunciation of an inferior grade. When the world became favorable once again, Zhe said: "For three thousand years..."
The kalpa does not diminish. Men and women give birth to one another until they fill Jambudvīpa. Then, for every hundred years, the life span decreases by one year, until it reaches twenty years.
At that time, the kalpa of disease arises; non-human beings emit poisonous vapors, and all people fall ill.

Then the kalpa of pestilence arises, and there is no medicine capable of curing it. Only after seven months and seven nights have passed does it finally subside. Those sentient beings, once again together...
They gather together and give rise to a middling degree of weary detachment (*nirveda*). Due to these causes and conditions, the lifespan decreases, and the calamities of disease subside.
Subsequently, as the lifespan gradually diminishes until it reaches ten years, the *śastra-kalpa* (the age of weapons) arises. When people see one another, they give rise to mutual anger;
whatever grass, wood, and other objects they grasp all transform into swords, with which they slaughter one another. This continues for seven days and seven nights before it finally ceases.
It passed. At that time, for sentient beings whose three types of decline reached the extreme of ten years of age, there was the decline of their physical bodies:
those who were tall were only one span (*vitasti*) of a Buddha in height, and their girth was but one handful. As for the decline of their requisites, at that time sentient beings...
They subsist solely on weeds, tares, and seeds of mugwort; this is the foremost among foods. They wear garments made of horsehair and human hair;
this is the foremost among clothing. There are no metals such as gold, silver, lead, or tin; they use only iron and wood for adornment, which is the foremost among ornaments.
Within the mountain dwell seers possessing the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*), who declare: "By your evil karma, you undergo such suffering."

One should practice the ten wholesome actions; only then will the kalpa increase. At that time, sentient beings gather together in succession, and later, having developed a superior degree of revulsion [toward worldly existence], the world becomes favorable once again.
Consequently, the son’s age becomes double that of the father’s, increasing until it reaches eighty thousand years (the above explains the increase and decrease according to the Mahāyāna).

Next, the subsequent decrease follows the explanation of the Hīnayāna, which differs. In the Mahāyāna, one cycle of decrease passes through the three calamities (*trīṇi saṃvartanīni*); these three calamities are identical [to those of the Hīnayāna].
The arising of the kalpa of decrease occurs once. In the Hīnayāna, it occurs once per kalpa of decrease, following each calamity.
In the Mahāyāna, famine comes first, followed by pestilence, and finally by warfare. In the Hīnayāna, warfare comes first, followed by disease, and finally by famine.

In the Mahāyāna, when the lifespan decreases to thirty years, one encounters the calamities. In the Hīnayāna, after each calamity, the lifespan must necessarily decrease to ten years before the kalpa begins again. Both systems agree on this.

Śāṇavāsa says: "When the lifespan reaches ten years, one calamity occurs. Furthermore, a verse states: "When it reaches thirteen [years], the three calamities appear—swords, pestilence, and famine—in that order;

they last for seven days, seven months, and seven years, respectively. Question: Are there minor calamities in the other three continents? Answer: In the northern continent (Uttarakuru), there are none at all.

The two continents of the East and West resemble the three calamities [of this world]. When the kalpa of famine arises here, hunger and thirst increase frequently in the two continents of the East and West.

When the kalpa of pestilence arises here, the physical strength of those in the two continents becomes weak and inferior. When the kalpa of weapons arises here, [the same occurs in the two continents].

The inhabitants of the eastern and western continents frequently encounter one another and give rise to increased anger and resentment. When asked what meritorious deeds must be cultivated to avoid such calamities, the answer is that the Sūtras state:
"By giving a single morsel of food to the Saṃgha, one will not fall into the kalpa of famine; by giving a single harītakī fruit to the Saṃgha..."

One will not fall into the kalpa of pestilence by upholding even a single precept against killing; one will not fall into the kalpa of warfare. (The former explains the three minor calamities; the latter explains the three major calamities.)

Regarding the statement that "sometimes twenty kalpas constitute one kalpa," it is asked: how is it that both the formation and the destruction of the world-world (loka-dhātu) each take twenty kalpas?

The answer is given in the *Abhidharmakośa*: "When the world is being destroyed, nineteen kalpas are spent destroying the sentient world (*sattva-loka*) and one kalpa is spent destroying the physical world (*bhājana-loka*).
When it is being formed, one kalpa is spent forming the physical world and nineteen kalpas [are spent forming the sentient world]."

Regarding the formation of the world of sentient beings, first as for the formation of the physical world (*bhājana-loka*), the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "The kalpa of formation begins from the rising of the wind. Master Lü says:
"From beneath the second dhyāna heaven, a skillful wind arises; this is called the initial sign of the world's formation. Now, concerning the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*):

It is formed from both ends. First, the palace of the Great Brahmā King of the First Dhyāna is formed; next, the palaces of the three abodes—the Brahma-pārṣadyas and the Brahma-purohitas—are completed.
Then, the palaces of the four classes of gods dwelling in the sky, beginning with Yāma, are formed in succession.
Having thus completed the seven palaces from the top down, wind arises from beneath the level of Yāma and descends directly downward, forming the wind-circle (vāyu-maṇḍala). This is the wind-circle.
It is firm and dense. Even if the *kiṃnara* gods were to strike it with a vajra-wheel, brandishing their power, the vajra-wheel itself would shatter while the wind-circle remains undamaged.

Next, the various circles are formed, extending as far as the Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*), the Seven Golden Mountains, and the High Mountains, up to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven (thus the completion of the receptacle world).
Next, regarding the sentient world below: from the second dhyāna, the Ābhāsvara Heaven, [the formation proceeds downward].
O Deva, there was once a son of heaven who was reborn in the First Dhyāna as a Brahmā King. This Brahmā King dwelt alone for ten kalpas. Then the Brahmā King thought, "I require attendants.
Subsequently, devas from the higher realms were reborn in the Heaven of the Brahma-Purohitas (Brahma’s Ministers), where their lifespan is forty kalpas.
He further reflected: "I must have a retinue. Then there were devas from the higher realms who came to be born in the Brahmakāyika Heaven with a lifespan of twenty kalpas;
next, those who became the Yāma Heaven and so forth, up to the four classes of gods dwelling in the formless realm; next, those born among humans in the four continents and the earth-dwelling gods;
next, those born as hungry ghosts, animals, and in the hells, until finally, the very last individual first fell into the Avīci Hell.
The *Nāsī* hell marks the conclusion of the first twenty intermediate kalpas (*kalpa*) of this world’s formation. Question: When this realm was first formed, what did sentient beings eat? Answer:

At the time of the initial formation of the kalpa, sentient beings ate "earth-cakes" (*pṛthivī-parpaṭaka*). These were as large as a hand-span, white as snow, fine and soft like clarified butter (*sarpis*) or sandalwood (*candana*), and tasted like rock honey (*śarkarā*).
After the essence of the earth (*pṛthivī-rasa*) had vanished, forest creepers (*vanalatā*) subsequently grew; these are also called "forests."
The stalks were like sprouts of parched grain; their flavor was fragrant and delicious, and after eating them, they would grow back again.

Later, when greed arose, the forest creepers ceased to grow, and there appeared non-glutinous rice (*śāli*), seven inches in length and free of husks. Once greed had arisen, it could not be digested once it entered the stomach;
because of this, excrement and urine first appeared. Thereafter, the rice required planting to grow. Subsequently, the ten unwholesome actions (*daśākuśala*) arose.
Karma. From the acts of killing and stealing, the position of the Field-Master (*kṣetrapati*) was established. In Sanskrit he is called *Mahāsamata*, which here means "Upright Mind" (*ṛjumanas*);

he possesses great impartiality and uprightness. (The above explains the formation of the world; the following explains its destruction). Question: What are the signs of the initial destruction of the world? Answer: The *Abhidharmakośa* states:
"Destruction begins when beings are no longer born in the hells, until the external receptacle world is completely exhausted. Now, as for that which is destroyed:
Sentient beings: first, having died from the Avīci hell, they are not reborn there again. If their karma is exhausted, they are born in other realms;
if their karma is not yet exhausted, they are transferred to another region of hell. This applies even if they further commit acts of immediate retribution while among humans.
They also receive [the results] by being sent from other directions; this is called the first sign of the destruction of the world. In this way, sentient beings only perish and are not reborn.
Thus, gradually, until all are exhausted—by the very nature of things, not a single sentient being is harmed—they wait until their retributions for sins are finished.
Next, the seven hot and eight cold hells are destroyed. Those who have finished their retributions are reborn among humans. Next, the hungry ghosts are destroyed. Those who have finished...

Those who have completed their retribution for sins are born among human beings. Next, the animals are destroyed; those who have completed their retribution for animal existence are born among human beings.
If there are animals living together with humans, they are destroyed along with them. Next, among the four continents of the human world, it is first the southern continent.

By the very nature of things, a person there spontaneously and without a teacher attains the first dhyāna of meditative concentration while seated. Arising from that concentration, he utters these words:

The joy and bliss born of seclusion are exceedingly pleasant and profoundly tranquil. Fearing that if people were to hear of this, they would all enter meditative absorption and, at the end of their lives, be reborn together in the Brahma world—just as it is in Jambudvīpa—those in the two continents to the east and west are unable to enter meditative concentration; they pass away according to the exhaustion of their own karma.
They are born in the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) before they are able to enter meditative absorption (*samādhi*). They are likewise born in the Brahma-world;

other heavens of the desire realm should be understood by this same principle. Thus ends the destruction of sentient beings in the desire realm. From this desire realm, they are reborn in the first dhyāna; from the first dhyāna...
Initially, there was one person who attained the second dhyāna. Having arisen from that meditative absorption, he thought to himself: "The joy and bliss born of concentration are truly tranquil.
Upon hearing this, all the other devas collectively practiced it as well. At the end of their lives, they were all reborn among the three heavens of the second dhyāna.
Thus concludes the destruction of the world of sentient beings. Next follows the destruction of the receptacle world (the physical universe). First, the destruction by fire.
At that time, nineteen kalpas pass during which the world of sentient beings is destroyed, and one kalpa during which the physical vessel-world is destroyed.

From the hells below up to the First Dhyāna heaven above, not two sentient beings remain. For a long time there is no rain; the great earth and its mountains cause the grasses and trees to wither and dry up so that they no longer grow.
Furthermore, a second sun disc appears, whereby the ditches, ravines, and small ponds all lose their moisture. Thirdly...
The sun rises. The small rivers dry up. When the fourth sun rises, the four great rivers flowing from Lake Anavatapta are all exhausted.
When the fifth sun rises, Lake Anavatapta itself is exhausted. When the sixth sun rises, the waters of the four great oceans are reduced by half.
When the seventh sun rises, the waters of the four great oceans are completely exhausted; fires break out across the great earth, and mountains and rivers are utterly consumed in an instant.
Fire arises, starting from the wind-circle below and reaching up to the first dhyāna heaven above; it becomes one single mass of fire.

The flames from each respective level burn the palaces and the physical world (bhājana-loka) of that same level. The fire of the desire realm is coarse and cannot burn the subtle vessels of the form realm;

the fire of the form realm is subtle and cannot burn the coarse vessels of the desire realm. Nevertheless, the fierce flames of the desire realm fire rise upward and act as the condition [for the destruction].

It draws forth the flames of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) to incinerate the palaces of the first dhyāna (*prathamadhyāna*), which are consumed over the course of one kalpa before they are finally exhausted.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* asks: "From where do the six sun-discs come? There are five explanations.

First, it is said that during the period when the world has not yet been destroyed, the remaining six sun-discs are stored beneath the great ocean. Second, it is said that they are stored beneath Mount Yugandhara, dwelling there in concealment; however, only...
One day, the sun rises into the sky and circles Mount Sumeru, its radiance shining until the end of the kalpa.
Regarding the remaining six [suns], there are five views: (1) the single sun becomes seven times hotter; (2) what was originally one sun is divided into seven suns;

(3) the calamity arises only in that specific location, and there need not necessarily be seven suns; (4) the former explanation is correct; and (5) it is said that sentient beings perceive it through the power of their karma.
It is destroyed. Subsequently, seven solar discs appear. At that time, throughout the Desire Realm and the intermediate space of the First Dhyāna, there is not a single thing remaining;
it remains empty for twenty kalpas. Thus far, we have explained one kalpa of fire, comprising the phases of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness.
The Brahmakāyika devas [live for] twenty kalpas; the Brahmapurohita devas, forty kalpas; and the Mahābrahmā devas, sixty kalpas.
These are all [measured by] kalpas of increase and decrease. When the world was first formed, the Brahmā King was born and dwelt alone for ten kalpas.

As the Brahmā King remained in silent seclusion, he thought of assistants. Then, from the Ābhāsvara Heaven of the upper realm, beings were born down into the Brahmapurohita Heaven, where their lifespan is...
His lifespan is forty *kalpas*. He first dwells for ten *kalpas* during the period of formation (*vivarta-kalpa*), then remains for another twenty *kalpas*, totaling thirty *kalpas*.
Furthermore, he extends his presence for ten *kalpas* into the period of destruction (*saṃvarta-kalpa*), thus totaling forty *kalpas*.

Afterward, the Great Brahmā King again forms this thought, reflecting upon his retinue: "There are further devaputras from the higher realms who descend to become members of the Brahma assembly. Thus it is said.
During the kalpa of abiding, he comes and undergoes twenty sub-kalpas of increase and decrease within that kalpa of abiding. The life span of the Great Brahmā King is sixty kalpas;
this is according to the total count. If one were to examine it closely, he perishes after fifty-nine kalpas, at the time of the twenty kalpas of destruction.
During the first nineteen kalpas of destruction, the Brahmā King remained present as the world of sentient beings perished.

Upon entering the twentieth kalpa, the Brahmā King saw the fires of destruction arising from below; he did not undergo this one kalpa but was reborn in a higher realm. Therefore, the commentator says:
"Either twenty kalpas constitute one kalpa, or forty kalpas constitute one kalpa, or sixty kalpas constitute one kalpa."
Regarding the statement that "these eighty [kalpas] constitute one kalpa," this refers to the calculation from the preceding void kalpa:

twenty kalpas of emptiness, twenty kalpas of formation, twenty kalpas of abiding, and twenty kalpas of destruction. The final fire disaster, when reckoned against the preceding eighty kalpas, constitutes one fire disaster.
Regarding the enumeration of the "Luminous" (Ābhāsvara) heavens and so forth: the Heaven of Limited Light (Parīttābha) is the lowest of the three heavens within the Second Dhyāna.
Its lifespan is two *kalpas* of fire-disasters (*kalpoddāha*), calculated as one hundred and sixty *antarakalpas* of increase and decrease.

This Heaven of Limited Light is not burned by these fire-disasters; indeed, these very fire-disasters constitute its lifespan. This doubling continues up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception (Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana). That is to say:
Regarding this second dhyāna: among its three heavens, the lifespan in the Heaven of Limited Radiance (Parīttābha) is two fire-catastrophe kalpas;
in the Heaven of Immeasurable Radiance (Apramāṇābha), it is four fire-catastrophe kalpas; and in the Heaven of Utmost Purity of Radiance (Ābhāsvara), it is eight fire-catastrophe kalpas.

Among the three heavens of the third dhyāna, the lifespan in the Heaven of Limited Purity (Parīttaśubha) is sixteen fire-catastrophe kalpas, and in the Heaven of Immeasurable Purity (Apramāṇaśubha), it is thirty-two kalpas.
In the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, there are sixty-four kalpas; in the fourth dhyāna, nine heavens;
and in the Anabhraka Heaven, one hundred and twenty-eight kalpas—excluding three kalpas subtracted from the Anabhraka, there are only one hundred and twenty-five kalpas. Question:

Why are three kalpas subtracted? Answer: The commentary states that it may be because the cultivation in the lowermost grade of the fourth dhyāna heaven is inferior, and thus three [kalpas] are subtracted.
Regarding the *kalpa*: Miǒu says there are two explanations. First, that one transcends the transformed sensations (*vipariṇāma-vedanā*) of the lower three dhyānas;
since the cultivation here is inferior, the fruit is also diminished, just as when a person reaches the summit of a mountain, they must rest.
Second, it is said that it exists in order to establish the five hundred *kalpas* of lifespan for the Bṛhatphala Heaven and the sixteen thousand *kalpas* for the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
It decreases as follows: in the Cloudless Heaven (Anabhraka), there are one hundred and twenty-five kalpas; in the heavens above the three calamities of fire, the number doubles successively.
In the Heaven of Merit-Born (Puṇyaprasava), the lifespan is two hundred and fifty kalpas; in the Vast Fruit Heaven (Bṛhatphala), it is five hundred kalpas.
In the Avṛha Heaven, the lifespan is one thousand kalpas; in the Atapa Heaven, two thousand kalpas; in the Sudṛśa Heaven, four thousand kalpas;
in the Sudarśana Heaven, eight thousand kalpas; and in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, sixteen thousand kalpas.
In the Mahāmaheśvara Heaven, the lifespan is thirty-two times ten fire-disaster kalpas. Next, in the Formless Realm: in the Sphere of Infinite Space, twenty thousand [kalpas].

Forty thousand *kalpas* for the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), sixty thousand for the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), and eighty thousand for the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Regarding the statement that one water-disaster *kalpa* corresponds to the Ābhāsvara Heaven: its lifespan is that of the third heaven within the Second Dhyāna.
Question: For what reason does one water-disaster occur after seven fire-disasters? Answer: Because it accords with the lifespan of the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
The lifespan [of the gods in the second dhyāna] is eight great kalpas. Previously, seven cycles of destruction by fire have already destroyed the first dhyāna.

Next, it is destined that there will be an eighth cycle of destruction by fire destroying the first dhyāna. Only when the destruction by fire of the first dhyāna does not arise will there be a destruction by water, which destroys the second dhyāna.
The lifespan of the Ābhāsvara gods of the second dhyāna is one *kalpa* of water-destruction, together with seven cycles of fire-destruction.

*Kalpa*. Question: Why, among the three heavens of the second *dhyāna*, is the lifespan of the first, the Parīttābha Heaven, two fire-disaster *kalpas*, while the third, the Ābhāsvara Heaven, has a lifespan of one water-disaster *kalpa*? Why is this not mentioned for the intermediate heaven (*ekadhyāna*)?
Answer: This is not a suitable place for such an explanation. If one were to speak of the lifespans of the various heavens, it would not be problematic.

This is a general statement. Now, here we rely on human beings to clarify the kalpas. Therefore, since the fire calamity first arises in the Second Dhyāna Heaven, it is necessary to specifically mention the Third Heaven.
Since the water calamity is about to arise, it is likewise necessary to specifically mention it.
Regarding the statement "eight, seven, fire, one, seven, etc.," this refers to the lifespan of the Śubhakṛtsna (Pervasive Purity) Heaven.
After seven cycles of destruction by fire have ruined the First Dhyāna, it then encounters a single destruction by water that ruins the Second Dhyāna.

Following forty-nine cycles of destruction by fire—seven times seven—which ruin the First Dhyāna, it encounters another seven cycles of destruction by water that ruin the Second Dhyāna. Beyond this, there is yet more...
There are seven calamities by fire that destroy the first dhyāna. When the eighth calamity by water is due to occur, it does not come;
instead, a calamity by wind arises and destroys it. This continues up to the third dhyāna.
Thus, there are eight sets of seven fires (fifty-six fires), seven calamities by water, and one calamity by wind within the third dhyāna.
The three heavens refer to the Ābhāsvara Heaven, whose lifespan is one *vāyu-kalpa* (wind-disaster eon). Question:
Why do the water-disasters and wind-disasters both take the third heaven within the second and third dhyānas respectively, rather than taking the third heavens of the lower [dhyānas]? Answer:
Because the water-disaster reaches its full extent in the third heaven of the second dhyāna, and the wind-disaster reaches its full extent in the third heaven of the third dhyāna.

This is because it is explained in a partial manner. Question: For what reason do eight cycles of seven-fire calamities and one cycle of seven-water calamities occur, followed by one wind calamity? Answer:
This accords with the fact that within the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, a lifespan of sixty-four kalpas constitutes a single lifetime.
Thus, there are eight sets of seven, totaling fifty-six fire calamities; the one wind calamity is therefore the sixty-fourth. As for the water calamity: [it occurs]... (and so forth).

At the time when the world is destroyed, from the second dhyāna there arises a rain born of co-nascence that is cloudless; this serves as the condition for the production of the water calamity in the desire realm.
When this rain falls, its drops are like axle-trees, pervading the entire world and pouring down simultaneously and evenly.
First, it submerges the four continents; next, it submerges the seven golden mountains; and finally, it submerges Mount Sumeru, the palaces of the Four Great Kings, and the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Next, the devas of the Yāma Heaven perish; next, those of the First Dhyāna perish; finally, those of the Second Dhyāna perish.

When the world is submerged and destroyed by the poisonous waters, it is like salt dissolving in water. Once the Second Dhyāna has been destroyed, the waters gradually descend, submerging and destroying the First Dhyāna.

The waters descend further, submerging and destroying the Desire Realm (kāmadhātu), continuing until they descend and submerge the wind-circle (vāyumaṇḍala). Thus the force of the calamity of water comes to an end. The world—
The destruction of the realms: when the world is about to be destroyed by the wind-disaster of the third dhyāna, that wind is fierce and sharp, like a sword-blade;
whatever it blows upon is reduced to fine dust. Yet as the wind blows through the celestial palaces, they overturn one another like two great men clashing two bronze gongs.
First the third dhyāna is destroyed, then the two lower dhyānas, and finally the desire realm is destroyed.

When the abodes of the gods up to the wind-circle have been destroyed, the world undergoes dissolution. Question: How do the three calamities each destroy the first, second, and third dhyānas respectively?

Answer: Sentient beings in the first dhyāna possess the affliction of vitarka and vicāra; externally, there is the calamity of fire. In the second dhyāna, because there is internal joy (*prīti*), there is externally the calamity of water.
In the third dhyāna, because there is internal breathing (*śvāsa-praśvāsa*), there is externally the calamity of wind. Question: Regarding the arising of these three calamities...
Question: At that time, there are no sentient beings; who then brings about this calamity? Answer: It is through lateral transformation (*pārśvavikāra*).

When the three calamities appear, although there is no transformation through birth (*upapatti-vikāra*), the increased karmic power of the sentient beings of the same level within the trichiliocosm transforms this world into a calamity.

Because their karma is identical, the Hīnayāna speaks only of what is brought about by karma and does not speak of lateral transformation. Question: In the Mahāyāna, do the self-world and other worlds share the same level?

Sentient beings possess karma that causes their own realm to be destroyed; why do they not themselves transform their own realm so that the calamities arise, rather than having to transform another realm? Answer:
It is the nature of things (*dharmatā*) that sentient beings of a particular realm and the calamities of that realm do not coexist. Therefore, they transform another realm. Question:

From what do the three calamities fundamentally originate, and from what are they born? Answer: The three calamities arise from the co-emergent designations and names (*nāma-vikalpa*) within the *ālayavijñāna* of sentient beings.
The seed is the direct producer. Although there is a difference in the proximity or distance of the conditions from the previous kalpa, it nevertheless relies upon sentient beings;
furthermore, because it is the karmic seed of another realm, it is directly inseparable [from them]. Question: After seven fires, how much time elapses before one reaches the calamity of water?

Answer: Once the seventh universal destruction by fire has occurred, there is emptiness. After the period of emptiness, the world is formed. Once formed, it remains stable. Thus begins the kalpa of abiding.

This is the calamity of water. When the second dhyāna is destroyed, it passes through eight cycles of seven [destructions] by fire that destroy the first dhyāna; this constitutes seven cycles of water destroying the second dhyāna.
During the seventh cycle of water, the destruction of the second dhyāna occurs, continuing down until the first dhyāna and below are completely exhausted.

Once they are exhausted, there is again emptiness. When emptiness has been established, it remains for the duration of the kalpa. When the kalpa is full, there is then the calamity of wind that destroys the third dhyāna. It destroys the third...
At the conclusion of the section on meditation, it says:

"Counting these until they become uncountable. This refers to the question: among fire, water, and wind [calamities], how many eons (kalpas) must be counted to constitute a *saṃkhyeya-kalpa*? The answer is:
a wind calamity (*vāyu-saṃvarta*) is formed by accumulating the lifespans of the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven; thus, it constitutes an "uncountable" number, which is precisely what is being counted.
The *vāyu-kalpa* (wind-disaster aeon) differs from that of the Hīnayāna, which merely accumulates *tejaḥ-kalpas* (fire-disaster aeons). Zhiyou states:
"In the Hīnayāna reckoning of fire-disaster aeons, one counts from one up to a hundred, and so on until the fifty-second, which is called an *asaṃkhyeya*.
Counting in this manner three times until reaching the uncountable is termed the 'three great *asaṃkhyeyas*.'"

Regarding the statement that one generally passes through these three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*: Question: From the initial cultivation of practice until the attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood, how many *kalpas* are required to achieve Buddhahood?

Answer: The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Generally, one passes through these three [levels]. The Mahayana tradition and the intent of the Commentary seek to manifest the difficulty of attaining Bodhi;
therefore, they take the *vāyu-saṃvarta-kalpa* (wind-disaster kalpa) as the unit for calculation. Thus, it is known that those non-Buddhist outsiders who hold views of nihilism lack the proper cause.

These masters of treatises, practitioners of the *dhūta* who boil gruel, those who wander the markets ringing gongs and striking copper and earthenware—such as these—eat their meals and put on their robes, yet they wear their *kāṣāya* draped backward.
Holding iron staffs in their hands, they claim that "the mind itself is Buddha" and that there is no need for cultivation. Their hearts are filled with greed and anger;
how could they possibly maintain a compassionate thought toward others? The sutras and śāstras are entirely untraceable in them; even if there are those who lecture, they constantly seek out faults.
It has been lost. Make every effort to cease its practice; do not wish for it to circulate. How painful this time is! The Dharma is destined for extinction.

Yet you force yourself to transmit and receive it, enduring suffering to proclaim it. Your resolve must not be slight; endure their insults and slanders. Do not follow the example of those who pass their time merely chasing after the moment.

Regarding the phrase "including the Bhadrakalpa and others," He [Hé] says: these are immeasurable; however, when the emergence of one thousand Buddhas is complete, that constitutes the end of the kalpa.
There are ten categories in total, as the Bhadrakalpa has no distinct count of its own. The commentary states: the nine preceding ones are called the *Vyūhakalpa* (Adornment Kalpa);
the present is called the *Bhadrakalpa*; and the future is called the *Tārakakalpa* (Star Kalpa). As for the ten categories: the first is named *Sūryacandramāsavarṣa* (Sun, Moon, and Year).
[The categories are: 1. Number; 2. Increase and decrease; 3. Twenty kalpas; 4. Forty kalpas; 5. Sixty kalpas; 6. Eighty kalpas—referring to the kalpa of the fire disaster. Answer:
At the time when the world was first formed, a son of the Ābhāsvara Heaven descended from that realm and arrived at this world.
He saw that there were one thousand lotus flowers in this world, emerging [and facing] toward the rear. There were one thousand... [the text continues].
When the Sages appeared, the various devas of the Form Realm conferred upon them the name "Worthy Kalpa" (Bhadrakalpa). There are both Great Worthy Kalpas and Small Worthy Kalpas. Lü Fu stated:
"In the initial Great Worthy Kalpa, one thousand Buddhas appear; we are now in the ninth period of decline. When this decline is complete..."

The aeon increases until the lifespan reaches eighty thousand years. From that point, as the aeon decreases from eighty thousand years, at the very beginning of this decrease, Maitreya Buddha appears in the world.
From the tenth decrease through the fifteenth decrease, nine hundred and ninety-four of the one thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa appear simultaneously.
From the sixteenth decrease onward, until the time of the destruction of the aeon, no Buddhas appear.
He appears in the world. Subsequently, during the Minor Bhadrakalpa, he appears among the thousand Buddhas as the Tathāgata Ruci (Louti).
(The above clarifies the distinctions.)

Regarding the mention of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* and other texts, this refers specifically to the Liang dynasty version of the *Samuccaya*. The *Samuccaya* (Treatise on the Compendium), fascicle ten, states that within the stage of skillful means (*upāya-bhūmi*), there are three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas:
first, the *asaṃkhyeya* of the mind of faith; second, the *asaṃkhyeya* of the mind of diligence; and third, the *asaṃkhyeya* of the mind of aspiration.
First, establishing a vow through body and speech and believing in the Tathāgata’s correct teaching is called "faith. Second, it is the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).

It becomes increasingly firm. One gains the certain knowledge that the fruit will surely be attained; the mind is already clear, and through the diligent application of energy born of weariness with suffering, it is called "mind.
With the supreme orientation toward *sambodhi*, the mind that seeks through true contemplation gives rise to a continuous succession of births, for there is no weariness or abandonment.
These are called the "minds of progression," each constituting one kalpa; they are also not assigned to specific stages.

As for the statement that each of the ten stages is divided equally, this refers to the mind of entry, the mind of abiding, and the mind of emergence, which serve to eliminate those afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Entering the first stage (*bhūmi*) means removing the internal obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*). Abiding in the first stage means removing the mental obstacle of afflictions.

Exiting the first stage—and likewise for each of the ten stages in succession—involves three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas per stage; these are added to the three *kalpas* prior to the first stage. Thus, the ten stages comprise thirty *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.

This completes the thirty-three [categories]. The first three minds are called *mahākalpas* (great eons). The twenty-one moments of mind prior to the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) are called *antarakalpas* (small eons).
The nine moments of mind in the eighth, ninth, and tenth stages are called *madhyamakalpas* (middle eons).
These minute divisions are termed "small," like a one-foot object divided into three segments, or twenty-one segments, or nine segments; thus, the three segments are taken as the *mahākalpa*.
As in the stage prior to the [first] ground (*bhūmi*), twenty-one segments constitute a minor eon (*antarakalpa*). As in the seventh ground, nine segments constitute a medium eon.

Regarding the mention of "eight, nine, or ten eons," although such statements exist, they are intended as a harmonious interpretation of the sūtra’s meaning. Question: The sūtra says "immeasurable, boundless, and... [the text is truncated].
Regarding the phrase "inconceivable asaṃkhyeya kalpas," it is not yet clear which of the ten types of kalpas this refers to. The commentary answers:
although there are such [classifications] where the durations of the kalpas differ, we now rely on our own treatise and others;
we follow the measure of immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable asaṃkhyeya years, rather than other great kalpas. According to the Lotus Sūtra, a single assembly speaks of five kinds of kalpas.

The Master of the Commentary (*śāstrakāra*) takes the general intent [of the sūtra], yet his interpretation is not fixed. Although the treatise states that there are five kinds [of kalpas], it does not say that the kalpas throughout the upper and lower sections of this sūtra all rely upon these five types.

For instance, regarding the account of the threefold bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) to attain Buddhahood, the Buddha cannot be constrained by the measurements of days, months, years, or kalpas.
This is as seen in the passage here and in the subsequent mutual inquiries among the various bodhisattvas.
Regarding "faith": during such a period, after fifty small kalpas and so forth, one attains the enjoyment of kalpas measured by days, months, years, and so on.
The commentator of the sub-commentary (*śāstrakāra*) also does not provide a definitive judgment, as he explains it according to five different perspectives.

Regarding the statement "to reveal that all Buddhas, etc.": Question: Since it is said that the commentators take [the measure of time] as months, days, years, and eons (*kalpa*), why is it called "appearing after incalculable great eons"?
Answer: Since it is said to be "incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* years," when these are accumulated, they again constitute a great eon.
Question: Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva need only speak of the past Lamp-Light Buddha (*Dīpaṃkara*) to suffice; why is it necessary to speak of so many?
[Kāśyapa] asked. The Master of the Commentary replied: "This is intended to reveal that all Buddhas are equal.
Regarding the statement, "This praise of the name is rare, etc.," [Kāśyapa] asked: "Since Mañjuśrī said he had seen [the Buddha] for a long time, I wonder what the name of the one he saw was?
[The Master] replied: "The Sūtra says: 'At that time, there was a Buddha named Candrasūryapradīpa,' and so forth" (Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra).
It is said: "The merits of all Tathāgatas are equal to one another, with the exception of four things: first, lifespan; second, name; third, lineage; and fourth, time.
There was a Buddha named Candrasūryapradīpa (Moon-Sun-Lamp-Brilliance); this is his specific name. The title "Tathāgata" and those that follow are general names.
During immeasurable and boundless kalpas, it is rare for a Buddha to appear, and even rarer is the occurrence of such a name. It is also rare to have but a single name.
One is called "Sun. Second is called "Moon. Third is called "Lamp. These three characters are all able to lead forth light and destroy darkness;

therefore, these names are also rare. Question: What is the distinction between a "name" (míng) and a "title" (hào)? Answer: If we rely on secular writings, a "name" is established based on one's physical substance (tǐ), while a "title" is established based on one's virtue (dé).

For example, when young, one is named "Spring" (Chūn); this is established based on substance. When one grows up and understands literature, one is named "Wén-gàn" (Literary Backbone); this is established based on virtue. [The text continues: "Understands..."
The name "Martial" (Mu) signifies martial prowess (Jun). Mo says: "It is like saying 'fire' when one calls for the substance of fire;

it is like saying 'warmth' to express its intrinsic nature (svabhāva), thereby manifesting its virtuous function. Now, speaking in terms of the Buddha-body, everything is established in reliance upon virtue; thus, the names and titles are not distinct.
Regarding the statement "the Buddhas such as Candrasūryapradīpa," terms such as "king," "son of heaven" (deva-rāja), "lord," "holy lord," and "sovereign" are general names.
If one says "Venerable Father," "Wu-xian," or "Xiao," these are specific names. Question:
Of the twenty thousand Buddhas, is the name Candrasūryapradīpa also a specific name, while the other Buddhas are not named Candrasūryapradīpa?
Question: What is meant by the rarity of the name? Answer: It is not rare for there to be the sun and no moon, or for there to be no lamp;
however, today the three meanings of sun, moon, and lamp are fully present. Therefore, the name is rare.
Regarding the statement that "the sun has two capacities," the *Fahua jing zhu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra) says: First, it guides illumination. The eye can only see objects when there is light;
on dark ground, one cannot see objects. Thus, it requires the guidance of sunlight, which is why it is called "guiding illumination.

The Buddha’s wisdom is likewise able to lead sentient beings toward untainted noble wisdom (*anāsrava-āryajñāna*). Second, it brings to fruition the myriad things of the world. Sunlight shines upon and causes them to open.

Flowers and fruits each differ from one another; the Buddha’s wisdom is likewise. He proclaims the teachings of the three vehicles and the five vehicles to enable sentient beings to attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Furthermore, he uses the sun as a metaphor for the Mahāyāna, for its light illuminates the four continents and its teaching is the most extensive.
The moon illustrates the *pratyekabuddha*, who becomes manifest only at night, just as the solitary realizer delights in tranquility. The lamp serves as a metaphor for the *śrāvaka*, who awakens...

Because their principle is shallow, that which they illuminate is not extensive; this is because they expound the Dharma of the Three Vehicles. Question: Since all Buddhas also expound the Three Vehicles, why are they not called "Sun," "Moon," and so forth?
Answer: This is because [the former] is merely a positive designation (*vidhi*), not a negative exclusion (*paryudāsa*).

Regarding the statement that the moon has two capacities and so forth: first, it removes heat; second, it provides coolness. If the myriad things of the world were not illuminated by the moon, they would lack this coolness.
The Buddha’s wisdom is likewise: it can eliminate the feverish afflictions of birth and death for sentient beings, enabling them to attain the coolness of nirvāṇa.

Regarding the statement that "a lamp has two capacities," etc.: first, it can dispel darkness; second, it can transmit illumination. A single bright lamp, when lit, causes the thousandfold layers of darkness throughout the hall to vanish entirely.
The Buddha’s wisdom is likewise: it cuts through the dim alleys of afflictions (*kleśa*) and destroys the nocturnal gloom of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Second, its capacity to transmit illumination means that from a single lamp, hundreds of thousands of lamps are kindled.

Regarding the phrase "The Tathāgata, first, is the general [designation]," the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Because it is said that his merits are equal, all Buddhas are identical in their ten titles.
"Tathāgata" is the general summary; the following nine titles are the specific summaries.

Within this, the two characters "Tathāgata" constitute the general, while the remaining nine titles are the particular. Question: What is meant by "general"? Answer: By merely saying "Tathāgata," one encompasses the three [titles].

The term "body" (*kāya*) encompasses the remaining nine titles. For instance, such names as "Tathāgata, Arhat," "Tathāgata, Samyaksaṃbuddha," and "Tathāgata, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna"—a single title such as "Tathāgata"—pervades all nine titles; therefore, it is called a general enumeration.
If one were to cite any one of the other nine titles, the remaining eight would be lost. This is just as when one says "Arhat," it generally encompasses them all.

Fifteenth, the meaning of "correspondence" (*yathārtha*). Question: As it is said that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses all titles collectively, why is he referred to specifically as "Tathāgata"?

Answer: There are two explanations. First, the name "Tathāgata" is pervasive, while the other nine titles are collective. Second, it is the first among the ten epithets; therefore, it is called "collective.
This is like the *nidāna* (introductory) section of a sutra: because it is the very beginning, it alone receives the name "introductory. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "As..."
This serves as a general introduction. The *Udānavarga* (Chuyao jing) explains the Tathāgata through four meanings. First, he comes from the past Buddhas.
All past Buddhas came from amidst the diligent cultivation of ascetic practices; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata.
Now, the present Śākyamuni Tathāgata, like those past Buddhas, likewise comes from amidst the diligent cultivation of ascetic practices over three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas; therefore, he is so named.
Tathāgata. Second, he is called Tathāgata because he comes from the two benefits [of self and others]. As the Sūtra says:
"Whether giving away kingdoms, cities, wives, children, heads, eyes, marrow, or brains, he is able to deliver himself and others; because he comes from this, he is named Tathāgata.

Third, he is called Tathāgata because he comes from the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature). As the Sūtra says: "Furthermore, because he accomplishes worldly purposes from the *dharmatā*, he is named Tathāgata. Fourth...
"Thus, like all the World-Honored Ones, he comes in reliance upon his virtues. As the Sūtra says:

"Just as the Buddhas of the past were fully endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities, and extensively saved all beings through their compassion without departing from the nature of Suchness (tathatā), so too am I now;
therefore, he is called the Tathāgata. (The above is based on the Śāstra.)
Regarding the statement in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* that "it is like the past," etc., the name "Tathāgata" is established by means of four kinds of dharmas. First, based on the teaching (*śāsana*).
The sūtra says: "It is like all Buddhas of the past. "Like" (*tathā*) means "in accordance with. It accords with what was taught by the Buddhas of the past. "Like" also means "resembling";

it resembles the sūtra-dharma taught by the Buddhas of the past, namely, the dharma of the twelvefold division of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*), which is the teaching of the twelvefold division of the scriptures.
Secondly, it refers to the practice of the *pāramitās*. This involves cultivating the six perfections, such as the practices of giving, ethical discipline, patience, and so forth.

Regarding the eleven kinds of emptiness, these refer to the principle (*tattva*): first, internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*), which is the contemplation that the five internal sense faculties are without self; second, external emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*).

Contemplating the five external objects (*pañca-viṣaya*): 3. Emptiness of the internal and external (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*): Because they are not subsumed under the five internal sense faculties (*indriya*), they are called "external";

because they are not subsumed under the five external objects, they are called "internal. These are precisely the objects of the internal body. 4. Emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*): This is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). 5.

Emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*): This is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). 6. Emptiness of the beginningless (*anavarāgra-śūnyatā*): Because there is no prior limit (*pūrvakoṭi*). 7. Emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*): All [phenomena].

Dharmas have no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). This refers to the three categories of phenomena (*dharmaskandha*). Eighth is the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*), which is the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

Ninth is the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), which is *nirvāṇa*. Tenth is the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*): mountains, rivers, and the great earth are the objects that are empty; now, the subject that grasps them is also empty.

Therefore, it is called "emptiness of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*). Eleventh is "great emptiness" (*mahā-śūnyatā*): this refers to all phenomena being like illusions and transformations; the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) are collectively termed "great emptiness.

Question: What is the distinction among these eleven types of emptiness? Answer: The first nine are the objects of observation, while the tenth is the observing wisdom which is also empty; therefore, it is called "emptiness of emptiness.
Within the first nine, the first seven are the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), and the last one is the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

Among the seven [types of emptiness], the first six contemplate the emptiness of phenomena in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-śūnyatā*). The latter one is the emptiness of nothing whatsoever (*akiṃcana-śūnyatā*). That which arrives at nirvāṇa is the fruit (the *saṃbhogakāya* as the retribution-body based on nirvāṇa).
Regarding the statement that the *prajñā* is "the Tathāgata and so forth," this explains the Tathāgata as the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). As for the Tathāgata: he comes from nowhere and goes nowhere;
therefore, he is named Tathāgata. "Coming" means there is no place from which he comes, signifying that he does not come from the future.
"Going" means there is no place to which he goes, signifying that he does not go to the past. This non-coming and non-going is precisely the Buddha of the Dharma-body.

Furthermore, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states regarding the term "vehicle" (*yāna*) and so forth: "One who rides the vehicle of reality (*yathābhūta*) does not mean that 'reality' (*tathatā*) itself is the vehicle;

rather, it is called 'reality' because one comes from the true path of the vehicle to achieve perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), and is therefore named a Tathāgata. (The aforementioned treatise).

Regarding the statement that "the meaning is briefly explained": the Master of the Commentary (*śūstrakāra*) introduces the doctrines of other Hīnayāna schools; these are not the tenets of this Mahāyāna school, nor are they its primary focus.

Therefore, he says they are "briefly explained. The masters of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* were originally disciples of the Sāṃkhya heretics and later went forth as monastics within the Sautrāntika school.
Although the divisions of their doctrinal positions are similar to those of the Mahāyāna, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:
There are three bodies (*kāya*). First, the fivefold dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), consisting of precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Second, the body sixteen feet tall made of gold, which was formed from the physical body of Prince Siddhārtha through the cultivation of causes;
thus it is called the *saṃbhogakāya* (the Body of Recompense). According to the Mahāyāna doctrine, this refers to the body that attained Buddhahood from the physical body of Prince Siddhārtha.

This refers to the *nirmāṇakāya*. The Master of the Commentary (*Sūzhǔ*) states: "Although the meaning is briefly clarified, this is an interpretation based on the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra).
It is not the tenet of this school [the Yogācāra]. This means it is not the tenet of the Yogācāra school within the Mahāyāna;

therefore, it is not adopted. Question: Since it is not adopted, why was it cited? Answer: It was intended to clarify the number of the Tathāgata’s bodies and fingers, borrowing from another [source] within the Hīnayāna.
"Coming by means of the path of reality" refers to the meaning of attaining perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*); "coming" is a designation for the meaning of the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body).
He said: "All Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have three similarities and four differences. The three similarities are: first, similarity in the provisions (*saṃbhāra*);

second, similarity in merit (*guṇa*); third, similarity in the three bodies (*trikāya*). The four differences are: first, difference in physical form; Śākyamuni is one *zhàng* and six *cun*, while Maitreya..."
First, they differ in stature: [Śākyamuni is] one thousand *zhàng* tall. Second, they differ in name: the names of Śākyamuni and Maitreya are distinct.
Third, they differ in lineage: Kṣatriya and Brāhmaṇa. Fourth, they differ in lifespan: Śākyamuni’s is eighty years, while Maitreya’s life is long.

Regarding the statement "should be correctly and equally [attained]," if this is explained according to the specific chapters, it refers to being "worthy of offerings" (Arhat) by severing the afflictive obscurations and realizing *parinirvāṇa*, and being "correctly and equally awakened" (Samyaksaṃbuddha) by severing the cognitive obscurations and realizing *bodhi*. Now, it is explained according to the general meaning.
The afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*) also obstructs bodhi and nirvāṇa, and the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) likewise obstructs bodhi and nirvāṇa;
for this reason, they are explained together in one place. In the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the term "should" (*yīng*) is used alone, without the character "to offer" (*gòng*).

This encompasses the three meanings found in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*. If the character "to offer" were included in the same passage, it would encompass only the aspect of "should" among those three meanings.
Regarding the meaning of "receiving offerings": it loses the other two meanings (as discussed in the upper section of the treatise and explained in the lower commentary).
As for the phrase "The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says, etc.," the question is: how many meanings should there be? The answer is: the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* explains it through three meanings.
The *Fahua lun* (Treatise on the Lotus Sūtra) explains the term "worthy" (*ārya*) through fifteen meanings. The intent is that possessing these three meanings constitutes the name "Worthy One.

Question: The meaning of "worthy" is a common designation for the Three Vehicles. Now, since the Buddha is named "Worthy," how does he differ from the three types of "worthies" in the Lesser Vehicle? Answer:

Although there are three types of "worthies" across the Three Vehicles, the "worthies" of the Great and Lesser Vehicles are distinct. Specifically, regarding the three types of "worthies" in the Two Vehicles, they are those who have eternally severed [the afflictions].

Because of the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*); second, because there would otherwise be no birth in segmented succession; and third, because he ought to receive the vast offerings of the people of a single trichiliocosm.

Now, as for the Buddha possessing these "ought-to-be" qualities: he ought to have eternally severed the two obstacles; he ought to be free from both segmented and transformational birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*);
and he ought to receive the sublime offerings of the ten directions and the trichiliocosm. As for the Two Vehicles in the present, they do not transcend [these limitations].
Three thousand. Regarding the past and future, there are no more than eighty thousand [kalpas].
As for the mention of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and this sutra, etc., in which part of this sutra is it that one should eternally destroy the thieves of the afflictions?
Answer: In this sutra, the phrase "all outflows (*āsrava*) are exhausted" explains the Arhat, which is precisely the eternal severance of the thieves of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
This is identical to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (as explained above regarding the character "should").
Regarding the statement "Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says 'A' and so forth," this serves to distinguish the underlying reasons. The *She-wen* (Explanatory Questions) states:

"According to the *Yogācāra-bhūmi-śāstra*, Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is also a common quality (*sādhāraṇa-guṇa*). Why, then, does the Master of the Commentary (*shuzhu*) judge Perfect Enlightenment to be an uncommon quality?

There are two explanations for this: first, it is said that the Master of the Commentary has erred regarding the text of the treatise; second, it is said that there are two types of common qualities. The *Yogācāra* states: "Arhat..."

The Arhat is a "shared virtue" (*sādhāraṇa-guṇa*). In terms of the persons of the three vehicles, they equally sever the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and equally realize the principle of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*);

thus it is called a shared virtue. Furthermore, the Perfectly Awakened One (*samyaksaṃbuddha*) is also a shared virtue: having attained that which all Buddhas equally sever—the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)—and equally realize the principle of the two kinds of emptiness (*dvaya-śūnyatā*), it is called a shared virtue. Moreover, the Master of the Commentary states that the Arhat is a shared virtue in relation to the three vehicles.
It is shared. As for "the Perfectly Enlightened One is unshared," this refers to the sense of being unshared; since [these qualities] exist in persons of the two vehicles, it is called "unshared.
It is not that the Master [of the Commentary] erred in examining the text.

Regarding the statement that the old [translation] says "perfectly equal" (*samyak-samā*), one asks: what is the distinction between "perfectly awakened" (*samyak-saṃbuddha*) and "perfectly all-knowing" (*samyak-saṃvid*)?

The commentary (*śū*) replies: "Perfectly all-knowing" refers to perfect awakening; it distinguishes [the Buddha] from the heterodox who possess false and partial awakening, and it distinguishes him from the two vehicles who possess limited awakening.

Furthermore, "perfect awakening" distinguishes him from the incomplete awakening of bodhisattvas. Thus, they are said to be one entity and identical in name. Mǔ says: "All-knowing" refers specifically to the thorough knowledge of the four inversions.
Based on what phenomena do these arise? Answer: They arise based on two views. The view of permanence and the extreme view (antagrāhadṛṣṭi) arise [based on the view of self].
The two inversions of pleasure and purity arise based on the adherence to views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa). The inversion of self arises based on the view of self (satkāyadṛṣṭi).

If that is so, since the followers of the Two Vehicles also eliminate these four inversions, they should be called "Perfectly All-Knowing" (samyaksaṃbuddha). Answer: Regarding the past and future limits, the followers of the Two Vehicles only know eighty thousand [kalpas]; therefore, it is not called "all-encompassing. Furthermore—

It is said: "Ordinary beings give rise only to the four inversions; the followers of the Two Vehicles know only the four inversions of ordinary beings; and the Buddhas also know the four inversions of the followers of the Two Vehicles.

Therefore, it is called 'universal' (*sarva*). Zhiyou says: "'Correct' (*samyak*) means the sense of being non-inverted. 'Universal Knowledge' (*abhisambodha*) means that regarding these four inversions, there is nothing to which one does not have universal penetration.
Thus, one is called a 'Perfectly Universal Knower' (*Samyaksambuddha*). Question: What are named the four inversions? Answer: The followers of the Two Vehicles cling to...
Regarding the Buddha’s body, it is characterized by suffering, impermanence, and so forth.

As for the statement that his "knowledge and conduct are perfected" (*vidyācaraṇasampanna*), this is termed a "reason" (*hetu*) by the author of this treatise. If, however, in this sūtra it says "one who is perfected in knowledge and conduct," [it refers to the same].
If one follows the explanation of the fruit of the ten thousand virtues in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it is called "endowed with clear vision" (*vidyā-cakṣus*). There are two meanings:

first, the "feet" (*pāda*) refer to the two dharmas of precept (*śīla*) and wisdom (*prajñā*); these constitute the vehicle, for by means of the feet of precept and wisdom, one attains *bodhi*. Second, [the other meaning is...]
The term "endowed with" (具足) is what the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* call "perfection" (圓滿). While the sutra text simply says "feet" (足), the latter meaning is correct.

The phrase "the so-called 'clear knowledges' refers to the three clear knowledges (*vidyā*), etc. is an explanation from the *Śāstra*. The three clear knowledges are three of the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). The six supernormal powers are:

the power of knowledge regarding the miraculous realm (*ṛddhiviṣaya-vidyā*), the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*), and the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). The three clear knowledges are:

first, the clear knowledge of the wisdom of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānavidyā*), which has as its nature the fifth supernormal power, that of recollecting past lives. "Past" (*pūrva*) refers to the past world; "lives" (*nivāsa*)...
This refers to past events. "Events" refers to Bodhisattvas and Buddhas, such as the Bodhisattva Sadāparibhūta and others; this is what is meant by "events.
Regarding these events, that which was named in former lives is called "past" (*pūrva*). It is the object transformed through mindfulness and conditions.

The untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) that, in accordance with those conditions, takes past objects as its domain is called the "clear knowledge of the recollection of past abodes" (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñānābhijñā*). If it takes past objects as its domain...

It is not exhaustive; it merely receives the name "clarity" (*vidyā*) but does not attain perfection. Second is the clarity of knowledge regarding birth and death (*cyutyupapādajñāna-vidyā*). Its nature is the second supernormal power (*abhijñā*), that of the divine eye.
The Tathāgata’s wisdom takes future births and deaths as its object—dying here and being born there—which is termed "birth and death.
