Regarding the statement that "some enter the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) and so forth," this is also called "non-retrogression due to the cause.

This is because those eight princes had not yet entered the first stage when they were taught by Prabhāketu, after which they finally entered the first stage; the commentator holds these two interpretations.
Regarding the statement "the fourth is the cause for entering": that which is able to enter consists of the two causes, namely merit and wisdom;
that which is entered into is the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood and Bodhi.
Regarding the statement on "the fifth cause of recollection," this refers to Mañjuśrī’s own recollection of past events. The Sūtra says:

"The last among them to attain Buddhahood was named Dīpaṃkara. Question: Since all eight princes attained Buddhahood, why is it that the last one alone is specifically mentioned as attaining Buddhahood, while the previous seven are not? Answer: It is because the eighth prince was named Dīpaṃkara.
This is the teacher of Śākyamuni. As for the other seven, they are distantly related to Śākyamuni; therefore, he mentions him specifically. Question:
Why were the eight princes previously cited all together? Answer: Because the eight princes were disciples of Mañjuśrī.
To establish the connection with Mañjuśrī, who is the ninth-generation ancestral teacher of Śākyamuni, these rain-flowers now all proceed from Mañjuśrī.
Since the Bodhisattva has come to study this, he has verified that what Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said is not false. How could the Nine Generations of Patriarchs have dared to forget these words?
As for the statement regarding preaching the Dharma and so forth for others, it was Mañjuśrī himself who saw his own past life as the Dharma Master Miaoguang.
After eighty minor kalpas, he preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and attained Buddhahood; this is called "benefiting others.

As for the statement that, according to principle, this passage should belong to the preceding section: the preceding part of the sūtra text describes how the eight princes, after making offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis [of Buddhas], all attained the Way of the Buddha; here again it says he was the last to attain Buddhahood. Both are...
The teaching on the eight princes attaining Buddhahood is collectively integrated into the preceding section on the causes for entering [the path].
It is solely because of this proclamation that the name of the eighth prince’s attainment of Buddhahood must be specifically clarified; thus, this is a specific clarification.

If one discusses the ten causes, they are collectively combined under "recollection. Because doubt arises through these conditions, Mañjuśrī first speaks, while the questioning is exclusively the work of Maitreya alone.
In the past, he sought renown, causing Maitreya to remember [him] so that it might be known that Mañjuśrī’s prediction was not erroneous;
knowing that the Buddha would certainly preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he called to mind the eighth prince, identifying Śākyamuni as his grandson;
and he called to mind eight hundred disciples, identifying Maitreya as one of his own disciples. (The above concludes the recollection of the eight princes.)
Regarding the phrase "this is the first": among the account of the eight hundred disciples attaining Buddhahood, this refers to the initial cause of defilement. As the Sūtra says:
"Among the eight hundred disciples, there was one person... and so forth.
Regarding what is called "lack of fluency": while currently engaged in reciting the sutra, one fails to maintain auspicious names and thus lacks fluency;
furthermore, those already mastered are entirely forgotten, and many names are lost to forgetfulness.
Regarding the statement that "inner sublime practice is not pure": this explains that although one may read and recite many sutras, one does not master them thoroughly.
Regarding the statement that "externally one is greedy for reputation": this explains that because one forgets much of what has been learned, one is called a "seeker of fame."
The commentary states: "You are called 'One Who Seeks Fame. This is a citation from the sūtra text. It demonstrates that Mañjuśrī knows events from the distant past;
thus, it intentionally says that while Maitreya formerly sought fame and profit, Mañjuśrī now understands every detail of those past events.
This serves as proof for Mañjuśrī’s response: because the Buddha Dīpaṃkara’s method of teaching was unerring, he spoke thus. Therefore, it is said:
In the past, when Maitreya sought fame, he asked Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva about the practice of the bodhisattva path;

yet he did not perceive that [Mañjuśrī] had previously suppressed evil and extolled the good. Now, in the midst of the great assembly, [Maitreya] proclaims that he himself seeks fame, profit, and so forth.
It is not a matter of disparaging others or envying their fame and profit; how then can one be called a Bodhisattva? The answer in the *Shu* (Commentary) states:

"Regarding the phrase 'You are named,' etc., this is not a disparagement of the Bodhisattva Maitreya. Therefore, the *Shu* says: "If it were otherwise, it would constitute the fault of directly accusing and disparaging another."
Regarding the statement "this is the cause of purity and clarity": [Question] Since Maitreya Bodhisattva has already attained Buddhahood, how can he have attained Buddhahood through a defiled cause?
[Answer] There is indeed a pure cause. As the Sūtra says: "This person also, by virtue of the causes and conditions of having planted various roots of goodness..."

Regarding the phrase "planting both merit and wisdom," a sutra states: "Having planted the roots of all virtues under tens of millions of Buddhas" means that one has encountered excellent conditions and resolutely cultivated merit and wisdom.
To say "this is the beginning" refers to the person. To take the present as the past, Mañjuśrī was formerly known as Prabhāsa;
to take the past as the present, the former Prabhāsa is none other than the Great Being Mañjuśrī today.
Again, to take the present as the past, Maitreya was formerly the seeker of fame (Yaśaskāma); to take the past as the present, that former seeker of fame is still [Maitreya] today.
Regarding the present Maitreya, the *Śāstra* states: "You are named 'Seeker of Fame' (Qiú míng), yet you manifest knowledge of past events; therefore, you are indeed a person.
It further states: "As for those who plant various roots of goodness," the commentator explains that these refer to the Dharma.

Regarding the commentary stating that this is a summary answer according to the Dharma: "According to the Dharma" refers to the sūtra itself. The sūtra says, "The present manifestation of these auspicious signs is no different from before," and so forth.
This means that seeing the rain of flowers and other such signs on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa at this time must signify that Śākyamuni is preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

It is said that when he was the monk Wonderful Light, he saw the Buddha Lamp-Light enter meditative concentration and rain down flowers, and so forth. Later, when he left the household life, he preached the Lotus Sutra.
Now, at this time, Śākyamuni displays these auspicious signs; one must know that Śākyamuni has emerged from concentration and will preach the Lotus Sutra (in prose).

Regarding the statement that the first two causes are not restated in verse: these refer to the cause of the great meaning as directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*) and the cause of the profound meaning of the words and phrases.
Regarding the statement that the latter two verses are not included in the response and so forth: this refers to what the Sūtra says, beginning with "O people, you should now know," and so on.
Regarding the statement "by this, they are further divided into two": this is merely a restatement pointing to specific matters.
Since the ancient and the modern coincide in referring to these two answers, it is called "by this."
Regarding the statement that "the seven causal factors are divided into three," there are three types of responses:

the response of praising what is rare and marvelous, the response of manifesting subsequent excellence, and the response of detailing shared activities. In the verse, only the first and last two responses are mentioned, while the middle one is omitted.
The response manifesting subsequent excellence refers precisely to the excellent cause. The Sūtra says: "Next, there was another Buddha, also named Candrasūryapradīpa."

Next, there were further Buddhas also named Candrasūryapradīpa and so forth; their names were identical to those of the Wondrous One, their nature was identical to that of the Wondrous One, their titles were identical to those of the Wondrous One, and their Dharma was identical to that of the Wondrous One—even down to the teachings they expounded, which were excellent in the beginning, middle, and end. Thus it was; yet they did not manifest the causes for such supreme excellence.
This merely describes the six causes.
Regarding the phrase "praising the rare and marvelous" and so forth, the sutra says: "I recall past lives," and so on.
Jin states that, briefly, there are five meanings by which something is called "past": first, momentary past, which refers to each preceding moment among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).

Thereafter, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) pass away in five ways: first, passing away through the two types of death, namely, the death of the constituent parts within various groups of sentient beings;
second, passing away through dissolution, namely, the destruction of the physical world (*bhājana-loka*) by the three calamities;

third, passing away through retrogression, namely, because one has not yet attained the four kinds of non-retrogressive qualities; fourth, passing away through exhaustion, namely, the *sopadhiśeṣa* and *nirupadhiśeṣa* nirvāṇas; and fifth, passing away through cessation.
When afflictions are exhausted, it is *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder). When the maturation [of karma] is exhausted and ceases, it is *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa without remainder).
Regarding the phrase "this is the first": the first verse is formed by the assembly [of the preceding]. The prose commentary has two parts:

the first concerns his time as a layman, and the second concerns his life after renunciation. As for the period as a layman, the prose sutra states: "Before that final Buddha had renounced the world, there were eight kings."
The sons were: first, named Yǒuyì (Possessing Intent); second, named Shànyì (Good Intent). Each ruled over four continents. Regarding those two who left the household life, the Sūtra says:
"When these princes heard that their father had left the household life and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they all relinquished their royal positions."

They also followed him into the homeless life. Here, the verse likewise consists of two parts. The first two lines concern their lay life; as the Sūtra says: "When the Buddha had not yet left the household life, eight princes were born to him.
This merely mentions the number of sons without listing their individual names. The latter two lines clarify their entry into the monastic order after the King’s transformation; as the Sūtra says:
"Seeing the Great Sage leave the household life, they also followed him to practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*). [The prose commentary follows. Home.

There are three forms that follow true companions; by practicing within the midst of the mundane world, one attains a favorable condition for returning [to the path]. One should steadfastly cultivate merit and wisdom.

Among the three sections, only the section on "practicing within the midst of the mundane world" is described here. The prose portion of the sutra states: "One should resolve upon the Great Vehicle and constantly practice the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*). This differs from the presence or absence [of such practices] in other contexts.
Regarding the statement that it was accomplished during the second period, the prose portion of the sutra says:

"At that time, the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa preached a Mahāyāna sūtra titled *Anantārtha*, up to the point where it was 'protected by the mindfulness of the Buddhas. In the present verse, the phrase "at that time the Buddha preached the Mahāyāna," etc., refers to this.

Regarding the statement that the prose (*dīrgha-pada*) and the verse (*gāthā*) differ in their sequence: in the prose, the shaking of the earth is mentioned first, followed by the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*).

In this present verse, however, the sentient beings are mentioned first, and the shaking of the earth is mentioned later; thus, they differ in their sequence. Furthermore, regarding presence and absence:

"The celestial drum sounds spontaneously" is not in the prose, but it is in the verse; thus, they differ in what is included and excluded. "Heaven rains *māndārava* flowers" is expanded upon in the prose.
The verses are consistent, though they differ in their breadth and brevity.
Regarding the phrase "all buddha-lands," etc., this indicates the scriptural text.
Regarding the phrase "also only the Buddhas Candrasūryapradīpa," etc., one asks: how is this known? The commentary (*śāstra*) replies: as stated previously—
Because this world undergoes six kinds of tremors, it is said that although all Buddha-fields are mentioned,
these tremors are merely the movement within the own-realm of the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa, and not a universal shaking of the realms of the ten directions.
Regarding the statement "the nirmāṇakāya, saṃbhogakāya, and so forth": Question: Since the lamp-light is a single Buddha-field (*buddhakṣetra*), how can one speak of "many"?
Answer: This clarifies that all Buddha-fields are in motion. Because the lower levels of the *nirmāṇakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya* are not one, they are called "many.

Within the stage of accumulation (*sambhārāvasthā*), the *nirmāṇakāya* is contrasted with the *saṃbhogakāya* of the first bhūmi; thus it is termed a "lower level. Within one great realm of the *nirmāṇakāya*, there are ten billion small [realms].
The transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). At the first stage (*bhūmi*), one further transforms and attains one hundred great transformation realms.

Within each great transformation, there are ten billion small transformations. Thus, the hundred great transformations manifested by the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*) at the first stage constitute one hundred times ten billion small transformations.
This refers to when the Buddha Dīpaṃkara was about to preach the Dharma, he moved one hundred times ten billion small transformation realms; these are called "the various [realms]."
Regarding the phrase "these first two": as for the first, the emission of light, it refers to the Tathāgata emitting light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows.
As for the second, the illumination of the object, it refers to the illumination of eighteen thousand Buddha-lands in the eastern direction, such that there was nowhere it did not pervade.
Regarding the statement that the verses do not describe the entry into parinirvāṇa or the construction of a stūpa:

within the prose (gadya) of Śākyamuni’s life, there are seven matters, and the subsequent verses of Maitreya do not recount the entry into parinirvāṇa, although they do recount six matters. Later, in the prose of Dīpaṃkara, there are seven matters, yet the current verses recount only five;
thus, both the entry into parinirvāṇa and the construction of the stūpa are omitted. Question: In the prose of Dīpaṃkara... [text ends]
Regarding what is seen now, how can one know that there are seven matters? Answer: Within what is seen now, these seven matters are made to be present.
Alternatively, taking Śākyamuni as an example, although the prose section does not mention the Lamp-Light Buddha, the prose section should likewise contain the seven matters.

Regarding the phrase "this is the first": the first half-verse says, "going toward sentient beings. The Sūtra states, "He shows all sentient beings the places of karmic retribution for birth and death.

The term "place" (*sthāna*) refers to the retributive state toward which one goes; that is, the bodies within the five destinies (*gati*) in the future, which are termed "places. This [refers to] those with fur and horns...
The "body with horns" is called a *sthāna* (place). It is the destination to which those characterized by a lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and a lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*) resort.
As for the statement that "or *sthāna* refers to principle (*yukti*) and so forth," it is named *sthāna* because it serves as a cause;

based upon this, the place of the fruit is established. A virtuous cause is the place where a virtuous fruit is induced; an unwholesome cause is the place where an unwholesome fruit is induced. This is the principle, and it is termed a "locus" (*sthāna*).
Regarding the phrase "or 'place' refers to a location": the iron walls and iron ramparts of hell are the "places of enjoyment," which are the bases of reliance;
these two interpretations are distinct. Regarding the phrase "this is the first":
it refers to first seeing the Pure Land. As the Sūtra says, "Furthermore, one sees the various Buddha-lands," and so forth. This is precisely [that].
This is the buddha-field seen by the light emitted from the Buddha Dīpaṃkara. Question: With what things is that buddha-field adorned? Answer:
The sūtra says, "It is adorned with various jewels. Question: When Śākyamuni illuminates the buddha-fields of the eastern direction, they appear golden;
what color does that buddha-field of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara have? Answer: The sūtra says, "The color of lapis lazuli and crystal," which refers to the color blue. Question: [Continues...]
Question: Why is that Buddha blue in color? Answer: This is due to the illumination of the Buddha’s light; it is for this reason that he appears as blue.

Regarding the statement that the light of Śākyamuni illuminates all things as golden in color and so forth: Question: What are the differences in the colors of the objects illuminated by the light emitted by Śākyamuni?

Answer: There are four explanations. First, it is said: The light from the *ūrṇā* (tuft of hair between the eyebrows) is white; [the light] of red and white colors illuminates the world and makes it [appear as such].
[The first view] says: It is golden in color, like a torch illuminating snow; the red and white are distinct from one another. The second [view] says:
The hair-tufts (*ūrṇā*) emit white light and golden light, which illuminate the world, making it entirely golden in color. The third [view] says:

The hair-tufts emit white light, while the red [parts] emit white light that illuminates the world, making it the color of lapis lazuli (*vaidūrya*) or crystal (*sphaṭika*). Question: For what reason does white light illuminate the world?

Regarding the realms (*dhātu*): "What colors do they take? Even the color of lapis lazuli? The answer is given in the Sūtra: "Adorned with various jewels, possessing the colors of lapis lazuli and crystal;
this is due to the light of the Buddha’s radiance. It does not hinder the white light from illuminating the world, yet it causes the world to appear as the colors of lapis lazuli and crystal.
The fourth [section] states: "The *ūrṇā* (tuft of hair between the eyebrows) emits white light, which takes on the color of lapis lazuli and illuminates the world, likewise appearing as..."
[The color] is like lapis lazuli. It is as if one were holding a torch and entering a mountain to illuminate and see various forms and colors.

Regarding the statement "intending to reveal the Mahāyāna, etc.," the question is: "If the realm illuminated by Śākyamuni is golden in color, how is this so? The answer in the commentary states: "Intending to reveal, etc.

This indicates that among the fruits of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), there is no second vehicle; it signifies that which is most worthy of honor, just as gold is the most excellent among the seven treasures.
The first phrase concerns "treasures. Because one's own possessions are held in high esteem, this indicates that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is likewise worthy of being valued and esteemed;
therefore, it is exclusively golden in color. Regarding the statement "all virtues are perfectly complete," etc., one asks:

Why is the realm illuminated by the Buddha Dīpaṃkara adorned with various jewels and made the color of lapis lazuli and crystal? The Commentary answers: The phrase "all virtues are perfectly complete," etc., intends to signify this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
This is a sutra that is complete with all flavors.

Regarding the phrase "mutually reflecting and manifesting": when it says the light of Śākyamuni illuminates [the world] as golden, it implies by reflection that the Lamp-Light World (*Dīpapradyota*) also becomes golden;
when the Lamp-Light World illuminates [itself], it becomes the color of lapis lazuli (*vaidūrya*), which implies by reflection that the world illuminated by Śākyamuni also becomes [that same color].
It is the color of lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*).
As for the statement that in Sanskrit it is called *vaiḍūrya* and so forth, these refer to the colors blue, yellow, red, and white. Zhangjing says:
"Tradition holds that Śākyamuni said it comes from the jewels of the mountain—that is, the jewels on the southern face of Mount Sumeru—and this jewel is blue in color. All [of these]...
True jewels cannot be destroyed; nor can they be melted or cast by smoke or flames. Yet, because ghosts possess supernatural powers, they break them into vessels.
Some say that these are the sounds of garuḍas, which ghosts and spirits shatter and sell to the human world.
Regarding the statement that "the Western regions are hot," etc., this records Master Xuanying’s refutation. [The argument is: "In the Western regions it is hot;
the land has no ice. Since there is already *sphaṭika* (crystal) in the West, yet there is still no ice, it is clear that [the object] is made of stone.

The above constitutes Master Xuanying’s incorrect interpretation within his *Jīngyīn* (Phonetics of the Scriptures). The Master of the Sub-commentary previously cited the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, which states that *sphaṭika*...

This [ice] is transformed from snow. Since there is already snow on the Snow Mountains (Himavat) in the west that does not melt even during the summer, and the severity of the cold is particularly extreme, how could there be no ice?
What prevents there being ice formed by the transformation of ice that has existed for a thousand years?

Regarding the mention of "scorching heat," this is stated according to the general principle. Question: These lapis lazuli and other items are all things seen in the east within the light of Lamp-Light Buddha;
why, then, does it speak of the west and so forth? Answer: This commentary merely explains the meaning of *sphaṭika* (crystal) as found in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*;
it is not intended to explain the text of this sutra. However, this is simply the commentator citing another source; it is not [the intent of the sutra].

This refers to our own position. If it were not so, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* would have merely stated that there is ice for a thousand years within a stone chamber, without specifically specifying the Western region.
How, then, could one use the Western region to challenge us? Therefore, we know that this passage is describing that [other] location.
Regarding the statement "this refers to hearing the Dharma," the Sūtra says: "As if within pure lapis lazuli," and so forth.

As for the statement "the Buddha emits light that illuminates itself," this is the commentary by the Master of the Sub-commentary (*Sū*). At the assembly on Vulture Peak, he saw from afar the Buddha attaining enlightenment in a world in the eastern direction;
upon his body, which was the color of purple-polished gold, he further emitted a light that pervaded his entire being, reaching as far as a *zhang*.
The six rays of light from the four sides each extend sixteen feet, converging into this bodily radiance.
Within it, one sees a body of purple-gold hue, like a statue of pure gold seen through a tube of lapis lazuli; it is self-illuminating.
Regarding the statement "or the multitude outshines the Buddha and others," this is the second interpretation.

In the world-system of the east, there are bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, Brahmā kings, and Śakra devānām indra seated around the Buddha; each possesses their own bodily radiance, yet from afar they behold the Buddha, who is the color of purple-polished gold.
The multitude saw him sitting within the light, like a true golden image appearing inside a tube of lapis lazuli.

Regarding the phrase "one verse on diligent precepts," this refers to both diligence (*vīrya*) and the observance of the precepts (*śīla*). The Sūtra says: "There may be certain bhikṣus dwelling in mountain forests," and so forth.
Zhen (Zhenhui) says: "If the pearl remains within the oyster shell, then its life is preserved; if the oyster loses the pearl [it dies]."
At that moment, he immediately perished. A bhikṣu who upholds the precepts is like a pearl-bearing oyster; when he breaks the precepts, he is like a dead oyster. Question:
Why does the commentary state that this clarifies the bodhisattva, while the sūtra speaks of a bhikṣu? Answer: Because the bhikṣu is indeed the bodhisattva.
This is intended to show that those living at home who practice the conduct of a bodhisattva are all likewise able to uphold the precepts.

Regarding the statement that "vigor universally stimulates [the other faculties], such as ethical discipline": Question: Why does vigor come first, while maintaining ethical discipline follows? Answer:
Vigor comes first because it universally stimulates the three types of action (body, speech, and mind). Ethical discipline is the foundation of training; therefore, it follows.

Regarding the statement that "one verse [summarizes] generosity, patience, and so forth": within generosity, there are the three types of giving—material giving, the giving of Dharma, and the giving of fearlessness. As for patience, there are three:
the patience of accepting the profound Dharma, the patience of enduring enmity and harm, and the patience of being at peace with suffering.

Regarding the phrase "reciting the dhyāna-concentrations," the Sūtra says: "Those who deeply enter the various dhyāna-concentrations. Here, "deep entry" refers to the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
Regarding the phrase "reciting one verse of wisdom," it further states: "Seeing that all Bodhisattvas know the mark of the quiescence of phenomena.
Mǔ (Mù) says: "All phenomena are fundamentally without intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); being without intrinsic nature, they are unarisen; being unarisen, they are unceasing; being unceasing..."
This is primordial purity. Purity is itself *svabhāva-nirvāṇa*. As a sutra says: "All phenomena, from the very beginning, are eternally characterized by quiescence."
Regarding the statement "desiring to hear the fulfillment," the Sūtra says: "At that time, the fourfold assembly...
Regarding the phrase "as in the preceding prose section," it is asked: The prose section mentions only twenty billion bodhisattvas and does not mention the fourfold assembly;
why, then, does the preceding [prose] speak of bodhisattvas while the verse speaks of the four assemblies? The answer, as stated in the Commentary, is: "This refers to the four divisions."
Because the assemblies manifest one another: the prose states that there are twenty billion bodhisattvas, which implicitly indicates that the fourfold assembly is also present in the prose;
the verse mentions the fourfold assembly, which implicitly indicates that bodhisattvas are also present in the verse.

Regarding the statement that they were previously based on their initial resolve (*cittotpāda*) and so forth: originally, these were the fourfold assembly (*catasraḥ parṣadaḥ*). Since they had already generated the resolve and engaged in practice during the prose section (*gadya*), they were designated as bodhisattvas.
The verse (*kārikā*), however, refers to their original status and thus mentions only the fourfold assembly.
Regarding the statement that there are four parts to the prose section (*gadya*): first, the lineage of the lamp; second, the reason for preaching this sutra; third, the duration of the time;
and fourth, the well-being of the great assembly.
Regarding the phrase "this refers to the beginning," it describes the causal context for this sutra. The long prose version states:
"At that time, the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa arose from samādhi and, on account of the Dharma Master Varaprabha, preached a Mahāyāna sūtra named the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Now, the verse says: "The Honored One, revered by devas and humans, has just arisen from samādhi," and so forth. [This] asks: when Candrasūryapradīpa preached the *Lotus Sūtra*,...
The *Sūtra* states that after the World-Honored One had offered praise, he caused *Prabhāketu* to rejoice; Śākyamuni preached the *Lotus Sūtra*, and Mañjuśrī was the witness.
If this is so, since Dīpaṃkara praised *Prabhāketu* and Śākyamuni [praised him], why did [Śākyamuni] not praise Mañjuśrī?
Answer: When Mañjuśrī had finished realizing the sutra, he departed for the palace of the Sāgara Dragon King in the eastern ocean and was no longer present at the assembly;
therefore, he did not offer praise. Because Prabhāketu remained at the assembly, he praised it. Question: For what reason did Śākyamuni preach this sutra?
Śāriputra was censured for his lack of faith, whereas the bodhisattva created by Dīpaṃkara was praised because of his sharp faculties. Question:
While those seen within the light were not moved even by the eight winds [of worldly fortune], why did the Dharma Master Miaoguang feel joy upon receiving the Buddha’s praise? Answer:
He manifested this appearance of joy; yet Miaoguang was likewise free from the eight winds.
Regarding the statement that [the teaching] can lead sentient beings to Bodhi and so forth: Question: What is called the "Eye of the World"? Answer: The sun and moon bear witness;

the eight sons of the Buddha were all disciples of Prabhāsa (Wonderful Light). Through Prabhāsa’s instruction and transformation, they were made to remain firm in their pursuit of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
It gives rise to the wisdom of sentient beings.
Regarding the length of the time period, the *Dīrgha Āgama* states: "For sixty minor kalpas he did not rise from his seat;

those in the assembly who were listening also remained seated in one place for sixty minor kalpas, their bodies and minds unmoving as they listened to what the Buddha taught, as if it were the duration of a single meal."
Recently, in this current two-line exposition of the sutra, it says: "The World-Honored One, having already praised [them], etc.
This is an attempt to exhort one's practice. Question: Why is there an exhortation to diligence alone? Answer: Because, among all practices, diligence is now established as the foremost;
it is able to universally stimulate all practices of the three karmas. Therefore, it is exhorted first. All supramundane states arise from diligence.
Regarding the statement that "the world is empty and void," one asks: why is there such grief and distress?
The answer, as stated in the Commentary, is that this first verse encourages one not to give rise to sorrow because "the world is empty and void. The Sūtra says:

"The Holy Lord, the King of Dharma, comforts immeasurable multitudes," because there is a refuge to rely upon in the future. Furthermore, while manifesting entry into extinction, he is in reality eternal, blissful, and self-sovereign.
Because of my own purity, and because the benefit of all Buddhas is identical, we together benefit sentient beings.
Regarding this bestowal of prophecy, the long prose section states: "He addressed the bhikṣus:
'This Bodhisattva Guṇakara will next become a Buddha, named Śuddhakāya Tathāgata. Now, in this verse of the sutra, this Bodhisattva Guṇakara, in the absence of...

Regarding the "true nature" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of the outflows: because the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) state of the untainted (*anāsrava*) is eternally abiding, and because the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) state of the untainted is free from inversion, it is called the true nature. Within this principle, the bodhisattva attains complete penetration.

Regarding the statement that the first verse manifests the entry into *nirvāṇa* and so forth: the prose commentary (*dīrghapaṅkti*) of the sutra states, "After the Buddha had given the prophecy, he entered *nirupadhiśeṣanirvāṇa* during the middle watch of the night.
Now, as for the phrase in the verse, "The Buddha attained parinirvāṇa this very night; like fire when the fuel is exhausted," "fuel" (*kāṣṭha*) refers to firewood.

The commentary to the *Yueling* (Monthly Ordinances) says: "That which is large enough to be broken is called 'fuel' (*xín*); that which is small enough to be tied into a bundle is called 'firewood' (*cǎo*)."
It is said: "The burning of wood. Mochizuki [Mō] says: The wood is like sentient beings who are capable of being moved; the fire is like the Tathāgata’s wisdom-body that responds to them.
When the conditions of sentient beings are exhausted, they are like the absence of wood; when the Buddha’s wisdom ceases, it is likewise like the extinguishing of the fire.

Alternatively, "wood" is a metaphor for the roots of goodness of all sentient beings, and "fire" is a metaphor for the Buddha. If there is a stimulus from sentient beings, the Buddha does not [cease].

Nirvana. If there are no sentient beings with roots of goodness, the Buddha enters nirvana. The Tathāgata appears in the world fundamentally for the purpose of teaching and transforming sentient beings;
once all sentient beings have been delivered, the Tathāgata enters nirvana.
Regarding the statement that the final verse reveals the loss of the excellent physician and so forth: the Sūtra says, "Bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, their number like the sands of the Ganges.
In the parable of the physician, the Sūtra states: "At that time, the sons heard of their father’s death and were deeply distressed in heart. They thought to themselves:
'If our father were still alive, he would have compassion for us and been able to protect and save us. Now, however...'"
He abandoned me and died far away in another land. Thinking of myself as orphaned and exposed, with no one left to rely upon, I was constantly filled with sorrow. My mind then became awakened;
I realized that this medicine possessed a beautiful color, fragrance, and flavor, so I immediately took it and consumed it, whereby my toxic illness was entirely cured.

Regarding the phrase "the second [group], the virtuous and firm," the Sūtra says: "These eight princes, transformed by Prabhāsa, have become firm in the unsurpassed Way; they shall behold countless Buddhas."
Regarding the statement "if one relies on the Hīnayāna, it refers to the three [Buddhas]": within the sūtra text, there are the words "innumerable Buddhas.
To explain the origin of these innumerable Buddhas, coming from the end toward the beginning is called "reversal" (*pratīpa*).

As for "Vipaśyin," this refers to the Buddha encountered at the beginning of the first eon of marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana-kalpa*). "Dīpaṃkara" refers to the Buddha encountered at the beginning of the third eon, corresponding to the eighth, ninth, or tenth stage (*bhūmi*).
Śākyamuni was first encountered at the beginning of the first great asaṃkhyeya kalpa prior to the stages [of the bodhisattva path].
In the past, when Śākyamuni was a potter, he encountered the ancient Śākyamuni. From the perspective of the Mahāyāna, this counts from cause toward fruit;
from the perspective of the Hīnayāna, it counts from fruit toward cause.
Regarding the statement that "in the first kalpa one encounters Śākyamuni and others": at the beginning of the first kalpa, one does not see only the single Buddha Śākyamuni;
rather, one encounters seventy-five thousand other Buddhas as well, and in the presence of each of those Buddhas, one makes offerings, pays respect, and practices all the various spiritual paths.

In the past, Śākyamuni was a potter. He encountered a Buddha named Śākyamuni Buddha, along with two disciples named Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, and an attendant disciple named Kāśyapa Ānanda. Having seen them, the potter...
He then made a vow: "May I attain Buddhahood exactly as this Śākyamuni has; may my disciples all be the same.

From that point on, he practiced the path until his causes were perfected and his fruit was fulfilled, whereby he attained Buddhahood and was likewise named Śākyamuni. This continued until the end of the third *kalpa*, at the beginning of the hundredth *kalpa*, when he encountered a Buddha named Vipaśyin.
This was the *Kalpa of Physical Marks and Excellences* (*lakṣaṇavyañjanakalpa*), during which he encountered only this one Buddha’s teaching and transformation before—

One attains Buddhahood. Regarding the "hundred kalpas of cultivating the marks and signs," according to the Mahāyāna, one cultivates the marks and signs for a thousand kalpas and studies majestic deportment for ten thousand kalpas.
Regarding the phrase "standing on tiptoe in praise," according to the third chapter of the *Buddhacarita*, the "Chapter on the Arousing of the Mind and Making Offerings," it says:
"I recall that in the past there was a Tathāgata who appeared in the world named Puṣya.

At that time, the Buddha had two disciples who diligently practiced the holy life (*brahmacarya*): one was named Śākya and the other was named Maitreya. At that time, that Buddha observed his two disciples..."
Before and after the Son attained Buddhahood, he beheld that Maitreya would attain Buddhahood first and Śākyamuni afterwards.

[He saw that] the disciples and sentient beings to be converted by Śākyamuni had their faculties ripened earlier. The Tathāgata then reflected: "How can I cause those whose faculties have ripened to meet with him?"
It is easy when it concerns a single person whose faculties are mature, but difficult when it concerns many. He then said to Śākyamuni, "I wish to travel to the mountains;
you may follow me. On the way, he instructed Śākyamuni to take up his *niṣīdana*.

At that time, the other Buddha arrived at the mountain first and sat within a lapis lazuli cave, entering the fire-element concentration (*tejodhātu-samādhi*). When Śākyamuni saw this, joy arose in his heart, and he joined his ten fingers in homage.
With palms joined and standing on one foot, he praised that Buddha: "In the heavens above and the earth below, there is none like the Buddha;

throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there is no equal. Having seen all that exists within the world, I find that none at all can compare with the Buddha. (The new translation reads as follows:)

"In this world, throughout the heavens, the earth, the abode of the learned (Śakrāvatāra), the celestial palaces, and the ten directions—nowhere is there a peer to this Great Śramaṇa, the Bull among Men, who has searched the lands, mountains, and forests.
That Buddha then gave a prophecy: 'In a future age, after ninety-four kalpas have passed...'"
He shall attain Buddhahood and be named Śākyamuni. According to the *Buddhapiṭaka-sūtra*, Maitreya first resolved his mind [for enlightenment] forty kalpas before Śākyamuni did so.
If this is so, how is it that Śākyamuni attained Buddhahood first? The answer is:

because Śākyamuni was courageous and vigorous, he surpassed Maitreya by forty kalpas and thus attained Buddhahood first. It is said that he praised the Buddha Tiṣya and thereby surpassed him by nine kalpas.
Therefore, a sutra states: "It is often said that ninety-one kalpas ago, there was the Buddha Vipaśyin.

As a youth of the Snow Mountains, he sacrificed his body to seek half a verse and thereby transcended twelve kalpas. As Prince Sattva, he sacrificed his body to a starving tigress and thereby transcended eleven kalpas.
As the Good Rishi, he spread his hair over the mud and thereby transcended eight kalpas. Thus, on three occasions, he collectively transcended [kalpas]."
Forty *kalpas*. Furthermore, by applying this principle, the periods of time thus bypassed are not limited solely to those within the hundred *kalpas*.
While the praise of the Buddha Tiṣya for bypassing nine *kalpas* certainly occurred within the hundred *kalpas*, the remaining [bypasses] must fall within the three *kalpas*.

The act of spreading one's hair to cover the mire occurs at the completion of the second *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*; as for the remaining two stages, they may pertain to all three *kalpas*, yet one must still undergo the removal of suffering. (7)
Prior to the [Bhūmi] stages, at that time, one was still unable to relinquish body and life.
Regarding the statement, "If one relies on the Mahāyāna, it is based on the Bodhisattvas and others," Master Yin said:

"The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* contains sixteen sections of meaning from beginning to end, which definitively establish the heterodox and the orthodox, just as a worldly scale has sixteen *liang* to definitively determine weight."
Nothing is omitted. He said: "There are eight [teachings] prior to the ground, and eight on the ground. First, regarding the eight prior to the ground:

for the sake of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), he teaches the Four Truths—suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self—to counteract the attachment to the body as being permanent, blissful, self, and pure.

Furthermore, to counteract the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), he teaches Prajñā to eliminate the inversion of grasping at a self. For the sake of those who have abandoned all hope (*icchantika*), he teaches faith to eliminate the inversion of lack of faith."

For the Śrāvakas, he teaches Great Wisdom (*mahājñāna*) to eliminate attachment and remove obstacles to meditative concentration (*samādhi*). For the Pratyekabuddhas, he teaches Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) to remove the obstacle of seeking personal quiescence.

This is termed "prior to the stages" (*bhūmi-pūrva*). Regarding the "eight on the eight stages above": upon entering the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), one is freed from death by fragmentation (*vibhava-maraṇa*) and afflictions (*kleśa*), and through partial realization of True Suchness (*tathatā*), one attains permanence, bliss, self, and purity. These four qualities constitute the eight [aspects] on the stages. This refers to the stages above the ground.
The preceding establishes the meaning of the sixteen divisions.

As for the statement that "in ancient times it was assigned to the tenth stage and so forth," this refers to the fourth reliance upon Bodhisattvas, who made offerings to Buddhas as numerous as eight *gaṅgā* rivers.

The intent of the Commentary (*Śāstra*) is to assign [this stage] to the fourth reliance (*āśraya*), which occurs during the kalpa of the primary marks and secondary signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*). Ancient masters assigned it to the tenth stage (*bhūmi*);

therefore, it is said that this is also not yet fixed. Citing the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha, it is held that within the fourth reliance, its placement during the kalpa of the primary marks and secondary signs is correct.
Regarding the statement by Tripitaka Master Paramārtha that "the first kalpa," etc., refers to the assignment of stages (*viniyoga*), there are two interpretations.

The first says: the period prior to the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) is the first reliance; the first, second, and third grounds (*bhūmi*) are the second reliance; the fourth, fifth, and sixth grounds are the third reliance;
and the final four grounds are the fourth reliance. The second says: the period prior to the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrva*) is the first kalpa...
The first reliance (*āśraya*) extends from the first stage (*bhūmi*) to the seventh stage; the eighth, ninth, and tenth stages constitute the second reliance;

and the eon of marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) constitutes the fourth reliance (the upper [first] corresponds to twenty, and the second corresponds to six *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka*). Furthermore, another teaching states: in the first reliance, a bodhisattva makes offerings to five *gaṅgā* Buddhas;
in the second reliance, to six *gaṅgā* Buddhas (merely adding one to the previous five); and in the third reliance, he makes offerings...
Regarding the seven rivers: simply add two to the five above. Regarding the fourth [stage], it relies on the offering of eight rivers; simply add three to the five above.

This accords with the commentary’s statement that "one shall see countless Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of eight Ganges Rivers. If one were to calculate based on the sands of twenty-six rivers, [the number would be even greater].
The principle is also different. If the Eight Princes were bodhisattvas of the eighth stage or above, they would attain Buddhahood by further making offerings at eight rivers;

this is called "seeing countless Buddhas. If they were bodhisattvas of the first stage, they would attain Buddhahood by further making offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of twenty-one Ganges Rivers; this is called "seeing countless Buddhas."

Regarding the statement that one "attains entry" and so forth: this is because it cites the understanding of the True Dharma (satyadharma). It is clearly understood that during the third kalpa, there are seven *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas of Buddhas;

thus, the eighth *asaṃkhyeya* kalpa refers to the kalpa of the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*). For this reason, one attains entry into the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), and it is therefore said that one shall see innumerable Buddhas.
Regarding the phrase "this is the first": one verse commemorates the eight princes. The prose commentary states that the last among them to attain Buddhahood was named Dīpaṃkara (Dīpananda).
As for the verse’s expression "God among Gods" (*devātideva*): among all classes of sentient beings, gods are the most supreme;
yet the Buddha is honored by all gods and is more exalted than the gods. Therefore, the Tathāgata is called "God among Gods."
Regarding the statement "possessing the six faults," this refers to the six lines of the sūtra beginning with "the mind constantly harbors indolence," which constitute the six faults.
Regarding the phrase "second, attachment to gain and so forth," this means not relinquishing gain and fame already obtained, and further seeking them when they have not yet been obtained.
The fifth [cause of failure] is failing to practice what one has learned. The sixth is forgetting what has already been recited. Regarding the term "clan" (*jù*):
it refers to a category or class. As for "equal" (*děng*): four *lǐ* (neighborhoods) constitute a clan; a *lǐ* is equivalent to a *lì* (village).
Five households form a neighborhood (*líng*), and five neighborhoods form a *lì*. Twenty-five households constitute one *lǐ*, and four *lǐ* amount to one hundred households.
Regarding the statement that "there are two kinds of causes for purification," the prose section of the sutra says:

"Because this person has also planted various roots of goodness as a causal condition, they encounter immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas, making offerings to them, honoring them, respecting them, and praising them."
Now, the verse says: "Also practicing various wholesome deeds," and so forth.
Regarding the two fruits: attaining Buddhahood and being named Maitreya is the fruit of self-benefit; extensively delivering all sentient beings is the fruit of benefiting others.

It is also the fruit of benefiting others. The fruits belonging to the category of pure causes are called the two types of pure fruits. Question: Since these two fruits exist in the future, how can they be called "recollection"?
Answer: Mañjuśrī’s recollection allows him to perceive the future; what fault is there in calling this "recollection"?
Regarding the phrase "this refers to the beginning": the first verse refers to the person. The prose section of the sutra states: "Maitreya, you should know:
was that Bodhisattva Wonderful Light at that time anyone else? It was my own self. The Bodhisattva Seeking Fame was none other than you.
Now, the verse says: "After that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa," and so forth.
Regarding the statement "this is precisely the Dharma," the prose section of the sutra says: "Now, seeing this auspicious sign, it is no different from before;
therefore, I reflect that today the Tathāgata shall preach a Mahāyāna sūtra named 'The Sublime' (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*). The present verse says: "I see the Buddha Dīpaṃkara... and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "this constitutes the formation [of the seal]," the Sūtra states: "Now, the signs are as they were in the original auspicious omens. The falling of flowers and the shaking of the earth are what are called the original auspicious omens.

As for the meaning of the *dharmatā* (true reality): the principle and wisdom (*prajñā*) of the One Vehicle constitute the *dharmatā*, while the emission of light and the shaking of the earth serve as its supportive manifestations.

Regarding the phrase "the rain causes the sprouts of the path to grow" and so forth: just as there are, in brief, four kinds of rain in the world—first, the wind that stabilizes, because it removes the wind of wrong views;
second, the settling of dust, because it removes the dust of afflictions and karma; third, the nourishing of sprouts, because it causes the superior mind to arise;
and fourth, the increase of all seedlings, because it causes the superior dharmas to flourish—the intent here refers to what the Buddha taught in the *Upāya-paryāya* (Chapter on Expedient Means).
The One Vehicle is called the "Rain of Dharma. Śāriputra’s turning of his mind and ripening of his faculties is called the "Sprout of Wisdom.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva asks Maitreya Bodhisattva with the underlying intent that the Tathāgata wishes to resolve the doubts of Śāriputra and others within the "Expedient Means" chapter.
To preach the One Vehicle is called the "Rain of Dharma. Within the gateway of the first stage of the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena, it causes the sprouts of bodhi-wisdom to grow.
*The Essential Compendium of the Profound Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra*, Fascicle 14.
In the winter of the sixth year of the Qiánfú era, the bhikṣu Hóngjǔ of Kāiyuán Monastery in Wènzhōu lectured on the *Mahākaruṇāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and transcribed this copy for veneration.
It was completed on the twenty-second day of the first month in the third year of the Gen’yu era, the Bingyín year.
This is solely for the purpose of causing the Buddha-dharma to flourish and bringing benefit and happiness to sentient beings.
[Compiled by] the Jing-shui Śramaṇa Xi-fu (born at age fifty-eight), *The Essential Compendium of the Profound Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra*, Scroll Fifteen. Compiled by Xi-fu.

Regarding the statement that the "Expedient Means" chapter (*Upāya-paryāya*) is brief: the sūtra is divided into three sections. Now, within the main body of the text, eight chapters are explained in three cycles.

Herein, the "Expedient Means" chapter represents the Dharma-exposition (*dharma-deśanā*). This chapter shall be analyzed according to three headings: first, the purpose; second, the explanation of the title.

Third, the exposition of the essential nature (*svabhāva*). Among the twenty-eight chapters, only this chapter contains no [explicit] explanation of obstacles; it possesses a section for the exposition of the essential nature. Regarding the three reasons for its inclusion, they are:

first, the eight preceding chapters as the reason for its inclusion; second, the twenty-ninth chapter as the reason for its inclusion; and third, the proponents of the *Śāstra* (the treatise) as the reason for its inclusion.
Furthermore, within the eight chapters, the first three parts serve as the reason for its inclusion: the introductory section (*nidāna*) and the main body (*samyak-artha*).
[The text] has been transmitted. Now, the explanation of the introductory section (*nidāna*) is complete. Next, the main body (*saddharma*) is elucidated.

Within the main body, the "Expedient Means" chapter (*upāya-paṭala*) comes first; therefore, it follows the introductory section. This is the first reason for its inclusion: it follows the preceding introductory section.
Second, the eight chapters of the main body constitute the reason for its inclusion. Since this chapter is the very first among those eight, there is thus the "Expedient Means" chapter.
Come. Within the third section consisting of eight chapters, there are three cycles of exposition. Now follows the first cycle, the Exposition of the Dharma (*dharmadeśanā*).

Since this Exposition of the Dharma is the very beginning, it follows the "Introductory Chapter" (*nidāna-parivarta*) and precedes the "Chapter on Expedient Means" (*upāya-kauśalya-parivarta*). (This concludes the general topical outline.)

Regarding the statement that "the one" takes the eight chapters as the main body of the teaching: this means that the eight chapters are designated as the main body in order to distinguish them from the nineteen chapters, which are not taken as the main body;
thus, the character "an" (安) is used here.

Regarding the statement that "the lotus flower emerges from water" and so forth, this refers to the essential substance (*tattva*). Now, we intend to take the main body of the teaching (*samyak-artha*) as the underlying purpose (*āgama-arthatā*).

There are two versions of the main body: one consisting of eight chapters and another consisting of nineteen chapters. We shall first determine the boundaries of the eight-chapter version as the main body, and subsequently explain its underlying purpose.
Question: Why does the Master of the Commentary (*śāstrakāra*) specifically select the eight chapters as the underlying purpose?
[Question: Is it so? [Answer: According to the *Fahua lun* (Treatise on the Lotus Sūtra) and the eight chapters of the *Lotus Sūtra*, these constitute the purpose for the coming [of the teaching];
thus, they are superior to the nineteen chapters. The Master of the Commentary (*shuzhu*) says: "Now, in discussing the meaning [of a sūtra], one first examines the title.

Since the title speaks of the 'Wonderful Dharma Lotus Flower' (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*), one must take the 'lotus flower' as the primary teaching (*zhengzong*). A lotus flower has the meaning of blooming and emerging from the water; it signifies abandoning the provisional and adopting the real, and destroying duality."
The two assemblies occur only within the eight chapters; beyond these eight chapters, there is no other place where they are taught.

One might intend to take the subsequent eight chapters as the "True Teaching" (zhengzong). Therefore, the reason for first explaining the "Lotus" here is that wherever the Lotus exists, that is precisely the True Teaching.
Question: Regarding the explanation of the intent behind the "Expedient Means" chapter here, why is it necessary to speak of the True Teaching? Answer:
Regarding the division into eight chapters as the "Main Body" (zhengzong): this intends to clarify that immediately following the Introductory Chapter (xupin), the Main Body is expounded.
Within the Main Body, the "Expedient Means" chapter (fangbianpin) should logically be discussed first; therefore, we deliberate upon it here at the outset.

This statement is made because one intends to explain the three fruits and the single cause through the sequence of "opening," "showing," "awakening," and "entering. A lotus flower possesses two virtues: emerging from the water and blooming; since—

It possesses the quality of emerging from water and blossoming; thus it serves as a metaphor for the two capacities of the Sublime Dharma (*saddharma*): bearing excellent fruit and having lofty conduct.

Bearing excellent fruit is analogous to emerging from the water, while lofty conduct is comparable to blossoming. This refers to the causal practice of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), which proceeds directly from the lower stages up to the supreme fruit of Buddhahood;
hence it is called "lofty conduct. The *bodhi* of the Buddha-fruit is exceedingly high, vast, profound, and far-reaching.
This practice of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) can directly attain the fruit of Buddhahood. Its height transcends the three realms;
its breadth pervades the ten directions; its depth is immeasurable; and its distance is long and difficult to reach.

Thus, although the fruit of Buddhahood is high, broad, and profoundly deep, there is nothing that can reach it or attain it, except for the causal practice of the One Vehicle, which alone can attain this height, breadth, and depth.
To be far removed from the fruit of Buddhahood and Bodhi is called *xíng sǒng* (行竦), which carries the meaning of "blooming" (*kaifū*).

Therefore, the eighth chapter extensively clarifies the meaning of the practice and its fruit as emerging from the water and blooming. Thus, the eighth chapter is titled the "True Main Body of the One Vehicle.

The *Guóyǔ* states: "Sǒng means 'good' and 'to restrain evil. The *Guǎngyǎ* states: "Sǒng means 'reverence,' referring to being lofty and superior. This implies that through practice one is able to honor what is good and ascend to the heights.

One ascends to attain the fruit of Buddhahood; therefore, it is said that "the practice is lofty" (*xíng sǒng*). Some versions use the character *shū* (sparse) instead, which accords with the meaning of the lotus flower blooming.

This does not preclude [the interpretation based on the treatise regarding] the meaning of blooming and emerging from the water. Question: Why are the teachings and principles not taken as the lotus flower, but only the excellence of the fruit and the loftiness of the practice—this "practice-fruit lotus flower"—are mentioned?
Answer: If one discusses the essence of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), there is no impediment to taking both the teachings and the principles together.
If one discusses the meaning of "Lotus" (Padma), from the perspective of practice and fruition it is superior, whereas from the perspective of doctrine and principle it is inferior.

If one takes doctrine and principle as constituting the "Lotus," then since doctrine and principle were already explained at the beginning of the first week’s *Upāya-parivarta*, it could be named "Lotus";

however, if that were the case, the second and third weeks—which speak only of practice and fruition—would not be the "Lotus. Furthermore, the three stages of opening, showing, and awakening in the first week are the fruition; [the entry into the Buddha's knowledge...]
The vision is this practice; the second circuit of the ox-cart is this practice; the third circuit to the place of treasure is the fruit.

Thus we know that the lotus primarily takes up both practice and fruit; hence it is said that "practice is to be uplifted. To be uplifted means to cease evil and apply oneself to good, to advance. Some say:
"Loose" (*śū*) refers to the loose branches and stalks supporting [the flower]; it is through these loose branches that the fruit is obtained. Bian states: "Loose" means to open.
Because the practice (*caryā*) is able to open the fruit, it is metaphorically called the "blooming practice. If the fruit blooms, it immediately emerges from the water.

Just as in the world there has never been a fruit that does not arise from a flower, nor a flower that does not bring forth fruit, if this flower does not exist, then it is simply non-existent; but once it exists...

Thus, both flower and fruit are contained within; this is discussed in the context of the Dharma. If this practice does not exist, then that is that; but if it exists, it will inevitably bring about the fruit of Buddhahood.

There has never been a practice that does not bring forth its fruit, nor has there ever been a fruit that does not arise from a cause. The commentary states that the fruit of Buddhahood cannot be accomplished in vain;

it is only through karmic practice that it is attained. The character *sǒng* (to stand upright/erect) has a basis for its usage here, whereas the character *shū* (sparse/thin) does not accord with the meaning of "opening and blooming" (*kāifú*).
(Taking both is superior).
Regarding the phrase "furthermore, in the sutra... and so forth: in this present sutra, only one vehicle is taught, thereby excluding the two vehicles.
Regarding the statement, "Therefore, by refuting duality and reconciling the two vehicles," the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) is the primary teaching (*samyak-artha*).

Since this sutra takes the refutation of duality and the reconciliation of the two vehicles as its primary teaching, and there is no place outside of these eight chapters where such refutation and reconciliation occur, only these eight chapters are taken as the primary teaching.
Forty years ago, [beings] clung to the two vehicles as supreme; the World-Honored One refuted this, saying:
Within the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the Single Vehicle; there is neither a second nor a third. The second week states:
"It is like that elder who first used three carts to entice his children, and afterwards gave them only the great carts. The third week states:
"The great city mentioned previously was created by me as an emanation," thereby knowing that the city grasped is provisional, and [knowing] the mind that grasps it.

It is also "destroyed," hence it is called "the destruction of the two. "Reconciling the two" means that forty years prior, within the path of the One Vehicle, he provisionally taught three [vehicles].
He reconciled the provisional to enter the real, and reconciled the two to return to the one; this is the primary theme of the *Lotus Sūtra*.
"Theme" refers to the central doctrine (according to the topical outline of the commentary, the eight chapters constitute the "central theme").

Regarding the phrase "therefore, it is taught in three cycles," the intended meaning is as follows: based on the treatise and according to the classification of the sūtra, this is taught in three cycles within the eight chapters.
"Cycle" (*zhou*) means complete or sufficient; because all four parts are fully complete, it is called a cycle. The three cycles are:

the teaching by way of the Dharma, the teaching by way of parables, and the teaching by way of past causal conditions. Regarding the character "to" (*dou*), the dictionary states it means to linger or delay. [This refers to] the teaching.
The character "wen" (文) means "superior. In the local dialect, it means "to dwell. Some say that "dòu" (逗) means "to unravel" or "to explain"; this interpretation is excellent.

It refers to changing the minds of those who cling to the Two Vehicles and causing them to return to the stage of the One Vehicle. Regarding the three cycles of teaching for the three types of faculties:

first, when the World-Honored One spoke in terms of the Dharma, he intended for all the śrāvakas to understand it collectively; yet by the time he finished speaking, only the son of the Vulture Peak (Śāriputra) understood. Taking...
It is said that the World-Honored One spoke solely for the sake of Śāriputra alone, while the remaining five hundred, one thousand, and two hundred people did not understand at all.
It was impossible to explain the Dharma further through abstract teaching, so he consequently employed a parable. When it came to the explanation by way of a parable, only four people understood;

it seemed as though the parable were intended specifically for those four. These four of middle capacity attained faith and understanding, and thus the Buddha preached the Parable of the Medicinal Herbs.
In the *Parīndanā-parivarta* (Chapter on Entrustment), the Buddha reiterates and confirms [the teaching]. In the *Vyākaraṇa-parivarta* (Chapter on Prophecy), he bestows prophecies upon them.

As for the remaining twelve thousand two hundred people of duller faculties, they did not understand when they heard the discourse on the Dharma, nor did they understand when they heard the discourse through parables; thus, they could not escape the karmic conditions of their past lives.

Therefore, the events of their past connections were recounted, serving as the beginning of the third cycle of forming karmic connections through which they finally attained awakening and understanding. Furthermore, regarding the principle of cause and effect in the first cycle:
The wisdom of both is taught [in the first cycle]. The second cycle specifically teaches the wisdom of causes; the third cycle specifically teaches the principle within the fruit.
Therefore, these are called the "three cycles of teaching," intended to accommodate those of the three faculties.

Regarding the statement that this chapter first expounds the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) and so forth: Question: Among the three cycles of teaching comprising eight chapters, why was the "Expedient Means" (*upāyakauśalya*) chapter spoken first, rather than the other chapters?
Answer: The commentary states that the beginning of this chapter expounds the One Vehicle for the sake of Śāriputra.
Having first arisen from meditative concentration (*samādhi*), he proclaimed two profound [teachings]. The Sūtra says: "At that time, the World-Honored One, having peacefully emerged from samādhi..."
[The Buddha] rose and addressed Śāriputra: "The wisdom of all Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable; the gateway to that wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to enter.
Next, there are three instances of Śāriputra’s request. First, he requests because of his narrow-minded doubts regarding himself and others. As the sutra says: "Since the distant past, I..."
"I have never before heard such a teaching from the Buddha. Next, he requested that the great assembly plant the seeds of causality, for the Sūtra says:
"At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying: 'World-Honored One, we only pray that you will speak of this; we only pray that you will speak of this. Why is this?
Because there are in this assembly countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of asaṃkhyeya persons who, having been transformed, are now capable of hearing it.'"
Please [note that] the Sūtra says: "In this assembly today, there are thousands of myriads of koṭis of those like us.

The Tathāgata made three pauses. The first was the pause praising what is rare; the Sūtra says: "Śāriputra, to speak in brief, the Buddha has fully accomplished immeasurable, boundless, and unprecedented dharmas.
The Śāstra says: "The first pause serves as a sign, causing the true noble ones to inquire about and grasp the One Vehicle."
First, it was to cause those who falsely claim to be noble ones to withdraw from their seats. Second, it was to prevent the assembly from being startled;

as the Sūtra says: "At that time, the Buddha said to Śāriputra: 'Stop, stop! There is no need to speak further. If this matter were to be spoken, all the devas and humans in the world would be struck with alarm and doubt.
Third, it was to prevent them from falling into a great pit; as the Sūtra says: "The Buddha again stopped him, saying: 'Śāriputra, if...'"
When this matter is spoken, all the world—including devas, humans, and asuras—will be struck with wonder and doubt.

This third [section] opens up this true reality (*dharmatā*) and reveals the gate of skillful means (*upāya*). It is divided into two parts: first, the bestowing of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), because it permits the gathering and guidance [of beings]; second, the granting of the prediction, which is the actual formal proclamation.
These six sections of text cause that which was not heard to be heard. Śāriputra, such a wondrous Dharma belongs to the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas.
At that time, he spoke of it. Second, he spoke of how Śāriputra [had realized] that the intent of the Buddhas’ teaching of the Dharma according to what is appropriate is difficult to understand.

Third, regarding which meaning: that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, act solely for the sake of the one great cause and condition (*ekamahākaruṇāhetupratyaya*), and so forth. Fourth, causing them to abide [in this].
The Sūtra says: "Śāriputra, it is solely by means of the One Buddha Vehicle that the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma for sentient beings," and so forth.
Five: The Reliance on the Sūtras. The Sūtra says: "The Buddhas of the past, through immeasurable and innumerable skillful means of various kinds," and so forth. Six: Prohibitions.
The Sūtra states: "Śāriputra, in the worlds of the ten directions, there is not even the Two Vehicles, let alone three.
Therefore, it is said that at the beginning of this chapter, the One Vehicle and so forth are taught.
Regarding the statement "first, in the Parable Chapter (*Dṛṣṭānta-parivarta*) and so forth," it is divided into two parts. First, the indication that joy arises upon hearing the Dharma:

the Sūtra says, "At that time, Śāriputra leaped for joy and was filled with gladness; he immediately rose, joined his palms, gazed up at the Honored One’s countenance, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'Now, having heard this sound of the Dharma from the World-Honored One, my heart leaps with joy; I have attained what I have never had before. Second, the explanation of that joy.
The reasons for his joy are divided into four parts: First, lamenting over the loss of the Great Dharma. The Sūtra says:

"In the past, I heard such a Dharma from the Buddha and saw various Bodhisattvas and others. Second, sighing upon occupying a minor stage. The Sūtra says: "I have always dwelt alone in mountain forests and beneath trees," and so forth.
Third, rejoicing that his afflictions are now exhausted through hearing [the Dharma]. The Sūtra says: "And now, having heard it from the Buddha..."
Regarding such dharmas as those never before heard or encountered, the four knowledges show that the Son of the Buddha has accomplished the Way.

As the Sūtra says: "Today I finally know that I am truly a Son of the Buddha," etc. (This is the section on "Understanding"). Next, the description of the fulfillment [of the path] is divided into three parts. First, the account of the past encounter; as the Sūtra says:
"At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra: 'I now, among devas and humans... Second, the account of the present meeting; as the Sūtra says: "By me..."
Through skillful means, I have led you so that you might be born within my Dharma; later, I shall manifest [the truth] to cause you to rely on the provisional to grasp the real. As the Sūtra says:
"I now wish to cause you to recollect your original vow," and so forth (as established above). Fourth, the section on bestowing the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) has two parts.
First, the prediction based on causes. The Sūtra says: "Śāriputra, in a future age, after passing through immeasurable and boundless..."
For inconceivable eons, he made offerings to several tens of billions of buddhas. Subsequently, he was granted the prediction of his attainment of fruition. The Sūtra states:
"He shall become a buddha named Padmaprabha."

Regarding the phrase "and so forth," the Sūtra states: "In the past, at Vārāṇasī, I turned the wheel of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, analyzing and explaining the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates, and so on (the first cycle was completed)."
Regarding the request made by Śāriputra in the "Parable Chapter," the sutra states: At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I now no longer have any doubt or regret;
in the presence of the Buddha, I have personally received the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi...
(and so forth). At that time, the Buddha told Śāriputra, "Did I not previously say that all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, by means of various..."

"Śāriputra, regarding these various causes and conditions, I shall now further clarify this meaning by means of a parable (etc.). Next, the section on the formal exposition of the parables is divided into two parts:
first, the parable of the past expedient means; second, the parable of the present reality. Regarding the four aspects of the past expedient means:

first, the parable of the Buddha’s existence within the three realms. The Sūtra says: 'Śāriputra, it is as if there were an elder who possessed a large house. Second, the perils of the five destinies..."

There is no analogy [to illustrate this]. The Sūtra says: "A great multitude of people... This is the third: the analogy of establishing skillful means. The Sūtra says: "He saw that great fire... This is the fourth:
the analogy of escaping danger by relying on words. The Sūtra says: "At that time, the sons heard what their father had said...

Regarding the subsequent section on the actual realization, there are four parts. First, the sons request the three [vehicles]. The Sūtra says: "Then the sons each addressed their father, saying, 'Father...'"
1. Regarding what was previously promised and so forth: the two fathers gave only one [chariot]. The Sūtra says: "At that time, the elder bestowed upon each of his sons equally one great chariot.
2. Explaining the fulfillment of the father’s intention: the Sūtra says: "At that time, the elder saw that his sons had safely emerged [from the fire].
3. Transcending the sons’ original expectations: the Sūtra says: "At that time, the sons each mounted a great chariot. They attained...
It is unprecedented; it was not what was originally expected (the preceding metaphors clarify this).

Regarding the statement that four individuals of middling faculties attained realization, it is divided into three parts. First, the description of the joy and reverence of these four persons is as stated in the Sūtra:
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti and Mahākāśyapa, having heard from the Buddha this unprecedented teaching—
the World-Honored One’s bestowal of the prophecy of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon Śāriputra— were moved by a sense of rare wonder.

They were filled with joy and exultation. Next, the four leaders among them recounted their situation, saying: "We occupy the foremost positions within the Saṃgha, yet our years are all worn out and advanced.
Subsequently, the four expressed their gratitude, saying: "O World-Honored One, by your great kindness, you have performed this rare and marvelous deed."
Out of compassion, you have taught and transformed us, benefiting us in ways that no one could repay for immeasurable billions of kalpas. (This concludes the understanding.
Regarding the statement that the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" chapter is a reiteration and confirmation, it is divided into three parts. First, the praise and seal of approval:
the Sūtra says, "At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahākāśyapa and the great disciples," and so forth. Second, the section on the reiteration and confirmation.
II. First, the Section on the Exposition of the Dharma, which is divided into four parts: 1. The Buddha’s Appearance in the World. The Sūtra says:
"Kāśyapa, you should know that the Tathāgata is the King of all dharmas; whatever he speaks is never false. 2. The Dharma Benefits Sentient Beings. The Sūtra says:
"Regarding all dharmas, he expounds them through wisdom and skillful means. 3. Differences in Receiving the Path. The Sūtra says: "The Tathāgata..."

One contemplates and knows the ultimate destination of all phenomena. Fourth, [the Bodhisattva] cannot reach it by himself. The Sūtra says: "Furthermore, regarding all phenomena, he has reached their ultimate limit and is thoroughly enlightened.
Next, the section on parables has four parts. First, the parable of the emergence of the Dharma King. The Sūtra says:
"Kāśyapa, it is as if, for example, in a trichiliocosm, there were mountains, rivers, valleys, and the lands where things grow—herbs, trees, and forests."

And the various medicinal herbs. The above constitutes the general metaphor; what follows are the specific metaphors. 1. "Dense clouds spread everywhere" is the metaphor for the appearance of the Three Dharma Kings in the world.
The Sūtra says: "They cover the entire trichiliocosm. 2. "The teaching universally nourishes" is the second metaphor. 3.

"Those who receive the moisture differ" is the third metaphor. The Sūtra says: "At one time, [the rain] falls equally, and its moisture universally permeates the grasses, trees, thickets, forests, and all medicinal herbs."

Section Four: The Parable of the Lack of Self-Awareness. The Sūtra says: "Though they grow from the same earth and are moistened by the same rain, the various grasses and trees each have their own distinctions. Later, it concludes: "I now speak for you of the true reality;
none of the assembly of Śrāvakas has attained final Nirvāṇa," and so forth.
Regarding the statement "he immediately conferred the prediction upon them" and so forth: Mahākāśyapa was named Prabhāsa;
Subhūti was named Nāmanimitta; Kātyāyana was named Jambunadaprabhāsa;
and Maudgalyāyana was named Tamālapatracandanagandha. (The second cycle is concluded.)
Regarding the statement that the "Parable of the Magic City" chapter speaks of past connections with sentient beings and so forth:
the sutra says, "O bhikṣus, when we were śrāmaṇeras, each of us taught and transformed immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

It further states, "Those immeasurable beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges who were taught and transformed at that time—these are you, O bhikṣus, and those who will exist after my parinirvāṇa."

These are the śrāvaka disciples who will appear in future ages. Regarding what was previously stated—that I manifested a great city (the aforementioned "establishing the connection") to benefit those of inferior faculties such as Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra—this is divided into three parts. First, Pūrṇa’s realization through mental reflection. The Sūtra says:
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra heard from the Buddha this teaching of wisdom and skillful means given according to what was appropriate;
he further heard the bestowal of the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon the great disciples (the receipt of the predictions);
he further heard matters concerning causes and conditions from past lives; and he further heard that all Buddhas possess great sovereign supernormal powers (the reception of transformation).
[The city is finished).
Regarding the statement that "the Buddha’s seal of approval was concluded," it is divided into three parts. First, asking the assembly if they see [him]. The Sūtra says:
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, "Do you all see this Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra? Second, praising his present virtues. The Sūtra says:
I have always declared him to be the foremost among those who preach the Dharma. Three times I have extolled his past virtues.
As the Sūtra says: "Do not say, 'Pūrṇa is merely able to protect and assist in proclaiming my Dharma.
He has also, in the presence of ninety billion Buddhas of the past, protected and assisted in proclaiming the true Dharma of the Buddhas."
