Regarding the statement "he immediately conferred [the prediction] upon five hundred others" and so forth: Pūrṇa shall become a Buddha named Dharmaprabhāsa;
Cunda and his five hundred followers shall be named Samantaprabhāsa; and two thousand others shall share the name Ratnākara. (The third cycle is concluded.)

Regarding the statement that "from this point downward there is no further mention of the One Vehicle," this distinguishes [this section] from the main body of the teaching. This concludes the refutation of each individual point;
in the second assembly, the two are established as the essence of the One Vehicle, with both ends corresponding. Thus, we know that the eight chapters constitute the main body of the teaching.
The phrase "Now that the assembly has gathered" and so forth concludes the purpose of returning [to the main topic]. "The assembly has gathered" refers to the fifteen classes of beings.
"Harmony of conditions" means that the Tathāgata is the transformer and the assembly being transformed is also at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa;

because the transformer and the transformed meet on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, it is called the harmony of conditions. Furthermore, it is said: since demonic activities are absent, if even a single person were to act as a demon...
When such events occur, it is not called "harmony. Now that there are no demonic disturbances, it is called "harmony" (the first interpretation is superior).
Regarding the phrase "having completed the awakening," the shaking of the earth, the raining of flowers, the emitting of light, and so forth, are what is meant by "awakening having been completed."

Regarding the phrase "the faculties and the vessel," this does not refer to the physical body meeting with the Buddha; rather, it refers to the maturation of the faculties such that one is fit to hear the *Lotus Sūtra*.
This is called the "congruence of the faculties and the vessel. It means that the faculties and the *Lotus Sūtra* correspond and accord with one another.

Now, one may properly set forth the central theme: namely, the teaching of the One Vehicle of the *Lotus Sūtra*. Since the introductory section (*nidāna*) has already been explained, it is now appropriate to present the main body (*samyak-artha*). This chapter constitutes the main body.
First, it follows the Introductory Chapter (Nidāna-parivarta), and thus the Chapter on Expedient Means (Upāya-kauśalya-parivarta) follows.

Regarding the statement, "The second [division] consists of nineteen chapters and so forth," this is a general classification. From the Chapter on Expedient Means downward, the first twelve chapters clarify the realm (*viṣaya*) of the One Vehicle;

here, the Master of the Commentary (*Sūtra-vyākhyātṛ*), following the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, establishes the three categories of realm, practice (*pratipatti*), and fruit (*phala*). Within this sutra:

The three designations—object (*viṣaya*), practice (*caryā*), and fruit (*phala*)—are merely established by the author of the *ṭīkā*. Among the twelve chapters, those corresponding to the cognizing mind are termed "objects";
two chapters clarify "practice": the "Chapter on Peaceful Abiding" concerns the practice to be performed, while the "Chapter on the Emergence" concerns the person who performs the practice.
There are no separate persons apart from the formations (*saṃskāra*), for it is by grasping the dharmas that a person is constituted; thus, "person" is also called "formations. Regarding the "fruit":

the *Tathāgata-āyus-pramāṇa-parivarta* is the fruit among fruits; the remaining four chapters are fruits within the cause. The *Tathāgata-āyus-pramāṇa-parivarta* is the fruit of ultimate purity, perfection, and clarity;
the *Guṇa-vibhāga-parivarta* is the fruit of partial realization through the noble path as a cause; and the *Anumodanā-guṇa-parivarta* is the fruit of benefit and merit.

"Transcending superior fruits," "the inconceivable fruits through the power of the *Dharmabhāṇaka-guṇa-parivarta* Sūtra," and "the fruits already realized in the past as cited in the *Sadāparibhūta-parivarta*"—these refer to making known the objects of verbal expression and so forth;
this is the interpretation of the Commentator (*Sūzhǔ*). It is also said that this correctly clarifies the intention behind the teaching. Question: Why?
To explain the objective realm (*viṣaya*), the Commentary states: "The explanation of the realm is intended to make known the provisional and the ultimate nature of the vehicles. Question:

How can the two dharmas—the provisional and the ultimate—be called the objective realm of the One Vehicle? Answer: Regarding the teachings, principles, practices, and fruits of the Two Vehicles attained by Śrāvakas during the forty years prior [to the Lotus Sūtra], they did not know them to be provisional;
rather, they clung to them as being final. In contrast to the cognitive mind of the Two Vehicles, these are designated as "provisional."

Regarding the "object" (*viṣaya*): at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, [the Buddha] proclaimed that the profoundness of the *Āgamas*—that is, the wisdom elucidated by the three previous teachings—is exclusively the True Vehicle.
Thus, both the profoundness of the *Āgamas* and the knowledge they elucidate are collectively termed the "real object. Now, speaking to the *śrāvakas*, he says:
"That which you attained forty years ago is provisional and not ultimate. He exhorts them to recognize this as provisional.

Abandoning [the provisional], one knows that which is real is to be grasped. This is why the first eight chapters clearly elucidate the provisional and the real: the first cycle was taught for those of superior faculties.
The Sūtra says, "In the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the One Vehicle," thereby causing them to grasp the real object.

The Sūtra says, "There is neither two nor three," thereby causing them to abandon [the provisional]. The Sūtra says, "Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there is not even the Two Vehicles; how much less..."

Furthermore, there are three stages. In the second stage, the ox-cart is taught for those of middling faculties; this is the actual realm (bhūta-artha) which they are to grasp, while the sheep-cart and deer-cart are provisional realms which they are to relinquish.
As the Sutra says: "It is solely by the power of the Tathāgata’s skillful means that, within the single Buddha-vehicle, he distinguishes and speaks of three.
In the third stage, the treasure place is the actual realm which they are to grasp, while the conjured city is the provisional realm.

[The text] instructs [them] to relinquish it. Regarding the subsequent three categories concerning "praising the excellence of the Dharma" (*dharmasaṃstuti*), "excellence of the Dharma" (*dharmapravaratā*) is itself the praise of the Dharma;

this is because the preceding phrase contains the word "praise" (*saṃstuti*), while the following phrase states "excellence of the Dharma. In the first prose section and the first verse of the "Chapter on the Excellence of the Dharma" (*Dharmaparyāya-praśaṃsā-parivarta*), there is a praise.
Regarding the person: subsequently, one prose section and one verse praise the Dharma. As for the person, the Sūtra states:
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, if there were an evil person who, with a malevolent mind, stood before a Buddha for an entire kalpa constantly reviling and abusing him, his transgression would still be light.
However, if a person were to utter a single evil word to disparage a layperson or a monastic who recites the Lotus Sūtra, that transgression is far more severe."

[This is] important. Furthermore, it says: "If one draws near to a Dharma Master, one will swiftly attain the path of a bodhisattva" (and so forth). Regarding the excellence of the Dharma, the Sūtra states:
"That which has been taught, is being taught, and shall be taught—among these, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is the most difficult to believe and the most difficult to understand.
It further says: "O Bhaiṣajyarāja, I now tell you: among all the sūtras I have preached, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the foremost."
Regarding the exhortation to recruit practitioners: it is asked when the Buddha summoned them to receive their mandate from the "Chapter on the Retainers" (*Dhāraṇī-pāla-parivarta*).

The answer is that the "Chapter on the Jeweled Stupa" (*Ratnakoṭa-parivarta*) states: "Although the Holy Lord, the World-Honored One, has long since entered parinirvāṇa, he still comes for the sake of the Dharma while remaining within the jeweled stupa;

why then do you people not diligently strive for the Dharma? Furthermore, the "Chapter on Devadatta" (*Devadatta-parivarta*) states: "Throughout immeasurable kalpas of the past, I have sought the Dharma."

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "There shall be no weariness or indolence. It further says: "If there are those with profound resolve who believe and revere [the teaching] without giving rise to doubt, they shall not fall into hell," and so forth.
Both chapters constitute exhortations and recruitment. "Exhortation" (*quan*) means to encourage; "recruitment" (*mu*) means to summon and enlist.
Furthermore, in the "Chapter on the Jeweled Stupa," it speaks of exhorting and recruiting by means of a great voice to announce universally to the fourfold assembly:
"Who among you can extensively expound the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in this Sahā world-system? The Buddha wishes to entrust this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to someone.
In the "Chapter on Devadatta," he exhorts and recruits with his own person. The sutra says: "Gathering fruit, drawing water, collecting firewood, and preparing food," and so forth.

Using one’s own body as a bed and seat, the body and mind remain free from weariness. The first two chapters speak of exhorting the body and exhorting the mind; "exhortation" (quàn) here refers to the act of summoning through mental visualization.

Second, it is said that in the "Chapter on the Dharma Master," both the person and the Dharma are praised together; in the "Chapter on the Jeweled Stupa," the Dharma alone is praised; and in the "Chapter on Devadatta," the person alone is praised. Bian states:
in the "Chapter on the Jeweled Stupa," the Dharma is uniquely honored; in the "Chapter on Devadatta," the person is uniquely honored. This constitutes the exhortation.
The exhortation also extends through the three grades. Within these three grades, the "Exhortation" (Quàn-mù) chapter implicitly explains their existence through its meaning.
The "Dharma Master" (Fǎshī) chapter offers a dual praise of both person and Dharma, which likewise serves as an exhortation to those who uphold the sutra.

The "Jeweled Stupa" (Bǎotă) chapter specifically praises the Dharma, while the "Devadatta" (Tiānshòu) chapter specifically praises the person; both are exhortations to those who uphold the sutra. These are collectively termed "exhortations. If...

According to the Buddha’s intent, the exhortation and recruitment apply generally to all three chapters. However, according to various commentaries, the exhortation and recruitment pertain only to the two chapters on the Jeweled Stūpa and Devadatta.
Based on this, the passage where the Śrāvakas receive their mandate to relinquish provisional means and uphold the practice of the true Dharma occurs only in the Chapter on Upholding (Jiechi pin).
Furthermore, the two characters "upholding" (chi) and "practice" (xing) appear only in the final chapter.

Regarding the phrase "subsequently maintaining even a single chapter," etc.: based on this, the śrāvakas receive the mandate to relinquish the provisional and maintain the practice of the true Dharma, while the bodhisattvas receive the mandate to maintain [the provisional].
This means that these twenty thousand bodhisattvas maintain it here in this land, while the four classes of śrāvakas maintain it in other lands;
and the eighty quadrillion nayutas of bodhisattvas maintain it both here and there. (The above is the general summary.)

Regarding the phrase "the first eight chapters, etc.," this refers to the specific classification [of the text] below. The intended meaning is that among the three categories of object, practice, and fruit, these eight chapters likewise classify the provisional and the real according to the exposition of the Dharma, the exposition through parables, and the exposition of past-life causes and conditions. Therefore...

Within the nineteen chapters of the main body (*śarīra*), eight chapters constitute the main body itself; in terms of their underlying principle, these eight chapters are no different from the main body as a whole.
Within these nineteen chapters of the main body, the first is the "Expedient Means" chapter (*upāya-paṛiccheda*); therefore, it follows the "Introduction" chapter (*nidāna-paṛiccheda*).

Furthermore, among the three categories of object (*viṣaya*), practice (*caryā*), and fruit (*phala*), since practice and fruit have not yet been elucidated, the object is explained first. Within this section on the object, there are twelve chapters of the sutra.
The "Expedient Means" (Upāya) Chapter is where the realm of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) is first expounded; therefore, it follows the "Introduction" (Nidāna) Chapter.

Furthermore, among the twelve chapters, the first eight chapters primarily clarify the provisional and the real. Within these, the provisional and the real are first explained through the Dharma-discourse, then through parables, and finally through the account of past causes and conditions.
Thus, the "Introduction" serves to first clarify the provisional and the real as presented in the Dharma-discourse. Therefore, [the "Expedient Means" Chapter] follows.
Following the [previous] chapter, the "Expedient Means" (Upāya) chapter arrives.
Regarding the statement "from here on," the *Śāstra* says that "from here on" refers to the title of the "Expedient Means" chapter.
From this point onward, the general purport of the author of the *Śāstra* is that all subsequent content belongs to the eight chapters of the main body (*samyak-artha*).

This is included within the middle [section]. To provide a general explanation: the treatise states that in the first cycle, the teaching (śāsana), principle (nīti), practice (caryā), and fruit (phala) constitute cause and effect;

in the second cycle, the cause is taught but the fruit is not; and in the third cycle, the fruit is taught but the cause is not. These four dharmas—teaching, principle, practice, and fruit—all possess both cause and effect.

Regarding the statement, "This meaning follows from the preceding Introduction Chapter (*nidāna-parivarta*) and so forth," the commentator briefly explains the term *lakṣaṇa* (characteristic) within the treatise;
there are three masters who provide interpretations, each differing from the others. The first master takes the teaching (*śāsana*) and the principle (*naya*) as cause and effect.

Based on the manifest cause and effect, he explains the essence (*svabhāva*), the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and the mode (*ākāra*). He holds that the expressive teaching is the cause, while the expressed principle is [the effect].

The fruit is that which is expressed by the teachings as conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); the cause consists merely of names and characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*). Within the principle (*tattva*) that is expressed, there is the twofold distinction between the conditioned and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

The principle of logical reasoning (*yukti-tattva*) constitutes the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), while the principle of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-tattva*) constitutes the essential nature (*svabhāva*).
The second master takes the fruit of practice as the essence, characteristics, and marks of cause and effect. Practice is the cause; the fruit is the effect.

Within practice, from the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward, untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) is merely termed a "mark" (*lakṣaṇa*); that which is realized through the ten stages, namely *tathatā*, is the essence and characteristic (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*).
Within the cause, the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) serves as the mark, while the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) within the cause serves as the essence and characteristic. This is the fruit.

The bodhisattva in the middle stage constitutes the characteristic marks (*lakṣaṇa*), while nirvāṇa constitutes the essential nature (*svabhāva*). Therefore, it is called the "characteristic marks of the essential nature of cause and effect.

Specifically, the three stages of opening, showing, awakening, and entering constitute the fruit. "Opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision" simultaneously opens both the wisdom-body (*jñāna-kāya*) and the dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*), encompassing both types.

The general names—essence (tǐ), nature (xiàng), characteristic (xiàngzhuàng)—demonstrate the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*). Specifically clarifying essence and nature leads to awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;

specifically clarifying characteristic and state leads to its realization. According to the third master’s teaching, both practice and action are the cause, while both principle and fruit are the result; therefore, they are termed essence, nature, characteristic, and state.
(This is the commentary by the Master of the Subcommentary [Sūzhǔ] on the Treatise.)

Regarding the phrase "as stated by the One Cloud" and so forth, this is the heading. First, the Teacher of Doctrine and Reasoning (Śāstrārthavādī) explains it as follows: the teaching of the characteristics of cause and effect serves as the cause;
that is, it is the cause for elucidating the principle. Therefore, it is called the "characteristics of cause and effect."
Regarding the statement, "Speech is like a door for entering [the truth]," etc.: Question: How can the teaching that expresses [the truth] be called a "door"? Answer: The commentary states:

"Just as a door is the means by which one enters a room," this explains the meaning of a "door. The teaching is the locus through which the principle is revealed; it is the sense of being the cause for what is to be understood.

There is no principle that is not expressed by the teaching, just as there is no person who exits a house without passing through the door. This clarifies that [the teaching] is not the direct [object].

Regarding cause and effect: when speaking of the place where the principle is revealed, the principle thus revealed consists precisely of the teaching through dharmas and the teaching through similes.
As for the statement that "the lotus merely speaks," etc., the first master [notes] that the sixteenth chapter of the *Anantamukha-sūtra* (The Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings) is titled "The Lotus."
Regarding the adoption of the teaching (*śāsana*) and the principle (*yukti*): why does this sūtra adopt the lotus as its metaphor for the teaching and the principle?

The Master of the Treatise explains that the teaching is "opening" (*vikaśana*) and the principle is "emerging from the water" (*udaka-niḥsṛti*). The teaching is likened to the opening of a flower, and the principle is likened to the lotus emerging from the water.

If the upward-turning lotus is explained as having four meanings, it does not preclude the adoption of these same four dharmas for the upward-turning Sublime Dharma (*saddharma*). Since the upward-turning lotus...
This explains the meaning of "blooming above the water. Regarding the Sublime Dharma (*saddharma*), it is metaphorically represented solely by the teaching (*śāsana*) and the principle (*naya*).

Therefore, it is said that the lotus flower expresses only two meanings: namely, "rising above the water" and "blooming. These two capacities of the Sublime Dharma correspond precisely to the teaching and the principle.
Because they are cause and effect, the "wisdom" (*jñāna*) is the expression (*vyākhyāna*), and wisdom itself is the principle. The expression is the teaching. Alternatively, wisdom is the fruit.
Exegesis is the cause; therefore, according to the principles of the teaching, the cause and the effect are mutually identical, and the teaching and its principles constitute the lotus.

Regarding the statement "the second [teacher] says three," this refers to the period after the three requests. The second teacher takes practice and the fruit as the mutual relationship between cause and effect. The "three requests" are:

the request to resolve doubts and eliminate delusions, the request to provide offerings to the Buddha as the cultivation of causes, and the request to hear the Dharma with joy. It is also said that the first was narrow.
First, he requests out of doubt on the part of both himself and others; next, he requests by stating that the great assembly has already planted the causes under other Buddhas;
finally, he requests by describing how both himself and others are now capable of hearing [the teaching] through the transformation of this present Buddha.
Regarding the statement "clarifying the one great matter" and so forth: this refers to the intent of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) concerning cause and effect as elucidated in this sutra.

In terms of practice and fruition, it is called the One Vehicle. The first three [aspects] are the fruition, while "entry" is its cause. This is based on the causal relationship of the producing cause (*janakahetu*); that is, cultivating from the cause until the fruition is reached.

Specifically, the wisdom of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) is termed the producing cause, which is able to realize *nirvāṇa*. That which is realized is termed the fruition. Alternatively, it may be understood as follows:

The former refers to the "revealing cause" (*vijñapti-hetu*). The wisdom that illuminates the fruit of the cause—that is, *nirvāṇa*—is also called the revealing cause; this applies to both interpretations.
Regarding the phrase "first raising the gate of wisdom," etc., it is an explanation of an objection. The first master asks the second master:

"If you take only the fruit of practice as the lotus flower and do not take the teaching and principle [as such], then when the Tathāgata emerges from meditative absorption and proclaims the two profundities, this..."

"What is that dharma? The second master, who provides a comprehensive explanation, replies: "First, regarding the intent of opening the gate of wisdom," and so forth. First, concerning the proclamation of the teachings and principles:
because Śāriputra clung to the Two Vehicles as ultimate, his state of doubt was easy to remove, but his state of clinging was difficult to sever.
This is why the Buddha turned his clinging mind into a mind of doubt. Without doubt, there would be no request; without a request, the Buddha would have no occasion to preach the sūtra.
This is why he proclaims the two profound teachings to resolve doubts. First, regarding the "proclamation of the gateway of wisdom": wisdom is the gateway to the principles and teachings.

As for the statement "desiring to arouse the doubts of Śāriputra and others," the term "others" includes the textual accounts of the doubts of the three faculties; that is to say, it causes them to give rise to new doubts.

Regarding the phrase "commanding him to make a firm request," Master Lu says: it refers generally to "because of a request. It means that only after commanding him to request [the teaching] does the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) come to be expounded;
hence, it is called "because of a request. There is a version of the text that reads: "Because of a request" refers to the three requests made with unyielding persistence.

The *Hanshu* states that Ban Gu’s commentary defines this as "repeatedly" (*zàisān*). When the Tathāgata first declined, Śāriputra immediately requested [the teaching]. The World-Honored One... [text ends].
Twice [the Buddha] declined. Śāriputra requested again. The World-Honored One declined for a third time. Śāriputra requested yet again for a third time.
Seeing that he would not cease, the Buddha finally acceded to his request and preached the One Vehicle. Thus we know that he did not disregard the principles of the teachings.
It correctly adopts the results of the lower practices as the doctrine of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). This is indeed the meaning of "earnestly and repeatedly.
The first master asked the second master: "How can you claim that Vasubandhu Bodhisattva himself adopted the teachings and principles of the *Padma* [Lotus Sūtra]?
Why, then, do you, the second master, not adopt it? The second master replied: "You, the first..."
The Master himself corrected [the text], stating that the *Lotus of Immeasurable Meanings* refers to the lotus of the bodhisattva, while this "nature-lotus" refers to the lotus of the śrāvaka.
The lotus of the bodhisattva pertains to the teaching and principle (*śāstra*), whereas the lotus of the śrāvaka pertains to practice and fruition (*pratipatti-phala*).
One must not use the lotus of the bodhisattva to explain the lotus of the śrāvaka. Furthermore, the first master challenged the second master, saying: "I..."

This takes the meaning of a lotus flower opening upward and emerging from the water as its basis; how much more so for the teaching and the principle? The teaching is the opening flower, and the principle is the emergence from the water.
How could you apply the meaning of "opening upward and emerging from the water" to the fruit of practice? The second master replied:

"The meaning of 'opening upward and emerging from the water' in the *Dharmapada-śāstra* (Fahua lun) is intended to explain the lotus in the *Ananta-artha-nirdeśa-sūtra* (Wuliangyi jing); it does not explain this [present case]."

Regarding the lotus flower in the sutra: if you insist that its meaning lies in the upward blooming of the fruit of practice emerging from the water, then my fruit of practice also possesses this quality.
To say that the two meanings of the lotus are equal is a general rebuttal of such objections. Question: If one takes "opening, showing, awakening, and entering" as the cause...
[Question]: Why, in the treatise, are the two meanings of the lotus used as metaphors for the teaching (*śāsana*) and the principle (*naya*), representing cause and fruit?

[Answer]: The commentary states, "The two meanings of the lotus," and so forth. Although the two meanings of the lotus are explained in the *Anantārthasūtra* (the *Lotus Sūtra*), here [they refer to] the practitioner’s conduct and the upward-directed fruit.
The stalk rising above the water represents the lotus; the spreading of the conduct is the blossoming of the flower. Therefore, the lotus is taken as a metaphor.

Regarding the fruit of practice, the meaning of "blooming above the water" is not at variance with the general principle of the two meanings of the lotus flower found in the *Anantārthadharmaparyāya-sūtra*.
Furthermore, the meaning of "blooming above the water" is universally present across all four dharmas.
"Name" refers to penetrating the principle. "Discrepancy" (*shuǎng*) arises from error; it means to deviate. It does not mean failing to penetrate the common path of principle.

It means that one's understanding of the teachings and principles of the *Anantārthasūtra* need not necessarily coincide with another's practice and realization. Even if their practice and realization were identical, there would still be no logical discrepancy or error.
Therefore, although it is so stated, the two meanings of "emerging from water" and "blooming" discussed in the *Wenlun* merely serve as metaphors for the doctrine (*jiao*) and the principle (*li*).

Now, we clarify that the practice and its fruit are called the "lotus flower. It is not yet clear under which of these two categories—doctrine or principle—the former two are subsumed. The answer is: the principle is subsumed within the fruit.
By means of practice, the teaching is subsumed; thus both teaching and practice are brought into full bloom. Principle and fruit both emerge from the water.

This also does not contradict the two meanings of that [lotus]: emerging from the water and blooming (the first part above clarifies the gate of wisdom; this generally addresses the first objection. The two meanings of the lotus address the second objection).
Regarding the statement, "The first [teacher] says 'wisdom,' etc.," this refers to the third of the four masters. Question: What is the difference between these three interpretations? Answer:
The first interpretation has already been clarified according to the treatise, yet it is not the correct one, because that treatise is an exegesis of the *Anantamukha-sūtra*.

Although the second is correct, it speaks only from the perspective of what is predominant and is thus not a comprehensive principle. The third master offers no further distinct meaning; he simply compiles...
The former two masters [hold views that] constitute the correct meaning for the third master. Separated, both are flawed; combined, both are excellent.

The four dharmas collectively constitute the characteristics of cause and effect, like the case of Hou Bai and two other men traveling together. Two intermediaries each bought one steamed bun (*zhengbing*).

Hou Bai had no money to buy one, so each person was half an intermediary. As for those two who paid the money— *Note: This passage appears to be a commentary on the relationship between the four dharmas (cause, condition, fruit, and effect) and their mutual dependence, using a colloquial anecdote as an analogy for how these elements must function in concert to produce a complete result.*
One person obtains half a measure, while Hou Bai alone obtains one full measure; it is the same within this context.
As for the phrase "the initial wisdom and the gate," "initial" refers to the presentation of the fundamental principle (*zong*). "Wisdom" is the principle (*li*); "gate" is the teaching (*jiao*).
The gate is the cause (*yin*), and wisdom is the fruit (*guo*).
The phrase "to cause [them] to recognize the former [teachings], etc. explains the underlying intent. Jin says: This proves that all four dharmas are collectively named "Lotus.
It teaches the principle so that one may understand the skillful means; although there are three teachings, the principle they elucidate is but one.

It discusses practice and the fruit so that one may recognize that while practice and the means are threefold, the essence of the fruit is but one. First, it teaches the principle, which is like the first [chapter].
The chamber has three gates. Later, one discusses the fruit of practice, just as a single pond has three channels for its water. The Chancellor said:
"One should know that discussing the two kinds of profundity as real indicates that the three [vehicles] taught in the past were expedient means. Thus, the provisional and the real intersect."

To cause them to engage in what is to be adopted and what is to be abandoned, he has taken up the four dharmas of teaching, principle, practice, and fruit; thus, the principles are complete and sufficient.

Now, by explaining the profundity of the Teaching, he causes [beings] to know that the teachings of the past were provisional; now, by explaining the profundity of Practice, he causes them to know that the practices of the past were provisional.
Regarding the statement that "the teachings of the Three Vehicles were heard," etc.: for forty years prior, it was taught that the practices were provisional while the ultimate is singular.
For forty years prior, one heard the teachings of the Three Vehicles; at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, one realized the principle of the One Vehicle.
Practicing the conduct of the Three Vehicles, one attains the fruit of the One Vehicle. Therefore, among the four dharmas, the two of teaching and principle are proclaimed first.

Profound. If the principles of the teaching were not first proclaimed, by what means would those of the Two Vehicles know that there are provisional and ultimate [truths], so as to abandon the provisional and resort to the ultimate?
To abandon the provisional and resort to the ultimate must necessarily rely upon the principles of the teaching. The meaning here is this:

it is in contrast to those of indeterminate lineage that the causes of the Three Vehicles are used to realize the fruit of the One Vehicle. If one considers those of determinate lineage, they practice the causes of the Three Vehicles and realize the fruits of the Three Vehicles.
This is the fruit [of that practice]. One understands the teachings of the three vehicles and realizes the principles of the three vehicles. As for those of indeterminate lineage, the Sūtra says:
"That which you practice is the path of the Bodhisattva. Furthermore, although they were previously Śrāvakas, they later become Bodhisattvas.

The phrase "as previously explained" refers to the detailed expositions by the three masters found within the section on the derivation of the title in the *Sūtra-vyākhyāna* (Jie jing pin) and within the section on the seventeen names.
The phrase "this chapter fully elucidates," etc., constitutes the third point regarding the purpose of this chapter; according to the *Dharmapada-śāstra*, this serves as its underlying intent.
The reason for the introduction [of the *Upāya-parivarta*] is based solely on the three cycles [of teaching], not on the "Introductory Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*).

This chapter provides a general exposition of the four dharmas, presenting both cause and effect together; therefore, it is taught at the very beginning. The other chapters do not possess these features, and thus they follow later. Consequently, the "Chapter on Expedient Means" (*Upāya-parivarta*) follows after the "Introductory Chapter."

Regarding the term *biàn* (便): it is pronounced with the initial *qiè* (切) and the final *fú* (符), meaning "habituation" (*xí*) or "ease" (*ān*). It is not negative; furthermore, when pronounced with the initial *bì* (婢) and the final *miàn* (面), it means "sharp," "appropriate," or "excellent.

As for the statement that "Buddha-wisdom has two aspects": [the interlocutor] asks, "Since we are currently explaining the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*), why is it necessary to say that Buddha-wisdom has two aspects?"
Answer: In wishing to explain the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*), one must necessarily discuss the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) as well.

Subsequently attained wisdom relies upon fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). Because fundamental wisdom exists, subsequently attained wisdom arises; because subsequently attained wisdom exists, skillful means can finally emerge.

The wisdom of skillful means is the provisional and skillful functioning of subsequently attained wisdom. When intending to employ it, one must necessarily incorporate its essence (*tattva*). The essence has already been clarified.

This is precisely true wisdom (*tattvajñāna*). True wisdom is itself fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). If one intends to explain subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), it is necessary to discuss fundamental wisdom as well.

Furthermore, it also encompasses the untainted true wisdom of subsequently attained wisdom. Later, "expedient means" (*upāya*) is explained; this is simply another name for skillful means (*kauśalya*).
Because the sublime function of subsequently attained wisdom extends throughout the three vehicles, it is said that "Buddha-wisdom is twofold. Jin says:

True wisdom (*tattvajñāna*) comprises both the fundamental and the subsequently attained [wisdoms]. These two untainted (*anāsrava*) wisdoms are collectively termed "true. The *She lun* (Compendium) states:

"To explain the Buddha's wisdom in general, there are these two wisdoms; furthermore, they are divided into three: first, the fundamental; second, the subsequently attained; and third, the expedient (*upāya*)."

Regarding the statement that "real dharmas are also twofold": since the cognition of mental discourse is of two types, its objects are likewise divided into two kinds. Question: This passage clarifies the cognizing wisdom (*ālambaka-jñāna*);
why is it necessary to clarify the real dharmas that serve as the objects of cognition (*ālambana*)? Answer: There are two reasons.

First, the modes of activity (*ākāra*) of these two types of wisdom are profoundly subtle and difficult to discern; if they were not distinguished by reference to their objects, there would be no means by which the two types of wisdom could be made manifest. Therefore...
First, regarding the object (*viṣaya*). Since wisdom arises in dependence upon an object, one first discusses the reality and the object; only after that does one speak of the two [wisdom and faith].
Wisdom does not arise in isolation; it is produced only by relying on an object. The arising of wisdom is established based on the object, just as in the explanation of faith:
it is first stated that one has "deep forbearance and aspiration toward the reality, qualities, and capabilities," which refers precisely to the objects of faith.

Regarding the phrase "the substance is real": "substance is real" distinguishes it from the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature). Both the *paratantra* (dependent) and *pariniṣpanna* (perfected) natures are subsumed under the category of reality because they arise from seeds.
The conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is the dependent nature; the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is the perfected nature. The *Bhūmivastu-śāstra* states:

"The conditioned and the unconditioned are called 'existent. 'Self' and 'what belongs to self' are said to be empty. This means there are ninety-four conditioned phenomena and six unconditioned phenomena. There is...

The dependent nature (*paratantra*) and the unconditioned perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*) are both subsumed under the category of reality. Question: Within the conditioned, resentment and malice depend upon hatred; they are like length and shortness, or square and round, which depend upon form (*rūpa*).
In what sense can these [mental states] be said to have a real essence? Answer: Because that which resembles [the real] is subsumed by the real, it is also called "real.

Second, "ultimate reality" refers exclusively to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), while simultaneously excluding the dependent nature. [This is] the question regarding the real essence.

Since this already encompasses both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), as well as the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), why is it necessary to separately mention the "object of reality" (*tattvārtha*)? Answer:

It is precisely because there are two types of cognizing wisdom (*ālambaka-jñāna*). Accordingly, on the level of the object of cognition (*ālambana-viṣaya*), two distinct categories are differentiated.

While the former [the conditioned] is substantially real and common to both fundamental (*mūla*) and subsequently attained (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*) wisdom, the present "object of reality" refers exclusively to that which is preeminent for fundamental wisdom alone. As for the conditioned [factors] mentioned previously...
These are dharmas that possess a substantial body (*tattva-śarīra*), yet because their substance is merely nominal, they cannot be called "true reality" (*bhūta-tattva*).

They are termed "substantial bodies" because they sustain and depend upon other-dependent dharmas (*paratantra-dharma*) which, like illusory phenomena, are contrasted with the false. However, when contrasted with the dharma of *tathatā* (suchness), they are not called true reality.

Question: Within the "substantial body," there are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas; how do these differ from the *tathatā* within "true reality" in terms of their subtle principle? Answer: There are two interpretations. First, the "substantial body"...

"Unconditioned within the middle" refers to the first five of the six unconditioned phenomena. "The wondrous principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*) within reality" refers to the sixth unconditioned phenomenon among the six, namely the unconditioned of True Suchness.
Another interpretation states: "Unconditioned within the reality of essence" refers to that which is revealed by relying on linguistic expression (*vyavahāra*);

whereas "unconditioned within the lower reality" abandons expression to discuss the ultimate meaning (*artha*). The latter is merely that which is confronted [by the mind] according to the nature of things (*dharmatā*), and thus differs from the former.

The term "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*) is used in opposition to the "imagined" (*parikalpita*); the subsequent term "true suchness" (*tathatā*) is used to distinguish it from the "dependent" (*paratantra*).
Because they differ in this way, they are thus divided into two types. (The section on objects concludes.)
Regarding the statement that "the wisdom of reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) is also thus": the word "also" refers to the object of cognition (*ālambana*).

Just as there are two aspects to the essence of reality—namely, the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*)—these are collectively termed the "essence of reality. The *Shè* (攝) commentary states: "Wisdom arises in dependence upon its object.

Since the real objects are twofold, wisdom is also twofold. The underlying intent is to distinguish their essential nature; if this were not clarified by contrast with the True [Suchness], how could it be defined?
The Dharma is termed "expedient means" (*upāya*); therefore, the ultimate truth is presented first, followed by the explanation of expedient means.
Since the objects of cognition (*ālambana*) are of two kinds, the cognizing wisdom (*jñāna*) is likewise of two kinds (as indicated above).

The phrase "that which is said to be the observation of the reality of the essence" is an explanation. Its meaning is that the observation of the reality of the essence is untainted, true wisdom (*anāsrava-bhūta-jñāna*).

In contrast to the deluded wisdom of ordinary beings, which does not know names as they truly are, it concludes by stating: "When both the fundamental [wisdom] and the subsequently attained wisdom are both suchness (*tathatā*)," this refers to the sense of being in accordance with reality;

knowing by way of its very essence is called "wisdom that accords with reality" (*yathābhūta-jñāna*). If this subsequently attained wisdom takes conditioned phenomena as its object, then regarding those conditioned phenomena—
To thoroughly understand that which is dependent on others as being like an illusory phenomenon is also to know it as the essence of suchness (*tathatā*).

When fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) realizes suchness, it is free from conceptual discrimination (*nirvikalpa*). Among the objects of perception (*ālambana*), there is the object possessing substantial reality, which constitutes the true object.

Since there are thus two kinds of objects, the wisdom that perceives them likewise consists of two types of wisdom; therefore, the commentary states that "real wisdom is also thus. The word "also" refers to the two types of perceived objects.

Regarding the two types of wisdom: first is the wisdom that accords with the reality of the essence (*tathatā*). This refers to the collective designation for both fundamental and subsequently attained wisdom as "wisdom that accords with the reality of the essence.

This is the wisdom that acts as the subjective perceiver (*ālambaka*). It is the contemplation of the phenomena of the preceding "reality of the essence," namely, the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);

these are the objective objects (*ālambana*). Question: Fundamental wisdom directly realizes *tathatā*. One can know the essence of *tathatā* through it; however, how does subsequently attained wisdom [know it]?

Question: Since the wisdom that takes the transformed image as its object does not accord with the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), how can it be called "wisdom that accords with the true nature of reality"? Answer:

Although the two types of wisdom—the fundamental and the subsequent—differ in terms of their directness or indirectness, when discussed in relation to the true nature of phenomena, they are collectively termed "wisdom that accords with the true nature of reality.

Question: What is meant by "real wisdom" (*bhūta-jñāna*)? Answer: First, because it takes real phenomena as its object; second, it receives the name "real" in contrast to the deluded wisdom of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). This is because the deluded wisdom of ordinary beings—[is false].

It does not accord with the object and wisdom; it provisionally gives rise to discrimination and thus cannot attain the name of "real wisdom. Therefore, the Commentary states: "In contrast to the deluded wisdom of ordinary beings which does not know [the truth], it is called 'real wisdom'";

this means that all contaminated (sāsrava) wisdom is termed "deluded wisdom of ordinary beings. However, the relationship between these proximate and remote aspects of the true and the false is not fixed, and can be categorized into four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
First: that which is not proximate is the true. This refers to the unchanging aspect of the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna), which conditions three kinds of objects.
Second, that which is direct is true: this refers to fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna) taking suchness as its object, because it does not produce a reflected image.
Third, that which is indirect is false: this refers to the first seven consciousnesses, which rely on the original substance to produce a reflected image. Fourth, that which is indirect is true:

this refers to the non-outflow subsequently attained wisdom (prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna), because it produces a reflected image while taking suchness as its object. Although this subsequent wisdom does not directly realize suchness, it is nonetheless considered true because it resembles it.

It is like fire in a mirror. Now, regarding these two types of wisdom—the fundamental and the subsequently attained—which take objects as their domain, although there is a difference in the degree of intimacy with those objects, both are nonetheless real.

Therefore, the Commentary states: "Both are correct. The meaning is that this is like the wisdom of the actual substance (*tattva-vastu-jñāna*), which encompasses both the fundamental and the subsequently attained wisdoms.
Fundamental wisdom takes only the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as its object, whereas subsequently attained wisdom takes both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned as its objects.

Regarding the phrase "realizing the true reality (*tattva*) and so forth," this distinguishes it from *paratantra-dharma* (dependent phenomena). Since *paratantra-dharma* is like an illusory object, it cannot be called the wondrous principle of *tathatā* (suchness).
This refers precisely to the wisdom that realizes true reality in this context; it is also the fourth level of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Setting aside the verbal expression to discuss the intended meaning, the "wisdom of the single dharma-realm" observes that both conditioned and unconditioned phenomena among the objects of cognition are [empty].

Regarding the term "reality" (*satya*): in relation to what is it called reality? Answer: It is in relation to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Both the dependent (*paratantra*) and the perfected (*pariniṣpanna*) natures receive the name "reality.

The *Śīlasamvara-sūtra* states: "The conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) are called 'existent' (*bhāva*); 'self' (*ātman*) and 'what belongs to self' (*ātmīya*) are called 'empty' (*śūnya*).

Question: The perfected nature may be called real; why is the dependent nature called real? Answer: Because the dependent nature possesses substantial existence (*dravya-sat*), it is called real. Question: This...
Regarding the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) as objects of cognition (*ālambana*), how many entities does each possess? Answer: The perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) has two aspects:

first, the perfected nature free from inversion (*aviparyāsa-pariniṣpanna*), which is the untainted (*anāsrava*); second, the ultimate perfected nature (*atyanta-pariniṣpanna*), which is suchness (*tathatā*).

Here, it is suchness that serves as the object of cognition. The dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) relies upon causes and depends upon conditions; for example, when the mind arises, it necessarily possesses four factors: first, arising from seeds as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*); second, depending upon an object...
It arises as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). Third, the preceding mind induces the subsequent mind as the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

Fourth, non-obstruction serves as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). There are likewise four types of conceptual construction (*parikalpa*): first, natural conceptual construction, such as that of the Sāṃkhya outsiders.
1. Grasping sentient beings as arising spontaneously from a primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and so forth; this is the pervasive conceptualization of names and expressions (*nāma-vikalpa*).

It is like a worldly person who, having been granted the name "Buddha’s slave" by the Buddha, subsequently clings to that name and gives rise to the notions of "self" and "other. 2. The pervasive conceptualization of mutual attachment (*lakṣaṇa-sambandha-vikalpa*);
it is like the worldly clinging to things such as "this is my field" and so forth. 3. The pervasive conceptualization of moments (*kṣaṇa-vikalpa*); it is like [the clinging to] the body.

Arising and ceasing in every moment; this is how the ignorant and deluded conceive of permanence and so forth. Question: What is the difference between "this-worldly reality" (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and the "substantially non-existent essence"?
Answer: Wisdom is differentiated according to its objects. That which is named "post-attainment" (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*) is so called because it does not realize [the ultimate];

the wisdom of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-jñāna*) is established in contrast to the deluded wisdom of ordinary beings, rather than being based on the actual nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Now, citing "reality" (*tattva*), this refers exclusively to the fourth [category], which discards the conventional expression to discuss the intended meaning (*artha*).
Regarding "wisdom," it is said that there are five pairs. First, the Tathāgata’s subsequently attained wisdom (prsthalabdha-jñāna) takes a single object while encompassing five types of objects;
according to the objects observed, this observing wisdom receives five distinct names of wisdom. Second, the fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna) does not follow [the distinctions of objects].

Subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) takes five kinds of objects; it merely receives the name "wisdom of reality" (*tattva-jñāna*). It is that which can confront [the ultimate], and the wisdoms it confronts are fivefold:
first, knowing the delusory; second, knowing phenomena (*vastu*); third, knowing characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); fourth, knowing designations (*vyavahāra*); and fifth, knowing expedient means (*upāya*).

Fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is realized solely within and does not follow subsequently attained wisdom in its knowing of the delusory, phenomena, characteristics, designations, and expedient means.
The fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) regarding these five types of knowledge is also designated as "true wisdom" (*tattva-jñāna*).

Herein, the Lord briefly sets forth the eight truths (*aṣṭasatya*) so that students may easily attain realization. Within this meaning, there are first the general names and subsequently the specific names. Regarding the general names:

first is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), which is also called the truth of concealment and manifestation. "Conventional" (*saṃvṛti*) means "concealed," in the sense of being destructible. "Worldly" (*loka*)...

This refers to manifestation. It signifies that which conforms to worldly convention while obscuring the principle of emptiness; it is the manifestation of characteristics, such as when a handkerchief is tied into the shape of a rabbit’s horn.
Just as the original handkerchief is concealed and the appearance of a rabbit manifests, so too is this case. Now, I shall follow the ancient interpretation.
The first is called conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). It is also called the truth of concealment and manifestation. The second is ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Its former name was the truth of the primary meaning (*paramārtha-satya*), and it is also called true truth. Regarding its specific classifications, according to the *Yogācāra-vijñaptimātra*, there are four types for each of the two truths:
1. Worldly conventionality, also called the truth of having a name but lacking reality. 2. Rational conventionality, also called the differentiation according to phenomena.
The truths: third, the conventional truth of realization, also called the truth of conventional establishment through skillful means;

fourth, the ultimate conventional truth, also called the truth of conventional establishment by designation, which is the ultimate truth of the two kinds of emptiness. There are four types of ultimate truth: first, the worldly ultimate truth.
It is also called the "truth of the manifestation of essence and function. Second is the "ultimate truth of principle," also called the "truth of the differentiation of cause and effect.
Third is the "ultimate truth of realization," also called the "truth of manifesting reality by means of the gate.

Fourth is the "ultimate truth of the ultimate," also called "discarding the expression to discuss the intent. These four conventional truths and four ultimate truths together constitute the eight truths.
The first [of the three] is exclusively conventional; the last one is exclusively ultimate; the remaining middle three are both ultimate and conventional.

When these three dharmas are contrasted with the preceding examples of the jar, the basin, and the vehicle, they are called the latter three ultimates. When contrasted with the latter single ultimate—the dharma-dhātu—they are called the former three conventions.
As for their essence, they are merely the post-attainment wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) of the Tathāgata directed toward various phenomena.

This is one. Because it can know these five kinds of matters, five names for wisdom are established. That which can serve as the antidote is solely the single, primary essence-wisdom (*svabhāvajñāna*);
this is the true wisdom that realizes the ultimate meaning by setting aside conventional designations. What are the five? First, the wisdom that knows delusory cognition:
this is the Tathāgata’s subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). This is the wisdom that is capable of knowing; delusory phenomena are the objects known. Wisdom is able to...
Knowing conventional phenomena as false is called "knowledge that knows the false. "False" refers to things such as armies, forests, jars, basins, and vehicles;
these constitute the first, mundane conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Ordinary people and non-Buddhists do not understand this and falsely grasp them as being truly existent.

The subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of the Tathāgata can know these false phenomena; this is called "knowledge that knows the false. The fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) of the Tathāgata is realized only through internal realization.
In the one true dharma-realm, one knows the real but does not know the delusory. In contrast to that wisdom which knows the delusory, this is called "actual wisdom" (*bhūta-jñāna*). Question:

Since the nature of the thoroughly imagined (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is entirely non-existent, how can it be said to be the sphere of activity for the noble ones (*ārya-gocara*)? Answer: That is stated with respect to the substance of the thoroughly imagined.

Regarding the statement that "knowledge does not take [conventional objects] as its object": we now know this to be a false conceptualization, because subsequently attained knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) does take them as its object.

As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Ordinary fools cling to existence, while noble ones realize non-existence; since it is admitted that the Buddha takes them as his object, they may also be said to be the cognitive domain of both ordinary and noble wisdom.

Second, regarding "knowledge of things" (*vastu-jñāna*): "things" refers to the essential entities of the three categories (*triskandha*). This is precisely the second type, the conventional truth of principle (*yukti-saṃvṛti*), also called "according with things" (*anuvastuka*).

Regarding the truth of differentiation (*viśeṣa-satya*): phenomena such as the three aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) manifest as distinct entities and characteristics.

These are objects that can be known through their differentiated aspects; yet within these aggregates, bases, and elements, there is absolutely no self (*ātman*). Ordinary beings do not realize this and falsely cling to a self, imagining it to have the function of a sovereign master.

Through his subsequent cognition (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), the Tathāgata knows that the substance and phenomena of these three categories arise from conditions and are entirely devoid of a self; he is able to know this.

Wisdom is defined as the knowledge of phenomena (*vastu*). The fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) of the Tathāgata exclusively knows the principle (*tattva*); it does not follow after the phenomena known by subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), which is called "actual wisdom" (*bhūtajñāna*).

Regarding the third [type], the wisdom that knows characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-jñāna*): "characteristic" refers to the modes of activity (*ākāra*), namely the sixteen modes of activity under the four noble truths.

This is the third [wisdom] which realizes conventional reality; it is also called the "conventionally established truth" (*upāya-prajñapti-satya*). Its characteristic consists of the causes and effects of defilement and purification.

That which appears is called the "characteristic" (*nimitta*). Subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) is known as the knowledge of the name and the knowledge of the characteristic. The fundamental wisdom of the Tathāgata knows the nature (*dharmatā*) but does not know the characteristic.

In contrast to that wisdom which knows the characteristic, it is called "ultimate wisdom" (*tattva-jñāna*). Regarding the four types of wisdom that express [the ultimate], "expression" (*abhilāpa*) means to express or reveal;

that is, by means of the gateways [of language], one realizes suchness through the two kinds of emptiness, which is termed "expression. This is the fourth, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which is the basis for the noble ones (*ārya*).

This wisdom, by relying on these two gates of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), is able to manifest ultimate truth; it is called "the wisdom of expression" (*prajñapti-jñāna*). Subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) cognizes this, and is thus termed "the wisdom that knows expression.

The Tathāgata’s fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) sets aside expression to discuss the ultimate intent (*artha*); it does not follow subsequently attained wisdom in its cognition of expression, and is therefore termed "real wisdom" (*tattva-jñāna*).
Among the four pairs of wisdoms mentioned above, that which is confronted is subsequently attained wisdom, while that which confronts it is fundamental wisdom. Subsequently attained wisdom...

Wisdom that conforms solely to objects receives five names; it has no other designation. Fundamental wisdom does not follow after the subsequently attained wisdom to take the five types of objects as its conditions;
it only receives the name of the five types of true wisdom.

Regarding these four types, they are mentioned in order to exclude over-extension (saṃkara). It is feared that people might interpret the statement in the *Vyākhyā*—from "knowing the false is called real wisdom" up to "knowing the signifier is called real wisdom"—as implying that the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) is being designated as "real wisdom. Thus, these four are specified to prevent such confusion.
Therefore, the Commentary states that these four kinds of actual wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*) all exclusively observe the fourth, true wisdom;
this is the wisdom that realizes the single true *dharmadhātu*, which is precisely the fundamental wisdom (*mūlajñāna*).

Regarding the phrase "the other four objects of cognition and so forth," this refers to the four types of knowledge: knowing the false, knowing phenomena (*vastu*), knowing characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and knowing designations (*prajñapti*).

The intent is to clarify that the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of the Tathāgata alone is termed "conventional wisdom" (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) because it can know these four conventionalities.

In reality, however, both the Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas may be said to possess knowledge of the false, phenomena, characteristics, and designations. Nevertheless, the present discussion seeks to explain expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).

Therefore, we take the *prṣṭhalabdha* (subsequently attained) [wisdom] of the Tathāgata; for it is this subsequently attained wisdom of the Tathāgata that possesses such skillful and wondrous functions.

Question: What is the distinction between the essence of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) and the essence of wisdom (*jñāna*)? Answer: Although their essence is one, they are distinguished according to their functional meanings. Illuminating and clearly perceiving is called "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*).

Resolute determination is called "wisdom" (*jñāna*). Discerning and selecting is called "insight" (*prajñā*). Sealing and maintaining is called "patience" (*kṣānti*). Thus, while their essence is identical, their names differ according to their distinct functional meanings.

Regarding the statement that "knowing the five pairs as provisional names and reality" means: the Tathāgata’s subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) knows that the two vehicles’ provisional attainments and realizations—the sheep, deer, and illusory cities—are merely provisional establishments for a specific time. Because the Tathāgata’s subsequently attained wisdom knows these provisional names, it is called provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).

The Tathāgata’s fundamental wisdom realizes the principle of the One Vehicle; this is called "knowing the real. It is not that subsequent wisdom is called "real" because it follows [the realization of] the provisional.
Question: Why was it not stated that the preceding four kinds of wisdom know the One Vehicle, yet here it is said that the wisdom and principle of the One Vehicle are realized?

Answer: This is said in response to the provisional wisdom of the two vehicles, in order to reveal that this ultimate reality is the principle of the Single Vehicle alone; hence it is called the "Single Vehicle.

As for the statement that this relies on realized wisdom (*pramāṇa-jñāna*) and so forth, this refers to fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). The fourth truth is the fourfold ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
The middle ultimate refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which is to say, setting aside the expression to discuss the intended meaning (*artha*).

Regarding the phrase "in contrast to the latter three conventional knowledges," this refers to the second triad of categories: the four truths and the two gates of emptiness. These correspond to the three types of knowledge:

knowledge of phenomena (*vastu-jñāna*), knowledge of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-jñāna*), and knowledge of the expression (*abhidhāna-jñāna*). Question: Since the latter three conventional [knowledges] are identical to the former three true [knowledges], why are they not contrasted with the former?

Question: The first three are true [wisdoms], while the latter three are called conventional. Why are the latter three conventional knowledges also termed "expedient wisdom" (*upāya-jñāna*) and "conventional wisdom" (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*)?

Answer: This is precisely because the two dharmas of the true and the conventional, and the expedient and the real, are set in opposition. By taking the fourth true wisdom and setting it against the conventional nature of the latter three knowledges, why is it not set against the first conventional [knowledge]?
Answer: Because that first conventional knowledge has no substantial essence as its object; it is merely a false dharma and is not the conventional wisdom of realization.

Therefore, it is not opposed [to the ultimate]. If that is so, when those of the two vehicles realize the principle of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), they likewise transcend linguistic expression;
why then is this not the fourth truth? Answer: When those of the two vehicles realize the principle, although they attain the truth, they themselves do not know it.

Therefore, the provisional wisdom (*prajñā*) of the two vehicles is not the fourth truth. Question: Since those of the two vehicles lack the wisdom of the gate of the twofold emptiness (*dvaya-śūnyatā*), how can they also be said to be "opposed" [to the ultimate]?

The fourth is the conventional [truth]. Answer: Although the two types of emptiness are not cultivated simultaneously, because one has partially attained the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), they must be contrasted.

If one proceeds by way of entering into the third conventional [truth], it refers to the third conventional wisdom. This consists of the sixteen aspects (*ākāra*) of the Four Noble Truths and the seven preparatory stages (*prayoga*).
These are the means of entry for the two vehicles, as well as the four fruits of the śramaṇa and the fruit of the pratyekabuddha. Third.
True wisdom (*tattvajñāna*) is the gateway of the two emptinesses; it is the genuine entry of a bodhisattva into the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) at the first stage (*bhūmi*).
The subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of a Tathāgata, which can know the entry into the Mahāyāna, is called "wisdom that knows the real.

The subsequently attained wisdom of a Tathāgata, which knows the entry into the two vehicles (*hīnayāna*), is called "wisdom that knows the provisional. Both this [subject] and its object are the subsequently attained wisdom of a Tathāgata, and not [the fundamental non-conceptual wisdom].
The preceding explanations all take the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) as the fundamental [wisdom]. Question:

Why is the third, the ultimate (*paramārtha*), not paired with the first and second, which are conventional (*saṃvṛti*)? Answer: The first conventional is merely a false phenomenon (*mṛṣādharma*) and lacks substantiality; thus, the second conventional is not taken up.

Furthermore, the phenomena of the three categories (*triskandha*) do not constitute the mode of entry (*praveśa-lakṣaṇa*) for practice; therefore, they are not taken up. Question: Regarding the distinction between the ultimate and the conventional...
What is the distinction? The answer is that there are four distinctions: First, the distinction regarding phenomena (*dharma*). Profound and subtle phenomena are termed *paramārtha* (ultimate truth);

coarse and shallow phenomena are termed *saṃvṛti* (conventional truth). Second, the distinction regarding persons. That which is known by superior wisdom is *paramārtha*; that which is known by middling or inferior wisdom is termed *saṃvṛti*.
Third, the distinction regarding essence. That which possesses a real intrinsic nature is termed *paramārtha*; that which lacks a real intrinsic nature is termed *saṃvṛti*.

Fourth, there is the distinction between the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and the outflow-free (*anāsrava*). Outflow-free phenomena are termed the ultimate (*paramārtha*), while outflowing phenomena are termed the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).
[The section on] "real wisdom" concludes here.

Regarding the statement that expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) is either threefold or fourfold: the intention of the commentator (the *shuzhu*) is to provide an interpretation of the "expedient" (*upāya*) mentioned in this sutra.

However, the term "expedient means" (upāya) appears throughout all sūtras; [this section] first cites it in its general sense, and subsequently explains the specific expedient means of this particular sūtra.

To begin with, let us explain expedient means in its universal application across all sūtras. The essence of the wisdom of skillful means is one and the same, and it is subsumed within the seventh of the ten pāramitās.
Alternatively, there are three types: first, the expedient means of progress and approach; second, the expedient means of performance and action.
There are three accumulations of skillful means; alternatively, there are four. Within the second category, "the practice of giving," the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) are distinguished;
when condensed, there are three, but when expanded, they become four.
Regarding the term "progressing toward through skillful means" (*upāya-prasthāna*): progress itself is the skillful means. Xiu says:

"In the Lesser Vehicle, it is said that for both Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—namely the two vehicles—while they abide in the two stages of the *sambhāra-mārga* (provisioning path) and *prayoga-mārga* (path of preparation), they cultivate the seven skillful means.
From the point of progressing toward the *darśana-mārga* (path of seeing) onwards, the four stages of approach and the four fruits are called 'progression'."
Regarding the statement "prior to the path of seeing," etc., there are seven stages: first, the contemplation of the five cessations; second, the mindfulness of specific characteristics;

third, the mindfulness of general characteristics; fourth, heat; fifth, summits; sixth, patience; and seventh, the supreme mundane dharma. As for the five cessations: first, for sentient beings with excessive greed, one causes them to practice the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
This is because sentient beings do not understand that the objects of the five sensory realms (*pañca-viṣaya*) are all illusory transformations.
Furthermore, they do not realize that their own bodies are originally composed of the four great elements, the five aggregates, and thirty-six constituent factors.

Consequently, they become addicted to the five sensory objects and cling to their own lives, unable to free themselves from defilement. Because of this, they remain submerged in saṃsāra for long kalpas;
therefore, out of great compassion, the Buddha wishes to cause them to transcend attachment and defilement, leading them to contemplate the impurity of all phenomena. Thus, he performs [this act].

The meditation on purity (*śubha-vipaśyanā*) can eliminate four kinds of craving: First, craving for form and color (*saṃsthāna-varṇa-rāga*). This refers to the arising of a craving mind upon seeing [objects] that are long, short, square, round, or possess beautiful features.

One counteracts this by taking as one's object the perception of decay and putrefaction (*pūti-bhāva-saṃjñā*). Second, craving for manifest color (*varṇa-rāga*). This refers to [craving] directed toward cosmetics, powders, and clothing.

One counteracts this by cultivating the perception of blueness and other such colors, practicing the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*). Third, craving for exquisite touch (*sparśa-rāga*). [One counteracts this by reflecting on the repulsiveness of the body.]

Regarding greed: when one gives rise to a greedy mind toward objects such as the body’s smoothness or massage, one should counteract it by forming the perception of [the body] being infested with worms and maggots.
Fourth is greed for offerings: this refers to the arising of a greedy mind due to the presentation of services, such as bedding, or through songs that bring pleasure and delight;
one should counteract this by contemplating a corpse so motionless that it cannot be moved. The *Abhidharma-śāstra* states: "Afflictions arise according to the power of their respective objects."
It is brought before one. When this contemplation is accomplished, one views all objects as impure. If food enters the mouth, the perception of impurity arises and one immediately spits it out;
thus, this contemplation is perfected. Second, for sentient beings with excessive anger, one should practice the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion.
Regarding the overcoming of anger: since beginningless time, sentient beings have constantly habituated themselves to anger, which continues in an uninterrupted succession.
When anger arises, all wholesome dharmas within the bodies of sentient beings are completely extinguished, for it can destroy the wisdom-life of their Dharma-body.
The *Sutra of Bequeathed Teaching* says: "One should know that an angry mind is more fierce than a raging fire; one must desire to sever it."
Hatred is the ultimate source of all that is unwholesome; one should regard sentient beings as one’s own children and cultivate loving-kindness and compassion.
Third, for sentient beings who are dominated by delusion, one should practice the contemplation of dependent origination, leading them to observe the twelve links of causality.
Fools do not understand cause and effect in this regard and thus extensively create evil karma. For their sake, one should explain how worldly grains and seeds produce such causes and effects.
Birth is uninterrupted; this is a metaphor for the continuity of cause and effect within one's own person. Ignorance initiates the process, while craving and grasping moisten the birth.
Subsequently, one enters the Path. Fourth, regarding those sentient beings who are attached to a self, they practice the contemplation of the analysis of the elements (*dhātu-vibhāga-darśana*).

This is because these sentient beings do not understand that this body is a composite formed by the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), and the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*); it is truly devoid of a self, yet they falsely conceptualize it as such.
There is a self; because of the conception of a self, one undergoes the suffering of birth and death.

Out of compassion for these beings, the Buddha causes them to contemplate that this body consists only of phenomena—namely the five aggregates, twelve bases, and eighteen elements—and that in reality there is no self. This is called the contemplation of the analysis of the elements (*dhātuprabhedabhāvanā*).

For the five types of distracted sentient beings who practice the meditation on counting the breath (*ānāpānasmṛti*), it is because sentient beings lack a point of focus for their minds that they become dissolute and unrestrained.
The mind lacks restraint; therefore, one counts the breaths to stop such distraction. "Counting" means to count repeatedly. "Breath" (āśvāsa) means to cease and rest.

Because various objects of attachment lead to an abundance of evil deeds and a complete lack of wholesome cultivation, one is instructed to count the breaths in order to suppress this upward-distracting state.
This refers to that wind of the breath as it either exhales or inhales, which momentarily ceases in the interval; this is called "breathing" (āśvāsa). However...
There are six causes by which [the practice] becomes perfected. First is counting (*gaṇanā*), which means reckoning the mind’s object as the inhalation and exhalation.
One merely recollects and maintains the count of the breaths from one to ten. Regarding this, there are three faults: first, the fault of undercounting, when taking two as one;
second, the fault of overcounting, when taking one as two; and third, the fault of confusion, when taking inhalation for exhalation or exhalation for inhalation.
A person who is free from these three faults is said to have correct counting (*saṃkhyāna*).

If the counting becomes confused in the midst of ten, one should again begin from the start and count in sequence, beginning anew until meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is attained. Second, regarding "following" (*anugama*):

this means binding the mind to the object of the inhalation and exhalation, proceeding with the breath without applying further effort (*prayoga*), following it as it moves. Where does it reach? When the breath enters, it enters...

Within the body, it circulates throughout the entire body; if it emerges outside the body, extending from one span (*vitasti*) up to one fathom (*vyāma*), mindfulness shall follow it wherever it goes.
Regarding the three types of cessation: when not counting the breaths, one must not allow the mind to become distracted.

One must necessarily restrain the mind and fix the attention upon the tip of the nose, or between the eyebrows, or even down to the toes; wherever the mind is attached, one should restrain it by counting.

Regarding the "fourfold observation": this means that after having observed this wind of breath, one further observes the body of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), including both the primary elements (*bhūta*) and the derived elements (*bhautika*), taking the twelve bases (*āyatana*) and eighteen elements (*dhātu*) as its objects. Regarding the "fivefold turning": [the mind] turns...

This refers to "transferring. When taking the breath-wind as the object, one establishes oneself in progressively superior stages of the noble faculties (*āryendriya*), up to and including the stage of the "first worldly dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*).

All of these involve this mode of practice. Regarding the "six purities" (*ṣaḍ-viśuddhi*): it means that subsequent advancement into the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and so forth, up to the "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣaya-jñāna*), is termed "purity.
Question: What is the meaning of "stopping" (*ting*)? Answer: The commentary states it means "to level" or "to align. It intends to refer to the "five stopping minds" (*pañca-sthāpana-citta*).

Contemplating that their power and efficacy are equal, one enters the Path of Seeing by practicing any one of these contemplations; their functional utility is identical. Ximing states: "To 'stop' (ting) means to dwell and cease.
These five contemplations bring the body and mind to rest; "to stop" (ting) here means to dwell. Through these five stops, the practitioner causes the mind to abide.

Second, as for the contemplation of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇasmṛtyupasthāna*), the treatise calls it the contemplation of individual characteristics (*svabhāvalakṣaṇasmṛtyupasthāna*). [Regarding] the body...

Regarding sensation, mind, and mental factors: their respective individual natures are called "specific characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa*). The body is the specific nature of the body, which is composed of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derivatives;
sensation is the specific nature of sensation; and mind is the specific nature of mind. Apart from these three understandings, all other teachings on phenomena are called "without specific nature.
