Thus, even the teaching of the One Vehicle may be termed provisional, for in reality there are no three vehicles; rather, the names and so forth of the three vehicles are skillfully established as provisional devices.
The phrase "generally indicating the real and the provisional" serves as a double conclusion for the two distinctions between the principles and teachings of the real and the provisional.

To proclaim that "the wisdom of all Buddhas is profound and immeasurable" is the indication of the real. If one takes what is near at hand, it corresponds to the five kinds of wisdom and the five kinds of profundity mentioned below.
This explains the reality (*tattva*). If one takes the distant perspective of the three turnings (*triparivarta*) where the practice and its fruit are taught, this explains the reality;

this also applies equally to the two chapters on the fruit of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). To proclaim that the gate of wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to enter is the designation of the provisional (*upāya*).

If one takes the proximate perspective of the five difficulties and the eight profound depths, this explains the provisional. If one takes the distant perspective within the three turnings and the twelve... [the text continues].
In the section concerning the object of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), wherever it speaks of provisional teachings, it is entirely an explanation of the provisional. Yuyun states:

"The wisdom is exceedingly profound and the gate of teaching is difficult to enter"; this indicates that the principle and teaching of the Mahāyāna are such that the two vehicles truly do not understand the Tathāgata’s provisional exposition.
This indicates that the principle and teaching of the Two Vehicles are provisional (*upāya*).

Regarding the statement, "desiring to cause the followers of the Two Vehicles to abandon the provisional," one asks: In the opening of the "Expedient Means" chapter, the World-Honored One provided a general outline of the provisional and the real.
What is the intention behind proclaiming two kinds of profundity? The commentary answers: it is intended for the sake of those of the Two Vehicles and others.
Therefore, it first proclaims the profundity of wisdom (*jñāna*), so that those of the Two Vehicles may know the reality (*tattva*) and thus accept it;

it first proclaims the profundity of the gate of teaching (*śāsana-mukha*), so that those of the Two Vehicles may know the provisional (*upāya*) and thus relinquish it. Furthermore, the former commentator explained: "The teaching that expresses [the truth] is called the provisional."

The means (*upāya*) are that which is taught, while the wisdom (*prajñā*) they convey is called the "True Vehicle" (*bhūta-yāna*). Within this True Vehicle, because one desires to cause those of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) to practice the causes and attain the fruits, it is said:
"As for the *Śrīmālā[-sūtra]... and so forth; this citation from that sūtra serves as a direct proof. Question: How is it known that the World-Honored One [spoke for] forty [years]?

In the past, for the sake of those of the two vehicles (*dvayāyānika*), he taught the provisional (*upāya*), causing them to relinquish that provisionality upon entering the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. The commentary answers by stating: "The *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* says, 'By these [means],' etc.
That sūtra speaks of the four knowledges (*jñāna*) of the two vehicles, which are precisely the knowledge of the Four Noble Truths (*catur-āryasatya-jñāna*) of the two vehicles.

This knowledge of the Four Noble Truths is itself bodhi; it corresponds to the sheep and deer carts in this present sūtra. Those who attain nirvāṇa correspond to the "transformed" (or "emanated") beings in this sūtra.
Regarding the city, that sutra states: "The fact that those of the two vehicles attain nirvana through four wisdoms that are not ultimate is a skillful means (*upāya*) of the Buddha.
This skillful means intends to cause those of indeterminate lineage among the followers of the two vehicles to attain the four wisdoms of the sheep and deer carts and the illusory city.

After attaining nirvana, they are made to abandon the four wisdoms of the sheep and deer carts and take up the ox cart; they are made to abandon the nirvana of the illusory city and take up the place of jewels. Thus it is said.
To say that this is the Buddha’s skillful means is precisely in accord with the intent of this sutra.

To say "desiring to cause them to abandon the two" means to abandon the wisdom and principle of the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā) of the two vehicles, and to adopt the wisdom and principle of the twofold emptiness (dharma-pudgala-śūnyatā) of the one vehicle.
This is precisely ascending the ox-cart and reaching the place of treasure.

Regarding the statement that there are two meanings for "realizing the profound treatise," this is a brief indication. When Bian He presented the jade, it was as difficult to comprehend as it was for the King of Chu;
he did not recognize the excellence of its substance. Only Buddha-to-Buddha can know what is difficult to comprehend, even for the followers of the Two Vehicles.
It is to be measured.
As for the statement that it is "even more profound," it means that the wisdom of all Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable, such that it cannot be known by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
The gateway to that wisdom is also profoundly deep and immeasurable; [it cannot be known] by any śrāvakas...
This is something that even Pratyekabuddhas cannot know. Translators, intending to be concise, speak only of "extreme profundity" (*gambhīra*) regarding the principle (*tattva*).
However, this profundity on the level of the teaching (*śāsana*) is transformed into five difficulties; these five difficulties are themselves the profound.

That the two vehicles do not know it pertains solely to the teaching. To explain them together, the meaning is that while the two vehicles do not know it at the level of the teaching, they do reach [it] at the level of the principle.

The Master was clearly unaware. Since he does not yet understand even the coarse outlines of the teachings, how much less could he know the principle, which is far more profound? Indeed, he truly did not know.

Regarding what are called the "five profundities," if one now relies solely on the perspective of ultimate truth (*tattva*), the two characters for "profound" (*shen-shen*) must be distinguished as pointing toward the transcendent.
This explains the five kinds of profundity. Regarding the first, "profundity of meaning":
because there are distinctions in meaning directed toward True Suchness (*tathatā*), there are various names. One name is the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*);

it is also called the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) and the Reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*). It possesses manifold meanings such as permanence, bliss, self, and purity; thus, it is called the profundity of meaning.
Regarding the profundity of the two natures: this refers to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). It serves as the intrinsic nature of all phenomena and is eternally abiding and indestructible;
thus, it is called the profundity of essence.
Regarding the three types of internal realization: ordinary beings do not realize it at all, Śrāvakas realize it incompletely, and only the Buddha realizes it fully; therefore [it is profound].

It is called "profound" because it is realized only by fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*); other wisdoms, such as preparatory wisdom (*prayoga-jñāna*) and subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), do not realize it, for they do not directly apprehend it.

Regarding the profundity of the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*), they serve as the basis for both delusion and awakening. While ordinary beings are deluded regarding birth and death (*saṃsāra*), True Suchness (*tathatā*) likewise serves as their basis.

When deluded, it serves as the basis for sentient beings; when they awaken and realize it, they become sages, and thus this True Suchness also serves as the basis for awakening. Furthermore, another interpretation states:

it is called the *dharmadhātu* (Dharma-realm) because it serves as the basis for the twelvefold teaching; it is called *dharmatā* (Dharma-nature) because it serves as the basis for the ninety-four conditioned phenomena;
and it is called the "original source of all Buddhas" because it serves as the basis for the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya* of oneself and others.

Regarding the statement "the five unsurpassed profundities," because their essence is most supreme, this explains the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). That which is called "Great Enlightenment" (*mahābodhi*) is the meaning of "unsurpassed.
That which is "expounded" is the meaning of "profound. Regarding these five profundities, traditionally they have been understood solely according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
If one follows this interpretation, the first four profundities and the fifth, which is the realized [fruit], are [unconditioned].

The "Supreme Perfect Enlightenment" (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) and the nature of perfect enlightenment—true suchness (*tathatā*) is also called "enlightenment. It is solely the principle of true suchness;

its essence is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Later, it is designated as "Great. According to the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras* and various treatises, the fifth [topic], the profound and supreme perfect enlightenment, encompasses both bodhi and nirvāṇa, and both essence (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, according to the previous commentary by the Master:
Regarding the selection and rejection in the commentary: however, according to various teachings, among the five types of profundity, most consist solely of the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*).

Since the word "most" is used, it implies that a small portion also includes both the nature and the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). This refers to the first four profundities herein, which are exclusively the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*);

whereas the fifth, the unsurpassed profundity, encompasses both nature and characteristics—that is, four of them in their entirety and a small portion of one, which constitute the nature of wisdom, while the remaining portion does not.

This is the general characteristic. Question: Nirvāṇa is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and may thus be called "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*). But bodhi is conditioned; for what reason is it also called "unsurpassed"? Answer:
Because the nature of the means of realization and that which is realized are inseparable, they may both collectively be termed "unsurpassed.

The means of realization serves as the cause, while that which is realized serves as the fruit. Unsurpassed awakening (*anuttara-bodhi*) is unconditioned, whereas perfectly equal awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is conditioned.
(The former [the first five] rely exclusively on the understanding of True Reality).

As for the statement "if it includes the contemplation of illumination and so forth," this refers to the understanding that encompasses both nature and characteristics. If illumination is included, then the nature of wisdom and the characteristics of wisdom are combined and termed "profound.
The intention of the Sub-commentary is that although ancient masters took True Suchness alone as the five profundities, the present [explanation] additionally includes the nature of wisdom.
The characteristic of wisdom (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*). Taken together, these are called the five profound depths.
Regarding the statement that "their meaning is profound" and so forth: "meaning" refers to functional utility. The essence of *tathatā* (suchness) is extremely subtle;

yet, when it encounters fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), it possesses the functional utility of severing delusions and realizing the truth. Having directly realized the essence of *tathatā*, it then turns back toward...
The superior wisdom explains the profound efficacy; this is called the profundity of name and meaning, which is the characteristic of wisdom.

As for what is called the profundity of essence: True Suchness (tathatā) serves as the essential nature of all phenomena. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "From the root of non-abiding, all dharmas are established.
Only Buddhas and Buddhas can exhaustively fathom this; thus it is called the profundity of essence. This refers to the transformative body of True Suchness.
It is profoundly deep; this is the second nature of wisdom (*jñāna*).
Regarding the statement that it is "deeply realized within" (*pratyātma-adhigama*) and so forth: although space is vast and infinite, it cannot be fully illuminated by the light of the sun.
Since space is boundless, the sunlight likewise becomes boundless. This refers to the realization of suchness (*tathatā*) through preparatory wisdom (*prayoga-jñāna*).
It is not attained. Subsequent wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) does not realize it. The two vehicles and bodhisattvas have partial realization;
their internal realization is limited and cannot be called "profound. Only the Tathāgata’s fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) realizes it exhaustively.

Yet, regarding this very wisdom that is capable of realization, one speaks of a functional capacity, which is termed "internal realization is profound. This is the characteristic of wisdom. Question: Is this [wisdom] the same as the first [wisdom]? Both are...

Regarding "Right Knowledge" (samyag-jñāna): what is the distinction between these two dharmas? Answer: The former refers to the functional application of wisdom (*jñāna*) in its superior sense; the latter refers to the vastness of the essence (*svabhāva*) of wisdom.
As for the phrase "relying upon the profound," it means that [this wisdom] serves as the basis for all conditioned and unconditioned, *saṃkhyeya*-fold myriad virtues, and for all [phenomena].
The Buddha is the basis (*āśraya*). Question: Since this fourth [basis] and the second are both truly existent, how are they distinguished? Answer:

The former refers to being the essential nature (*svabhāva*) and the root of qualities for all phenomena; this present fourth refers to being the support (*āśraya*) for all phenomena. Therefore, they are distinct.
Regarding the phrase "unsurpassed and profound," its essence encompasses both nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "Asanga and others," one asks: upon what sacred teaching is it based that unsurpassed *bodhi* encompasses both nature and characteristics? The answer is:
the works of Asanga, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, and so forth.
Regarding the statement that the substance of these two kinds pervades all: among conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), bodhi is supreme, and its substance pervades all conditioned things;
nirvāṇa is supreme among unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*), and its substance pervades all unconditioned things.
This is the commentary master’s account of the original intent of the Tripitaka Master of the Tang Dynasty. The commentary master was a disciple of the Tripitaka Master.

His intention was to state that if one were to grasp only the supreme and profound emptiness—the true mark (lakṣaṇa)—it would be too narrow; therefore, one must also include contemplative insight (vipaśyanā).
This is what the commentary master has related as the fundamental intent of this sutra.

Regarding the meaning of "universal" (*sāmānya*): in terms of what is expressed (*vācya*), among the four types of wisdom, there are the nature of knowledge (*jñāna-svabhāva*) and the characteristics of knowledge (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*).

By means of these two, one understands the five profundities. If explained according to the universal meaning, the four types of wisdom that are expressed possess both the nature and the accompaniment of their objects;

each has its own meaning, substance, and realization based upon the four kinds of profundity. First, regarding the nature of wisdom, there are distinctions among myriad virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
First, its meaning is profoundly deep. Second, it serves as the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena; thus, its essence is profoundly deep.
This does not mean that its essential nature is to be taken as something static, neither arising nor ceasing—this is what is meant by the profundity of its essence.

Third, it is realized only by fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and cannot be accessed by other forms of cognition; thus, its realization is profoundly deep. Fourth, it serves as the support for all phenomena.
This is called the profundity of the basis (a single-layered explanation). First, it is the characteristic of wisdom;

because this characteristic possesses the functional utility of realizing the principle and severing delusions, it is called the profundity of meaning. Second, its essence is untainted (*anāsrava*); therefore, it is called the profundity of essence.
Third, because it is that which realizes, although the principle is universal, when wisdom realizes it, it merges with *tathatā* (suchness) like a box and its lid. Thus, it is profound.

It is called "profound realization" because it realizes the ultimate depth. Fourth, it is called "profound reliance" because it serves as the basis for myriad virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges (the second level of clarification).
It is called "profound meaning" because its accompanying wisdom possesses the sense of differentiation. It is called "profound essence" because each possesses its own intrinsic nature.
It is called "profound realization" because it realizes the principle in common with fundamental wisdom. Conditioned and unconditioned phenomena each...
It has an essence; thus its essence is profound. Because it is that which is realized and known by the wisdom of the fundamental and subsequent [stages], its realization is profound.
Because it serves as the basis for all meanings, its basis is profound (the threefold understanding). It is the object of wisdom; "object" refers to the differentiation of meanings.

Because it differentiates manifold meanings, its meaning is profound. Because it possesses a distinct essence as both conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), its existence is profound.

The essence is profoundly deep because it is that which is realized; since it is realized and penetrated by the wisdom of the Buddhas alone, exhausting its very source and bottom, it is called "profound depth of realization.

The qualities and dharmas of all Buddhas rely upon one another; this is called "profound depth of dependence" (the explanation of the fourfold understanding of the upper section, concerning the meaning of "penetration," is now complete).
Regarding the statement "the nature of wisdom, its characteristics, and so forth": first, the nature of wisdom corresponds to the profundity of meaning;

second, the characteristics of wisdom correspond to the profundity of essence; third, the companions of wisdom correspond to the profundity of realization; fourth, the objects of wisdom correspond to the profundity of the basis.
Regarding the phrase "only the unsurpassed, profound, etc.": "only the unsurpassed and profound" refers to the Great Bodhi (Mahābodhi), as it is the locus of all supreme virtues;

thus, it does not correspond to the meanings of the four types of wisdom discussed previously. While the previous [section] concerned the realization of the essential nature and its basis, this section discusses the four profundities in terms of their relative superiority and inferiority, correlating them with the four wisdoms that take the nature, the companions, and the objects as their respective domains, while encompassing the fifth, the unsurpassed profundity.
Bodhi and nirvāṇa are exclusively superior; therefore, they are not assigned to the four types of wisdom (*prajñā*), as the four wisdoms are inferior.

Because the unsurpassed and profound is the sovereign of all virtues, it is comprehensive: it acts as the sovereign within the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) sphere and among the conditioned, and it acts as the sovereign within the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) sphere and among the unconditioned. Bodhi is the sovereign of the conditioned, while nirvāṇa is the unconditioned.
Master, the meaning is that if one speaks solely of the upward direction toward Bodhi and Nirvana, then one fully explains the unsurpassed profundity; this is entirely absent elsewhere.
If one were to speak of "profundity" in a general sense, it would not preclude the presence of the other four types of wisdom in total. Only the unsurpassed profundity is the primary subject.
The remaining four [aspects of] profundity are designated as "profound" in accordance with the wisdom of others; they are not the primary subject itself.

Regarding the statement, "Furthermore, it is not that which is illustrated by the metaphors," etc.: the preceding explanation of the meaning of profundity, which provided three types of interpretations for the meaning of profundity, was entirely the Master of the Commentary’s own exposition of the treatise.
Now, these final two lines below represent the Master’s own personal intention in explaining profundity.
These are two words that cannot be illustrated by worldly things; therefore, it is said that they are "that which cannot be illustrated by metaphors.

When not contemplated, discursive thought ceases; when not deliberated upon, speech is lost. When speech is lost and thought has ceased, no metaphor can illustrate it; therefore, it is called "profoundly deep."

Question: Regarding the fifth profundity, why is it not correlated with the four types of wisdom? Answer: Within this unsurpassed profundity, both the nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are fully present.

Because it is the primary subject of the qualities (*guṇa*), it is not merely that which is illustrated by metaphors; rather, it simultaneously manifests the two entities of nature and characteristics.

This differs from the previous four [profundities], where there was nature without characteristics, or characteristics without nature; here, in this unsurpassed [profundity], both nature and characteristics are manifested together.
Therefore, they are not individually correlated. Question: Are the preceding four kinds not themselves the stage of fruition (*phala*)?
Why then do you speak only of "unsurpassed profundity"? Answer: To speak according to the ultimate reality, these five profundities all have wisdom as their precursor.

Since the four kinds also pertain to both cause and fruit, their "unsurpassed profundity" exists solely in the stage of fruition; thus, they are not separately correlated. The meaning of this single phrase is...
The remaining profound and collective virtues are the masters [of these qualities], and therefore they are not individually correlated.
As for the preceding explanation of "profound" and so forth, this is the Master of the Commentary’s exegesis based solely on the meaning of the scriptural text;
it is explained according to one particular principle, referring exclusively to the dimension of principle (*tattva*), wherein it is said that the wisdom of all Buddhas is profound and immeasurable.
Regarding the gate of wisdom (*jñāna-mukha*), it does not speak of anything above it as being profound or immeasurable.

As for the phrase "interpreting the sūtras according to the śāstra," the gate of wisdom used to interpret the sūtras according to the śāstra likewise possesses five profundities; this is the interpretation of the masters of the śāstras.

If one follows the literal text of the sūtra, the two characters "profound" (*śen-shen*) are the general term; they refer exclusively to what is described as "profound" upon the basis of the principle of wisdom.

"Profound meaning" (*gambhīrārtha*) is a general term. If distinguished specifically, it applies to both the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*) and the principle (*tattva*); in both cases, the two characters "profound" (*shen-shen*) should be present. Question:
How is there "profundity" in the direction of the teaching (*śāsana*)? Answer: The meaning of "profound" refers precisely to the five difficulties (*pañca-praśna*).
According to the intent of the scriptural text, for the sake of the smoothness of the phrasing, the first phrase already contains "profound"; it cannot be [applied] to the subsequent phrase.
It is repeated here for the purpose of reformulating it as the "Five Difficulties. Furthermore, the previous explanation by the treatise author regarding wisdom stated:

first, its essence is subtle; second, it is difficult to comprehend. The subsequent explanation concerning the gate of teaching likewise states: its essence is subtle and difficult to comprehend. The sūtra author [focuses] on the principle of emptiness.

Regarding the term "profound" (*gambhīra*): this is the general statement. Question: Since it has already been established that there is profundity throughout the entire teaching, where in the text is "profundity" presented as a specific category?

Answer: The commentary cites the text: "The *āgama* is profound. This refers specifically to the five difficulties (the former explaining the upward profundity of wisdom, and the latter explaining the upward immeasurability of wisdom).
Regarding the phrase "immeasurable and so forth": among the five kinds of wisdom, one is the teaching that expresses (the *nirukta*), while four are the principles expressed (the *lakṣya*).

Here, "immeasurable" refers specifically to the four wisdoms as the principles expressed. According to the intention of the treatise, "immeasurability" belongs specifically to the principles expressed, whereas the "gate of wisdom" belongs specifically to the teaching that expresses. Furthermore, the profound depth of wisdom is also its function; it is wisdom.
The upward aspect of immeasurability is also its function (the latter point follows the commentary). First, the essence of the nature of wisdom is all-pervasive; therefore, it is called immeasurable.

Second, the characteristics and functions of wisdom are broad; therefore, they are called immeasurable. Since the reality realized is already pervasive throughout the dharma-realm, the wisdom that realizes it is likewise boundless.
Like a box and its lid, there is nowhere it does not pervade; therefore, its function is said to be broad. Third, the companions of wisdom... [total]...
Encompassing the myriad virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, it takes wisdom as its companion; thus, it is "endowed with name and virtue.

Regarding the four objects of wisdom—conditioned and unconditioned, empty or existent, and the objects of the ultimate and conventional truths—it pervades the ten directions; therefore, it is called "vast in phenomena" (*dharmavipula*). "Vast" means "much."

The first three [categories] establish the "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) by focusing on the upward-directed function of the essence of wisdom (*jñāna*). The latter one establishes it as "immeasurable" by focusing on the vastness of the essence of the dharma and its objective sphere (*viṣaya*).
Regarding the statement "like space, it is limitless," Zhangjing says: "The nature of wisdom is such that its essence is all-pervading, like space. Wisdom...
The characteristic of wisdom (*prajñā-lakṣaṇa*) is expansive and limitless; its companion, wisdom itself, is fully endowed with virtues, and these virtues are infinite in number.

The sphere of wisdom (*prajñā-viṣaya*) consists of the vast and manifold phenomena (*dharma*), which are ultimately inexhaustible. Furthermore, it is said that just as space is limitless, both nature (*prakṛti*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) correspond to this.
Nature, when directed upward, is likewise like space and limitless; characteristics, when directed upward, are likewise like space and limitless.
It is limited. Furthermore, as the accompanying objects ascend toward virtue, their number is infinite and reaches no end or conclusion.
The number of virtues accompanying wisdom is infinite and reaches no end or conclusion. The number of objects accompanying the virtues of wisdom is infinite and reaches no end or conclusion.

The commentary concludes by stating: "Therefore, they are called 'immeasurable' (*apramāṇa*). Among the five kinds of wisdom discussed previously, the commentator relies on the four wisdoms according to what they signify.

The previous correlation was based on profundity; now, it is correlated with the immeasurable. This also relies on the four wisdoms to ascend toward the ultimate, correlating them with the pervasiveness of essence, the breadth of function, the completeness of virtue, and the vastness of the Dharma.

Regarding the statement, "However, now we speak only of equality," the Master of the Commentary previously, in his explanation of the section on profundity, stated in the second interpretation: "If..."
The union of the wisdom of simultaneous observation with its nature and characteristics is called "profound. Taking either the nature or the characteristics alone is also called "profound.

Now, this explanation of the immeasurable aspects also adopts the second interpretation. "Essence" (*tǐ*) refers to the essence of principle; "virtue" (*dé*) refers to the myriad virtues. Lù says: "Essence and virtue correspond to the nature of wisdom.
The nature of wisdom is the essence of all phenomena, possessing merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; this is termed 'essence and virtue. 'Function' (*zuòyòng*)."
This corresponds to the aspect of wisdom (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*). Because it possesses the functional activity of penetrating principle and realizing the truth, it is called "activity" (*vṛtti*).

Question: Why is it called "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*)? Answer: Regarding the nature of wisdom (*jñāna-svabhāva*), its essential qualities (*deha-guṇa*) are immeasurable; thus it is called immeasurable. Regarding the aspect of wisdom, its functional activity is immeasurable; thus it is called immeasurable.
Regarding its essential qualities, its virtues are complete and its phenomena are vast, like the boundlessness of space; thus it is called immeasurable. As for its activity...
Because its upward-reaching virtue is infinite and its ultimate completion is inexhaustible, it is named "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*).
Mǔ states: "The essence is pervasive, the function is broad, and the Dharma is vast; being equal to space—these four phrases are all the meaning of 'immeasurable.

These eight phrases, when explained collectively one by one, do not depart from immeasurability; each and every one is itself immeasurable. This commentary follows this collective explanation in its arrangement.
The *Jin* (金) [commentary] relies on a different principle; thus, there is no contradiction between them.

Regarding the statement that "all possess the infinite," one asks: why are both "the infinite" (*wuxian*) and "the inexhaustible" (*wujinqjin*) applied to both "nature" (*xing*) and "characteristics" (*xiang*)?

The answer is given in the sub-commentary (*shu*) with the words "all possess," etc. Lu says: in the sub-commentary, "one" refers to the infinite, while "two" refers to the number of virtues being inexhaustible.
Exhausted. The three [sections] conclude without end; the single phrase "like space" is omitted for brevity. Only the three phrases accord with the principle, though there should be four.
Regarding the statement that "its gates are profound and also twofold," the *Commentary on the Sūtra* says: "In the past, the words of the Three Teachings penetrated the ultimate aim of the One.
The *Opening of the Middle* says: "Know that wisdom resides in the teaching; the teaching is itself the gate. Since wisdom is profoundly deep, the gate is likewise so.

It is difficult to comprehend. Furthermore, it is said: "The inner sanctum must be reached through the gateway; the realization of wisdom is truly manifested through the teachings (naming and instruction).
Without a gateway, one cannot enter the inner sanctum; lacking the teachings, wisdom cannot be realized. Is not the meaning of a "gateway" precisely this?
The "gateway of wisdom" is explained by the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound. This gateway is profoundly deep, and it also...
There are two meanings. First, the essence is wondrous; this is like Bian He presenting his jade—the essence itself is wondrous. Second, it is difficult to comprehend;
because the King of Chu did not recognize that the essence was wondrous, there are five difficulties regarding the teaching. These five difficulties constitute the meaning of profundity.

That it is difficult to comprehend means that the followers of the Two Vehicles cannot fathom it. According to the Sanskrit original, it should be stated in full: "The gate of its wisdom is profound."
It is immeasurable, beyond the knowledge of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Its teaching is coarse and manifest, like yellow leaves that cannot be recognized as gold;
its realization of principle is profoundly deep, like fine purple-gold that is difficult to discern. Regarding the true nature of an infant’s conduct:
it relies upon this—just as when a child is crying, the mother passes a bar of pure gold to him, yet he continues to cry even more.
Much later, he gave me a single yellow leaf, whereupon I laughed with joy and remained silent. For forty years, those who followed the Śrāvaka path had cherished the artificial and disliked the real;
when I preached the Mahāyāna Dharma to them, it was as if a child were afraid of pure gold.

At the assemblies of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, they were like the deaf or the intoxicated. Yet, at the assemblies of the various Mahāyāna sūtras, I was present in the audience, though my body grew weary.
They become indolent, just as a child fears real gold. The Tathāgata preaches the Dharma of the Two Vehicles for them, using only provisional names to guide all sentient beings.
Having heard this, those of the Two Vehicles joyfully practice it, just as a child loves yellow leaves.
When the commentators cite the Sanskrit sūtras, they speak of the "five difficulties" only in relation to the gateways of the teaching (*śāsana-mukha*). This has two intended meanings:
first, because there are five kinds of profundity in the wisdom that is expressed (*lakṣya*), there are five difficulties in the teaching that expresses it (*lakṣaṇa*);
second, because śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), and others do not understand these five kinds of wisdom, there are five [difficulties] regarding the teaching.

Regarding the phrase "there are also two meanings": because the preceding realization of the profound already possesses two meanings, and the gate of wisdom likewise possesses two meanings, it is said that "there are also [two meanings]."
Regarding the phrase "The Discourse quotes the Sūtra," etc.: it asks, "What are called the five difficulties? It answers: "The Discourse quotes the Sūtra," and so forth.

This means that because the wisdom expressed (*vācya*) is profound, its expression (*vācaka*)—namely, the five difficulties—is likewise profound. (The preceding [section] concludes the brief introduction.)

Regarding the statement "the first is due to the objects [of expression] and so forth," there are two meanings in the commentary. First, because the five kinds of profundity pertain to the expressed meaning (*vācya*), there are five difficulties regarding the teaching.
Second, because it is unknown by the wisdom of ordinary beings and sages, there are five difficulties regarding the teaching itself. Now, as for the first point:
because the expressed meaning contains infinite meanings like grains of dust, it is called "profound"; the expressive teaching (*vācaka*) then accords with its gateway.

It is difficult to see. That which is difficult to see means that the followers of the Two Vehicles cannot fathom its origins within this teaching; therefore, it is called "difficult to see. This refers to the insight (*darśana*).

Regarding the phrase "secondly, by way of the essence of wisdom": because the essence of wisdom is profound upon the reality (*tattva*) that is explained, it is called "the essence is extremely profound. This refers to the expressive [words].
The teaching that elucidates this gate is difficult to awaken to. As for the mental discourse, the two types of wisdom of the Tathāgata are not perceived by those of the Two Vehicles;
thus, regarding this gateway of the teaching, it is likewise difficult to awaken to. Since what is elucidated is not understood, the means of elucidation is also difficult to comprehend.

Regarding the statement that "the three are realized internally through wisdom": this means that within the reality that is expressed, there exists the essence of wisdom; because its internal realization is profound, its gateway is difficult to know.
Right wisdom realizes suchness (tathatā), truly accords with all things, and its essence is identical to the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). It is non-different from reality.
For this reason, the followers of the two vehicles cannot understand it through their own doctrinal gateways.
Regarding the statement that "the four are based on wisdom": because the principles they express serve as the basis for all meanings, these gateways are difficult to understand.

The teaching expresses wisdom, and this wisdom is profoundly deep, being the very essence of the Tathāgata; thus, the two vehicles do not comprehend it, and so these gateways of expression are truly difficult to understand.
However, the underlying principles within the teaching are easily manifested. Since even the profound principles are difficult to clarify, how much more so is this [wisdom]!
Because there is much confusion and error regarding the causes of the teaching, the gateway of the teaching is difficult to understand.
As for the statement that it is "fifthly, unsurpassed by way of wisdom," this is because the principles to be expounded—namely, *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*—are unsurpassed and profound.

Its gate is difficult to enter. Because even the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha), though they contemplate the sixteen aspects with discernment, cannot take it as an object and thus do not know it, it is called "difficult to enter.

"Entering" means understanding. Question: For what reason are these five profundities specifically assigned to the five difficulties? Answer: It is because one wishes to reveal that [the profundity] arises from the depth of the expression;

since these are the gates of the teaching (*deśanā*) that expresses them, they are said to be "difficult to see," "difficult to realize," and so forth. Question: How is it that the expressed meaning (*vācya*)...

Regarding wisdom (*prajñā*), it is described only as "profound" (*gambhīra*) and not as "difficult to see," "difficult to realize," and so forth. Regarding the teaching that serves as the means of expression (*vyañjana-dharma*), it is described only as "difficult to see" and so forth, and not as "profound.

Answer: According to the treatises, "profundity" also applies to the teaching as a means of expression. However, the scriptural text emphasizes the predominant aspect and thus speaks only of wisdom as being difficult to see, difficult to realize, and so forth;
it merely describes the expressive teaching by citing what is easy to understand as a contrast to what is difficult. This refers to the teaching within the *piṭaka* (the scriptural collection).
Consciousness itself does not even know the principle that it expresses; that principle is profound, obscure, and remote, making it clearly difficult to fully comprehend.
One can only speak of its difficulty to perceive and realize by means of the expressive gateways [of language], such as "awakening" and so forth.

The phrase "teaching the five difficulties and so forth" serves as a conclusion. It refers to teaching the aforementioned five difficulties by specifically correlating them with the five kinds of profound wisdom.
In the current Qin edition of the sutra, there are only two [difficulties]: "difficult to understand" and "difficult to enter."

The statement, "Furthermore, there are two types of wisdom: first, that of ordinary beings, and second, that of noble ones," represents the second point. Regarding the first, "manifest" refers to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of an object before one;
knowing it in accordance with the object and apprehending the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the phenomenon is called direct perception. Ordinary manifest wisdom does not know this.
It is called "difficult to see.

Regarding "inferential knowledge" (*anumāna-jñāna*): it is the process of inferring a prior object; this is termed "inference" (*anumāna*). When one compares this with that—such as seeing smoke and so forth—it is called inferential knowledge.
That which is not known by such inferential knowledge is called "difficult to realize."
Regarding the term "noble wisdom" (āryajñāna): this refers here to the minor noble ones of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha), and not to great bodhisattvas or Tathāgatas.
Regarding the term "with outflows" (sāsrava): that which is not known by wisdom with outflows is called "difficult to know."

Regarding the statement that there are two types of untainted (*anāsrava*) [wisdom]: first, the fundamental [wisdom], and second, the subsequently attained [wisdom]. Not knowing through the initial untainted fundamental wisdom is called "difficult to understand" (*durvigāhya*).
Not knowing through the subsequently attained untainted wisdom is called "difficult to enter" (*durgama*). "Entering" refers to realization and understanding. Question:

The fundamental wisdom of the two vehicles internally realizes the principle of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), yet they do not know it from the standpoint of the teaching; this is called "difficult to understand. As for the Bodhisattvas... [the text continues].
The fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) of emptiness internally realizes the principle of the two kinds of emptiness; how could it possibly know the teachings that express [that principle]?
Since it does not take external objects as its conditions, why further reproach it for not knowing? Answer: This is explained by way of a successive transmission.

The fundamental wisdom of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas doubly realizes the principle of the two kinds of emptiness; this principle is precisely that which is expressed (*vācya*). Since the fundamental wisdom of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas knows that which is expressed...

"Explanatory" (詮) refers, by contrast, to the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, which also cognizes the teachings that serve as the means of expression (*abhidhāna*).

The fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) of the two vehicles realizes only the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and does not realize the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*); this is precisely why those of the two vehicles do not know that which is expressed (*abhidheya*).

Since the fundamental wisdom of those of the two vehicles does not know what is expressed by the Mahāyāna, it serves by contrast to reveal the subsequently attained wisdom of those of the two vehicles.

Furthermore, they do not understand the teachings that express [the truth]. Question: Do the followers of the Two Vehicles possess the post-attainment wisdom (prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna) that is untainted (anāsrava)?
If you grant that they do, how is it that the "sheep" and the "deer" do not ascend? If you say they do not, how can it be said that this [wisdom] is unknown by post-attainment wisdom?
If this is so, what can be said of not knowing it? The answer is that, according to reality, it does exist. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only), fascicle five, states:
"That is to say, the defiled manas has, from time immemorial, functioned as a subtle, uniform, and spontaneous flow; it cannot be suppressed or extinguished by any of the mundane paths."

The noble paths of the three vehicles possess the sense of "suppressing" and "extinguishing. This is because the true understanding of selflessness contradicts the grasping at a self. The commentary explains:

the untainted right knowledge (*anāsrava-samyagjñāna*) of the three vehicles suppresses [the afflictions] according to their respective capacities, as it contradicts the attachments of the two vehicles; therefore, it does not merely suppress them.

Furthermore, it is said that when subsequent untainted knowledge (*prṣṭhalabdha-anāsrava-jñāna*) manifests, it is the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of that [right knowledge], and thus it also contradicts this [grasping]. The commentary explains: this subsequently attained knowledge...
It is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*). This is induced by the contemplation of the two emptinesses (*dvaya-śūnyatā*) and, as appropriate, opposes the attachments of the two vehicles.

Therefore, according to this text, there exists untainted subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*). However, when practitioners of the two vehicles realize the principle, the subsequently attained wisdom arises through impact;

because it takes conventional designations (*prajñapti*) as its object, its scope of objects is not broad or pervasive. Thus, it is said that in the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), there is no untainted subsequently attained wisdom.
Furthermore, the *Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta* states: "All śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, by means of their untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), cannot conceive of or know its limit.
Thus we know that the two vehicles possess post-attainment untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). If this is so, how do you know it is not original wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*)?

Answer: Original wisdom exclusively takes the internal as its object; it does not take external objects as its domain. If this is so, how do you resolve the previous objection? Answer: [It is resolved by] the Dharma...

In the *Huayan jing shu* (Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra), it is stated that those of indeterminate nature (*aniyata-gotra*) who turn their minds toward the Mahāyāna do so in order to seek the Buddha-wisdom; they therefore conceal their subsequently attained cognition (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) and block off that [Hinayāna] mind.

This is like the instruction of a physician who commands that both [the disease and its cause] be severed. Thus, it is said that while the sheep and deer carts have names, they do not actually ascend [to the destination].

Regarding the phrase "only [the term] 'etcetera' (*ādi*) in this present sutra," one asks the Master Vasubandhu, who commented upon the Sanskrit original: "In the gateway of the teaching, there are five difficulties;
I do not yet know how many of these difficulties are fully contained within this sutra. The commentary answers: "In this present sutra, etc.

First, that which is unknown to non-outflow wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) is called "difficult to understand" (*durvigāhya*). Later, that which is unknown to non-outflow wisdom is called "difficult to enter" (*durgama*).

Regarding the statement "the term 'all' generally reveals both realization and teaching," the Master of the Treatise explains the meaning of "not knowing. "Realization" refers to the wisdom that realizes the signified meaning;
"teaching" refers to the pedagogical gateways that signify it. Previously, the author of the treatise also stated that [the nature of] realization is difficult to comprehend.

Regarding the phrase "also said to be difficult to understand in terms of the teaching," this refers to not knowing the meaning. Now, in the Qin edition of the sutra, there is only one instance of "not knowing" occurring in the context of the teaching;
therefore, it is said to be a general manifestation. If it were divided into two locations, it would constitute a specific manifestation.
The phrase "all śrāvakas and so forth" introduces the passage concerning their lack of knowledge.
The phrase "only a Buddha can know" is the conclusion. It means that because this is an object of knowledge known only by a Buddha, it is not known by those of the two vehicles.

Regarding the statement that the Buddha now offers praise: one asks why the World-Honored One does not directly reveal the teaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, but instead first praises wisdom and subsequently praises the profundity of the gateway.
The commentary answers: "The Buddha’s present praise, etc., serves to express the intent behind proclaiming these two kinds of profundity.
This is intended to cause Śāriputra and the others to give rise to doubt; for if they did not give rise to doubt, there would be no [need for the subsequent] chapter.
The third section, "The Division on the Doubts of the Great Assembly," concerns Śāriputra and others who originally clung to their own vehicle as ultimate.

Such clinging is difficult to remove, whereas doubt is easy to dispel. This is why the Tathāgata turned their minds from clinging into doubt, causing Śāriputra and the others to give rise to doubt and request the teaching of the Dharma.
This continues until the two kinds of profundity are praised, at which point it is confirmed that they indeed possess doubt. [End of] Sūtra.
It is said: At that time, among the great assembly were various śrāvakas, arhats whose outflows were exhausted, and others who harbored doubts, thinking:
"For what reason does the World-Honored One now so earnestly praise the foremost skillful means of the Buddhas? This was their doubt regarding the wisdom of the former Buddhas.
That which is spoken has an intention that is difficult to discern; this refers to the doubt regarding the gate of his wisdom, which is difficult to understand and difficult to enter.
"Doubt" here refers to the doubt concerning the two preceding [sections on] profundity. "Please explain" likewise merely requests an explanation of those two profundities.

The three stages of "opening, showing, awakening, and entering" constitute the wisdom of all Buddhas, while the provisional teachings given over the three weeks constitute the gate of that wisdom. Therefore...

Regarding the Buddha’s praise of the two profundities, the treatise itself explains: it is for the sake of causing the great assembly to give rise to respect and yearning, desiring to hear the Tathāgata’s teaching. Second, it says: "Praising the two profundities" is the heading.

Regarding the phrase "to speak for the sake of those below, etc.," the question is: Why are both [aspects] praised as profound, and why is wisdom praised first? The commentary answers: "For the sake of those below, etc.
Praising wisdom is because it serves as the basis for gradually teaching the One Vehicle—the true Dharma attained by the Buddha—through the three successive turnings (the Three Wheels).
Therefore, the profundity of wisdom is praised first; that is to say, this wisdom is precisely the reality of the Three Wheels.

Regarding the two fruits of bodhi and nirvāṇa, the first assembly revealed the three stages of opening, showing, and awakening. These lead to the two supreme fruits, and even further to the true principle of the jewel-treasury in the third assembly.

This is why he first praised the profundity of his wisdom; it was intended to indicate that the Dharma attained by the Buddha, which he was about to explain below, is exceedingly profound and difficult to understand. Therefore, he first extolled his wisdom.

Regarding the phrase "the words manifest what is praised below," this praises the teaching gate (*śāsana-mukha*). It serves as the reason for the gradual unfolding of the provisional [teachings] in the three subsequent turnings of the wheel.

Because one intends to explain what follows below, the underlying intent of the discourse is difficult to discern; thus, the reality of the Dharma proceeds gradually, which is why the depth of the gate is praised first.
Question: Why is the depth of wisdom praised first, and the depth of the gate praised later? Answer: [It is because of] joy and revulsion.
Because they differ, [the Buddha] first praises wisdom to cause the śrāvakas to rejoice, and later explains the gates of teaching to cause them to feel weary [of their limited state].

Furthermore, because taking up and discarding differ, he first praises the profundity of wisdom to cause them to take it up, and later praises the profundity of the teaching to cause them to discard [their former views].

This serves as the preliminary sequence for the provisional teachings of the two vehicles expounded in the three subsequent weeks. That is to say, within this first week, it is said: "There is neither two nor three. The second...

The second turning of the wheel states: "The two vehicles of the sheep and the deer exist in name only, but lack substantial reality. The third turning states: "That great city mentioned previously was created by my transformation;
it was spoken of as two merely because they were places of rest. Since this is a provisional teaching, it is intended to induce weariness [with saṃsāra].
Regarding the statement "it is not so; it should only be [understood as] 'equal' and so forth": this refers to comprehending through the profound wisdom and the profound teachings that preceded it.
Thus, herein one understands the various characters for "Buddha" (*buddha*). By synthesizing these two characters, one understands the various characters.

One understands the character for "Buddha" by means of the myriad virtues that constitute a Buddha. A single Buddha is constituted by the myriad virtues; a single Buddha is formed by the myriad virtues. A single Buddha is formed by the myriad virtues.
The Buddha explains the character "Buddha" (*buddha*). First, a single Buddha is constituted by ten thousand virtues; all Buddhas likewise take up these ten thousand virtues to form their bodies.
Second, it means that the World-Honored One praises the profundity of wisdom. Within wisdom, there are five kinds of wisdom.

Within the causes of wisdom, the teachings that express it are already subsumed; thus, when one praises wisdom as being fully understood (*parijñāta*), the gateways of the teachings are also praised as being fully understood.

Why, then, is it necessary to separately praise the gateways of the teachings apart from wisdom? Answer: The World-Honored One did so because he wished to give rise to the explanation of provisional means (*upāya*) through a gradual process.

It was precisely for the sake of giving rise to the explanation of provisional means through a gradual process that he separately praised the gateway of wisdom. If it were not so, [he would have] merely...
If one merely praises wisdom, it is immediately attained; why then emphasize that the gate is profound?
As for the meaning of the phrase "Why is this so?": it refers to the discourse on the Buddha’s wisdom, up to and including the gates of wisdom, which I have attained.
I have attained liberation; I have immediately attained the wisdom of all Buddhas and realized the profound. Furthermore, I have attained the teachings of skillful means:
the Śrāvakas attain the teaching of the Four Noble Truths, and the Pratyekabuddhas attain the teaching of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination.
Why, then, do you now say that both of these are unknown to the Two Vehicles? What is the reason for this ignorance?

Furthermore, the meaning of this inquiry is as follows: [The questioner] thinks that if the wisdom of all Buddhas is called "profound" because it is not yet attained by those of the Two Vehicles, then within the gateway of wisdom, how can the provisional teachings of the Two Vehicles—whom I have already mastered—be called profound? This is the intent of the inquiry.

Regarding what is called "attained liberation": it merely involves abandoning the *paricchinna-bhava* (segmented existence), severing the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), and realizing the principle of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

Although these are the same [as in the Lesser Vehicle], the Great Liberation of the Great Dharma-body of Mahāprajñā—the wisdom that is identical with the wisdom-aspect and whose nature is the Dharma-body—is that which you have not yet attained; you certainly do not yet know it.

Regarding the terms "receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting," one is able to receive [the teaching] through faith; one is able to uphold it through mindfulness. To open the text is called "reading" (pāṭha);
to recite from memory is called "recitation" (svādhyāya). These constitute three of the ten dharmas.
Regarding the statement "this reveals [the case of] the Blessed One and others": for three great *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, they made offerings to twenty-six *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* Buddhas;
during the stages prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*), they made offerings to five *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* Buddhas; from the first ground to the sixth ground, to six *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* Buddhas;

from the seventh ground to the ninth ground, to seven *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* Buddhas; and on the tenth ground, they made offerings to eight *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* Buddhas. Having thus encountered many Buddhas over such a long period of time...
To receive and uphold it accumulates merit beyond the reach of thought; therefore, it is called "profound.

As for the statement that it is not like the brief [teachings] of the two vehicles and so forth: for Śrāvakas, those of sharp faculties require three lifetimes, while those of dull faculties require sixty kalpas;
for Pratyekabuddhas, those of sharp faculties require four lifetimes, while those of dull faculties require one hundred kalpas. Since these timeframes are not remote, such encounters are also rare.
Therefore, even upholding [the teachings] and so forth are not termed "profound. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, chapter twenty-three, states:
"For those who have planted the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*), at the very fastest, they will attain liberation in three lifetimes:

in the second life they will give rise to the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), and in the third life they will enter the state of a noble one (*ārya*) and eventually attain liberation. Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, chapter sixty, states: "By means of the Śrāvaka vehicle..."
If one practices for the longest duration, it takes sixty *kalpas*, at which point the fruit will necessarily be realized. The commentary explains:

"For those who practice with fierce intensity, it takes three or six lifetimes, or up to sixty *kalpas*; if it is not otherwise, it may take a thousand *kalpas*. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vol. 7) states:
Those who have planted the factors conducive to liberation may wander through birth and death for as long as a thousand kalpas. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* also states:
"Even for a śrāvaka of the most diligent and sharp faculties, it takes at most three births; the next [category] sixty kalpas; and the next, immeasurable kalpas. Now, according to the preceding text:
Those of sharp faculties [attain it] in three lifetimes; those of dull faculties, in sixty kalpas.
Regarding the merit and wisdom of the Buddhas, the *Ninth Chapter of the Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "The sublime practices cultivated are, in brief, of two kinds:
namely, merit (*puṇya*) and wisdom (*jñāna*). Furthermore, based on the six *pāramitās*, their general characteristics are both twofold; as for their specific characteristics, the first five are..."

Regarding merit (*puṇya*): the sixth [perfection] consists solely of wisdom (*prajñā*). Alternatively, the first three consist solely of merit, the sixth consists solely of wisdom, and the remaining two pertain to both.
According to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, the first three are the path of superior birth and are termed merit; the latter three are the path of definitive excellence and are termed wisdom.

Regarding the terms "pure" (*viśuddha*), "courageous" (*vīra*), and so forth: "courageous" indicates superior progress and distinguishes [this energy] from all defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*). "Firm" (*dhīra*) indicates purity and distinguishes it from the pure-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).

This explicitly reveals diligence (*vīrya*), because it is comprised solely within the nature of the wholesome (*kuśala*) and because it ensures that all virtuous deeds to be performed are brought to fulfillment.
*Fahua jing xuanzan yaoji*, Scroll Fifteen.
In the winter of the sixth year of the Qianfu era, the Bhikṣu Hongju of Kaiyuan Monastery in Wenzhou lectured on this text and transcribed it for offering.
Copied on the twenty-first day of the third month in the second year of the Shōgen era.

Written by Gyōen and others. May the merit [of this] continue through successive excellent and virtuous outflow-results, reaching to the end of the future, to benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings.
*Fahua jing xuanyan ya ji*, Scroll 16, Compiled by the Śramaṇa Xifu of Jingshui Temple.

Regarding "decisive fruition" (*guo jue*), ten matters are briefly cited as examples of decisive fruition: first, cutting one's own flesh to feed a hawk; second, casting oneself down for a starving [creature].
1. To tear out his heart as the Dharma; 2. To gouge out his eyes and give them to others; 3. To flay his skin to make paper; 4. To carve his bones to make pens;
5. To cut his face to make ink; 6. To grind his head to express gratitude to the King; 7. To light a thousand lamps with his arms; 8.
To burn his body as an offering—these ten deeds are truly difficult to accomplish. Because they were all performed for the sake of seeking the Dharma, they are called "resolute fruits" (*guo-jue*).
Regarding the statement "one who casts a single word into the fire": if one can cast their body into a fire-pit seven fathoms deep, I shall bestow the Dharma upon you.

Upon hearing this, the Bodhisattva was filled with joy and leaped for gladness. He reflected: "For the sake of the Dharma, I ought to remain even for a long time in the Avīci Hell and undergo immeasurable suffering in all the evil destinies;
how much more so when merely entering a human fire-pit? Thus he immediately—
"I have heard the Dharma; please speak it for me alone. Even if I must enter a pit of fire, I shall not consider it a hardship.
Furthermore, in the past, when the Buddha was the Rishi Jñānaprabha, he transformed himself into a hare and cast himself into a fire to seek the Dharma.
Regarding the phrase "giving up half of one's body": when the World-Honored One was first in the stage of the *saṃkhyeya* provisions, he acted as a youth in the Snowy Mountains;
for the sake of seeking half a verse, he gave up his entire body to five rākṣasīs.
Regarding the "mind of increase," there are two meanings. First, it refers to the mind that increases one's own merit.

For example, as with a great virtuous person of today who, being bound by reputation and status, fears that their name may not match their deeds and thus devotes themselves exclusively to performing wholesome acts; this is called "increasing oneself. Second, it refers to the far-reaching resonance of one’s own name.
When others hear of it, they come to admire their lofty conduct and, seeing the worthy, desire to emulate them, diligently cultivating wholesome acts; this is called "increase."
This is to praise the merits of others.

Regarding the phrase "by means of the dharmas to be accomplished," Xiu says: this refers to the nature of wisdom (*jñāna-svabhāva*) and *nirvāṇa*. This is something unprecedented, termed a "wonderful and sublime matter.

The mind capable of accomplishing this—the four wisdoms of enlightenment—is called the "wonderful and sublime mind. It is so named because it is derived from the wonderful and sublime principle that is realized.
This is the reason. The wisdom capable of realization is called "excellent" (*pranīta*). That which is spoken by the excellent is difficult to understand within the teaching;

thus, it is called the "severance of great wisdom. Body and function are distinguished: while one comprehends the conventional, the other realizes the ultimate, and because these are not contradictory, [they are unified].

Regarding the phrase "unsurpassed and profound," Yongtai says: "Excellence and subtlety" refers to the grasped and the grasper; the intent is to take the wisdom that realizes [the truth] as the grasper.
"Unsurpassed and profound" refers to the grasper and the grasped; the intent is to seek the principle realized, which is called the non-dual nature.
These meanings mutually illuminate one another, as they are taught so that realization may be attained. The first interpretation takes the grasper, while the latter interpretation takes the grasped.
Regarding the statement that "some teachings are difficult to understand," Xiu says: these all pertain to principle (*li*). Only a Buddha can know them; they are of profound meaning.
It is because of this profound principle that the teachings are subsequently expounded, and thus they are called "profound."
Regarding the phrase "entering the profound": "entering" means understanding. There are two aspects of the mind: first, entering by oneself as it naturally arises;

second, being able to lead others to enter through words, phrases, and sentences. The meaning is difficult to grasp, as for example when it is said that "all sentient beings shall all become Buddhas," yet one does not understand my intended meaning.

Regarding the statement that "the Buddha personally maintains [this]," Xiu says: "Such difficult matters as these are personally undertaken and sustained by the Buddha within his own person; because he sustains them, they are not lost.

Regarding the statement that "he is not the same as the non-Buddhists," it means that the Tathāgata’s principles concerning the causes and conditions of preaching the Dharma are expounded only after having realized them through direct personal realization.
[The Buddha] says: "Unlike the non-Buddhists, who cannot understand [this] themselves, how could they enable others to understand?

Regarding the statement that 'the principle of dependent origination is extremely equal,' the meaning of the principle of dependent origination is precisely the names, phrases, and sentences spoken by the Tathāgata.
This principle is exceedingly profound; the Buddha can personally realize it and also cause others to understand it, just as he transforms sentient beings."

From the beginning to the end, he expounds the Dharma for them according to their individual capacities, enabling them to attain the fruits of the Path; this is called the extremely profound teaching of the Dharma of causes and conditions.

Regarding what is called "teaching according to suitability," there are five aspects: first, knowing the time. When speaking to others, one must also know the proper occasion and not exceed the appropriate limit.
Second, knowing the place. For instance, one need not preach the Dharma in border regions or places where discipline is absent.
Third, because one knows the faculties, dispositions, and inclinations [of beings], and thus imparts the medicine according to their capacity, teaching in accordance with what is appropriate.
Fourth, if there are those who do not understand the profound and secret Dharma, one causes them to understand by employing worldly analogies.

Fifth, for those who are devoted to the extremely profound principle and have studied for a long time, one teaches the deep Dharma. Due to these five reasons, one teaches in accordance with what is appropriate; thus, the underlying intention is difficult to fathom.
It is known.

Regarding the statement "that which is performed and maintained": it is called "that which is performed" (*kṛtya*) because it benefits others externally; it is called "that which is maintained" (*dhāraṇa*) because it consists of internal qualities that benefit oneself.

That is to say, the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) for others constitute benefiting others and are thus called "that which is performed"; the [Enjoyment Body] for oneself...
The merit of self-benefit through one's own body continues until the end of the future, being uninterrupted and inexhaustible; this is called "sustaining" (sthiti-dhāraṇa).
However, because the bodies of śrāvakas generally do not exceed a lifespan of fifty or a hundred years, they lack the merit of sustaining their own self-benefit.
Furthermore, they are unable to extensively transform sentient beings; because they lack the activity of benefiting others, these are called "unshared" [qualities].

Although the śrāvakas and others deliver people—such that the tally sticks fill the stone chamber—this is still not considered much. It does not equal the infinite and boundless number of sentient beings delivered by the Tathāgata.

Regarding the statement that this is not the same as the Two Vehicles (*dvayāyānika*), Xiu says: "The practices of the Two Vehicles initiated through conditions based on the teachings, as well as those of beings born by transformation (*upapāduka*) and so forth, are called 'external activities.
If one realizes the principle to be realized, or upholds the scriptural teachings, the precepts, and so forth, these are called 'internal benefit and sustenance' (*adhyātma-arthasthiti*).
Although they perform such benefits, they are all narrow and limited, and thus are not called 'profound. In contrast, the Tathāgata’s external benefit consists in preaching the Dharma."

Through hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates, he extensively benefits all classes of beings. His internal benefit enables the realization of the unsurpassed, pure abiding in the *dharmadhātu*, possessing merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
this is called "profound depth. Furthermore, his external benefit consists of the perfection of altruistic conduct.
Because his internal benefit—the conduct of abiding—is the fulfillment of self-benefiting conduct, it is called "the profound depth of abiding."
Regarding the phrase "the foregoing general exposition," etc.: by means of the proximity to the Buddhas, it concludes that the upholding, receiving, reading, and reciting are profound.
Regarding the term "practice," it concludes that practice is profoundly deep. As the Sūtra says: "To fully practice all the immeasurable path-dharmas of the Buddhas."
Regarding "resolute fruit," this concludes the profundity of the practice that bears fruit; the Sūtra says, "valiant and energetic.
Regarding "the mind that increases merit," this concludes the profundity of the mind that increases merit; the Sūtra says, "his fame is heard everywhere."
Regarding the statement "the mind that realizes delightful and wondrous matters," this concludes the profundity of the mind that realizes delightful and wondrous matters. The Sūtra states:

"One accomplishes profound and unprecedented dharmas. Regarding the statement "accomplishing the unsurpassed dharma," this concludes the unsurpassed profundity. The Sūtra states: "As for dharmas that are difficult to understand, the Tathāgata is able [to realize them]."
"Knowing" refers to the difficulty of understanding what is taught according to suitability; this concludes the seventh profundity.
"The two vehicles do not comprehend" refers to the eighth profundity. These are established by the Buddha's accomplishment of the first four profundities.
The fifth and sixth are the causes; once the fruit is accomplished, the seventh profound [level] is taught externally for the sake of sentient beings.
Because the Buddha has preached the Dharma, the eighth profound [level] is that which cannot be known by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Question: How do these eight profundities correspond with the categories of teaching (śāsana), principle (yukti), practice (pratipatti), fruit (phala), and the two profundities?
How is this so? The answer is: the first and seventh are the teaching (*śāsana*); the sixth is the principle (*nyāya*); the second is the practice (*pratipatti*);
the fifth and eighth are the fruit (*phala*); and the third and fourth are the common application of the fruit. Regarding their mutual inclusion within the two profundities:
the first and seventh are the profundity of the *āgama*; the second is the profundity of practice; and all others are the profundity of realization (*adhigama*).

Regarding the statement, "How much more so is the Buddha’s wisdom not exceedingly profound?": this means that the eight types of profundity discussed above have only explained the gate of *prajñā* (wisdom), not *jñāna* (gnosis).
If even the gate of *prajñā* is itself exceedingly profound, how much more so is the Buddha’s *jñāna*; how could the followers of the two vehicles possibly fathom it?
Regarding the statement that the Tathāgata praises what has been realized and the Dharma taught: the sublime Dharma is that which is realized, and the Tathāgata is the one who realizes it;
the Dharma is that which is taught, and the body of the Tathāgata is that which can teach it.
Regarding the phrase "exclaiming that the Tathāgata is able to realize and able to teach," etc.: Question: The two types of profundity have already been explained previously.
Now, to again praise the merit of the Dharma-preacher—what is the intention behind this? Answer:

For forty years prior, the Śrāvakas clung to what they had attained as being identical to that of the World-Honored One, and they even clung to their own bodies as being no different from the Buddha’s. Since the dharmas they had attained were thus considered the same, they [clung to] the person who attained them as well.

The body, moreover, is not different [from the Tathāgata]. Previously, two types of profundity were praised to make known that the Dharma is distinct; now, the merit of the Dharma-preacher is praised to make known that one's own person is distinct from the Tathāgata.

Regarding the statement "citing the sūtras and so forth based on the śāstra," according to the Sanskrit version of the sūtra, following the eighth section on profundity, there should immediately follow a single phrase:

"For what reason? This is a single interrogative term that calls into question the aforementioned wisdom regarding the five types of profound teaching gates and the eight types of profundity—why is it said in all cases that the two vehicles do not know them? The answer states: "Śāriputra..."
No. Because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have achieved mastery in their teaching of causes. This is the Sanskrit text of the sutra above.

"The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have achieved mastery" constitutes one section; furthermore, "the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have achieved mastery in their teaching of causes" constitutes another section.
Mastery is the profound wisdom of internal realization. From the achievement of mastery comes the teaching of causes.
This refers to the profound nature of the gate of teaching (*śāsana*). Furthermore, the accomplishment of mastery (*vaśitā-sampad*) establishes the preceding three phrases.

The accomplishment of causes (*hetu-sampad*) establishes the fourth [phrase], namely the fourfold sevenfold eloquence (*pratibhāna*), such as various verbal expressions. This is solely because of the accomplishment of mastery.

Therefore, the wisdom of all Buddhas possesses five kinds of profundity. It is precisely because it is established through the explanation of causes that these five difficulties and eight profundities directed toward the ultimate are unknown to those of the Two Vehicles.
Regarding the statement, "Śāriputra, the Tathāgata is equal [to all]," the question is: what is meant by "the accomplishment of the causes and conditions for teaching with mastery"?

The answer is provided in the commentary, citing the Sūtra: "Śāriputra, the Tathāgata is accomplished in various skillful means (upāya), various knowledges and visions (jñāna-darśana), various mindfulnesses and contemplations (smṛti-vipaśyanā), and various modes of expression.
These constitute four general categories. What are these termed "skillful means, knowledge and vision, mindfulness and contemplation"?
Regarding the words: the respondent below explains these four general phrases through three sections and five points.
Jin Cheng states that there are three types of differences between this Qin dynasty translation and the Sanskrit original: first, omissions; second, lack of sequence;
and third, divergent combinations. As for the omissions, they concern the sixth point, "the difficult-to-understand dharmas," which the Tathāgata is able to know.
It further states: "That which cannot be known by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Next, there is another interrogative inquiry:
"For what reason? The sūtra author answers: "Śāriputra, because the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, have achieved mastery in their teaching of causes.
Thus, these four preceding sections of the sūtra text are present in the Sanskrit original but are absent from the Qin translation; this is the [first]... [section].

First, a slight deficiency. Second, regarding the lack of sequential order: if it were the Qin (Chinese) version of the scripture, it would first state, "Śāriputra, since my attainment of Buddhahood," and only then introduce the general phrases of the sutra text with its various causes, conditions, and parables.
If it were the Sanskrit original, it would first state, "Śāriputra, since my attainment of Buddhahood," and subsequently proceed downward to introduce the specific [details].
The scriptural text of the *Sūtra* extensively expounds the verbal teachings through innumerable skillful means; this is what is meant by "the sequence of before and after being disordered.

Third, regarding the differences in combination and separation: the Sanskrit version of the *Sūtra* states, "various skillful means, various knowledges and views, and various mindfulnesses and contemplations."

The Qin translation combines various causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). The Sanskrit manuscript says "various expressions" (*vicitra-vākya*), while the Qin manuscript says "various similes" (*vicitra-upamā*).
This is because in the Western lands, expressions frequently employ various similes; thus, "expressions" are rendered as "similes.

There are three types of differences here, arising from the fact that four lines in the Sanskrit manuscript correspond to two lines in the Qin translation, due to variations in how they are separated or combined.
This is not the same [as the previous explanation] (according to the *Lunji* commentary on the *Jing*).

Regarding the phrase "successive mental verbalizations" (*zhuanzhuan yiyen*) and so forth, this briefly sets forth the general meaning. The section beginning with "successive mental verbalizations" consists of distinct clauses.
This explains the preceding general statement, which is termed "successive progression" (*krama*). There are three stages of this successive progression.

First, by means of the four meanings—such as the "attainment through treatises" (*śāstra-siddhi*) and so forth—one explains the four preceding general phrases. Second, by means of the specific phrases beginning with "the Sūtra," one elucidates the preceding general statement.
