Regarding the statement here that "subsequently attained wisdom" (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) is called "all-encompassing":

it is so named because it can universally know all phenomena (*dharma*) and takes all objects as its cognitive domain. Regarding these "all-encompassing" aspects, Zhangjing states there are four meanings:
first, taking all realms as its object; second, taking all entities as its object; third, taking all categories as its object; and fourth, taking all times as its object. Within these four...
The object-field functions without obstruction; this is called "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñā*). Within all realms there are two: first, the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*);
second, sentient beings (*sattva*). Within all phenomena there are two kinds of distinctions: first, the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); second, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Within all categories there are five kinds: first, the distinction of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*); second, the distinction of common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*); third, the distinction of cause and effect (*hetu-phala*); fourth... [text fragment].
There are distinctions among the realms and destinies; there are distinctions among the five and the three natures; and as for time, there are three periods: first, the past; second, the future;
and third, the present. Because one knows all such realms, all phenomena, all categories, and all times exactly as they truly are, it is called "omniscience" (sarvajñatā).

Regarding "unimpeded wisdom" (*asaktajñāna*): it refers to that which, for a moment, relying upon the mental faculty, is universally pervasive across all things, unobstructed and swift; this is called unimpeded wisdom.
To state it concisely: it is so named because one is not humiliated or defeated by the challenges and interrogations of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Regarding "pure wisdom": because all afflictions (*kleśa*) and the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of cognition have been ultimately and forever severed, it is pure wisdom.

The mundane [wisdom] of the two vehicles is with outflows (*sāsrava*) and is not called pure; now, the mundane [wisdom] of the Buddha is without outflows (*anāsrava*) and free from craving and hatred, and is thus called pure.

Regarding the phrase "free from overweening pride (*adhimāna*) and so forth": this means that unlike the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), who claim to have attained what they have not attained, the Buddha has realized the perfection of merit and wisdom and possesses all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*);
thus he is said to be free from overweening pride. This refers to being free from the conceit of claiming to have attained much when one has attained little.

Regarding the meaning of "the power of speech" (*vāg-bala*), it is as explained previously. The first ten knowledges constitute the essence, while these four knowledges represent the ascending significance.

By means of these three subsequent knowledges (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*), the Tathāgata is able to know the former two. The knowledge of what is possible and what is impossible is called the power of knowledge (*jñāna-bala*).

Regarding the phrase "each according to their own actions" and so forth: the power of knowledge regarding one's own karma (*svakarmajñānabala*) means that one knows, as it truly is, that one experiences the results of one's own actions and that the merit of giving can be transferred, such that one obtains results without having performed the action. As for the "transference of the merit of giving," the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) claim:
"If one practices giving in this life, one will experience the fruit of poverty in a future life; if one commits theft in this life, one will be wealthy in a future life."
The fruit of the noble ones; the fruit of hungry ghosts who observe the fast; the fruit of long life in the heavens resulting from sacrificing a horse to worship a deity;
and even the case where one performs causes of suffering yet obtains the fruit of happiness, or performs causes of happiness yet receives the retribution of suffering.

For example, there may be those who prostrate before the Bodhi tree and practice giving, while others do not go. If one attempts to purchase [the merit] with gold coins, they cannot obtain it, leading to various disputes. This is now explained.
The power of karma subdues these defilements; one must know that all karma is experienced by oneself. Question:
Within the Buddha-dharma, when descendants prepare a vegetarian feast for the deceased, is it not the case that this person creates merit while another receives the fruit? Answer:

Even when a white banner appears in the intermediate state of hell, this matter must likewise require the deceased themselves to generate the aspiration; if it were otherwise, throughout the worlds of the ten directions...
The cultivation of the Bodhisattva realm is infinite. Each and every one makes a universal vow: "May all sentient beings, without exception, become Buddhas just as my own body has.
If one were to allow another to create karma while this person undergoes its retribution, that would be the way of an ordinary person;

yet, once all have collectively attained Buddhahood, we ordinary people cannot avoid birth and death. Therefore, one must act for oneself and experience the results for oneself. Thus it is said: "Each [must act for themselves]."
It is that which is performed by oneself.
Regarding the "three times," these are the past, future, and present. Regarding the "three types of karma," they are either meritorious karma, non-meritorious karma, and immovable karma;

or alternatively, they are karma that ripens in the present life, karma that ripens in the next life, and karma that ripens in subsequent lives. Karma is that which can bring about fruition, and fruition is that which is brought about.

Karma is that which accords with its own name, "one's own karma. There are three types of karma: first, non-meritorious karma, which leads to the three miserable realms; second, meritorious karma, which leads to the four continents and the six heavens of the desire realm;

and third, immovable karma, which leads to the form and formless realms. Non-meritorious karma has three grades: the superior grade results in rebirth in hell, the middling grade in the realm of hungry ghosts, and the inferior grade in the animal realm.
Meritorious karma has two grades: the inferior grade results in rebirth in the four continents, and the superior grade in the six heavens of the desire realm. Immovable... [text fragment ends]
There are two categories of movement: the lower grade belongs to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the superior grade belongs to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Alternatively, there are actions of body, speech, and mind. Or, there is karma to be experienced in the present life: when one performs an action in the present life and receives its retribution in the present life, it is called "karma to be experienced in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman*).

Or, when one performs an action in the first lifetime and receives its retribution in the second lifetime, it is called "karma to be experienced in the next life" (*upapadyavedanīya-karman*). Or, one may perform an action in this life and receive its retribution from the third lifetime onward.

Regarding "reception" (*vedanā*), it is called "conforming to the subsequent. As for indeterminate karma (*aniyata-karman*), there are three types: that which is determinate in time but indeterminate in its retribution; that which is indeterminate in time but determinate in its retribution; and that which is indeterminate in both.

The Tathāgata’s subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) knows each and every one of these. Within the bodies of sentient beings, they themselves perform actions and themselves receive their retribution.
This is designated by the name of its cause and is called the "power of knowledge regarding the results of one's own actions" (*karmasvakatva-jñānabala*).

Regarding the phrase "the maturation (*vipāka*) of good and evil karma in this [life]," Zhangjing says: This refers to the power of knowing the maturation of karma in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*; it cites both cause and effect together. Question:
What is the difference between this "one performs the action oneself and receives the fruit oneself" and the principle of "what is possible and what is impossible" (*sthānāsthāna*)?

Answer: The former principle of "what is possible and what is impossible" excludes the views of others regarding causelessness, bad causes, and unequal causes; it does not allow for spontaneity (*svabhāva*).
One obtains happiness through the cause of happiness. This is like the realization that the nature of reality (prakṛti), Brahmā, Śakra, and so forth, are the maturation (*vipāka*) of karma;
this refers to performing an action oneself and subsequently experiencing its result oneself. Question: Upon what scriptural authority do these two preceding interpretations rely? Answer:

If one follows the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and similar treatises, only those actions that can induce the three types of karma—such as karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) and so on—are termed "one's own karma" (*svakarma*). However, if one relies upon the *Prajñāpāramitā*...

The Sūtra names this the "power of knowing the maturation of karma. The former [power] is able to know karma; this one, however, is distinguished because it is based on the ability to know the fruits produced by karma.
As for the statement that it is also called the "knowledge of the maturation of karma": the maturation of karma belongs to sentient beings, whereas the power of knowledge belongs to the Buddha.

Regarding the phrase "the four dhyānas, liberations, and so forth": because they are able to investigate thoroughly (*pravicaya*) through the tranquility of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and since the essence of this investigation is wisdom (*prajñā*), while concentration possesses the function of tranquility that can give rise to the investigative wisdom, they are called *dhyāna* (meditative absorption). There are four interpretations. First, *śamatha* (calm abiding), which is also called *samādhi* (equipoise);
it encompasses both concentrated and non-concentrated states, and includes everything that is focused and undistracted. Dullness (*styāna*) and agitation (*auddhatya*) are...
It is not uneven. By means of the application [of effort], one subdues lethargy (*styāna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*), holding the mind evenly so that it proceeds toward a single object;
this is called *samādhi*. Second, regarding *samāpatti*: briefly stated, *samāpatti* is translated here as "equilibrium" (*dengzhi*).

It encompasses both states with mind and without mind, and is exclusively meditative concentration (*samāhita*) rather than distraction (*vikṣipta*). This has two types: first, the mind in a state of meditative equipoise, which is peaceful, harmonious, and comfortable.
Pliancy is called "equanimity" (*samatā*). This is because, through the power of the preceding concentration, it leads the body and mind to this state of peace and equilibrium;
thus it is called "attainment. A second interpretation states: "Equanimity" means equality. Lethargy and restlessness are termed "inequality."
Through the preceding preparatory application, the categories of lethargy and agitation are eliminated; this mind of preparatory application is itself the category of equanimity.

When this mind is in a state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita*) and reaches a stage of serenity, it is able to lead [the practitioner] equally [to that state]; this is called "attainment" (*samāpatti*).

Regarding the statement that "these various meditative absorptions (dhyāna) pertain to both the fulfilled and so forth": contaminated (*sāsrava*) absorptions encompass both the defiled (*saṃkliṣṭa*) and the pure (*viśuddha*);

uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) absorptions are exclusively pure. If one speaks merely of the "defiled," this refers only to those characterized by relishing (*āsvādana*), and does not extend to pure absorptions.

If one speaks of the "defiled" in its broader sense (*saṃkliṣṭa*), it then encompasses both contaminated pure absorptions and those characterized by relishing. To distinguish them more precisely, there are two types within the defiled: first, those that constitute obstacles (*āvaraṇa*).

Regarding defilement (*saṃkleśa*): when seeking the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), because one lacks skillful means (*upāya*) and because various hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) arise in an intermingled fashion, there is first "defilement of one's own stage" (*svabhūmi-saṃkleśa*).

Although one has abandoned the defilements of a lower stage to attain a higher meditative absorption, one remains bound by the envelopers (*paryavasthāna*) and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of one's own stage and thus does not attain purity.
This consists of four sets; two are pure and two are defiled. As for the two that are pure: first, skillful means; second, [the result of] that].

"Excellently purified. Regarding the two types of defilement: first, being free from active entanglements (*paryavasthāna*); second, being free from latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). Thus, there are four [categories].
This section of the commentary reconciles the fact that the names for "wisdom" (*jñāna*) in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and "yoga" in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* differ;
its intent is to state that the Tathāgata is able to know all the distinctions among these various meditative absorptions (*samādhi*).

Regarding the statement "the faculties refer to faith and so forth," this refers to the power of knowing the superior and inferior faculties (*indriya-parāpara-jñānabala*). "Faculty" (*indriya*) has the meaning of growth and development; therefore, they are called "faculties. These faculties are the five:
faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. The *Jianyao* (Essentials) states: "This reveals that the five faculties, such as faith, have degrees of superiority and inferiority.

Those that are superior are termed 'excellent' (*śreṣṭha*), and those that are inferior are termed 'inferior' (*hīna*). Among these two types of faculties—the excellent and the inferior—the Buddha [possesses the power to know them]."
Because he is able to know all of these, it is called the power of the superior faculty (*indriya-vaiśāradya-bala*).

Furthermore, these five faculties—whether pertaining to the path with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*), and whether superior, middling, or inferior—are such that the five faculties of a Bodhisattva are superior, those of a Pratyekabuddha are middling, and those of a Śrāvaka are inferior.
The middle and lower faculties are described collectively as "inferior" (*hīna*). The superior ones are distinct and preeminent; these are the Bodhisattvas.

This refers to the general discussion of the two categories—superior and inferior—within the three vehicles (*triyāna*). According to the intent of the commentary (*śāstra*), each of the three vehicles possesses its own soft, medium, and superior grades.
"Soft" (*mṛdu*) means inferior, which is to say "low. Hearing the teaching for the first time is called soft; subsequently practicing the path is called middling;
and finally maturing the fruit is called superior. This interpretation is generally not correct. Rather, within the body of a single person, there exist the five faculties such as faith;
naturally, among these, there are those that are superior, middling, and low. The middling and low are termed "inferior," while the superior grade is termed "excellent."

Regarding the phrase "if [the power] comes from others" and so forth: Question: Since the five faculties, such as faith and the rest, are of a single kind, how can there be distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior?

Answer: The Commentary states, "If [the power] comes from others," etc. If one discusses the wisdom regarding the superiority or inferiority of the faculties (*indriya*), the text has already concluded that section; thus, it should properly belong to the subsequent passage.

However, according to the flow of the Commentary, it is correct to attribute this to the power of knowing the superiority or inferiority of the faculties (*indriyaparāparajñānabala*). Although it was previously concluded...

[This concludes the section. However, this portion of the commentary serves as a concluding summary of the text. If one follows others as a precursor, they are called "followers by faith" (*śraddhānusārin*);
they possess dull faculties and are inferior. Although the seeds of the three vehicles exist within their bodies, they are unable to awaken to them.

One must rely on the instruction of others before faith can arise; because this faith originates from another, such a person is called a "follower by faith" (śraddhānusārin), who is of medium capacity.
Alternatively, those who take the contemplation of all phenomena as their primary practice are "followers by dharma" (dharmānusārin); these are persons of sharp faculties.
First, one observes and gives rise to faith within oneself, without depending on a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra); such a person is called one of "keen faculties" (tīkṣṇendriya). Question:

In this context, does this refer only to the five faculties beginning with faith, or does it also include the other faculties? Answer: It is explained that this refers to entering the Path of Vision (darśanamārga).
Furthermore, regarding the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*): if one speaks generally of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), these may be included among the twenty-two faculties.

Because the essence of the five faculties beginning with faith is wholesome (*kuśala*), they possess distinct names and distinct entities. This distinguishes them from the preceding eight faculties, which are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

The mental faculty (*manas*) and the five sensations (*vedanā*) are distinguished by their pervading all three moral natures (*tridhātu*). As for the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), because their essence is identical to wisdom (*prajñā*), [they are not counted separately]. Thus, among the twenty-two faculties, only...
This much has been explained; it is not that [the Buddha] is unaware of anything else.
Regarding the phrase "delightful resolve" (*adhimukti*) and so forth, this refers to the power of knowledge regarding the various types of resolve (*nānādhimukti-jñāna-bala*). Master Xiangguo says:

"Within the three vehicles, each according to their own inclination, they take delight in, aspire to, and cultivate and study [the path]; this is called 'various convictions' (*nānā-adhimukti*). The mind excels..."
The objective sphere (*viṣaya*) is termed "superior" (*viśeṣa*). To hold it with certainty is termed "resolution" (*adhimukti*).

To hold fast to the Triple Gem as a fertile field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), to cherish the practices of the Three Vehicles, and to seek the fruits of the Three Vehicles is termed "delight. First, through superior resolution, one certifies the preceding object;
this certainty is the cause, which cannot be diverted. That this result can be known by the Tathāgata is termed "the power of knowledge" (*jñānabala*). Sentient beings...
The three vehicles and five natures differ in their excellence; this is collectively termed the "power of knowledge regarding the various inclinations.
Whether one delights in the wholesome or delights in the unwholesome, the Buddha is able to know it all.

Regarding the phrase "if established extensively" and so forth, this refers to the power of knowledge regarding the various elements (*nānādhātu-jñānabala*). It means that sentient beings possess diverse natures:
whether they belong to the Single Vehicle (*ekayāna*), the Five Vehicles (*pañcayāna*), or all three natures; whether they possess seeds that are wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate;

and even up to the eighty-four thousand types of conduct (*carita*)—the Tathāgata is able to fully comprehend them all. "Establishing" (*vyavasthāpana*) has the meaning of designation (*prajñapti*); it refers to the various elements.
"Element" (*dhātu*) has the meaning of "cause" and also the meaning of "nature. It refers to the seeds of the three vehicles and the five vehicles.

As for the mention of "four vehicles," this is the three vehicles with the addition of the indeterminate vehicle. As for the "five vehicles," this is the four vehicles with the addition of the human and celestial vehicles;
these refer to those of no lineage (*agotra*). This is based on the seeds of the five vehicles. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* speaks of four kinds of elements: first, [the element of the lineage].
1. The element of the naturally abiding lineage (*prakṛtisthagotra*). 2. The element acquired through practice (*samudānītagotra*). 3. The element that is susceptible to counteraction;

this refers to the counteraction by untainted wisdom (*anāsravajñāna*) against defiled seeds. 4. The element that is not susceptible to counteraction; this refers to the counteraction by untainted wisdom against the innate seeds (*dharmatābīja*) within the bodies of those who lack the lineage.

Regarding the phrase "or greed, anger, and so forth": there are those in whom greed alone predominates, those in whom anger alone predominates, those in whom delusion alone predominates, and those in whom all three are present;
therefore, they are called "of equal parts" (*samabhāga*).
Regarding the phrase "up to eighty thousand [dharmaskandhas] of sentient beings," Bian explains that this refers to the total number. Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa* states:
"The Muni taught eighty thousand dharma-aggregates; they are also like the three hundred [stanzas] of poetry. This too cites the total number.

In truth, there are eighty-four modes of conduct; the *Shijing* consists of three hundred and five poems; and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* speaks of the eighty-four thousand gates of affliction (*kleśa*).
These various categories are called "lineages" (*gotra*). Lineage means the "elemental realm" (*dhātu*).

One knows that among all sentient beings, there are those with a lineage of excessive greed, a lineage of excessive anger, and so forth, up to a lineage of excessive delusion—namely, the eighty-four thousand types of illness.
The Buddha’s wisdom knows each and every type of lineage of practice; this is called the power of knowing the various elements (*nānādhātu-jñānabala*).
The phrase "if it is precisely thus" refers to the practice of entering the noble path (*āryamārga*). The phrase "if it is precisely thus" points to the seeds within the preceding section.
The phrase "within the gates of the various realms of existence" points to the manifestation of the seeds of defiled phenomena within this present section.

The gates of the various realms of existence (*gati*) are themselves that which is to be reached. That which is to be reached is the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) known by the Buddha. There are four such objects of knowledge: greed, hatred, delusion, and their equal portions (*sabhāga*).

Regarding the phrase "one who practices in accordance with correctness" (*yoniśo-pratipanna*): one part refers to that which is capable of reaching [the goal], while greed, hatred, and delusion are that which is to be reached.

The cultivation of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā-bhāvanā*), and the contemplation of the analysis of the elements (*dhātu-vibhāga-bhāvanā*) constitute the practice capable of reaching [the goal]. Now, we take only this...
The "conduct that leads to" (*pratipat-pratipadana*) refers to the conduct that leads everywhere within this world. This is a *tatpuruṣa* compound, meaning "the conduct that encompasses all-leading.
Here, the word "leading-to-everywhere" (*sarvatraga*) belongs to the Tathāgata. It is the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) of the Tathāgata’s gnosis that knows all things;
because it can universally know the conduct by which sentient beings proceed, it is called the "conduct leading everywhere" (*sarvatragā pratipat*).

Regarding the statement "or all the gates of the five destinies": meritorious karma is the practice leading toward the human and celestial realms; imperturbable karma is the practice leading toward the higher realms;
the karma of stinginess and greed is the practice leading toward the realm of hungry ghosts; shamelessness and lack of remorse are the practices leading toward the realm of animals;
and wrong views and slandering the Dharma are the practices leading toward the realm of hell.

Regarding the phrase "or various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and so forth," this refers to the practice of moving toward and adhering [to views]. This interpretation differs from other interpretations;

here, we instead take the "practice toward which one moves" as the meaning. Within the body, which is a mere designation of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), there are divergent views that act as the "agent of movement," while the practice itself is the "object of movement.

The divergent views of non-Buddhists move toward such practices as self-mortification, lashing oneself with wooden staves, or lying upon beds of thorns. The divergent views of śramaṇas move toward the three vehicles (*triyāna*).
They practice and cling to magical arts, talismans, incantations, the twelve Vedas, and various technical crafts.
They form diverse factions and distinctions, each practicing what is heterodox and contradicting one another. Each clings to their own conduct as superior, regarding all others as inferior and wrong.
Regarding the expression "either this world or other worlds," this refers to the practice of seeking *nirvāṇa*. "This world" is the present;

"other worlds" refers to the past and future, which together are termed "other worlds. Ha states: for those of the three vehicles (*triyāna*), the practice of proceeding toward *nirvāṇa* throughout the three periods of time is called "blameless proceeding.
The essence of *nirvāṇa* is itself blameless; thus, it is the proceeding toward that which is blameless.

This is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (dependent determinative compound). To summarize: because the untainted (*anāsrava*) noble path transcends birth and death, it is called "the course of action that is without fault" (*anavadya-gati-caryā*).

Here, "without fault" is the "course of action," forming a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound). However, this interpretation is too narrow as it takes only the untainted [path]. If one says "the course of action that is without fault," [it is broader].

This exhaustively encompasses both the untainted (*anāsrava*) and the tainted (*sāsrava*). Among the three types of action, tainted wholesome actions that accord with the Noble Path are all non-offensive actions.
The Buddha’s wisdom can know each of these four types of action; this is called the power of knowledge regarding the paths leading everywhere (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad-jñāna-bala*).
Regarding the phrase "as for those that are universally pervasive" (*sarvatraga*), this refers to the terminology found in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

This "path leading everywhere" (*sarvatragāminī pratipad*) is the sphere traversed by the Tathāgata’s subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*); thus it is called the "practice of practice. As for "the wisdom that is capable of thorough knowledge," it is named according to its object of knowledge;

thus it is called the "universally pervasive practice. The State Counselor (Xiangguo) said: "In the former interpretation, 'universally pervasive' refers to the Buddha's wisdom that takes [phenomena] as its cognitive object."

The term "pervasive" (*vyāpin*) refers to this present explanation of pervasiveness, which pertains to the object of cognition (*ālambana*). The movement toward various realms of existence (*gati*) is called pervasive. Question:

What is the distinction between the power of knowledge regarding the movement toward realms (*gati-gāminī-jñānabala*) and the power of knowledge regarding what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*)? Answer: The *Saṃgraha* states: The former has a broad range of cognitive objects, while the latter—concerning the movement toward realms—is narrow.
The former is broad because it includes as its objects even what is impossible (*asthāna*), whereas the latter is narrow because it concerns only what is possible (*sthāna*).

Regarding the phrase "if, with respect to various sentient beings," etc., this refers to the power of knowledge consisting in the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānabala*), which takes past objects as its domain.

The aforementioned power of knowledge regarding the paths leading everywhere (*sarvatragāminīpratipajjñānabala*) is the wisdom of the Tathāgata that can know the movements within the bodies of sentient beings;

here, however, it is stated that the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge can know the bodies of sentient beings themselves. "Past" (*pūrva*) means former lives; it refers to the world of phenomena that have passed away.

This refers to the "power of recollection" (*anusmṛti-jñānabala*). Its object of focus (*ālambana*) resides in the past. The two dharmas of mindfulness (*smṛti*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) both take the past object as their focus and perform discernment;
this is wisdom. Mindfulness follows wisdom, taking the same object at the same time; this is called the power of the knowledge of recollection.

Regarding the interpretation that "recollection follows wisdom," the character *sui* (follow) belongs to mindfulness. Another explanation states: that which can correctly take the past object as its focus is called mindfulness, while [the discernment] is wisdom.

It cannot take past objects as its cognitive object (*ālambana*). Because all [cognitions] are led by mindfulness (*smṛti*), this knowledge follows mindfulness and likewise takes past objects as its cognitive object;

thus it is called the "power of the knowledge of recollection" (*pūrvenivāsānusmṛtijñānabala*). Regarding the subsequent explanation that "this knowledge of liberation follows mindfulness," the character *sui* (follow) belongs to the knowledge. The former explanation is correct.

The knowledge of conditions (*pratyaya-jñāna*) and mindfulness (*smṛti*) are dharmas that arise simultaneously. The fact that the power of knowledge is not mentioned here is an explanation based on immediate proximity (*upapada-vigraha*).
The remaining nine [powers] are all *tatpuruṣa* compounds. Regarding "seeds" and so forth: each one is collectively designated as "various.
This refers to the vocal sounds of sentient beings and names from the four directions—the names of all sentient beings in the eastern world, such as Zhang San and Li Si.
The Tathāgata is able to know individually all the names of sentient beings in the southern, western, and northern directions.
As for "the self-substance," it refers to the physical bodies of sentient beings; "substance" here is synonymous with "body."
Regarding the phrase "the eight types of discourse" (*aṣṭau vyavahārāḥ*), this refers to the complete enumeration of the past:
there are eight kinds of matters that serve as the causes for discourse, and each of these is explained individually; thus they are called the "eight types of discourse. First, such names:
for example, the name of Śakra in the past was "Jambuka. Second, such classes of birth: such as Brahmins and Kṣatriyas.
The three types of lineage (*gotra*): the lineage of the clan, such as the six clans of the Brahmins and others, which are like the surnames Zhang, Wang, and so forth.
The four kinds of food: such as the *sudhā* nectar in the palace of Śakra, and the naturally occurring non-glutinous rice of the Northern Continent (*Uttarakuru*).

Fifth, the experience of suffering and pleasure: this refers to suffering and pleasure. The loss of wealth and reputation is called suffering; the acquisition of wealth and reputation is called pleasure. Sixth, long life:
for example, if a person is destined to live for one hundred years, after passing through infancy, they continue to live until the age of sixty or seventy.

The first is called "life" (*āyuṣ*). The second, lasting from seventy to eighty or ninety years, is called "long-abiding. The third, lasting from eighty to the end of one's natural lifespan of a hundred years, is called the "limit of the measure of life.
Regarding these eight [stages], wisdom follows mindfulness as it takes past objects as its objective support; this is precisely mindfulness following after recollection.

Decisive discernment is what is called wisdom (*jñāna*). Mindfulness (*smṛti*) is that which is able to recollect. This is a concise expression for "the practitioner who practices what has been traversed. Question:
Why were eight factors previously mentioned, while later they are abbreviated into six? Answer: Xiu said, "In the general sense, within the bodies of sentient beings, there are eight past matters."

Now, they are briefly categorized as six. Since the eight types are condensed into six, and because the practices undertaken do not exceed six kinds, the previous [categories of] long life and long endurance are subsumed collectively under "life-span"; thus, there are only six. This merely abbreviates the number, but does not abbreviate the practices themselves. Question:

What is the difference between the eight "phrases of discourse" (*vyavahāra-pada*) and the "briefly summarized practices"? Answer: The former refers to the teaching that serves as the expressive medium (*vācaka*).
The six abbreviated practices (*ṣaḍ-saṃkṣepa-caryā*) are the principles to be explained. Both of these are objects of knowledge known by the Tathāgata’s wisdom.

Regarding the eight verbal expressions, there are eight types based on the essence of the phenomena (*dharma-tattva*). The six abbreviated practices, as discussed in the treatise, are what the Buddha knows, and thus they are synthesized into six types.
Because the lifespans are combined into one, it is called "abbreviated. That is to say, the six kinds of various objects are the spheres of activity traversed by the knowledge of past lives;
thus, they are called the "abbreviated spheres of activity."
Regarding "the first, summoning, etc.": this refers to the aforementioned names. Regarding "the second, Kṣatriyas, etc.":
this refers to the aforementioned classes of birth, such as "I was formerly a Kṣatriya or a Brāhmaṇa. Regarding "the third, parents": this refers to the aforementioned lineage.

Regarding "the fourth, food and drink, etc.": this refers to the aforementioned food and drink; that is, the transformation of the raw into the cooked, which is likewise like [the transformation of] the cold.
"Tao bu cha" and so forth are termed "the correct path. Fifth, regarding "flourishing and decline": flourishing refers to happiness; decline refers to the aforementioned suffering.
Sixth, regarding "life span": this refers to the aforementioned limit of long life and enduring residence.

The phrase "these [knowledges] such as the recollection of past lives" is the conclusion. When wisdom (*jñāna*) and mindfulness (*smṛti*) arise simultaneously and are able to take the past as their object, it is called the power of wisdom associated with mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna-jñānabala*).
This refers to the power of wisdom that is concomitant with mindfulness, according to the commentary.
Regarding the phrase "the various classes of sentient beings," this refers to the power of knowledge regarding death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādajñānabala*).
While the aforementioned power of recollecting past abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānabala*) takes the past as its object, this power of knowledge regarding death and rebirth takes future objects.

That is to say, it knows that three types of śrāvakas will, after the passage of a certain number of kalpas in a future age, attain Buddhahood; and it also knows which of the disciples who perform virtuous deeds will [attain such results] in a future life.
Those who create wholesome karma will be born in a favorable realm. Those who commit evil deeds will be born in the three miserable destinies in future lives.
Furthermore, the Buddha’s words can subdue those who cling to the view of annihilationism, for he says: "In future lives, there will be no further body."
One may speak of annihilation; yet the future is immeasurable. How can one maintain that the body undergoes annihilation?
Regarding the phrase "when about to pass away," death refers to the final moment of consciousness of the *pūrvakālabhava* (existence prior to death) being present.
There is only this single moment, and no subsequent thought-moment; this is called death. Mǔ (Mokṣala? says: "The desire to die and the actual dying are termed..."

"Death. Regarding the statement "dwelling in existence (*bhava*) and so forth," Cien says: one takes the final moment of consciousness at the end of the intermediate state (*antarābhava) and names it the "one thought-moment at birth.

At that time, the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) grasps the physical body inherited from the parents and abides; this is precisely what is called "the time of birth. It does not refer to the actual moment of being born.
The fetus is what is called "birth. In this context, the intention is merely to speak of birth and death, as well as the subduing of those who hold to the view of annihilationism.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "A bhikṣu who was unfilial and used harsh speech [in a previous life] remains in the womb for sixty years; in his mind, he perceives this as being like sixty kalpas.
All such states are termed "abiding," and the Tathāgata knows each and every one of them; this is called the power of knowledge regarding death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādajñānabala*).
The phrase "regarding the good and evil destinies, etc. explains the meaning of the power of understanding (*pratisaṃvid*).
The phrase "all dharmas, etc. refers to the paths of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning; this is called the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).

Now, it is explained that if correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) is combined with skillful means (*upāya*), it also encompasses the knowledge of the accumulations (*saṃbhāra*), the preparatory application (*prayoga*), and the skillful means of subduing afflictions to achieve the path; this is called the [exhaustion of] outflows.
Exhaustion. Whether as seeds or as manifest activity, all outflows (*āsrava*) are exhausted. This manifest activity, together with its latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), constitutes the seeds;
thus, when both seeds and manifestations are exhausted, it is called the power of knowledge regarding the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānabala*). Question:

If outflows are seeds, the Tathāgata universally contemplates and knows the exhaustion of outflows within the bodies of those in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) of the three vehicles. He likewise knows that the outflow-dharmas within the bodies of noble learners (*śaikṣa*) have not yet been exhausted.
Question: If one knows the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*), it may be called the power of knowledge regarding the exhaustion of the outflows.

Why is it not also called the power of knowledge regarding the non-exhaustion of the outflows when one knows that the outflows have not been exhausted? Answer: Because it is taught by way of implication, or because it is spoken of according to what is predominant.

Question: Within the Buddha’s own person, all outflows have already been exhausted. Does the Buddha know this for himself? If he does know it, what is this called as a power? If you say it is "knowledge and vision," what are its characteristics?

Why? Answer: Because it perceives the mind. Within the fruit [of cognition], the activity is predominant; thus, the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) is also obtained. Furthermore, the seeing-part also mutually perceives the self-witnessing king (*svasaṃvedana-rāja*).
This is because it is not the same as the cause. Thus, one attains the ability to know oneself and is sufficient for the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*). If that is so, [then...]
What is meant by "having the same object"? Since it is impossible for a present mind to reflexively take its own mind as an object, the answer is:

when the King (the subject) takes the perceived portion as an object, it does not conflict with the cause of self-cognition, because [the latter] takes this very perception as its object; thus, there is no fault.
Regarding the statement, "Wisdom is the essence," and so forth: all ten kinds of wisdom are the essence, and all ten powers are the function.
Wisdom is itself power; this is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.

Regarding the phrase "the knowledge of former abodes (*pūrvanivāsa*) and so forth" herein, Xiu says: "However, wisdom (*jñāna*) does not take the past as its object; it is mindfulness (*smṛti*) that is able to know the events of former lives.
Because wisdom and mindfulness are conjoined, mindfulness also takes the past as its object in accordance with [that wisdom]. Thus, it receives its name from its auxiliary associate.

Therefore, the power of the knowledge of recollecting former abodes is explained by way of proximity (*upacāra*); or rather, it is able to take past objects as its domain because it is conjoined with that mindfulness."
Both are derived from proximity; those names are obtained through association with that [proximity]. This is an *upapada* compound (where the subsequent member is predominant).
Regarding the phrase "the possible and the impossible" (*sthānāsthāna*), etc., these are all *tatpuruṣa* compounds based on the northern [tradition].
The statement, "Although they are situated in three different texts," serves as a transition from what precedes. The phrase, "However, its essence is fivefold," introduces what follows.
Regarding the expression, "the single most excellent essence": if one asks what is meant by "most excellent," the answer is that among the Buddha’s merits, wisdom (*prajñā*) is the most excellent.
This refers to the most excellent essence.

Regarding the statement that the Buddha possesses the faculty of knowing all (ājñātāvīndriya) and wisdom (*prajñā*), the Buddha’s faculty of knowing all comprises nine factors, namely the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*).

Together with mental joy (*saumanasya*), pleasure (*sukha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*). Now, from among these nine, the five faculties (*indriya*) and from among those five, the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), are taken as the essence of the ten powers (*daśabala*).

There are three untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*): first, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñātāvyajñāsyāmīndriya*), which refers to the period prior to the fifteenth moment of mind within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), because one is about to know what was previously unknown;
second, the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*), which refers to the period from the sixteenth moment of mind up to and including the diamond-like mind (*vajropamasamādhi*).
Regarding those prior to the fifteenth moment of mind: because they have already been known, these three are "possessors of full knowledge" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).

This refers to the stage after the path of liberation; therefore, it is called the faculty of one who has fully known. Question: Are these three faculties conventional (*saṃvṛti*) or ultimate (*paramārtha*)? Answer:

According to the Hīnayāna, both are provisional phenomena and are all termed "conventional," etc. The treatise states: "Although the four objects (*viṣaya*) are with outflows (*sāsrava*), they are called 'ultimate' because they are real. The three [faculties]...

Although the faculties (*indriya*) are untainted (*anāsrava*), they are called "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*) by way of designation. According to the Mahāyāna school, since they are untainted, they are subsumed under the ultimate (*paramārtha*).

Regarding the statement "the two [factors] induce the extraction of the essence," there are two explanations: first, that which definitely induces wisdom is called "inducing production" (*ākṣepa*); second, meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
This forest of merit can also produce merit; this is called "inducing production" (*āvedha*). Wisdom is the sovereign of all virtues and can also induce the production of all dharmas;
thus, wisdom is also termed "inducing production. Therefore, the ten powers (*daśabala*) take concentration and wisdom as their essence.

It is further stated: "From meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the fundamental [wisdom] arises; from the fundamental, the subsequently attained (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*) arises; and through the subsequently attained wisdom, one attains supreme and wondrous function, which is called 'power' (*bala*).

Regarding the statement, "The three overcome the substantial entity," etc.: if it is asked, "Since they overcome the substantial entity and take the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) as their nature, why is this not explicitly stated?"
Regarding the powers of faith and mindfulness, they answer that wisdom is supreme; thus, the term "power of knowledge" (jñānabala) is used according to what is predominant.
In reality, however, faith and the others may also constitute its essence.

Regarding the essence of association (*saṃprayoga*): at the moment wisdom arises, there must necessarily be the eleven mental factors—the universal, the object-specific, and the wholesome—that arise simultaneously with it. Therefore, the treatise states: "and association."
Regarding the statement "the four aggregates, etc.": when wisdom arises, there must necessarily be pure consciousness (*viśuddha-vijñāna*). The mind-king (*citta-rāja*) is consciousness itself;

simultaneously, there are the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-caitta*), which constitute the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*); perception (*saṃjñā*) constitutes the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*);

and the remainder of the universal factors, as well as the eleven [mental factors] such as the object-specific (*viniyata*) and the wholesome (*kuśala*), are all the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). At the time wisdom arises, it is associated with these [factors] within sentient beings; therefore, it is so named.
Correspondence. Although there are many dharmas, they do not depart from the four aggregates as their nature.

Regarding the statement that "the five [aggregates] have the same substance as the retinue," this substance is the most extensive; by adding the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) to the four aggregates, one arrives at the five aggregates.

The commentator takes the two types of restraint—those of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the path (*mārga*)—as the aggregate of form. One may ask: how can the Buddha’s body be established through the restraint of concentration and the path?

Second, regarding the precepts: the answer is that if one follows the Hīnayāna school, it is taught that the *samādhi-saṃvara* (precepts concomitant with meditative concentration) are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*), while the *mārga-saṃvara* (precepts concomitant with the Path) are exclusively uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

According to the Mahāyāna school, the *samādhi-saṃvara* applies to both the contaminated and the uncontaminated, whereas the *mārga-saṃvara* is exclusively uncontaminated. Here, we adopt the Mahāyāna position.
The Buddha’s body is without outflows (*anāsrava*). His morality (*śīla*) follows that of the Buddha; thus, his concentration-morality (*samādhi-śīla*) is also exclusively without outflows. Question:
Among the two types of morality—concentration and the path—within the causal stage, they are established based upon manifest volition (*cetanā*).

When this manifest volition possesses the capacity for restraint and prevention, such that the functional power to give rise to the sevenfold unwholesome bodily and vocal matter (*rūpa*) is absent, it is termed non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*). If this is so, then in the state of Buddhahood, there is no such unwholesome matter to be prevented.

How is it that this is also called "form" (*rūpa*)? There are three explanations. First, it is said: although there is no form to be prevented, that which can produce wholesome form is also called "form.
Second, it is said: because the capacity for prevention and production exists within the fruit, it is also called "form."
Third, it is said: "It is called 'form' (*rūpa*) because it is described as that which is protected from afar.

Regarding the phrase "although there is no textual passage for this," the commentator of the *Śāstra* (the *Sūtra-vṛtti*) has added this interpretation of his own. He establishes the principle by stating:

"Although there is no textual passage for this, it logically ought to exist, because it serves to prevent the defilement of violating the precepts and assists in crushing the enemy [of afflictions]. The nature of violating the precepts is termed...

These constitute defilements (*mala*). Because the unmanifest precept (*avijñapti-śīla*) is able to prevent these defilements and ensure they never arise again, it is called "preventing the defilement of transgressing the precepts.

Since these defilements have been prevented, the various afflictions (*kleśa*) do not arise; this is called "assisting in the destruction of the enemy. Here, the "enemy" refers to the afflictions, which act as enemies to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
Regarding the phrase "the remaining three gates," this refers to the meaning of the other gates. Next is the third gate, which analyzes the aspects of practice (*ākāra*);
following the analysis of the names, it has been briefly explained and concluded.
Regarding the fourth sequence: when the Tathāgata first attains unsurpassed bodhi, he does so instantaneously; subsequently, however, he arises [in stages].
First, he establishes the non-erroneous cause and effect and gives rise to the power of knowledge regarding what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*).

Subsequently, seeking their aspiration for the maturation (*vipāka*) of the desire realm, he teaches them to distance themselves from all unwholesome karma and to practice wholesome karma, thereby giving rise to the power of knowledge regarding one's own actions (*karmasvakatā-jñānabala*).

Power. This continues until, next, one brings about the permanent abandonment of all afflictions (*kleśa*) and gives rise to the power of knowledge regarding the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñānabala*).
Regarding the fifth, the various gateways: there are five gateways. First, the gateway of differentiation; second, the gateway of non-commonality;

third, the gateway of equality; fourth, the gateway of distinction; and fifth, the gateway of elicitation. As for the first, the gateway of differentiation, there are three types: first, differentiation by time.

First, the classification of the three periods of time, because one enters into realization in accordance with them. Second, the classification of categories, because one enters into realization regarding every single phenomenon according to its specific and general characteristics.

Third, the classification of bodies, because one enters into realization regarding the distinct continuities and all matters and meanings of sentient beings throughout the ten directions. As for the uncommon gate, it is not shared by the two vehicles.
[This power] is absent [in others]. Bodhisattvas attain it partially, while only the Buddha alone is fully perfected. Regarding the gate of equality:
all Tathāgatas are entirely equal, fully possessing this power without any distinction. Regarding the gate of differentiation:

as explained extensively in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, its characteristics are too numerous to describe here for fear of prolixity. Furthermore, there are three types of elicitation: first, skillful means; second, the faculties (*indriya*).

The root, the three inducements, and the preparatory means: these refer to the meditative concentration directed toward the teachings, wherein one repeatedly contemplates their aspects until they are fully perfected.
Regarding the root: although it exists in all dhyānas, because the Tathāgata frequently dwells in the fourth dhyāna, it is specifically called the "root.
As for the gate of induction, there are two kinds: first, arising in the presence [of the object];...

The function [of the subsequent knowledge] has the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) as its essence. The second, the function of abiding in the fundamental nature, has supramundane correct wisdom as its essence;
this is precisely the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).

Regarding the enumeration of names and so forth: the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) of a Buddha are listed in the commentary itself, while the four grounds of self-confidence (*catur-vaiśāradya*) of a Bodhisattva are as follows:

These are: first, fearlessness regarding the dhāraṇī; second, fearlessness regarding knowledge of the faculties; third, fearlessness regarding answering questions; and fourth, fearlessness regarding severing doubts.
These are explained as in the "Chapter on Never-Disparaging" (Sadāparibhūta-parivarta); they are now the four kinds of fearlessness of this Buddha.
The statement that "the four" refers to their numerical designation is an explanation of the names. Regarding "fearlessness": in these four matters, the Tathāgata is able to know them for himself;

this is a general discussion of fearlessness. In these four matters, when someone poses a question, the Tathāgata is able to know it for himself and is entirely without any trace of fear; therefore, they are called "fearlessnesses."
To speak of being "serene and fearless" refers to fearlessness of body. To speak of the mind being "without cowardice or inferiority" refers to fearlessness of mind.
To speak of being "without doubt or hesitation" refers to fearlessness of speech. Alternatively, "serene and fearless" is a general term for fearlessness;

"the mind being without cowardice or inferiority" is fearlessness of mind; "being without doubt or hesitation" is fearlessness of speech; and "being entirely without timidity or dread" is fearlessness of body.
It is called "fearless" because it is free from fear; this is a summary term.
Regarding the phrase "perfectly awakening to all dharmas," the word "perfect" (正) distinguishes [this awakening] from the mistaken awakenings of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

If "perfect" refers to the correctness of being right versus wrong, it distinguishes [the Buddha] from non-Buddhists. If "perfect" refers to the perfection of being complete and correct, it simultaneously distinguishes [him] from Bodhisattvas, as their awakening is not yet perfected.

Regarding the phrase "perfectly awakening to all phenomena" (*sarvadharmābhisambuddha*), this distinguishes [the Buddha] from those of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*). "Partially awakening to all phenomena" refers to the objects of knowledge (*jñeya-dharma*).

Discussing them together, one speaks of "Perfectly Equal Awakening" (*samyak-saṃbodhi*); if analyzed, one speaks of "Perfect Awakening" (*samyak-bodhi*) and "Equal Awakening" (*saṃbodhi*). The aforementioned "Fearlessness of Perfect Equal Awakening" refers to the abandonment of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

Regarding the statement that the seeds and manifestations of the various afflictions (*kleśa*) have been exhausted, this refers to the fearlessness of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-vaiśāradya*).

Having severed the obstacle of afflictions, one knows that the outflows—whether as seeds or as manifest states—within the bodies of others are entirely exhausted; this is called the fearlessness of the exhaustion of outflows. Question:

Since the outflows within the bodies of others may not yet be exhausted, why do you not also speak of a "fearlessness regarding the non-exhaustion of outflows"? Answer: In reality, he knows them all; however, this is spoken of from the perspective of what is predominant.
Furthermore, when asked whether one knows the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) within one's own continuum, the answer is that one does indeed know it.

Regarding the phrase "obstructions to the teaching of the Dharma" (*dharmadeśanā-āvaraṇa*), these are the fearlessnesses regarding the obstructions to the Dharma. First is desire (*rāga*); second is the afflictions (*kleśa*) of all realms;

these collectively are termed "obstructions. The afflictions of discrimination within the three realms, in relation to the vision of the path (*darśanamārga*) for those of the three vehicles, are collectively termed [the third].
They are obstructions. The first six grades of innate afflictions constitute obstructions to the second fruit; the latter three grades constitute obstructions to the third fruit;
and the innate afflictions of the two upper realms constitute obstructions to the fourth fruit. In summary, as for defiled phenomena acting as obstructions, they consist of the two obstructions:
the afflictive obstruction (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

Regarding the statement "the path of deliverance and so forth": this refers to fearlessness concerning the path that leads out of suffering. Specifically, the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and the ultimate path (*niṣṭhāmārga*) are called the path of deliverance.

Furthermore, by extension, the paths of preparation (*prayogamārga*), equipment (*sambhāramārga*), and application (*anantaryamārga*), which also suppress the afflictions, are likewise called the path of deliverance.
For Śrāvakas, this involves the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths; for Pratyekabuddhas, it involves forty-four knowledges (*jñāna*) or seventy-seven knowledges.

The path for emerging from suffering consists of the Bodhisattva’s wisdom of the two emptinesses, up to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the six perfections, the four means of attraction, and so forth.

The Buddha has completely abandoned both obstacles; this is called the fearlessness of the path for emerging from suffering. Emerging from the noble paths of the three vehicles is the dharma of the path for emerging from suffering.
The four [fearlessnesses] of perfect enlightenment are not themselves the fearlessnesses, nor are the fearlessnesses identical to the four [attributes] of perfect enlightenment and so forth. This...

These four dharmas are the objects [of fearlessness]. Because the Tathāgata is physically and mentally fearless regarding these four, they are so named. Regarding the phrase "in these four," the *Jianyao* (Essentials) states:

the first two are qualities of self-benefit—namely, the Buddha’s own state of being a perfectly awakened one (*samyaksaṃbuddha*) and his fearlessness as a perfectly awakened one, and his fearlessness regarding the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). The latter two are qualities of benefiting others.

The fearlessness regarding the dharmas that obstruct [liberation] and the fearlessness regarding the path leading out of suffering apply to those who follow the three vehicles, as they concern both the path leading out of suffering and the dharmas that obstruct the three vehicles.
Since these fearlessnesses belong to the Buddha himself, there are the fearlessness regarding the path leading out of suffering and the fearlessness regarding the dharmas that obstruct [liberation].
All [of these] are *tatpuruṣa* compounds.

Regarding the statement "the nature of the substance is produced," the principle for the fivefold production of the substance is consistent with what was explained previously in the section on the ten powers.
Regarding the statement "if it functions," Jin says: "To equally awaken to all phenomena and to sever both seeds and manifest [defilements] constitutes abiding in its own nature."

It has correct knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) as its essence; this is none other than fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). To speak of the factors that obstruct [enlightenment], the path for emerging from suffering, and so forth, constitutes its active function (*kāritra*).
Subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭha-jñāna*) is its nature (*svabhāva*). Regarding these four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), each possesses its own specific nature and function.

Regarding "initiation": because one gives rise to wisdom based on meditative concentration (samādhi) and thereby attains the four [analytical knowledges], it is called "induced. Thus, its essence consists of meditative concentration and wisdom.
This meaning of "induction" is also the same as that explained within the context of the ten powers (daśabala); the remaining meanings are likewise the same.
Regarding the phrase "discourse on reality and so forth," it means, as before, to ascertain the actual substance.
Regarding the phrase "as stated in the sūtras," this refers to the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra*.
Regarding the phrase "furthermore, there are śramaṇas or non-śramaṇas, etc.," this asks: in the World-Honored One’s scriptural teachings, it is said that the Buddha is endowed with...
The All-Knowing One knows all things; there is nothing he does not know. Why? Because when a bhikṣu came from another region, the Buddha asked him, "Are you dwelling in peace and comfort?
Is almsfood easy to obtain? This was a case where his actions did not accord with his teaching.

Regarding the statement, "Thereupon, within this context, some raise an objection," etc.: Since the World-Honored One has posed a question that appears as if he were unaware, bystanders immediately raise an objection, saying:
"If the Buddha knows, why does he need to ask? If he asks while not knowing, how can it be said that he possesses all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*)?
In reality, however, the Tathāgata’s cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) have been exhausted; it is merely that the Tathāgata demonstrates [this].
This serves as a gateway for mutual guidance and establishes a precedent for future generations; therefore, I set forth these matters.
When I say, "In this matter, I have no basis for right view," and so forth, the *Abhidharma* states: "I have no cause (*ālambana*) for right view regarding this matter.
Here, "cause" (*ālambana*) means "basis" (*yō*). The intended meaning is: "When I examine your objection, there is no source or reason for it; it lacks truth."
This is the causal basis of the true principle. "Abiding in security" means that the body is without fear or dread. "Fearlessness" refers to the mind being without fear.
"Declaring of oneself, 'I abide as a Great Sage'" and so forth refers to fearlessness through vocal action.

Regarding the phrase "welcoming those who come," it means that when one asks whether alms-seeking for a bhikṣu is easy or difficult, the arising of a joyful mind in the present moment is nothing other than beneficial;
all such instances are the Wheel of Dharma.
Regarding the statement that he wished for all people to examine things with impartiality: he asked Ānanda, "Is it raining? This was intended to cause Ānanda to scrutinize the matter with precision.
If the Buddha, who already knows the answer, still asks, how much more so should those who do not know?

Regarding the statement that "his words also serve as a model for later generations," this is like the example of the Master [Confucius] entering the Grand Ancestral Temple and inquiring about every matter;

he served as a model for those who followed, yet this was also the Master’s own practice of propriety (*li*). However, all the speech of the Buddha is for the sake of benefit and constitutes the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*).

This is unlike the ten sections of the Hīnayāna, such as the *Bahudhātuka*, which maintain that not all words of the Buddhas are beneficial—as, for instance, in the case of the inquiry concerning the festival (*kai*).
[The Buddha] asked, "Is it raining? and "O bhikṣus, is alms-seeking easy? What is the benefit of this?
What wheel of Dharma is being turned? He replied, "The ten divisions of the Hīnayāna, such as the Mahāsāṃghika, etc. The Buddhas said, "All is for the sake of benefiting [beings].

He asked about the rain, etc., in order to cause the matters of the preaching to be examined. Even though the Buddha already knows, he asks so that those who seek alms, such as Nanda and others, may resolve their minds to practice; it is not without purpose.
All that is beneficial is the Wheel of Dharma. Among the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), the first three pertain to the Buddha, while the last one pertains to his disciples.
Nevertheless, because the World-Honored One declared, "I have full knowledge regarding these four matters and am without fear," the World-Honored One has thus sounded [the drum].
These statements regarding the activities [of the Buddha] frequently contradict the scriptural texts; therefore, an objection arises.
As for the objection stating "all outflows (*āsrava*) and so forth," the question is: how was it that he first attained the Way and subdued the celestial Māra?
The Buddha then narrowed his eyes and spoke with anger to King Māra and the other wicked māras; it was as if the Buddha himself were possessed of wrath.

Furthermore, when Devadatta saw that the Buddha had left to become a renunciant, he said, "I have given birth to Rāhula through an illegitimate union. When the Buddha heard these words, [he remained unperturbed].

He immediately became angry with Devadatta, thinking, "This foolish and ignorant man! Although the sūtras say his outflows are exhausted, his greed, anger, and delusion are still manifest in his outward appearance.
He rebuked Devadatta for having both anger and attachment.
[Beings] are swept away and drowned by joy (*prīti*). To counteract this joy of the second dhyāna, the factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-aṅga*) is established in the third dhyāna.
This fourth absorption (*dhyāna*), being a superior pleasure compared to that of the third dhyāna, acts as an obstacle that prevents transcendence;

therefore, the Blessed One exhorted [beings] to abide in right mindfulness, and thus the factor of mindfulness is established in the fourth dhyāna. This question and answer concerns the fruits of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. Question: First...

Question: What is the distinction between the bodily radiance of the first dhyāna and that of the second dhyāna? Answer: The bodily radiance of the first dhyāna is like a maṇi jewel; it is dark within and bright without.
The bodily radiance of the second dhyāna is like the light of a lamp; both within and without are clearly illuminated. Now, according to this context:

if following the Hīnayāna, there is no feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*) in the first two dhyānas; what is called "pleasure" therein is actually pliancy (*praśrabdhi*). If following the Mahāyāna, it is indeed [the feeling of] pleasure.

Regarding the statement that these are definitely the four formless [attainments] (*ārūpya*) and so forth, it is divided into two parts: first, the explanation of the name; second, the presentation of their essential nature (*svabhāva*).

Within the explanation of the name, there is first the explanation of the general name and then the specific names. As for the general name: the general name is "formless" (*ārūpya*). *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 141.

Question: Why are these four called "formless" (*ārūpya*)? Answer: Because they transcend all phenomena that possess form (*rūpadharma*), and because there is no room for the presence of form-dharmas therein, they are called "formless.
"Four" refers to their number. Regarding the term "formless": "no-form" means the absence of form;
this refers to the four fundamental stages and the three preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*). These seven locations are termed "formless."

The preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) receives this name because it takes the form (*rūpa*) of the lower stages as its object and still possesses the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*).
According to schools such as the Mahāsāṃghika and the Mahīśāsaka, they maintain that there exists a subtle karmic-resultant form (*vipākaja-rūpa*) in the form realm;

because this form is subtle, the name "formless" (*ārūpya*) is established. As for what is called "formless," it means that those coarse forms are absent. According to the Mahāyāna, however, "formless" means that karma is absent.

Regarding the "fruit": it is admitted that there is the matter of the fruit. As for the term "formless" (*ārūpya*), this is discussed in reference to the karmic fruit. (The above constitutes the general designation). To explain the specific names hereafter:
first, as for the "Sphere of Infinite Space" (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), it fully relies upon the preparatory concentration (*sāmantaka-samādhi*) of the Sphere of Infinite Space.
Having first counteracted and eliminated the form (*rūpa*) of the fourth dhyāna and below, the *Fayuan* states: "Space" means to empty out form; "infinite" refers to the ten directions.

The various characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are indivisible; this is precisely the boundless space (*ākāśa*). Regarding "sphere" (*āyatana*): the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) together with the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) is called the sphere.

Boundless space is the object (*viṣaya*). The sphere is the cognizing mind (*ālambaka-citta*). Because it takes the boundless sphere as its object, it is explained according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound.
"Form" (*rūpa*) has the meaning of substantial obstruction. If one does not contemplate form as empty, then even when the spiritual power (*ṛddhi*) moves to and fro, there will be obstructions.

Obstruction. When the practice of contemplation is accomplished, that which is the object of one's mental engagement is the aspect of the "Infinite Space" (ākāśānantya). Question: What is meant by "sphere" (āyatana)?
Answer: There are two interpretations. The first states: with respect to the person practicing meditative concentration, the mind that takes space as its object is called the "sphere."
Second, regarding the "base" (*āyatana*): it refers to the concentrated mind capable of cognition, which is the locus for the arising of spiritual qualities.

Second, regarding the "Base of Infinite Consciousness": at that stage, the mind capable of cognition takes the "Base of Infinite Space" as its object; thus, the consciousness that cognizes space becomes the objective field.
Since the space of the lower stage is already infinite, the consciousness capable of cognizing it is likewise infinite. Third, regarding the "Base of Nothingness": [it is] small...
This is explained through two points. First: observing this stage, one sees that "I" and "mine" do not exist; thus it is called the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). Question:
Since "I" and "mine" are absent in all stages, why is this stage alone named the Sphere of Nothingness? Answer:

Although they exist in other stages, their influence is weak, inferior, and diminished, unlike in this stage. Second: "Nothing" refers to the observation of consciousness, which is the same as in the lower stages. In this stage...
Within this [state], one does not observe any object at all, but dwells in tranquility; this is called "nothingness" (ākiṃcanya). In the Mahāyāna, it is not so:

the twenty-two factors of that stage serve as the subjective perceiver (ālambaka), taking the consciousness of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana)—which itself takes infinite consciousness as its object—as its own objective field (ālambana).

Furthermore, it is said: "Alternatively, there is the Sphere of Nothingness, which takes the infinite consciousness that is the object of perception as its field. (These two [explanations] together constitute the primary [definition]).
Upon this consciousness, one contemplates and examines that apart from consciousness, there is not even a single dharma;

because it takes non-existence as its object and possesses nothing whatsoever, it is called "nothingness" (*ākiṃcanya*). Question: Since a mind does not arise by taking non-existence as its objective condition (*ālambana*), how can it draw forth and give rise to the cognizing mind?
Answer: Although one contemplates with non-existence as the object while practicing resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*), in practice, it must...
Based on the above observation, one forms the understanding that nothing exists. One contemplates that not a single dharma exists outside of consciousness.

It does not take emptiness as its object, nor does it take consciousness as its object; it takes only "nothingness" (*akiṃcanya*) as its objective sphere. Fourth, regarding the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*):

it takes the Sphere of Nothingness as its object, and this subjective mind is able to take that [sphere] as its mental object. Regarding the first character, "non" (*na*), it does not mean by way of non-existence. This...
Within this meditative concentration, the coarse perceptions of the lower stages are absent; thus it is called "non-perception" (*asaṃjñā*). The second character "non" (*a-*) does not mean "not";
the third character "non" (*a-*) does not mean "without. That is to say, it is not a state of non-existence. Rather, it refers to the extremely subtle internal mind of that stage.
Mental perception is not non-existent; therefore, it is called "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). The *Fayuan* states:

"In the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), the extremely subtle mind and mental factors—twenty-two dharmas in total—are not non-existent; therefore, it is called 'neither-perception-nor-non-perception'. Next, regarding the essential nature (*svabhāva*): the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* says there are two types:

first, that obtained through cultivation (*bhāvanā-labdha*); second, that obtained by birth (*upapatti-labdha*). If it is obtained through cultivation, it possesses the form resulting from meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*), which includes matter (*rūpa*).

Regarding the aggregates (*skandha*): if it is acquired by birth, its nature consists of four aggregates; thus, the *Mahāyāna-dharmayāna-vana* states that its nature consists of the five aggregates as its retinue.
Furthermore, regarding what is called "formless concentration" (*ārūpya-samādhi*), this refers to the four fundamental [formless attainments] and the first three preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*).

These take only the formless concentrations as their objects. However, the preparatory stage for the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-sāmantaka*) takes the form-objects of the lower realms as its object, because it still possesses the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*).

It is not that the object of focus is non-existent; rather, it is formless. Question: What is the difference between the characteristics of the meditative absorptions of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and those of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)?

Answer: When entering the meditative absorptions of the four dhyānas, the physical appearance of one's body is as if remaining within a room. When entering the formless absorptions, the physical appearance of one's body— *Note: The provided text ends abruptly. The sentence regarding the physical appearance in the formless absorptions would typically continue with a description of being like empty space.*

It is as if dwelling in empty space. Question: Why are there only these four meditative attainments (*dhyāna*) among the formless realms? Answer: They are established as four kinds based on the attainment of birth separated from the lower stages.

Separated from the fourth *dhyāna*, one attains birth in the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*). Separated from the Sphere of Infinite Space, one establishes the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).

Separated from the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, one establishes the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). Separated from the Sphere of Nothingness, one establishes the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

Regarding the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*): there is another explanation that, according to the duration of birth, there are four locations— namely, twenty thousand kalpas for the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*),

forty thousand kalpas for the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), sixty thousand kalpas for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), and eighty thousand kalpas for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (this concludes the explanation of the dhyānas and liberations).

Regarding the statement "liberation refers to the eight liberations, etc.," the *Fayuan* provides a tenfold analysis: first, enumerating the names; second, revealing the characteristics (*ākāra*); third, identifying the essential nature (*svabhāva*);

fourth, explaining the etymology; and fifth, the objects of focus (*ālambana*). Among these, the commentary contains three gates [corresponding to the first three]. Fourth is the explanation of the name; fifth is the objective sphere (*viṣaya*).
Six: Attainment by ordinary beings and sages; seven: Distinctions regarding the removal of hindrances; eight: Arising based on the physical body; nine: The two types of attainment of the fruit; ten:
Distinctions between the out-flowing (*sāsrava*) and the non-out-flowing (*anāsrava*). *Fahua xuanzan yaoji*, Scroll 16.
In the winter of the sixth year of the Qiánfú era, the bhikṣu Hóngjǔ of Kāiyuán Monastery in Wenzhōu transcribed and made offerings of this [text] while lecturing on the *Mahākaruṇāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
It was completed on the tenth day of the seventh month in the first year of the Hóngcháng era (the Year of Xīnyǒu). By Yǒngshí.
Completed on the second day of the tenth month of the same year.
*Fahua jing xuanzan yaoji*, Scroll Seventeen,
compiled by the Shamen Qifu of Jingshui.

Regarding the statement "based on the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, chapter twelve, etc.," this is a citation of the text to explain the general name. The old Śrāvaka treatises speak of the "eight liberations" (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*). Lü Fu states:
"The first two liberations turn away from the pure and move toward the impure; the third liberation turns away from the impure and moves toward the pure;
the fourth liberation turns away from form (*rūpa*) and moves toward space (*ākāśa*); the fifth liberation turns away from space and moves toward consciousness (*vijñāna*)."
The sixth liberation turns away from consciousness and moves toward the formless; the seventh liberation turns away from the coarse and moves toward the subtle;
