the eighth liberation turns away from perception and feeling and moves toward cessation. The commentary states: "The first three liberations are entirely distinct from those of the Mahāyāna, whereas the latter five appear similar to the Mahāyāna.
The *Jiàn yào* says: "According to the Mahāyāna interpretation, the first three liberations attain liberation by contemplating form (*rūpa*)."

The next four [liberations] attain liberation regarding the mind; the final one attains liberation regarding both the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). Furthermore, the practitioners of the Hīnayāna cultivate the first three liberations:

next, they eliminate craving for visible forms (*varṇa-rāga*) by forming the perception of impurity (*aśubha-saṃjñā*); they eliminate the obstacle to transformation (*nirmāṇāvaraṇa*) by forming the perception of light (*āloka-saṃjñā*).

As for Mahāyāna liberation, it must involve contemplating that one has already become free from attachment to color. In contrast, the Hīnayāna liberation involves contemplating that which is not yet [free].

Regarding the "liberation from the taints" (*vairāgya-vimukti*): Zhiyun states that the first three remove the obstacles to transformation; the next four induce the production of the merits of the "conflict-free" (*araṇā*) and "wish-fulfilling" (*praṇidhijñāna*) concentrations;
and the final one is the ultimate fulfillment of liberation. Thus, there are eight liberations. Furthermore, the first seven are both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
The last one is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*). According to the Hīnayāna, all eight liberations (*vimokṣa*) are tainted.

However, when a Mahāyāna practitioner cultivates liberation, they must first rely on the preliminary concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*) of the first dhyāna to suppress and sever the defilements of the desire realm.

All the faculties and objects of the desire realm are then already free from the taints of passion. If one were to call this state "liberation" immediately, it would not yet be the actual thing required.

Furthermore, when one takes this perception of form and makes it luminous, it is then called "liberation" (*vimokṣa*). It is liberated from the obstacles to meditative concentration and attains mastery over its objects;

because it is both "understanding" (*vi*) and "liberated" (*mokṣa*), it is termed "liberation. Eighth is the numerical designation: they are called the "eight liberations. (The above is the general explanation; the following is the specific explanation.)
Regarding the passage beginning with "There is the contemplation of form" (*rūpasaṃjñin*), although many versions of the sacred teachings have been cited previously, none were fully comprehensive.
Only the *Fayuan zhang* provides an extensive explanation. Among its ten sections, the commentary cites the first three; however, this text lacks a section on the "Explanation of Names.
Instead, the names are explained directly at the point where they are listed. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that there are two causes and conditions by which it is so named.
There are those who possess form (*rūpin*). First, those born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) who attain the meditative absorptions of the form realm (*rūpadhyāna*) are called "possessors of form.
Second, those who produce the perception of light (*ālokasaṃjñā*) within the stages of the form realm are called "possessors of form. Furthermore, there are three meanings of "existence" (*bhava*):

first, those who are free from the defilements of the desire realm and attain the meditative absorptions of the form realm are called "possessors of form"; second, those who do not produce the perceptions of smallness or greatness, but produce [the perception of] light...

The clear perception is called "having form" (*rūpi*). Third, when one has not yet relied upon the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) to counteract the defilements of the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*), but dwells amidst those defilements of form, it is called "having form.

This refers merely to contemplating the internal and external forms of the sense faculties and objects within the desire realm (*kāma-dhātu*), and engaging in mental cultivation and resolute conviction (*adhimukti*);
this is what is meant by "having form. Question: Regarding "having form," why is it not stated as "having internal form"? Furthermore, regarding the contemplation of all forms, why...

It does not say "contemplating external forms. The answer is: it is solely because the person in the first liberation contemplates both the five internal sense organs and the five external sense objects together.

If one were to say "internal," there would be the fear of confusion with contemplating only the five internal sense organs; if one were to say "external," there would be the fear of confusion with contemplating only the five external sense objects.
Therefore, while there are forms, they are not called "internal"; when contemplating various forms, they are not called "external. Regarding the contemplation of various forms, there is...

The contemplation of form (*rūpa*) is explained according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound. Furthermore, if "external" is defined by having already abandoned defilements, then the five sense faculties (*indriya*) are internal;

yet they may also be termed external. Conversely, if "internal" is defined by not having abandoned defilements, then the five sense objects (*viṣaya*) are external; yet they may also be termed internal.

In the fifteenth chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, fearing that [the practitioner] might erroneously assume that [contemplation] only takes the five external sense objects and the five internal sense faculties as its object, it does not differentiate between internal and external when taking form as the object.
This refers to the external.
Regarding the statement "the two internal [liberations] are without form," etc., one asks: why is the word "internal" specifically applied to the second liberation? The answer is:
among the first liberation, a practitioner who is initially training has only abandoned the defilements of the desire realm, but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the form realm.
If the character "internal" (內) were added [to the first liberation], it would likely imply that one has not yet abandoned defilement; thus, it is called "internal.

It was thought that for a beginner who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the desire realm, the character "internal" should not be added. Regarding the second liberation, it does not distinguish between those who have newly practiced and those who have practiced for a long time;
rather, it includes those who have abandoned the defilements of the form realm. To distinguish it from the former, the character "internal" is added. Question: What is meant by "signless" (無相)?
Regarding the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*), the answer "internally possessing the perception of no-form" (*adhyātma-arūpa-saṃjñin*) is based on three causes and conditions:

first, being free from the defilements of the two realms of desire and form is called the perception of no-form; second, attaining the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) is called the perception of no-form; third, not producing light is called the perception of no-form.

This second liberation first relies upon the meditative concentration of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-samādhi*); having already abandoned the defilements of the realm of form, it now relies upon this [sphere of infinite consciousness].
Having become detached from passion, one establishes an external designation. Taking this luminous color as being either small or large—this is the second liberation (*vimokṣa*).

Although here one relies on the concentration of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-samādhi*) to become detached from the passions of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), when one contemplates external colors as being small or large, one immediately returns to rely on a concentration of the form realm, once again taking the colors detached from the form realm as being small or large.

Regarding perception (*saṃjñā*): contemplative reflection (*manasikāra*) is superior. Because those formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) cannot contemplate form as being "little" or "much," and because the perception that takes form as its object within the internal mind is incompatible with the formless sphere attainment (*ākāśānantyāyatana-samāpatti*), it has already been counteracted and eliminated.
Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "The formless attainments do not manifest. Question: What are these two aforementioned types called? Answer: They are called liberations (*vimokṣa*).
The first liberation relies on the concentration of the form realm (*rūpadhātu-samādhi*) and is called "liberation" because it is free from the defilements of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-kleśa*).

The second liberation attains the concentration of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-samādhi*) and is called the "second liberation" because it is further removed from the defilements of both the desire and form realms.

The above concludes the explanation of being internally without the perception of form. Below follows the explanation of contemplating external forms. Question: What is meant by "contemplating external forms"? Answer: It is explained through three meanings regarding the internal.

Regarding external forms (*bāhyarūpa*): first, the five sense faculties (*pañcendriya*) are called internal forms; second, sentient beings (*sattva*) are called internal, while non-sentient things (*asattva*) are called external;
third, those who have already abandoned the taints of passion (*rāga*) are called external forms, while those who have not yet abandoned them are called internal.

Now, this liberation involves contemplating forms that have already abandoned the taints of passion, and by forming mental images—whether small or large—it is called the contemplation of external forms.

Regarding the statement "the three pure liberations and so forth," the *Yogācārabhūmi* says: "Having attained equanimity and mindfulness that are perfect and pure, one takes this as a basis and cultivates the cultivation of pure, supreme conduct to perfection; this is called 'attaining liberation. The intended meaning is that one attains the fourth dhyāna."
Because one has abandoned the obstacles of the three stages—vitarka, vicāra, and joy (prīti)—one is said to have "attained the perfection of equanimity and mindfulness, which is pure and bright.
Furthermore, because all agitation has been stilled and one is free from the obstacles to the transformation of the pure and the impure, it is called "liberation" (vimokṣa).
This also involves observing external forms while being formless oneself, producing various signs such as the pure and the impure; this has already been explained previously.

Because there is no internal form and so forth, these are not discussed in detail. The first two are collectively termed "pure liberations" (*śubha-vimokṣa*) because they are described according to their predominant quality.

The third alone is specifically named the "pure liberation," as it is called "pure" (*śubha*) due to its freedom from defilement (*vairāgya*). There are three meanings of "purity": first, it is pure because it has previously abandoned defilement;
second, it is pure because its supporting meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is free from the three calamities and eight afflictions; and third, it functions as purity itself.
The luminous and fresh aspect transforms so as not to be an impure aspect; this is called "purity" (*śubha*).

Regarding the phrase "realizing with the body" (*kāyena sākṣātkṛtvā*) and so forth, the *Jianyao* (Essentials) states: there are two explanations. First, it is named according to its metaphorical application among the five faculties (*pañcendriya*).

The body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) apprehends its object most intimately; thus it is called "body" (*kāya*). When the sixth consciousness attains this liberation, it intimately realizes the principle, just as the body-faculty intimately perceives its object.
Second, it is named according to its essential nature: the "body" here is the mind itself; because the concentrated mind intimately realizes [the object], it is called "body.
Third, because the third and eighth liberations each reside on the side of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), [they are so designated].
The third [liberation] is the limit of the four fundamental dhyānas; the eighth is the limit of the nine successive attainments (anupūrvavihārasamāpatti).

Because noble wisdom directly realizes them, it is called "realization" (sākṣātkriyā). This third liberation is personally accomplished and attained by the sixth consciousness; thus, it is called "bodily realization" (kāyasākṣitva).

Question: Since the first two liberations are also directly attained, why are they not called "bodily realization"? Answer: Because the first two involve conceptual mental cultivation and have not yet been termed "actual.
Upon reaching this third liberation, one truly attains and achieves the reality itself; therefore, it is so named.

Regarding the phrase "attaining realization through the body" (*kāyasākṣātkriyā*) and being "fully endowed" (*paripūrṇa*): only the third liberation and the eighth liberation of the bodhisattva uniquely receive the designation of "attaining realization through the body and being fully endowed.

Question: At the time when the eighth liberation—the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodhasamāpatti*)—is attained, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) has already ceased. How [can there be realization through the body]?

It is called "direct attainment" (*pratyakṣalābha*). Answer: If one speaks in terms of the stage of perfection (*pariniṣpanna*), there is no mental consciousness, and thus it is not called direct attainment.
Now, speaking in terms of the time when the mind is present, [the attainment] has already been accomplished; it is only during the state of non-mental-consciousness that it becomes manifest.

This is also called "bodily realization" (*kāyasākṣin*). Question: Why is it called "complete"? Answer: The third liberation is the stage of fulfillment for the four fundamental dhyānas. Subsequently, it must...

Because all preceding stages are fully accomplished, it is called "complete" upon reaching the fourth dhyāna. The exhaustion of the eighth consciousness is the culminating stage of the nine successive attainments;
therefore, it is termed "complete. "Complete" (paripūrṇa) carries the meaning of being fully endowed. Question: What is meant by "abiding"? Answer:
Briefly stated, this term "liberation abides" means that it draws forth various meritorious qualities and causes them to dwell within the body.
Therefore, it is called "abiding" (*sthiti*). Alternatively, this liberation is the place where the noble ones (*ārya*) dwell;

thus it is called "abiding. The Noble Ones often provide these two interpretations. Because the first two liberations are characterized by a concentrated mind that is obscured and a weak engagement with a distant object, they are merely termed "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*). This third liberation alone is termed "abiding. Furthermore, regarding the first two liberations...
This liberation is the cause of application; the third liberation is the fulfillment of the fruit.

Regarding the "sphere of infinite space": the characteristics of the two realms of desire and form are easy to understand, whereas the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) is difficult to discern;

thus, it is designated by the name of its specific sphere. That is to say, it is the objective field (*ālambana*) that serves as the antidote to form, wherein all signs (*nimitta*) of the ten directions [are absent].

It cannot be conceptually differentiated. That which is called the "sphere of infinite space" (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) refers to the various phenomena, such as meditative concentration (*samādhi*), within that stage, which serve as the basis;

thus it is termed a "sphere. Regarding this explanation of "sphere," with respect to the practitioner who is able to cultivate it, the sphere refers to the space upon which they rely and the place where they rely.
The intended meaning is that the single aggregate of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) of that stage is the basis for cultivation, while simultaneously being the object.
Regarding its basis: when one attains the mind of that stage, the sphere of space first manifests; this is called the "base.

This occurs because, having previously attained the concentration of the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-samādhi*) and already abandoned the defilements of that stage, one now contemplates the aforementioned object once more to further effect liberation.
The same applies to the other four [formless attainments].

Regarding the "sphere of infinite consciousness" (*vijñānānantyāyatana*): one first attains the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of that specific level and becomes detached from the defilements of that level.

One then repeatedly contemplates the consciousness that takes the sphere of infinite space as its object; since space is infinite, consciousness is also infinite. This is because the "sphere" (*āyatana*) is precisely the perceiving mind.

Regarding the "liberation of the sphere of nothingness" (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-vimokṣa*), there are two explanations in the Hīnayāna: first, observing that within this state there is no self or what belongs to a self, it is called "nothingness"; second, not observing any object at all, it is called "nothingness.

This is not like the observation of emptiness in the lower stages, nor is it like the observation of consciousness as an object in the lower stages; because one dwells in tranquility within this state, it is called [the liberation of] nothingness.
All [other schools] maintain that there are external objects; the Mahāyāna is not so. It observes only that there are no objects apart from consciousness.
There is not a single dharma that exists outside of consciousness. Question: Is this not the contemplation of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*)? Answer: It is not.

The contemplation of Consciousness-Only observes that all phenomena arise from consciousness; that is the contemplation of Consciousness-Only. This "non-existence" means that nothing exists apart from consciousness. At first glance, it seems like a contemplation.
Regarding "consciousness" (*vijñāna*): in reality, one does not contemplate it. Rather, contemplating that there is nothing external to consciousness constitutes its mode of activity (*ākāra*).
As for the phrase "the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), the first "non" (*na*) does not mean "absence.

Within this meditative absorption, the coarse perception of the lower stages is absent; that is, having transcended to the perception of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), it is called "non-perception. The second...
"Non-character" (a-saṃjñā) does not mean "not by means of. The third term, "non-character," does not mean "not by means of non-existence.

There is only the ability of the mind in that stage to take internal objects as its focus; the extremely subtle mind and mental factors—the twenty-two dharmas—are indeed not non-existent. This is called "non-perception" (a-saṃjñā).
"Non-perception" is itself the mind.

Regarding the phrase "the cessation of perception and feeling" (*saṃjñā-vedita-nirodha*) and so forth: perception and feeling are two factors that act as obstacles; among all mental factors (*caitta*), they alone are termed "mental formations" (*citta-saṃskāra*) because they strongly assist the mind.
When one becomes weary of their toil and deliberation, they temporarily cease. Merely being free from feeling is called the "liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling. Question:

Within the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), since the sixth and seventh consciousnesses do not function, how can it be said that one "bodily realizes" (*kāyena sākṣātkaroti*) it? Answer: [The body is the basis for this realization.]

In reality, it has already been attained during the state of mind (*cittavasthā*), yet it must rely upon the state of no-mind (*acittaka*) to be manifested. Question: What is meant by "abiding" (*sthiti*)? Answer:

Some say that it refers to abiding in the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the absence of conflict (*araṇā*), and the merit of vows (*praṇidhāna-guṇa*); while within those meditative concentrations, it is called "abiding.

Furthermore, it is called "abiding" because it is the place where the noble ones (*ārya*) travel and dwell. Question: It was previously stated that what is directly grasped by the noble ones is called the "body" (*kāya*). How is this so?
This is the realization. In this eighth liberation, mental images (*saṃjñā*) do not function. How is this self-realized? Answer: Because it pervades the physical body (*rūpakāya*).

Regarding the passage in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, chapter twenty-nine, beginning with "internally [having] the perception of form" (*adhyātmaṃ rūpasaṃjñī*), the commentary omits the word "perception" (*saṃjñā*). According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, it says "internally having the perception of form. Question: What is meant by "internally having form"? Answer: The *Shō* (Commentary) states:

The Small Vehicle practitioners only contemplate [this state], yet they have not yet abandoned the defilements of form (*rūparāga*). Question: Why is it called "internally having form"? Answer: The *Shō* says:
"Having internal form" (*antar-rūpin*): "internal" (*antara*) refers to the internal body, so called because it possesses the forms of the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*).
Because one has cherished and loved this internal body since beginningless time, one does not attain liberation. Second, wives, children, and men are also termed "internal.

When one has not yet practiced contemplation, one's craving and attachment toward external wives and children are just as they are toward the internal body; therefore, they are termed "internal. This explains "internal."
[This refers to] the term. When there is within the internal mind the perception of those forms of desire, it is called "having form," and thus it is termed "internal possession.
Question: What is meant by "contemplating external forms"? Answer: As for contemplating external forms, from time immemorial one has craved and loved the internal body;
because greed and defilement arise toward the internal body, one does not attain liberation. If one is to be transformed, one then contemplates one's own body as impure. Thus...
Difficult. One must proceed from the easy toward the difficult, and observe from the outside toward the inside. This has two meanings: first, because it is outside the body, it is called "external";
one performs the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) upon both animate and inanimate forms. Second, this very internal body is also termed "external.
When the practitioner’s contemplation of the mind has become mature, they contemplate the internal body as if it were external.
The object is also called "external. For now, that which is outside the body is termed the "external world.

One should conceive of both sentient and insentient things as impure, or practice the five contemplations for settling the mind (*pañca-vastu-praśamana-bhāvanā*), such as the contemplation of the bloated corpse, the contemplation of worms, and the contemplation of putrefaction, thereby subduing the mind of craving.
Regarding the statement, "As for saying that internally one has not yet subdued and eliminated views, etc.," this is a citation from the *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya*. Question:

The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* belongs to the Mahāyāna, whereas the *Abhidharmakośa* belongs to the Hīnayāna. Why does the Master of the Commentary cite a passage from the *Kośa* to explain a Mahāyāna treatise? Answer:

It is precisely because the path described in the *Abhidharmakośa*—namely, "internally possessing form while contemplating external forms"—corresponds to what is stated in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* as "internally not yet having subdued... [the defilements].

The meaning of "the perception of form in the seer" (draṣṭuḥ rūpasaṃjñā) is the same [as previously explained]. This is why the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* is used here to explain the *Abhidharmakośa*. "Internal" refers to the internal body.

Regarding the various things that can see, the "seer" is a conceptual construct (*prajñapti*). Within this conceptualized internal body, there exists the perception of form characterized by desire; this is called "the perception of form in the seer."
Regarding the statement that one contemplates external forms as impure: according to the perspective of the Hīnayāna, when there is a mind of craving for form within, this is called "possessing form.
To eliminate this craving, one contemplates external forms as impure. There are two kinds of "external": first, the forms of the five external sense objects are considered external;
second, once the contemplation of the mind has been perfected, one subsequently contemplates one's own body as well, realizing it does not belong to oneself.
The four great elements are a provisional combination; in the end, they return to the great earth. Why, then, must one harbor greedy attachment?
With deluded consciousness as the "internal," such things as form and so forth are called the "external. Question: How can there be greed for form within the internal body?

Regarding the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), one contemplates external objects within the internal body to eliminate internal greedy thoughts. Answer: For those of the Two Vehicles, their contemplation of the mind is subtle and weak, and thus they are unable [to achieve this].
Furthermore, one contemplates the internal body as impure. This practice must proceed from the easy toward the difficult. Contemplating from the external toward the internal is easy;
alternatively, one may proceed from the derivative toward the fundamental. Since beginningless time, the arising of greed in the internal mind has been induced by external observation.
When the internal mind arises, it is always due to external objects. Therefore, by observing the external, one quiets the internal phenomena. Question: What is the first stage of the Hīnayāna?
First, the accomplishment of liberation. Answer: When first practicing contemplation, one contemplates a single corpse from head to foot as it becomes bloated and putrefied;

subsequently, one no longer gives rise to desire for this object. Next, one contemplates five corpses, ten persons, and so on, until contemplating them throughout an entire province or a nation, yet still no desire arises.
Then, one again proceeds from the broad to the narrow, focusing on a single corpse.
Furthermore, one does not give rise to desire for these superior objects either. Gradually shifting one’s observation, the mind turns inward and contemplates one’s own body as impure;
this is called the first accomplishment of liberation for a practitioner of the Hīnayāna.
It is also said that it is incorrect to observe only external objects belonging to others as impure while failing to observe one's own internal body.

Regarding the statement, "Now it is not so": this refers to the previous claim that those who have not yet internally subdued and eliminated the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*) are the same as those described in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, which agrees with the *Abhidharmakośa* and the Mahāyāna.
Question: Why is it stated here, "Now it is not so," when the Mahāyāna doctrine—in which the commentator [Sthiramati] actually refutes the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*—appears to be similar?
Answer: Although there is partial agreement regarding the internal non-subjugation and non-elimination of the perception of form, within this context...

There are many differing interpretations; therefore, it is said that "now it is not so. First, the Mahāyāna forms the perception of light, whereas the Hīnayāna practices the contemplation of impurity.
Second, the Mahāyāna eliminates the obstacle of transformation, whereas the Hīnayāna eliminates craving for form.

Third, the Mahāyāna contemplates that which is already free from the taints of passion, whereas the Hīnayāna contemplates that which is not yet free from the taints of passion; hence it is said that it is "not so. Fourth, the Master of the Commentary explains: "Now it is..."
If it were not so, then within the liberation of the Mahāyāna, the Abhidharma would be identical to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and not the same as the *Abhidharmakośa*;
therefore, it says "if it were not so. Fifth, it is not merely emptiness; this differs from the *Abhidharmakośa* and also differs from the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.
The preceding explanation of the phrase "it is not so" is the Master’s own interpretation. Question: Since the Mahāyāna has already abandoned the obstructions, what further use is there for...?
[The author] replies: It is not so, because one wishes to purify the mind and cause obstacles to recede further.
Regarding the statement "the initial practitioner according to the *Abhidharma* text," this refers to a person at the beginning of practice for the first liberation. Question:

The *Abhidharma-kośa-śāstra* does not distinguish between "initial practice" and "long-term practice. Examining the treatise, it states: "Regarding those who have not yet subdued [defilements] within..."
"Perception of form" (*rūpa-saṃjñā*), or "the perception of form established in the viewer" (*draṣṭu-rūpa-saṃjñā*). This is the heading of the treatise (*śāstra*). The commentary below explains:

"That is to say, within one's own body, before relying on the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), one has not yet suppressed and eliminated the perception of form in the viewer, or the perception of form in the viewer is established and manifests before them.

Since there is no explicit text in the treatise regarding the words "initial cultivation" (*ādikarmika*) and "long-term cultivation" (*bahulīkṛta*), by what authority did the Master of the Commentary (*ṭīkākāra*) state them? Answer: [The answer follows].

Although the text is not explicit, the principle admits of both interpretations. The Master of the Commentary (Soshu), embodying the intent of the treatise, placed the word "or" (*vā*) within the text.

If it were intended as a single meaning, why would he have placed the word "or"? Therefore, we know that these two meanings correspond to the distinction between "initial cultivation" and "long-term cultivation.
This is because the treatise contains the two characters "inner body" (*adhyātma-kāya*); the *Chao* [Commentary] first explains "inner" at this point.

Regarding the body: as for the "internal body," there are three interpretations. First, it is said that the intended meaning of the treatise refers to the body itself; the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is called "internal.
Second, the apprehension of the five sense organs and the five sense objects is called the internal body, as they are not separate from the physical body.

Third, the apprehension of the manifest colors within the two realms of desire and form—both sentient and insentient—is termed the internal body, because one has not yet relied upon the meditative absorptions of the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhyāna*).

Having subdued and eliminated the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*), one dwells within that very perception of form; this is called "the internal body" (*adhyātma-kāya*). [This is] the subsequent commentary.
According to the initial practitioner described in the *Abhidharma* (the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*), this is the arrangement established by the author of the commentary (*ṭīkākāra*).
Regarding the phrase "the body is in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and so forth," this refers to the treatise (*śāstra*). Specifically, it concerns a person who has first cultivated liberation;
their body is in the desire realm, thereby distinguishing them from those in the two higher realms.

The phrase "having already abandoned the desires of the desire realm" refers to the object of observation within meditative concentration; it does not refer to the concentrated mind that performs the observation simultaneously.
If expressed fully, one should say: "Having relied upon the dhyāna of the form realm, one has already abandoned the desires of the desire realm. This is how the text should be read.
For a beginner, it is necessary to rely on the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*) of the first *dhyāna* to subdue, eliminate, and sever the desires of the desire realm.
The nine grades of afflictions are called "leaving the desire realm" because one has already abandoned craving; thus, this state is termed "having already left the desires of the desire realm.
The *Miǎochāo* (Miscellaneous Excerpts) states: "This refers to ordinary beings, followers of the Two Vehicles, and Bodhisattvas who still abide within the desire realm."
Regarding those who do not reside in the upper realms: when such a person again cultivates liberation, their body remains in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Since they rely on the "not-yet-attained" concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*) of the first dhyāna to distance themselves from all visible objects (*rūpa-viṣaya*) of the desire realm, this is collectively termed "detachment from defilement" (*vairāgya*).

"Is this not liberation? He replied: "Although form is free from defilement, it is not yet called liberation. One must rely upon the fundamental dhyāna of the first dhyāna to further contemplate the desire realm;
having already abandoned the perception of form-color, one cultivates the perception of light. Once the perception of light is accomplished..."
This is called the accomplishment of liberation (the first two lines of the commentary on "liberating the body" are reversed).
Regarding the statement, "not yet relying on the formless [realms]," etc., the question is: what further name is given to this initial cultivation?

The answer is that the commentary states, "not yet relying on the formless [realms]," etc., for one and a half lines, which serves as a further refinement concerning the person who is initially cultivating. The commentator divides and clarifies the person who is initially cultivating, saying: "Not yet..."

Relying on the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), one suppresses and eliminates the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*). This perception of form is not the perception of craving for form; rather, it is a defiled phenomenon (*kleśa-dharma*).
Here, the term "perception of form" is used specifically to distinguish it [from craving]. The perception of form is the cognitive engagement (*ākāra*) that takes form as its object.
For example, a beginner who has this cognitive engagement of the perception of form has not yet suppressed and eliminated it by relying on the formless attainments. Question:
"What is meant by 'view' (*dṛṣṭi*)? What is meant by 'the one' (*ya*)? Answer: "View" refers to the capacity to see. "The one" refers to the conventional designation (*prajñapti*).

As for the term "perception of form" (*rūpa-saṃjñā*), it refers to the cognitive engagement (*ākāra*) that takes form as its object. Therefore, it is said that "the view is the perception of form. Question:

Since this is not the perception of craving for form, why does the commentary (*śāstra*) speak of "subduing and eliminating" it? Answer: Because when the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samādhi*) are present...

The perception, mental formations, and conceptualizations regarding form have already ceased. Now, at the time this concentration arises, the perception, mental formations, and conceptualizations regarding form have already ceased;
therefore, it is called "subduing and eliminating. In reality, however, form and the formless do not see one another.

Regarding the phrase "not yet free from desire for the realm of form" (*rūpadhātu-vītarāga*): Question: If that is so, why does this single line of the commentary say "not yet free from desire for the realm of form"?

Since it specifically mentions "desire for the realm of form," it is clearly understood to refer to the perception of greed for form. Answer: This is the intended meaning of this single line of the commentary.

For a beginner who has not yet attained the formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samādhi*), it is known that they have not yet abandoned desire for the realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu*) because they have not attained the formless absorptions.

When a beginner practicing the first liberation (*prathama-vimokṣa*) relies upon the realm of form to suppress and eliminate the defiled greed of the desire realm, all forms such as the sense faculties and objects of the desire realm are forms that have been detached from defilement. Therefore, [it is said] only...

This is a distinction made regarding those who have not yet attained the formless realm; it does not mean that they actually possess greed for form. They have attained a conceptual understanding (*saṃjñā*) that takes form as its object.
Therefore, the commentary states: "Because they have not yet abandoned desire for the realm of form."

Regarding the phrase "if one has long practiced the karma," etc., it should be stated in full as: "having relied upon the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) and having become detached from the desire for the realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu-kāma*).
As for the term "desire for the realm of form," this refers to the conceptualization and mental engagement (*saṃjñā-vitarka*) regarding form, not to sensual craving (*rāga*). Question: How so?

Regarding the attainment of detachment from the desires of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*): the procedure must first rely upon the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) of that respective level. One must first suppress and sever the defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭadharma*) consisting of the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the form realm;
these forms of the form realm are precisely what constitute the objects of detachment. Nevertheless, at the time of detaching from the defilements while taking form as an object—

Regarding form (*rūpa*), one still forms a conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) and an application of mental attention (*manasikāra*) toward it as "form. If this very conceptualization and application of attention become an attachment, it is not called liberation;

it must likewise be countered through an antidote (*pratipakṣa*). Therefore, within the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), one counters the conceptualization and application of attention toward form.
Question: Why does [the text] not simply state that the seer has no conceptualization of form, yet instead says "the seer"?

Regarding the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*): the answer is that it is actually the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-samādhi*) that truly serves as the antidote to the perception of form; thus, the perception of form has already ceased.

It is only because, while one is precisely in the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space, one contemplates only that which cannot contemplate form. This is due to two reasons.
However, one must further establish the contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). This serves two purposes: first, to cause the hindrances to recede; second, to cause the contemplation to increase in clarity.

Therefore, one again relies on the *dhyāna* of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), taking the previously attained detachment from the taints of form as the basis to establish and perform present mental engagement and observation.
This involves merely establishing the perception of form (*rūpasaṃjñā*), yet not yet the perception of light (*ālokasaṃjñā*). (The above concludes the establishment of the present state.)

Question: Since both the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are free from defilement (*vītarāga*), it is not yet clear whether, at the time of repeated contemplation (*punar-vipaśyanā*), one contemplates the forms of the desire realm or the forms of the form realm.

Answer: There are two explanations. First, according to the *Abhidharmakośa* (Dharma-lakṣaṇa), when the forms of the desire and form realms have already been freed from defilement, if the faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*) are suffering, one repeatedly contemplates them as light (*āloka*). Second, it is said that according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*: [The text continues with the second explanation.]
One contemplates all internal and external forms within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and forms the perception of light (*ālokasaṃjñā*). (The second [method] is correct. Question:

How is this known? Answer: A person who has long practiced liberation does not contemplate the desire realm when forming the perception of light; the practice must necessarily rely upon the forms of the desire realm.

Regarding the statement "contemplating all [forms] of the desire realm and so forth": for a beginner, this is based on the first or second dhyāna; for one who has practiced for a long time, it is based on the fundamental dhyānas of the four dhyānas.
One contemplates all internal and external forms of the desire realm as a whole by forming the perception of light, because the lower portion consists of both the internal and external.
A question is raised: the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that one contemplates all [forms] as being free from the taints of color and as light.

Regarding the clarification of the perception (*saṃjñā*): it is not said that one who repeatedly contemplates the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) must necessarily be a person of the first liberation (*prathama-vimokṣa*).
Is it not possible that one might merely attain detachment from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) without attaining detachment from the taints of the form realm?

Answer: The first yoga speaks only of the desire realm because it is explained in reference to the beginner (*ādikarmika*). Second, it is named according to its broader scope; if one speaks of the "desire realm," it refers to both the initial cultivation and the long-term cultivation.
[This] encompasses all people. If one speaks of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), only those who have practiced for a long time attain it;

beginners do not. Third, because the objects of the form realm are subtle, they are easy to train and refine; one attains them through a single contemplation and does not require repeated contemplation.

In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the obstacles of form obstruct concentration strongly, making it rigid; therefore, it is necessary to practice repeated contemplation. Question: Why does one not rely on the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*)?
[Question: Regarding the observation [of the earth], why does one not form the perception of male or female, but only the perception of the phenomenon (*dharmasaṃjñā*)?

[Answer: It is because one wishes to transform the great earth into gold, silver, and so forth. If one were to form the perception of male or female instead of the perception of the phenomenon, one would lack mastery and would be unable to transform the great earth and so on.
If one forms the perception of the phenomenon, whenever one wishes to transform it, one can transform it; thus, one attains success.
Because of mastery, one must produce various signs. That is to say, for this person who has long practiced, the cravings of both the desire realm and the form realm have been completely severed.

Desiring to give rise to supernormal powers—such as passing through stone walls as if they were open spaces and causing obstacles to recede to a great distance—one further relies upon the established visualization of "form already abandoned.
One forms the perception of light. Regarding the perception of light, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Twelve Stages) asks: "What is light?"
Regarding "perception" (*saṃjñā*): it refers to a certain person, namely a practitioner of meditation, who, within a dark room, gives rise to this antidote toward all lights.
With a diligent mind, he correctly grasps their signs and reflects upon them thoroughly. Just as it is with the lower direction, so it is with the upper direction;
in this way, because he treats all dark signs, he establishes this perception. Furthermore, within meditative concentration, he repeatedly...
One repeatedly takes up the sign of light; that is to say, either the light of a lamp, or the radiance of fire, or the light of the solar disk, or the light of the lunar disk.
Thus one observes, proceeding from the small to the great.
Regarding the statement "by means of the first three liberations, etc.": herein, light draws forth the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*).

First, the meanings of the bases of mastery and totalities are described individually; subsequently, the text is analyzed and explained. Question: Regarding the object of the first liberation, the treatise states it consists of "all forms" (*sarvarūpa*).

Why, then, is it said here that they "comprise the small and the many"? Answer: The bases of mastery specifically involve the cultivation of meditative observations of the small, the many, and so forth.
Now, these are collectively subsumed as "light"; therefore, this does not contradict the statement in the treatise that one contemplates all forms (*rūpa*). Question:

Why is it necessary here to cite the eight spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*), and furthermore, how do they differ from or agree with the objects of focus (*ālambana*) for the liberations (*vimokṣa*)?

Answer: Because they are mutually dependent causes. Thus, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states: "One practices based on liberation; one initiates skillful means by means of the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*);

and one brings them to thorough completion by means of the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*). It further states: "If one achieves completion regarding those [spheres of totality], then one reaches the ultimate regarding liberation," and so forth.
For this reason, it is necessary to induce the qualities of the spheres of mastery. Question: Although it is said that they are mutually dependent, even if there are two...

Question: What fault is there in [the objects of] the spheres being distinct? Answer: As in the case of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), which, in order to induce the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), performs signless contemplation (*animittadhyāna*) and contemplates true suchness (*tathatā*) and so forth—though they differ in terms of proximity—their focal objects must be identical because of liberation. Thus, the stages of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and so forth arise.

The subsequent bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*) and the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) are likewise mutually dependent for their fulfillment and completion. This clarifies the limits of the objects of focus;
it distinguishes [these] from the eight bases of mastery and ten bases of totality of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*).

Since they take form (*rūpa*) as their object and conceive of it as small, large, and so forth, and since the first three are capable of inducing [the subsequent ones], it is clear that both take form as their object. These objects of focus for this liberation (*vimokṣa*) subsume the eight bases of mastery.
[These] are the forms of the ten spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) and so forth. Question:

Since it is said that the "spheres of mastery" (*abhibhvāyatana*) and so forth are induced by the first three liberations (*vimokṣa*), why are they not explained immediately after the third liberation, but rather clarified within the first liberation?

Answer: In reality, it should indeed be so. However, there are briefly two reasons for placing them here. First, it is said to distinguish [this teaching] from the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), which [only] concerns greed...

Regarding form, one practices the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*). Now, in the Mahāyāna, those who have long cultivated their practice—because they have eliminated the obstacles to the transformation-body (*nirmāṇa-āvaraṇa*)—subsume within the meaning of the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭāv abhibhv-āyatanāni*) the notions of "small," "large," and so forth, while forming the perception of light within liberation (*vimokṣa*).
If one speaks of the eight bases of mastery, one takes the light from within liberation and forms the notions of "small" and "large" within the eight bases of mastery; these two are mutually related.

Because they involve entering [into the object], these two are cited here. It is said that by means of the first liberation, one immediately gives rise to the first two of the eight spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*);
therefore, it is not discussed further within this context. If one says "liberation," it refers to the essential state of detachment.

If it is said that the "bases of mastery" (*abhibhvāyatana*) induce superior qualities, one asks: since this refers to the first liberation (*vimokṣa*), why speak of the first three liberations? Answer:

With respect to the eight bases of mastery, these are distinguished from within the first three [liberations]. Because they are clarified by the first, they are collectively subsumed under it. Question:

The latter two "totalities" (*kṛtsnāyatana*) do not belong to the first three [liberations]; how then can these three also induce the totalities? Answer: The three [liberations] induce them beforehand.

One attains all eight spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the ten spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*). This is because the first eight spheres of totality are cited here, as they are spoken of in their majority.
Question: Which liberations (*vimokṣa*) induce the eight spheres of mastery? Answer: The first liberation induces the first two spheres of mastery;
the second liberation induces the third and fourth spheres of mastery; and the third liberation induces the latter four spheres of mastery. This is based on the expression "the first two."
There is one with form. The next two are called "formless. The final four involve being internally formless while observing external forms that are blue, yellow, red, or white. Question:
How does the first liberation induce the first and second spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*)? Answer: It is because the first sphere of mastery involves the perception of internal form.

One contemplates external forms as small—whether beautiful or ugly, inferior or superior—and regarding those forms, one possesses superior knowledge and superior vision, subsequently forming a perception in accordance with reality.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Small forms" refers to the requisites and so forth of sentient beings;
"many" refers to forms such as palaces and dwellings; "beautiful forms" refers to exquisite primary colors that are consistently pure and sublime.
Therefore, that which is contrary to this is called "unwholesome form" (*akuśala-rūpa*). "Inferior" refers to forms of sound, odor, taste, and touch that are disagreeable;
that which is contrary to these is "superior form. Through the concentration (*samādhi*) of the path of calm abiding (*śamatha*), it is called "superior knowledge" (*jñāna*);

through the wisdom (*prajñā*) of the path of insight (*vipaśyanā*), it is called "superior vision" (*darśana*). Within these two types—the superior and the non-superior—there is no [concept of] supremacy (*adhipatya*).
Pride. The arising of the thought of subduing [them] is called the "thought of reality as it is" (*yathābhūta-saṃjñā*). This is the second sphere of mastery (*abhibhv-āyatana*):

having the perception of internal forms, one contemplates external forms that are manifold—whether beautiful or ugly, inferior or superior—and regarding those forms, one knows them and sees them with mastery, attaining the thought of reality as it is.
Because these two spheres coexist, this emerges from the first liberation (*vimokṣa*). (The next two spheres of mastery emerge from the [second] liberation...)

Regarding the second liberation (*vimokṣa*): He said, "Since the first two spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) are drawn forth from the first liberation, why does the first [sphere] contemplate internal and external forms while forming the perception of light?
Furthermore, both the first and second [spheres] speak of contemplating external forms, yet differ in being 'small' or 'vast. What is the answer? [Response:

The liberations are still inferior because they take both internal and external objects as their conditions. Because one gradually attains superiority through the cultivation of the spheres of mastery, one contemplates only...
This refers to external forms.

Regarding the statement "one then contemplates those spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and so forth," the intended meaning is that since the spheres of mastery are produced by the liberations (*vimokṣa*), one is made to again contemplate those objects of the spheres of mastery as being small or large.
The question asks: what is the purpose of contemplating both internal and external forms prior to this?

Regarding the "perception of light" (*āloka-saṃjñā*): now, when one forms the perception of the "small," "large," and so forth within the *abhibhvāyatana* (bases of mastery), why is this called a "common observation"? Answer:

The commentary states that one observes those very objects by encompassing the colors of the small, large, and so forth, and views them as the perception of light; therefore, there is no contradiction.

This is like encompassing the Four Noble Truths through the contemplation of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) and dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), which does not prevent the three vehicles from observing the same object. The present case is likewise the same.

Next, the specific *abhibhvāyatana* (bases of mastery). Regarding the bases of mastery: if one asks what is meant by the "eight bases of mastery," the answer is that because one attains liberation within these eight bases of mastery, they are called "bases of mastery.
They are also called "mastering the objects of focus" (*ālambana*). Prior to attaining liberation, the observing mind has not yet attained sovereignty;
the objective field is powerful, and consciousness is constantly dragged along by the field, sinking into the six realms of existence. Now, the observing mind has matured.
Consciousness is powerful; all inferior objects follow the mind. Because it can temporarily subdue preceding objects, it is called "surpassing the objective support" (*ālambana-vibhūti*).

Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that there are five meanings for the term "sphere of mastery" (*abhibhvāyatana*): first, superiority through the displacement of the inferior, as in the case of a handsome person [overcoming] an ugly person, and so forth.
Second is the excellence of subduing the weak, such as when a strong person strikes others who are inferior.
Third is the excellence of obscuring the superior, such as when the sun rises and obscures the stars, the moon, and the light of lamps so that they no longer appear.

Fourth is the excellence of wearying with regard to the object of focus, such as when one grows weary of the lower and delights in the higher; the dharma attained through that delight is what is called "superior. Fifth is the excellence of turning back, such as when a person...
O King and others, because one must teach for the sake of sustaining life so that the poor and wealthy may act with freedom according to their will, this constitutes the third [topic]:
the two superior meanings of concealment (*abhibhava*) and mastery (*vaśitā*). It is superior to the previous liberation (*vimokṣa*); it is the superiority of concealment.

Regarding the observation of whether [the object] is large or small, it is the superiority of mastery. As for the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭāv abhibhv-āyatanāni*) regarding all things within the mind's engagement with objects, they consist of those eight locations.

Because they can be turned at will, they are called "victorious" (*abhibhvāyatana*). This is an *adhikaraṇa-svāmin* (locative determinative) compound. Alternatively, "sphere" (*āyatana*) refers to the mind that acts as the perceiver;
since those objects—whether small or large—are the objects of perception for this mind, the perceiver itself is the sphere. This is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional determinative) compound.

Prostrating to remove obstacles such as congestion and blockages, these are subsumed under the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Because the latter is superior to the former, they are called "bases of mastery" (*abhibhvāyatana*).

There are eight distinct bases of mastery: first, having internal perception of form, one perceives external forms as small; second, having internal perception of form, one perceives external forms as large.
3. Internally perceiving no form, one views external forms as small; 4. internally perceiving no form, one views external forms as large;

5. internally perceiving no form, one views external forms as blue; 6. internally perceiving no form, one views external forms as yellow; 7. internally perceiving no form, one views external forms as red.

Eighth: being internally non-visualized of form, one contemplates external forms as white. This contemplation concerns the forms of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), categorized as "small" or "vast," such as blue, yellow, red, and white.
"Small" refers to the forms of sentient beings and their requisites; "vast" refers to the forms of mountains, rivers, the great earth, and so forth.

When contemplating those small and vast forms of mountains and rivers in this manner, there are further seven points of meaning. For instance, regarding the first *abhibhvāyatana* (sphere of mastery), one contemplates external forms.
1. "Minor" refers to that which is good, meaning beautiful visible forms (*varṇa*), because they are exclusively pure and exquisite. 2. That which is the opposite of this is called "bad color. 3.
"Inferior" refers to the five sense objects—sound, odor, taste, touch, and so forth—that are disagreeable. 4. "Superior" refers to those that are excellent.

This refers to agreeable sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and so forth; the five superior knowledges; śamatha concentration; the sixfold vision through the path of vipaśyanā; and the attainment of knowledge as it truly is.
Regarding these two types—the superior and the non-superior—one must be free from overweening pride (*adhimāna*) and give rise to the perception of mastery.
If one claims that the mind is superior when the object is not yet superior, then this essential meaning is lacking. This...
The seven objects [of the first three *abhibhvāyatanas*] function as the basis for the subsequent seven *abhibhvāyatanas*, and the same applies to the ten *kṛtsnāyatanas*.
Regarding the five *abhibhvāyatanas* that contemplate blue, yellow, red, and white, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "That is to say, 'blue-blue,' 'blue-manifesting,' and 'blue-light.

Herein, the initial 'blue' is the general term (*sāmānya-pada*), while the others are specific terms (*viśeṣa-pada*). 'Blue-manifesting' refers to innate blue, such as the color of a blue flower; 'blue-appearance' refers to... [the result of] mixing.
"Blue combined" refers to blue garments and the like. "Blue light" refers to the fresh, pure radiance present upon those two types [of objects].
This means that when explaining blue garments, it is said they are like the deep indigo dye of Vārāṇasī and so forth. As for the ten spheres of totality (*daśa kṛtsnāyatanāni*):
They are also called the ten *kṛtsnāyatana*s (totalities). When practicing this meditation, each [object] is taken as having the characteristic of pervading all places.
This means that one causes the object of observation to transform with mastery, becoming vast and filling every single place.
Question: For what reason are earth, water, fire, and so forth established as *kṛtsnāyatana*s? Answer: Because by means of this observation of the *kṛtsnāyatana*s...

Because the four great elements and the derived matter that depends upon them both pervade all outflows (*āsrava*). If one were not to establish the pervasive nature of the locations of earth, water, fire, and so forth, then even apart from the four great elements which serve as their basis, one would be unable to contemplate the derived matter—such as blue, yellow, red, and white—as having the characteristic of pervasiveness.
Therefore, because one contemplates both the basis and that which depends upon it as being entirely pervasive, one establishes earth, water, and the others. Thus...
1. The universal meditation on blue; 2. The universal meditation on yellow; 3. The universal meditation on red; 4. The universal meditation on white;
5. The universal meditation on earth; 6. The universal meditation on water;
7. The universal meditation on fire; 8. The universal meditation on wind; 9. The universal meditation on space; 10. The universal meditation on consciousness.
If one does not establish the earth, water, and so forth, then one cannot contemplate the derived forms (upādāyarūpa), such as blue and yellow, as having the characteristic of pervasiveness.
Because the basis is absent, the dependent [forms] could not properly exist in their full extent; however, since this is a universal contemplation, one contemplates only the dependent [forms].
In this context, one also contemplates the provisional characteristics of earth and so forth. Question: What is the superior function of contemplating this earth and so forth? Answer:

It means that one desires to tread upon earth as if it were water, to enter water as if it were earth, and for the body to emit water and fire. A noble one (ārya) shakes the great trichiliocosm by contemplating wind;
or, because one may manifest the conflagration at the end of an eon, one must contemplate fire. If one wishes for lapis lazuli to become the ground or for gold to [become the ground]...
The stalks are made of *cintāmaṇi* gems and the pericarps of *jambūnada* gold; the petals are made of white silver. One should perform visualizations of blue, yellow, red, white, and so forth.

If one wishes to destroy afflictions, as well as all [obstructions] whether pertaining to form or mind, one emerges from the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) and enters the fourth dhyāna.

Because it brings forth various merits such as the knowledge of non-contention (*araṇājñāna*), the knowledge of vows (*praṇidhijñāna*), and the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), one therefore performs the visualization of consciousness. If...
Because one wishes to induce unimpeded movement back and forth, passing through stone walls as if through open space, one therefore practices the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).
Question: Why does one not contemplate odors, tastes, and the five sense faculties? Answer: The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Seventy [Verses]) states:

"Because these two objects (visible forms and sounds) are common to both one's own body and those of others, they pervade both the internal and external, and pervade the entire realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) without constant interruption. The five sense faculties, however, belong exclusively to one's own body. If that is so, [why focus on emptiness?]

Question: Previously, you instructed one to contemplate the internal and external, which refers to the transformation of the five sense faculties (*pañcendriya*). Since these do not transform their own characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), why is it necessary to contemplate them?
Answer: Because they transform their basis (*āśraya*), they must be taken as objects (*ālambana*). As for odor and taste among the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), they are not omnipresent;

sound is intermittent; therefore, they are not mentioned here. Question: Why are the two bases of space (*ākāśa*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) established? Answer: Because the objects of perception (*ālambana*) are all-pervasive and do not exceed the nature of space. As for the subject...
Because their objects are all-pervasive and do not exceed the scope of consciousness, these two dharmas are established as *kṛtsnāyatana* (totalities). Question:

Since one is already able to transform [objects] such as gold and silver through the practice of the *abhibhvāyatana* (mastery bases), why is it necessary to further practice the *kṛtsnāyatana*? Answer:

The *abhibhvāyatana* of the Śrāvakas can only transform a single room’s space or a small portion of gold and silver; however, if one practices the *kṛtsnāyatana*, one is able to transform them universally. Only...

These spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) can be accomplished only by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; Śrāvakas possess only the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*). As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"Pressing the earth with his foot, he transformed the land in three ways, making the eight directions pure and adorned. Question: Why is it necessary to perform these three types of contemplations?
Answer: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: It is like a worldly potter who, wishing to make jars and other vessels, first prepares the clay.
Just as one constructs a mound by means of liberation; having been fired within the fire, one applies skillful means by means of the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*);
and once the vessel is completed, it is used according to one's will through the ten spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), whereby transformation is exercised with mastery.

Therefore, the treatise says: "By means of liberation, there is the actual construction and cultivation; by means of the eight bases of mastery, there is the application of skillful means; and by means of the ten spheres of totality, [there is] thorough examination."
[The spheres of totality] are perfected. If one follows these eight [bases], the śrāvakas also cultivate the *kṛtsnāyatana*s (spheres of totality).
Although they cannot pervade everything universally, they nonetheless belong to that same category. If it were not so, they would have no functional efficacy.

If this is the case, why does the Sūtra mention only the three knowledges (*vidyā*), the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and the possession of the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), but does not mention the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the ten spheres of totality? [Answer: It is because...

Because the former subsumes the latter: that which pervades is the mind, and that which is pervaded is the sphere (*āyatana*). This is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (locative compound). Alternatively, the pervader is itself the sphere; this very contemplative mind is the locus (*āśraya*) of the object.

It is like the term "formless sphere" (*ārūpyāyatana*), which is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound). Question: Upon what mind and what meditative absorption do these ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*) depend? Answer:
Those based on objective phenomena have subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) as their nature; those based on true suchness (*tathatā*) have direct knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) as their nature.
If the first eight universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*) rely upon the fourth dhyāna, the latter two universal bases rely upon the two stages of space and consciousness.
Regarding the phrase "by means of eliminating transformations and so forth," Sthiramati says there are two explanations: first, if one is a beginner, they rely upon the first and second dhyānas.

Regarding the fundamental dhyānas (*mauladhyāna*): if one has practiced them for a long time, relying on the fundamental dhyānas of the four *dhyānas*, one contemplates all internal and external forms of the desire realm as a whole, forming the perception of light.
Obstacles cause what is short to become long and what is day to become night; this is called the transformation [obstacle].
Because there are obstacles within the body that are known to exist, they prevent one from attaining mastery over the time of transformation. This is the obstacle to transformation.
This is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (dependent determinative compound). Regarding the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), it is said in two ways:

when one has not yet engaged in contemplation, if one perceives all visual objects with a mind of resentment or aversion, they all appear as impure; if one gives rise to a mind of craving and attachment, all visual objects appear as pure.
Because the internal body possesses hatred and love, one perceives an increase in what is good and what is evil; this is precisely transformation (*nirmāṇa*). Transformation is...
"Obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*). This is a *karmadhāraya* compound. It refers generally to both the afflictive and cognitive obstructions (*kleśa-jñeya-āvaraṇa*). The former interpretation is correct.
If one contemplates the transformations of the mind and so forth as external objects, yet does not form the perception of light, then there will be obstruction within those transformations.

This is because the transformed objects revolve according to the mind. When the mind forms the perception of light, the understanding of the object likewise follows the mind in forming the perception of light. Question:

Why, within the perception of light (*ālokasaṃjñā*), is the obstacle of transformation (*nirmāṇāvaraṇa*) eliminated? The answer is given in the *Abhidharmapāda* (Treatise on the Higher Dharma), Chapter Three:

"Because it is solely the matter that is obstructed; [the perception of light] is the direct antidote to that, as it serves to counteract the obstruction of mutual resistance. Therefore, one contemplates it."
This proceeds from the shallow to the deep.

Regarding the statement that one does not eliminate desire and so forth: first, it is because this differs from the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), which eliminates desire; therefore, one does not cultivate the perception of impurity (*aśubha-saṃjñā*).

Second, it is because one contemplates that one has already become detached from stained colors; therefore, one does not cultivate the perception of impurity. Furthermore, as for the practitioner: if...
When one wishes to contemplate internal and external forms while forming the perception of light, one must first establish the mental image of form within the mind so that it appears before one;
only then does one contemplate internal and external forms and the like, forming the perception of light. Question: Why does one not contemplate the forms of the higher realms?

Answer: There are three explanations. First, because the body resides in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Second, because the transformation of objects follows the mind, thereby providing relief for those in existence. Third, because the forms of the higher realms are subtle and difficult to perceive.

Because of their nature as afflictions (*kleśa*), these three dharmas of the desire realm obstruct meditative concentration (*samādhi*) with great force; therefore, one must repeatedly contemplate them so that these obstructions are turned far away.

These obstructions consist of inferior sensations (*vedanā*), lack of pliancy (*akarmanyatā*), rigidity, hardness of mind, and so forth, which are able to obstruct concentration but cannot transform earth, water, and the other elements.

When one contemplates form (*rūpa*) at this time, these obstructions are naturally dispelled, and one is immediately able to perform transformations. If one does not contemplate form, these obstructions [will persist].
That which is able to obstruct transformative activities is called the "obstruction to transformation" (*nirmāṇāvaraṇa*).
Regarding the statement in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* that "one has not yet attained [the formless attainments]," etc., this refers to the first section of that treatise.

That text explains that those who have not yet abandoned the defilements of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are speaking from the perspective of a beginner practitioner (*ādikarmika*). As for the statement in the *Abhidharma*, "the four formless attainments," it refers to those who have already abandoned the defilements of the form realm.
Regarding the defilement of the realms (*dhātu*), this is explained in reference to those who have practiced for a long time. For these two treatises, there is likewise no contradiction.

As for the statement "contemplating external forms and so forth," this is from the twelfth section of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. [Question: In the preceding section where the names were enumerated...
The first liberation does not mention "internal" or "external. Why, then, is it stated here that the first liberation involves contemplating external forms?
Answer: A person who has attained the first liberation contemplates both internal sense-bases (*indriya*) and external objects (*viṣaya*) as a whole.

If the word "external" were used [exclusively], there would be a risk of confusion, implying that one contemplates only the five external objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) and not the five internal sense-bases (*pañcendriya*). This is why the twelfth passage does not distinguish between internal and external.
The fifteenth passage of the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "There are external characters (*bāhya-akṣara*). These are called 'external' by way of having already abandoned defilement (*vītarāga*).

If they are called 'external' by way of having already abandoned defilement, then the five sense faculties (*pañcendriya*), though internal, may also be called 'external. If they are called 'internal' by way of not yet having abandoned defilement, then the five objects (*pañcaviṣaya*), though external, may also be called 'internal.'"
Regarding the statement "only based on the beginner": this refers to a person who is first practicing the first liberation (*prathama-vimokṣa*).

A beginner has not yet attained the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) and has not yet abandoned the defilements of the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*). As for one who has practiced for a long time, they have already attained the formless attainments and have abandoned the defilements of the form realm.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, chapter twelve, states: "The person of the first liberation has not yet attained the formless attainments and has not yet abandoned the defilements of the form realm. This [text] refers specifically to the beginner.
This is the explanation by the practitioner (the first treatise on liberation).
Regarding the statement "the second liberation," etc., the *Jianyao* says: "The first liberation of the Hīnayāna takes only external objects as its cognitive object."
One visualizes impurity without taking the internal body as the object; this is the second liberation. To claim that one visualizes the internal body alone as impure is incorrect.
In reality, the first liberation involves practitioners of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) contemplating external objects as impure to suppress and eliminate internal craving.
Gradually, they extend this contemplation of impurity to include their own bodies as well, until reaching the second liberation. Internally...
The body, too, attains freedom from defilement.

Regarding the statement "internally subdued and eliminated, etc.": in that first liberation, internal defilement has not yet been eliminated. The word "not yet" is used because the characteristic of form (rūpa-lakṣaṇa) still exists.
Therefore, it is said that for a person in the first liberation, the small vehicle (Hīnayāna) practitioner has not yet discarded the characteristic of the body. Second...

Second, regarding liberation: having already attained freedom from defilement within one's own internal body, one now contemplates that the body does not exist, but consists only of the four great elements;

therefore, it is said that "internally there is nothing. Because there is no internal body, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "The practitioner, from this point forward, gradually eliminates the signs associated with the internal.
That is to say, through the perception of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-saṃjñā*), he [visualizes] his own corpse after death being carried away."

The charnel ground where corpses are abandoned, continuing until the body no longer exists and only the four great elements remain; this is called "the liberation by contemplating external forms while being internally formless.
The *Abhidharmakośa* states: Having attained the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), one has already suppressed and eliminated the perception of form within oneself as a seer.

The mind then once again turns outward toward objects free from defilement, including one's own body, establishing it as a gift and forming the perception of impurity, thereby subduing the outward [tendency].
The covetous mind does not arise; this is called the accomplishment of the second liberation-phenomenon (*vimokṣa-nimitta*) of the Hīnayāna.

"Seeing" (*dṛṣṭi*) means the ability to see. The "perception of form" (*rūpa-saṃjñā*) is the perception of attachment to form. Having already detached from the taints of form, one establishes and arranges [the object] as an impure perception (*aśubha-saṃjñā*).
Following the inclination of the mind, one causes obstacles to recede and the contemplation to become increasingly clear. For this reason, one contemplates only external objects. One practices...

The perceptions of impurity—such as the bluish, the festering, and the decaying—are called "the perception of internal formlessness" (*adhyātma-arūpa-saṃjñā*). [Question: Since internal defilements have already been eliminated, external defilements likewise do not exist; why then is it necessary to further contemplate them? [Answer: The *Abhidharmakośa* states: Although greed has already been removed, one contemplates the external impure colors of the bluish, the festering, and so forth, in order to make the contemplating mind firm and stable, thereby ensuring that greed does not arise. There are two explanations for "abandoning" (*śūnya*). First, "without the perception of form" means there is no perception of craving for form. Second, it is said that "without the perception of form" means the perception of form is entirely absent;

this is called being without the perception of form. One contemplates the end of this body, from its becoming bluish and festering, through the stages of maggots and bones, until it is completely dissolved and exhausted.
Not even a single part is seen; it is identical to empty space. This is collectively termed [the meditation on] emptiness.
"Internally, there is no perception of form; there is only the mind capable of taking [form] as its object. Bian states that between these two interpretations, the latter is correct;
it represents the position of the master Saṃghabhadra in the *Nyāyānusāra*. However, according to the intention of the commentator [of the *Śāstra*], he adopts the former interpretation:
