As for "neither-non-perception," this means that when one investigates the objective sphere above the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), one perceives only the mind and mental factors taking the Sphere of Nothingness as their object; because these are extremely subtle, the mind and its concomitants are in a state of extreme tranquility.
In the preceding Sphere of Nothingness, the object of focus was consciousness; there, one contemplates that nothing exists outside of consciousness. This is the minor [explanation].
The parts are also non-existent. This is the stage of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). It takes as its object only the mind and mental factors of the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

Because it is unlike the lower stages which possess coarse perception (*saṃjñā*), it is called "Non-perception" (*asaṃjñā*). Yet, because there still exist extremely tranquil states of mind and mental factors, it is called "Non-non-perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñā*);
this is not due to their absence. Since they are not entirely non-existent, Mochizuki [the commentator] says: "The first 'non' (非) does not mean..."

It is not so. This Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) lacks the coarse perceptions of the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*); therefore, it is called "Non-perception" (*asaṃjñin*). The second character "non" (*a-*) does not mean "not by way of";
the third character "non" (*a-*) does not mean "not by way of absence. There still exist within the mind extremely subtle mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) that are not non-existent;
therefore, it is called "Neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). Question: Is the perceiving mind of the Stage of Non-perception...
Regarding the twenty-two factors: the objects of focus (*ālambana*) are also these twenty-two factors.

When one has not yet examined them thoroughly, does one contemplate and examine by directing the mind toward the higher stages based solely on the coarse perceptions (*audārika-saṃjñā*) of the lower stages, or does one do so while simultaneously relying upon the twenty-two factors of the mind that serve as the subject (*ālambaka*) within the same stage? The answer is that both explanations apply. One school says: "Only..."

One contemplates and observes twenty-two factors by ascending from the objects of perception. Second, it is said that one simultaneously contemplates and observes the most subtle twenty-two factors of the respective stage while ascending;
thus, both the perceiving subject and the perceived object are fully examined.
This is called the aspect of the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana-vimokṣa*).
Regarding the phrase "no longer [directed] toward anything else": it means that one contemplates with resolute conviction solely upon the mind that takes the sphere of nothingness as its object;
it does not proceed further by taking empty consciousness as its object, nor does it extend beyond these two stages. Thus, it is said, "no longer toward anything else."
Regarding the phrase "extending even to the sphere of perception" (*saṃjñā*): "perceptible" (*kṣeya*) refers to the designation established in relation to its object.
In the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), the single aggregate of mind and mental factors is extremely lucid; therefore, it is called "capable of producing perception.

In the stages of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), the mind and mental factors are extremely obscure and thus lack the power to arise spontaneously. Consequently, they must depend upon the Sphere of Nothingness as an object to be drawn forth and produced. Only then...

It is able to take an object as its focal point. Through contemplation and resolute conviction, this constitutes the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) of the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
It is the locus where twenty-two mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) arise as the perceiving faculty.

Since the mind must rely upon an object in order to arise, the perceiving mind of the stage of the Peak of Existence takes as its object the twenty-two factors of the Sphere of Nothingness that serve as the perceived object.
Because it is the condition for the arising of perception, it is called the "place where perception can arise. The answer is: the two spheres of infinite space and infinite consciousness.

Therefore, one does not form a resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) toward anything else, but receives its name from the state of "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), as it is established in contrast to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

One must contemplate that [sphere] as liberation; unlike the lower stages which possess coarse perception, this is called "non-perception" (*asaṃjñā*). Nevertheless, there is still an internal mind, which perceives only...
Because this extremely tranquil mind remains present, it is called the "liberation of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Question:

Since there is no further dharma external to consciousness that can be taken as an object, it is called "nothingness" (*ākiṃcanya*); thus, it does not include the twenty-two factors of its own meditative stage, but rather consists solely of the contemplation and resolute conviction regarding the twenty-two factors within the sphere of consciousness. Now, in contrast to "nothingness," why is it called "neither-perception"? Why is this so?
One merely contemplates and resolves upon the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana), which includes oneself as well.

The answer is that the sphere of nothingness establishes its name solely because there is no phenomenon external to consciousness; therefore, one contemplates and resolves upon it only with respect to oneself and others.
Since the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) can be designated in terms of both oneself and others, one contemplates and resolves upon it in both respects.
Regarding the statement, "One should know as follows below," there is no further place for explanation in this commentary. Zhangjing says:

"This is merely a phrase from the *Fayuan zhang* (Chapter on the Garden of Dharma). That work contains ten sections; the first three are the same as these four explanations in the 'Section Explaining the Names.
Therefore, it says, 'One should know as follows below.'"

Regarding the statement, "As for what was said above concerning the attainment of detachment (*vairāgya-prāpti*) and so forth," this distinguishes the temporal stage of contemplation. "As for what was said above" refers to the explanation based on those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), not concerning those still in training (*śaikṣa*).
The suppression of afflictions (*kleśa*) is termed "detachment. Even if one attains the suppression of afflictions, it is not included within this specific category of "attainment of detachment.
Question: How is it known that only the attainment of the abandonment of afflictions by those beyond training is called the "attainment of detachment"?

The commentary answers: "The aforementioned discussion regarding the departure from defilement (*vairāgya*) and so forth refers to what is attained by those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), not based on those still in training (*śaikṣa*), because those in training have not yet departed from defilement.
Question: Since those beyond training have already departed from the afflictions (*kleśa*), what obstacle do they now subdue when cultivating liberation (*vimukti*)?
Answer: They subdue the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Furthermore, regarding the objects already liberated, those beyond training...
Because it involves the resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) that [the object] has been transformed, it is called "liberation" (*vimokṣa*).

Regarding the statement "the first seven liberations, etc.," this refers to those such as the Arhats (*aśaikṣas*) who have already abandoned the defilements of affliction and are thus called "already liberated.

This means that by inducing superior qualities, they attain mastery through the resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) in contemplating the objects free from defilement, thereby distancing themselves from the hindrances to meditative concentration (*samādhi-āvaraṇa*). This is called [liberation].

For the sake of liberation. Question: How can it be known that this is not an attainment through the separation from defilements by one who is still in training (*śaikṣa*)? Answer: It takes the seventh liberation as its object;
this belongs to the stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). It is the liberation of that very stage.

As for the afflictions of the stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, even if a person of the third fruit suppresses them with tainted wisdom (*sāsravajñāna*), they remain suppressed and do not manifest. Even if they were to be severed by untainted wisdom (*anāsravajñāna*), they could not be severed. If they were indeed severed—

Yes, they attain it and thereby become those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). Since the afflictions of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) are not currently manifest (as stated above regarding those beyond training), one who is called a "body-witness" (*kāyasākṣin*) is also a person who has realized the third fruit, having suppressed the afflictions and attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

It is not attained through the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa*). Since the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is attained by suppressing the afflictions, this conversely reveals that the seventh liberation is also attained by suppressing the afflictions.

However, while it is clarified that the attainment of cessation necessarily possesses the preceding seven liberations, possessing the preceding seven does not necessarily entail the attainment of cessation.
From the first dhyāna up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), all are suppressions and not abandonments.
In the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the mind and mental factors are extinguished; because this is realized by means of the body, it is called "bodily realization" (*kāyasākṣin*).

The present mention of the "bodily-realized *anāgāmin*" serves to distinguish them from others of dull faculties who do not attain it. This clarifies that while such an *anāgāmin* attains liberation, they do not yet attain the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

Yet one is free from defilement. Regarding the stage of "having-perception" (saṃjñā-bhūmi), it is certainly not suppressed or abandoned; because this is the stage of one in training (śaikṣa), it is not abandoned. As for that which is unsurpassed and worthy of aspiration, it is not suppressed.

If this is so, and the defilements of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) still remain, how can it be called liberation? Answer: Although the afflictions (kleśa) remain, they are merely obstacles to meditative concentration (samādhi-āvaraṇa).
In the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), by suppressing them, one obtains the name of "liberation. If this is so, since those afflictions have not yet been eliminated, how can [one] attain [it]?

Regarding the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*): the answer is that by merely suppressing the obstacles to concentration, one immediately attains that absorption because, through the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one is able to give rise to it.

Question: What is meant by "bodily realization" (*kāyasākṣin*)? Answer: It means direct realization. It refers to personally entering fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), severing the afflictions, and attaining the third fruit [of Arhatship].
Regarding the statement, "If one relies on the *vijñaptimātra* [theory], there are two types [of abandonment]," this refers to the stages of subduing and severing. Question:

According to the intent of these two masters, why is it that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) do not even subdue [the defilements of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*)]? Should it not be admitted that they can attain those meditative absorptions? Answer: The first master says:

Because the seeds of afflictions in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are of two natures and are manifold, they strongly obstruct meditative absorption; therefore, they must be severed. This is unlike the higher realms, where [afflictions] need only be subdued.
One attains entry. Second, it is said: from the third dhyāna downward, including the desire realm, the afflictions and the transformed sensations are both seeds of affliction;

because they strongly obstruct meditative concentration, they are specifically severed. From the fourth dhyāna upward, including the formless realm, the delusions of the lower three stages must be suppressed, while those of the single stage of the Peak of Existence (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) are neither suppressed nor severed, thereby allowing entry into the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti). Although those in training (śaikṣa), though not...

[The opponent] submits: "Even if one does not admit that those at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) attain the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), they still attain liberation because their mental factors are extremely subtle.
Question: Since the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* discusses only the meditative absorption of cessation, how does it establish the meaning of the defiled and the undefiled?

Answer: One must first attain the seven liberations before realizing the eighth, the liberation of the meditative absorption of cessation. By mentioning the latter to clarify the former, there is no error. This is the intended meaning.

Regarding the statement that an Anāgāmin has not yet abandoned defilement, it is accepted that they attain the realization-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-sākṣātkriyājñāna*). Among the first seven liberations (*vimokṣa*), there are cases where one attains them without having abandoned defilement;

however, these are of a single nature—obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*)—because they do not obstruct meditative absorption. By suppressing [defilements] through these, one attains the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

Regarding the statement that "the single stage of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) has not yet been subdued": this means that there is nothing higher to be desired. Here, one still desires what is above and feels aversion toward what is below; it is through this [state] that subdual occurs.
As for the "Peak of Existence," it is so called because it is the summit of the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*). Question: If this is so, why is it called "liberation"? Answer:

Because the perceptions (*saṃjñā*) in that stage are subtle and the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are not powerful, there is no need for further subdual to attain liberation and the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). However—

The following [passage] explains that one enters the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) by means of untainted wholesome wisdom (*anāsrava-kuśala-prajñā*) which abandons those obstacles to concentration (*samādhi-āvaraṇa*).

Regarding the statement "Thus, in the *Yogācārabhūmi*, the twelfth [chapter], etc.," it is asked: How is it known that one attains the meditative attainment of cessation without having suppressed the defilements of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*)?

The commentary answers: "The *Yogācāra*, etc. The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Regarding the two liberations of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣa*) and consciousness (*vijñāna-vimokṣa*), some say they are separated from..."
Regarding the defilements of one's own stage, the [text] mentions the two higher stages but does not explicitly state the phrase "separation from the defilements of one's own stage.

This is because it is stated by way of elliptical abbreviation, referring to both the learner (*śaikṣa*) and the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*). Regarding the first two liberations—those of space and consciousness—some say that the phrase "separation from the defilements of one's own stage" applies;

these are obtained through the separation from defilements by a non-learner. By implication, this also includes the latter two liberations, which are likewise obtained through the separation from defilements. As for the latter two liberations, there is no [explicit statement].
The phrase "detached from the defilements of its own level" indicates that this is attained by a *śaikṣa* or an *anāgāmin* who has not yet abandoned those defilements.
By implication, the first two liberations (*vimokṣa*) are likewise attained by those who have not yet abandoned the defilements; therefore, it is said that [the text] is abbreviated.

Regarding the statement that they exist only in the fundamental dhyānas (*mauladhyāna*): one must rely on the fundamental dhyānas to enter the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), not the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*).

This means that while these eight liberations (*vimokṣa*) may pertain to both the preparatory stages and the fundamental dhyānas when considered in terms of freedom from defilement (*vairāgya*), when it comes to the actual practice of contemplation (*manasikāra*), they must necessarily reside in the fundamental dhyānas.

Regarding the term "liberation through the meditative attainment of cessation" (*nirodhasamāpatti-vimokṣa*): it refers to the time when, during the cultivation of meditative concentration, one develops a superior aspiration within the preparatory application (*prayoga*) of that concentration due to weariness toward coarse and agitated mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
This aspiration obstructs the mind and mental factors, causing them to become increasingly subtle and minute.

At the moment the mind becomes extremely subtle, it perfumes the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), forming seeds of an exceedingly predominant mind of weariness. The functional capacity of these seeds [then] impairs...

Subsequently, one subdues the coarse and agitated thoughts of the subsequent moment so that they do not manifest for a time; based on this state, the "attainment of cessation" (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is established.
This passage clarifies that both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) enter the attainment of cessation.

Thus, both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna alike speak of the attainment of cessation as the place where perception and feeling cease, which is precisely the aspect of liberation (*vimokṣa*). Regarding the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*), the first seven have objects of perception (*sālambana*). The eighth...
The eighth [category] is that which lacks an object of focus (*anālambana*).

Regarding the statement "speaking without the aspect of mental activity (*ākāra*) and so forth," this refers to the perceptions (*saṃjñā*) and feelings (*vedanā*) that are abandoned; this is common to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, and is termed "lacking the aspect of mental activity.

Because the mind is strengthened by the assistance of these two—perception and feeling—it is uniquely designated as "mental activity" (*citta-saṃskāra*) among the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
Now, being weary of and afflicted by mental exertion, one temporarily brings it to cessation; because this state must be attained by severing obstacles, it is called "liberation" (*vimokṣa*).

This refers specifically to the liberation consisting in the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedita-nirodha-vimokṣa*), analyzed according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound. The preceding seven liberations are all *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compounds: the observation of various forms is itself the liberation. Question:
When entering the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), why is it necessary to abandon perception and feeling? Therefore, one enters [the attainment].

[Question: Regarding meditative absorption (*samādhi*), [the answer] is that because the mind is strengthened by the preparatory application (*prayoga*) of perception (*saṃjñā*) and feeling (*vedanā*), these must necessarily be extinguished when entering the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

[Question: How many types of preparatory applications are there? [Answer: There are three. First, vitarka and vicāra constitute the preparatory application of speech; second, inhalation and exhalation constitute the preparatory application of the body;
third, perception and feeling constitute the preparatory application of the mind. [Question: At what time are these three types of preparatory applications extinguished? [Answer: The first...

In the second dhyāna, the preparatory application for speech is ceased; because speech arises from vitarka and vicāra, and the second dhyāna is devoid of vitarka and vicāra, the preparatory application for speech is ceased.

In the third dhyāna, the preparatory application for the body is ceased; because of inhalation and exhalation, and because the body-faculty remains established in its position, the preparatory application for the body is ceased.

In the fourth dhyāna, the preparatory application for the body is ceased due to inhalation and exhalation. Upon reaching the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (asaṃjñisattva), the preparatory application for the mind is ceased, because [of the presence of...]

Because perception and feeling assist the mind, they enable the mind to function; therefore, when entering the meditative attainment of cessation, the mind does not arise, as one has abandoned perception and feeling.
Regarding the statement that there are two types [of entry] when one is about to enter [the attainment of cessation], it is asked: what are the two modes of activity? The answer is:

entering the attainment of cessation, first, one enters by relying on a mind of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*); second, one enters by relying on the realm of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*). It is asked: what kind of person enters the attainment of cessation by relying on these two minds? The answer is:

if it is a beginner (*ādikarmika*), they necessarily enter by relying on a mind of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; if it is one who has long practiced, [they may enter by either].
There are two [ways]. First, entering by relying on the signless realm (*animitta-dhātu*), for the signless realm is precisely suchness (*tathatā*).

Because those who have practiced for a long time direct their minds toward the signless realm, they immediately enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). Regarding the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), these two are taught. For one who has practiced for a long time, they enter the absorption of cessation at any location.
If it is a beginner who is still in training (*śaikṣa*), they must rely on the contemplation of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) as their preparatory practice (*prayoga*).

It enters. Because it occupies the very last position within the successive meditative absorptions (*anupūrva-samāpatti*). Question: If one enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) by means of the mind of *tathatā*, why does the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* state that one enters it by employing uncontaminated wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) of contemplative observation as the preparatory application (*prayoga*)? Answer: Regarding the uncontaminated wisdom of contemplative observation...

This is not the severing of afflictions; rather, it is the attainment of subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). When desiring to enter meditative absorption (*samādhi*), one becomes weary of coarse conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) and brings all mental activity to rest before entering the concentration.
According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) takes true suchness (*tathatā*)—the signless realm—as its object;

the mind then becomes weary and ceases, coming to a temporary rest as one enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). This is explained from the perspective of long-term cultivation. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

When entering the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), one enters the attainment either by relying on the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) or by relying on the perception of the attainment of cessation itself.
When entering the attainment of cessation, there are two aspects: first, one takes three kinds of objects as conditions; second, one contacts three kinds of contact.
Regarding "taking three kinds of objects as conditions": first, one takes existence (*bhava*) as an object, because the mind is not disturbed by the conceit of "I am" (*asmimāna*).

One touches the touch of immovability. Second, regarding the objects of the six sense bases: because there is no greed, hatred, or other such afflictions, one does not give rise to longing or seeking;

thus, one touches the touch of non-existence. Third, regarding the object of cessation: because one does not engage in mental construction (*vitarka*) toward any signs (*nimitta*), one touches the touch of signlessness.

As for "having an object," this refers to the objects of the six faculties, the mind, and mental factors. Regarding "the two objects of the six bases," this refers to the six sense-fields (*ṣaḍāyatana*). Regarding "the object of cessation," it refers to...

Regarding the signless (*animitta*): Question: At what stage of existence does one first cultivate this meditative absorption? Answer: One first gives rise to this absorption among human beings. As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"Because it is produced through the power of the teachings of the Buddha and his disciples, and because the wisdom and understanding among humans are extremely sharp.

[In cases where] it arises slowly, it extends to the two higher realms. The treatise says: "Thereafter, it may also manifest in the two higher realms. This refers to the case of the novice monk Udāyin.

Once, while the Buddha was still in the world, Śāriputra was preaching the Dharma. A person who could believe in the Mahāyāna entered the *nirodha-samāpatti* (attainment of cessation) while relying on the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
At that time, this śrāmaṇera challenged Śāriputra, asking: "How can one enter the *nirodha-samāpatti* from the formless realm?

The Buddha rebuked this notion in various ways, [explaining that] one realizes the formless realm and thereby attains entry into the *nirodha-samāpatti*. [The question is: among the eight consciousnesses, how many cease?

"Is it consciousness? He replied: "It is that which ceases and that which does not constantly function, as well as a portion of that which constantly functions. Regarding those that do not constantly function, this refers to the first six consciousnesses.
Regarding the portion that constantly functions, the Western masters explain: the teacher Vijñānakāya states that "a portion" refers to the *ālayavijñāna* and the *manas*.

Both [types of grasping] are constantly active; however, because only the latter is extinguished, it is said to be "one part. Second, the master Śīlabhadra says that [this grasping] pervades both the grasping at persons (*pudgala-grāha*) and the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).
Since those in training (*śaikṣa*) among the two vehicles extinguish only the grasping at persons and do not extinguish the grasping at phenomena, it is said to be "one part."

The extinction concentration (*nirodha-samāpatti*) of those in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) within the two vehicles merely extinguishes the non-constantly active mind and mental factors; it does not extinguish the constantly active portion of the uninterrupted clinging to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*).

Therefore, for a Bodhisattva proceeding directly [to Buddhahood] from the first ground (*prathamabhūmi*) upward, if they enter the extinction concentration by relying on the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*), they only extinguish the manas that clings to a person;
if they enter the extinction concentration by relying on the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), [they extinguish both]. The clinging to persons and...

The two aspects of the *manas* are both extinguished. The pure aspect of the *manas*, together with the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), takes the grasping at phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) as its basis, because the grasping at a person (*pudgalanairātmya*) exists therein.

When the two [graspings] are severed, the grasping at phenomena is eliminated and the grasping at a person follows suit and ceases. If one were to sever only the grasping at a person, the grasping at phenomena would necessarily remain;

therefore, it does not eliminate the fruit of the wisdom of the emptiness of persons. If one enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) by means of the Tathāgata’s contemplation of the two kinds of emptiness, then the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) and...
The Wisdom of Equality functions in conjunction with meditative absorption. Question: What is the intention for entering the attainment of cessation?
Answer: In the Hīnayāna, one seeks the perception of cessation; in the Mahāyāna, one seeks merit (the two aspects are thus clarified).
Regarding the statement "The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* says, etc.," Huadù states: The first three liberations (*vimokṣa*) in the *Kośa* have non-attachment (*alobha*) as their nature;

this is one among the eleven wholesome mental factors (*kuśala-dharma*). This is because the first two liberations involve non-attachment toward impure objects, while the third liberation involves non-attachment toward pure objects;
thus, these three types take non-attachment as their essential nature.

Regarding the statement that the "retinue" consists of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and so forth: by means of the first three liberations (*vimokṣa*), one takes form (*rūpa*) as the object; this is thus the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).

The absence of craving toward these objects is the nature of non-attachment (*alobha*), which is subsumed within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). As for the two factors of feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*), each is comprised of its own respective name.
When mental factors arise, they necessarily rely upon the mind-king; therefore, there is the aggregate of consciousness. Thus, it is said that the five aggregates constitute its nature.
Regarding the subsequent four formless absorptions: because the four formless absorptions are exclusively of a wholesome nature, they possess only four aggregates.
Furthermore, the immaterial aggregate (ārūpya-skandha) and the eighth liberation, the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), have as their essence that which is neither matter nor mind;
they are subsumed under the aggregate of formations dissociated from thought (viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha).
Regarding the phrase "the middle [vehicle] within the Mahāyāna," this is explained in the seventy-third fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

The five dharmas are: first, marks (*nimitta*); second, names (*nāman*); third, discrimination (*vikalpa*); fourth, correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*); and fifth, suchness (*tathatā*). Zhiyou states: "The first four are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), while the latter one is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Furthermore, among the first four, there are two types: the first three are with outflows (*sāsrava*), and the last one is without outflows (*anāsrava*). Moreover, the first three are further divided into two; the first..."

Two are the objects of cognition (*ālambana*), and one is the cognizer (*ālambaka*). Of the former two, there are again two: "characteristic" (*nimitta*) is that which is signified, and "name" (*nāman*) is that which signifies.

Furthermore, among these five factors, "name" is the teaching that signifies, and "characteristic" is the principle that is signified. "Conceptualization" (*vikalpa*) refers to all minds and mental factors within the three realms.
Regarding the statement "mundane, supramundane, and so forth," there are two types of correct knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*):
first, exclusively supramundane correct knowledge; second, mundane-supramundane correct knowledge. As for exclusively supramundane correct knowledge:
when Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas realize suchness (*tathatā*), it is termed exclusively supramundane correct knowledge. Mundane-supramundane correct knowledge...
This refers to the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas who, first, penetrate *tathatā* (suchness) through correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*).

Thereafter, by means of the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), they take the established truths (*vyavasthāna-satya*) as their object and become weary of the faults and afflictions of the three realms; this is called mundane and supramundane correct wisdom.
As for "suchness" (*yathā-yathā*), it refers to the sublime principle of *tathatā* (as indicated by the treatise above).
Regarding the phrase "with outflows" (*sāsrava*) and so forth, Xiu states: "Wisdom with outflows is called mundane; wisdom without outflows is supramundane. In fascicle 73, it asks:
"What is the essence of the eight liberations? It answers: "They take mundane and supramundane right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) as their basis.

Because they take True Suchness (*tathatā*) as their object, they are subsumed under right knowledge. Contemplative minds that possess outflows are subsumed under conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*). — Master of the Commentary.

To explain the meaning of the treatise: the two characters "mundane" (*loka*) encompass the conceptualization (*vikalpa*) among the five dharmas; this conceptualization is precisely the mundane, outflowing (*sāsrava*) mind of conceptualization.
The three characters "supramundane" (*lokottara*) encompass the two wisdoms: the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

All of these are untainted (*anāsrava*). Question: Since the preceding seven liberations (*vimokṣa*) involve both tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted cultivation, how can they be called "right knowledge" (*samyagjñāna*)?

Answer: The Master of the Commentary (*śūstrakāra*) has taken the general meaning and distinguished tainted right knowledge as well. However, according to the intent of the Treatise (*śāstra*), it refers exclusively to untainted right knowledge.

Regarding the statement that "it has wisdom alone as its nature," this does not distinguish between the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), nor between the fundamental (*mūla*) and subsequently attained (*prṣṭhalabdha*) [wisdom]; all take wisdom as their essence.

Regarding the statement "taking form and non-form as objects, etc.," one might ask: while the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*) are all supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), yet...
If the meditative hindrances can be removed and superior qualities can be induced [by other means], why are these eight liberations necessary? The answer is:
one must take as objects forms, non-forms, and the realm of suchness (*tathatā*) before one can finally abandon all meditative hindrances and induce superior virtues; liberation is the foundation.

Pure concentration (*śuddha-samādhi*) arises only then. Question: What is meant by taking as objects both the material (*rūpa*) and the immaterial (*arūpa*), as well as suchness (*tathatā*)? Answer: The first three liberations take material form as their object;
however, they treat it as light, whether small or large, in mutual relation, and as entering into a single flavor (*ekarasa*). In total, these all take material form as their object.
The next four liberations take as their objects non-material space, infinite consciousness, nothingness, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
and the realm of suchness (*tathatā*).

Regarding the phrase "being free from all obstacles to meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and so forth," the *Dharmārāma* explains that there are eight liberations (*vimokṣa*) which counteract six obstacles: the first two liberations remove the obstacle to transformation (*nirmāṇa*);

the third liberation removes the obstacle to the supreme dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*); the fourth liberation, the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), removes the obstacle to going and returning;
and the fifth liberation, the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), removes the obstacle to the absence of conflict (*araṇā*) and the prayer of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*).

The obstacles to the various merits of wisdom are removed by the sixth and seventh liberations; these consist of the outflows, which are the afflictions (*kleśa*), as well as the obstructions, which are karma.
The eighth liberation removes the obstacle to the most supreme dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).

The phrase "because it cannot be accomplished by anything else" reveals the functional capacity of wisdom (*prajñā*). This means that all previously mentioned inducements of merit and the elimination of the obstacles to meditative concentration (*samādhi*) are, in their essential nature, wisdom;
therefore, it is said that they cannot be accomplished by anything else. (This refers to the actual substance.)

Regarding the statement "if they correspond in substance and so forth," this refers to the correspondence between the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*). Together, the king and its factors constitute the four aggregates (*skandha*).
The first seven liberations (*vimokṣa*) have these four aggregates as their essential nature. If, however, the retinue is included, they have all five aggregates as their essential nature.
Regarding the phrase "according to the Abhidharma-samuccaya and other treatises": it is asked how the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) can also consist of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
The intended meaning is that the first three liberations (*vimokṣa*) take form as their object. *Fahua jing xuanyan yaoji*, Scroll Seventeen.
*Fahua jing xuanzan yaoji*, Scroll 18,
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Xifu of Jingshui Temple.
It is said that "this Dharma cannot be shown" refers to the teaching of the initial provisional and subsequent ultimate [truths] as expounded by the Tathāgata, according to what is appropriate.
What has been explained cannot be expressed to others, for the principles of causes and conditions transcend language;
it is like the pain in a person's body, which words cannot reach, as it must be personally realized.
Regarding the phrase "the characteristics of words are quiescent," the *Yājiàoyào* states: It means that the dharma of *tathatā* (suchness) cannot be pointed out to others.
Why? Because the characteristics of its words are quiescent; furthermore, because its nature as a name is empty and it is unattainable.

According to various commentaries, this is explained in terms of *tathatā*. However, if one follows the intent of the *Shū* (the sub-commentary), even the dharmas of the *paratantra* (dependent nature) cannot [be pointed out].

To demonstrate this, it is said that one "attains the four forms of verified purity" (*catur-avetyaprasāda*). The older tradition calls these the "four unbreakable faiths," while the newer tradition calls them the "four verified purities.

These four are the objects—namely, the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and the precepts. These four objects themselves constitute the focal points (*ālambana*), and the faithful mind that takes them as its object is the subject that perceives these four.
At the time of encountering the object, this faith cannot be destroyed; it is called "firm. Because "firm" has the meaning of being indestructible, it is termed the "firmness of the power of faith.
This is first attained at the stage of the first dhyāna. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, which is the object of this faith, is the Dharma within the four kinds of indestructible faith.

Regarding the statement "but not yet fully realized": [The questioner asks] why it is said that those with firm power of faith are able to know this, yet it is also said that non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas are all unable to know it.
The commentary (*shu*) states: "But not yet," etc. The intended meaning is that those who do not know have not yet attained full realization; thus they are said to "not know."

Regarding the statement "though prior to the path of seeing": Question: Since those prior to the [first] bhūmi are also able to believe and know [this], why is it said that only the first bhūmi does so?

Answer: The commentary states, "Though prior to the [first] bhūmi," etc. The meaning is that Bodhisattvas prior to the bhūmis possess only inferential knowledge (*anumāna*), which differs from the realized belief and knowledge of the first bhūmi.

Regarding the answer stating "the four types of verified purity" (*avetyaprasāda*): when untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) realizes this and penetrates the principle, it is termed "verified" (*sākṣāt-kṛta*). It is untainted...
Wisdom conjoined with faith takes the four dharmas as its common object; because they are called "pure," they are termed the "fourfold verified purity" (*caturvidha avetyaprasāda*).

Regarding the phrase "the assembly of the Buddha’s disciples," this refers generally to both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). It does not depend on the number of individuals, nor does it concern the breadth or narrowness of their location.

It makes no distinction between those of sharp or dull faculties, nor does it specify the duration of time—whether earlier or later—but rather points collectively to the followers of the Three Vehicles.
"I do not know. Regarding the passage in the Sūtra beginning with "Suppose," Śāriputra thought to himself: "This teaching is for others of dull faculties;
it was not spoken for me, Śāriputra. While he was reflecting thus, the World-Honored One said, "Suppose... This means: suppose one *trichiliocosm*...

Among them, Śāriputra was one of those with sharp faculties; yet, as a provisional being composed of the five aggregates, even when his spirit was exhausted through contemplating the Buddha’s wisdom, he could not know it.

Regarding those who have attained such single-mindedness together: it is simply a matter of taking the wisdom of the pratyekabuddhas of the ten directions, gathering and uniting it in one place, which is termed "single-mindedly seeking together."
Regarding the phrase "Pratyekabuddhas, etc.": in Sanskrit they are called *pratyekabuddha*, which here means "Solitary Realizer. One who realizes [enlightenment] alone is termed a "Solitary Realizer.

This contains two categories: first, in comparison with *śrāvakas*; second, in comparison with those who travel in groups (*vargacārin*). Those of sharp faculties become rhinoceros-like (*khaḍgaviṣāṇakalpa*), while those of duller faculties become group-travelers.
Because they move in a group or faction, they are called "group-travelers" (*vargacārin*).

Regarding the phrase "if they have not yet entered [the path]," etc.: if one abides in the roots of merit conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) of a Śrāvaka, a Pratyekabuddha is far from the fruit and requires a long period of cultivation;
because their refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) has already been prolonged, they become a "Rhinoceros-like" (*khadgaviṣāṇakalpa*) Pratyekabuddha.

However, if one who has entered the four Śrāvaka roots of merit turns back toward the Pratyekabuddha path, they only become a "Group-dweller" (*vargacārin*); they are near to the fruit and their period of cultivation is brief, as their application of effort is...

It is few; therefore, it is called dull faculty (*mṛdv-indriya*). For example, when people in the world practice their craft for a short duration, with few repetitions, and the phrasing is coarse and difficult, they are considered to have dull faculties.
Regarding the statement "in the stage conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) and so forth": within the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), there are three categories, namely:

those not yet fixed for rebirth, those already fixed for rebirth, and those who are in the process of being reborn. If one is not yet fixed for rebirth and dedicates [the roots of merit] toward [enlightenment], one becomes a rhinoceros-like pratyekabuddha;

because the number of births is many, it is possible to refine the faculties over a hundred kalpas. If one is already fixed for rebirth and becomes a pratyekabuddha in this very life, one does so at the time of being reborn.

All these constitute the *vargacārin* (group-practitioner). The stage of the five *smṛtyupasthānas* (foundations of mindfulness) is called "not yet determined birth. The stage of the *svalakṣaṇasmṛtyupasthāna* (distinct-characteristic mindfulness) is called "already determined birth.

The stage of the *sāmānyalakṣaṇasmṛtyupasthāna* (general-characteristic mindfulness) is called "birth in this very life. If one who has entered the stages above the four roots of goodness (*catvāri nirvedhabhāgīyāni*) subsequently turns toward [the Mahāyāna], they all become *vargacārins*.
Question: Do Pratyekabuddhas not also have their own vehicle through which they generate the resolve, practice, and attain the fruit? For what reason must this be so?
Is it those among the śrāvakas who have turned their minds [toward the Mahāyāna]? Answer: Among them, there are also those who practice within their own vehicle and attain its fruit;

these mostly become rhinoceros-like (khadgaviṣāṇakalpa) pratyekabuddhas. If they are those who turn their minds toward the śrāvaka path, they comprise both categories: the group-practitioners (vargacārin) and the rhinoceros-like.

This is designated by way of its broadest sense; for now, it refers to those among the śrāvakas who turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna]. Question: At which mental states do the four stages of the roots of goodness (*catur-kuśalamūla*) occur? Answer:

It may be so for the lower and middle levels, but not for the highest level of patience (*kṣānti*), because its duration is too brief to permit further refinement. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states that within the middle and lower levels of patience, they are termed "transitions" (*saṃkrānti*).

Regarding the statement that "bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds" are "endowed [with these qualities]," this refers to ordinary bodhisattvas in the two stages of the path of accumulation (*sambhāramārga*) and the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*), which precede the [first] bhūmi.
The prose version does not mention "bodhisattvas," whereas the verse does; thus, they differ in what is present or absent.
Regarding the "numerous multitudes": rice may serve as food; hemp may serve as clothing; bamboo is solid on the outside; and reeds are hollow within.
For one who has resolved their mind [on enlightenment], benefiting sentient beings takes this true emptiness as the foundation; thus, these things may be used as metaphors.
Regarding the term "field" (*tián*): it means "to emit. It emits all things; all things are born from the earth. This is the functional capacity of the field.

Regarding the term "translated meaning" (*yìyì*): if one asks what is meant by "translated meaning," the answer is that taking Sanskrit words and rendering them into the language of Táng (Chinese) is precisely what is called "translated meaning."
Regarding "land" (tǔtián): if one says "country" (guótǔ), it is not correct. This was translated according to its meaning from the Sanskrit original;
the phonetic transcription is *chā* (with the tone indicated by the character 疏煞).

Regarding the ten kinds of generating the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, fascicle 49, states: first, the immeasurable, boundless, and vast mind that makes offerings to all Buddhas;
second, the mind that liberates all sentient beings; third, the mind that causes all moments of existence (*kṣaṇa*) to enter the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*);
fourth, the mind that contemplates all phenomena as being like empty space; fifth, the mind that contemplates all the practices of Bodhisattvas... [sixth]...
1. To maintain right mindfulness of all Buddhas of the three periods of time; 2. To thoroughly comprehend the inconceivable fruition of the Dharma-realm;
3. To adorn and purify the lands of all Tathāgatas; 4. To enter deeply into the great assemblies of all Tathāgatas; 5. To observe the wondrous voices of all Tathāgatas;
in each and every one of these, there are immeasurable ways of perceiving the Buddha-nature. By means of these...

Those born blind [do not see it]. Those of the Two Vehicles see the Buddha-nature like an infant seeing the moon. Bodhisattvas prior to the stages (bhūmi) see the Buddha-nature like a person with an eye ailment.
From the first stage to the seventh stage, it is like a flash of lightning, for they see it as soon as they enter meditative contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
In the eighth and ninth stages, it is like seeing the moon through a fine silk gauze. In the tenth stage, one sees only one's own nature and does not yet see the Buddha. If one reaches...

Regarding the stage of Buddhahood: one perceives that one’s own body and the bodies of others are entirely equal. Although one is currently at the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*), one is still unable to know the Buddha-wisdom.

Question: Since this section speaks of wisdom (*prajñā*), why is it said that one “sees the nature” (*dharmatā*)? Answer: Among the five kinds of wisdom, True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the very nature of wisdom;
because it is precisely wisdom itself, it is cited here as proof. Previously, the power of faith was firm and stable.
This is explained from the perspective of faith; because realization and understanding have not yet reached perfection, one does not know the Buddha-wisdom. Question:

Why is it said that from the first bhūmi onward is called "arousing the mind" (bodhicitta)? Answer: According to the ten kinds of arousing the mind in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, these are collectively termed "arousing the mind" (as cited previously).
Regarding the statement that the preceding section is "profound": Question: The eight types of profundity mentioned previously were all praises of the profundity of the teaching (*śāsana*).
Why, then, is it said here that wisdom (*jñāna*) is unknowable? Answer: The Commentary states, "The preceding section," etc.

The intended meaning is that when praising the Buddha’s wisdom, because the wisdom itself is profound, its gateway (*mukha*) is also profound. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that within this current section on the uncommon profundity, the eighth and ninth sūtras...

The text exclusively extols the Buddha’s wisdom, appearing to describe the profound nature of the realized wisdom; it was written as a second benefit so that there might be no fear of later refutations of this commentary.
Regarding the statement "or fourteen and a half verses" (up to) "the first six," etc., this should be understood according to the previous distribution.
Regarding the phrase "the very last among them," this refers to the final verse among the six stanzas;
it corresponds to the first one and a half stanzas among the nine stanzas. This refers to those disciples who have previously made offerings to various Buddhas.
Regarding the phrase "the eight verses following," this refers to the eight lines of prose beginning with "Even if the world were filled...
Regarding the phrase "according to the meaning and the structural divisions (*kośa*)," the preceding eight profound points in the long prose (*gadya*) constitute the teaching-gate (*dharma-mukha*).
Now, these verse lines (*gāthā*) likewise describe the teaching-gate. Within this teaching-gate, the Buddha’s wisdom is mentioned repeatedly; thus, they are categorized according to their meaning.
Regarding the statement "generally praising [the passage] up to the verse on non-discrimination," etc.: Question: What is meant by "general" (total)? Answer:

The Sūtra states that from the words "Since my attainment of Buddhahood" onwards, these four lines constitute a single verse and a half; because this specific portion of the sūtra text describes it, it is called "general.

Therefore, it is said that there are no separate verses. Question: If only one verse and a half describe it, then there *is* a verse; why do you say there is none? Answer: According to the standard...

In the prose (*gadya*), there are general phrases such as "various causes and conditions," and the sections beginning with "extensively expounding" below are specific phrases. There are ten verses in total, comprising both the general and the specific;
these are all not described here, and thus they are called "verses without distinct [explanations]."
Regarding the scriptural statement, "I have now fully attained": this refers to being able to realize and to teach, which is termed "full attainment.

This demonstrates the possession of both the profound principle (*nyāya*) and the profound teaching (*śāsana*). "Only I know these marks" refers to self-knowledge; "the Buddhas of the ten directions are likewise" refers to the knowledge of others.
This is something that only Buddhas and Buddhas can know.

When the sutra states that "the words of all Buddhas are not different," it means one should not perceive a discrepancy between what was taught forty years ago—where two vehicles were spoken of—and what is taught today, where one vehicle is spoken of.
This distinction between the provisional and the real regarding the One and the Three is not taught exclusively by this Buddha alone; it has been taught by all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
All are like this: first provisional, later real; only Buddhas and Buddhas know this, while others do not. You need only give rise to the power of faith; the words of all Buddhas are no different.
Referring to the two types of profound depth, the teachings of the past forty years ago and the present teaching are not the same as those spoken at the assembly on Vulture Peak;
these are collectively termed "the long-term. "The long-term" refers to the ultimate and final duration.
The meaning [of this] is that, in the end, he speaks of the true Dharma and exhorts them to give rise to faith. "Śāriputra, even you have entered into this sutra by means of faith.
Furthermore, after a long time, the Dharma of the World-Honored One must necessarily speak the truth; thus the Tathāgata implicitly grants permission for Śāriputra to speak.
If he had not given his implicit consent, how could Śāriputra have desisted three times without withdrawing?
When he said, "Since you have not yet attained equality," this refers to the provisional and ultimate teachings; I have realized each of them one by one, so you need only give rise to faith.
Regarding the scriptural statement, "and those who seek the state of a pratyekabuddha": a pratyekabuddha is an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, in the section on the Stage of the Solitary Realizer (*Pratyekabuddhabhūmi*), states that there are five characteristics of this stage. First is the spiritual lineage (*gotra*): by nature, they are solitary realizers.

Due to these causes and conditions, their minds find no delight in places of sensory clamor, while they develop a deep attachment for places of tranquility. Second is the path (*mārga*): this refers to a certain class of solitary realizers.
Regarding the lineage (*gotra*): having passed through a hundred eons, one encounters the appearance of a Buddha in the world and repeatedly draws near to serve him;

thus, the continuity [of the lineage] is perfected, and with single-minded devotion, one seeks to realize the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha. Third is cultivation (*abhyāsa*): this refers to a certain class who, having first practiced for more than a hundred eons, appear in a world devoid of a Buddha;

without a teacher, they spontaneously cultivate the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*) and realize the direct vision (*abhisamaya*) of the Dharma. They thereby attain...
The Pratyekabuddha-bodhi: without severing the afflictions, one becomes an Arhat. Fourth is the dwelling, which has two further categories:
first, the rhinoceros-like, who delight in dwelling in solitude within secluded forests; second, the group-practitioners, who also delight in dwelling together in mutual dependence with a community.
Fifth is the conduct: dwelling in various villages and towns, they well protect their bodies and deliver sentient beings.
Sentient beings are not transformed by means of words; this refers precisely to the second path.

When the Sūtra says, "I cause them to be liberated from the bonds of suffering," those in the three fruits and four stages of realization are collectively termed "liberated from the bonds of suffering."
Regarding the passage "The Sūtra says that by means of skillful means," etc.: Question: This passage clarifies that the term "skillful means" refers to the teaching of the three vehicles (*triyāna*).
For what reason did Śāriputra hesitate, not knowing where they were headed? Answer: There are two points of interpretation.

First, it is said that this merely describes the wondrous function of the Tathāgata’s subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*), which leads sentient beings and causes them to become attached in various places; this is called what is taught through skillful means, namely, the existence of the three vehicles. Second, ...

As for this, although three [vehicles] were initially mentioned within the "intentional concession" (*abhiprāya*), in the end there is only one. At this time, it has not yet been clearly stated that two are not true;
therefore, it is called an "intentional concession. Taking Śāriputra’s lingering mind as an example, he asked the World-Honored One:
"If you have already excluded the two vehicles by means of this [teaching], why is it necessary to speak of the two vehicles to others? The Sūtra answers: "The Buddha, by means of skillful means..."
This refers to the four-line sūtra.

Regarding the statement that "the three requests [to teach] up to the point where [the Buddha] ceased were all as before": if he had not first ceased [speaking], Śāriputra’s three requests would not have been fulfilled.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One’s initial cessation served as a sign to cause the true noble ones to inquire about the One Vehicle, and to cause the nominal noble ones... [to understand].

He rose from his seat and departed. This occurred even up to three instances of the Master’s refusal. Had the Master not uttered the word "stop" (*zhi*) beforehand, [the Buddha] would have had no occasion to speak after those three requests;
according to the sutras, he should have waited for the fourth request before preaching the Dharma.

It is precisely because the Master’s utterance of "stop" preceded the third request that it coincided with the Tathāgata’s permission to speak. Therefore, the instances of "stopping" all occur first, while the requests all follow afterward. This is the explanation of the first [point].
This is the intended meaning of "riding" [the vehicle].
Regarding the statement that the Buddha’s *śamatha* (calm abiding) is also threefold: it refers to the *śamatha* that extols the marvelous. The sutra says:
"Śāriputra, to speak in brief, the Buddha has fully accomplished immeasurable, boundless, and unprecedented dharmas. Śāriputra, there is no need to speak further. Second.
"Fearing they might be startled, I have previously refrained from speaking. At that time, the Buddha said to Śāriputra, "Stop, stop! There is no need to speak further.
If this matter were to be spoken, all the devas and humans in the entire world would become startled and doubtful. Fearing they might fall into a great pit, I have stopped;
the Buddha has again stopped, Śāriputra. If this matter were to be spoken, all the devas, humans, and asuras in the entire world..."
One should be startled and doubtful; the bhikṣu of overweening pride (*adhimāna*) is about to fall into a great pit.

As for the statement "requesting that all remain behind," initially the doubt was raised and set aside, or it was requested; alternatively, it is said that the request was made because of the narrow-minded doubts concerning oneself and others.
"Since time immemorial, I have never heard the Dharma from the Buddha. Now, the fourfold assembly all harbor doubts (and so forth).

Together with the verses on the Sun of Wisdom and others, this subsequent presentation of how the great assembly planted causes under other Buddhas is also called 'the request to cultivate causes together with the Buddha.
The Sūtra says: Śāriputra addressed the Buddha again, saying: 'World-Honored One, we only pray that you will speak it; we only pray that you will..."*

I shall explain this. Why is that? Because in this assembly there are countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* beings who have previously seen various Buddhas, whose faculties are sharp and keen, and whose wisdom is clear and lucid. Together with the verses and so forth, these three [sections] describe both themselves and others;
since they are now capable of hearing through the transformation of the present Buddha, their request is also called the "Request with Joyful Hearing of the Dharma. At that time, Śāriputra again...
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, we pray that you will speak; we pray that you will speak.

In this assembly, there are hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of those like us who, life after life, have already received transformation from the Buddha. As the verse says: "The Unsurpassed Honored One among Two-Legged Beings," and so forth.

Regarding the statement "the initial act of ceasing": Question: What is called the characteristic of the initial act of ceasing? Answer: There are two interpretations. First, the act of ceasing and not speaking is the characteristic of preaching the Dharma.
Second, the act of ceasing and not speaking is the characteristic of not preaching the Dharma. At first glance, this appears to be a refusal to speak;
yet, the very manifestation of this characteristic of refusing to speak is, in fact, the precursor to preaching the Dharma. Therefore, it is called a "characteristic."
This was accomplished. He did not manifest the appearance of preaching the Dharma, intending to cause Śāriputra to give rise to doubt.
Because for forty years he had clung to his own vehicle as ultimate, that clinging mind was difficult to sever; however, doubt is easily removed.

Therefore, he turned this mind of clinging into a mind of doubt, which is why he proclaimed the cessation [of teaching]. This was because most śrāvakas are arrogant toward the Dharma; if he had not waited for an invitation, [they would have failed to listen].
The aspiration [to hear] is difficult to generate. Therefore, immediately after the Tathāgata praised his own wisdom, he said, "Stop; there is no need to speak further. Śāriputra thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One has been speaking from the very beginning, and no one requested him to stop. To whom, then, was this command directed? The answer is twofold:
first, to instruct Śāriputra so that doubt would arise in his own mind; second, to cause doubt to arise in the minds of the assembly.
In the course of his speech, he paused, saying: "I only pray that you will speak it; I only pray that you will speak it, World-Honored One!
For what reason do you so earnestly praise skillful means? This is called seeking the profound realm; this is the first meaning.
To thirst for and yearn to hear it is the second meaning. [The Sūtra continues: With palms joined and gazing up in reverence, he waited expectantly for the sublime [words] to emerge.
At that time, he spoke according to reality. There were devas, nāgas, spirits, and others, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
there were also bodhisattvas seeking buddhahood who wished to hear this Way.

Regarding the phrase "stopping afterwards": when this discourse was being spoken, there were among those in the assembly bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who immediately rose from their seats, paid homage to the Buddha, and withdrew.
Regarding the statement "first, myself and others": it means that from the past until now, I have never heard such teachings as these from the Buddha.

Regarding the statement "addressing the great assembly and so forth": it means that the World-Honored One spoke only to them, saying, "Do not worry that people will not believe. As the sutra says: "Why is this?
Because the countless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya sentient beings in this assembly have all seen various Buddhas... (and so on).

Regarding the subsequent description of oneself and others, the Sūtra says: "In this assembly now, there are those like us who, throughout hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of lifetimes, have already been transformed by the Buddha."
Regarding the statement "the three requests made by Śāriputra," it refers specifically to the three requests made by Śāriputra alone, from which [the three instances] are distinguished;

they are not categorized as being attached to the text of the three refusals (*tri-niṣedha*). This is because the refusals proceed in tandem with the requests. Therefore, the Master of the Commentary (Sū-zhu) assigns the three refusals to correspond with the three requests.
This is included within the three requests. Therefore, the Commentary states: "The text follows three sections; this is the text on 'Cessation,' which follows the text on the 'Requests.

As for the statement that the initial 'Cessation' belongs [to the first section], it is because it stands at the beginning of the first section. Second, the 'Profound' is first proclaimed in the middle; this is the praise of wisdom."
The excellence of the Dharma of wisdom and the excellence of the Dharma Master constitute the One Vehicle. Regarding the first [section], it is subsumed under "Cessation" (*śamatha*);

regarding the remaining two [sections], they are subsumed under "Cessation" within the portion concerning the merits of the Dharma Master. In the three subsequent passages of request, the phrase "subsumed under the two cessations" means they are included within those two cessations.
This second [section] concerns the arousal of wonder and doubt among the fourfold assembly, found within the passage of Śāriputra’s request.
Regarding the statement "the manifestation of the threefold meaning": this clarifies the meaning of the divisions. First is the meaning of certainty;

it refers to the meaning of the minds of those of the Two Vehicles attaining certainty regarding their own realization prior to forty years [ago]. The Buddha taught the single meaning of liberation. Second is the meaning of doubt;
it refers to the two kinds of profound meanings praised by the Buddha, which were previously mentioned as being unknown. Regarding these meanings, there is...

"Doubt" refers to doubting the meaning. The Sūtra says: "As it is now, one does not know where this meaning leads. Third: regarding what matter does one doubt the meaning? For what cause and for what condition?
Diligently extolling the foremost skillful means of the Buddhas is called doubting the meaning based on what matter.

Question: What is the difference between "doubting based on what matter" and "doubting the meaning"? Answer: There is a distinction in their breadth and narrowness. Doubting the meaning refers exclusively to...
The second [point], "profound," gives rise to a new doubt. Regarding what matter does this doubt concern the meaning? Because it concerns both the new and old doubts, it applies only to Śāriputra.
As the Sūtra says: "The twelve hundred [people]... had this thought. Question: Previously, when the assembly was enumerated, there were twelve thousand; why is that mentioned here?

Why does the text mention only one thousand two hundred people? Answer: If one discusses the total number of the assembly of doubters according to both their gravity and their status, there were twelve thousand people.
As for the specific mention here, it refers to those one thousand two hundred who doubted both with their minds and their speech.

The Sūtra speaks of "śrāvakas" three times, using the terms *caishan* (repeated praise), *chanshan* (laudatory praise), and *zanshan* (praise). It praises two kinds of profundity. Regarding "expedient means" (*upāya*):
the gateway of the teaching is called expedient means; the wisdom that is expounded is also called expedient means;

and that which connects the lower [levels] to reveal the upper [levels] is all called expedient means. "The wisdom of the Buddhas is profound and immeasurable" reveals the superior expedient means. Its...
The gate of wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to enter. It employs skillful means; it is called "skillful means" because it contains [the ultimate].
To say this is to point to the words spoken from within the Buddha's own mouth.
Regarding the scriptural statement "attaining nirvāṇa," this refers to nirvāṇa with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).
Regarding the scriptural statement "knowing the doubts in the minds of the fourfold assembly," one asks:

since a śrāvaka knows the mental states of others only when in a state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), how can he know the doubts in the minds of the fourfold assembly while in a distracted state (*vikṣipta-citta*)? The answer is: it is through the Buddha’s empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Below...

Having spoken of the One Vehicle, he departs. Previously, he had implicitly granted his consent to explain his intention; now, Śāriputra perceives that the minds of the assembly are filled with doubt and quickly requests [an explanation].
Second, because there are signs of doubt upon the outward appearances of the assembly, he shows them how to destroy their hesitation.
Regarding the doubt concerning the "cause" (*hetu*) among the causes of arising: here, "cause" refers to the reason or the underlying motive, not the causal factor in the sense of cause-and-effect.
Why is it that the Tathāgata repeatedly proclaims the profound realm—first speaking of the profound and later speaking of the profound?

It is because this [repetition] differs from the aforementioned reasons and motives, which gives rise to doubt. (In the prose section, the former is called "profound," while in the verse, the latter is called "profound.")
Regarding the statement that "liberation is the same," this refers to the sense of attaining liberation through the abandonment of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*);

it is in this sense that they are said to be the same. The treatise states: "However, the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) does not obstruct liberation, because it lacks the capacity to initiate karma and moisten rebirth.

If one speaks generally, however, the afflictions can also obstruct great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*). The treatise states: "It is said that the afflictive hindrances obscure suchness; how could it be otherwise?"
It should be understood that the holy teaching speaks in terms of predominant function, for in reality, both [obstacles] are capable of obstructing both fruits.
As it says below: "In what is this person liberated? They are liberated merely by being free from delusion;
in truth, they have not yet attained complete liberation."

Regarding the category of attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*): it refers specifically to the seeds of attachment to phenomena. Among these, the one hundred and twenty-eight types of doubt constitute one such class.
That which is "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*) arises from the true matured consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*); its essence is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

This doubt concerning the matter of what is subsumed under the indeterminate born of maturation—such as when those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) do not recognize black salt and so forth—is one instance thereof.

Regarding the passage from the Sūtra, "From the past until now," concerning the phrase "the fourfold assembly and others," Jin says: The three rounds of requests differ in their breadth and narrowness.
In the first round, Śāriputra and others made the request; since the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings all likewise requested that he preach, it was the broadest.
The intention here is that Śāriputra requested alone, fearing that the World-Honored One might not preach for the sake of a single person; therefore, he presented the request universally.
The doubts of the multitude were such that they merely requested that the World-Honored One definitively explain [the matter].

He spoke of the profound and subtle wisdom that is difficult to understand and so forth; this refers to the gate of wisdom (the second three-week period seeking the vehicle, followed by the third three-week period seeking the city, which is the most narrow).

Regarding the statement that "the Buddha himself spoke," this verse arises following the preceding prose section concerning the causes and conditions. It shall now be explained through eleven and a half verses.
Within the preceding section where the Buddha himself spoke, he first praised the merits of the Dharma Master; yet, no one had requested him to preach.
This is titled "The Buddha’s Own Declaration. The Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision are vast, profound, immeasurable, and unimpeded; these are precisely what is being asked about.

"O Great Holy Honored One, Sun of Wisdom," after a long time you have finally preached this Dharma. You yourself declare that you have attained such powers, fearlessnesses, and samādhis, up to the inconceivable.
This refers to the wondrous Dharma realized at the beginning of the "Chapter on Questions," as well as the Dharma-master who is able to realize it.
"Exquisite! This has already been fully elucidated by the immeasurable verses of the World Hero. Why, then, is this question restated? Answer:
At first glance, it might seem as though this refers to the characteristics of the eightfold merit described within the previous praise of the Dharma Master's excellence;
however, such is not the case. That previous section praised the Dharma Master’s merit in order to focus attention on a single point, which was solely his wisdom."
It opens up and brings forth the wisdom realized by the Dharma Master that is capable of realization; it should be gathered together and placed in one location.
This is precisely the wisdom of the prose commentary (*gadya*) on this question. It is the wisdom of the immediately preceding prose section which asks:

"For what cause and for what reason do you so earnestly praise the Buddhas' foremost skillful means and their profound, subtle, and wondrous wisdom? [This is] the dharma difficult to understand; it is the gateway of wisdom. Now...
These one and a half verses from the Great Holy Honored One, the Sun of Wisdom, describe the preceding prose teachings and principles (*śāstrārtha*). Question:

Since the prose teachings and principles are merely that which is realized (*sākṣātkṛta*), why does this verse text describe them by exhaustively explaining the qualities of the realizing Dharma-master’s mindfulness and contemplation?
Answer: Although both were asked together within the prior presentation of doubts, it was because the Tathāgata has achieved [them].
Because one contemplates and observes its merits, that which was previously explained and realized is both termed "profound. Now, this verse cites the means by which it is manifested;
its intent is to take up what is realized. Although the verse praises the excellence of the Dharma-preacher, it remains distinct from the excellence of the Dharma that accomplishes [the realization].
"Self-illumination" refers to self-benefit; "benefiting all those in darkness" refers to benefiting others.

"Ming" (冥) is pronounced as *mo* (莫) with the rhyme of *jing* (經), meaning a dark night. It is also pronounced as *mo* (莫) with the rhyme of *ding* (定), meaning evening. Following the initial interpretation: [the former is for oneself, the latter is for others].

The statement that "there is nothing it cannot illuminate" means that illumination belongs to the Buddha’s wisdom; it universally illuminates all sentient beings, and thus there is nothing it does not shine upon.
The statement that "it is like a donor" uses a farmer as a metaphor for a patron and the cultivation of merit as a metaphor for tilling a field; this refers to the field of merit that is the Buddha.
In this middle [state], merit and goodness increase; one is first born into a happy realm and later attains the true world.
When the sun rises, it is precisely the time for farmers to perform their labors; when the sun rises, it is precisely the time for donors to cultivate merit.
The mention of the hundred birds singing is a metaphor for the appearance of a Buddha in the world. A Dharma Master of high virtue assists the Buddha in propagating the transformation [of beings].
Having first appeared, he has already delivered one thousand two hundred arhats; he travels to various kingdoms to transform and deliver immeasurable sentient beings.
Regarding the metaphor of the "evil Māra": "evil" (pì) means either "to employ" or "wicked"; here it takes the sense of wickedness because he destroys virtuous matters.
When a grandson sees his mother leave, he weeps; when Māra sees the Buddha emerge, he weeps out of fear that his own followers will be delivered.
The "Mountain King" refers to Mount Sumeru.
The "long night" refers to the long night of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

"Many years" means that it is only after forty years have passed that one may speak of them as many years. As the Sūtra says: "For a long time I have kept this essential [teaching] silent. It does not... [text continues].
"Explain it quickly. "The reason I have not yet explained it is that the time for its explanation has not yet arrived.

Regarding what is attained at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), this refers to the profundity of wisdom (*prajñā*). Based on this, it is the *Anuparipṛcchā-svayaṃbhāṣita-sūtra* (The Sutra Spoken Spontaneously Without Being Questioned).
"My intention is difficult to fathom" refers to the depth of the gateway of wisdom. "Intention" (*manas*) refers to both wisdom and the gateway; [this concerns] the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
I do not know. This is why I am unable to ask.
There are sūtras spoken without being asked; these are the *Aparipṛcchā-sūtra* (Sūtras Spoken Without Being Asked). To praise the practice of the Way refers to the Way of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
