Regarding the statement "the general words of the treatise": the scripture itself is a single unit, yet there is a distinction between those who are startled and those who are not.

The commentary provides five types of definitive explanations, which are ultimately subsumed under two categories. Because these are presented as a comprehensive summary, they are called "general words."

Regarding the term "causal prediction" (*hetu-vyākaraṇa*): this explains the intended meaning of the latter two types of cessation mentioned in the treatise. While the sūtra author refers to them as "cessation-cessation," the master of the treatise cannot likewise call them "cessation";
thus, he changes the term to "causal prediction. Within the section on the analysis of the *vyākaraṇa* (prediction) in the treatise, it is further divided into four parts:
first, the determination of the mind; second, causal prediction; third, receiving the prediction; and fourth, bestowing the prediction. First, the determination of the mind.
Regarding the "Mind": the commentators do not categorize it here. The Sūtra’s general meaning extends to the subsequent passage. Second, regarding "because of the prediction" (*vyākaraṇa*):

the Commentary states that the preceding section on "because of the prediction" refers to the Sūtra’s words, "Stop, stop; there is no need to speak further," while the following two sections on "stopping" refer to the point where [the disciples] become startled and doubtful.
This is so. The second revised section concerns the "Prediction Based on Causes" (*hetu-vyākaraṇa*). Regarding the meaning of "based on causes" (*hetu*):

it is called "prediction based on causes" because the act of bestowing the prediction is explained by way of its causal basis. (The preceding section concludes the topical outline for the prediction based on causes; the following is the actual explanation of the prediction based on causes.)

Regarding the phrase "should listen" and so forth: it is asked, "Since the Blessed One has already finished the first round of prohibition, what further purpose is served by a second round of prohibition?
The answer is: If there were no second round of prohibition, for what reason would [the teaching] arise? First, it serves the purpose of investigating and seeking the profound realm.
Second, it is intended to cause the great assembly to give rise to a mind of reverence and a desire to hear it thoroughly. Therefore, [the second round is necessary].
The above constitutes the two meanings regarding those who should hear [the teaching]. First, as for seeking the profound realm, the Sūtra says:

"I only pray that you will speak it! I only pray that you will speak it! This refers to those who, with reverence and longing, desire to hear and give rise to a mind of rare aspiration. The Sūtra says:
"In this assembly, there are countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* sentient beings. What is the second time of cessation? It is attained immediately.
What is the purpose of the third round of cessation? Answer: If there were no third round of cessation, for what reason would those who are wicked people arise and withdraw from their seats?
This means they are unfit to be listeners and thus withdraw. As the Sūtra says: "When these words were spoken, there was a bhikṣu in the assembly who prostrated to the Buddha and withdrew.
Therefore, based on these three meanings, the [phrases] "emerging" and "bestowing a prediction" are established upon the latter two cessations.

Because it serves as the cause, it is called the "prediction based on the cause" (*hetu-vyākaraṇa*). If one finds these vernacular expressions cumbersome, one may simply say "the prediction of the cause.
Furthermore, some commentaries read the character *kāi* (開) instead; however, since that character has two meanings, it is better to read it as *wen* (聞). Regarding "taking" (*qǔ*) the prediction:

this means granting that one shall receive a prediction. There are two senses to this "taking": first, the sense of granting permission, which is called "taking"; second, the sense of encompassing (*saṃgraha*).
"Bestowing meaning" (*śāsana*) is termed "taking" (*upādāna*). First, "taking" refers to granting permission to speak. Second, "taking" refers to the sense of receiving and bestowing;
it refers to the sense of receiving Śāriputra’s request. This is precisely taking as the cause and the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) as the fruit. As the sutra below states:
"Since you have earnestly requested three times, how could I now not speak? This is it.
Regarding the "bestowal of the prediction" (*vyākaraṇa*), the following six sections of the text provide a formal analysis and explanation (examining four matters).
As for the phrase "among the four types of definitive predictions," whereas previously the definitive mind was not correlated with the scriptural text, here it appears to be so correlated.
Regarding the phrase "because of the subsequent bestowal of the prediction" (*vyākaraṇa*): it is because of that prediction that there are the two subsequent cessations (*niṣedha*).
Since these two subsequent cessations are the causes for the two subsequent requests, it is said that they indicate the basis for the repeated request.

At the place where the World-Honored One ceased speaking for a second time and Śāriputra requested for a second time, he caused Śāriputra to investigate the profound realm, giving rise to a yearning desire to hear it.

With a mind of earnest devotion, the World-Honored One stopped him a second time with "Stop, stop. Śāriputra requested a third time. This was to cause those of evil intent to withdraw from their seats;
only when these three conditions were fulfilled was he fit to preach the sutra, hence it is said, "on account of the bestowal of the prophecy.

Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the World-Honored One’s second "stop, stop" occurred at the point where Śāriputra first made his request; this is termed "stopping," which serves as the basis for the single request. The World-Honored One...

The third "cessation" (*nirodha*) refers to the place where Śāriputra made his second request; thus it is called "cessation. It is so named because it is the point from which the repeated requests arise.
Now that the wicked person has risen and departed during this third cessation, it is finally fit to preach the sutra;

therefore, the third cessation is called the "Cessation Due to the Bestowal of Prophecy" (*vyākaraṇa-nirodha*). It is also simply called "cessation," as it is the point from which the repeated requests arise. The former interpretation is correct. If one follows the latter...
[Commentary: It appears that the section on the bestowal of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) is categorized under the third *viniścaya*.

Furthermore, the third *viniścaya* only encompasses the single meaning of those who are unfit to be listeners; it loses the two meanings of seeking the profound realm and yearning to hear [the Dharma].
There are also commentaries that treat this as the reason for the request [to teach]. If one takes the literal characters, they apply to the latter two *viniścayas*: Questioning and Decision.

The concentrated mind is the cause for the bestowal of the prophecy. How do both of these relate to the modes of activity (*ākāra*) of *śamatha*? Answer: Because their respective referents differ. "Concentrated mind" refers to the Buddha’s mind;
it is determined by the proclamation of cessation (*śamatha*). By means of the cause for the bestowal of the prophecy, he causes Śāriputra to request [the teaching] swiftly.
"From 'Śāriputra' until 'I only pray that you will speak of it; I only pray that you will speak of it,' this is the general request.
Because the World-Honored One had twice declined previously, the current request follows the preceding text and likewise states 'I only pray that you will speak of it' twice."
The Sūtra says: "For what reason? Śāriputra requests the teaching again and again, seeking to clarify the intent of his previous request.
In his response, Śāriputra fears that he alone may not succeed in requesting the teaching; therefore, he further cites many people to join their strength and request it all at once.
The phrase "countless in this assembly" and so forth indicates the number of people. Śāriputra says: "Even if one were to spend thousands of millions of billions of kalpas..."
They have not heard the name of the Buddha, nor have they heard the True Dharma. If such beings as these were present, I would not dare to request [the teaching].
However, the many beings currently in this assembly have all seen various Buddhas; their faculties are sharp and their wisdom is clear.
Regarding those who possess ultimate reverence and faith:
"Wise" (yì) refers to being earnest and sincere.
What the sutra calls a "great pit" is likewise so; for those with faith who hear it, it is a potent medicine, but for those without faith who hear it, it is not.
This is like poison. Water can carry a boat, yet it can also overturn a boat. The wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle is likewise.
If one practices in accordance with it, one will swiftly attain liberation. If Śāriputra had heard that he would become a Buddha named Padmaprabha, he would have slandered it and sunk forever.
If those fifty disciples had heard it and lacked faith, they would have fallen into hell. Though the great ocean is vast and immeasurable, it cannot—
Once they have dwelt among corpses, how could those who practice the One Vehicle—which is vast and boundless—tolerate lack of faith?
Among blessings, there is none higher than encountering a request to turn the Wheel of Dharma; among sins, there is none more grievous than encountering the slandering of the Dharma.
The Avīci Hell is called the Great Pit; the Avīci Hell is the bottomless pit. The seven hot hells and eight cold hells are but minor pits. "World-Honored One, stop! Śāriputra!"
No. There is no need to speak further; one cannot find what one seeks by speaking. This will surely lead to falling into a great pit.
There are two kinds of great pits. One is according to reality: beneath this earth, at a depth of thirty-two thousand *yojanas*, there is the Reviving Hell (*Saṃjīva*);
and passing another four thousand *yojanas* below that, there are the other seven. Is this not a great pit? Beneath the eight cold and eight hot hells, it is called "Great."
"Avīci" (the Uninterrupted). "Avīci" refers to the location that is without interval. Question: What is meant by "Great Avīci"? There are three meanings for "Great":
first, because it gives rise to great delusions; among the ten afflictions (*kleśa*), false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is the greatest. Second, because it creates great karma;

thus it is called "Great," referring to the five heinous acts (*ānantarya-karma*). Third, because the retribution is great; due to giving rise to false views and not believing the True Dharma, one dies and enters Avīci. This is called [Great Avīci].
This is to repay [the debt of] the Great Pit. The Great Pit is the Avīci Hell; the Small Pits are the other seven hot hells.

Miu asked: "Since these beings have attained the fourth dhyāna, the Great Pit must necessarily involve the arousal of karma in the Desire Realm, as the afflictions of the lower realms have already been suppressed."
Why is it said that they have fallen into a great pit? The answer is: it is because one fears that after hearing the sutra, they might give rise to a lack of faith;
like slandering liberation, they would fall away from the superior meditative concentrations and immediately enter the great pit—hence the expression "about to fall."
Regarding the phrase "fearing that they harbor overweening pride (*adhimāna*) and so forth": it means fearing that after hearing the sutra, they will give rise to slander;
this is called "fearing that they harbor overweening pride. As for "the *tiṣṭhantika* bhikṣu": one who does not investigate the holy teachings of the Tripiṭaka is called a *tiṣṭhantika*.

Upon hearing the World-Honored One say that there are four fruits of śrāmaṇya, he suppresses the afflictions through the six modes of practice, feeling revulsion toward the lower states as being painful and coarse, while rejoicing in the higher states as being pure and subtle; thus he attains worldly tranquility.
He reflected: "Because they possess outflows (*sāsrava*), they are called 'worldly. One might think these are the fruits of the four stages of *śrāmaṇya*.

Having given rise to the thought that one has already transcended [the world] and so forth, one cultivates karma of the higher realms and is reborn there. Upon experiencing the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one then gives rise to slander, saying:

'I have heard that once an Arhat has passed away, he is immediately born in hell. When questioned by others, those in the assembly would all refuse to say, 'I am one of overweening pride (*adhimāna*')."
For what reason do people call him one of "overweening pride" (adhimāna)? How can they know for certain that he will slander the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* upon hearing it? Answer:

Because he has attained the four dhyānas and is permitted [to claim] the four fruits of the śramaṇa, these are all states of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) who will inevitably slander [the teaching].

Fearing that he might fall into a great pit, the commentary (*śāstra*) says: "He is not a noble one in training (śaikṣa). Question: How can we know he is not a noble one in training? Answer: The commentary...
It says: "The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states... and so forth. Question: For what reason is it stated that there are bhikṣus who claim for themselves [attainments] based on what they have heard?

Answer: The commentary says: "Because of overweening pride (*adhimāna*). Question: How do we know that the noble ones (*ārya*) do not claim for themselves [attainments]? Answer: The commentary says: "Because they lack false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*)" and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "all treatises state," this refers to the *Abhidharmajñānaprasthāna-śāstra* and others.

Regarding the phrase "at the end of life" and so forth, Zhe (攝) says: Mahayana and Hinayana each have different explanations. In the Sarvāstivāda school of the Hinayana, there is the theory of "existence prior to birth" (*pūrvabhava*), which gives rise to slander;

it is because one perceives the body of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) while in that state of prior existence that slander arises. In the Mahayana, it is the intermediate state itself that gives rise to [slander].

Regarding slander: it is asked, when slander arises within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), how many afflictions (*kleśa*) arise? It is answered: five afflictions arise. Specifically, there are three that are discriminative (*vikalpita*):
false view, hatred, and delusion; and two that are innate (*sahaja*): the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*), because these are able to moisten rebirth.
However, according to the actual principle, all afflictions arise. As the treatise states: "The various afflictions of the lower stages arise for one born in a higher stage."

The others and those that arise simultaneously are all capable of manifesting. If this is so, since the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) possesses five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), would there not then be two fundamental consciousnesses (*mūlavijñāna*) for a single sentient being, such that the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*) would increase or decrease?

Regarding the scripture’s phrase, “I only pray that you will speak it! I only pray that you will speak it! Jiguang states: the repetition of these words signifies the dual benefit of oneself and others.

Regarding the scripture’s mention of “hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, millions,” etc., one should take the single phrase “hundreds, thousands, millions” and connect it with “those such as ourselves.”

If read as a separate phrase, it refers solely to the number of people. If one reads "hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, millions, and billions" as a single phrase extending downward to "life after life," this refers to time and not to the number of people.

Of these two interpretations, if one assigns "hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, millions, and billions" to the preceding phrase "like us and our equals," it accords with the subsequent verse; this would mean that immeasurable multitudes are able to reverently believe in this Dharma.

"Many" means numerous; "hundreds of thousands of billions" continues through successive lifetimes. Reading [this] in accordance with the verse text, it indicates that the Buddha has already taught and transformed beings such as these in every lifetime.

It refers merely to the timing. The question is: did Śāriputra remember the Mahāyāna teachings during the time of the twenty thousand Buddhas of the past, or did he remember the teachings of the Hīnayāna? If he remembered the teachings of the Hīnayāna, how [is this to be understood]?
"Please explain the Mahāyāna. If one can recall the transformations of the Mahāyāna, how could one possibly recall [the details of] such a long duration?
The objects of the past and future conditions of the Hīnayāna do not exceed eighty thousand [kalpas]. Answer: "If we rely on the underlying principle, one can recall the Hīnayāna.

Question: "If that is so, why do you request that the Mahāyāna be explained? Answer: "Śāriputra merely requested [an explanation]; he did not specify whether it was such-and-such a Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna. It arose in his mind..."
“Doubt” is a general request. Second, the Buddha’s empowerment causes [the Bodhisattvas] to remember the Mahāyāna teaching; thus, they request the exposition of the Mahāyāna. Question:
As stated in the *Vyākaraṇa* (Prediction), "In the past I taught you to resolve upon the Buddha-way, yet now all that is false.

How can it be said here that they have remembered it? Answer: Where it was called "false," it referred to their original state of mind. What is said here—that they have remembered it—is due to the Buddha’s empowerment.
Regarding the statement that "birth and death are long," it is asked: Since Śāriputra has already transcended birth and death, how could he possibly speak such words?

The answer is: Until one attains true awakening, one remains constantly within the dream-state. For Śāriputra, this was his final body of the *pariccheda-śarīra* (segmented existence), yet even while in the midst of *pariṇāma-cyuti* (transformational birth and death), he was not yet able to eliminate it;
therefore, he spoke of wishing to benefit others throughout the long night of birth and death. It is asked: What further... Śāriputra?

The body of subsequent existence (*paścādbhava*) is immutable, and the death-and-rebirth of fragmented segments (*paricchinna-vaipakṣika-jāti-maraṇa*) has already been exhausted. How, then, can it be called the "long night"? Answer:

Although the fragmented [death-and-rebirth] has been exhausted, the transformational [death-and-rebirth] (*nairmāṇika-parivṛtti*) still persists; this is also termed the "long night of birth-and-death. Because they have received the Buddha’s transformative teaching, it is said that they are at peace and benefited.

The Sūtra speaks of the "Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings. This is explained through three meanings based on principle (*li*): first, because the Buddha is fully endowed with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), he is called "two-legged";

second, because he possesses internal wisdom while externally manifesting supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); third, because his inner body is endowed with the four types of knowledge (*jñāna*) while outwardly possessing merit and virtue (*puṇya*), these are termed the "two.
Next, according to the perspective of phenomena (*vastu*), it clarifies that among the six destinies and four modes of birth in the present world, there are none who possess fewer than two legs.
Among those with four feet and many feet, humans and devas are the most excellent. Question: Why is this so? Answer:

Because among bipeds, humans and devas are superior in entering the Path; therefore, they are called "venerable. Among bipeds, the Buddha’s body is the most excellent, and thus he is named the "Venerable One Among Bipeds" (Dvipadottama).
Regarding the statement in the Sūtra, "I am the eldest son of the Buddha": one who possesses the untainted noble wisdom born from the Buddha's own mouth is called a "son.
Among all the śrāvakas, Śāriputra’s wisdom is the most preeminent; therefore, he is called the "eldest son."

Regarding the statement, "If one follows the self-commentary (*svavṛtti*) and so forth," it would follow that the prose (*gadya*) at the beginning of the chapter and the subsequent verse (*śloka*) should be joined together.
Why did the commentator (*ṭīkākāra*) not divide them? Answer: Because the three lines of sutra text at the end of the chapter belong to the fourth section, which exhorts the arousal of joy.

Since the sutra text does not describe this in prose, the commentator has separated it here to avoid confusing it with the three lines at the end of the chapter, which are intended to join with the prose.
There are two parts to the practice (*caryā*). First, the two records are elucidated; second, the four sections are refuted. As for why it is not discussed here:
the structure of the text involves difficulties regarding the concealment and manifestation [of meaning], which is why this section is not opened up at this point in the text.
The Sūtra states, "You have already made your earnest request three times. This permits the meaning of "earnest" as being "delighting in three.
Question: For what reason must there be three requests? Answer: If the three requests are not fulfilled, the intent of the request has not reached its ultimate limit.
If the three requests were exceeded, the intent of the request would be exhausted. Therefore, there are exactly three—neither more nor less.

Regarding the term "grasping and supporting" (*saṃgṛhīta-parigraha*): it refers to the Buddha’s act of taking one under his care. Having been requested three times, he granted permission to preach; thus it is called "taking.

When the Sūtra says "listen attentively" (*sādhu śṛṇu*) and so forth, hearing [the teaching] gives rise to the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*); reflecting well upon it gives rise to the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*); and contemplating it gives rise to the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* is like one who, parched with thirst, longs for cool water; like one who, hungry, longs for delicious food; like one who, ill, longs for excellent medicine;
and like a swarm of bees relying upon honey. We, too, are just like this. We pray that you will open the Dharma of the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*).

Vasubandhu’s commentary states: "These four metaphors illustrate four kinds of dharmic meanings: first, upholding; second, providing assistance; third, distancing oneself [from defilements]; and fourth, abiding in peace. Upon hearing these words—

The teaching is like a person drinking water without using a cup; they drink as soon as it is obtained. In this way, the wisdom of hearing (śrutamayī-prajñā) accepts immediately upon first hearing and retains it according to the text.
The wisdom of reflection (cintāmayī-prajñā) receives the teaching like food entering the mouth and being chewed, with physical strength assisting its digestion.

In this way, the wisdom of reflection chews the Dharma that was heard. The wisdom of cultivation (bhāvanāmayī-prajñā) hears the Dharma like taking excellent medicine; as the medicine takes effect, the illness is eliminated. In this way, [the wisdom of cultivation] practices.
Wisdom conforms to the true meaning and practices according to the Dharma, remaining far removed from all afflictions and habitual tendencies.

The three types of wisdom produce their fruits; just as honey is that upon which bees depend, so too the three wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation are the locus upon which the noble ones rely.
Furthermore, "listening attentively" causes one to abandon distraction; "reflecting well" causes one to abandon negligence; and "mindfulness" causes one to abandon perversion.

Moreover, the three types of wisdom are like four vessels, each serving a different purpose. First, because of the absence of the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), one does not hear, just as water poured onto the bottom of a basin does not remain.
Second, because of the absence of the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), one hears but does not reflect, just as...
It is like pouring water into a leaking vessel; because one lacks the three types of wisdom cultivated through meditation, one merely reflects but does not practice.

This is like filling a foul-smelling vessel with water. If one possesses the three types of wisdom, it is like filling a well-crafted vessel, a complete vessel, or a precious vessel with water, which then drenches the body and mind of lust.

Regarding the phrase "listening to the sound with attentive ears": *qieyun* (phonetic rhymes) defines "to listen" (*ling*) as taking up a sound with the ear. Furthermore, it means to attend to the sounds one hears, entrusting them to the ears capable of perceiving them.
Now, there are five characteristics of one who listens to the Dharma: first, seeking awakening and understanding; second, focusing single-mindedly on the object of contemplation;
third, listening to the sound with attentive ears; fourth, clearing away distractions and maintaining composure; and fifth, concentrating the mind in one-pointedness while listening to the sound.
"Entrusting to the ear": taking sound with the ear is called "listening. Entrusting the sound that is heard back to the ear that is capable of hearing it is called "entrusting" (*zhù*).
"Entrusting" means to entrust or consign.
Regarding the term "sweeping and cleansing": "sweeping" refers to clearing away; "cleansing" refers to washing away. One sweeps away distraction and cleanses away sinking and agitation.
One sweeps away defilements and hindrances, thereby gathering and maintaining the mind from distraction.
Regarding the term "thirsty": it means being like one who is thirsty. At the time of drinking, one experiences only the small amount [of water] and has no other thoughts.

Likewise, the listener enters exclusively into the meaning of the Dharma without any other interpretations; with a single mind, they enter into the words and their meanings—the teaching that expresses [the truth].

Regarding the statement that the mind experiences both sorrow and joy: this refers to those who possess the spiritual lineage (*gotra*). Because it accords with their faculties as a matter of natural law, they feel deep compassion upon hearing it;
like a living being struck by a whip, a sense of poignant distress arises within them spontaneously.
Regarding the statement "if one does not admonish them," [the interlocutor] asks: "World-Honored One, you speak only for their sake; why is it necessary to instruct them to listen attentively?
The commentary answers: "If they are not equal [in capacity]."

Regarding the statement that the mind may become unsettled, there are three meanings: first, the dharma of a distracted mind is like an overturned vessel; second, the dharma of a conceited mind is like a leaking vessel;
third, listening to the dharma with a biased mind is like a defiled vessel.

Regarding the passage in the Sūtra that says, "When these words were spoken... [they] paid homage and withdrew": at the beginning of the *Pratyaya-varga*, two points of profound depth were proclaimed;

others did not understand them, and those with overweening pride (adhimāna) were unwilling from the start. Furthermore, seeing Śāriputra make his three requests while the World-Honored One made three refusals, five thousand people said, "All the teachings from forty years ago were consistent with our own views; today, he suddenly says we do not know them."
Furthermore, he was invited three times, yet he still refused to listen; he simply rose and departed. How could one use this as a reason for not prostrating before the Buddha?

The answer is that by prostrating, one bears the responsibility for his having heard the previous teaching and then departing without rejoicing in the subsequent discourse. This was because prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* assembly, he had already turned away from the presence of the Tathāgata.
To hear the Dharma and practice it, thereby attaining the four dhyānas, is merely a mistaken calculation; it is to hope for that which is truly real within the center [of the mind].
As the Sūtra says: "For what reason? This is the Tathāgata’s self-inquiry. Why? Because among the five difficulties, four have already been fulfilled;

there remains only the difficulty of hearing the Dharma. As for why one would then arise and depart, the Commentary answers: "First, a human body is difficult to obtain, like [a flower on] Mount Kunlun..."
1. It is as difficult as casting a mustard seed onto the point of a needle. 2. It is difficult to be born in the Central Land (Jambudvīpa), like a blind turtle encountering a floating log.

3. Regarding the sense faculties (*indriya*): first, it is difficult to possess all five physical faculties, such as the eyes; second, it is difficult to possess the five spiritual faculties, such as faith—like seeking fire by rubbing water.

4. It is difficult to encounter the appearance of a Buddha, like a *utpala* flower blooming along a path. 5. Although one may encounter the appearance of a Buddha, it is difficult to hear the True Dharma, like [climbing] a suspended...
Sandān was hungry. In the city of Rājagṛha there were nine hundred million people: three hundred million saw the Buddha and heard the Dharma;
three hundred million saw the Buddha but did not hear the Dharma; and three hundred million neither saw the Buddha nor heard the Dharma.

Furthermore, although they possessed the faculties of the eyes, ears, and so forth, if upon hearing the Buddha’s Dharma they do not give rise to faith, they are also said to be incomplete in their five faculties—namely, the five beginning with faith.
This is the root. Of the five difficulties, the first four have already been established. Why, then, does he arise and depart just as he is about to hear the Dharma?
What is the reason for this arising and departing? (The following is the commentary from the *Shu*).

Regarding the phrase "this group" (cǐ bèi): *bèi* (pronounced either bù mèi or bù bèi) originally referred to those who were not of low status in ancient times, whereas nowadays it refers to those of low status.
According to the *Guǎngyá*, *bèi* also carries the meaning of "kind" (*lèi*) and denotes a "faction" or "group."
Regarding the term "one hundred pairs" (*bǎiliǎng*): the first character *liǎng* is pronounced with a high tone (*yīn*). It is read as *chējū* (車居) and *hèshè* (賀攝). One pair refers to two chariots;
saying "one hundred pairs" thus means two hundred chariots. Mou says: one chariot has two wheels, which is called one "pair"; thus, "one hundred pairs" refers to one hundred chariots.
The character "fan" (番) [in "fanqu"] refers to the *prajñā*. As for the term "crime" (*zuì*), this is the ancient form of the character for crime;
it was originally composed with "xīn" (辛) at the bottom and the character "xiān" (仙) from the constellation Xīnxīng (辛星) at the top.

This was later modified into the current character for "crime," which carries the meaning of that which may be destroyed, as found in Buddhist scriptures. Question: What is the meaning of "crime"? Answer: The commentary states:

Regarding "blameworthy" (*sāvadya*) and so forth: some interpret that while the causes of transgression possess the quality of being blameworthy and so on, the results of transgression likewise possess the sense of being blameworthy and so forth.
This interpretation is incorrect. Both cause and effect are fully endowed with all four meanings. Question: How is it known that both cause and effect are fully endowed with all four meanings?
Answer: The sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) states: "Whether it be the cause or the result, they are blameworthy and so forth."
Regarding the statement, "If one relies on the Hīnayāna, these offenses are numerous," up to the mention of the "three obstacles" (*trividha-āvaraṇa*): Question: This explains the roots of offense;

why then are the three obstacles, such as the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) belonging to others, mentioned? Answer: Regarding the phrase "up to the three obstacles": Question: This explains the roots of offense.

Why are the three obstructions—the affliction-obstruction and so forth—expounded? ZHANGJING replies: The affliction-obstruction is called "sin" because it is the causal condition for the sin of karmic obstruction;
thus, it is named "sin. The retribution-obstruction is called "sin" because it is the fruit of that sin; thus, it is named "sin."
Regarding the statement that all afflictions are generally categorized into two types: first, those that arise repeatedly are termed "diligence" (*tīkṣṇa*);
second, those that arise but are not intense are termed "sharpness" (*tīkṣṇa*). This explains the meanings of "diligence" and "sharpness."
Regarding the division into four propositions: first, diligence without sharpness. "Diligence" means arising repeatedly; "sharpness" means intensity.
Although it may arise repeatedly, it is dull and not intense. Second, sharpness without diligence.

This refers to killing three times or five times in a single lifetime, or killing three thousand or five thousand creatures in one instance. Here, we take the first of these four propositions: diligence.
And it is not beneficial. The third phrase is both diligent and beneficial; this refers to that which is both an affliction and an obstacle, encompassing the remaining two phrases.
That which is an affliction but not an obstacle allows for the possibility of initiating preparatory application (*prayoga*) because of the presence of the path of counteraction (*pratipakṣa-mārga*).

Regarding the "five deeds of immediate retribution" (*pañcānantarya*): they are killing one's father, harming one's mother, killing an arhat, causing a schism in the Saṃgha, and shedding the blood of a Buddha.
These are called the deeds of immediate retribution. Among these five, four are bodily actions (*kāyakarman*), while causing a schism in the Saṃgha is a verbal action (*vākkarman*).

Among the five, four constitute the fundamental act (*maula*), whereas one constitutes the preliminary application (*prayoga*). This is because it is impossible to sever the life-force of a Buddha; therefore, [shedding his blood] does not constitute a fundamental act.

This is the fundamental offense. First, regarding the immediacy of retribution (*avīci*): it is experienced only in the next life. Having committed this karma, one is reborn immediately without being separated by another body or another realm;
thus it is called "immediacy of retribution. "Immediacy" (*antara*) means "separation" (*vyavadhāna*). Second, regarding the immediacy of lifespan:
one possesses a full intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*), during which there is no premature death. Third, regarding the immediacy of physical form: one enters the earth.
First, it is "uninterrupted" because its body is all-pervasive and equal [to the size of the world]. Second, it is "uninterrupted" regarding the suffering of pain;

while in other hells there are intervals of cool breezes during the experience of intense agony, in this hell there is pure suffering with no further interval. Third, it is "uninterrupted" regarding location;
there is no other distinct location that serves as a separation between them.

Regarding the "three miserable realms and eight difficulties": first, the hells; second, animals; third, hungry ghosts; fourth, the northern continent (Uttarakuru); fifth, the long-lived heavens (Ābhāsvara);

sixth, being before or after a Buddha—meaning that because there are those who attain [the path] by relying on the Dharma when a Buddha has not yet appeared or has already passed away, this is changed to "before the Dharma" and "after the Dharma";
seventh, worldly wisdom and eloquence; and eighth, the long-lived heavens, which refers specifically to the Heaven of No-Thought (Asaṃjñisattva). Eighth.

The sense faculties are incomplete. Question: What is meant by the "obstruction of maturation" (*vipākāvaraṇa*)? Answer: This body of the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*) can obstruct the Noble Path;
therefore, it is called an obstruction. The commentary concludes: "These three obstructions, etc."
Regarding the statement that, according to the Mahāyāna, there are two roots of offense—namely, the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*):

the cognitive obstructions, as appropriate, obstruct entry into the noble stages (*āryabhūmi*) of the Mahāyāna. Among the cognitive obstructions, the conceptualized (*parikalpita*) type obstructs the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) of the first stage (*bhūmi*).
The innate (*sahaja*) type obstructs the ten stages and the Buddha stage; thus, it obstructs all eleven positions. The first ten [stages] are obstructed by these [conceptualized] obstructions.

There are ten stages (*bhūmi*). The final [obstruction] obstructs the state of Buddhahood. 1. The obstruction of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*) obstructs entry into the first stage, the *sarvatraga-tathatā* (all-pervading suchness).

2. The obstruction of wrong practice obstructs entry into the second stage, the *parama* (supreme). 3. The obstruction of dullness and ignorance obstructs the third stage, the *pravara-āśraya* (excellent flow). 4.

The obstruction of the manifestation of subtle afflictions obstructs the fourth stage, the *anupādāna* (non-appropriation). 5. The obstruction of parinirvāṇa by means of the Lesser Vehicle obstructs the fifth stage, the *jāti-viśeṣa* (distinction of lineage). 6. The obstruction of the manifestation of coarse signs obstructs the sixth stage.

(1) Lack of purity through non-attachment; (2) the obstacle to the manifestation of subtle characteristics (*dharmāvikalpa*); (3) application of effort toward the signless (*animitta*); (4) lack of increase or decrease;
(5) lack of desire to act for the benefit of others (*jñānavasitā*); (6) not yet having attained mastery over all phenomena (*karmavasitā*);
(7) the subtle cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). These are explained as the eleven successive obstacles in relation to the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and suchness (*tathatā*).
Therefore, it is said that they "accord with what is appropriate. Regarding the phrase "obstructing entry into the noble stages of the Mahāyāna" (the realization of the knowable):

as for the phrase "afflictive obstructions accord with what is appropriate," there are two types of afflictions: first, the discriminative; second, the innate. The discriminative obstructs entry into the first stage (*bhūmi*);
at the time of entering the first stage, it is directly severed. The second, the innate, is [severed] suddenly from the first stage onward.

They do not arise spontaneously. From the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) onward, they arise through the power of intentional effort (*abhiprāya-bala*), yet they do not constitute an obstruction. Question: Since these arise through the power of intentional effort, why are they called "affliction-obstructions" (*kleśāvaraṇa*)?
Answer: The seeds of affliction obstruct the state of Buddhahood; at the time of attaining Buddhahood, they must be completely severed. Next, regarding the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*):

The *vikalpita* (conceptualized) [afflictions] obstruct the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the first fruit (*phala*) of the Lesser Vehicle. The *sahaja* (innate) [afflictions]... [obstruct the Path of Cultivation].

The former six [categories of afflictions] obstruct only the second fruit; the latter three categories obstruct the third fruit; the eighty-one categories (nine times nine) of the two upper realms obstruct the fourth fruit.
For a *pratyekabuddha*, both the discriminative and innate [afflictions] constitute obstructions. For one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), there is nothing further to be realized.
For a Mahāyāna Bodhisattva of gradual enlightenment, these afflictions are first severed within their own vehicle; if [they are of] sudden [enlightenment], [the process is otherwise].

For the awakened, the afflictions of conceptual discrimination are eliminated upon the path of seeing; however, among the innate [afflictions], their seeds are not severed, but merely obstruct the vajra-mind.
They are severed simultaneously with the subtle objects of knowledge (at the lower stages).
Regarding the statement "one hundred and twenty-eight": in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are ten for each of the four truths and six for the path of cultivation, totaling forty-six;

when doubled, this makes ninety-two. In the two higher realms (*rūpadhātu* and *ārūpyadhātu*), ten instances of hatred (*dveṣa*) are excluded, leaving eighty-two. When these are added to the forty-six of the desire realm, the total is one hundred and twenty-eight.
In total, there are one hundred and twenty-eight afflictions (*kleśa*). This count refers exclusively to the fundamental afflictions.

As for the phrase "together with the secondary afflictions" (*upakleśa*): in the desire realm, all twenty secondary afflictions are present; in the two upper realms, there are eight major secondary afflictions.
There are sixteen major secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), along with *śāṭhya* (deceit) and *māyā* (guile) from the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and *mada* (pride) from both realms;
these twenty secondary afflictions, together with the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) when combined according to their lightness or heaviness, are termed the "affliction-obstruction" (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "karma and so forth produced by speech," a question is raised: how can the resulting fruit also be an obstruction?
If the bodies within the three realms are collectively termed obstructions, then there would be no humans or devas who could enter the Path of the Sages. Furthermore, it is asked:
while unwholesome and non-meritorious karma may be called obstructions, how can wholesome and immovable karma also be obstructions? The Commentary answers: "The meaning of this is..."

Regarding the statement "and so forth," the intended meaning is that these are the outflows (*niṣyanda*) of the categories of those afflictions (*kleśa*), and are collectively termed "obstructions" (*āvaraṇa*). This is not based on what is most predominant.

For example, although the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is not directly summoned by afflictions, it is called an "obstruction of retribution" (*vipākāvaraṇa*) because it is summoned by delusion (*moha*).

Furthermore, when it is said that the two obstructions do not include the fruit of karma, that refers to what is predominant; this [present case] does not refer to what is predominant. Question: How is the obstruction to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) [defined]?

"Does it give rise to [karma] and induce its fruition? Answer: "If explained in terms of indirect succession, it serves as the basis for the afflictions, like a remote object-condition (*parokṣālambana*).
It is also called the 'basis of deliberation' (*ālambanādhiṣṭhāna*). Furthermore, it is like a person who is confused by a pillar; just as one who grasps a rope as a snake also grasps the hemp.
If explained separately, there is no giving rise to karma. Furthermore, the treatise says: "However, the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) does not obstruct liberation."

They are liberated, because they lack the capacity to initiate karma or to moisten rebirth. If one considers them as conditions for the induction of the *nirmāṇa-citta* (transformation mind) and so forth, this is also possible, because their power of meditative concentration and vows supports that [mind], and thus no new karma is initiated. Question: As for the karma previously initiated, what is its essential nature?
Answer: Discriminative ignorance directly initiates karma; other afflictions, both discriminative and innate, all assist in its initiation.
Therefore, the treatise states: "If they are innate, they assist in the initiation of unwholesome conduct and are likewise subsumed under the unwholesome."
Regarding the statement that "it is not based on what is weighty," this refers generally to both karma and its fruits, which are the reasons for the existence of afflictions (*kleśa*). Question:
The Master [Vasubandhu] commanded the composition of this treatise so as to produce correct understanding and to sever the two weighty obstructions (*āvaraṇa*).

Since these weighty obstructions consist of the afflictive (*kleśa*) and cognitive (*jñeya*) obstructions, why is the cognitive obstruction not included here? Answer: That was stated according to a specific meaning. There are four such meanings: first, as in... (text fragment).
1. Because they are as difficult to sever as a vajra; 2. because it is difficult to cross over the stream of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) within them;

3. because they are the place where sentient beings are oppressed and submerged; and 4. because they give rise [to suffering]. Fourth, because they cause sentient beings to sink and fall, drowning in the three realms (*tridhātu*), their faults are censured and they are established with the name "heavy.
The afflictions (*kleśa*) and the objects of knowledge (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*) are collectively termed "heavy," for all four possess these various meanings. This is explained in terms of their capacity...

That which obstructs entry into the stage of the noble ones is termed "heavy. Since that cognitive obscuration (jñeyāvaraṇa) does not obstruct the noble stages of the two vehicles, it is not termed "heavy.
This scripture applies to all three vehicles; thus, it speaks from a broad perspective.

Regarding the statement that there are four heavy obstacles based on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the intention is that while the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* includes both light and heavy obstacles, here we take only the heavy ones.
These are established based on the faults of disparagement and blame, and are designated by the name "heavy."
Regarding the statement "and their outflows, the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), etc.": "outflow" (*niṣyanda*) has the sense of similarity;
that is, the secondary afflictions are of the same category as the root afflictions, and are thus called "outflows."
Regarding the phrase "according to what is appropriate": here, "according to what is appropriate" differs from its usage in the preceding and following sections.

These afflictions, according to what is appropriate for each of the three vehicles (*triyāna*), all obstruct the noble path (*āryamārga*). This is because, within each vehicle, the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) of those who practice all obstruct the noble path;
thus, it is said "according to what is appropriate. The *Jianyao* states: "If one possesses [them] in full, there are one hundred and twenty..."

8. Each and every one of these is capable of obstructing the Noble Path; even a single one can obstruct the Noble Path (the former being the afflictive hindrance [kleśāvaraṇa], the latter being the hindrance of karma based on wisdom).

Regarding the statement that there are five karmic obstructions in the *Satyaka-irreṇya-putra-sūtra*: when the World-Honored One was still alive, this person asked the Buddha, "If I were to leave the household life, how would I compare to Śāriputra?
The Buddha replied, "You would not equal him. Thereupon, he did not leave the household life. The Buddha then gave him a prophecy, saying:
"One hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, this person will appear in the world, named Upagupta. At that time, people...
He was known as the Buddha Without Marks (A-lakṣaṇa-buddha). As for the one called the Nirgrantha-putra, he was the previous incarnation of Upagupta. Question:

Does one become guilty of a transgression against the fundamental precepts (ānantarya) by committing all of them together, or does one become guilty of such a transgression by committing even one or two? Answer: One becomes guilty of a transgression against the fundamental precepts by committing any one of them.
The aforementioned killing of one's father and so forth are transgressions common to the Three Vehicles.

Regarding the statements on "destroying stupas and ruining monasteries": if one gives rise to an evil mind and takes even a single brick or tile, it is all subsumed under the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*).
Or, if one does not permit their construction, this is also a transformation of the five heinous crimes, as explained in the *Huàdù* (Transformation and Deliverance).

If a person casting [an image] sees that the Buddha’s face is not upright and breaks it to recast it, there is no offense. However, if one strikes and destroys it out of a mind of anger, it immediately constitutes a heinous crime.

Regarding the term "stealing and using": "stealing" refers to taking for oneself in private; "using" refers to doing so by means of official authority. Whether acting as a private accomplice or as the principal leader, employing expedient means to destroy [the property] is likewise this karma.

Regarding the terms "obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*) and "impediment" (*vighna*): when one intends to act but is not permitted to act, it is called an "obstruction"; once the action has already begun and is subsequently cut short, it is called an "impediment.

Regarding the phrase "its debt is the mobilization" (*tad-ṛṇam udyogaḥ*): Miyou states that "mobilization" (*udya*) refers to labor service (*yō*), while "adjustment" (*tiao*) refers to the head of a household (*zǔ*).
Regarding the statement "the three evil realms, the eight states of non-leisure (*aṣṭāvakṣa*), and so forth," this means that there is no leisure to cultivate the Noble Path;

therefore, they are described as obstacles. The phrase "and so forth" includes those who are *paṇḍaka*, those without sexual organs, and hermaphrodites. Question: Can those born from moisture or from eggs attain the fruits of sainthood (*āryaphala*)?
Lü said: Lady Tiwei gave birth to a crane-egg; the daughter of Sudatta gave birth to an egg, and from its birth, a thousand sons were produced.

All of them attained the Noble Path. That [statement] refers to the Hīnayāna; in the Mahāyāna, such a thing certainly does not exist. It merely states that those with bodies from the three miserable realms do not enter the Noble Path.
Since Tiwei was a human body, what prevents him from entering the Noble Path? For instance, ghosts are of two types: those born from a womb and those born by transformation;
even if they were womb-born, they still cannot attain the Noble Path.
Regarding the Buddhas who appear in the interim: it is asked when the Dharma of Śākyamuni will be extinguished. The answer is given in the *Zhufa ji* (Record of the Duration of the Dharma):

"From the period of decrease until the period of increase, when the human lifespan reaches sixty thousand years, the Dharma of Śākyamuni Buddha will come to an end. At that time, it is called the 'extinction of the Dharma' (*dharmavyaya*)."

Regarding the "karmic action that obstructs the Dharma," the *Sūtra* states: If a person is stingy with the Dharma—fearing that others might understand it and thus surpass them—they do not teach it to others.
There are six kinds of retribution for this: first, blindness; second, folly; third, being an enemy of the Buddhas of the ten directions;
fourth, committing every kind of evil; fifth, being shunned by virtuous people; and sixth, falling away from the noble embryo (*āryagarbha*). Mou says: "Blindness means the extinction of wisdom."
Because it is the eye; because ignorance is the obstacle to be countered; and because an enemy has the sense of turning away from awakening. Regarding "losing the noble embryo":

the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is the womb, and the seeds of wisdom are the embryo. Listening for one great eon is like the fulfillment of ten months, culminating in the stage of penetration (*prativedha-avasthā*).
This is what is meant by "initially arising. Now, because one is stingy with the Dharma and lacks faith, the "sacred embryo" (āryagarbha) is lost.
Regarding "outflow" (niṣyanda), there are two kinds: first, the "true outflow," which is the arising of actual manifestations from seeds.

When unwholesome or evil seeds produce unwholesome actual manifestations, they are called "true outflows" because their nature is identical; they directly produce their own results. Thus it is termed "equal outflow."

This means "equal. "Outflow" (*niṣyanda*) refers to a category or type. These two types of conventional outflows do not necessarily require identity of nature; they merely take up the sense of similarity.
Because in a previous life one obstructed others from hearing the Dharma, in this present life one does not oneself hear the Dharma;

thus it is called "similarity. Because the fruit resembles its past cause, and the cause resembles its fruit, it is called the "fruit of outflow" (*niṣyandaphala*). This is what is being discussed here.
It is similar to the result of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*). The dominant result (*adhipati-phala*) also has two types. First, the concordant dominant:

when another person wishes to hear the Dharma, one provides assistance and support so that they may hear it; consequently, in this present life, one's own self also hears the True Dharma—this is called the concordant dominant.
Second, the discordant dominant: when a person wishes to hear the Dharma, one creates obstacles and prevents them from hearing it—this is called the discordant [dominant].

Predominance (*adhipati*). Predominance is the cause; the fact that one does not hear the Dharma oneself in this present life is the result. Because it is the result of a predominant [cause], it is called the "predominant result" (*adhipatiphala*);

this is according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) analysis. Question: What is the distinction between these two results? Answer: From the perspective of their similarity, it is called the "result of outflow" (*niṣyandaphala*).
The fruit, when viewed in relation to its cause, is called the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*). Mūla says: "That which can induce the deficiency of the Dharma is the cause;

the present non-hearing of the Dharma and so forth is the essence of the transgression, and this is the fruit. The Sūtra says: "The King of All Sages preaches the Dharma to teach and transform [beings]."
Such a person of sin shall be born in difficult places and the like.
Regarding the statement "yoga and so forth," up to the seven types: first, the conceited toward those inferior;

this refers to one who considers himself superior to those who are actually inferior to him, further clinging to the notion that he is superior to them. Second, or one who considers himself equal to those who are his equals.
Question: Since it has already been stated that regarding equals and considering oneself equal is in accordance with reason, why is it called pride (*māna*)? Answer:

In the Noble Teachings, it is said that pride occurs when, within the process of weighing and measuring, one applies equality or inequality across various levels and paths; at such times, this is pride.
Second is overweening pride (*adhimāna*), which consists in considering oneself superior to those who are equal, regarding all their personal qualities, activities, and so forth.
To consider oneself equal to those who are actually one's equals is pride (*māna*). To consider oneself superior to those who are actually one's superiors is overweening pride (*adhimāna*).

To consider oneself equal to those who are actually one's superiors is overweening pride. To consider oneself equal to others when, in reality, one is actually superior to them—this concealing of one's own superiority and claiming equality with others is called overweening pride (*adhimāna*).

*Manātimāna* (conceit beyond conceit) refers to regarding oneself as superior to those who are actually superior; even when another person is hundreds of thousands of times superior to oneself, one reckons oneself to be even more superior than that person—this is called *manātimāna*.
*Asmimāna* (the conceit "I am") has the characteristic of being haughty while relying on one's own physical existence (*ātmabhāva*).

Even though there is no horse upon one's body, one maintains a state of empty stomach and high ground. *Adhimāna* (overweening conceit) refers to claiming to have attained much when in reality one has acquired very little.
There are many types. Inferiority-conceit (*ūnamāna*) refers to regarding oneself as slightly inferior when others are for the most part superior.
As the Śibī child said: "The Prime Minister excels me in riding a saddle and possessing a horse; however, if we discuss rising early and sleeping late, he is not my equal.
This is called regarding oneself as slightly inferior to another. False conceit (*mithyāmāna*) refers to claiming to have attained what one has not attained at all; this is false conceit.

This refers to their characteristics. Regarding the statement "those who now harbor hatred and arrogance," since these five thousand followers already possess the characteristic of arrogance (*māna*), it is not yet clear which of the seven types of pride they are subsumed under.
The answer in the *Śū* (Commentary) states: "The 'arrogance of superiority' (*adhimāna*) and so forth" means that the five thousand people [possess] superiority...
Pride (*māna*). This corresponds to the fifth [type] mentioned previously. Question: What is its mode of activity (*ākāra*)? Answer:

Having attained the four dhyānas, one gives rise to a mind of outflow-tainted wisdom (*sāsrava-prajñā*) and, having obtained little, claims to have obtained much. In a state where afflictions do not arise because they have been suppressed by the six modes of practice (*ṣaḍ-abhibhv-ākāra*), one realizes non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and, having realized little, claims to have realized much, and so forth.

Regarding the statement that "attainment" refers to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*): Question: Since one has not yet fully realized the four [fruits], what kind of practice or fruit is it to say that one has attained even a small portion of the fruit?

Answer: How could there be any false conceptualization regarding the attainment of even a small portion of the noble fruit (*āryaphala*)? Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "All noble ones have no self;
they merely claim to have attained [the fruits] and so forth."
Regarding the phrase "the eyes behold," this refers to the divine light emitted during the Introduction Chapter (*Nidāna-parivarta*).

Regarding the phrase "the ears hear the sublime chanting," this refers to hearing the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* (*Ananta-nirdeśa-sūtra*). Alternatively, it is said that the "sublime chanting" refers to Maitreya’s questions and Mañjuśrī’s answers.
Regarding the phrase "the common mind has not yet been transformed": "common" (*yōng*) carries the sense of being inferior or base. "Transformed" (*gé*) means changed.

If the common mind has not been changed, then to expound the wondrous and proclaim the difficult will cause one to deviate from the intended meaning. The wisdom of all Buddhas is called "expounding the wondrous. Explaining the gates of wisdom is called "proclaiming the difficult.
Alternatively, chanting the two "extremely profound" [verses] is called "expounding the wondrous," while the three instances of ceasing to speak are called "proclaiming the difficult."

Regarding the phrase "hearing within the introduction," this refers to the exchange of questions and answers that occurs after [the initial stage], serving as the primary cause for eventually abandoning the provisional and attaining the real at the beginning of the Great Transformation.

Regarding the phrase "listening within the main body of the teaching" and so forth, it refers to what is deeply expounded within the main body of the teaching; that is, the two aspects of the provisional and the one aspect of the real.
This is contrary [to reason], and thus slander arises. Therefore, the Commentary states: "To crush and destroy," and so forth. Śāriputra is like fine rice, for he can alleviate hunger;
thus those five thousand remaining followers are like chaff and husks, left to be carried away by the wind.
Śāriputra is like clear wine, for he can bring delight to the body and mind of others; thus those five thousand remaining followers are like dregs and sediment, turbid and heavy.
They must immediately be discarded. The Tathāgata stirred the frosty wind of the three *śamatha* concentrations, which shattered and withered the perilous leaves of the five thousand [monks].
Śāriputra was like a sturdy tree; as he remained unmoved by the fan and the whisk, he was thus preserved. As the subsequent scripture says: "The dregs and chaff among the assembly."

Regarding the phrase "the worldly and the silent" spoken by the Buddha’s majestic power: the intended meaning takes this silence as correct. If one makes it mundane at the edge of the mouth, it should instead be made "stopping" (zhǐ) as correct.
If one writes "zhì" on paper, both are incorrect.
Regarding the phrase "all treatises state," the question is asked: Why does [the text] not stop there? The answer given in the commentary (*shu*) states:

"The 'treatises' refer fundamentally to the *Abhidharma* and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*. The *Saṃgraha* says: 'The Buddha has attained mastery over all phenomena, yet he alone lacks mastery in two respects:
first, the certainty of experiencing the fruition of maturation (*vipāka-phala*). For example, in the past, there was a pond of fish in a village..."* (The text continues with the story of the fish).
People gathered together and ate the large fish from the pond; those who were the remaining small fish became King Virūḍhaka.
The soldiers he led were the people of that village, who are now the Śākyas. Thus, they were eventually slaughtered by King Virūḍhaka.
Second, Maudgalyāyana used his supernormal powers to take the Śākya clansmen up and place them within the constellation of Puṣya;
as they sat inside a bowl, the Śākyas looked down at that bowl and their heads fell off, whereby their retribution was rendered certain. Second.
The certainty of karmic action is as follows: King Bimbisāra was constantly engaged in hunting and frequently went into the mountains, yet he could never catch any game or beasts.
Later, he saw a *ṛṣi* and thought to himself, "I have failed to catch any game; I shall therefore dispatch this man.
He then gave the oral command to have him killed, his body and head severed from one another. Thereupon, the *ṛṣi* made a vow: "In the future..."
The world then put the king to death by means of a verbal decree. The king of the past was none other than the father-king;
the rishi was none other than King Ajātaśatru. Furthermore, the Abhidharma states: "First, due to the powerful force of past karma, one obtains a human body and so forth."
The continuity of the maturation-body (*vipākakāya*) is determined; it gives rise to various derivative evils (*niṣyandakarma*).

Second, through the power of past karma such as the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*), which assist in human wholesome karma, one obtains the continuity of a human rebirth and simultaneously gives rise to derivative evil karma.

Because this karma arises, the performance of action is determined, as in the case of King Ajātaśatru’s killing of his father or King Virūḍhaka’s slaughter of the Śākyas—all of these constitute the performance of action.
This refers to karma.

To say that "the roots of sin are deep" means that, according to the masters of the treatise, the maturation of the fruit is certain. Having committed many acts in past lives that obstruct the Dharma constitutes the root of sin;
"root" here signifies cause. That one does not hear the Dharma in the present life constitutes the fruit of sin. It was caused by others in previous lives... [text truncated]

Regarding the hearing of the Dharma: in this life, they themselves do not hear the Dharma. These five thousand people, together with the kinsmen of the Śākyas, belong to the same category of those receiving retribution;
they are called the "definitive class."

Regarding those called "those with overweening pride" (*adhimāna*): they belong to the category of those whose karmic actions are fixed. If one remains attached to such fixity, one gives rise to slander against the three types of karma and the Dharma;
this is entirely the category of fixed karmic action. The World-Honored One observed these five thousand people and King Ajātaśatru [in this light].

This is because they belong to the same category of those whose karmic actions are fixed. There are two reasons: first, due to the power of their karma, namely that their roots of transgression are deep and heavy, making it unfit for them to hear the Dharma;
second, because their faculties are not yet matured, these people of overweening pride (*adhimāna*) would inevitably slander the Dharma upon hearing it.
For this reason, these five thousand rose from their seats and departed. Although the Buddha possessed supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), he did not stop them.
Regarding the phrase "it might be permissible" (*chakaku*): Question: Why did the World-Honored One not remain for a while longer so that [the disciple] might hear even a little more of the Dharma?

For what reason did he instead cause him to depart immediately? Answer: The commentary states, "It might be permissible," etc. The intended meaning is that regarding the Dharma, there is no stinginess;

however, had he remained, it was feared it would have been of no benefit. Thus, it was deemed "permissible" to let him depart. As for the previous point concerning the fixed karma, it was not rejected because it could not be overcome by the Buddha’s power.
This refers to the power of the Buddha’s restraint. If one were to commit a grave offense despite such restraint, it would constitute a heavy karma;

therefore, [the Buddha] does not stop them. Regarding the statement that "he generates the resolve," one asks: if a king commits a *ānantarya* (immediate) offense, this is also the performance of an action (*karma*), and the reception of its fruit is certain.
Why, then, does the Buddha emit rays of compassionate light to touch him, causing his sin to diminish so that he does not fall into hell? The commentary (*śāstra*) answers: If he...
Regarding the arousal of the bodhicitta and so forth: for example, King Ajātaśatru, having repented for killing his father, developed boils over his entire body.
He declared himself a person destined for the great hells; yet, through such earnest repentance and self-reproach, his body and mind became pure, and all his retinue likewise became pure.
The Buddha emitted the Moon-Love Light Samādhi, which illuminated the king’s body; he was immediately healed. This demonstrates that even fixed karma can be transformed.
Regarding the statement that "the mind is not easily changed," it is as when King Virūḍhaka slaughtered the Śākyas and killed his own father. The Buddha said to the Great King:
"Seven days from now, your life will surely come to an end. If you do not repent, you will certainly fall into hell. The King said, "A great man—how could he repent?
He then remained within the water for a full seven days; when he emerged from the water, he was consumed by fire and reduced to ashes.
Because he had not resolved his mind [to seek awakening], the power of the Buddha could not repel his fate. As the Sūtra says: "And it cannot be restrained."
"Cease! Though the rain from heaven is moistening, it cannot cause flowers to bloom upon withered wood. Though the sun and moon are bright, they cannot open the eyes of the blind.

Therefore, do not cease. Second, it is an exhortation to later students to exert their efforts. Even while the Tathāgata was present in the world, there were still many who felt resentment and jealousy."

Regarding the phrase "the Buddha permitted [him] to speak," etc., it means that by using words of permission and acceptance, he immediately awakens the listener's mind.
Regarding the statement "it would be better to withdraw," there are two benefits in departing: first, one does not incur the fault of slandering the Dharma in the present;

In immeasurable and boundless kalpas, a single Buddha appears in the world and preaches the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, like the udumbara flower. (The text continues with "one...")

Even until this present life, it has been for forty years since [the Buddha] first attained enlightenment; he has long kept this essential teaching in silence, not being in a hurry to preach it.
Śāriputra asked: "Why is this rare Dharma not praised by speaking of emptiness? The World-Honored One [replied]:...

since the World-Honored One has already praised [this teaching] with such earnestness and intends to expound a dharma never heard before, the *Treatise* states that it is called "never heard."
Question: What is meant by "making heard that which has not been heard"? Answer: It refers to the Dharma not previously heard, which is made to be heard today.

Second, taking the recent past as a measure, for forty years since [I began] intending to preach it, I have been unable to preach it; this is also called the Dharma of making heard that which has not been heard. This is precisely...

Venerable Sir, it is only because I have not heard the profound [teachings] that the teachings which express them—being expressed for those who have not yet heard the Dharma—have their underlying intent difficult to understand.

If I were to explain them directly, sentient beings would easily comprehend them; however, it is precisely because they are taught according to what is appropriate, and the teachings are presented in accordance with the faculties [of the listeners], that this is called "teaching according to what is appropriate.
When the three [vehicles] are taught, there are actually three great [truths] that are easy to comprehend; it is only because...
When the three are spoken of, the three cannot be found; when the three are spoken of, there is only one. For this reason, the underlying intention is difficult to understand. [A question is asked:

"Does the World-Honored One not speak directly so that others may easily comprehend? The World-Honored One replied: "Forty years ago, I sought to speak directly, but it could not be attained. As the Sūtra says:
"If I were to praise only the Buddha Vehicle, sentient beings would be submerged in suffering; therefore, I do not avoid bestowing peace [by teaching the three vehicles]."

This is an expedient teaching. Since there are already countless expedient means in the higher teachings, the principle they elucidate is a dharma that cannot be understood through discursive thought or conceptual discrimination.

Regarding the question of "in dependence upon what meaning": it is asked, in dependence upon what meaning did the World-Honored One preach the Dharma for the sake of Śāriputra? The answer is:
he took the first section, the Dharma that had not yet been heard and was now being made to be heard, and in dependence upon the names, phrases, and sentences within the second section, he spoke.

First the provisional and later the ultimate; this is explained as the application of the rules and methods. Therefore, the commentary states: "To cause those who have not heard to hear, and to teach through skillful means. Question:
Since the second section explains that these are the teachings that express [the meaning], I wonder upon what expressed meaning they rely?

"For the sake of Śāriputra, it is said. The answer is: based on the third reliance (*pratisaraṇa*), within which meaning, the fourfold process of opening, showing, awakening, and entering is revealed—the meaning expressed by the cause and fruit of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*)—and this is what was taught for the sake of Śāriputra. This is precisely what the commentary states:

"It refers to attaining, in the presence of the Buddha, the profound and difficult-to-understand Dharma; that profound and difficult-to-understand Dharma is itself the 'One Great Matter' (*mahābhidheya*) consisting of the four knowledges and insights."
Yao and Rou both say: "In what sense does this rely? This passage is either redundant or erroneous. Mou says: "This interpretation is not correct.

Since the first instance already states 'in what sense does it rely' and there is no further distinction, one should simply take the preceding two passages as being subsumed within 'in what sense does it rely'.
He (He) says: "What sense contains the preceding two senses? The meaning is that the preceding two..."
Regarding the meaning (*artha*): by what principle is it so stated? Therefore, the third [verse] says: "It is spoken solely in reliance upon the Great Matter (*mahā-vastu*).

Furthermore, the first [verse] relies upon a certain meaning to establish [the subject], while the second relies upon a certain meaning to explain it. Now, as for what the first relies upon as its meaning:
The interrogative phrase: "In what way does one cause others, such as Śāriputra, to hear what they have not yet heard that accords with the Dharma?

By what meaning is it clarified that the intent of the taught Dharma is difficult to understand? Next, the second part, which follows, is the actual interrogative phrase: "By what meaning [is this established]? The answer states:

"It is based on the previously attained Dharma, namely *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*. This answers the previous point regarding causing others to hear what they have not yet heard; the following sentence [proceeds from there].
"The clouds are deep and the Dharma is difficult to understand. This answers the second line above. Regarding "expedient teaching" (*upāya-deśanā*):

the phrase "abiding" refers to causing [beings] to abide in the fourth [stage]. Because of what was taught in the preceding second section—namely, the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles—it causes those of the Two Vehicles to know that the provisional may be abandoned and to rely upon the third.
Based on what meaning? It is based on the ultimate reality of the One Vehicle, whereby one comes to know the truth.

It may be accepted that the fourth section exhorts [the disciples] to come and abide within the One Vehicle (ekayāna), teaching that throughout the worlds of the ten directions there is no other vehicle, whether dual or triple;
it thus exhorts Śāriputra and others to abide within the One Vehicle.
Regarding the term "Dharma," it refers to the fifth reliance. It is not only I who first employ provisional means and subsequently reveal the ultimate truth;
all sentient beings likewise abide within the One Vehicle. All Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time act in this same manner.

As the Sūtra says: "Śāriputra, all Buddhas of the ten directions... (The phrase "the ten directions" here refers upward to the ten quarters). Regarding the "three periods," the Buddhas of the past also [taught] by means of...
By means of immeasurable and innumerable skillful methods, various causes and conditions, parables, and expressions, he expounds all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings;
these dharmas are all for the purpose of the Single Buddha Vehicle. It is the same for the future and the present as well.

Regarding the term "prohibition" (*pratiṣedha*): in the sixth section, the ten directions of the world are prohibited. It might be said that there is a possibility of falling back into the two vehicles or the three vehicles;
however, within the two vehicles, beyond the ten worlds, there is no second Śrāvaka vehicle above them—how then could there be a third Pratyekabuddha vehicle?
Regarding the term "negation" (*pratiṣedha*):

the treatise states that "negating and destroying the two attachments" refers to the following. The followers of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas) cling to the notion that the wisdom realizing ultimate truth is supreme.
These followers of the Two Vehicles all possess a mind that clings; to destroy that clinging mind is what is meant by "destroying the two."

Regarding the statement "rejecting the two truths": there is no truth in the Two Vehicles. During the forty years prior [to the Lotus Sūtra], the teaching of the Three Vehicles held that there were three [truths].

However, beneath the teaching of the Two Vehicles, there has fundamentally been no ultimate principle; it was merely borrowed from the principle found beneath the Mahāyāna teaching and applied to the teaching of the Two Vehicles.
It is not that a principle was established in its entirety within the teaching of the Two Vehicles. When it is said that there is "no principle," it means there is no ultimate [principle].
This is the principle. It is like the water channels found before the doors of every household; everyone takes from them for use.
If one were to call this "the water of the Penglai Pond," it would necessarily belong only to the house of the Son of Heaven.

If one were to call it "the Great Truth," it would necessarily exist only within the Mahāyāna teachings and not below [in] the Two Vehicles. Therefore, it is called "expelling the two truths. "Attachment" refers to the mind, while "truth" refers to—

This is the object [of the teaching]. The preceding six sections constitute the second part, which concerns the profundity of the gate of explaining wisdom; the remaining four sections concern the profundity of wisdom (linked like a fishing hook and chain).
Regarding the expression "praising its rarity": the Buddha told Śāriputra, "Such a wondrous Dharma as this is preached by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, only at rare intervals."
Furthermore, it is said: "Throughout billions upon billions of kalpas, even unto the inconceivable, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, occasionally preach this sutra.
As for the statement that those without wisdom do not rejoice, it is because their capacity to receive the Dharma is limited."

Regarding the term "Banyun" (梵云): in the Jin [dynasty] it was translated as "Numinous Auspicious Flower" (靈瑞華), which is somewhat similar [in meaning]. It is also translated as "Flower Arising from Emptiness" (空起華).

Regarding the phrase "the great ocean recedes": according to tradition, when the human lifespan is eighty thousand years, the waters of the great ocean gradually recede until they reach the knees of the Four Heavenly Kings (Cāturmahārājakāyika), at which time a golden wheel appears, thirty feet high and one hundred and fifty [feet] wide.
"Ten feet.

Regarding this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, Lü says: "It revolves throughout the four continents. Along both sides of the path, there are *udumbara* flowers growing in pairs facing one another as adornments.
