The "Responsive Flower" (yinghua). As for the "Auspicious and Wondrous Flower," it is the auspicious sign of a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin).

The *Lotus Sūtra* is the precursor to the attainment of Buddhahood. When a Wheel-Turning King appears, this flower manifests; when the Buddhas appear in the world, the *Lotus Sūtra* then unfolds. Thus, the manifestation of the Auspicious and Wondrous Flower occurs.

It causes those who have not seen [the truth] to see it, for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* has opened [the way]. It causes those who have not heard [it] to hear it. Therefore, the Commentary (*Śū*) states:

Thus, it is said that the ocean of birth and death gradually diminishes. Question: Within the holy teachings, it is stated that the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*) does not decrease. Why is this so?

As for the phrase "the path of the One Vehicle is manifest": because the faculties of those in the Mahāyāna have matured, it is called "the manifestation of the path of the One Vehicle. Thus, the Wheel-Turning King appears.
Birth and death gradually diminish, and the path of the One Vehicle becomes manifest; it is at this point that he expounds it. This is indicated by three signs:

first, the gradual receding of the ocean waters, which symbolizes the diminishing of the ocean of birth and death upon the Buddha’s descent into the world; second, the appearance of the path of the golden wheel, which represents those beings to be converted.

The path of the One Vehicle is revealed, and only then does the Buddha preach it; the three udumbara flowers appear, and only then does he ascend the royal throne. This represents the sentient beings to be transformed:

when the blossoms of awakening open in splendor, the Buddha appears in the world. Now, examining the udumbara flower in detail, since it serves as a metaphor for those to be transformed, what is the meaning?

It is used as a metaphor for this sutra. Furthermore, it says "the path of the One Vehicle is revealed"—what, then, is this path of the One Vehicle? Herein, we explain that the "path" refers to the way [of practice]. That is to say:

The *udumbara* flower is a metaphor for the ripening of the faculties; this sutra is what it represents. The sutra states that it is preached only at rare intervals, just as the *udumbara* flower appears but once in a long while.

This signifies that the ocean of the mental continuum has diminished, such that there is no longer a path for those to be converted through the cycle of birth and death (*paricchinna-janma-maraṇa*). It reveals that the capacity of the Mahāyāna roots has matured.

The *udumbara* flower is the wondrous Dharma that is taught. When the *udumbara* flower appears, it symbolizes that the emergence of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) is not in vain, and likewise, the wondrous [Dharma] is not in vain.
Dharma. If one proclaims and makes it heard, one will certainly attain Buddhahood. As for the "Wheel-Turning King" (Cakravartin), this represents attaining Buddhahood in the future;

As for the statement that Śāriputra had previously heard it: although he had already heard it during the time of the twenty thousand Buddhas following the sixteen princes, he has now completely forgotten it;

The reason for this is as follows: what is the evidential statement? For what reason is the Buddha’s underlying intention in teaching the Dharma so difficult to understand?

only the Buddhas are able to know it.

As for the statement regarding "those of the three vehicles" and so forth, the intended meaning is that within the teachings of the two vehicles, there exists only the principle of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Furthermore...
This is the principle of our Mahāyāna school; it does not exist within the teachings of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha). It is called "ineffable" for the following reasons:

second, because the *tathatā* (suchness) and *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) contained within the Mahāyāna teachings themselves transcend all words, they are termed "ineffable. Being beyond words and devoid of marks, they are nevertheless expressed through names and speech.
It is not so. It is called "ineffable. These three vehicles of the Dharma possess only names, chapters, and phrases; there are no separate three essences.

Regarding the statement that there are no three distinct entities (this explains the meaning of the title’s difficult-to-understand intent; it refers to the "Gate of Wisdom" at the beginning of this chapter). Question:
At the beginning of the chapter, wisdom was first clarified, followed by the Gate of Wisdom. Why, in this section, is the Gate of Teaching explained first, and wisdom explained later? Answer:

The previous section relied on the prior wisdom to subsequently explain the Three Vehicles in order to manifest the One Vehicle, while internally acknowledging the existence of the Three Vehicles. In this section, the teaching is explained first.
The subsequent explanation concerns principle (*li*). This means that the three manifest vehicles and their teachings ultimately converge in the single vehicle (*ekayāna*) of principle.
Because the intended goals differ, this second explanation refers specifically to the teaching of the three vehicles (*triyāna*) given during the forty years prior.
The principle explained therein is subsumed within the third [section], "Based upon what meaning. As the Sūtra says: "For what reason? What is the one..."

Regarding the analysis of the textual passage, the phrase "arising from the preceding text" and so forth indicates that this is a formal inquiry (*paripṛcchā*). That is to say, it inquires into the first section, which concerns what has not been heard before;

it inquires into the second section, which concerns the speaker: for what reason was it taught according to what is appropriate? The underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) of such teaching is difficult to understand.
What is the reason for this? Is it because this Dharma cannot be reached through deliberation or discrimination, and its understanding can only be known by a Buddha?

The answer is: It is taught according to the principle of cause and effect based on the one great causal condition (*ekamahākaruṇā-hetu-pratyaya*), and it is taught based on [the four stages of] opening, showing, awakening, and entering.

What is the reason for this response by the Sūtra compiler? Next, regarding the response from the perspective of the Śāstra author as to "in accordance with what meaning" [the teaching was given], the Commentary states:

"In accordance with what meaning does he preach the Dharma in such a way that its underlying intent is difficult to understand? Preaching the Dharma in accordance with what meaning is beyond the scope of deliberative discrimination;
only a Buddha can know it. The answer is: "In accordance with the meaning of what matter? It is the one great causal condition (*ekamahākaruṇā-hetu-pratyaya*)."
It is said: "If the Tathāgata were to speak for the sake of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), the two vehicles would easily understand;

however, because he speaks based on the one great cause and condition (ekamahā-kṛtya-hetu-pratyaya) and based on this meaning, it is difficult to understand. In this regard, the meaning upon which the *śāstra* (treatise) relies constitutes the question, while the "one great cause and condition" of the *sūtra* (scripture) constitutes the answer.
Regarding the statement "the substance of things, such as phenomena (*dharma*) and so forth": the "great matter" does not transcend nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

If the great matter is a characteristic, it is a thing-phenomenon (*dharmavastu*); if the great matter is a nature, it is the substance-phenomenon (*svabhāvavastu*). If the great matter is an object, it is the meaning (*artha*);
if the great matter is in relation to the expressive teaching (*vyañjana*), it is the principle (*yukti*). Thing-phenomena are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); the substance-phenomenon...
It is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). The meaning of the matter is unconditioned; the principle is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

If one follows these four meanings, only when they are fully complete is it called the "Great Matter" (*mahā-kṛtya*). Explaining it according to three meanings: first, the "Great Matter" refers to things and matters. "Things" (*vastu*) refers to *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*.
This is the general meaning of "true reality" being called "things and matters. Second, it is said that the "Great Matter" refers to the essential matter (*tattva-vastu*), which is *bodhi*.
Nirvāṇa. That which is a dharma possessing a substantial entity (svabhāva) is called a "substantial matter" (vastu). Regarding the three great matters: first, the meaning of "matter" (vastu);

second, the meaning of "object" (viṣaya)—that is, when bodhi and nirvāṇa are contrasted with the wisdom that takes them as conditions; this very meaning of "object" is itself termed a "great matter. Third, the two characters for "principle" (nyāya):

these correspond to the aforementioned three meanings from the sutra—either the principle of things and events, or the principle of substantial entities, or the principle of [the aforementioned] matters.

Regarding the principle of "meaning" (*artha*), the two characters "second" (*di er*) or "principle" (*dao li*) explain the principle of the fundamental dharma of causes and conditions within the sutra.
The intention of the *Shu* (Commentary) is that it need not necessarily take all four meanings to be designated as the "One Great Matter.
It may be understood accordingly as the wisdom of the principle of phenomena (*vastu*), the wisdom of the principle of substance (*ātman*), or the wisdom of the principle of meaning (*artha*).
The Sūtra says, "appearing in the world. The Commentary states that this is for the sake of these great causes and conditions, which is why he appears in the world.

Regarding the phrase "proclaiming his own virtuous title," this refers to the two characters "World-Honored One" (*Bhagavān*) in the Sūtra. The question asks: why does the World-Honored One speak of himself?
Question: How can he say this himself? It seems as though the World-Honored One is boasting. Answer: He proclaims his own virtuous title for one great purpose:
to appear in the world and extensively benefit all living beings. This is why he proclaims his own virtuous title.
Furthermore, he does not take other matters as his object of focus.
To say "it would not be so" means that if he did not appear in the world for the sake of great causes and conditions, he would be identical to those of the two vehicles who enter extinction;
they seek only their own benefit, do not transform sentient beings, and do not require the title of their own virtue. It is solely for the sake of all [sentient beings].
That sentient beings attain Buddhahood is called the "Great Matter"; this is why [the Buddha] designates it for himself.

Regarding the passage in the Sūtra that says, "To reveal the Buddha’s knowledge and vision," etc., one asks: does "revealing" mean the Buddha reveals it for himself, or does he reveal it for sentient beings?
If it means he reveals it for himself, the Buddha has already revealed it long ago; why then does the Sūtra speak of "the Buddha’s knowledge and vision"? This implies that [it is not yet attained].

Indeed, the sutra text explicitly states: "To open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and cause them to become pure. This clearly shows that it is only the knowledge and vision within Śāriputra’s own body that is being opened.

If the knowledge and vision within the bodies of sentient beings could not be called the "Buddha-vision," then the two natures—principle and practice—existing within sentient beings would not be called the "two kinds of Buddha-nature.
Since those [two kinds of Buddha-nature] are already established as a matter of course, why is this [the case here]?

Agreed. However, this nature and characteristic of knowledge and vision has existed among sentient beings since beginningless time, obscured by the two hindrances. The Tathāgata has revealed and expounded it, clearly explaining that within their own bodies there are two unsurpassed [qualities], so that they may know them and aspire toward them. Since Śāriputra already knows these two dharmas, I do not yet know what sequence of exposition he used to demonstrate how they can be realized;

I shall therefore exhort him to cultivate them. Thus it is said: ... (The remainder of the passage follows) ... I have now briefly explained the meaning of the title. As for the main body of the treatise, it is divided into three parts: first, the introduction; second, the main exposition; and third, the conclusion. Regarding the introduction, it consists of two sections: first, the homage; and second, the statement of intent. Regarding the homage, it consists of two parts: first, the homage paid by the author; and second, the homage paid by the translator. Regarding the statement of intent, it consists of two parts: first, the general statement of intent; and second, the specific statement of intent. Regarding the main exposition, it consists of two parts:

first, the explanation of the two types of bodhicitta; and second, the explanation of the stages of practice. Regarding the conclusion, it consists of two parts: first, the summary of the meaning; and second, the dedication of merit. This concludes the brief outline. Now, let us proceed with the detailed explanation. [The text continues with the detailed commentary on the specific points mentioned above.]

Third: All [the bodhisattvas] abide in the stage of fruition and have entered the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; this is the cause for their attainment. Therefore, it is next explained that they have "entered the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

This concludes the first cycle. Regarding those who were equally granted the ox-carts: these are the untainted causal practices (*anāsrava-hetu-caryā*) consisting of the fundamental and subsequent two wisdoms.

If one is a bodhisattva of the fifth stage according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the two wisdoms of the ultimate and the conventional are mutually contradictory in their modes of activity; to unify them so that they correspond is extremely difficult to master.
Therefore, by merging the two realms of the ultimate and the conventional with the two wisdoms of the fundamental and the subsequent, this "ox-cart" becomes a single entity.
It causes all the sons—the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages—to spend their days and nights throughout kalpas, specifically for two *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.

If they obtain the "instruction-carts," they may also pass through the first kalpa. This concludes the third cycle: the destruction of the illusory city and the leading [of the children] to the place of treasure. Third.
This is why it is named "Opening the Buddha’s Knowledge and Vision.

To say that this explains the Great Matter means that its essence is precisely knowledge and vision. As for the two characters "knowledge and vision," the compilers of the sutras have assigned them four names.

Because they are explained as "opening, showing, awakening, and entering," they are called the "knowledge and vision of opening, showing, awakening, and entering"; this is the meaning of the upward direction. According to the masters of the *Śāstras*, there are four [aspects].
I shall explain this according to its meaning. "Opening" refers to the unsurpassed meaning; "showing" refers to the meaning of sameness; "awakening" refers to the meaning of non-knowing;

and "entering" refers to causing one to realize the meaning of non-retrogression. Thus, through these four meanings, one understands and perceives [the truth], for the essence of such knowledge and vision is itself a great matter.
Regarding the passage from "The discourse says" up to "the Tathāgata can realize," the *She* (攝) commentary states: "Tathāgata" refers to the person who realizes;

"one of suchness-knowledge" (*yathābhūtajñāna*) indicates the knowledge that realizes; "knowing that meaning" indicates the dharma realized, which is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). The *Mu* (牟) commentary states:
"The Tathāgata can realize suchness" marks the principle realized by the knowledge that realizes. It says "knowing... [to indicate the realization].

"Because of that meaning" (*tadarthatvāt*) is the explanation; it refers to the meaning of the term *tathatā* (Suchness), which is the objective realm of principle (*nyāya-viṣaya*). The phrase "a single cognition" (*ekajñāna*) applies generally to both the cognizer and the cognized.
Question: What is called "the realization of reality as it is" (*yathābhūtaprativedha*)? Answer: The commentary states: "Because of knowing that meaning. Regarding "meaning" (*artha*):

if it is contrasted with the realizing wisdom (*pramāṇa-jñāna*), it is called "meaning" because it is the object (*viṣaya*). If it is contrasted with the expressive teaching (*deśanā*), it is called... [text ends]

The "meaning" (*artha*) refers to the object expressed. It is called "meaning" because it is a principle (*naya*). Furthermore, it is explained as that which the Tathāgata can realize, namely the conventional person.
Because one knows that meaning as it truly is, this is simply the fundamental wisdom realizing the principle of *tathatā*. The two characters "as it truly is" (*yathābhūta*) refer to *tathatā*.
The three characters "knowing that meaning" (*taj-jñāna*) are likewise the principle of *tathatā*.

Regarding the terms "dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*), "true suchness" (*tathatā*), and so forth: first, the two characters for "dharma-nature" explain the word "real" (*bden pa*) in the aforementioned treatise;
it refers to the actual fundamental nature of all phenomena. Second, the two characters for "true suchness" explain the character "such" (*de bzhin*) in the aforementioned treatise. Third, it says:

The commentary on the latter two phrases states: "Because it is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of reality as it is. These two phrases specifically conclude the two characters "as it is" (*yathābhūta*) from the preceding treatise.
Regarding the phrase "that which is realized... is the meaning": this is an explanation; that is, it explains the text of the treatise because one understands its meaning. Meaning (*artha*).

The term "name" (nāma) encompasses both explanations. The principle of True Suchness (tathatā) is one; however, when contrasted with the teaching that expresses it, it is the name and meaning that are expressed.
When contrasted with the wisdom that realizes it, it is the name and meaning of the object known.

Regarding the statement, "The essence of correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) is fundamentally [this]," this refers exclusively to fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), which is termed "knowledge-and-vision" (*jñāna-darśana*).

This concludes the two characters "capable of realizing" (*neng zheng*) from the preceding treatise. Regarding the statement, "Capable of knowing the principles and so forth," this concludes the character "meaning" (*yi*) from the preceding treatise.
The statement "that which can immediately realize perfect enlightenment" summarizes the meaning of the sūtra regarding the means of realization and that which is realized.
The statement "enlightenment as cessation" refers to that which is revealed through the abandonment of hindrances; for this reason, it is also called enlightenment.
Regarding the term "locus of knowledge" (*jñānasthāna*): it is the locus of the object of cognition (*ālambana*) and the locus upon which knowledge relies;

therefore, it is also called "knowledge. Regarding the statement that "knowledge is the primary essence": this means that the nature and function [of the mind] are predominant. Fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is termed "knowledge," while subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) is termed "vision.
These two together are called "knowledge-vision. Taking the principle of *tathatā* as the nature of knowledge-vision—this is the relationship between nature and function.

Regarding the attainment of the nature through its function: if one knows it, that intimacy is known only by oneself and does not extend to being known by others; it is similar to events occurring in a dream.

The principle of *tathatā* (suchness) is realized by fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), whereas subsequent wisdom (*prṣṭha-labdha-jñāna*) takes it as an object; because this involves the transformation of mental images, the connection is remote. Therefore, it is known only by oneself.

Fundamental wisdom illuminates the true realm (*tathatā*), while subsequently attained wisdom illuminates the conventional realm. Therefore, taking the nature (*svabhāva*) as it conforms to its manifestations (*lakṣaṇa*), they are collectively termed "knowledge and vision" (*jñānadarśana*).
Question: If knowledge is proximate and vision is remote, then among the five eyes, since this is called the "wisdom eye" (*prajñācakṣus*), why is it not called "vision"?

Answer: Those [five] objects are designated as "eyes" based on the distinction between the fundamental and subsequent wisdoms in relation to their conditions; this [present case], however, is distinguished by proximity and remoteness, and is therefore not the same as those.

Regarding the statement that "these two are function and so forth": these two are themselves the essence and function of cognition. If one considers the actual nature of wisdom (*jñāna*), it is precisely suchness (*tathatā*).
It is like a knife, which has the function of cutting objects while taking the four elements as its substance. If one refers to its underlying nature (*āśraya-svabhāva*), [it is suchness].
This refers to taking empty space as the essence.

Regarding the statement "taking the nature (xing) to accord with the characteristics (xiang)": Question: Since knowledge and vision (zhìjiàn) have already been assigned to the latter two wisdoms (jñāna), how can True Suchness (tathatā) be combined with and designated as "knowledge and vision"?
Answer: It is by taking the nature [of the latter two wisdoms] and so forth... [as explained in the following passage].

Regarding the statement, "desiring to make the two equal": it is asked, since various sutras and treatises only advocate for subsuming the derivative into the fundamental and bringing the characteristics back to the nature, why is it that here one brings the nature toward the characteristics?

Answer: It is because one desires to make them equal and accord with that school’s tenet, which takes the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñatā*) as the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*); therefore, this is explained first.
Regarding the phrase "Śrīmālā and others": Question: This sutra’s central tenet clarifies the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), and the One Vehicle is the Knowledge of All Modes (sarvajñatā).
For what reason are three names from the Śrīmālā-sūtra—each of which is *tathatā* (suchness)—cited here to authenticate this sutra? Answer: The Commentary states: "Śrīmālā and others."

The Master of the Commentary states: "Precisely because this sutra’s primary tenet clarifies the apprehension of the *sarvajñajñāna* (all-knowing wisdom), there may be a fear that one will suspect it intends to take *sarvajñajñāna* alone as the essence of the One Vehicle.
It does not merely take *sarvajñajñāna* as its essence; it also takes *tathatā* (suchness) as the essence of the One Vehicle."
Regarding the statement "the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and so forth," the intended meaning is that the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* encompasses both principle (*li*) and wisdom (*zhi*) as the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
This differs from the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, which takes only true reality (*zhēn lǐ*) [as the One Vehicle]. Here, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* includes both practice (*xíng*) and principle as the One Vehicle.

Because its myriad practices are vast and extensive, it is called "Great" (*mahā*); because this very great essence possesses the function of transporting [beings], it is called a "Vehicle" (*yāna*). Thus, being both a vehicle and great, it is termed [Mahāyāna].
Because it is "Great," taking its essence as its function, the Great is also the Vehicle (*yāna*). Because it takes its function as its essence, the Vehicle is also Great.

Alternatively, because one rides upon the Great Vehicle, it is called the "Great Vehicle" (*Mahāyāna*). "Great" is established in reference to *tathatā* (Suchness); the character "Great" is applied to the Vehicle.

Since this conditioned name "Vehicle" possesses the nature of the Great, it is called the "Great Vehicle. The intended meaning here is that the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) of the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* is the true [One Vehicle].

As for "inclusion," the Mahāyāna consists of the myriad practices. Since it is taught as the One Vehicle, it is clearly understood that the Mahāyāna subsumes the nature (xing) by means of its characteristics (xiang).
Question: Why does the Master of the Commentary explain the function of nature through principle and wisdom? Answer:
The *Śāstra* states that the three characters "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñā*) pertain exclusively to both nature and characteristics.
Regarding the statement "knowing the meaning of the One Vehicle" (up to the point of "the essential doctrine"): this refers to the teaching of the One Vehicle across three cycles.
In the first cycle, both principle (*li*) and wisdom (*zhi*) are taught together; in the second, wisdom is taught but not principle; and in the third, principle is taught but not wisdom.
Thus, one knows that the teaching of the One Vehicle across these three cycles encompasses both principle and wisdom.
Regarding the "ox-cart in the burning house," ancient masters took the Truth (*tattva*) to be the substance of the cart.
Here, the author of the *Śāstra* (the Subcommentator) refutes these ancient masters by stating that the "burning house" and so forth are, in fact, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
Regarding the mention of "the perilous path" and "the place of treasure," these refer to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); therefore, their being "made" is not mentioned. Question:
Since the place of treasure is unconditioned, it is said that its making is not mentioned; yet the conjured city (*nirmāṇa-pura*) is also unconditioned—why then is its making mentioned? Answer:

The place of treasure is fundamentally unconditioned, and that which is unconditioned does not speak of being made. The conjured city is a provisional designation (*prajñapti*), and for this reason, its making is mentioned. Question:
The "constructed city" (*nirmāṇa-pura*) is said to be "made," yet it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). The "ox-cart" is also said to be "made"; should this likewise be considered unconditioned? Answer:
The ox-cart is called "made" because both its name and its substance are made; therefore, it is conditioned. The constructed city is called "made" because its name is made while its substance is not;

therefore, it is unconditioned. Question: The "jeweled destination" (*ratna-sthāna*) is unconditioned. Since it is placed above [the constructed city], should the character "destination" (*sthāna*) also be considered a name for something made?

Answer: Regarding the term "created city" (*nirmita-pura*), there are two meanings. First, it is because the World-Honored One himself stated in the sutra, "That which I have created. Second, the term "created" refers to the act of creating rather than the substance itself; this is not the case for the "Jewel Place" (*ratna-sthāna*), and therefore it is not said to be "created. It possesses a real substantial nature (*dravya-svabhāva*), and thus it is simply called the "Jewel Place. Question: The ox-cart has both a name and a substance as a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta*) precisely because it is something created. As for the sheep and deer carts, however—[one asks] why they are not so? Answer: [Because they are merely expedient means. Furthermore, the ox-cart is a true vehicle because it can carry one to the destination. The sheep and deer carts are not true vehicles because they cannot reach the destination. Moreover, the ox-cart is a true vehicle because it is a great vehicle (*mahāyāna*). The sheep and deer carts are not true vehicles because they are small vehicles (*hīnayāna*). Furthermore, the ox-cart is a true vehicle because it is a vehicle of liberation (*vimukti-yāna*). The sheep and deer carts are not true vehicles because they are vehicles of bondage (*bandhana-yāna*). Furthermore, the ox-cart is a true vehicle because it is a vehicle of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). The sheep and deer carts are not true vehicles because they are vehicles of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Furthermore, the ox-cart is a true vehicle because it is a vehicle of the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*). The sheep and deer carts are not true vehicles because they are vehicles of the Two Vehicles (*dvaya-yāna*). Furthermore, the ox-cart is a true vehicle because it is a vehicle of the Buddha-vehicle (*buddha-yāna*). The sheep and deer carts are not true vehicles because they are vehicles of the Two Vehicles. Furthermore, the ox-cart is a true vehicle because it is a vehicle that reaches the other shore (*pāramitā-yāna*). The sheep and deer carts are not true vehicles because they are vehicles that do not reach the other shore. Furthermore, the ox-cart is a true vehicle because it is a vehicle that leads to the cessation of suffering (*nirodha-yāna*). The sheep and deer carts are not true vehicles because they are vehicles that lead to the accumulation of suffering (*samudaya-yāna*). Furthermore, the ox-cart is a true vehicle because it is a vehicle that leads to the attainment of Nirvana. The sheep and deer carts are not true vehicles because they are vehicles that lead to the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Furthermore, the ox-cart is a true vehicle because it is a vehicle that leads to the attainment of Buddhahood. The sheep and deer carts are not true vehicles because they are vehicles that lead to the attainment of Arhatship or Pratyekabuddhahood. Furthermore, the ox-cart is a true vehicle because it is a vehicle that leads to the attainment of the Dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*). The sheep and deer carts are not true vehicles because they are vehicles that lead to the attainment of the form-body (*rūpa-kāya*). Furthermore, the ox-cart is a true vehicle because it is a vehicle that leads to the attainment of the Wisdom-body (*jñāna-kāya*). The sheep and deer carts are not true vehicles because they are vehicles that lead to the attainment of the body of limited wisdom. Furthermore, the ox-cart is a true vehicle because it is a vehicle that leads to the attainment of the Body of Liberation (*vimukti-kāya*). The sheep and deer carts are not true vehicles because they are vehicles that lead to the attainment of the body of non-liberation. Furthermore, the ox-cart is a true vehicle because it is a vehicle that leads to the attainment of the Body of Joy (*sukha-kāya*). The sheep and deer carts are not true vehicles because they are vehicles that lead to the attainment of the body of suffering. Furthermore, the ox-cart is a true vehicle because it is a vehicle that leads to the attainment of the Body of Eternity (*nitya-kāya*). The sheep and deer carts are not true vehicles because they are vehicles that lead to the attainment of the body of impermanence. Furthermore, the ox-cart is a true vehicle because it is a vehicle that leads to the attainment of the Body of Purity (*śubha-kāya*). The sheep and deer carts are not true vehicles because they are vehicles that lead to the attainment of the body of impurity. Furthermore, the ox-cart is a true vehicle because it is a vehicle that leads to the attainment of the Body of Self (*ātman-kāya*). The sheep and deer carts are not true vehicles because they are vehicles that lead to the attainment of the body of non-self. Furthermore, the ox-cart is a true vehicle because it is a vehicle that leads to the attainment of the Body of Bliss (*sukha-kāya*). The sheep and deer carts are not true vehicles because they are vehicles that lead to the attainment of the body of suffering. Furthermore, the ox-cart is a true vehicle because it is a vehicle that leads to the attainment of the Body of Wondrousness (*adbhuta-kāya*). The sheep and deer carts are not true vehicles because they are vehicles that lead to the attainment of the body of ordinariness. Furthermore, the ox-cart is a true vehicle because it is a vehicle that leads to the attainment of the Body of Sovereignty (*vaśitā-kāya*). The sheep and deer carts are not true vehicles because they are vehicles that lead to the attainment of the body of dependence. Furthermore, the ox-cart is a true vehicle because it is a vehicle that leads to the attainment of the Body of Freedom (*svatantra-kāya*). The sheep and deer carts are not true vehicles because they are vehicles that lead to the attainment of the body of bondage. Furthermore, the ox-cart is a true vehicle because it is a vehicle that leads to the attainment of the Body of Non-obstruction (*anāvaraṇa-kāya*). The sheep and deer carts are not true vehicles because they are vehicles that lead to the attainment of the body of obstruction. Furthermore, the ox-cart is a true vehicle because it is a vehicle that leads to the attainment of the Body of Non-duality (*advaya-kāya*). The sheep and deer carts are not true vehicles because they are vehicles that lead to the attainment of the body of duality. Furthermore, the ox-cart is a true vehicle because it is a vehicle that leads to the attainment of the Body of Non-conceptualization (*nirvikalpa-kāya*). The sheep and deer carts are not true vehicles because they are vehicles that lead to the attainment of the body of conceptualization. Furthermore, the ox-cart is a true vehicle because it is a vehicle that leads to the attainment of the Body of Non-arising (*anutpāda-kāya*). The sheep and deer carts are not true vehicles because they are vehicles that lead to the attainment of the body of arising. Furthermore, the ox-cart is a true vehicle because it is a vehicle that leads to the attainment of the Body of Non-extinction (*anirodha-kāya*). The sheep and deer carts are not true vehicles because they are vehicles that lead to the attainment of the body of extinction. Furthermore, the ox-cart is a true vehicle because it is a vehicle that leads to the attainment of the Body of Non-birth (*ajāti-kāya*). The sheep and deer carts are not true vehicles because they are vehicles that lead to the attainment of the body of birth. Furthermore, the ox-cart is a true vehicle because it is a vehicle that leads to the attainment of the Body of Non-death (*amaraṇa-kāya*). The sheep and deer carts are not true vehicles because they are vehicles that lead to the attainment of the body of death. Furthermore, the ox-cart is a true vehicle because it is a vehicle that leads to the attainment of the Body of Non-decay (*ajara-kāya*). The sheep and deer carts are not true vehicles because they are vehicles that lead to the attainment of the body of decay. Furthermore, the ox-cart is a true vehicle because it is a vehicle that leads to the attainment of the Body of Non-sickness (*aroga-kāya*). The sheep and deer carts are not true vehicles because they are vehicles that lead to the attainment of the body of sickness. Furthermore, the ox-cart is a true vehicle because it is a vehicle that leads to the attainment of the Body of Non-ageing (*amara-kāya*). The sheep and deer carts are not true vehicles because they are vehicles that lead to the attainment of the body of ageing. Furthermore, the ox-cart is a true vehicle because it is a vehicle that leads to the attainment of the Body of Non-defilement (*asaṃkleśa-kāya*). The sheep and deer carts are not true vehicles because they are vehicles that lead to the attainment of the body of defilement. Furthermore, the ox-cart is a true vehicle because it is a vehicle that leads to the attainment of the Body of Non-purification (*avyavadāna-kāya*). The sheep and deer carts are not true vehicles because they are vehicles that lead to the attainment of the body of purification. Furthermore, the ox-cart is a true vehicle because it is a vehicle that leads to the attainment of the

Question: These are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*). Why, then, do the two vehicles not see themselves ascending [the vehicle]? Answer: Because the two vehicles, having attained the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) which is free from outflows (*anāsrava*), do not realize that this [wisdom] is conditioned.
Therefore, the World-Honored One, following their state of non-realization, concealed it by saying it does not exist;
yet this does not preclude its actual existence.
Regarding the statement "the opening" and "the unsurpassed": it establishes that there are two dharmas, namely *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*, and nothing else.
If there were yet another dharma, how could these two alone be called "unsurpassed"? Question: *Nirvāṇa* is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and may thus be called unsurpassed;
however, *bodhi* is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). How can it be called unsurpassed? Answer: They are distinguished in relation to one another as conditioned and unconditioned. There is...
It cannot be called "unsurpassed" [in an absolute sense]. Rather, it is discussed in terms of the category of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) themselves;
within the conditioned, it is called unsurpassed because the Noble Ones possess these two dharmas: awakening (*bodhi*) and nirvāṇa. Thus, it is termed "the unsurpassed meaning of the opener."

Regarding the phrase "the wisdom of all-knowledge" (*sarvajñajñāna*): the upward-pointing "wisdom" refers to the Buddha-wisdom. The Buddha is a provisional designation for the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
Within the person who is the all-knower, this wisdom exists; it is therefore called the "wisdom of all-knowledge.

The downward-pointing character "wisdom" (*jñāna*) encompasses both fundamental wisdom (*mūlajñāna*) and subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdhajñāna*). The upward-pointing character "wisdom" (*jñā*) refers to the body of the provisional designation of the five aggregates. It is not [the case that...].
The character for "wisdom" (*jì*) above [in the compound] merely serves as a phonetic lead-in from the preceding context; here, we take the character for "wisdom" (*zhì*) below.

The three dharmas—the fundamental wisdom, the subsequently attained wisdom, and *tathatā* (suchness)—are collectively termed "knowledge and vision" (*zhìjiàn*). Regarding the interpretation of this meaning:
regardless of the extent of the analytical wisdom involved, the matter must necessarily be accompanied by *tathatā*. (This refers to the realization of the Dharma of the Superior Person.)
Regarding the statement, "Furthermore, all-encompassing wisdom [extends] to the sublime principle": Question: Why is it that wisdom is cited as encompassing the principle? Answer:
When wisdom realizes the principle, it should illuminate the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*), just as a pearl and its radiance are inseparable. Therefore, wisdom is cited;
at times, the principle follows along with it, which is why it is called "opening up the Buddha’s knowledge and vision" (the original [nature] and the subsequent understanding).
The term "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*) is an expression of praise for excellence. This pair opens up both *bodhi* (enlightenment) and *nirvāṇa*.
There are some transcribed commentaries which claim this refers specifically to the *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa* of Śāriputra; however, that is not the case here.

Regarding the essence of this *bodhi*, there are two aspects for each—dharma and metaphor—and within the two types of wisdom and principle, each has its own dharma and metaphor. In the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha* is taken as [the basis].
Regarding "knowledge and vision": in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, the apprehension of the empty Tathāgatagarbha constitutes knowledge and vision.
As for the statement regarding "inherently existing seeds," one asks: if Nirvāṇa is the inherently existing essence, it is an unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) seed;

how then can that which exists be called "inherently existing"? The answer is: it is simply said that Nirvāṇa, being unconditioned, is inherently existing; it does not mean that all things which exist are unconditioned.

Regarding the phrase "perfuming through extensive learning," a concise summary states: from the first generation of the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), one draws near to virtuous friends;

initially relying upon bodhisattvas, one makes offerings to the Buddhas of the five Ganges-sands and hears the teachings of the True Dharma. During the stages of accumulation (*sambhāra-mārga*) and application (*prayoga-mārga*), one cultivates the ten thousand practices over the course of one great... [kalpa].

For kalpas, these [wholesome roots] nourish the untainted seeds within the fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). It is only within the stage of the first ground (*prathamabhūmi*) that the two wisdoms—subtle and equanimous—arise as actual manifestations (*pravṛtti*), whereby one enters the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
Prior to the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), there are only tainted states; from the first ground up to before the seventh ground, [the state is mixed].

There is cultivation that is both with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*). From the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) onward, there is exclusively cultivation without outflows. It is effortless and consists of signless (*animitta*) cultivation.

When one attains Buddhahood, in the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), one abandons the inferior outflow-free states; within the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), the four wisdoms (*jñāna*) and bodhi arise in their full perfection.
This is the result of the growth produced by the cultivation of the permeations of hearing (*śruta-vāsanā*); its essence is the four wisdoms, which are themselves the causes of the four wisdoms.

This is called the "non-empty Tathāgatagarbha. Question: How can that which is with outflows (sāsrava) serve as a support for that which is without outflows (anāsrava)? Answer: There is no contradiction;

prior to entering the stages (bhūmi), during the first eon, the outflowed serves to support the outflow-free. Once one has ascended to the stages and beyond, it is the outflow-free that supports the outflowed, enabling the attainment of the fruits of those ten kings.
Regarding the statement "arising from causes and conditions": this is discussed here in general terms. Nanda [the seed] only arises; Candragarbha [the seed] only grows;

Dharmapāla [the seed] is both originally present and newly perfumed. If one follows the commentary (*śāstra*), it speaks of the originally present seeds (*bīja*) as arising before entering the stages (*bhūmi*) and growing upon entering the stages.
Question: Are the two wisdoms produced by the mirror old or new? Answer: They are only originally present.

Regarding the statement that the *ālayavijñāna* is "with outflows" (*sāsrava*): although it is not itself [identical to] the outflows, it is called "with outflows" because the seeds of the outflows arise within it and because it is perfumed by the consciousnesses associated with the outflows.

Regarding the statement that it "can contain all that is without outflows" (*anāsrava*): this explains the sense of destroying the outflows. It is like when ordinary people, during a time of turmoil, [are suddenly freed from it].

The prince was captured. Having arisen through his present actions, he became king; once he had entered the palace gate, he was struck with one hundred blows and saw the gallows at the corner of the hall.
What is called the *tathāgatagarbha* is the seed of the four wisdoms; it is the future *saṃbhogakāya* Tathāgata.
Regarding the statement "due to associating with virtuous friends," this refers initially to the Bodhisattva’s practice of making offerings at the five rivers and so forth.
Regarding the statement "much learning" and so on, this refers to the transformation that diminishes power and increases capability.
Regarding the statement "the *ālaya* is the cause of containment," *ālaya* means "to contain"; this explains the eighth consciousness, which is named "Empty-like."
The *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) refers to the meaning of "causal nature. To understand the term "seed" as "storehouse":

if one takes the seeds of wisdom to be the causal nature, then the eighth consciousness, the *ālaya* capable of containing consciousness, is precisely the storehouse of the causal nature of emptiness. Here, the "storehouse" (*ālaya*) is itself the causal nature.

If the seeds of wisdom possess the functional capacity to produce [results], they are termed "containing and storing"; acting as the cause for the present, they are called "nature" when the cause is transcended, which is non-emptiness.

If that is so, then the "containing" (saṃbhāra) is itself the nature; why then must they be assigned separately? Only the characteristic (lakṣaṇa) is assigned to the non-empty, because this [position] takes only the non-empty as the storehouse (ālaya). (This adopts the second interpretation.)

Regarding the statement "it is like one who plants a tree": it is like the seed of a nyagrodha tree, or like a mustard seed, which, through four conditions—wind, sun, rain, and so forth—gives rise to sprouts and the like.
Once it has been entwined by creepers for many years, its branches and trunk gradually flourish, becoming vast, well-spaced, and perfectly full.
Its shade spreads over the measure of five hundred chariots; even if used solely for shading, it is not exhausted. Such is the nature of seeds.
It is like the seed of a nyagrodha tree residing within the eighth consciousness, as if hidden within a rock. The afflictions and defilements are like drifting dust.

The hearing-perfuming (*śruta-vāsanā*) prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) is like the bright sun and the nourishing rain. Upon reaching the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), the active manifestations arise like the growth of young grass.

The afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*) act as obstacles, analogous to coarse cloth. As the path is cultivated repeatedly, it is like branches and trunk gradually flourishing until the fruit is attained.
Abiding in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), it is swift, vast, and perfect. This is the body of self-enjoyment (*svasaṃbhogakāya*). The Buddha-seed arises from conditions;
after the attainment of enlightenment, its substance transcends the three realms and its causes extend throughout the ten directions. Thus, it does not perfume the seeds [of the other two bodies].

Regarding the statement "realizing distinct [nirvāṇas] upon encountering conditions": if one encounters the stage of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), at the point where afflictions of conceptualization (*parikalpita-kleśa*) are exhausted, one realizes a portion of the *svabhāva-viśuddha-nirvāṇa* (intrinsic purity nirvāṇa) through that condition.
If one encounters the point where innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) of the three realms are exhausted, one realizes the *nirvāṇa* attained through that condition;
this is called *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder). If one encounters the point where the physical body, which is the basis of suffering, is exhausted, through that condition...

The realization of nirvāṇa is called *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa without remainder). If one encounters the assistance of the two factors of increased compassion and increased wisdom, the nirvāṇa realized through those conditions is called *apratisthita-nirvāṇa* (non-abiding nirvāṇa).
If one encounters the fulfillment of these three conditions, the realization attained is called *mahāparinirvāṇa* (great parinirvāṇa).
Therefore, it is said that "one encounters [these] and so forth."
Regarding the statement "the two kinds of Tathāgatagarbha": here, wisdom (*jñāna*) is the subject that takes as its object; the two kinds of empty Tathāgatas are the objects.

Because wisdom takes these two kinds as its objective sphere, it is called the "wisdom of the two kinds of emptiness. This very [wisdom] is what is termed the "empty Tathāgatagarbha" when it exists amidst the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Furthermore, True Suchness (*tathatā*) itself is also called the "empty Tathāgatagarbha" when it exists within the afflictions. Question: How can True Suchness be called "empty"?

Answer: It is called "emptiness" because it severs false and delusive afflictions and is manifested by means of emptiness; secondly, it is also called "emptiness" because it is the very nature of emptiness.
Wisdom that takes these two as its object is termed the "wisdom of the two kinds of emptiness."

Regarding the term "if separated" (*yad-vivikta*): if it arises separately from delusive phenomena, it is called "separated. Because it is easily relinquished by the Noble Path, it is called "relinquished.
Because it is that which is to be abandoned, it is called "abandoned. Because it can be transformed, it is called "different" from the storehouse of all afflictions.

It conceals True Suchness (tathatā) and is called the "storehouse of all afflictions" (sarvakleśakośa). Regarding why True Suchness is called a "storehouse," the Commentary states that it is "not afflicted" because it is not a false dharma;
it is called "not separated" because it cannot be easily removed; and it is called "not detached" because it is not something to be severed.

It is called "uninterrupted" because it undergoes transformation. It is called "undifferentiated" because it transcends the sphere of objects and mental states. It is called "inconceivable" because it is wondrously beyond the reach of thought.
Regarding the statement that "afflictions and outflows... are called the empty tathāgatagarbha," this designates the "empty treasury."
The statement "Nirvāṇa is untainted... it is not a false dharma" is the thesis (*uddiṣṭa*). The statement "By proximity to virtuous conditions...

it is called Nirvāṇa" explains the empty Tathāgatagarbha. The meaning is that the expressive wisdom (*abhilāpaka-jñāna*) is termed "expedient means" (*upāya*) in relation to the realized principle (*adhigama-tattva*).
The manifestation of realization through these expedient means is termed "Nirvāṇa. This is its essential nature (*svabhāva*).
It is not non-empty, because it is the nature of emptiness manifested by means of emptiness. First: the nature of afflictions is false and unreal, which is called "emptiness";

the severance of afflictions is called "the emptiness that serves as the cause for emptiness. When one realizes true suchness (*tathatā*) based on this emptiness, true suchness is also called the "empty tathāgatagarbha.

Second: furthermore, it is the nature of emptiness with respect to the principle of the two kinds of selflessness (*anātman*). Since persons and phenomena are fundamentally non-existent, [this] is true suchness.
It is the nature of the emptiness of intrinsic nature; therefore, it is also called the "empty Tathāgatagarbha.
Regarding the statement that its essence is not empty: [the questioner] asks, "If the conditioned and unconditioned are designated as having a 'real essence,' why is it called empty?
The answer in the Commentary states: "Regarding the essence of the name," and so forth.
Regarding the meaning of the state of being obscured by afflictions (up to its nature as a cause): this explains the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*.

It refers to the essence of *tathatā* (suchness); because it is not false or deceptive, it is called "non-empty. Because it is hidden within the afflictions, its very substance is termed a "garbha" (womb/storehouse).
It takes that which is hidden within as *tathatā* (Suchness); thus, it is called a "storehouse" (*garbha*). Question: Why is *tathatā* called a storehouse? Answer:

Afflictions (*kleśa*) act as the concealer, while the principle of *tathatā* is that which is concealed; this is the *tathāgatagarbha*. Second, it is called a storehouse in the sense of being a causal nature (*hetubhāva*).
The untainted seeds (*anāsravabīja*) and the *tathatā* while still enveloped in afflictions are termed the "storehouse of causal nature. This very [tathatā] while enveloped in afflictions...
It is no different from the *tathatā* that has emerged from bondage; the *tathatā* that has emerged from bondage is precisely this *tathatā* while in bondage.
It is able to manifest the *dharmakāya* of the myriad natures within the fruit. As for the *dharmakāya*, it is called a "treasury" (*garbha*) for two reasons:

first, because it is that which is manifested; second, because it is that which manifests. Question: Why is the essence of *nirvāṇa* called the "causal nature"? Answer: Because it is the nature within the cause.

It is called the "nature as cause" (*hetutva*). Furthermore, this nirvāṇa is without cause or effect; yet, because it can act as a cause for causes and effects, and because it is the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*), it is the nature of the causal stage.
This is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive) compound. Second, it is called the "nature as the cause of realization" (*pariniṣpanna-hetutva*); thus it is named the "nature as cause.
The untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) serve as the cause for the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*); it is also named the "Treasury of the Nature as Cause" (*hetutva-garbha*).
Regarding the statement "this very dharmakāya, etc.," the intended meaning is that this very dharmakāya is neither empty nor existent. Based on these two senses, it is described as empty;
yet its emptiness differs from the previous designation of the afflictions as empty, because the practitioner contemplates those persons and phenomena.

Second, it is the emptiness of the principle of universal imagination (*parikalpita-śūnyatā-tattva*). Because this [emptiness] is revealed by means of that [principle], it is described as "the emptiness of the essence" (*svabhāva-śūnya*) rather than "non-empty.
In Sanskrit, it is called *śūnyatā*. Such emptiness is the nature of the two types of emptiness; it is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (possessive compound).
Regarding the term *Dāṭhika* (pronounced with the initial *d* as *tiáo*): this is raised as a metaphor. Long ago, there was an elder named Dāṭhika who possessed great wealth;
however, he was deeply stingy by nature. During his lifetime, he buried gold beneath a wooden block used for pounding grain. After he died, he was reborn as a dog in that very same household.
Due to the latent causes of his past miserliness, he would lie beside the block; none of the family members, whether young or old, dared to disturb him.
Approaching, the Buddha knew that the elder’s faculties were ripe, so he went to his gate and called out, "Dāgineyya! Dāgineyya! Hearing this, the dog leaped for joy and ran before the Buddha.
The Tathāgata comforted him, while the family members looked on in amazement. The Buddha explained the reason for this: beneath the threshing floor, they had unearthed a hidden treasure of gold;
only then did they realize that their dog was none other than their venerable master. This has two meanings. First, because of...

Finding gold underground reveals the *kuntapitaka* (a type of weapon); this is like the father of the aforementioned person who, by severing the afflictions (*kleśa*), reveals the Tathāgatagarbha-nature within his own body.
Gold represents the afflictions; the dog is a metaphor for the Buddha-nature; and digging for treasure is a metaphor for severing the afflictions.

The second [master] says: "The dog illustrates afflictions (*kleśa*), while the gold is a metaphor for the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*). Because of that dog, one comes to know that there is treasure beneath the ground;

likewise, by severing afflictions, one manifests the *tathāgatagarbha* within oneself. Mou says: "If one follows the commentary (*shu*), it appears that the gold is a metaphor for afflictions and the *daitya* (the dog) illustrates the Buddha-nature.
It is because of digging up the treasure that one finally realizes the dog was one's father in a previous life."

It is only through the severing of afflictions (*kleśa*) that the Buddha-nature within the body is revealed. Just as goodness cannot be manifested without evil, so too is the subsequent understanding of "good" and "conformity.

It is because one knows gold by means of the dog, and because the Buddha-nature is revealed by means of afflictions, that it is called the "Treasury of Emptiness" (this is a re-examination of the *ālayavijñāna* and the name "treasury" in relation to afflictions).
Because the seeds of those four wisdoms and suchness (*tathatā*) are named the "treasury," the meaning of "gold" is ultimate.

It is accomplished; it is not further realized (the following clarifies the gateway of the virtues of cultivating the causes through teaching). Because it takes the *ālayavijñāna* and the afflictions as its conditions, it is called "store" (*garbha*).
The characteristics and the virtues of the teaching are therefore explained again in detail.
Regarding the mention of the *ālayavijñāna* and so forth: both of these two scriptural authorities possess both scriptural evidence (*āgama*) and logical reasoning (*yukti*).

Question: Why is *tathatā* (suchness) and the untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) called a "store" (*garbha* or *ālaya*)? And how can unwholesome phenomena (*akuśala-dharma*) be called a "store"? Answer: As it says in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*:

"That which has not yet been attained is called the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). [The commentary] *Shè* (攝) states: "Wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-dharma*) are of three kinds: first, the tainted (*sāsrava*); second, the untainted (*anāsrava*); third, the... [text ends].
Among the outflows (*āsrava*), there are two: first, the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); second, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

The conditioned refers to the non-empty Tathāgatagarbha and the four wisdoms of enlightenment (*bodhi*) mentioned in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*. The unconditioned refers to the non-empty Tathāgatagarbha mentioned in the *Śrīmālādevī Siṃhanāda Sūtra* (the aforementioned untainted dharmas).
Question: It may be so for untainted wholesome dharmas; however, how can one speak of the Buddha in relation to tainted wholesome dharmas?

[Question on] Nature (*dhātu*). The *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) answers: Within the stage of application (*prayoga*), those contaminated wholesome dharmas that accord with the arising of the truth of the Path of Seeing are called the "cause of Buddha-nature.

Because one achieves and attains uncontaminated noble wisdom through the cultivation of contaminated [practices] within that stage of application, these contaminated wholesome dharmas receive the name "Buddha-nature.
[Question: If it is thus for contaminated wholesome dharmas, why is it not so for contaminated unwholesome [dharmas]?
Is the Dharma also called Buddha-nature? The answer states: "The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says...
Regarding the phrase "the false body (*pseu-shen*) and so forth," the *Jianyao* states: "The view of a transitory collection (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) is translated as 'false body.

The Sautrāntika school calls it 'false,' referring to one's own lineage (*gotra*). The Sarvāstivāda school calls it 'the body of existence' (*satkāya*). According to the Mahāyāna, it is called 'transmigration' within the three realms."
The body is empty, false, and unreal; it is called a "false body. Within the seeds of this very false body, there exists the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha;
therefore, it is called "Buddha," just as gold exists within ore.

Regarding the "seven stations of consciousness" (*vijñāna-sthiti*): that which has not yet established itself in the desire realm seeks to establish itself; having established itself, it does not wish to depart from this—this is the characteristic of consciousness.
Within the three miserable realms (*durgati*), suffering is abundant and joy is scarce; these are detrimental to consciousness, and consciousness does not find pleasure in dwelling there.

Ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), and noble ones (*ārya*) are all born there together. As for ordinary beings being born there, they reach the Heaven of the Signless (*asaṃjñisattva*) within the fourth dhyāna. First.

This is the dwelling place of ordinary worldlings and non-Buddhists, where both [the coarse and subtle] forms of mental perception are extinguished. If it is a noble one (*ārya*), they reach the fourth dhyāna and are born in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens;
most of these are *anāgāmins* of fixed nature who turn their backs on birth and death, seeking to realize *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
Therefore, consciousness does not delight in abiding in the fourth dhyāna. "One body with diverse perceptions" refers to the differences in joy and sorrow among humans and devas in the desire realm.

The distinction of physical form (*kāya-vibhāga*). In the three southern continents, physical forms are unequal; this is called "difference of body" (*kāya-nānātva*). Mental conceptions and perceptions differ;
this is called "difference of perception" (*saṃjñā-nānātva*). Among the six classes of desire-realm devas, the sizes of their physical forms differ; this is called "difference of body.

When a long-established *devaputra* manifests the five signs of decline, he experiences intense suffering, whereas a newly born *devaputra* experiences pleasure; this is called "difference of perception. Second, difference of body with unity of perception (*kāya-nānātva-saṃjñā-ekatva*).
This refers to the beginning of the kalpa of formation (*vivartakalpa*), when Brahmā alone dwelt there. Later, the Brahmā-purohitas and Brahmapārṣadyas were born.
Brahmā thought, "I have produced them," while they thought, "We have been born from him. This shared perception is called "sameness of perception" (*saṃjñā-ekatva*).

As for "difference of body" (*kāya-nānātva*): Brahmā’s body is superior, while the bodies of the others are inferior. Thus, there is "sameness of perception" and "difference of body. In the second dhyāna, the bodies are large.
There is one type of body and one name-body. When a newly born deva sees the fire below and is struck with fear, an elder deva knows that it will not reach him and is not afraid;
thus their perceptions (*saṃjñā*) differ. There are four cases where there is one body and one perception:

this refers to the third dhyāna, where the physical form is of one kind, the name-body is one, and the shared experience of bliss constitutes one perception. This is further augmented by the spheres of infinite space, infinite consciousness, and nothingness.
The *Abhidharmakośakārikā* states: "Those with different bodies and different perceptions; those with different bodies and one perception; the reverse of these, with one body and one perception;

and the three lower [realms] of the formless realm—therefore, there are seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*). The others are not [stations] because they involve impairment. These stations of consciousness must necessarily contain the seeds of the *ālayavijñāna*.
Therefore, desire, hatred, and delusion, as well as the ten unwholesome paths of action, constitute the seeds of the Tathāgata."

Regarding this, the *Mahāvyūha-śāstra* provides two interpretations. First, it is said that because it is precisely when afflictions (*kleśa*) are [realized as] the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*) that the latter is manifested, afflictions are spoken of as the seeds of the Tathāgata. Second, afflictions are the dependent and the Buddha-nature is the basis;
by referring to the dependent afflictions in terms of their basis, afflictions are also called the seeds of the Tathāgata. Question: Are wholesome dharmas not [seeds]?
"Wholesome dharmas are collectively termed the lineage of the Tathāgata. I do not yet know whether indeterminate dharmas constitute the lineage of the Tathāgata. The answer is:
"It is precisely the ālayavijñāna; it is indeterminate."

The phrase "the aforementioned Bodhi" refers to the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*. The Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) arises through cultivation; the cultivation of mindfulness gives rise to its manifest activity, thereby perfecting the Reward Body.
Mou states: the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom constitutes the self-enjoyment body; the Wisdom of Equality constitutes the other-enjoyment body;
and the Wondrous Wisdom, within both pure and impure lands, preaches the Dharma to sever doubts and rains down the great rain of the Dharma.

Regarding the statement that "the cultivation and manifestation of the dharmakāya" refers to the realization attained through the severance of afflictions, this is called cultivation and manifestation. Muni says:

This is precisely the fruit of the two-fold transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) at the stage of Buddhahood. The *mahāprajñā* that constantly illuminates the dharmakāya is the cause of realization, and that which is realized is the fruit;

therefore, it is said to be "the cause of realization and the realization itself. The arising of the uncontaminated seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) into their active manifestation (*samudācāra*) is the cause of production.
That which is produced is the fruit. This means that the seeds of the four wisdoms of bodhi produce the manifest activity (*pravṛtti*) of the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*).
It is precisely this manifest activity that serves as the cause for the realization of the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), acting as the "cause of realization" (*sākṣātkāra-hetu*).

Furthermore, these very seeds of the self-enjoyment body act as the cause for the production of the manifest activity, acting as the "cause of production" (*janana-hetu*). Therefore, it is said that they are "produced by the cause of production."
Regarding the statement that it is attained through the cultivation of causes based on the teachings: "Teachings" refers to the two types of teachings, namely the *Laṅkāvatāra* and the *Śrīmālādevī*.

"Cultivation" means the generation of the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) through practice and the manifestation of the Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*) through practice; this is termed "cultivation. "Causes" refers to the cause of realization and the cause of generation; thus, it is called "teaching."
Cultivating the cause is the means of attainment; the cause itself is the attainment.

Regarding the statement that there are four [sections] within the preceding treasury: the first two treasuries concern the cause and fruit of the *saṃbhogakāya*, which correspond to the aforementioned *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*;

the latter two treasuries concern the cause and fruit of the *dharmakāya*, which correspond to the aforementioned *Śrīmālādevī Siṃhanāda Sūtra*. These two texts have been brought here and divided into four types.

This refers to the "son" (the *tathāgata-garbha*). As for the statement that it is "able to contain and store," this connects back to the previously mentioned *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, where the *ālaya-vijñāna* is named for its capacity to contain and store.
This "store" (*garbha*) is like a treasury; the untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) rely upon the eighth consciousness, just as husked barley and the like [rely upon their sheaths].

Regarding the phrase "capable of producing the treasury of virtues": this refers to the aforementioned *Laṅkāvatāra*, which states that the complete permeation (*vāsanā*) and so forth are the untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*);
these are called "capable of producing. "Virtues" refers to the four wisdoms (*catur-jñāna*), which are the resultant merits produced by those seeds.

The untainted seeds within the causal stage are stored and concealed within the eighth consciousness; thus, they are called the "treasury" (*kośa*) of its own essence. Furthermore, they contain the manifestation of the four wisdoms of enlightenment (*bodhi*).

"Practice" is named "storehouse. This is the distinction between the two. Because the cause can produce the fruit of those meritorious qualities, it is the *svasaṃbhoga-kāya* (self-enjoyment reward body).
As for the statement "capable of concealing," this concludes the preceding section on Śrīmālā; whether separated, liberated, severed, or distinct, it conceals [the nature].
Because it is the truth, it is called "concealment" (*saṃvṛti*).
Regarding the statement that afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth are like earth covering an object: the earth is the concealer, while weight and so forth are the concealed;
the afflictions are the concealer, and the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*) is the concealed.

Regarding the statement "that which can manifest virtue": this summarizes the preceding [passages] from the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* such as "not separate," "not detached," "not severed," and "not different. Question:

Since it is said that severing afflictions manifests the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), this already contains the sense of "that which is manifested" (*lakṣya*). How, then, can it be called "that which can manifest" (*lakṣaka*)? Answer:

One explanation states that within the state of fruition, True Suchness (*tathatā*) emerging from its entanglements is the "manifestor," while the sands-of-the-Ganges virtues are the "manifested. Therefore, it is called the Dharma... [text ends].
The second [position] states: that which exists within the causal stage—the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha* enveloped by adventitious defilements—is called the "manifestor";
that which exists at the resultant stage—the empty *tathāgatagarbha*—is the "manifested."

Regarding the statement "it is like the nature of gold": just as swords, bracelets, and so forth are only manifested through gold, so too, although the myriad virtues are distinct, they are manifested only through the Dharmakāya.
All noble ones and sages possess their distinctions by virtue of the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). When compared with afflictions (*kleśa*), [the virtues] are...

In reality, it is that which is manifested; however, because it is now viewed as being identical to the virtues, it is called "that which manifests. This is because, having emerged from the entanglements, it is able to manifest the myriad virtues, just as gold extracted from ore is able to manifest [the form of] a vessel.
Regarding the term "great state" (*mahāpada*): according to the treatises, one realizes Great Nirvāṇa by severing the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) that cause the continuity of rebirth;

one realizes Great Bodhi by severing the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that hinder understanding. Although both obstructions are severed to manifest these two fruits, this is true in principle for both.
How could those afflictions not obstruct Bodhi? One should know that the sacred teachings rely upon their predominant functions.

This is explained according to the superior teaching; therefore, it is called the "great stage. The meaning is that at the time of attaining bodhi, one must also sever the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), and at the time of attaining nirvāṇa, one must likewise sever the afflictive obstructions.

Regarding the statement that "the Buddhas appear in the world" [up to] "that which is attained": Question: Since the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) does not initiate karma, how can it be said to initiate karma and thereby summon its fruit?
Answer: There are three explanations. First, the karma initiated by the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*) is itself the cognitive hindrance.

Second, it is said that Bodhisattvas on the first stage (*bhūmi*) may commit transgressions of the three types of action; this delusion is the cognitive hindrance, which initiates what is experienced [as retribution].

The transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) does not attain brilliance or mastery. Thirdly, it is said: precisely because it is a transformation body, karma is also termed the "outflow" (*paryavasthāna*) of the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

This is because incomplete conceptualization serves as the causal support for karma; thus, from the perspective of its capacity to provide assistance, the seeds of karma—which are themselves cognitive obscurations—are also termed the "outflow of karma.
The fruit obtained therefrom is the transformation body (the former [explanation] clarifies that one thereby attains purity).

Regarding the phrase "knowing and seeing based on this" (as explained in the *Shu*), the term "opening" refers to the arising [of bodhi] and so forth. Before the Buddha appeared in the world, bodhi did not arise and nirvāṇa was not manifested or realized;
this is called being "closed and unopened. Now that the Buddha has appeared in the world, he desires to cause sentient beings to sever the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and realize nirvāṇa.
[The Buddha] severs the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and gives birth to bodhi; this is called "opening the opening" of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*).
Question: Of what kind of person does this knowledge and vision open within the body? Answer: This is merely a general description praising the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) of the Buddha's person.

Śāriputra and others truly give rise to a mind of joyful aspiration toward the Dharma-body, bodhi, nirvāṇa, and the *śarīra*. If Śāriputra joyfully aspires toward the opening of the Buddha’s vision, [he shall attain it].

Nirvana. To speak specifically of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*): if one joyfully aspires toward the Bodhi within the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, this is specifically called the awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Regarding the statement "excluding these two," there is only Bodhi and Nirvana, and no other dharmas; therefore, it is called "without remainder" (*anupadhiśeṣa*).
Regarding that which surpasses the two dharmas: bodhi surpasses all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), and nirvāṇa surpasses all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
Within these two dharmas, there is nothing further superior; therefore, it is called "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*). As stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, fascicle 29:
"To be mindful of by the Buddhas, to increase the roots of goodness of the Buddhas, to abide in the vows of the Buddhas, and to perform the deeds of the Buddhas. According to this:

This is to cultivate within one's own person the roots of goodness for attaining Buddhahood. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* speaks of cultivating the Buddha’s roots of goodness; it is to cultivate the dharmas of the roots of goodness within one's own person.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says, "To open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision," which means to open the knowledge and vision within one's own person.

Regarding the term "demonstration" (*śāsanam*): "demonstration" means pointing out. Previously, when praising *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*, Śāriputra gave rise to a mind of longing and admiration, thinking that these did not exist within his own person.

It was for this reason that the Buddha pointed back to what had been said before, stating that the vehicles of the three *yānas* are equal and that all equally possess this nature. Therefore, "demonstration" carries the sense of "sameness."
Regarding the statement "it is like a milch cow" up to "there is no distinction": ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are like milk that has not yet been milked, where blood and milk are mixed together;
*śrāvakas* are like milk that has been milked and is white; *pratyekabuddhas* are like curd; and lesser *bodhisattvas* are like fresh butter (*navanīta*).
The Great Bodhisattvas are like clarified butter (*sarpis*), and the Buddhas are like the finest cream (*maṇḍa*). What is cited here in this commentary represents only the general meaning;

it intends to express their shared significance and does not further differentiate the various stages. Just as one takes the white color of milk while the colors of the cows differ, so too do the sentient beings of the Three Vehicles and Five Vehicles each have their distinctions, yet the Buddha-nature is one.
This concludes the section on "Subsuming Questions and Opening the Buddha’s Knowledge and Vision."

Question: How does the *tathatā* (suchness) within the "opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision" differ from the *tathatā* within the "partial manifestation of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision"? Answer:

The *tathatā* within the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is stainless (*vimala*), whereas this *tathatā* within the partial manifestation of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is with-outflow (*sāsrava*).

This is naturally understood from the commentary on the section following "opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision," where the word "pure" (*viśuddha*) appears; thus it is said to be stainless. As for the other three [phrases], they are not.

To speak of "purity" would imply that the Buddha’s knowledge and vision possess defilement. According to the intent of the commentary (*shu*), this is merely a matter of the general and the specific regarding the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
the phrase "opening and revealing both" refers to taking the Dharma-body principle from within the opening of the Buddha and distinguishing it separately.
Therefore, it is incorrect to categorize the three fruits as entering the cause and further divide them into "with defilement" and "without defilement."

Regarding the statement that "the three awakenings do not know the meaning," the sūtra speaks of awakening as knowing the meaning. When the masters of the śāstras comment on the sūtra, they say that awakening does not know the meaning.
Why is there this discrepancy? Answer: What the sūtra says refers to correctly knowing the meaning; it is not that one does not know the meaning at all.
When the śāstra says "does not know," it is citing the state of the dharmas at the time of awakening: that which is awakened to today was previously unknown.
To realize today that which was not known in the past is called "awakening. One awakens to what was previously unknown.

Furthermore, within the bodies of those of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas), there exist innate, untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*). Previously, these followers of the Two Vehicles believed their own persons were forever devoid of the Buddha’s portion;

therefore, they spoke of what is not the locus of reality as being the locus of reality. The locus of reality is precisely the awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddha-jñāna-darśana*), which they did not possess in the past.
To know the Dharma. That which was not realized in former days is realized today; therefore, it is said that "one who has awakened does not know" [in the conventional sense].
As for the phrase "it is as if there were a person," this refers to the three types of śrāvakas, using them as a metaphor for one's own person. "A close friend" [refers to...].
These are none other than the sixteen princes who were his true and virtuous friends. Hearing the Mahāyāna is their home.
