third, the self is both finite and infinite; fourth, the self is neither finite nor infinite. Third set: first, the self is eternal; second, [the self is non-eternal].
1. The self is impermanent; 2. the self is permanent; 3. the self is both permanent and impermanent; 4. the self is neither permanent nor impermanent.

These four [positions] constitute twelve [when applied to each aggregate]. Since it is thus for the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), each of the remaining four aggregates likewise has twelve propositions. Thus, the five aggregates together comprise sixty [propositions].
When combined with the two types of external self-theories, they constitute the sixty-two views (*dvāṣaṣṭidṛṣṭi*).
Regarding the statement "the spirit and the self": the spirit is that which grasps, and the self is that which is grasped; these two are distinct from one another.
Thus, they constitute two types (as distinguished in the preceding section).
Regarding the statement "due to the grasping at a self-entity" (*ātman*): to speak briefly, the self-entity is precisely the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

Having grasped that the body possesses a self and given rise to the view of a self, one subsequently gives rise to the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). Based upon these two views—extremism and false views—one takes them as the root and gives rise to the sixty-two views.
Among these, the attachment to views and the attachment to precepts and rituals are merely their attendants; they do not directly produce the [sixty-two] views themselves.
These are the two views.

Regarding the phrase "the subsequent views and so forth," the treatise states: fourth is the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*). This refers to clinging to various views and their underlying aggregates as being supreme, [thinking] they can bring about purification;
its function is to serve as the basis for all conflict. Fifth is the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), which refers to...

Its function is to serve as the basis for fruitless exertion, consisting in the grasping of views, ascetic rules and observances, and their underlying aggregates as supreme and capable of bringing about purification.

Regarding the phrase "clinging to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and so forth: according to the treatise, this refers to the grasping (*upādāna*) and its supporting aggregates (*skandha*). It consists of the five aggregates by nature, including the concomitants of views and precepts, as well as their retinues such as form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*).

Regarding the statement "clinging to these false dharmas" (*mṛṣā-dharma*), if one follows the first interpretation, false dharmas refer exclusively to the view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*);
that is, the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīla-vrata-parāmarśa*) is the cause from which the view-grasping arises, and the remaining afflictions (*kleśa*) are produced.
If one follows the second interpretation, false dharmas refer to one and a half verses, which specifically clarify the arising of the five views.
Regarding the phrase "relying on one's own pride" (*māna*): "to rely" (*shi*) means to take as a basis; "to boast" (*jing*)—Zheng says that boasting refers to self-importance;
"to exaggerate" (*kuada*) refers to grandiloquent speech; and "to despise" (*mie*) means to treat others with contempt.

Regarding the phrase "one who is thus possessed by such craving": the two characters for "craving" (*tanyù*) conclude the preceding one and a half lines of scripture concerning being submerged in the five desires while still dwelling amidst worldly dust.

The two characters for "clinging to what is heterodox" (*zhéxié*) conclude the preceding two and a half stanzas, which describe seeking a false way out of suffering through erroneous study and confused practice;
therefore, this is not the same as the seeking that occurred forty years ago when he requested the Buddha to reveal his knowledge and vision, which he had not yet attained.

Those living at home are attached to desires; those who have left the home life are heterodox practitioners who confuse themselves with erroneous learning. As the Sūtra says, "By means of the causes and conditions of various desires," and so forth—this refers to the four types of practice.

What are called the "four practices of close approach" (*catvāri upaniṣad-gatāni*) are precisely the four means of integration (*catvāri saṃgraha-vastūni*). Because they belong to the Tathāgata, the four practices of close approach belong [to him].
Regarding sentient beings: first, because the Buddha practices giving, sentient beings draw near to him as a virtuous friend;
second, because of his kind speech, they hear the sublime Dharma; third, because of his beneficial conduct, they reflect upon it according to principle; and fourth, because of his purposeful deeds.

Practice according to what has been taught. Furthermore, among the four [types of wisdom], the first produces merit, while the latter three produce knowledge. Within knowledge, there are three divisions:
first, hearing; second, reflection; and third, the wisdom of cultivation.
Regarding the statement that there are no four types of wisdom arising from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*): when one listens to the True Dharma, wisdom arising from hearing is the primary cause.

Since this primary cause—wisdom arising from hearing—is absent, the two other forms of wisdom, those arising from reflection (*cintāmayī*) and cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī*), cannot be attained either. Now, with these four practices lacking, the three wisdoms do not arise.
Such evil persons are extremely difficult to deliver.

Regarding the phrase "I have established skillful means for them": teaching the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) during the forty years prior is called "establishing skillful means," as it serves as a preparatory means for the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the "path that exhausts suffering": this refers to *nirvāṇa with remainder*, wherein the suffering of the segmented [birth-and-death] (*paricchinna-duḥkha*) has been stilled;

thus it is termed the "path that exhausts suffering. As for the expression "because it is thus," these two characters represent the correct interpretation within the sūtra. Question: Since there is still a body that serves as the basis for suffering...
What is meant by "nirvāṇa as the cessation of suffering"? Answer: Although there remains subtle suffering because its basis has not yet been extinguished, the obstacles are forever stilled;
therefore, it is called nirvāṇa.

When the Sūtra says, "Although I have spoken of nirvāṇa," and so forth, this refers to the teaching of the *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder) of the Hīnayāna given during the forty years [of his ministry].
Furthermore, to say that this is not true cessation means it is not true cessation, because there remains the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) which has not yet been eternally extinguished.
Question: What is called true cessation? Answer: All phenomena, from the very beginning, have always been characterized by quiescence.

Regarding the scriptural passage beginning with "The sons of the Buddha, having practiced the path," etc.: anyone who is able to turn their mind toward the Great Vehicle is entirely a cause for Buddhahood.

Based on those whose faculties have matured in the Mahāyāna and who turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle to sever the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), it is said they will become Buddhas in a future life; this is designated by the name they will eventually bear.
Regarding the statement "exhorting the relinquishing of liberation, etc.," the intended meaning is to cause one to attain the Buddha-fruit, which is the Dharma-body and the true principle (*tattva*).

This statement exhorts the relinquishing of that grasping mind; it does not mean relinquishing the essence of the *nirvāṇa* of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). As the treatise states:

"The fruit of the two-fold transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) attained by the two vehicles merely consists in the permanent separation from the fetters of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*); because it lacks the sublime qualities [of a Buddha], it is called the 'body of liberation' (*vimukti-kāya*). I...
The two fruits attained by the Honored Muni are eternally free from the two obstacles and are also called the Dharma-body,
because they are adorned with immeasurable and boundless great qualities such as the powers and fearlessnesses.
Regarding the statement "the Dharma is from beginningless time," etc., this explains that all phenomena have been so from the very outset, thereby revealing the truth of the *dharmakāya*.
From beginningless time, its self-nature has been quiescent; this is precisely the primordially pure *parinirvāṇa* by nature.
Its essence is not something newly arisen, for it has existed from the beginning; it is thus the "Jewel Repository" (*ratnasthāna*) and constitutes true cessation (*nirodha*).

Regarding the phrase "having already practiced the path": the path is itself wisdom (*jñāna*). Within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), one repeatedly cultivates that path; this is called "having already practiced the path.

One will become a Buddha in a future life, realizing the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). This is the realization of the principle of the *dharmakāya*, the dharma of the inherently quiescent nature.
Regarding the phrase "My original wisdom," etc., this refers to the skillful means (*upāya*) within the Tathāgata’s wisdom. It explains the two lines of scripture, "I possess skillful means," etc.;
it is not that the preceding and succeeding [teachings] of the Two Vehicles are themselves the skillful means of the Mahāyāna.

Herein, the Dharma of the Two Vehicles taught during the forty years prior is cited, while the Dharma of the One Vehicle was taught at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Taking these four...
The Dharma ten years ago was as follows: at the assembly of the Lotus Sūtra, the One Vehicle was established in a single place and designated as the "Three Vehicles.
These Three Vehicles are all skillful means for attaining Buddhahood in the future.
The Sūtra states: "Now, in this great assembly... there are no followers of the two vehicles. This means that it is not only I who alone preach the One Vehicle;
all Buddhas preach the One Vehicle. If they did not preach the One Vehicle, then they would not first employ provisional means and subsequently reveal the ultimate reality.

Since it is taught that the provisional comes first and the real follows, it is clearly known that this explains the One Vehicle. If one were to teach only the initial provisional without teaching the real, the words of the Buddhas would differ;
however, since the provisional is taught and the real must necessarily be taught, the words of the Buddhas do not differ. This holds true for the Buddhas of the past and the Buddhas of the future.
"To ultimately cause all sentient beings to attain all-knowledge—this statement is without discrepancy. Question:
Since the verse states that "doubts are removed," in which part of the prose commentary (longxing) does this removal of doubt occur? Answer: The prose commentary says: "Śāriputra..."
"You all should with one mind believe, understand, accept, and uphold the Buddha’s words. The words of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are without falsehood.

There is no other vehicle; there is only the Single Buddha Vehicle. This is identical to that [previous teaching]. Since you have not yet reached the stage of practice, I urge you not to give rise to doubt;
this is precisely the removal of doubt. Therefore, the Commentator says: "Since it is said that there is only one [vehicle]," and so forth.
Regarding the scriptural passage mentioning "devas, humans, and so forth": according to the first interpretation, "the multitudes of sentient beings" refers to those of indeterminate nature.

According to the second interpretation, it is an immediate statement using diverse skillful means (*upāya*). If one follows the first interpretation, "diverse" refers to the skillful means; that is, the initial is provisional (*prajñapti*) and the subsequent is real (*tattva*).

If one follows the latter interpretation, it differs from that preparatory means (*upāya*); it refers to the sudden awakening (*tad-ekakṣaṇābhisambodhi*) taught as the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), analyzed according to the *tatpuruṣa* compound.

Regarding the former interpretation, which analyzes it as a *karmadhāraya*, [Master] Xiū says: "Those śrāvakas of indeterminate lineage (*aniyata-gotra*) who have turned their minds [toward the Mahāyāna] are called 'those of indeterminate lineage'. This refers to...

Regarding the gradual awakening to karma, those who speak of "fixed nature" do so because the bodhisattvas of sudden awakening have a fixed lineage within the Mahāyāna; there is no longer any admixture of the lineages of the two vehicles.
If it were for those of indeterminate nature, one would first teach the three vehicles and subsequently teach the one reality. If it were for...
Regarding the determination of the nature [of beings]: the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) is taught all at once, because there is no sequence of before and after.
As for the statement "by means of diverse skillful means" (*upāya*): now, for the sake of sudden awakening, the One Vehicle is taught directly; this is called "diverse skillful means.

It is called "diverse skillful means" because it differs from previous skillful means. Although the skillful means are one, they are distinct according to what is intended. Alternatively, it may be that the skillful means...

Because of the distinction between the great and the small: directly teaching the One Vehicle is called the "distinctive skillful means" (*upāya*), while teaching the Two Vehicles is called the "lesser skillful means.

Since provisional verbal teachings are used to elucidate the ultimate principle, and because there would be no way to manifest the principle without relying on verbal teachings, one knows that verbal teachings are the skillful means for manifesting the principle.
For this reason, the verbal teachings of the Mahāyāna are also termed "skillful means"; they are called "distinctive" because they differ from the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle.

Regarding "expedient means" (*upāya*): Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā states that teaching the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) all at once is what is distinct; teaching it all at once is "straightforward," while teaching it gradually is "expedient.

Now, when it says "distinct expedient means," this is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning that what is distinct is itself the expedient means. Alternatively, it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "distinct from that expedient means," where the term belongs to the possessor.
However, one must not say that the "capable of being distinct" is itself the expedient means; for the "capable of being distinct"—namely, the sudden teaching—is not the expedient means.

Therefore, the sutra says: "Directly abandoning the provisional means, he taught only the unsurpassed path. However, this does not mean that the means themselves are rejected as being different [from the goal], for this is a teaching of sudden realization.

Regarding the statement "aiding the manifestation of the One Vehicle": what is meant by "aiding the manifestation of the ultimate truth" (*paramārtha*)? The answer, as recorded by Jiguo, is that even causes can ultimately return to the Great [Vehicle];

thus it is called "aiding the manifestation of the ultimate truth. Because the provisional teachings of the Two Vehicles aid in manifesting the meaning of the One Vehicle, they are said to "aid the manifestation of the ultimate truth.
Subsequently, based on the Bodhisattva of Sudden Enlightenment, the interpretation of the Mahāyāna of Sudden Teaching is termed "different expedient means" (*upāya*).
This teaching differs from the Hīnayāna; it is distinct from the provisional teachings of the Hīnayāna and is thus termed "extraordinary skillful means" (*viśeṣopāya*).

Question: In what sense is the Mahāyāna called "skillful means"? Answer: The teaching that expresses [the truth] is the skillful means for elucidating the principle. It is through the teaching that the principle is expressed and revealed.
This is because it assists in manifesting the ultimate meaning of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).

The mention of "True Suchness" (*tathatā*) and so forth refers to the Bodhi of the four wisdoms. Since this pertains to the Sudden Teaching of the Mahāyāna, one cannot indiscriminately include the provisional teachings.

Regarding the scriptural statement that "meditative concentration (dhyāna) and wisdom (prajñā) are equal," the term "equal" (等) refers to internal equality and parity; it simply means that the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) are equal.

Furthermore, there is another interpretation of the term "equal," which includes the four means of attraction (catvāri saṃgrahavastūni) and the four immeasurables (catvāry apramāṇāni); the latter interpretation is superior.

Regarding the phrase "meeting the Buddha and hearing the Dharma," this clarifies that sentient beings meet past Buddhas and hear the Dharma, cultivating immeasurable dharma-gates and various practices;
these are termed "various merits. Planting various roots of goodness is termed the "cause of Buddhahood.

This sequence of guidance and reception also simultaneously indicates the goodness of a single youth, which must accumulate until it reaches the fruit of Buddhahood, Bodhi. There are those who do not cultivate merit and wisdom.

This meaning can also be understood in this way. Since it connects with the preceding discussion of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) and the four means of integration (*catuḥsaṃgrahavastu*), there is nothing therein that is not both merit and wisdom.

As for the phrase "there are those who are good yet rigid," this refers to goodness within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*); it is not goodness that accords with principle and benefits all beings. To distinguish this by means of the four logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*): first, there is that which is good but not pliant;
this refers to the followers of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*), who possess wisdom but lack the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Second, there is that which is pliant but... [text fragment].

1. Wholesome: This refers to ordinary worldlings who are bound by their attachment to wives and children; although they possess a heart of compassion, they lack the wholesome intention for application toward the world.
2. Both wholesome and supple: This is the mind of a bodhisattva. 3. Neither wholesome nor supple: This belongs to the followers of external paths.

Regarding the statement that "to accord with principle and benefit beings": those of the Two Vehicles accord with principle but do not benefit beings; ordinary worldlings benefit beings but do not accord with principle.

When they associate with others to eat meat and drink wine, they provide benefit to those people before them, yet later fall into hell. A Bodhisattva, however, both benefits beings and accords with principle.

Regarding the phrase "the latter text says 'merely,'" the question is: Why does one not practice wholesome deeds and cultivate a gentle mind while the Buddha is still alive, but instead do so after his parinirvāṇa?
The answer is: Because it is difficult for those living after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa to practice wholesome deeds and cultivate a gentle mind; therefore, this is specifically cited.

Furthermore, the practice of the six perfections is the general practice, whereas this cultivation of a wholesome and gentle mind is a specific practice; thus, these were not performed during the Buddha's lifetime.
[These practices] are not causes for Buddhahood because they were easy to cultivate during the lifetime of the Buddha.

Regarding the statement "following the six perfections as above": a question is raised concerning the preceding scriptural passage which states that during the lifetime of past Buddhas, sentient beings practiced the six perfections and thereby attained the Way of the Buddha;
yet after their parinirvāṇa, it is said that one should only practice wholesome and gentle thoughts, without mentioning the six perfections. Is this not [contradictory]?
[Question: Is practicing the six pāramitās after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa not also a cause for attaining Buddhahood? [Commentary] The sub-commentary answers:

According to the aforementioned six pāramitās, the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa represents the general practice (*sāmānya-caryā*), while cultivating a mind of gentleness and pliancy represents the specific practice (*viśeṣa-caryā*). By practicing this general practice, one also attains the Way of the Buddha;

it is not the case that one cannot attain Buddhahood by practicing the six pāramitās after his parinirvāṇa. Whether during his lifetime or after his passing, there are these two types: the general and the specific.
[These] practices are all causes for Buddhahood.
The statement that they are "adorned and polished with the eight treasures" (the character *ying* being pronounced *u-ding*) differs from the introductory chapter (*Xùpǐn*).

Furthermore, among the seven treasures, this [passage] lacks the coral and *maṇi* found there, while it lacks the crystal and *móguī* (rose quartz) found there; this also differs from the section on Avalokiteśvara below, which includes amber.

Regarding the statement in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* that the seven treasures number seven, this is because it distinguishes between lapis lazuli (*vaidūrya*) and pearls (*maṇi*), thereby forming seven treasures.

In this present sutra, since rose-colored gems (*musāragalva*) are mentioned, this indicates that lapis lazuli and pearls are combined into one. If lapis lazuli were [counted] as one [separate category], [the total would differ].
A single pearl immediately becomes the eight treasures. If lapis lazuli is combined with the pearl, they form a single lapis lazuli bead.
Furthermore, when rose quartz is added, they become the seven jewels.
Regarding what is called "red pearl": it is that which is spat out by red insects; it is named "red pearl" because its substance is red and it is a pearl.
Question: The sutra mentions only the seven treasures; how can the commentary categorize them as the eight rarities? Answer: Within the eight rarities, the seven treasures are included.
Regarding the term "intermediate colors between blue and white," this refers to the color azure. Red and white form vermilion; blue and yellow form green; red and black form purple.
These are all not primary colors. Blue, yellow, red, and white are the primary colors.
Regarding the statement that there are many types of agate: in Sanskrit it is called *aśmagarbha*, which is translated here as "thunderbolt-treasury" (*chǔ-zàng*) or "womb-treasury" (*tāi-zàng*).
It takes the sense of being firm and solid; because it resembles coral (*mǎnǎo*), and because it belongs to the category of jade, the character is written with the "jade" radical (*yù*).
Alternatively, as it may belong to the category of stone, it is written with the "stone" radical (*shí*).
Regarding the statement that "móguī" (玫瑰) is red in color: *huǒqízhū* (火齊珠) is simply another name for *móuguī*. The character *qí* is pronounced with the departing tone (*qùshēng*).
*Méilánggān* (玫琅玕) originates from Mount Kunlun. Question: Since *móuguī* is of one kind and is stone, what is the distinction between them? Answer:

If both superior and inferior qualities are described together in one place, it is called *méi*. If it is exclusively round and beautiful, it is called *guī*. This takes only the superior quality into account.
Regarding the term "Ekottara" (Increasing by One): there are four types—first, the Long; second, the Increasing; third, the Grouped; and fourth, the Miscellaneous.
Regarding the phrase "a stūpa never before erected": the fruit obtained from this is precisely Brahma-merit (*brahmapuṇya*).
Regarding the term "repairing" (*pu-chi*): if one repairs a temple that has fallen into ruin, there are two merits.
First, it causes the merit of the original founder of the temple to continue uninterrupted and increase ever further. Second, it causes one's own merit to likewise grow.
If one were to build a new temple from scratch, one would obtain only the merit of self-benefit, lacking the merit of benefiting others.

Regarding the phrase "the threefold harmony" (*trisaṃnipāta*): Question: Since the Noble One is already free from contention (*araṇa*), how can one speak of harmony? Answer: Jin says: It is merely said that there is harmony;
it is not that the disciples of the Noble One and the assembly of the Noble One are distinct from the harmony—the Noble One is himself the assembly.
On that day, Devadatta asked the Buddha for his own followers but did not obtain them; he then led five hundred foolish men away at night. After [the Buddha] had departed...
It shall be explained separately. Alternatively, these may all be ordinary bhikṣus who are disciples of the Noble Ones.

When it was asked, "How is it that the Noble One, the Aśaikṣa, is without dispute? [it was answered: "Just as King Aśoka extinguished the dispute, on that day the Noble One was in fact without dispute;
it was only Mahādeva who had the dispute, while the rest of the noble assembly were without dispute. Nevertheless, they persisted in their error, for originally...
This violates the teachings of the Tathāgata. Through such reconciliation, one cannot attain the merit of Brahma. There are two meanings of "reconciliation" (*saṃgha*):
first, the principle (*li*); second, the phenomenon (*shi*). Within the phenomenon, there are two types: first, when the Saṃgha has a dispute, one uses the principle to exhort and persuade them;
second, when the Saṃgha lacks food and intends to disperse, one provides food so that they may remain together.
Regarding the statement that the Buddha was first accomplished [as a king]: for this reason, after death he returned to become a Brahmā King.
Regarding the statement that he shall attain Bodhi: having brought forth the fruit of Brahmā-merit, the Buddha is also called a Brahmā King.
The Sūtra states that there may be those who erect stone shrines, just as a state maintains ancestral temples.
Those who wish to cause their descendants to flourish by enshrining the Buddha’s remains in a stūpa do so to increase the field of merit for sentient beings.
Regarding the "nine materials" and so forth: first, stone; second, sandalwood; third, *candana* (sinking water), which is agarwood; fourth, *kālānusāri* (muguka);
fifth, miscellaneous timber, referring to various types of wood; sixth, brick; seventh, tile; eighth, mud; and ninth, when these are mixed and fashioned into bricks or slabs to construct a stūpa.
The ninth [section] describes the construction of the foundation steps.
Regarding the term "lingmiao" (spiritual temple): according to the *Qieyun*, the character *zhào* (召) is pronounced as *guǎng* (廣). *Guǎng* here refers to its appearance.

Regarding the term *Baihūtong* (White Tiger Tong): in ancient times there was the White Tiger Hall (*Baihùdiàn*), where various worthy scholars were assembled within this hall to discuss and penetrate [the principles of governance].
He understood all characters. It is further said that this was a man surnamed Bái (White) and named Hǔ (Tiger), who also compiled the *Yùpiān* (Jade Lexicon).
Regarding the statement about piling sand to make a Buddha: when the Buddha was in the world, countless youths were playing with sand on the road, calling it flour;
or they would take ash and call it roasted grain powder (*mǎocháo*). Suddenly they encountered the Buddha coming, and the countless youths [raised] both hands...
He gathered sand and made it into flour and meal to offer to the World-Honored One. Out of compassion for his sincere devotion, the World-Honored One accepted it and departed after stroking his head.

By virtue of this meritorious retribution, he became an Iron-Wheel-Turning King. This refers to those who possess the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), have resolved their minds on enlightenment, and practice;
by making offerings, they all attain Buddhahood. The boy was then seven years old.

Regarding the phrase "not those who are ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and so forth": this excludes those without the spiritual lineage (*agotra*) and those with a fixed lineage (*niyatagotra*). It also excludes śrāvakas of fixed nature (*niyatabhūmi*).
Even if one were to make offerings to those of the lineage who have not yet resolved their minds for enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), they would not become Buddhas.

This is because ordinary persons act solely for their own sake, and those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) seek only their own fruition; therefore, making offerings to them does not result in Buddhahood.
The scripture states, "If a person acts for the sake of the Buddha," which refers to performing [the act]. It specifically means creating images of the Buddha.
The phrase "establishing various forms and images" refers to making Buddha images through painting, embroidery, wood, or clay.

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of seeking to become a Buddha," etc.: Question: What is the intention behind creating images of the Buddha? Answer: The commentary states, "for the sake of seeking to become a Buddha," etc. The meaning is twofold:
first, one creates Buddha images for the purpose of seeking to attain Buddhahood in the future; second, one creates Buddha images for the purpose of contemplating and honoring the Buddha.
For example, when the Buddha went to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to observe the rains retreat and preach the Dharma to his mother, at that time King Udayana...

Prince Wenshi, having already contemplated the Buddha, realized that since he lacked supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), he could not reach him directly. He therefore commissioned Qiaojin and Maudgalyāyana to ascend to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

There, they carved an image of the Tathāgata out of sandalwood. Upon beholding, gazing upon, and paying homage to it, the World-Honored One bestowed his response and gifts upon them. This concluded the matter.
After the summer retreat, [the Buddha] descended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven via the three jeweled stairways and returned to Jambudvīpa.
At that time, the sandalwood image also rose to meet him and pay homage to the World-Honored One. The World-Honored One stroked its head and bestowed a prophecy:
"In a future age, you shall perform extensive meritorious deeds for the sake of sentient beings. From this, the teaching of the image arose.

The phrase "furthermore it is said" constitutes the second interpretation. If a person, for the sake of the Buddha (the character "佛" is pronounced with a departing tone), establishes various images—including those of the Buddha, Vajrapāṇi, the Lion, and so forth—all of these are for the sake of the Buddha.
Regarding the phrase "life after life": because he fashioned an image, his physical appearance became upright and handsome; by this cause, he attained eyes that were clear and bright.
Regarding the phrase "born later in the Brahma Heaven": it praises how, over a long duration of time, he established [merit] throughout ten *kalpas*, or twenty *kalpas*.
One kalpa refers to the Brahmakāyika heaven; alternatively, forty kalpas constitute one kalpa, or sixty kalpas constitute one kalpa, as appropriate in each case.
Regarding the statement "ten times the four continents," since it mentions the great ocean of the four continents, this refers to the eighth [ocean], the salt sea.

Regarding the "ocean," it does not refer to the preceding seven [categories]. There are two meanings: first, because one creates images in this life, through the power of habitual tendencies from past lives, one further creates merit by frequently casting images and transcribing scriptures.
These exceed the ten-fold multiples of the great oceans and the four continents;

taking what is currently small as the cause, one creates even more later, such that the number of items becomes vast. Second, within the body, [the quantity of] these exceeds that of the great oceans and the four continents.
"Ten accompaniments.
Regarding the statement that there are ten items in two verses: first, the seven treasures; second, brass; third, red and white copper; fourth, bronze; fifth, lead.
Sixth, tin; seventh, iron; eighth, wood; ninth, clay; tenth, lacquer-cloth. These ten materials are used to fashion a Buddha image.
Regarding their classification: red copper and white copper both belong to the category of copper and are thus combined.
If red and white copper were grouped as one, then silver would differ from tin and must therefore be listed separately. If lead and tin were considered similar and thus combined into one, then...
"Opening" refers to red and white copper. "Glue, lacquer, and cloth" are used together as one unit;
they are not opened separately. Regarding lead and tin, there are two explanations: first, that lead and tin are of the same category and thus combined; second, that they are distinct.
Between silver and lead, some say that the superior is silver, the inferior is lead, and that which is neither superior nor inferior is tin. The *Shangshu* (Book of Documents) says: "Qing..."
The term "zhou" (洲) refers to lead. A question is raised: *The Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* states that one is not permitted to use glue to make images; how is this [the present usage] justified?

The answer is twofold: first, it is said that animal-hide glue is prohibited, whereas wood-glue alone is permitted. Second, because the prohibitions and allowances differ, there is no fault in using it.
Regarding the sūtra’s statement that the marks are "adorned by a hundred merits": because one cultivates a hundred merits during the causal stage, these serve as the adornment;
since they induce these marks, the marks are what is adorned. Among the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks, there are both general and specific causes. If it refers to the general cause:

The six perfections are the myriad practices. If these were distinct causes, then regarding the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks, for each mark cultivated, it is accompanied by the adornment of a hundred merits.
The *Abhidharmakośa* asks: "What is the nature of the cultivation of sublime karma? The verse states:

"A male of Jambudvīpa, facing the Buddha, [cultivates] that which is produced by the thought of the Buddha; over the remaining hundred kalpas, one cultivates each [mark], adorned by a hundred merits. The prose commentary [explains this].

[Answer: It is explained that the cultivation of the karma for the primary and secondary marks occurs only on this continent (Jambudvīpa), because the awakening wisdom here is superior. To distinguish males from females, it refers only to those facing a Buddha;

they contemplate the Buddha and give rise to volition, which is subsumed under the category of "that accomplished through volition" (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). Outside of the three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), one cultivates the karma for the excellent marks during the remaining hundred great eons.
Such is the natural law regarding the causal stage of all Buddhas. However, each of the thirty-two marks is adorned by a hundred merits (*śata-puṇya*).

"Yan. One hundred wholesome volitions (*cetanā*) are called "one hundred blessings. For example, when cultivating the mark of the soles being level and full, one first gives rise to fifty volitions to purify the body;
next, one gives rise to one volition that directly draws forth that mark; finally, one gives rise to fifteen volitions to bring it to completion.
It is like a farmer who first prepares the furrows and ridges, then sows the seeds, and afterwards uses a hoe—*tong*—to weed them.
One should wash it with water and treat it thoroughly. Since this characteristic is thus established, the remaining characteristics are to be explained by analogy.

Regarding the fifty volitions (*cetanā*), these constitute the ten paths of wholesome action (*daśa-kuśala-karmapatha*), each possessing ten volitions. For instance, at the time of the first volition of non-killing, there are five volitions:

(1) the volition of abstaining from killing; (2) the volition of exhortation; (3) the volition of praise; (4) the volition of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*); and (5) the volition of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). This applies likewise up to right view.
Thus it is. What is now called "adorned with a hundred merits" refers precisely to the thirty-two marks produced by those hundred merits.

To say that [this practice] must invariably be accompanied by a compassionate mind refers to the third of the seven supreme excellences (*saptavidha-paramatā*), namely, the supremacy of intention (*āśaya-paramatā*).
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "When practicing the six perfections, one must be embraced by these seven supreme excellences before they can be established as *pāramitās*."
Maitreya: First, the excellence of abiding, which means one must abide in the bodhisattva lineage (*gotra*).
Second, the excellence of reliance, which relies upon the great mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*). Third, the excellence of intention, which is compassion for all sentient beings.

Fourth, the excellence of activity, which consists in performing all activities by taking up objects such as giving (*dāna*) and so forth. Fifth, the excellence of skillful means, which is non-conceptual wisdom (*animitta-jñāna*).
It is that which is embraced by others; it is the purity of the three spheres; it is the most excellent of the six dedications, dedicating toward unsurpassed enlightenment;
it is the most excellent of the seven purities, being unmixed with the two obstacles and free from regret throughout the three times.

Regarding the statement "bestowing the flowers," this refers to mindfulness (*smṛti*), investigation of phenomena (*dharmavicaya*), diligence (*vīrya*), joy (*prīti*), pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), concentration (*samādhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*). Clear recollection of the object is called mindfulness.
Because it discerns virtues and faults, it is called investigation of phenomena. Being fervent and subsequently wholesome, it is called diligence.
That which brings satisfaction to the mind is termed joy. The harmonious refinement of body and mind constitutes pliancy. Focused attention upon the object of observation is called concentration.

Concentration (*samādhi*)—which is free from lethargy and agitation and characterized by equanimity and tranquility—is designated as "equanimity" (*upekṣā*). Question: The discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) is wisdom (*prajñā*), and it is specifically named a factor of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).

Since the remaining factors are not subsumed under wisdom, how can they be called factors of enlightenment? Answer: The factor of mindfulness (*smṛti*) is so called because it is the basis upon which the factors of enlightenment rely.

The discernment of phenomena is so called because it is identical in essence to enlightenment itself. Diligence (*vīrya*) is so called because it is the factor of enlightenment that brings about deliverance. Thus, [these factors] consist of both wisdom and non-wisdom.

Wisdom is collectively termed the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*). Question: Why are these seven called "flowers"? Answer: Within the stage of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), one cultivates the seven factors of enlightenment;
because they are similar to flowers in that they lead to the ripening of fruit, they are called flowers.
Regarding the statement that by giving incense one obtains the fragrance of the fivefold Dharma-body: incense is able to eliminate foul odors;
likewise, these five constituents of the Dharma-body—concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—are able to eliminate the foul dharmas of the afflictions.
Regarding the statement that one should give banners as an offering: a banner is able to rotate and inspire wholesome thoughts in people.

Just as a *dhāraṇī* can transform evil karma and lead to the attainment of wholesome karma, the *Sūtra on Rebirth* states that when a banner rotates once, it [yields] the rank of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*).

Regarding the gift of a canopy: if one offers a flower canopy to the Buddha, one attains the four immeasurables—compassion, pity, joy, and equanimity—because it provides shade and protection for the four modes of birth.
Regarding the statement "during the era of the Yellow Emperor, Ling Lun and others," [the questioner] asks: For what reason did music arise? [The respondent] answers:

The commentary states, "During the era of the Yellow Emperor," meaning that during the reign of the Yellow Emperor, he commissioned the man of the Ling Lun clan to go to the north of Mount Kunlun, west of the Great Marsh.
Within the ravines, he felled bamboo; six for the males and six for the females, with which he fashioned the twelve tubes.

Listening to the cries of the phoenix, he established the twelve pitch-pipes, known as the six *liǎo* (lutes) and the six *lǜ* (pipes). Línghún was a music official skilled in tuning the musical scales.

In the first month, the pitch-pipe *Zhōngcuò* vibrated in resonance. According to the Imperial Commentary on the *Monthly Ordinances*, a "pitch-pipe" (*lǜ*) is a tube used to gauge the wind, made of bamboo. It is central...
It corresponds to the *Ying* (Response). It is used for blowing ashes. The pipe is eight inches long, with an internal diameter of three *fen* and a width of nine *fen*.
Gao You says: "When things first emerge from the earth in clusters, it is called *Da-cu* (pronounced *cang-dou*).
In the second month, the *lü* is *Jia-zhong*. The pipe is seven and four-tenths inches long. Gao You says: "In this month, all things depart from the yin and are born; therefore, it is so named."

Jiāzhōng (Clamping Bell). This is the *lǜ* (pitch-pipe) for the third month; it is "Gūxǐ" (Abandoning the Old and Washing New). The pipe is seven cun and one fēn long. Gāo Yòu says: "Gū means 'old' and xǐ means 'new.
In this month, the yang qi and yin qi disperse; they are both outside and within. The myriad creatures abandon the old and move toward the new.
The *lǜ* for the fourth month is Zhōnglǚ (Central Lü), six cun and six fēn long. Gāo Yòu says: "It is by means of the yang qi that the yang [spirits] are gathered."
Success. Therefore it is called Zhonglü (Central Lü). In the fifth month, the pitch-pipe is Rǔbīn, measuring six cun and three fen;
in this month, the yin qi withers and retreats below, while the host—the yang qi—is within, and the guest—the yin qi—is outside.
In the sixth month, the pitch-pipe is Línzhōng, measuring six cun and seven fen. In the seventh month, the pitch-pipe is Yízé, measuring five cun and six fen; "Yí" (Level) signifies an image.

"Ye" (也) means "it is so. "Ze" (則) refers to the law (*dharma*). When the Great Yang is within and the Great Yin qi emerges, all things wither and suffer; thus they respond to the law and complete their nature.

In the eighth month, the *lü* (pitch-pipe) is Zhonglü, measuring five cun and three fen. The Yin qi is stored within; the Yin *lü* acts upon the Yang, fulfilling its function through its true essence.
In the ninth month, the *lü* is Wusheshi, measuring four cun and nine fen. The Yin qi ascends, and the Yang qi...
The [Yang] descends. All things flourish following the Yang. Wu-ye (pronounced yi) appears. In the tenth month, the pitch-pipe in use is Yingzhong, measuring four cun and seven fen;
the Yin night operates within the Yang, turning its work into fruition. In the eleventh month, the pitch-pipe in use is Huangzhong, measuring nine cun.
The Huangzhong (Yellow Bell) is the beginning of the pitch-pipes (*lü*). Gao You said: "Yang energy is drawn from below, while Yin energy abounds above;
it is planted beneath the multitude of the Yellow [Earth], and thus it is called Huangzhong. In the twelfth month, among the pitch-pipes, the Dali is eight cun and four fen long.
This implies that once Linglun had felled the bamboo and established the twelve pitch-pipes, the Way of music proceeded from this point onward.
It flourishes; hence it is called "producing music.
Regarding the so-called five notes (*pañca-svara*) and eight tones (*aṣṭa-tantrī*): the five notes are gong (*gāndhāra*), shang (*shang*), jiao (*jiao*), zhi (*zhi*), and yu (*yu*).
The *Hanshu* states: "The five notes cleanse away the depraved intentions of people and restore their most upright nature. Gong signifies the center; from the center, it flows forth.

"Four Directions" (*Sìfāng*): It proclaims the beginning of the generation of life; it is the foundation of the four directions. "Shāng" (*Shāng*) means "manifestation" (*zhāng*); because the myriad things reach fulfillment and can thus be manifested.

"Jué" (*Jué*) means "contact" (*chù*); things contact the earth to grow, bearing the wilds as their horns. "Zhǐ" (*Zhǐ*) means "blessing" (*zhǐ*); when things flourish and expand, they are said to be "prosperous.
"Yǔ" (*Yǔ*) means "universe" (*yǔ*) and "covering"; [it refers to] the canopy. According to the *Hànshī wàizhuàn*, the music of the Yang [note] is named "Great Protection" (*Dàhù*).
"Guardian" (hu) has the meaning of "protecting and rescuing. Hearing the sound of Gong causes people to become gentle, kind, and magnanimous.
Hearing the sound of Shang causes people to become broad-minded and fond of righteousness. Hearing the sound of Jiao causes people to feel compassion and be benevolent and loving.

Hearing the sound of Zhi causes people to delight in nourishing others and be fond of good faith. Hearing the sound of Yu causes people to be respectful, frugal, and fond of ritual propriety. One asks: why are there only five?
The answer is that they were granted the Five Rites.
Regarding the term "gan-qie" (shield and axe): Zheng Xuan stated that *gan* is a shield and *qie* is a battle-axe (held by warriors). *Yu* refers to wings;
*mao* refers to ox-tails (held by those of civil rank). He further stated that holding a side-shield in the left hand is called *gan*, while holding a spear in the right hand is called *qie*.
The shield is called the *qi* (spear). Holding these two types of implements, one performs a dance characterized by a heroic and fierce bearing;

this is called the "Dance of Joy" (*wule*). As for the "Patterned Music" (*wenle*), it involves feathers and furs. One holds a staff in the left hand adorned with bird feathers, and in the [other] left hand, one holds [an implement] adorned with animal fur.
Performing the dance while holding these two types is refined and elegant in its style; this is called Patterned Music. This was the practice during the time of Tang.
Music: "Martiality first, followed by culture" is the sequence for governing a state.

As for the phrase "the eight musical instruments harmonize," this refers to metal, stone, silk, bamboo, gourd, earth, leather, and wood, which symbolize the Eight Trigrams and the eight seasonal nodes.
Regarding "sound" (*yin*): the Preface to the *Mao Shi* states, "Emotion issues forth as sound; sound is formed into patterns, which are called 'music' (*yin*). This means that...
The notes gong, shang, jiao, zhi, and yu correspond to one another in high and low registers; this is what is called the formation of patterns.
Question: Why are only eight [instruments] mentioned? Answer: The vernacular explanation says: metal moves them; strings and bamboo lead them;
gourds, shaped like large beasts, proclaim them; earth praises them; leather and wood regulate them. When things attain their proper function, this is "capability" (keng); it is "harmony" (xiehe).
When high and low notes correspond to one another, it is called "sound" (*yin*); this is precisely the meaning of harmony. The *Yueli* (Record of Music) states:
"All that arises originates from the human heart. When the heart moves, it causes external things to respond accordingly.

Therefore, it speaks of "the sounds that govern the world," "the sounds of Zheng and Wei," and furthermore, "the sounds of Sangjian and Dishang," which are the sounds of a perishing state. If one discusses Great Music (*dàyuè*), however, it is without sound.
The nature of harmonious balance is difficult to capture in images and difficult to grasp in form;

therefore, one resorts to metal and stone to produce concordant sounds, describing the power of Heaven and Earth in their generation and growth. As for the flow of strings and bamboo: "metal" refers to bells, chimes, and the like;
"stone" refers to stone chimes and the like, which are struck to produce sound; "strings" refers to categories such as lute strings; and "bamboo" refers to the transverse flute.

These are the categories of wind instruments. As for the *bō* (flute): the *shēng* (reed organ) is held upward like a sauce ladle; that which is blown is the *bō*. As for the *tǔ* (earthen instrument):
this refers to the *xuān* (clay ocarina), made from baked earth, which produces sound when blown. As for the *gé* (membranous instrument): this is the drum. As for the *mù* (wooden instrument):
this refers to the *cù yǔ* (one-beat) and *èr yǔ* (two-beat). The *cù* is a wooden object resembling a lacquered bucket; a tongue is placed inside it, and by shaking it, sound is produced.
All the musical instruments were struck simultaneously. As for the second type, the *mei*:

its shape is like that of a crouching tiger, with twenty-four teeth on the upper jaw representing the twenty-four vital energies (*prāṇa*). It is made of bamboo; when the teeth are struck, they produce sound. All the musical instruments then ceased playing at once.
(The above explains the general names.)
Regarding the term "drum" (*bherī*): when it is struck and produces sound, it is called "the drum resounds. If it has leather on only one side, this is the type of drum that is struck.
If it can be struck, it is named a drum; "drum" refers to the act of striking. Here, we take the drum as that which is struck. Generally, anything that emits sound is called a drum;
it is not limited to musical sounds alone. Even a field-clearing mallet is called a drum. Here, we take it to mean all things that produce sound when struck.
All sounds are produced by drums; thus, they are called "general sounds. The *I Ching* says, "It is stirred by the movement of thunder.
As for the term "horns," their curved shape resembles ox horns; when blown, they produce sound.

Regarding the term "conch" (*śaṅkha*): it is a species of aquatic creature found in the ocean. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states, "Blowing the conch to know the time," which means knowing when a musical piece has reached its conclusion.
In India, all musical sounds are produced by blowing the conch.
Regarding the term "xiāo-guǎn" (flute and pipe): the xiāo is a type of guǎn. It was created by Shùn, modeled after the wings of a phoenix;
it produces a whistling sound (*xiāoxiāo*). According to the *Shìmíng*, "xiāo" means "solemn" (*sù*); the sound of the guǎn is solemn and clear.
The *Guǎngyǎ* states that it consists of twenty-four pipes without bottoms, or sixteen pipes with bottoms; those without bottoms are for tuning. It is also said that the xiāo is two feet long.
Regarding the character *shāo* (pronounced *suǒjiǎo*): the intended meaning is that this character also shares the pronunciation of *xiāo*, yet it is not that character.
If one adopts the reading *suǒjiǎo*, then to strike a person with a counting-stick (*suan*) is called *shāo*; because the sounds are identical, it is cited [as such]. *Yinyìnyìyě*.

Regarding the term "dí" (flute): it refers to a seven-holed *yè* (transverse flute); conversely, *yè* refers to the *dí*. "Dí" is a general name, and it is also called "zhí" (straight), as its sound is upright.

The *Fengsu Tong* states: "The *dí* was created by Qiu Zhong during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Han. 'Dí' means 'to cleanse' (*dí*); it is so named because it cleanses away depravity and impurity."
It is included among the refined and correct [instruments]. *Yue* (籥) is pronounced with the *zhe* (切) rhyme; it is a musical instrument. According to the *Erya*, the *dayue* (大籥) is called *yue*.

The commentary states it is like a *di* (笛), having three holes and being short and small. The *Guangya* says it has seven holes. The *Chuxueji* states that while the *di* is fixed, all stringed instruments and songs originate from the *di*;
thus, in the present day, the Han section takes the *di* as primary. As for the Hu (foreign) section, it uses the *sheng* (笙).
It comes first. It is one chi and four cun long. Its seven holes represent the seven luminaries; its five holes represent the five elements;

its three [main] holes symbolize the Three Powers (the Heaven, Earth, and Human). All other musical instruments follow the sound of the flute; the flute does not follow the sounds of others. It is the primary sound of music.
Regarding the term "qin-jin" (琴禁), Bai Shantong stated that it means "prohibition. It is so named because it restrains lustful depravity and rectifies the human heart.

The *qin* was created based on the principle of subduing [the passions]; originally it had five strings, where the larger represented the ruler and the smaller represented the minister, with the large and small corresponding to one another like a ruler singing and a minister responding.
Later, King Wu added one string, and King Wen added another; these were altered to the *gong* and *bian-gong* tones to further command the relationship between ruler and minister.
It is said that the sixth [string] was named "Wenxian" (Civil String) and the seventh was named "Wuxian" (Military String); records state these were created by Shen Nong.
The *Guangya* says: "The *qin* is three chi, three cun, and six fen long."

Regarding the term *kōng hóu* (箜篌): according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to the seductive music composed by Shi Yan. Later, when he was born among the mulberry trees (*sang jian*) and washed away by the waters of the Shang River, he created this *kōng hóu*.
When it was first completed, he presented it to the feudal lords. They listened for one day but were not satisfied; even after many days, they remained dissatisfied.
The feudal lords all came [to hear it], and thus it emptied the states of the lords. Therefore, it is named "Empty" (*Kong*).
The character "Hou" (侯) has a beautiful sound; once heard, it does not leave the mind. There remains only the state of Hou, which is called Konghou (空侯). Another explanation says:

the state of Konghou is called Konghou because when the state of Hou presents its tribute, the other states have no cause for concern, whereas the state of Konghou has cause for concern; thus it is named Konghou.

The *Tong* (Comprehensive Record) states: One name for it is *kanhou*. When Emperor Wu of the Han dynasty was performing sacrifices at Mount Tai, he ordered the musician Hou Tiao to create the *kan* based on the *qin*.
Hou remarked that this *kan* corresponds to the rhythm (*jie*). "Hou" is his surname; its twenty-four strings represent the twenty-four qi (energies).

As for what is called the *pipa*: it was originally a musical instrument of the Hu (Central Asians), played while on horseback. Mou said: "Pushing the hand forward is 'pi'; drawing the hand back is 'ba.
Its interior is hollow and its exterior is solid; thus it is named 'pipi,' which represents the vital breath (*qi*) of Heaven and Earth."
The sounding board is round and the handle is straight; this represents the sequence of Yin and Yang. It is three chi and five cun long:

the three chi symbolize the Three Powers (Heaven, Earth, and Humanity), the five cun symbolize the Five Elements, the two holes symbolize the Sun and Moon, and the four strings symbolize the Four Seasons.
Regarding the statement that the *niao* is like a bell: its shape resembles a bell and it may be struck like a cymbal; its size is permitted to vary. The *zheng* is the same as the *niao*;
it resembles a *niao* but is larger than a bell. The larger ones are called *niao*, and the smaller ones are called bells (*ling*).

Regarding what is called "military law" (*junfa*): in ancient military law, one person among ten would hold the signal device to startle the other nine, so that they could advance when it was time to advance and halt when it was time to halt.
The Senior Commandant (*cháng sīmǎ*) held the *duó* (a clapper), which is the same as the head of a unit (*duìtóu*).
By striking it to produce a sound, he signaled the order; the *duó* is thus equivalent to a bell (*líng*). As the *Lúnyǔ* says: "Heaven uses the Son of Heaven as its wooden bell (*mùduó*)."
Regarding the statement that "five men form a *wu*": five times five makes twenty-five men, which constitutes a *liang*. Five men form one *wu*;
five such groups of five make twenty-five men, which is called a *liang* (pronounced *liáng-cháng*). According to military law, twenty-five men have a *simǎ* appointed over them;
this is equivalent to the head of a unit (*duìtóu*) in the present day. A *simǎ* is simply the head of a unit; in ancient times, they were called *sī*.
Regarding the horses: two *sīmās* hold the *duo*. A *duo* is a circular object with three holes; its body is bronze and its tongue is wood.

When struck, it produces sound to call out to twenty-five men. The *duo* is larger than the *niao*. Although the *niao* is cited here as a point of reference, it is not relevant to the meaning of this context.

Regarding the term *tongba* (cymbals): it refers to two copper plates that are struck against each other from the left and right; this is called *tongba*. There is no source for the character *ba* being used here as *ba* (in the sense of "striking").

Regarding the phrase "the *Faputi jing* (Sūtra on Arousing Bodhicitta) and others," the *Faputixin lun* (Treatise on Arousing Bodhicitta) states: "Music and female forms corrupt and disorder the pure mind."
Regarding how this is to be offered as an offering, the commentary answers by citing the *Sūtra on the Arising of the Bodhicitta*:

"The pleasure of sexual misconduct destroys the pure mind; therefore, it must not be given as an offering. As for the pleasure of the righteous, it praises virtue and promotes goodness; what harm is there in offering it?
It is just like the sounds of Zheng and Wei in this land, which are called 'licentious music,' while Yunshao and Dafu are called 'righteous music. If it is righteous, one cultivates it."

One establishes virtue through the body. If one is depraved, the state will perish and the family will be ruined. Furthermore, that sutra prohibits [the acceptance of offerings] out of fear that the recipient might corrupt their pure mind;
this sutra, however, intends for the offering to be made to the Buddha, and thus there is no fault.
Regarding the phrase "as in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*": the intended meaning is that the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* permits such matters as musical offerings and the like.
Regarding the term "chanting" (*gāyana*): chanting is precisely the music within the Dharma; it refers to names and phrases within sound used to praise and extol the Buddha.
Virtue. This is identical to the description of the manifestation of sublime virtue found in the *Shijing* (Book of Poetry). One commentary states: "The singer sets forth virtue;
when it moves, heaven and earth respond, the four seasons harmonize, the stars and constellations are regulated, and the myriad things are nurtured.
According to the *Dharmapada*, chanting praises the virtues of the Buddha; that is, within the causal stage, one uses these musical sounds to sing in praise of the Buddha’s virtues.

Among the fruits [of Buddhahood], one attains the mark of the Brahma-voice; as among the thirty-two marks of the World-Honored One, the mark of the Brahma-voice is the most preeminent, enabling the preaching of the Dharma to deliver sentient beings.
Regarding the statement "one shall attain the state of a Great Being" and so forth: for example, while in the causal stage, Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara delighted in providing musical offerings;
upon reaching the resultant stage, he skillfully expounded the Dharma to benefit sentient beings.
Regarding the term *Vāsa* (pronounced *Pohé* [qùhū]), some teachers have erred in their interpretation. As for the mention of the Prince of Chen-si and others:
it is asked why the *brahma-gāthā* (Banzhai) exists in this land. The answer, as set forth in the commentary, refers to the Prince of Chen-si and others.
According to the *Lìdìjì* (Record of the Successive Emperors), Cao Pi, the Wen Emperor of Wei, was the son of Cao Cao, the Wǔ Emperor of Wei; he reigned for seven years.

Emperor Wu had two sons. The elder was named Cao Pi; the second was Cao Zhi, whose courtesy name was Zijian. Since Cao Pi succeeded to the throne as the ruler, his younger brother Cao Zhi was enfeoffed as the Prince of Chen-si (Chensiwang).

Chen-si was the name of a commandery. Cao Zhi possessed a beautiful appearance and was gifted with literary talent. His elder brother Pi treated him with exceptional honor and respect, even constructing a pavilion for him named Zhuan.
Consequently, he was subjected to harassment and coercion by Empress Dowager Zhuan, yet he refused to comply. He bit his own arm until it bled. His virtue—

While washing his hair, he was exhausted. When his elder brother saw that the arms of the consort and the queen were bitten and damaged, he inquired about how this had happened. He then intended to kill him, decreeing: "Let him walk seven paces;

if the poem is completed, he shall not be executed, but if it is not completed, he shall be executed. The poem said: "Boiling beans, one burns the beans themselves; Using those very beans to cook within the cauldron.
Of the same kind and sharing the same roots, Why do you roast one another so urgently? Once the poem was completed, [he was released]. Thus...
He was exempted from the [ritual] execution. The reason for his exclusion was that he was awaiting his [true] destiny. Initially, he was enfeoffed as Prince of Hedong;

after the King passed away, he was posthumously enfeoffed as the Prince of Chen-si. At the age of ten, he composed literary works; once his pen had touched the paper, they were complete verses, requiring no revision whatsoever.

Whenever he praised the Buddhist scriptures, he would invariably sigh with admiration and contemplate them, regarding them as the ultimate pinnacle of the True Way. Consequently, he devised the "Seven Tones" for chanting, thereby modulating the melodic inflections.
...the resonance [of that sound]. Therefore, I have now composed the "Chengning Chapter" (Chapter on Accomplishing Peace) for recitation.

Regarding the phrase "rocky grottoes" (*yanxiu*) and so forth: when King Dengxiang was in the region between Mount Yu (*Yushan*) and the western part of the continent, he heard the recitation of the sutra in a rocky grotto.
He subsequently imitated that sound to create the *Brahman* (Sanskrit) language; it was named after the mountain, hence it is called "Wu-fan" (Barbarian Brahman). The *Erya* states: "Mountain..."
There is a deep cavern that forms a grotto; it is heard that within this cavern the sutras are being recited. Regarding the term *qiú* (遒):

the character is pronounced with the *xiù* (袖) rhyme [and the *jǐ* (几) radical]. *Wǎn* (婉) is pronounced with the *xǐ* (洗) rhyme. Some write it with the character *qiū* (酋); these are combined into a single form. It is not used in the sense of "encircling" (*zhuó-rào*).

Writing it as a single character conveys the meaning of "extending" or "circling at length," which is to say, it indicates a drawn-out tone. If it were written with the "encircling" (*zhuó*) radical attached, its definition would be...
This refers to the meaning of "exhaustion. The commentary takes "exhaustion" to mean that the breath is harmoniously expansive and all contractions are fully exhausted;

this is the distinction between the high and the low. "Sound" means clarity; it is the sound of reciting sutras within mountain caves, where the pure and beautiful tones are completely resonant, causing the echoes to flow through the valleys.
Regarding the phrase "míng hé xī děng" (冥合西等): *míng* (pronounced with the *mo* and *jīng* initials reversed) means darkness or night; it refers to the dark union with the Western [Land].

*Qiè* (契) means to contract or bind together. *Jiūrú* (糅) states: Whenever one wishes to recite a sutra, one must first produce three rhythmic sounds to praise the virtues of the Buddha and the merits of the sutra, and only then recite the scripture.
When subsequently reciting the text as spoken, there are likewise three rhythmic sounds for dedicating the merit and making vows.
The first three and the last three share the same number of recitations; therefore, they are collectively termed *qǐ* (invocations). *Qǐ* means "to open.
The formal exposition in the middle consists of seven sounds. There are three [categories]: the Three Jewels constitute the three invocations.
Regarding the seven sounds, the Four Truths are added to the Three Jewels, which are thus called the seven sounds.
Regarding the term "Koṭīkarṇa," Zhi Shou notes that in the Western Regions it is called *Śrūpama*, which should correspond to *Koṭī*;
in the Tang language, this means "two hundred billion. The ancient transcription "Yi'ěr" (Ear of a Billion) is an error. The *Xiyu zhuan* (Records of the Western Regions) states:

In the past, in the country of Irṇavata in South India, there was an elder who was noble, prestigious, and immensely wealthy; however, in his later years, he had no heir to continue his lineage. At that time, someone came to inform him [of the birth of a son].

The stepmother sent a messenger to inform her father. Upon hearing this, the father was filled with joy and bestowed upon him two hundred *koṭis* of gold coins—which is equivalent to twenty thousand strings of cash.
Ten strings constitute one *wan*; one hundred strings constitute one *yi*; one thousand strings constitute one *ji*; and ten thousand strings constitute one *bai*.
Thus, two hundred *koṭis* equals twenty thousand strings. Because of this, the son received the name "Two Hundred *Koṭis*" (*Er-bai-ji*).
It is like the sons and daughters of a common family who, at the time of their birth, are given names such as Five Jin, Six Jin, or Seven Jin based on their weight.
Yet, when they have grown up and reached maturity, there grows beneath each of their feet a single hair more than a foot in length, which never touches the ground.
It was lustrous, fine, and soft, with a color like that of gold. Later, King Bimbisāra heard of it and desired to see it;

he issued a summons to the elder to bring it from his home to the city. He had a canal dug for transport and filled it with mustard seeds, then moored his royal barge there to send the jewel to his son.
Hoping to avoid the calamity of overturning in a boat, he first paid homage to the World-Honored One (Bhagavān). The World-Honored One demonstrated the *paryaṅka* (cross-legged) posture for him.

He presented his affairs to the King, who approved of his conduct and instructed him to return home. He subsequently took refuge in the Tathāgata; this family attained the fruits of the Path, reaching the point where they were able to chant the *brahmaghoṣa* (sacred hymns).
This term "Kūṭi" is also used in the sense of "faithful and righteous"; the character "er" (耳) is a particle used to assist the phrasing of the sentence.
The word "etc. includes Nanda the cowherd, who was also able to produce the Brahma-sound.
As for the sutra’s statement, "If a person with a distracted mind [offers] flowers," this speaks only of those who have already generated the aspiration for enlightenment;
even with a distracted mind, one may still behold the Buddha.

Regarding the statement that it is "equal to the previous four matters," a question is raised: what is the difference between this offering of seasonal flowers and the offerings of the previous four matters? The answer is:
the former is based on a concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*), while this refers to a distracted mind (*vikṣipta-citta*). Alternatively, they differ as follows:

the former consists of prostrations and offerings involving various objects, whereas this consists solely of the offering of seasonal flowers. Even if one offers but a single flower with a light mind and few materials, the merit of this single, subtle act is nonetheless complete.
All shall attain the Buddha-way.
Regarding the statement that "briefly speaking, offerings are equal," the intended meaning is that images of other materials also attain Buddhahood.
Whether these images are made of gold, silver, copper, iron, clay, wood, or other substances, all such images attain Buddhahood.

Regarding the scripture’s statement that one “gradually sees innumerable Buddhas,” this refers to bodhisattvas of the four reliances (*catur-pratisaraṇa*), such as those who made offerings to twenty-six *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* Buddhas.

As for the scriptural mention of “some performing prostrations, raising their hands, and so forth,” the *Record of the Western Regions* (*Xiyuji*) states that the ritual for paying respect is as follows: [text continues].
There are nine [grades of salutation]: first, greeting with words; second, showing respect by lowering the hand; third, raising the hands high in a bow;
fourth, joining the palms in a level, respectful manner; fifth, bending one knee; sixth, kneeling for a long duration; seventh, resting both knees upon the ground; eighth, bending all five limbs;

ninth, prostrating the entire body to the ground. Raising one hand now corresponds to the third grade, the high bow. Within this sutra, there are five [grades of salutation], the first being the formal prostration (*praṇāma*).
Second, join the palms; third, raise the hands; fourth, slightly bow the head. Recite "Namo Buddha" once; this is the first verbal expression of greeting.

When the Sūtra says, "one spontaneously attains the unsurpassed path," this clarifies that one makes offerings to oneself as a Buddha. When the Sūtra says, "extensively deliver [beings] without... [end of fragment].
Regarding the term "etcetera": [the Buddha] further transforms sentient beings before finally entering parinirvāṇa and accomplishing the turning of the wheel of Dharma.

As for the scriptural passage stating that he enters *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder) until the fires are extinguished: one asks, how is it that the Buddha manifests in accordance with the followers of the Hīnayāna by entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*?
Furthermore, regarding the sequence of provisional means followed by ultimate reality—the ritual standard for the three periods of time—why is this so?
Entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* further increases the affliction of fixed determination. Answer: Although "without remainder" (*nirupadhiśeṣa*) is the same, the analogies of fuel and fire differ.
In the Hīnayāna, the fuel is a metaphor for the *ālayavijñāna*, and the fire is a metaphor for the body and wisdom.

When entering *nirupadhiśeṣa*, since the *ālayavijñāna* is severed, the body and wisdom that depend upon it are likewise extinguished; just as when the fuel is gone, the fire also follows and is extinguished. If one refers to the Mahāyāna, sentient beings...

The roots of goodness are like firewood; the body and wisdom of the Tathāgata are like fire. If the roots of goodness of sentient beings remain, it is as when there is fire because there is firewood, corresponding to the appearance of a Buddha in the world.
When sentient beings have perished and the roots of goodness are gone, it is as when the fire is extinguished because the firewood is exhausted, corresponding to the Tathāgata’s entry into nirvāṇa.

Regarding the scriptural passage, "If a person with a distracted mind," and so forth, the intended meaning is that it does not speak of those who are in meditative concentration (*samāhita*) or those who have repeated [the name] many times.
If this is the case even for one with a distracted mind, how much more so for one in concentration or one who has repeated it many times?
Regarding the statement, "I always recite the names of the fifty-three [Buddhas]": in the past, there were three thousand people who constantly recited the names of these fifty-three Buddhas.

One thousand of them attained Buddhahood in the past *Vibhūṣaṇakalpa*; one thousand will attain Buddhahood in this present *Bhadrakalpa*, with Krakucchanda Buddha as their leader; and one thousand will attain Buddhahood in a future kalpa.
Furthermore, the Sūtra states: "If there are those who hear this Dharma, or those of the lineage (gotra) who hear this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, they shall attain the Buddha-way.
This indicates that it is not the case that those without the lineage who hear it will become Buddhas.
Regarding the scriptural statement "all Tathāgatas," this refers to all [Tathāgatas] within the future.
As for the statement that Buddhas and sentient beings are both spoken of together, *Miù* (糅) says:

"All Tathāgatas" refers to those who transform (*nirmāṇa-kāya*), while "those who hear the Dharma" refers to those who are transformed. This is because they are clarified as being situated in this same single location.

Regarding the statement that "the explanation here is consistent with what was said above," this is because the preceding and succeeding sections are identical. Now, I say it is not so. The meaning here is that the future Buddhas will deliver all sentient beings and cause them to enter the Buddha’s untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*); this is precisely what the Buddha taught. This constitutes one layer. Once the sentient beings being transformed have themselves attained Buddhahood, they in turn preach the wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) and Prajñā to others; among those who hear it, there is not a single person [who does not attain it]. This constitutes another layer. Thus, the two layers are distinct. Therefore, the former is called the "Buddha's teaching" (*buddha-deśanā*), while the latter is called the "teaching by the Bodhisattvas. Because these two teachings are mutually inclusive, they are collectively termed the "One Vehicle. It is for this reason that the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The One Vehicle is the Buddha Vehicle. This is not established. This is likewise the case when the beings transformed by future Buddhas attain Buddhahood.
It is the collective teaching of the wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle. [One layer. The Commentary states that "beings" refers to those beings who shall attain Buddhahood.
It is like Śākyamuni transforming Śāriputra into Padmaprabha, and Padmaprabha further merging with Drdhavīrya to become Padmottara.
This is the practice of peace, because it accomplishes the turning of the wheel of Dharma.

If one were to say that these two are explained together, otherwise—since the first four lines have already stated that all sentient beings are delivered and enter into untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*)—what need would there be to further state in the final two lines that "not a single one fails to become a Buddha"? Therefore, this belongs to the second section.
These are persons manifested by the Buddha. "Combined" (*he*) should be understood in its proper sense: first provisional and later real; the transformation of those of indeterminate nature.

This is the case for every Buddha. It also carries the meaning of "conjunction" (*zhonghe*): the two layers of the transformers are both Buddhas, and the two layers of the transformed are both sentient beings.
Since this is clarified in this single location, it is called an "explanation by combination."
The scriptural passage beginning with "The original vows of all Buddhas," etc., explains the meaning of first employing provisional means and subsequently revealing the ultimate reality. Question:

For what reason must the Buddha’s appearance in the world necessarily involve first teaching through provisional means and later through the ultimate reality? Answer: The scripture states: "The original vows of all Buddhas...

[omitted] ...they likewise attain this same path. This is also like the case of Padmaprabha appearing in the world; although it was not a time of evil, by virtue of his original vow, he taught the Three Vehicles.
This is the Dharma.

Regarding the statement "to clearly awaken to the three natures": it is by means of this awakening to the three natures that one is able to explain the provisional and the real. How does one awaken to the three natures and thereby become able to explain the provisional and the real?

It is because one clearly awakens to the fact that the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) exist; therefore, [the Buddha] spoke [of them] during the first period.
There is. Because one realizes that the nature of the imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva) is non-existent, emptiness was taught in the second period.
Because one simultaneously realizes both of the former two natures, neither-emptiness-nor-existence was taught in the third period.
