Regarding the "destinations" (*gati*) of all phenomena, there are three: first, knowing that the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is the destination of all delusive phenomena;
second, knowing that the nature of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is the destination of all dependently arisen phenomena;
and third, knowing that the nature of perfected reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is the destination of all eternal phenomena. Thus, the provisional is taught first, followed by the ultimate.
First, the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Second, the clear realization that the three natures ultimately converge in the One Vehicle. The One Vehicle is precisely the attainment of Buddhahood.

By knowing that the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is non-existent, one understands the illusory phenomena of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and cultivates its pure aspects;

by relying on the dependent nature, one realizes the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), culminating in the three bodies (*trikāya*) and ultimately converging in the *dharmakāya* and *tathatā*. Therefore, the commentary states "clear realization."
This refers to the progression from the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) up to the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

Regarding the phrase "the wondrous principle of *tathatā* (suchness)": it explains the meaning of the character "nature" (*svabhāva*). It serves as the essential nature of all phenomena; this quiescent nature is precisely the untainted (*anāsrava*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharma.
To speak of the "eternal nature" is to explain the character "eternal" (常). Now, as for *tathatā* (True Suchness): "True" (*zhen*) means reality, signifying the absence of falsehood;

"Such" (*ru*) means suchness, signifying the absence of change. It is not like conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), which are impermanent and subject to change, and thus cannot be said to be eternal.

Regarding the statement that "the Buddha is able to realize and know," this refers to understanding the two characters for "nature" (*xing*); it is the knowledge of the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
Regarding the two phrases beginning with "thoroughly imagined" (*parikalpita*), these refer to understanding the two characters for "phenomena" (*fa*).

Regarding the statement that "the essential nature is non-existent," this explains the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). As for "pervasive conceptualization" (*parikalpa*): "pervasive" (*pari*) means all-encompassing; "conceptualization" (*kalpa*) means discursive construction.

It refers to that which universally takes all things as objects and gives rise to discursive discrimination. Among the three natures, this is the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

First, that which is pervasive but not conceptualizing is the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*). Second, that which is conceptualizing but not pervasive is the seventh consciousness (*manas*), which takes only the *ālaya* as its object.

Because it gives rise to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). The third [nature] is both pervasive and conceptually constructed. The sixth consciousness pervasively objects to all things and gives rise to conceptual construction. The fourth is neither pervasive nor conceptually constructed;

that is, the five sensory consciousnesses object only to the five dusts (*pañca-viṣaya*) and lack conceptual construction. Within the Tathāgata’s fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), he realizes and penetrates the nature of pervasive construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*);
within his subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*), he understands dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) to be like illusory phenomena. (The above explains one phrase of the sutra.)

The statement that "the Buddha realizes selflessness" concludes the preceding discussion on the nature of permanence. Its meaning is that the World-Honored One is able to realize the principle of the two kinds of emptiness (*dvaya-śūnyatā*).
He knows that the nature of the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) is fundamentally non-existent; he also knows that the *parikalpita-svabhāva* is the false attachment of ordinary beings.

Thus, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "Based on a rope, the cognition of a snake arises; upon seeing the rope, one realizes its [snake-nature] is non-existent. This refers to realizing and seeing that.

When the rope is divided, one realizes that the cognition of a snake was a delusion; the confused mind failed to understand that the fundamental substance is hemp and falsely conceived it to be a rope—this is a metaphor for the attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).

Furthermore, upon that very rope, one again falsely conceives it to be a snake and gives rise to the thought of being bitten by its venom—this is a metaphor for the attachment to a self (*ātma-grāha*).
That is to say, the mind of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-citta*) is the grasper (*grāhaka*), while the two kinds—self (*ātman*) and phenomena (*dharma*)—are the grasped (*grāhya*).
The phrase "and knowing that these are non-existent," etc., concludes the preceding discussion on the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).
The phrase "the uncontaminated dependent nature" (*anāsrava-paratantra*) is the heading. Question: What is meant by the "uncontaminated dependent nature"? Answer:
The commentary states that the four characters "retribution-buddha-seed" (*vipākabuddhabīja*) explain the character "buddha" in the sūtra; "seed" explains the character "seed" in the sūtra;

the two characters "causal conditions" (*pratyaya*) explain the two characters "from conditions" (*pratītya*) in the sūtra; and the two characters "that which is produced" explain the character "arising" (*utpāda*) in the sūtra. Furthermore, another explanation says: "from conditions."
That which arises is called "conditioned" (*pratyaya*). It is called "arising" (*utpāda*) because it is produced through cultivation.

Regarding the statement "the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dependent nature," one asks: The treatise states that the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is produced from the conditions of conceptualization (*vikalpa*);

how then can it be established as uncontaminated? In response, there are two interpretations. First, the verse speaks in reference to the defiled portion (*saṃkleśa-bhāga*). Thus, the verse of the treatise says: "Conceptualization and conditions..."

Regarding "that which is produced": it should be understood that this refers, for the time being, to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) in its defiled aspect; however, the pure aspect of the dependent nature is also included, as it is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Second, regarding "discrimination" (*vikalpa*): it is not only the deluded mind that is capable of objective cognition (*ālambana*) that is called discrimination;

therefore, it applies generally to the untainted (*anāsrava*) as well. Alternatively, all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), whether defiled or pure, are termed discrimination because they engage in objective cognition.

Regarding that which is "produced by causes and conditions": the seeds existing from the beginning serve as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*); the permeation of the three types of wisdom through hearing serves as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*);

the supreme mundane dharma (*laukika-agra-dharma*) serves as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*); and the universally pervasive true thusness (*sarvatraga-tathatā*) serves as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
The seeds of the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha arise in the first stage (*bhūmi*); from this point onward, throughout the causal path of the ten stages, one repeatedly cultivates those newly perfumed.
Regarding "that which gives birth": that which inherently exists gives rise to the two wisdoms of the Sublime and the Equanimous. The former and the latter reach equality.
Within liberation, one relinquishes impermanent form and attains the permanent aggregates. Through the seeds of the four wisdoms, the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*) is brought forth.
That the reward body is able to arise is entirely due to cultivation. "Cultivation" means to initiate; it is only through the cause of practice that [the reward body] can arise.

Regarding the statement "by means of realizing the true principle," this refers to the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature). If one is on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), one realizes *tathatā* (suchness);
if one is at the stage of Buddhahood, one realizes Great *Nirvāṇa*.
Regarding the statement "severing the mind that clings," once the clinging subject is severed, the grasped objects—the self and dharmas—are likewise without obstruction.

Since defilement no longer exists, there is no longer any outflowing *paratantra* (dependent nature) characterized by the defiled portion; instead, one relies upon the seeds of the four wisdoms belonging to the pure portion of *paratantra*.

From these, the manifest activities arise, forming the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) and realizing the principle of the *dharmakāya* (truth body). This is termed the "One Vehicle" (*ekayāna*), which here specifically refers to the principle of *tathatā* (suchness).

Regarding the "One Vehicle" (Ekayāna): the intention is to cause sentient beings to sever the defiled aspect of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), cultivate the pure aspect of the dependent nature, and realize the principle of the Dharmakāya; therefore, it is called the One Vehicle.
As for the question, "What is the One Vehicle? the answer is: it refers to the re-manifestation of the eternal dharma, namely the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature).

If one distinguishes based on the categories of eternal and non-eternal, true suchness (*tathatā*) alone is identified as the perfected nature. If one distinguishes based on the categories of outflowing (*sāsrava*) and non-outflowing (*anāsrava*), this excludes not only the outflowing but also the non-outflowing *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature).
The intention of the commentator (*śāstrakāra*) is to take true suchness as the One Vehicle, as indicated in the second line of the verse.
Therefore, he first poses the question: "What is the One Vehicle? The answer below explains that True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the One Vehicle.

Regarding the phrase "further clarifying the eternality of phenomena" (*dharmāṇām nityatvam*), this refers to the four characters "knowing that phenomena are eternally without nature" (*jñātvā dharmān nityān nihsvabhāvān*) from the preceding verse;
these are precisely the "True Suchness of phenomena" (*tathatādharma*) within the second verse. This is because, in the preceding verse, one knows that phenomena are eternally without nature.
This explains the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature). It is now explained once more; therefore, it is called "revelation.

Regarding the phrase "the dharma abides in its station" (*dharmasthititā*), this simultaneously indicates the two dharmas of "abiding" and "station. True Suchness (*tathatā*) exists within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*);
because its essential nature is eternally constant, it is called "the abiding of the dharma" (*dharma-sthiti*). The intended meaning is that True Suchness pervades all things.

Among all phenomena, the lush green bamboo is, in its entirety, True Suchness (*tathatā*). It is further said that True Suchness is primordially present and dwells within the realm of birth and death;

this is called the "abiding of the Dharma" (*dharmasthiti*). To speak of the abiding of the Dharma means that the Dharma of True Suchness abides within the stages of the three levels of worthies (*trayaḥ śaikṣa-pudgalāḥ*), the ten stages of sages (*daśa-āryapudgalāḥ*), and the two vehicles (*dviyāna*);
by severing defilement and attaining purity, these various stages are manifested. All worthies and sages take the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as their basis.
The Dharma has distinctions: when enshrouded by afflictions, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha*; when free from these shrouds, it is called the virtues of the *dharmakāya*.
As for the statement that "the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding," this refers to the aforementioned Dharma abiding in its own place within the world;
since this very world takes true suchness (*tathatā*) as its essence, and that essence is eternal, the world is also eternal. This is termed "the eternal nature of the characteristics of the world."
It abides. As the Sūtra says: "One does not perceive the three realms as the three realms.

Regarding all such matters that arise and abide within the characteristics of the world, from the very beginning one does not see these worldly characteristics. In the Dharma-nature school, the characteristics of the world are themselves eternally abiding;
delusion is birth-and-death, while awakening is nirvāṇa. They are like waves and water; their essence is not separate. If...

When deluded, the world is birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*); when awakened, the characteristics of the world are themselves *nirvāṇa*. Upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood, both birth-and-death and *nirvāṇa* are equal;
therefore, it is said that "the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding" (the divine wisdom of liberation relies on the nature).

To be confused about the characteristics of the world as being non-eternal is to fail to realize that they are the eternally abiding *tathatā*. Abiding within the characteristics of the world, one encompasses those characteristics.
It returns to its fundamental nature. Because one brings the characteristics of the world back to this nature, it is said that "the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding.

The characteristics of the world refer to the phenomenal appearances of both sentient and insentient beings, which are themselves impermanent *tathatā*. However, the characteristic that constitutes the essential body of the world is eternally abiding;
therefore, it is said that "the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding."
Regarding the phrase "in the Vajra-maṇḍala" and so forth: having understood [the meaning of] "maṇḍala" within the sūtra, one asks, "What is called a maṇḍala? The answer is:

the four wisdoms (catur-jñāna) are called the "path" (mārga), and the unconditioned principle (asaṃskṛta-dharma) is called the "field" (kṣetra). Because one realizes the principle of the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), one subsequently accomplishes the wisdom of the Reward-body (saṃbhogakāya);
this field where the path is attained is called a "maṇḍala. Furthermore, it is like the place where rice is grown or the place where wheat is grown; it is so named.

It is like a granary for grain or a threshing floor for wheat. Within the fruits [of practice], it is the principle of the *dharmakāya*, for it is the locus upon which the myriad virtues, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, depend.
The dharmas of merit are called the "path" (*mārga*), while the principle that serves as their locus is called the "field" (*kṣetra*). The *dharmakāya* in its essential nature is itself the path;
alternatively, the *svasaṃbhogakāya* is called the path, and the principle of the *dharmakāya* is called the field. The fruit of the *svasaṃbhogakāya* is realized upon the field of the *dharmakāya*.

Because it is attained there, it is called the place where the Way is realized; this is what is meant by a "site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Within that site of enlightenment, one knows that this Dharma abides in its own dharma-position and is eternal in the world.

This is explained from the perspective of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), which attains perfect enlightenment through thirty-four moments of mind within a single period of transformative manifestation;
thus, it is said that "one has known [it] at the site of enlightenment."
Regarding the phrase "within namelessness and signlessness," this explains the skillful means (*upāya*) by which the Teacher speaks within the sūtras.

If one were to discuss the quiescent nature (*śānta-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena, it could not be proclaimed through words. Now, within that which is nameless and signless, he speaks by means of names and signs.
When discussing phenomena that are nameless and signless, the mouth wishes to speak but words fail; the mind wishes to contemplate, but thought ceases. This is what is now being taught.
This refers to merely attaining the name and essence [of reality], like a person calling out "fire" while the fire does not burn their mouth and so forth. The Four Noble Truths are the names;

within each truth there are four aspects (ākāra), which are the characteristics (lakṣaṇa). (The section on the meaning of the three natures in the preceding section on meditative concentration is concluded.)

Regarding the statement that, "Briefly, among all phenomena," emptiness refers to the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature), while existence refers to the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) and the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature).
The *Śīlasamvara-sūtra* states: "The conditioned and the unconditioned are called 'existence'; 'self' and 'what belongs to self' are said to be 'emptiness.'"
If the school of Bhāviveka asserts that within the conventional gate all three natures exist, while within the ultimate gate all three natures are empty;
whereas the school of Dharmapāla asserts that within the ultimate gate they are neither empty nor existent, yet may be said to exist when distinguished according to their verbal expression.
To say that "emptiness is without differentiation" and is established as a single nature refers to the *parikalpita-svabhāva*.
To say that "there are phenomena with differentiation" and so forth—within this context, this is the most restricted [category]—refers to the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*, which is termed "the eternal."
It is solely the principle of *tathatā* (suchness).
As for the statement "the impermanent is permanent," this refers to the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature). The dependent nature cannot be subsumed within the category of permanent phenomena;

rather, that which is contaminated (*sāsrava*) is subsumed within the dependent phenomena. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, fascicle eight, states: "The uncontaminated conditioned [phenomena] are free from..."

Reaching the ultimate, its supreme function is all-pervasive; it is also called the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature). True Suchness (*tathatā*) possesses three meanings, and for this reason it is named the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*.
First, its essence is pervasive, which is the meaning of "perfect" (*pari*). Second, its essence is eternal, as it is not subject to arising and ceasing;

thus, it is "accomplished" (*niṣpanna*). Regarding these three meanings: its essence is not false or erroneous, being the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena; this is the meaning of "real" (*satya*).
Furthermore, the dependent nature of the pure division (*śuddha-paratantra-svabhāva*) also possesses these three meanings. First, its supreme function is all-pervasive;

that is, it can universally sever all defiled phenomena and universally take all suchnesses (*tathatā*) as its object. Therefore, this constitutes the meaning of "perfection" (*pariniṣpanna*). Second, it is ultimately able to sever all defiled phenomena;
this is the meaning of "accomplishment. Third, its essence is free from falsehood and non-delusory; this is the meaning of "reality. Because it possesses these three...
The meaning is as follows: the pure portion of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is also termed the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

To speak now according to the previous gate, within the aforementioned gate of the permanent and the impermanent, we additionally take the pure portion of the dependent nature—the untainted (*anāsrava*) manifestations and seeds—which arise by depending upon various conditions;
therefore, it is said that "the seeds arise from conditions."

The statement, "The meaning is to clarify that it can realize the principle of non-self," is a further explanation of the two characters "knowing the permanent nature of phenomena" (*dharmāṇāṃ nityatva*) in the sutra.

The statement, "It means being able to fully understand that the two selves are non-existent," explains the two characters "knowing the absence of nature in phenomena" (*dharmāṇām asvabhāvatva*) in the sutra. This is the intended meaning.
To clarify the one who realizes [the truth], the question is asked: what is the sequence of the three natures?

If, according to the former, one first realizes suchness and subsequently abandons the afflictions (*kleśa*), why does the treatise explain the "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*) and "liberation" (*vimukti*) [samādhis] as distinct from the abandonment of afflictions and the realization of the true mind? If, on the other hand, one first abandons the afflictions...

Why does the treatise state: "Without directly perceiving this perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), one is nonetheless able to fully comprehend the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*)"? Answer:
By repeatedly cultivating the superior contemplation of the two kinds of emptiness, the power of the perfuming of untainted seeds becomes strong.

When this wisdom arises, the afflictive obstructions do not manifest, whereby one comes to dwell eternally within the state of non-arising and spontaneously realizes the single true Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). This is precisely...

The nature of things is called "the real. When speaking of realization within the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), there is no sequence whatsoever. Within subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), one speaks of a sequence by following conventional models.

If one speaks of the true seeing (*tattva-darśana*), the first is the path of non-interruption (*ānantarya-mārga*), the next is the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), and the last is the path of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*).

Therefore, it is said that the afflictions are severed during the path of non-interruption, while on the path of liberation, one realizes the principle of cessation (*nirodha-satya*) and eliminates the residual habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

If one speaks of subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), it means that only after first realizing suchness (*tathatā*) can one perceive that dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) as being like illusory phenomena and so forth.
This is because within fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), one has realized the emptiness of what is imagined by the conceptualizing nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Therefore, the treatise states:
"Once non-conceptual wisdom has realized suchness, only then, within subsequently attained wisdom, can one fully comprehend the dependent nature as being like illusory phenomena and so forth. Thus...

It is realized first and then attained. It is severed first and then realized. This is because, according to the discussion of the true path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), one first sees the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) and subsequently the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*);

whereas this is explained according to the path of seeing the signs (*nimitta-darśana-mārga*). Question: Since beginningless time, one has perceived objects through their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).

How is it that only later does one attain "clear understanding" (*pratividha*)? Answer: Because since beginningless time, the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*) have coexisted; thus, although one perceives their own objects, [they are not truly understood].
One realizes that objects are empty, like encountering people in a marketplace whom one does not know by name. Thus, the Treatise says:

"Although from beginningless time the mind and mental factors have already been able to take their own characteristics, such as the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), as objects, they nevertheless constantly function in conjunction with the two types of grasping—of self and phenomena—and do not know things as they truly are.
They fail to realize that these are merely the false manifestations of one's own mind and mental factors, induced by various conditions."
Regarding the statement "relying on others, such as virtuous friends," this explains the *dharmapada* (dharma-position) within the sūtras;

that is, during the one eon prior to the [first] bhūmi, the power of the seeds of the *saṃbhogakāya* gradually increases through the permeation of the three types of mundane wisdom (*trividhā prajñā*) derived from hearing, until they first arise at the initial stage of the first bhūmi.

Through the gradual cultivation of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), one reaches the state of fruition, which is termed "the fulfillment of awakening. This corresponds, among the four types of practices for drawing near (*catvāraḥ upaniṣad-pratipattayaḥ*), to the practice of drawing near to virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra-upasevana*);
and among the four superior powers (*catvāri balāni*), it is the power of virtuous friends.

It is explained through explicit teaching: twelve years ago, he taught existence; he taught emptiness through implicit teaching.

Now, at this assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, he explicitly teaches existence and explicitly teaches emptiness. Because he teaches them collectively during this third period, it is called the "Ultimate Truth."

Regarding the statement that "the meaning of the three natures is as explained elsewhere," this refers to the explanation of the three natures within the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (The Treatise on Consciousness-Only), specifically in the "Twelve Gates of Analysis.

As for the scriptural passage stating, "Worshipped by devas and humans... [omitted] ...he also teaches such a Dharma," it means that he also teaches the single reality which is worthy of being so called.
Because sentient beings [attain this], it is called "peaceful security.
To say that the sutra reveals various paths is to open up the provisional (the *upāya*). That "in reality they are equal" is to manifest the ultimate truth (*tattva*).
This is also the same as the passage below which proclaims the Buddha-way through various Dharma-gates; it is also the same as the previous section which further employs diverse skillful means.
This serves to clarify the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

The Sūtra states, "knowing the various activities of sentient beings. The Commentary explains this as the general phrase concerning the characteristics of mental activity (*citta-saṃskāra*). The word "knowing" (*jñā*) extends throughout all the subsequent phrases.
Regarding the phrase "or resolve" (*adhimukti*): it is asked, by what power of knowledge does one know the various formations (*saṃskāra*)?
The answer is: all formations are initially the mind. "Formations" is a general term; this understanding of formations is precisely the resolve of sentient beings.

Through the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding resolve, he knows the pure and impure differences in the resolves of all sentient beings, understanding them as they truly are. Pure... [text ends]
Causing [wholesome qualities] to increase and causing one to abandon the impure, etc., while delighting in the practices of the three vehicles and so forth, is called "pure resolve.
Delighting in killing and so forth is called "impure resolve."
Regarding the phrase "the thoughts and mental states of others" (*cetaḥparyāya-jñāna*): it refers to knowing the distinct paths toward which each individual inclines.

This differs from the power of knowledge of the course leading everywhere (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad-jñānabala*), which knows, exactly as they are, the practices by which sentient beings can emerge from all suffering.

Regarding the power of karma: all sentient beings create their own karma and experience its results themselves; this the Buddha knows through his power of knowledge regarding the wisdom of one's own karma.
Regarding the power of desire: it refers to the arising of aspiration and longing; this the Buddha knows through his power of knowledge regarding the wisdom of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).

Regarding the "element of nature" (*dhātu-bala*): among those who are inferior in various ways, one understands their faculties (*indriya*) as they truly are according to the distinctions of their respective elements (*dhātu*).

Without relying on specific instructions for each particular gateway of entry, one establishes them accordingly. This refers to the four kinds of elements in the *Mahāśāstra*: first, the element of the naturally abiding lineage (*prakṛtistha-gotra-dhātu*);

second, the element formed through cultivation (*samudānīta-dhātu*); third, that which is susceptible to counteraction (*pratipakṣa-karaṇīya*); [and fourth, that which is not susceptible to counteraction].

The various realms (*dhātu*). Those who have already planted the roots of merit conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*). The four unremediable realms (*apratikāra-dhātu*), namely those persons lacking the spiritual lineage (*agotra*).
Regarding the power of diligence (*vīryabala*), some say it is subsumed within the power of knowing what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*), because that power is broad in scope:
in the Buddha’s Dharma, the correct cause is called "possible" (*sthāna*), while the false causes of non-Buddhists are called "impossible" (*asthāna*). Within the term "etc. (*ādi*):
The power of knowing the results of one’s own karma (*svakarma-vipāka-jñāna-bala*) is as follows:

it is the aspect of the power of knowing what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñāna-bala*) that the Tathāgata can know—namely, that by means of a sentient being’s diligence, a wholesome fruit is experienced, and by means of performing unwholesome conduct, an unwholesome fruit is experienced.
This is called a "power. Second, it is said: "Or the power of diligence, etc. The phrase "etc. includes faith, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom; the intended meaning is the power of diligence.

This is precisely power (*bala*). Since the essence of the lineage (*gotra*) is the five faculties (*pañcendriya*), and diligence (*vīrya*) is counted as one of those five faculties, it is said that the essence is identical to the power of the lineage.
In the former interpretation, the three powers of desire (*chanda*), lineage, and diligence were explained as being distinct;

in the latter interpretation, the power of diligence is identical to the power of the lineage, and since the power of the lineage is the five faculties, the power of diligence is not separate from them.

Regarding the phrase "the power within the word": the character "power" (*li*) in the latter term is understood to penetrate through to the "power" in the former term; it carries the meaning of not being subdued or defeated.

As for the mention of "past and future Buddhas" and so forth: Question: Why is it that the aforementioned Buddhas spoke only of awakening to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), yet did not speak of knowing the faculties of sentient beings, whereas this present Buddha knows the faculties of sentient beings but does not speak of awakening to the three natures? What is the reason? Answer: [The text continues with the response.]
The Commentary states: "Because they mutually reflect and illuminate one another, the meaning of the provisional first and the real last is identical.
The scriptural passage from "Now I am also like this" up to "proclaiming the Buddha-way" constitutes a single recitation of the sūtra text, which is assigned to the teaching of the Real.
Question: The phrase "various dharma-gates" seems to refer to the provisional; why, then, is it said to be the Real and the Provisional?

The answer states: Some say that "various Dharma-gates" refers to the events in the Introductory Chapter—such as the raining of flowers and the shaking of the earth—and the intent behind the Bodhisattvas' questions and answers, which merely proclaimed the Buddha-way.
Alternatively, "various Dharma-gates" refers to what was taught prior to the forty years [of the Lotus Sūtra], which were expedient teachings (*upāya*).
"Proclaiming the Buddha-way" refers precisely to the assembly where the provisional is merged into the real; it is the teaching of the ultimate reality itself.
Regarding the statement, "I am also equal to Śākyamuni," there is no textual passage in the preceding prose section stating that he is equal to Śākyamuni.
This topical division is merely the Master of the Commentary’s own interpretation of the sutra’s intent, asserting their equality with Śākyamuni.
According to the *Vyūha-śāstra*, for three reasons, all Buddhas of the three periods of time are identical in their initial provisional and subsequent ultimate teachings.
The three bodies are equal: first, because their basis is the same, the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas is equal, for the *dharmadhātu* is without distinction;
second, because their mind is the same, the *janmakāya* (birth-body) of all Buddhas is equal, for they are identical to the Buddha-mind without distinction;
third, because of their activity, the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation-body) of all Buddhas is equal, for they share the same objects to be converted. Now it is said:

"Identical" refers to the identity of their karma. Because the provisional and the real are identical, they transform beings of indeterminate nature. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Now I am also like this," which signifies the identity of the teaching masters.
Regarding "bringing peace and security to sentient beings," the intention is to employ various identical Dharma-gates;

this reveals the identity of the three vehicles and proclaims the single Buddha-way, manifesting the identity of the One Vehicle. "By my power of wisdom" signifies the identity of the power of wisdom.

One who knows the dispositions and desires of sentient beings observes their faculties to be identical and employs skillful means to preach the Dharma, establishing teachings that are identical so that all may attain them;

thus, the benefit is identical. For instance, if the faculties are not yet mature, one rejoices upon hearing a small teaching; if the great faculties are mature, one rejoices upon hearing a great teaching. Each of the Three Vehicles accords with its respective faculty, and this is called universal rejoicing.

Although the forms of rejoicing are not uniform, they are all termed "universal. As for the term "universal" (jie): [it refers to... (Note: The final sentence fragment "As for the term 'universal' (jie): appears to be an editorial note or a partial gloss left over from the source text, as it does not form a complete thought within the provided passage.)

"Both. Regarding the phrase "I request you to bear [this] in mind," etc.: "Request" refers to the entreaty of the various devas for the teaching; "bear in mind" refers to the contemplation of the signs [of the teaching];
"expedient means" refers to skillful inducement.
Regarding the statement that the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras* explain [this], Zizhou distinguishes it by means of five gates:

defining its essence (*svabhāva*), explaining its name (*nāman*), identifying its person (*pudgala*), its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and its inclusion within the five categories (*pañca-saṃgraha*). As for the general name: in Sanskrit it is called *prajñācāra*.

*Pra* (or *pañca*) here means "five" (*pañca-artha*); *jñā* (or *cāra*) means "exhaustion of practice. *Jñā* is "practice" (*caryā*), and *cāra* is "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*). This refers to the practice regarding objects.
Because it perceives all forms, it is called "eye" (*cakṣus*) by extension from this function; however, this is not the primary etymological explanation. "Eye" carries the meaning of "illuminating";

thus, the term is established according to its essential nature and function as used in the Tang [Chinese] tradition. "Five" refers to a number; this is an explanation based on a numeral (the preceding explains the general name, while the following explains the specific names).

Regarding the statement "the single flesh eye" (*māṃsa-cakṣus*): here, we take the sense faculty (*indriya*) to be the eye, not the consciousness (*vijñāna*) to be the eye. It is definitively stated: "flesh" refers to the matter that is the maturation (*vipāka*) of karma;
"flesh" is itself the eye. This is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound. Alternatively, according to Zhangjing, that which can perceive those objects is called "flesh."
The physical sense-faculties that serve as the basis are called "fleshly eyes" when based upon the physical eye; this is an explanation according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound.
The statement that they do not arise from meditative concentration indicates that they are produced by the retribution of karma.

Regarding the statement "produced by the four great elements" (*mahābhūta*), the interpretation that the Prefecture of Lu takes both the producing great elements—earth, fire, water, and wind—as its nature is incorrect.
Here, we take only the produced matter (*upādāya-rūpa*)—namely, visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility—as its nature, and do not take the producing elements.
Regarding "nourishment" (*āhāra*), there are two types of nourishment: first, nourishing the emaciated so as to make them plump; second, nourishing the stunted so as to make them grow.
These are called "nourishment. There are four kinds of nourishment: first, food and drink; second, sleep; third, the holy life (*brahmacarya*); and fourth, meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).

The *Fayuan* states: "There are two further types of nourishment (*puṣṭi*). First, that which is extensive in scope, namely: food and drink, sleep, and the meditative attainments of the holy life (*brahmacarya*).

Second, that which increases through characteristics, which also arises from food and superior mental attention (*manasikāra*); this refers to the universal [factors] of mind and mental concomitants, as it causes them to become lucid.
Now, flesh and sleep possess the first two types of nourishment—namely, food and drink and sleep—[the latter being] the type of nourishment consisting of morsels (*kavaḍīkāra*)."

Food is the preliminary practice for sleep; therefore, it is called "nourishment. For example, Aniruddha lost his eyesight because he did not sleep, which was due to his failure to obtain nourishment.
Regarding the statement "or maturation, purity, etc.": these five material sense-faculties (*pañca-rūpīndriya*) are the eighth aspect of the objective field (*nimitta-bhāga*).
Drawn forth into this present life by the power of prior karma, they mature at a different time, mature as a different category, and mature through transformation;

thus, they are called "maturation" (*vipāka*). Maturation is itself matter (*rūpa*). Question: What is the distinction between nurtured matter (*aupacayika-rūpa*) and maturation matter? Answer: It is said that one type is...

Matter such as food and drink that assists what has been produced is called "nourished matter" (*aupacayika-rūpa*). That which is induced by past karma is called "retributive matter" (*vipākaja-rūpa*).
Regarding the phrase "two kinds of divine eyes," there are two: first, the divine eye obtained at birth, which is termed "divine" because it arises from the body of a deity.

The eye. Here, that which is acquired by birth (*upapatti-labdha*) is not taken. Second, regarding that which is acquired through cultivation (*bhāvanā-labdha*): it is definitively stated that although the names of the heavens are the same, only that acquired through cultivation is taken.

It is universally accepted that cultivation occurs among the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the three continents of the southern region. This refers to the fundamental meditative concentrations (*mauladhyāna*) of the four dhyānas.

It is called the "divine eye" (*divyacakṣus*). It is the eye arising from meditative concentration (*samādhi*). [In the sense of] "the eye of a deva" (*devasya cakṣuḥ*), it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound; or, since the light and purity [produced by] concentration itself is called "divine," [it is] "the divine which is the eye," a *karmadhāraya* compound.

By means of sitting, one attains the [form-sphere] of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); through the assistance provided by this power of concentration, relying upon the physical faculty of the eye (*māṃsacakṣus*), one is able to produce the divine faculty of the eye (*divyacakṣurindriya*), which is able to see objects beyond obstructions. This is called the "divine eye."

Regarding the phrase "severing the hindrances to meditative concentration (*samādhi-āvaraṇa*) and so forth," this refers to the severance by the Master [of the Commentary]. There are two types of hindrances to concentration:

first, inferior experience, which involves the reception of objects belonging to lower stages and a lack of aspiration for the concentrations of higher stages; second, lethargy and restlessness (*styāna-auddhatya*). To speak according to the actual reality:
Afflictions such as greed can generally obstruct meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Therefore, the treatise states: "This [contemplation] merely deludes regarding phenomena;

it functions according to the external gate, being coarse and agitated in its state of distraction. Because it directly obstructs concentration, this is merely an observation of phenomena where the mind is coarse;

it cannot subdue those delusions regarding principles, nor the innate [afflictions], but can only subdue those that arise from delusion regarding the five external sense objects. It cannot subdue those [other afflictions]."
It arises simultaneously with seeing.
The phrase "arising from cultivation" indicates that it is not produced by the karma of the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*).
Regarding the statement "though it nourishes the four great elements," "nourishing" here does not refer to the nourishment provided by food, drink, or sleep. The *Jianyao* says: "From [itself]..."

Regarding the statement that there is "meditative concentration and holy life" (*dhyāna-brahmacarya*), it is definitively explained: because one cultivates concentration by means of this, it is termed "nourishment" (*puṣṭi*). He asked:

"Since the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*) has wisdom (*prajñā*) as its intrinsic nature, how can it be said that its intrinsic nature is derived pure matter (*upādāya-rūpa*)? He replied: "Because the hindrances to concentration (*samādhi-āvaraṇa*) have been abandoned."

One attains the higher meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*). Based on these absorptions, one induces the pure matter of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), which resides within the body. However, wisdom (*prajñā*) arises in turn by depending upon this faculty of the divine eye;
thus, it is called the "supernormal power of the divine faculty" (*divyendriya-abhijñā*), and there is no contradiction.

Regarding the statement "observing existence and so forth": observing existence is wisdom that takes existence as its object in contrast to fundamental gnosis (*mūla-jñāna*); this is called "observing existence. In contrast to the observation of emptiness, it is called the "object of wisdom regarding existence.
It is also the teaching. The eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*) is fundamental gnosis; the dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*) refers to subsequently attained gnosis (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).
Subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) is of two kinds: first, that which takes principle as its object; it manifests images and takes suchness (*tathatā*) as its object.
Second, that which takes phenomena as its object; this is what is now referred to as the "Dharma-eye" when it takes phenomena as its object within the One Vehicle.

It universally takes all things as its object—whether form or mind—and is able to contemplate all the one hundred and forty kinds of merits of the Buddha-body and all phenomenal dharmas. It is also said that this subsequently attained wisdom is able to...

Taking the hundreds of thousands of teachings as its object is called the Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*). Taking principle as its object is subsumed under the Wisdom-eye (*prajñācakṣus*); both have wisdom as their essential nature.

Regarding the four types of the Wisdom-eye: only the fundamental wisdom that takes ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) as its object and realizes the principle of the two kinds of emptiness is called the Wisdom-eye.
Furthermore, Zhangjing said: "According to the scriptural text, wisdom comes first and the Dharma follows; the commentary has inverted this order.

As for the statement that the fruit results from the accumulation of causes: the three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas are called the 'accumulation of causes,' and it is through this that the fruit is perfected."
Regarding the statement "grasping the preceding four": grasping the preceding four is collectively termed the "Buddha-eye. Apart from these four, there is no separate essence. Question:
Since the fleshly eye and the divine eye are contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena, how can they be termed the "Buddha-eye" by grasping these four eyes? Answer: It is a matter of terminology.

It does not grasp a physical body. Question: Why is there the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) within the stage of Buddhahood? Answer: Within the stage of Buddhahood, there are the first fifteen elements (*dhātu*).
Having abandoned impermanent form, one provisionally attains permanent form; it arises as actualized activity (*pravṛtti*) from the seeds of the five untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).

Question: How can there be the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*) within the stage of Buddhahood? Answer: The divine eye faculty within the stage of Buddhahood is induced by meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Its nature is pure form (*rūpa*). Bian states: "Because it is induced by the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), within the fruit [of Buddhahood], it is able to encompass the former four [aggregates].
Although the superior and inferior aspects are entirely distinct, it merely encompasses their names; therefore, there is no error."
Regarding the mention of "Nāgārjuna and others": Question: How is it that the preceding four [eyes] are collectively termed the "Buddha-eye"? Answer: The commentary states: "Nāgārjuna and others.

Nāgārjuna Bodhisattva composed the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Great Commentary on the Perfection of Wisdom) to explain the *Pañcaviṃśati-sāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Large Sutra). In explaining the meaning of the five eyes, he refers to the "great ocean" as a "celestial pond" (*tiantai*).
Within a celestial pond, there are no names for the four rivers; likewise, when the four eyes reach the stage of Buddhahood, they become the eye with nothing remaining [beyond them].
There are four names. Just as the four rivers have distinct names before they reach Lake Anavatapta, but once they flow into that lake they are collectively called the great ocean;
so too, the four eyes have distinct names before they reach the Buddha’s body, but once they flow into the Buddha’s body, they are collectively termed the Buddha-eye.
(The above clarifies the names; the following sets forth their essence.)
Regarding the statement that "the substance of the first two is matter": both the result of karma and the result of meditative concentration are matter. Mou says:

However, the faculties of the physical eye differ according to various schools. For the Lokāyata and the Tīrthikas, the four great elements in their purified state constitute its substance; for the Sāṃkhya and the Vaiśeṣika, [it is otherwise].
According to the [Sarvāstivādins], fire, space, earth, water, and wind serve as the essential natures (*ātman*) of the faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body, respectively.

According to the Mahāsāṃghikas, flesh is the essential nature. According to the Sautrāntikas, the subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*) are the essential nature. According to the Ekavyavahārikas, they exist as names but lack substantial reality.
Regarding the Mahāyāna school, there are two positions. First, Master Nanda holds that its essence consists of the seeds of consciousness.

Second, the doctrine of Dharmapāla holds that its essence consists of the primary and secondary pure matter (*rūpa-prasāda*). Within this, there are three divisions: first, those consisting solely of seeds; second, those consisting solely of manifest [matter].
The second [interpretation] is correct. Therefore, the Abhidharma states: "The eye faculty refers to that which has previously seen or currently sees forms, as well as their seeds.

Second, the divine eye (divyacakṣus) has as its nature the translucent matter (rūpaprasāda) produced by the four great elements (mahābhūta) arising from meditative concentration (samādhi); for it is the fruit of supernormal power (abhijñā-phala).
Zhangjing asked: "In the causal stage, both the flesh eye and the divine eye have form as their substance. In the state of Buddhahood, how do these two substances differ?
He replied: "There is a distinction at the level of the cause, but none at the level of the fruit."

Regarding the statement that "the two subsequent bodies of wisdom" (dvitīya-kāya-jñāna) encompass both the fundamental and the subsequent [wisdoms]: the Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*) is exclusively subsequent wisdom, while the Wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*) is fundamental wisdom.

Regarding the statement that "the subsequent one encompasses both": this refers solely to the Buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*), which takes the preceding four as its essence; therefore, it encompasses both the material (*rūpa*) and the non-material (*arūpa*).
Each has two. According to the meaning of the *Śāstra*, "pervading both" refers to pervading both form (*rūpa*) and cognition (*jñāna*).
Regarding the phrase "humans, etc., have the flesh [eye]," the word "etc. includes the other four [realms]. This is because all four destinies possess the physical eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*).

Alternatively, that which is visible—the sense object (*viṣaya*)—is called "flesh," and the material sense organ (*rūpīndriya*) is so called because it depends upon that flesh; thus, the eye of the flesh is called the "flesh-eye."
It refers to the eye.
Regarding the statement that "the gods and others possess the divine eye," the word "others" (等) includes the inhabitants of the three continents. Master Zizhou says:

"Humans [of the three continents] and those of the six heavens of the desire realm who have attained the fundamental dhyāna of the fourth dhyāna are all able to produce the divine eye. This is because they have attained it.
Because it is pervasive, it belongs to the eye of the heavens; thus it is also called the "heavenly eye" (*divyacakṣus*).

Regarding the statement that the two vehicles possess the "wisdom eye" (*prajñācakṣus*): because the two vehicles realize the principle of the emptiness of sentient beings (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), they possess the wisdom eye.

However, the two vehicles lack the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) and do not establish the "dharma eye" (*dharmacakṣus*). Although they do indeed take dharmas as objects to a small degree, this is omitted from discussion and remains hidden.

Regarding the statement that a bodhisattva possesses the Dharma-eye: because the bodhisattva possesses that knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) and takes hundreds of thousands of teachings as its object, [the Buddha] possesses the Buddha-eye.
It is for this reason that five [eyes] are taught. Question: If the Buddha possesses the Dharma, it may be designated as the Buddha-eye.

Question: A bodhisattva possesses the dharma-eye; should it not therefore be called the "bodhisattva eye"? Answer: The Buddha-eye exists only in a Buddha; it is named the "Buddha-eye" after the Buddha.
The dharma-eye is not possessed by bodhisattvas alone; its name is established based on its object, and thus it is called the "dharma-eye. Question:

Since the Dharma is not possessed by bodhisattvas alone, why is the dharma-eye not called the "bodhisattva eye"? Furthermore, the divine eye is not possessed by gods alone; how then can it be named the "divine eye"? Moreover...
Furthermore, divine vision (divyacakṣus) is not restricted solely to devas; it may still be called "divine vision. Likewise, fleshly vision (māṃsacakṣus) is not restricted solely to humans;

it ought to be called "human vision. Answer: Fleshly vision exists throughout other realms of existence (gati); because it is common to all, it is not specifically "human vision. Divine vision belongs exclusively to the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) of the devas; therefore, it is called "divine."
Regarding the phrase "able to illuminate and reveal what is manifest," this refers to the visual faculty (the fleshly eye) taking an object as its condition; here, "manifest" means a clear condition.
Regarding the phrase "without obstruction," this refers to the condition of space. Alternatively, "manifest" refers to form, while "without obstruction" refers to the open expanse.
Visible form and space are manifested as one color.

As for the statement that the two types of divine eyes can illuminate both the hidden and the manifest: the divine eye does not depend on space; rather, it is because the two conditions are pervasive that it sees both the hidden and the manifest—namely, the presence or absence of obstructive matter.

Regarding the phrase "illuminating all aspects": when subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) takes as its object that which is form (*rūpa*) or that which is mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), these are termed non-form;
this is also subsequently attained wisdom taking as its object that which is suchness (*tathatā*), which is termed non-form, as it is taken as an object solely by fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
Regarding the statement that "the essence of the Dharma-eye is wisdom": the essence of the Dharma-eye is exclusively wisdom; it has no other distinct essence. Therefore, wisdom is combined into one.
This single essence of the Wisdom-eye also subsumes the Dharma-eye; thus, it is said that the essence of the Dharma-eye and wisdom are combined into one. Question:
Among the five eyes in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the wisdom [eye] is fundamental gnosis (*mūla-jñāna*), while the Dharma-eye is subsequently attained gnosis (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).

The essence of these two knowledges (*jñāna*) is wisdom (*prajñā*). Why, then, does the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* explain that the first and last of these two knowledges are collectively termed the "eye of wisdom" (*prajñā-cakṣus*)?
The commentary answers: "The essence of the eye of phenomena (*dharma-cakṣus*) is [wisdom], etc. Furthermore, it asks:

"If the essence of these two eyes is one, and the eye of phenomena is subsumed within the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*)—since both are of the same kind, namely wisdom—why is wisdom not subsumed under the eye of phenomena? The answer is: The eye of phenomena...

The essence is wisdom (*prajñā*). It is logically appropriate that [the faculty of] phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) be subsumed within the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*). Since the eye of wisdom does not take phenomena as its object, it is therefore impossible to subsume wisdom under the eye of phenomena (*dharma-cakṣus*).

Regarding the statement that [the objects of] the fleshly eye and the divine eye are not the same as the objects of the [eye of] form (*rūpa-cakṣus*), one asks: both the fleshly and divine eyes are indeed forms; yet, in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*,...

[The opponent] then asks: "The two eyes of Dharma-wisdom (*dharmaprajñā*) are both wisdom; why are they not divided into two distinct eyes? Furthermore, the two colors of 'this' and 'that' are each opened into two types;
why are the two wisdoms of 'this' and 'that' not likewise opened into two kinds? The Commentary answers: "They are not the same as color and so forth.

One [type of wisdom] takes manifest color as its object, while the other takes hidden color as its object. Thus, there is a distinction between the two: the intentional expression (*manojalpa*) and the teaching through principle (*yukti*)."
They are not identical in color, because some are hidden and some are manifest.
Regarding the statement that "the Buddha-eye is identical to [the others]": Question: In the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the Buddha-eye is established separately by encompassing the preceding four eyes.
Why, then, does this sūtra not establish the Buddha-eye as separate from the four eyes? Answer: The commentary states: "The Buddha-eye is identical to the preceding four."

Regarding the statement "or discussing the causes, etc.," this is the second interpretation. It refers only to the three eyes—namely, the fleshly eye, the divine eye, and the wisdom eye—and does not mention the Buddha-eye because it is currently discussing the stage of a causal practitioner (hetu-bhūmi);
thus, it is omitted for brevity. Therefore, one should know that within those three eyes mentioned in that treatise...
This fully encompasses the five eyes.

Regarding the statement that "the single fleshly eye sees all things" and so forth: Question: Among all forms, there are those that are concealed or manifest, and those that are obstructed by external or internal barriers.
How is it that the fleshly eye can see them all? Answer: Because within that fleshly eye, there is contained a portion [of the divine eye].
Regarding the objective sphere of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*): it is explained in one place that the divine eye only perceives the objects of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
As for the statement that "the divine eye sees dying here and being born there," a question arises: the divine eye should only be able to see present forms that are hidden or distant.

"How can one perceive future births and deaths? The deity replied: "Among the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), the divine eye power (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*) is coarse; among the three knowledges (*tisro vidyāḥ*), the divine eye is subtle.

It is also called the 'knowledge and vision of birth and death' (*cyutyupapādajñāna-vidyā*), for its essence is wisdom (*prajñā*). Because it is wisdom, it is able to take birth and death as its object.
Through this knowledge and vision of birth and death, which serves as the gateway for the divine eye, the divine eye is induced to take future births and deaths as its object."

Regarding the phrase "the eye of wisdom sees all through the three objects": Question: Why was it that previously the eye of wisdom contemplated principle (*li*), whereas here the wisdom contemplates the differences in the faculties and natures?
Answer: The former is fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*); this is subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) contemplating the faculties.
Regarding the statement that "the four dharma-eyes see all": "all dharmas" refers to the true reality of all dharmas.
Huàdù explains: because they perceive everything, encompassing both cause and fruit.

Regarding the statement that "the five Buddha-eyes see the ten powers of a Buddha": among the aforementioned five eyes, the dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*) is subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), which is able to perceive the one hundred and forty unique qualities (*āveṇika-guṇa*) of the Tathāgata. When it is now said that they "see the ten powers," this takes a portion of the objective domain of that dharma-eye as its essence.
Regarding the "six eyes of wisdom," these are also subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) that comprehends all types of phenomena.
Regarding the "seven eyes of clarity," these are also wisdoms capable of seeing the light of all Buddhas, both for oneself and others.

Regarding the statement that the "eight eyes transcend birth and death": seeing only the principle is the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). At the moment of initial enlightenment, one enters the nirvana of the three aspects (*tri-niṣṭha-nirvāṇa*).

Regarding the "nine unimpeded eyes," some say they perceive only phenomena (*dharma*), while others say they perceive only principle (*li*); this also encompasses both the fundamental and the subsequent [wisdoms].

Regarding the "ten universal eyes," the *Jianyao* states: these refer to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) realized, which pervades the entire Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), as well as that which realizes it.
This wisdom is likewise universally without eyes; therefore, it is called "universal" (*pu*).
Regarding the phrase "the first among the ten," one asks: how is it that the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) among the ten also encompasses the heavenly eye (*divya-cakṣus*) among the five?
The answer is: the heavenly eye has two capacities: first, it can see obscured and hidden forms; second, it can see this [world's] death and rebirth.
Since it is stated among those ten that the fleshly eye sees all forms, we know that it encompasses a portion of the domain of the divine eye;
because the part is designated by the whole, it is collectively termed the "fleshly eye."
Regarding the statement that "the second among these is the middle one of the five," this means that the second of the ten fully subsumes those five;
specifically, it subsumes the second of the five, which consists of a portion of the two middle ones among the five—the objects of dying here and being born there.
Regarding the statement "the third through the ninth among these," the five eyes refer to the Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*) among the aforementioned five eyes. Mou states:
"The third eye among the ten is the Wisdom-eye (*prajñācakṣus*); it perceives the differences in the faculties (*indriya*) of all sentient beings, taking only their faculty-natures as its object.

The Wisdom-eye among the [first] five takes only ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) as its object, which is different from the former. The Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*) among these ten perceives the Buddha."
Regarding the ten powers: among the five [eyes], the Buddha-eye takes as its object both form and non-form, taking the first four objects as its domain.
As for the statement "or the fourth, eighth, ninth, etc.," these three eyes all apprehend a portion of that which takes principle (*li*) as its object.

The fourth [eye] perceives the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) of all phenomena; the eighth is the eye that emerges from birth and death, perceiving the dharma of nirvāṇa. The Commentary states: "The fourth..."

The ninth is the unimpeded eye (*anāvaraṇacakṣus*). That which is unimpeded regarding principle is subsumed under the wisdom-eye (*prajñācakṣus*); that which is unimpeded regarding the teachings is subsumed under the dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*).

Regarding this, Zhangjing provides a further explanation in three sections: first, the explanation of the names; second, the sequential order; and third, the basis of vision. The explanation of the names has already been understood. As for the sequential order:
first, the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*) sees what is near but not what is distant; it sees what is coarse but not what is subtle; it sees what is bright...

It is not darkness. Because one sees what is within the obstruction but not what is outside the obstruction, there is a deficiency in its function; therefore, one cultivates the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).

Once the eye has attained the divine eye, although the aforementioned fault is absent, one merely perceives the false conceptualizations within forms and does not see the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena;

thus, one has not yet transcended birth and death, and for this reason, one cultivates the wisdom-eye (*prajñācakṣus*). Although one attains the wisdom-eye, because there is still no thorough comprehension regarding all phenomena, one therefore cultivates...

The Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*). Although one has attained the Dharma-eye, because it is not yet all-encompassing regarding that which is to be known, one cultivates the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*). Regarding the three types of vision:

the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that among the physical eyes (*māṃsacakṣus*) of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), none are superior to those of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), who can see for a hundred *yojanas*.

The physical eyes of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) are explained as being the same as those of ordinary beings. The physical eyes of a Bodhisattva are as described in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*; [they are] slight... [text ends].
Those who have long upheld the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* see for a hundred *yojanas*; the great ones see the trichiliocosm.

With their physical eyes (*māṃsa-cakṣus*), they see the trichiliocosm and also perceive the causes and conditions of the good and evil of sentient beings; this is similar to the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*).
Regarding the divine eye, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that ordinary persons who cultivate and attain it see one four-continent world system (*cāturdvīpaka*), while lesser *arhats* see...
A minor [Arhat] sees a small chiliocosm; a great Arhat sees a medium chiliocosm; Aniruddha sees a great trichiliocosm.
A minor Pratyekabuddha is equal to a great Arhat; a great Pratyekabuddha spontaneously sees a great trichiliocosm.
As for the divine eye of a Bodhisattva, the least sees a hundred *yojanas*, up to the greatest Bodhisattva, who sees the boundless worlds of the ten directions as well as the three worlds. Wisdom—

The eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*) perceives the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena; the Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*) perceives phenomena; and the Buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*) perceives both principle and phenomena in their entirety.
When it is said that "one observes with the Buddha-eye," this refers here to the observation by the Buddha-eye among the five eyes described in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Alternatively, it may be...

The self-enjoyment body dwells in the self-enjoyment realm, or the other-enjoyment body dwells in the other-enjoyment realm, observing the sentient beings of the six paths and the śrāvakas of the three faculties.
These beings are poor and lack both merit and wisdom: they lack merit because they do not cultivate the first five perfections;
they lack wisdom because they do not cultivate the sixth pāramitā. They are called "poor" because they lack merit, and [they lack wisdom] because they lack wisdom.
The names are exhausted.
Regarding the "Buddha-eye" among the ten [eyes]: it is asked, why not take the Buddha-eye contemplation from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*?
The answer, as stated in the commentary, is that the Buddha-eye among the ten sees the ten powers of the Buddha, but does not see sentient beings.
Regarding the statement "not cultivating the two causes of merit and wisdom," this refers to the passage in the sutra from "I observe with the Buddha-eye" up to "lacking merit and wisdom.
Regarding the "seven kinds of noble wealth," these are faith, ethical discipline, learning, relinquishment, wisdom, shame, and dread of blame.

Because these seven types of resources benefit and sustain the practitioner, enabling them to reach the further shore, they are called "wealth. The seven dharmas of the wealth of humans and devas are generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, [wisdom, and relinquishment].
Wisdom and skillful means benefit sentient beings; because they involve the coming and going between humans and devas, they may also be called "wealth.

However, because they do not correspond with the seven most excellent [qualities], but merely seek the retributions of humans and devas and thus accord with birth and death (*saṃsāra*), they are only termed the "seven dharma-wealth.

They do not fulfill the meaning of "deliverance" (*tāraṇa*) and are not called *pāramitās*. They are merely comprised within the "wholesome acquired by birth" (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*). Question: Since they accord with birth and death, why are they called "skillful means"?
It is appropriate to answer that practicing generosity, precepts, and so forth, while seeking the fruits of human and celestial rebirths, also possesses a slight degree of skillful means.
As for the statement regarding those "sunk in present suffering," the Buddha’s eye perceives the sentient beings of the six realms; these are precisely the three grades of śrāvakas.
Within the six realms of existence, one is submerged by manifest suffering. Thus, the sutra says: "By reason of various desires, one falls into the three evil paths."
Regarding the statement that those who seek the essential path of liberation may instead practice erroneously and act in confusion:

the Sūtra says that people of meager merit and few virtues, oppressed by manifold sufferings, enter the dense forest of false views—such as [the extremes of] existence or non-existence—and fall into the three evil realms.

When the Sūtra speaks of entering the perilous path of birth and death, it means that all perilous paths do not exceed these two types of birth and death; these are also precisely [the paths] from the hells...
They emerge [from the hells] and shall fall among the animals and other realms. The perils of heaven cannot be ascended; the perils of earth consist of mountains, rivers, hills, and mounds.

Kings and dukes establish fortifications to defend their states. Who would say that the *tu* plant is bitter? It is as sweet as shepherd’s purse (*cai*). One might say the perils of heaven are as level as a smooth plain.
Regarding the statement that "the suffering of continuity is uninterrupted": once the preceding maturation (*vipāka*) has been exhausted, another maturation arises again.
Ji Guo says: "Entering the perilous path of birth and death, one sinks into the state of suffering; the suffering of continuity is uninterrupted.

One sinks into the fruit of suffering by being deeply attached to the five desires, and sinks into the instruments of suffering like a yak that loves its tail. This sinking into the heart of suffering is identical to what was previously described as being 'within evil.'"
Because they dwell amidst the secular dust of the world and are submerged in the five desires, they are unlike [the noble ones].
It is said that the worldly yak, out of self-love, becomes entangled in thorns upon its own tail and refuses to move.
Consequently, when the yak passes by, a hunter suspends thorns along its path; the yak likewise becomes caught by its tail, and the man moves forward to kill it. Upon reaching...

If one does not act [properly] when facing death, it is like the ox that loses its life because of its love for its tail. Sentient beings, out of greed for the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), fall into the evil realms (*durgati*) due to that greed.

Regarding the phrase "hiding the body to protect the tail," Miǔ (糅) states: "Hiding the body" has the meaning of being deluded and obscured; because one is deluded and obscured by greed regarding the tail.

He cherished his tail so dearly that he was eventually killed by it. Had the yak known early on that the tail was the very cause of his own destruction, he ought to have discarded the tail to preserve his life.
Likewise, if sentient beings knew early on that the body is the cause of saṃsāra, they ought to feel revulsion and renounce it immediately.
There is honey upon a blade; one must not crave its sweetness. A poisonous plant has flowers; one must not be attached to them. There is poison within food; one must not consume it.
One must not eat it. There is a pearl before the beast; one must not take it. The bird in the net regrets that it cannot fly high;

the fish on the hook regrets that it cannot endure its hunger. Birds lose their lives for food; humans lose their lives for wealth. Man dies for the sake of riches; the bird perishes for the sake of food.
Every creature loses its body for wine; the clam and the oyster lose their bodies for the pearl. The *miao* ox [loses its life for its tail-hair].
The ox loses its body because of its tail; sentient beings, for the sake of craving and attachment, lose this very body and lose their bodies as humans or devas, thereby sinking into the evil realms.
Mou said: "The ox symbolizes sentient beings; 'craving' symbolizes the peripheral mind, which is precisely the greedy mind. Thus, one loses the body.
Sentient beings crave the five sensory objects and consequently sink into the evil realms; furthermore, the peripheral mind craves the tail, and thus [it perishes]."
He then killed his body. Because of the mutual arising of affectionate attachment, they were submerged in the evil realms.
The two characters "bì" (to obstruct) and "bì" (to cover) both signify the vertical path.
Regarding the term "Southwest Barbarians" (Xinan Yi): if explained according to specific names, there are the Eastern Yi, Western Rong, Southern Man, and Northern Di;
if explained according to the general name, the four directions are called the "Four Barbarians. Therefore, they are termed the Southwest Barbarians.

The Sūtra says: "Not seeking great power... [down to] the dharma that cuts off suffering. This refers to the golden complexion and the thirty-two marks, the ten powers and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, as well as the dharma that cuts off suffering—the untainted noble path of the three vehicles. Furthermore, for Śrāvakas, it refers to the seven preparatory stages (*saptaprayoga*);

for Pratyekabuddhas, the forty-four knowledges and the seventy-seven knowledges; and for Mahāyāna practitioners, the stages prior to the *bhūmis*, namely the *sambhāra-mārga* (path of accumulation) and the *prayoga-mārga* (path of preparation).
The two stages are the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).

Regarding the statement, "Those who enter deeply into various false views and seek to abandon suffering through [the perception of] suffering," consider for a moment the three disciples of Kāśyapa who served fire, the dragon, and practiced asceticism.
Jiguō says: "Those who do not seek the Buddha of Great Power" refers to those who are deluded regarding conditions and causes. And with...

Regarding the dharma for severing suffering: it is to provide the excellent medicine to those who are deluded; to enter into the conditions of suffering for those who have deeply entered various false views;

to initiate ascetic practices for those who already suffer and desire to abandon suffering; to feel compassion for those who suffer for the sake of such sentient beings; and to arouse the intention to uproot suffering by giving rise to great compassionate mind.
To say that the Buddha possesses supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and so forth means that the Buddha has the power to deliver sentient beings.

To say that he possesses wisdom and so forth means that the Buddha has the capacity to enable sentient beings to sever suffering. It is because sentient beings are unable to seek for themselves the Dharma for severing suffering that [the name of the Buddha] arises.
Regarding the statement "not seeking rebirth and so forth," this refers simply to the wisdom of the two kinds of emptiness within the bodies of sentient beings;
it is taught to sentient beings to enable them to practice in reliance upon it, and for this reason it is called "given by the Buddha."

Regarding the phrase "reversing [the path] and falling into the non-Buddhist paths (tīrthika) and so forth": this refers to non-Buddhists who observe the precepts of the cock or the dog, such as sleeping on thorns or scorching the body with five fires, and who, in their interpretation of the sūtras, have deeply entered into various false views.

Regarding the reason for the six-year period: it asks how sentient beings, being attached to false views, fail to transcend birth and death. The commentary answers that "six years" and so forth refers to the analogy of a dog chasing a clod of earth;
here, the dog represents the non-Buddhist (tīrthika), while the clod of earth is a metaphor for ascetic practice. Engaging in such ascetic practices is like the behavior of a dog.
"Chasing after clods of earth": the bitter fruits of the future will not cease; it is like being struck by a clod as it comes toward you. The cause of suffering is ascetic practice;
the fruit of suffering is the three miserable realms. One clod departs and another arrives; the cause of suffering ends and the fruit of suffering arrives.
As for the term "lion," it is a metaphor for the Buddha’s disciples who sever those evil views; this is called "chasing away the person.

That they do not invite bitter fruits is called "not being a clod. Entering into the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) is like biting the person so that the clod does not come back; by severing the cause of origination, the bitter fruit is naturally extinguished.
Regarding the statement, "Contemplating and giving rise to causal practices": Question: Previously it was said, "I, with the Buddha-eye, observe the sentient beings of the six realms.
This refers to the realization of the fruit [of Buddhahood]. Why, then, at this time, does one again contemplate and give rise to causal practices?

Answer: This refers to the past, when he was the sixteen princes. In reality, he had already attained Buddhahood long ago; however, he manifested as dwelling within causal practices, giving rise to great compassion. And...
This is for the purpose of teaching and transforming others; therefore, there is no fault. This is identical to what is said in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*:

"Although one has attained the Buddha-way and turns the wheel of Dharma, one does not abandon the path of the bodhisattva. The intended meaning is that this Prince [Mañjuśrī] manifests as dwelling within the realm of causes.

This may be verified by the *Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta* (Chapter on the Lifespan). Furthermore, it says: "The mind of great compassion is called causal practice," which refers to the manifestation of the present life. Thus, it arises.

This cause is the mind of compassion (*karuṇā-citta*). It demonstrates the eight signs and so forth, all of which are transformational marks (*nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa*), showing the arising of causal practices.

Furthermore, it is said that when the Buddha was formerly an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*), he saw sentient beings dwelling in suffering; he reflected upon practicing the path himself, intending to save them only once his fruition was fulfilled.

Regarding the scriptural statement, "For the sake of these sentient beings," the word "for" (故) carries a profound meaning. What is this profound meaning? It means that one perceives all sentient beings as being distinct.

This is what the scripture refers to when it says, "They do not seek the Buddha of Great Power, nor the Dharma for severing suffering," and further states, "Due to the causes and conditions of various desires, they fall into the three evil realms," and also, "Of meager virtue and little merit."
People are oppressed by manifold sufferings. Furthermore, seeing that all sentient beings lack wholesome roots, this corresponds to what the sutra says:
