"The place where the Wheel of Dharma is turned" means that even if there is realization of the Deathless (amṛta) among the devas, if it does not exist among humans, it is not called the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma. Therefore, only these [five] are mentioned.
Question: When the five men turned the wheel of Dharma, all five saw it; why was it only Cunda who did so? Answer: Cunda saw it first;
therefore, the other four were still at the stage of the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśala-mūla*).
Regarding the statement, "The teaching has already been turned correctly," when Kauṇḍinya also entered the path of seeing (darśanamārga), he thought, "I have understood the Dharma.
Thereupon, the earth spirits announced this to the gods of the Four Great Kings; thus it was passed on in succession from those dwelling on earth to the gods dwelling in the sky, proclaiming:

"The World-Honored One has turned the wheel of the sublime Dharma (saddharmacakra). Therefore, it is known that the path of seeing is called the wheel of the Dharma. Question: Within the assembly, there were also various...
Question: A celestial voice was transmitted. Why was it said that only the earth deity spoke? Answer: First, because the earth deity sat near the World-Honored One;
second, because she was the first to utter a sound, according to the sequential principle of the Dharma. Question: Why did the sound reach only as far as the Brahma Heaven? Answer:

Because the Brahmā King requested the World-Honored One to turn the Wheel of Dharma, the sound reached the Brahma world so that the Brahma deities might hear it and give rise to profound joy. Question: If...

Regarding the statement that "only the Noble Path is called the Wheel of Dharma": [one might ask] since it was already designated as "turned" when the Buddha preached the Dharma to the merchants under the Bodhi tree, for what reason is it only at Vārāṇasī that the Wheel of Dharma is said to have been turned? (This is an objection based on the Buddha’s own conduct.
Answer: There are two kinds of turning: first, by oneself; second, for others. Since the Buddha takes the benefit of others as his primary task, this refers to turning it for others. Question:
If the noble path arises in another, it is called "turning the wheel of Dharma. Why is it said that the Buddha turns it? The answer is: this is spoken in terms of his capacity to turn it.

That is to say, although the noble path exists within that person's body, if the Tathāgata does not provide verbal instruction as the cause for its turning, that person’s own noble path would arise without a cause.
Since the arising of that noble path is entirely due to the power of the Buddha, it is said that the Buddha is the one who turns it. As it is said:
Regarding the treasure of the Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*): before the king has placed the wheel in his left or right hand and turned it, even the various devas are unable to turn it.
If one asks what constitutes "turning" for others, it is only when he speaks of it that it is called turning.

During the second seven-day period, [the Buddha] gave the three refuges and the five precepts to Trapusa, and taught the Dharma. According to the Mahāsāṃghika school and others, all the words spoken by the Buddha constitute the Dharma.

[The wheel. Answer: That [previous point] refers to the truths observed in common by the three vehicles, as it is not a universal path; now, this is discussed in terms of the universal path shared by the three vehicles.
Regarding the statement "according to the Sautrāntika school, etc.," the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu was originally a native of Gandhāra. Regarding the sūtras...
He entered the monastic order within a particular school and later traveled to the kingdom of Kaśmīra, where he studied the *Vibhāṣā* treatises.

As he listened to the teachings, he committed them to memory at a rate of one verse per day, completing six hundred lines. However, within those verses, he praised the doctrines of the Sautrāntika school and refuted those of the Sarvāstivāda.
Because the master Vasubandhu was using the tenets of the Sautrāntika school to challenge the Venerable [Saṃghabhadra], the Venerable was unable to penetrate his arguments.
He entered meditative absorption to observe the matter and realized that Vasubandhu was covertly refuting the Sarvāstivāda school through the Sautrāntika perspective.
He then said to Vasubandhu, "Return to your country at once; those who have not yet abandoned desire may fear you and seek to harm you. Vasubandhu then took a copper leaf...

He transcribed the treatises he had composed and was about to return to his own country. In the kingdom of Mi-lo, there was a master of the Sāṃmitīya school who kept the treatises he had authored secret;
he commanded a yakṣa deity not to allow those treatises to be disseminated. Vasubandhu then recorded them and departed.

At that time, the masters of the Sāṃmitīya school congratulated one another with joy, saying, "The Sāṃmitīya school is flourishing! Buddhasimha said, "That Vasubandhu intends to propagate the Sautrāntika school and will refute your 'existence' (bhāva)."
The Master’s verse is a traditional transmission that seems merely to harmonize [the views]. If you do not believe this, please ask Vasubandhu to explain it, and you will know for yourself.

There was an Arhat of the Sarvāstivāda school who was equal in status to the Emperor; he requested the Celestial Being (Vasubandhu) himself to provide an explanation. When the explanation was given, it was exactly as had been stated.
This, then, is the Sautrāntika refutation of the tenets of the Sarvāstivāda school.
Regarding the statement that "the aspect of the three turnings is not merely [the path of seeing]," this directly refutes the previous claim by Vasumitra (Ghoṣaka), who said:
"The Wheel of Dharma exists only in the path of seeing; when the path of seeing arises in Kauṇḍinya and others, it is called 'already turned. Vasubandhu refutes this, saying:
"It is not only the path of seeing."
Regarding the question of how this can be explained, it refers to the reasoning established by the master Vasubandhu. He states:

"Therefore, it should be understood that these three types [of turning] are themselves threefold. The first consists of the three turnings of self, and the second consists of the three turnings of others.

The first is the turning of the seal of realization (*saṃjñā-parivarta*): knowing as it truly is, "This is the Noble Truth of Suffering," and knowing as it truly is, "This is the Noble Truth of the Origin [of Suffering]" (and so forth).
1) Turning through the Seal: Because it seals the characteristics of the Four Noble Truths, it is called "turning through the seal. 2) Turning through what ought to be practiced:
"This is suffering; I should fully know it. This is the origin; I should fully abandon it. This is cessation; I should fully realize it. This is the path; I should fully cultivate it.
3) Turning through what has already been done: "This is suffering; I have fully known it. This is the origin; I have fully abandoned it..."
"It has been abandoned. This is cessation; I have fully realized it. This is the path; I have fully cultivated it.

Regarding the two others, there are three turnings: first, the turning that indicates the characteristics: "This is the noble truth of suffering; this is the noble truth of the origin [and so forth]. Second, the turning that exhorts practice.
"This is suffering; you should fully understand it. This is its origin; you should completely abandon it.
This is its cessation; you should fully realize it. This is the path; you should fully cultivate it. This is the turning of the wheel through realization.

"This is suffering; you have fully understood it. This is its origin; you have completely abandoned it. This is its cessation; you have fully realized it. This is the path; you have fully cultivated it."

Question: Under each Truth (satya), there are four aspects (ākāra)—namely, vision (cakṣus), knowledge (jñāna), clarity (vidyā), and awakening (buddhi). Thus, four times four makes sixteen, and with three turns (parivarta), there would be forty-eight.
How can it be said that there are twelve? Answer: For now, let us consider that under each Truth, there are four [aspects] and three turns.
It is said to be twelve because the number is the same; thus, it is provisionally called twelve. In reality, however, there are forty-eight.
If discussed vertically, they are called twelve; if discussed horizontally, there are forty-eight. This is suffering, which is seen, known, clarified, and realized.

"This is the origin; through eye, wisdom, clarity, and awakening... (and so forth). "2. This is suffering; you should fully understand it through eye, wisdom, clarity, and awakening. This is the origin;
you should completely abandon it through eye, wisdom, clarity, and awakening. This is cessation; you should fully realize it through eye, wisdom, clarity, and awakening. This is the path;
you should fully cultivate it through eye, wisdom, clarity, and awakening. 3. "This is suffering; through eye, wisdom..."

Regarding "clarity, awakening, and so forth": however, the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) school explains that within the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), the "Dharma-patience" (*dharmakṣānti*) is called the "eye," the "Dharma-knowledge" (*dharmanirjñāna*) is called "knowledge," the "subsequent patience" (*anvayakṣānti*) is called "clarity," and the "subsequent knowledge" (*anvayanirjñāna*) is called "awakening. These distinguish the four noble truths individually.

Furthermore, there is another interpretation: "seeing directly" is called the eye (*cakṣus*); "decisive discernment" is called knowledge (*jñāna*); "illumination" is called clarity (*vidyā*); and "vigilant awareness" is called awakening (*buddhi*).
In the Mahāyāna, the single untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) is collectively termed the Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*), because there are distinctions based on the past, future, and present;

it is not that four distinct knowledges arise separately regarding a single truth. This is because the true path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) lasts for only a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), which differs from the sequential stages of the Hīnayāna.

Regarding the term "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*): that which takes the past as its object is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*); that which takes the future as its object is called "clarity" (*vidyā*); that which takes the present as its object is called "awakening" (*buddhi*).

That which takes all three periods of time as its object is called the "eye" (*cakṣus*). The eye is the general [term], while the other three are specific. Question: The three—suffering, origin, and the path—are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

Because the wisdom that penetrates the three periods of time takes this as its object, that object is called "the clear awakening of wisdom" (*jñānāloka-vibodha*). Since the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it neither comes nor goes; how then can one speak of the three periods of time? Answer:

It is explained by way of conventional designation (*vyavahāra*). It also penetrates the three periods of time. When the subject-wisdom takes that Truth of Cessation as its object, it is called "the clear awakening of wisdom.

This refers to both the understood and the not-yet-understood. The two afflictions are termed "obscuration" (*paryavasthāna*) and "hindrance" (*nivaraṇa*). Regarding the Truth of Cessation, the afflictions...
The afflictions (*kleśa*) pertain to all three periods of time. When untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) takes past afflictions as its object, it is called "knowledge" (*jñā*);

when it takes future afflictions that obscure *tathatā* as its object, it is called "clarity" (*vidyā*); and when it takes present afflictions that obscure *tathatā* as its object, it is called "awakening" (*buddhi*).

Thus, the three periods are established. Therefore, the Commentary states: "For this reason, it should be understood that this very [wisdom] extends to the ultimate principle. This is the Wheel of the Dharma.
Question: Since the practice of the Dharma involves the sense of crushing and destroying, it may appropriately be called a "wheel. How is it that the teaching of the Dharma is also called a "wheel"?
Answer: Regarding the teaching of the Dharma, because it possesses the sense of being expounded and the sense of being turned, it is therefore called a "wheel" and called a "turning."
Regarding the statement that it "should correspond to correct principle," this refers to the principle of the three turnings (*tri-parivarta*).
As for the question, "What is meant by 'turning' (*parivarta*)?"—since the teaching is called a "wheel" (*cakra*), how can it be termed a "turning"? The Commentary (*ṭīkā*) answers:

"By means of this dharma-gate, etc. Here, "continuity" (*saṃtati*) has the sense of the body; because it causes [beings] to understand the meaning, it issues from the mouth of the World-Honored One and enters [the mind of] Kauṇḍinya.
It is so called because it turns; thus, it is named "turning.
As for the phrase "or the various noble paths," this is Vasubandhu’s second interpretation, which explains the Wheel of Dharma of Practice.
As for the phrase "toward those to be converted," it refers to the presentation of such [teachings].
Regarding the phrase "turning within one's own continuum," this explains the meaning of "turning" (*vartana*), which refers to the manifestation of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).

Regarding the phrase "in the continuum of others," a question is raised: since the Sautrāntika school maintains that it is called the "Wheel of Dharma" (*dharmacakra*) because it turns through all three paths, how is it that the World-Honored One’s turning [of the wheel] for Ājñātakauṇḍinya—occurring at the very first moment of entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*)—is already designated as the Wheel of Dharma? The commentary answers: "In..."

Regarding "his mental continuum" and so forth: it is simply that one sees what has never previously turned throughout the past now turning for the first time today; this is called the "initial turning.

There is an interpretation which claims this refers to the latter two turnings, but that is incorrect (as [the elder] Tianqin [Shangtianqin] raised the objection and [the master] Zhongxian [Zhongxian] provided the defense).
Regarding the statement "there is an explanation by this [author]," it refers to the master Saṃghabhadra.

Since Vasubandhu had used the Sautrāntika doctrine to refute the Sarvāstivāda school, his teachings did not prevail for many years. Saṃghabhadra lamented these refutations and sought to defend the Sarvāstivāda.
He composed a treatise in eighty fascicles titled *Abhidharmakośa-vajra* (The Thunderbolt Against the Abhidharmakośa).

Later, from the kingdom of Kaśmīra, he tied the *Vajra* to the head of an elephant and the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* to the elephant’s tail, pursuing Vasubandhu with the intent to defeat him face-to-face.
Vasubandhu avoided him, always maintaining a distance of one *yojana*; though he followed, he could not catch up. Vasubandhu’s disciples said to their master, "Why..."
Therefore, he avoided the master Vasubandhu, who remarked, "It is like a lion king avoiding a boar. Whether near or far, superior or inferior, the wise should understand this.
Subsequently, Vasubandhu contracted dysentery; consequently, Saṃghabhadra took his gold, silk, and the treatise he had composed [and departed].
He sent a letter to Vasubandhu, saying: "I have composed this treatise; I pray that you will deign to examine it. You may then transmit it so that it may circulate.
If it is not so, I am content to be reduced to ashes. Upon reading it, Vasubandhu remarked: "This is precisely in accord with my own school.
He subsequently changed the title to *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (The Treatise in Accordance with Correct Reasoning), which remains extant in the canon today. However, Saṃghabhadra...

The Master [Vasubandhu] generally rejects this, asserting that it is not the correct tenet of the Sarvāstivāda that the Wheel of Dharma (dharmacakra) refers exclusively to the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga).
This claim that the term "Wheel of Dharma" applies solely to the Path of Seeing is an incorrect tenet within our own Mahāvibhāṣā;
it does not represent the original intention of the Sarvāstivādins.

Regarding the statement, "The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* also describes [this]," etc.: Question: Does the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* also state that the name "Wheel of Dharma" (*dharmacakra*) is established only with respect to the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*)?
Answer: The commentary states, "The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*, etc., are also not the correct tenets within our own school.
Since these are already not the correct tenets in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, how could their presentation in the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* be considered correct?
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* further states, "Alternatively," citing the *Kośa* to establish the correct doctrine (*siddhānta*) of the Sarvāstivāda school.

The phrase "or the various noble paths" refers to the three paths of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning; these are properly named the Wheel of Dharma, which is why they are called "various. This is the fundamental intention of the Sarvāstivāda (Sabbatthavāda).
The above represents the interpretation accepted by the masters of the *Nyāyānusāra*.
The statement "Hence the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* says 'Vibhāṣā'" is the Master of the Commentary’s own explanation; it also recounts the original intent of the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.
Regarding the phrase "by means of three cycles," some say "by means of three turnings of the teaching," but this is an error.

Regarding the phrase "in the mental continuum of another, such as [the stage of] seeing," a question is raised: "If the Wheel of Dharma turns through all three paths, how is it that when one first enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the Buddha asks whether [the listener] has understood?
The commentary answers: "Regarding 'in the mental continuum of another,' etc., this is stated provisionally with reference to the initial turning that leads one into the state of an Arya;
it does not yet refer to the turning in which the fruit is fully perfected. This clarifies that the Wheel of Dharma is not designated solely by the name of the path of seeing alone.
Regarding the statement that it is "not only the Path of Seeing [that establishes the Wheel of Dharma]," etc.: Question:

Since the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that the Wheel of Dharma is established only upon the Path of Seeing, is this not the correct interpretation? Is it not rather the case that the hub, spokes, and rim—corresponding to the three [aspects]—is the correct interpretation?

Answer: The commentary states, "not only the Path of Seeing," etc. This indicates that Vasumitra (Miaoyin) considers the hub, spokes, and rim to be established solely upon the Path of Seeing; however, this too is refuted.
Regarding the phrase "The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* says, etc.," Cope states: "Upon examining the upper and lower sections of that treatise, nothing is found exactly as cited in the commentary.

However, the commentator [Suzong] has stated this based on the general intent. In the twenty-third chapter of that treatise, the 'Chapter on the Three Wisdoms,' it says: 'The arising of mutual dependence is exhausted. This refers to..."

Regarding the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), the three turnings have already been explained. Furthermore, the *Ekasatyavarga* states: Question: If one does not attain the path by means of the Four Noble Truths, by what dharma should one attain the path?
Answer: One attains the path by means of a single truth; that is to say, the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*). As it is said in the Sūtra: [text follows].

The practitioner contemplates these five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as being without self (*anātman*). Just as a bottle is called "empty" because it contains no water, so too, because there is no divine self (*pudgala-ātman*) within the five aggregates, they are termed "empty.

The Minister of State said: "The first turning extends up to the contemplation of the five stages of cessation (*pañca-vinodana-citta-bhāvanā*), whereby the wisdom born of hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*) arises.
The second turning extends up to the general and specific mindfulness-contemplations (*smṛty-upasthāna*), whereby the wisdom born of reflection (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*) arises. The third turning..."

Upon reaching the stage of the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśala-mūla*), cultivation arises; one contemplates only the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*) and only the aspect of selflessness (*anātman*) within the aggregates (*skandha*).
It proceeds solely as "emptiness" (*śūnya*) and lacks the other twelve aspects (*ākāra*). The Sautrāntika master Siṃha says:

"The meaning of Master Ma is that he originally left the household life within the Sāṃkhya school, yet like the Hīnayāna, he accepts that there is a path for abandoning afflictions prior to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*). From the five stabilizing practices (*pañca-sthāpanā*)...
The mind and so forth are observed equally, because there is the sense of transformation.
Regarding the statement that "now, the Mahāyāna is collectively equal": the *Yogācārabhūmi*, the *Saṃdhinirmocana*, and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* all clarify the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*).

Nevertheless, both the Great and Small Vehicles speak of both general and specific [turnings]. As for the general [turning] of the Mahāyāna, it refers to the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) and the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).

They pertain to the paths of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning; only the ten knowledges (daśajñāna) reside in the path of no-more-learning, and do not pertain to the former two [paths], which is the same as in the Hīnayāna.

If one follows the distinction of the Mahāyāna, the seven factors of enlightenment (saptabodhyaṅga) reside in the path of seeing, the eightfold noble path (āryāṣṭāṅgamārga) resides in the path of cultivation, and the ten knowledges reside in the path of no-more-learning.

Regarding the distinctions within the Hīnayāna: the Eightfold Noble Path pertains to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*); the Seven Factors of Enlightenment pertain to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*);

and the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*) pertain to the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). As for their general characteristics, they are the same in both the Great and Small Vehicles; as for their specific characteristics, there are differences between the Great and Small Vehicles. The ten knowledges exist only in the stage of no-more-learning, which is the same in both the Great and Small Vehicles.
Regarding the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the Wheel of Speech: the first intrinsic nature accords with Saṃghabhadra; the latter eight branches accord with Ghoṣaka. Question:

In what way do these accord with the teachings of the Hīnayāna schools? Answer: They accord because they comprehensively synthesize various textual passages. Now, I say this is not so. Within the commentary (*śāstra*), there are two interpretations:

the first concerns the distinct characteristics of practice according to the three paths; the second concerns the allocation of the total practice to the hub and other parts [of the wheel]. This is the enumeration.
They are not the same. How could this be called an interpretation that accords with the *Suyāma-sūtra*? Moreover, the *Śāstra* itself explicitly states that it differs from the Hīnayāna.

If one argues that the former interpretation concerns a distinct cultivation (*pṛthag-bhāvanā*) according to the treatise, why does the *Śāstra* state that it "comprehensively includes the paths of seeing and cultivation" (*dṛg-bhāvanādi-sāmānya*)? Answer: That treatise’s wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*) is not restricted solely to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
It is not based on the three paths [of seeing, meditation, and no-more-learning] being cultivated simultaneously in the seventh and eighth consciousnesses.

Regarding the term "dharma-vicaya-sambodhyaṅga" (the awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena): among the seven awakening factors within the wheel of the Dharma of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), it takes the awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena as its essence.
This investigation of phenomena is precisely the non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) within the path of seeing; it is thus called the awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena.

Within the wheel of the Dharma of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), it takes right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) from the eightfold noble path as its essence. Within the wheel of the Dharma of the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*), it takes correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*) from among the ten knowledges as its essence.

This constitutes the essence. As for what are called the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), they are: investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), diligence (*vīrya*), joy (*prīti*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), and pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
"Enlightenment" (*bodhi*) refers to wisdom; "factors" (*aṅga*) has the meaning of "parts. Among these, the single factor of investigation of phenomena is both enlightenment and a factor.

The other six are factors but not enlightenment, because they assist enlightenment or because they are of a nature associated with enlightenment. Regarding the eightfold noble path, there are right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) and right intention (*samyaksaṃkalpa*).
The Eightfold Noble Path consists of right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. "Right" (*samyak*) means noble (*ārya*).

"Path" (*mārga*) has the sense of traversing or walking upon. Within the Eightfold Noble Path of the Mahāyāna cultivation, only the single factor of right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) is taken as the essential nature of the wheel, because its substance is wisdom (*prajñā*).
The [tradition of] Lu Prefecture also includes right thought (*samyaksaṃkalpa*), but here we take only [right view].

There is one dharma that realizes the actual substance, which is solely right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*). Regarding the ten knowledges (*jñāna*), according to the explanation of the Hīnayāna, they are as follows: the knowledge of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path constitute four;

the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), and knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) constitute another four; and the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) constitute two.

These are the ten knowledges. Question: Within the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*), there are ten knowledges. What, then, is the noble realization-knowledge (*ārya-prativedha-jñāna*) referred to here?

[Question: What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the wheel? [Answer: It is precisely the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*); these are designated as "right knowledge" (*samyagjñāna*). [Question:

Why, among the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), is only the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) taken; why, among the eightfold right path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*), is only right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) taken;

and why, among the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*), are only the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising taken? Why are the remaining seven [factors]—six from the [seven] factors of enlightenment, eight from the [eightfold] path, and eight from the [ten] knowledges—not so designated? Why is this?

[The interlocutor] does not accept [this]. The answer is that the characteristic of being able to sever delusions (*kleśa*) is precisely the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*). These three types have wisdom (*prajñā*) as their essence;
because it is through contemplation that they can sever delusions, wisdom constitutes their essence, while the remaining factors merely assist in the severing.

Within the Three Paths, each of the first two paths possesses both the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) and the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*); the Path of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣamārga*) likewise possesses these two.
Furthermore, within the state of Buddhahood, if these were not fully present, the state of Buddhahood would lack the seven factors of enlightenment and the eightfold noble path.

Question: Do the ten knowledges of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna) also pertain to the paths of seeing and cultivation? Answer: They exist only in the state of Buddhahood; they do not pertain to the former two [paths].
The latter necessarily includes the former, but the former does not necessarily include the latter.
Regarding the mention of "right view," "right knowledge," and so forth, Mou says: These terms merely conclude the three preceding meanings. It is like when one announces a person's name and title;
these refer only to what is internal and not to what is external. They pertain solely to the three paths and do not include other categories such as names.
This is based on their essential nature (*svabhāva*); other factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are included in subsequent passages.
Regarding the statement in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (95) that "it consists of right view and so forth": Question:

How does the commentator know that right view and right knowledge constitute the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the wheel? Answer: The commentary states, "The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (95), etc. As for the nature of being accomplished (*sādhyatva*):

the two paths prior to the path [of cultivation], namely the path of equipment (*saṃbhāra-mārga*) and the path of application (*prayoga-mārga*), act as the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), while the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) is that which is accomplished (*sādhya*). Thus, the path of seeing is what is to be cultivated.

The path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is that which is cultivated; the path of cultivation is that by which one trains, while the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*) is that which is to be trained in.

Within the state of no-more-learning, awakening (*bodhi*) is that which brings about accomplishment, and nirvāṇa is the nature of that which is accomplished. This great treatise cites the text up to this midpoint to illustrate both the beginning and the end.

It mentions right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) and the other factors of the Eightfold Path of the path of cultivation, and it takes up the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), as well as [the path of] no-more-learning.
That which is the nature accomplished by the Middle Way’s Right Wisdom through the study of the Path is precisely the *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa* of the fruition.

Regarding the "three turnings for oneself and others": within the World-Honored One’s own progression from cause to fruition, there are three turnings, as these encompass the paths of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning.
The "sage's eye of wisdom" refers to the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) pertaining to each of the Four Noble Truths; this is called the true sage’s eye of wisdom.
This refers to vision, knowledge, clarity, and awakening. Question: Since the cause possesses the sense of crushing and destroying, it may be called a "turning" (*vartana*).

But since the fruit lacks the sense of crushing and destroying, why is it called a "wheel" (*cakra*)? Answer: Because within the fruit there is the sense of having been firmly established and then repeated, and because of its sense of perfection, it is also called a wheel.
The statement "the *Abhidharmakośa* also says 'and so forth'" serves as proof for the Wheel of Dharma of the three paths.

The statement "or its essence consists solely of the eight noble [paths], etc. reveals the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the wheel. Regarding the aforementioned three turnings for oneself and others, these pertain to both the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
Within the categories of self and other, both seeing and cultivation are included; within seeing and cultivation, both self and other are included. Thus far, it is exclusively...

The essential nature [of the factors] is established based on the characteristics of the path of practice (*pratipad*). Both the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*) pervade all three paths (the upper [path of seeing] being the path of cultivation; the lower [paths of meditation and no-more-learning] being the characteristics of distinct practice).
The essential nature is established based on the eightfold noble path, because the eightfold noble path possesses the complete sense of the three parts—the hub, spokes, and rim—of a wheel.

This addresses the objection. The objection states: "If the Mahāyāna path of vision (*darśanamārga*) takes only the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) as the intrinsic nature of the wheel, how can it possess the meaning of a 'Wheel of Dharma' (*dharmacakra*), given that it lacks a hub, spokes, and rim? If the commentary says: "Alternatively, its essence consists only of the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*) and so forth."
Regarding "right view" and "right intention": right view is the essence (*tattva*), and right intention is the function (*vṛtti*).
Since both essence and function are wisdom (*prajñā*), they are called the "root," like the hub of a wheel. One is able to maintain the precepts through the discernment of wisdom;

thus, right speech, right action, and right livelihood take the precepts as their essence. The precepts are the spokes of the wheel, for the precepts arise from wisdom, just as spokes depend upon the hub.

With the hub present, once the precepts are pure, concentration (*samādhi*) manifests before one. Mindfulness (*smṛti*) is able to maintain and retain [the object], while diligence (*vīrya*) further exerts itself universally.
Because concentration is single-minded, it is able to gather and sustain the other factors of practice, just as the rim gathers the spokes so that they do not become scattered or disordered.

The statement that it "is not the same as the Lesser Vehicle" (Hīnayāna) serves to distinguish it from the latter. It is not the same as the Lesser Vehicle in its assignment of the three names—hub, spokes, and rim.
Within the conditioned vehicles, wisdom is the most supreme; if one does not first possess wisdom, it is called a "slack vehicle.

Among the practices for self-benefit, precepts are proclaimed as the foremost; if one does not first possess precepts, it is called "slack precepts. Therefore, the Great and Small Vehicles differ. Question:
One type of wheel is defined as the perfection of the Eightfold Noble Path. What is the distinction between the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna in this regard?

Answer: First, regarding the distinction of essence: in the Mahāyāna, wisdom (*prajñā*) is taken as the hub; in the Hīnayāna, ethical discipline (*śīla*) is taken as the hub. Furthermore, the specific allocation of numerical factors within these systems differs in both quantity and nature.
Second, regarding the distinction of the path: the characteristics of the practice differ. In the Hīnayāna, the eight branches of the Noble Path are cultivated individually.

The seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) pertain to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), while [the eightfold noble path] pertains to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). In the Mahāyāna, the seven factors of enlightenment pertain to the path of seeing, and the eight branches of the noble path pertain to the path of cultivation.

Among the Mahāyāna seven factors of enlightenment, because the factor of joy (*prīti*) accords with the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), one cultivates the seven factors of enlightenment on the path of seeing at the first stage.
The eight branches of the noble path—right speech, right action, and right livelihood—pertain to the path of cultivation.

These are the three types of action (*karma*). Because a bodhisattva practicing the myriad deeds must necessarily rely upon these three types of action; furthermore, the factor of reflection (*saṃkalpa*) accords with those bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) who benefit sentient beings by preaching the Dharma;
and the cultivation of the path refers to the cultivation of the eight branches of the noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).
Regarding the distinction of these eight branches of the noble path: it is asked, "In the Mahāyāna, these eight branches of the noble path exist only on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*);

for what reason are they now said to pervade all three paths? The answer is: there is a distinction among these eight branches of the noble path. If one relies upon their specific modes of activity (*carita-lakṣaṇa*), [they are so designated].

The eight factors of the noble path exist only within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). However, if one considers their general characteristics as a universal practice, the eight factors of the noble path extend across all three paths—those of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning (*darśana*, *bhāvanā*, and *aśaikṣa* mārgas). If this were not the case, the Blessed One would not possess the eightfold noble path.
When discussing their application across these paths, both the Mahayana and Hinayana are identical.

"Speech" refers to that which can produce the subsequent noble path (*āryamārga*). The "subsequent noble path" is precisely the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). "Teaching" refers to the teaching prior to the path of seeing;
because this teaching can produce the subsequent noble path, it is designated as the cause of the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra-hetu*).

First, through hearing, the wisdom born of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) arises; through the wisdom born of hearing, the wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) arises; and through the wisdom born of reflection, the wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) arises.
Within this stage of the preparatory application (*prayoga*) of the accumulations (*sambhāra*), one hears the teachings that "this is suffering" and "this is the origin," and so forth.

Taking the three types of wisdom—arising from hearing, reflection, and cultivation (*śruta-maya*, *cintā-maya*, *bhāvanā-maya*)—which are associated with outflows (*sāsrava*), as the cause, one produces as the result the untainted noble knowledge (*anāsrava-āryajñāna*) of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

Alternatively, taking cultivation as the cause, one produces the fruit of Buddhahood as the result. Furthermore, taking these two as the cause, one produces the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*) as the result. Moreover, if not...

Having heard the teachings, how does one perceive the principle? If one does not perceive the principle, how can one practice? How can one realize the fruit? Therefore, the teachings serve as the cause.

Regarding the phrase "all teachings": since the teachings are not uniform, they are called "all teachings. Alternatively, the teachings may encompass the three paths; thus, they are also termed "transformations" (turnings).
These are called the various teachings.
Regarding the statement "the *Anantārthasūtra*": Question: How is a teaching designated as a "Dharma-wheel"? Answer: The commentary states:
"The *Anantārthasūtra*, etc."
Regarding the various sutras and treatises, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* is named the Dharma-wheel (*dharmacakra*). It speaks of the three turnings of the Dharma-wheel, namely:
turning, illuminating, and maintaining. Furthermore, it states later: "In the past, at Vārāṇasī... [and so on]... until again turning the unsurpassed, greatest Dharma-wheel."
The phrase "also the Abhidharmakośa" refers to the cause for turning the Wheel of Dharma. The teaching serves as the cause for the arising of practice.
Regarding the statement "one attains what is to be attained": that which is attained is what is attained by the attainer; the attainer is the attainer of that which is to be attained.
The means by which one attains is the expedient (*upāya*), and this expedient is precisely the cause. That which is attained is the fruit (*phala*); the attainer is...
The "skillful means of the household attained" refers to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound.
Regarding the statement that "the former serves as the cause for the latter": the teaching is solely the cause and not the fruit; the Buddha-fruit is solely the fruit and not the cause.

Therefore, it is said that the former serves as the cause for the latter. Alternatively, the primary teaching is the cause and the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) is the fruit; the wisdom derived from hearing is the cause and [the wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) is the fruit].

Wisdom (*prajñā*) is the fruit; wisdom through reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) is the cause. Wisdom through cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) is the fruit. The three types of wisdom with outflows (*sāsrava*) are the cause;

the Wheel of Dharma of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) is the fruit. The Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) is the cause capable of attaining [the fruit]. Among the fruits, the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the Bodhisattva are the fruits that are attained.

Alternatively, it may be explained that the enlightenment (*bodhi*) within the fruits still belongs to the three cycles and is subsumed within the twelve aspects (*ākāra*); thus, it remains that which is capable of attainment.
This refers to the skillful means (*upāya*). Afflictions (*kleśa*) are the results that have been attained.

Regarding the statement that these are combined as "result-causes" (*phala-hetu*), Huìhuà states: "That is to say, within the aforementioned stage of training (*śaikṣa-bhūmi*), whether they be causes or results, all serve as causes for the stage of no-more-training (*aśaikṣa*); therefore, they are termed 'combined result-causes'."
Regarding the statement that "the three cycles are precisely turned," it is asked: what is the difference between this interpretation and the previous one? It is answered:

the previous interpretation includes the stage prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), as all [stages] therein are brought forward as causes. This subsequent interpretation takes only the paths of seeing and cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
The first turning and the second turning serve as the causes for the third turning; therefore, they are called "expedient means" (*upāya*).
Regarding the phrase "in accordance with their sequence," this refers to correlating the sequence of the three turnings with the clear realizations (*abhisamaya*) of knowledge and vision.

As for the statement that these are called "expedient means," there are three interpretations. The first follows the sequence: the character "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is correlated with the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).

"Seeing" (*darśana*) refers to the Dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) within the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*). The character "seeing" is also assigned to the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), where it refers to Right View (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*) among the Eightfold Noble Path.

The two characters "clear observation" (*abhisamaya*) are assigned to the Ultimate Clear Observation (*atyanta-abhisamaya*) within the Path of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*). These two are assigned in reverse order to the Path of No-More-Learning;

within that path, there are the Knowledge of Destruction (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the Knowledge of Non-Arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), which are assigned to "knowledge. "Seeing" is assigned to... [the Path of Seeing].

The path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Within the path of cultivation, right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) is correlated with the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), as it constitutes a clear realization (*abhisamaya*).

Even within the stage of the path of seeing, there is untainted clear realization, which is also termed "clear realization. Regarding the sequential correlation of these three, Jin says: "There are three types of the path of seeing."
In the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), correct cognition (*samyag-jñāna*) is termed "knowledge" (*jñāna*); subsequently attained cognition (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) is termed "vision" (*darśana*);

and the realization of the principle is termed "clear observation" (*abhisamaya*). Regarding the three aspects of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*): fundamental cognition is termed "knowledge"; subsequent cognition is termed "vision"; and the realization of that cognition is termed "clarity.

Regarding the three aspects of the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*): fundamental cognition is termed "knowledge"; subsequent cognition is termed "vision"; and the ultimate state is termed "clarity. This interpretation cited from the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra* intends to take...
It is the means for attaining what is to be attained. The two characters "means" (*upāya*) are the cause of the Wheel of Dharma. Question:

How is it that wisdom and vision (*jñāna-darśana*) and clear realization (*abhisamaya*) are called the means of attainment? Answer: There are two interpretations. First, within the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*), the wisdom of enlightenment (*bodhi-jñāna*) is the agent of attainment.

The skillful means (*upāya*) constitutes that which is attained. When the wisdom of the two types of enlightenment (*bodhi*) is first acquired at the higher level, the single thought-moment serves as the skillful means for attainment, while the two subsequent moments and those thereafter constitute what is attained. The intent of the present commentary is simply this:

insight-wisdom (*jñāna-darśana*) is the cause, and manifest vision (*abhisamaya*) is the fruit; vision and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā*) are the cause, and the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) is the fruit. The treatise speaks of the "three turnings."
These are all skillful means (*upāya*). "Skillful means" has the sense of a cause; this is stated according to its general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "the retinue of the three wheels," the intention is that, apart from wisdom (*jñāna*), it refers to all the co-arising five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and so forth.
All are called "retinues" (*parivāra*).

Regarding the phrase "all the noble paths": since the three paths are not one, they are termed "all. Within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), with the exception of the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*);

within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), with the exception of right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) and right thought (*samyaksaṃkalpa*). Right view is the essence of wisdom (*prajñā*); right thought is...
Regarding the function of wisdom: since both are wisdom, within the paths of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and so forth, correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) is excluded.

These three [the wheel, its rim, and its hub] are subsumed under the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the wheel itself; all other factors that serve as its associates, such as the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), are entirely its retinue.

Regarding the statement that the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts refer to the "unmanifest [action] associated with the noble ones" (*ārya-samprayukta-vijñapti*) and so forth, this refers to the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). It has three names:
First, the old term is "unmanifest [action] co-existent with the Path" (*mārga-sahabhū-avijñapti*), which takes the volition (*cetanā*) manifesting simultaneously as its basis;

it is so named because it prevents evil. The new term is "precept co-arising with the Path" (*mārga-sahaja-śīla*), whose essence is untainted (*anāsrava*). It is also called the "precept cherished by the noble ones" (*ārya-kānta-śīla*), because the noble ones hold it in high regard. This is the first interpretation.

This refers exclusively to the precepts co-arising with the Path (*mārga-sahaja-śīla*). Second, Huàdù states: "The precepts cherished by the Sages" refers to the precepts co-arising with meditative concentration (*samādhi-sahaja*) and the precepts co-arising with the Path;

their essence is untainted (*anāsrava*), and they are what the Sages preserve and cherish. If the precepts were tainted (*sāsrava*), the Sages would loathe them; here, only the untainted precepts are taken.

Regarding the mention of dharmas such as faith (*śraddhā*) and so forth: "faith" refers to the four indestructible faiths (*avetyaprasāda*), which is the realization through faith (*śraddhābhisamaya*).

This is the second of the six realizations (*ṣaḍabhisamaya*) in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*. The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the twenty-two dharmas consisting of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).

Regarding the statement that "the aids to the path remove delusions," some say that the precepts cherished by the noble ones aid clear observation (*abhisamaya*), while increased clarity, faith, and other factors aid the path to sever delusions.
This interpretation is incorrect. The intended meaning is that both the precepts and faith assist observation to increase its clarity, thereby aiding the path to remove delusions;
for that right knowledge cannot sever them alone, just as when the precious wheel-treasure (*cakraratna*) subdues enemies, it is the king who acts.
The thousand sons likewise descend together.

Regarding the realm of the Wheel of Dharma (dharmacakra), it is like when a fierce general of the world defeats an enemy; he takes the blue canals and yellow embankments as the boundary for defeating the enemy.
Regarding the statement "the four noble ones, etc.": the principle of the Four Truths (*catur-ārya-satya*) is the locus for severing afflictions (*kleśa*), and is thus termed the "object" (*viṣaya*).

Just as in the world, the place where a king resides who has subdued various kingdoms, or the site of a fierce battle where enemies are slain, is called a "site" or "locus," so too the principle of the Four Truths is termed the "object" because those of the Three Vehicles (*tri-yāna*) equally contemplate it.
Furthermore, those of the Three Vehicles equally sever the afflictions belonging to the Four Truths.
Affliction is termed the "object" (*viṣaya*). Although all equally contemplate the Four Noble Truths, here they are explained specifically according to their predominant focus:
Śrāvakas take the Four Noble Truths as their object; Pratyekabuddhas take the twelve links of dependent origination as their object;
and Bodhisattvas take the three natures and the three absences of nature as their object.

Regarding the statement "Furthermore, it is said in the *Yogācāra*": the meaning has already been cited previously within the section on the causes of the wheel. Now, we take up the fruit for those who practice the skillful means (*upāya*).
Previously, the cause was taken up; now, the fruit is explained, as the respective objectives differ.

Regarding the statement that this sūtra also teaches [this]: at that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū received [the teachings] from the ten directions, up to that which cannot be turned back.

Regarding the mention of the *Saṃdhinirmocana* and other sūtras, the scripture states: "At one time, by means of the characteristics of the Four Noble Truths, he turned the wheel of the sublime Dharma."

Next, at one time, he turned the wheel of the true Dharma by means of the hidden mode (*saṃdhāya*). Now, the World-Honored One turns the wheel of the true Dharma by means of the explicit mode (*vibhajya*);
that is, the teaching that is neither empty nor existent. During the second period, he taught the three natures of non-essence;

this was a hidden teaching, spoken with intentional language, and not of explicit meaning. During the third period, [he taught that] "non-existence" refers to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), while "existence" refers to...
Because it relies on the perfected nature, it is manifest.

As for the statement that the *Yogācārabhūmi* says "that which is obtained by means of attainment," this refers to Great Bodhi as the result obtained through the causal conditions of the means of attainment;
that is, it is the result of Nirvāṇa obtained [through practice]. It is the "obtained" within the category of the "attainer," and it is the "attainer" within the category of the "obtained."

Because it is capable of attaining [the goal], it is called "attaining that which is attained. Regarding this, there are two interpretations: first, both *bodhi* (enlightenment) and *nirvāṇa* are the objects;
second, *nirvāṇa* is that which is attained, while *bodhi* is the cause capable of attaining it.

Regarding the subsequent mention of the four fruits of śrāmaṇya: although the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) enumerates four fruits, the intent here is to take the stage of training (śaikṣa) as the cause and the stage beyond training (aśaikṣa) as the fruit.
The first three fruits constitute the skillful means for attainment, while the fourth fruit is that which is attained.
Regarding "that which is embraced": the fruits embraced are Śrāvaka-bodhi and Pratyekabuddha-bodhi;
that which embraces them is the skillful means (*upāya*).
Regarding the phrase "again, the three cycles," etc.: here we take only that which is attained, not that which attains; the latter belongs to the preceding dharma.

The wheel is the cause (the preceding section has five parts). First, the wheel as self-nature that accords with reality is called a wheel. Second, the wheel as the skillful means of the cause of the Dharma is called a wheel.
Third, the wheel as the retinue and associates is called a wheel. Fourth, the wheel as the objective sphere of the Dharma is called a wheel.
Fifth, the wheel as the fruit obtained through the practice of the Dharma is called a wheel (the five names have been enumerated).

Regarding the statement, "Thus, these five bodies, etc.," their essence consists of the teaching (*śāsana*), principle (*nyāya*), practice (*pratipatti*), and fruit (*phala*). This encompasses the aforementioned five wheels of Dharma (*dharmacakra*):

First, the wheel of Dharma subsumed under the teaching: this includes a portion of the teaching within the causal stage (*hetu*) and a portion of the Brahma-voice characteristics within the wheel of Dharma of the fruit;
both are categorized as the teaching. Second, the wheel of Dharma subsumed under the principle: this refers to the object (*viṣaya*) and the portion within the fruit of the wheel of Dharma.

It refers to the principle of *nirvāṇa* and the principle of the Four Noble Truths. The three types of practice (*traya-yoga*) comprise a portion of the intrinsic nature of the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*), namely:

the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) within the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) within the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and the three wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation (*śruta-cintā-bhāvanā-prajñā*) which constitute the causes of the Wheel of Dharma.

Regarding the retinue (*parivāra*), only that portion belonging to the causal stage is taken; this includes the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) that serve as its attendant associates. All of these are...

They are subsumed within the various practices. Regarding the four fruits: they include the bodhi and nirvāṇa within the fruit of the wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*), as well as the characteristics of the Brahma-voice.

Furthermore, they include each individual part within its own nature, namely, right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) and the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) that constitute the retinue of the wheel within the fruit;
all these are subsumed under the fruit. Moreover, the aforementioned cause of the wheel of Dharma is the teaching (*śāsana*), while the object of the wheel of Dharma is the principle (*nīti*).

The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*) together with its retinue (*parivāra*) constitutes the dharma of practice (*pratipatti-dharma*). The fruit of the wheel (*cakra-phala*) constitutes the dharma of fruition (*phala-dharma*) [corresponding to the five *prajñās*].

The intrinsic nature of the wheel is contemplative insight (*vipaśyanā*). The cause of the wheel is the written word (*vyañjana*). The retinue of the wheel is the assembly (*parivāra*). The object of the wheel is the objective sphere (*viṣaya*).
The fruit of the wheel is the *prajñāpāramitā* of the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa-prajñā*).
Regarding the term "Brahma-wheel" (*brahma-cakra*): it is a wheel of persons; because it is the wheel of the Dharma-Brahmā, it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound.
Regarding the term "Brahma-designation" (*brahmādhivacana*), there are three explanations by Zhang Jing: first, the Tathāgata is neither Brahmā nor non-Brahmā;

yet, for the sake of transforming sentient beings, he provisionally relies upon the name "Brahmā," and thus it is called a designation. Second, the Dharma turned by the Buddha is called the Brahma-wheel; [the prefix] "Brahma" is an intensifier.

Regarding "speech" (*vāc*), it implies an increase. The essence of the Dharma is originally free from words and transcends all marks; it is only when there is no speech and no explanation that it is truly "without increase.

Now, by placing the names of the Brahma-wheel (*brahmamaṇḍala*) upon this [Dharma] through phrases and sentences, one increases its verbal expression; therefore, it is called the "Brahma-increasing speech" (*brahmavardhanī vāk*).
As for the "threefold increase," it signifies the sense of being unsurpassed (*anuttara*). The Tathāgata is addressed as "Brahma" because he is endowed with the supreme qualities of Brahma.

The four immeasurable minds are called *brahmavihāra* (the virtues of Brahma). Although all sentient beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas possess loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), these are merely conventional and not ultimate.
When they reach the stage of a Buddha, their loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity truly enable the uprooting of suffering and the bestowing of happiness.

Because these virtues of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity are most preeminent within the person of a Buddha, they are called *brahmottara* (supreme Brahma). This is the teaching of the Buddha.
The teaching of the Dharma is called the "Brahma-designation. Question: In the preceding verses, there were three mentions of the nature of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas;
why is it that here one does not explain emptiness, but instead explains the Brahma-wheel? Answer:

Because in the context of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, the character for "wheel" (cakra) does not appear below [the name], it is not explained. Only the Brahma-wheel and the Dharma-wheel possess the character for "wheel."

Regarding the statement that "the two are called the Wheel of Dharma" (*dharmacakra*): just as for a Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*) with a golden wheel, the gold is the means of accomplishment and the wheel is the result of accomplishment;

so too, the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), and so forth, constitute the means of accomplishment, while the wheel constitutes the nature of the result of accomplishment. According to the Hīnayāna school, if there is ethical discipline (*śīla*)...
The myriad virtues arise from the precepts; that is to say, right speech, right action, and right livelihood constitute the three hubs.

Right view, right thought, and right effort serve as the spokes, while right mindfulness and right concentration serve as the rim. According to the Mahāyāna school, the myriad virtues arise in dependence upon view;
therefore, right view and right thought are taken as the hubs, while right speech, right action, and right livelihood [serve as the spokes].

The spokes are right effort and right concentration; the rim is the Dharma. Because it uses the Dharma as its wheel, it is called the "Dharma-wheel" (*dharmacakra*). "Dharma" is the wheel [this is a *karmadhāraya* compound].
"Guidance" (*naya*) refers to the guiding principle that causes beings to produce understanding; "sustenance" (*dhāraṇa*) means to maintain its own essence.

Uncontaminated wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) is the essence, while the sense of destroying [defilements] and so forth is its function. These three paths of the Dharma-wheel all possess the meaning of guidance and sustenance, not only...
It destroys [the afflictions], yet it also possesses a sustaining principle (*dhṛti*).

Regarding the phrase "the meaning of being one and complete," this refers to the investigation of dharmas (*dharmapravicaya*) among the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), as well as [the right view] among the eight branches of the noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).
It possesses a hub, a rim, and spokes; because it has the sense of being complete, it is called a "wheel" (as explained extensively above).

Regarding the phrase "or the awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) and so forth": [this] asks whether the eight branches of the noble path, possessing the sense of completeness, may be called a wheel.
If the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) are not fully perfected, how can they be called a "wheel"? The commentary answers:

Alternatively, the factors such as the factor of investigation (*vīmaṃsā-sambojjhaṅga*)—the seven factors of enlightenment within the path of vision (*darśanamārga*)—are designated as a wheel because their essence (*svabhāva*), function (*kāritra*), and utility (*pariniṣpatti*) are complete.

These seven factors of enlightenment possess both essence and function throughout all three paths. Question: Since afflictions (*kleśa*) are not abandoned during the fruition stage (*phalamārga*), how can [the wheel] exist there?

[Question: Is it [a wheel] by virtue of its essence (*tattva*) and function (*vṛtti*)? [Answer: In the state of fruition (*phala*), the realization of principle (*tattva-prativedha*) is exhaustive in its aspect, and the penetration of phenomena (*vastu-prativedha*) is also exhaustive;

for this reason, it is also called a "wheel" (*cakra*). [Question: If that is so, then in the causal state (*hetu*), because the realization of principle and the penetration of phenomena are not yet universal, and because the wisdom of the cause (*hetu-jñāna*) is not yet perfected, it should not be called a "wheel," as it lacks the sense of perfection.
[Answer: This is also not the case. It is simply by virtue of possessing both essence and function that it is termed "complete" and "perfect," and thus called a "wheel."

Who says that the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is entirely complete? If it were not so, why would the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*) be called the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*)? Does the Master of the Commentary (*śāstrakāra*) lack wisdom?
Because his wisdom was not yet fully perfected, his intention was merely to take the sense of "perfection" [as the definition], and not to restrict it solely to the Eightfold Path.

Even the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) and so forth possess the sense of having their essence and function perfected. The Master of the Commentary’s intention is that if one considers only the hub, spokes, and rim [of a wheel]...
Regarding the term "perfection" (*paripūri*): fearing that the essential meaning of the preceding three paths might be lost, it is explained as perfection by way of essence and function.

These four types of phenomena are the teaching, the principle, the practice, and the fruit. Whether it be the subduing [of afflictions] through the teaching, or the severance [of delusions] through the principle, or...
It is an auxiliary practice (*sahakārin*). If it is the actual fruit (*phala*), then it corresponds to the "correct" (*samyak*) [as in the preceding classification].

If one relies on this section, the intention of the commentary (*śāstra*) seems somewhat abrupt, as it suddenly provides these correspondences here after not previously discussing doctrine, principle, practice, and fruit (*śāsana-yukti-caryā-phala*).

However, it is simply that untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) possesses these four meanings and is thus termed "the meaning of destruction. Furthermore, if it is "subduing," it subdues the active manifestations (*samudācāra*); if it is "severing," it severs the seeds (*bīja*); if it is "auxiliary," it assists the mind (*citta*).
If it is correct untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), the essence of wisdom can correctly sever [afflictions], while its retinue acts as an aid for severing them.
Mǔ says: "Whether 'subduing' or 'severing' refers to the afflictions; whether 'aiding' or 'correct' refers to the counteracting factors (*pratipakṣa*). 'Aiding' is precisely the retinue."
"Correct" refers to intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). The intention is that when these two are compared to those afflictions, both are subject to suppression and severance;

therefore, they are called "crushing. (Otherwise, there would be no objective aspect [ākāra]; further inquiry is required). *Miyou* says: These four all pertain to both the fundamental and subsequent wisdoms.

Among them, when fundamental wisdom correctly severs the delusions regarding principle (*li*), it simultaneously suppresses the delusions regarding phenomena (*shi*); the simultaneous five aggregates are termed "auxiliaries. Subsequent wisdom does not sever delusions regarding principle.

When subduing the afflictions of phenomena (*vastu-kleśa*), the simultaneous subduing of the delusions regarding principles (*tattva-moha*) is likewise so; one should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*):

1. Subduing but not abandoning: those prior to the stages (*bhūmi*). 2. Abandoning but not subduing: the diamond-like path of immediate succession (*vajropama-anantarya-mārga*). 3. Both abandoning and subduing: from the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) upward, prior to the diamond-like path of immediate succession.
4. Neither subduing nor abandoning: all ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).

Regarding the meaning of "suppressing" (*vighna*) within the three stages: although the afflictions are not yet severed during the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), they have already been suppressed;
thus, it is like a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*), whose golden wheel rests upon the king’s head, causing all that has been subdued to never rise again.

Now, in this uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*), the two obstructions are severed and forever exhausted, while the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) suppresses them so they do not arise. The uninterrupted path is like driving out thieves.
The path of liberation is like closing a door; "closing the door" carries the meaning of suppression.

Regarding the statement that it causes the force [of the afflictions] to turn away and become distant: once the afflictions have been severed, they abide forever in non-arising, which is termed "distant. There are two aspects to this: first, causing the delusions to turn away and become distant.
Once the delusions have been suppressed, noble wisdom increases in clarity and the power of the antidote becomes strong; thus, those [delusions] are said to be "distant. As for example...
It is said that the sun can eliminate evil; secondly, the power of wisdom increases as it moves further away. Furthermore, once those [afflictions] have been treated, they fall away moment by moment;
in relation to the path that treats them, they also receive the designation "distant. This is like saying that wisdom grows along with its fruit, which refers to their becoming equalized.
Regarding the meaning of the four indeterminate factors: just as a chariot, once completed, cannot remain stationary and must necessarily move, so too is the wheel of Dharma.
From one's own view to one's own path of cultivation, and from one's own path of cultivation to the path of no-more-learning—this constitutes the three revolutions (the "upper" three revolutions).
Regarding the statement "following one's own wisdom of no-more-learning" (*aśaikṣajñāna*): this refers to Ājñātakauṇḍinya, for whom [the Buddha] performed the three turnings.

The Buddha took the Dharma he had realized within his own mind and expounded it to Ājñātakauṇḍinya, causing the wisdom of the three moments to arise within Kauṇḍinya’s body. He then turned his own realized mind and entered the bodies of others.

Through these verbal instructions, the other [disciples] understood the principle of the Truths (*satyārtha*) and became identical to Ājñātakauṇḍinya; having already entered the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), they proceeded onward.

From the principle of the Truths, one gives rise to right practice; that is, from one's own view one proceeds to one's own cultivation, and from one's own cultivation one proceeds to the stage of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
Regarding the phrase "thus proceeding by succession," this refers to Ājñātakauṇḍinya attaining Buddhahood in the future and then teaching others, whereby they attain the fruit.
Furthermore, because one teaches it to others, it is called "successive" (*saṃtāna*); thus, it is called "indeterminate.

Regarding the phrase "like a wheel-turning monarch" (*cakravartin*), this provides an analogy to conclude four meanings: 1. "Like a wheel-turning [monarch]" concludes the meaning of "perfection" mentioned previously. 2.

Because one is able to subdue those afflictions (*kleśa*) not yet subdued, it concludes the meaning of "crushing and destroying" mentioned previously. 3. Because one is able to stabilize those already subdued...
The phrase "and so forth" concludes the preceding meaning of suppression. The phrase "fourfold going and returning" concludes the preceding meaning of indeterminacy.
Regarding the expression "going and returning": when the Tathāgata established the Noble Path within the person of Ājñātakauṇḍinya, that constituted one instance of "going.
When Ājñātakauṇḍinya, in turn, transmitted it to other persons, that constituted another instance of "returning," making it a double cycle of going and returning.

Regarding the statement "the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says, etc.," this serves as proof for the meaning of "indefinite. That is to say, the Blessed One spoke it to Kauṇḍinya, and Kauṇḍinya spoke it to others.
As for the statement "the Dharma itself is [the wheel]," the Dharma that is here transformed is the wheel; this is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound).
Regarding the term "turning" (*vartana*): if the Dharma is called a "wheel," how is it that it is called "turning"? The sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:
"Turning" means movement, manifestation, operation, and arising.

Regarding the phrase "the declaration of the teaching through speech and movement": this refers to the words of the Blessed One, such as "This is suffering" and "This is the origin," which constitute the proclamation of the teaching.
Regarding the term "Manifesting" (khyāpana): Question: What is meant by "manifesting"? Answer: The commentary states that it means manifesting the sublime principle (*naya*).
Regarding the term "Conveying the Noble": Question: What is meant by "conveying"? Answer: The commentary states that it means conveying the noble path (*āryamārga*) so that it precedes the voice.

Regarding the phrase "arising of true wisdom" (*tattvajñāna*): the question is asked, "What is meant by 'arising'? The commentary (*śūtra*) answers: "The arising of true wisdom refers to the fruit that follows after words.
This, then, corresponds to the sequence of teaching, principle, practice, and fruit.
Regarding the statement, "The noble path is conveyed before the sound," the Lu-fu commentary says: The holy wisdom of the listener arises prior to the sound of the speaker’s preaching;
this is called "prior" in relation to that [sound]. True wisdom arises after the words; this is called "subsequent.

If one speaks specifically of the individual Śāriputra, when the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) arises, this is "prior" in relation to that [attainment]; thus it is called "conveying the noble path," and so forth.
If we consider it in terms of the Tathāgata’s voice: [the voice] has already passed away, and only then do the other four persons attain the Way;
this is called "arousing true wisdom prior to the words. This is the first interpretation. According to the second interpretation, Ājñātakauṇḍinya alone attains it, while the other four do not;
this is called "operating the Noble Path prior to the sound. At the time of turning the Wheel of Dharma, the listeners hear it...

Those sounds, names, phrases, and syllables repeatedly acquire seeds that descend into the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). Only when the summer retreat concludes does one finally attain the Noble Path (*āryamārga*).
The Tathāgata’s voice is present, while the Noble Path arises in the future. This is like the common usage of referring to the future as "matters ahead.
Since the present Noble Path exists in the future relative to the sound—because it precedes the sound—it is called "prior to the sound" (*śabdapūrva*).

This interpretation is correct. Regarding the third [reason], because the Tathāgata first personally attained the Noble Path within his own body and had never before spoken of the Noble Path to anyone, it is called "carrying the Noble Path prior to the sound" (*śabdapūrvaṃ nayanam*) because it occurs before the sound of the teaching.
It is intended that the Tathāgata himself speaks so that true knowledge arises after his words; thus the Tathāgata speaks with full clarity. For those who listen, noble wisdom arises after his words.

Regarding the phrase "perfectly destroying hindrances and afflictions": "perfect" (*pari*) has the sense of completion, and "destroying" (*varta*) has the sense of crushing. This is because that Wheel of Dharma is turned upward in its perfection.

The sense of "overwhelming" (parājaya) is predominant; therefore, it is specifically termed a "bond" (*saṃyojana*). The senses of "suppressing" (*nirodha*) and "indefinite" (*aniyata*) are not predominant, and thus they are not mentioned.

As for the statement that "that which is turned is the Dharma": *dharmacakra* is a *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "the wheel of the Dharma," or else "Dharma" refers to the sound of the teaching, while "wheel" is [the instrument].

Regarding "outflow-free knowledge" (*anāsrava-jñāna*): when Kauṇḍinya hears the voice of the Tathāgata’s teaching, he gives rise to outflow-free knowledge and severs the afflictions; this is called a "wheel.

It is a *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "the wheel of the Dharma family. Alternatively, when outflow-free knowledge arises and is able to sever the afflictions, the Dharma itself is the wheel; this is a *karmadhāraya* compound.
Regarding the statement "by way of five kinds of aspects," [the question is: What kind of activity does the turning of the Wheel of Dharma (dharmacakra-pravartana) possess that enables it to turn?

The answer in the commentary states: "By way of five kinds, etc. The first three turnings pertain to the Buddha’s causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*); whether as the *nirmāṇa-kāya* (emanation body) or the *saṃbhoga-kāya* (enjoyment body), these all belong to his own turning for the sake of attaining what is to be attained.
The latter two types, however, pertain to the World-Honored One [turning] for Ājñātakauṇḍinya and others—these are the three for others.
Because it causes others to enter the paths of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning, these five are the very foundation of the Mahāyāna Wheel of Dharma.

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of attaining that which is to be attained": "for the sake of attaining" refers to skillful means (*upāya*), while "that which is to be attained" refers to *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*.
As for what is called the "object of focus," it refers to the principle of the three natures, the twelve links of dependent origination, and the four noble truths.
As for what is called the "expedient means for attaining that which is to be attained," "for the sake of attaining" refers to the three cycles of twelve aspects;
these twelve aspects are the expedient means for attaining nirvana.
Regarding the phrase "attaining what one ought to attain for oneself," this refers to *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*. Jin says:

the fruits of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*) of the three vehicles are called "what one ought to attain for oneself. Furthermore, this third characteristic is solely that which is attained; it is not the means of attainment.
(The above three [characteristics] clarify the Buddha’s turning of the wheel.)

Regarding the statement "as for the four [turnings], having attained them, etc.," the two subsequent questions concern the three turnings for others. Question: What is the purpose of the latter two turnings?

Answer: It means that after the Tathāgata has first attained the three preceding turnings and fulfilled the fruits of the path, he returns and teaches the dharmas of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and so forth that he has realized to Cundabhadraka and others.
After Cundabhadraka and others have attained them, they likewise possess the three aforementioned characteristics.
"Afterward, one may explain it to others.
To speak of "establishing in another's continuum" means to set it up. "Continuum" (saṃtāna) has the meaning of "body" (deha). The Tathāgata himself has realized this;
he wishes to transfer this realized mind toward the body of Ājñātakauṇḍinya—can it be established there? Answer: It is the establishment of names and teachings, the provision of verbal designations.

It is said that when he spoke for the sake of Ājñātakauṇḍinya, Kauṇḍinya attained enlightenment upon those words. This means that the Tathāgata’s own mind of liberation turned and entered the body of Ājñātakauṇḍinya.

Question: Since it was his own liberation, why is it called "the Buddha’s turning"? Answer: It is precisely this mind of liberation that, by reason of the Buddha’s verbal teaching, is termed "the Buddha’s turning."
Regarding those who "give rise to deep faith and understanding in self-realization," this refers to Ājñātakauṇḍinya and others.
When they first saw the Prince practicing austerities and all abandoned him, they said to one another: "Why did we see him so late? He is merely a man of reckless folly."

Because these five men had conceived a lack of faith toward the Tathāgata and did not know that the Tathāgata’s body possessed the three turnings of the path and the perfection of the fruit, they were possessed of pride.
