Regarding the "vehicles" and so forth: if their minds have not yet turned toward the [Mahāyāna], each seeks the vehicle of their own vehicle.

As for those called "persons of the two vehicles": if one asks why persons of the two vehicles, having already left the house and perfected the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), would further seek a vehicle, the answer is that *prajñā-vimukta* arhats seek to eliminate the hindrances to meditative concentration (*samādhi-āvaraṇa*) by entering the fundamental dhyānas (*mauladhyāna*), and they seek superior supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

"Attainment. The meaning is the same as "seeking the vehicle. Even if one has attained supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), if they are a "liberated-in-both-ways" (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*) practitioner, they still seek the extensive qualities of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
This is because such a *ubhayatobhāgavimukta* Arhat, like the case of the Black Salt (*kālalavaṇa*), still harbors doubts and remains possessed of delusion;

they only know the Four Noble Truths in general, but cannot extensively know the immeasurable characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) within the Four Noble Truths. This is also called "seeking the vehicle" (as explained in the *Xiàngyīnjiǎnyàojiě*). Bian states: "It is certain..."

This refers to the period before they had turned their minds [toward the Great Vehicle], when they followed the Tathāgata, heard his teachings, and sought after the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

This meaning is identical to that of "seeking the vehicle. The intent of the Commentary is as follows: while the Buddha was at the Deer Park, he preached the Dharma of the three vehicles, causing each to practice and attain the fruits of their respective vehicles;

this is called "the father’s prior promise. When the two sons attained these fruits, yet remained outside the scope of the teaching and its practice, this is called "leaving the gate of the house of the分段 (limited) realm. However, regarding all...

Even regarding the Dharma, they are still unable to know it; this is called "not seeing the chariot. Therefore, in the presence of the Buddha, they cultivate the three types of wisdom to seek what they have not yet realized;

this is called "wishing for it to be bestowed at that time. The mental discourse [of these practitioners] is that the followers of the Two Vehicles seek their own sheep and deer within their own minds, yet they do not realize what it is they are seeking.
However, it is the ox-cart; the ox-cart is precisely that which the father previously promised. This means that the two vehicles do not sever the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

Because the cognitive hindrances are not severed, they do not know all phenomena, and thus they are said to have "no cart. Now, because they seek to thoroughly penetrate all phenomena, they are merely seeking the ox-cart;
this is the intended meaning here. Question: Since the two vehicles lack the seed of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), one might say they are "seeking a cart," but [how can this be said of a Bodhisattva]?

Since the Bodhisattva already possesses the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñatā*), why does he still seek it? Answer: It is because the Bodhisattva seeks the vehicle of the fruit—the various knowledges and the stage of Buddhahood—beyond what he has already attained.

Although he has attained these in the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), there is no harm in seeking them further as he looks toward the subsequent stages. (The above is a general explanation; the following is an explanation based on the commentary. Question:

Does he seek this within the house or outside the house? Answer: He seeks it outside the house. As for what is permitted within [the house], [it refers to] the Pratyekabuddha. Question: Regarding the Pratyekabuddha...

Question: Since there were no humans at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, where could they have sought the carts? Answer: Some say that although there was no attainment of the fruit [of Buddhahood], there were those who first resolved their minds [to seek it].
This is incorrect. These people were seeking outside the gate for the vehicle of their own fruition—the vehicle of merit within the fruits of the [three] vehicles.

All commentaries are confused regarding this; they claim that the seeking of the carts occurred only at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. This explanation is not so. Seeking the carts does not necessarily occur only at Vulture Peak.
On the Vulture Peak Assembly, there were those of the Two Vehicles. Under the Bodhi tree, the World-Honored One had promised them the sheep and deer carts;

subsequently, for forty years prior [to this assembly], they had attained fruits and joyfully pursued them, seeking superior merit—this is collectively termed "seeking the carts. If one were to explain it in this way, it would not be so.
Seeking the carts does not necessarily occur only at the Vulture Peak Assembly; rather, it refers to those of the Two Vehicles under the Bodhi tree.

The World-Honored One permitted the sheep-drawn and deer-drawn carts. Subsequently, for forty years prior [to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*], those who attained the fruit and joyfully strove toward it, seeking superior merit, were collectively termed "those who seek the carts.
If one explains it in this way, then forty years prior there were pratyekabuddhas who attained the fruit; their seeing the World-Honored One approach was precisely the occasion of seeking the carts.
If, however, one restricts it solely to the assembly of the *Lotus Sūtra*, then it is called the occasion where the pratyekabuddhas sought the carts.
Furthermore, if each seeks their own vehicle, it does not preclude their being in accord with the various sūtras. If one rejects the two carts and takes the ox cart, that is precisely this sūtra.
Question: The learners (*śaikṣa*) of the two vehicles seek superior merit; why are they not said to be "seeking a cart"? Answer:

Because the practitioners on the stages of the learners have not yet reached the point where one seeks a cart. In the previous explanation, before the two younger sons turned their minds [toward the Great Vehicle], each sought...
To mount one's own vehicle is like having already turned the mind [toward enlightenment] and seeking a bullock cart.
As for the statement that "Bodhisattvas rely on this fundamental treatise and so forth," according to the meaning of the commentary, it refers to the two vehicles entering the city.

They do not board the vehicle either. According to the interpretation of the ancients, the followers of the Two Vehicles do not board the vehicle when entering the city; this accords with the principle established in the *Śāstra*.
The ancient masters, however, also permitted that the Bodhisattva’s vehicle may enter the city, which constitutes a distinction. An ancient question states:

"The followers of the Two Vehicles have brought to rest the three faults of afflictions (*kleśa*), suffering (*duḥkha*), and karma (*karman*) pertaining to the *paricchinna-bhava-jāti-maraṇa* (segmented birth-and-death), and thus they enter the City of Transformation after traveling three hundred *yojana*s. As for the Bodhisattvas..."

In the gateway of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), one mounts the chariot; having thus departed from outside the gate of the house of *paricchinna-bhava* (segmented existence), this signifies that one has brought to rest the segmented birth-and-death (*paricchinna-jarāmaraṇa*).

It is permitted that the Bodhisattva also enters the city. The commentary on the response states: "The person who is a Bodhisattva," etc., refers to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-śāstra*’s instruction to realize the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*).
The intended meaning is that when an Arhat’s person realizes the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*), they subsequently attain...
Liberation occurs when afflictions (*kleśa*) are exhausted. Since Bodhisattvas remain in the causal stage (*hetvavasthā*), their afflictions are not yet exhausted;

they have not attained liberation, nor have they attained the exhaustion of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) or the two types of *nirvāṇa* within the fruit. Therefore, they are not said to have "entered the city. Because they do not experience weariness, they do not enter *nirvāṇa-with-remainder* (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).

Furthermore, it is not taught that Bodhisattvas enter the "transformed city" (*nirmāṇa-pura*). Thus, [this applies only to] the fruits of the two vehicles' state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*).
Attaining the exhaustion of hindrances and liberation at this stage, and realizing *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, is called "entering the city.
Since Bodhisattvas are in the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*) and have not yet realized liberation, they do not give rise to weariness regarding suffering, nor do they enter *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
Therefore, it is not said that Bodhisattvas enter the illusory city; according to the scriptural text, it is likewise not stated that Bodhisattvas enter the illusory city.
Regarding the statement that "entering non-abiding nirvāṇa is also cessation," this is the interpretation of the ancients. The Master of the Commentary (*Sūshǔ*) says:
"Since it is not permitted for Bodhisattvas to enter the city of *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder), the ancients say: 'I permit Bodhisattvas to enter the city of *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.'"
An ancient said: "I allow bodhisattvas to enter non-abiding nirvana. The intent of this ancient was as follows:
since the two vehicles possess the nirvana with remainder, one allows them to enter the illusory city; what prevents a bodhisattva from attaining non-abiding nirvana?
Both are indeed nirvana, and thus both are called "entering the city."
The statement, "If that were so, it would also follow that [the two cases] are equal," is the Master of the Commentary’s counter-interrogation of the ancient [opponent].

Regarding the principle of the two kinds of emptiness realized by a Bodhisattva, one portion—the principle of the emptiness of persons—is identical to that of the Two Vehicles; thus, it is granted that the Bodhisattva enters the non-abiding [nirvāṇa], which is termed "entering the city.

Since the Bodhisattva has already realized the wisdom of the two kinds of emptiness, the wisdom of the emptiness of persons within that [realization] is likewise identical to that of the Two Vehicles.
One should admit that the Bodhisattva likewise mounts the sheep and deer carts (Pu). When the Bodhisattva attains non-abiding, he is said to be permitted to enter the city;

when the Bodhisattva attains the Knowledge of All Modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), he should likewise mount the sheep and deer [carts] (also stated as: the Bodhisattva attains non-abiding for himself but not for others;

he cannot have others construct an entry into the city). The followers of the Two Vehicles attain [non-abiding] for themselves but not for others, and they do not attain the Knowledge of All Modes upon mounting [the vehicle].
Regarding the sheep and deer [carts]: it was asked that while a Bodhisattva obtains a cart but does not enter the city, one instead takes the Bodhisattva and enters the city together.
If those of the Two Vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) board their carts at the foot of the city wall, should it be permitted that they likewise board the sheep and deer carts?

Thus it is said: the "transformed city" (nirmāṇa-pura) is used to entice Bodhisattvas of inferior capacity; since it is equally stated that they "enter" the sheep and deer carts, those of inferior capacity should likewise ascend them. Furthermore, the Sūtra says:
The commentary says: "It does not state that the eldest son entered the city; now it permits him to enter. The scriptural text does not state that the two sons mounted the carriage;
now it permits both to ascend along with the deer.

By saying 'therefore we know it is merely equal,' the Master of the Commentary establishes a principle to refute the views of former scholars. His intention follows the previous separate interpretation."
Among these, the followers of the Two Vehicles enter the city but do not mount the carriage; the Bodhisattva mounts the carriage but does not enter the city.
Regarding the statement that "having already subdued the afflictions, he emerges," etc., this refers to the Bodhisattva seeking the ox-cart. Question:

Since the Bodhisattva has already attained the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), he should immediately mount the carriage. Why is it necessary to say he "seeks" it? Answer: Although the Bodhisattva has attained it partially, it is not yet fully perfected.

"Full" (pūrṇa) refers to the stage of fulfillment; seeking it there, one finds no discrepancy. According to reality, each of the ten stages involves the meaning of joyfully seeking the wisdom of the fruit.
From the initial departure from the household, this is designated by the name "rope" (śulka). Emerging from the death of the segmented realm (*bhavāgra*), one also realizes the Four Truths;
that is, one contemplates the Four Truths based on the three natures and the three absences of nature. This universal wheel of Dharma is called the "rope."

Regarding the statement that "the three sons were equal," why did the middle and youngest sons enter the city while the eldest son did not? He entered [the state of] extinction, which is equivalent to entering the city.

Regarding the statement that he "answered without weariness" and so forth: because the Bodhisattva is free from weariness and does not find suffering loathsome, he did not enter the city, whereas the Śrāvaka [did].
Because they loathe suffering, it is for this reason that it is said they enter the city.

Regarding the statement that although they subdue the afflictions (*kleśa*), these include those of the *pariccheda* (segmented) realm and so forth: Question: Since Bodhisattvas do not loathe suffering, they do not enter the city; how then can it be said that Bodhisattvas leave their homes? Answer: The commentary states "subduing the afflictions" and so forth. This means that while they do not loathe suffering, they nonetheless subdue the afflictions associated with the various realms, such as the *pariccheda-bhava*. Thus, although they remain within the cycle of existence, they are said to have "left home" because they have transcended the power of the afflictions that bind ordinary beings to the household life. Therefore, there is no contradiction.

As for the statement regarding "entering the city," it is solely because the three sons left the house together that the younger two entered the city while the eldest did not, resulting in this difficulty.
Had the ancients permitted the eldest son to enter the city, this difficulty would not have arisen.
Regarding the phrase "weary of suffering" and so forth: the eldest son was not weary of suffering, nor did he seek to cease from it.
When the Bodhisattva entered the city, he sought only a slight respite from suffering; therefore, it is said that he entered the "transformed city."

Regarding the statement, "Because it speaks of places of rest, it says 'two,' etc.," the intended meaning is that the scriptural text mentions only two places of rest and only two vehicles entering the city;
the fact that it does not mention three means that the scriptural text does not state that bodhisattvas enter the city.
Regarding the statement that "vehicles and so forth are set up outside the gate," there are three types of vehicles and two types of cities; this constitutes a contradiction or obstruction.
As for the statement that "two vehicles face the Great [Vehicle]," the Great [Vehicle] refers to the ox-cart (*go-ratha*); turning the mind toward the Great [Vehicle] means taking that ox-cart.
The true and the false are combined; thus, it is said that there are three vehicles.
Regarding the statement that the "provisional city" corresponds to the "real," the principle attained by those of the Two Vehicles is provisional.

When the provisional and the real are contrasted, the provisional principle is called the "transformed city" (*nirmita-pura*), while the real principle is called the "jeweled destination" (*ratna-sthāna*). When this provisional principle is set against the real principle, there is only...
The two vehicles do not have three cities. "Actual fruit" refers to the actual principle (*tattva*).
Regarding the statement that "the principle should be similar," the intended meaning here is that the two carts likewise represent the two cities of the provisional and the real;
because they are contrasted as the provisional and the real, they are said to be "similar."

Regarding the phrase "the distinctions of what is confronted," this refers to the two chariots. These are the provisional means (upāya) in contrast to the real cause. The ox-cart and the two cities represent the provisional means in contrast to the real fruit.

The jewel-treasure site represents the fruit in contrast to the cause; because these contrasts differ, they are called "distinctions of what is confronted. As for the road established within the transformation city, it is posited in relation to the five hundred *yojanas*.

If one were to posit the cities solely in relation to the three—afflictions (*kleśa*), suffering (*duḥkha*), and birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*)—then they would pertain to the birth-and-death of segmented existence (*paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa*).

It is also said that the three carts outside the gate correspond to the *parināmi-śūnyatā* (transformative death). This is also called "provisioning midway. Because the objects they correspond to are distinct, the arrangements differ.

Specifically, the carts correspond to the *bheda-śūnyatā* (segmented death), hence they are said to be "outside the gate. The city corresponds to the *parināmi-śūnyatā*, hence it is said to be "midway.
The carts are described as "inducements" because they lead one out of the house, thus being "outside the gate"; because one retreats within the city wards, two are "provisioned midway."
Furthermore, because they were lured by the chariots, three cities were established to alleviate their suffering; thus, two [types of people] are mentioned.
When it says "those who possess the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) lack it," this refers to the absence of such knowledge among the followers of the Two Vehicles.

The exhortation to take the sheep and deer carts and the subsequent dedication toward the great vehicle constitute the cause for the ox-cart. This is why the three vehicles were set up outside the gate.
Regarding the statement that entering non-abiding is not called "entering [a city]": Question: When a bodhisattva enters non-abiding, what prevents them from entering a city?
Answer: Non-abiding is the reality; it is not a conventional designation. Therefore, it is not called "entering a city."

Regarding the statement that "the three vehicles are all sought," this refers to seeking the vehicles rather than seeking the city. Originally, one seeks the vehicle with the hope of perfecting the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
That which does not hope for the two types of cessation is precisely not seeking the city.

Regarding the phrase "attaining the fruit spontaneously," etc.: Question: Since it is not said that the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) requested the city, does this not mean they did not seek the cessation of suffering?

Answer: The commentary states, "Attaining the fruit spontaneously, etc. This means that because they do not speak of longing or seeking, this is equivalent to the "requesting of the city" mentioned below.

The various types of wisdom (jñāna) based on the vehicle arise each from their own seeds; therefore, one must request the vehicle. Once the request has been made, one merely cultivates until wisdom is perfected.

When wisdom is perfected, one can personally realize cessation (*nirodha*). This principle of cessation points upward; "downward" refers to seeking. Furthermore, because the city has already been attained, there is no need to seek the chariots;
because they have not yet been attained, it is necessary to seek them.

Regarding the statement that "the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñatā) has not yet been attained," this refers to those of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha). It is simply a matter of concealing the fact and saying it does not exist.
As for the statement, "If one interprets it in this way regarding the two vehicles and so forth," the intention is to challenge the two vehicles:

they have already entered the illusory city (the city of transformation), so it may be said they do not seek the city; however, since Bodhisattvas have neither entered the city nor yet reached the place of treasure, they must still seek the place of treasure. This is not yet... [text ends].
Because there is no difference between having arrived and not yet having obtained the vehicle, the followers of the Two Vehicles seek the vehicle because they have not yet obtained it;
likewise, a Bodhisattva who has not yet reached the place of treasure must also seek that place of treasure.

Regarding the statement that "this meaning may be so," this means the Master of the Commentary (Sūzhǔ) grants that it may be so. What prevents the granting of what has been obtained without being sought?
It is precisely because they did not seek it when previously approaching the City of Transformation (hóuchéng) that [the Buddha] speaks of seeking the place of the treasure (bǎosuǒ).
The phrase "seeking with single-minded devotion" and so forth refers to searching. The Sūtra says: "He immediately extinguished the conjured city and said to the multitude:

'Come, you all! The place where the treasure is located is near. That great city you previously saw was created by me as an illusion. Although the scriptural text does not explicitly mention "searching," it carries the sense of searching.
Regarding the statement that the sutra text merely speaks of exhortation: one might ask, "Since they did not request it, why was there a need to exhort them?

The answer is: the Buddha acts as an uninvited friend for sentient beings; thus, although they did not request it, he exhorted them. As the sutra says: "I saw that you were utterly exhausted and intended to turn back midway;
therefore, by the power of skillful means, I provisionally manifested this city. Now I urge you to apply yourself with diligence. When one applies oneself with diligence, one shall...

Together they arrive at the place of treasure. The Long Discourse says: "You all, go and come," and so forth. According to the reality of the matter, even from the perspective of a Bodhisattva, one must likewise seek to realize Great Parinirvāṇa.
In the sutra, this is merely stated in reference to those who have turned their minds [toward the Mahāyāna]; the Buddha acts as an uninvited friend and does not say that they must request it.
Regarding the phrase "as transmitted in ancient tradition," the intention of the ancient masters is as follows: Both the city and the chariot are what those of the Two Vehicles cultivate.

However, the conjured city is a real provision; because it can truly bring rest from suffering, one does not seek it. The chariot is a false pointer, for there is none outside the gate; therefore, one seeks it.
If one were to interpret it in this way, it would directly refute the ancients. If the chariot and the city were distinct entities, then the meanings of "seeking" and "not seeking" would differ.
Since the ancients took *nirvāṇa* as the essence of the chariot, and the essence of the chariot is itself *nirvāṇa*, then at the time of seeking the chariot, they would also be seeking the city.
As the ancient masters testified: "To seek *nirvāṇa* for oneself is called the Śrāvaka vehicle."
Just as those sons, seeking the sheep-carts, emerged from the burning house and so forth, we know that the carts are themselves nirvāṇa.
At the time they sought the carts, the city was also sought.
Furthermore, there is an interpretation stating that [the passage] beginning with "the chariots set forth" reflects the intention of the ancient masters.

Their view is that the three chariots are now provisionally established so that the children within the house may be led out once they have emerged; thus, they were previously indicated only in empty words. Now, their minds are stirred, and because they hear that there are chariots, they resolve to seek deliverance.
Therefore, this is called the stage of the beginner (*ādikarmika*).

Regarding the statement "this is also not the case," etc.: at the time when those of initial capacity seek the chariots, they are already those beyond training (aśaikṣa), for they have already departed from the house.
How, then, can it be said that the chariots set out for those of initial capacity?
Regarding the statement, "Furthermore, since the substance is not distinct," etc.: In the past, the city and the chariot were both considered names for the substance *nirvāṇa*;

they were not distinct substances. Since they are not distinct, what difference is there between a false designation and a real one? If there is a distinction between seeking and not seeking, then that is the difference.
A hollow reference and a literal establishment are not the same. If they were distinct and not the same, what would be the nature of that entity? You admit that the two entities are identical;
how then can you distinguish between the real and the false? If the chariot and the city were different, there ought to be an entity of the "chariot" apart from the city.
Regarding the phrase "Furthermore, there is an interpretation that says... and so forth: the manifestations are not of a single path, which would obstruct the intention of the ancient masters.
The city should also be sought. Because the manifestations are not of a single path, one should not seek it; whether to seek it or not is a matter of timing.

This is called "the manifestations are not of a single path," and therefore it is not discussed here. Question: Does the ancient master say that there are places in the sutra text where it is sought? Answer: The commentary states: namely, below.

The commentary states, "This refers to the place where the treasure is sought," which is a refutation by the Master of the Subcommentary (*Sū*). This is the place where the treasure is sought; it is not the passage concerning the search for the illusory city (*nirmāṇa-ratha-pura*).
Although this passage is cited, it refers to the ancients; when one cites the sūtra text itself, there is nothing that does not accord [with it].
However, because the characteristics of the text are obscure, even though this passage is cited, the meaning remains difficult to understand.
Regarding the statement "the words 'should be stated' refer to the following passage," the Master of the Commentary (*shuzhu*) is correct; the ancients who cited this text were in error. Question:
Since the Master of the Commentary admits that [the text] should be sought and furthermore cites the passage, his position is identical to that of the ancients. He ought not to refute the ancients.
Answer: This is based on the interpretation of the ancient masters. Both the chariot and the city are the single essence of *nirvāṇa*. Why, then, do they seek the chariot and not the city?
At the time of seeking the chariot, the city is also sought. According to the intent of the commentary (*śūtra*), the chariot is conditioned wisdom (*saṃskṛta-jñāna*).

The scriptural text is explicit in stating that the city of jewels was sought; the "transformed city" (nirmita-nagara) is unconditioned (asaṃskṛta). Although the wording is not explicit, the meaning implies that there was indeed a seeking.
This does not mean that the ancients' seeking for the city was entirely disallowed.

Regarding the phrase "or [the discussion of] the parable of the chariot and so forth," there are further obstacles concerning the *sopadhiśeṣa* (with remainder) and *nirupadhiśeṣa* (without remainder) [nirvāṇas].
As for the statement, "If that is so, since the Bodhisattva now... and so on, this is the Master of the Commentary (*shuzhu*) refuting the views of the ancients.

Regarding the statement that the two vehicles have no remainder and so forth: for instance, when a person of the two vehicles attains the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), at the time they possess the "with-remainder" [nirvāṇa], they have already attained "remainderless nirvāṇa" (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*). This merely indicates a sequence of before and after; why then should one seek it further?

Regarding the statement, "Therefore, it should simply be as previously explained," the *Jianyao* (Essential Summary) states: This refers to the attainment of the fruit within the fourth question-and-answer section of the preceding "Correct Explanation.
Therein, it is said that the spontaneous realization of cessation (*nirvāṇa*) upon entering the city does not require verbal explanation; rather, such matters must depend on the vehicle.

Since these various types of knowledge (*jñāna*) each arise from their own respective seeds, they must be sought. Once they have been sought and obtained, one merely cultivates wisdom, until that wisdom becomes perfected.

It is fulfilled; it is naturally realized as cessation (*nirodha*). Regarding the principle of cessation, there is no need for further seeking. If one interprets the meaning according to the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra*, one takes wisdom (*jñāna*) as the body of the vehicle, with the sheep and deer carts distinguished by their sharpness or dullness.
However, the ancient masters took *nirvāṇa* as the vehicle. Since *nirvāṇa* has no differentiation, how could the sheep and deer carts be distinct?
If the vehicle were identical to the city, then these sheep and deer carts—which are *nirvāṇa*—should not possess any characteristics of distinction between sharp and dull faculties.

Regarding the statement that the ox-cart of the Buddha-fruit consists of the four wisdoms (*jñāna*) and so forth: this commentator [the Sub-commentator] explains that the essence of the cart pertains to both the causal and resultant stages.

As for the resultant cart: the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, the Wisdom of Equality, and the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation—these three comprise both the fundamental and subsequent [wisdoms]—and the Wisdom of Accomplishing Activities, which is exclusively subsequent. These three wisdoms, as fundamental wisdoms, constitute the body of the ox.

The four wisdoms (*catur-jñāna*) obtained subsequent to [enlightenment] constitute the body of the chariot. Therefore, the commentary states: "The four wisdoms have the wisdom of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) as their nature" (the preceding clarifies that the fruit-chariot consists entirely of the four wisdoms, while one part of the cow is borrowed from the cow to draw it).
The phrase "taking the chariot as the cause through wondrous contemplation" and so forth explains the chariot within the context of the cause.
The phrase "although there are five wisdoms" and so forth refers precisely to the fivefold categories of essence, characteristic, cause, companion, and object.
Regarding the phrase "within the characteristics of bodhi": if it issues from the essence of the One Vehicle, it is broad and pervasive because it encompasses the five wisdoms.
If it issues from the ox-cart, it defines the nature by taking only the characteristic of wisdom; it is exclusively the wisdom of the [Buddha-]seed.
"Omniscience" (sarvajñatā) refers to fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). Because the Mahāyāna possesses the wisdom of the two emptinesses, it is broad;

because the Two Vehicles possess only the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), they are narrow. Furthermore, within omniscience, the Two Vehicles attain only the single wisdom of analytical observation and do not attain the others;
thus, they are narrow. It is also termed "the wisdom of a single consciousness."

Regarding the phrase "knowledge of all modes" (*sarvākārajñatā*) and so forth, the intended meaning here is as follows: the knowledge of all modes of the two vehicles is not the same as that of the Buddha.
This knowledge of all modes—which discriminates the four truths, each with immeasurable aspects—is not known by those of the two vehicles; it is called an "unshared virtue.

When a person of the Mahāyāna attains this knowledge of all modes, they are able to transform mental images and know both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) four noble truths.

The Noble Truths. If a śrāvaka knows the four truths with effort (*saṃskṛta*), but does not know the four noble truths without effort (*asaṃskṛta*), and is unable to observe the faculties and bestow [teachings accordingly], this is collectively termed an "unshared virtue" (*āveṇika-guṇa*).
Among the one hundred and forty kinds of merits, it is the "sublime wisdom of all aspects" (*sarvākāra-prajñā*).
Question: Since Bodhisattvas also partially attain this, why is it called an unshared virtue? Answer: Because Bodhisattvas give rise to both [the conditioned and the unconditioned], it is so named.

Regarding "shared" (sādhāraṇa) and "unshared" (asādhāraṇa): when these qualities arise exclusively in the two vehicles, they are called "unshared. Furthermore, because Bodhisattvas actually attain them, they are called "shared";
yet, because the two vehicles conceal them by claiming they do not exist, they are termed "unshared."
Regarding the term "non-conceptual wisdom" (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), it refers to the meaning of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).

As with the case where a cow is not itself the actual body of a chariot, concerning the statement "like the manifest and the unmanifest," etc., one asks: regarding the chariot of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), one must take fundamental wisdom as the vehicle;

what wisdom then serves as the leader for the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*)? The answer is given in the commentary: "Like the manifest and the unmanifest, etc. This is the intended meaning.

Regarding the statement that the remaining three types of wisdom are "induced" (*ākṣepa*) by the subsequent wisdom (*pṛṣṭhaja-jñāna*), and that the vehicle is induced [by it]: for an action to be accomplished, one must obtain the ox and the rope; subsequently, one obtains the wisdom.

For an action to be accomplished, one must obtain the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). Therefore, the commentary states, "as in the case of the manifest [action] (*vijñapti*) and so forth. This is like when receiving the precepts:

the precept that is maintained takes only the future unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) as its essential body (*śīla-tattva*). As for the manifest precept (*vijñapti-śīla*), it refers to the verbal expressions and phrases used when requesting the precepts.
At that time, speech constitutes a vocal intimation (*vijñapti*), while acts such as prostration constitute a bodily intimation.

Regarding the third instance—the final moment of the *karmavācanā*—once one has received the precepts from the Saṃgha, from that point forward until the end of this life, the sustained state is exclusively non-intimation (*avijñapti*).

This remains so until it is relinquished due to four conditions: death, the arising of both sexual organs, the severance of the roots of goodness, or the performance of a formal act of abandonment. Now, regarding this non-intimation, according to the Hīnayāna...
Explanation: Its substance is subtle matter (*rūpa*). It is produced by the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of the very first moment.
These primary elements are able to directly project the non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) for the entire duration of one lifetime into the future.

The projecting primary elements perish in that single moment, but the projected non-informative matter continues from the second moment onward, depending indirectly upon the primary elements of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*). This is like a wheel thrown by hand, which continues to roll depending upon the ground. If...

According to the Mahāyāna, the substance of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) is defined as a form-substance (*rūpa-dharma*) derived from volition (*cetanā*) insofar as it is that which is prevented [from arising].

It is established upon the seeds of the sevenfold volitions. According to the master Nanda, it is established solely upon the stage of the increase of the seeds of volition through new perfuming (*navasaṃskāra*).

This refers to the final moment of the third *karmavācanā*. At that point, upon the seeds of volition (*cetanā*), there arises the functional capacity to prevent [evil] and initiate [wholesome action] across seven branches;

these are then conventionally designated as the "seven branches. Upon reaching the second moment, no further distinct seeds are produced; rather, the continuity of their own kind proceeds with increasingly superior functional activity.
The seven branches are established [as follows]: the *Śukla-candra-maṇi-garbha* (Pure Moon Essence Treasury) establishes them solely in the stage of the increase of the original seeds;

however, although those original seeds do not increase in substance, they increase in function, and thus it is spoken of based on that function, whereby something "unprecedented" is attained. The Bodhisattva Dharmapāla establishes them by way of both the new and the old stages of increase.
There are the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) of the Prātimokṣa, and the two unmanifests of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the Path (*mārga*). Liberation...

Non-manifest (avijñapti) is established upon the seeds of volition (cetanā-bīja), because even when the mind is distracted or absent, non-manifest continues to function constantly during the flow of pure or impure states.
Second, the two types of non-manifest—those of meditative concentration (dhyāna) and the path (mārga)—are established upon the actual activity (samudācāra) of volition.
That which exists while in meditative concentration (*samādhi*) but ceases upon emerging from it is called "precept that follows the mind" (*cittānuvartin-śīla*).

To say "this chariot is also like this" means that correct knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) is like the manifest action (*vijñapti*), while subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭha-jñāna*) is like the non-manifest action (*avijñapti*).

Although the non-manifest action arises based on the manifest action, it proceeds from a single moment toward the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), just as a shadow exists because of a tree; although the shadow arises from the tree...

It arises; it is likewise produced from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). This refers to the unmanifest precept (*avijñapti-śīla*), which must be induced by the manifest precept (*vijñapti-śīla*).
Just as the vehicle of subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) must be induced by the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).

Regarding the phrase "the one great matter before words," etc.: it is asked that while previously the One Vehicle was said to take both principle (*li*) and wisdom (*zhi*) together, why does the essence of the One Vehicle here take only wisdom and not principle?
Furthermore, in the later "Parable of the Phantom City" chapter, it takes principle directly.

"And yet, why is wisdom not grasped? The commentary answers: "Each is based on a single meaning," and so forth. This means that in the first cycle, both phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*li*) are explained in general;

in the second cycle, only phenomena are explained and not principle; and in the third, only principle is explained and not phenomena. These are what are called "each being based on [a single meaning]."
Regarding the statement that it is the same as *Nirvāṇa* and the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*: in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the One Vehicle is identified as Buddha-nature;

in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, the One Vehicle is identified as the Mahāyāna, and the Mahāyāna is identified as the realm of *nirvāṇa*. To take only *tathatā* (suchness) as the body of the vehicle would thus involve contradiction and obstruction; this is untenable.

Regarding the statement that "each is granted a distinct body," how can it be that they are each granted one? If wisdom (*jñāna*) is taken as the body of the vehicle, then because wisdom is subsequently planted and seated [within the ground], it could be established that each is granted one.
However, if True Suchness (*tathatā*) is taken as the body of the vehicle, since its essence is without differentiation, how can it be said that each is granted one?
Wisdom arises from its own seeds and is distinct; thus it is said to be "distinct. Since the essence of ultimate truth (*tattva*) is without differentiation, how can one say it is "distinct"?

To speak of it as being adorned by distinct qualities is difficult. Furthermore, regarding the statement "how could one possibly explain it": if wisdom is taken as the body of the vehicle, then it possesses the characteristic of adornment.
If one takes True Suchness (tathatā) as the body of the chariot, how can it be said to have embellishing features? Space is not stained by smoke, nor is it said to be adorned with color.
Since True Suchness is devoid of manifold characteristics (lakṣaṇa), how could it adorn the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu)?

Regarding the statement "how is it that the ox-drawn vehicle is as swift as the wind": this is a critique based on a deficiency in reasoning. If one takes the wisdom of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), since the essence of that wisdom is in motion, one may say it is as swift as the wind.
However, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is immovable; how can it be said to be as swift as the wind?

If it is said to be "as swift as the wind" because it can realize [all things] instantaneously (*kṣaṇa*), this is merely a metaphorical expression for its swiftness. Since the ultimate truth is immovable, how can it be described as "swift"?

Regarding the statement "how can it be said [they are immeasurable]": this is a challenge based on the inclusion of numerical categories rather than a challenge regarding their ultimate reality. Since the entities of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are each distinct, one may say their number is immeasurable.

However, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) do not fall within any numerical categories; how then can it be said that their number is immeasurable? Because the entities of conditioned phenomena differ in nature, they are each designated by the name "immeasurable unconditioned.
They do not fall under the category of a single dharma. Now, the Master of the Commentary (the *Śū*), for the time being, relies upon his own school's tenet for this purpose.
[Response: This is refuted. If the ultimate truth taught by [your] single-nature school were different from this, then one might resolve this difficulty according to that doctrine.
First, as for the fact that the *tathatā* (suchness) and the bodhisattvas of the ten stages each realize it individually, what prevents them from each being granted [their respective realizations]?

Second, as for the emptiness of form-attributes and the emptiness of the adornments, they serve as attributes of form; this is like the teaching of the "transformed city" (*nirmāṇa-pura*), so what prevents them from being adorned? Third, it is like riding upon the Great Nature (*mahā-bhūta*). With...

Wisdom is the reliance. It is instantaneous and swift; what prevents us from saying it is "quick"? (4) Just as seven is like ten, what prevents us from using numerical designations to describe its immeasurability?
Because it is like a place of rest, two are spoken of; is this not a matter of principle and number?

Moreover, although principle and wisdom differ in essence and function—like a pearl and its luster—they are not separate from the *dharmatā*. Thus, True Suchness (*tathatā*) possesses the function of responding to conditions; there is no discrepancy.
To speak separately of the absence of non-simultaneous conditions is a thesis that departs from the nature [of things]. Rather, they should be distinguished while ultimately forming a single essence;

thus one knows that *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) and *dharmalakṣaṇa* (the characteristics of phenomena) can both function in tandem. To dogmatically adhere to a single path is not the mark of a person who has attained realization. If one follows the principles of one’s own school, one should simply negate the positions of others for the time being.
Regarding the statement that "the small and medium [capacities] are like children," this is a general rebuttal.

For instance, when a sage of the five fruits turns their mind toward enlightenment, it takes eight, six, four, or other such kalpas before they reach the initial stage of the ten faiths; furthermore, after another great kalpa, they enter the first bhūmi, where they finally "board the vehicle."
Question: How is it that from the very moment they first turn their minds [toward enlightenment], one says they each receive an equal "great vehicle"?
Answer: The commentary states that there are two senses in which they are said to "each receive" it: first, the vehicle of the present superior teaching; second, the vehicle for future practice.
Because the present and the future differ, they are collectively termed "receiving. This refers to riding the One Vehicle for one great *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* prior to the [first] stage (*bhūmi*).

This refers to the vehicle of the teaching. From the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward, the superior wisdom-vehicle of the Bodhisattvas—the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) wisdom that serves as the mount for those who have received the body of transformation (*nirmāṇakāya*)—is collectively termed the "vehicle. This is what is meant by "being able to board the vehicle. As this sutra states:
"Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas ride upon this precious vehicle and proceed directly to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*)."
Regarding the phrase "the essence of the wisdom that is the referent," this refers precisely to the seed-wisdom of the two kinds of emptiness in the first bhūmi.
In contrast to the teaching-vehicle of the expressive words heard prior to the bhūmis, the first bhūmi is therefore called the "essence of the wisdom that is the referent."

"Speaking words like giving a bright pearl" is an illustration. Since that initial turning of the mind occurs while still on the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*), the Mahāyāna teachings heard at that time are called "giving the pearl of the teaching.
Later, upon entering the first ground (*prathamabhūmi*), one obtains the substance of the pearl itself.

Regarding the mention of the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* and other texts, this explains the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*). It also explains the passage where [the Buddha] announces that he will bestow upon each of his sons a single great vehicle (*mahāyāna*). Question: Although they were previously śrāvakas, they are not bodhisattvas later on; therefore, at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, they receive the name of the "teaching-vehicle" (*deśanā-yāna*). I do not yet understand where they obtain the actual substance of the vehicle (*yāna-bhāva*) thereafter. Answer: The commentary states "the *Śrīmālā* and others. The word "others" includes the *Mahāyānasamgraha* and so forth. This refers to the fact that although they were previously śrāvakas, they are now bodhisattvas. Therefore, it is said that they have obtained the substance of the vehicle. Furthermore, regarding the statement that they obtain the substance of the vehicle, it means that although they were previously śrāvakas, they are now bodhisattvas. Thus, it is said that they have obtained the substance of the vehicle. The above relies on the sūtra, which speaks of the "three kinds of mind-made bodies" (*manomaya-kāya*): namely, the arhats, the pratyekabuddhas, and the bodhisattvas who have already attained mastery.
These three constitute the "three children. This is identical to what this sūtra states regarding the vehicles of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and non-retrogressive bodhisattvas.

It is the precious vehicle (*ratnayāna*). Question: The *Śāstra* states that one is caused to realize the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*). At which stage does one attain non-retrogression such that it is called "ascending the vehicle and leaving the house"?

Answer: Initially, being in the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) is called non-retrogression. Citing the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* to prove gradual enlightenment, the intent is to speak of the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) of the three vehicles.
This is attained prior to the stages by those of the two vehicles, while for Mahāyāna bodhisattvas, it is attained at the first stage. This is the third [point].

This refers to departing from the house and ascending the vehicle. For the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), departing from the house and ascending [the vehicle] prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) is called the "teaching-vehicle" (*nāmopadeśa-yāna*).

For the Mahāyāna, departing from the house and ascending [the vehicle] upon the stages is the "practicing-vehicle" (*caryā-yāna*). This refers to the realization of non-retrogression above this point and the attainment of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), which is consistent with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra-upadeśa*.
"Entering into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

Regarding the statement "furthermore, as for sudden enlightenment (*tunwu*) and so forth," the question is: If it is gradual enlightenment where wisdom (*prajñā*) predominates, one may speak of the first stage (*bhūmi*);

but if it is sudden enlightenment where compassion (*karuṇā*) predominates, how is this to be understood? The answer in the commentary states: "Furthermore, as for sudden enlightenment and so forth," which refers to taking the contaminated practices (*sāsrava-caryā*) prior to the stages as the basis.

The first is named "the initial resolve" (*prathamacittotpāda*). The second is "the resolve realized through direct perception" (*sākṣātkṛtacittotpāda*), which refers to the stages from the first bhūmi onward (both interpretations are acceptable).
Although it is said that these are also like the "chariot" and so forth, the resolve realized through direct perception in the first bhūmi is termed the "initial resolve.

This is because, although there are untainted (*anāsrava*) teachings and practices from the first bhūmi onward, they are not included [in this category] because they are identical in their abandonment [of afflictions], involve the transformation of support (*pariṇāmikī upapatti*), and are not yet definitive. Therefore, they are not taken [as the initial resolve].
Regarding the statement, "Now, taking those from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) onwards," etc., this is the second interpretation.

Its meaning is that those of the three vehicles who have attained both gradual and sudden enlightenment, and whose wisdom has increased, equally receive the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Taking pure outflow-free conduct (*anāsrava-caryā*) as their causal vehicle, they are already situated in the eighth stage.

Regarding the phrase "prior to the seventh stage," this refers to what is called the Bodhisattva whose compassion increases; although they have realized the two kinds of emptiness, they still abide in the realm of birth-and-death (pariccheda), as they have not yet attained the transformation body (pariṇāmanakāya).
Regarding the statement, "Therefore, we now adopt the former interpretation," this means taking the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) as the stage of non-retrogression.

This is because those of sudden enlightenment generally have an increase in compassion (*karuṇā*), whereas those of gradual enlightenment generally have an increase in wisdom (*jñāna*). Thus, by adopting the former interpretation of the first stage, one obtains the superior ox-cart.
Regarding the statement "the Laṅkāvatāra by means of these," the Sūtra says:

"The three types of mind-made bodies (manomayakāya)—those of Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas of great power—both enter the first stage (prathamabhūmi). Thus, it is stated that the three types of mind-made bodies originate from the first stage.
They immediately mounted the vehicle together. The intent of that sutra states: those from the fifth stage and below are called the "body born of the mind through the joy of samādhi";

those of the sixth, seventh, and eighth stages are the "body born of the mind through the self-nature of the joy of awakening to dharmas"; and those of the ninth, tenth, and eleventh stages attain the "body born of the mind through effortless action, which is co-arisen with its kind."
Regarding the statement that the parable illustrates the seed of Buddhahood, Xiang says: "To cite the fruit while discussing the cause is also not correct. Mou says:

"In the second week, the substance of the ox-cart encompasses both cause and fruit; the cause is entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, while the fruit is the distinct realization of the manifestation of the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*)."
Regarding the "activity of immeasurable wisdom," the intent of the treatise follows the verse: "Riding this precious vehicle, one goes straight to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
Therefore, it pertains to the cause. If one follows the prose commentary, which praises the virtues of the chariot, it refers exclusively to the vehicle of the fruit.

As the Sūtra says: "That chariot is high and broad" (and so forth). Furthermore, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "It is constantly [attended] by immeasurable devas, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, non-humans, and so forth."
Because it is attended by [the Bodhisattvas], we know it is the Vehicle of the Fruit (*phala-yāna*). Jiaxiang says: "To emerge from the realm of the two kinds of birth-and-death is 'High';

to be replete with the ten thousand virtues is called 'Vast. To emerge from the two deaths means there are no afflictions that are not exhausted; to be replete with all virtues means there are no qualities that are not perfected."
The *Zhongjing* (Combined Sūtras) states: "I possess the immeasurable and boundless power of wisdom, the fearlessnesses, and so forth—the dharmas of all Buddhas.
This means that subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) serves as the carriage, while the myriad virtues, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, serve as the accompanying ornaments.
These are precisely the immeasurable and boundless wisdoms; "immeasurable" refers to their height, and "boundless" refers to their breadth.

Regarding the statement that "the substance [of the body] is high in three respects": each of the sense organs and marks of excellence is boundless, as they are produced by the induction of limitless roots of goodness;
thus, experiencing one's own body and experiencing the bliss of the Dharma for oneself is called "high. This continues until the limit of birth and death, throughout the entirety of future time.

Therefore, it is called "vast. Furthermore, regarding the Body of Enjoyment for Others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*), its eyes are like the waters of the four great oceans, and its *ūrṇā* hair-tuft is like the five Mount Sumerus.

The phrase "capable of both illuminating and transforming" serves as a conclusion. "Illuminating" refers to the manifestation of reflected images (*pratibimba*), which is like exhausting the source and reaching the very bottom; "transforming" refers to...

Benefiting others and engaging with sentient beings; the differentiation of the seeds of wisdom regarding objective phenomena; the capacity for all dharmas to be subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*); and the function of the two benefits (*dvaya-hita*).

Regarding the phrase "adorned with various jewels," this refers to the sūtra’s description of the powers (*bala*), fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), and other such qualities.

This is the Dharma. To use the analogy mentioned above regarding the elder’s carriage, it is entirely adorned with the seven treasures—namely, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, coral, and diamond.
Likewise, within the Dharma, the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision are vast and profound, possessing immeasurable, unimpeded powers and fearlessnesses.
Furthermore, when wisdom arises, twenty-two factors arise simultaneously; moreover, there is...
It is adorned with the countless, dust-like myriad virtues of the conditioned and unconditioned.
Regarding the term "railing" (*varanda*): that which runs lengthwise is called a "balustrade" (*varaṇa*), and that which runs crosswise is called a "fence" (*śūnya*).
As for the statement "it is the four *dhāraṇīs*": this current explanation takes these to be the railings on the chariot, used as a metaphor for the four *dhāraṇīs*. [Sanskrit: *varaṇa-śūnya*]

It is called *dhāraṇī*. This is translated as "total retention" (*zongchi*). There are two types of total retention: first, gathering (*she*); second, dispersing (*san*). Gathering means to hold; it refers precisely to this "retention through hearing.
One hears the words and their meanings, transforming them so they are held without forgetting; all the dharmas one has heard can be retained. Its essence consists of mindfulness and wisdom.
Dispersing means to bestow (*shi*). It has four kinds: first, the Dharma, which is the teaching that expresses [the truth]; its essence is...
1. Sound, name, phrase, and syllable; 2. Meaning, which refers to the meaning expressed and the principles of the ultimate and conventional truths;

3. Mantras, such as the *ṣaḍgatika-dhāraṇī* and others found in the *Saddharma-puṇḍarīka-sūtra*; 4. The ability to attain the bodhisattva’s patience, namely the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Within the three natures of phenomena, all possess the characteristic of non-arising: the characteristic of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is non-arising, and the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is non-arising...

It arises spontaneously; it is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Since afflictions and suffering do not arise, that which can express this is called the "dharma of non-arising" (*anutpāda-dharma*).

"Patience" (*kṣānti*) refers to the seal of certification. Regarding this dharma of non-arising, before the stages (*bhūmi*), one has heard of it but has not yet given rise to the wisdom-seal (*jñāna-mudrā*);

at the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), one is able to certify it, which is termed "Bodhisattva patience. This is what is attained; here, the means of attainment is fully taken as the attainment itself. Jiguō says: "On the elder’s chariot..."
"Zhoujie" (周迊) means "entirely surrounded by railings. The railings hold the internal members so they do not go out; the balusters prevent outsiders from entering.

Upon the Tathāgata’s wisdom, there is likewise a total enclosure of *dhāraṇīs* (total-holdings): they maintain internal goodness so it does not depart, and they ward off external evil so it does not enter.
Regarding the mention of "girdles, bells, and so forth," the Sūtra states: "Bells were suspended on all four sides. On the ox-carts were bird-bells;
on the four types of carriages, both large and small, there were great bells sounding *tu-tu* and small bells sounding *ti-di* and *ling-ling*.

The great bells resounded *chi-chi*, *lang-lang*, and *cuo-cuo*, while the small bells chimed *zi-yin* and *da-da*. The carriages of the elders had bells suspended on all four sides to provide warning.

O Son, when the Dharma-sound is proclaimed from the Tathāgata’s supreme wisdom, it gladdens the hearts of the assembly; when the bells ring, all the sons rejoice; and when the Dharma-teachings are heard, the eight classes of beings are brought to goodness.
Furthermore, one hears the Buddha’s gentle voice, profound, far-reaching, and most subtle. It is also said that it is clear and resonant, heard from afar.
Regarding the meaning of the commentary: wherever the mind is directed is called the "face. With a compassionate heart, one contemplates the four [directions].
"Birth" refers to the four directions. The sevenfold eloquence is like a bell, pervading the four realms of birth; thus it is called "four-directional suspended bells.

Eloquence expounds the teachings through sound like a bell. Beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of seventy-two Ganges Rivers, one hears the characteristics of the Brahma-voice at the assembly on Vulture Peak, which is like the sound of a bell.
Regarding the scriptural passage, "furthermore, from above it reaches the canopy," Jiaxiang says:
"The elder’s canopy is high-raised and covers below, just as the Tathāgata’s fourfold impartial mind rises above the two vehicles and covers the six realms of existence.

Although it is called 'covering the carriage,' it actually covers the children of the three vehicles within the carriage. The character for *xiǎn* (canopy) is pronounced *xū yǎn* (虚偃). The scripture also continues with "with rare treasures" and so forth.
Regarding the adornments: when asked why, within this description, the canopy (*vitāna*) is directed upward and separate miscellaneous jewels are mentioned, the answer is as follows:
the canopy has the four immeasurables—compassion (*maitrī*), pity (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)—as its essence.

Within that, because there are distinctions in the characteristics of the modes of practice regarding compassion for sentient beings (*sattvālambana-maitrī*), compassion for phenomena (*dharmālambana-maitrī*), and objectless compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*), they are separately distinguished. As for the excellence of the canopy mentioned above, it pertains to the essence.

Adorned with various jewels, it discusses within the Dharma the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*). Regarding their essential nature, there are distinctions such as compassion directed toward sentient beings (*sattvālambana-karuṇā*) and compassion directed toward phenomena (*dharmālambana-karuṇā*).
These specific modes of activity also accord with the subsequent text. A net of pearls is spread over its top;
this is why it is described separately.
Regarding the statement "each [type] has sentient beings, etc.": when taking sentient beings as the object of observation, one perceives their suffering and so forth, and thereby delivers them.

If, however, it is a case of taking phenomena (*dharma*) as the object, one does not perceive sentient beings; rather, one observes those [objects] by forming the conceptualization of the three categories (*triskandha*) of phenomena for the sake of benefiting them.
If there are no objects of perception, having already dispelled the two types of grasping, one does not perceive a self, persons, or the characteristics of phenomena;
rather, one contemplates true suchness (tathatā) and gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness and so forth, as previously distinguished.
Regarding the scripture’s statement that "precious cords are interlaced," Jiaxiang says: "If the carriage canopy were not lashed down, it would flutter and fly away;
therefore, cords are secured to keep it from moving. The Tathāgata’s vehicle of wisdom is likewise: if wisdom lacked the great vows, its principle of universal grasping would be lost;
yet by skillfully driving with the Four Great Vows, the mind of vast transport remains ever-stable."
Regarding the term "supreme certainty": it is called "supreme" because by generating the great vow, one shall attain the fruit of Buddhahood, which is superior to all other fruits.
It is called "certainty" because it is sustained by the power of that vow, ensuring that one does not fall back or lose it.
Regarding the mention of the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra* and others: these also concern the making of vows to uphold the True Dharma (*saddharma*).

A son of good family is capable of bearing the four kinds of heavy responsibilities, as described in this same sutra: "interlaced with jeweled cords. If there were no vow, [there would be nothing for] all sentient beings.
Generally, one is captured and led away by non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Now that there is this vow, one will not be moved by false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) nor turned by indolence (*kausīdya*).

Regarding the passage "the sutra hangs with various flower-garlands," Ji Guo says: "When the flower-garlands hang down, one is delighted; they collectively constitute the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*)."

Bowing in accordance with all things is like a forest; this is analogous to the chariot described above, which is further adorned with flower tassels hanging from its four sides—this refers to the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) within the Dharma.
Regarding "generosity" (*dāna*): first, gathering the poor through generosity, by distributing one's own wealth and possessions to sentient beings; second, [loving speech]...

Speech encompasses the removal of ill-will; that is, to be free from frowning, to speak with a smile and as the first to address others, to invite them forward and inquire after their well-being, to offer timely consolation, and to always speak words that are pleasing and beneficial.
One should cause others to rejoice by teaching the supreme Dharma so that they may attain liberation.

Regarding the three types of beneficial conduct (*artha-caryā*), those previously mentioned were the "receiving of the prediction" (the teaching of the Dharma); now, the "beneficial conduct" refers to the actual practice and cultivation.
[He] acts [in this way]. Yet he causes sentient beings to obtain present benefit in the form of wealth and status, and subsequent benefit through renunciation;

as for "benefit in both respects," it means that they are born in the five Pure Abodes and subsequently attain liberation. Fourth, "common purpose" means sharing in all the activities performed by all sentient beings.
First [one acts] in common with others, and later one exhorts them; thus the practice becomes firm and steadfast, such that no regression arises.

Regarding the phrase "flower-sound" (*huāyīn*) and so forth: it refers to a fillet (*sìng*) adorned with flowers. There are two distinct meanings for "flower" and "fillet. If they refer to a fillet that is itself an adornment of flowers, then there is but a single meaning.

Regarding the statement that "the character *wèi* (綩) is used as a synonym," the Master Mou’s intention was this: the original scripture uses the character with the "silk" (*sī*) radical on the left; its etymological source is unknown.
Now, it should instead be written with the "grass" (*cǎo*) radical below as *xián* (莚).
Regarding the statement that "the ancients had an interpretation such as this," Jiaxiang takes meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) to mean "layered" (*yuanqian*).
Because meditative concentration is supple and serves to settle the body, and because there are four types of meditative concentration, it is called "double-layered."
"To say that this principle is not so" is the Master of the Commentary’s refutation. Because the principle contradicts the sacred prophecy, he says it is "not so.

Regarding the phrase "as stated in the Vimalakīrti," according to the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) serves as the bed; here, "bed" refers to the wooden planks of a carriage.

Regarding the phrase "pure livelihood" (*pariśuddhājīva*) and so forth, this refers to right livelihood (*samyagājīva*) within the Eightfold Noble Path. Pure livelihood serves as the bedding. Lü states:

"Mental action (*manas-karman*) produced by the absence of greed and delusion is called pure livelihood; bodily action (*kāya-karman*) produced by the absence of hatred is called right action (*samyakkarmānta*)."

Vocal action (vākkarman) produced by non-attachment (alobha) is called right speech (samyagvāc). Regarding the term "repeatedly laid out" (*punarukta*): if that is so, what is meant by "repeatedly laying it out to cause [the gift] to be bestowed"?

Non-attachment and non-delusion (amoha) act as the motivating mental actions (*manaskarman*), while the [actual] bestowal is the action they motivate. The conjunction of these two types of motivation is termed "repeatedly laying it out."
The mention of "body, speech, and mind" explains the meaning of "pure livelihood. The three types of action (trikarma) constitute the "repeated layering.
Alternatively, taking body and speech as primary, they are all subsumed under mental action; thus, it is called "repeated layering."
The phrase "the mind wanders upon the *huán*" explains the meaning of the *wǎnzhèn*.
The statement regarding "constantly practicing pure livelihood" (*śuddhājīva*) and so forth explains the double-layered matting.

The scripture’s mention of "placing a red pillow" refers to spreading out the mat and positioning the pillow; this is the ritual for reclining and sleeping. Upon entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the mind is extinguished.
Regarding the physical state of resting, as for the phrase "the ancient interpretation," Jiaxiang says that *nirvāṇa* can rest the cycle of birth and death, and thus it is called a "pillow.

As for the phrase "the present explanation," the commentary takes this to refer to the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). Before entering this meditative state, the mind and spirit are exhausted by anxieties and attachments.

Contemplation: Since the mind that clings to external objects is mostly tainted (*sāsrava*), the seven consciousnesses do not function; by means of this, one enters meditative absorption (*samādhi*), ceasing weariness and indolence, thereby increasing the Noble Path—this is called the "Red Pillow" (*dan-zhen*).
Regarding the phrase "pillow of the immortal elixir" (*xiāndān*) and so forth: Question: What is meant by the "elixir-pillow"? Answer:

According to ancient exegesis, it refers to a pillow within which the divine elixir of the immortals—the ninefold-transformed *śreṣṭha-rasāyana*—has been formed, causing one's lifespan to increase. The meditative concentration of the outflow-free (*anāsrava-samādhi*) is likewise so called, because it increases the Noble Path (*ārya-mārga*).
Regarding the statement that this principle is incorrect: although the intent of the *Shu* (Commentary) borrows from ancient interpretations, I have not yet dared to reach a definitive conclusion.
As for the absence [of wooden pillows] in the Western Regions, Master Xuanying held that because there were no wooden pillows in India, they used only red-dyed cotton cloth as pillows;
these were stuffed with *tūla* cotton, hair, and so forth to form a pillow, which was dyed red and thus called a "vermilion pillow" (*danzhen*), upon which one would lean.
This is the pillow. The preceding section provides the correct explanation.
Regarding the phrase "supporting the noble path": all noble ones rely upon faith and the other faculties;

the arising of faith is the root, just as trees and the like depend on soil and water for their growth, with those elements serving as the root. Soil can support the five faculties beginning with faith, and thus it can support the noble [path].
The Path is untainted (and thus not grasped).

Regarding the statement that "the essence of the white ox is equal [to the chariot]," it means that just as a chariot must be drawn by an ox, the activity of subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) must be drawn by fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
Jiguō takes fundamental compassion as the power of the ox and takes the roots of goodness as the ox itself, because they constitute the very body of the ox. This is the interpretation of Jiā.
Xiang takes "Great Wisdom" (*mahāprajñā*) as the ox.

Regarding the phrase "non-conceptual wisdom" (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) and so forth: Question: In the household of a wealthy man, there are oxen for pulling carts, oxen for pulling mills, and oxen for plowing fields.
I do not yet know what kind of ox this is. Answer: The commentary states that non-conceptual wisdom and the like are the "oxen for drawing the cart."
It is an ox. He asked, "For what reason does the householder’s family keep a white ox? He replied, "Plow-oxen, yellow oxen, and black oxen are common;
even the poor can obtain them. As for this white ox, only the householder’s family can provide it; other families do not have one.
Among all oxen, those that are white are the most supreme, being the source of all colors."

The phrase "Lord of Ten Thousand Virtues" refers to the *knot* (the result). Since all the ten thousand virtues within the Tathāgata’s fruition exist because of the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), this wisdom is said to be the "Lord.
This is the *dharma*. The white lotus flower is the *metaphor*. The essence of this wisdom is untainted (*anāsrava*) and is named the "Sun."

Regarding the statement that the Bull-King possesses three virtues, these are: abandonment (*prahāṇa*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and benevolence (*anugraha*). Abandonment is that which is realized; knowledge is its intrinsic nature;
and benevolence is its functional activity. Therefore, all three are cited together.

Regarding the term "vanquishing enemies": its dewlap hangs down to the ground and its long horns reach toward the heavens; whenever it encounters an enemy, it must fight, and in fighting, it is always victorious, like a water buffalo battling a tiger.
This is a metaphor discussed within the Dharma: the Buddha’s power of severed virtue is able to vanquish the two obstacles and the māras.
Regarding the description of his majestic virtue and other qualities: the ox’s polished horns startled the heavens, appearing like the emergence of a Dragon Spring sword;
as it leaped and cast itself to the ground, it was like the soaring peak of Mount Lingling; its roar encompassed the thunder of spring, vibrating deeply beyond a hundred *li*.
Its breath charges through the autumn mist, vast and pervasive, shrouding the corners of the eight directions. Its tail is like a long pine tree hanging downward;

its eyes resemble shooting stars, each reflecting the world with dual clarity. The Prime Minister said, "The ox possesses five virtues: first, its single horn; second, its hump; third, its hooves; fourth, its dewlap."
The five characteristics of a bull: one who possesses such a bull desires it to have four features—a capacity like a peck (*dou*), a relaxed [belly], a tight [body], and a warm [nose].

As for its mouth, it should resemble a peck; the area of the tail should be like an overturned ladle, capable of holding one peck. Furthermore, it is said that its four hooves should be like those capable of holding one peck;
its belly should be relaxed while its legs are tight, its dung should be dry, and its nose should be warm.
Regarding the phrase "adorned with manifold virtues": when correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) arises, the twenty-two mental bases (*citta-rāja-āyatana*) are termed "manifold virtues.

Because they are all of a wholesome nature (*kuśala-svabhāva*), they receive the name "virtues" (*guṇa*). Within the state of fruition (*phala-avasthā*), the distinction between essence and function constitutes all the virtues, which together adorn wisdom. This illustrates the virtues of the Buddha's wisdom.
Regarding the phrase "delivering oneself and others": "self" refers to self-benefit, and "others" refers to benefiting others. If one wishes to benefit others, one must first benefit oneself;
this is likened to a debt of gratitude. Because the Tathāgata’s wisdom possesses these two modes of transport, it is likened to an ox.
Because this sutra possesses three virtues, it is likened to the Mahāyāna, and not to other sutras.

Regarding the statement that the horse is like the "noble steed of the Mahāyāna," the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "To harness a horse to a cart, to control and drive a team of four"—this is what it refers to.
Regarding the statement that it is not compared to a donkey-cart, [the interlocutor] asks: "In which sūtra or teaching is the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) compared to a donkey-cart? The answer is: none.
The *Bhaya-dharmanī-sūtra* states: "Śrāvakas are like donkeys on vehicles. This refers to the actual practice.
As for the mention of the elephant and so forth, it is said that the *Suśīla-sūtra* agrees with the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*: the elephant chariot is a metaphor for non-abiding nirvāṇa;

the ox, horse, and deer represent the other three types of nirvāṇa. The ox symbolizes the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because it possesses manifold virtues; the horse symbolizes... [text fragment ends].

There are those with remainder (*sa-upadhiśeṣa*), because they have not yet severed suffering; there are those like deer (*mṛga-upamā*), who are without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*), because they dwell in seclusion and tranquility.

As for the sūtra’s statement that “the complexion of the skin is full and pure,” this means the skin is full and the complexion is pure: "full" signifies being replete, and "pure" signifies being clean.

Regarding the phrase "inner virtues are perfected": this refers to the simultaneous realization of the two emptinesses (*dvaya-śūnyatā*), which is unlike the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas who realize only the principle of the emptiness of sentient beings (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and thus possess incomplete inner virtues.
Regarding the phrase "the three colors are pure": this means purity; it signifies that the three obstructions—of afflictions (*kleśa*), karma (*karman*), and suffering (*duḥkha*)—have been exhausted.

Regarding the phrase "endowed with the virtue of precepts": since one has already severed the two obstacles, one is in accord with the virtue of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), and is thus called "shared" (*sādhāraṇa*).
To say it means "majestic power" (*vibhūti*) is incorrect.
Regarding the mention of the dialects of Zhao, Wei, and so forth, Shen Zhi states: "Zhao is located in the regions of Xu and Ru;

Wei is located in the prefectures of Yuan, Ding, and others; Yan is in Youzhou; and Dai refers to Daizhou. These prefectures produce women of exquisite beauty; Yan and Zhao abound with such fine ladies."

Regarding the phrase "The quiet maiden is beautiful" (*jing nü qi shu*), the *Mao Shih* says: "The quiet maiden is beautiful; she awaits me at the corner of the city wall. "Quiet" (*jing*) means pure and still.
A woman must be pure, still, and possessed of proper measure before she may be wed. "Beautiful" (*shu*) refers to lovely appearance. "Awaits" (*si*) means to wait for.

"City corner" (*cheng yu*) is used to signify height, implying it is impassable and cannot be stepped upon. The virtue of a woman is pure and still, yet she may be cherished; her lovely appearance brings peace.

Furthermore, they are able to be submissive and wait for ritual propriety before acting; they defend themselves as if with a city wall, and thus there is affection. Though there is affection, because one does not see [the beloved], one tosses the head and paces back and forth.

The words "the will goes forth" mean to pace back and forth; "the movement stops" means to have affection for them but not go to see them.
