The eighth consciousness has existed from time immemorial until the present; therefore, it is called "long. The manifesting consciousness arises and ceases instantaneously;

therefore, it is called "sudden exhaustion. Lu Fu says: "If discussed vertically, it refers to the beginning of the aggregate of consciousness, where the four phases of a single *kṣaṇa* arise and perish in every thought-moment;
this is called 'long. If discussed horizontally, it refers to the four phases of a single lifetime of the aggregate of consciousness; thus, it constitutes 'sudden exhaustion.'"

Vertically, this refers to the four subtle phases—arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing—that have existed since beginningless time. Horizontally, it refers to the four coarse phases of a single lifetime:

birth, aging, illness, and death. When discussing the vertical four subtle phases, because they have been in a state of endless arising and ceasing since beginningless time, the duration is so vast that they are termed "long-standing. When discussing horizontally, these refer to the coarse four phases pertaining to the present life.
Internally, birth, old age, sickness, and death shift and turn without ceasing. The Chancellor said: "From time without beginning, one dies in the lower realm and is born in the upper realm;
one dies in the upper realm and is born in the lower realm. This is called 'long-standing' because it has endured for so long. This begins from the very first birth and ends with the final death.
These two stages of birth and death occur instantaneously without gradual transition, and are thus termed 'sudden ruin,' meaning they collapse all at once. This is the intended meaning.
It is said that [this state] has arisen from inversion since beginningless time; it is called "long-standing" because it is like something decayed by wind and rain over many years.

It is called "suddenly worn out" because it is abruptly discarded all at once within a single kṣaṇa, like a forest collapsing. Furthermore, it is said that being seventy, eighty, or ninety years old is what is meant by "long-standing," which refers precisely to this sudden wearing out.

Regarding the phrase "the hall and the dwelling are high and precarious," an ancient master said: "The body in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is like a hall; if one is born in the two higher realms, it is like a dwelling.
According to the interpretation of the *Śāstra*, the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) is large and constitutes the hall, while the other faculties are small and constitute the dwellings.
That hall is vast and pervades the dwellings, whereas the dwellings are small and do not pervade the hall. Because the body-faculty is large, it pervades the other four [faculties].

Regarding the sense-faculties (*indriya*): because the four [sensory] faculties are small, they do not pervade the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*). While the absence of the four [sensory] faculties does not prevent the presence of the body-faculty, if the body-faculty is absent, the other faculties likewise do not exist.
Just as a dwelling (*śālā*) must depend upon a hall (*maṇḍapa*), the affairs of the remaining four faculties must depend upon the body-faculty.

The prose commentary states: "A multi-storied pavilion atop a hall. Since the term "dwelling" (*śālā*) is used here in place of "pavilion" (*maṇḍapa*), it is called a "hall-dwelling" (*maṇḍapa-śālā*). As for "lofty and dangerous":

The preceding analogy states that the hall and residence of the elder’s house were exceedingly high; being so high, they were prone to collapse, and such instability implies a lack of permanence—this is the mark of impermanence (*anitya*).
In the context of the Dharma, when the human body is at its peak, robust, and full of strength, this is itself a sign of impending decay.
It is not good for one who is suddenly flourishing to remain in that state; the seasonal miasma of heaven will first strike their door, and fever shall arise.
When illness arrives, there is increased chills and high fever; when cold-natured ailments arrive, the complexion becomes withered and yellow.

This is like a tree standing out from the forest—it will surely be the first to be toppled by the wind. Its appearance is like a mass of foam, for it lacks solidity. It is also like a house that has stood for a long time, where the timber and wood have all decayed.
Regarding the phrase "the enemy fears the reversal and applies various [remedies]," it means that as a person grows old, they rely on assistance. (10)
The pillar supports the branches; rising and sitting follow it in succession.

When it is said that "the root of the pillar is crushed and decayed," this refers to taking the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) as the root of the pillar.

Because the root of the pillar is crushed and decayed, the beams and rafters collapse. If the life-faculty were absent, sensation (*vedanā*) and the other aggregates would immediately perish. Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "It is like a person..."
As long as the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) exists, the remaining faculties are established; if the life-faculty ceases, all the faculties perish.

The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has seventy-three dharmas as its substance, and among these, none is more preeminent than the life-faculty. The life-faculty possesses the power to maintain the continuity of matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) without interruption;
were it not for this power of uninterrupted maintenance, the duration—whether long or short—would be determined solely by prior karma. As for the desire...

To obtain a long-lasting life-force (*jīvitendriya*), one must necessarily rely on a firm foundation; to obtain a beautiful body and longevity, it depends upon the sustaining power of other karmic forces.
As stated above, the foundation is able to support the root of karma; in the Dharma, the pillar of reflection (*cintā*) is able to sustain life.
Regarding the phrase "moment-to-moment transition and the cessation of karmic volitions," this means that if the causes of karma are exhausted, the fruit of life will not endure.

As one flows and transitions from moment to moment, there is no room for meditative absorption (*samāpatti*). When the sense faculties (*indriya*) are destroyed and decayed, how can there be any peace?

The two phrases "the pillar of mental expression" and "the roots and the foundation" both belong to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Because of the foundation, there are the pillars and roots; by reason of these [pillars], the beams [are supported].
Just as there are rafters and ridgepoles [in a house], so it is with this body. Within the volition of karma, there is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*);
because of this life-faculty, there are the causes and conditions of life, all of which are formations (*saṃskāra*). Question:

Since the meaning of the "collection" (*rāśi*) of the five aggregates (*skandha*) is identical, for what reason do the two aggregates of consciousness (*vijñāna*) and formations each encompass two phrases of the Sūtra, while the remaining three [aggregates] each encompass one? Answer: The aggregate of consciousness is the primary factor.

Because there is a distinction between horizontal and vertical [relationships], they are divided into two phrases. Regarding the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), it comprises seventy-three among the one hundred dharmas;
from within these, only the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is taken. Furthermore, within the life-faculty, both cause and effect are encompassed:

volitional action (*cetanā*) is the cause of life, and the life-faculty itself is the result of that volitional action. Because wholesome and unwholesome karma serves as the cause, it is able to induce wholesome [results] in the future.
The fruit of evil is that one's lifespan may be long or short; thus we know that both life and its fruits arise from the cause of karma.
Because causes and effects differ, they are divided into two phrases. Since this is not otherwise, each is treated as a single phrase.
Regarding the phrase "the beams and rafters are leaning," the "beam" (liáng) refers to the horizontal beam, while the "rafter" (dòng) refers to the vertical rafter.

If the beams and rafters remain upright, the upward-pointing rafters and eaves will persist; if the beams and rafters lean, how can the house remain standing? The beam relies upon the rafter, and the rafter relies upon the pillar.
The container depends upon the supported object, and the supported object depends upon the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). It is because there is a rafter-base that there are beams above it.

Because the eighth consciousness serves as the primary subject that experiences (*anubhava*) the preceding objects, it is only through its reliance upon the five [sensory faculties] that the five consciousnesses can arise to experience them.

Thus, they experience the objects of the five dusts (*pañca-viṣaya*), and these five dusts are all experienced by means of sensation (*vedanā*). These sensations of the first six consciousnesses exist only because of the primary sensation;

it is due to this that they are able to receive and tolerate their objects. The Commentary states there are two interpretations: first, the essence of consciousness is called "primary sensation" (*maula-vedanā*); second, it refers to the grasping...

Among the mental factors associated [with consciousness], that which experiences is called *vedanā* (feeling). The second interpretation is correct. Furthermore, within this second interpretation, there are two further explanations:
first, taking the feeling of the eighth consciousness as "correct feeling" (*samyag-vedanā*), because it is the master of the total retribution;
second, including the aforementioned feelings and subsuming them into one place, collectively designating them as "correct feeling."
Regarding the phrase "How can it be settled?", it means that it reveals how all sensations (*vedanā*) within the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are impermanent.
Furthermore, it says, "The loss of right concentration" refers to the sensation of the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). How can it be settled? Sensation occurs in the present moment;
like water striking a bubble, one arises and another perishes. When encountering a favorable object, there is a pleasant sensation (*sukha-vedanā*), which experiences that favorable object. Suddenly—
There are circumstances that conflict with the object; thus, the feeling of sorrow (*daurmanasya-vedanā*) also experiences [this]. While the preceding object ceases, the subsequent object arises;
while the preceding experience ceases, the subsequent experience arises. This arising and ceasing is unstable from moment to moment, like floating bubbles.
Regarding the terms "foundation" (*ādhāra*) and "steps" (*sopāna*), these refer to volition (*cetanā*) as the essence among the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*).

Since, according to the Mahāyāna, all karma is volition, and because it can sustain the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), it is likened to a foundation and steps. Just as when people build a house in the world, if the foundation is firm and solid, its pillars will endure for a long time;
if the foundation and steps are not solid, the pillars will soon collapse and be destroyed. This refers to the power and momentum of karma upon volition.

When the limit is exhausted, it is like the collapsing of a foundation or a flight of stairs; the Dharma is likewise. One sustains the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) through volitional karma (*karmacetanā*);

because of the cause that is the life-faculty, there is the attainment of meditative absorption (*samāpatti*); because of the existence of sensation (*vedanā*), one is able to experience, and only then does the arising of phenomena occur. Question:
Among the seventy-three factors within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), why are volitional karma and the life-faculty specifically mentioned? Answer: Volitional karma is...
The cause is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), and it is the fruit. Since cause and fruit are distinct, two dharmas are mentioned. Question: Why are other dharmas not mentioned? Answer:
Only these two are cited to include and explain all other dharmas; for all those dharmas therein depend upon the life-faculty.
Regarding the mention of "walls, partitions, and so forth": that which wards off the outside is called a wall (*kuḍya*); that which defends the inside is called a partition (*bhitti*). An Guo states:

"The substantial cause (*mūla-vastu*) as a remote condition is termed a 'wall,' while the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) as an immediate condition is termed a 'partition. Daoluo states: "Transformation based upon the substance is termed a 'wall'; transformation apart from the substance is termed a 'partition.'"
It is empty and not substantial; arising and ceasing from moment to moment, it is therefore said to be crumbling and collapsing.
*The Essential Compendium of the Profound Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra*, Fascicle Twenty-four;
*The Essential Compendium of the Profound Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra*, Fascicle Twenty-five.

Regarding the phrase "The śramaṇa of Jingshui Temple says that [the term] 'corresponding to what is appropriate' and so forth": the aggregates of form and formlessness exist throughout the two lower realms. As for the dharmas of the *manojalpa-bhūmi* (the stage of mental discourse), where they exist, they serve as metaphors;
where they do not exist, they do not serve as metaphors.
Regarding the phrase "by these three meanings and so forth": it is by virtue of these three meanings that emptiness is revealed;
namely, suffering, emptiness, impermanence, non-self, and impurity.
Regarding the expression "stripping the robe" (*tī*): the ancients said that "stripping the robe" means to shake it out; it refers to tossing it about. Now we follow the character *duó* (to strip).
The *Yīzhōu* says: "He bestowed upon him the *pán-dài*; throughout the morning, he was stripped of it three times. *Xī* (bestowed) is synonymous with *cì* (granted).

*Pán-dài* refers to the waist-belt. Within a single day, one is disrobed three times. As for the purple robe and golden belt, they were likewise removed three times. This further discusses what is obtained.
Regarding these garments, even in terms of their acquisition, they are not considered precious. *Tī* (褫) carries the meaning of stripping or peeling away color.

To say that one should now use *tā* (陁) is consistent with the *Shuowen Jiezi*. Based on its function, it is written as *tuó* (陊). *[(毤-八+ㄙ)-毛+ㄆ]* (with the phonetic *túhuó*) means to seize or take by force.
To speak of "wood grain" (*mùlǐ*) refers to the grain of the wood being smooth and regular.
Regarding the terms "covering with thatch" (*pāṭikā*) and so forth: when one is young, the skin possesses a radiant luster, which is called "covering with thatch.
After one has grown old, the skin falls away piece by piece, resembling parched barley; this is called "falling in disarray" (*vikīrṇa*).

Regarding the term "white canopy" (*báigài*) and so forth: it is homophonous with *hélì* (the second character being pronounced as the opposite of *fǎn*). Guo’s commentary states it refers to white *máo* grass.

This refers to thatching made by weaving bundles of white *máo* grass to cover a house, serving as a temporary shelter (*shānlú*). As the *Lǐjì* says: "He dwells in a thatched hut," referring to the grass hut where one who observes the mourning rites for a parent resides.
Regarding the terms "gou" (桷) and "duanmu" (端木): "gou" is a synonym for "chuan" (椽), which the *Erya* calls "qiang" (欀); the commentary states it refers to the rafters of a house.
What is now called "gou duanmu" is precisely what is currently known as the "lian-yuan" (連檐). Combined, these form the correct term "lian-mian" (連棉).
Regarding the term "què lǚ" (雀梠) mentioned here: it refers to the place where sparrows nest, roost, and dwell, hence it is called "lǚ," which is synonymous with "lǚ" (旅, traveler/guest).

Within the Dharma-body, the bone joints are like the rafters (chuán), and the sinews are like the eaves (lǚ). If one grows old and the sinews weaken, there is a loss of strength and the bone joints become dislocated.
Regarding the phrase "The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Chapter 19, etc.": Question: What scriptural authority states that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are a house?
Answer: The commentary states "the *Yogācāra*," etc. The text is correctly located in the nineteenth [chapter], not the seventeenth. The intention of this citation is as follows:
These three preceding phrases specifically correlate with the impermanence of the form-body (*rūpakāya*). Fearing that the meaning might lack a basis, this teaching is cited as proof.

Regarding the three phrases beginning with "mud and plaster," since that [previous] passage used the "city of the mind" as a metaphor for the body, this passage now uses the "house" as a comparison for the body;
it is for this reason that it is cited. At the conclusion below, flesh is taken to be the "mud and plaster."
Regarding the phrase "citing the verses of the sutra," this refers to the *Vimokṣa-sūtra*.

Regarding the term "dyong" (墉), it means a wall; it is pronounced with the rhyme of *zhōng* (鍾) and the tone of *yǎo* (饒). It signifies that the city of bones is plastered and adorned with flesh, sinews, and blood.
Looking upward, one sees the flesh, sinews, and blood used to plaster and decorate the bony city, much like the lime and mud plaster applied to the walls of a provincial or prefectural capital.

Regarding the statement that the "city" refers to the eight consciousnesses, the *Xiangyun* (Commentary on Characteristics) says: "A city is that which serves as a basis; it has the sense of warding off and gathering in.

Internally it gathers all things, and externally it wards off the external. It gathers what is within so that it does not go out, and wards off what is outside so that it does not enter. It gathers the four dharmas of greed and so forth within, causing them not to emerge."
The outer city represents wholesome qualities such as faith and understanding, which prevent [the mind] from entering [unwholesome states]; thus it is likened to a city.
The eighth consciousness is likened to the inner citadel, for it is able to grasp and maintain the five [aggregates], protecting them so they do not perish.

If the first seven consciousnesses are likened to the outer walled city, they can traverse difficult paths and effectively protect the body, ensuring that the eighth consciousness is never severed. Therefore, it is said that "bones fill the moats and stones," serving as a metaphor.
The aforementioned account of piling bricks and stones to build a city is a metaphor for the bones within the human body.
As for the term "cord" (shéngní)—the second character being pronounced with the *qie* rhyme *rèn*—it is because a city has cords that it is held together;
likewise, if one speaks of sinews (*jīn*), they hold the body together.
Regarding the phrase "the physical form and so forth," this refers to the gathering of numerous dharmas. "Hài" (skeleton) is a general term for the physical body (*rūpakāya*).
"Yōng" (wall) is a synonym for a city wall. According to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and other texts, the body is often taken as the city; here, however, it refers to the city of the eight consciousnesses.
The mind-king (*cittarāja*) constitutes the city, and these four types of dharmas are the dharmas sustained by the mind-king.

Regarding the statement that the Three Jewels go forth to transform others: the Buddha going forth to transform others is called the Jewel of the Buddha; the Saṃgha going forth to transform others is called the Jewel of the Saṃgha;
and preaching the Dharma with one's mouth is called the Jewel of the Dharma.
Regarding the "two kinds of mental citadels": the eighth consciousness constitutes the inner citadel, while the preceding seven consciousnesses constitute the outer ramparts;
therefore, they are called the two kinds of mental citadels. Here, "mind" is itself the "citadel," and "entering" means to understand.

Since beginningless time, one has been unable to comprehend the essential nature of these two kinds of mental citadels, remaining in inverted and false views; how then can one seek to attain the Buddha-dharma?
One cultivates the fruit of *vijñapti-mātra* and takes it as one's own. This interpretation accords with the preceding "city," namely the eight consciousnesses;

however, it does not accord with the subsequent explanation of the four dharmas. *Śamathadeva* summarizes these as three interpretations: first, those who live at home give rise to greed and anger, which is called the first;

those who have left home give rise to pride and concealment, which is called the second. These two types are not the city itself, but because they dwell within the city of the mind, they are also called the "city of the mind. Second.
It is said: first, the well-expounded Dharma; second, the Vinaya—these two are called the "city of the mind. Because they serve as a city for the mind, they are termed the "city of the mind.
Third, it is said: the well-expounded Dharma and the Vinaya are the two kinds [of teachings];
the mind that accords with these two is itself the city, and thus it is called the "city of the mind. Zhe (攝) says: the third interpretation is the most intimate, for it is the mind itself.
It is like a city formed with objects as its domain. If one follows the meaning of the various *Madhyamaka* [treatises], it refers to the mind of the person who can preach the Dharma;

this mind is that which takes two objects as its conditions. When the mind that conditions these two objects becomes the object itself, it forms a city for the mind, which is called the "city of the two kinds of minds.
Whether the listener be a monastic or a layperson, to give rise to understanding within this city of the two kinds of minds is called "entering the city of the mind. Question:
In what sense are "well-spoken teachings" (saddharma) considered identical? Answer: Well-spoken teachings refer to the Sūtras;
Abhidharma refers to the Śāstras; and Vinaya refers to the Discipline (Vinaya). If that is so, why are they combined and referred to as the "three cities of the mind," rather than just two?
Answer: The first two are combined; therefore, they are called two. Because the Śāstra-piṭaka is subsumed within the Sūtra-piṭaka of well-spoken teachings, there are only two.

Because there are two distinct categories—those who have left the household life and those who remain at home—the study of the Sūtras and Śāstras provides instruction for laypeople, while the Vinaya Piṭaka is for those who have left the household life.
As for the Sūtra and Abhidharma, they apply to both the laity and the monastics alike; since these are practiced by both groups, they are combined as two and not divided into three.

Regarding the phrase "how much less could they grasp," the intended meaning is this: since they are unable even to enter, understand, or examine the two types of "cities of mind"—those of householders and those of renunciants—how much less could they aspire toward them as their own? As for the wholesome dharmas taught by the Buddha, they cannot even take them up and claim them as their own;
how then could they themselves give rise to the intention to teach the Dharma? It is like a delicious meal that one cannot even... [consume].
It is difficult to find anyone who can do this for others. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 19, states: "Those who preach the Dharma well are the śramaṇas;
those who preach the Dharma poorly are the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*)."
As for "turrets" (lǒulǔ), these are things that can be placed atop [a structure] to repel the enemy;
they are called turrets because they are able to protect that city, just as a person's hands and feet are able to protect the body.
Regarding the term "mù" (目) being defined as "qiào kǒng" (竅孔): the character "kǒng" is pronounced with the initial *yú* (予) and the final rhyme *fǎn* (反).
It means "to pierce" (*chuān*) and refers to looking outward. Regarding the head being called a "hall" (*diàn*): because the head is most honorable, it is like a palace within a city;
the King of the Mind resides within this hall. Since various sutras already liken the bones to a city, what prevents the *Lotus Sūtra* from likening the bones to rafters?

"Rafters" (*gō*)—the phrase "bending enclosures and the like" is a metaphor for non-self (*anātman*). The intended meaning is that if there were a self within the house, it would possess mastery and could act according to its will without obstruction;
however, because there is no such [self], one's actions are constrained by bending and crookedness, and one does not attain sovereignty. There are many [such constraints].
Obstructed and contorted, it is clearly known to be without self.
Regarding the "thirty-six things," the verse says: "The external marks are three and four unwholesome; the body-vessel consists of two and six parts; within it are contained twelve impurities;
and the nine orifices foul the form. As for "three and four": hair, body hair, nails, teeth, fat, tears, mucus, saliva, and filth.
Sweat and excrement. Second, the six [impurities]: skin, blood and flesh, sinews, vessels, marrow, and bone. Fat and grease;

that which is above is called fat (*vapa*), and that which is below is called grease (*medas*). The twelve impurities: spleen, kidneys, heart, lungs, liver, gallbladder, abdomen, stomach, and the red, white, and pale fluids.
This refers to the two stores, the raw and the cooked.
Regarding these three meanings—first, impermanence; second, non-self; and third, impurity—they thus constitute emptiness.
As for the statement that there are twenty-nine verses, the extended prose of the metaphors consists of three lines of sūtra text. The extended prose of the application states: "The fool..."
The two lines, "The fire of the three poisons is shrouded by the darkness of delusion," are from the sutra. The verses consist of twenty-nine stanzas, differing in their expansion and brevity.
Regarding the phrase "concluding the aforementioned difficulties and so forth," the sutra says: "That house is thus terrifying, filled with poisonous harm and the fires of calamity."
The difficulties are not limited to one. This concludes the twenty-nine verses in summary.
Regarding the statement that "the prose account of the arising of calamities follows the fire [section] and so forth": Question: In the prose section, the fire arises and burns the house;
in the verse, insects and ghosts are added. What is the intention behind this? Answer: It is said that the prose section and so forth... [is intended to show... that they are afflicted.
Regarding the statement "the three poisons and so forth as they are spoken," these refer to greed, hatred, and delusion.

They are also called the "three stumps" (*trivṛkṣa*), the "three burnings" (*tridāha*), and the "three unwholesome roots" (*trīṇy akuśalamūlāni*). Seeking after various defiled objects is termed "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*); burning away the roots of virtue is termed "fire" (*agni*).
It harms the virtuous body; thus it is called a "snake. It entangles one far from the forest of merit; thus it is called a "creeper. The mind constantly seeks sensory objects;

thus it is called "turbidity. It obstructs birth beyond saṃsāra; thus it is called a "net. It perspires all meritorious qualities; thus it is called "poison. It moistens rebirth without end; thus it is called "water. It drags sentient beings into death and drowning.

It is called a river because it flows vertically through the three realms; it is called "lengthwise" because it extends vertically. It is called "broad" because it encompasses horizontally the four modes of birth. It is called a "needle" because it pierces through bodies of benefit and harm;
it is called a "thread" because it continuously binds together birth and death.

Regarding the statement that "the final one and a half verses collectively conclude these two," this refers to the two categories: the five dull afflictions (*pañca-mṛdu-kleśa*) and the five sharp afflictions (*pañca-tīkṣṇa-kleśa*).
As the Sūtra says: "Yakṣas, hungry ghosts, and various evil birds and beasts, driven by the urgency of hunger, look toward the four directions through windows and lattices."
Regarding the statement that it is concluded by a half-verse: the Sūtra says, "The house was so terrifying and its appearance thus transformed. This concludes the preceding six verses.

Regarding the statement that there is no corresponding allocation within this [text]: there is no such passage stated in the scriptural teachings; rather, it is the meaning that corresponds to the mode of practice (*ākāra*).

The pairings are as follows: the eight birds represent greed (*rāga*), and the ten insects represent hatred (*dveṣa*); this is because their modes of activity correspond. As for the phrase "following the ancients and thus remaining silent," it means following the chapters of the ancient masters and remaining silent.

Regarding the statement that "the root treatise does not explain [them]," this refers to the *Dharmapada-śāstra*, which does not provide an explanation at all; it does not necessarily mean that [the correspondence] is incorrect.

As for the phrase "because the meaning accords with [the tradition]," it certainly does not mean that [the correspondence] is entirely absent. How could the intention of the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) be that there is no aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) to be paired?
The abode is the dwelling; the remaining four aggregates are the rooms and halls. Birth, aging, sickness, and death form the four walls.
The seeds of the five destinies are likened to five hundred people. The untainted seeds of the three vehicles are compared to thirty children.
As for the remaining afflictions, there is no further place to assign them; they can only be considered as insects and ghosts.
Regarding the statement that there are four types of craving (*tṛṣṇā*): first is craving for the present existence (*bhavābhinandanatṛṣṇā*). To summarize:

this refers to craving for the body of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) in the present life—its various adornments, its clothing, and its concealment in fine dwellings so that others may see it. Second is craving for future existence (*punarbhavatṛṣṇā*).

One hopes to obtain such a body again in future lives. This present body is dignified and six feet tall, and the voice resembles a bell. Or, one may possess a celestial body that is radiant, pure, and sovereign.
Regarding these future bodies, one gives rise to craving. Third, craving that proceeds together with greed and joy:

this refers to obtaining the objects of the five sensory realms in the present, becoming greedily attached to them and cherishing them, giving rise to both greed and joy; therefore, it is called "proceeding together. Fourth, craving for various delights.
"Craving" refers to the arising of greedy attachment toward the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) when they have not yet been obtained; once obtained, one craves them even further.

Because what is not yet obtained is manifold, it is termed "this and that" (*tatra-tatra*). Of the four types [of craving], the first two arise conditioned by the body, while the latter two arise conditioned by objects.
Regarding the statement, "All [these] are based on the separate practices (*pṛthag-caryā*) and so forth": if one were to discuss the objects of craving, such objects exist everywhere.

However, here we rely on the characteristics of the separate practices and temporarily correlate them with the four types of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), because they are currently observable. Question: What is meant by "currently observable"? Answer:

The *Shulü* (疏路) states that this refers to the characteristic of craving manifest upon the bodies of the eight birds. This is not so; rather, it simply means that [craving] is already present and has been acquired within the context of the four types of craving.
The "unobtained object" refers precisely to the object currently visible.

Regarding the mention of "vultures, owls, and so forth," their assignment within the Commentary does not follow the sequence of the sutra text. Among the four types of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), there is a division into superior and inferior grades.
The four superior grades of craving—wherein craving is synonymous with greed—are assigned to the four great birds; the four inferior grades of craving...

This corresponds to the four small birds. Furthermore, regarding the four types of craving in the superior grade: the first is the vulture (*jīva*). The *Shuowen* says: "The vulture bird is black in color and has many offspring.
Shi Kuang said: "In the south there is a bird named the vulture; it has a yellow head and a red throat, possessing all five colors.

This bird is numerous in the Western Regions. Its plumage is naturally reddish; it craves only the dead, and constantly dwells among the mountains, hiding itself to protect its body as it scavenges for food."

Sustaining one's own body is like craving for the present; because it is the very essence of craving itself. Second is the *ulūka* (owl), which hoots after nightfall; appearing strange, it foretells misfortune.
It anticipates that people will throw objects for it to eat, just as craving for the future [foretells] the bitter fruits of future suffering, which is precisely what is called misfortune.
This is named "craving for the future" (*aparānta-tṛṣṇā*). Third is the *cilla* (kite), which gives rise to craving for objects obtained in the present; seizing them, it is most greedy.
*Piyā* (love). *Nandī* (delight). Making sounds in the trees, like craving that accompanies delight; one gives rise to craving toward objects already present and obtained.
Having craved, delight arises. The four vultures: they give rise to craving toward insects and rabbits not yet obtained.

Because their strength is great and their nature is prone to injury and killing, they give rise to craving toward various objects with the intent to kill; this is called "craving for this and that" (*tatra-tatrābhinandinī*). Upon obtaining one object...

Successively, one looks for more. Just as with those various forms of joy and craving, because one gives rise to hope regarding desirable objects not yet obtained (the preceding interpretation follows the commentary but deviates from the sequence of the sūtra).
According to the sequence of the sūtra, the four types of craving are assigned as follows: First, the *kāka* (crow): it provides only for the body of that very day and does not look further ahead;
this is like *pratyutpanna-tṛṣṇā* (craving for the present), because it craves its own self. Second, the *ulūka* (owl): it does not come out during the day; it thinks...
Seeking food at night, they are like those possessed by craving for future existence (*bhava-tṛṣṇā*), who crave that future body and things not yet obtained.
The three vultures, because of their strength, seize whatever objects are currently present and, having obtained them, do not let go; they are thus able to devour them, giving rise to greed and joy.

Because they do not let go of what has already been obtained, they act in conjunction with greed and joy. The four eagles know when a person has died and constantly contemplate the death of people in the future.
One partakes of them. Just as there are various forms of delight and craving for objects not yet obtained—since such objects are manifold—they are called "craving for various delights."

Regarding the mention of "crows, magpies, and so forth," these correspond to the four types of craving of the lower grade. First, the crow: it gives rise to craving for its present body, stealing other people's children and grandchildren to feed its own.
If it goes to another person's house, it picks up food to eat; it is easily startled and difficult to strike. As soon as one intends to hit it, it has already flown away early in the morning.
This is like having craving for what is presently manifest, cherishing and protecting the present body. Because there is such craving for what is presently manifest, [it is the first]. Second...
The magpie: Magpies are generally full of flattery and deception. They chirp auspicious sounds toward people's homes, calculating that the people will later throw things out for them to eat;
this is called "having affection for what comes later. The three types of doves: Doves are by nature soft and lacking in hardness or strength.
Upon finding a single grain of rice or wheat, they sigh with gratitude and coo with joy; they give rise to greedy attachment only toward the objects already obtained—this is called "greedy joy."

Co-arising craving. There are four types of *kulinga* birds. By nature, *kulinga* birds are highly lustful; their lustful minds are never satisfied, and thus they give rise to craving for objects not yet obtained.

Because this craving arises in various ways, it is called "craving for the joy of this and that" (*tatra-tatrābhinandinī tṛṣṇā*). Question: Regarding the division of greed into superior and inferior grades, two categories are acceptable.
But for what reason are the eight birds also divided into superior and inferior? Answer: As for the first four birds, the *ulūka* (owl) is able to eat its mother. This is evident.
The power of *māyā* (deceit) is particularly strong; because the other three powers involve the application of effort (*prayoga*), they are divided into superior grades.
These eight birds are classified as superior or inferior grades solely based on the magnitude of their power and application, not based on whether their nature is sharp or dull.

Regarding the phrase "or dull-witted," etc., this is the second section, which correlates [the parables] with the sūtras. One who is dull-natured and greedy is likened to an old owl that is dull-natured;
having much down but little flesh, it cannot catch a rabbit. It pursues the deer only toward dung-heaps, picking up dead old things from the top of mounds.

It is held in the hand of the youngest child; it slips from the belly of the sheep-master. It chases after places where there is no food, and as sentient beings hunger for food, it comes toward the street.
Seeking objects: when satiated, one wanders aimlessly through empty space. This is like a porter carrying a load for others in the world, or like picking up and tossing aside a plum pit;
it is called "dull-natured greed. Second is "manifesting strange greed," which is likened to an owl. An owl makes its sound after nightfall, which people consider inauspicious;
this serves as a metaphor for the underlying causes of craving. After nightfall, it approaches the gates of people's houses and expounds upon principles, manifesting strangeness.
Seeking money for use is also as the sorceress says: there are ghosts and monsters within her house, and she seeks money and goods from them.
The three types of those with great greed are likened to the eagle; the eagle possesses great strength, being able to seize the elk, carry off the deer, and kill the foxes and hares.
As Zheng’s commentary states: even if one has thousands or tens of thousands of coins, it is like an official who uses heavy shackles and large clubs to beat people in order to take [their wealth].
Money. Regarding the fourth type, greed for physical movement: this is likened to a vulture. A vulture seeking food must first circle and wheel in the air three or five times to exercise its body.
Only after night has passed and it hides in the mountains does it head toward the royal city at daybreak to search for food and eat various birds;
only when there are none left does it dare to seek more food. The merchant’s business is likewise like that of a vulgar lecturer-monk who merely spreads his nets thinly.

Seeking [teachings] and so forth from external places; fifth, the greed of unrighteous seeking is like a crow. When a crow seeks food, it often acts unrighteously, seizing other sparrows to sustain its own life.
It is like officials and others who strike people with coarse shackles and heavy clubs, or who steal and plunder money.
Sixth, the greed of vocal expression is like a magpie. First uttering a sound with intent, it charms the young wife of a commoner’s household.

The female magpie is fond of "good mornings" and "good rests. She throws things down for him to eat. This is like people in the world who practice flattery to seek fame and profit, or like travelers on a journey who, when undertaking great affairs, speak with words that are remarkably marvelous, claiming everything will be peaceful, secure, and excellent.
It is also like those who act as intermediaries or brokers, using clever speech and a pleasing countenance to seek money and goods. These are the seven types of base and greedy persons.
It is like the pigeon. When seeking food, the pigeon cannot take large or substantial objects; it only picks up stray grains and rice, obtaining three or five at a time.
Because it calls out "A-ku" (mother-in-law) while pecking for sustenance, it is like those in the world who dig from pits or remove filth;
though their affairs are base and inferior, they likewise give rise to greed. Eighth, those with much lustful greed are like pigeons; by nature, pigeons are full of lust.
As for lust: it is like the people of Chongren and Pingkang; it is like the reputation of a daughter;

it is also like the undisciplined sons of a household who let go of one and seize two, hooking three and grabbing four, refusing to withdraw their hands regardless of whether the object is desirable or loathsome.

Regarding the statement "relying on the *Śāsanāntima-sūtra*": the question asks whether the reference to the black short snake in the *Śāsanāntima-sūtra* serves as a proof for the preceding [section] on the black snake, or serves as a proof for the black short snake itself.
The answer to the black short snake in the latter part of the text provides two interpretations, neither of which is definitive.
Therefore, this opens up two perspectives to provide dual proof.

Regarding the "mysterious snake" (*xuánshé*) mentioned in the *Hànshū*, this follows the intention of the late Dharma Master Xuányìng, who takes it to mean a black viper (*hēiwán*) and does not take the character *wán* (viper) itself.
The reason for citing the *Hanshu* extensively to explain "xuán" (玄) is that it does not refer to a venomous snake. Regarding the two interpretations of the *Hanshu*:
Wei Zhao explains that "xuán" means black, and "wán" (蚖) refers to a centipede. Cui Bao explains that "xuán" refers to a "snake-physician" (*shéyī*).

It is said that when a person is injured by a snake, this snake spits water; if it touches the wound, the injury is immediately healed. Therefore, it is called a "snake-physician. The large ones are long.
Three feet in length; its color is dark purple (*kṛṣṇa-nīla*). "Dark" (*kṛṣṇa*) refers to black; "purple" (*nīla*) likewise refers to black.

It is skilled at possessing humans and can manifest transformations or cause confusion among people, such as when wild foxes and the like possess humans. Regarding the section on the magpie and leopard, there are six parts:
first, the explanation of the snake-doctor, which is large and three feet long, etc.; second, the enumeration of four names, beginning with *yaohuan* (the lizard); third... [text ends].

[The character] "jie" (knot/bind). The *Yupian* states: "Below 'she' (snake) and 'yi' (heal), four. This is a distinct name for the fourth [section]. "In the house, it is the guardian against harm," below;

fifth. Master Huìyìng re-establishes the previous meaning. According to this, the *Yìjiào* [Sūtra], below six. The commentary (*shù*) says: "The commentary on the explanation states: Now, the explanation of the *luán* (viper) has two [types], below."
According to the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* (Yijing jing) and other texts, Master Xuanying interpreted the meaning and selected the character "wuan" (蝮).

Thus, this master’s intention was that Wei Zhao, Que, and Bao interpreted the "black wuan" (*heiwuan*) as a venomous snake; since it can heal the effects of a snakebite, it is further called a "mei" (魅, a malevolent spirit).

Furthermore, it is said to possess people rather than being described as something that injures or kills, nor is it classified as a poisonous insect. In the *Hanshu*, the black wuan is not considered a poisonous insect. This is according to the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*.
In this context, the venomous insect should have been taken as the metaphor; it ought to have been the black *vṛścika* (scorpion), yet it was erroneously written as "snake" (*sarpa*).
Regarding the statement, "Now, in explaining the *vṛścika*, there are two types," the Master of the Commentary’s explanation therein contains profound significance.
This refers to two kinds of black *vṛścikas*: the first is non-venomous and has many names, while the second is venomous and is known solely by the name "different" (*anya*).
The snake has no other specific name; however, the Master of the Commentary selects here only those that are venomous, excluding the one that is non-venomous.
Whether selected or not, they are all collectively termed "black vipers" (*kṛṣṇasarpa*). When it comes to citing the text, one cannot cite both black vipers together.
The reason for excluding [the non-venomous one] is to distinguish it by its specific name, which is the *kṛkalāsa* (lizard). Second...
First, in the *Hanshu*, it states that the black *wuan* (viper) is non-venomous; next, it mentions the "black short snake," which is precisely what should be captured.
There is indeed a venomous snake named the black *wuan*, which is not of the same category as those interpreted by Wei Zhao and others.

According to the master’s intent in the commentary, the "black short snake" is identical to that mentioned in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* (Yijiao jing). Master Xuanying, upon seeing the term *wuan* in the *Hanshu*, [concluded...]

It is not poisonous; thus, he provides an interpretation based on the character *wán* (snake). This differs from the intended meaning of the *Shū* (Commentary). The intent of the *Shū* is merely that it is named the "black *wán*," not that it refers to the phonetic sound *wán*.

As for the mention of the *Yìjiào jīng* (Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching) and other texts, the author of the *Shū* concludes his own argument: a short black snake is a poisonous snake; therefore, [it is not].
This must be an error. That sutra says: "The poisonous snake of affliction sleeps within your heart, just as a black viper sleeps in your room.
You should use the hook of moral discipline to expel it early; once the sleeping snake has been driven out, you may sleep in peace."
Regarding the statement "only called the black viper (*kṛṣṇa-āśīviṣa*) and so forth," this refers exclusively to that [specific] name.
As for "these are water-insects and so forth," this refers only to the yellow snake, the *śara* snake, the *kāka* snake, ordinary snakes, and the like. Question:

Among the various types of snakes, how does this snake differ from the black snake mentioned previously and the *vṛścika* (scorpion/viper) mentioned later? Answer: The *āśīviṣa* snake is the black one with a bald tail; the *vṛścika* is—
"Repaying enmity": "ordinary snakes" refers to all other types of snakes.
Regarding the phrase "the three *vṛścika* and so forth," *vṛścika* (pronounced *fǎng fú* in the rhyme) refers to the scorpion.
Regarding the phrase "the *Erya* and so forth": "broad" (*bo*) means expansive or wide. "Head" (*shou*) means the top or beginning. "Splitting" (*bi*) is like a person spreading their fingers;
the *Guangya* states that "splitting" refers to separating the hands.
Regarding the mention of "needles," these are poisonous thorns.
Regarding the mention of "brocade ribbons," Mou says that today's sash-bands are the common designation for those with five-colored interlaced patterns.
Regarding the term "having bristles" (*liè*; the character *liè* is pronounced with the *liáng* and *shè* finals; it refers to hair): "If it stings the hand, one must immediately cut off the hand.
This means that when the venomous insect crawls upon the hand, the poison enters the heart in an instant and death ensues.
If one has been bitten, by cutting off the hand immediately, one may survive. The same applies to the foot.
Regarding the "four lizards": people of that time called the *tālajaṅgha* a "mother-finger" (*mūṣika*). Its great venom resides in its head;
the scorpion's venom resides in its tail. Regarding the "centipede": *jihvā* is another name for the centipede. When this insect eats a snake, it goes straight into a person's belly.
They devour hearts and livers, or eat brains and marrow. Regarding the *jīqū* (pronounced *zǐyú*), the *Erya* states: "The *jīqū* resembles a locust;
it has a large abdomen and long horns, and it feeds on the brains and marrow of snakes."

Regarding the "six kinds of centipedes": Question: What is the difference between a millipede (*śatapadī*) and a centipede (*gṛhagolika*)? Answer: One with a green body and yellow legs is a centipede;
one with a reddish body and red legs is a millipede. Those with red legs are suitable for use as medicine; those that are yellow are not.

Regarding the "seven kinds of geckos" (shǒugōng): as stated in the *Shū* (Sūtra/Commentary), when the Yellow Emperor was about to dispatch geckos [as messengers], he asked, "Since 'black viper' (*hēilán*) is already a general term, why is it not mentioned here?
Why instead take 'mantis lizard' (*yíngluán*) as the general term? The answer is: because the referents differ.
"Mantis lizard" is the general term for three types, while "black viper" is the general term for four types; thus, there is no contradiction.
Regarding the term "centipede" (*śatapada*): at that time, people saw that others had many feet and called them "centipedes"; it also refers to the fact that they actually possess one hundred legs.
Regarding the term "nine *yòu*": *yòu* (pronounced *diāo*), *shèng*, and *shí* refer to the *lìshǔ* (the field mouse). It has burrows in the fields; when it sees a person...
Yan Shou’s *Shu* says: "The stone rat possesses consciousness; man lacks consciousness—this is what is called 'death' (*ming-si*). (The *Xiangshu* says: 'The rat has propriety; man lacks propriety. "
"Hao" refers to the name of a commandery located in Jianping Commandery.
As for "Guo Pu and others," it refers to Guo Pu, who annotated the *Shanhai jing* (Classic of Mountains and Seas), and thus he is cited here.
Regarding the statement that one "should act like a wildcat" (*mārjāra*), the intended meaning is that there is no great partiality (*pakṣapāta*) [in one's practice].
Regarding the mention of the *Chunqiu* (Spring and Autumn Annals) and other texts: the *Chunqiu* records the affairs of the state of Lu.

Whenever the time for the suburban sacrifice to Heaven arrived, according to the rites, they would first nourish and feed oxen, sheep, and so forth, which were termed "sacrificial victims" (*sheng*). When performing a special sacrifice to Heaven, they used silks and brocades [to adorn them] and fed them with non-glutinous rice.
And so forth. If there is even the slightest damage, it is immediately unfit for use.

However, among those used for the sacrifice to Heaven, if the horns are as large as silkworm cocoons or grains of millet, and similar to these standards, those that are unfit are taken from the very best [bulls], which are called *jiaoniu* (sacrificial oxen).
Weasels are fond of eating their horns.
Regarding the statement that "one who reaches the limit does not know," it is like a bee devouring a green insect.
Regarding the specific characteristics of hatred (*dveṣa*), this explains hatred by taking up the reasons for its eleven [aspects], just as there are eight types of food.
These are correlated with the four types of craving and possess superior and inferior grades.
Regarding the first, when one perceives that harm touches or afflicts one's own person, anger arises immediately; or, even if one knows oneself to be at fault, anger arises immediately.
Second, regarding those who are beloved—namely one's wife, children, and so forth—some say that it is only when they are deceived, insulted, or humiliated that anger arises.
Anger (*dveṣa*). Or, it may be toward those who are objects of anger. Regarding the three types of unloved beings: first, one harbors resentment toward a person;
upon hearing them praised, one immediately gives rise to anger. Fourth, regarding the past: this refers to having a great enmity with someone from former times.

Once they have already passed away, one hears reports of their good or evil deeds and immediately gives rise to anger; or, after the parents have passed away, one hears others speak ill of them and immediately gives rise to anger.
The same applies by analogy to those yet to come and those currently living.
Regarding the "seven unpleasant things": that which is beloved among the five objects of desire is "pleasant," from which joy arises;
that which is unpleasant gives rise to anger, or it may arise conditioned by non-sentient objects, such as reviling the wind or scolding the rain.

Eighth, "jealousy" (*īrṣyā*): to harm the virtuous is called "envy" (*dveṣa*), and to harm their beauty is called "jealousy. Toward both the virtuous and their beauty, this is termed "anger. Ninth, "past habituation" refers to [that which has been practiced] extensively over many...
Having formed a bond of enmity, one does not let it go. Now, although meeting someone whom one does not recognize, one immediately gives rise to anger.
Regarding "the views of others": the views and understandings of others are actually superior in principle, while one's own views and understandings lack any principle whatsoever.
Seeing that one's own views are inferior to those of others, one immediately gives rise to anger—such as when disputing over principles, chanting, or bargaining.

Regarding the phrase "following the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) and so forth": Question: What are the "various evil insects" that cross paths with one another? Answer: The commentary states they are the "secondary afflictions and so forth," namely the five:
anger (*krodha*), resentment (*upanāha*), vexation (*pradāsa*), envy (*īrṣyā*), and harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*).

Regarding what is called "fierce and sharp": it is like cutting through a camp or breaking through an encirclement. A venomous snake may refrain from its wrath, but if it does become enraged, even the *bhaiṣajyarāja* tree cannot save one.
It is like a person who is difficult to offend; only when offended does their anger arise. Thus, the Regional Commander (Jiedushi) slaughtered all three armies.

Regarding what is called "being provoked": the nature of a snake is to remain neutral; it will only inflict poison if the practitioner touches or provokes it. It is like a person of a quick-tempered nature who cannot endure being offended;
he will cause harm immediately upon being provoked, but if he is not provoked, he leaves things as they are.

Regarding "retribution": it is like a venomous viper. If it is harmed this year, it does not seek retribution immediately; however, later on, it will inevitably seek vengeance regardless of distance or proximity.
This is like harboring a grudge that is never abandoned, leading to rebirth in the hells and other such realms.
Regarding the manifestation of signs: the movement of a scorpion’s tail and its venomous sting manifest the sign of anger.
Regarding "harmful poison": it is like when officials beat and kill thieves, or as when snakes that have already been poisoned are further harmed by centipedes.

Regarding what is called "inability to sever": first, one does not deviate from the vow of not lying even unto death, yet constantly harbors resentment, saying things such as, "In the future, I shall strike you with an iron-handled axe.
When each and every part of the centipede's body is severed, each segment moves; this is called "severing anger."

Regarding "jealousy" (īrṣyā): it refers to cases such as [the Emperor] envying Yuan Zai’s wife for cutting off the hand of a maidservant; that he kept the blood of this harmful act smeared upon his arm so that it would not wash away was precisely to envy others and to harbor resentment toward them.
Regarding what is called "frustration and vexation": it is like the dull fisherman who was distressed by his wife and thus compared himself to the nature of a centipede.
When the centipede walks, if it is lightly touched, it immediately becomes a single mass and grows angry with itself.

Regarding "intense anger" (*pradāśa*): it is like a new bride who, when scolded by her parents-in-law, feigns joy; yet later, in the inner chamber, she harbors resentment toward her husband and so forth.
Or like a weasel that, while hunting, hides near a burrow and uses its own tail to feign a joyful expression as it stalks its prey;
though the heart of anger remains within, this is called "intense anger."
Regarding "openly committing harm and slaughter": this refers to those who openly engage in such acts, like hunters or those who act with public violence during times of war and strife.
Regarding "secret plotting":
this refers to those who harbor dark schemes; their hearts are most venomous—they harbor anger within while smiling on their faces, and they harbor hatred in their minds.

Though its appearance was respectful, the *xi* mouse harbored poison within its heart; it devoured various birds and beasts until they were exhausted, yet remained unaware and unconscious of its own nature. It is also called "Sweet Mouth.
When it ate the horns of the sacrificial ox at the suburban altar, the ox felt no pain; this is termed "concealed calculation" (*qiàn jì*) anger.

Regarding the phrase "intermingled, etc.," this interpretation differs from the previous one concerning arising in encounter with conditions (*pratyaya*). In the former, they were assigned to the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*); here, they are merely fetters (*saṃyojana*).

Regarding the statement "arising as seven, nine, etc.," it means that within each of the three time periods (*adhvan*), there are two distinctions—upper and lower—which constitute both the specific and the general.

Furthermore, taken as a single aggregate, when the specific and the combined are discussed together, there are seven. If each of the three time periods has three—namely, superior, middling, and inferior—and these are combined, there are nine.
The mention of "seven and nine" here refers to two layers of paired explanations, each based on a distinct meaning.
However, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle nine, which states that there are nineteen types of delusion (*moha*) in total, the mention of "seven and nine" is an error.
Thus, these nineteen are condensed into seven categories: first, delusion regarding the world; second, delusion regarding phenomena; third, delusion regarding saṃsāra;

fourth, delusion regarding the supreme; fifth, delusion regarding reality; sixth, delusion regarding defilement and purification; seventh, delusion regarding overweening pride. As for the "nine kinds," [they are as follows:]...
According to the *Vyākhyā* (Commentary), nineteen types are selected. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle nine, states: 1. Ignorance regarding the past (*pūrvānta-ajñāna*):

namely, "Did I exist in the past? Or did I not exist? 2. Ignorance regarding the present (*pratyutpannānta-ajñāna*): namely, "Do I exist [now]? Or do I not exist? 3. Ignorance regarding the future (*aparānta*) is likewise.
4. Ignorance regarding the internal (*adhyātma-ajñāna*): namely, giving rise to incorrect views regarding one's own individual formations (*saṃskāra*).

1. Ignorance regarding principle (*yoniśo-manasikāra*): namely, conceiving of it as a self. 2. Ignorance regarding the external: namely, conceiving of the various formations (*saṃskāra*) as being "mine.

3. Ignorance regarding both the internal and external: namely, giving rise to improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) toward the formations within the continuum, thereby discriminating between enemies and kin;
this constitutes ignorance regarding all that is internal and external. 4. Ignorance regarding karma: namely, [ignorance] regarding the various karmas.
9. Ignorance regarding maturation (*vipāka*) for those who possess attention (*manasikāra*), and so forth; 10. Ignorance regarding karma and its maturation—namely, the aforementioned two; 11.
Ignorance regarding the Buddha, whether not reflecting upon him or reflecting upon him; 12. [Ignorance regarding] the Dharma; 13. [Ignorance regarding] the Saṃgha; 14.

Ignorance regarding suffering (*duḥkha*); 15. [Ignorance regarding] origin (*samudaya*); 16. [Ignorance regarding] cessation (*nirodha*); 17. [Ignorance regarding] the path (*mārga*). Regarding these Three Jewels and Four Truths, there is...

17. One knows [the cause], or does not reflect upon it; or although one reflects, due to ignorance, or due to negligence, or due to disparagement, one regards the cause as non-existent, or as being Īśvara, or as being the Puruṣa, or as an unequal cause. 18.

One is ignorant of the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) produced by the cause (the characteristics of these *saṃskāras* are as stated above). 19. One is ignorant regarding the spheres of contact (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*).
Reaching the state of non-cognition refers to those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*), who engage in inverted reflection regarding what has been realized.

There are three types of ignorance concerning the world (*loka-moha*): namely, ignorance of the prior limit, the middle limit, and the subsequent limit; that is, ignorance of the three periods of time, which is termed ignorance of the world.

There are three types of ignorance concerning the two matters (*vastu-moha*): first, ignorance regarding the internal; second, ignorance regarding the external; and third, ignorance regarding both the internal and external.

1. Delusion regarding names and things (*nāma-vastu-moha*). 2. Delusion regarding transmigration (*saṃkrānti-moha*). This delusion is twofold: first, ignorance regarding maturation (*vipāka-ajñāna-moha*); second, ignorance regarding karma and its maturation (*karma-vipāka-ajñāna-moha*).

These two are termed the delusion of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra-moha*). 3. Delusion regarding the supreme (*agrya-moha*) is threefold; that is, delusion regarding the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha. 4. Delusion regarding reality (*tattva-moha*) is fivefold;

that is, delusion regarding the Four Noble Truths, which constitutes four types. 5. Delusion regarding defilement and purification (*saṃkleśa-vyavadāna-moha*) is threefold. First, delusion regarding... [text ends]

The cause, the two fruits of delusion, and the three that encompass both cause and fruit of delusion—namely, the seventh, the delusion of overweening pride—are each one [of the six], which is precisely the six contacts (*ṣaṭ-sparśa*).

Among these, the first three divisions include them in their entirety; the next five include them as partials; and the textual passages on suffering, its origin, and the direct sequence, as well as the metaphors of excrement and insects, are all consistent with this.
The remainder do not contradict it.
