Once a karma has been exhausted, there is no other intervening karma to obstruct it, even if one is reborn in any of the five destinies (*pañcagati*) with various different conditions; since all such experiences are equally induced by the subversion of the sūtras, they are collectively termed "ripening in the next life.
The specific mention of emerging from hell is intended to demonstrate that realizing the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) can lead to many lifetimes. Otherwise, [it would not be so].
Does this statement mean that [the being] emerges from hell? Changjing said: "Now, the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) can lead many births.

This slanders the Mahāyāna sūtras and differs from the Dharma of the Hīnayāna; it is not like the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, which holds that a single karma leads to a single birth. Nevertheless, when viewed in terms of what is led,"
It should be understood as including both subsequent and later retributions; however, in this sutra, they are designated by their initial reception and are all termed "retribution upon birth.
This is precisely the Mahāyāna principle that a single karma may span many lifetimes, wherein a single karma is capable of bringing [the result] to full completion.

The character *xiù* (醜救反) is read as *qùhū* (秞去呼). It is also read as *xǔjiù* (許救反), with the same pronunciation as *xiù* (嗅). It is also read as *xǔyù* (許郁反). It means to raise livestock (*chù yǎng*) or to store (*zhù chù*).
It is read as *chǒu liù* (丑六反). It means to accumulate (*chù jī*).
Regarding the phrase "now, from the first two": *chǒu* (救) and *xù* (許) are homophones meaning "to save" or "to permit.
Regarding the term "Mahāyāna": it refers to the karma of slandering the sūtras, which is capable of inducing this fundamental ripening (*vipāka*) and its concordant flow (*niṣyanda*).
Therefore, it is said here that it is named after its origin.
Regarding the phrase "those mentioned herein": it refers to those who emerge from hell and are reborn as dogs, jackals, or camels; this conveys the sense of being pierced downward.
The character for "to lead" (領) is pronounced with the initial *k* and the final *-u* (as in *kǔ*), and its pronunciation is identical to that of the character for "cave" (窟).
Regarding the *Sāncāng*: it explains that having a sore on the head or not having a sore—being bald with the head lowered and hairless—is called "mí" (禿).
Regarding the *Qièyùn*, it says "báitù" (白禿); this refers to having a white, balding sore on the entire head, which is collectively termed "mí.
If that is the case, then being red-bald, hairless, and having sores would also be termed "mí."
Regarding the statement "or making it into a topknot" (*ji*, pronounced *xià*): its shape is like a thin topknot (the pronunciation is indicated by the character *qiǎo*).
It should be written with the character [肆-聿+(序-予+(比/舌))], and pronounced with the sound *ji*.
Regarding the term "unexamined" (未詳), it has not yet been seen [in authoritative sources].
Regarding the character [黑*奔], it should be written as the character [黑*(大/星)].
Regarding the term "yòu" (又), its pronunciation is the same as "tàn" (毯). Regarding the term "yú" (於), its pronunciation is the same as "jiàn" (檻).

Regarding the term "zuò niǎo" (作嬲), the character "niǎo" (嬲) has the phonetic reading "nú qiǎo" (奴巧); it means to disturb or agitate, and is written as "lào" (嫪), with the same phonetic reading as "náo" (撓).
Regarding the statement that there are ten fruits of being a jackal: the karma is unified as one, yet because of slandering the sutra, it brings about ten kinds of ugly retributions.

The sutra says: "Even for those who treat a scroll of the sutra with reverence, viewing it as the Buddha, if they slander the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* by giving rise to a mind of arrogance, they are therefore born as dogs.
If, however, one maintains a pure heart of faith and respect toward the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and does not give rise to doubt, one will not fall into hell.
As for the hungry ghosts and animals, because they gave rise to a malicious mind to slander the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, they were reborn with the bodies of jackals.

As for the statement "one bald patch": the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the head and chief of all sūtras; because of their slander, their heads are shaven and hairless, and thus their crowns are not adorned.
Regarding the mention of the "two emaciated": those who read and uphold this sūtra’s perfect teaching will attain a face of perfect fullness.
Conversely, by slandering this perfect teaching, one attains an emaciated and withered appearance, with the marks and signs of excellence being incomplete.
If a person who upholds this sūtra attains Buddhahood in the future, their wondrous form-body will be perfectly full in its seven locations.

Regarding the statement that "the three colors are dark-brown": because this sutra is the source of all vehicles, it is likened to the white ox and the white flower, which are the basis of all colors.
One who upholds this sutra will attain a complexion as fresh and white as these; however, by slandering the sutra, one obstructs the light of wisdom in others and thus becomes dark-brown in color.
Regarding the mention of "four types of leprosy": this sutra is the essence of all sutras, adorned with myriad virtues.
One who upholds this sutra will experience the attainment of high and long eyebrows, a broad and level forehead, and the full complement of human marks.

Conversely, by slandering this sutra, one will experience the affliction of leprosy covering the body. Or, because of slandering the sutra, it becomes a festering sore for the Buddha-dharma and a blemish for those who uphold the sutra.
Therefore, the body incurs illness.

Regarding the "five contacts": the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is a scripture revered by humans and devas. Those who uphold this sūtra are moved by its power to receive celestial youths as their attendants;
conversely, those who slander the sūtra are moved by its power to receive others who beat, strike, and harass them, and furthermore, [they themselves...]
Because of a single act of foolishness committed by a youth, he invited that youth to beat him.
As for the mention of "six people," this sutra is protected by all Buddhas and brings joy to all Buddhas; such is the person who upholds this sutra.
One will be pleasing to behold by others; yet, due to slandering the sutras and lacking reverence for the Mahāyāna, one will evoke loathing and disdain from others.
"Wù" (惡) is pronounced with the initial *wū* (烏) and the final *gù* (故). It signifies "to increase. The *Lunyu* says: "I hate how purple usurps the place of vermilion."
Regarding the "seven constant causes," this sutra possesses great power. It sustains the Dharma-food of sentient beings;
those who uphold this sutra find their physical bodies fully nourished and thus suffer no constant distress. Those who hear it rejoice, and the Buddha dispatches offerings. The sutra says:

"I shall dispatch the fourfold assembly of transformed beings to make offerings to the Dharma-preacher and to guide sentient beings. This is because [otherwise] one would cause them to be deprived of the Dharma-food due to slandering the Dharma.
Because the flavor of other dharmas does not satisfy them, they consequently suffer from constant hunger and thirst.
Regarding the phrase "bones and flesh": this sutra is a scripture that brings about a robust, powerful, and beautiful physical form.
One who upholds this sutra will obtain a full and perfect countenance; however, by slandering this sutra, one will experience withered bones and parched flesh.
Regarding the "nine births": this sutra is a scripture that brings forth liberation from the two kinds of birth and death.

One who upholds this sutra shall immediately go to the World of Peace and Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*) and be born through transformation within a lotus flower. However, by slandering this sutra, one will undergo bitter suffering upon rebirth.
Regarding the phrase "struck while dying": it refers either to being struck and killed by tiles or stones, or to being struck by tiles or stones upon a corpse;
this is called "being struck by tiles or stones while dying. Because of slandering the sutra, one undergoes suffering both in life and in death.
Regarding the phrase "one who carries a heavy burden": this sutra is a scripture for casting off the heavy burden of birth and death.
Because of slandering this sutra, one takes the form of a camel and constantly carries heavy loads. This sutra is the vehicle upon which all noble ones and sages ride;
because of slandering it, one is reborn among camels, or becomes a camel that serves as a mount for others, its body constantly bearing heavy burdens.

As for the mention of "staffs and whips": because one upholds this sutra, one experiences the result that blades and staves are not used against them; because one slanders this sutra, one experiences the result that staffs and whips are inflicted upon them.

Regarding the "three types of food through mindfulness": because one upholds this sutra, one attains the food of the joy of Dharma and the delight of dhyāna; whereas due to slandering it, one consumes only water and grass.

Regarding the "four types of ignorance": because one lacks knowledge of upholding this sutra, the radiance of wisdom is like the light of the sun; yet by slandering the sutra, [one remains in darkness].
Therefore, they think only of eating and drinking, possessing no other knowledge.

Regarding those called *luòyīn* (駱駝) and so forth—the pronunciation of *luò* being the same as that of *luò*—they travel three hundred *lǐ* per day and carry thousands of loads. By nature, they discern the flow of water veins;
when they brace the earth with their hooves, springs of water immediately gush forth.
Regarding the mention of "a *luò* horse": a white horse with a black mane is called a *luò*.
When the sutra says it came into the village as a *luò*, it was because of hunger and thirst.
Regarding the mention of "one with scabies": the mouth of one who upholds this sutra shall have no sores or chafing; yet, by virtue of reciting the sutra, scabies may cover [the body].
Regarding the statement that "two eyes are missing": the Mahāyāna sūtras constitute one eye, and the Hīnayāna sūtras constitute the other eye.
If one slanders both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, both eyes are lost. Now, because one only slanders the Mahāyāna, one eye is missing. This sūtra is...
The eyes of sentient beings: those who uphold this sutra will experience their eyes becoming entirely pure; conversely, due to slandering the sutra, one becomes sightless.
Regarding the phrase "three times struck and cast down": those who uphold this sutra will experience celestial youths serving as their attendants; [conversely], due to...
Because he slandered this sutra, he was beaten and struck by his own son until he died;
thus it is said that four such acts lead to death. If a person who is ill were to hear this sutra, their illness would immediately be extinguished, and they would neither age nor die.
Now, because he slandered this sutra, he has met with death once again.
Regarding the statement "the body is large": this sutra is the scripture that brings forth the cycle of birth and death within the five destinies.
Because of upholding this sutra, one attains the Dharma-body and the Reward-body; yet because of slandering the sutra with a mind of anger, one receives the body of a python.

Because of slandering the scripture that brings forth the cycle of birth and death in the five destinies, the body is five hundred *yojanas* in length, serving as the locus for all manner of suffering.
Regarding the mention of "two types of deafness": this sutra is the scripture for the ears and eyes of all sentient beings.
Those who uphold this sutra attain the faculty of pure hearing and can hear the sounds throughout the three thousandfold world-system. Because of slandering this sutra, one is reborn with deafness.

[Objection: It is heard that snakes originally have no ears; how then can one speak of them being deaf? [Response: Master Mu replied, "Although they lack a manifest physical locus, they nonetheless possess the faculty of hearing."
Regarding the term "three types of fools": this sutra is a scripture of wisdom. Those who uphold this sutra receive the empowerment of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva;
even if they forget the phrases and clauses, they will subsequently master them all. It is because of slandering this sutra that one becomes dull-witted and foolish.
Regarding the "four lackings" (*anartha*): this sutra is the cause for attaining Buddhahood. "Cause" carries the meaning of "foot.

Because one upholds this sutra, one realizes the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) and walks with feet treading upon lotus flowers. Those who slander the sutra drag their bellies along the ground, crawling as they go.
Some say that even snakes have feet, which they keep hidden within their bellies; by taking eight medicinal herbs, one can master the arts of sorcery.
Regarding the phrase "five kinds of minor insects," this sutra is the untainted dharma-food for all sentient beings; because of slandering it, one is devoured by these minor insects.

Regarding the phrase "one should follow from the hump," this refers to the body being bent. Because one slanders the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*—the practice of the upright body—one experiences the body being bent. [The word] *zha* (to sip) [refers to being consumed].
The two characters 唼 and [口* (唐-口+(走-土))] are pronounced as "she" (shè). In written form, they are transcribed with the phonetic value of "she."
Regarding the statement "one who is dull-witted": by upholding the sūtras, one attains sharp faculties and wisdom; by slandering the sūtras, one attains dullness of the faculties.
By upholding the sūtras, the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) become pure. Here, "faculties" refers to the five physical sense-faculties (*pañca-rūpīndriya*) along with their bases;
it does not refer to the five spiritual faculties (*pañcendriya*), such as faith and so forth.
Regarding the term "two dwarfs" (*cuo*): according to common usage, a dwarf is called *cuo*. If it were written as *cuo* (as in *chuang-cuo*), it would mean a carbuncle or boil;
this is not the meaning here. This sutra is the longest among the sūtras based on principle. One who upholds this sutra is moved by the manifestation of Anantagātra (Boundless Body);
conversely, because of the arising of slander, one is moved to receive a short stature.
Regarding the "three types of ugliness": this sutra is adorned with ten thousand virtues, and the ox-cart is embellished with various jewels;

those who uphold this sutra are moved to receive the adornment of the marks of a hundred blessings. Because of slander, one becomes ugly. Furthermore, this sutra is a teaching free from outflows (*anāsrava*);
because of slandering and being attached to it, one is harmed by outflows.
Regarding the "four": "hand-crippling" refers to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* being the hand that instructs all sentient beings; because of slandering it, one's hands are crippled.
Regarding the "five":
"leg-lameness" means this sutra is the foot of unsurpassed bodhi; because of slandering it, one's legs become lame. There is...
To have "addictions" (*pi*) is the same as having "perversions" (*bi*);
they are both illnesses. Regarding the "six blind": this sutra is the eye of human and heavenly beings; because they slander it, they are blind.
Regarding the "seven deaf": by slandering the sutra so that it does not circulate, they cause others not to hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and thus they are deaf.
Regarding the "eight hunchbacks": they slandered the practice of upright conduct and the *Zhengzhi shi fangbian jing* (Sūtra on Upright Abandonment of Expedient Means);

therefore, they became hunchbacks. Regarding the "nine people who do not believe": because they upheld this sūtra, they had attained faith and acceptance; now, by slandering it, they cause others to fall into wrong views. Consequently...
This illustrates that people who do not believe and accept [the teaching] will receive retribution.

As for the statement that "ten mouths are foul-smelling," those who uphold this sutra constantly emit the fragrance of blue lotuses from their mouths, and the fragrance of ox-head sandalwood constantly issues from the pores of their bodies;
conversely, because they slander the sutra, they consequently experience foul breath from their mouths at all times.
Regarding the statement "possessed by eleven ghosts": if those who uphold this sutra are harassed and disturbed by spirits and ghosts, their heads shall shatter into seven pieces.
I shall dispatch transformed members of the fourfold assembly—bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and pure laymen and laywomen—to make offerings to the Dharma Master.
Because of slandering this sutra, they will consequently be afflicted by malevolent spirits and ghosts, which will enter their bodies.
Regarding the "twelve kinds of poverty": this sutra is a treasury of conditioned phenomena and a storehouse of unconditioned phenomena—a scripture of wealth and nobility.
Those who slander it or become attached to it will experience the fruit of poverty.

Regarding the statement "thirteen types of low-born persons": those who uphold this sutra will attain the seat of Śakra, the seat of Brahmā, and will also dwell together with the bodhisattvas who possess dhāraṇīs.
Conversely, by slandering it, one invites rebirth among the low-born.

Regarding the statement "the fourteen ways of harming others": this sutra concerns those who possess sovereignty and are unbound, who have no dependence or seeking, and for whom the sons of gods serve as attendants.
Because of their slanders, they experience being driven by others and lack sovereignty.
Regarding the statement "many suffer from illness": this sutra is the excellent medicine for the ailments of Jambudvīpa.
If one hears this sutra, illness will be immediately extinguished; it is due to slander that one suffers much illness.

Regarding the "sixteen types of emaciation": because one slanders sūtras that describe others as being robust, strong, and possessing excellent physical forms, one consequently experiences many illnesses and emaciation.
Regarding the "disease of thirst," a sūtra states:
"When one gradually sees moist earth and mud, one knows with certainty that water is near. Because one slanders this [teaching], [one suffers from thirst].
The teaching is that the disease of thirst arises accordingly.
As for the "seventeen things without reliance," the wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle is the ultimate resort of the Great Nature;
it is the sutra upon which all sentient beings rely. Because they slander it, they have nothing to depend upon or take refuge in.

Regarding the statement "arising from being led by the mind": A question is raised: If the act of slandering the sūtras is a mental action (*manas-karma*), how can it be described as "hunchbacked and ugly," which is categorized as a bodily action (*kāya-karma*)?
The answer states in the commentary: "Because it is led by the mind," and so forth.
Regarding the statement that "two fruits may be known," Jin says: Because one does not cause others to become intimate with the sūtras, one attains the superior fruit;

because one causes others to forget them, one attains the inferior fruit. He further says: Because one does not personally cultivate the four practices of intimacy, the minds of those before one are not transformed or recorded.
Second, it is said: Even if those before one have already lightly memorized [the teachings] but subsequently forget them, it is due to [one's own lack of cultivation].
In one's birth, one causes others not to remember [one] or causes them to forget; thus, one invites this result.
Regarding the statement that "meager merit and protection have two results": first, the result of treating others without success; second, the result of being ill oneself without receiving treatment.
Regarding "treating illness by following its nature": treating a cold illness with hot medicine and treating a hot illness with cold medicine is called treating illness by following its nature.
Regarding "further increasing other ailments": first, when an old ailment becomes even more severe, it is called further increasing other ailments;

second, when one originally suffers from red eyes and, despite treatment, they do not improve at all, and furthermore, the pain shifts to the waist and legs, this is called further increasing other ailments. Or, due to...
The illness increases and leads to death. Second, the fruit of having an illness for which there is no physician:
if one has an illness oneself but no one provides medical treatment—due to slandering the sūtras—one causes others not to hear the Dharma and acts as a bad friend to others;

consequently, when one has an illness at home, no one comes to provide medical treatment. Due to [the failure to apply] the medicine of the Truthful Dharma, even if one takes excellent medicine, it further aggravates the condition, and the illness persists.
It is difficult to find a parallel.
As for those who have suffered calamity through no fault of their own: if they have committed offenses against others, it belongs solely to the state;

if they have acted in rebellion against their own kin, it extends to the elders within their own household. Those who openly seize titles and plunder by force, or who take names in secret and commit theft—such persons deserve death.

The *Amṛta* (不死) states: "There are those who receive [punishment] beside [the perpetrator]. It is said that they eat the staff [of punishment] to repay for their lives. From the perspective of the present life, this is considered 'unjust' (*heng*).

However, if one considers it in terms of karma from previous lives—specifically the karma of slandering the scriptures—it is appropriate that they receive it. This interpretation holds that one who did not commit the theft himself may yet be treated as a thief; this is called 'meeting with injustice' (*hengli*).
Second, it is said that being robbed, plundered, or stolen from by others is also called 'meeting with injustice. *Yang* refers to calamity; *fá* refers to punishment."
(The former interpretation is correct). Because those who slander the sūtras act contrary to principle, they consequently incur punishment, even though they do not commit acts of direct rebellion.
Regarding the phrase "reciting a single verse yet not seeing the Buddha": such sinful persons as these face the difficulty of being born neither before nor after a Buddha.
Regarding the phrase "reciting a single verse yet not hearing the Dharma": the first two lines refer to such sinful persons who are constantly born in difficult circumstances;

within these various difficulties, the five obstacles (*pañcāvaraṇa*) are subsumed. The latter two lines—being insane, deaf, or mentally deranged—mean that they will never hear the Dharma; this corresponds to the obstacle of worldly wisdom (*loka-paṇḍita*).

"Distinguishing through eloquence and intelligence" constitutes six difficulties within this single line of verse. Lu says: "It may be granted that one whose mind is distracted by worldly wisdom and eloquence [is called 'deaf,' but] how can this be applied to the 'blind'?
Answer: It is defined as being "deaf" with respect to not hearing the Dharma. Here, "deaf" implies "blind. One does not define deafness or blindness solely by the ears or eyes;
rather, because those with worldly wisdom do not hear the Dharma and do not see the principle, they are so designated. As Zhuangzi says:
Is it only those with physical bodies who possess deafness and blindness? Indeed, even those of great wisdom may have them.
As for the scriptural statement "like the sands of the Ganges," there are two interpretations. First, the sands of the Ganges refer to the aforementioned number of kalpas.

Second, it is said that "like the sands of the Ganges" refers to the number of future births. Among these sands of the Ganges, there are all those who are suddenly deaf and mute. Answer: Because of... [text fragment]
"Speech not obtaining the name 'immediate' (*sadyah*) also arises from birth from the womb; because one is immediately born deaf or mute, it is called 'immediate birth.

As for the difficulty of the non-intactness of the sense-faculties (*indriya*), this refers to the difficulty of the non-intactness of the sense-faculties; it is appended to the previous seven difficulties to form eight."

Regarding the statement that one "experiences increase and so forth throughout the four realms of existence," this is a summary inquiry. Previously, it was stated that one experiences the three miserable destinies as *vipāka-phala* (ripened results).

This case is the same; why, then, is it said here that one experiences "increase" (*adhipati*) and "outflow" (*niṣyanda*)? The answer is that there are three types of karma capable of producing results:
the root (*mūla*), the preliminary (*prayoga*), and the subsequent (*pṛṣṭha*). If one experiences [the result] from the root karma of slandering the sūtras...

The "result" (phala) refers to the distinct maturation (vipāka). If one experiences the result arising from the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) or the subsequent stage (*pṛṣṭha*), one experiences both the increased (*adhipati*) and the concordant (*niṣyanda*) results. Since karma is threefold, the way it induces its results is likewise distinct.

Slandering the sūtras takes doubt as the preparatory stage, wrong view as the fundamental stage, and perverse desire as the subsequent stage. For instance, shedding the blood of a Buddha constitutes the act of killing.
The Buddha’s preparatory action (*prayoga*) is also a grave offense that can bring about the concordant (*niṣyanda*), similar (*sabhāga*), and dominant (*adhipati*) results, such as rebirth in hell;
this is why the name is established in both places. Because the Buddha’s body cannot be killed, it does not constitute a fundamental course of action (*maula-karmapatha*);
rather, it is only a preparatory course of action that brings about a concordant result. Question: That which is called "false" resembles the "real. As for hell—
If one looks at the fruit in expectation of the cause of slandering the sūtras, how can it be called "similar" in meaning, and why is it termed a "pseudo-outflow" (*niṣyanda*)? Answer:
Because of slandering the sūtras, one severs the lineage of the Buddha; others fall into ruin, undergo the sufferings of the three miserable realms, and cause their own bodies to enter hell.
This is what is meant by "similarity. Just as in a previous life one committed killing and severed the lives of others, causing the lives of those others to be short and not long, so too now—

In this life, one personally obtains the retribution of a short lifespan; therefore, it is called "resemblance. Question: What is the difference between the two fruits of "outflow" (*niṣyanda*) and "increase" (*abhyudaya*)? Answer:
In a previous life, one lacked faith in the Dharma and gave rise to contempt, hatred, and jealousy as causes.

In this present life, when receiving the fruit, the increase of anger constitutes the result. Because the result resembles the cause, it is the fruit of outflow. The body is constantly foul-smelling and defiled.
Impurity is the dominant fruit (adhipati-phala).

Regarding the term "pleasure gardens" (*ārāma-vihāra*): it explains that those who constantly dwell in hell and so forth—specifically those who slander the sūtras—take refuge in hell as if they were visiting pleasure gardens.
They enter and exit from one hell to another without interruption, just like wandering through pleasure gardens. Or...
It is merely within a single hell that one cannot escape; this is called the "Garden of Wandering Views.
As for the phrase "other evil realms," it is explained as being like one's own house, namely the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*).

Just as a person’s own house belongs to them and they cannot cast it off, so too when one receives the body of a hungry ghost, one cannot cast it off; it is similar to one's own home. Furthermore, [it is said:]...
If one were to treat this as a guest-commentary, it would be merely temporary; however, within our own school (*svayūthya*), the text would be too long. Regarding the phrase "as previously cited":
in the previous general enumeration, those who did not believe in this sutra and gave rise to craving were few; thus, they were omitted and not discussed. Why, then, are they discussed here?
The commentary answers: "As previously cited," etc. The intended meaning is that those who previously slandered the sutra fell [into the lower realms].
Because hungry ghosts are few, they were not mentioned [previously]. Since they do exist in small numbers here, they are now singled out for mention.
Regarding those who are mute and dumb: if one asks what the distinction between these two types is, Huadu replied, "One who is entirely unable to produce sound is called mute (*mūka*)."

If there is a sound that the tongue cannot produce, it is called "dumb" (*mūka*). A dumb person may obtain sound through their own efforts; however, a mute (*mūka*) lacks both [the ability to speak] and sound.
As for the character *gǔ* (骨), the phonetic gloss states it is a sound of lamentation. The pronunciation of *yǎ* (啞) is the same as *wēi* (危).
Regarding the term "abscess" (*jū*): an abscess has its core within and its swelling without; thus, when the mind lacks faith, it is like an abscess.
When one speaks words that lack faith externally, it is like the swelling of an abscess. A person who upholds this sutra adorns themselves with the adornments of the Buddha;

however, because they slander the sutra, they are adorned with such things as deafness and blindness. Furthermore, the Tathāgata covers those who uphold this sutra with his robes; yet, because of their slandering of the sutra—
Therefore, such illnesses as these serve as their clothing.
As for the phrase "deeply attached to the view of self," this refers to the five sharp afflictions (*tīkṣṇa-kleśa*) among the ten afflictions.

Regarding the phrase "increase of delusion" (*moha*): its essential nature is not itself delusion; rather, it refers to being deeply attached to the meaning of the sutras due to the sense of "predominance. It also refers to the intensification of hatred (*dveṣa*).
When the sutra mentions "lustful desire" (*kāma*) and so forth, it refers to greed (*lobha*). This is because the person who upholds the sutra does not act for the sake of obtaining women.
Regarding "delusion":

although it is said that there are those of the nature of innate capacity (*prakṛti-gotra*) and those of the nature of cultivated capacity (*samudānīta-gotra*), these refer to the lineage-nature and the cultivated-nature.
Regarding "discerning right from wrong": this refers to discerning right from wrong within worldly affairs; that is to say, it is the engagement with phenomena.

Regarding the phrase "having previously planted the roots of learning" (*śikṣā-vana-ropita*): this refers to worldly arts, crafts, and literature; it does not necessarily mean that one has previously heard the Dharma and thus planted the roots of learning.

Regarding the phrase "preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and other [sūtras]": there are two interpretations. First, it means they do not seek after non-Buddhist paths (*tīrthika*). Second, it means their nature seeks awakening.
They do not seek the path of the two vehicles.
As for the statement, "If I, in past lives, etc., have seen Buddhas," this refers to the appropriation of roots of goodness; the commentary explains that these are the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
The Sūtra states that those who constantly cultivate a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) are necessarily individuals of keen faculties who possess diligence.

The Sūtra further states that they have "no divergent mind" (*ananyacitta*); focusing single-mindedly on one object is what is meant by having no divergent mind. A divergent mind is precisely distraction (*vikṣepa*).
Therefore, this is judged to be the cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Regarding the statement "abandoning [unwholesome] wisdom, [relying on] spiritual friends, and drawing near to virtuous conditions," these are precisely the conditions for upholding the precepts.

As set forth in the "Chapter on Peaceful Practices" (*Anupūrvavihāra-parivarta*), one should distance oneself from ten kinds of unwholesome conditions: not associating with kings, princes, ministers, or high officials;
not associating with non-Buddhist practitioners such as Brahmins or Nirgranthas; and refraining from composing secular writings or praising non-Buddhist texts. This is...
This refers to distancing oneself from adverse conditions before subsequently upholding the precepts; thus, it is called the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*).
As for the mention of "sincerity" (*rjuka*) and so forth, this clarifies the practice of patience (*kṣānti*). Sincerity corresponds to the patience of enduring suffering (*duḥkhādhivāsana-kṣānti*);

however, there are those who are sincere yet unable to endure suffering. Here, the discussion concerns those who are capable. A person of sincerity may encounter sudden circumstances, such as the case of Wei Sheng and the woman.
Regarding Ziqi, who died while embracing a beam, and others like him,

it is said that those who always take pity on all beings practice the patience of enduring enmity and harm; they do not discriminate against those who come to harm them, and they are able to endure even unto death.
Regarding the phrase "reverence and so forth," it is asked: how do reverence for the Buddha and the patient acceptance of the thorough investigation of the Dharma correspond? It is answered:

because the Buddha is able to teach the Dharma, one reveres the Buddha and listens to the Dharma in his presence; having heard the Dharma, one is then able to exercise patient acceptance toward its explanation.
This is called the patience of the thorough investigation of phenomena (*dharmavicaya-kṣānti*).

Regarding the statement that "the two and a half verses concern exclusive seeking," this means it is uninterrupted. Question: What is the distinction between "exclusive seeking" (*ekānta-paryeṣaṇā*) and "thorough seeking" (*tattva-paryeṣaṇā*)?

Answer: Exclusive seeking means not seeking the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*); thorough seeking means not seeking the non-Buddhist paths (*tīrthika*). Furthermore, exclusive seeking refers to continuity (*saṃtāna*), while thorough seeking refers to transmission (*paramparā*).
This refers to the application of the mind.

When it is said that the *Śīla-sūtra* speaks of the "internal," this does not mean that one has studied everything exhaustively and thus attained the ultimate; rather, it means that one has attained a fundamental understanding within a single text, which is termed "ultimate.
If one has not yet reached the ultimate in the study of the Mahāyāna, other vehicles are not permitted [as a substitute]. These other vehicles are...

Regarding the Hīnayāna: if one has practiced it for a long time, then during the three periods of the day, one should study Mahāyāna Abhidharma (inner science) during two periods, and study the Hīnayāna as well as the treatises on the four vidyās during one period.
As for the four vidyās, these together constitute the five vidyās. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, chapter twenty-five, states: "First is the field of inner science (*adhyātma-vidyā-sthāna*).
This has two characteristics: first, it reveals correct cause and effect; second, it reveals that which has already been realized..."

The science of craftsmanship (*śilpakarmasthāna-vidyā*) has two characteristics: first, the characteristic of not losing what has been done; second, the characteristic of not obtaining what has not been done. Second, the science of logic (*hetu-vidyā*) also has two:

first, the characteristic of demonstrating the excellence of refuting the arguments of others; second, the characteristic of demonstrating the excellence of escaping the arguments of others. Third, the science of grammar (*śabda-vidyā*) also has two characteristics:

first, the characteristic of demonstrating the establishment of meaning and the means of proof; second, the characteristic of demonstrating that language lacks excellence [when divorced from these]. Fourth, the science of medicine (*cikitsā-vidyā*).

There are also four kinds of characteristics: first, manifesting the nature of the disease; second, manifesting the cause of the disease; third, manifesting that which arises again after having been eliminated;

and fourth, manifesting that which does not arise again after having been severed. Fifth is the science of arts and crafts (*śilpakarmasthāna-vidyā*), which manifests the establishment of various distinct fields of skillful activity and their functions.
Regarding these various distinct characteristics, the thirty-eighth [fascicle] states: "The inner science (*adhyātma-vidyā*) refers to the speech of all Buddhas.

It is said that there are ten kinds of causes: first, the cause of conventional designation (*anuvyavahāra-hetu*); second, the cause of dependence (*apekṣā-hetu*); third, the cause of projection (*ākṣepa-hetu*); fourth, the cause of support (*parigraha-hetu*); fifth, the cause of birth (*abhinirvṛtti-hetu*);

sixth, the cause of origination (*abhinirhāra-hetu*); seventh, the cause of specific determination (*pratiniyama-hetu*); eighth, the cause of cooperation (*sahakāri-hetu*); ninth, the cause of opposition (*virodha-hetu*); and tenth, the cause of non-opposition (*avirodha-hetu*). These are condensed into two."
The first [category] comprises the first two [perfections], while the second, skillful means, comprises the latter eight. Furthermore, four conditions and five fruits are taught:

maturation (*vipāka*), outflow (*niṣyanda*), dominance (*adhipati*), human effort (*puruṣakāra*), and disjunction (*visamyoga*). Regarding these, the Bodhisattva [understands] the characteristics of correct cause and effect as revealed by inner science (*adhyātma-vidyā*).

By knowing things as they truly are and practicing with diligence, one causes the lineage of the power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible to gradually become purified and gradually increase.
What is called the second characteristic? It refers to the fact that although sentient beings perform their own actions, even after having performed them...
Throughout many hundreds of kalpas, the capacity to produce its fruit never perishes, nor does it fail to act; nor does a different action ever result in a different maturation.
By means of this, one gradually attains purification through the cultivation of the lineage of the power of wisdom of one’s own vehicle.
Regarding the clarification of characteristics: this refers to the desire to know, as they truly are, that the causal treatises composed by non-Buddhists are evil doctrines, for the purpose of...

To subdue the various heterodox arguments of others; to cause those who have not yet gained faith in this true and holy teaching to develop pure faith, and to cause those who have already gained faith to increase and expand it further;

and regarding grammar (*śabdavidyā*), if bodhisattvas [apply themselves] to grammar, it is for the sake of causing sentient beings who delight in formal language to generate deep respect and faith toward the person of the bodhisattva, and for the sake of awakening...
[The fifth category of] the *vyākhyāna* (exegesis) is called "the differentiation of words and phrases. This refers to explaining a single meaning through various categories and distinct sounds.
Regarding the science of medicine (*cikitsā-vidyā*), it is when Bodhisattvas seek to alleviate the various diseases of sentient beings and to benefit all the hosts of devas.
Regarding the science of arts and crafts (*śilpa-karma-sthāna-vidyā*), it is when sentient beings, by expending little effort, accumulate [great results].
Wealth and treasures. For the purpose of benefiting all sentient beings; for the sake of rare and marvelous signs among sentient beings;

and by means of skillful wisdom and impartiality, to distribute and offer them as sustenance and to gather in immeasurable sentient beings—the Bodhisattva practices all five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*), because the Mahāyāna sūtras are included within these sciences. If one studies with a mind directed toward the Mahāyāna, [one will] reach the ultimate end.
If one has not yet mastered the remaining four treatises after completing the study of them all, there is a fear that one will eventually abandon the Mahāyāna.

For this reason, the Tripiṭaka Master of the Tang dynasty translated only the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra* and did not translate the other four vidyā-śāstras, fearing they might cause the abandonment of the Great Practice.
As for the phrase "other sūtras," this refers to sūtras of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*), as well as the sūtras of the Hīnayāna, which are termed "other sūtras.
Furthermore, it reveals the characteristics of seeking the truth within this One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

Second, because there are also sūtras within the teachings of non-Buddhist paths—such as the *Mahāvaipulya* sūtras and others—and because in this land there are Confucian texts such as the *Classic of Filial Piety* (*Xiaojing*) and Daoist texts such as the *Laozi Daodejing* and the *Zhuangzi* (the latter being the Southern [School]).
The *Huajing*. "Jing" means constancy; it is a classic to be practiced constantly for a hundred generations.

Regarding the statement that "sincere resolve moves the spirits," sincerity arises from harmony. It is recorded that when Shun ruled the world for thirty days, the people of Miao rebelled against his mandate.
Yi turned against Yu and led troops to wage war against them. After many days had passed, they were unable to subdue them. Yu—
He asked the King, "Your Majesty’s sincere resolve has moved the divine; these three tribes have not returned to others.
The Emperor followed his words and extensively cultivated civil virtue. After seventy days had passed, these people of the three tribes spontaneously submitted their lives out of sincerity.
He was able to harmonize even the ghosts and spirits. The Book says: "The Emperor then extensively spread his civil virtue; after seventy days, the Prince of Miao submitted.

To "submit" (*ge*) means to arrive through the ultimate [influence]. That they would not submit to being attacked, yet came of their own accord when not attacked, clarifies that there was a Way in governing them.

The state of the Three Miao lay to the left of Lake Dongting and to the right of Lake Pengli, situated at the edge of the "barbarian territories" (*huangfu*). This explains the sense of "arriving" (*zhi*) within the scripture.
It is the mind.

Regarding the statement "to overcome [delusive] thoughts and become a sage," the *Book of Documents* says: "Only the sage, through thought, becomes mad; though mad, by overcoming his thoughts, he becomes a sage. The commentary states:
"If even a sage does not maintain mindfulness of the good, he becomes a madman; only a madman is capable of maintaining such mindfulness."
Regarding "good," one becomes a sage through the power of mastery; it means to excel and to take the place of another.
This implies that a person of superior wisdom cannot perform inferior deeds, nor can a person of inferior wisdom perform superior deeds.
A person of middling capacity becomes good when they encounter the instruction of a good person, and becomes evil when they encounter the instruction of an evil person.

Regarding the statement in the fourth chapter, the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding," that it follows the "Chapter on Parables": Question: When the Dharma was first expounded during the first week, why did Śāriputra not receive it through parables?
[The Buddha] taught by means of metaphors; why did the four great śrāvakas not understand through the Dharma? The answer is: because it accords with the Buddha’s intention.

When the World-Honored One taught by way of the Dharma, Śāriputra understood through the Dharma; when the World-Honored One taught by way of metaphors, the four great śrāvakas understood through metaphors.
Since the former Buddhas intended that all who possess wisdom attain understanding through parables, they understood by means of metaphors. If it were otherwise, it would contradict the Buddha.

This is a contradiction. This first section explains the teaching on those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). Second, regarding the statement "the treatise explains the seven," etc., this refers to the second point where the tenets of the treatise are confronted:

at the assembly on Vulture Peak, there was a class of ordinary śrāvakas prior to the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) who clung to the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣaphala*)—which they themselves were deluded about—as being ultimate, asserting that "my vehicle and the Tathāgata’s vehicle are neither distinct nor different. For [this reason, the treatise addresses them].
This chapter has been introduced in order to provide an antidote to this.
Regarding the seven parables: first, for those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*) who seek merit through perverted views, the Parable of the Burning House is taught.
Second, for those with one-sided overweening pride who seek the liberation of the *śrāvaka*, the Parable of the Poor Son is taught. Third...
1. For those who adhere to the Mahāyāna, it is taught that there is only the Mahāyāna, using the parable of the medicinal herbs.
2. For those with fixed resolve, the parable of the conjured city is taught. 3. For those without fixed resolve, the parable of the tied jewel is taught. 4.
For those who have accumulated merit, the parable of untying the jewel is taught. 5. For those who have not accumulated merit, the parable of the physician is taught.
Regarding the phrase "seeking merit through inversion": the karmic rewards of humans and devas are not true merit; to falsely calculate them as merit is called inversion.

The noble fruits of the Three Vehicles do not seek the rewards of humans and devas; this is called "arising in accordance with reality" rather than inversion. Only by turning back to seek the fruit of Buddhahood is it truly called arising in accordance with reality, not inversion.

Regarding the second type, those who seek the liberation of a *śrāvaka*: having heard the World-Honored One’s teaching that "my births have been exhausted and I shall not undergo further existence," there are those who, prior to the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*), are ordinary persons still in training (*śaikṣa*) seeking the fruits of the two vehicles;

this is called "seeking the liberation of a *śrāvaka*. Because they seek only the Lesser Vehicle and do not seek the Great Vehicle, it is called "exclusive. If one studies both types together, [it is otherwise].

This is called the Mahāyāna of the two directions; it is called "superior. To claim that one has attained what one has attained and thus neglects the cultivation of the Mahāyāna, saying, "My vehicle is no different from the Tathāgata’s vehicle," is pride.
The commentary states: "The vehicle for which I seek is called 'my vehicle'."
Because this person is one in training (śaikṣa). Question: Do those who seek the two vehicles not know the difference between the Buddha and the two vehicles? Answer:
According to reality, they are the same in that they have severed the afflictions and attained liberation through the principle of the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā).

Thus, these three types of people are reckoned as sitting together upon the bed of liberation; in every respect they appear identical, yet in truth they are not the same. To regard what is not the same as being the same is called [false conceptualization].
It is a perversion.

Regarding the statement that "taking such perversions as the object of antidotes," one asks: since this chapter is led and explained by the four great śrāvakas themselves, how can this chapter be called an "antidote"?
The answer is: the seven similes are each presented with two intentions; the first is for the sake of the four [great śrāvakas]...

The first refers to the great śrāvakas who attained understanding. The second refers, by way of secondary correspondence, to a certain class of ordinary persons still in training (*śaikṣa*) within the assembly on Vulture Peak;
while the text for the primary attainment of understanding is explicit, the text for the secondary correspondence is not so clear.
This is why Vasubandhu’s commentary does not specifically cite those who belong to the latter category.
This statement is taught as an antidote by means of the parable of the impoverished son. Question: What are the specific characteristics of this exclusive pursuit of liberation? Answer:

Those of the two vehicles who have attained the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) arise from the correct realization of the principle of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). Subsequently, they enter meditative contemplation (*samādhi-vipaśyanā*).

Because their minds were previously coarse regarding what was realized, they do not perceive the true wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) nor the suchness (*tathatā*) of the emptiness of persons; rather, they perceive that afflictions and suffering do not arise during the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga-mārga*).

The mind then transforms into the conceptualization and understanding of *nirvāṇa*. The manifested aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) that is transformed is mostly a "transformed city" (*nirmāṇa-pura*), yet the transforming mind of understanding reckons it to be a goat cart or a deer cart;

this is called "inversion. Having already fallen into inversion oneself, one turns toward ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) and speaks of this inverted mind.
Śrāvakas and ordinary beings then single-mindedly aspire for and seek it; this is the liberation of the śrāvakas.

Regarding the statement that "the vehicle of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-yāna*) and the subsequent vehicle" and so forth, this clarifies the basis for the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) giving rise to attachments.

The term "two vehicles" (*dviyāna*) does not differ [from its previous usage]; it applies universally, functioning across both the preceding section on the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the present section on the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Zhiyou states: "As for the persons of the two vehicles..."
Thirty years ago, I heard it said that three people sat together upon the bed of liberation; this was precisely the "identical vehicle" (avaiṣamya-yāna) of the past.
As for the "identical vehicle" of later times, this refers to what was heard during the assembly of the Lotus Sūtra:
that within the Buddha-lands of the ten directions there is only the One Vehicle (ekayāna), neither two nor three. This is the "identical vehicle" of the future. 10.

In the worlds of the ten directions, there are two or three [vehicles], which implies that there is a distinction between myself and the Buddha. However, in the worlds of the ten directions, there are neither two nor three vehicles;
thus, one knows they are not different. Question: Why is the assembly at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* called the "Final Vehicle"? Answer:
Why could it not be called the "Final Vehicle" in contrast to the assembly at the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*? Secondly, according to the teachings of Jincheng and others, previously there was none...
Regarding the fact that there is no difference among the vehicles (*yāna*), the "Expedient Means" chapter (*Upāya-paryāya*) is the first to teach this; therefore, it is called "prior.

It teaches that the Buddha-knowledge and vision (*buddha-jñāna-darśana*) reveal that the *dharmakāya* of the three vehicles is fundamentally equal. Furthermore, in the sixth [chapter], it negates [the existence of] a nirvāṇa for two vehicles, asserting that there is only the *dharmakāya*.
Moreover, it says: "The mark of the quiescence of all phenomena cannot be expressed in words"; therefore, it is called "non-existence" (*amala*).
This is because there is no difference in the vehicle.

To say that "there is no difference in the later vehicle" refers to what is called the "difference in the later vehicle" within the second turning [of the wheel]. The two vehicles of the sheep and the deer are not at all granted;
all the sons equally receive the ox-cart. Since they are equally bestowed with the ox-cart, we know that [in reality] there is but one vehicle (the *ekayāna*).

There is no difference. It was because the Tathāgata perceived that they possessed the lineage of the Mahāyāna yet were unwilling to turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle that he taught the single Buddha-vehicle alone, without a second vehicle; this is the intended meaning of the Buddha’s teaching.
Upon hearing this, Śāriputra and the four great śrāvakas attained realization and immediately abandoned [their former path] to turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle.
The phrase "he then becomes deluded and attached" encompasses the subsequent sense of not awakening; it refers to how one then insists:
"Since it is said that the three vehicles are no different, why bother seeking the Mahāyāna further? Therefore, one seeks the small and is given the small, which is no different from the great."

Regarding the statement that the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the initial vehicle (*ādi-yāna*) are distinct, the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) says: "The movement toward the objective is itself the fruit of Buddhahood, the Bodhi;

in contrast to the unconditioned principle (*asaṃskṛta-tattva*), it is called a 'vehicle' (*yāna*). As for the term "initial practice," this refers to the causal practices of the three vehicles (*tri-yāna*);

they receive the name "initial" in contrast to the subsequent fruit of Buddhahood. Alternatively, only the two vehicles are termed the "initial vehicle," receiving that name in contrast to the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*).

Based on the previous explanation, Lu said: "The meaning is that within the vehicle [of the bodhisattva], one seeks the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñatā). Within the unconditioned vehicle, one has not yet attained the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā).
The causal practices of the three vehicles are like the impoverished son, while the subsequent fruit of Buddhahood is called the elder. Question:
If the four great śrāvakas understood that the preceding unconditioned state and the subsequent vehicle are one and the same, why is it described as an "elder," as in the case of the Buddha?

The "poor son" refers to the śrāvaka. Does this indicate that the vehicles are different? Since it is stated here that one realizes the Small Vehicle and enters the Great Vehicle to seek the One Vehicle, for what reason is the Small Vehicle mentioned?
Answer: The śrāvaka describes his own past nature of greatness, yet he regrets and reproaches himself for seeking the Small Vehicle, just like the poor son.
The World-Honored One abides in greatness, like the wealthy elder, who teaches and transforms us, causing us to attain the same [Great Vehicle].
"Great! To explain the sutra: the great wealthy elder is the Tathāgata; we are all like the sons of the Buddha.
Since the Tathāgata has always said that we are his sons, this precisely explains that there is no difference from the previous vehicle."

Regarding the phrase "first, the removal of doubt": it refers to the resolution of the delusions of doubt that have been severed. Doubt (*vicikitsā*) has the nature of being hesitant toward the principles of the various truths (*satya*).

As stated in the *Pañcavastuka* (Treatise on the Five Categories), verse 58: "It arises in dependence upon five objects, because it arises from causes, effects, functions, the truths, and the reality of the Jewels.

Faith (*śraddhā*), by contrast, has the nature of mental purity characterized by deep conviction, delight, and aspiration toward objects such as the Three Jewels; therefore, it is called the "removal of doubt. This is its name.

Regarding the statement that faith "destroys delusion," this refers precisely to the fundamental ignorance (*moha*). The treatise states: "Ignorance has the nature of being confused and dark regarding the principles of the truths;
non-ignorance has the nature of clear understanding as its own characteristic. Since non-ignorance is the direct antidote to ignorance, it is so described.
To destroy delusion is called "understanding.
Regarding the statement "not rejoicing in the bodhicitta," the sutra says that one does not give rise to even a single thought of fondness or delight;
this cites the fruit of having joy, desire, and faith as a means of revealing the characteristics of lack of faith. Thus, one is unable to believe even in perfect enlightenment. Faith...
This means that one immediately awakens to and understands the Way of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), thereby emerging from the state of non-understanding.
As for the statement that "doubt and regret are both eliminated": the elimination of doubt signifies the attainment of faith, and the elimination of regret signifies the attainment of understanding.

Regarding the statement that "faith is [identical to] receptivity, aspiration, and so forth," this cites both the cause and the result. Through faith and acceptance, one is able to purify the mind; thus, faith serves as the cause, from which aspiration subsequently arises.
Aspiration is the result of faith, and faith is the basis for aspiration. Speaking in terms of the cause, it is termed "resolute belief" (*adhimukti*). The *Śāstra* states:
"It has the nature of a pure mind characterized by deep receptivity, delight, and aspiration toward reality, virtues, and capabilities. Here, "receptivity" (*kṣānti*) refers to...
Resolve (*adhimokṣa*) is the cause of faith. Aspiration (*chanda*) refers to the desire within the category of specific mental objects (*viśeṣa-viṣaya*);

it is the fruit of faith. Regarding the phrase "the sublime wisdom that seals and aspires": "resolve" means the determination and firm holding of resolve; because wisdom has already arisen, there is aspiration. Lu says:
"Although its essence is identical to faith and resolve, this [term] additionally takes up the function of wisdom. I now say: faith...
"Mutual wisdom" (jūjūchi) refers to the correct understanding that resolves the tenets. It is the capacity to understand through wisdom.
As for the statement "faith removes non-belief and so forth," this refers to the mental understanding that is capable of discernment.
Regarding the statement "the mind is pure and further known": it is not merely that the mind gives rise to pure wisdom; it is also able to understand and know the purity of the mind.
This faith and further knowledge is itself the understanding and faith of the mind’s purity; furthermore, this knowing is the understanding of that understanding.
Regarding the statement that faith is the mind capable of comprehension: by means of faith, the mind capable of simultaneous comprehension attains purity. Question:

If this is so, what is the distinction between making the mind pure and gradual [purification], etc.? Answer: This purity serves as a defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa) to avoid the error of confusion with the latter.

What is called the "clarification of the principle reached" refers to the principle of the identity of the one and the three; it is another designation for the function of wisdom that brings about understanding.
Regarding the "depth or shallowness of understanding and faith," at the initial moment of hearing, one first gives rise to pure faith, and only later does one attain realization and understanding.
Regarding the statement that "faith is compliance": having now heard the principle of the one and the three as taught by the Tathāgata, one endures and accepts it;
this is immediately raised as the exercise of faith, thereby manifesting faith itself.
Regarding the statement that "the three types of faith manifest through others and so forth," this refers to [faith] arising from others and through one's own awakening and understanding.
Regarding the statement that "one accords with others through mental purity," it means that by following the verbal teachings of others— the first and third [types of faith]—
one’s own mind attains purity.

Regarding the statement that "understanding reveals oneself," the Chancellor (Xiangguo) says: "This is known through inference (*anumāna*); it is not a matter of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) or realized through wisdom.

It is only at the time of the first stage (*bhūmi*) that one can directly know that one will attain perfect enlightenment. Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Cheng weishi lun), fascicle nine, states:

"When the Bodhisattva attains these two paths of vision (*darśana-mārga*), he is born into the family of the Tathāgata and dwells in the Stage of Supreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), having thoroughly mastered..."
In the dharma-realm, they attain all forms of equality and are constantly born within the great assemblies of all Buddhas.

Having attained mastery over many hundreds of gateways, they know for themselves that they will soon realize great enlightenment (mahābodhi), and are able to bring benefit and happiness to all beings throughout the future.
Regarding the phrase "with respect to others and with respect to the Dharma," Lü says: because one has faith in others, one gives rise to faith in the Dharma;
because of one's own understanding, one gives rise to understanding of the Dharma. The meaning is that "with respect to others" refers to having faith in both [others] and the Dharma;

"with respect to oneself" refers to having understanding in both [oneself] and the Dharma. Now, while "others" can be known [through external testimony], as for "understanding oneself," it means knowing one's own future state.
They come to become Buddhas. Furthermore, the testimony states: regarding persons, it is because they believe the Buddha’s words; regarding the Dharma, it is because they accord with this sutra.
First the person, then the Dharma.

Regarding the statement "four" and the two terms "faith" and "understanding": the "four" refers to the fourfold classification according to faculties (*indriya*), nature (*gotra*), stages (*avasthā*), and levels (*bhūmi*).
As for the statement "now there is a double exclusion," this refers to taking the third phrase from each of the two sets of fourfold propositions;
this is what is called "double exclusion."

Regarding the meaning of "increasing in accordance" (*anuvṛddhi*) and so forth: Question: Since faith (*śraddhā*) and understanding (*adhimukti*) are not different, should their essential natures (*svabhāva*) also not be distinct?

Answer: To speak according to reality, one has both faith and understanding regarding both the teaching (*deśanā*) and the principle (*naya*); however, it is only in terms of the sense of "increasing in accordance" that they are distinguished.

It is stated that they are distinct: understanding (*adhimukti*) pertains to the teaching (*śāsana*), while faith (*śraddhā*) pertains to the principle (*yukti*). Therefore, the Commentary says: "Understanding the teaching as real, provisional, and so forth. Question:
As previously stated, one both has faith and understanding regarding both the teaching and the principle; why is it now said that understanding pertains specifically to the teaching?
Does faith belong to the principle (*nyāya*)? Answer: If one bases it on what increases [afflictions], then understanding belongs to the teaching (*śāsana*) and faith belongs to the principle.
However, when discussed in terms of their general scope, both are common to both the teaching and the principle.

Regarding the statement "not yet realized in principle," Jin says: It is said that one "understands" the principle; however, fearing that this might be confused with "realization-understanding," it is not so stated.

Since the teaching consists of names and phrases, one knows it to be the teaching. Because it takes the common characteristics of names and signs as its object, it is the inferential cognition (*anumāna-jñāna*) of names and phrases;
there is no confusion to be excluded, and thus there is no fault in being attached to such understanding.
Regarding the statement that "the meaning is understood through discourse," this means that upon the level of verbal teaching, both faith and understanding are present;

however, upon the level of principle (*li*), there is only faith. Although verbal discourse can also lead to an inferential understanding of the principle, the point here is that the four great śrāvakas possess only inferential understanding and not realized understanding (*sākṣātkāra*). This is the intended meaning.

Regarding the phrase "both faith and understanding," etc., there are two interpretations. First, if we consider both the teaching (*śāsana*) and the principle (*yukti*) as the objects of focus, then faith and understanding may be termed *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound).

Why? Because faith is one among the eleven wholesome mental factors (*kuśala-citta-dharma*), while understanding (*avabodha*) is none other than wisdom (*prajñā*), which is one of the five object-specific mental factors (*viṣaya-pratiniyata-viśeṣa-citta-dharma*).
Although they are both mental concomitants (*caitta*), their essential natures (*svabhāva*) are distinct. How, then, can it be said that faith is [identical to]...?

Explanation: Now, regarding the two virtues of understanding (*adhimukti*) from the perspective of the subjective faculty that perceives: when these four great śrāvakas give rise to right faith, they simultaneously give rise to understanding;
at the moment of understanding, they further possess faith. This differs from what was previously distinguished, where there may be those who have faith but lack understanding.

Alternatively, one may understand [the teaching] but not believe it; this is not called "possessing both functions. However, these four types of persons possess the two qualities of being able to both believe and understand, and are thus called "possessing both functions" (*dharmadhara*).

Regarding the term "provisional" (*prajñapti*): when a single person possesses these two functions, it is called "possessing both functions," just as the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* explains the name "Mahāyāna" as being both "vehicle" (*yāna*) and "great" (*mahā*), hence "possessing both functions.
It is also like the explanation of the name "Bodhisattva": it is both "enlightenment" (*bodhi*) and "being" (*sattva*).
They are also *sattvas*, and are thus called Bodhisattvas. The subsequent explanation is clear.

Regarding the statement that "only those of superior faculties [belong to this category]," Jin says: Śāriputra is designated as "superior" because he has refined his faculties (*indriya-pariśodhana*).

Regarding the statement that those of medium faculties are also one: Maudgalyāyana is foremost in supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and has attained the four dhyānas; because he is liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*), he is called "medium.

Regarding the statement that they all belong to the inferior nature: this is because they are liberated through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukta*). However, there is such a teaching, which must be verified in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, as in the case of the ten [types of persons].
Among the great disciples, there is no one else who is liberated both ways (ubhayatobhāgavimukta).
As for the question, "How does this contradict that principle?"—how does it contradict the principles of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*? Alternatively, it may mean:

"How does this contradict these four [types of individuals] regarding the path of those with medium faculties? As stated below, the intended meaning is that if one practices only the path of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), one attains...

Regarding the Śrāvaka fruits, when divided into three grades based on the sharpness or dullness of their faculties, Śāriputra is of superior faculty, Maudgalyāyana is of middling faculty, and the rest are of inferior faculty.
Now, this [classification] is made by dividing those among the śrāvakas who have turned their minds toward the Mahāyāna into three grades;
therefore, Śāriputra is of superior faculty, the four individuals are of middling faculty, and the rest...

This is for those of inferior faculties. If one interprets it in this way, it does not deviate from the true intent; thus, this sutra does not contradict the principles of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.

As for the statement, "For example, Śūnyatāvataraka, Subhūti, and others," the intention of the commentator (*shuzhu*) is that Śāriputra was named "the foremost" because he had refined his faculties (*indriya-vaimalya*).

Furthermore, for instance, Ājñātakauṇḍinya, Subhūti, and the others each possess a particular excellence. Why does the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* not simply allow them all to be equally capable and collectively designated as "foremost"?
Since they were later categorized according to their respective meanings into three distinct grades, so too here, each is based on a single capacity.
What fault is there in designating these four individuals as being of middle grade?

The phrase "Why must those who are capable be identical? is a rhetorical question intended to test the premise. Its meaning is as follows: If among the ten great disciples all are called "foremost," why must their capabilities be identical?
Since they were not identical yet still received the title of "foremost," what prevents these four types from being of the same nature despite their threefold differences?
Just as with those ten people, although their specific abilities were not identical, they were all called "foremost. Even if...
It is not uniform. As for the four types of people with neutral dispositions, what fault is there?
The discourse follows the analogy of the impoverished son to cure the illness of clinging to the single vehicle (*ekayāna*). It is to destroy the attachment that constitutes the disease.
Regarding the scriptural statement "rejoicing and leaping for joy," there is rejoicing throughout all three cycles. In the first cycle, it says: "At that time, Śāriputra leaped for joy and rejoiced;
he immediately rose, joined his palms, gazed up at the Honored One’s countenance, and addressed the Buddha, saying... and so forth. The second cycle consists of this very passage.
Furthermore, in the third cycle, Pūrṇa attained what he had never experienced before, and with a pure mind, he leaped for joy. Moreover...
The text below says: At that time, the twelve hundred arhats who had attained mastery of mind thought to themselves: "We are filled with joy at having attained what we have never experienced before.
Would it not be most wonderful if the World-Honored One were to grant us each a prediction of enlightenment, just as he has for the other great disciples?

The sutra speaks of "that which was heard from the Buddha. What is meant by "that which was heard"? The answer is: it refers to that which belongs to the hearing; that is, the bestowal [of the prediction].
Regarding the matters of the predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) and so forth: as for the locus where they were heard, it was heard at the place of the Buddha.
This Dharma was heard concerning the Buddha’s bestowing of the prediction of the fruit upon Śāriputra due to his causal practice, and concerning Pūrṇa-maitrāyaṇīputra, Puṣpa, Prabhāsa, and others.
This is an unprecedented phenomenon (*adbhuta-dharma*): for forty years, the Buddha had never bestowed predictions upon any śrāvakas, as they had all been told that śrāvakas are like withered seeds.
"One cannot attain Buddhahood. Now, having heard that Śāriputra has received his prediction, he is filled with joy.

Regarding the statement "I vow that we shall both achieve [enlightenment] together," the commentary says: "The word 'together' (雙) signifies possessing two kinds of life-span, manifesting that his vow has been fulfilled; therefore, the Venerable One spoke thus."
This contains both meanings. If one were to speak only of "Wisdom-Life" (*prajñājīvita*), the meaning of "longevity" (*āyuṣmat*) would be omitted;

thus, it could not be called "Venerable" (*āyuṣmat*). Since it contains both meanings—both "Wisdom-Life" and "Longevity"—it is named "Venerable. Because both are fully possessed, it is called a "double accomplishment" (*ubhayasampad*).

This is because the vow has been fulfilled and because it is an expression of praise for that vow. The *Śū* (Commentary) points out: "If one speaks only of 'Wisdom-Life,' the meaning is deficient. Lu Ying says: "Wisdom-Life."

The pair [of terms] may be praised as belonging to the noble ones (*ārya*). For the noble ones take wisdom as their life, and these are what they collectively praise. They may be wished for as belonging to ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*).
For ordinary persons take the constant longevity of the body as their life, and these are what they collectively wish for. Now, the Venerable One possesses both of these lives equally.
Therefore, it is said that they are "doubly accomplished" (*dvaya-saṃpanna*). The *Chao* states: "The praise and the vow are exceedingly long; 'doubly accomplished' does not exhaust [the meaning].

The intent of the *Shu* is that "doubly accomplished" does not anticipate Subhūti’s understanding. The meaning is that since the worldly lifespan (*laukika-āyus*) and the noble life-force (*ārya-jīvita*) are each distinct, the single term "possessing a lifespan" (*āyuṣmat*) encompasses both meanings, namely, praise and the vow.
It does not refer to the expression "possessing wisdom-life" (*prajñājīvita*), nor does it employ the expression "possessing bodily lifespan" (*kāyāyus*). Therefore, it is so stated.
The Venerable One does not say "life of wisdom" (*prajñājīvita*). He speaks of understanding as the cause for being a Venerable One; this constitutes a pair of accomplishments.

Regarding the statement that one's name is manifested through virtue, the commentary says: Subhūti is foremost in understanding emptiness. The wisdom that understands emptiness belongs to *prajñā* (wisdom).
Because he is said to have "wisdom as his life," it is called "virtue. Question: Among the four great śrāvakas, Kāśyapa is the eldest. Why...
Therefore, Subhūti’s name is listed first. The answer is that this is done to first clarify the events within the Prajñāpāramitā assembly.
Formerly, he was also present there when the three gates of emptiness were established; since Subhūti was foremost in understanding emptiness, he is listed first.
This merely clarifies his preeminence and does not distinguish the sequence of the other disciples. Otherwise, how could Kāśyapa ever be placed after Candra-kumāra-bhadra?
Regarding the "near" explanation through parables, this refers to the aforementioned Parable of the Burning House.

Regarding the "far" hearing of the bestowal of predictions, this refers to the initial bestowal of the prediction upon Śāriputra at the beginning of the Parable Chapter. Alternatively, it refers to what is heard in the Chapter on the Expedient Means:
"Whether śrāvakas or bodhisattvas, if they hear the Dharma I preach, even so much as a single verse, they shall all attain Buddhahood."
There is no doubt that this is not because they have personally heard their own prediction (vyākaraṇa), for it has not yet been spoken.
As for the statement "the first rose from his seat": those of the two vehicles (dvayayāna) exclusively delight in nirvāṇa and loathe saṃsāra;
since they lack the activity of benefiting others, when they give rise to the Great Mind (mahācitta) as if being born anew, this is called "rising from one's seat."

Regarding what is called the Bodhisattva precepts: these are the *saṃvara-śīla* (precepts of restraint) among the three clusters of precepts (*tri-saṃvara*). It is not that they were not previously observed;
however, because those [previously] observed were for the sake of great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), this explanation is given.
Regarding the expression "performing auspicious acts": baring the right shoulder is the emblem of diligence; it signifies the performance of auspicious deeds.
Question: Why does one not bare the left shoulder? Answer: In all activities performed, the right side is used first;
the right is the direction of conformity. The newly translated *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "partially covering the left shoulder," which does not mention the right shoulder.
Regarding the term "concealing": because it is concealed in other places as well, it can be said to be partial.
Regarding the term "right knee": because one now generates the Great Mind (mahācitta), which is like the earth.

Regarding the phrase "the five, such as single-mindedness, etc.": in former days, one already generated the Mahāyāna mind, and within one's body there are also the seeds of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha).
By nature, it cannot be called "one mind. Today, by abandoning the Two Vehicles and returning to the One Vehicle, one no longer pursues other objects; this is what is called "one mind.
As for the phrase "the six directions within the palm," the Two Vehicles abandon the provisional to grasp the real, which is like a single hand. The Tathāgata accords with them in this way.

He preached the Lotus Sutra. "Joining the hands" is like the teaching of joining two hands; it is named "joining the palms" (*añjali*) because it is like two people in the world placing the palms of their hands facing one another.

As for "bowing with the body bent sevenfold," this signifies that both body and mind are humbly submissive; thus, while the inner mind accords with the Buddha, the external form is one of bowed reverence.

In the past, since his mind had not yet turned [toward the Dharma], his physical body was likewise haughty; thus, it is said that both body and mind were unwilling to comply with the Buddha, which is why he is described as "bending his body.
Regarding the phrase "eightfold gazing": internally he contemplates the principle, and externally his eyes gaze upon the Buddha; therefore, it is called "gazing. His mind gazes outward.
Regarding the principle underlying the teachings: by relying on this principle, one gazes upon the Dharma-body. The Buddha's teaching is spoken by the Transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya);

at the very moment one hears the teaching, one beholds the body of the Transformation Buddha. One contemplates the Dharma-body by relying on the principle, and contemplates the Transformation-body Buddha by relying on the teaching.

Regarding the phrase "saying nine and addressing the Buddha," etc.: since their inner minds were thus, they looked toward the Buddha with external gestures and spoke words expressing their faith and understanding of the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the phrase "dwelling at the head of the Saṃgha," etc.: the question is, why did they not aspire to the Mahāyāna in the past? The answer is from the Sūtra: "We..."
