Regarding the phrase "equal to others": since it is stated that they do not fall into the evil realms (*durgati*), how can it be that a "poor son" regresses and flows through birth and death (*saṃsāra*)?

The Commentary answers: "That [statement] refers to the superior grade (*uttama-prakāra) and so forth. Superior-grade right view is precisely wisdom (*prajñā*). The term "superior" (*adhimātra*) is intended to reveal that this is the mind of preparatory application (*prayoga-citta*).
The meaning of the treatise’s answer is that the superior-grade generation of the mind (*cittotpāda*) is indeed non-retrogressive, whereas the middle and lower grades of generating the mind are...
[The text] concludes. Since the impoverished son withdrew on that day, it is clear that this was the awakening of the middle or lower grades of mind. Question:
I do not yet understand whether these three grades are established in relation to the three vehicles, or whether there are three grades within each individual vehicle.
Answer: Within each of the three vehicles, there are three grades. However, we take only those three grades from within the Mahāyāna. If one awakens [the mind] in the Mahāyāna...
If one rides upon the superior grade of mind, then there is no falling back. If one gives rise to the middle grade of the Mahāyāna mind, one falls back and enters the Two Vehicles.
If one gives rise to the inferior grade of the Mahāyāna mind, one falls back into birth and death, entering directly into the three miserable realms.

A second interpretation states: giving rise to the mind of a Śrāvaka is the inferior grade; giving rise to the mind of a Pratyekabuddha is the middle grade; and giving rise to the Mahāyāna mind is the superior grade.
Third, it is said: "Only those with the Mahāyāna lineage (gotra) are fixed in the Mahāyāna; once they have resolved their minds, they do not regress.

Those with the Śrāvaka lineage, the Bodhisattva lineage, or the Pratyekabuddha lineage are inferior; this is termed 'lineage' (gotra), and because it belongs to the middle or lower grades of resolve, one regresses immediately.
Now, in contrast to that, when the supreme grade of right view (samyag-dṛṣṭi) is established through the Dharma, even if one passes through a thousand lifetimes, [one does not regress]."

Regarding "retrogression," it does not exceed the two interpretations mentioned above. Question: Experiencing a thousand lifetimes and flowing through birth and death with retrogression—both are birth and death;

what is the difference between them? Answer: "A thousand lifetimes" refers exclusively to the two realms of humans and devas. "Flowing through retrogression" refers to rushing through the five realms of existence (*pañcagati*).
Another explanation says: there are those who have generated the superior resolve (*adhimukti-citta*), and although they pass through a thousand lifetimes...

There is no falling back. Among these, there are those who have generated the aspiration for enlightenment at a middling or inferior level; though they may pass through a thousand lifetimes, they will nonetheless fall back.

There are those who, throughout these thousand lifetimes, remain within the two realms of humans and devas. There are also those who, after passing through these thousand lifetimes, advance to the stages of the Two Vehicles, yet it is not impossible that they may subsequently fall back.

Regarding the phrase "the mind is not yet firm": it is a metaphor for what was said above concerning an eight- or ten-year-old child who abandons his father, flees to another land, and does not return for fifty years.
In terms of the Dharma, the seed of the bodhicitta within the bodies of those of the Two Vehicles is called the "father," in reference to the principle expounded in the *Lotus Sūtra*.
To listen to the teaching with single-minded devotion is called "drawing near to the father"; if one does not do so with single-mindedness...
When the mind retreats from cultivation due to the causes of hearing [the teachings], it is called "abandoning the father.
Regarding the phrase "turning one's back on the teaching and departing," Zhang Jing says: "Turning one's back on the good is 'escaping'; following after evil is 'departing.

To be unwilling to diligently seek the principles of the Mahāyāna teachings is like a single instance of avoiding one's father; entering into birth and death is what is meant by 'escaping and departing.'"

What is called "another country" refers to *saṃsāra*. "Fifty years" signifies the meaning of dwelling for a long time. Long-term residence is not to be enjoyed; it is not a place where one grows and dwells in security.
While one could live freely within one's own home, for what reason does one act as a guest in another country? In every matter, one sighs that it is difficult to endure.
It is suffering beyond the limit of suffering, for it cannot be loved or delighted in. Thus, it is taught in the Dharma that there is no peace within the three realms.
Furthermore, one cannot remain because of the oppression of birth and death. A Hu horse longs for the north wind; a bird of Yueh dwells on the southern branch.
One constantly remembers one's native land as one's own dwelling place. Birth and death are a foreign land; the Buddha-dharma is one's own country.
To say that the Buddha-dharma is one's own country means that it is capable of enduring for a long time. Thus, a sutra says: "Gradually traveling on, he encountered his way back to his native land.
Furthermore, the *Awakening of Faith* says: "Returning to the source means returning to the root of birth and death; returning to the fountainhead of the Buddha-dharma."
This is because there exists within one's own body the original seed of bodhi.

As for the statement "in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*," this reconciles apparent contradictions in the text. Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* speaks of those who lack the spiritual lineage (*agotra*), for whom the Buddha-dharma is like a foreign land and not their own portion.
Regarding the phrase "by means of this and that": "this" refers to this very sutra; "that" refers to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

Regarding the phrase "by means of this having a nature": this refers to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, which takes the existence of spiritual lineage (*gotra*) and the arousal of the resolve for the Buddha-dharma as its own country, and takes birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) as another country.

Regarding the statement that they are "without nature": the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* regards the cycle of birth and death prior to the arousal of the mind—whether one lacks the spiritual lineage (*agotra*) or possesses it—as their own country, and the Buddha-dharma as another country.
The statement "previously, by means of the three grades" serves as a general response to external objections. Question:
Why, in the preceding Parable of the Burning House, did you say, "This triple world is all mine; all the sentient beings within it are my children"?
According to the preceding scriptural passages, all worlds are already the property of the Buddha. For what reason do you now divide the kingdom and treat others as outsiders?
The author himself answers in the commentary, saying: "Now, by means of 'other lands' and so forth," he answers the previous point regarding the Buddha’s other realms.

Within the three realms (*tridhātu*), one does not discuss defilement or purity; all are the dwelling place of the Tathāgata. When viewed from the perspective of the three realms in relation to the Master who performs the transformation, they constitute a single burning house.
This [point] is made from within the perspective of those being transformed, viewing the Buddhadharma of the Three Vehicles as pure; this is one's own land.
Viewing birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) as defiled is called "another country. If it is pure, one takes the Buddha-dharma as one's own country and birth-and-death as another country;
if it is defiled, one takes the Buddha-dharma as another country and birth-and-death as one's own country (just as a single object is perceived differently according to one's understanding).
Regarding the statement "furthermore, based on the explanation for ordinary beings": the Buddha’s [consciousness] is a transformation of that which is untainted (*anāsrava*).

Just as the transforming consciousness and its transformed objects are treated as one, here we speak of the Buddha’s transforming untainted mind as a whole, collectively termed "one's own realm" (*svadeśa*).

The transformations of the tainted consciousnesses (*sāsrava-vijñāna*) of ordinary beings are, with respect to the tainted objects they perceive, collectively termed "another's realm" (*paradeśa*). Furthermore, based on the sentient beings to be converted, it is said that there are two types of persons.
First, ordinary beings; second, noble ones. From the perspective of the noble ones, the Buddha-dharma is their own country and birth-and-death is another country;
from the perspective of ordinary beings, birth-and-death is their own country and the Buddha-dharma is another country (this interpretation is superior).

Regarding the phrase "based on great compassion" (*mahākaruṇā*): as for great compassion, it refers solely to taking birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) as one’s home; because one abandons nirvāṇa and enters into birth-and-death.
If great wisdom (*mahājñāna*) speaks, it describes birth-and-death as a foreign land and the Buddha-dharma as one’s own country; thus, one feels weary of birth-and-death and enters nirvāṇa.

Regarding the phrase "metaphorical explanations following the words" and so forth: this refers to the analogy of the names of countries, collectively clarifying the countries mentioned within this chapter.
As for the mention of "the first and the third": the first refers to abandoning one's father and fleeing to dwell long in another country;

the third refers to engaging in the lending and taking of interest throughout other countries. The second refers to traveling by stages until encountering one’s way back toward one's home country. The fourth... [text ends].
The four stages traverse the kingdoms and cities; these two are called "kingdoms" in relation to the Buddha-dharma of the Three Vehicles.
The fifth is the kingdom of the human king, which refers to kings, ministers, kṣatriyas, and householders. Alternatively, it may be explained through analogy:
the brahmins, kṣatriyas, and householders are analogous to the four assemblies of the Buddha-dharma.

Regarding the statement "ten up to fifty": within the five destinies (*pañca-gati*), there are five seeds for each destiny consisting of the five links—consciousness and so forth—which are produced by the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
As for those ten unwholesome paths of action (*daśa-akuśala-karmapatha*), they are of three grades; the ten wholesome paths of action have only two grades.
Now, superior-grade unwholesome paths of action provide the support for the five seeds of the hell realm. That which is supported [is as follows].

This refers to the ten [factors] that serve as the support for speech; it specifically concerns the seeds of names and phrases (*nāma-pada-vyañjana*) which serve as the support, and not the seeds of karma which serve as the support for speech.
Furthermore, it refers specifically to these very seeds of names and phrases.
The delimitation of matter and mind that maintains continuity is precisely the meaning of "fruit. Inferior unwholesome karma provides the seeds for the five constituents of the hungry ghost realm;
this is called the twenty [factors]. Inferior unwholesome karma provides the seeds for the five constituents of the animal realm;
this is called the twenty [factors]. Wholesome karma is divided into only two grades and not three. Inferior wholesome karma provides the seeds for the five constituents of the human realm.

The seeds are called "forty. When superior-grade wholesome karma provides the seeds for the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the five factors (*pañcāṅga*) of the upper realms, they are called "fifty years.
The word "or" (*vā*) is an indefinite term. It is analogous to the aforementioned impoverished son who goes to another country for either ten or fifty years;
in the discourse on the Dharma, it refers to going into hell, which is called "ten," or going into the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*).
The name "twenty" refers to those among the hungry ghosts; "thirty" refers to those among the animals; up to "forty" for those among human beings;
and "fifty years" for those among the devas. Alternatively, it may refer to the full cycle through the five realms of existence, which is why it is called fifty.
Regarding the statement that one "again sees the Buddha within [the state of] speech": this refers to seeing the Buddha once more before the Mahāyāna bodhicitta has yet regressed.
This is precisely what it means to have reached the city of the Mahāyāna—to hear the Mahāyāna Dharma and behold twenty thousand transformation bodies (nirmāṇakāya) of the Buddha. Question:

Previously, it was stated that falling back into the flow of birth and death constitutes a regression of the mind. How can it be said here, then, that this is "before the Mahāyāna [mind] has regressed"?
Before his heart, he again beheld the Buddha. Regarding the previous answer concerning those who "retreat and flow away":

this refers only to those who do not single-mindedly seek the Buddha and who turn their backs on the teachings to commit evil; it does not mean that they have retreated from the Great Mind (mahācitta).

The meaning is that once they have encountered a Buddha and generated the mind of Mahāyāna, they later retreat again; having retreated, they encounter a Buddha once more and generate the mind of Mahāyāna. In this manner, it continues for thousands of millions of times.
[They] turn back. Having already resolved their minds [for enlightenment], they yet regress. This scriptural passage concerns those of the Two Vehicles who encounter various Buddhas;
all are transformed by them through the Mahāyāna Dharma, and not yet through the Hīnayāna Dharma. All of these fall within the scope of being taught and transformed by twenty thousand Buddhas.
Therefore, it was previously stated that "in life after life, he had already received transformation through the Buddha.
The phrase "the nature of a single faculty" refers to the five faculties, such as faith and the rest.
The phrase "as his years grew large" is a metaphor for when the aforementioned impoverished son first fled, at the age of nine or ten, [referring to his] body.

His age was still young, yet he had been away for a long time. As his son grew up and reached adulthood, he did not return; as his years increased, his resources for sustenance were exhausted, yet he still did not return.
According to the Dharma, when he first heard the teaching from the sixteenth prince, he was perfumed by it and attained the seeds of the Great Vehicle’s perfect bodhicitta.
These newly perfumed seeds have grown day by day over the course of many years.
Therefore, it is called "grown large.
As for the phrase "furthermore impoverished," "furthermore" means to increase. Wearing a hemp garment in the twelfth month—here, "furthermore" (fu) means to smolder.

Because they have not cultivated merit, they are called "impoverished"; because they have not cultivated wisdom, they are called "impoverished and distressed. This is the same as what was said in the first cycle: "I observe with my Buddha-eye..."
The sentient beings of the six realms—those who are impoverished and lack merit and wisdom, and so forth—are likewise equal to those in the lower destinies.
It is, for example, like a poor person who goes to the house of a relative or friend; that house is exceedingly wealthy and fully provided with all necessities.

The phrase "galloping in the four directions" is synonymous with "running about. It refers to the arising of form and the arising of power within the midst of the four modes of birth—womb, egg, moisture, and transformation—which is termed "galloping in the four directions.
The commentary on the sutra states: "Birth, old age, sickness, and death circulate and succeed one another;
one is oppressed by the suffering of the four modes of birth."
Regarding the statement "the four rules for exiting suffering," this refers to seeking a way out. Observing fasts and precepts is called "seeking food and clothing.

Furthermore, because one partakes of the food of the True Teaching and the water of Right Principle, it is also termed "seeking. To grow weary of the three miserable realms while clinging to the human and celestial realms, and to loathe great suffering while hoping for minor pleasures, is called "seeking food.
As the Son of Heaven said: "I am one who is already satiated; how could I wear a belt? (i.e., I have no further need).
And they do not eat.
As for the phrase "wandering gradually," it refers to wandering at one's leisure. Because they do not single-mindedly seek the Buddha-dharma, it is called "gradual.
Driven by their spiritual lineage (*gotra*), they proceed spontaneously; because what they do is not ultimate, it is called "wandering."

Regarding the phrase "encountering the way back to one's native land": it refers to returning from within the teachings of the Three Vehicles (Triyāna). This is called "encountering the way back to one's native land.

As explained above, the impoverished son had no intention of returning; he was made to work as a hired laborer, yet through the power of his faith and his own footsteps, he suddenly arrived at his native land.

In terms of the Dharma, this means that while the impoverished son wanders through the cycle of birth and death across the five realms of existence (*pañcagati*), he intends merely to travel between the human and celestial realms to escape the three [lower] states.
Oppressed by the suffering of being smeared [with afflictions], one suddenly encounters the teachings of the Three Vehicles; this is like returning to one's own native land.

Regarding the statement that "the initial teaching arouses the great mind" and so forth, this applies generally to the preceding analogy of falling back into the flow of birth and death and then again seeing the Buddha.
Regarding the phrase "conforming to what was previously cultivated" and so forth: this does not mean that the Mahāyāna mind has regressed.

Rather, it is called "conforming to what was previously cultivated" because one has merely regressed into the cycle of birth and death; the original Mahāyāna mind has not regressed. Upon hearing the Mahāyāna once again, it is said to conform to what was originally practiced.
Regarding the scriptural passage beginning with "His father came first," it asks: Does the elder run after his son to seek him? The answer is:
Although the son travels a thousand *li*, the father’s heart remains with him from the start. For example, as the scripture says (and so forth): "The elder has only one son;
having lost him, he searches for him within the house. He cannot sit at ease; he suffers from feverish distress (*dausthulya*). How much more so for wealth and goods that have no owner?"
It is unavoidable that one must return to one’s country to build a city and dwell there.

Regarding the statement, "Although it was said previously that they were already equal," the question asks: if the teachings of the sixteen princes were originally about generating the resolve for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), why is it now said that they sought sons but could not find them?

The answer in the commentary states, "Although it was said previously," etc.; the intended meaning is that after initially generating the resolve, they subsequently regressed and turned their backs on the teachings and principles.
This is called "seeking and not obtaining. To lose it midway is the same as never having obtained it at all. Therefore, these twenty thousand Buddhas come again to teach the arousal of the mind;
this is called "stopping within the city. The city is located within the kingdom, not in another country.
Regarding the statement "seeking sons but not finding them": after the sixteen princes, [the Buddha] intended to further use the Mahāyāna to transform sentient beings;

however, they withdrew their minds and ceased their studies, refusing to resolve to generate the bodhicitta. This is called "seeking sons but not finding them. This refers to the period following their regression of mind;

it does not mean that they never studied at all, which would be called "not finding" in the sense of total failure. As the Sūtra says: "If I encounter sentient beings, I teach them all to resemble the Buddha."

As for the Way, sentient beings withdraw from it of their own accord; therefore, it is said that they previously sought it but could not obtain it. Their lack of single-minded pursuit is what is meant by "withdrawing.
It is not that [the Buddha] does not preach it to them; rather, when one looks toward the Buddha’s preaching, there is no cessation.

Regarding the phrase "stopping at one city": this refers to stopping at the city of the Mahāyāna within the midst of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). At first glance, it may seem as though birth and death are being called a "city," but that is not the intended meaning.
The two characters for "birth and death" (*saṃsāra*) serve to explain the meaning of the character "middle. As for "stopping" (*zhi*), some say it means to halt or abandon;
they claim that having abandoned the city of the Mahāyāna teachings and failed to find his son, he ceased speaking—this is called "stopping. This interpretation is incorrect.
This "intention" refers generally to the Buddha’s three vehicles as a kingdom; the Mahāyāna is like a city within that kingdom. "Abiding" means dwelling.
This is a metaphor for what was said above: the elder, unable to find his son, built a city in another country to dwell in himself while waiting for his son.
In terms of the Dharma, this means that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is left behind within the realm of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) according to principle.
Regarding "dwelling in the teaching": it is like a father being in a city. This means that the Buddha-body is the principle (*artha*) expounded by the Mahāyāna sublime Dharma teaching;
this is called "staying within the city. Question: From what perspective is the Mahāyāna spoken of as a "city" in relation to the teaching? Answer:

This sutra says, "The Buddha himself abides in the Mahāyāna," and the Many Treasures Stūpa (*Prabhūtaratna*) replies, "How much more so for the teaching within the stūpa—how much more so for the principle seen by the Buddha? Question: According to what follows below...

In the past, while in his own capital, he harbored anxiety and searched for one who resembled the Buddha; this was like seeking a son within one's own country rather than seeking him in another country.
[The interlocutor] replies: "Not so. For in the subsequent passage, he likewise seeks him within his own capital—seeking his son within the city of the Mahāyāna.

Regarding the phrase "about to expound the Mahāyāna," the *Chaoyi* (Excerpts) states: "Intending to expound the Mahāyāna so as to cause others to generate the Great Resolve is called 'about to expound.

This explains the reason for expounding the Mahāyāna. Now, I say this is not so. As it was previously stated, "I have constantly taught and transformed you," this constitutes what has already been expounded;
how then can it be said that he is "about to expound" it? Answer: My current interpretation of "about to" (*jiang*) is that it refers to the Mahāyāna which he is about to expound.
It is used as a city; it does not refer to taking other dharmas. "Jiang" (將) means to take. It is like saying, "I shall take this money to buy such-and-such an object.
Regarding the phrase "providing one's own resources," it refers to asking after the hundred insects and seven birds, all of whom were his children. Once the elder had sought out his children...
He built a city elsewhere to dwell, having finally found his son. [The father asks: "Do you not think of your kingdom, your wealth, and so forth?

The response in the commentary states, "From this point downward," etc. The intention of Jiaxiang is as follows: The impoverished son has turned his back on his father and wandered through the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), suffering in poverty and hardship.

Now, seeing that he has lost his son, the father’s fruit of fulfillment is such that he attains Buddhahood, endowed with all virtues; thus his house is called "greatly wealthy," possessing immeasurable riches and treasures.

Regarding the statement "conditioned granaries and unconditioned [treasuries]," that which contains grain, barley, and so forth is called a "granary" (*koṣṭha*); that which contains gold, silver, and so forth is called a "treasury" (*kośa*).
Grain, barley, seeds, and the like possess the quality of growth, just as the four wisdoms of enlightenment arise from seeds; thus they are called "granaries.

Specifically, the eighth consciousness is the granary that stores the uncontaminated seeds of the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body) enlightenment; thus it is called a "granary. [The same applies to] gold and silver.
It has the meaning of being equal and without growth. It is like *nirvāṇa*, which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and neither arises nor ceases.

As for the explanations of Kuījia: that which nourishes the life of wisdom is like a granary; that which houses the *dharmakāya* is like a storehouse. The meaning of "fullness" is like being filled to capacity; the meaning of "overflowing" is like the spilling forth of utility.
Furthermore, in terms of essence, it is called "full," while the arising of its function is like "overflowing."
Regarding what is called the *Bowuzhi*, it was composed by Zhang Hua, the Minister of Works during the Jin dynasty. It provides explanations and interpretations of written texts.
As for the term "dou" (斗), in ancient times three *chuan* (舛) were taken as one *dou*, and three *dou* were taken as one *hu* (斛). In the present day, one *shi* (石) is called one *hu*.
This merely takes the ancient measure of three *dou* being called a *hu* as a point of comparison.

Regarding the scriptural statement that there are "many servants": a questioner asks, "Since the householder’s family is so immensely wealthy with immeasurable assets, I wonder how many more servants he possesses?
How many strong elephants, horses, and chariots does he have? The answer is: the scripture states that there are "many servants," and so forth.
The mention of "whips and spurs" and so forth explains the meaning of servants and attendants. The one hundred and eight afflictions are called "many.
Regarding the phrase "skillful means" and so forth: a Son of Heaven may have seven ministers who remonstrate against him; even if he lacks the Way, he does not lose his realm.
That a minister may, in jest or in earnest, offer praise or criticism to their lord—bringing the lord to a level above Yao and Shun—is entirely due to these [skillful means].

Regarding the employment of wise ministers: a state takes its high ministers as its treasure. Ministers do not exist apart from the king; it is by relying upon the king that ministers first come into being.
Skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) does not exist apart from subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*); it is by relying on wisdom that skillful means and clever application arise.
Just as ministers assist the king in governance and transformation so as to bring his rule into parity with that of Yao and Shun, this is entirely due to the skillful means of the ministers.

Skillful means. Throughout three incalculable eons, he assisted the Tathāgata, enabling the Tathāgata to become the Great Teacher of the triple world and the compassionate father of the four modes of birth;
all of this was due to his skillfulness in expedient means.
Regarding the statement that the "wonderful vows and powers" are like this: the wonderful vows are like the officials, while the ten powers are like the common people.
The officials are the minor functionaries who, for the sake of the elder’s household, calculate the money and goods, knowing both expenditures and revenues. The common people are the subjects;
they are the laborers for the elder’s household. While the great elder sits comfortably on the ground, he causes them to mix the mud, carry bricks, and exert their physical strength.

Furthermore, regarding the discourse on the Dharma: the "wondrous vows" refer to the Four Great Vows. To vow to deliver sentient beings and then relinquish them once they have been delivered is called "knowing how to exit.
To cause those not yet delivered to be delivered and to cause them to enter into the Buddha-Dharma is called "knowing how to enter.
It is like a registrar handling cases and managing funds: when someone takes money out, it is called "knowing how to exit"; when someone pays interest, it is called "knowing how to enter."
"Qianlai" (錢來) means "knowing entry"; thus, it refers to an official who knows both income and expenditure.

Alternatively, on the Buddha’s body, self-benefiting merit is called "knowing entry," while merit benefiting others is called "knowing exit. As for "powers" (*bala*), these are the ten powers of the Tathāgata’s body, which can destroy the celestial Māras and subdue all non-Buddhists;
they include such feats as transforming the great earth into mountains of gold or swallowing the vast ocean with a single hair.

Regarding the statement that the five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā) are like elephants and so forth: just as worldly elephants, horses, and carriages can transport heavy loads over great distances, the Tathāgata’s five supernormal powers can transport ordinary beings to the state of sainthood.
While elephants and horses are ridden by common people, the five supernormal powers are mounted by the noble ones (ārya).
As they proceeded toward the world-system of Wild Horses (Aśvakarṇa), it rained down four kinds of flowers from the heavens, and the earth shook in six ways.
Regarding "movement" and so forth:
the five vehicles are called "carriages" because they transport and carry sentient beings across; they are also the implements for the play and recreation of all worthies and sages.
In the house of the elder, there were countless oxen for carriages; in ancient times, there were even those who possessed a thousand teams of horses.

Regarding the phrase "eighty-four thousand": just as a thousand sheep can eat grass and sever it, thereby causing households to become increasingly wealthy while providing for the poverty of others, so too do the eighty-four thousand modes of practice sever evil and provide nourishment for the roots of goodness in sentient beings.
Regarding the statement that "guest profits are abundant and extensive," this explains the profit derived from the circulation of capital in the householder’s wealth.
When the householder’s wealth goes out, it returns with profit; thus, it is called "having profit on the outgoing. When the wealth comes back in, it arrives with profit;
the goods brought in are acquired at a favorable price, which is called "having profit on the incoming."

Regarding the teachings on the ultimate and conventional truths (*paramārtha-satya* and *saṃvṛti-satya*): the teachings on the ultimate and conventional truths are like the original capital provided by a merchant for his business.

Using these teachings on the ultimate and conventional truths to transform sentient beings is called "income and profit. Within the teachings, that which elucidates untainted (*anāsrava*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) merit is called the teaching on the ultimate truth.

Within the teachings, that which elucidates the tainted (*sāsrava*) karmic fruits and retributions of humans and devas is called the teaching on the conventional truth. Within the teachings, [that which] speaks of cessation...

Cultivating evil leads to suffering, whereas cultivating goodness leads to the departure from suffering; this is called the benefit of exiting [samsara]. Within the teachings of the ultimate and conventional truths, it is said that for one who cultivates goodness, there is happiness;

this is called the benefit of entering [the path]. As for the statement "entering the Buddha-dharma" and so forth: when sentient beings resolve their minds and enter into the Buddha-dharma, this is called the benefit of entering. To speak of this for others...
The Dharma causes others to emerge from birth and death; therefore, it is called "benefit for emergence. Here, the teaching of the Dharma is taken as the benefit.

Regarding the phrase "or the teachings of the three vehicles," etc.: the teachings of the three vehicles are like wealth, and the Buddha is the owner of that wealth. The noble ones of the three vehicles are like merchants.
Within the Pure Land, the Buddha teaches the doctrines of the three natures, the three non-natures, and the six perfections, just as one sits at a shop.
O Wealthy Master, when a Bodhisattva attends an assembly to hear the Dharma, it is like a merchant displaying his wares.

Emerging from a pure land and entering into a defiled land, they travel through the marketplace of the three realms among the two destinies of devas and humans, selling their wares through their vows and practices.

Just as Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva manifests nineteen types of bodies to preach the Dharma and transform sentient beings—this is called "selling wares"—and in doing so, there is profit even upon emerging.

There is also benefit in entering [the path]. It is like a person who borrows capital from a sutra and, through its transformation, gains a share of the profit; the noble assembly of the Three Vehicles is likewise.
Furthermore, when one enters to study the Buddha-dharma, it is called "external benefit"; benefiting other sentient beings is called "internal benefit. When a Bodhisattva preaches the Dharma...

Attaining a portion of the merit of self-benefit is called "entering benefit. Question: Since the teachings for humans and devas involve remaining within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), how can this be called "benefit"?

Answer: It is called "benefit" because it is superior to the three miserable realms (*durgati*). By taking the observance of the five or eight precepts as the cause, one obtains the body of a human or a deva.
Relying upon this body, one subsequently enters the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*). As the Sūtra says: "To escape the calamity of fire and preserve one's life and limb is not a falsehood."

Why is this? If one were to preserve their life and body, they would have already obtained objects of pleasure; yet the elder’s wealth and goods would not yet exist, resulting in a fruitless journey without profit.
Likewise, if the Tathāgata’s Dharma-gates of the five vehicles do not yet exist, the merit of benefiting others will not be accomplished.
For example, when Bakula maintained the precept against killing, he was killed by his stepmother five times, yet he did not die; this is called the benefit of the Dharma (*dharmārtha*).
Furthermore, by observing a one-day fast, he obtained five hundred days' worth of surplus provisions; this is called worldly benefit (*artha*).

If one expounds the teachings of the Two Vehicles, sentient beings who hear them will attain the fruits of the Two Vehicles, quickly obtaining threefold or fivefold benefits. Moreover, [it is explained as follows]:
At the assembly on Vulture Peak, when the Tathāgata preached the Lotus Sūtra, he was like a wealthy merchant sitting in his shop;
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva hearing the Lotus Sūtra was like the goods in the shop being transported to and from the sea for the purpose of teaching and transforming others, like a traveling merchant.
He transformed the dragon girl so that she attained Buddhahood, and the multitude gathered at the ocean assembly was beyond what words can proclaim or what the mind can fathom.

It may appear as though one has gained a thousandfold or ten-thousandfold profit; yet, if one encounters sentient beings who lack the spiritual lineage (*agotra*), who refuse to resolve their minds toward enlightenment,

and who slander the Buddha and the sutras, falling into the great hells— this is called "violating the sutra and losing the path of the currency," like withered and rotten barley, which fundamentally results in a loss of three hundred.

Regarding the phrase "pervading birth and death" (*saṃsāra*), it is asked: Since the Buddha appears only within the human and celestial realms of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), how can it be said that his teaching pervades birth and death?
Answer: Although his physical body does not extend everywhere, it is like a king residing in Hao (Hào) who contemplates the distant frontiers;

though his person does not move, his law reaches all corners of the world. Changjing said: "A world where there is a Buddha is called 'one's own country' (*svadeśa*); a world where there is no Buddha is called..."
"Other lands. It is also said that the Buddha-dharma is one's own land, while birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is other lands. Question:

Since the Buddha-dharma does not reach the Northern Continent or the three miserable realms (*durgati*), how can it be called "pervasive"? Answer: From a general perspective relative to the noble ones of the Three Vehicles, it may still be called pervasive.
For example, in the case of Avalokiteśvara and others, there is no land throughout the ten directions where they do not manifest their bodies.

Regarding the "holy multitudes of the three vehicles," they are like a worldly master of wealth who manages enterprises everywhere; the ten stages and the three vehicles likewise engage in teaching and transformation in various directions.

Regarding the "merchants and appraisers," those who travel while selling are called merchants (*shāng*), while those who sit and sell are called appraisers (*gù*). The Great Transformation Body Buddha is like a merchant (*jià*).

The statement that "Mahāpratibhāna and others were like merchants" refers to Confucius and his peers. Emperor Wang Mang was also titled King Wenxuan; his parents sacrificed at Mount Nichu and thereby obtained this son.
He served as a *sīkǒu* (Minister of Justice) in the state of Lù, much like how today one might be appointed to a low-ranking official post. This is according to the "Zihan" chapter of the *Lúnyǔ*.
Zi Gong said, "Suppose there were a fine jade here; would one wrap it in a cloth and hide it away, waiting for a good price before selling it?
The *Jing* says: Ma [the commentator] states, "To 'wrap and hide' means to conceal it within a case; 'selling' refers to offering it for sale.
Having obtained a good price, how could one be unwilling to display and sell it? The Master said, "Sell it! Sell it! I am merely waiting for the right price. Ma says, "To sell..."
"Indeed! These are not words for self-promotion; I dwell here awaiting my price. The meaning within these words is this:
Zigong [thought], "Since Confucius possesses the virtue of a sage, even one as insignificant as I must have heard of him. Why is this so?
It is because he does not peddle his wisdom and talents, but keeps his virtue hidden. Thus, by means of this analogy, he sought to fathom his master's intent, comparing Master Zhongni to himself.
However, waiting for a price is the meaning of being a certified merchant. The subsequent statement, "firmly holding goods to wait for the people," means not seeking to sell oneself prematurely.
Within the Dharma, the intent is that the teachings of the Three Vehicles are like jade; their roots are not spoken of because they are hidden within a casket.
Their faculties are mature and capable of hearing [the Dharma], like goods of good value. It is proclaimed everywhere, as if they were being sold.

Regarding the term "gonghu" (public house), this character does not exist in the standard dictionaries. It is an archaic form; it appears only in the *Erya* (Classic of Elegant Phrases) in its phonetic glosses under the character "jia" (price/value). Therefore, I have cited it here.

The term "market tax" (*shi-shui*) is an introductory heading. Within this context, the characters *gu* (valuation) and *jia* (merchant) are identical. *Gu* refers to the broker (*ya*), who is so named because they appraise the value of goods, whether expensive or cheap.

Regarding the "nine occupations" (*jiu-zhi*) of the *Rites of Zhou*: among these nine matters, it corresponds to the sixth, the Great Treasury (*da-fu*), which oversees the market and the local districts. It is the Office of the Market (*shi-si*).

Xiang. Dou Shang. Bei is an assistant. What are called the nine occupations? First is the timely cultivation of the nine grains: millet, broomcorn millet, sorghum, rice, hemp, soybeans, wheat, and so forth.
Second is the management of the state’s forests and woodlands. Third is the Yu and Heng officials gathering mountain materials.

Fourth is the marshes and hunting preserves for raising birds and wild game. Fifth is the five superintendents overseeing the transformation of the eight raw materials. Sixth is the merchants who collect and circulate goods and wealth (upper and middle).

Seventh, the concubines and wives transform and process silk and hemp. Eighth, the handmaidens and servants gather and collect vegetable ingredients. Ninth, the common people lack constant knowledge and instead engage in shifting tasks and reporting matters.

As for what is called the *Baihutong* (Explanations from the White Tiger Hall): Emperor Gaozu of the Han established a hall named the White Tiger Hall (*Baitu Dian*). When there were difficult textual meanings throughout the realm, [scholars would discuss them there].
Yang Xiong provided a comprehensive commentary within this hall; therefore, the hall is named *Baitu Tong* (Comprehensive Explanation of the White Tiger).
As for the term "shang" (商): "shang" refers to deliberation (*shangliang*). What does it mean? It means to appraise goods and wealth and then trade them there; hence it is called "gathering" (*ju*).
Regarding the term "merchant" (*jia*): it refers to firmly holding onto goods while waiting for others to come, which is precisely "selling while sitting.

As for saying that "merchant" is also a general term, the meaning is that "selling while walking" (*xingmai*) is also called "merchant," and "selling while sitting" (*zuomai*) is also called "merchant";
therefore, it is said to be a general term.
Regarding the statement that Xun Ying was in Chu: Xun Ying was a high official of the state of Jin. The states of Jin and Chu were similar to one another in their alternating strength and weakness.
The records state that Jin and Chu frequently raised armies to attack each other. Xun Ying, as a Jin soldier, engaged in battle with the forces of Chu;
he was captured alive by the Chu and released, taken away without being harmed, and remained imprisoned there. A merchant from the state of Zheng entered [that territory].
The administration of the state of Chu was disrupted. Zheng had established friendly relations with Chu, and their diplomatic exchanges proceeded without hindrance.

In secret, they wished to escort Xun Ying back to his own country to devise a plan; they intended to send him out through Zhongguo (the Central States). This proposal has three interpretations in total.
First interpretation: "Chu" (褚) has the meaning of "storing. It refers to intending to place Xun Ying inside a clothing chest (*yilóng*), but he was brought out before it was completed;

thus, he is named "Chuzhong" (褚中). Second interpretation: The character "Chu" is pronounced level-tone (*píngshēng*). It means he was hidden and carried out within a wooden carriage used for infants (*bǎo mùchē*).

Third interpretation: There was a merchant surnamed Chu and named Zhong. He brought him out because the plan had not yet been finalized. In the interim, the State of Jin personally provided gold and silk.
"Ransomed. This means that Zheng was originally a merchant; since he had already been defeated by the Chu, he sold himself to gain wealth—thus one understands the character "jia" (merchant).
He also traveled about selling goods.
As for the mention of Yangzhai, it is the name of a commandery, located two hundred li east of Luozhou. These two layers of meaning prove [that the account] is not [authentic].
"Only sitting while selling" is also a general practice.
Regarding the phrase "the internal path" (up to the "general statement"): Question: What is meant by a "general statement"? Answer:

The intention here is that wandering through various villages and traveling through kingdoms and towns share the same essential nature; therefore, it is called a "general statement. If distinguished according to specific cases, there are differences in their breadth and narrowness.
Therefore, separate settlements are established.
Regarding the phrase "all the teachings of the Dharma and so forth," this specifically designates the essential nature of the kingdoms and settlements.
Regarding the phrase "the intended meaning herein," the "inner path" refers to the Buddha-dharma of the three vehicles; by contrast to the teachings of external paths, one attains the inner path.
This is the name for the dwelling places of those who practice the three vehicles; it is the essence of the "village" (*grāma*).
Regarding the phrase "seeking the essential way of transcendence," this correctly explains the character *you* (to travel). "Traveling" (*you*) carries the meaning of traversing or walking upon.

This is analogous to what was said above regarding the impoverished son who, heading toward his own country, traveled through various prefectures and districts, performing labor and selling his strength—this is called "traveling through various villages. In the context of the Dharma, [it refers to the practitioner's journey].
Commentary: When the impoverished son enters among the Three Vehicles of the Buddhist Dharma to listen to the sutras and receive the precepts, this is called "wandering through the village.
Regarding the phrase "as previously explained in the preceding text," etc., this refutes the ancient masters who assigned the teachings of non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) to the village.

Regarding the phrase "or listening to the preaching of the Dharma, etc.": first, at the time of the general summary, the preaching of the Dharma and the supernormal powers are correlated with the kingdoms and cities.

This is analogous to the aforementioned impoverished son who, for the sake of food and clothing, travels through various kingdoms and cities; he has previously traveled through them while heading toward another country.
It is like returning from the Tubo (Uighur) kingdom after having traveled through various prefectures and districts;
as one goes back and forth, gradually arriving at one’s own country, it is similar to passing through those prefectures and districts. The way of father and son is the nature of Heaven.
Upon reaching one’s own country and passing through its prefectures, one originally has no intention of returning home. This is how the Sixteen Kings are discussed within the Dharma.
"Son, during the time of twenty thousand Buddhas, you were taught the Mahāyāna, yet you fell back into the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

Pressed by the suffering of birth and death, you sought the essential way out and once again encountered the Dharma of the Three Vehicles; however, you could not discern it through analytical selection.

At times you received the precepts, at times you practiced fasting, and at times you paid homage to the Buddhas—this is called 'traversing kingdoms and cities. This is the first interpretation, which generally takes the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of preaching the Dharma as the basis for fear."

"States and towns are not distinguished" means that states and towns are distinct. Regarding the "shallow or deep nature of the Dharma taught": the teaching of the Two Vehicles is shallow, while the teaching of the Mahāyāna is deep.
The supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) of Bodhisattvas are superior, whereas those of the Two Vehicles are inferior; this is termed "traveling through states and towns."

Regarding the phrase "the metaphor of traveling through countries" and so forth: when the impoverished son listens to the Dharma, this is termed "traveling through countries and cities. One might ask:

since this impoverished son has not yet withdrawn his mind from the Mahāyāna, how could he travel through various villages and pass through countries and cities while hearing the teachings of the Hīnayāna?
The answer is: it does not preclude the son from also listening to the Hīnayāna teachings and observing the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.

Regarding the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*): it is simply that [the Great Vehicle] is unwilling to abandon the great for the sake of the small. For example, when the Dharma Master descends from his seat during a lecture on the Vinaya, he refuses to study the Hīnayāna.

As for the statement, "To know whether sentient beings are good or evil," this refers to reaching the City of the Father; it is a metaphor for the aforementioned impoverished son who has no intention [to return].
Returning to his home, within his own kingdom—whether east, west, south, or north—he sought food and clothing by performing manual labor as a hired servant.

Unbeknownst to him, he encountered the city where his father resided. In the Dharma, it is said that the impoverished son has no intention [to hear the teaching], yet he listens to the Mahāyāna through the power of his roots of goodness.
Having encountered the Buddha-dharma, he cannot distinguish between the teachings of the Three Vehicles and the Five Vehicles; he simply listens to them according to his capacity. Suddenly—
Listening to the Mahāyāna teachings is called arriving at the city where his father resides. As for "ou-zang" (否臧): "ou" (否) derives from following [the wrong path] and signifies evil;

"zang" (臧) derives from goodness and signifies the good. It refers to one who, while within the Three Vehicles, encounters followers of the Two Vehicles and hears them preach the Dharma of the Two Vehicles.

Encountering a person of the Mahāyāna and hearing them preach the Mahāyāna Dharma is called "Zang" (Treasure), as it signifies abundance through goodness. Suddenly hearing the teaching of the Middle Way Mahāyāna is called "Arriving at His Father’s House.
Regarding this, there are three interpretations: first, by listening to the depth of the Dharma being preached, one understands "wandering through various villages";

second, by observing the superiority or inferiority of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), one understands "traversing kingdoms and cities"; third, by recognizing the multitude of sages, one understands [the arrival].
Regarding the phrase "by means of Yi-ou-zang": Jie eventually arrived at the city where his father resided.
As for the statement "relying on the subsequent Jie," etc., "Jie" refers to the city and "she" (house) as distinct entities. Question: What is the difference between the city and the house? Answer:

The commentary states, "relying on the subsequent Jie," which indicates that he subsequently encountered his father’s house and stood by its side; it is at that location that the name "Yi" (relying) is applied.
This will be explained later; it shall be chanted here. The *Śāstra* states: "Fortunately encountering the Buddha-dharma, one first hears the Mahāyāna.
This is merely called 'reaching the city,' but not yet 'entering the house. Below, regarding those who have practiced for a long time, it is called 'arriving at the father's house.
Furthermore, the Mahāyāna in its general aspect is called the 'city,' while the Mahāyāna of the Middle Way is like the 'house. Question: Why is the Mahāyāna teaching here called the "city"? Answer:
The Buddha himself abides in the Great Vehicle. Regarding this, Lu Fu states that it should be chanted within [the main text];
it is incorrect to claim that the subsequent commentary cannot be understood and thus the four lines are redundant.
Regarding the scriptural passage, "The father constantly thinks of his son," this refers to Śākyamuni Tathāgata. "Separated from his son" refers to the three classes of śrāvakas.
"More than fifty years" refers to wandering through the five destinies; the term "remaining years" refers to the asuras. Regarding the phrase, "Never having spoken to anyone," the question is:
when asking about illness and desiring a staff or a shoulder-strap, why is it not explained to others? The answer is: because there is a tear in the lining of the robe.
It is as if he were a human being. He pulls at his ears without letting them leave his cheeks. He has never visited the houses of neighbors to the east or west to speak of things intimately.
"My son has been away for a long time without returning. According to the Dharma, he has not awakened for forty years.

He has never, before the assembly of the Buddhas of the ten directions, the great Bodhisattvas, and the multitudes of devas and humans, spoken of the three types of *śrāvakas*. When I was among the sixteen princes...
Regarding this teaching: he had never before spoken of such matters to others. His heart was filled with despondency; though he sought words to express it, he could find none.
When the World-Honored One was a prince among the sixteen sons, he preached the Lotus Sūtra for eighty-four thousand *kalpas* to transform those who were retreating from the path.
At that time, he endured eighty-six thousand *kalpas*, and because his transformative influence was so profound, he ought to have remained non-retrogressive.

On that day, fearing he might retreat, I did not dare say more. Furthermore, I regretted that the Śrāvakas had not earlier conceived the mind of the Mahāyāna, and I lamented that he had not returned home sooner.
A man does not return for three reasons; because of this, more than fifty years have passed since that day.

Regarding the statement "not manifesting speech through speech," Master Mu said: "To manifest means to manifest as a segment. When one contemplates a matter within the mind, that matter does not yet constitute a transgression.
However, if one utters words with the mouth, those words become a segment of action; therefore, one must not fail to restrain speech. This explains the mind harboring regret."
Regarding the scriptural passage on "reflecting upon one's own aging" and so forth: A certain elder reflected that his years had surpassed those of the *púliǔ* tree;

his hair was turning gray, he was distant from heaven and near to earth, and the clatter of his head-dress echoed above him. His sons and daughters had not returned for a long time, and he desired to see them with his own eyes.
His wealth was immense, yet there was no one to whom he could entrust it; fearing it would be lost or scattered, he departed. This is not [the case].
For half a day in the morning, I have gathered together my life’s work of forty-five years; the money and goods I have accumulated, I now intend to distribute today among my sons and daughters.
May these children live for ten thousand generations, with descendants succeeding one another so that the lineage shall never be severed.
For this reason, I have always remembered his son with deep earnestness. As it is said in the *Dharmaparyāya*: "Perhaps even a single phrase [is worth more than] a great mountain... (and so forth).
Furthermore, when one observes the trichiliocosm, there is not even a space the size of a mustard seed that was not a place where a bodhisattva sacrificed his body and life.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "for those such as Jū (Long-lived)" and so forth: this refers to having attained enlightenment many years ago, which is termed "aging.

If referring to the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body), it has been since the attainment of enlightenment for aeons (*kalpas*) as numerous as motes of dust, and is thus termed "aging. Even in the case of the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body), from the perspective of the assembly at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, forty years have passed since the attainment of enlightenment, and this is termed "old age.
Alternatively, even if an emanation body was manifested in a previous previous life, it is likewise termed "a long time since attaining enlightenment."
This is called "old age.
Regarding the statement, "Although there are bodhisattvas and so forth," [the questioner] asks the Buddha: "If all sentient beings are your children, why do you say that you have no offspring?
The commentary answers with the word "although": the intended meaning is that although sentient beings are immeasurable, they have not yet been [given] the voice [of the Dharma].
Because they have heard the prophecy [of their own future enlightenment], it is said that [the Tathāgata] has no sons.
As for the statement "or having few sons," one asks: since the Tathāgata already possesses Bodhisattvas as his sons, why is it said that he has no sons?

The commentary answers by stating "or having few sons" and so forth. This means that regarding the Buddha-dharma attained through the Tathāgata’s cultivation over three great *kalpas*, there is a fear of [its extinction in] *nirvāṇa*...
"Because there was no one to whom he could entrust [the estate], he therefore remembered his son, the śrāvaka.

As for the phrase 'having thought of him, he rejoiced': [the interlocutor] asks, 'The elder possesses no small amount of wealth; he can certainly support himself. Why does he need to seek out his son?'"
The Sūtra answers: "Furthermore, he thought: 'If I obtain a son, I shall personally bestow all my wealth and possessions upon him;
even if it costs me my life, I will submit to it now. But if the son does not come, I shall die without intending to divide [the inheritance].'"

Regarding the statement that he saw his father and then fled in the morning: previously, while traveling through various villages and passing through kingdoms and cities, he had arrived early at his own country.

Yet, within his own country, he originally had no intention of returning home; it was only because he sought food and clothing by performing labor for hire that he traveled back and forth until he reached his father’s house.
Having been there for a long time, he did not return [to his original dwelling], and all his former residences were completely [abandoned].

Unaware, they discourse upon the Dharma; originally having no intention to listen to the Mahāyāna, they hear the sūtras from those who are excluded by their spiritual lineage (gotra), hear the Hīnayāna from those who have received the precepts, and hear the Mahāyāna from others.
Without realizing it, they come to listen to the Middle Way Mahāyāna teaching—this is called "encountering one's father's house."
Regarding "physical and mental diligence," it is stated below that one seeks the essential way of deliverance with a pure body and mind;
this is equivalent to what is said in the analogy: "pushing one another and vying with one another to run."

Regarding the statement "it is not his original mind" (up to) "arriving at his father’s house": it is asked, what is the distinction between first mentioning a "country," then a "city," and finally a "house"? Answer:

This is because those whose faculties awaken to the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) have varying degrees of proximity to its principle. Thus, the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) of the sentient beings to be converted are of three grades.
If those with inferior roots of goodness hear the teaching, they are far from the principle of the One Vehicle, like being in a "country. If...
Those with medium-grade roots of goodness who hear the teaching are relatively close to the principle of the One Vehicle; this is likened to reaching the city.

Those with superior-grade roots of goodness who hear the teaching are closest to the principle of the One Vehicle; this is like arriving at the father’s house. As stated above, within the kingdom there is a city, and within the city there is a house.
In the discussion of the Dharma, the Three Vehicles of the Buddha-Dharma as a whole are like the kingdom, while the Mahāyāna as a general characteristic therein is like the house.
Within the city, there is further the Mahāyāna of the definitive Middle Way, like a father’s house.
Regarding the statement that "the near is born and the distant is matured": "Lufu" (the birthplace) refers to the state of being raw.

When one first possesses the mind of Mahāyāna as an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), one practices for sixty *kalpas*; gradually maturing, one becomes distant from the stage of an ordinary person, which is thus called "distant."

"Ripened" (*pakva*). "Near-ripened" (*upapanna*) refers to those who, in a previous birth prior to Śākyamuni, were born with a disposition toward the dry and arid [states], but upon encountering conditions, fell back and entered the Two Vehicles;

they are called "near-ripened. Second, it refers to looking toward the future: for instance, Śāriputra has only now begun to enter the stage of a śrāvaka and so forth, thus he is called "near-ripened.
After turning the mind [toward enlightenment] and passing through three great eons (*mahākalpa*), one finally attains Buddhahood; this is called "distant ripening."
Regarding the phrase "practitioner of the Mahāyāna teachings": the first clause is the heading; it is also the name of the gate of interpretation.
Regarding the statement that "it can express the principle and can realize the fruit": these two clauses constitute the explanation.
To say that "name" is called a "gate" is a term for designation.

To say "at that time they were unable to," etc., means that although those śrāvakas may have practiced a small portion of the Great Practice and also believed in the Mahāyāna, they were unable to practice it universally or believe in the Mahāyāna in its entirety; thus they are said to "dwell by the side of the gate. This has already been examined and questioned.
This refers to standing at the side.

As for the statement that "the time has not yet fully arrived," if one can universally practice the Great Practice and universally believe in the Mahāyāna, one will then attain entry into the gate and stand upright.
"Standing" is the posture of being about to act; it signifies that one should prepare to extensively hear and extensively practice the conduct of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna). Therefore...
"Standing by the side of the gate" means this.
Regarding the phrase "when walking, one is at ease," etc., within the Mahāyāna, being settled while walking is called "abiding.
Regarding the phrase "furthermore, those of small capacity have not yet realized," Jin says: "Those who are newly learning the Mahāyāna are called 'small,' not those of the Hīnayāna."
It is "small. At that time, one has not yet sought the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna); this is the meaning of being "initially small.

Because the faculties for the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) have not yet grown, they are called "small-capacity" (hīnendriya). Since one has not yet realized the Great Vehicle, it is not called "entering the gate. It indicates a subtle faith and practice; therefore, it is the "side of the gate."

Regarding the scriptural statement "seeing from afar" and so forth, there are three interpretations. First, it is said that while one is still in the stage of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), because their faculties and nature are not yet mature, it is called "seeing from afar";
if they turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*), it is then called "seeing intimately.

Second, it is said that this refers to the stage prior to the [first] bhūmi, where one is distant from the true nature of reality (*tathatā*) as the pervasive principle; hence it is called "seeing from afar. Third, it is said that if one reaches the first bhūmi, one realizes the principle of *tathatā*.
To claim that this is not distinct from the principle within the Buddha’s body and thus is called "direct" (*pratyakṣa*) is incorrect.
The principle of the first stage is a principle within the causal state; because the causal and resultant states are distinct, it is merely called "near-seeing," not "direct seeing."
Now, for those on the stages prior to the bhūmis (*bhūmi-pūrva*), being in proximity [to the Buddha], they are said to "see from afar.

Even if practitioners of the two vehicles (*dvayāyānika*) are in the same location as a *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha, it is still called "seeing from afar" because cause and effect are distinct; thus, it is not called "seeing directly. Third, it is said that this refers to the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*);

in relation to the great *nirmāṇakāya* of the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*), it is also called "seeing from afar. Once one has reached the first bhūmi and beyond, one sees the *saṃbhogakāya*.
The *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body) is called "seeing from nearby.
Regarding the statement "because it departs from the Mahāyāna, etc.," this refers to the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), and is thus called "seeing from afar.

Regarding the statement "the Buddha [possesses] the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) and so forth," the intention is to take the meaning of "fearlessness" itself as the lion; it does not refer to the four fearlessnesses.

"Fei" (畏) refers to the bed (*śayana*). If one were to take the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) as the bed, it would contradict the teachings of other sages. Now, the four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) are taken as the bed.

Regarding the statement "using a jeweled footstool to support [it]," the shape and proportions are closely modeled after a footstool; the stool is placed facing downward, and the cushion is set upon it facing upward.
"Son, 'the feet for one who upholds fear'—the *Jianyao* says: In the discourse on the Dharma, non-greed and non-hatred are taken as the precious footstool to support the feet of the precepts.
For all violations of the precepts arise mostly from greed and hatred; if one is free from greed and hatred, one will be able to maintain the precepts.
Thus, non-greed and non-hatred are like the feet for the training in the precepts."

Regarding the "tracks of training in morality" (*śīla-śikṣā-pada*): non-greed and non-hatred constitute the tracks of training in morality; morality constitutes the track of training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*); and concentration constitutes the track of training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*).
As for the term "brahmin," it carries the meaning of "one of pure conduct. How much more so, then, does this apply to the training in morality?
Regarding the term *kṣatriya*: it refers to the royal lineage who possess sovereignty over affairs; it is a metaphor for wisdom, which is able to exercise sovereignty through discernment.

Regarding the term *gṛhapati* (householder): it has the meaning of "tranquility. This class of householder includes those with few private possessions and great forgiveness, such as Dan-zai Mie-ming (Dantai Memyō).
Unless it was for public business, he never visited Yan’s chamber. This is like the causal conditions prior to the established dharma:
surrounded by the ministers and brahmins on his left and right, within the dharma he discusses the Buddha’s body and its surroundings, adorned with the three trainings.
Furthermore, regarding the term "Mahāyāna": it is sometimes used as a metaphor for the assembly of the three vehicles;
the Mahāyāna is like a brāhmaṇa, the pratyekabuddha is like a kṣatriya, and the śrāvaka is like a householder.
Regarding the "three foundations of mindfulness" and so forth: ordinary persons experience pleasant sensations; because these are agreeable and gratifying, they give rise to attachment.
Because they experience painful sensations, which are oppressive and contrary, they give rise to aversion. Because they experience neutral sensations, which are indifferent, delusion arises.

To illustrate what was said above regarding the elder’s body being adorned with a necklace of genuine pearls: in the Dharma, the three applications of mindfulness (*tri-smṛtyupasthāna*) upon the Buddha’s own body are compared to that pearl necklace.
One person on the left strikes him with a sword; one on the right anoints him with gold; and between them is a third person who neither anoints nor strikes him.
The Tathāgata regards these three people as perfectly equal and without any distinction whatsoever.
Regarding the statement that "ministers and attendants provide protection," this is explained briefly here and not elaborated upon;

it is none other than the three trainings of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom, which are inseparable from subsequently attained gnosis (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*). Furthermore, this is identical to the aforementioned skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).

Just as ministers and attendants do not exist apart from a king, and the existence of ministers and attendants depends upon the king, so too skillful means exists in dependence upon subsequently attained gnosis.
"Officials and people" refers to the wondrous vows, which are the Four Great Vows; "power" refers to the Ten Powers.

Regarding the statement that the mind maintains the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) and so forth, according to the sutras, this is analogous to the description above of the elder’s attendants on his left and right.

"Holding a whisk in his hand" refers to the meaning within the commentary: the elder himself holds the whisk in his hand. This signifies that the mind maintains the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), never being separated from them.

Even if [the whisk] is held in the left hand, it is because it is not separated from the mind. When the mind corresponds with the four means of integration, this is what is meant by "not being separated from either side.
As for the "mind," it is the vow to deliver sentient beings with the whisk, as well as the mind that corresponds with the ten directions and so forth.
Relying on that mind which accords with his sublime vows and powers, he practices the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*);
for it is through the power of those very eyes that he practices the four means of attraction, just as white whisks are held by officials and commoners.

Regarding the phrase "the essence is pure" (*tǐjié*) and so forth: the merit of the Buddha-dharma does not coexist with that which is outflowing (*sāsrava*); thus it is called "pure essence. This is the explanation of its own meaning.

By means of these four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), one gathers and assembles sentient beings; to deeply cleanse the defilements of sentient beings is the meaning of "brushing away" (*fù*).

Regarding "not being separated": it means to be constantly in accord with the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*); this is called "not being separated. Holding a white whisk in his hand, though he passes through [the crowd], it does not touch the body of the elder.
Through the power of his vows, he is in accord with the four means of integration; thus, stinginess, greed, and harsh speech have no cause to arise.
Furthermore, when a person holds a white whisk in their hand, they can always summon a pure breeze. The power of his vows is likewise in accord with the four means of integration.
They should be applied. To attract and lead others among sentient beings: giving to those who are destitute is called "attraction"; kind speech toward those who are angry is called "attraction";

beneficial conduct toward those who are stingy and greedy is called "attraction"; and working together with all people by first engaging in their activities and subsequently leading them away from them is called the "four means of attraction" (*catvāri saṃgrahavastūni*).

Regarding the statement that the four immeasurables are "jewels," these are loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. They provide shelter and protection for sentient beings like a jeweled canopy.

It is also said that when sentient beings uphold the Dharma as their object, it is called a "jeweled canopy"; alternatively, taking the objectless [immeasurable] directly constitutes the jeweled canopy.

Regarding the statement that the seven purities (*saptaviśuddhi*) are flowers: this explains the various flower banners. The seven flowers of purity are: first, purity of ethical discipline (*śīlaviśuddhi*);

second, purity of mind (*cittaviśuddhi*); third, purity of view (*dṛṣṭiviśuddhi*); fourth, purity through overcoming doubt (*tīrṇavicikitsāviśuddhi*); fifth, purity of knowledge and vision regarding what is and is not the path (*mārgāmārgajñānadarśanaviśuddhi*); sixth, purity of knowledge and vision regarding the practice (*pratipadājñānadarśanaviśuddhi*);

seventh, purity of knowledge and vision regarding the abandonment of the practice (*pratipannājñānadarśanaviśuddhi*); eighth, purity of unconditioned cessation (*anupādhiśeṣa-nirvāṇaviśuddhi*); and ninth, purity of the buddha-field (*kṣetraviśuddhi*). Zhiyou states: "Among the nine purities..."
Excluding the latter two purities, one takes the former seven; these are the seven pure flowers.
It is said that the dhāraṇī serves as the banner and revolves. Questioning the absence of delusion, its nature is similar to that of the dhāraṇī; the banner is thus continuous and uninterrupted.

There are two meanings: first, gathering; second, dispersing. To record without omitting the substance means that mindfulness, wisdom, phenomena, meaning, phrasing, and eloquence are like four kinds of colored silk.
Mindfulness is like thread, and wisdom is like a needle; they can constantly hold these together, long employing these four to save sentient beings.
It is like flowers and banners being gathered and spread out.
As for what is called the fivefold dharma-body: the fivefold dharma-body is like incense, and wondrous concentration is like water; thus they are combined as scented water.

The mind is like the earth; it serves as the basis for this [body]. Because the fivefold Dharma-body and sublime meditative concentration moisten the body and mind, it is like water sprinkled upon the earth.
As for the fivefold Dharma-body, there are the fragrance of precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the fragrance of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
These are able to submerge all other fragrances; thus they are called "fragrances."
Regarding the phrase "instructing others" and so forth: it refers to teaching the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) to sentient beings, which is like scattering various flowers.

"Flower" here carries the meaning of "cause. This is analogous to what was previously described as proceeding toward the jeweled canopy; just as it is appropriate to sprinkle water upon the ground, one subsequently arranges precious objects upward.
In terms of the Dharma, this refers to the practice of merit within time and space, which is like the precious objects. Their external manifestation of activity is like the brilliance of jewels.
Wu Huaduo said: "It was only after [the Buddha] attained the Ten Powers that he subdued the celestial Māras and manifested the six supernormal powers to defeat the heterodox teachers;
this is what is meant by 'fierce'."
Regarding the phrase "taking up [the meaning] within the Śākya," the intention is that the character "take" (qu) is to be applied above the character "internal" (nei).
To "internally take up for oneself" means to employ the Dharma as it has been realized to deliver sentient beings.

The statement "the words 'giving' and 'receiving' are as before" means that the two characters for "giving" (出) and "receiving" (內) were already understood in the preceding practice; therefore, it says "as before.
This directly explains the two characters for "giving" (與) and "receiving" (取), which refers to such things as the ripening of the faculties of sentient beings.

Regarding the statement that the nature of his fetters (*saṃyojana*) is noble and sublime, Jiaxiang says: His myriad virtues are not merely one; they are termed "various" (*nānāvidha*). They adorn and embellish the *dharmakāya*, which is synonymous with "ornamentation.

The Ten Powers (*daśabala*) crush the celestial Māras, which is termed "accomplishment" (*siddhi*); the Four Fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*) subdue the non-Buddhists, which is termed "virtue" (*guṇa*).

Among the beings of the seven assemblies and the masters of the eight classes of spirits, he is peerless throughout the three realms; the four modes of birth look up to him in reverence. For this reason, he is especially...
"Venerable sir.
Regarding the pronunciation of *sǎ* (灑): it is also read as *suǒ mǎi* (所買反) and, according to the phonetic analysis (*qièyùn*), as *suǒ jiě* (所解反) or *suǒ mài* (所賣反).
It means that when water falls to the ground and settles the dust, it is called *sǎ*. The phonetic analysis thus admits both pronunciations.
Regarding the term "xùn" (訊): it is pronounced with the *qie* (phonetic guide) *xī jìn* (息晉); it is erroneously written as *sī jiàn* (思見). "Xùn" [with the radical "mouth"] means to scatter.

As for the statement that this refers to the initial manifestation of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and so forth: this is not what is seen with the eyes; this is the stage of accumulation (*sambhāra-mārga*), which only allows one to see a small portion of the transformation body.
Since what is now being seen is the great transformation body, one runs away. There are those among the ancients who saw the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and ran away.
[The Master] Yun said: "According to the principles elucidated in the sutras, this Buddha is merely a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). In the Pure Land, there are few transformation Buddhas;
his physical dimensions do not correspond to those of the Great Transformation Śākyamuni, who is one thousand *zhang* tall. Therefore, the Commentary states:

'The Reward Body (*sambhogakāya*) has not yet been seen,' nor does it mean that there are few transformation bodies in the defiled land. Mo said: "Alternatively, through the power of the Buddha, he was added to the assembly of the *Lotus Sūtra* and saw the purity of the eastern direction."
This is the empowerment of the Buddha of the Earth.

As for the passage in the Sūtra concerning the impoverished son who saw his father: the impoverished son did not return home; for a long time he remained separated [from his family], failing to recognize that this was his own father or the nature of his father’s wealth and status.
Consequently, upon seeing him, he was struck with alarm, fear, and regret at having come.

Regarding the statement that "it is known through inference and not seen by the eye," at the time of those twenty thousand Buddhas, the sixteenth prince was a śrāvaka in the stage of a *kṣānti* (patience) seeker.
When he heard the exposition of the merits of the Mahāyāna Buddha-lands and pure realms, it was not necessarily seen by his eyes;
rather, it was through the two types of wisdom—listening and reflection—within this defiled land that he inferred it was not perceived directly by the eye. Nor was it...
