This is a realization through wisdom (*jñāna-sākṣātkriyā*). It is not a realization through wisdom of a bodhisattva on the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*). Since it is described as "inferential knowledge" (*anumāna*), it is not something seen with the eyes.

This is explained in reference to the Great Transformation Body (*mahā-nirmāṇa-kāya*) and its pure land. Only upon reaching the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*) through cultivation does one behold the Great Transformation Buddha.

Now, these followers of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka-yāna* and *pratyekabuddha-yāna*) are in the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*); they hear, contemplate, and infer [the existence of the Buddha], and thus it is said that they "regret their coming. Question: If it is inferential knowledge, why is it only the Great Transformation Body?

On that day, it was not heard that the teaching of the two bodies (the Dharma-body and the Reward-body) was being expounded. The answer is: on that day, the impoverished son was unable to contemplate the Mahāyāna teachings extensively;
having gained only a slight understanding, he spoke merely of the "Great Transformation" (the *nirmāṇakāya*) and did not mention the Dharma-body or the Reward-body.
Some say: according to the force of the scriptural passage here, the dimensions are very small; thus, it should only be the merits of a small *nirmāṇakāya* Pure Land. [Question: Why?
This is called "inferential knowledge" (anumāna). Answer: When the impoverished son was in the defiled land, he heard descriptions of the merits of the transformed pure land and its manifestations;
however, he had to wait until his future rebirth in that pure land to actually see them. The period prior to that birth is collectively termed "inferential vision" (anumāna-darśana).

Regarding the statement that one may "see the Buddha with the eyes" and so forth, this refers to the transformation Buddhas seen within the defiled lands who emit light and manifest supernatural powers;

this is called "seeing their power and majesty," meaning seeing them directly with the eyes. It does not mean that each and every such event must occur after one has been born in a pure land to see it.
Regarding the statement that "thought cannot bring it into practice": if one cannot practice it on the level of the cause, how can one realize it on the level of the fruit?

Regarding the statement that "it is called 'regret'": the poor son of the Pure Land originally intended to exert his strength in the impoverished village; he did not expect to have inadvertently trodden upon such high ground.
Gate. Although they have had the good fortune to see a Great Being, they give rise to thoughts of possessing but meager skills.

Fearing his majesty while also hoping for personal gain, they previously sought advancement but now regret having come; thus they seek the liberation of the Two Vehicles. Those who seek such liberation are likewise so:

originally intending to direct their minds toward minor reductions [of affliction], they fail to realize it and instead tread upon the Great Way. Though they hear the principle of the One Vehicle, they—
Their attachment to the pleasures of the two vehicles is profound; since they cherish the path as being remote and difficult to advance upon, they look instead for great benefits that can be sought.
Thus, they fear a long journey in advance and loathe hearing the Great Teaching, which is why they say they regret having come.
Regarding the phrase "conceiving a thought," it means to secretly form this thought; "secretly" (siqie) implies in private.

Regarding the phrase "the king and others," the impoverished son says, "This is truly the residence of a high minister; this is truly the residence of a camel. [The mention of] Shi Chong's residence serves as an analogy for what was said above regarding the king being the Son of Heaven.
As for "others," these refer to the brothers of the Son of Heaven, such as the Prince of Guangling and the Prince of Shu.
The term "equal" (等) refers to the King of the Descent (降王).
To say that "equal" has the meaning of "similarity" (相似) means that although the brothers of the Son of Heaven are inferior to the Son of Heaven, they resemble him.
In the discourse on the Dharma, the "King" is the Dharmakāya Buddha; "equal" refers to the Sambhogakāya Buddha. "Equal" carries the sense of similarity. The Sambhogakāya...
The merit of the body resembles the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), because it is non-different from that which the Buddha has realized and is capable of realizing it. Question:

How do the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) resemble one another? Answer: They resemble each other in their non-conjunction; this is said here on account of their sovereignty and unsurpassed nature.
This refers to similarity of name. For example, Emperor Wenzong and Emperor Wuzong are neither superior nor inferior to one another.
As for the statement "or kings," this refers to those such as the present Sage King (the Buddha), whereas other kings of different lineages differ in terms of superiority and inferiority;

therefore, two categories are cited to illustrate this similarity. Just as a king in the world—referring here to a king of a different lineage—is used as a metaphor for the Nirmāṇakāya (Emanation Body).
Regarding the statement "it is not my diligent effort," the impoverished son reflects: "According to this person’s doctrine, it is not a place where one can act with ease.
Instead, I must exert my strength in vain; I gain no wealth, yet my hands and feet grow weary, and I am further beaten with a staff.

It would be better to work as a hired laborer at the home of the impoverished son’s child, where I may rest and have freedom. This is discussed in the Dharma: when sentient beings hear the Mahāyāna teaching...

In the middle [section], it speaks of the power of the various Buddhas' supernatural penetrations (*abhijñā*). I privately reflect: this may perhaps be the meaning of the merit of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), or the merit of the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*).
Such matters must necessarily require three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* of renouncing one's head, eyes, marrow, and brain; only then can that which is sought be attained.
Therefore, it is said: "This is not for those like us."
The term "poor neighborhood" (*pīn-lǐ*) refers to those of the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*). Question: Why is it called a "poor neighborhood"? Answer:
It is called "poor" because they lack the principle of the wisdom of the emptiness of all phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā-jñāna*). Regarding the term "neighborhood" (*lǐ*), Master Muzhe says:

five households constitute a neighbor (*líng*), and five neighbors constitute a neighborhood (*lǐ*); this refers to twenty-five households. The sages of the Five Fruits possess the capacity to transcend the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*).
Having transcended, there are two categories of transcendence; this is called "going to the poor village.

"Liberating oneself" means to exert one's full strength. That is, the teachings and practices of the Two Vehicles, as well as conditioned and unconditioned meritorious dharmas, are called "the ground.
After three lifetimes and sixty kalpas, or four lifetimes and a hundred kalpas, one attains the fruits of the Two Vehicles; this is called "food and clothing."
It is easy to understand.
As for the statement, "If he were to dwell long in the Great [Vehicle]," it means that if the impoverished son did not run away, he would be constrained and exhorted to practice the Great Deeds;
this is called being coerced or forced to act against one's will.
"Self-examination" (zìchuǎn) means to gauge, to measure.
"The words 'not yet staying' mean that, as stated below, he runs swiftly to seize him and has not yet let him go; therefore it is said 'not yet staying, not yet arrived.
Second, among the two vehicles, it is like a destitute son who suddenly flees and has not yet found a place to settle his livelihood; at that time, the wealthy elder..."
The sixteenth prince saw his son and recognized him immediately; the impoverished son did not recognize his father, yet the father recognized his son. Upon seeing him, he also recognized him at once.
People of the time said, "When an object meets its owner, the eyes become fixed and firm. Furthermore, the way of father and son is a matter of innate nature (*t'ien-hsing*). Someone asked:
"How is it that upon seeing his son, [the father] runs away, yet his heart is filled with joy? He replied: "This is the behavior of one who does not understand the underlying principle."
This is the interpretation of the meaning. Based on a superficial reading of the momentum of the scriptural passage, such an objection arises. However, according to the actual facts:

when the elder saw [the boy] standing by the side of the gate from afar, he immediately began to speak out of affection. Because the elder’s family was wealthy and noble, the narrative flow of the scripture was interrupted;
at the end, the boy ran away, and his father rejoiced. The sequence of the textual phrasing suggests that the father’s joy was upon seeing him run away.

Regarding the statement that those of the Mahāyāna lineage are "near" [to awakening]: Maudgalyāyana asked, "If these father and son possess right view at this time, yet are unwilling to cultivate the great causes, how can their Mahāyāna seeds be said to be mature?
If they are already mature, why do they not give rise to the Mahāyāna mind? The answer is as follows: This refers to the intention of turning toward the Mahāyāna.

All such cases are due to having resided for only a short time [in the Mahāyāna]. Now, since they have retreated into the two vehicles (Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha), this is the subsequent condition for turning back toward the great cause.

When the season for ripening arrives, it is said that "the conditions for birth are near and have matured. Alternatively, it may mean that while the nature of the fruit was previously unripe and near [to being born], it has now matured over a long period.
Because one recognizes that it has ripened, one feels joy.

Regarding the statement that [the capacity] suddenly comes of its own accord: when Lü asked about his previous illness, [the person] ran away; because he pushed [the teaching] aside and refused to cultivate the Great Vehicle, he immediately withdrew from the great mind (*mahācitta*).
Now, the third section explains that it "suddenly comes of its own accord," which means the roots [of capacity] have matured; thus, there is no contradiction. Answer:

The previous instance of running away was based on the recent withdrawal from the Great Vehicle due to a mind with outflows (*sāsrava-citta*); the present coming of it refers to that which has been fundamentally present since beginningless time.

Regarding the Mahāyāna teaching on the seeds of the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) as untainted (*anāsrava*): when these five faculties mature, it is called "suddenly coming of its own accord" (*akasmāt svayam āgata*).
Question: What is meant by "suddenly"? Answer: This is explained through an analogy. A wealthy man sought a son for a long time within the city, yet he could not find one.

Now, having encountered him unexpectedly, it is said that [the son] has "suddenly come of his own accord. Question: If this refers to one who is unwilling to cultivate the Mahāyāna, how can you further speak of the faculties?
"Ripened. This response correctly explains the matter of seeing twenty thousand Buddhas again within that [intermediate state]. Therefore, it says "the faculties are ripened.
If this were not the case, then the phrase "running away" in the preceding analogy would be followed by the phrase "suddenly coming back"; thus, it cites the previous analogy.

Reflecting back upon the preceding text, the phrase "the conditions for birth nearby have ripened" likewise cites the previous instance of seeing the Buddhas again within that state. This does not contradict the present section. Not.
This refers to being willing to practice the Great [Vehicle].
As for the statement "still coveting and begrudging," it means that the elderly are often poor. The setting sun declines in the west; the wandering waters flow eastward.

When the Sūtra says "immediately dispatching bystanders," this refers to the Buddha’s subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*). This teaching is the principle (*tattva*); thus, the principle becomes [the means].

It can be explained as follows: "Urgency" refers to this mind, because it causes speech to arise; therefore, it is called an "impulse" (*anuśaya*). As for what was said regarding the One Vehicle being an "impulse," it means that the teaching arises from a heart of compassion;
thus, it is called "suddenly pursuing. The statement in the teaching that "all are suddenly pursued" refers to the urgency of the bystander.
In the analogy, the bystander is the person who seizes the matter; the heart of compassion is the one running; and the verbal teaching is the person who assists the elder at his gate.

The bird before me does not fly away; why does it encounter such a desperate and impoverished son who dares to linger at my gate? The practice of the One Vehicle teaching is difficult for a Bodhisattva of sudden enlightenment to perform.
You are an ordinary person of gradual enlightenment; why do you begrudge your efforts? Since you have come here, truly let go of your eastward and westward wandering.
If you can give rise to the great bodhicitta, you must be exhorted with stern words so that you do not return again to the cycle of birth and death. Therefore—

Regarding the phrase "he immediately dispatched [messengers]," the sutra says, "He ran swiftly to seize him. This is a metaphor for the aforementioned treatise. Once the impoverished son had run away, the messengers suddenly pursued him.
In the Dharma, it is said that the Buddha, knowing he was urgently entering the two vehicles, was compelled to preach forcefully for his sake; therefore, it is so named.
This is urgent; it is explained in secret and serves as the present corroborative cause.
Regarding the statement that "the principle is fundamentally beyond words": the principle of the One Vehicle is primary, while the teaching of the One Vehicle is secondary.
Regarding the statement "speech or practice may be cultivated," etc.: if practice can correctly sever delusions and thereby attain the fruit of sainthood, it is called the primary agent.
If the teaching can only assist in severing delusions, it is termed a peripheral factor.

Regarding the phrase "compassion arises swiftly": if we follow the analogy, and since the aforementioned teaching spoke only of bystanders, the "compassion arising swiftly" mentioned here in the commentary refers to the Buddha’s subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). Teaching the doctrine of the One Vehicle is what is called "sending away the bystanders."

Regarding the statement that "compassionate teaching involves urgent transformation": this is illustrated by the previous case where the elder saw the impoverished son refusing to submit and fearing he might flee, so the messenger pursued him urgently.

Within the Dharma, one frequently sees those who wish to retreat from the Great Vehicle and fail to practice it; for them as well, one must forcefully preach the teaching. Therefore, it is called "urgent transformation."
This is precisely what serves as the present evidence; thus it is stated in the *Guhyasamāja-tantra*. Regarding the phrase "running swiftly to seize":

this refers to suppressing [the recipient] and bestowing the Mahāyāna, which is called "running swiftly to seize. If one follows the circuitous path of the Hīnayāna, practice is slow and the seizing is delayed;
therefore, the Mahāyāna teaching is termed "swift seizing" (*kṣipra-grahaṇa*). It is as if saying: "If you do not take [it], [then...]"

"Later you will surely experience grief and regret," and so forth. From those born in the realms of compassion above down to the universal monarchs below, according to their respective lifespans, they ultimately sink back into the ocean of birth and death.

This is also as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: "In the midst of a night dream, [the Buddha] manifests forms such as a vajra and says, 'If you do not resolve to attain bodhicitta, I shall take your life,' and so on. You have traversed the evil realms for many kalpas; there is no..."

If one can transcend even the suffering of diligent effort for the sake of benefit, and attain the state of a Bodhisattva through the cultivation of even a small measure of superior practice, then one should not give rise to despondency regarding the great benefit.

As for the statement that "the mind and mouth do not submit," it means the mind does not delight in practicing the Great Vehicle; this is termed "calling out," which refers to being uncompliant with the practice of the Three Vehicles.
The meaning of "enmity" (怨) is that of non-submission, just as when one captures a thief in the world—if there is no means to extinguish [the offense] or sever [the connection] with others, then...

It causes one to become an enemy; therefore, one does not submit. If one were to submit, there would be no enmity. Furthermore, "qu" (屈) means to be wronged or oppressed. To be "qu" is the meaning of submission.
To suppress me and force me to submit is called "enmity" (怨). That which I do not desire is imposed upon me; being thus wronged and suppressed is what is named "enmity."
Alternatively, when one engages in worldly discourse with the mouth, it is called "loud shouting.
Regarding the offense of not responding appropriately, some say: "It is clearly an offense; the instances of such offenses are numerous," as discussed in the aforementioned treatise.

Originally, he was raised by you, and it was through you that he could have inherited the family lineage. Yet, because he turned his back on his father and fled to another land for more than fifty years, no news of him has been heard.
When the impoverished son arrived at the gate of the elder’s residence, he hurried past; this was so that their names would not be defiled [by an improper encounter].
On the gate of the elder’s residence, these words were inscribed: "If there is business, knock on the door and request admittance; do not enter directly. Why?
Therefore, one enters directly into the interior of another's house and stands there. Furthermore, there are boundaries between the inner and outer areas of a person's home;

why then do you enter the interior of the house at will? As for those who go inside and see the elder’s precious canopies within the residence, or the arrayed treasures spread out before them, and then take those treasures—this is precisely an act of transgression, this is a fault. How can you say that there is no transgression? According to the Dharma...
Treatise: Fundamentally, it was never said that merely generating the mind of the Mahāyāna and practicing Mahāyāna deeds constitutes "not violating the precepts.

During the time of the twenty thousand Buddhas, within the assembly of the sixteen princes, you heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, which taught you to attain Buddhahood. You were thus perfumed with the seeds of the bodhicitta;
through hearing and wisdom, the two evils were daily transformed into goodness, and you succeeded to the lineage of the Mahāyāna Dharma-treasure. It is because of this that you [are here] later.
To retreat from the Mahāyāna and fail to practice it is an extreme violation of one's commitments. Furthermore, you previously made a formal promise, pledging to do a great many things for the elder;
yet since then, you have done nothing at all. How can your deceit and arrogance be so extreme? Within the assembly of princes, you made four great vows:
first, the vow to deliver infinite sentient beings. Yet, not a single being has been delivered, and their afflictions remain boundless.
I vow to sever all afflictions; though they have not yet been severed. I vow to study the boundless Dharma gates;

though among the Six Perfections and myriad practices I have not yet studied them all, I shall first take up the practice of giving. Should someone come to beg for my eyes, I would rather retreat than ever commit such an offense.
I vow to achieve the unsurpassed Buddha-way; this occurs after one has passed through the sixth mind of the Ten Faiths and beyond. The first...

When he was at the sixth stage, while standing by the side of the gate, he suddenly retreated and fled; this did not constitute an offense. Regarding his four great vows, he had not yet fulfilled even one in total.
Subsequently, he regressed from his study of the Mahāyāna and deceived the Buddhas of the ten directions to no small degree (as described in the *Śīla-prakaraṇa*, etc.).

Regarding the statement, "The application is for the present time": A question is raised—since the Buddha possesses superior and inferior faculties and his power of wisdom can know the minds of sentient beings, why does he forcibly suppress others and compel them to study?
The commentary answers: "The application is for the present time," and so forth.

Regarding the statement "resting the mind and not practicing," etc.: this refers to entering into birth and death, which is called "falling to the ground. It means that the six consciousnesses do not cultivate goodness.
Because one does not sever the roots of goodness, one does not perceive death.
The Sūtra states that those who will certainly die are so called because, even if they were instructed to practice the ten thousand deeds by means of their heads, eyes, marrow, and brains,
or if they were told to abandon their bodies for a single phrase or half a verse of the Dharma, they would nonetheless inevitably meet their end.
Regarding the statement that the fifth section involves converting [beings] by means of the Two Vehicles, the commentary states:

Since they could not be converted by the Great Vehicle in the preceding fourth section, the Buddha now provisionally teaches the Two Vehicles in this fifth section as a skillful means to guide them. This is precisely what was previously stated:
"I lead you by means of skillful means so that you may be born within my Dharma. It is also consistent with the parable of the burning house. Contemplate this.
The *Fangbaji* (The Means of Deliverance) states: "I shall now employ skillful means to enable my sons to escape this harm.
Therefore, the six sections of the commentary on this parable all explain the stages of practice according to the Hīnayāna.

Regarding the statement that "the first teaching arouses the provisional mind": this refers to the teaching of upholding the three refuges and the five precepts, whereby one may temporarily escape the three miserable realms, attain birth among humans or devas, and experience superior, wondrous bliss. This constitutes the prior cause for the two vehicles; therefore, it is taught at the beginning.

Regarding the phrase "arousing the minor intention": this refers to those who, from among humans and devas, give rise to the intention of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) desiring liberation.
This is why it is explained next.

Regarding the phrase "causing them to cultivate the factors conducive to liberation" (*mokṣabhāgīya*): since those individuals have already aroused the intention of the two vehicles, they do not yet know what practices to cultivate at which stage of the path.

Practice. Thus, that which causes one to cultivate the stages conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) herein refers to the stages of the provisions (*sambhāra*) and application (*prayoga*) of the Hīnayāna.

As for the statement "the son then relies on practice," this refers to the five contemplations for settling the mind (*pañca-viṣaya-sthāpana*), the general mindfulness-contemplation (*saṃmānyasmṛtyupasthāna*), and the specific characteristic mindfulness-contemplation (*viśeṣalakṣaṇasmṛtyupasthāna*), which constitute the stage of the correct position (*samyagavasthā*).

"Exhorting entry into the wholesome" refers to proceeding from the completion of the previous stage of accumulation (*sambhāra*) into the stage of application (*prayoga*), followed immediately by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and so forth.
"Attaining the state of an Arya" refers to entering the fruits such as Stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) from the previous stage of application. Furthermore, these are the first six sections.

Among these, the first four sections constitute the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*). The next section constitutes the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*). The final section constitutes the stages of the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*), the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), and so forth.

Regarding the statement that "the stage and practice are still far," this is because from the initial generation of the mind (*cittotpāda*), one is distant from the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*), and because the ultimate truth (*tattva*) is distant. Furthermore, it is said:

"The Buddha abides in the stage of fruition (*phala-avasthā*), while he perceives his children in the causal stage (*hetu-avasthā*); since the stages of cause and fruit are distinct, it is called 'seeing from afar.'"
Regarding the phrase "Do not force them to come," etc.: previously, because his compassion was so intense, it was called "forcibly dragging them back.

Now, as for saying "do not," the Buddha said: "I possess a compassionate heart; though I wish to look up to them and cause them to study the Great Teaching and practice the Great Path, they do not accept or receive it.
Therefore, the father stopped him. Thus, the Sūtra says "do not," meaning: "For now, let them rest from being [drawn] toward the Mahāyāna."

The Teaching does not say so. Question: Since the Buddha’s compassionate mind should abandon sentient beings, why does he speak? Answer: Bestowing the Way according to their faculties is precisely the functioning of compassion.
To cause others to instead produce transgressions would not be compassion; fearing harm to sentient beings, he therefore desists. Small kindness obstructs great kindness;
a good heart that is not impartial receives no good retribution—such as wearing a tattered felt hat on one's head and so forth.

Regarding the statement "employing the Two Vehicles": the Dharma of the Three Refuges and Five Precepts is termed "provisional" when viewed from the perspective of those with the Buddha-nature, as it must lead them to attain the fruit of sainthood before it can be called "real.
However, when viewed from the perspective of those without the Buddha-nature, it is not termed "provisional" at all.
Regarding the phrase "to moisten the mind": the Three Refuges and Five Precepts can extinguish the burning afflictions of the three miserable realms; thus they are called "cool.
By attaining the bodies of humans or devas, one is mostly associated with the two feelings of joy and pleasure, which nourish and benefit both body and mind;
these Five and Eight Precepts are therefore termed "water. To bestow this teaching is termed "sprinkling," and it is spoken according to what the heart desires and toward which one inclines.
That [mind] is the "face. Furthermore, the arousal of the bodhicitta is called the "face," while lack of faith is called the "back.

Regarding the statement, "First cause them to repent and extinguish [their faults]," etc., it is because one fears that followers of the Two Vehicles might regret cultivating Mahāyāna practices and thereby fall into hell.

I shall preach the teachings for humans and devas, so that they may at least be spared from suffering. Regarding the ten *paryavasthānas* (envelopments): based on the eight *paryavasthānas*, two additional ones are added to make ten. The eight are:

lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), envy (*īrṣyā*), vexation (*pradāśa*), remorse (*kaukṛtya*), torpor (*middha*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), and lethargy (*styāna*). To these, either anger (*krodha*) or concealment (*mrakṣa*) may be added to constitute the ten.

As for the temporary cessation of the eight difficulties (*aṣṭākṣaṇa*): by upholding the three refuges and the five precepts, one obtains the body of a human or a deva; this is what constitutes subduing them.
This refers to the eight difficulties. To be born among humans or devas is what constitutes awakening; to fall into the three miserable realms is called being in a state of stupor. Question:

Why are the Three Refuges and Five Precepts termed the teaching of the Two Vehicles? Answer: For those who lack the spiritual lineage (gotra), these represent the ultimate fruit of the human and heavenly realms.
However, for those of indeterminate nature, the Three Refuges, Five Precepts, and Ten Wholesome Actions serve as the skillful means (upāya) for the Two Vehicles.

Regarding the phrase "suspension of instruction, etc.": Question: What is meant by "do not speak with him again"? Answer: It refers to the suspension of being [treated as] equal, which is to say that one does not provide great instruction, just as one does not speak.
The Sūtra asks: "For what reason? Question: Why is it that one does not speak with him at all? Answer: The Sūtra says: "For what reason?"

This is a citation. The response to the scriptural passage regarding the intention behind the difficulty raised is as follows: The elder was filled with regret, thinking that his retinue was too large.
At first, he believed that no one could surpass him in wealth and status; he did not know that this very body would instead become a great source of hardship and remorse for his son.

He sat upon a lion throne with a jeweled footstool supporting his feet (and so forth). On that day, I wore a tattered shoulder-cloak, fastened a tongue-shaped waistband, put on sandals with worn-out soles, and wrapped my feet in socks.
With my forehead smeared with ashes, I rode a donkey worth twelve hundred cash and sat in a humble, dilapidated hut.
This poor son was not afraid; I spoke with him every day and had no objection to giving him money and goods. Ask [him].

Since they are unwilling to come, could it not be that they are the children of the Elder? The Sūtra answers: "I know for certain they are my children. This means one knows they possess the seeds of a Bodhisattva.

According to the discourse on the Dharma, I shall provisionally employ various means to teach and transform them. How can they be compared to monkeys or hemp-horses? Following their respective types, there is no end to the transformation of other bodies;
I manifest great transformation-bodies and dwell in transformed pure lands. Furthermore, upon hearing the Unsurpassed Right [Dharma] but once...
Equal enlightenment is extremely difficult to cultivate; this is why it is considered difficult for a son.

When the sutra says "by means of skillful means," it refers to the elder who, knowing he was his son, did not immediately speak out, fearing that upon hearing it, the impoverished son would be terrified, faint, and fall into despair.
Although the Tathāgata knows that the great nature [of Buddhahood] exists within him and whether its maturation is near or far, he does not yet [reveal it].
One may simply say: "I was once initiated into the Mahāyāna," yet to conceal this and not speak of it is called skillful means (*upāya*).
As for saying, "I see that you should release him," one asks: since a wealthy elder or a person of high status understands all matters, why did he first order his capture?
Thereafter, he immediately ordered him to be released. The answer in the *Shu* (Commentary) expresses the intent of this release.
*Fahua jing xuanzan yaoji*, Scroll 26; *Fahua jing xuanzan yaoji*, Scroll 27.

Regarding the statement "the consciousness of the śrāvaka-nature, etc.," first, as for the interpretation in terms of the meaning of arising: one first generates the mind of the Mahāyāna, and subsequently generates the mind of the Hīnayāna.

Because the Hīnayāna mind intervenes between [the previous] Mahāyāna mind, when the minds of the two vehicles arise thereafter, they are termed "distant arising" in relation to the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
It takes sixty kalpas for the fruition to reach maturity. *Ying* says: "Falling back from the sixth stage, in relation to an ordinary person..."
Now, the status of "name" arises from a distance. Furthermore, compared to the attainment of the fruit by those of the Two Vehicles, it is called "ripening near.

As for the statement that one knows there is a "great lineage" and so forth: this means knowing that the lineage of the Mahāyāna has not yet ripened; thus, one first teaches the Hīnayāna and later teaches the Mahāyāna.
This is known only by the Buddha; other people do not know it, and thus it is called "hidden."
The Sūtra says: "The messenger says to him, 'I now release you. This is a metaphor for the aforementioned discourse on abiding:

"Go back to your own country; do not go to other lands to work as a hired laborer. Within your own country, you shall find stability and ease; I shall no longer exercise supervision over you. In terms of the Dharma, this means:
"I permit you to cease practicing the Great [Vehicle]; I now release you to practice within the two vehicles. This is called [the stage of] *śaikṣa*.
"Let them go wherever they wish. Grant them all that they previously desired; do not exhort them toward the Mahāyāna. This is what is meant by 'releasing.

It is like not pursuing someone—this is what is meant by 'releasing. It is not necessary to issue a formal command for their release, because at this time they are judged as attendants who will later undergo transformation."
Regarding the scriptural statement that "the impoverished son rejoices," Bian explains: "The impoverished son rejoices" means he eliminates disbelief of the mind;
"rising from the ground" means he eliminates disbelief of the body; and "since there are no words" means he eliminates disbelief of speech.
To say that it accords with their original capacity means that it conforms to their fundamental minds.

To say that they have first developed a small mind means that they had never before developed the mind of the Two Vehicles; that they develop it for the first time today is called "attaining what was never before attained."

Regarding the phrase "coming from the ground of birth-and-death": it refers to those who have gone among the followers of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), who, following their practice, have attained the state of having residual existence (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*) and are now seeking food and clothing.

Regarding the phrase "causing them to cultivate the factors conducive to liberation" (*mokṣabhāgīya*): it is as in the previous case of Śāriputra, who, because of the gift of his eyes, became terrified [of cyclic existence] and undertook the great practice; now...
There is no need to sacrifice one's head, eyes, and so forth; it is sufficient merely to practice the contemplation of the impurity of the body and the like.
This is precisely the wholesome liberation of the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*) in the Hīnayāna, which corresponds to the time of Kāśyapa Buddha.

The statement regarding the "secret dispatching of two persons" refers to the teaching of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*). In the aforementioned parable, this corresponds to the elder dispatching two men to lead the impoverished son away.
In terms of the Dharma, the Buddha’s great compassionate mind establishes the teaching of the Two Vehicles; this is precisely what is meant by the elder dispatching the two men.
Tanying asked: "For what reason was it said that after first dispatching the messengers of majestic power, the bystanders immediately pursued and brought them back?"

The messenger ran swiftly and seized him with increasing urgency. Later, he dispatched a messenger lacking majestic power; why then did he claim to have sent him secretly and speak to him gently, rather than dispatching him urgently?
The answer, as Zang said, is that the Mahāyāna teaching is what the Buddha constantly employs. Because they are close to the Buddha, they are called "attendants.
When the Buddha first attained enlightenment, he immediately preached the Mahāyāna, desiring to cause them to return to their original nature and cultivate themselves.
"Great" means to pursue and bring back. "Great teaching swiftly bestowed" means to run quickly to seize [the person].

Because the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) cannot transform them directly, it provisionally establishes the Two Vehicles; hence it is said to be "secretly dispatched. Since the Mahāyāna transforms beings by taking Buddhahood as its goal, it is called "urgent pursuit.
Since the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) teaching takes a distant goal, it is called "slow speech" (or "slightly superior").

Regarding the scriptural passage concerning "the withered appearance of form and color" (*rūpa-vivarṇatā*), it is asked: Since the householder’s family possesses abundant clothing and ample food, and among those who have come forth from the household—whether elders or young—there is not even one lacking clothing or food, for what reason are there those whose form and color appear withered? The answer is twofold:

First, some say they may be people from the householder’s eastern or western neighbors whom he has invited and brought here. Second, some say they may be those from his own household who have dressed up [for the occasion].
"Equipping and setting forth. Forty years ago, following all the Buddhas, he employed the power of skillful means (*upāya*).
Through these provisional teachings of skillful means, he borrowed and requested [the Dharma] from the mouths of the Buddhas of the ten directions. Thirdly, it is said:

"Forty years ago, within the path of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), he differentiated and taught the Three Vehicles; this is called 'equipping and setting forth. Although he manifested various paths, in reality..."
It is for the sake of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

Furthermore, those of inferior wisdom who delight in limited teachings—what is called the teaching of skillful means (*upāya*)—is termed "skillful means" because it serves to entice and lead those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
Because the Buddha’s intention in establishing his teachings is difficult to discern, it is called "secretly dispatched. There are two kinds of teachings, which are referred to as "two persons."

Regarding the phrase "wisdom is narrow" and so forth: the ninefold teaching (navāṅga-śāsana) explains only the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā). This interpretation is stated from the perspective of the fruit attained by the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha).
Regarding the phrase "or because the teaching is partial" and so forth: this is explained based on the doctrine and reasoning of the two vehicles.
Regarding the phrase "or one's own virtue is deficient," this refers to what was previously stated concerning the practices of the two vehicles (*dvayāyānika*).

That is to say, it refers to the complete fulfillment of the teaching, principle, practice, and fruit (*śāsana-yukti-caryā-phala*) of the two vehicles. By way of analogy, as stated above, the impoverished son lacks clothing and food; his face is darkened and sallow, which is termed "a haggard appearance.

In terms of the Dharma, the names, phrases, and syllables (*nāma-pada-vyañjana*) of the Hīnayāna are established based upon sound (*śabda*); since sound is form (*rūpa*), they are designated as "names" (*nāman*).
"His physical appearance is haggard.

Regarding the phrase "let the messenger deliver a message": it means that when the Tathāgata teaches the Hīnayāna doctrine, it reaches the ears of the śrāvakas; [the messenger] says to them, "You may go to him."
Regarding the terms "expedient means," "gradual," and so forth: the Mahāyāna teaching is called "running swiftly," while the teaching of the two vehicles is called "speaking slowly.
It involves circuitous approaches to practice and the guidance of expedient means.

Regarding the phrase "the two vehicles and so forth": within the teachings, that which explains the severance of afflictions is called the "place of activity" (*kṛtya-sthāna*). Alternatively, the teaching that is directed toward those with the faculties of the two vehicles is called the "place of activity."
Regarding the phrase "the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) and so forth": this refers to the stage of the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣa-bhāgīya*).

Although one has not yet actually attained the untainted state while still prior to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), it is called "untainted" because it is the cause for that [attainment] and will certainly be obtained. Because these practices accord with that [untainted state], they are called "conducive to liberation" (*mokṣa-bhāgīya*).
This is also termed "doubling" (*bhūyo-dāna*); the transformation of their characteristics is what constitutes "doubling."

Regarding the phrase "intending to engage in questions and answers," it means that the elder, fearing that his messenger might be clumsy of speech or dull of wit and thus unable to manage the dialogue, provides these instructions.
If the impoverished son consents to be brought back to work for him, [the messenger] should ask what kind of livelihood he intends to pursue.
"You may speak with him thus: 'I will hire you to remove the dung; the two of us will also work together with you. Furthermore, it is said:
"Hearing" (*śruta*) is called the question, for it refers to the teaching that can express the principle (*nīti*). "Principle" is called the answer, for the principle can establish the teaching.

Because the expressed principle reveals the expressive text, one is then able to realize its meaning; therefore, it is called the answer. Question: Regarding the teachings of the various schools of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, why is this so?
The teachings and practices of the Two Vehicles are uniquely called "dung-removing vessels," whereas the teachings and practices of the Mahāyāna are uniquely called "precious vessels. Answer:
The teachings of the Two Vehicles for one's own benefit are solely called "dung-removing vessels. The teachings of the Mahāyāna have two names:

first, because they can remove the dung of afflictions (*kleśa*), they are also called "dung-removing vessels"; second, because they contain the dharmas of benefiting others—namely, loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—they are called "precious vessels."
It is like a vessel for the Dharma.
Regarding the statement "not only practice, etc.": what was previously called the "Dharma-wheel" serves as the cause; this is to borrow its majestic power.

When practicing to sever delusions, one must necessarily rely on hearing the teachings of the Dharma to awaken to the principle before one can begin to give rise to practice that severs delusions; this is termed "borrowing the majestic power."
This is the "power" (śakti). Teaching is called "assistance. For example, when it says, "The three realms have no peace," and so forth;

regarding the phrase "knocking with the teaching," this refers to using the teachings for the two vehicles to exhort them to resolve their minds [for enlightenment], which is termed "seeking the impoverished son" and "knocking" (the pronunciation is *kǒu*).

Regarding the statement "describing the severance of afflictions": within the teachings, the five contemplations for settling the mind (*pañca-vastuka-vipaśyanā*) are explained, specifically detailing the various modes of practice for severing afflictions;
this is what is meant by "fully recounting the aforementioned matters."
Regarding the phrase "first taking the price": it means that the impoverished son first secures the money and only then engages in his livelihood.

In the Dharma as well, one hears the teachings of the Two Vehicles and cultivates the two types of wisdom—wisdom derived from hearing and wisdom derived from reflection—but has not yet engaged in actual practice; this is called "first taking the price.

Once those [two types of] wisdom derived from hearing and reflection are attained, one then proceeds to contemplative cultivation, specifically practicing the five stages of mental abiding (*pañca-sthāna-citta*) and the distinct characteristics of mindfulness (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa-smṛti*), which is like "seeking to remove the filth."

Regarding the phrase "this truly superior virtue": the outflowing (*sāsrava*) wisdoms of hearing and reflection, when compared to the roots of goodness of humans and devas, are called "truly superior virtues.
Although they are outflowing, they can serve as the cause for the fruit of the stage beyond training (*aśaikṣa-phala*) in subsequent stages.

Cultivating the five stabilizing minds, the specific-characteristic mindfulness, and the general-characteristic mindfulness during the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), and cultivating the four truths during the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*), is called the gradual subduing of afflictions; this is termed "seeking" (*mīmāṃsā*).

Regarding the *Sūtra on the Sweeper*, it says: "His father saw his son," and so forth. This means that when the elder saw his son, he took pity on him because his appearance was haggard and his face lacked luster.
Furthermore, he marveled that the boy had gone to the stable instead of coming to collect the money and goods. As discussed in the Dharma: as...

Coming to take pity on the sons of the two vehicles, he sees their physical marks and signs and is deeply concerned; seeing that they have today reached the stage of the provisions (*sambhāra-avasthā*), he immediately causes them to turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle.
For those who are gradually enlightened Bodhisattvas, he is concerned because they do not turn their minds to seek the Great Vehicle; thus, while taking pity on them, he is concerned for them.
Regarding the statement "pitying those who lack the marks and signs": this is analogous to the elder mentioned above, who was unwilling to enjoy his own children, grandchildren, and wealth.

You have undergone so much hardship because of your deep affection for your kin; therefore, you are grieved. Within the Dharma, the Buddha pities these sentient beings who are mostly clumsy in their minds:
seeing that they do not seek unsurpassed *bodhi*, but instead merely delight in the *nirvāṇa* of the two vehicles.
This refers to the minor fruit; thus, it is seen with compassion.

As for the statement that it is strange to seek nothing: if one does not cultivate the myriad virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges found in the Mahayana Buddha-fruit, why would one need to cultivate the inferior practices of the Hinayana?
Regarding the phrase "having already removed the filth" and so forth: this refers to the distance of the time [of conversion].
The intended meaning is that the six sections of the sūtra beginning from "From when his father saw him from afar" are collectively termed "conversion by means of the two vehicles.

Among these, the first four sections correspond to what the commentary calls "having already removed the filth" and above; because these represent conversions during immeasurable past lives, they are here termed "distant."

This is transformation through the world (*loka-vivarta*). The fifth [section] encourages entry into the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), and the sixth constitutes the stage of becoming a noble one (*ārya*);

these two segments refer to those transformed in the immediately preceding life and in this present life, and are thus called "transformation through the proximate world" (*āsanna-loka-vivarta*). If we discuss the three lives, in the first life one cultivates the goodness of liberation (*vimukti-kuśala*);
in the second life, one cultivates the four stages of preparatory application (*prayoga-mārga*); and in the third life, the actual task must again begin from the fourth [stage].

Only upon reaching the stage of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) does one enter the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and gradually become an Arhat (*aśaikṣa*). Regarding the four roots of goodness that are "similar," they are similar for two lifetimes;
the first of these lifetimes is called the "distant" stage, while the second and third lifetimes are the "near" stage. The same applies to the four lifetimes of a Pratyekabuddha.
Furthermore, Pratyekabuddhas require one hundred kalpas and Śrāvakas sixty kalpas to complete the practice of the provisions (*sambhāra*), or it may take several lifetimes.
Fifty kalpas are called "distant time. Alternatively, practicing during the stage of application (prayoga) for ten or twenty kalpas is called "near time.

The statement regarding "initially establishing the teaching so that others may enter the four roots of goodness" and so forth explains a future occasion. Of these two explanations, the first concerns the stages (bhūmi).

Explanation: "Another day" (*tad-anya-divasa*) refers to two interpretations. First, regarding the sequence of days: the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*) is called the "first day," while the subsequent stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*), wherein one further beholds transformation Buddhas (*nirmāṇa-buddha*), is called "another day.
Because the Buddhas encountered in the earlier and later stages are distinct, it is termed "another day. Second, regarding the interpretation by time:

"day" refers to the period of thirty or twenty *kalpas* spent practicing in the stage of equipment, which is called the "first day"; the subsequent period of ten or twenty *kalpas* spent in the stage of application is [called "another day"].

Taking the distant in contrast to the near, it is designated as "another day. The stage of the four roots of goodness differs from what preceded it; the stage of liberation is distinct from the former, and is thus called "another day.
The intent of the *Śāstra* (Sūtra-commentary) is merely that by contrasting these two stages with one another, the meaning of "another day" is already established.
How much more so since all these refer to those who have practiced for many kalpas, and especially since the stage of liberation is only entered after having already passed through many kalpas.
Regarding the preparatory stage (*prayoga*):

since the meaning of "another day" is already well-established, the separate mention of "time" indicates that there is a distinction between concentration (*samāhita*) and distraction (*vikṣipta*), and that the contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*) is likewise distinct.

In this stage, one performs the contemplation of the five faculties (*indriya*), the five powers (*bala*), and the four truths (*catuḥ-satya*). This explains the phrase "another day" found in the sutras.
Regarding the statement "the faculty of knowledge (*jñānendriya*) is not yet matured," this explains the meaning of the "window" in the sutra. Zhangjing said:

"When the great faculties are matured, the manifestation of transformation is like seeing one's child through the main door; as it is taught in the Mahayana doctrine of the two kinds of emptiness, one contemplates the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
Since it is not yet matured now, the secret transformation serves as the window, established through the power of the Tathagata’s compassionate mind and skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*)."
"Lost" refers to the window and the casement. Second, regarding the teaching of the Two Vehicles, it is called a "window and casement" because it is a vision through a narrow tube.

The "son" is the principle of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) expounded within that teaching, like seeing a son through a window. The "casement" (*yǒu*) is the Path (*mārga*); the teaching can lead forth wisdom, and thus it is called the "Path.
This teaching on the principle of the emptiness of persons is the direction toward which the Tathāgata’s great compassionate mind is oriented; hence it is called "direction" (*xiàng*).

Regarding the phrase "nor by means of equality" and so forth, the intended meaning is the same as before; however, while the previous explanation was based on those of indeterminate nature and thus termed "secretly bestowed," this explanation does not speak of "secret bestowal," but rather explains it in relation to those of determinate nature.

Regarding the term "windows and casements," there are two interpretations. The first states: "Within the elder’s precious canopy there are windows; through these windows one looks outward and sees the son.
This interpretation is incorrect. If it were windows on top of the precious canopy, then that would be the name for the "True Gate" (Saddharmamukha) in the Mahāyāna teachings.

It is not appropriate to call it a "window" (chuāng). Another interpretation states that this refers simply to a window within a horse stable; "window" here signifies something private or hidden, meaning one does not look directly at the object.
In this case, the elder [the Buddha] stealthily positions himself toward the window inside the horse stable and looks inward to see the impoverished son.

According to the discourse on the Dharma, he conceals his *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body) and manifests his *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body) to appear within the teaching of the emptiness of birth (*jīvakāya-śūnyatā*), thereby seeing the sons of the Two Vehicles.

If it includes the teaching on the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*), it is called being "within the main gate. For the time being, regarding the partial teaching on the principle of the emptiness of persons (*pudgalasūnyatā*), it is like a window.

As for the statement "when about to attain the Way," this refers to the five bhikṣus in the Deer Park who, upon seeing the sixteen-foot golden body, attained the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*);
therefore, it is called "seeing from nearby. Zhang Jing says: "This 'nearby seeing' of those in the state of no-more-learning, conversely, constitutes 'seeing from afar.'"

[The text] says: "Seeing. Now, since the Deer Park (Mṛgadāva) is called "near seeing," it conversely constitutes the stage of the four roots of goodness (catur-kuśala-mūla), which is not [the result of] this present life;
collectively, it is termed "distant seeing. Only within the Deer Park of this present life is it termed "near seeing. This is the first interpretation.
In this present life, the Deer Park is termed "near seeing," whereas previously, while in the stage of the four preparatory practices (catasraḥ prayoga-bhūmayaḥ), it was termed "distant seeing."

Regarding the phrase "or by departing from that," there are two interpretations. First: Within the Deer Park (Mṛgadāva), one further passes through another great asaṃkhyeya kalpa to reach the stage of a Bodhisattva on the First Ground (Prathamabhūmi).

Having been born into the family of the Tathāgata, one dwells in the Ground of Supreme Joy (Pramuditābhūmi); this is called "seeing nearby. The Deer Park is also referred to as "seeing from afar. Second:

It is said that [the Deer Park] is distant from the state of sainthood (*āryatva*). This is spoken with reference to the *buddhaphala-bodhi* (the enlightenment of the fruit of Buddhahood) when viewed from the Deer Park.
In this context, being far from the fruit of Buddhahood and Bodhi is called "seeing from afar. When the impoverished son eventually attains Buddhahood, it is called "seeing clearly.
The first explanation pairs "seeing from afar" with "seeing nearby," while the latter explanation pairs "seeing from afar" with "seeing clearly.

This refers to viewing the fruit of Buddhahood from the perspective of the Two Vehicles, which is termed "far"; it does not mean viewing the cause from the perspective of one's own vehicle's fruit. This is because the previous passage states that the father saw the son from afar.
If considered according to one’s own vehicle (svayāna), this is the child seeing the child.
As the Sūtra says: "He immediately discards his necklaces, fine soft garments, and so forth," thereby concealing the eighty-four thousand marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) of the *vipākakāya*.
Upon the *vipākakāya*, there are eighty-four thousand marks; each individual mark further possesses eighty-four thousand [sub-signs].
Regarding the secondary marks of excellence (*anuvyañjana*): each mark is further accompanied by eighty-four thousand rays of light that pervasively illuminate the worlds of the ten directions.
Moreover, his eyes are like the waters of the four great oceans, and the hair-treasure (*ūrṇā-kośa*) is like the five Mount Sumerus.

Therefore, it is said that he immediately cast off his necklaces, fine soft garments, and ornaments for adorning the body, and manifested upon another body the thirty-two marks of a great man (*dvātriṃśan mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*). Thus, it is said that he "again donned" them.
Thus it is said. When manifesting as a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics cannot be defiled by afflictions;

therefore, they are called "ornaments for the body. However, the marks and characteristics of a transformation body can be stained by external conditions, and thus they are likened to "soiled garments.
A wealthy elder would most certainly not wish to wear tattered clothes while entering a horse stable, yet he did so because he had no choice in the matter of gathering up the children.
The Buddha’s body is likewise. Although he does not personally desire to manifest the thirty-two marks, he does so for the sake of sentient beings.

As the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* says: "He teaches the Dharma that the poor delight in, in order to transform sentient beings. [The text] asks: "Where can one obtain coarse, tattered, and greasy garments from the houses of the wealthy?
There are two interpretations of the answer. First: "From the eastern house, the western neighbor, the southern village, or the northern quarter—borrow them from the homes of the poor."
Furthermore, in the discourse on the Dharma, it is said that the Buddha’s body possesses eighty-four thousand marks. In reality, the Tathāgata originally did not possess the thirty-two marks;
he borrowed them from the house of a Cakravartin king. As a sutra states: "If one were to see the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks, then a Cakravartin king would also be a Tathāgata.
Secondly, it is said that he went forth dressed in tattered clothes, just as in the case of the Tang [dynasty].

The "costumes of the Guoshan (State Mountain) troupe" represent the emergence of the princes of the Six Kingdoms. This was originally non-existent in the land of Tang; it is merely a matter of costumes being produced.

[These costumes] cause my Tathāgata to conceal his eighty-four thousand marks. Just as a destitute son might appear identical to a wheel-turning monarch, possessing the thirty-two marks, yet these marks are identical to those of the outflows (*āsrava*);
thus, he relies upon the womb of Māyā and others. Therefore, it is said that they are "produced through costumes."
Regarding the statement that it "shows the existence of afflictions, evil karma, and so forth": *rajas* (dust) refers to dust and grime, which is to say evil karma;
*pāṃsu* (soil) refers to excrement and earth, which is to say afflictions. Jiguō says: "Taking a consort and fathering a son shows being defiled by greed;
practicing austerities for six years shows being defiled by delusion; reviling Devadatta shows being defiled by hatred. Bian says: "Although these afflictions are cited..."
It is vexing, and it also involves evil karma.

Regarding the phrase "first establishing provisional teachings" and so forth: it is like how, because the right hand is more stable and convenient, all people first use their right hand, and only later do they turn toward the great [teachings]. The Mahāyāna teaching is like using the right hand. Jiaxiang said: "Right..."

The hand serves as a means for grasping and acting; true wisdom possesses the capacity to gather the aggregates (*skandha*) and fetters (*saṃyojana*). Because the hand grasps a vessel, it removes filth;
because wisdom accords with principle, it severs delusions.
Regarding the phrase "removing filth and vessels," this is a metaphor for the aforementioned removal of filth, which requires obtaining vessels such as baskets and containers.

[The character] *jù* (also read as *dān* or *qián*) refers to the treatises on the Dharma within the *Jìguó* [school]. The three types of wisdom (*trividya*) are likened to vessels for removing filth:

the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) is the vessel for holding aloft; the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) is the golden vessel; and the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) is the pure vessel. The teachings of the Two Vehicles expound these three wisdoms;

they are thus compared to the act of grasping, and are therefore called "grasping the vessel for removing filth. The power of these three wisdoms is able to sever the afflictions (*kleśa*). This is compared to...

Regarding its exclusion [from the path of seeing], it is further stated that the vision, knowledge, clarity, and awakening within the context of the Four Noble Truths constitute the factors capable of severing [the afflictions].

This specifically refers to the wisdom of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*). At this stage, one merely suppresses and severs the afflictions by means of contaminated wisdom (*sāsrava-jñāna*), just as it is explained in the case of the attainment of the "clearly manifest" concentration (*vibhaṅga-samādhi*);
for this is due to the functional power of that [uncontaminated wisdom].
Regarding the statement "expressed through teaching": this refers to the capacity for transformation. It means that the teachings of the two vehicles indicate the practice for severing afflictions.

Regarding the statement "the Buddha himself shows identity": this refers to the thirty-four moments of mind and so forth, which are termed the severance of afflictions; it is the transformational aspect of severing delusion.
"Name" indicates identity.

Regarding "expounding provisional teachings and the like," this refers to teaching that one relies on these practices to sever afflictions, thereby encouraging those to be converted to conform to oneself;
this is the conversion through "common purpose. It is, for example, like an elder who personally holds a vessel for removing filth. This is also [the same].
This summarizes the preceding intent.
The Sūtra says, "appearing as if he were afraid," meaning that he dressed himself up as a poor man before entering. The point is that the impoverished son was not afraid of working for hire anywhere.
Mǔ said: "If he did not manifest an appearance of fear, the impoverished son would not believe that this was the removal [of his suffering]."
He was a man of filth. This refers to the Prince who, while going out through the four gates, saw the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death and became disillusioned;
his state of mind was characterized by fear. The elder, feigning the role of a hired laborer, acted as if he were afraid of his master’s anger;

his state of mind was likewise characterized by fear. By means of this skillful expedient, he was able to draw near to the impoverished son. He then came to know that the hundred insects and seven birds were the son's dependents. Thus it was with the elder.
For the sake of his son, he cast off his precious and elegant robes and donned tattered, filthy garments. As the sutra says:
"He immediately removed his necklaces, fine soft upper garments, and ornaments for adorning the body; he further put on coarse, worn-out, and greasy clothes, with dust and dirt covering his person.
Holding a refuse-removal tool in his right hand, appearing as if in a state of fear, he spoke to the laborers: 'All of you, work diligently; do not be indolent.'"
By means of skillful expedients (*upāya*), he was able to draw near to his son. The Tathāgata is likewise:

for the sake of sentient beings, he conceals the true virtues of the *saṃbhogakāya* and manifests the provisional forms of the *nirmāṇakāya*; he hides the profound texts of the subtle principle and proclaims the coarse teachings of superficial meaning.
Not remaining in the Pure Land, he comes to this defiled realm. [Therein] men and women fall into cesspools, and their parents leap into them to rescue them.
"Save me! I only wish to save my son and daughter; I do not fear that their clothes will be soiled by filth.

The Buddha’s heart takes pity on sentient beings, just as the elder pities his children. As the Sūtra says: "To employ skillful means is to feign an appearance of fear; this is called 'skillful means.'"
It was solely through skillful means that he was able to approach his son.
Regarding the statement "showing [him] the terrors of various sufferings," one asks: what is meant by "having fear"? The answer is: for the sake of Prince Siddhārtha.
He went out through the four gates and beheld an old man, a sick man, a corpse, and the appearance of a śramaṇa. He contemplated his father the king’s palace as being like a cemetery;
seeing the female musicians, he perceived them as being like corpses and cried out three times, "Alas! At midnight, he leaped over the city wall and practiced asceticism for six years.
The attainment of equal and perfect enlightenment through thirty-four moments of mind beneath the Bodhi tree is truly a state of having something to fear.

To point to the current body of the Buddha as the locus of these superior modes of activity is erroneous; it refers to his previous births. As the Sūtra states, "In life after life, he received transformation from the Buddha," meaning that in each successive birth, the transformed bodies and transformed marks were all like this.
"Regarding the passage 'You should always practice here and not go elsewhere,' practicing the contemplative cultivation within the two vehicles is what is meant by 'you should always practice here.
Not being heedless and retreating into the state of an ordinary person or into the paths of non-Buddhists is what is meant by 'do not go elsewhere.
As for 'I shall increase your price,' this refers to the four stages of the roots of goodness (*catur-kuśala-mūla*), wherein the wisdom you cultivate now is superior to your previous understanding."
The wisdoms of hearing and reflection during the stage of liberation are therefore called "added value" (*ādhāna*).
As for the term "addressing by name," it refers to calling someone by their given name.

Regarding the statement, "I shall bestow upon you the wisdom of cultivation": if one asks what is meant by "future" (*bhaviṣyat*) in relation to the present application of effort (*prayoga*), the answer is that this refers to [the future result].
This was previously discussed. Since it is said that one is "encouraged to enter" the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), what fault could there be in the term *māṅ*?
If we follow the subsequent passage, since it says "I shall increase your price," this is precisely what should be called *māṅ*, *rāṅ*, *zhēnāṅ*, and *yìāṅ*. Thus, it is correctly named *māṅ*.
Regarding the term "jar-like vessel," it refers to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) being like a jar.

Regarding the phrase "that which exists by reason of concentration," this refers to all meritorious qualities such as liberation (*vimukti*) and the stages of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), which exist by reason of concentration, just as rice and flour exist depending upon a jar.
Meditative concentration is like the jar, while rice and flour serve as metaphors for the various meritorious qualities.

Master Lu said: "The aforementioned liberations are common to both ordinary beings and sages; those who attain the eighth liberation, the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), are restricted to five types of persons:
namely, those in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) of the three vehicles, non-retrogressive bodhisattvas, and those with sharp faculties who are *anāgāmins*. Others cannot attain it."

Regarding the statement, "This stage is also [described as] 'learning' (*śaikṣa*) and so forth": Question: In various sūtras and śāstras, it is fully explained that the three knowledges (*vidyā*), the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*) are attained only by those who have become arhats. How is it that a "poor son" (the practitioner) attains these meritorious qualities already at the stage of the four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*)? Answer: The commentary states, "This stage is also [described as] 'learning' and so forth. This means that prior to the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), one practices impure contemplation (*sāsrava-bhāvanā*) and trains in [the realization of] the truths. Thus, because this stage involves training, it is designated as "learning. Furthermore, since the practitioner has not yet abandoned all afflictions (*kleśa*), it is also called "learning. It is not until one reaches the fruit of arhatship that one is no longer subject to training and is therefore termed "beyond learning" (*aśaikṣa*). Consequently, although these qualities are not yet fully perfected, they are provisionally established as being present in this stage. This is similar to how the term "arhat" is applied to the stage of the "non-returner" (*anāgāmin*) who is destined for parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*); although they have not yet abandoned all afflictions, they are provisionally designated as "arhats" because they will certainly attain the fruit of arhatship in the future. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Moreover, because the practitioner at this stage possesses the capacity to cultivate these qualities, they are said to "attain" them. This is like saying one "attains" the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) while still on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Thus, there is no error in the teaching. Furthermore, because these qualities are cultivated through the power of the path of vision, they are said to be attained at this stage. This is similar to how the "four foundations of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are said to be attained upon entering the path of vision, even though they were already cultivated previously. For this reason, there is no fault in the statement that these qualities are attained at the stage of the four roots of goodness. This concludes the explanation. The following section concerns the "path of seeing" (*darśanamārga*). Regarding the phrase "The path of seeing is the first moment of the dharma-knowledge of suffering," and so forth: the meaning is that the path of seeing consists of fifteen moments of mind. These are the four moments of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*)—namely, the dharma-knowledge of suffering, the dharma-knowledge of origin, the dharma-knowledge of cessation, and the dharma-knowledge of the path—and the eleven moments of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*)—namely, the subsequent knowledge of suffering, the subsequent knowledge of origin, the subsequent knowledge of cessation, the subsequent knowledge of the path, the subsequent knowledge of the dharma-realm, the subsequent knowledge of the origin-realm, the subsequent knowledge of the cessation-realm, the subsequent knowledge of the path-realm, the subsequent knowledge of the peak of existence, the subsequent knowledge of the cessation of the peak of existence, and the subsequent knowledge of the cessation of the peak of existence. These constitute the fifteen moments of the path of seeing. As for the statement, "The first moment is the dharma-knowledge of suffering," this refers to the initial moment of the path of seeing, which is the dharma-knowledge of suffering. Because this knowledge directly perceives the truth of suffering within the desire realm, it is called "dharma-knowledge. The various meritorious qualities such as the *abhibhvāyatana* (bases of mastery) and *kṛtsnāyatana* (bases of totality), as well as loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity within the Three Vehicles, are called the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*).

Regarding the mention of "salt, vinegar, and so forth," Zhe says: prior to this path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one trains in the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), taking it as the primary and subsequent characteristics.
However, these are with outflows (*sāsrava*) and are not the two true knowledges (*jñāna*). The two knowledges are attained only upon entering the state of a noble one (*ārya*).
Regarding the mention of "harmonizing" and so forth: all delicious foods and drinks require salt and vinegar;

likewise, among the merits of the emptiness of arising (*utpatti-śūnyatā*), all arise because of wisdom. Since wisdom is primary, it is only by contemplating the self as empty that one subsequently attains merit.
As for those things mentioned in the Sūtras, they are used as metaphors for what was explained above: such as pepper, ginger, salt, fermented soybeans, asafoetida, oil, and so forth.

Regarding the discussion within the Dharma, it refers to the simultaneous mind and mental factors of both the fundamental and subsequent wisdoms; these constitute desire, just as clarified butter and oil can bring forth various [qualities].

Taste and touch are like [the sensation of] touching; they are like kneading dough. The resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) that the phenomena of faith and observation are inseparable is like a melon seed.

Within each individual concentration, salt and vinegar are consumed exclusively; discursive thought (*vitarka*) is like a laborer chopping wood; the establishment of the boundaries of the object is like a cauldron or pot;
volition (*vicāra*) acts as the process of transforming the raw into the cooked; and the reception of phenomena (*vedanā*) is like a bowl that successively holds various other things.
Regarding the phrase "an old and decrepit servant": the elder said, "I do not refuse to give you a strong and capable hand;
however, I fear you will be unable to command others. I shall now give you this old and decrepit servant for you to employ.
He may be driven about in light and easy tasks, but he cannot endure the hardships of heavy labor. If you send him to the marketplace, you must have another person follow behind him. [End of] Dharma.
Treatise: When an Arhat transforms his staff into a person, it must be through a concentrated mind and so forth; this follows subsequent conditions.

Even if one were to cause [a being] from the Wild Horse World (Gandharva-loka) to come here, they could not avoid it. My Tathāgata has thoroughly matured those of the Two Vehicles and taken them away;

their supernormal powers remain present, yet they do not transcend the three thousand [worlds], nor do they reach back eighty thousand eons into the past or future—they are called "old and decrepit messengers. As for the five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā):...

Among the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), excluding the power of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayābhijñā*), the four bases of psychic power (*catvāra ṛddhipādāḥ*)— namely, those of desire, effort, mind, and investigation—
are called "worn-out servants" because their functional efficacy is weak.

Regarding the statement that this refers to those of sharp faculties who "leap over" [the stages], the Minister of State (Xiangguo) said: In the Hīnayāna, it is only permitted to leap over the first two fruits and take up the third fruit.

It is not so in the Mahāyāna. Furthermore, as for the Hīnayāna: during the four stages of preparatory application (*prayoga*), one suppresses the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm so that they do not manifest;

subsequently, upon entering the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), these are abandoned simultaneously with the afflictions of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpavāsanā*). Thus, [one attains the fruit] all at once.

One who attains the third fruit becomes a body-witness *anāgāmin*. They obtain the four fundamental dhyānas, the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and so forth;
all of these arise based upon meditative concentration. According to the Mahāyāna, however, it is held that one may skip the two intermediate fruits and attain the fourth fruit directly.

For example, there is a certain class of those with sharp faculties who, as a first-fruit [srotāpanna], groups the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the three realms into nine stages.
The highest-of-the-high grades are combined into one, and this applies down to the lowest-of-the-low as well.

Just as when one or two [grades] are severed, one simultaneously severs all three realms, so too when the six grades of the desire realm are completely severed, it is not called the second fruit, because this includes the severing of the six grades belonging to the two higher realms.
If the nine grades of the desire realm are completely severed, it is not called the third fruit, because this likewise includes the higher [realms].
Because it involves the two realms and nine grades [of afflictions], it is called the fourth fruit. This is precisely what is meant by "leaping over the middle two.
The cultivation of the afflictions of the three realms is like splitting bamboo stalks.
Regarding the statement "attaining the fruits in succession": herein, these are all the fundamental stage virtues within the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśalamūla*).

"Rice, flour, and so forth" refers to the contemplations on the Four Truths, the five faculties (*pañcendriya*), the five powers (*pañcabala*), and so on. Jin says: "In the stage of patience (*kṣānti*) of the Hīnayāna, one cultivates the five faculties."

In the stage of the "Worldly Supreme Dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*), one cultivates the five powers (*pañca-balāni*). In the Mahāyāna, during the two stages of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and "Summit" (*mūrdhan*), one cultivates the five faculties (*pañcendriyāṇi*); in the stages of "Patience" (*kṣānti*) and "Worldly Supreme Dharma," one cultivates the five powers.

In these four stages, one universally cultivates the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths. Within the Mahāyāna, among the four modes of practice, one performs the mental aspects (*ākāra*) of both the established (*prajñapti*) and non-established (*aprajñapti*) truths.
In the Hīnayāna, one performs only the established truths; furthermore, one is able to contemplate the eight [realms] above and below.

The "aspects of the truths" (*satyākāra*). The word "etc. includes all other meritorious qualities. The commentary states that "not yet reached" (*anāgamya*) refers specifically to the first dhyāna when it has not yet reached the higher absorptions;

these are collectively termed "preparatory stages" (*sāmantaka*). Because this first dhyāna is the initial attainment of meditative concentration and has not yet reached the fundamental absorption (*mauladhyāna*), it is called "not yet reached.
However, while every stage within the higher realms possesses its own "not yet reached" state, they do not receive the specific name "not yet reached."
