Furthermore, since they share the same meaning through the analogy of the rain as the gate of delight and aversion, it could be combined with the "Parable Chapter.

Likewise, since these medicinal herbs share the same meaning in terms of curing illness, they could be combined into the "Medicine Herb Parable Chapter. The principle is essentially the same in either case.
Regarding the two verses at the end of the chapter: I now declare to you the most ultimate truth: none of the assembly of śrāvakas has attained final nirvāṇa;
the path you have been practicing is the bodhisattva path. By training and studying gradually, you shall all become buddhas.

Regarding the phrase "first praised and extolled": this refers to the section on the "Poor Son" (*daridraputra*), where the four great *śrāvakas* compared the elder to the Tathāgata and themselves to poor sons, thereby understanding and accepting the Tathāgata’s merits.

This is why the World-Honored One offered praise and confirmation at the beginning of the "Simile of the Herbs" (*tṛṇauṣadhīparivarta*). As for the initial praise: at that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahākāśyapa.
At the beginning of the preceding chapter, Subhūti was addressed because he was able to expound the *Prajñāpāramitā* Sūtra;
this is precisely the occasion for the fourfold assembly of the *Prajñā* to receive the teachings, as described by Subhūti.
For these two reasons, Subhūti was specifically addressed. Now, here alone Kātyāyanīputra is addressed.
The name "Kāśyapa" has two meanings: first, he is the eldest among the year; second, the verse-text of the preceding chapter was spoken by Kāśyapa.
When the sound of the verses ceased, the Buddha then spoke this chapter to him. Because the momentum of their speech was continuous, he addressed Kāśyapa alone.
As for the phrase "and the other great disciples," it refers to the remaining three individuals, not to many others, because those three shared a common mind and were united.
The intention is to lead [beings] by means of the parable of the impoverished son; this is why it is cited concurrently.
As for the scripture’s statement, “Excellent, excellent, Kāśyapa! You have well explained,” and so forth: “Excellent, excellent, Kāśyapa!
You have well explained the true merits of the Tathāgata” is a praise.
The Sūtra says: "It is truly as you have said. "Truly" means according to reality. This single phrase, "as you have said," is a seal of approval.

Question: Why does it say "Excellent! Excellent! twice? Answer: Jiexiang says that the two utterances of "Excellent! describe the skillfulness of his words, while "truly as you have said" confirms the reality of the matter.
Jiguo says that the first praise acknowledges the provisional (expedient) teaching, while the latter praise acknowledges the ultimate (real) teaching; therefore, it is repeated.
Ah! Regarding the question on the preaching at Vulture Peak: if the Buddha’s body consists entirely of manifested marks (*nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa*) of merit, how can it be called "real" merit?
The answer is: this is merely to praise Kāśyapa for grasping the Tathāgata’s principle of the provisional and the real.

Even if these are manifested marks, because they are taught based upon the real—the provisional and the real within the "one and three"—they are also termed "true merit. Furthermore, one may take the parable of the elder as an analogy.
Come! The followers of the Two Vehicles are comparable to the impoverished son. Because the merits of the Mahāyāna are manifold, its wealth and resources are immeasurable;
the merits of the Two Vehicles are deficient and meager, like a poor village. The four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*) serve as a jeweled canopy, which the Elder honors and reveres.

The *nirvāṇa* of the Two Vehicles is like a thatched hut where one stays overnight outside the gate, dwelling there while preoccupied with thoughts of poverty. The seven noble riches (*sapta-ārya-dhana*) are gold, silver, and precious jewels.
The Jewel: The fivefold Dharma-body is like water sprinkled upon the ground; the virtues of the seven factors of enlightenment are like scattered flowers;

the noble assemblies of the Three Vehicles proclaim them everywhere, like guests enjoying abundant and extensive benefits; because the merits of the state of fruition are complete, they are like granaries overflowing with grain;
the sublime vows and powers are like ministers, officials, and subjects; and the eighty-four thousand modes of practice are like oxen.

His sheep are innumerable. He maintains the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) in his mind, as if holding a white fly-whisk. His merit for the dual benefit [of self and others] is like the act of taking out and putting in, or receiving and giving.

Because he rides upon the teaching of the emptiness of the living being (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), his manifestation of principle is not complete; he is like one with a squinting eye. Because his noble wisdom is deficient, he is called "dwarfish" (*vāmana*); because his marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) are incomplete, he is like one who is ugly.
Regarding the phrase "the words are marvelous because they accord with reason," this refers to the World-Honored One’s praise of Kāśyapa: "Excellent, excellent!

Kāśyapa, you have well spoken of the Tathāgata’s true merits. The character *ya* (pronounced *wuya* in the fifth tone) signifies admiration; it is called *ya* because it expresses the beautiful qualities of a person.
Thus, he admired Kāśyapa’s speech, noting that it accords with the principles of both provisional and ultimate truth, being truly as he has stated.
As for what was said, Changjing stated: "Sincerity arises from faith; this is precisely the meaning of patience (*kṣānti*).

If one fears that followers of the Two Vehicles might think, 'I have fully known the merits of the World-Honored One,' or if one fears that followers of the Two Vehicles might give rise to arrogance, it is for this reason that the third section further extols the merits of the Tathāgata’s own person.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: 'The Tathāgata furthermore possesses exhaustiveness, etc. As for what you have said..."
A small portion has been spoken; that which remains unsaid is vast. Therefore, it is said that there are further immeasurable and boundless merits.

That which cannot be fully expressed is as stated in a verse from the *Gaganagañja-sūtra*: "The empty space of the ten directions might be traversed by foot, The waters of the four great oceans might be measured, And the minds of all sentient beings might be made one, But the merits of the Tathāgata can never be fully told."

Furthermore, it is said: even if there were one thousand heads, each head having a thousand mouths, and each mouth a thousand tongues capable of producing various sounds, and if for a thousand kalpas they were to praise the Buddha’s merits, that which was praised would be as little as a single mote of dust, while that which was not praised would be immeasurable.
"It is like a speck of dust on the great earth.
The phrase "to show that he is still equal [to them]" explains the third section of the sutra. The Buddha is identical to the elder;

you have taken the elder as an analogy for the Tathāgata, using the small to illustrate the great, as they share partial similarity. You are identical to the impoverished son; even though the Sage’s virtue is subtle, it is permitted [to be compared].

The same. First: comparing the persons of the two vehicles to the impoverished son, they do not necessarily resemble him in every respect; however, because they resemble him to some small degree, it is permitted that they are "slightly the same.
Second: the noble virtues of those of the two vehicles are slight; in reality, they are the same as the impoverished son. Therefore, it is said that they are "slightly the same."

As for those who say that there is also a gradual [attainment]: this refers to the period after the turning of the mind (*cittavivarta*). Once the mind has been turned, one gradually becomes integrated and at ease;

just as the gold, silver, and treasuries gradually become the same as those of the elder, so too, once the merits of the two vehicles have been turned toward the Great Vehicle, they gradually become identical to those of the Tathāgata.
It is well said that after taking charge of the household affairs, one attains Buddhahood.

Regarding the statement that there are four types of equality within the Dharma: in Master Fashu’s commentary, he divided these into four sections, yet their thematic characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are extremely inconsistent.

The Master [of the present work], following the subsequent analogies, has extracted and recorded these passages from the current scripture as they correspond to them. Therefore, he has categorized them as such.
By correlating the upcoming analogies with the explanatory text and reflecting back upon the meaning of this sutra, one will come to understand it clearly.
Regarding the phrase "sovereign over the Dharma," the sutra says: "If there is anything taught, it is because the Buddha has appeared in the world;
if he did not appear, how could there be any teaching?"
The Sūtra states that the Tathāgata is the King of all dharmas. "King" carries the meaning of sovereignty. Because his speech is not false, he is called a king.
If his words were false and deceptive, how could he be termed sovereign? If he were not sovereign, he would not be called the Dharma King.
It is also like a lecturer who, within what they understand, can only proclaim the teachings without impediment.
Regarding the statement that "the two dharmas benefit all sentient beings," the sutra says: "One employs wisdom regarding all dharmas to arrive at and expound them."

It is called "Dharma" because it benefits all sentient beings. When the Sūtra speaks of "all dharmas," it means that True Suchness (tathatā) serves as the basis for all dharmas, and is thus termed "all dharmas.
Regarding the phrase "by means of great compassionate wisdom," what is meant by "wisdom-convenience" (jñānopāya)? The answer is: with respect to the ineffable Dharma, [one employs] names.

Because they are explained through characteristics, they are called "expedient means" (*upāya*). Question: Originally, these are dharmas that are without names or characteristics; yet one forcibly establishes names and characteristics, superimposing them upon the essence of all dharmas.
Why is this called "expedient means"? Answer: If the teaching of the Dharma does not accord with the essence of the dharmas, it is not called "expedient means.
When the taught Dharma is identical to the realized Dharma, it is therefore called "expedient means."

Regarding those who are "able to explain well": they understand the sūtras and expound upon them. "Expound" (*yan*) refers to the manner of water flowing in a long stream. From the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), one realizes the principle of *tathatā* (suchness).

Within this principle, there are myriads of virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. From this fundamental wisdom, the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) arises; this is called "self-benefit.

The subsequently attained wisdom transforms and conditions appearances, which are like the myriads of virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; all of these belong to this self-benefit subsequently attained [wisdom].
Attaining wisdom, one brings it forth from within; it is like an image in a mirror. For the sake of benefiting others, it is well to establish names and provide explanations. Question:
Should one not speak of the realized Dharma that is free from attachment? Answer: All the teachings he expounds reach the stage of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*).
"Phenomena apart from names and marks" refers to "all phenomena" (*sarvadharma*) in the sutras. Master Xiang states that these are the phenomena of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).

The fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*) of the Tathāgata realizes the nature of the *ālayavijñāna*, which is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpannasvabhāva*). Within subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), one discerns the marks of the *ālayavijñāna*.

By relying on others [the teachings], one takes the two kinds of emptiness as the gateway; one discerns that the imagined nature (*parikalpitasvabhāva*) has no reality despite its appearance, while the dependent nature (*paratantrasvabhāva*) possesses reality. Having discerned this—

The Dharma is fully realized through fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). Taking fundamental wisdom as its basis, subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) arises by means of skillful means (*upāya*).

This subsequently attained wisdom is able to expound the twelvefold teachings (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*). These are no different from the dharmas realized by fundamental and subsequently attained wisdom, just as the four great rivers flow into the celestial lake (*deva-saras*).
Regarding the phrase "the principle spoken of accords with [reality]," this explains the attainment of the stage of wisdom (*jñānabhūmi*) within the sūtra. There are two interpretations.

First, after the fundamental wisdom (*mūlajñāna*) has realized [reality], one speaks of the accord between what was said and what was realized; therefore, it is called "attainment. The "stage of wisdom" refers exclusively to the principle of *tathatā* (suchness).
The second [interpretation] says: Sentient beings hear the Tathāgata’s teaching; they contemplate the principle and give rise to practice; relying on practice, they give rise to wisdom;

they realize and become attached to True Suchness (tathatā), reaching the stage of Buddhahood which encompasses both Bodhi and Nirvāṇa—this is called the Stage of All-Knowledge (sarvajñatā-bhūmi). This latter interpretation indicates that it encompasses both principle and wisdom.

When the verbal teaching accords with principle, it is because it is spoken in accordance with realization. This differs from the non-Buddhists who claim, "I have attained the medicine of immortality by drinking nectar";
such teaching does not accord with principle. Riding this precious vehicle, one proceeds directly to the site of enlightenment;

since the practice is not in vain, it is called "practice that accords with principle. Furthermore, it says: "Once the Son of the Buddha has practiced the Way, he shall become a Buddha in a future life. If one applies these two...
The teachings of the *yāna* (vehicles), when compared to the principle of the Mahāyāna and so forth, are all not in accord with it; the same applies when the Mahāyāna is compared to them.
As for the statement "thereby universally nourishing," it refers to the Dharma that leads to the stages (*bhūmi*), which moistens and nurtures those of the three vehicles and five natures.
Regarding the statement that "the phenomena of emptiness and existence arise from consciousness," this explains that there are distinctions in the reception of the Path.

The Sūtra states: "The Tathāgata perceives and knows all dharmas, even those within the sphere of activity of the profound mind. This precisely refers to the distinctions in the reception of the Path.

If one does not know the faculties (*indriya*), how can one receive the Path? Question: By what cause does the Tathāgata preach the Dharma and attain omniscience (*sarvajñatā*)? Answer: The Tathāgata perceives and knows [all things] as one...
The ultimate destination of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*). All phenomena do not exceed emptiness and existence; they encompass all phenomena exhaustively.

To know that all delusive phenomena lack intrinsic substance is to understand that phenomena return to the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (the nature of universal imagination) and the *parikalpa-citta* (the mind of universal imagination).

Between the object of universal imagination and the intermediate [subject], there is no substantial mark or aspect; this is the *parikalpita-svabhāva*. It is like people in a marketplace who, throughout the entire day, do not recognize one another’s names or surnames.

Throughout the day, one distinguishes the object-aspect (ālambana-bhāga) from the image-aspect (nimitta-bhāga), yet fails to realize that the image-aspect is non-existent. It is like a person with cataracts seeing flowers in the sky;
though there are fundamentally no flowers in the sky, the appearance of the flower-aspect arises from the mind. This above explains the Tathāgata’s ultimate refuge. Question:
When does the Tathāgata perceive and know this? Answer: He perceives and knows it upon attaining enlightenment. Second, knowing that all dharmas exist: first, conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma).
The Dharma takes the dependent nature as its refuge; the two unconditioned dharmas take the perfected nature as their refuge.
These three natures are that to which all empty phenomena and existent phenomena return.
Regarding the term "ultimate true nature": these three natures ultimately converge in *tathatā* (suchness).

Regarding the phrase "knowing the minds of sentient beings and so forth": the mind of sentient beings is that which tends toward [the goal], while the practices of the Three Vehicles are that which is tended toward.
Dharmodgata understands that because the Buddha’s penetration of the faculties of the consciousness of phenomena causes those beings to be converted who receive the Path to differ,
each attains the growth of superior understanding among men.
Regarding the phrase "Vimalakīrti said, etc.," there is that which has no destination. According to this sutra, the Tathāgata perceives and knows the ultimate destination of all phenomena.
As for the "destination of the intended disposition," it means that by realizing this sutra, one also knows the conduct of the deep minds of all sentient beings.

Regarding the statement that "speech is precisely the three natures," the meaning is that apart from the three natures, there are no further dharmas. Emptiness is the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), while existence refers to the dependent and perfected natures (paratantra- and pariniṣpanna-svabhāva).

Regarding the phrase "the destination of the mind," Lü says: "The mind is itself the activity (*caryā*), while 'destination' (*gati*) is the fruit. Therefore, according to the sūtra, it refers to what the mind travels toward;
'activity' is precisely the place where the mind goes. The intent is to grasp that which is traveled toward—to know the minds of sentient beings."

The power of knowledge regarding resolute conviction (*adhimukti-jñānabala*) knows this. Furthermore, it knows the mental activities of sentient beings; this is the power of knowledge regarding the paths leading everywhere (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad-jñāna*).
Regarding the phrase "in principle" (*li*): "principle" refers to the objective sphere (*svabhāva-viṣaya*), while "knowledge" refers to the mental activities of sentient beings.
In relation to the Tathāgata’s wisdom, he is able to know and penetrate them without obstruction.
Regarding the statement, "Or it is by means of the Buddha’s realization (*buddha-adhigama*)," etc.: [The question] asks what distinguishes this from the previous [explanation]. [The answer] is:

The previous explanation held that the realization of the Dharma (*dharma-adhigama*) and the wisdom of the faculties (*indriya-jñāna*) belong to the Buddha, while the beings to be converted each receive the path within their own rational and cognitive capacities.
This present explanation holds that the reception of the path belongs to the Buddha himself; having first received it, the Buddha is then able to cause those of the three vehicles to attain it.
This serves to distinguish the three vehicles.

As for the statement that "they cannot reach [enlightenment] by themselves," the Sūtra demonstrates that all sentient beings possess all-encompassing wisdom precisely because they are unable to realize it on their own.

If they were able to realize it by themselves, why would it be necessary for the Tathāgata to reveal this wisdom? Furthermore, regarding all phenomena, one must investigate them to the ultimate limit and attain clarity.
As for "the realized": because the Buddha has thoroughly investigated all phenomena, there are distinctions in the provisional and the real teachings of the three vehicles and five vehicles.

For those of the bodhisattva lineage, he teaches them to attain the wisdom of the *bodhi* of the Buddha-fruit; for śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, he teaches them to attain the wisdom of the emptiness of self-nature.
This is the distinction shown between the three vehicles and five vehicles. [There are] few bodhisattvas who possess their own innate capacity.
Furthermore, because [the Buddha] does not fully know the faculties and dispositions of others, he maintains that there is no distinction between the vehicles (*yāna*).

Regarding the statement "the subsequent metaphor and its application" (*yanxia yu ji he*), the question is: How does the Master of the Commentary (*shuzhu*) categorize this sutra into four sections? The answer is:

The Master’s statement "the subsequent metaphor and its application," etc., intends that the four divisions within the subsequent metaphor correspond to these [four categories]. This refers to the subsequent Dharma...

The analogy of the King’s appearance in the world corresponds to this first section: the Buddha’s emergence in the world. The subsequent analogy of the teaching universally nourishing all corresponds to this:

the Dharma benefiting sentient beings. The subsequent analogy of receiving moisture differently corresponds to this: the differences in how they receive the Way. The subsequent analogy of being unaware of it oneself corresponds to this:
the inability to reach realization on one's own. Thus, because the exposition of the Dharma consists of these four segments of analogies, they are all fully present here.
There are four sections. This corresponds precisely to the four sections established by the Master of the Commentary (Sū-zhǔ) in his *Fǎshù* (Exposition of the Dharma).
Regarding the phrase "Furthermore, there is an interpretation... and so forth, this refutes the ancient school and the classification of Jiguó (Jiguo).

This is the first recitation of the *Fǎshù*: "Kāśyapa, you should know that the Tathāgata is all dharmas... up to 'not false'. This section as a whole clarifies that what has been taught is not false; it is not [to be] individually assigned.

This is also the scriptural text. From the passage "By means of wisdom and skillful means, [the Tathāgata] expounds all dharmas" down to "all-knowledge," this corresponds to the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddha-jñāna-darśana*).
Second, the Tathāgata’s contemplative knowledge of the ultimate destination of all dharmas corresponds to the revealing of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Third, the unimpeded penetration into the deep mental activities of all sentient beings corresponds to the awakening to the Buddha’s [knowledge and vision].
Knowledge and vision. Fourth, having thoroughly investigated and clearly understood all phenomena, one reveals to all sentient beings all-encompassing wisdom;
this is assigned to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

Although these interpretations are made here in accordance with [the preceding], they will be fully detailed below in the section on the parables, where it describes the Dharma King appearing in the world to preach the teaching.

The four sections of text beginning with "Universally nourishing" (*pǔzī*) constitute an interpretation that addresses those [previous points]; this is precisely the "distinctive intent" (*biéyì*), which accords with what Kenjō has explained.

Furthermore, another interpretation holds that although this explanation conforms to the passage on the "opening, showing, awakening, and entering" (*kāishì wùrù*) of the One Vehicle, it does not conform to the present text.
Because it breaks through the common ailment of [conflating] the vehicles, it is called the "distinctive intent."
The statement, "Furthermore, it separately reveals that [the teaching] is not false," represents the Master of the Commentary’s own self-reliant interpretation;

the topical outline (*ko*) follows that of the ancient masters, while the meaning within it differs. Of these, the first section provides a general clarification that [the teaching] is not false, citing the Sūtra:

"The Tathāgata is the King of all dharmas; whatever he speaks is entirely not false. Following this general introduction, the subsequent four sections separately reveal this point. First, the thorough...

Regarding the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the Sūtra states: (1) through wisdom and other faculties, one is able to know both emptiness and existence regarding all phenomena; (2) the Tathāgata perceives and knows all things as they are;
(3) he knows the inclinations and pleasures of the minds of sentient beings, and also knows the deep-seated mental activities of all sentient beings;
(4) he is able to manifest the provisional and the ultimate, and has reached a thorough, exhaustive, and clear understanding of all phenomena.

Regarding the statement that "the reality of dharmas transcends words": although it is expressed through speech as the Dharma taught by the skillful means of wisdom, it is not itself the ultimate truth.
The names and designations of all phenomena are merely provisional existences; when one calls out the word "fire," the fire does not burn one's mouth.
Although this is not the ultimate truth, the Dharma that is spoken accords with the Dharma that is realized, and the Dharma that is realized is non-existence (*abhāva*).
Regarding "dharmas of names and signs": this refers to the teaching that within words one speaks of dharmas that are devoid of names and signs.

However, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all dharmas is entirely beyond the reach of verbal expression; conventional cognition and verbal expression operate only in reliance upon common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), such as when one calls out "water" or "fire."

Question: True Suchness (*tathatā*) is also like this. What is the difference between these two dharmas? Answer: For instance, when fire is defined as having heat as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it is thereby designated as "fire.

Although it does not necessarily burn, heat is established as its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). Similarly, if one says that the true dharma is neither pure nor defiled, and is free from the middle and the extremes, [it is established as such].
When it is spoken in this way, it likewise does not accord with the essence, because it cannot be expressed.

Regarding the statement "it is thus" and so forth: the question is, when correct wisdom realizes the truth, all things are entirely non-existent; yet when one reaches the subsequent explanation, the myriad phenomena are clearly manifest.
How can you say there is no difference? The answer is: that which is realized is precisely the three natures (*trisvabhāva*); as for that which is explained...

The one is precisely the three natures; what further distinction could there be? It is just as when a Bodhisattva of the fifth stage realizes the conventional and attains the ultimate—there is no difference at all.
How much more so when the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma, where could there be different realizations? However, the intent of the commentary is as follows:

Fundamental wisdom realizes principle, while subsequent wisdom realizes phenomena; these are designated as "Buddha-wisdom. Although they are conventionally described as "fundamental" and "subsequent" based on the distinction between principle and phenomena, at the time each is realized, there is no difference in their realization (as explained by Mou).

Regarding the term "ground" (*bhūmi*), it refers to the basis upon which one understands all the teachings that have been expounded, such that they all reach the ground of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*).

"Ground of wisdom" (*jñāna-bhūmi*) has the sense of being a basis; its true nature (*tathatā*) is called the "ground," for there is only fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) that reaches this ground of wisdom.

Regarding the term "Buddha of mental discourse" (*manojalpa-buddha*): this refers to the teaching that accords with realization; therefore, it is called a "ground" (*bhūmi*). Because this wisdom realizes [the truth], it is termed "reaching" (*prāpta*).
As for the phrase "or the teaching can be equal," this means that the four—teaching and so forth—are all termed "reaching the ground."
Regarding the statement that "one who can know emptiness and existence" understands the ultimate destination of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) as taught in the sūtras:
it means that the Tathāgata is able to know the destination of all phenomena—both empty and existent—as being the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature). Furthermore, all phenomena are twofold:

conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) take refuge in the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature), and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) take refuge in the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature).
These three natures (*trisvabhāva*) are the locus to which all phenomena—whether empty or existent—ultimately tend.
Regarding the phrase "the ultimate destination" and so forth, it refers to the *tathatā* (suchness) as the final destination of the three natures.
This is because the Tathāgata establishes all things within ultimate emptiness; thus, all phenomena ultimately tend toward emptiness.
This is because it is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of reality (*tathatā*). Just as the nature of space is revealed only by depending upon material phenomena (*rūpadharma*), so too is this the case.
Regarding the statement "knowing the conduct of the mind": this means that one understands the scriptures and also knows the profound mental conduct of all sentient beings.

Because there is a mind corresponding to the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), the mind experiences joy; since it takes delight in the Vehicle of the Hearers (*śrāvakayāna*) and the Vehicle of the Solitary Buddhas (*pratyekabuddhayāna*), it is called the "profound mind" (*adhyāśaya*).
If the mind excels the object, it is the power of knowledge regarding resolute conviction (the former being the profound mind and the latter being the objects of practice).

If the mind is that which practices and practice is that which is practiced, this is the power of knowledge regarding the paths leading everywhere. Furthermore, one knows that these sentient beings are creating karma for the hells.
They undergo the retribution of the hells; this applies to all six realms of existence alike.
As for the statement "having already realized that all dharmas are equal," this is an explanation of the scriptural passage concerning the thorough exhaustion of all dharmas.
It refers to the doubts of sentient beings: "How is it that in the past, forty years ago, you taught the three vehicles, yet today you teach the one vehicle? Therefore...
It is said that for forty years following his enlightenment, the Tathāgata observed that the faculties of sentient beings had matured in three ways;
therefore, the Tathāgata taught the Three Vehicles. Today, on this Vulture Peak, it is only the nature of the One Vehicle that has matured;
this is why the Tathāgata now teaches the One Vehicle. Because the Tathāgata skillfully knows the faculties and natures of sentient beings, he initially taught the Three [Vehicles].
Regarding "expedient means" (*upāya*): later, he speaks of the one reality; the Tathāgata knows each and every thing without error.

As for the phrase "the aforementioned meanings and words," the commentary on the four lines concludes the preceding four points: first, exhausting the true nature of phenomena; second, being able to know emptiness and existence;
third, knowing the mental inclinations of sentient beings; and fourth, being able to manifest the provisional and the real.
Regarding the phrase "by these four meanings," Mou states there are two meanings: first, because the Buddha’s teaching is not false, his merits cannot be fully extolled;

second, because he possesses these merits, he is able to expound upon the provisional and the real. Since sentient beings lack such merits, how could they attain the non-differentiation of the three vehicles?
This follows from the previous fourth point regarding "lack of self-awakening," and it brings forth the preceding distinction.

This is the source of the mind’s activity. Because the teaching is not in vain, it further clarifies that there are distinctions among the vehicles (*yāna*) in order to refute the attachment to the notion that the vehicles are identical.
The Sūtra says, "Kāśyapa, for example, as for the trichiliocosm," which is the general description;
"mountains, rivers, streams, and valleys" is the specific description. Within the mountains there is land, within the rivers there is land, within the streams there is land, and within the valleys...
Upon reaching the land, this is the locus of the mind within the trichiliocosm. Within this location, there are no material objects;
there are only mountains, rivers, streams, and valleys. These four types have existed since antiquity. Throughout the trichiliocosm, what is not a mountain is a river;
what is not a river is a stream; and what is not a stream is a valley. Thus it is throughout the three thousand worlds.
The realms, mountains, rivers, valleys, and lands are that which can produce; the herbs, trees, forests, and various medicinal plants are that which is produced.
The trichiliocosm is the capacity for existence, while the seeds of the Three Vehicles are the contents thereof.
If we take this as a general metaphor, there are grasses that are medicinal and grasses that are not medicinal, yet all arise from the earth.

"Born from the ground" refers to the discourse on phenomena. This is explained in terms of the Tathāgata’s great compassion; all six destinies and four modes of birth are the objects of the Tathāgata’s teaching.
The two characters "born" (所生) belong to the following phrase.
The Sūtra speaks of "various kinds" (nānāprakāra): the kind of small grass, the kind of medium grass, and the kind of large grass.
In terms of the Dharma, these refer to the kind of bodhisattva, the kind of the two vehicles, and the kind of humans and devas; this is called "various kinds."

Regarding the statement in the Sūtra that "names and forms are each distinct": licorice, yellow-barked tree (berberis), yellow astragalus, and wild cowhage have distinct names; this refers to their being different within the Dharma.
Among Bodhisattvas, there are those of the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten transferences, the first bhūmi, the second bhūmi, and so forth.

Among Śrāvakas, there are those of the first fruit, the second fruit, and so forth. Among Pratyekabuddhas, there are those who are like rhinoceros horns and those who travel in groups. [Likewise] among humans and devas...
Śakra, Brahmā, and the Wheel-Turning King each have distinct names.
When the Sūtra speaks of "different forms" (*rūpa*), it refers to the three types of grasses opening their flowers and attaching their leaves, each with different colors—blue, yellow, red, and white.

In the discourse on the Dharma, this refers to the differences in the magnitude of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of those of the Three Vehicles; thus, their names and forms are said to be distinct.

Regarding the statement "the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system" and so forth: there is an interpretation that this refers to the realm ruled by a Great Transformation Body (*mahā-nirmāṇakāya*).

This is incorrect, because a Great Transformation Body is seen only by Bodhisattvas in the four stages of application (*prayoga*). What is here called the "realm transformed by a single Buddha" refers only to what is ruled by a minor transformation body.

Although it is seen by Bodhisattvas in the stage of equipment (*sambhāra*) as pervading the four continents, in this context, we are referring to the minor transformation body as the sovereign ruler of the entire realm.
A single trichiliocosm. This is mentioned because it is the same as the domain of the King; thus, it is said that the realm of the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha is the trichiliocosm.
Regarding the statement "Gen is the mountain," this is the name of a hexagram. However, when the Sages established the hexagrams, they did so to observe their images (*xiang*).

These are the names of the hexagrams according to human convention: Qian is Heaven, Kun is Earth, Xun is Wind, Kan is Water, Li is Fire, Gen is Mountain, and Dui is Lake. Mountain signifies production; it produces.

It gives birth to the myriad things; it is that which proclaims and emits. "Qi" refers to mountain miasma (*ārdra-gandha*). Within the crags and ravines, this mountain miasma disperses and gives birth to the myriad things.
The two rivers are the Guàn River; its character is a pictograph representing its form, signifying flowing water. The three gullies (*xī*):
according to the *Erya*, "water that pours into a river is called a gully. The four valleys (*gǔ*; ancient pronunciation *lù*, with the phonetic *yú yù* [homophonous with *yù*]).

Regarding the phrase "analogous to the great trichiliocosm" and so forth: this is an analogy for what was stated above—that within the three-thousandfold great thousand-world system there are mountains, rivers, valleys, and ravines;

within these mountains, rivers, valleys, and ravines there is earth; and both the mountains, rivers, valleys, ravines, and the earth are capable of producing, while the herbs, trees, and medicinal plants are all that which is produced.
In terms of the Dharma, the modes of birth—womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born—are capable of producing, while the seeds within the body are that which is produced.

They serve as the basis for birth. Now, the four types—mountains, rivers, valleys, and gullies—are used as metaphors for the four modes of birth: egg-born, womb-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born. This is merely a correspondence based on numerical similarity;
there is no distinct correspondence regarding their specific characteristics. Alternatively, if one correlates them according to the number of conditions required:

egg-birth possesses all four conditions, as the embryo is enclosed within an eggshell; moisture-birth relies upon the favor of humidity, and thus is likened to mountains. Second, womb-birth possesses three conditions, as the embryo is enclosed within a womb.
Because moistening volition is like a river; third, moisture-born beings possess two conditions, and because their moistening volition is like a stream;
fourth, transformation-born beings possess one condition—volition—and are therefore likened to a valley.
Regarding the statement that "herbs" (*huì*) constitute three and "trees" (*mù*) constitute two: some say that grasses have thickets and trees have forests.

The intention of the *Shū* (Commentary) is that both grasses and trees possess thickets and forests. Master Lùfǔ asked: if medicinal herbs are distinguished from grasses and trees, they have no separate essence apart from them.

Why does the sūtra employ the word "and" (*ca*)? The answer is that within the dharmas being illustrated, seeds and manifest activity (*samudācāra*) are distinct; therefore, the sūtra places the word "and.

According to the commentary, the "trees and shrubs" (*vanaspatis*) metaphor illustrates manifest activity, while the "medicinal herbs" (*oṣadhi*) metaphor illustrates seeds. Alternatively, "trees and shrubs" may separately illustrate the Mahāyāna.

The medicinal herbs serve as a general metaphor for the three vehicles (*triyāna*). Since there are differences between the seeds (*bīja*) and their manifestations (*vṛtti*), as well as between the universal and the particular, the word "and" (*ca*) is employed.

As for the phrase "although these are numerous," this serves to distinguish the specific dharmas. What has been presented thus far constitutes a general metaphor; it is a general metaphor for the seeds of the six destinies and the four modes of birth.
However, according to the requirements of this specific sutra, what is essential here refers exclusively to the seeds of mundane and supramundane wholesome dharmas.
This collectively serves as a metaphor for medicinal herbs.

To say that their "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) and "functions" (*vṛtti*) differ means that "characteristic" refers to the practice on the stages (*bhūmi*), while "function" refers to the activity of cultivation, namely the severing of afflictions (*kleśa*).
This is what is meant by the difference in their functions (the above constitutes the general metaphor).
Regarding the statement that the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) conceals the *dharmakāya* (truth body): "concealing" (*mi*) refers to being hidden or latent; "pervasive" (*mi*) means extensive.

This is because the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha, as a sovereign of a single *trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*, as well as his various emanations corresponding to different types of beings, pervade the entire *trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*.
The phrase "dense clouds spread everywhere" (*mimǔ mí bù*) does not refer to sudden, violent clouds, but to dense clouds. "Mí" (everywhere) means pervasion; "biàn" (pervasion) means spreading.
This is a metaphor for what was stated above: clouds arise from dragons, and rain is obtained from clouds. At that time, people see only the clouds and do not see the dragons.
In terms of the Dharma, transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) arise from the body of self-enjoyment (*svasaṃbhogakāya*). At that time, people see only the transformation bodies.
The *svasaṃbhogakāya* (body of self-enjoyment) is not seen; the rain comes from the clouds of others. The Dharma teaching likewise proceeds from the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body).
It might be possible for there to be clouds without rain, but it is impossible for there to be rain without clouds.

It might be possible for there to be an emanation body that does not preach the Dharma, but one has never seen a preaching of the Dharma without an emanation body. The Commentary states: "The emanation body conceals the reality; reality is [the *dharmakāya*]."
The *svasaṃbhogakāya* (self-enjoyment body) is called the "concealed reality. Its eight phases gradually manifest:

as a *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body), he acts as an infant for eight years, a youth for seven years, studies the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) for four years, enjoys sensual pleasures for ten years, leaves the household life at twenty-nine, and attains enlightenment at thirty-five.
From the manifestation of these successive birth-phases up until the attainment of enlightenment, he exerts himself within this very body.
The householder Śreṣṭhi Sela aroused the aspiration for enlightenment upon seeing the Teacher’s three-fathom body; five hundred brahmins gave rise to faith upon seeing his body reduced to ashes.
As a king over the three thousandfold world system, not only did his body pervade it, but his voice likewise pervaded it.
Regarding the statement "one transforms three thousand," this is a metaphor for the teaching’s universal nourishment. The sutra states that it covers the trichiliocosm;

since the sound has already filled it entirely, the sounds of the Dharma resonate one after another. Turning the Wheel of Dharma thrice within the great chiliocosm, that wheel is able to bring quiescence, for its fundamental nature is itself quiescent.
This rare Dharma-wisdom is realized by devas and humans, whereby the Three Jewels appear in the world. It is like clouds spreading everywhere.
Wherever it rains, it follows; wherever the body pervades, the sound of the Dharma also pervades.
Regarding the phrase "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*), this is explained by the preceding analogy. The preceding explanation states that when it does not rain, it has ceased;
once it rains, it necessarily falls at one time, neither before nor after. Therefore, "time" (*kāla*) is established. "Equal" (*sama*) means impartiality. Even on dry ground, it descends everywhere.

It rains. Rain falls everywhere upon the upward-facing trees and forests; it also rains upon the upward-facing three kinds of grasses and two kinds of trees. Therefore, it is said that the rain falls equally (*samavarṣa*).

It is the same with the discourse on the Dharma: when the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma, there has never been a case where the faculties of sentient beings were matured and he did not preach the Dharma.

There has never been a case where the roots of beings are not yet matured for the teaching of the Dharma. "Simultaneous" (ekakāla) means that which is neither before nor after. To use the previous analogy of rain:

it must also be during the third or fourth month, when grasses and trees begin to sprout; only then is the falling of rain upon the grasses and trees called "simultaneous. If it rains in the eleventh month, it is "untimely.
Likewise, the preaching of the Dharma must also occur when the faculties of the assembly are matured. There are two meanings of "simultaneous."

First, it is precisely the time when the faculties of sentient beings have matured. Second, when the Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, sentient beings attain awakening and understanding simultaneously;
this is also called "simultaneous. The metaphor of "pouring down equally" illustrates preaching the Dharma with impartiality, making no distinction between śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
The Great Root and the Small Tree are taught with equal Dharma; hence it is said that [the rain] falls equally.
As for "timely rain," this refers to the time of great equality, the thirty-six rains, where the rain does not break up clods of earth.

If, in the final age, the rain is untimely, now it is revealed that [the teaching] accords with the faculties [of beings], being like that timely rain. (This concludes the general heading; below follows the horizontal nourishment.)
Regarding the scriptural passage that mentions "small roots, small stems, small branches, small leaves," and so forth: Question: What is meant by "horizontal growth" (*hengzi*)? Answer:

The scripture mentions "small roots" and so forth as a metaphor for the three types of grasses mentioned above receiving rain. Each attaches itself to its respective root, stem, branch, and leaf, spreading out horizontally; this is called "horizontal growth.

The mention of the "three grasses" and so forth manifests the horizontal aspect, while the listing of "attaching themselves" and so forth manifests the opening of flowers and the spreading of leaves as they extend horizontally; this is what is meant by [horizontal growth].

"Horizontal growth" (*hengzi*) refers to when [trees] grow both thick and tall; this is discussed in terms of vertical growth only with respect to a single type of grass. It is the same within the Dharma:
when those of the three vehicles and five natures hear the teaching, they are all able to practice the causes and attain the fruits within each respective vehicle—this is called horizontal growth.
If, however, one speaks only of the various trees within the Mahāyāna, according to their size as superior, middling, or inferior, this is called vertical growth.
The phrase "the natures of the three vehicles differ" is the heading; "the nature of the faculties" is the explanation; and "nirvāṇa, etc. is the proof.

Regarding the statement "whether one encounters [conditions] or does not encounter them," there are certain patients in the world who, if they meet a physician and take medicine, are cured immediately;
if they meet a physician who provides food and restorative care, they are also cured. This refers to those of great bodhi.

"Sā" means "if one encounters inequality," which refers to the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha). Question: It may be so for the śrāvakas; however, as for the pratyekabuddhas who do not encounter the appearance of a Buddha, how can they also be said to have a difference?
If we consider the stage when they first cultivate the wholesome roots conducive to liberation (mokṣabhāgīya), it is necessary that they encounter a Buddha.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that these three vehicles are equal in name: Question: Sentient beings possess their own innate spiritual lineages (*gotra*).

Why, then, are they described in terms of the teaching, principle, practice, and fruit as being like roots, stems, branches, and leaves? Answer: The spiritual lineage serves as the basis; the four factors, beginning with the teaching, serve as...

The "supporting" (āśraya): based upon these seeds, it is explained that there are subsequently roots, stems, branches, and leaves. When the Buddha’s teachings are heard, they nourish and adhere to the seeds within consciousness;
because this occurs first, it is called the "root. Second, when the Tathāgata teaches the dharmas of the fruit, they nourish and adhere to the seeds within consciousness;
this is called the "stem. Based upon a single seed, when categorized according to the four dharmas of teaching, principle, practice, and fruit:
This establishes the roots, trunk, branches, and leaves.

Regarding the statement "relying on the teaching to realize the principle," etc.: it is like relying on the root to attach to the trunk; relying on the principle to give rise to practice is like relying on the trunk to attach to the branches;
and attaining the fruit by relying on practice is like the sequential order of the production of branches and leaves. Question: Up to this point, you have only taken up practice.

The Dharma is like medicinal herbs. One does not take the fruits of the teachings and principles [as the primary focus]. Why, then, are the fruits of the teachings and principles now assigned to the roots, branches, and leaves?
Answer: The previous section concerned that which is nourished. Among the three types of grasses, the practice of the *śrāvaka* (the "root") is what can directly attain the fruit;

it possesses the sense of growth and the sense of curing illness. Therefore, it was specifically selected. The three meanings of non-arising (*anutpāda*) do not constitute the direct means for curing illness; therefore, they were not selected.

Now, the three aspects of teaching (*śāsana*), principle (*yukti*), and fruit (*phala*) exist in dependence upon [the Dharma]. Since all of them are dharmas that nourish, they are taken collectively. Question:

Previously it was stated that the teaching is that which nourishes, while principle, practice, and fruit are the three things to be nourished. Why, then, are all four dharmas now said to be that which nourishes? Answer:
The previous statement that "only this is that which nourishes" was designated from the perspective of the beginning. In reality, it must be so from the very outset.
One hears the teaching, and only then realizes the principle; through practice, one attains the fruit. Thus, there must first be the initial [stage of] teaching before the subsequent three can exist;
for this reason, it is taught that the teaching alone is "that which nourishes. However, according to reality, the teaching, the principle, the practice, and the fruit are all "that which nourishes."

Regarding the statement "furthermore, based on superiority and inferiority": hearing the teachings on the *dharmas* of the fruit is superior, and thus it nourishes and adheres to the seed-nature (*gotra*) like a root.

Hearing the teachings on the *dharmas* of practice is next in inferiority, and thus it nourishes and adheres to the seeds like branches. Hearing the teachings on the *dharmas* of instruction is the most inferior, and thus it nourishes and adheres to the seeds like leaves. These are to be assigned accordingly.
To speak of "horizontal" refers to the three vehicles, which are like the large, medium, and small grasses.

To speak of "vertical" refers to the four categories, which are likened to the roots, stems, branches, and leaves. Within these dharmas, all receive [the teachings] regarding doctrine, principle, practice, and fruition.
These are called the four vertical stages.
As for the statement that "categories exist based on nature," "nature" refers to the spiritual lineage (*gotra*). Without seeds, there can be no growth upon roots, stems, branches, and leaves;
therefore, there are four categories, which likewise exist based on nature. Why are these not called horizontal? The answer is: two trees depend upon that [same ground].
The vertical nature does not rely on the horizontal nature; these two natures, horizontal and vertical, will be distinguished below.

As for the statement that some also speak of four [stages], these refer to the two stages prior to the grounds: the stage of equipment (*sambhāra*) and the stage of application (*prayoga*). The stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*) is called the root of the tree;
the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) is called the trunk; the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) is like the branches; and the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*) is like the leaves.

Regarding the statement that "this meaning is not universal," the Master of the Commentary refutes the ancients. Although roots, stems, branches, and leaves exist, they are not found among all small herbs;

therefore, he does not adopt [that classification]. Likewise, prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) of the two vehicles, there is no designation of the stage of resolute conduct (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*);
furthermore, for those of the human and celestial vehicles, these four stages do not exist either.
Regarding the term "vertical growth" (*shùzhǎng*): among the two types of wood, the distinctions in the growth of the three grades—superior, middling, and inferior—are called "vertical growth.

Mǔ (Móu) says: because the three grades flourish and benefit from the bottom to the top, it is named "vertical. Thus, the Sūtra states: "In accordance with the superior, middling, and inferior [capacities], one speaks of the superior, middling, and inferior;
only then is it called 'vertical. In that passage concerning the three types of grass, the text does not state that there is a superior grade.

The commentary categorizes this as "horizontal. In reality, if one were to discuss the superiority or inferiority, or the depth or shallowness, of grasses and trees, there would be no distinction between horizontal and vertical.
As for the mention of "large trees" and so forth in the discourse, this explains the intent of the Sūtra; the Sūtra states: "Among all trees, large and small, each receives its own [share]."
This seed is unsurpassed. The scriptural passage does not belong to the section refuting [the view of] illness. The scripture itself states that there are superior, middling, and inferior [levels].
Therefore, we know that the two types of wood are called "upright and long. The seeds of the four wisdoms and bodhi are not separate from the Buddha-body;

this is what is meant by "not being separate from my own body. Because this is not taught among the followers of the Two Vehicles, only in the Mahāyāna is there the meaning of the unsurpassed nature of the seed.
Regarding the phrase "before the stage of non-retrogression" and so forth: Question: For what reason do the two types of wood (the small and the large) have two different masters' interpretations?

Answer: Because the scriptural text is concise yet all-encompassing; it speaks of "turning the wheel of non-retrogression" and "delivering immeasurable billions," without further distinguishing the stages or positions. Both [interpretations] are therefore permitted.
"Transformation. From the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*) onward, it is called a "large tree"; prior to that, it is called a "small tree.
This merely reflects the difference in the assigned stages of non-retrogression; this is why there is a divergence in the views of the two masters (the above quotation indicates this).
Regarding the statement "one [type] and seven [types] prior to the seventh stage," this master combines the large and small wood into one place and divides them into three grades.
According to the lower verse of the sutra, "all trees—superior, middling, and inferior"—are categorized according to their size;

thus, he does not distinguish between the two types of wood (large and small). Therefore, he generally divides them into three grades based on the three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomayakāya*). This is the characteristic.
It is said: From the first stage to the fifth stage is designated as "lower. This is called the *samāpatti-sukha-manomaya-kāya* (body made of mind born of the bliss of meditative attainment).
Because it is a birth of transformation (*pariṇāmi-janman*) that arises according to one's will, it is called the "mind-made body" (*manomaya-kāya*). Why is it called the "body formed by mind"?

The sixth, seventh, and eighth stages are designated as "middle. Those who attain the *dharmatā-svabhāva-avabodha-manomaya-kāya* (body made of mind through awakening to the self-nature of phenomena) are able to contemplate conditioned things as an illusion.

All phenomena (*dharma*) are entirely without substantial reality. To observe and realize that all phenomena, such as illusions and the like, are utterly non-existent is called "the joy of awakening to phenomena.

However, upon attaining the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta*), one is immediately able to awaken to the fact that phenomena are like illusions and lack intrinsic substance; this occurs in the sixth stage (*bhūmi*) without requiring a long period of time.

The seventh stage involves preparatory effort (*prayoga*); therefore, the sutra specifically refers to the eighth stage. In reality, however, this principle applies throughout the preceding seven stages as well.

Regarding the statement that there are ninety-two stages: it means that according to the various diverse types of sentient beings, Bodhisattvas are able to manifest bodies identical to them, arising simultaneously.
Although they arise simultaneously, they do so without preparatory effort, arising spontaneously and effortlessly.
To exert effort is called "unconditioned practice" (*anabhisaṃskāra-caryā*). The meaning of "body" is the same as before.
Just as various images can appear simultaneously within a mirror without any deliberate application (*prayoga*), so it is here as well. Question: What is meant by "various types"? Answer:

From the eighth stage upward, in a single moment, based upon the body of transformation (*pariṇāma-kāya*), one is able to manifest hundreds of thousands of millions of types of bodies throughout the lands of the ten directions.

"Earth. Because one should transform sentient beings according to their faculties, it is called "species" (*jāti*); because many different types of bodies are manifested simultaneously, it is termed "species.

What is meant by "simultaneous arising" (*sahaja*)? Answer: Because there is no sequence [of before and after]. Manifesting hundreds of thousands of millions of types of transformation bodies and so forth all at once in a single *kṣaṇa* is called "simultaneous arising.

Question: What is meant by "effortless activity" (*anābhoga-vihāra*)? Answer: From the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) onward, there is no longer any preparatory application (*prayoga*); this is called [effortless activity].

Regarding "effortless practice" (*anabhisamskāra-caryā*): although within the gate of self-benefit there is no effortful practice, when teaching and transforming sentient beings, there remains a subtle cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Because one relies on the practice of benefiting others, one is not yet able to be precise and thorough regarding the gate of the medicine and the illness;

this is due to the need for provisional investigation and reflection (*vitarka-vicāra*) to contemplate the faculties and natures of sentient beings. Since there is no further application of effort within the practice of self-benefit, it is called "effortless."
This is indeed so.

As for the statement that this is not the case according to the meaning: regarding the first and second sections here, the former states, "I have already categorized the two types of wood, large and small.
[It continues: "A Bodhisattva prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) practices with outflows (*sāsrava*) for one great eon; it cannot be directed toward the small."
[The text] collects [the categories] within the "grass. This is why the subsequent classification includes terms such as "returning" (*pratyāgama*) and "not so" (*apratyāgama*).

The intention of this master is that he does not merely take those from the first bhūmi upward to represent the two types of "wood"—large and small. If only the preceding seven bhūmis were taken to represent "small wood," then under what category would bodhisattvas prior to the bhūmis be subsumed?
They would be subsumed under "small grass" or "medium grass. Within "small grass" and "medium grass," there are two types of "wood. The second...

Furthermore, since "wood" does not encompass those [beings] prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), where else could they be included? If small wood were not included, then the dharma of the three types of grass would be incomplete.
According to this principle, one takes the Bodhisattvas prior to the stages as "small wood.

Based on this, they are divided into three grades: those prior to the stages are the inferior grade; from the seventh stage back to the first stage are the middling grade; and the eighth stage... [is the superior grade].
The above refers to those of the highest grade. "Gathering the causes" refers to the great wood of the bodhisattva, which encompasses both types of wood.
If one follows this meaning, then "small wood" is designated as the lower grade in response to the preceding question;
"wood on the ground" is designated as the great wood, thereby distinguishing between the middle and the high grades.
Regarding the statement "exclusively impure cultivation": this refers to the impure perfuming through hearing (*śrutavāsanā*) during the one *kalpa* prior to the [first] stage (*bhūmi*).

Even when one hears the essential teaching (*dharmatā-deśanā*) that is pure (*anāsrava*), its reflection (*pratibimba*) remains constantly impure, as it is interspersed with outflows (*āsrava*) because it is produced by impure faculties (*indriya*). Thus, it is entirely impure.

The preceding section explained how the two types of wood—great and small—are each divided into three grades, due to the differences in the superiority and inferiority of the three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*).
This is divided into three grades.

Regarding the statement that "the first two refer to those prior to the First Ground," the Sūtra says: "To know for oneself that one will certainly become a Buddha without doubt—this is called a 'small tree.
Bodhisattvas prior to this ground are called 'small trees. Question: At the Eighth Ground, one severs doubts regarding both principle and phenomena (*tattva* and *dharma*).

[The doubt regarding principle is] exhausted. At the first stage (*bhūmi*), the doubt regarding principle is exhausted. How can one be free from doubt prior to the stages? Answer: Previously, one did not believe that one could become a Buddha oneself;
once the mind has been turned [toward awakening], one believes that one can become a Buddha oneself. Furthermore, a Bodhisattva of sudden enlightenment doubts others but does not doubt himself.
Hearing that śrāvakas become Buddhas is likewise free from doubt. The great branches and small branches each have three grades.
As for the three grades of the small branches, they are the ten abodes, the ten practices, and the ten stages of dedication.
Regarding the statement that "the ten faiths are the first [of the stages]," it is asked: why are the forty minds not mentioned? The answer is:
they are precisely the tenth, which is subsumed within the immeasurable dedication of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-apramāṇa-pariṇāmanā*).
Regarding the statement "by these [sūtras] such as the *Avataṃsaka*," this refers to the realization of the thirty minds. Question:

If that sūtra contains the thirty minds, why does it further speak of the bodhisattva of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) and the manifestation of the eight phases of enlightenment (*aṣṭa-mahā-prātihārya*)? Answer:

It is because the eight phases are accomplished within the very first stage, the Abiding in the Initial Resolve (*prathama-cittotpāda-vihāra*). Thus, they are subsumed under the ten stages of faith, for one enters the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*) from there.
Regarding the statement that it mentions only Śāriputra: the question is, how can we know that the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) are subsumed within the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*)?
The answer is given in the commentary: "It mentions only Śāriputra," etc. The *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* states that the ten stages of faith are subsumed within the ten abodes.

If there were a separate stage of "slight faith" (*mṛdu-śraddhā*), why would this sūtra mention [Śāriputra] having practiced for one hundred and sixty kalpas? It is because he cultivated that single stage of faith.

After ten kalpas, one reaches the sixth stage (bhūmi) and immediately regresses into two positions; since this takes only sixty kalpas, we know that the ten faiths cannot be established as a separate stage.
Regarding the statement that this refers only to the thirty-three [asamkhyeyas]: there are three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*).

First, the *asaṃkhyeya* of the stage of practice through faith (*śraddhācaryā*); second, the *asaṃkhyeya* of the stage of practice through vigor (*vīryacaryā*); and third, the *asaṃkhyeya* of the stage of practice leading toward [the goal] (*abhimukhacaryā*). Within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), there are three for each stage, namely:

the mind of entry (*praveśa-citta*), the mind of abiding (*sthiti-citta*), and the mind of emergence (*niṣkramaṇa-citta*). These respectively eliminate the internal obstacles of those stages. Since it has already been stated...
The stages prior to the *bhūmis* are three; it is not said that there are four. Therefore, there is no separate stage [for them].

Regarding the mention of the *Abhidharma-samuccaya* and other treatises (*ābhidharmika*), they subsume the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśalamūla*) and the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*).

After the first *kalpa* is completed, one cultivates the four roots of goodness. Although it is said that they are "fulfilled," the word "fulfillment" merely refers to the conclusion of the first *kalpa*; there is nothing further distinct from this.

When explaining [the stages], one does not speak of kalpas separately; it is clearly understood that the four roots of goodness are merely the immeasurable, universal inclusion within the dharma-realm (as explained above regarding the "small wood" analogy).

Regarding the statement that "the characteristics are the same as those of the world": on the first, second, and third stages, they are the same as the world because ordinary worldly people are also able to practice giving, ethical discipline, and patience;

thus, their characteristics are said to be the same as the world. On the third stage, the Bodhisattva achieves superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the Great Dharma-dhāraṇī, and is able to radiate the light of boundless sublime wisdom; therefore, it is said that [the characteristics] are "conformable" (*anuloma*).

Regarding the statement that they are "identical to those who have transcended the world" [in the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages]: the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages are similar to the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas).

In the fourth stage, bodhisattvas cultivate the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma); in the fifth stage, they contemplate the Four Noble Truths; and in the sixth stage, they contemplate dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda). Therefore, the Treatise states:

"Abiding securely in the most excellent factors conducive to enlightenment, they burn the fuel of afflictions, for the flames of wisdom increase. In the fifth stage, the two types of knowledge—of the ultimate and the conventional—are mutually interpenetrating in their activity.

This is incorrect; they should be made to correspond. Because it is extremely difficult to overcome, the wisdom of dependent origination in the sixth stage induces the most excellent non-conceptual *prajñā* to manifest.
The preceding five [stages] consist of the wisdoms of the ultimate and the conventional, which observe the four truths: first, defilement; second, purification.

Within the first four stages, one constantly contemplates the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena as objects of aversion, while regarding awakening and the path as objects of aspiration. In the fifth stage...
One is able to unify the ultimate and conventional realms, yet defilement and purity remain as the objects to be unified. It is like a single mirror reflecting both water and fire simultaneously;

water and fire exist in mutual relation. Only upon entering the sixth stage (*ṣaṣṭhī-bhūmi*) and abiding in the contemplation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-darśana*) is there finally neither defilement nor purity.

Regarding the statement that there are three grades among the "middle" [practitioners]: Question: Since those who follow the path of the pratyekabuddha attain the fruit in a single sitting, how can their levels be distinguished? Answer:

This is also based on whether they have not yet severed or have already severed [the afflictions]. Furthermore, when discussing pratyekabuddhas in relation to śrāvakas, there are likewise three grades.
Regarding the phrase "these [categories]": horizontally, they span the three vehicles—namely, the roots, stems, branches, and leaves of the great, medium, and small capacities.

Vertically, they correspond to the various trees of different sizes, each receiving nourishment according to its superior, middling, or inferior nature. Furthermore, this passage clarifies the difficulty regarding the division of two types of wood into three grades, which is termed "vertical growth.
As for the division of the three types of grasses into three grades, it should not be considered "horizontal flourishing. Therefore, this text provides a comprehensive explanation.
The above. *Hokkekyō Genzan Yōshū*, Volume 27.
Completed copying on the second day of the eighth month in the first year of the Gennin era at Fukō-in.
This is solely intended to cause the Dharma to endure for a long time and to benefit humans and devas.
Pseudo-monk Ningyuan (born in the year [blank], age fifty-eight).
*Fahua jing xuanzan yaoji*, Scroll Twenty-Eight.

Regarding the statement that "the reception of moisture varies," the Sūtra says: "The rain from a single cloud accords with their respective seed-natures (*gotra*). Here, "a single cloud" refers to the Buddha-body (*buddhakāya*).

The Buddha-body is the "rainer," while the "rain" is the Dharma-teaching that is rained down. "Accords with their respective seed-natures" means that it corresponds to the specific capacities of sentient beings.

This refers to what is nurtured and grown. That which attains growth consists of: first, hearing the teaching and generating the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), whereby one perfumes and acquires the seed of *bodhicitta*;
this is called "birth. Practicing for a long period of time is called "growth. Regarding the phrase "flowers and fruits unfolding and bearing fruit":

the character "unfolding" (*fū*) corresponds to "flowers," and the character "bearing" (*jitsu*) corresponds to "fruits. The unfolding of flowers is a metaphor for hearing the teaching; the blossoming of flowers reveals their fragrance, which is a metaphor for spiritual practice.

When the flowers of various practices bloom, one will surely see the *zhǐ* (fragrant herb). Once they have blossomed, they will surely produce lotuses. If the teaching is fully unfolded, one will surely practice the conduct that leads to nirvana.

Regarding the statement, "Comparing the teaching to the principle, etc.," this refers to the explanation of the distinctions between the Three Vehicles and the Five Vehicles based on this scriptural passage, which leads to a discussion of the differences among the various *yāna-piṭakas*.
Question: Since the teaching is, after all, a single uniform one, how can there be two distinct differences in what is called the *yāna-piṭaka*?
Answer: The commentary states, "Comparing the teaching to the principle, etc. Here, "teaching" refers to the single rain, and "principle" refers to the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Regarding the statement "or by means of the teaching, etc., subsequent to [the turning of the mind]," this refers to the faculties achieved after the turning of the mind (parāvṛtti).
Since there is only a single Mahāyāna faculty, it is called "one rain" and is also termed "one sound."

Regarding the statement that "the principle of the Dharma taught has but a single aspect," this concludes the preceding section by correlating the teaching with the principle, while disregarding the specific capacities [of the listeners];
this is termed "one rain.

Regarding the statement that "those of regressive nature and those of ultimate nature both become Buddhas," this concludes the preceding section by correlating the teaching with the subsequent stage, wherein those of indeterminate nature achieve [enlightenment].
Regarding their faculties, it is called "one rain" and also "one sound.

To say that the teachings are applied according to the faculties while setting aside the underlying principles and dharmas is termed the "Three Vehicles. This above serves as a general conclusion concerning the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas of both determinate and indeterminate natures.

Regarding the statement that "teachings or instructions are directed toward those with initial faculties at an immature stage": those of indeterminate capacity who have not yet turned their minds [toward the Mahāyāna] are called "those with initial faculties.
That which is set in motion for them is termed the "Three Vehicles" (triyāna) and is also called the "Three Chariots" (trivāhana).

The phrase "according to the suitability of their faculties, first [teaching] the lateral [vehicle], etc. is the conclusion. Question: What is meant by the "initial lateral method of induction"? Answer:
The teaching of the Hīnayāna during the forty years prior [to the Lotus Sūtra] is called the "initial method of induction" and is also called the "lateral method of induction.

The teaching of the One Vehicle on the Vulture Peak assembly—wherein "the direct [path] abandons expedient means"—is also called the "correct method of induction" and the "subsequent method of induction. Mou said:
If the teachings of the three vehicles are expounded for those of fixed capacity, they are collectively termed the "Directly Inducing Dharma" (*samyak-ākarṣaṇa-dharma*).

If the teachings of the two vehicles are expounded for those of indeterminate capacity, they are termed the "Indirectly Inducing Dharma. Expounding the One Vehicle is termed the "Directly Inducing Dharma. (The above clarifies the distinction between the vehicles; below clarifies the distinction between the treasuries.)

If one says that the teachings encompassing practice constitute the Tripiṭaka, they are precisely the three trainings: ethical discipline (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).

Teaching that elucidates the practice of ethical discipline is called the Vinaya Piṭaka; teaching that elucidates the practice of meditative concentration is called the Sūtra Piṭaka; and teaching that elucidates the practice of wisdom [is called the Abhidharma Piṭaka].

It is called the *Piṭaka* of Names (*nāma-piṭaka*). Regarding the statement "if the teaching contains the principle (*tattva*) and so forth": because the teaching contains the principles of the emptiness of sentient beings (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), it is called the Śrāvaka-piṭaka for those with the capacity of a śrāvaka.
Because the teaching contains the principles of the two-fold emptiness (*dvi-śūnyatā*), it is called the Bodhisattva-piṭaka for those with discerning faculties. Question: Why is this not stated?

Regarding the "Pratyekabuddha-piṭaka," there are two explanations. First, because among the Pratyekabuddhas the teachings are few, they are subsumed within the Śrāvakas by taking the few from the many.

Alternatively, because they hear [the Dharma] arising from sound, Pratyekabuddhas may also be called Śrāvakas. Question: Since they are collectively termed Śrāvakas, why are the Pratyekabuddhas not mentioned first?
[One might argue that] the Pratyekabuddhas are the most sharp-witted. Answer: They are subsumed by taking the narrow from the broad. Therefore, they are included [within the Śrāvaka category].

This refers to entering the stage of the śrāvaka. Those who are pratyekabuddhas are few, while those who are śrāvakas are many; thus, the narrower category is subsumed under the broader one. Furthermore, pratyekabuddhas possess sharp faculties (tīkṣṇendriya), whereas śrāvakas possess dull faculties (mṛdvindriya).

If one were to speak only of those with sharp faculties, those with dull faculties would not be included. Therefore, when speaking of those with dull faculties, those with sharp faculties are also included. Question:
Since there are three types of "grass," why is the teaching for the "small grass"—consisting of humans and devas—not called a "piṭaka" (basket)? Answer: Regarding the teaching for the small grass...
It may be understood that [the King] was not granted the title of "Tripiṭaka.
Regarding the statement "King Ajātaśatru," it serves as proof that he possessed the Three Piṭakas.
As for the phrase "now, matching the teaching with the principle," one asks: since the *Ajātaśatru Sūtra* already contains the Three Piṭakas, why is this...?

The Sūtra speaks of "one rain. The answer is: in this Sūtra, the teaching is contrasted with the principle (*tattva*), and because the faculties of the subsequent [beings] are fixed as one, it is called "one cloud and one rain.

Regarding the statement that there are currently present capacities (*indriya*) to be addressed: "principle" refers to the *tattva*. Alternatively, within the principle of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), there are both shallow and deep levels.
Regarding this, the distinction between the two vehicles is clarified.

As for the principle of the teaching corresponding to the capacity of the recipient: the principles of the teachings addressed to the three types of faculties, such as the śrāvakas, are termed the Śrāvaka-piṭaka and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "the teaching that will reveal the principle," etc., this concludes the preceding section on the basis for naming the vehicle attained through the teachings.
