This is what is realized within the fundamental contemplation of an Arhat and is termed the "transformed city" (*nirmāṇa-pura*). Those who are learners (*śaikṣa*) of the two vehicles and ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) of the seven stages of preparation are termed "other people."

Regarding the phrase "endowed with speech and so forth": the question asks how one knows this does not refer to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), those in training (*śaikṣa*), or ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).

The answer is that the commentary on the passage beginning with "speech and so forth" serves as the proof. These first seven sections of the commentary explain the first section of the opponent’s treatise.

Regarding the statement "Furthermore, there is an interpretation concerning 'existence' (*asti*) and so forth": the eighth [point] specifically concerns ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), distinguishing them from those in training (*śaikṣa*) who aspire toward [the higher realms].
This is precisely the intended meaning of the second heading in the *Vyākhyāyukti*. As for the term "existence" used by the author of the treatise, it refers to various types of persons.
The preceding discussion on the seven stages of preparation (*saptaprayoga*) for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) has already been explained.
Within this second category, there are four types, all of whom are ordinary beings who have attained meditative concentration (*samādhi*). The first consists of two types:

(1) those ordinary beings who, having performed non-agitated karma (*āniñjya-karman*), are born in the higher realms and attain the concentration of those higher realms; and (2) those whose bodies remain in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) yet, while seated, attain the stage of the higher realms.

Regarding "concentration" (*samādhi*): this refers only to ordinary persons who have attained concentration, not to non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). This point remains entirely unrefuted. Second, there are two further categories:
first, those non-Buddhists who suppress their afflictions through the six practices and attain concentrations of the higher stages, yet reckon each individual concentration to be *nirvāṇa*.
This is subsumed under wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), and this too is not refuted. Second, those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*).

When a person suppresses their delusions through the six practices and attains the four dhyāna concentrations, they reckon these as the four fruits of śrāmaṇya. To claim one has attained much when one has attained little is called *adhimāna* (overweening pride).
This [text] specifically refutes those who possess such overweening pride. The commentary states that from the words "the text contains an explanation" (*yixia*) onwards...
The intent of the Commentary (Sū) is the same as that of Jiaxiang. The reason for citing this is that the Master [Jiaxiang] said:
"Since the treatise states 'persons of overweening pride' (*adhimāna*), these are ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) who cling to the four dhyānas. Lu asked:

"The five thousand persons of overweening pride already departed during the 'Expedient Means' chapter (*upāyakauśalya-parivarta*); why are there more now? He replied: "Pride is of two types. The first is... (the text continues with the five types of pride).
The thousand [monks] who possessed transgressions of the precepts and overweening pride (*adhimāna*) were not present in the assembly when the previous chapter began and departed.

Second, those who possessed the precepts were called "overweeningly proud," and they were indeed present in the assembly. Therefore, the Commentary states: "Furthermore, there is an interpretation, etc., which refutes those with overweening pride by regarding the four dhyānas and samādhis as a 'transformed city' (*pariṇāmika-nagara*)."

Regarding the statement that the Buddha spoke of the non-learner (aśaikṣa) stage of the two vehicles and so forth: this refers to the transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya) and its cessation. Therefore, even when the Buddha preached the sūtras, he also refuted [this notion].

This is fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna), which realizes the principle of the emptiness of persons (pudgala-nairātmya). It is a skillful means (upāya) to lead others into [realization], like a conjured city (gandharva-nagara).
Compared to the three types of nirvāṇa, it is called "unreal. How much more so, then, regarding the four dhyānas and samādhis you have attained—would you cling to them as a true cessation?
This correctly refutes the four dhyāna-samādhis clung to by those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*), who grasp them as actual cessation.
Regarding the phrase "those who are still in training" (*śaikṣa*) and so forth, this is a further refutation of those in training so that they do not give rise to such a clinging.

[The view] that the four dhyāna-concentrations constitute the four fruits of śramaṇaship is held only by those with overweening pride; therefore, among those in training, [this has already been] attained.
The three preceding fruits and those on the seven stages of preparation (saptayoga) all do not give rise to grasping (*abhiniveśa*).

Regarding the phrase "the guide and so forth," the commentator concludes the tenets of his own school. Because the previous exposition of ancient interpretations was interrupted, he reiterates the conclusion here.
The passage cited is from the section on the extinction of the illusory city (*nirmitapurī*). An ancient master stated that the illusory city is the guide.

It was established by supernatural power (*ṛddhi*). Its destruction was likewise extinguished by that same supernatural power. Here, the commentator of this treatise explains it as "transformed" (*nirmita*) and "extinguished.

Within the passage concerning the establishment of the city in the Deer Park, and within the passage concerning its "establishment" (*prajñapti*), he does not say it is a transformation; rather, he merely exhorts one to enter the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
He simply states that the city was a transformation and was subsequently destroyed.
Regarding the statement "to break the attachment of those of the Two Vehicles," this refers to the transformation [city].

Regarding the statement "for the sake of extinguishing ordinary beings," this is called the extinction of the transformation. Herein, the true transformation city—though called "extinction"—is an extinction whose essence is non-extinguished.

The name and essence of the "transformed city" (nirmāṇa-pura) both perish. As for the "transformation," it is merely a provisional establishment; the remaining nirvāṇa is the extinction of that provisional name, which was the transformed city.

Furthermore, regarding the objects sought by those of the three preceding fruits who subsequently attain the wisdom of subsequent realization (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), it is not said that they themselves perish.
Moreover, the provisional cities sought by those of overweening pride (*adhimāna*) are entirely extinguished.
The statement "it should also be like the protector of the Dharma" (Dharmapāla) correctly accords with the interpretation of the ancients.

If one takes the person of overweening pride (*adhimāna*) who clings to the four dhyānas as being like a conjured city (*nirmāṇa-pura*), this is still like the protector of the Dharma’s position that there is no clinging within meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

The intended meaning of the Dharmapāla school is that, regardless of whether they are those in training (*śaikṣa*) or ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), all give rise to conceptual clinging within the distracted mind; for [they hold] that meditative concentration is wholesome, and... [there is no... clinging.
This is because it allows for the arising of unwholesome attachments (the meaning of the path).
Regarding the statement "the three," as the treatise treats them collectively, the commentary provides a threefold explanation.
Regarding the statement "therefore he is called Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū": this one practiced the path for one great kalpa and three incalculable kalpas;
when he was about to attain Buddhahood, the Buddha-dharma did not manifest before him, and he sat idly at the site of enlightenment for another ten kalpas.

This is intended to reveal that the Bodhi of the Mahāyāna is difficult to attain and its practice is likewise difficult to cultivate, unlike the two vehicles (Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha), which attain the fruit after practicing for sixty kalpas over three lifetimes. It is not so.
It is called "Supreme.

Regarding the statement that this constitutes a textual fragment (*vyañjana-śeṣa*) and so forth: from the beginning of the chapter up until the parable of the conjured city (*nirmāṇa-pura-upama*), it exhaustively explains the ancient and recent periods of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū.
The text of the parable of the conjured city does not specifically refute [the notion of] illness; rather, it merely reveals the essence of the Dharma (*dharma-tattva*).
"Venerable and exalted. Thus, this is a fragment of the text.
As for the statement, "Some speak of the Buddha-activities of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū," this refers to the sixteen princes. Regarding the phrase, "Your power of practice is unsurpassed":
when the sixteen princes first heard the sutra and began their cultivation, many kalpas passed; today they are oriented toward bodhi.
Beneath the tree, it is said that he attained Buddhahood through his practice, which is called "unsurpassed.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "all the śrāvakas and so forth," this is explained in three ways according to the three faculties of the śrāvakas. Śāriputra and others were taught on that very day;
they had already reached the stage prior to the sixth abode. How could they have practiced for such a long duration of time and yet still be directed toward the state of a śrāvaka?
He sat within the earth. Now, as the roots of beings in the Mahāyāna are finally ripening, we know that his practice is unsurpassed.

Regarding the statement that he did not preach the Great Pervading [Wisdom] (Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū) and so forth: the commentator fears that people might be confused, thinking that the latter two sections of the commentary—one explaining the practice of the sixteen princes and the other explaining the practice of the śrāvakas—are merely general explanations of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū’s cultivation.
[The text] proceeds. Fearing that people might fail to discern [the meaning], the commentary briefly states in a single phrase: "It does not speak of the practice of the Buddha of Great Pervasion.

Regarding the statement, "That which is about to be explained is the essential [practice]," this is a general response to an objection. The question asks: Within this chapter, the power of cultivation is being explained.

It is unsurpassed. Furthermore, the parable of the conjured city (*nirmita-pura*) is taught. Why is the title of the chapter not "The Chapter on Practice," but rather "The Chapter on the Conjured City"?
The Commentary answers: "That which is about to be explained now... and so forth. "Ancient" refers to the deeds of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū during his practice.

The intention is that while the parable of the conjured city is intended to be explained, it is necessary to recount the ancient events of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū; this is because the conjured city was situated three hundred *yojanas* away.

The external exposition: it is said to extend for three hundred *yojanas*. One must necessarily relate ancient events; by drawing them forth with the hook, one speaks so as to cause the present intention to be redirected toward what is truly taught.
Although one takes the realization of the past and present as the substance, even when taking the present fruit as the category, one takes the realization of the past and present as the substance.
This chapter is titled "The Parable of the Conjured City. It describes the conjured city established beyond three hundred *yojanas*.
It then explains the causes and conditions for establishing this conjured city; these "causes and conditions" refer to the practices performed in the distant past.

This is precisely the cause of the Mahāyāna, which is also contained within this chapter. Since cause and effect are inseparable, it is likewise included in this chapter, where its name is proclaimed.
Regarding the statement that "the power of increase is unsurpassed": it refers to the destruction of the illusory city (*nirmita-nagara*) and the leading [of beings] to the Mahāyāna.

Although two types of *nirvāṇa* are taught, these are merely provisional designations for analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). That [teaching] serves to transform and lead them to the Mahāyāna, thereby intending to increase the power of the practice of those of the Two Vehicles.
Their [former] great practice was called "exhaustion"; now, by reversing that and increasing the power of wisdom (*jñāna-bala*), it is termed "increase."
As for the statement "previously mentioned the illusory city (*tathāgatagarbha*) and so forth," this refers to the subsequent sutra.

Since the subsequent sutra first speaks of the illusory city and later speaks of the supreme increase of power, it is called "previously mentioned. Therefore, the subsequent sutra says: "Having formed this thought, by means of the power of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*)."
In the midst of the perilous path, after they had traveled three hundred *yojanas*, he manifested a city. Only later did he say:
"At that time, the Guide, knowing that these people had found rest and were no longer weary, immediately caused the manifested city to vanish and addressed the multitude, saying:
'You may proceed; the place of jewels is near. That great city you saw previously was created by me as a place for rest.'"
[The Buddha] said: "This power of increase is unsurpassed.

Regarding the statement, "It has not yet been told to the caravan leader and others," this explains the scriptural passage on the unsurpassed power of increase. This unsurpassed [power] does not have a separate scriptural passage;
it simply takes the passage concerning the extinguishing of the illusory city as being the power of increase itself.
Regarding the statement that "this is a remainder of the meaning": the Buddha established the "transformed city" (nirvāṇa-city) originally to provide rest for merchants who were weary and exhausted;
both [the city] and cessation (*nirodha*) are metaphorical texts. Since metaphorical texts belong to others, the text on the transformed city belongs to the section on destroying the illness.

In the *Dharmaparyāya*, it is taught that the nirvāṇa of the two vehicles is provisional, intended to increase the attainment of the Mahāyāna mind. The text on the destruction of the transformed city belongs to others. It destroys [the illness].
The treatment for the illness has already been completed. Within this, one portion increases the minds of merchants; when contrasted with the Two Vehicles, it is named "Unsurpassed.
This is like a household harvest that is not uniform; such is the meaning of the "residue" (śeṣa).

Regarding the phrase "warding off bandits" (*yu kou*) and so forth: "bandits" refers to calamities. The calamity of the bandits of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) allows for the attainment of *nirvāṇa* with remainder;
the cessation of the suffering of birth-and-death is called "warding off bandits. Those exhausted by birth-and-death—being boiled and scorched within the six realms—are called "the weary.
The bliss of tranquil extinction is *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding the statement, "Now, this is called 'analogical discourse' (aupamya-viniścaya)": it is called "analogical discourse" when an analogy is used to explain a doctrinal discourse (*dharma-viniścaya*), referring to them as being in the same category.

Alternatively, the analogy itself is the doctrine; among the twelve divisions of the teaching (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*), there is the *avadāna* (parable), wherein the analogy may also be designated as "doctrine.
This specific term "analogical discourse" clarifies that it is not a "doctrinal discourse."
Regarding the statement that "that which was originally non-existent now possesses the *abhiṣeka* and so forth," this refers to forcibly clinging to what is non-existent as being existent;

it is not Nirvāṇa, and is thus called "originally non-existent. To claim that this is true cessation is to be said to possess "arrogance" (*adhimāna*). This means to consider one's meager attainment to be a great attainment.

Regarding the statement that one clings to non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and so forth: at the stage of the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of an Arhat, as well as the provisionally established objective parts (*nimitta-bhāga*) sought by the two vehicles and ordinary beings, they cling to these as true analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). The Master of the Commentary points out that these are not true analytical cessation;
rather, they are the true analytical cessation realized within fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). This is what is called "non-analytical cessation."

To say that the presently explained "cessation through deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is the "transformation" (*nirmāṇa*) means that cessation through deliberation is liberation (*vimukti*), and liberation is nirvāṇa;

thus, while the names differ, the essence is the same. The intended meaning is that one says the true transformation-city has no substantial reality; by removing it, the provisional transformation-city naturally vanishes.
Thus, having simultaneously abandoned the true transformation-city, one proceeds toward the place of jewels.

Regarding the statement that one does not perform it as a "Buddha-activity" (buddhakārya): this refers to the supreme power of cultivation that thoroughly penetrates past events; this is what is called a Buddha-activity.

Regarding the statement that this present sutra does not [do so] and so forth: because it is remote, it is not taken up there; here, we take up the manifestation of the fruit as the title of the chapter. That is to say:
This is the conjured city.
To say that it is not by means of hidden causes refers to the fact that they had previously, in the past, resolved their minds upon the Mahāyāna.
Regarding Pūrṇa’s realization, the Sūtra says: "He then spoke these words: 'The World-Honored One is most extraordinary; what he has performed is rare.'"

There is. In accordance with the various dispositions of the world, through skillful means and insight, reaching down to the fundamental vows of the deep mind, it is said that the Buddha reiterates and confirms this. As the sutra states: "At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
'Do you see this Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra? I have always praised him as being foremost among those who preach the Dharma.'"
First: Regarding the bestowal of the prediction (vyākaraṇa). The Sūtra says: "O Bhikṣus, Pūrṇa was foremost among those who preach the Dharma under the seven Buddhas;
now, among those who preach the Dharma under me as well, he is likewise foremost. This concludes the title.
It is called the "Light of Dharma.

Regarding the passage in the sutra that speaks of "immeasurable" and so forth: "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) means exceeding the portion of calculation; "boundless" (*ananta*) means exceeding the portion of time;
"inconceivable" (*acintya*) means exceeding the portion of intellectual estimation; and "asaṃkhyeya" is translated here as "innumerable," meaning that one cannot calculate this asaṃkhyeya.
Reaching the immeasurable (*apramāṇa*). Counting these *asaṃkhyeya* [kalpas] until they reach the boundless (*ananta*), it is called the boundless *asaṃkhyeya*.
Counting these *asaṃkhyeya* [kalpas] until they reach the inconceivable (*acintya*), it is named the inconceivable *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*.
Regarding the mention of the three [qualities] for future generations, Jin says: "Tong" (通) means thorough penetration; it refers to the principle of the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*).

Because the wisdom capable of such penetration is untainted (*anāsrava*), it is called "Victorious Wisdom" (*jñānavijaya*). The name of the land is "Good Accomplishment" (*Sukhāvatī*); it carries the sense of being perfect and complete. Since all the great dharmas of the Buddhas are entirely perfected therein, it is named "Good Accomplishment."

Regarding the "great signs" (*mahānimitta*): during a kalpa, great signs of the Buddha’s activity appear; because these appearances are vast, they are called "great signs. Regarding the "initial calculation":
[the questioner] asks, "World-Honored One, as previously stated, 'boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable' (*asaṃkhyeya*)—is this a large number?

The Sūtra answers: "O Bhikṣus, suppose one were to take all the earth-element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) and grind it into ink until no earth-element remained. As for the term *mudi-dhātu*, it refers to the earth-element.
These are the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). Among these four great elements, one does not take water, fire, or wind; one takes only the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*).

Within the earth element, there is that which is provisional and that which is substantial. That which is perceived by the eye is provisional; that which is apprehended by the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) is substantial.
Earth has hardness as its nature, and water has moisture as its intrinsic nature. This true earth element is the tangible object apprehended by the body-faculty.

That which is gathered by dust cannot be seen by the eye. Herein, that which is taken as what the eye sees—what can be ground and rubbed—is the "earth-element" (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) in a conventional sense.
Second, "earth" refers to the supporting ground, and "element" (*dhātu*) refers to the category; mountains, rivers, valleys, grasses, and trees are collectively termed the "earth-element.
Taking the former meaning is correct. Suppose there were a person who took the entire trichiliocosm...
Prepare some ink. Grind it thoroughly to make ink. Following this method, travel toward the east for a full thousand lands and drop a single dot.
Travel another thousand lands and drop another dot. When the ink is exhausted by this method, it is called "exhausting the seeds of the earth" ink.
Regarding these "seeds of the ink," there are two explanations. One says that after grinding it into water, one travels for a thousand lands and then drops [a dot].
"One dot. Second, it says "grind" (mò). This means taking minute particles by grinding them to form the dot.

Regarding the statement that there is no character "grind" (mò) used with the phonetic value of "ma" (mó), Zhangjing says: this means that the character "grind" (mò) possesses only the departing tone (qùshēng).
Regarding these questions and answers: the question asks, "What do you think?
Whether it be the master mathematician or his disciples"—the term "many" implies that even a single person cannot know exhaustively, nor can many people together know exhaustively.

Changjing says: "The intent clarifies that the disciples are as proficient as the master in calculation and examination, and it demonstrates the path of learning and transmission through which they mastered calculation."
"A great city is not like that. Why must you mention the teacher and his disciples? Do you know their number? These are the words of the question.

"No, World-Honored One," is the phrase of the answer. The Sūtra says: "If they were equal to a single point, then even if one did not mark the first thousand, the number of lands equal to the remaining nine hundred and ninety-nine dust motes would still be unknowable; how much more so for those beyond that?"
This is the enumeration.

Regarding the statement that "the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*) is called 'knowing'": the intention of the *Śāstra* is that the subsequent wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) is termed "knowing," while the Buddha’s five eyes (*pañcacakṣus*) are termed "seeing.

Furthermore, the knowledge of past lives is termed "knowing," and the wisdom-eye (*prajñācakṣus*) is termed "seeing. Lü [Cheng] says: The *Śāstra*’s commentary on the sūtra speaks according to what is predominant; in reality, however, the Buddha—
The eyes also see.
Regarding the statement that Śākyamuni’s practice did not exceed [the initial resolve], Mou says: "At that time, he was already clearly called a prince.
The commentary states that "yet" (猶) means "still" (尚). The intent of the question is: even if one were to first generate the aspiration for enlightenment during the era of the Buddha Mahāvīra.

Up to the present time, three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* have already passed—by a factor of hundreds of thousands of millions; how much more so for the kalpa prior to Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, when he had already long since resolved his mind [on enlightenment].
It was only upon reaching the time of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū that he became a prince.

Since the status of a prince is not the stage of initial resolve (*prathama-cittotpāda*), how could it be said that he only attained Buddhahood after such a vast period? One should rather say that he had already been a prince long ago. This is the intended meaning.

At that time, the sixteen princes had already practiced for a long duration and reached the first bhūmi or above. It was only after the passage of countless *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas that they first attained Buddhahood.

Why, then, would their birth have been so late? At that time, they were already princes; on that day, they were still ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), yet they would have already attained Buddhahood long ago—let alone having been called princes from the start.
Regarding the statement that "there are four types of intended meaning (*abhiprāya*)," the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* explains that there are four intentions which interpret the four secrets (*saṃdhi*).
Within all the extensive Mahāyāna teachings, nothing exceeds these four secrets; thus, the Tathāgata interprets them by means of the four intentions.

The first is the intention of establishment (*vyavasthāpanābhiprāya*). "Intention" refers to the Buddha’s cognitive mind, which has the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) as its essence.
The secret is the teaching; its essence consists of the aggregates of form and formations, namely phonemes, names, phrases, and sentences (2. Defining the essence).
Within this, there are four [equalities]. To summarize: first, the equality of the single syllable, because the past [Buddhas] and the self are identical in being named "Buddha.
Second, the equality of speech, because all past Buddhas as well as the present Śākyamuni possess sixty-four kinds of exquisite vocal tones and language for their teachings.

The Dharma is identical. First is the equality of the three bodies (*trikāya*), because there is no difference between my own Buddha-body and the *dharmakāya* and *rūpakāya* adornments of all Buddhas.
Second is the equality of the Dharma, because I and all Buddhas have attained the same merits, such as the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).

Third is the equality of secret teachings, which serve as proximate skillful means for the task of teaching and transforming sentient beings. Fourth is the equality of the four intentions (*abhiprāya*), which serve as remote [skillful means].
This is the skillful means (*upāya*). The harmonious integration of these meanings is called "the secret. Next, the four intentions (*abhiprāya*) are used to explain the four secrets.
Although the thousand Buddhas and ten thousand Buddhas are each distinct, their *dharmakāya* is identical in principle; that Buddha is my own body—this is the intention of the Buddha.
Regarding the statement "the intention of equality" up to "because they are equal": The Victorious Vision Buddha (Vipaśyin) of the distant past was my own body.
In reality, the Victorious Vision Buddha and Śākyamuni Buddha are indeed distinct; however, this is spoken from the perspective of the intention of equality.
To identify the other Victorious Vision Buddha as one's own body is based on the identity of their *dharmakāya*. This does not preclude the sixteen princes of the past [from being my emanations].
This is the Buddha’s intended meaning (*abhiprāya*). The sixteen princes of the past were, in fact, those very Buddhas who were practicing the causes [of enlightenment] at that time;
yet, having long since attained Buddhahood, they identified others' paths as their own bodies—this is called "secret" (*guhya*). By what teaching is this explained?
The answer is: by means of the "intentional meaning of equality" (*samatābhiprāya*) in conjunction with the "harmonious synthesis."
Regarding the phrase "the intention regarding a different time" (*kāla-antara-abhiprāya*) and so forth: although the words refer to the present, the intended meaning refers to a different time.
For example, when it is said, "May I attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss," and one immediately attains rebirth, this serves as a remote cause for future rebirth;

if actual rebirth were to occur, one would still need to further cultivate wholesome deeds and mindfulness of the Buddha before it could be achieved. Thus, the statement that by making a vow one attains rebirth is an instance of the intention regarding a different time.
When the words and the intended meaning differ, it is called an "intentional teaching regarding a different time" (*kālavimukty-abhiprāya*). For example, as it is said:
"By recollecting Ānanda, haṃ khaṃ," or "By briefly hearing the name of the Buddha Vimalacandraprabha throughout the entire *Tripiṭaka*, one attains Buddhahood.

Such matters are difficult for ordinary people to understand; they must be explained by means of the principle of intentional teachings regarding a different time. What is cited here in this commentary is precisely [an instance of this].
In the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, it is stated that by merely making a vow, one attains rebirth in the World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*).

This meaning serves to nurture roots of virtue from previous times; it is like the worldly saying that one obtains a thousand coins simply by means of a single coin. This is an intention regarding a different time (*kāla-antara-abhiprāya*).
If one wishes to be born in the Pure Land, it is necessary to practice the causes; how can one do so by merely making empty vows? Question:

It is stated in detail throughout the sutras that by reciting the name of Amitābha, one attains birth in the Pure Land, so there is no room for solitary doubt. How, then, can this secret method be accomplished?
Answer: Holding the Name and making vows are both causes. When one is about to reach the end of life, one will certainly be reborn in the Pure Land.

The Pure Land is the fruit, and making vows is the cause. Based upon the present cause, the future fruit is proclaimed, so as to enable sentient beings to accumulate practices until their merit is perfected.
The commentary on the shadows explains cause and effect; thus, it constitutes a secret teaching. This refers to both the general and specific meanings.

Regarding the statement that "the three distinct meanings refer to the intent and so forth": when speaking generally regarding the three natures, they are all said to be empty; this is termed "secret. However, the matter must be explained according to their specific meanings:

namely, that the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) is empty, while the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) and *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature) are not empty. This is called "distinct meaning."
Although this meaning is discussed, the intention lies in another meaning; because the verbal expression differs from that intended meaning, it is called "a different meaning" (*arthāntara*).
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "If one serves as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, one can then understand the Mahāyāna Dharma.

Asṅga’s commentary explains: "This refers to the meaning of the Mahāyāna Dharma characterized by realization (*adhigama-lakṣaṇa*) and the meaning of the Mahāyāna Dharma characterized by teaching (*deśanā-lakṣaṇa*)."

There are distinctions between them. Regarding the mental verbalization that understands the meaning, there are two types. First, it is only at the time of realizing the principle that one is said to "understand the meaning";

this refers to those who have realized the characteristics of the Mahāyāna, namely Bodhisattvas from the first bhūmi upward. Second, at the time of hearing and reflection, it is also called "understanding the meaning."
That is to say, the Mahāyāna according to the provisional teachings (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*) is that which is heard by ordinary beings prior to the stage of the ten faiths.

Because there are differences between the stages of the noble ones and ordinary beings, it is called "distinctive. This means that, according to the Mahāyāna of the provisional teachings, it is not difficult to understand;

however, because it is said that one can only attain realization and understanding after encountering many Buddhas, it constitutes a "secret. When the Tathāgata speaks of the meaning of that realization and understanding, it appears within his words as if he were speaking of awakening.
This is the meaning of "explanation"; thus there is this distinction.

Regarding the phrase "the inclinations (*āśaya*) of the fourfold assembly," it is asked: what is meant by "esoteric" (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*)? It is answered: when the Buddha preaches the Dharma, if he were to praise something, he would praise it extensively;
if he were to disparage it, he would disparage it extensively. Yet, in a single practice, he may either praise or disparage; this is called "esoteric. This is because...

This is the explanation regarding the intentions and underlying purposes of the Buddha’s words for sentient beings. For those who are stingy, the Buddha praises generosity and the act of giving, so that they may develop contentment and cease seeking other practices.
However, because he wishes to cause them to fully cultivate superior qualities of virtue, he subsequently disparages that very same generosity.
Thus, while his own statements appear contradictory and inconsistent, they are in fact intended as a secret teaching (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*).

The esoteric [meaning] is that one observes the faculties to receive the Path, for such is the nature of the Dharma; thus it is called the "intention" (*abhiprāya*). To remedy greed, one praises giving;

to be constantly delighted by seeing [the teacher], one draws near; and to honor and respect [him], one seeks a good reputation. Furthermore, these act as causes for future times; this is called the "excellent benefit of giving."

If there are those who do not seek the Dharma, for their sake one should say: "Even if worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were filled with precious jewels and offered as gifts to all the Tathāgatas, it would not equal the gift of a single Dharma.
If there are those who violate the precepts, one should say: "A person of wisdom can protect the precepts and thereby attain three kinds of happiness:
renown, gain and offerings, and after death, rebirth in the heavens. If there are those who delight in observing the precepts but do not delight in the Dharma, one should say: "What is the use?"

If one possesses the foundation of ethical discipline (*śīla*), though it be weak or inferior, yet is able to explain the Dharma for the benefit of many, such a person should be honored like my Great Teacher.

If one delights in much learning (*bahuśruta*) but does not cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they are like a poor man who counts another's treasures while possessing not even half a coin of his own.
If one cultivates concentration but does not delight in much learning, how can it be said that "much learning increases wisdom"? For it is through much learning that [wisdom] is made possible.
It draws forth joy. Through much hearing, one abandons what is meaningless; through much hearing, one attains nirvāṇa. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, in the "Chapter on the Inquiry into Knowledge," states:
"The Buddha knows that the dispositions and inclinations of sentient beings differ; according to how each should be delivered, he thus preaches the Dharma: to those who are stingy, he praises giving;

to those who violate the prohibitions, he praises upholding the precepts; to those with much anger, he praises patience; to those who are indolent, he praises diligence; to those who are distracted..."
The mind praises meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), while ignorance praises wisdom (*prajñā*).
Regarding the statement, "Now, relying upon equality," it means that Śākyamuni had already attained Buddhahood previously. If one refers to him by the distinct name Vipaśyin, [the question arises:
Is he that very same Buddha, or is it not so? The answer, as stated in the commentary, is that he relies upon this [equality] here.
This was spoken with the intention of equality (samatābhiprāya). In reality, it is not that those Buddhas [did not exist] (as the State Councilor Xiangguo interpreted);

rather, because the inclinations of sentient beings were such that they should hear accounts of other Buddhas' deeds, "other Buddhas' deeds" refers to the sixteen princes. This does not preclude that these were times when those other Buddhas were cultivating the causes [of enlightenment].
Now, based on the intention of equality, it is said that the deeds of other Buddhas are none other than my own person; for I have attained the intention of equality.
Regarding the statement "furthermore, the continuity of a virtuous mind" (extending to) "the Prince": this means that among the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), there is no unwholesome or neutral mind;
there is only a virtuous mind that continues from moment to moment. By accumulating these moments, the three great *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* are completed.

Now, the time remaining until the fruit of Buddhahood is short; thus, if one were to calculate the total duration of all moments during which the three natures arise in succession, [it would be as follows].

Therefore, even after such a vast number of kalpas have passed, there is no contradiction with the sutras. Furthermore, it is said that although the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya) has long since attained Buddhahood, it manifests various appearances for the sake of sentient beings.
Regarding Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, he was a prince, just like Mañjuśrī and others.
According to the *Ayuḥpramāṇa-parivarta*, the time of his attaining Buddhahood is clearly shown to be prior to that of the sixteen princes; [he did so] five hundred thousand million times.
[The number of eons] is equal to the atoms in hundreds of millions of nayutas of asamkhyeyas of trichiliocosms.
Since my attainment of Buddhahood, more than hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of asamkhyeya kalpas have passed. Why is there this contradiction? The answer is:

that [calculation] refers to his actual attainment of Buddhahood, whereas this prince’s account is based on the manifestation of signs. At the time of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, he manifested as a bodhisattva, just like Mañjuśrī.
These are not actual Bodhisattvas.

Regarding the phrase "furthermore, based on days and nights," if days, nights, months, seasons, and years were reckoned as kalpas, it would not conflict with the notion of kalpas as numerous as motes of dust.
However, if one speaks in terms of *mahākalpas* (great kalpas), they fall entirely within the three great kalpas of Śākyamuni.
Regarding the prose sections that follow: from this point onward, the prose and verse texts provide a commentary. At the end of the chapter, the scripture states:
"The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū sat at the site of enlightenment for ten *kalpas*. The verse begins from this point. The prose section following "The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
'The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū... is what follows that [verse]. Within this, as for each of the Brahma Kings of the ten directions:
The verses spoken at the beginning are merely recitations; they are not *geya* (verses corresponding to prose).

The Sanskrit verses found within the prose sections do not serve as verses corresponding to that preceding prose. Rather, the meaning is that the prose passages interspersed within the *geya* sections contain descriptive texts, which are termed "prose verses" (*gāthā*) containing descriptive text.
Regarding the statement "the first assembly’s own affairs," this is the second [section] which correctly clarifies those affairs.

At first glance, based on the outline of the commentary (*śū*), it might seem that this refers to the "first assembly’s own affairs" within the section correctly clarifying those affairs; however, that is not the case. The "affairs of the disciples" have already been categorized and presented previously;
it is simply according to the interpretation of the *Lù* (Road) that this is correct.
Regarding the scriptural passage stating that "the Buddha sat upon his seat," etc., it means that as long as the path of liberation has not yet arisen, the Dharma is said not to be manifest.

Regarding the statement that "the Reward Body (Sambhogakāya) attains enlightenment," if this refers to the attainment of enlightenment by the Self-Enjoyment Body (Svabhogakāya), it is indeed difficult to believe from a logical standpoint.

Jin says: "When the three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas are fulfilled, one studies the marks and signs for a hundred kalpas, studies majestic deportment for a thousand kalpas, and [studies] for ten thousand kalpas."

One studies transformative practice. If the causal practices are not fulfilled, one will not achieve Buddhahood. If it were said that one has already attained Buddhahood, why would it be necessary to sit empty at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas?
Whether a year is reckoned as a kalpa, and one further passes ten years; or whether a day is reckoned as a kalpa, and one further passes ten days—how could this be considered too long?
The commentary answers by stating that the attainment of the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body) and so forth provides a comprehensive reconciliation of these points.
Regarding the statement that the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) attains enlightenment: this transformation body is not a small or minor transformation body;
rather, it is manifested from the enjoyment body (saṃbhogakāya), which is the fruition body (vipākakāya), and is thus called "transformation."

Regarding the phrase "now, the other recompense body" (*paranirmita-vipāka-kāya*): this distinguishes it from the *svasaṃbhoga-kāya* (self-enjoyment body), and "recompense" (*vipāka*) distinguishes it from the *nirmāṇa-kāya* (emanation body).
Question: How is it known that this is the recompense body and not the emanation body? Answer: It is because the Buddha’s lifespan is stated to be five hundred and forty million *nayuta* years;

therefore, it is the recompense body. Thus, the commentary (*śāstra*) says: "Now, the other recompense body manifests its marks. Question: If it is the recompense body, how could it have [such a short]...?

The Patriarch [Wu] responded: "From the seventh stage downward, Bodhisattvas whose compassion has increased possess present retinues, because those with increased compassion still abide within the realm of birth-and-death (*bhavasaṃdhi*).
The commentary states: 'The other *saṃbhogakāya* is not as described; it is the other *saṃbhogakāya*.
This is because the phrasing accords with the preceding passage concerning the *nirmāṇakāya* attaining enlightenment and so forth."

Regarding the statement that awakening (bodhi) is difficult to attain, the Sūtra says: "One is on the verge of attaining awakening, yet the various Buddha-dharmas do not manifest before one," and so forth.

The five dharmas are not identical; they are called the "various Buddha-dharmas. Alternatively, the dharmas possessed in common by the Buddhas of the three periods of time are called the "various Buddha-dharmas.
These are precisely the awakening attained and the nirvāṇa realized—the dharmas of all Buddhas. Awakening...
Because the Bodhisattva manifests within his own body but has not yet attained perfect clarity, it is called "not appearing before [the eyes].

Regarding the statement "according to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and other texts," this refers to the ten matters concerning sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). For what reason does he sit at the site of enlightenment?
What are these ten matters? First, it is said that he causes all Buddha-fields to tremble in various ways. Second, he illuminates all...
1. Because of the world; 2. because of eliminating all evil realms; 3. because of transforming all lands into vajra; 4.
because of observing the lion’s roar of all Buddhas; 5. because of being free from all deluded minds and being pure like space;
6. because of manifesting a body and deportment that accord with purity; 7. because of conforming to the vajra-perfected samādhi.

Therefore, for nine reasons: because he accepts the pure seat of all Buddhas; and tenth, because by the power of his roots of goodness, he is able to bestow [benefits] upon all sentient beings—therefore, he sits at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).

Regarding the phrase "shattering the armies of Māra" and so forth, that sūtra asks: "What are the ten? First, it is because sentient beings in the world of the five turbidities delight in mutual warfare;
[the Buddha acts] to manifest the power of the Bodhisattva’s merit. Second, to completely extinguish all doubts and delusions of devas and humans.
Third, because he desires to transform and deliver the retinues of Māra. Fourth, because devas and people of the world delight in warfare...

1. "Conquest" means causing [beings] to submit and be transformed. 2. Fifth, having manifested the power of the Bodhisattva’s merit to the devas and humans, it is indestructible, for the purpose of taming sentient beings.
3. Sixth, because it gives rise to the power of all sentient beings. 4. Seventh, because of compassion for all future sentient beings. 5.
Eighth, even when demonic activities currently exist at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), one is able to completely transcend them.

Because it is the realm of the various Māras; ninth, because it reveals that the power and momentum of the afflictions (*kleśa*) are weak and inferior, whereas the power of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) of great compassion is exceedingly strong;
tenth, because it accords with the sentient beings of this turbid world. By virtue of possessing these ten meanings, he manifests the subduing of Māra.

Furthermore, the *Mahāyānapratipattisāra-sūtra* (The Great Vehicle Sutra) states that this is the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Moreover, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "Under the Bodhi tree, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni had not yet attained supreme enlightenment when Māra..."

They come to cause disturbance, fearing that [the practitioner] will transcend the three realms. The Bodhisattva enters the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*) and gives rise to the *Rāvaṇa-huṃkāra* (Thunderous Roar) Samādhi, whereby he immediately destroys the celestial Māras.
Regarding the statement "not otherwise, O Māras," Master Lu says: A Bodhisattva of the tenth stage manifests as a Māra-king, appearing before one's eyes with a form that fills the mind.
They are not even able to compete in strength, let alone against a Buddha; therefore, it is said that they are "not so.

Regarding the statement, "Furthermore, Śākyamuni Buddha destroyed [the Māras]," this refers to the eight phases of the Great Prajñāpāramitā, wherein he only defeated the celestial Māras after attaining enlightenment.

In this present sutra, however, only the Great Penetrating (Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū) Buddha is described as defeating the Māras and completing the realization of the Way; thus, the full text of the scripture contains these two accounts.
It is said that this matter is not fixed. If one attains the Way first and subsequently defeats Māra, then Māra competes in power with the Buddha;

if one defeats Māra first and subsequently attains the Way, then Māra competes in power with the Bodhisattva. This is because there are differences according to individual faculties and circumstances.
There is no need for reconciliation.
As for the statement "Furthermore, Maitreya and others," this serves as a general rebuttal to the objection. The *Sūtra on the Descent [of Maitreya]* states:

"At that time, King Śaṅkha, together with his various ministers, took a magnificent jeweled terrace and offered it to Maitreya. Having accepted it, Maitreya bestowed it upon the brahmins. The brahmins...
Having received it at the gate, they immediately destroyed it and divided it among themselves. Maitreya realized that this wondrous terrace was impermanent in an instant;

knowing that all phenomena are likewise subject to decay and extinction, he cultivated the mark of impermanence, left the household life to study the Way, and sat beneath the Dragon-Flower Bodhi tree.
With its trunk and leaves reaching fifty *li* in height, on the very day he left the household life, he attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Bodhi asked: "Why is it that Maitreya attained the Way on the very day he left the household life, whereas Śākyamuni practiced austerities for six years and sat at the site of enlightenment for ten great kalpas?
How can their speed and slowness be so unequal? He replied: "Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū waited for the faculties of sentient beings to ripen."
It takes ten kalpas to realize bodhi; this is not the case for Śākyamuni and Maitreya.

Each of these three Buddhas acts according to what is appropriate, causing sentient beings to conceive a sense of wonder toward the Buddha so that they may easily enter the Dharma. There is also such a matter as this:

during the time of Maitreya Buddha, the common people will mostly treat one another with arrogance based on their sharp intelligence; therefore, Maitreya will be born into a Brahmin family among those of keen faculties.

Because he is the most supreme and exalted. If one were of the Kṣatriya caste, who are highly esteemed for their great power and influence, people of the time would often have overwhelmed them with displays of valor.

Therefore, the Buddha was born into a Kṣatriya family because he is the most superior among those who possess valor. Furthermore, Śākyamuni appeared as a means to subdue the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).

He demonstrated various ascetic practices; for six years he consumed only hemp and wheat daily, yet his diligent austerities surpassed theirs. Therefore, the ways in which the Buddhas attain enlightenment each differ.
Regarding the phrase "spreading seats and so forth," Mou says: Some claim that this passage appears to be inverted; it should read, "sitting at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas.

However, since the preceding scriptural text contains the character "prior" (xian), it is not inverted. At first glance, it might seem as though the various devas collectively spread a single seat, but that is not the meaning.
Rather, each of the devas individually spreads a seat, and each perceives the World-Honored One receiving [offerings] at their own home.
He sat. He did not perceive himself as receiving the seat; the Buddha’s mind was impartial and accepted it universally. Question:
For what reason must one obtain the Vajrāsana (Diamond Seat) to accomplish the task of becoming a Buddha? Answer: Apart from the Vajrāsana, the World-Honored One cannot ascend upon any other object.
As for the seats now offered by the various devas, these are small secondary seats placed atop the Vajrāsana.
Regarding the phrase "the three scatterings of flowers," the word "適" (shì) in the sutra means "as soon as. As for the "one hundred *yojana* on each side," there are two explanations:

first, that each flower is square and circular, measuring one hundred *yojana* on each side; second, that when the flowers fall like fine rain, they circle the Buddha’s Bodhi tree, covering one hundred *yojana* on each side.

Regarding the term "jìyīn" (伎音): it is written with the radical "hand" (扌) and the character "zhī" (支), referring to formal arts and crafts. When referring to female musicians, it is written as "jì" (妓).

As for the phrase "the text of the sūtra follows the context," this merely refers to the continuity of the literary flow. To say that music was performed after [the Buddha's] passing is slightly less obscure than the other reading.
One interpretation states: it simply means that the performance of music continued until his parinirvāṇa; the limit is set at the time of his parinirvāṇa, precisely at the moment of his passing.
Dudo asked, "If one says that serving [the Buddha] throughout one's life is like reaching its conclusion, how can one serve him?

The second [master] replied, "It is like when Śākyamuni entered parinirvāṇa: the śrāvakas wept, while the bodhisattvas rejoiced. Knowing that the Buddha neither comes nor perishes, it is not an obstacle to making music."
Regarding the statement that first clarifies the sixteen princes: Question: Why are the sixteen princes listed first, followed by their ancestor, the Wheel-Turning Sage King?
Answer: It is precisely because one wishes to establish a karmic connection (*saṃbandha*) with the sixteen princes that the princes are listed first.
Regarding the phrase "relatives and so forth": Question: For what reason did the sixteen princes request the turning of the wheel of Dharma first? Answer:

The commentary states that because their relatives were present before them, they were not [treated as] equals. The *Miù* (Concordance) says that the sixteen princes requested the turning of the Mahāyāna wheel of Dharma.

The Brahma Kings of the ten directions requested that the Wheel of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) be turned. When the Brahma King *Raudra* made his request, the sixteen princes were also present in the assembly.

After the turning of the Wheel of the Lesser Vehicle was completed, a great deal of time passed; it was only after twenty thousand *kalpas* had elapsed since the request that the sixteen princes finally requested that the Wheel of the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) be turned.
It was only after this request, and following another twenty thousand *kalpas*, that he preached this sutra. For this reason, the Brahma Kings cannot be considered equal [to the princes].
To hear the Dharma-wheel of the Mahāyāna is called "not being present. This interpretation is irrational. Rather, it is because the prince is a kinsman while the son of Brahmā is not;
thus, the son of Brahmā is called "not a kinsman. When the prince arrives first and requests the turning of the Dharma-wheel, it is called "being present.
When the son of Brahmā arrives later and requests the turning of the Dharma-wheel, it is called "not being present."
"Manifestly present" means being right before one. Regarding the name "Zhijí" (Jñānakuṭa), Jiāxiáng says: Because the great wisdom of equality has already been accumulated, he is named Zhijí.
Regarding the phrase "King Drum-Sound (Duṇḍubhisvara) and others": Question: In which sacred teaching is it stated that the Enjoyment Body (saṃbhogakāya) has parents?
Answer: The Commentary states "Drum-Sound and others. Question: How can the Reward Buddha (vipākakāya) have parents, wives, and children? Answer:

When contrasted with those Bodhisattvas from the seventh stage downward who increase their compassion and receive a body of segmented birth (paricchinnabhava), the Lord who manifests such transformations does possess parents.
Regarding "wife and children": if one has attained the transformation-body (pariṇāmika-kāya) at the eighth stage or above, the sovereign who performs emanations has no parents, wife, or children.

As for the statement that these Buddhas and patriarchs are *cakravartins*, Zhiyou says: since other Enjoyment-Buddhas (*saṃbhoga-buddha*) appear throughout the periods of increase (*vivarta-kalpa*), [they may have such relations].
The Buddha’s father was a Golden Wheel-turning King (*cakravartin*). In relation to Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū Buddha, he is called "father"; in relation to the sixteen princes, he is called "grandfather.
Regarding the phrase "the two visited the Buddha," the sutra states that "rare and extraordinary" refers to taking exquisite treasures and jewels to go and make offerings to the Buddha.
Regarding the phrase "the three mothers and so forth," the Sūtra states: "The various mothers wept. Here, "various" refers to both the birth mother and the foster mother.
Because their affection was so deep that they wept, he sent them away in accordance with their emotional desires.
According to ancient rites, in former times the Son of Heaven had three *gong*, nine *qing*, twenty-seven *zhangfu*, and eighty-one *yuanshi*. The Empress had three *fu-ren* and nine...

The *pín* (ladies-in-waiting) numbered twenty-seven, the *shìfù* (ladies of the second rank) eighty-one, and the *yùqī* (concubines) [eight hundred and one]; these were collectively termed "the mothers.
To shed tears silently is called *tì*; this is from the *Zuǒzhuan*. To shed tears without sound is called *qì*; this is from the *Shuōwén*.
Regarding the phrase "the five approaches to the mind," the sutra states, "all draw near," and so forth. "All" means "every.
These consist of the bodily action of making offerings, the mental action of reverence, and the verbal action of praising.

Regarding the scriptural passage beginning with "The World-Honored One of Great Majestic Virtue" and so forth: "throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas" does not exceed the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.

This precisely clarifies the cultivation of the causes. As for "all vows already fulfilled": among the Four Great Vows, the vow for the benefit of others (*parārtha*) was not yet fulfilled, whereas the other three were already fulfilled;
therefore, it is said generally that they are "fulfilled. "Auspicious" (*kalyāṇa*) means auspiciousness, which is to say, the attainment of Buddhahood.

In brief, they do not exceed two types of vows: first, the vow for one's own benefit; second, the vow for the benefit of others. While the vow for one's own benefit is fulfilled, the benefit of others is not yet complete.

Regarding the passage from the Sūtra beginning with "World-Honored One, it is most rare," which consists of two verses and so forth: "The body, along with the hands and feet, is tranquil, peaceful, and unmoving"—this refers to the concentration of the body (*kāya-samādhi*).
"His mind is always serene and composed, never becoming distracted"—this refers to the concentration of the mind (*citta-samādhi*).
"Ultimately and eternally extinguished"—this refers to *nirvāṇa*. "Abiding securely in the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*)"—this refers to *bodhi*.

Regarding the phrase "praising the excellence of cultivating the causes" and so forth: Lü says that although it clarifies the Buddha sitting at the site of enlightenment, because he has not yet attained Buddhahood, it is called "praising the virtues of the cause.
Mǔ says that it is precisely praising the future buddha-activities.

Regarding the phrase "as stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*," Lü says: "The ten seats (*āsana*) explained therein—whether walking or standing—may also be designated as 'seats' by way of their excellence.

The first five seats are all the mental domains traversed and the mental abodes of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; they are designated by the name of those 'seats' in a figurative sense, and are not the seats of wheel-turning kings (*cakravartin*) or others, for they are [the manifestations of] their very bodies.
As for the latter five, such as the Seat of the True Dharma (*saddharmāsana*), they are so named according to their meaning."
It is named for its purpose. "Sitting" refers to the mind abiding; it differs from the preceding five, which are named after the persons [who established them].
Some say that while the postures are fixed, there are ten distinct activities, and thus they are divided into ten types of sitting. One should consult that commentary (*śāstra*) for further details.
To speak of "dàn-pà" (恬怕) means the sense of tranquility; it is also similar [to "dàn-jìng"].

To say that the phonetic rhyme lacks flavor and is thus written as "dàn" (淡)—if the original scripture uses this character "dàn," it does not carry the meaning intended here; rather, it refers to "dàn-bó" (淡泊), which signifies detachment and simplicity.

Regarding the statement that "one who acts with tranquility (*tiánjìng*) is called tranquil (*tián*)," the sūtra speaks of "tranquil serenity" (*tiánpò*), which likewise carries the meaning of stillness and quietude. This [term] is derived from the mind and applied to the tongue;
it shares the same pronunciation as the character *tián* in "delicious flavor" (*tiánměi*). This character *tián* does not admit the pronunciation *dàn*.
Regarding the *Yùpiān* and other sources: "tú gǎn" (徒敢反) and "tú làn" (徒濫反). It distinguishes between the shallow and the deep; this is the meaning of "tranquil stillness" (*ān jìng*).
As for those who write it as "tán" (惔), "tán pà" (惔怕) is pronounced "tú gān" (徒甘反); this carries the meaning of "sorrow," not the meaning of "quiescence."
Regarding the character *dàn* (惔) in the dictionary: it is said that this character also carries the pronunciation *dàn* (憺), with the phonetic transcription *tú-làn-fǎn*.
Regarding those who say the pronunciation is *pà* (怕), etc., the phonetic transcription is *xǐ-bái-fǎn*; the pronunciation *pà* also carries the meaning of "tranquility."
Regarding the statement that "words and letters are unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*): it is not that True Suchness (*tathatā*) is called unconditioned;
rather, it is because they are produced through conditioning. Since there is no fixed standard [in words], and all things are not conditioned, this also carries the meaning of quiescence (*śānti*).
The two characters *dàn* (dull) and *pà* (fear) combine to form the sense of "tranquil stillness. One should use the character *dàn* (dull) as the correct form.
Regarding the phrase "the suffering of suffering" and so forth, the Sūtra states: "Sentient beings suffer and are afflicted," and so on.

This means that the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya) constantly dwells within the body composed of the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) and constantly resides in the locus of the four sense-objects, which are instruments of suffering. "Blind and dark, without a guide" refers to the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya).

Ignorance initiates the process of karma; through delusion one enters into darkness and accumulates evil karma. "Not knowing the path to the exhaustion of suffering" refers to the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
Since beginningless time, one has been unable to give rise to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*); this is called not knowing the path to the exhaustion of suffering.

"Not knowing how to seek liberation" refers to the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*). Liberation is the principle of cessation, which is fundamentally impossible to realize; this is called not knowing how to seek liberation.

Tuo (Deshan) said: "Sentient beings are constantly suffering and distressed. They lack the power of the cause; they are blind and ignorant, lacking the power of a guide; they lack the power of a virtuous friend;
they do not recognize the path to the exhaustion of suffering, lacking the power of provisions; they do not know how to seek liberation, lacking the power of mental application (*manasikāra*).

In the first phrase, 'lack the power of the cause' means: if one is a person without the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), there is no innate cause; if one is a person with the spiritual lineage, there is no [innate] cultivation."

Because of these causes, those who increase their rebirths in the evil destinies throughout the long night have previously cultivated evil causes based upon the Four Noble Truths; now, receiving the fruit, they pass from darkness into darkness.
That is to say, the three miserable realms (the *tricāṭu*) and the human and heavenly realms are called "luminous places" (*prakāśasthāna*).

The term "míng" (冥) is pronounced with the *qie* (切) as *mò* (莫) and *jīng* (經) reversed [i.e., *jìng* (經)]. It means darkness; it means night. It is formed from the character for "sun" (日) with the departing tone (*qù yīn*). It corresponds phonetically to "eyes closed" (*miǎn*).
*Miǎn* also commonly occurs with the level tone (*píng*).
Regarding the phrase "because of meeting with benefit," the Sūtra says: "For the sake of attaining the greatest benefit. The character *wéi* (爲) is pronounced *yīn-róng-wēi-fǎn*.
It means "certainly," "to attain," or "properly. The people of the five vehicles each attain ultimate benefit; this is termed "the greatest."
Regarding the initial long passage on the request to turn the wheel of Dharma, the sutra states: "Out of compassion, for the benefit of all devas and humans.

Why does it not mention sentient beings of the three miserable realms? The answer is: the sound of turning the wheel of Dharma is intended to bring increase [in merit and wisdom], yet those [beings in the three realms] lack the leisure [to receive it];
therefore, they are omitted. It is not that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, does not benefit them; he is indeed the Teacher of Devas and Humans.
The scriptural statement that one is "adorned by a hundred blessings" refers to external qualities (*bāhya-guṇa*). "Unsurpassed wisdom" refers to internal qualities (*ādhyātmika-guṇa*). Question:

Since adornment by a hundred blessings is an internal quality, why is it called external? Answer: The hundred blessings are the cause, while the [physical] marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) are the fruit. Thus, because they are the causal basis for the physical marks and signs, they are designated as external.

To explain that causes lead to results is termed "external. The section on the "Expedient Means of the Hundred Merits" has been explained; now it shall be stated briefly. Regarding the "hundred merits":
the Buddha possesses the thirty-two marks, and for the cultivation of each mark, one hundred merits serve as the cause.

Now, in discussing these hundred merits, they are explained according to the ten paths of wholesome action (*daśa-kuśala-karmapatha*). For the cultivation of each path, one possesses ten intentions (*cetanā*); when calculated, these constitute the hundred merits.

For example, when practicing the first path of action, non-killing, there are five volitions: first, the volition of distancing the mind from killing; second, the volition of exhortation; third, the volition of praise;
fourth, the volition of sympathetic joy; and fifth, the volition of dedication. Thus, the initial practice of the path of non-killing consists of these five volitions.
Each of the remaining nine paths of action likewise possesses these five volitions, thereby constituting fifty volitions in total for each practice.
At the time of [the formation of] one mark, fifty volitions (*cetanā*) first arise to purify the vessel of the body.
Next, one volition arises to project [the mark], followed by fifty subsequent volitions that bring it to completion. It is like planting vegetables:

first one prepares and levels the furrows, then sows the seeds, and finally irrigates them with manure and water. Through these hundred merits, one mark is collectively accomplished; this is called "adorned by a hundred merits."
The marks. In this manner, they successively develop into the thirty-two marks, which are called the "pure body.

Regarding the statement that the Buddha’s consciousness is penetrating and thus [the marks] are requested, etc., there is one interpretation based on the sūtras that correlates them with the five powers (*pañcabala*):

first, it is said that the World-Honored One knows the thoughts in the deep minds of sentient beings; this is the power of mindfulness (*smṛtibala*). Second, it is said that he also knows the path they practice; this is the power of wisdom (*prajñābala*). Third, he further knows their knowledge...

The power of wisdom (*prajñā-bala*) refers to the power of insight (*jñāna-bala*). With the exception of the phrase "removing desire for pleasure and cultivating merit," this corresponds to the final [power].

The phrase "the karma performed in past lives" from the sutra text is divided into two parts. Regarding "past lives" (*pūrva-nivāsa*): this refers to the power of knowledge regarding former abodes (*pūrva-nivāsānusmṛti-jñāna-bala*), which is the fourth power.
Fifth, regarding "the karma performed": this refers to the power of knowledge regarding one's own karma (*karma-svaka-jñāna-bala*). Finally...
"Desire for pleasure and the cultivation of merit" refers to "desire for pleasure," which corresponds once again to the power of mindfulness that was previously emphasized as being deeply held.
The two characters "cultivation of merit" correspond once again to the actions performed below, which is the power of one's own wisdom. The following is based on the commentary (*shu*).
Regarding the phrase "a single object of recollection": if one asks what is meant by "object of recollection," it refers to desire, inclination, and resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).

That which sentient beings delight in and recollect constitutes the known object (*jñeya-viṣaya*), while the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge consisting of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-jñāna-bala*) is that which knows it.

Regarding the "two objects of practice": the paths practiced by sentient beings constitute the object of knowledge, which the Tathāgata knows through the power of knowledge regarding the paths leading everywhere (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad-jñāna-bala*).

Regarding the "three powers of wisdom": the wisdom of sentient beings constitutes the object of knowledge, [which the Tathāgata knows] through the power of knowing the superior and inferior faculties (*indriya-parāpara-jñāna-bala*).
The power of wisdom (*jñānabala*) is that which knows.

Regarding the phrase "four types of past lives": the past lives of sentient beings are the objects known by the Buddha; the Tathāgata possesses the power of wisdom regarding past abodes (*pūrvanivāsajñānabala*) by which he knows them.

Regarding the phrase "the five karmas, etc.": sentient beings' own karma is the object known by the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata possesses the power of knowledge regarding his own karma and is thus able to know it.

Regarding the phrase "their inclinations, etc.": this is a summary. The two characters "inclination" (*yùlè*) summarize the power of knowledge regarding the faculty of resolve (*adhimukti-jñānabala*). The two characters "what is contemplated" (*suǒniàn*)... [text fragment]

[This is] the word. It is the power of the force of focused mindfulness (*smṛti-bala*). Cultivating wisdom is the activity. This refers to the aforementioned power of knowing one’s own karma (*svakarma-jñāna-bala*).
Regarding the statement "briefly citing these," the question is: "The Buddha possesses ten powers; why speak of five powers? The commentary states: "Briefly citing these" refers to the five powers:

the power of knowing what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñāna-bala*), the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-jñāna-bala*), the power of knowing various elements (*nānā-dhātu-jñāna-bala*), the power of knowing birth and death (*saṃsāra-jñāna-bala*), and the power of knowing the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya-jñāna-bala*). These are the five powers.

Regarding the statement that "light illuminates the dark recesses," the phrase "passing through the midst of their lands" refers to this world’s circuit of the four continents and the Lesser Iron Encircling Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*), where the sun and moon are not obstructed from shining upon them.

Master Xiang states that one must take the Iron Encircling Mountains outside the Great Trichiliocosm, which are of ultimate height and breadth, where even the sun and moon cannot reach with their light;
this refers to the space between the two Iron Mountains of this world-system and the next.

There are sentient beings who, dwelling in perpetual darkness, cannot see one another. Suddenly beholding the radiance and marks of a Buddha, they are struck with wonder and astonishment, and speak to one another:
"How is it that these sentient beings have suddenly appeared? [The opponent] asks: "To which realm are these beings assigned? [The respondent] asks: "If they are so, what fault would there be?
If they are not included within the three realms, that would also contradict the holy teachings. For the holy teachings state that outside the three realms, there is no other gift [of existence].

Question: Regarding the place of transformation (*nirmāṇa*), there is the objection that it would not be fully included among sentient beings. Answer: It is like an object situated within [the three realms];

although it is not itself of the three realms, it is nonetheless an object within the three realms. Sentient beings are also like this: although they are not themselves of the three realms, what prevents them from being likewise subsumed within the three realms?
Because their experience of karma is bound to the three realms, they are also subsumed within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) of the three realms. This is due to the Iron Ring Mountains (*cakravāḍa*).

This is because the mountain resides within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Question: By what karma is one born there? Answer: A sutra states that by using oil for a lamp for the Buddha, one is born among the Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*).

That "his speech and movements illuminate the Brahma palace" refers to the Buddha’s intention. Question: Once he has attained enlightenment, he should be able to achieve this immediately; why is it necessary for him to cause the earth to shake and emit light? Answer:

It is because he fears sentient beings may not know that a Buddha has appeared in the world. His intention is to cause them to know [of his appearance] so that they might make offerings and request him to turn the Wheel of Dharma.
Question: If they emit light, they will know [he has appeared]; why is it necessary to move the realms? Answer: Sentient beings are of two kinds: first, those with eyes; second, [those without].
Such a person is sightless. Being sightless, they do not see the radiance being emitted; therefore, it is necessary to move the realm.
Regarding the analogy of the six directions, the sutra states: "From the southwest direction down to the nadir, it is likewise."

Regarding the statement "excluding the last two directions": the textual sections for the last two directions are all incomplete. In the fourth example among the other directions, four sections are entirely missing.

Within the fifth, the upper direction, there are only three textual sections; the fourth is absent, and it is tacitly permitted [that it is not recited]. Question: Why is the fourth section missing? Answer:
Because at the very end, the Brahmā King made his request, and [the Buddha] granted permission orally; therefore, it is not present.
The fourth [point] is silence.
Regarding the statement that "all these [beings] have access to the four dhyānas": according to what follows below, since it says, "We have come from five hundred myriads of koṭis of lands;

having abandoned the bliss of profound meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi) for the sake of making offerings to the Buddha," and since it speaks of "abandoning bliss," how could this not apply to all four dhyānas? [This is the answer. To him, he replied:
This is the pliancy and bliss within meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Regarding the phrase "or only the first dhyāna," etc., the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra* states: "For example, it is like a flood of water that reaches as far down as the Golden Wheel (*kāñcanacakra*) and extends upward to the Brahma-world (*brahmaloka*), filling all three realms with water. Suppose there were a person who took a single cow-hair and divided it vertically..."
Divide it into three parts and take one part. Dip it in water and wipe it dry; dip it again in water until the water is gone. Yet the merit of Brahmā remains ultimately inexhaustible. Lu said:

"That which is induced by requesting the turning of the Wheel of Dharma is the merit of the first dhyāna. If that is so, why is the merit from the second dhyāna and above not also considered the merit of Brahmā?
Answer: In the Āgama sūtras, the merit of the gods and humans of the desire realm is used merely as a standard for comparison with the first dhyāna.
First, because it constitutes a single *brahmā-puṇya*; second, because from the second dhyāna upward, it cannot be compared [to lower realms]. For these reasons, it is not mentioned.

Regarding the question of "each going to one another," does this refer to the Brahma-kings of five hundred million *koṭi* lands meeting and deliberating together, or does it refer to the Brahma-kings within a single *trisāhasra-mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu* meeting and deliberating together? At that time, it was likewise among that assembly; was it [the Brahma-kings of] five hundred...?
"Is this among the multitudes of ten trillion lands, or rather among the assembly of Brahma-kings of the trichiliocosm? The answer is:
it refers precisely to the Brahma-kings and the Brahma-multitudes of the trichiliocosm coming together.
Regarding the scriptural statement that [the Buddha] appears "at intervals" in the world, and that he does so for the sake of those of great virtue—this refers to the opposite of their decline.

As for the statement that they "follow the light to seek the Buddha," the scripture says there were "five hundred myriads of koṭis. This refers to those who inquire about the three vehicles and whose transport is unimpeded;
even they do not exceed the three thousandfold world system. How then could ordinary beings or Brahma-kings reach such a distance? There are two interpretations: first, it is mostly...
The Bodhisattva Brahmā King was permitted to receive the fruit of the ten kings; therefore, he was able to travel so far. Mou [Zixuan] said: "This interpretation is far too narrow.
Is it only a Bodhisattva who acts as the Brahmā King? Are there not ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who do so as well? The second [explanation] says:

"He arrived here through the Buddha’s empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "If it were by the power of meditative concentration, supernormal powers, and so forth, it would not be certain," as in the case of the *Daśabhūmika-bhāṣya*.

The *Dharmadhātu-parivarta* of the *Saṃyuktāgama* states: "I once traveled to the world-system called Wild Horse (*Aśvājana*), which is located seventy-two billion *Ganges*-sands of Buddha-fields away from here.

My disciple Maudgalyāyana, foremost in supernatural powers, went to that world-system and emitted a great sound that pervaded the trichiliocosm, expounding the sublime Dharma. This was because the Tathāgata empowered him to go; had it not been so..."
