Regarding the statement that the answer arises from those truths such as the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*): the four inversions (*viparyāsa*) are namely permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Sentient beings do not understand that the body composed of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) is impermanent, without bliss, without self, and impure;

they falsely calculate it to be permanent, blissful, self, and pure. Therefore, these are inversions. The text [uses] "suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self" to eliminate those four inversions. First...
Contemplating the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). Because the Truth of Suffering is the basis for the four inversions (*viparyāsa*), one is made to know the Truth of Suffering.
It is said that by means of that Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) and so forth, one knows that the Truth of Suffering is suffering;

this simultaneously entails knowing the Truth of Origination. It is not that one first fully knows the Truth of Suffering and only thereafter knows the Truth of Origination; rather, at the very moment one correctly knows the Truth of Suffering, one simultaneously knows the Truth of Origination. The summary states: "By means of karma and afflictions..."

Affliction (*daurmanasya*) resides in the eighth [consciousness]. Since it is the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), when one knows the Truth of Suffering, one simultaneously knows the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*). Some say: "This is not so.

Within the Truth of Origination, there are the characteristics of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing; from the perspective of its nature as a state of oppression, it belongs to the other [Truth], the Truth of Suffering."
Therefore, one knows that at the time of knowing suffering (*duḥkha*), one simultaneously knows the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).

Regarding the statement "though [the knowledge] is universal," it is asked: since one already simultaneously knows the truth of suffering, why is it necessary to simultaneously abandon origination? The commentary answers:
although one universally knows suffering and so forth, among the seeds of the afflictions (*kleśa-bīja*) there is ignorance (*avidyā*), which possesses eleven types of excellence.
The tenth is the superiority of following along (*anuvartana*). From the highest realm of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception down to the Avīci Hell, all are pursued by ignorance;

it is not merely afflictions (*kleśa*), but the seeds of karma (*karma-bīja*) are likewise so. It is like people in the world who, knowing someone to be an enemy or a thief, must kill that enemy if they do not wish for them to ultimately harm others.
Thus, although one has already understood suffering (*duḥkha*), one must necessarily abandon its origin (*samudaya*). As the Sūtra says: "Those who are dear will inevitably [bring about] mutual..."
[They] are separated; only karma is not abandoned. Good and evil follow one throughout all times in future lives. Question:

If the seeds of afflictions and karma are the *ālayavijñāna*, why are the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) of afflictions and karma not the *ālayavijñāna*? Answer: In relation to the seeds, the manifestations are precisely their fruits.

Their substance subsequently oppresses [the person] and is subsumed under the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*). This is the basis for the explanation that the characteristics [of phenomena] are gathered back into their nature.
To subsume those active manifestations (*samudācāra*) back into their seeds (*bīja*) is clearly explained in meaning; how can this be considered a difficulty?

Regarding the terms "contact" (*sparśa*), "realization" (*sākṣātkriyā*), and so forth, they carry the sense of "directly seeing" (*pratyakṣa-darśana*) and the sense of "initially observing. When initially observing the form as it arises independently, this is precisely the interpretation of the treatise.

Previously, it was stated that one knows suffering (*duḥkha*), abandons the origin (*samudaya*), realizes cessation (*nirodha*), and cultivates the path (*mārga*); here, it should be said that one knows in this manner.

"Suffering is thus abandoned, its origin is thus realized, and its cessation is thus attained. "Touching and realizing" (sparśa-sākṣātkriyā) has the meaning of direct perception. "Touching" serves as the manifestation; "realizing" is synonymous with seeing directly.
This is stated to distinguish it from indirect conditions; hence the term "touching and realizing. It is the internal realization of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). A second interpretation states:

"Touching" refers to the five sense faculties (*pañcendriya*) apprehending their objects. The body faculty (*kāyendriya*) is the most intimate; it intimately apprehends the object of touch. This is like the present wisdom.
It is realized through principle. It is called "contact-realization" (sparśa-sākṣātkriyā) because it resembles the body-faculty contacting its preceding object.
Before the truths have been realized, one conceives of the Truth of Cessation as being like a precipice; once realization has been attained, birth and death are severed.
Since I have now joyfully accepted that Truth of Cessation, it is therefore called "contact-realization."

Regarding the statement "if one diligently cultivates the path," it is asked: why is it necessary to cultivate the Truth of the Path? It is answered: because it accomplishes three meanings, one cultivates the path;
that is, the Truth of the Path is that which can know suffering, abandon the origin, and realize cessation—these three meanings.
The question, "Why are the Four Truths presented in this manner? concerns the sequence of the questions and answers.

The underlying meaning is that while all phenomena generally follow the order of cause first and effect later, why is it stated here that the effect comes first and the cause later? The answer is that the teaching is delivered according to what is appropriate, and thus varies from case to case.
One cannot apply this as a universal rule.

As for the phrase "because of this," it refers specifically to the fruit of suffering that is associated with outflows (*sāsrava*), because its nature is one of oppression; thus, it is mentioned first. Second, it says:

Based on the preceding section, it is intended to say that the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) is the locus upon which the four inversions (*catur-viparyāsa*) depend; therefore, it is mentioned first.
Regarding the phrase "in this manner" (*evam-ādi*), there are two meanings. The *Śāstravyākhyā* states: First, "in this manner" (*evam*) is a term used for specific designation.

Just as this Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*)—with karma and afflictions (*kleśa*) as its causes—is able to summon and bring about the fruit of suffering, [it is mentioned] after the Truth of Suffering.

Now, the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya) is explained. Second, it is said: "Like" (*tathā*) means similarity. Because the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) causes of origination possess the quality of being oppressed by outflows, they resemble that Truth of Suffering; therefore, it is said to be "thus."
Regarding the phrase "by means of these two," etc.: there are dharmas of birth and death called the "black category" (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*). "Ultimate" means exhaustion; it means fulfillment.
The causes and effects of unwholesome karma are called the black category; this is identical to what is referred to as "black karma" in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
The phrase "for this reason, one delights in [it]" and so forth refers to the Dharma. "Delight" (*sukha*) is precisely the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*);

that is, the Truth of Cessation is itself delight. This explains the essential nature of the Truth of Cessation. Because this Truth of Cessation is an outflow-free fruit (*anāsravaphala*), it is therefore listed as the third noble truth.
Regarding the statement, "Because it is thus, bliss is the fourth": "thus" means similarity.

Regarding the term "bliss," this refers to the bliss of realizing the Dharma (*dharmapravicaya-sukha*), because it resembles the upward-directed tranquility (*śānti*) of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*).
Because it is thus, bliss is the fourth; that is, the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).

Regarding the statement that "these two encompass the ultimate consummation of the white category (*śuklapakṣa*)," "ultimate" means "exhaustive. The intended meaning is that they exhaustively encompass all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) merits.
This total inclusion is realized through the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*), wherein the cause and fruit of untainted suchness (*tathatā*) are perfected.
This is called the ultimate (the upper part explains the Dharma; the lower part clarifies yoga).

As for the statement "for example, a serious illness" and so forth: the suffering of the serious illness is the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*); the cause of the illness is the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*); the healing of the pain is the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*); and the excellent medicine is the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).
Regarding the phrase "furthermore, like the sequence of encountering suffering": it is like the suffering experienced by people in the world.

For example, when a person enters prison, this is the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*). First, one directs the mind toward the place of suffering and investigates the cause of entering prison, asking:

"What fault was committed? Next, regarding the cause of encountering suffering, the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*) is established. Next, regarding liberation from encountering suffering, this is the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*); one seeks its realization.
"Deliverance" means to be liberated. Regarding "the means to liberation hereafter," this refers to the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).

As for the statement that "one [truth] is subsumed within several aggregates while the three truths, etc., are [subsumed within others]," this simply means that among the five aggregates, the three truths are subsumed under the aggregate of suffering (*duḥkha*).
The Truth of Cessation and the Truth of the Path [are included]. Among these three truths, the five aggregates are not subsumed. Question:

If this is so, how can one speak of their mutual inclusion? Answer: It is like the statement that the five elements generate one another: wood generates fire; fire generates earth; earth generates metal; and metal generates water.

Water gives rise to wood; how could fire, on the contrary, give rise to wood and the like? It is simply that the aggregates (*skandha*) subsume the truths (*satya*); this is a subsumption based on their characteristics.

Since the aggregates are accumulations (*caya*), and the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*)—being unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)—is a single dharma that is not an accumulation, the truth of cessation is not included within the aggregates.
Furthermore, while the unconditioned is quiescent, these [aggregates] are clamorous; thus, their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are incompatible. Moreover, suffering is characterized by three...
Suffering is its essence. To speak of it in general terms, the entire five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*) are subsumed within the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).

To explain the Truth of Suffering in detail: the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death, as well as the eighth—the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging—among these are subsumed within the five aggregates of clinging.
Furthermore, separation from what is loved and the failure to obtain what is sought are states of craving; the encounter with the hated is a state of aversion. These...

In which aggregate (*skandha*) are these three collectively subsumed? Regarding the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*): speaking in terms of its essential nature (*svabhāva*), karma and afflictions (*kleśa*) are called "origination" and are subsumed within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

Furthermore, there is an interpretation that it extends to form (*rūpa*) and formations; thus, by means of the five aggregates, karma is identified as volition (*cetanā*). If one considers the function in terms of its substance, it is the aggregate of formations.
If one distinguishes between substance and function, volition in its active manifestation possesses the capacity to either restrain or incite; regarding that which can restrain...

Regarding what is said to be "that which is guarded against": it generally includes both matter (*rūpa*) and non-matter (*arūpa*), and is subsumed within two aggregates (*skandha*). If its simultaneous attendants (*parivāra*) are included, it also extends to all five aggregates.
As for the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*): the five untainted aggregates (*anāsravaskandha*) are able to encompass the path; this refers to including its attendants as well.

If one takes the Truth of the Path in its essential nature—that is, untainted wisdom (*anāsravajñāna*)—it is subsumed within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*). Question: Why are unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) not included among the Four Noble Truths?

[Question: It is included [in the truths], but it is not included among the aggregates (*skandha*). [Answer: "Truth" (*satya*) has the meaning of reality; because it is ultimate reality, it is included within the truths.

Since it does not correspond to the meaning of the aggregates, it is not included therein. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is not included among the aggregates, because its meaning does not correspond."

Regarding the statement that the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) is not like that, there are three interpretations: First, it is said that when the place where the two truths of suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) have ceased and the dharma of tranquility is accomplished, the contaminated five aggregates (*sāsrava-pañcaskandha*) are already termed "mutually tranquil" with that [cessation]. Second, it is said that the nature of the contaminated five aggregates is clamorous;

because one realizes the Truth of Cessation through the realization of the dharma of separation (*visamyoga*), they are termed "mutually tranquil" with that [cessation]. Third, it is said that as for the aggregates, they must... [text truncated]
It possesses the meaning of flux. The Truth of Cessation is called "quiescence" because it is free from those [characteristics] of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing.

Regarding the question, "What are the two? Who [possesses them]? How many are there for each?"—the intention is to ask how many combined aspects of practice (*ākāra*) each of the Four Truths possesses. The commentary answers that they are "each according to their respective order."

Regarding the statement "it refers to impermanence and so forth," the *Lüshe* (Record of the Lineage) says: "This meaning is elucidated in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. Now, following the *Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā*, it shall be briefly clarified.
First, as for the four aspects (*ākāra*) of the Truth of Suffering: the first is the aspect of impermanence (*anityatā*). This, moreover, has twelve types.

The first is the aspect of non-existence (*abhāva-lakṣaṇa*): that is, the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) never, at any time, possess the nature of a self (*ātman*) or what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*)."

Because they exist, those two characteristics of permanence do not apply; therefore, they are called "impermanent. Second is the characteristic of destruction, which means that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), having arisen, are severed;
they momentarily exist and then return to non-existence. Third is the characteristic of transformation, which means that conditioned phenomena proceed through a succession of dissimilar states.
Fourth is the characteristic of separation, which refers to [the loss of] conditioned phenomena due to the dominant influence of others or by being seized by another.
One's requisites and so forth naturally perish or are seized by others because they belong to oneself. The fifth is the sign of manifestation, which refers to the actual experience of impermanence;
it is the moment of experiencing the present object, wherein impermanence is experienced due to the persistence of its causes.

Sixth is the characteristic of natural law (*dharmatā-lakṣaṇa*): because one must inevitably experience the future impermanence due to its causes, it reveals that the nature of impermanence is certain to be experienced;
this refers to the fact that those very things persist until now. Seventh is the characteristic of momentariness (*kṣaṇa-lakṣaṇa*):

this means that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) do not abide for even a single moment thereafter, but necessarily disintegrate immediately, which is what is meant by "the past. Eighth is the characteristic of the impermanence of continuity (*saṃtati-anityatā-lakṣaṇa*).

This refers to the arising and ceasing of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) from time immemorial; the uninterrupted continuity of all dharmas, which successively transmit one another so that saṃsāra is never severed.

The nine types of illness and their characteristics refer to the disharmony of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the exhaustion of vitality during the period of abiding. The tenth refers to the various modes of mental activity and their successive transformations.
That is to say, at all times, one may give rise to a mind of greed, or a mind of anger, or a mind free from greed and anger; the same applies to the mind of delusion and so forth.
Eleventh is the characteristic of the rise and fall of the eleven requisites, meaning that all prosperity ultimately returns to decay and transformation.

Twelfth is the characteristic of the formation and destruction of the receptacle world, meaning its disintegration through the three calamities. Second is the characteristic of suffering: the five contaminated aggregates (*pañca-skandhāḥ*) are all...

Suffering refers to that which is contrary to one's aspirations and involves oppressive conditions; it is termed "suffering" (*duḥkha*). This includes the three types of suffering, the eight types of suffering, and so forth.

Third is the characteristic of emptiness (*śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa*): within the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), both the self (*ātman*) and what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*) are empty; this is called the characteristic of emptiness. Furthermore, there are three kinds of emptiness. *Cai* states:

first is emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), which means contemplating that the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is not dualistic, as in the contemplation of the emptiness of nature.

Because the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) is entirely non-existent; because the three true natures are empty, as one contemplates the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature) as emptiness itself, as well as the eighteen kinds of emptiness and so forth;

and fourth, regarding "selflessness" (*anātman*), it is called selfless because it is free from the arbitrary imputations of external non-Buddhists who claim a self exists within the aggregates (*skandha*), and because there is no creator or sovereign.
As for the four aspects of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*): first is the aspect of cause (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*). Only...

Regarding karma and afflictions, they possess the capacity to project the seeds of the five future branches, beginning with consciousness; thus, they have the functional power to bring about future arising.
This is the definition of the cause (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*) when speaking of karma and afflictions from the perspective of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).

This is the projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*). Second is the characteristic of origination (*samudaya-lakṣaṇa*): karma and afflictions serve as the co-arising causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) for the future body within the five destinies. "Co-arising" (*sahabhū*) means...
The meaning of similarity: it causes those sentient beings to resemble humans among the five destinies in having round heads and square feet;

and it causes them to resemble animals in having hair and tails. Because karma gathers together these capacities, it is called the "characteristic of accumulation. Third is the characteristic of birth (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*):
through karma and afflictions, it acts as the differentiator for those sentient beings within their future state of rebirth. It is non-existent [without them].
The types of measurements differ from one another; humans and devas are not alike. Even among humans, their forms differ in size, color, and complexion;
therefore, this is called the characteristic of birth (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*). Regarding the characteristic of conditions (*pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*):

with karma and afflictions as causes, the continuity of the five destinies of those sentient beings in birth and death remains uninterrupted. One abandons a human body and attains a celestial body; once the previous maturation (*vipāka*) has...

Exhausted. Furthermore, other resultant maturations (*vipāka*) arise. "Condition" (*pratyaya*) has the meaning of being a condition through mutual dependence. Because this mutual dependence is uninterrupted, it is called the "characteristic of conditions.

Regarding the four aspects (*ākāra*) of the Truth of Cessation: first is the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*). This is not the essential substance of the Truth of Cessation; rather, one takes the functional capacity inherent in the Truth of Cessation and names it "cessation.
This occurs because, by departing from the karma and afflictions belonging to the preceding Truth of Accumulation, one moves toward the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) Truth of Cessation.

The first is the characteristic of excellence (*praṇīta-lakṣaṇa*). The second is the characteristic of tranquility (*śānta-lakṣaṇa*); because it extinguishes the oppressive clamor and manifold sufferings beneath the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), it is described as having the characteristic of tranquility with respect to the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*).

The third is the characteristic of subtlety (*praṇīta-lakṣaṇa*); by being doubly free from the two truths of suffering and its origin (*samudaya-satya*), one realizes the body of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

It is called "wonderful characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*). Fourth is "characteristic of detachment" (*viveka-lakṣaṇa*): because it is a permanent transcendence, once attained it is never again lost; thus it is named "characteristic of detachment.

This is not like the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) obtained by suppressing afflictions through the methods of external paths or ordinary worldlings, which may later give rise to afflictions again and is therefore not called "characteristic of detachment.

Regarding the four aspects (*ākāra*) of the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*): first is the "aspect of the path" (*mārga-ākāra*), meaning it is thorough penetration; it also carries the sense of being a cause.
By means of this noble path, the various noble ones realize the true meaning; thus, it is called the characteristic of the path (*mārga-lakṣaṇa*).
Second is the characteristic of suchness (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*): all afflictions (*kleśa*) are irrational. Through ignorance regarding the Truth of the Path, one abandons these irrational afflictions;

subsequently, one speaks of the characteristic of suchness. This is not [the ultimate] True Suchness (*bhūta-tathatā*), but rather it is called "suchness" because it accords with [the truth]. Third is the characteristic of practice (*pratipatti-lakṣaṇa*): in contrast to...

To remedy the four inversions and awaken to the meaning of reality—this is called the aspect of practice. Regarding the four aspects of emergence (*niḥsaraṇa*): True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the dharma of emergence;
the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) is that which can realize this emerging *tathatā*. Turning back toward the path that realizes it, one speaks of its functional capacity.

Regarding the question, "Why are there four aspects for the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and so forth?"—that is, why must one cultivate four aspects under the Truth of Suffering? The answer is:

because ordinary beings do not understand that the body composed of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) is suffering, they conceive it as permanent, pleasurable, self, and pure, thereby giving rise to the four inversions (*catur-viparyāsa*).
In order to eliminate those four inversions, one cultivates the four aspects.
Regarding the statement that "impermanence eliminates the inversion of permanence" and so forth: Question: For what reason can a single [truth of] suffering eliminate two inversions? Answer:
Now, that which is called "suffering" must necessarily be *sāsrava* (with-outflows). All *sāsrava* phenomena are entirely suffering. By knowing them to be suffering, [the inversions are eliminated].
Because one knows that these places of suffering are entirely impure, a single aspect of suffering can eliminate two inversions;
namely, the two inversions of [perceiving] pleasure and purity. Question: Why do the two aspects of emptiness and non-self eliminate the inversion of self through the aspect of suffering? Answer:

Within the aggregates, bases, and elements, there is no such eternally permanent self as is grasped by [the ignorant]; this is called "non-self. Furthermore, those very aggregates and so forth lack...
The "self" as conceived by those non-Buddhists is, in fact, called "non-self. Since there is non-self, all things are entirely empty.
Through these two [concepts], the single delusion of self is counteracted.

Regarding the statement "the four contemplations of the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya)," etc.: Question: Why must the Truth of Origination necessarily possess these four aspects? Answer: The Commentary states, "the four contemplations of origination," etc.
According to An-guo, the four aspects of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) are as previously explained in the *Fire-House* analogy. Based on these four inversions (*viparyāsa*), the four [aspects of] craving arise;

craving, which is the essence of receiving [existence], is properly named the Truth of Origination. Now, these are formulated as the four contemplations of the causes of origination and the conditions for arising.
Excluding those four types of craving, at the time each individual craving is excluded, all are fully present as the four aspects of the causes for accumulation and the conditions for arising.

One must not assign these four aspects individually to the four types of craving. Because one previously failed to understand the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya), one clings to suffering as being permanent, pleasurable, self, and pure;
from this, the four kinds of craving arise. Due to the misconception that the Truth of Suffering is permanent, the subsequent [cravings] are produced.
There is craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Craving for a future body (*punarbhava-śarīra*)—that is, craving for a future body that is long-lived and handsome—is called "craving for rebirth" (*punarbhava-tṛṣṇā*).
This arises based on the two inversions of pleasure (*sukha-viparyāsa*) and purity (*śubha-viparyāsa*), giving rise to craving accompanied by greed and joy (*rāga-prīti-sahagata-tṛṣṇā*). Muzhou says:
"With respect to other sentient beings and their requisites, which are in reality outflows (*āsrava*) and impure phenomena, one gives rise to [this craving] through the inversion of purity."

Craving (*tṛṣṇā*). At the time of attaining what is sought, it is simultaneously associated with joy (*nandi*); because craving and joy exist at the same time, it is called "concomitant" (*sahagata*).
Regarding the phrase "and that various joys and pleasures," some say it refers to craving that is concomitant with joy, which [arises] toward wealth and property already acquired for oneself.

Regarding form (*rūpa*), one gives rise to various forms of delight, pleasure, and craving. Because these arise toward various objects regarding material wealth and form that have not yet been obtained, they are called "various" (*tatra-tatra*).

As for the statement that next, based on the inversion of self (*ātma-viparyāsa*), one gives rise to grasping (*upādāna*): this means that one no longer gives rise to craving merely for material wealth, physical form, or requisites, but rather due to clinging [to them as a self].

The body possesses a self. One gives rise to craving only toward this self; one craves and is attached to the body that possesses a self, falsely calculating it to be the self and thereby giving rise to craving.
Therefore, it is called "exclusive craving" (*ekānta-rāga*). Muni says: "To be the sovereign master is the meaning of 'exclusive' (*eka*).
Because craving arises from this exclusivity, it is named "exclusive craving. This refers to the present existence of craving.
Regarding the statement that "extinction consists of the four contemplations, etc.," this refers to extinction as tranquility, excellence, and detachment. These arise from the Truth of the Path;

however, because they have not yet severed the four types of craving belonging to the lower realm of origination (*samudaya*), the attainment of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) at the point where those four cravings are extinguished constitutes the Truth of Extinction (*nirodha-satya*). Thus, Master Mu said:
When the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is manifested through the abandonment of any single object of craving, it is characterized by four aspects:

the aspect of cessation, the aspect of tranquility, the aspect of excellence, and the aspect of detachment. These four aspects cannot be individually assigned to the cessation of each of the four types of craving.
Regarding the statement that "the Way consists of four contemplations": the principle of the Truth of Cessation regarding the four cravings is that which is realized;
this is the Truth of the Path, wherein the four cravings are extinguished by means of the path that realizes them.
Regarding the question of who understands the four doors of liberation and so forth, Xuānmù cites the second chapter of the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* as follows:

"If one speaks only of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), this refers to both meditative concentration and non-concentration, the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*), and all three types of wisdom (*prajñā*). If the term 'samādhi' is added, it refers only to concentration and not non-concentration;

only cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and not hearing or reflection (*śruta-cintā*); and it includes both the tainted and the untainted. If the word 'door of liberation' (*vimokṣamukha*) is added, it refers only to..."
This cultivation is neither through hearing nor reflection; it is exclusively meditative concentration without distraction, and exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*).

Regarding the sixteen aspects (*ākāra*) of the Truths, how many does each possess? The answer is: there are three gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*). As for the names of these gates and the sixteen types of aspects, how many are there?

First, within the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), the initial gate of emptiness liberation (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*) subsumes two aspects of the Truth of Suffering: namely, emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and selflessness (*anātman*). Next is the gate of signlessness liberation (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*).
The four aspects under the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) are subsumed [by the door of emptiness]. The subsequent door of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣa-mukha*) subsumes ten aspects:
namely, two under the Truth of Suffering—first, suffering, and second, impermanence—and four each under the Truths of Origination and the Path, totaling ten aspects. Question:
Why is the Truth of the Path not an object of aspiration? Answer: Since the Truth of the Path is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), even those of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) do not aspire to it.
This was explained according to the three types of contemplation of the Śrāvakas. Now, according to the Mahāyāna, these are subsumed under two gates of liberation within the Abhidharma:

the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*) subsumes two [factors], namely emptiness and selflessness under the Truth of Suffering; the gate of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*) subsumes six, namely the two [factors] under the Truth of Suffering... [and so forth].

The first two—suffering and impermanence—are the same as in the Hīnayāna. Together with the four under the truth of origination (samudaya-satya)—namely, cause, origin, production, and condition—there are six.
There are eight included under the signless (animitta), namely the four each for the two truths of cessation (nirodha) and the path (mārga), because both are signless.
Since the truth of the path relies upon the truth of cessation, it is also called signless.

Regarding the statement "the five entries into the clear realization of the truths" (*satyābhisamaya*), the answer is that the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Chapter Nine) states there are six types of clear realization.

An-guo says: First, the clear realization through reflection (*cintā-abhisamaya*). This refers to the four stages—Heat (*ūṣmagata*) and so forth—which are induced by the wisdom of superior patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) and serve as the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for entering the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

Within this path, the investigation of all phenomena is called clear realization. Second, the clear realization through faith (*śraddhā-abhisamaya*). This refers to taking the Three Jewels as one's object; it is supramundane and pure.

1. Faith (*śraddhā*): It assists contemplation so that one does not regress; thus it is designated as a "clear realization" (*abhisamaya*). 2. The clear realization of the three types of restraint (*trividha-śīla-abhisamaya*): This refers to the concentration-restraint, the path-restraint, and the untainted (*anāsrava*) restraint.

Because they can eliminate the defilement of violating precepts and cause contemplation to increase in clarity, they are also called "clear realizations. 3. The clear realization of the knowledge of the truths (*jñāna-satya-abhisamaya*): It takes the non-conceptually established truth (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*), suchness (*tathatā*), as its object.

Its essence consists of the fundamental and subsequent knowledges. 4. The limit of the clear realization (*abhisamayāntika*): [This refers to the subsequent knowledge arising from the limit of the clear realization.]

The clear realization of the truths through wisdom (*jñāna-satyābhisamaya*). This refers to the conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) that takes established phenomena as its object, which arises subsequent to the clear realization of the truths through wisdom.
Regarding the six culminations (*niṣṭhā*), these refer to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*). Question:

How are this fifth clear realization of the truths mentioned here and the six clear realizations of the treatise related to one another? Answer: Among the six clear realizations, the first three do not correspond at all to this [fifth clear realization]. As for the sixth...

Clear realization (*abhisamaya*) belongs exclusively to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and is not included within this [category]. Among the six clear realizations, it consists of the fourth and a portion of the fifth;
for within the fourth, there is the penetration of true vision (*darśana-mārga*), and the fifth clear realization also partially penetrates the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).

Regarding the statement that there are four truths (*catuḥsatya*) within both the small vehicle and the two [higher] vehicles on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), this is said because all three vehicles possess them.

As for the phrase "the six [vehicles] and the three vehicles observing the truths," the answer is: on the day when the Buddha Mahāvairocana turned the wheel of the Dharma of the four truths, there were followers of the three vehicles present in the assembly.

Since it is stated generally that there are four truths, they are categorized as the aspects of the four truths according to their essential nature; thus, although they are the same, they are differentiated.

The vehicles differ according to each individual. Upon hearing the teaching, a śrāvaka then contemplates above the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). He practices the contemplation of the Four Truths (*catuḥsatya*):

he regards the five contaminated aggregates as the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) because they are impermanent and oppressive; he regards the afflictions (*kleśa*) as the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*);

he regards the cessation of suffering and its origination as the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*); and the wisdom capable of realizing this as the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*). Alternatively, he contemplates within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) that there is no...

Outflowing wisdom (*āsrava-prajñā*) constitutes the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*). When Pratyekabuddhas hear this teaching, they contemplate the Four Truths (*catvāri satyāni*) based on the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*).

Ignorance (*avidyā*) and a portion of the constituent of existence (*bhava-aṅga*) constitute the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*). The five constituents beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the constituent of birth and old age (*jāti-jarā*) constitute the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).

The cessation of suffering and origination constitutes the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). The wisdom capable of realizing this constitutes the Truth of the Path. Having heard this, Bodhisattvas contemplate the Three Natures (*trisvabhāva*).

Regarding the Four Noble Truths: the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is viewed as the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*); the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*);

the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*); and the wisdom that realizes [the latter] is the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*). Furthermore, the pure portion of the dependent nature, being conditioned and untainted (*anāsrava*), is also the truth of the path.

Regarding the statement that these seven [categories] are the Four Noble Truths as conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) and so forth: the Tripiṭaka master’s direct translation renders them as the "hidden and manifest truths" (*gūḍha-prakāśa-satya*).

"Hidden" (*gūḍha*) means concealed; "manifest" (*prakāśa*) means revealed. Because they conceal the real and reveal the false, they are called "hidden. Because they are manifestly subject to destruction, they are called "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*).
As for "ultimate" (*paramārtha*): "supreme" (*parama*) means preeminent. There are two kinds of "meaning" (*artha*): first, the meaning of object; second, the meaning of principle.

Regarding the name and meaning: it is therefore called the *paramārtha-satya* (Ultimate Truth). It was formerly termed the *paramārtha-satya* (First Principle Truth) and is also called the *tattva-satya* (True Truth).
Fayuan states that both the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and the ultimate each have four names. Having already explained the general names above, as for the specific names:

first, the worldly conventional (*loka-saṃvṛti*), also called the truth of "having a name but lacking reality"; second, the rational conventional (*yukti-saṃvṛti*), also called the [truth] according to the differentiation of things.
The distinct truths: third, the conventional truth of realization (*adhigama-saṃvṛti*), also called the conventionally established truth of skillful means (*upāya-prajñapti-satya*);

fourth, the conventional truth of the ultimate (*paramārtha-saṃvṛti*), also called the conventionally established truth of provisional designations (*prajñapti-prajñapti-satya*). Regarding the specific names for the ultimate: first, the worldly ultimate (*loka-paramārtha*), also called the truth of the manifestation of essence and function (*svabhāva-kārya-prabhāsvara-satya*);

second, the ultimate of reasoning (*yukti-paramārtha*), also called the truth of the differentiation of cause and effect (*hetu-phala-viśeṣa-satya*); third, the ultimate of realization (*adhigama-paramārtha*).

It is also called "the truth of reality revealed by means of the gateways. The fourth is the ultimate ultimate truth (*paramārtha-paramārtha-satya*), also called "the truth that discards the expression to discuss the intent.

This refers to the one true *dharmadhātu*, where the first three are the established ultimate truths (*prajñapti-paramārtha*) and the fourth is the non-established ultimate truth (*aprajñapti-paramārtha*).

Zhangjing said: "The two sets of four truths are combined into five categories: first, [conventional objects] such as armies, forests, jars, and basins; second, the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*)."
[The categories are: 1) the three types of suffering and the four truths such as the origin of suffering; 2) the two kinds of emptiness and true suchness (*tathatā*); 3) the one true *dharmadhātu*.

Of these, the first [category] is exclusively conventional (*saṃvṛti*), possessing only a nominal designation; therefore, the last is exclusively ultimate (*paramārtha*), as it is beyond verbal expression. The three intermediate types are both ultimate and conventional:

the ultimate is not ultimate in itself, for it is ultimate only in dependence upon the conventional; the conventional is not merely conventional, for it is called conventional only in dependence upon the ultimate. By virtue of this...
Because of this opening and closing, the Eight Truths (aṣṭasatya) are established.
Regarding the mention of "fifty-five" and so forth, the term *yogācāra* refers to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, while the two characters for *nirvāṇa* refer to the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.

This is because it is stated in both the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and the fifty-fifth [section] of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*: regarding the Four Truths, there are collectively the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), and the ten... [dhātus].
Regarding the eight realms (*dhātu*), when contrasted with the Four Noble Truths, they are conventional; when contrasted with the other three [truths], they are the ultimate (*paramārtha*).

When contrasted with the non-established [truth], these Four Noble Truths are said to be conventional. Now, since the Four Noble Truths pertain to both the conventional and the ultimate, the Commentary states that "in reality, they encompass both types.
Thus, the Four Noble Truths are both true and conventional; they are the third [truth] within the conventional, and [the first] within the true.
Second, this therefore encompasses both truths (*satya*).

Regarding the statement "the eight truths" and so forth, Master Lu says: "The two truths, ultimate (*paramārtha*) and conventional (*saṃvṛti*), each have four aspects, hence they are called 'the [eight] truths. In the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, there is only one truth;
in the *Ratnaketuparivarta* and the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-alaṃkāra*, two truths are taught; and in the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* and the *Madhyānta-vibhāga*, three truths are taught."
Regarding the Truths (*satya*): both the *Yogācāra* and the *Vijñaptimātra* schools explain the four truths. To correctly distinguish their characteristics, it is briefly stated:
these sixteen aspects (*ākāra*) of the four truths are subsumed under the second truth, the Truth of Ultimate Meaning (*paramārtha-satya*) by way of principle, among the four ultimate truths;

and they are subsumed under the third truth, the Conventional Truth of Realization (*prāpti-saṃvṛti-satya*), among the four conventional truths. This precisely clarifies the four truths pertaining to the fruits of the noble ones (*ārya-phala*).
This is the principle.
Regarding the question of how many grades there are within the nine sufferings, the Chancellor (Xiangguo) said: "To speak briefly, there are three sufferings, five sufferings, and eight sufferings.

Furthermore, suffering is of three kinds: first, the suffering of that which is grasped (*parigraha-duḥkha*), which depends on the mind that clings through the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*)."

Because it is that which is grasped. Second is the suffering of phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-duḥkha*), which refers to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). Third is the suffering of conjunction (*saṃyoga-duḥkha*), because it is conjoined with the characteristics of suffering.
Since the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is precisely suchness (*tathatā*), yet it is mixed with all the characteristics of contaminated suffering, it is called "conjunction.
There are three aspects of the Truth of Suffering. Lü [Cheng] says: "The accumulation of habitual tendencies consists of the seeds of the two attachments to self and phenomena."
The causal collection (*hetu-saṃcaya*) refers to the mind that acts as the object-condition (*ālambana-citta*); this is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

The mind that acts as the object-condition for the two types of grasping—namely, grasping at self and phenomena—carries those grasps and perfumes [the consciousness] to acquire seeds; this is called the collection of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā-saṃcaya*). Second, the collection of co-emergence (*samutthāna-saṃcaya*) refers to karma and afflictions (*kleśa*).

Afflictions give rise to karma, and karma gives rise to its fruit; because they arise simultaneously and equally, it is called the collection of co-emergence. Third, the collection of non-separation from fetters (*avisaṃyoga-saṃcaya*).
That is, suchness while still entangled [in afflictions]. There are three kinds of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*): first, cessation by nature (*svabhāva-nirodha*).

Because the objects of perception—the defiled phenomena consisting of the two attachments to self and dharmas—are fundamentally non-existent, it is called cessation by nature. Second, cessation of the two graspings (*dvaya-grāha-nirodha*). Because both the grasper and the grasped are non-existent, it is so named.

Third, cessation of the fundamental nature (*prakṛti-nirodha*). This is because it is the very essence of suchness itself. Regarding the three aspects of the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*): first, the universal...

First, the path of knowledge, because it can know the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Second, the path of permanent abandonment, because it can sever the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

Third, the path of realization, because it realizes the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Furthermore, there are four paths, namely the path of application (*prayoga-mārga*) and so forth; or alternatively, the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅga-mārga*) and so forth.

Regarding the statement that "the ten [aspects of] space are not equal," An-guo says: The six kinds of unconditioned phenomena have true suchness (*tathatā*) as their actual substance, while the remaining five are all provisional and are established based upon true suchness.
If one subsumes the provisional into the real, all five are included within the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).

However, the manifestations transformed by the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) follow the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), whereas the manifestations transformed by the tainted mind (*sāsrava-citta*) are subsumed under the Truths of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and Origination (*samudaya-satya*); thus, they pertain to all four truths. This...

These two types encompass both the wholesome (*kuśala*) and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); therefore, they are specifically excluded here, as [the present discussion] concerns only that which is wholesome by nature.

Regarding the statement that there are "two kinds" herein: according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, each of the defiled (*saṃkleśa*) and the purified (*vyavadāna*) has both forward and reverse orders, thus resulting in four modes of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-mukha*).
In this sutra, however, there are only two: the forward contemplation of the defiled and the forward contemplation of the purified.

The non-cessation of birth and death is called defilement (*saṃkleśa*). When ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease, and so forth; this is the cessation of that very birth and death, and is thus called purification (*vyavadāna*).

To say that "this defilement is in accordance [with the teaching]" means that the Sūtra states: "Ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form," and so on.

This is the forward contemplation of the process of affliction (*saṃkleśa*). Regarding the reverse contemplation of the process of affliction: one contemplates from the effect toward the cause, which is called "reverse contemplation" because it does not follow the sequence of successive arising.

The member of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇāṅga*) is the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*). From what does old age and death arise? Old age and death exist conditioned by the member of birth (*jātiaṅga*).
From what does the member of birth arise? The member of birth exists conditioned by the member of existence (*bhavāṅga*). From what does the member of existence arise?

The existence-factor (bhava-aṅga) arises conditioned by the grasping-factor (upādāna-aṅga). ... [and so on] ... from what does the formations-factor (saṃskāra-aṅga) arise? The formations-factor arises from the ignorance-factor (avidyā-aṅga).
This is called the inverse contemplation of affliction (saṃkleśa).

Regarding the statement on "purity and conformity": with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form cease;
and so on, until with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair cease.
Regarding the sequence of purification: because old age and death cease, birth ceases;
because birth ceases, becoming ceases; because becoming ceases, grasping ceases; because grasping ceases, craving ceases; and because craving ceases, sensation ceases.

Because the link of sensation ceases, there is the cessation of the links up to volitional formations; because volitional formations cease, ignorance ceases. This is the reverse contemplation of purification.
Regarding the statement that "the birth and death [links] arise in sequence," one asks: why does the sutra text describe only the forward progression of defilement and not its reverse?
Yes. The answer is: the contemplation of the impure (*aśubha*) follows the sequence of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Contemplation in the reverse order does not follow the sequence of birth and death.
Since the scriptural text does not explicitly state this, it cites the contemplation in the forward order as an illustration for the reverse order. Question:
Why does the scriptural text only mention the forward order of purification and not the reverse order of purification? Answer: That commentary states: "First, one cuts off..."
"Because of birth and death. This refers to an analogy with the reverse contemplation (*pratiloma*). When first practicing the preparatory stage (*prayoga*), one seeks to sever birth and death;

therefore, one first performs this pure forward contemplation (*anuloma*). Upon attaining the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), one emerges from the fundamental contemplation (*maula-dhyāna*) and only then performs the method of reverse contemplation.
Here, because we are taking up the initial seeking to sever birth and death—which accords with that preceding stage—it is said to be analogous to the reverse. Thus says Master Lu.

There is also the case where ignorance conditions formations (*saṃskāra*), yet it is not said that formations give rise to ignorance; likewise, up to birth conditioning old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), yet old age and death cannot give rise to the branch of birth.
How, then, can this be called "mutual arising" (*anyonya-janman*)? Answer: One should say that this is because the nature of birth and death is such (*dharmatā*).

This, however, is not correct. What is here called "mutual arising" is merely a general summary; it refers specifically to the ten branches of the past as the causes acting as the capable [conditions].
Birth (*jāti*) takes the two present factors as that which is produced. Furthermore, ten causes arise upon the fruit of these two present factors.

It is not necessary for each factor to be considered in relation to every other factor for it to be called "arising" (*janman*). As for arising, it refers simply to ignorance being the condition for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*);
the meaning of the "birth-factor" (*jāti-aṅga*) is likewise. This is a matter of designation (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*), just like the five characteristics of arising, or like a mother giving birth to a child.

Regarding the statement "first severing birth and death" and so forth: at the time of first practicing the preparatory application (*prayoga*), one seeks to sever birth and death and first performs this visualization of purification (*viśuddhi-vipaśyanā*).

Once the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*) has been attained, one emerges from correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*) and subsequently contemplates the branches of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) either in forward or reverse order.

Here, we take the perspective of the very first stage when one seeks to sever birth and death; because this follows the sequence of the initial stage, the forward-order visualization (*anuloma-vipaśyanā*) is presented.
This is an example of a reverse contemplation (*pratyavekṣā*).

Regarding the "discrimination by way of six gates," the eighth chapter of the treatise explains it through ten gates: first, listing the names of the factors and discerning their general and specific natures;
second, clarifying the general and specific names and the reasons for their designations; third, the basis for their sequential order; and fourth, the functions of the general and specific factors.

5. The distinction between cause and effect; 6. Mutual functioning as conditions, analyzed through four propositions; 7. The relationship between the producer and the produced, as elucidated in various treatises;
8. The refutation and establishment of increase and decrease, resolving various objections; 9. Determining the time periods and refuting errors; 10. Analysis through various categories.
Within this analysis, there are seventeen further categories of detailed explanation. These six categories correspond to those [seventeen], being either present or...
None. This citation refers to that passage; the passage will be pointed out one by one in the subsequent text.

Regarding the "extraction of the essence" (*svabhāva*), there is both a general and a specific extraction. As for the general extraction of the essence: it consists of the "characteristic" (*nimitta*) and "discrimination" (*vikalpa*) among the five dharmas.

Among the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), it refers exclusively to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); among the three aggregates (*triskandha*), it pertains to each of the categories in part.

In this commentary, however, it is discussed solely in terms of its distinct essential substance (*svabhāva*). Regarding the phrase "among the afflictive obstructions" (*kleśāvaraṇa*), first the various types and distinctions of ignorance (*avidyā*) are analyzed, and subsequently the text of the commentary is explained.
Now, first, the seven questions distinguish two types of karma; sixth, they differentiate the varieties of ignorance (*avidyā*); and seventh, they categorize them according to the realms (*dhātu*).
To briefly distinguish them by way of the two obstructions (*āvaraṇa*), one takes only the afflictive obstruction (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and not the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

This corresponds to the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vihāra*) in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, wherein only the first four stages of dwelling are taken and the fifth, the stage of the dwelling of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*), is excluded. Regarding the stage of the dwelling of ignorance:
This refers to the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). It cannot initiate karma. The first four *vihāra-bhūmis* (abodes) can initiate various karmas. As for these four *vihāra-bhūmis*:
the first is the abode of views (*dṛṣṭi-vihāra*), which consists of the discriminative afflictions of the three realms; the second is the abode of all desire (*kāma-sarva-vihāra*).

These are the innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). The third is the ground of all abidings (*sarvatraga-bhūmi*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), which is innate to the form realm.
The fourth is the ground of all abidings of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), which is innate to the formless realm. However, these first four grounds of abiding can give rise to various karmas;
among them, the [first] sees all locations as they truly arise, while the remaining three assist in their arising, as distinguished in the second section.

Regarding the five *avidyā-vāsabhūmis* (grounds of the abiding of ignorance) that do not initiate karma: Question: The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states that the *avidyā* of the knowable (*jñeya*) initiates karma;

furthermore, the bodhisattva on the first stage commits errors regarding the three types of action due to delusion. Is this not, then, initiated by the *avidyā* of the knowable? Answer: This does not contradict reason because it does not induce a general rebirth.
Furthermore, while the *avidyā* of the knowable is considered defiled (*kliṣṭa*) in relation to the bodhisattva, it is not termed defiled in relation to others. Therefore, there is no contradiction.
It is not grasped. Regarding the second type, co-nascent discrimination (*sahaja-vikalpa*): the co-nascent serves as the auxiliary, while discrimination is the primary factor.

If one follows the Sarvāstivāda school, they hold that karma is generated merely by perceiving phenomena (*vastu*), whereas discrimination does not generate karma through delusion regarding principles (*tattva*). This contradicts the Mahāyāna. Question:

What is meant by "co-nascent discrimination"? Answer: The treatise states: "Co-nascent self-clinging (*ātma-grāha*) has, from beginningless time, been perfumed by false imaginings (*abhūta-parikalpa*)."

The innate [ignorance] arises by the power of internal forces; it is always present with the body and cannot be diverted by false teachers, false teachings, or false conceptualizations, proceeding spontaneously.
This is called "innate" (*sahaja*). The second, the conceptually constructed [ignorance], only begins to arise subsequently due to the power of external conditions in the present.

Furthermore, according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, this differs from the view of Master Sthiramati, who maintains that [the innate ignorance] is sharp and intense, and that a portion of gods and spirits possesses it.

It is distinct. It refers to karma that can produce a collective retribution (*sādhāraṇa-vipāka-karman*). For example, a powerful ghost pointed at Śāriputra’s head, and he entered hell while still in his physical body;
likewise, Sūdarśana’s parrot heard the Dharma of the Four Truths, and ten thousand fish heard the name of Ratnaśrī Buddha, and they were all reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
All such cases as these involve the production of collective retribution karma. Furthermore, it is acknowledged that among human beings there is a portion of sentient beings who are dull-witted.
There is no discrimination. The Bodhisattva Dharmapāla says: "Discrimination exists in the realms of humans and devas; there is no discrimination in the three evil realms.
For example, when a great ghost enters hell, or a parrot is born in heaven, and so forth—all such cases are merely manifestations. If it were not so," [it would contradict the principle].
If one were able to create karma that results in total retribution within the three miserable realms, there would be no occasion for sentient beings to be born among humans or devas;

thus, the Bodhisattva who protects the Dharma is correct [in his view]. Third, regarding the analysis in terms of consciousness: it is the ignorance associated with the sixth consciousness that serves as the primary and auxiliary impeller of karma.
Although the seventh consciousness possesses innate ignorance, it cannot impel karma; therefore, even within the sixth consciousness, one must further distinguish [the types of ignorance].

The primary factor is the [volition], while the co-nascent factors act as its auxiliaries. Therefore, the *Śāstra* states: "The primary [factor] takes conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and the associated innate ignorance (*sahaja-moha*) as its essence.
(The following describes the four types. Regarding the fourth, the karma that initiates [rebirth]: excluding karma conducive to the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-vedanīya-karman*). As the treatise says:

"Only those karmas capable of inducing good or evil in future lives constitute this limb [of dependent origination]. Thus, excluding karma conducive to the present life, the remainder consists of karma conducive to the next life (*upapadya-vedanīya*) and karma conducive to subsequent lives (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya*).
Regarding karma that is indeterminate (*aniyata-karman*): this refers to the limb of ignorance (*avidyā*).

As for the fifth [limb], the "arising of both general and specific karma," ignorance gives rise to general retribution and is capable of giving rise to both general and specific retribution; only then does it constitute this limb.

If it gives rise solely to specific retribution, it is not this limb. The treatise states: "That which specifically assists the future fruit is not this limb. Question: How is it that giving rise to specific retribution is not [this limb]?

Regarding the limb of ignorance: the answer is that because the fruit of individual retribution (*pratiniṣyanda-phala*) involves interruptions, whereas the ten causes and two fruits are uninterrupted;

furthermore, while the fruit of collective retribution (*sādhāraṇa-phala*) is restricted solely to the current realm of rebirth, the individual fruit is received throughout other realms as well; moreover, the karma of collective retribution is also termed "projecting karma" (*ākṣepaka-karman*).

Because the power of karma can induce the eighth consciousness as the branch of the total retribution (*vipāka*), and because the specific retribution is also called the "fulfilling karma" (*paripūri-karman*) as it serves as an ornament.
Furthermore, according to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* alone, a single karma can induce only one birth and does not induce multiple fruits. As the treatise says:
A single karma draws forth one birth, while multiple karmas can bring it to completion; "completion" refers to the distinct retributions.
According to the Mahāyāna Yogācāra school, while a single karma can draw forth one birth, they also allow that a single karma can draw forth the collective retribution of multiple births.
Furthermore, as stated in the sūtras, a single act of slandering the sūtras results in many lifetimes in the hells, as well as many lifetimes among animals, and so forth.
This refers to how a single karma can project multiple births (the distinctions among types of karma will be explained below). Sixth, regarding the classification of ignorance (*avidyā*):

this refers to what the sub-commentary states below, namely that it comprises four types—namely, associated (*saṃprayukta*), non-associated (*asādhāraṇa*), active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*), and latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
"Associated" means arising simultaneously with the other nine [afflictions] of discrimination; it is called "associated. "Non-associated" refers to the single dharma of ignorance itself.
When it arises, it does not arise simultaneously with the other nine root afflictions; thus, it is called "unshared" (*āveṇika*). The treatise states:
"Associated ignorance is deluded in the same way as the nine [afflictions], whereas unshared ignorance is directly deluded regarding the principle of suffering.

Among the unshared types, that which is associated with the seventh consciousness is the "constantly active unshared ignorance" (*sadā-anuśayin āveṇikī avidyā*). Because it has continued as a single category since beginningless time, it is called "constantly active. It is exclusively...

This consciousness exists; it is called "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*). Question: Regarding the seventh [consciousness], which is associated with the four roots, why is it called "unshared"? Answer: First, one says:
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the root, while view (*dṛṣṭi*), pride (*māna*), and craving (*tṛṣṇā*)—these three—are secondary; thus it is called "unshared. Second, one says:

However, all four are indeed roots, but because they are predominant (*adhipati*), it is named "unshared. Third, one says: Only the consciousnesses exist; that which is prior to the six [consciousnesses] is...

[Question: There is none [that is not associated with ignorance]; this is what is meant by "unshared" (*āveṇika*). If that is so, then the first six [mental factors] are unshared because the seventh ignorance does not correspond with them;

thus they are called "unshared. [Answer: This is not so. Just as the "unshared Buddha-qualities" (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*) are called "unshared" because they belong exclusively to the Buddha and no other person possesses them, so it is here.
[Question: Since there are four factors [of ignorance], why are they called "unshared"? [Answer: It is also like the Buddha’s one hundred and forty kinds of unshared qualities.
Because all such dharmas are termed "unshared" (āveṇika), the sixth [type of] ignorance is called the "solitary unshared. Within this, there are two types of ignorance:

that which is associated with the eight major secondary afflictions (mahābhūmika) is called the "principal solitary unshared ignorance"; if it is associated with the minor secondary afflictions (parīttakleśabhūmika), [it is likewise so termed].
It is therefore called "non-dominant" (*asvāmika*), because it is eclipsed by the minor derivative afflictions (*upakleśa*) with which it co-arises.

Furthermore, when the major derivative afflictions (*mahābhūmika-kleśa*) arise, the presence of the minor ones is not certain; however, when the minor ones arise, the major ones must necessarily be present, as the major ones pervade all defiled minds (*kliṣṭa-citta*).

For this reason, it is non-dominant. In relation to the minor derivative afflictions, ignorance (*avidyā*) is not dominant; yet, simultaneously with the major derivative afflictions, it is also termed "dominant. [This applies to] the *paryavasthāna* (envelopments).

Regarding ignorance (*avidyā*): it should manifest as two distinct types that function non-concurrently. Since beginningless time, it has bound sentient beings. Regarding the latent tendency (*anuśaya*):

it is the seed of ignorance that follows along with sentient beings, lying dormant within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) (the rest is explained elsewhere). Regarding the seventh [consciousness] in terms of persons and realms:
one asks how the four kinds of ignorance—belonging to sentient beings of the three realms, and to the internal and external ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*)—arise.

[Question: Regarding karma: [Answer] In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) give rise to karma of the five destinies (*pañcagati*) of the desire realm through all four types of ignorance (*avidyā*).

Furthermore, they give rise to karma from the first dhyāna upward. From the second dhyāna upward, it is not produced by the ignorance of the desire realm; rather, from the third dhyāna upward, it is produced by the ignorance of the higher realms.
Moreover, among the karmas produced by the ignorance of the desire realm, the karma thus produced includes both the wholesome (*kuśala*) and the unwholesome (*akuśala*).

Those of a wholesome nature can give rise to ignorance, yet all [such instances] are of an unwholesome nature. The *Śāstra* states that for external dharmas and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), the four types of entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) arising from improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) and the ignorance of ordinary beings are all of an unwholesome nature.

Furthermore, regarding the karma produced within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), with the exception of the karma of the Heaven of Contentment (*saṃtuṣita-deva*), if one cultivates the karma of the Heaven of Contentment, the ignorance therein is of an obscured (*nivṛta*) nature. Through the power of faith...

Because [ignorance] is dormant. Furthermore, ignorance gives rise to karma that leads to the three evil destinies; it is admitted that ignorance and formations (saṃskāra) are simultaneous and are of an unwholesome nature.

However, regarding the wholesome karma of humans and devas, ignorance and formations arise sequentially because their natures are different. There are two types of ignorance that can give rise [to karma]:
namely, delusion regarding the fruit of maturation (vipākaphala-moha) and delusion regarding the true meaning (tattvārtha-moha). There are three types of formations that are set in motion.

This refers to the meritorious and the immovable [karmas]. Furthermore, among the four types of karma commonly practiced by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), manifest action (*vartamāna-karman*) is primary, while seeds (*bīja*) serve as its auxiliary.

(The preceding section clarifies the external ordinary beings; from the stages of "Heat" and "Summit" onwards, they are internal. Within the second category, the ordinary beings who dwell in the internal Dharma, there are again two types:

first, those who are negligent (*pramatta*); second, those who are non-negligent (*apramatta*). One interpretation states that the stage of the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśala-mūla*) is termed "non-negligence," as one dwells within the internal gate.
Therefore, in the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), it is termed "heedlessness" (*pramāda*) because one dwells predominantly in the outward-facing gates.

Second, it is said that "exertion" (*pragraha*) is non-heedlessness, while "lack of exertion" is termed heedlessness. Although these two types differ, among the four kinds of ignorance (*avidyā*), that which consists of non-offering is excluded from both, as it involves delusion and denial regarding the Truths (*satya*).
Consequently, for the heedless person, the associated ignorance is precisely [that which is present].

It produces the seeds. It assists in producing non-negligence, because it causes the seeds to manifest as actual activities (*samudācāra*) and assists in producing the manifestation [of those seeds] that arise during the preparatory stage (*prayoga*).
Question: What kind of fruit does that which is produced induce? Answer: The seeds that have been cultivated manifest as actual activities.

Because it assists in bringing forth the manifestation [of the path] during the distant preparatory stage (*dūraprayoga*). Question: What kind of fruit does that which is produced bring about? Answer:

The karma performed brings about the retributive fruit of the ten kings and their retinues. Thus, the karma cultivated prior to this stage serves as the ripening cause (*vipākahetu*) for the ripening fruit of the ten kings;

it serves as the predominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) for the wisdom of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*); and with respect to the fruit of Buddhahood, it serves as a remote predominant condition.

Regarding the higher objects of focus: for example, those from the first fruit (srotāpanna) upward, such as those with seven more births or one who returns once more, all have already attained [the path] within the seven preparatory stages (saptaprayoga).
Since they have entered the state of the noble ones (ārya), they no longer create new karma. Question: Of how many factors does this member of ignorance (avidyā) consist?
Answer: It has the single dharma of ignorance alone as its essence. This differs from [the theory of] dependent origination with parts and stages, which encompasses other dharmas as well;

furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* describe it as a "single-category gate" (*eka-vastu-mukha*). If that is so, why does the fourth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* state:

Ignorance (*avidyā*) and volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are [mutually] causal conditions. Because the seeds of wisdom that coexist with ignorance are designated as the "member of ignorance," it is asked:
by what means of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) do they become the causal condition for volitional formations? Furthermore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

regarding the claim in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* that ignorance is a causal condition for volitional formations, this refers to the habitual tendencies of karma (*karma-vāsanā*) at the time of ignorance; these are metaphorically designated as "ignorance," though in reality they are volitional formations.
(Regarding the general refutation above and the subsequent clarification below).

As for the phrase "among the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*)," this excludes the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Mochizuki states that he cites the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, which speaks of five levels of abiding afflictions (*pañca-vāsabhūmi-kleśa*).
Since the first four afflictions are able to initiate karma, they are classified as afflictive hindrances; the fifth level of abiding affliction is not included.

This is as explained extensively above. Question: Why is the ignorance that constitutes the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) not included? Answer: There are two types of ignorance: first, that which can produce birth and death;
second, that which can obstruct the noble path, namely the cognitive obscuration. The noble path does not produce the birth and death of the fragmented existence (*prādeśika-jāti-maraṇa*).

Furthermore, [the cognitive obscuration] only obstructs the Mahāyāna and does not obstruct the lesser fruits. Now, the afflictive obscuration (*kleśāvaraṇa*) applies to all three vehicles and also produces...
Because it pertains to birth and death, it refers to ignorance (*avidyā*) among the afflictions (*kleśa*). Question:

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* also states that in the second bhūmi, one abandons the delusion regarding the three types of karmic action through transgression, which is a cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). How can you say that it does not initiate karma? Answer: Zhangjing says:
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states that although the cognitive obscuration can initiate karma, it cannot bring about the retribution of birth and death. If we discuss transgression...
Regarding the commission of the three types of karma: it does not hinder the arising [of the path], though it cannot induce the attainment of rebirth within *saṃsāra*.

As for the statement that "one primarily grasps the discriminating karma," this is because it is precisely this that can initiate karma; thus, it is "primarily grasped. That which arises simultaneously and assists in its initiation is called "secondarily grasped.
All instances where ignorance initiates an action constitute the very essence of this limb; delusion (*moha*) is simply another name for the limb of ignorance (*avidyā*).
This is the name. The afflictions of discrimination arise by relying on three conditions; what is now called "spontaneous" refers to that which is innate (*sahaja*).
Question: How is it known that this also takes innate ignorance as its essence? Answer: Zhangjing says: It quotes the tenth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, which states:
A person who has attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) abandons one portion of the twelve links of existence (*bhavāṅga*).

If the link of ignorance (*avidyā*) were exclusively conceptual (*vikalpita*), then it would follow that the person in the first fruit has abandoned it entirely. Since it is stated that they abandon "one portion," it is clear that this includes innate ignorance (*sahaja-avidyā*) as its substance.
Question: Does the link of ignorance in this context take the self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma*) as its substance, or does it take other phenomena? *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle [number].

The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, Chapter 8, state that [the ten stages] constitute a single matter (*eka-artha*). This differs from the Hīnayāna approach, which discusses attainment (*prāpti*) in terms of distinct states (*avasthā*) and thus allows for its application to other dharmas (the heading above refers to the "body").

The phrase "establishing consciousness-only" (vijñaptimātratā) refers here specifically to the section in the treatise concerning the twelve links of dependent origination, namely the "projecting" (ākṣepaka) and "projected" (ākṣipta) factors.

The term "capable of producing" (janaka) refers exclusively to those [factors] that are capable of producing; it does not include those of a single category that are incapable of producing karma. Furthermore, it says:
The ignorance associated with the seventh consciousness and the ignorance of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) cannot initiate karma.

Regarding the phrase "that which truly induces": among karmas, there are those that truly induce the collective retribution (*sāmānyavipāka*), and those that truly induce both collective and individual retribution (*viśeṣavipāka*).
Since karma is thus, ignorance is likewise; one takes only the ignorance that initiates the collective retribution as the essential nature of this link [of dependent origination]. If...

Among the karmas, only those that yield specific retribution (*vipāka*) and only those that are concordant with the present life constitute the constituent members of the link of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). Ignorance (*avidyā*) in this context is likewise:
it only triggers specific retribution and only triggers ignorance concordant with the present life; it does not constitute the constituent member of the link of ignorance itself.
Regarding the phrase "future lives," "future" excludes [karma] that conforms to the present life, which is not included here.

Regarding the phrase "good and evil," Zhangjing says that because it does not include the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), among the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), only those that produce good and evil are taken.
