Regarding the statement "there are also places where it is taught," etc., this reconciles apparent contradictions; that is, it refers to what is taught in the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*.

In the commentary, the branches of birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) are taken [as the fruit], while the intention is to take the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) in their present manifestation as the essence. How, then, does this accord with the seeds mentioned in the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*?

Yes. The answer is that the text of that sūtra states: "If one speaks in terms of stages (*avasthā*), the seeds of the five members beginning with consciousness and the seeds of the future members of birth and old age/death are substantially distinct from their actual manifestations (*samudācāra*) across different lifetimes.

Now, when these seeds of the five members have been moistened and proceed to directly produce the actual manifestations of the members of birth and old age/death—this is precisely how the commentators interpret the sūtra regarding the arising [of the members].
Regarding the simultaneous nature of the projecting and projected factors: it is for this reason that the members of birth, aging, and death are said to encompass both seeds and their manifestation.

As for the statement that the projecting and the projected arise simultaneously, ignorance (*avidyā*) and volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are the projectors; the five members beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*) are the projected.

Craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*) are the producers; the members of birth and aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*) are the produced. Here, we take the five projected members [as the subject].
Because it includes both the [causal] branch and the two branches that arise from it, the branches of birth and aging are said to pertain to the seed.
Regarding the phrase "explained in successive order," the branches of birth, aging, and death are also manifest activities (*pravṛtti*). Manifest activities necessarily arise from seeds.
Since the five branches beginning with consciousness were explained first, followed by the branches of birth, aging, and death, they are called "successive."
Regarding the statement that there is no distinction between the categories [of the members]: apart from the five members, there are no separate members of birth and old age/death;
and apart from the members of birth and old age/death, there are no separate five members. Therefore, it is said that there is no distinction.

This is stated according to the general sense of non-differentiation, wherein the members of birth and old age/death are also understood to include the seeds. However, if explained according to their specific distinctions, it is not the case that these two members also include the seeds.
This refers to actual manifestation (*samudācāra*).

Regarding the mention of "sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction" and so forth, this explains that they are not constituent links (*aṅga*) [of dependent origination]. Question: Among the twelve links, why is aging established as a separate link?
Why is it not explained in one place together with the link of death? Answer: Although aging pervades all three realms, it is not determinate.

In the human realm of the desire world (*kāmadhātu*), there are those with white hair and wrinkled faces; although these specific signs do not exist in the higher realms (*ūrdhvadhātu*), all beings possess the signs of decay at the time of old age.
The fact that the factors of form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) differ from what they were before is the characteristic of aging (*jarālakṣaṇa*).
This exists throughout the three realms. Among them, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) does not age; because its duration is not fixed, it is not established as a separate category.
Question: Why are the characteristics of illness (*vyādhi-lakṣaṇa*) not established as a separate limb (*aṅga*)? Answer: Because two conditions are lacking.
First, it exists only among humans in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), whereas it does not exist in the higher realms. Second, although there is illness among humans, it is not determinate;
there are those who die while free from illness, such as the Bhikṣu Bakula, who had never been ill throughout many lifetimes. Thus, [the first condition] is not universal, and the second—

No; therefore, it is not established as a separate member [of dependent origination]. Question: Within the mode of miraculous birth (*upapāduka*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are present all at once.

Since this is subsumed under the member of the six bases, there is no prior stage [of name-and-form]. How, then, can there be the member of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*)? Answer: There are two explanations. First, although the member of name-and-form does not pervade all modes of miraculous birth, it does pervade all except for those born from a womb (*jarāyuja*);

thus, it is also established as a member even for those born from moisture (*saṃsvedaja*). Second, although the six sense bases are present all at once in miraculous birth, [the member of name-and-form is still applicable].
In the first and second moments, the function of the limb of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) is not yet established.

Prior to the arising of contact (*sparśa*), that initial stage is designated as the limb of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Question: The holy teachings state that improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) is the cause of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair are the fruits of old age; why are they not established as separate factors? Answer:

Because improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) serves only as the cause for their non-interruption, while sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair serve only as the fruits of their continuity. Furthermore, because they are both causes and effects, they are not established as separate factors.
Moreover, since the causes of sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair exist within the body of old age and death, they are not established as separate factors. Question: Where [are they located]?

These sorrows, lamentations, sufferings, and afflictions arise from old age and death. The commentary answers that sorrows, lamentations, sufferings, and afflictions arise because of old age and death;
they are not themselves included among the [twelve] links.
As for the statement regarding the mutual relation of the sense-faculties (*indriya*), this refers to the time of death, when one’s own faculties face those of other relatives, wives, and children.
"Children," etc., refers to the arising of sorrow, suffering, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "in the two lower realms," according to the *Śāstra*’s section on the classification of the three realms, it states that although [these afflictions] all pertain to the three realms, [they are specifically discussed here in relation to the lower ones].

Regarding the "with-portion" (sabhāga) and "entire" (sakala): in reality, the factors of ignorance (*avidyā*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), becoming (*bhava*), and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) all pertain to all three realms (*dhātu*).

As for the factor of formations (*saṃskāra*), mental karma pertains to all three realms; for example, verbal karma exists in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and thus its name pertains to two realms, whereas its substance exists only in the realm of form.
Among the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), the five physical bases exist in the two lower realms, while the mental base (*manāyatana*)...

It pervades the three realms. Regarding the explanation of the name: this explains only the general name. This is called "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and is also called "dependently arisen. The *Pañcāśatikā* states:

"The fruit is called 'condition' (*pratyaya*), and the cause is called 'dependent origination' (*pratītyasamutpāda*). It further states: "There is no sovereign, no agent, and no experiencer; there is no self..."
Functioning without autonomy, arising from causes, and evolving in dependence upon various conditions;

originally non-existent yet existing, and having existed, then dispersing and ceasing—manifested solely by phenomena, moistening that which is to be moistened and following along with the continuous stream of dharmas—is called "dependent origination."

Regarding the statement that there are five interpretations: the first four explain it in terms of the phenomena of contaminated birth and death (*saṃsāra*); the fifth interpretation explains that awakening serves as the condition, and its proclamation is termed "arising" (*udaya*).
Regarding the statement "one [type] is due to afflictions": it means that with the bondage of afflictions as a condition, they arise repeatedly;

this is called "arising" (*utpāda*). Without the condition of delusion, the fruit cannot arise; therefore, it is called "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*). When the previous maturation (*vipāka*) has already been exhausted, this constitutes the condition.

The further arising of other maturations (*vipāka*) constitutes "origination. Only the twelve factors of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-dharma*) within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), which are exclusively with outflows (*sāsrava*), receive this designation as "dissimilarity" (*visadṛśa*).
This is according to the correct tenet of the Mahāyāna.

Regarding the phrase "the two rely upon the assembly and so forth": this distinguishes [this teaching] from the reliance on various conditions found in the Hīnayāna; it explains the term "understanding" (*jie*).
Once the essence has rapidly perished, it arises again in conjunction with others; this explains the term "arising" (*qi*).
The statement "it is called dependent origination" serves as the conclusion. Conditioned phenomena rely upon causes and depend upon conditions;
each individual link possesses a multitude of conditions to arise, and there is nothing that arises without possessing its conditions, as was already explained in the case of the link of ignorance.

There are then associated factors—namely, the specific outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) and latent dispositions (*anuśaya*)—as well as the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), which arise by way of the four conditions.
Since this is the case for ignorance, and so on up to old age, which exists only by depending upon various conditions, it is called "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
When conditions are lacking, the preceding momentary aggregate of phenomena ceases; this is termed "condition. When conditions are complete, the subsequent momentary aggregate of phenomena continues.

Arising through combination is called "origination" (*samudaya*). When a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛtadharma*) arises, it must necessarily take the cessation of the preceding moment as a condition;
only by inducing the subsequent moment can it be brought into existence. That the preceding [moment] ceases to serve as a condition for the subsequent arising is "origination.

There is an interpretation that takes the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*) as the condition for the existence of the link of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); this interpretation is incorrect, as it merely provides a general definition of the twelve links. (1)

Within a single series (*saṃtāna*), because the preceding moment ceases, it acts as the condition; because the succeeding moment arises, it acts as the origination. This is called "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Regarding the phrase "to exclude the Mahāsāṃghika and other schools," the word "other" includes the teachers of the Mahīśāsaka school. These teachers of that school maintain:
The twelve links of existence depend upon the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); that is, the twelve links take the unconditioned as their essence.
Although the twelve links arise and cease and are subject to interruption, within them cause and effect are eternally fixed, never becoming confused, disordered, or lost.
This is entirely due to the sustaining power of the unconditioned. The unconditioned is like a saw, which remains unbroken; the twelve links are like—
"Saw-teeth" (*sāra*) means the severing of saw-teeth. Question: The Mahāyāna also teaches that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) serves as the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena.
Why, then, is it distinguished from the Hīnayāna? Answer: In the Mahāyāna, the myriad phenomena take the unconditioned as their essential nature;

however, this is merely a condition—specifically, a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). [Phenomena] arise each from its own distinct seed. This is the tenet of the Mahāsāṃghika masters. "Non-" (*a-*)... [text ends].
It serves as the direct support for the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). The twelve links of existence have the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as their direct support.

This is said in order to exclude that [wrong] attachment; therefore, it is stated that they "rely upon and depend on manifold conditions" (*pratyaya*), arising and ceasing moment by moment, each produced from its own seed.

They take impermanent phenomena (*anitya-dharma*) as conditions, not taking permanent phenomena (*nitya-dharma*) as conditions, because the unconditioned is merely their true nature (*dharmatā*). It is like space, which exists for the purpose of removal.
This is the basis. If one follows the *Sectarian Doctrines* (*Śāsanaprakaraṇa*), the four schools—the Mahāsāṃghika, Ekavyāvahārika, Lokottaravāda, and Gokulika—all maintain that there are no seeds.

That is to say, they hold that the two types of cessation (*nirodha*), space (*ākāśa*), the four formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*), dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and the noble path (*āryamārga*) all have the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as their essence.

Regarding the statement that "the Sāṃmitīyas and others also [hold this]," Master An states: There are two types of the four characteristics (*catur-lakṣaṇa*). First, the four characteristics of a single moment (*kṣaṇika-catur-lakṣaṇa*), which pertain to mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*).

Second, the four characteristics of a single lifetime (*eka-kāla-catur-lakṣaṇa*). Within this, there are again two: first, the grasping of the internal sense faculties (*indriya*) as abiding for a single lifetime;
second, the reckoning of the external vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) as abiding for one eon (*kalpa*) without ceasing in the interim. This is within the context of the Hīnayāna.
The four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of each moment are the same as those in the Mahāyāna; this [text] does not further distinguish them.

Here, we only exclude the grasping at the internal sense-faculties and the physical body of sentient beings, as well as the external vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*). Within the four characteristics of a single lifetime, there is no further arising and ceasing moment by moment.
This explains dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*): the preceding moment serves as the condition, and the subsequent moment is what arises. Thus, the Middle Way is attained.
Regarding the statement that "the three groups [of factors] take the past and so forth as conditions," Zhangjing says:

The *Yogācāra-bhāṣya-ṭīkā* states that if one relies on the perspective of stages (*avasthā*), the first ten members serve as conditions and the final two members serve as the arising. Although the single aggregate of dharmas belonging to the past has already fallen away and no longer exists, [it still functions as a condition].
This is termed "conditioning by various causes. Because the seeds of past conditions exist within the eighth consciousness and are not abandoned, these very seeds act as conditions;
relying upon one's own continuum, they give rise to the manifest state once again. Therefore, this is termed "arising."
Regarding the term "continuity" (*saṃtāna*): it refers to the meaning of one's own continuum. Conditioned phenomena rely upon causes and depend upon conditions;

the preceding moment does not perish, yet the succeeding moment does not arise [independently]. A prior aggregate of mind and mental factors arises from seeds; these very seeds alone serve as the condition.
To arise again as actualized activity within one’s own continuum is called "origination" (*samudaya*); thus it is termed "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

The phrase "as it is said, 'when this exists, that exists'" is a term of specific designation. The statement "because this exists, that exists" reveals dependent arising without an agent (*akartṛka*).

Because ignorance exists, the factor of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) exists; because the factor of volitional formations exists, the factor of consciousness (*vijñāna*) exists. This demonstrates the absence [of a creator].

The factor of ignorance (*avidyā*) serves as a condition only for the factor of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). If viewed from the perspective of the factor of consciousness (*vijñāna*), it lacks power.

This refutes the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) position that the twelve links of existence (*bhavāṅga*) possess real functional activity; such activity consists merely of ignorance serving as a condition for volitional formations, and volitional formations serving as a condition for consciousness.
While the Small Vehicle schools reckon this activity to be real, although the Mahāyāna does indeed acknowledge functional activity, [it is not ultimately real].
Originally, it is false. Question: The holy teachings state that ignorance (*avidyā*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) serve as conditions for one another. Answer:

If one speaks in terms of proximate conditions, the member of ignorance serves as a condition only for the member of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). If one speaks in terms of remote conditions, in the sense of not obstructing birth, it serves as a condition for the subsequent twelve members.
The statement "because this exists, that exists," and so forth, refers to the meaning of dependent origination without an agent (*anabhisaṃskāra*). An-guo says:

"It is like the materialists (*Lokāyatika*), who maintain that sentient beings are all produced by the four great elements, parents, and atoms (*paramāṇu*), which possess real causal efficacy (*kāritra*) capable of generating sentient beings;
this is what is called 'causal efficacy. Furthermore, it is like the Sāṃkhya and Vaiśeṣika masters who posit a creator, [claiming] 'I' am able to produce [them]."
Regarding the cause of death: it possesses a real function. Since we are now refuting that [notion], there is no "unmanifest" (avijñapti).
Each of the twelve links arises from seeds through the conditions of causes and conditions; they possess no real function. Because function is merely conventional, it is said to be "unmanifest."
The statement "because this arises, that arises" reveals dependent origination through impermanence. Because ignorance arises, the constituent of volitional formations (saṃskāra) arises;

if ignorance does not arise, the constituent of volitional formations likewise does not arise. That which is capable of producing [an effect] is entirely an impermanent phenomenon. This refutes the eternalist views of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).

The phrase "not other than" (*na-anyat*) serves to cite and explain the treatise’s argument. It means that [the nature of dependent origination] is not like the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) entities of the Hīnayāna, nor is it like the eternal dharmas of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) which are said to produce all things;
therefore, it is called "not other than. Master Lu says: the two characters "not other than" serve as the heading, while the passage beginning with "only by" (*kevalam...

yataḥ*) explains what precedes. "By" (*yataḥ*) here means "relying upon. Relying upon ignorance (*avidyā*) and volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) as conditions, the resultant dharmas such as consciousness (*vijñāna*) arise.
It is precisely because of this that it exists.

Regarding the statement, "Because this arises, that arises," which clarifies impermanence and so forth, the Minister of State (Xiangguo) said: "With ignorance as the cause, the *saṃskāra* limb is produced as the result;
with the *saṃskāra* limb as the cause, the *vijñāna* limb is produced as the result. This continues in the same manner for all subsequent limbs."

That which produces and that which is produced—the cause and the fruit—are both impermanent phenomena. This refutes the false attachments of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), who hold that the essence of Brahmā, primordial nature (prakṛti), the self (ātman), and so forth, is eternal; that it does not arise from causes, yet can act as a cause to produce other resultant phenomena.

Now, in order to refute them, [it is said that] "the four are impermanent. Furthermore, this also refutes the doctrine of the Mahāsāṃghika school regarding the arising of conditioned phenomena (*pratyaya-dharma*), because [such phenomena] do not [exist]...
This refers to the nature of the agent (*kartṛ*).
The statement that "it does not arise from conditions such as real entities" means that sentient beings do not arise from conditions such as parents or atoms; nor are they mere non-actors (*akartṛ*).

Rather, the self possesses real functional activity capable of producing effects. This is stated to further distinguish [the Buddhist position] from the aforementioned materialist (*Lokāyata*) tenets.

Regarding the statement that "it is also not the case that [the cause] is unarisen, such as the nature of dharmas," they [the opponents] reckon that eternal dharmas do not arise from subsequent causes; therefore, they are called "unarisen.

Furthermore, it is not the intention [of this teaching] that the Brahmā King or the Primordial Nature (*prakṛti*) acts as the cause, whereby the producer is vast while the produced is small—even down to a single dharma, which is termed a "small dharma.
There is not a single dharma that arises [in this manner]. Master Lu says: "The producer is vast, while the..."

That which arises is "small. Even down to a single dharma, it is designated as a "small dharma. There is not a single dharma that, at the time of its arising, is established without depending upon causes and conditions.

Regarding the statement "the four [factors] repeatedly perish and so forth," the fourth meaning concerns the sequential progression according to the realms (*dhātu*). Because they are repeatedly destroyed and cease, it is termed "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Question: What is the distinction between this and the second of the two preceding [meanings]? Answer: In the former case, that which has already perished in the past serves as the condition.

The arising of present phenomena is "origination" (*samudaya*); this is the meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Now, the fourth [section] does not explain the meaning of dependent arising, but merely reveals impermanent phenomena:

that within the bodies of sentient beings of the six realms and four modes of birth, there is a moment-to-moment flux and instability, characterized by the destruction and cessation of numerical designations. This differs from the second [section].
Regarding the statement "the five [factors] in the past and so forth," the World-Honored One himself explained them as conditions.

He taught this arising for the sake of sentient beings, meaning that when the Buddha was practicing the causes in the past, he heard such a teaching from a virtuous friend concerning conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
All arise from hearing through conditions (*pratyaya*). Awakening leads to the attainment of perfect enlightenment (the character *jie* [解] is interpreted as "understanding conditions").
Regarding the phrase "having awakened to the nature of conditions, etc.": "equal" (*sama*) means similarity; it is called "equal" because it is taught in a similar manner.

The continuous arising of the awakening to the nature of conditions is termed "conditions. The continuous arising of that which is equal is termed "arising" (*samudācāra*). Conditions belong to awakening; arising belongs to...

It is called "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda) because it is an explanation [of how things arise]. An-guo says: that which is realized is called the "condition" (pratyaya), and the explanation itself is called "arising" (samutpāda).
As for the term "successive" (kramaśas), this precisely refers to the conditions; the explanation itself is called "arising. Thus, "successive" is precisely the meaning of dependent origination.
Regarding the statement that "there is no self-natured self apart from sentient beings," An Guo says:

The Vaiśeṣika school posits that outside the bodies of sentient beings there exists a separate *puruṣa* (self), which acts as the recipient of the results of performing good and evil deeds; it is this self that merely knows the reception of the fruit.
Therefore, the commentary refutes this, stating that there is no self-natured self. Furthermore, the meaning of "that which is produced by oneself" is the meaning of "conditionality."

Regarding the phrase "in other continuities (*saṃtati*) and so forth," this refutes the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). [The claim that] "this person performs wholesome deeds while another receives the merit" is untenable.

"Continuity" has the meaning of "body. To perform an action oneself is called the "condition" (*pratyaya*); to experience the fruit oneself is called the "arising" (*utpāda*). It is impossible for that which one has performed oneself to be the condition for another.

The experience of another receiving the fruit is called "arising. One's own experience is not [the same as] that of devas or humans, and so on, down to ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*).
The branch of formations creates karma which serves as a condition; thus, the experience of receiving the fruits of merit or demerit is called "arising. Question:

If one performs the action oneself and receives the fruit oneself, why is it appropriate for men and women to perform meritorious deeds for the sake of deceased ancestors? Answer: There are three reasons. First, it is said that [one cannot receive the fruit]. [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly.]

Regarding merit: this is merely a teaching given by the Buddha within the context of the gate of manifested forms (*nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa*). In reality, the deceased do not obtain such blessings. As a sutra states:
"In the past, there was an elder who was by nature extremely stingy and greedy; after he died, he fell into the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*).

After his wife had completed the meritorious deeds on his behalf, she turned her attention to other matters that she enjoyed. At that time, the deceased husband spoke a verse: 'I formerly accumulated precious wealth...'"
Whether right or wrong, others now enjoy happiness while I alone endure poverty and suffering. The ghost said:
"It is not that you alone are excluded from clarity; if another person performs good deeds, you yourself should alone receive the benefit.

Otherwise, there would be no hells or the three miserable realms in this world, for within the ten directions of the Dharma-realm, Bodhisattvas practice for the sake of all sentient beings, diligently seeking the Great Dharma."
Furthermore, within every moment of thought, one should make a vow: "May all sentient beings be liberated from suffering.

If this is so, why do sentient beings still undergo suffering? [Question: If it is as you say, then must not the Bodhisattva be deceiving sentient beings? [Answer: It is necessary for a Bodhisattva to make such a vow;
even if they cannot save them, they shall take this aspirational mind with them when they attain Buddhahood. Second, the sevenfold discrimination.

One obtains one [seventh], yet it is not fully encompassed. Question: Since one obtains one-seventh out of seven parts, this is also a case where another person creates the karma, while this individual receives the benefit disproportionately.
Answer: When one obtains one-seventh out of seven parts, the matter must necessarily originate from the deceased person themselves, who must have harbored a mind aspiring for merit.
Since this mind already exists, it is produced by oneself and experienced by oneself; it merely takes others as conditions for its arising.

Regarding the statement "each has eleven explanations," etc., the *Abhidharmakośa* explains that there are eleven meanings for the term "conditioned" (*pratītyasamutpanna*). As for these eleven [meanings] in the *Abhidharma*:

first, the sense of being uncreated (*akṛtaka*); second, the sense of having causes (*sahetuka*); third, the sense of being devoid of a sentient being (*niḥsattva*); fourth, the sense of dependence on others (*paratantra*); fifth...
1. The meaning of being devoid of agency; 2. The meaning of impermanence; 3. The meaning of momentariness; 4. The meaning of the uninterrupted continuity of cause and effect;
5. The meaning of the correspondence between cause and effect; 6. The meaning of the differentiation between cause and effect; 7. The meaning of the determination of cause and effect.
These are called dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Regarding the statement that the Abhidharma (Dharma-paryāya) also speaks of "unconditioned dependent origination" (*anabhisamskāra-pratītyasamutpāda*), this refutes the twelve links as having functional activity (*kāritra*) in the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna).

In the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna), the twelve links are provisional; the link of ignorance (*avidyā*) serves merely as a condition for the link of formations (*saṃskāra*), but it lacks power with respect to the other links.

Regarding the statement that they arise through conditions and are impermanent: the link of ignorance produces only the link of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). If one considers it in relation to other links, it cannot produce them;
therefore, it is said to be "powerless."

Regarding the statement, "Because it arises through the conditions of causal efficacy (*śakti-vṛtti*)," this is a further explanation of the third distinct category. The Master of the Commentary (*Sūtra-śāstrin*) cites three points from the *Abhidharma-samuccaya-vyākhyā* (or *Dharmapada-śāstra*).

Since the first two—arising without activity (*akriyā-pratītyasamutpāda*) and arising through impermanence (*anitya-pratītyasamutpāda*)—are identical to those in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, he does not explain them further.
He explains the third, "arising through causal efficacy," in order to distinguish it from the non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*) attachment to a single cause that can produce many effects.

[The section on] Result. Question: What is meant by "conditioned arising through functional power"? Answer: Ignorance initiates the formations (*saṃskāra*). It serves as a condition for the branch of formations only by its own power;

once that power reaches the branch [of formations], it no longer has the capacity to extend further and serve as a condition for the branch of consciousness (*vijñāna*). This continues until the branch of existence (*bhava*) lacks power.
Even when the branch of existence possesses power, it serves as a condition for birth and death (*jātimaraṇa*) only by its own power, and does not look toward aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
This is the condition (*pratyaya*). It reveals the functional power of the dharma of impermanence, whereby these twelve links arise in mutual dependence.

An-guo says: According to the *Āryadeva-śāstra*, in recounting these various views, it states that the master Guṇamati asserts that from the navel of the god Nārāyaṇa there arises a great lotus, and within that great lotus there arises Brahmā, the progenitor. That Brahmā...
He is capable of creating all things, both animate and inanimate. From the mouth of Brahmā, the Brāhmaṇas were born;
from his two arms, the Kṣatriyas; from his two thighs, the Vaiśyas; and from his two feet, the Śūdras.
The great earth is the sacrificial ground for cultivating merit; by making offerings to Brahmā upon this sacrificial ground, one attains birth in that realm, which is called [the World of Brahmā].
Nirvāṇa is, moreover, eternal in essence. Some say it is time, space, the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*), or spontaneity (*svabhāva*).

This would mean that a single cause can produce multiple effects; however, we now refute this view. We demonstrate that ignorance (*avidyā*) and the other factors merely possess the functional capacity to give rise to their respective *saṃskāras* (formative forces).
They cannot universally produce all other links of dependent origination. The same applies when these factors are considered in relation to one another. Question: For what reason does the yogin...
Kātyāyanīputra says that the link of ignorance serves as a condition for everything up to old age and death. The answer is that there are two kinds of conditions:
first, proximate conditions; second, remote conditions. If one considers them in terms of proximate conditions, they exist in immediate succession.
If one relies on remote conditions, then ignorance also serves as a condition for old age and death. In the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, both the remote and the proximate are taught.
Now, in relation to the Abhidharma, [the teaching] is proximate rather than remote, and thus there is no contradiction.
Regarding the statement "although all dharmas," the question is: Does the previous statement that there is no unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) or impermanence mean that nothing at all is produced?

The answer, as stated in the commentary, is: "Although all dharmas," etc. This is not like the non-Buddhists who claim that a single cause can produce everything; it clarifies the twelve [links of dependent origination].
Each individual limb arises through the power of various conditions, and their respective capacities differ; this is called "dependent origination by way of capacity and function.

One should analyze the proximity and distance [of these limbs] using a fourfold categorization (*catuṣkoṭi*): first, there are those that have ignorance as a condition, but are not themselves formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and so forth;

second, there are those that are formations but do not have ignorance as a condition, such as untainted (*anāsrava*) consciousness and the like. The remaining limbs should be understood accordingly, as all possess both aspects.

The four lines (the first line provides the general name). Next, to clarify the specific designations: Ci'en states that for the single dharma of ignorance (*avidyā*), there are no six types of etymological analysis (*nirukti*).

Since its substance is a single dharma, there is nothing to be distinguished; it receives its name from manifesting its own essence, which carries the meaning of "constructing" (*saṃskāra*). It is also designated according to its functional capacity. "Consciousness" (*vijñāna*) is named from its function of discerning and distinguishing.

"Feeling" (*vedanā*) is named from its function of experiencing and receiving. "Craving" (*tṛṣṇā*) is named because its substance is defiled. "Grasping" (*upādāna*) is named because it involves the desire for [continued] existence. "Existence" (*bhava*)... [text ends].

The fruit is called "existence" (*bhava*). The arising of the aggregates is called "birth" (*jāti*). "Name-and-form" (*nāma-rūpa*) is a *dvandva* compound (a copulative construction), because name and form are distinct in their essential nature;

thus it is called a "contradictory" compound. Regarding the limb of the "six sense bases" (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), the bases where matter and mind arise and grow are called "bases. Because there are six such meanings, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound (a possessive construction) expressing a number.
"Aging" (*jarā*) has the meaning of transformation; "death" (*maraṇa*) has the meaning of cessation and non-existence. The things signified by these terms are each distinct. Furthermore...
This is a *vyadhikaraṇa* (non-appositional) compound.
Regarding the phrase "characteristics of conditions" (*pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*), it refers to the mode of functioning (*ākāra*) of the twelve links as conditions.

Regarding the statement "ignorance has two kinds," etc., this correctly clarifies the mode of functioning of ignorance. [The author] asks: what is the intended meaning of the term "characteristics of conditions"? Why is this so?
Following the link of ignorance (*avidyā*) is the link of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); following the link of volitional formations is the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*);
and so on, until following the link of birth (*jāti*) is the link of aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*). Why, then, was the link of ignorance mentioned first? The answer is: ignorance is twofold.

First, regarding the ultimate reality (*tattvārtha*), which is the principle of the Four Noble Truths; to give rise to delusion with respect to that is called "delusion regarding the ultimate reality. One who is deluded regarding the ultimate reality—

This refers to the delusions regarding: first, suffering; second, impermanence; third, emptiness; and fourth, non-self. The term "delusion regarding true reality" (*tattvārtha-moha*) is a *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "delusion concerning true reality.
All contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*) within the three realms are suffering, yet ignorance perceives them all as pleasure.

Now, with respect to the fruits of the two higher realms and the human and celestial realms of the desire realm, one fails to understand that these are suffering, impermanent, and non-self, instead accepting them as permanent and pleasurable, and further calculating [them as such].
For the sake of *nirvāṇa*, they seek to accomplish meritorious karma (*puṇya-karman*) and immovable karma (*āniñjya-karman*), desiring to be born in that body.

This [desire] is also subsumed under the Truth of the Origin of Suffering (*duḥkha-samudaya-satya*) within this very life. Since they seek that body, they become deluded and attached to the true principle of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self as found within the Four Noble Truths;
therefore, this is called "delusion regarding the true meaning" (*tattvārtha-moha*).
Regarding the "delusion concerning the two types of ripened fruits": the bodies of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals are properly termed "ripened fruits.
Because one does not believe that these fruits arise from killing and stealing, it is called "delusion concerning the ripened fruit. An-guo asked:

"Why is the delusion of ignorance regarding the retributive fruits of humans and devas called 'delusion regarding reality,' while the delusion of ignorance regarding the fruits of the three miserable realms is [called]..."

Is this the delusion regarding maturation (*vipāka-moha*)? The answer is: when one is about to create the causes for rebirth as a human or a deva, and while seeking the fruits of human or deva existence, one does not know that these fruits are suffering, but falsely conceives them to be happiness;

being thus deluded and attached to the principles of suffering, emptiness, and impermanence within the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), this is called the delusion regarding the true meaning (*tattvārtha-moha*).
Furthermore, if one does not believe that killing or stealing are the causes for the state of maturation, and does not understand maturation...

If one obtains the fruit from killing, this is merely called ignorance regarding the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*), not ignorance regarding the true meaning (*tattvārtha*). Furthermore, speaking in terms of what is predominant:
when that person performs the karma of killing, they simultaneously lack conviction that there is a fruit in hell; this is why they perform the karma of killing.

Their delusion regarding the characteristics of the ripening fruit is predominant, while their delusion regarding the true meaning is inferior. If, however, they maintain ethical discipline, they possess conviction...

There is the delusion regarding the meaning of seeking the fruits of human and celestial existence; this is called "delusion regarding the true meaning. There is the delusion regarding the fruits of the three evil realms;
this is called "delusion regarding the fruit of maturation" (*vipāka-phala*).

Regarding the statement that [ignorance] is "only of the superior grade," some say that the delusion regarding the true nature of reality (*tattvārtha-moha*), which arises in relation to the bodies of humans and devas, is actually ignorance of the middling and inferior grades.

Xuānmó says: "It is only the superior grade that is deluded, because its faults are grave. If one speaks in terms of the meaning of "increasingly adhering" (*anuśaya*), [it refers to the superior grade].

The delusion regarding the true meaning and the delusion regarding the fruit of maturation arise from distinct bases; however, when considered collectively, they are both termed the "delusion regarding the fruit of maturation.
The statement that "both take the internal body and so forth as their object" serves to distinguish them from external dominant fruits (*adhipatiphala*).
Regarding the statement that "there are two kinds of conduct," etc.: first is wholesome conduct, which refers to the ten wholesome courses of action, such as abstaining from killing;
second is unwholesome conduct, which refers to the ten unwholesome courses of action, such as killing and stealing.

Regarding the statement that [karma] may be divided into three types: first, immovable karma (*āniñjya-karman*). Second, the explanation: one interpretation states that karma created by moving the ground and thereby attaining [a result] is called immovable karma;
alternatively, karma belonging to those who are immovable is called immovable karma. A second interpretation states that it refers to the karma that is created.
Unlike the karma of the desire realm, which can be shifted, this karma cannot be altered; thus it is called "immovable karma" (*āniñjya-karma*).
Among these, the interpretation that it refers to "immovable [karma]" (*aniñja*), "karma of immovability" (*aniñja-ja*), or "sustaining karma" (*dhṛti-karma*) is correct.

Second, karma created through meritorious action (*puṇya-karma*) is called "meritorious karma" because its intrinsic nature and its fruit are desirable. In reality, however, all wholesome karma within the three realms collectively constitutes meritorious karma. For now...
With respect to the heavens of the desire realm and among human beings, because the enjoyment of sensual pleasures is predominant, it is specifically termed "meritorious karma" (*puṇyakarman*).

As for the third type, "non-meritorious karma" (*apuṇyakarman*), the karma produced by it—both its intrinsic nature and its fruit—is undesirable and not to be relished; thus, it is named non-meritorious karma.
To say that this is the "perfuming of the constituent parts" (*bhāgīya-vāsanā*) explains the branch of the cultivation of practice (*bhāvanā-aṅga*).

That is to say, it refers to the seeds of karma capable of summoning [rebirth] within the three realms as constituent parts. There are two types of perfuming: first, the seeds of wholesome karma, which are capable of summoning desirable fruits.
Second, the seeds of all unwholesome karma are those which can summon undesirable fruits. "Bhava-bhāgīya" (existence-portion) means that which pertains to the three realms of existence;
"vāsanā" (perfuming) is a name for seeds. Therefore, it is called "existence-portion perfuming."
Regarding the phrase "the five kinds beginning with consciousness," it is asked: what is meant by "name-and-word" (*nāma-vyañjana*)? It is answered: there are two types of name-and-word.

The first is the name-and-word that expresses meaning. "Expressing" (*vyañjana*) means manifesting or making known; it refers to the characteristics of the teaching that serves as the signifier. "Name" (*nāma*), "phrase" (*pada*), and "syllable" (*vyañjana*) are what constitute the expression.
"Meaning" (*artha*) refers to principle; it is the doctrine that is signified. When the sixth consciousness hears the teaching, it understands and grasps the signifier.
Regarding the principles of the teachings: when the mind arises through understanding, seeds are perfumed. These seeds are perfumed by two types of linguistic expression (*nāma-vyavahāra*):
first, the linguistic expression that signifies meaning; second, the linguistic expression that reveals objects, which refers to the minds and mental factors that apprehend objects.

The seeds formed by being perfumed according to these two types of linguistic expression serve as the respective causes and conditions for all conditioned phenomena (the first [type] is for apprehension). Second, there is the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*).

Perfuming (*vāsanā*) refers to the seeds of the false attachment to "self" and "what belongs to self. Because of this attachment to a self, one also perfumes the seeds of the contaminated five aggregates within the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*);
this is precisely what is called the perfuming of names and phrases (*nāma-pada-vāsanā*). Because it perfumes the seeds of self-attachment, it causes the distinction between self and others;
therefore, it is established separately (the perfuming of the three realms of existence was explained previously). Question: Are these three types of perfuming identical or distinct?
The answer is that the meaning is not fixed. The latter two types of perfuming are "existent as verbal designation" (*prajñapti-sat*). These latter two may or may not be verbal designations;
specifically, those which are non-defined by speech (*vāk-avyākṛta*) but are not grasping (*anupādāna*), as well as untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*), are not the latter two.

If one were to contrast self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*) with the links of existence (*bhava-aṅga*), it could be formulated as follows: first, there is that which is self-grasping but not a link of existence, namely, the obscured-non-defined (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) grasping. It is not...

Regarding the *bhavāṅga* (existence-factor): first, that which is associated with *manas* (the ego-thought); second, those two *bhavāṅgas* that are not characterized by self-clinging, namely, wholesome and unwholesome minds that do not give rise to clinging;
third, the category of association with existence, namely, those associated with unwholesome clinging;

fourth, the category of neither, namely, seeds of the non-obscured neutral nature and untainted seeds—these are the *bhavāṅga-vāsanā* (existence-factor habit-energies) among the three types of habit-energies. Thus ends the section on the existence-factor.
The various names refer to different aspects of the same entity; they are all synonymous terms for karma.

Regarding the statement "these five neutral factors (*avyākṛta*) and so forth": these five branches—consciousness and the others—within this eighth consciousness are extensively perfumed within that consciousness.

They are neutral by nature and do not arise through their own power; rather, it is only after being summoned and induced by the force of karma that they are subsequently able to follow [their conditions].

Regarding the arising of karma, as for the statement "by means of the superior grade": [Question] Since it is initiated by the power of discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna*) that gives rise to meritorious and immovable [karma], why is it said that ignorance (*avidyā*) is its condition?
[Answer] The *Mahā-śāstra* (Daśabhūmika-bhāṣya), fascicle 10, states: "Because one does not clearly understand conventional suffering (*saṃvṛti-duḥkha*), [one initiates] non-meritorious [karma]."
Meritorious karma arises from a failure to comprehend suffering in its ultimate sense (paramārtha-duḥkha), thereby giving rise to meritorious and immovable formations.

The sufferings of the three miserable realms are easily understood and are thus termed conventional suffering (saṃvṛti-duḥkha). Because the karma of humans and gods is difficult to discern, it is termed ultimate suffering.
Furthermore, the suffering of change (vipariṇāma-duḥkha) is called conventional suffering, while the suffering of conditioned existence (saṃskāra-duḥkha) is called ultimate suffering.

Regarding the phrase "following the initiation of karma" and so forth: according to whether the karma is wholesome or unwholesome, and which realm or stage (*dhātu-bhūmi*) it is projected into, these five factors are subsumed within the seeds of *saṃskāra*.

That which is drawn forth by the factor of *saṃskāra* belongs to the place of future birth; these very seeds are precisely the seeds for the factors of birth (*jāti*) and aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*) in the future.

Regarding the statement that "the seeds and stages are fixed and simultaneous," this means that when these five factors—the seeds—act as the *saṃskāra* (formative) link during the stage of projection (*ākṣepa*), they are projected all at once without any sequence of before or after.
Prior to the "taking up of water" (the moisture of grasping), the preceding six links transform into the *bhava* (existence) link.

Question: Since there is no sequence of before and after, why does the previous sutra state: "Ignorance conditions formative forces (*saṃskāra*); formative forces condition consciousness (*vijñāna*); consciousness conditions name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*)"?
[Question: [Regarding the statement] "and so forth," [the answer is: It is explained that there are distinctions of priority and sequence based on the temporal stages of their arising in the future.

Although they are actually simultaneous, they are categorized according to principal and attendant, general and specific, superior and inferior, and cause and effect. Among the factors, the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the principal; the other links are its attendants.

Name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is the general; the other three are the specific. The six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are the superior; the other two are the inferior. Contact (*sparśa*) is the cause; feeling (*vedanā*) is the effect.

Furthermore, regarding the statement in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Cheng weishi lun) beginning with "That is to say" (*yue*), it refers to the delusion regarding the internal fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*). This establishes the member of ignorance (*avidyā*).

The mental states that can summon various karmas leading to future existence establish the members of existence (*bhava*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) as conditions, which then induce and directly produce [the result].
The seeds of the five fruits in the states of future birth, aging, and death constitute the seeds of the five links beginning with consciousness.
Here, the term "predominant" (*pradhāna*) carries the sense of dependence; the sense of dependence necessarily requires this reliance upon ignorance as the inducer.
The phrase "furthermore, based on delusion regarding external objects" refers to gardens, fields, houses, family members, the five elements, and so forth.

The phrase "conditioned by the perception of objects" means that the perceiving faculty experiences and receives the object; this establishes the existence of the "feeling" (vedanā) limb [of dependent origination].
The statement "giving rise to craving" (tṛṣṇā) proves the existence of the link of feeling (vedanā).
The statement "conditioned by craving, the four [realms] such as the desire realm arise again" proves the existence of the link of grasping (upādāna).

The statement "the combination and moistening of craving and grasping" refers to this combination and moistening of the two links, craving and grasping, of the seeds of prior karma—both the projecting karma (ākṣepaka-karman) and that which is projected (ākṣipta).
The seeds of the five factors beginning with consciousness are re-designated as the "existence" (bhava) link.

This proves that regarding the existence link, when it says "from this [intermediate state] and so forth," the existence link gives rise to its own active manifestation, whereby the "birth" (jāti) link subsequently arises.
What is referred to as "decline, change, life, and so forth" is precisely the link of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇāṅga*).
Due to the link of old age and death, there subsequently arise various forms of sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction (as stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*).
The statement, "This explains [the process] through delusion regarding the internal and so forth," is the Master of the Commentary’s explanation of the conditions (*pratyaya*).

The phrase, "From that point on, the five factors and so forth," intends to mean that the seeds of karma, having been moistened, possess only the functional capacity to project and elicit [a future existence].
Regarding the statement "the three explanations of Yoga," Huaduo says: First, the twelve links are established based on the twelve causal conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
The first six links are established based on internal bodily conditions, while the latter six links are established based on external objective conditions.
Second, it is said that the twelve links are established by virtue of the three types of sentient beings; the first [set] is established based on worldly sentient beings.
Six branches. Second, regarding sentient beings who delight in and cling to sense objects, the latter six branches are established.

Third, regarding sentient beings who delight in transcending the world, all twelve branches are established in total. It is said: "Due to ignorance, one is deluded regarding what ought to be done in the world, and only then do various formations arise.
Because various formations arise, the mind becomes inverted. Because the mind is inverted, one undergoes birth."
Death leads to continuity; because of continuity, the sense faculties become complete; because the sense faculties are complete, one experiences objects;
because one experiences objects, there is attachment and longing; because of attachment and longing, afflictions increase;
because afflictions increase, the karma for future existence increases; because karma increases, the fruits of the five destinies arise; and once born, they undergo transformation and decay.

Thus, old age and death arise; for this reason, the thirteen links follow this sequence. These three explanations all concern the order of causes as they pertain to the stage of the fruit that is to be born.
This is because when the five causes—consciousness and so forth—are first perfumed by past karma, they do not possess such a sequential order;
therefore, it refers to the stage of what is to be born. The *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* states: "They exist simultaneously, yet are taught in a sequential manner."
Regarding the statement "relying on the world" (*loka*), relying on the world means relying on the body; all [worlds] are defined by the birth and death of the body.

As for the reference to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* regarding the "ten causes" and so forth: from the fruit of the link of ignorance, there are the ten links as causes in the present and two links as fruits in the future.
This is what is meant by the certainty that cause and fruit do not belong to the same world-period. Furthermore, regarding the ten links as causes in the past, the preceding...
In this world, ignorance gives rise to formations; these, whether wholesome or unwholesome, draw together the five links beginning with consciousness.

At the time of death, craving again arises, taking up moisture like water, and being proximate to the fruit to be experienced, it is termed the link of existence (*bhava*). These constitute the ten causal links of the past.
In this present life, the factors of birth, aging, and death constitute the fruit. Furthermore, within this very body, one again initiates activity through ignorance;
the factor of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) then gathers the five factors beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*), which belong to the state of being bound to the place of rebirth.
At the time of death, craving arises and takes up moisture, transforming into the factor of becoming (*bhava*). These constitute the ten causal factors of the present life. After the body has died—

The two future branches of fruit—aging and death—are themselves the ten present branches of cause. These two future branches of fruit constitute the principle of a single layer of cause and effect in this Mahāyāna teaching;
they differ from the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), which, following the *Sarvāstivāda* school, establishes two layers of cause and effect across the three periods of time.
The two past branches of cause refer to ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*). The present...

Regarding the fivefold fruit, this refers to the five links beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*). Regarding the threefold causal factors of the present, these are craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*).
Regarding the twofold fruit of the future, these are birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*). This is explained in detail in the *Abhidharmakośa*. To summarize:

a question is asked as to why the Hīnayāna specifically teaches two sets of cause and effect across the three time periods. The answer is: there are non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who deny the existence of the past and the future, asserting that only the present exists.

Phenomena arise naturally from within the Dharma. Because they are ignorant of the past limit (*pūrvānta*), one asserts that all phenomena are eternal; because there is no teaching regarding the future limit (*aparānta*), one asserts that all phenomena are annihilated.

Within the Buddha’s Dharma, in order to refute these views, dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is taught: by taking ignorance and formations of the past as causes, the view of permanence is refuted;
by taking old age and death of the future as effects, the view of annihilation is refuted; and by [identifying] the five effects and three causes of the present, both extremes are refuted.
It arises spontaneously. Therefore, the Mahāyāna Vijñaptimātra school refutes this, saying:
"These twelve links constitute a single cycle of cause and effect that avoids the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism; if one were to posit two such cycles, it would be truly useless."

It is said that because the cause is permanent, the fruit is refuted as being annihilated. Question: In the Mahāyāna, there are ten branches of causes in the past and two branches of fruits in the present;
ten branches of causes in the present and two branches of fruits in the future. Is this not a double-layered structure? Answer:
Although it appears to be double-layered, fundamentally it does not depart from a single layer.

Regarding the statement that "birth [in the next life] and subsequent retribution, etc., are required," the intended meaning is that present retribution (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) is not a constituent part [of the cycle], as it does not fulfill the sense of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) nor accord with the sequence of cyclic existence.
When karma is created in this very life and one receives the result in this very life, without being separated by another birth, it is called "concordant with the present" (*dṛṣṭadharmika*).

If one creates karma now that is to be experienced in the very next birth, it is called "karma to be experienced in the subsequent life" (*upapadyavedanīya*). If one creates karma in this life that is to be experienced in a third birth or beyond, it is called "karma to be experienced in a later life" (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*).
Regarding the statement that the first seven factors within the causal phase are necessarily co-existent with the factor of craving (*tṛṣṇā*):

for instance, when ignorance (*avidyā*) initiates activity and one performs an action (*karma*), in a single moment the seeds of the five factors beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*) are gathered. Together with the preceding two factors [ignorance and formations], these are called the "first seven within the causal phase.
It is only at the time of approaching death that craving arises to provide the moisture of water, whereby they transform into the factor of existence (*bhava*). This [craving] is the moistener.
Those who are moistened [by karma] are all destined to be born in the same world in their next life; this is explained in terms of karma ripening in the very next birth (*upapadya-vedanīya*).

As for what is said regarding karma ripening in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya*) being different, it is like the case of Udraka Rāmaputra, who sat and attained the meditative absorption of the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

While he was entering that concentration, having fully perfected the seven limbs of immovable karma (*āniñjya-karma*), he was disturbed by the clamor of various birds in that forest, and consequently gave rise to [thought].
Due to a mind poisoned by anger, he manifested as the body of a flying-fox *yakṣa* and devoured birds and beasts.

At the time he made his vow, the seven factors of his lineage were fully matured among the flying-foxes; yet, by the power of fixed karma, he was forcibly reborn in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
After eighty thousand kalpas had passed, as his life there was ending, he finally gave rise to craving for water.

Rūṇi: Eighty thousand kalpas ago, among the flying foxes (*ulūka*), the seeds of the seven factors [of dependent origination] exhausted their retribution in the heavens, and he then received the body of a flying fox.
This constitutes: the first birth, wherein the karma of a flying fox was created; the second birth, wherein the heavenly retribution was received;

and the third birth, wherein the fruit of being a flying fox was received. These seven factors constitute one lifetime; the factors of craving, grasping, and becoming constitute one lifetime, while the factors of aging and death constitute [the subsequent] lifetime.
The fruit is a single lifetime; this is based on karma to be experienced in a subsequent life (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya*). Regarding the dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) of three lifetimes:

if it is karma to be experienced in the next life (*upapadya-vedanīya*), the ten links belong to one lifetime, while the links of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) belong to another—this is the dependent origination of two lifetimes. If it is karma to be experienced in a subsequent life, it is the dependent origination of three lifetimes.
Within these three lifetimes, it is the case that one body creates the karma, another body moistens the rebirth (*pratisandhi*), and yet another body receives the fruit. Thus, [the seven links...].

Because the three members and the two members are necessarily of different time periods, they are designated as "subsequent retribution" (*paścādvipāka*), which differs [from other types]. Mochizuki states: "They also extend across the three time periods.
This is because the causal force of the seven members of the past is similar; thus, the three members of the present serve as the cause, while the two members of the future constitute the fruit."

Regarding the phrase "as for the various [types of] dependent origination," this refers to the fact that within all the scriptures, the explanations differ from one another; hence the term "various dependent originations.

The commentary cites four versions of the treatises—namely, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the *Madhyāntavibhāga*, the *Yogācārabhūmi*, and the *Abhidharmakośa*—and thus divides this section into four parts.
Regarding the term "discrimination of self-nature" (*svabhāva-vikalpa*), there are several types of discrimination: first, that which explains and interprets [names] is called discrimination;

second, that which takes mental phenomena as its object of cognition is called discrimination; third, that which involves analytical differentiation is called discrimination. Here, it refers to the third meaning, not the former two.

*Cheng weishi lun* (Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only) states: "Discrimination means the sense of analytical differentiation. The seeds of the three natures give rise to the three manifestations.

The activities proceed such that each belongs to its own kind without mutual confusion. Turning back toward the seeds, the capacity to produce actualized manifestations (*samudācāra*) is termed "discrimination" (*vikalpa*).
There are two interpretations of this: first, discrimination is the cause and self-nature (*svabhāva*) is the result;

discrimination is the seed, while self-nature is the actualized manifestation. Question: Why are the seeds of the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate called "producing actualized manifestations"?
They are not mutually confused. Answer: Because seeds ascend [to the level of manifestation], each has its own distinct discernment (*vikalpa*).

The manifest resultant phenomena have distinct intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*); thus, this discernment is called the "condition" (*pratyaya*), while the intrinsic nature is called the "arising" (*samudaya*).

That is to say, the seed is the condition and the manifest phenomenon is the arising. Another interpretation states: "Intrinsic nature" has the meaning of cause, which is the seed; "discernment" refers to the differentiation (*vibhāga*).
This refers to another sense: namely, the manifest resultant dharmas. Question: Why do the produced results differ from one another? Answer:

Because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the seeds produces results according to their specific causes; each possesses its own propelling portion (*ākṣepa-bhāga*). The intrinsic nature of the seed of form produces the manifestation of form.

The term "discrimination" (*vikalpa*) refers to the manifestation of mind arising from the seeds of mind; this is called discrimination. Here, the seed is termed "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*), while the manifestation is termed "discrimination.
According to the first interpretation, discrimination is the cause as the seed, and intrinsic nature is the result as the manifestation.
According to the second interpretation, intrinsic nature is the cause as the seed, and discrimination is the result as the manifestation.

First, it is explained that discrimination (*vikalpa*) serves as the condition, from which arising itself proceeds. Later, it is explained that self-nature (*svabhāva*) serves as the condition, while discrimination is the arising.

This latter explanation is considered more comprehensive, as it applies to both types of perfuming—seeds and manifestations (the above explains the phrase "discrimination of self-nature" from the treatise).
Regarding the statement "it refers to that which relies upon the *ālaya-vijñāna*," etc.: the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) is the locus of support for those various phenomena.
By mentioning the supported consciousness, the intention is to reveal the seeds that rely upon it, not the consciousness itself.
The phrase "the arising of all phenomena" refers to the fruits that are produced; therefore, it is called the "dependent origination of the discrimination of self-nature.
Regarding the phrase "the two types of discrimination, craving, and so forth," these are also seeds. Master Mu said: "This interpretation refers exclusively to wholesome and unwholesome karma."

Although wholesome and unwholesome karma serves as the condition, it is that which brings about desirable and undesirable fruits that constitutes the "arising. This distinguishes it from indeterminate phenomena.

Compared to the previous analysis of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), this definition is narrower. While the former explains how seeds of the three natures each produce their respective manifest activities, this second [explanation] refers only to the perfuming of specific portions of wholesome and unwholesome karmic seeds, which bring about the arising of the maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*) of good and evil. The pleasant fruits experienced by devas and humans are called...

The desirable is so called; the bitter fruits of the three miserable realms are called the undesirable. Now, that which is discriminated is explained: these are the fruits of the two destinies of good and evil.
That which is capable of discriminating is the karmic seed of the good and evil destinies, termed "perfuming with constituent parts" (*bhāgīya-vāsanā*).
The term "seed" refers to discrimination, while actual manifestation is the fruit of the desirable and undesirable.
The phrase "Now, this correct explanation," etc., serves as a critical analysis (*paryeṣaṇā*) of the two preceding interpretations; it is also termed "acceptance and rejection. Question:

Why is the former interpretation not accepted, while the latter is adopted? Answer: Because the latter interpretation [explains] that dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) correctly gives rise to wholesome and unwholesome karma.
Regarding the seeds of wholesome and unwholesome karma in relation to the twelve links [of dependent origination], this is the primary clarification.

As for the statement that "the meaning also includes the former," it refers back to the seeds of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) within the previous explanation, which give rise to their own nature’s active manifestations (*pravṛtti*).

This is because the seeds of the preceding moment give rise to the manifestations of the succeeding moment; since this inclusion is broad, and because it is broad, it is taken in its entirety, and thus it is called "meaning."
It also includes that which was previously induced by karma; this refers precisely to what is explicitly explained within the twelve links.
That which among them is not induced by karma is excluded and not taken up; therefore, it is said that it is not explicitly explained.
The intended meaning is that this present link of consciousness includes one portion of the preceding dependent origination, and thus it is said to "include the preceding."

Regarding the statement "furthermore, three types are taught": these twelve links, according to their actual nature and underlying principle, further include the conditions of acquisition (*prāpti*) and enjoyment (*upabhoga*);
thus, they are designated as the "three types."

Regarding the phrase "distinguishing the *Madhyāntavibhāga* and others," this refers to specific classifications. Question: What is meant by "the dependent origination of enjoyment" (*paribhoga-pratītyasamutpāda*)?

Answer: The commentary states, "distinguishing the *Madhyāntavibhāga* and others. The treatise says: "The dependent origination of enjoyment refers first to what is called 'conditioning consciousness' (*ālambana-vijñāna*). This explains the meaning of the dependent origination of enjoyment:
because the eighth and seventh consciousnesses exist as conditions, the first six consciousnesses arise, along with the other evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*)."

It is called "consciousness as a condition" because it serves as the causal condition for their arising. The second is named the "experiencer" (*vedaka*) because it experiences the objects of the five sensory realms.

That is to say, when the six internal bases give rise to the six consciousnesses and they take the preceding six objects as conditions, they are collectively called the "experiencer" because they are able to receive and apprehend those preceding objects.

Question: Why, among all the mental factors (*caitta*) that arise simultaneously, is only one dharma—feeling (*vedanā*)—mentioned here, while the others, such as emptiness (*śūnyatā*), are not? Answer:

Feeling (*vedanā*) is specifically mentioned because it is predominant in its capacity to experience the preceding object. This is the second interpretation. It refers to the six consciousnesses as "feeling.

Consciousness itself is not feeling; rather, it is the master of feeling. When consciousness perceives an object, among the mental factors (*caitta*), the factor of feeling has the stronger function of experiencing the object.

Now, following the predominance of the master, this is attributed to the consciousness. By attributing the function of feeling to the consciousness, the consciousness is called "feeling. Question: Why?
Therefore, consciousness is called "feeling" (vedanā). In response to the question regarding the second name in the *Prakaraṇapāda* treatise, the term "feeling" (*vedanā*) here signifies the subject.

Because mental factors (*caitta*) are subordinate, they cannot receive the title of "subject"; thus, the six consciousnesses, which are the sovereign mind-kings (*cittarāja*), are designated as "feeling."
Regarding the statement "that which can experience within this": Jin Yun says that the first phrase clarifies the producer, which is the first sentence of the treatise;
"the first" refers to the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness). The subsequent three phrases are the produced.

Within these three phrases, that which clarifies the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) is the second sentence of the treatise, called "the experiencer. The final two phrases clarify the mental factors (*caitta*), which are the [remaining] sentences of the treatise.
Among these, "that which can experience" (*anubhavitṛ*) and "discrimination" (*vikalpa*) refer to the mental factors (*caitta*). Mochizuki states:

"The two characters 'among these' (*atra*) point dualistically to the preceding two phrases concerning the object-condition and the experiencer. The three characters 'can experience' are precisely the *vedanā* (feeling) within the mental factors.

As for the fourth phrase, 'discrimination refers to the mental factors,' the two characters 'discrimination' (*vikalpa*) are the *saṃjñā-skandha* (perception aggregate). "Refers to" (*tarka*)... [text truncated].

The single character "this" (之) refers to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Because volition (*cetanā*) and attention (*manasikāra*) possess the functional capacity to initiate, urge, and exert effort, they are designated as "driving" (*pra-√vṛt*).

The two characters "mental factors" (*caitta*) refer to the remaining phenomena within the aggregate of formations. Since both the mind and these mental factors experience the perceived object (*ālambana-viṣaya*), they are so called.
The phrase "the dependent origination of experience" (*upabhoga-pratītyasamutpāda*) serves as a summary. This refers to the dependent origination of experience.

Regarding the statement "it is also of this same meaning," some say that it is now clarifying dependent origination because, among the twelve links, the six evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and their associated mental factors (*citta-caitta*) have corresponding meanings;
thus, they are included within this same meaning by virtue of reaching [that state]. It is not [included] in this particular context.
This is precisely the point; therefore, it is said that this is not a definitive exposition.

As for the statement that the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* further speaks of four kinds [of conditions] and so forth, that treatise states there are four types of dependent origination, namely: the "projecting" (*ākṣepaka*) and the "projected" (*ākṣipta*), and the "generating" (*abhinirvartaka*) and the "generated" (*abhinirvṛtta*), and so on.

Regarding the statement that the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* also says "equal" (*sama*), it is simply because the seeds of karma within consciousness serve as the link of consciousness (*vijñāna-aṅga*) for the locus of the seeds of consciousness.
Now, since consciousness itself is also that which projects (*ākṣepaka*), the intent here is to take the karmic seeds within consciousness;

these karmic seeds are the projectors, while the seeds of consciousness are certainly the projected (*ākṣipta*). Because the karmic seeds reside within consciousness, they are referred to as "karmic seeds."

Regarding the formation of the seed of the consciousness link (*vijñāna-aṅga*): it also takes the seed of karma as its object and becomes blended with the seed of the consciousness link in a single location, like two bundles of reeds leaning against one another.
The seed of karma is that which projects (*ākṣepaka*), while the seed of the consciousness link is that which is projected (*ākṣipta*).
Because the seed of karma is metaphorically designated as the seed of the consciousness link, it is said that consciousness is also "that which projects."

Regarding the phrase "the seeds of the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) and so forth": Question: Since the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* cites the seeds of karma as the seeds for the member of consciousness (*vijñānāṅga*), under what category are the actual seeds of consciousness subsumed?
Answer: The commentary states "maturation-consciousness" and so forth; the seeds of consciousness are instead subsumed within the member of name-and-form (*nāmarūpāṅga*).

This is based on the classification of the members according to their composite nature (*miśraka-svabhāva*). In this system of composite nature, there is an intrinsic seventh consciousness which serves as the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) within "name."

Regarding the statement that the Sūtra teaches the "consciousness link" (*vijñāna-aṅga*) and so forth: the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* explains both the seed of karma and the seed of consciousness. Question:
The first volume of the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* states that consciousness encompasses both the "projecting" (*ākṣepaka*) and the "projected" (*ākṣipta*). How is this to be reconciled? Answer:

That Sūtra states that because both the seed of karma and the seed of consciousness are the consciousness link, they both encompass the projecting and the projected. Question: If the seed is designated as the consciousness link, why... [text ends]

The seeds of the non-maturing consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) are included within the "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) section of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*. Are the seeds of consciousness collected in the same location as the seeds of karma?
The answer is that Dharmapāla, interpreting the intent of the Sūtra, states: "Consciousness is the support for 'name' (*nāman*); it is not subsumed under 'name-and-form' (*nāmarūpa*)."

The ālayavijñāna is the root; it serves as the basis for name-and-form (nāmarūpa), while name-and-form is the derivative. This definition of their essential nature is established to avoid confusion. Question:

Regarding the statement that all five categories are "derived," why does the first fascicle of the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* state that one portion of name-and-form—namely, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling—is also called "produced"? Answer: Because they exist as actual manifestations (*samudācāra*), they function as seeds.
This refers to that which is produced. Question: Why does that sūtra also state that one portion of the limb of sensation (*vedanā*) is the limb that produces?
