Answer: There are two types of manifesting sensation: first, internal maturation sensation (*vipākavedanā*), which the sūtra classifies as being subsumed under the limb that is produced;

second, objective sensation (*viṣayavedanā*), which gives rise to craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and so forth, and which the sūtra classifies as being subsumed under the limb that produces. These are distinct in terms of their respective meanings, and furthermore—
This is a contradiction.
Regarding the mention of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, chapter nine and so forth, this reconciles the tenets of the Hīnayāna as presented in the *Kośa*. Master Kuang states:
"A single moment" (*kṣaṇa*) refers to one and the same moment. "Continuous" means succeeding one another in connection. "Divided" refers to the twelve [links] preceding and following.
Regarding the state of the constituent parts (*aṅga*), as for what is distant, it refers to the continuity [of parts] separated by preceding and succeeding intervals.
As for the question, "What is a moment (*kṣaṇa*)?", because two constituent parts are complete within a single moment, it is called "momentary dependent origination" (*kṣaṇika-pratītyasamutpāda*).
Regarding the definition of the essence [of the twelve links], there is the sense of their being simultaneous; this is not according to worldly treatises.

When the Commentary asks, "What is meant by 'one moment' (*kṣaṇa*)?", the Master of the Sub-commentary answers: "Within a single moment, if one gives rise to a mind of greed and commits killing, one is already complete with all twelve links.
The *Jianyao* (Essentials) states: "If one commits killing with a mind of hatred, the twelve links are not complete within a single moment."

If one commits killing with a mind of hatred (*dveṣa*), there is certainly no mind of greed (*lobha*). Since the factor of greed is absent, the "limb" (*aṅga*) of grasping (*upādāna*) is likewise absent.

Furthermore, regarding the case where one commits killing with a mind of greed and possesses all twelve limbs: when one commits killing with a mind of greed, it is first associated with ignorance (*avidyā*);
this is precisely ignorance associated with greed. At the very moment of exerting force to kill a living being, it is associated with the mind of greed.

[The aggregate of] volition (*cetanā*) arises simultaneously with this branch of formations (*saṃskāra*). The sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*), which is able to cognize the preceding object, is precisely the branch of consciousness (*vijñāna*) associated with craving.

The three aggregates that coexist with this consciousness collectively subsume name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Since the Lesser Vehicle does not believe in the existence of the seventh or eighth consciousnesses, it takes the sixth consciousness as the branch of consciousness;

since the five sensory consciousnesses are included within "name" (*nāma*), and the sixth consciousness is taken as the branch of consciousness, the consciousness aggregate thus refers to the present [moment].
Furthermore, if the seventh and eighth consciousnesses were absent, there would be no mental faculty (*manas*) within the branch of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*);

there would only be the five internal faculties constituting the branch of the six sense bases. Question: Since the sixth sense base, the mind-base (*mana-āyatana*), is missing, how can the six sense bases be established? Answer: By taking the few from the many, they still constitute the branch of the six sense bases.
This is because, within a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), one apprehends dharmas; it is not appropriate to apprehend the preceding moment. However—
The sixth [member] is the faculty within the link of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

Regarding the phrase "the three aggregates co-arising with consciousness," all commentaries state that among the five aggregates, the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) is excluded, because it is established as a separate member [of dependent origination].
The three aggregates consist of the entirety of the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) and a small portion each of the aggregates of form (rūpa-skandha) and formations (saṃskāra-skandha).

Among the eleven types of form, the five sense-organ forms are excluded, as they are subsumed within the limb of the six internal bases (ṣaḍ-āyatana); furthermore, the form included in the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana-rūpa) is not taken here.

Only the four internal sensory objects—form, odor, taste, and touch—are taken as the "form aggregate co-arising with consciousness" (vijñāna-sahabhū-rūpa-skandha). Within the universal mental factors associated with consciousness, contact (sparśa) is excluded.

Feeling (*vedanā*) consists of two [types]. It is established as a constituent (*aṅga*) in its own right. The remaining mental factors—attention (*manasikāra*), as well as desire (*chanda*), resolve (*adhimokṣa*), mindfulness (*smṛti*) among the object-specific mental factors (*viśeṣa-viṣaya-ka*), and other such mental concomitants (*caitta*)—constitute the aggregate that accompanies consciousness (*vijñāna-sahabhū-skandha*).

These three aforementioned aggregates—the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) in its entirety and portions of the aggregates of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*)—together constitute the three aggregates which are collectively termed the member of name-and-form (*nāmarūpāṅga*).
Regarding the statement, "Abiding in name-and-form and the faculties," "name-and-form" is the general category and the "five faculties" are the specific instances.
Because the specific abides within the general, it is said that they "abide in name-and-form and the faculties. These five faculties are designated as the limb of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

Because the six sense bases exist in conjunction with the other three—faculties, objects, and consciousness—they are called the limb of contact (*sparśa*). The experience resulting from mental contact and so forth is called feeling (*vedanā*).
The phrase "greed itself, etc. refers to the primary intention to kill.

The phrase "associated with this, etc. refers to those factors associated with greed, such as lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*), lethargy (*styāna*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*).
This refers to the link of grasping (*upādāna*).
As for the phrase "the bodily and vocal actions that arise": the two types of karma—bodily and vocal—that arise simultaneously in the same moment as craving are called the link of becoming (*bhava*).

Regarding the statement "these dharmas are thus" and so forth: when these dharmas arise correctly, it is called birth (*jāti*); the characteristic of change is called maturation (*jarā*); the transformation of decay is called aging (*jarā*);

the characteristic of cessation is called extinction (*nirodha*); and the time of disintegration is called death (*maraṇa*). This is discussed in terms of the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) within a single moment (*kṣaṇa*). [The interlocutor] asks:
since the temporal periods of the characteristic of birth and those of aging and death are distinct, how can the twelve [links] be complete within a single moment?

Master Zhi answers by citing two interpretations from the *Śāstraviniścaya* (攝釋論). The first states: "This is called one *kṣaṇa* based on the completion of the activity of the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

Therefore, the twelve links possess the sense of being complete [within a single moment]. The second states: "The four characteristics are integrated in essence; they are collectively referred to as the characteristic of birth (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) without regard for their individual activities.

It is simply because the essence manifests before us that the link of birth (*jāti-aṅga*) is said to exist. The essence of the link of birth shares the same characteristics as the activity of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*)."
According to the present Dharma-śreṣṭha (the Lesser Vehicle interpretation): furthermore, when the eye sees a form, the ear does not arise.
In what moment could the two factors of consciousness (*vijñāna*) and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) coexist? In the Mahāyāna, the eight consciousnesses and their afflictions arise simultaneously.
Regarding the statement that "others say": a *kṣaṇa* (moment) consists of arising, abiding, change, and cessation.
The statement "now, the Mahāyāna" refers to the refutation of the Hīnayāna. Its intent is to refute [the claim] that the twelve links are not complete within a single *kṣaṇa*.
Question: Why are they not complete? Answer: In the Hīnayāna, consciousness does not arise simultaneously; there is a sixth moment without the preceding five, as in:
At what moment is the consciousness link simultaneous with the aggregate of consciousness within "name"?
*Fahua jing xuanzan yaoji*, Scroll 29; *Fahua jing xuanzan yaoji*, Scroll 31.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Xifu of Jingshui Temple.

Regarding the characteristics of the four lands (*catur-bhūmi-lakṣaṇa*), the Sūtra states that the assembly of Bodhisattvas is exceedingly vast. There are six aspects of these land-characteristics in the prose section:

first, breadth and narrowness; second, physical appearance; third, the presence of goodness and the absence of evil; fourth, the characteristics of devas and humans; fifth, sustenance through food; and sixth...
The section from "the retinues of the three vehicles" onwards all constitute mutual inclusion. In this verse, the characteristics of the land (*kṣetralakṣaṇa*) are categorized;

specifically, the bodhisattvas within that pure land are categorized under a single aspect of the land's characteristics. It does not include the Buddha’s lifespan or the stūpas mentioned in the preceding prose.
Alternatively, some explain that the two verses and one line beginning with "the assembly of bodhisattvas is exceedingly vast" describe the preceding prose.
Regarding the characteristics of the soil: within the six sections of the text, the sixth concerns the retinue of the three vehicles. The prose of the sūtra states:
"There were immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya, thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas of bodhisattva assemblies who had attained great supernatural powers and the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge."
They are well able to teach and transform the various classes of sentient beings. Regarding the three virtues of a bodhisattva mentioned in the verse, the Sūtra says:

"All possess great supernatural powers and are fully endowed with majestic virtue and strength. [The phrase] "well able to teach and transform the various classes of sentient beings" is omitted [in that specific verse].

Regarding the three virtues of a śrāvaka, there are countless śrāvakas and bodhisattvas who possess the three types of higher knowledge (trividyā), the eight liberations (aṣṭavimokṣa), and have attained the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ). It is by means of these [virtues] that...
Regarding the Sangha, it describes the three virtues of the śrāvakas, omitting the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and adding the four unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).

The scripture states: "The sentient beings of that land... (three phrases). This verse corresponds to the preceding section on "having good and no evil," specifically the phrase "born by transformation without desire.

It does not correspond to the section on "humans and devas seeing one another. The scripture states: "A body adorned with the marks of excellence" (one phrase). This verse corresponds to the second [phrase] within the preceding section on "the characteristics of humans and devas."

The seven marks and signs: they are entirely golden in color and adorned with the thirty-two marks. While these are praised in verse, the attainment of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and so forth are not.
The Sūtra states: "Exclusively born through transformation. This refers to Bodhisattvas in the lands of retribution prior to the seventh stage who still possess parents and are born from them;
their birth is still accompanied by sorrow. "Exclusively born through transformation" here refers to the lands of retribution from the eighth stage upward.

Furthermore, when the Sūtra says, "The food of Dharma-joy and the delight of dhyāna," and so forth, it describes the fourth category of humans and devas mentioned in the preceding prose section. The Sūtra states:
"Attaining great supernormal powers, their bodies emit radiance. ... down to: "First, the food of Dharma-joy; second, [the food of dhyāna-delight]."
They feed on the joy of dhyāna. Therefore, the present verse says: "Delighting in the Dharma and feeding on dhyāna, they have no further thought of food.
To say "this is the first" refers to the mind’s aspiration.
The Sūtra says: “At that time, the twelve hundred arhats... [up to] ...those who were mindful. This refers to what was previously heard:
when the Bodhisattvas heard this Dharma, their nets of doubt were all removed, and it was declared that the twelve hundred arhats would all likewise become Buddhas.
Furthermore, they heard that among the disciples of the Buddha, those endowed with majestic virtue, numbering five hundred, would all become Buddhas; moreover, they saw this with their own eyes.
I, a person, have received a prediction regarding my own mind; yet, hoping for a formal prophecy, I have not yet dared to fully anticipate it, which is why I reflect upon it.

If the World-Honored One were to grant each of us a prophecy, as he has for the other great disciples—namely, Śāriputra of superior faculties, the four of middle faculties, and Pūrṇa, who was previously mentioned—would that not be most joyful? For we have already obtained our predictions.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra that says "these one thousand two hundred," etc., it specifically points to the one thousand two hundred as being recorded separately;
thus, we know that the five hundred are included therein.
As for the phrase "among these one thousand two hundred," since the "Chapter on the Questions" already mentions five hundred Arhats, why [is this said]?
The Sūtra says, "He made this thought," and then mentions "one thousand two hundred people. Regarding this, there are two interpretations.
First, some say that the five hundred and the one thousand two hundred are distinct groups; the five hundred are outside of the one thousand two hundred.

Second, the *Zhengyi* (Correct Meaning) states that the five hundred are included within the number of the one thousand two hundred. As for these one thousand two hundred people, they consist of two categories: first, the five hundred...

First, those who were present at the assembly received a personal prediction from the Buddha himself. Second, the remaining seven hundred who were not present at the assembly were granted predictions by the Buddha through others.

Whether they were present or absent, they are included in the general enumeration; thus, the scriptural text mentions one thousand two hundred people. This count is based on those who were present at the assembly.
Because the Buddha personally bestowed the prediction upon them, the title specifies "five hundred people. Question:

If that is so, and there were only five hundred in the assembly, why does the sutra state, "The twelve hundred people each had this thought"? Answer: It is like a matter commonly sought by a multitude of people in the world.
If one person goes first, the minds of the multitude likewise agree; this case is also like that. Although they are not present in the assembly, they still harbor such thoughts:
"Since the other seven hundred people are not in the assembly, how can it be known that the Buddha has bestowed the prediction upon them?

The answer is: by successive transmission, they are also said to have received the prediction. The Sūtra permits this by stating that the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is bestowed in succession.

Commentary: Since the World-Honored One spoke of bestowing predictions in successive order—first to Pūrṇa, next to the twelve hundred, and finally to the five hundred—it follows that these five hundred are taken from among those twelve hundred and are considered part of that primary group. Question:

Why is it that within the five hundred, Ājñātakauṇḍinya is given a prediction separately? Answer: Because Ājñātakauṇḍinya was the very first to leave the household life and the very first [to attain realization].
Because this was understood [as such], the Buddha specifically marked it.
As for the statement "this is called Black Light" (*kṛṣṇābhāsa*), the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* calls it "Black Radiance. The *Āgama* Sūtras state: "His body was extremely black.
While he was walking at night to beg for food, the time happened to be shrouded in dark clouds. A pregnant woman saw him amidst a flash of lightning."
Thinking it was a malevolent spirit, she was startled and fell, thereby injuring her fetus. He then said to her, "What kind of spirit are you?
She replied, "I am a disciple of Gautama; I have come here to beg for food. After the woman had finished speaking, she addressed her with coarse words and harsh abuse.
The Tathāgata, knowing this, commanded the bhikṣus: "From this day forward, you must not eat past midday, nor may you go out to beg for food in advance."
Regarding the phrase "this appearance," Jin Yun states that he attained enlightenment at the time of sunrise; therefore, he is called "Appearance.
He was a disciple of Ānanda.

Regarding the phrase "Cūḍapanthaka" and so forth, Xiang Guo states that this person was a slave named Sēnù (Snake-Slave); some say his father was a slave. [From] the *Buddhacarita-sūtra* (Benxing jing).
He was called Senu (Snake-Slave), which is also translated as "By the Roadside. Long ago, there was the daughter of an elder who had a secret affair with a slave.
They subsequently fled to another country, and after some time, she became pregnant. As her delivery drew near, she longed to return home; while traveling halfway there, she gave birth to her son.
Because he was born by the roadside, he was thus named. This happened twice, resulting in two sons in total. The elder son was named Panta, and the second son was named Cūḍapanthaka.
Bandhaka is the same as the names found in the sutra texts, such as Cunda and Śākata; they were so named because they were born by the side of the road in succession as brothers.
Another explanation states that Śākata (pronounced with the initial *ś* as in "sheng" and the final *-ta* as in "go") means "by the side of a small path."
Because the younger brother derived his name from his elder brother, it does not necessarily mean that each one was born by the roadside.

As for the name *Sāgata* (in the Tang dialect pronounced as *Ye*; also written as *Jie*), its phonetic rendering is translated as "Welcome. This title was established by the Buddha upon meeting him and following his teacher.
If you ask why he is named *Samantaprabha*, "Prabha" means light, and "Samanta" means universal or pervasive; thus, his radiance illuminates the ten directions and is eternal.
The benefit of preaching the Dharma pervades the mind. As for the phrase "successively" (*zhuan ci*) in the sutra, it does not mean "to transmit" as it does in the subsequent passage.

Regarding the phrase "rejoicing and leaping for joy" (*huan xi yong yue*) and so forth, Jiaxiang says: inner rejoicing refers to rising from one's seat and so forth, which is outwardly manifesting respect.
As for the phrase "repenting and reproaching oneself," [it means] the Buddha said: "In the past, he taught me to resolve my mind [for enlightenment]."
"May you cause me to practice so that I may seek the great fruit. Yet I have been deluded, turning my back on the Great and heading toward the Small; this is my first fault.
From the beginning of the first week, at that time the World-Honored One arose serenely from samādhi and addressed Śāriputra, and so forth.
"The Tathāgata likewise taught us the same [teaching] for our opening, showing, awakening, and entering; yet we harbored doubts and did not awaken.
Furthermore, it was the same during the second round as well. Having thus troubled the World-Honored One on two occasions, this is our second fault."
During the third week, he invited the World-Honored One to bestow a prediction of his own enlightenment.
Because of my dull faculties, at that time I repented and reproached myself, just as Śāriputra had done. From then on, throughout the day and night, I have constantly reproached myself, saying:
"This is our fault, not the World-Honored One's. During the second week as well, he spoke of his former mind with self-contempt, likewise repenting and reproaching himself.
The preceding section concerned internal remorse and reproach.
Regarding the statement that there are two types of "comprehension through acceptance," this is because at the point where Pūrṇa accepted the Dharma previously, the five hundred [monks] did the same.
The preceding section was for one person as the primary subject; the same principle applies to the others. Based on these three cycles of teaching, the stages differ.
The comprehension of the text across the three cycles also varies in its progression: in the first cycle, one comprehends through the Dharma; in the second, one comprehends by means of an analogy;
and in the third, one comprehends through both Dharma and analogy. The former was comprehension through the Dharma over a long period; this is comprehension through an analogy.
Regarding the initial section on the former provisional teachings, there is a transcribed outline divided into six parts: first, the analogy of approaching a virtuous friend; the sutra says:
"World-Honored One, it is as if someone went to the house of a close friend and fell asleep while intoxicated. Second, the analogy of being taught to arouse the great vow.
The Sūtra says: "At that time, the kinsman has official business to attend to" constitutes four phrases. Third, the metaphor of being unconscious and unaware:
the Sūtra says, "That person lies drunk and does not perceive anything at all. Fourth, the metaphor of falling back and hanging down:

the Sūtra says, "Having risen, he wanders abroad and arrives in another country. Fifth, the metaphor of attaining a minor nirvāṇa: the Sūtra says, "For the sake of food and clothing, he strives and seeks with diligent effort."

It is extremely difficult and arduous. Sixth is the simile of self-declaration of completion. The Sūtra says: "If one obtains even a little and considers it sufficient," and regarding the phrase "about to leave the perilous path," the Sūtra says:
"World-Honored One, it is as if there were a person who went to the house of a close friend and became drunk."
He lay down to sleep. At that time, a friend who had business to attend to tied a priceless jewel inside his garment and gave it to him before departing.
The analogy of "leaving midway and only then withdrawing" refers to what the sutra says: the man was intoxicated and lying down, completely unaware of it.
Regarding the statement that he established a "transformed city" for their benefit, the Sūtra says: "Having set out on his journey, he arrived in another land;
for the sake of food and clothing, he labored diligently, until he finally considered himself satisfied."
Regarding the statement that the fourth assembly does not accept [the teaching] because they are weary: this was not included even in the preceding combined prose section. That text states:
"This is not for the purpose of clarifying the two paths of the provisional and the real; rather, it is precisely to clarify the matter of ceasing suffering. For this reason, it was not accepted.

Regarding the phrase "this is the first": this summarizes the initial parable of departure. The Sūtra says: "World-Honored One, it is as if there were a person who went to [a friend's house] and then departed.
Here, the "friend" refers to the śrāvakas of the three roots; "going to the house of a close friend" refers to the residences of the sixteen princes.
If one encounters non-Buddhists, they are called "evil friends"; if one encounters those of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), they are called "provisional friends."

Now, meeting one who practices the Mahāyāna is called "meeting a kinsman and friend. Because the seeds of the four wisdoms and the Buddha-nature are identical, it is called "kinsman" (*jñāti*), just as in the world those of the same clan are called brothers of the same lineage. Those with the same name are called "kinsmen," and those with the same aspirations are called "friends.
Having the same pursuit of Bodhisattva practice is what constitutes a "friend. The Middle Way Mahāyāna is termed the "lineage" (*gotra*).
Regarding the scriptural statement that "one lies down after being intoxicated by wine," the ancient master Jiaxiang explained: "The poor man was not originally drunk;
he went to the home of a kinsman or friend and encountered wine upon the mats, which he then consumed. As the verse below states: "For example, a poor man goes to the home of a kinsman or friend;
that house is exceedingly wealthy, and they have prepared all manner of delicacies. [The author] asks the ancient master about this.
By what is "alcohol" defined? Answer: Taking the teachings of the signless Mahāyāna as the substance of the alcohol. Question: Why is it necessary to take the teachings as the alcohol? Answer:
Because they can cause confusion and bewilderment, leading one to fall prostrate; therefore, they are likened to alcohol. As the Sūtra says:

"They become even more terrified, faint, and collapse upon the ground. A verse in the Sūtra states: "Holding the vessel of the samādhi of emptiness, one fills it with the wine of signlessness. Now, one practices...

Various practices nourish and develop the Dharma-body. Furthermore, it is said that wine has the power to bring joy and satisfaction; this is a metaphor for how, upon hearing the teaching, one leaps with exuberant joy.
Second, the Guangzhai Commentary states: "The poor man was originally intoxicated; he merely lay down upon arriving at the house of a close friend.

This does not mean that he became intoxicated and fell asleep only after reaching the house; rather, this poor man was already intoxicated from the start, and only upon arriving at the house of his close friend did he lie down.
Only then is intoxication revealed. It is like a person walking in the street who does not collide with or offend others; how could one know they are drunk?

Only when they arrive at the home of a close friend and their speech becomes incoherent is their intoxication revealed. In the discourse on the Dharma, the original arising of ignorance is called intoxication.
Upon reaching the home of the Mahāyāna friends and hearing the Mahāyāna teachings, the inner mind becomes deluded by those teachings; this is called intoxication. One is unwilling [to accept them].
"Cultivation" is called "reclining. To recline means not to act (this concludes the commentary on the sutra).
As for the statement regarding the sixteen princes, these were none other than Śākyamuni himself when he was a prince in a past life.
Regarding the phrase "those who have persons, etc.," this refers to the śrāvakas comparing themselves to others.

Regarding the phrase "friends and equals," one asks: what is meant by "friend"? The answer is that the *Shu* (Commentary) states: "Those of the same school are called companions (*peng*); those of the same aspiration are called friends (*you*).
That is to say, sharing the same gate of awakening is termed 'clarity' (*ming*"); sharing the same resolve is termed 'friendship' (*you*)."

Regarding the phrase "colleagues and friends" (*liáo yǒu*) from the *Líjì*: "colleagues" (*liáo*) refers to officials and functionaries of the same bureau or office who attend to one another's affairs.

Regarding the term "friends" (*yǒu*) used to describe those who possess benevolence: "holding" (*zhí*) means to maintain; because they share the same will, they rely upon and support one another, and thus are called "friends."

As for the term "fraternal" (悌), it does not refer specifically to brothers; rather, it means to instruct one another in virtuous deeds, which is what is called "fraternal. As for "reaching" (至), it refers to relying on the two types of wisdom—learning and reflection;
hearing the teachings and contemplating the principle is what is meant by "resolute meaning" (志義).

Regarding the statement that "the Buddha-dharma is taken as the nation," this explains the meaning of the household. It is analogous to the previous description of an intoxicated person coming and going from various places to a friend’s house;
within the Dharma, it refers to proceeding from the midst of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) toward the Buddha-dharma.

Regarding the statement "at the time [of speaking], one is still like an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*)," this explains the meaning of being "drunk and lying down. At this stage, the afflictions (*kleśa*) of an ordinary person have not yet been severed;

the mind is shrouded by ignorance and is in a state of stupor and intoxication—this is the meaning of "drunk. One constantly slumbers within birth and death (*saṃsāra*), and even upon encountering the Buddha-dharma, refuses to practice—this is the meaning of "lying down.
Zhangjing said: "Being deluded regarding the teachings is called 'drunkenness'; lacking in practice is called 'lying down. To lie down is precisely not to practice."
Question: If ignorance (*avidyā*) constitutes intoxication, and ordinary beings have possessed ignorance from the very beginning, why is it only now that they are said to be intoxicated?
Answer: Although it was not severed previously, it arises once again now. Since they were initially deluded by the Great Teaching, what harm is there in this new intoxication?

Regarding the metaphor of intoxication, it was previously explained that the poor man first drank wine and subsequently fell asleep in a state of intoxication. In the context of the Dharma, the Great Teaching is called "wine," and hearing [it] is called...
Drinking: being deluded and obscured by ignorance is called "intoxication. No longer practicing cultivation is called "lying down.

To say, "At this time, the Prince’s work of transformation has ceased," and so forth, refers to his *nirmāṇa* (emanation). Entering *nirvāṇa* means that he has manifested his body in other realms to transform others. As the Sūtra says:
"At this time, a friend had official business to attend to," and there is also the teaching that says: [he entered *parinirvāṇa*].

Transforming those of the two vehicles and ordinary beings is called "private affairs. Teaching and transforming bodhisattvas, causing them to enter the equality of the Mahāyāna, is called "official affairs.
Second, benefiting oneself is called "private affairs," while benefiting others is called "official affairs.

Third, not regarding the Triple Gem of the Buddhas of the ten directions and the teachings of the Three Vehicles as one's own is called "official affairs"; the Buddhas of the ten directions are called "officials" because they teach and transform.
"Sentient beings" refers to "official business. The affairs of an official household are called "official business.
It is said, "It is also like one traveling in a swift boat. [The questioner asks: In the previous analogy, it was said that when one must go on official business, one travels to various places.
According to the Dharma, the Buddha fundamentally has no coming or going; why then is it called "must go on official business"? [The answer: The commentary states, "It is also..."
Regarding "floating on swift currents" and so forth: "swift current" (*kai*) refers to the rapid flow of water; "advancing" (*mai*) means to go forward; and "boat" (*shu*) refers to a vessel.
Regarding the phrase "gazing at a stagnant pond" and so forth: "gazing" (*choku*) refers to seeing with the eyes; "stagnant pond" (*kyō-chō*) refers to a pool of water that does not flow.
As for "flowing westward," it means that the river’s natural course does not originally flow toward the west; rather, it is the boat that is heading eastward.
As he departed, it was as if one were seeing the waters of a frozen pond flowing westward. Guzhi said:
"The clouds and mountains upon the pillow—once reaching the mountain peak, the islands and counties have all shifted away. Falun said: "The Tathāgata is always present in the world;

it is simply because sentient beings ride the boat of birth and death, transmigrating through the three realms, that they falsely perceive the Tathāgata entering extinction. In truth, the Buddha does not perish. This is the meaning.
It is said that water does not actually flow; it is the movement of the boat that makes it appear to go. Thus, the Tathāgata always abides in the world, yet the mind pursues him, calling it Nirvāṇa.
The Buddha himself dwells in the Mahāyāna, like still, frozen pond water; when the minds of sentient beings regress, it is as if a swift boat were moving.

Regarding the phrase "the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and others" (the character 筮 is pronounced with a level tone): first, as for those who have heard the Dharma practice, such as Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, he said:
"In the land of the Buddha Ratnatejobhyudgatarāja, I heard from afar that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* was being preached in this Sahā world; therefore, I have come."

This is for the sake of practicing the Dharma upon hearing it. Alternatively, it may be that Gadgadasvara has come from the land of the Buddha Śubhavyūharāja to make offerings to Śākyamuni and to hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
Regarding the second point, the practice of preaching the Dharma: as was concluded in the questions and answers in the Introductory Chapter, Mañjuśrī no longer appears;
instead, he goes to the dragon palace to preach the Dharma and returns. Furthermore, when Gadgadasvara appears, he manifests various [transformations].
They do not weary their bodies, even when among the royal harem and other such places. Throughout all the worlds, they always delight in preaching the Dharma to benefit sentient beings.
Third, regarding "not following greed and the rest": the conduct of sentient beings is entirely associated with the three poisons, whereas that of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is not so.
Fourth, regarding "those who practice in the desire realm": these are those who come from pure lands to be born here in order to transform and guide living beings.
Therefore, it is as in the cases of Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and others. Regarding those in the five realms of form and the formless realm:

this refers to practitioners of the four dhyānas and the four *ārūpya-samāpattis* who are caused to practice meditative concentration so that they may swiftly advance. Regarding the six types of Dharma-practitioners:
as when Jñākūṭa asked Mañjuśrī, "When you went to the Dragon Palace, how many sentient beings did you transform and lead to the accomplishment of purity?"

7. Those who practice by swiftly observing the principles of meaning through wisdom; 8. Those who practice in all realms of existence, manifesting various bodies according to the classes of sentient beings within the five destinies;
9. Those who practice in all Buddha-fields, traveling throughout all lands to make offerings;
10. Those who practice toward nirvāṇa, delighting in the practice of nirvāṇa while remaining within saṃsāra; 11. Those who bring all Buddhas to fulfillment.
"Practice" refers to the fact that all practices for attaining Buddhahood are entirely perfected.

Regarding the phrase "should be explained according to the context," the Sūtra states: "One should engage in official affairs. This corresponds to the eighth of the ten [practices], the practice of all Buddha-fields;
it may also correspond to the ninth, the bodhisattva practice, or perhaps to the second, the practice of preaching the Dharma.
The statement that "the so-called great bodhicitta" refers to the priceless jewel of the sūtras is explained as follows. Question: Is the substance of this jewel contaminated (*sāsrava*)?

Answer: There are two explanations. First, it is said: The sūtra states that because it is a priceless jewel, it takes only the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) innate seeds (*bīja*) to be called "priceless.
If it were contaminated, how could it be called priceless? Second, it is said: It takes only the contaminated [seeds].
The seed of the bodhicitta is called the priceless jewel. Question: Why is a jewel that is *sāsrava* (with outflows) called "priceless"? Answer:
Although it is *sāsrava*, when compared with the jewels of the bodhicitta of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) and the Great Vehicle, it is also called priceless.
The merit of the two vehicles is like the price of a single day. Furthermore, it is said that taking both the *sāsrava* and *anāsrava* as wholesome is superior. Question: As for the jewel...
"Are these [seeds] newly perfumed (*navasaṃskṛta*), or are they innately present (*sahaja*)? The answer is threefold. The first master says: "All seeds exist by their very nature;
they do not arise from perfuming. As the Sūtra states: 'All sentient beings, from time immemorial, possess various elements (*dhātu*), like a cluster of akṣa fruits;
they exist as such by the nature of things (*dharmatā*). Here, 'element' (*dhātu*) is a synonymous term for 'seed' (*bīja*). Thus it is said.
He establishes that cause and effect are not disordered. The second [master] says: "All seeds arise because they are encompassed by their respective layers.

Since seeds are merely another name for habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), these habitual tendencies must exist through perfuming (*bhāvanā*). This is like the fragrance of sesame produced by the perfuming of flowers.
As stated in the Sūtras: "The minds of all sentient beings are perfumed by various defiled and pure dharmas. The *Tri-svabhāva-nirdeśa* (or *Tri-ratna-dharmapāla*) says: "All seeds are of two types:
first, those that are innate (*prakṛtistha*), which have existed naturally within the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) since beginningless time;
second, those that are acquired (*samudānīta*), which have arisen repeatedly from beginningless time through the manifestation [of dharmas]. As the first master [Vasubandhu] taught.

There is a teaching that introduces [the concept of] perfuming through practice, as in the case of the second master. Question: Is the priceless jewel something newly perfumed, or is it inherently present? Answer:
First, there is the position that it refers exclusively to the meaning of seeds newly perfumed. This is because the sutra states:
"On such-and-such a year, month, day, and time, a priceless jewel was tied inside his garment. Since there is mention of a specific time, season, month, and day, [it must be a new acquisition].

[This] knows the new. If [seeds] existed only as innate (*prakṛtistha*), they would exist by their very nature; how then could one speak of "binding"? Second, [the theory] includes both the innate and the newly perfumed (*navasaṃskāra*).
In this case, it is necessary to first establish the new perfuming based upon the innate. If the innate did not exist, how could the new perfuming be established?
Question: How can one speak of the timing of innate seeds? And how can one speak of the analogy of "tying a jewel"? Answer: It is obtained through the attainment of a stage (*bhūmi-pratilambha*).

During the first great *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*, the perfuming of hearing (*śruta-vāsanā*) associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) serves as the support for that which is innately present (*prakṛtistha*). This is also designated by a specific year, month, and day;

it is precisely at this time of support that it differs from what preceded, and this constitutes the "tying of the jewel. Taking the protection of the Dharma (*dharma-pāla*) as the primary [condition] is correct.
Taking the bodhicitta associated with outflows as the "jewel" is correct.

Regarding the statement that there are three kinds of precious jewels: first, the water-clearing jewel; second, the wish-fulfilling jewel; and third, the gold-spitting jewel. As for the three grades of the gold-spitting jewel:
the inferior grade spits out one *liang* of gold that increases a thousandfold; the middling grade spits out one *liang* that yields ten-thousandfold.

If one obtains one *liang* of the superior grade of spittle, it yields immeasurable multiples. The substance of the jewel is a metaphor for the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), which can produce the three vehicles (*triyāna*).
From within the One Vehicle, the Śrāvaka vehicle is differentiated, just as the jewel produces a thousandfold; from the One Vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle is differentiated.
Just as a pearl yields ten thousandfold, from within the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) the Mahāyāna is distinguished; just as a pearl yields immeasurablefold. Question:
What is the distinction between the "producing" One Vehicle and the "produced" Mahāyāna? Answer: The producing is the Mahāyāna of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* assembly;

the produced is the Mahāyāna [taught] during the forty years [of Śākyamuni’s ministry]. Because the Mahāyāna is established by being contrasted with the Two Vehicles (Dviyāna), it is thus [designated].

That which is produced is not the producer itself. Master Jin said: "The One Vehicle is likened to the jewel; the Three Vehicles are likened to the gold spat out [of the jewel] (as if one were to start from small and progress toward the great).
The lower grade is likened to the Śrāvaka-saṃgha; the merit and blessings bestowed by them are few. The middle grade is likened to the Pratyekabuddha;

the merit obtained from bestowing upon them is greater. The upper grade is likened to the Bodhisattva; the extraordinary retribution for bestowing upon them is inexhaustible. As for the two waters and the clear jewel..."
There are three grades. First is the inferior grade, which can purify a small amount of water; second is the middling grade, which can purify the great ocean.

The inferior grade is a metaphor for the teachings of the Hīnayāna, as the principles they elucidate are the shallowest. The middling grade is a metaphor for the teachings of the Hīnayāna, as the principles they elucidate are of intermediate depth.

The superior grade is a metaphor for the teachings of the Mahāyāna, as the principles they elucidate are the deepest. Third is the wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*), which serves as the primary metaphor herein. This...
The jewel itself has three grades. The lower grade rains jewels that fill half of Jambudvīpa; the middle grade rains jewels that fill one Jambudvīpa;
and the upper grade rains jewels that fill the four continents. The lower grade is a metaphor for the Buddha-nature (buddhadhātu) in the two stages of *sambhāra* and *prayoga*;
the middle grade is a metaphor for the Buddha-nature in the stage of *darśanamārga*; and the upper grade is a metaphor for the Buddha-nature in the stage of *bhāvanāmārga*. Now, regarding this...
"Binding the jewel" refers to the wish-fulfilling gem obtained prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), which is called "priceless.
While the preceding passages used the analogy of water clearing and spitting out gold, the present passage employs the wish-fulfilling gem as a metaphor.

Regarding the statement that "all prayers are fulfilled," this refers collectively to the attainment of the subtle discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*), the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*), the two types of emptiness (the emptiness of phenomena and the emptiness of self),
and the fundamental and subsequently attained wisdoms (*mūla- and prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

Regarding the statement that "the garment refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and so forth": this explains the scriptural passage, "Tie your garment inside. Here, "garment" refers to the mental consciousness; it takes the eighth consciousness as its object.

However, according to the commentary (*śāstra*), the mental consciousness should instead take the sixth consciousness as its object, because the arousal of the bodhicitta occurs within the mental consciousness.

Thus, using the metaphor of a garment, it is not appropriate to take the eighth consciousness [as the object]. This is because the seventh and eighth consciousnesses are subsumed under the category of the ten... [text truncated].

Because it is the mental faculty (*manas*) among the two bases, the eighth is called "mind" (*manas*). Furthermore, "mind" is understood through the sense of immediate succession (*samanantara*); thus, the eight consciousnesses are collectively termed "mind.

If one says, "It is bound within you," and since it is currently present, one further says, "It still remains," this does not refer to the capacity to maintain the seeds (*bīja*), but refers exclusively to the eighth consciousness.
If, however, one relies on the meanings of "binding" and "infusion" (*vāsanā*), then one takes the first two [consciousnesses] as the gateway.
The perfuming resides in the aggregate; that is to say, it takes the sixth consciousness as its object because it is characterized by discrimination.
Thus, it can represent the outer garment of the eighth consciousness, while [the eighth consciousness] itself can represent the inner lining of that garment. This is why both are taken together.

When the sixth consciousness hears the Mahāyāna and acquires the seeds of bodhi through this hearing-perfuming (*śrutavāsanā*), they are stored within the *ālaya-vijñāna*. As the subsequent sutra states: "Tied within the inner garment"—this is intended to convey that meaning.

It is a location. The place where the jewel is worn does not carry the meaning of "binding. When the Sūtra speaks of "wearing" and "binding" vows, one must take the sixth case (the locative), which signifies that which can bind and that which correctly binds—the meaning of binding the jewel.
Regarding the scriptural passage concerning "that person sleeping in intoxication" and so forth: "that person" refers to the śrāvakas of the three faculties.

"Sleeping in intoxication" means that although they have initially resolved upon the Mahāyāna mind, their minds are still entangled by the stupor of afflictions; this is the meaning of "intoxication."
The phrase "lying in the house of a Mahāyāna friend" explains the meaning of "lying.
The phrase "not being aware that one possesses the jewel of bodhicitta" explains the meaning of "not knowing at all.
In the commentary, the three meanings of "intoxicated," "lying," and "not being aware" are explained as being distinct from one another.
Regarding the statement "Citing the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* [on] 'stupefaction' (*mūrchana*) and so forth," the Sub-commentator (*ṭīkākāra*) distinguishes the essence of stupefaction:

there are two types of ignorance (*avidyā*), namely, that which is constantly active (*nitya-pravṛtti*) and that which acts independently (*kevala*). Which of these is taken here? Therefore, he cites the first principle from the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.

That treatise refutes the Hīnayāna to establish the existence of the seventh consciousness. As the verse of the cited treatise says: "The mind directed toward the true object shall arise; it is constant..."
It can act as an obstacle and accompanies all mental factors; it is the non-common (*asādhāraṇa*) ignorance.
If one understands that such a person is intoxicated and lying down, completely unaware, this precisely corresponds to the ever-active non-common ignorance within the seventh consciousness.

It is a single type of defilement that is constantly uninterrupted, for there is no awakening or cognitive awareness. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) always dwell [in this state]."
Throughout the long night, blinded by ignorance (*avidyā*), their minds are shrouded in a state of stupor and intoxication, never having awakened.

Therefore, the Commentary states that the ignorance associated with the *manas* is termed the "essence of intoxication. Question: If the ignorance within the seventh consciousness is constantly in a state of intoxicated slumber, how can it be said that [the consciousness] "arises and wanders"?
Furthermore, there is no principle of "tying a jewel" while in a state of intoxication. For this reason, the Master of the Commentary...

Following the treatise, a second interpretation is established. Its own thesis states: "Now, the non-shared ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*) within the sixth consciousness is taken as the essence of intoxication, because it possesses the quality of being intermittent.
Since the sixth consciousness encompasses all three natures (*tri-vidha-svabhāva*), we now take a single moment of mind;

the aspect in which understanding arises upon hearing the teaching is called 'tying the jewel. Question: If the aspiration is generated in association with a wholesome mind (*kuśala-citta*) of the sixth consciousness...
At that time, it is called "tying the jewel. How is it that the jewel is tied while one is intoxicated? The answer provides two interpretations from various commentaries:

First, regarding a single intermediate thought-moment which is a wholesome mind—while the preceding thought-moment is ignorance and the succeeding thought-moment is also ignorance—the two ends are unwholesome.

Because ignorance continues in a state of intermingling, this is called "the jewel within intoxication. Second, in terms of the actual phenomenon, one must also include the absence [of the jewel] within the seventh consciousness (*manas-vijñāna*).
Ignorance (*avidyā*) constitutes the essence of intoxication. The seven consciousnesses and the six consciousnesses serve as the root of contention, for they are the cause of birth and death.

Now, when the sixth consciousness hears the Dharma, it is unable to forget its objective marks; therefore, this is called "tying a jewel while intoxicated. This is said from the perspective of the sixth consciousness.
Having arisen, he wanders about. If one considers it in relation to the seventh consciousness (*manas*), it is said that the person lies drunk and does not perceive at all;

hence the phrase "tying a jewel while intoxicated. Only by taking both the sixth and seventh consciousnesses together is the meaning fully complete. According to the intent of the *Śāstra*, it specifically refers to the seventh consciousness;
according to the intent of the *Vyākhyā*, it specifically refers to the sixth consciousness. The subsequent mention of "wandering" is based on the wholesome state of the sixth consciousness.
Nevertheless, this is still walking while intoxicated. Only true untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) can be called sobering.
Since the commentary states that the sixth, the non-common ignorance (*āveṇika-avidyā*), is precisely the essence of intoxication, we know it includes the seventh ignorance as well.
This interpretation accords with the commentary.
The phrase "in the stage of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*)" and so forth refers to the assignment of stages. An "ordinary being" is simply a worldling (*bāla*). Huàdù (化度) says:
"Within the sixth consciousness, ignorance may arise intermittently. If it arises as unwholesome or neutral, if it arises as unwholesome, this is the time of being intoxicated;
if it arises as a wholesome mind, this is the time of wandering about. Since all such states belong to the stage of an ordinary being... [Thus] people say.

From the time after the regressive mind arose until the preaching of the *Lotus Sūtra* at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa—throughout all that interval between those two points—they were all merely "walking on faith.

Regarding the statement "having already regressed from the Great Mind," it is asked: "Since they have regressed from the Great Mind, what dharma do they seek? The answer is as explained in the preceding metaphor.
Seeking food and clothing according to the rules; this is discussed in the *Dharmapada*. It refers to withdrawing from the Mahāyāna to seek the Hīnayāna.

Precisely because one seeks the Hīnayāna, it is called "wandering. After practicing for sixty kalpas over three lifetimes and attaining the fruit of the Two Vehicles, one turns the mind toward the Great Vehicle.
Just as when one first sets out upon the Bodhi-path, traveling in vain without any objective is called "wandering.
As for the phrase "eventually reaching the Two Vehicles," this explains the "other country" mentioned in the sutra. The "other country" and the "one's own country" are distinct from one another.
There are three general explanations. First, it is said that the Mahāyāna is one's own country, while the Two Vehicles are another country.

This is illustrated by the previous account of rising from where one was intoxicated and sleeping in a friend’s house, then entering another country to seek food and clothing. In terms of the Dharma, hearing the Mahāyāna teaching is called "the friend’s house.
To retreat from the Mahāyāna mind and enter among the followers of the Two Vehicles is called "another country. As for "another country":
"Not having grown there" means that within the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha), great wisdom and so forth have never been cultivated; thus it is called "not a place of growth.
The phrase "formerly in saṃsāra" is the third interpretation: saṃsāra is one's own country, and the Mahāyāna is one's kinsman.
Abandoning [the Lesser Vehicle]. Taking the nirvāṇa of the two vehicles as a foreign land:
when it says "if one has already resolved [upon enlightenment]," etc., this refers collectively to the Buddha-dharma of the three vehicles as one's own country, and saṃsāra as a foreign land.
Regarding the phrase "before the aspiration has been generated," this refers to the passage from the sutra that is about to be recited.

If [the aspiration] has already been generated, then for those of the Two Vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha), the Buddha-dharma is their own country, while birth-and-death (saṃsāra) is another country. Question: Since those of the Two Vehicles have already once generated the mind of the Great Vehicle (mahāyāna), why are they called outsiders to the Buddha-dharma?
Answer: Because they have regressed from the Great Vehicle mind and remain instead in birth-and-death, they have not yet generated that mind again. It is for this reason [they are so called].
Therefore, it is called the Buddha-dharma. Outsiders take birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) as their own country, while the Buddha-dharma of the Two Vehicles is called another country.
A poor person, driven by intoxication, heads toward birth-and-death and lies upon the ground; this is the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) lying within birth-and-death.
Yet, rising from that intoxicated spot on the ground, he goes elsewhere to seek food and clothing—this is precisely entering the Two Vehicles from birth-and-death. For this reason:
The Commentary states: This passage explains the two preceding lines of the Sūtra. The Sūtra says: "Setting out on a journey, he arrives in another country.

Regarding the statement that this is also the same as *nirvāṇa*: in the previous "Parable of the Poor Son" chapter, it was cited from the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* that prior to the arousal of the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), saṃsāra is one's own country because it is one's own portion; the Buddha-dharma is another country because it is not one's own portion.
Therefore, this completes the explanation of this passage.
As for the statement "or by means of the Mahāyāna," it concludes the preceding point that the Mahāyāna is designated as one's own country and the Two Vehicles as other countries;
or alternatively, the Mahāyāna is the father’s house and the Hīnayāna is other countries.

As for the phrase "striving with diligent effort," this refers to the previous chapter on the Great House, where the three vehicles mutually encourage one another and are collectively said to be "running about";

thus it is called striving with diligent effort. To attain the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) after three births and sixty *kalpas*, or four births and a hundred *kalpas*, is what is meant by "extreme hardship."

Regarding the statement that this pertains to the causal stage of the Two Vehicles: it is precisely because these five desires constitute the very basis of negligence that it is said the Śaikṣas of the Two Vehicles encounter extreme difficulty in their diligent pursuit and seeking; they seek to sever defiled phenomena.
Regarding the phrase "having already conceived the thought that [birth] has been transcended," this explains that one considers what has occurred above to be sufficient.
Regarding the phrase "this is the beginning," it refers to the initial mastery over cessation and transformation. As the Sūtra says: "Thereafter, when friends and relatives arrive, it is as follows."
The close friend was none other than the sixteenth prince. Their meeting occurred today at the assembly on Vulture Peak, where Śākyamuni met him once again to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Regarding the name "Jian" (Meeting), Ji Guo explains: "The term 'Duōzāi' (Alas!
is an expression of reproach for his change of character, censuring him for failing to cultivate the Great [Vehicle]. The term 'Zhàngfū' (Manly Person) is a praise for his resolve."
Furthermore, those who establish their own principles, achieve merit, and accomplish great deeds may truly be called "great men" (puruṣa). Why have you made such grand vows?
In the past you failed in the Great Practice, yet today you labor in the Lesser Path. Why do you suffer so? Why, for the sake of food and clothing, have you come to such a state?
By "such as this," he refers to the Dharma of the Two Vehicles. For what reason do you seek food and undergo such hardships?
Śreṇika, you seek food and clothing; why not seek within the Mahāyāna the ten stages of faith, the ten abodes, the ten practices, and the ten dedications?
Why do you instead cultivate the sixteen mental states of the two vehicles, while still seeking food and clothing?
Why, for the sake of food and clothing, have you descended to such a low level that you are dragged away by the nirvāṇa with remainder?
Day and night they run, their feet never touching the ground; they perform all manner of tasks. What need have they for food or clothing?
It continues in this way. This meaning is extremely profound. This is identical to the transformation at cessation (*nirvāṇa*). As the Sūtra says: "At that time, the Guide knew these people."
Once they had attained rest and were no longer fatigued, he immediately extinguished the conjured city and spoke to the multitude, saying: "Come, you all!
The place of jewels is near. That great city you saw earlier was created by me as an illusion. (He led them away and extinguished the conjured city.)

Regarding the phrase "the pleasures of the five desires," that is, "the five [aggregates]," it explains the sutra’s statement: "In the past, I desired to enable them to obtain peace and happiness, indulging freely in the five desires.

Regarding the phrase "the pleasure of intrinsic nature," this refers to the essential nature of pleasure within the five types of sensation (*vedanā*). Second, "causal pleasure" refers to the sense faculties (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
The conjunction of the three [bases] gives rise to contact (*sparśa*). Because contact is the cause of pleasure, it is called "pleasure as cause.

Fourth, the pleasure of the cessation of the three feelings refers to the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedita-nirodha-samāpatti*). Fifth, the pleasure that is the antidote to suffering refers to the simultaneous arising of the cessation of cold, heat, and so forth;

the wisdom that arises simultaneously with the pleasant feeling is the very essence of this pleasure. Fifth, the pleasure free from affliction and harm has four aspects, the first of which is the pleasure of renunciation (*naiṣkramya-sukha*).

First is the joy of renunciation, which belongs to those who have left the household life and uphold the precepts. Second is the joy of seclusion, which consists of being reborn in the higher realms of form and so forth.
Third is the joy of awakening to the Dharma, which is bodhi. Fourth is the joy of tranquility, which is nirvāṇa, the pure dharmadhātu, and so forth.

Regarding the statement "or the five dharmas of the Buddha-fruit": this refers to the pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the two emptinesses, and the four categories of wisdom-mind (*catur-jñāna-citta-varga*);
these five combined constitute bliss.

Regarding the statement "or the untainted [dharmas] of the Mahāyāna," Jin says: this refers to the fivefold dharma-body (*pañca-dharmakāya*), which is the body of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-kāya*).

Vocal restraint is called the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīla-skandha*). The three types of concentration of one beyond training—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are called the aggregate of concentration (*samādhi-skandha*).
Right view and right knowledge of one beyond training are called the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*).

The liberation consisting of mastery over objects—the mind associated with the mental attention of one beyond training that has already attained resolve, is now attaining resolve, or will attain resolve—is characterized by the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).

One should resolve with conviction; this is called the aggregate of liberation (*vimukti-skandha*). The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are called the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana-skandha*).
As for the statement, "In the past, I acted so that you might obtain [it]," etc., it refers to a certain year, month, and day mentioned in the sūtra, when an invaluable jewel was [offered].
Various copies do not explain the specific year, month, and day. Shen-zhi (神智) says: "It occurred during the time of the sixteen princes, twenty thousand..."
At that time, the Buddha repeatedly preached the Mahāyāna in many different places rather than at a single location; thus, it cannot be specified as occurring on a certain year, month, or day.

As for the statement regarding the "responsibility for abiding in the provisional," this refers to the present explanation of the sutra, which demonstrates the location of the jewel, yet you remain unaware of it—this serves to reveal [your ignorance].
This is an error.
To say that one is "vainly worrying and toiling" explains the sūtra’s phrase "diligent suffering and distress.
To say that one "seeks self-benefit" explains the sūtra’s phrase "seeking to sustain oneself."

To say that "attachment to phenomena (dharmagrāha) is not extinguished" is a very foolish interpretation of the sutra; it refers to the ignorance regarding the knowable (*jñeya-avidyā*). [This is the first reprimand for abiding in the provisional.
To say that "this causes one to grasp at the real" refers to the sutra’s statement: "You may now trade this jewel for whatever you require.

The intention is that one shall take the pearl of the bodhicitta from former times and exchange it for the superior stage of the Mahayana—the pearl of the awakening mind that clarifies the nature of reality. Furthermore, [the text continues:]...
That which undergoes transformation through successive stages may be termed "trading" (mào).

Regarding the statement that the character is composed of "shell" (貝) and "mǎo" (卯): when one trades goods, the character for "trade" (貿) is formed. Some people claim that from the character "trade" (貿), the character "mǎo" (卯)—pronounced *yǒu*—is derived by adding a "basket" (簆) radical;
this is incorrect. The commentator, fearing that others might not understand, states that the sound of "mǎo" is "yǒu," for in ancient times, the character for "yǒu" (酉) was written as such.
This resembles the form of the character *mǎo* (卯) at present; it is for this reason that it was written erroneously.

In ancient times, the character *yǒu* (酉) was correctly used to signify "death" (*sǐ*), which corresponds to the image of *mǎo*. This is precisely the ancient character for "commerce" (*màoyì*). Some write it as the character *jiǎ* (賈), which is a personal surname.

Regarding the character *jiǎ* (pronounced *gē yǎ*), another interpretation states that there are three explanations for the meaning of "commerce": first, it refers to the time when the sixteen princes were taking [goods].

The contaminated (*sāsrava*) bodhicitta, having already undergone the perfuming of seeds, pertains to the stage of accumulation (*saṃbhāra-avasthā*). Having already undergone the perfuming of the two types of wisdom—those arising from hearing and reflection—it pertains to the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*), wherein it is easily attained.
It is easily attained as the contaminated wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) within the stage of application, and it is easily attained as the wisdom of cultivation in the first bhūmi.

Second, it is said that one exchanges the inferior uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) jewels of the ten bhūmis for the great wish-fulfilling jewel of the merit and wisdom of the higher stages of the Mahāyāna. This is precisely [the meaning].
It is said that one abandons impermanent form and attains eternal form. Thirdly, it is said that by taking the initial small jewel—

the jewel of the wisdom of emptiness of birth within the stage of the Two Vehicles— one dedicates it toward the Great [Vehicle] to obtain the jewel of the non-outflow seed-wisdom of the Mahāyāna emptiness of phenomena attained subsequently.
To speak of using the "small jewel of the initial resolve" refers to the jewel of the *sāsrava* (contaminated) bodhicitta.
To easily obtain the "great wish-fulfilling jewel of superior merit and wisdom" refers to the *anāsrava* (uncontaminated) wisdom-jewel of those who have ascended the stages (*bhūmi*).

Regarding the statement "this corresponds to the initial stage of separation," it refers to the simile in the Sūtra: "For example, there was a man who went to the house of a close friend and lay down after drinking wine.
At that time, the friend had business to attend to at the government office; he tied a priceless jewel inside the man's garment and gave it to him before departing.
The present correspondence states, "The Buddha is also like this," and so forth. This section provides long-standing proof for the existence of newly perfumed seeds (*navābhyāsita-bīja*).
This refers to the son.
As for the statement regarding "reaching the midpoint of the journey," it is a metaphor for the sutra’s description of the man lying drunk, completely unaware of anything;
it corresponds here to the mention of "seeking" and then "forgetting."
Regarding the statement that "the convergence [of the parable] constitutes the transformation of the *hīnayāna* city":

the preceding parable states that after setting out on his journey, he arrived in another land where, for the sake of food and clothing, he sought them with diligent effort, undergoing great hardship; yet if he obtained even a little, he considered it sufficient.
The present application of the sūtra says, "Having attained the path of an arhat, they consider themselves [equal to others]," which refers to the meaning of the three births and six [realms].
For ten kalpas, one seeks food and clothing; this too involves great hardship and difficulty, yet obtaining even a small amount is considered sufficient.

Regarding the phrase "wasted in vain" and so forth: from the perspective of one's own vehicle (Hīnayāna), it is not called wasted; however, when one turns the mind toward the Great Vehicle and practices through circuitous means, it is termed empty expenditure.

Regarding the term "nán" (pronounced with the ancient *hàn* rhyme): it means extremely difficult to cure (*chí* being pronounced as *hū*). It is the root of hardship. Both [terms] appear in the *Shìmíng*.

"Object-root" (*wùgēn*) refers to the ear being as difficult to pull out as an object; "ear" is an auxiliary phrase. There is the character "tooth" (*yá*) in some commentaries, but one should further consult multiple editions.
As for the term "difficult to endure" (*nàndàn*), it is pronounced *tā* (with the second tone).
Regarding the term "timidity" (*jìtàn*): those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) were formerly full of timidity in their pursuit of food and clothing;
this is termed "difficulty" (*jiānán*), where "difficult" is pronounced with a departing tone (*qùyīn*) and "timid" with a level tone (*dànyīn*).
Regarding the phrase "this is the initial [application]," it means that the initial [analogy] should be applied to the cessation of the transformation. The preceding *Dṛṣṭānta-sūtra* states:
"Later, his kinsmen and friends encountered him and said, 'Alas, O man! What do you mean by food and clothing? and so forth. Now, applying this to the present *sūtra*, it says:
"Now, World-Honored One, you have awakened me and others," and so on.

Regarding the statement, "This is what should be received; now I shall speak of the reality," there are three parts to the preceding metaphorical text. First, it speaks of the beginning. The Sūtra says:
"In the past, I desired to bring you peace and happiness, allowing you to indulge freely in the five desires. From such-and-such a year, month, and day until now, [that time] remains present."

Next is the reprimand regarding the provisional [teaching]. The Sūtra says: "That you did not know how to strive with diligence and endure hardship and distress in order to seek your own livelihood was truly foolish.
This refers to the subsequent reception of the ultimate [truth]. The Sūtra says: "Now you may trade these jewels for whatever you require;

you shall always have as you wish, without any lack or deficiency. This is the summary of what accords with the intention. The Sūtra says: "World-Honored One, it is only now that I have come to know... and so forth.

Regarding the statement that "one verse indicates the prostration," the prose of the sūtra says: At that time, the five hundred arhats, having received their predictions in the presence of the Buddha, were filled with joy and exultation;
they immediately rose from their seats, went before the Buddha, and prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet.
Repenting and reproaching oneself: now, with one verse, [the text] describes how we heard "the unsurpassed," etc.
Regarding the subsequent one and a half verses of self-reproach, the prose of the sūtra states: "World-Honored One, we have constantly harbored this thought."
I previously thought that I had already attained ultimate *parinirvāṇa*, but now I realize it is as if I were ignorant.
As the verse says: "Now, before the World-Honored One, I repent for all my transgressions."

Regarding the statement that the first seven lines describe the metaphors for the initial teaching on the arousal of the bodhicitta: the prose of the sūtra says, "For example, there was a person who went to the house of a close friend and lay down, intoxicated by wine.
At that time, the friend had business with the authorities," and so forth. The present verse says, "For example, a poor man went to the house of a close friend," and so forth.
Shen-zhi (神智) comments: "He is 'poor' because he lacks the wealth of the Dharma; he is 'destitute' because he lacks the treasure of wisdom."
Alternatively, "poverty" refers to the absence of merit, while "indigence" refers to the absence of wisdom. Muzhou said: "In worldly metaphor, it is like being drunk and lying down in silence.
In the Dharma, it refers to the initial arousal of the mind at that time, which serves as the cause for attaining the treasure; therefore, this stage is called 'silence.

Furthermore, what was previously taught was general and did not distinguish between the Great and Small Vehicles. Those of the two vehicles who take the small fruit as their goal are the gradual path for the present, and thus it is called 'silence.'"
Regarding the statement that "the last line of the verse was only halfway through when he withdrew," the prose sūtra says: "That person lay drunk and did not perceive anything at all.
Now, one line of the verse describes this, saying: "At that time, lying down, he did not perceive [anything]."

Regarding the statement that the two verses refer to the establishment of the "transformed city" (*nirmita-pura*), the prose of the sutra says: "Having set out on his journey, he arrived in another land;
for the sake of food and clothing, he sought them with diligent effort, undergoing great hardship. If he obtained even a small amount, he considered it sufficient.
The verse sutra now says: "This person, having already set out," and so forth. This is what is meant.
Regarding the statement that the first verse indicates the causes cultivated in the past: the prose of the sutra says, "Later, a kinsman encountered him and said, 'Alas, O man!
How do you provide for your food and clothing? and so forth. The corresponding verse of the sutra is this single verse concerning the kinsman who gave the jewel.

Regarding the statement that the subsequent verse clarifies the arising of joy: the prose of the sūtra says, "In the past, I desired to enable you to obtain peace and happiness, indulging at will in the five desires;
on such and such a year, month, day, and time, [I gave you] an invaluable jewel, etc. Now, the verse of the sūtra says, "When the poor man saw this jewel, he was exceedingly joyful," and so forth.

The phrase "although present and future" is a general response to the objection. Question: The essence of the jewel consists of the latter two wisdoms (*jñāna*), which are first attained at the Mahāyāna path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
How is it that one now possesses an abundance of various wealth and indulges freely in the five desires? Answer: The commentary states, "although present."
Regarding the statement, "Just as seeing a tree standing in white [snow], one sees only its smoke and must know there is fire; one sees only the heron and must know there is water;

so now, seeing only its teaching, one must see its principle"—the seven treasures of the noble ones and so forth mean that by obtaining the pearl of the teaching through mental discourse, one will subsequently necessarily obtain the pearl of wisdom.
Some say this is also a verification of the existence of Buddha-nature. But if there were only Buddha-nature, what [would be the point]?
Do not worry. This refers to seeing white egrets, which indicates the presence of water.
Regarding the statement that "the first verse corresponds to the initial 'bringing forth,'" the preceding prose commentary correlates with the sutra by stating: "The Buddha was also like this;
when he was a bodhisattva, he taught and transformed us, causing us to resolve upon the mind of omniscience. Now, the verse of the sutra says: "We also..."
Regarding the phrase "in this way, one line is thus," the subsequent half-verse combines the summary with the intermediate sections and so forth. The prose of the sūtra states:
"Yet we sought and forgot, being unaware and unconscious. Now the verse says: "Because we were without wisdom, we were neither conscious nor aware."
Regarding the statement that the latter half of the verse collectively explains the establishment of the "provisional city" (*nirmita-nagara*):

the prose commentary of the sutra states, "Having attained the path of Arhatship, they consider themselves to have reached *parinirvāṇa*; their livelihood is difficult to maintain, and they are content with what little they have obtained.
Yet, their aspiration for omniscience remains undiminished. Now, the verse of the sutra says: "Having obtained a portion of *nirvāṇa*, they are self-sufficient and seek nothing more."
Regarding the statement that the first verse refers to the parinirvāṇa of Śāriputra: the prose sūtra says, "Now, the World-Honored One has awakened us by speaking these words:
'O bhikṣus, what you have accomplished is not ultimate extinction. For a long time I have caused you to plant roots of merit for Buddhahood;
it was through skillful means that I displayed the appearance of nirvāṇa, yet you believed you had truly attained it.'"
[The Buddha] entered parinirvāṇa. Now, regarding the verse: the sutra says, "Now the Buddha has awakened me;
this one practice is it. As for the statement that the subsequent verse clarifies the arising of joy, the prose portion of the sutra says:
"World-Honored One, I now truly know that I am indeed a bodhisattva who has received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. For this reason, I am filled with great joy. Now...
The verse of the sutra says: "I have now heard from the Buddha the matter of the adornment of the prediction [of enlightenment]; this is the first practice.

Regarding the "Chapter on Bestowing Predictions upon Those in Training and Those Beyond Training," the phrase "those of high renown" refers to Pūrṇa and the five hundred, two thousand, and one hundred people; it does not refer to those who are merely famous.
Regarding these individuals, this chapter and its commentary record the questions of Zhangjing and the holding of the day by Qingxi; how could it be that their names were not high? The answer is:
although these two persons were indeed of high renown, in terms of their capacity to guide, these two venerable ones were transformed śrāvakas who led actual śrāvakas.
Thus, they merely served as the objects of guidance; they did not speak of themselves as the guides. Therefore, the two thousand [followers] were not of high renown, as previously stated.
The same applies to Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra; he should not be categorized among those of inferior faculties. This is also based on the predictions made for those being exhorted.

Furthermore, although both of these individuals were held by Ānanda to be well-known to the masses, they were nonetheless of high renown. The Sūtra refers to "those not of high renown" in relation to the majority of people.

Regarding the explanation of the names: the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states this in the chapter "Bestowing Predictions upon Ānanda and Rāhula. That [text] relies on two sages, while this concerns two thousand people.

As for the phrase "advancing in practice and fulfilling cessation," the precepts, concentration, and wisdom constitute the very essence of study; advancing in the cultivation of understanding constitutes the meaning of being a learner (*śaikṣa*).

The progressive training that is perfectly fulfilled is called "Aśaikṣa" (One Beyond Training). Regarding the meaning of "Aśaikṣa," Zàn says: "It refers to those who have not yet reached perfection but are already complete among the assembly.

It is correct to understand it according to both these meanings. Since this depends on meditative concentration (*samādhi*), why is it said exclusively that concentration is fulfilled, rather than mentioning wisdom (*prajñā*)?
