This is because such an act causes one to lose the practice of self-benefit and prevents others from hearing the sutra, thereby undermining the practice of benefiting others. Thus, the resulting transgression is heavy.
To say that the Buddha is without love or hatred is the second meaning. The Buddha abides in the three mindfulnesses and is equal toward both enemies and kin;

thus, even if he is reviled, it does not hinder his correct transformation of others, and therefore the sin of reviling him is light. Ordinary people have not yet abandoned love and hatred; if they encounter revilement, [the consequences are grave].
The mind immediately regresses and feels regret; one is unable to uphold the sutra. Since the sutra is not upheld, there is no way to become a Buddha.
Because this cuts off the seed of the Three Jewels, the offense is grave.

To say that one further reviles the Buddha constitutes the third difficulty. To see the Buddha’s golden body adorned with the thirty-two marks, surrounded by the eight classes of devas and nāgas, and yet to utter words of abuse—this is extremely difficult; therefore, it is said that the offense is light.
However, if one reviles an ordinary person who upholds this sutra, one may do so at will because such an act is easy. For this reason, there is a strict admonition not to do so. Thus [it is said].
It is said that the fault of such an act exceeds even that of reviling the Buddha.

Regarding the phrase "when the Buddha was still in the world," this refers to the distinction between the superior and inferior capacities of beings. When the Buddha was present, the faculties of sentient beings were superior;

thus, if someone reviled the Buddha, others who heard it would not believe it, knowing it to be slander, and their own wholesome minds would not regress. It would merely cause harm to the reviler himself.

One does not harm others, and for this reason the offense is light. However, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when the faculties of sentient beings are dull, if someone reviles a holder of this sutra and others hear it, they will all retreat from their wholesome minds; thus, the person who reviles them harms both themselves and others.
Therefore, the offense incurred is extremely grave.
Regarding what is called the "light of the Great Dharma": when the Buddha preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, it is termed the light of the Great Dharma.
To now extinguish the bodhicitta is precisely to extinguish that great light.
Regarding the phrase "exceeding the five immediate [sins] (*ānantarya*) and so forth": among the five immediate transgressions, there is no [sin] that destroys all the Buddha-dharma;
therefore, it is said to "exceed" them. This [act of] slandering the Buddha-dharma cannot be subsumed within the five immediates, for its transgression is even more grave.

This is explained in terms of the common immediates shared across the three vehicles (*triyāna*). If one speaks specifically of the Mahāyāna’s distinct immediate karmic offenses, there is the slander of the Mahāyāna.

Regarding the karmic offenses of the sūtras: if one relies on the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) of the Hīnayāna—namely, the five beginning with patricide—they are all subsumed within a single heinous crime in the Mahāyāna.

Even if one has committed the sin of destroying the teachings of the Hīnayāna, that offense may still be mitigated; however, if one slanders a person who can propagate the Mahāyāna sūtras, the Dharma itself will consequently perish.
Therefore, this offense is grave.

Regarding the phrase "furthermore, after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa": in this degenerate age, people are unwilling to uphold the sutra; even if there are those who do uphold it, they find it difficult to do so.
Therefore, their disparagement exceeds that of reviling the Buddha himself.
Regarding the statement "reciting the Buddha’s adornments," one asks: when does one obtain the Buddha’s adornments? The answer is that there are two [ways], the first being external:
if one currently upholds the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, one immediately possesses the Buddha’s adornments. All the merits of the Buddha’s bodily adornments are contained within this sutra;
the person who is able to uphold it receives and maintains the merits of the Buddha’s body, thereby possessing the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) of the Buddha’s adornments.

The first refers to the present. The second refers to the future: by upholding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in this life, one will in the future be endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics;
this is called "attaining the merit and adornment of the Buddha-body. The Sūtra says, "They shall be borne upon the shoulders of the Tathāgata.
The first instance of the level tone (pingyin) means "because of being covered"; the second instance of the level tone means "because of."

This is the composition. Regarding the previous scripture’s mention of what is taught in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*: this refers to the *Śrīmālā* (the "Victorious Garland"), pronounced with a departing tone (*qùyīn*), meaning it is based upon that [sūtra]. The scripture states:
"A son of good family who upholds the True Dharma is capable of bearing four kinds of heavy responsibilities; only the great earth can sustain these four heavy burdens."
Furthermore, there are four kinds of sentient beings who can only be transformed by the Buddha’s teaching; they cannot be transformed by others.

These are those who give rise to the mind of the two vehicles and attain the fruits of the two vehicles, and those who give rise to the Mahāyāna mind and attain the Bodhi of the Mahāyāna Buddha-fruit.

This explains how the Tathāgata acts as a carrier for sentient beings, transporting them so that each may take up the fruit of their own vehicle. Thus, the Tathāgata serves as a carrier for sentient beings.
To "bear" (dàn) means that one becomes a Tathāgata; it signifies "to bestow" (yǔ). One who upholds the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* bestows the burden of the Tathāgata.
This indicates that not only can the upholder of the sutra bear the four modes of birth, but even before I myself upheld the sutra, I entrusted the Tathāgata to act as my bearer.
"May you transport me. Now that I uphold this sutra, I shall repay the diligent efforts of the Tathāgata above.

I venture to take up the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as a burden, acting as a substitute for the Tathāgata to transport beings of the four vehicles and deliver them to the fruit of Buddhahood and Bodhi.
Thus concludes the explanation based on the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*.
The statement that "they are also borne upon the shoulders of the Buddha" is explained according to this very sutra. Initially, "píng" (平) is read as "hū" (呼), meaning "to be covered by.
When the Buddha takes those who uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and places them upon his own shoulders, it is termed "being borne upon the shoulders of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha’s body resides beneath the teaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* elucidates the two benefits [of self and others].
Practice. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the means of expression (*vācaka*), while the practice of the two benefits (*dvaya-hita*) is that which is expressed (*vācya*).
The practice of the two benefits constitutes the two shoulders of the Tathāgata; since the Tathāgata’s practice of the two benefits is that which is expressed, it is placed below.

Since the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the means of expression, it is placed above. Furthermore, the sūtra is that which is upheld and is thus placed below; the person is the one who upholds the sūtra and is thus placed above. Taking...
The mind takes the teaching as its object and upholds the Dharma with certainty, as if sitting upon the Buddha’s shoulders.

It is like parents picking up their child and placing them upon their shoulders without recoiling from the smell. This is the same as in the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra*, where the word is pronounced with a departing tone (*qù*).
The phrase "that which the Buddha values" indicates the underlying reason. The question asks: "Is this the intention of bearing [the burden] upon the shoulders of sentient beings?
The answer in the commentary states: "That which the Buddha values," and so forth.
Regarding the meaning of "to act" (*zuò*): this is the second interpretation. It is read with a level tone (*píngyīn*). It means "to act" because one acts for the sake of others.
When the Buddha acts as a bearer, he acts as that which is borne upon the shoulders of the Tathāgata; the sentient beings bear the Tathāgata upon their own shoulders.
Those who uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* are first able to uphold it themselves, and second, they expound it for others. This is precisely the mind of twofold benefit. This is...
Upon the two shoulders of sentient beings' own self-interest and interest in others—their two-fold altruistic mind—they establish the fruit of Buddhahood and Bodhi.
It is as if the Buddha’s body were sitting upon the shoulders of sentient beings; because the cause is able to attain the fruit, they are called "those who shoulder the burden of the Tathāgata.

Alternatively, the two-fold altruistic mind of sentient beings constitutes the two shoulders; the mind is the two shoulders. The mind upholds the teachings of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, and these teachings are able to...

Regarding the elucidation of principle: when one receives and upholds the teaching that expresses [the truth], one simultaneously grasps the principle expressed therein; within that expressed principle, the merits of the Tathāgata’s three bodies are already contained within the teaching itself.
When the practitioner of the sutra focuses their mind on the words and meaning, it is as if they were sitting before a Buddha who has placed [his presence] upon their shoulders.
The former interpretation relies on the teaching, while the second interpretation also relies on the teaching; both interpretations are excellent, yet the latter is superior to the former.
To speak of "shouldering the great Bodhi" refers to the Buddha-body itself.
To say that "those in these four places should be praised and venerated" refers to the person who upholds the sutra; such a person is superior.

One ought to pay respectful homage to them according to their location, just as when one sees a white elephant on the road, everyone—regardless of whether they are a monastic or a layperson—bows to the elephant. Now, one should pay homage upward [to this person].
This refers to venerating the sūtras within one's person.
As for the "fourfold offerings," they are: lodging, food and drink, bedding and clothing, and medicine.

Regarding the term "true field of merit": it is asked, "Only those who have attained Arhatship are called 'Worthy of Offerings' (Arhats). As for those in the first three stages of fruition, they are metaphorically referred to as 'borrowing from the superior.
If an ordinary person merely upholds the sutras, how can they constitute a true field of merit? The answer is: "A person who upholds the sutras is no different from the Buddha;
they are worthy of receiving offerings. How can one compare them to the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna)?"
The Sūtra states that "the highest offerings among humans" refers to the finest and most exquisite food and drink; these are called the highest offerings.
The Sūtra states that "one should present celestial jewels and the like"; these are celestial offerings.
The term "compiler" (*zhuànzhě*) also carries the meaning of "one who collects.
As for the reason for this explanation: it refers generally to the preceding five invocations of the sutra text.

Why is it that by upholding this sutra one obtains the adornment of the Buddha’s merits? Why is it that by upholding this sutra one obtains what is borne upon the shoulders of the Buddhas, even unto the heavens?
"O Jewel-Heap, you should offer this to him. Why? Because wherever he is, he should be praised and honored. The answer is: because such a person joyfully expounds the Dharma;
it is not necessary to listen and receive it for a long time. Having heard it for but a moment, one immediately attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This is because the person who upholds the sutra is superior; they obtain the adornment of the Buddha's merits and are borne upon the shoulders of the Tathāgata by humans, devas, and others."
It is also various offerings.

Regarding the statement that "this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is most profound and secret," etc., it is because the preceding scriptural passages repeatedly addressed Bhaisajyarāja, and furthermore, the subsequent scripture states:
"I now tell you: among all the sūtras I have preached, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the foremost."
"Furthermore, one must not distribute it or grant it to others recklessly. Moreover, the *Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta* states:

"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, I entrust this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to you. Question: If this sūtra was not entrusted to Ānanda, how could he have compiled it so as to fulfill the meaning of the formula "Thus have I heard"?
Answer: He was able to do so simply by means of compiling the treasury, recording it, and maintaining it in memory. If...
The teaching should be explained according to the faculties [of the listeners]. Using poison as medicine is something they do not understand; for this reason, it was not entrusted to Ānanda.
Because he was to uphold this sutra to transform the śrāvakas, it was therefore entrusted to the bodhisattvas.
Regarding the phrase "for example, using poison," the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "It is called nectar (*amṛta*), and it is also called poisonous medicine.

This sutra is likewise so. If one can receive and uphold it, its heavy sins are extinguished; it is then like nectar. If one slanders it, one falls into the Avīci Hell; it is then called poisonous medicine.
On the Snowy Mountains there is a grass: when cows eat it, it becomes milk; when snakes eat it... [the text continues].
It becomes poison. Just as water can carry a boat, it can also capsize a boat.

Regarding the statement that "the words accord with ultimate truth": Question: Why does one rejoice when the Dharma is preached? Answer: One rejoices because the speaker of the Dharma’s words accord with ultimate truth;
one rejoices because one attains the fruit for oneself; furthermore, it accords with others hearing it and accords with the ground upon which the fruit is attained. Therefore, [one rejoices].
This is joyful. Question: This chant speaks of "no Medicine King" (A-bhaiṣajyarāja); why then does it say the Dharma is entrusted to the Medicine King? Answer: The sutra below states:

The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja: "The sūtras I have spoken—those already spoken, those currently being spoken, and those yet to be spoken—numbering immeasurable thousands of billions—are themselves the entrustment."
Regarding the term "general summary" (*sāmānya-nirdeśa*) for the Dharma Master: it refers to both those who address the Buddha face-to-face and those who do not;
hence, it is called "general. Regarding the first verse, which attains spontaneous wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*): the Sūtra states, "If one wishes to abide in the Buddha-way," etc., two lines.

The ancient sūtras and śāstras refer to this as "natural wisdom" (*svayambhū-jñāna*), while the new sūtras and śāstras call it "spontaneous wisdom. This is because the non-Buddhist schools (*tīrthika*) maintain that the self (*ātman*) is natural.
In order to distinguish this from the non-Buddhists, it is called "spontaneous wisdom" (*anābhoga-jñāna*).

As for what is called "natural wisdom" (*svayambhū-jñāna*), it refers to the wisdom that realizes the truth of the two kinds of emptiness; because it is the very nature of wisdom, it is named natural wisdom.

The rational nature (*nyāya*) is inherently present; it does not arise from cultivation. Now, by virtue of upholding this sūtra and making offerings, it occurs spontaneously and is thus termed "natural" (*svabhāva*).

Regarding the statement that the final verse attains the "True" (*tattva*) and so forth, the sūtra says: "The wisdom of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is the characteristic of wisdom (*jñānalakṣaṇa*). This is its division.

There are two types of wisdom: the wisdom of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) and subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). The single character "wisdom" (*prajñā*) refers to fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).

These two verses of the scripture clarify that by first performing offerings to those who uphold the sutra, one attains natural wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*), and it is also clearly understood that one attains the wisdom of all aspects.
If, in the subsequent practice, one clearly upholds the sutra oneself and makes offerings to others who uphold the sutra, one attains [all].
The wisdom of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) also attains natural wisdom (*svayambhūjñāna*). Zhiyou states: "The natural wisdom practiced previously is fundamental wisdom (*mūlajñāna*);
the wisdom of all modes practiced subsequently is subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdhajñāna*). The former interpretation is superior.
Regarding the statement that "the wisdom is divided into two," this means that a single phrase of the sutra is divided into two types of wisdom.

Regarding the statement "as for the wisdom of spontaneity," it merely means rejoicing in and making offerings to those who uphold the sutra; if one were to further personally receive and uphold it oneself, what doubt could there be?
Regarding the statement that the first verse refers to the Buddha’s messenger, the Sūtra says: "If there is anyone who can receive and uphold even a single verse... Mochizuki states:
This verse separately describes the virtues of the Master and does not recount the prose section; the description of the Buddha’s messenger in the prose section naturally occurs later in the verse.
Regarding the statement that follows the verse about relinquishing the Pure Land, the prose says:

"It should be known that such a person, having personally relinquished the retribution of pure karma, will, out of compassion for sentient beings, be born in an evil world after my parinirvāṇa to widely expound this sutra. Now, the verse says:
Regarding those who are able to receive and uphold even a single verse,
the statement that "the subsequent verses follow according to one's wishes" means that, as the Sūtra says, it should be known that this person has extracted [the essence] from within a single verse.

It is said that through the accomplishment of ten recitations of the mind, one attains rebirth in the same manner as those of the nine grades. By observing the eightfold precepts, one reaches only the three assemblies at the Dragon Flower [Buddha’s] enlightenment;
however, by upholding the Lotus Sutra, one attains the power to take birth with sovereign mastery.
Regarding the statement that "one verse reiterates the teaching," the prose (*gadya*) of the sūtra says: "One should hold celestial jewels and scatter them;
one should offer up a heap of celestial treasures. Now, the verse says: "One should [offer] celestial flowers and incense.
This single verse describes the matters of the fourth section of the prose regarding material offerings (*āmiṣa-pūjā*).

Regarding the statement, "If one possesses the precepts, though they may be equal," the question is asked: "If making offerings to a Dharma teacher who possesses the precepts brings merit, does making offerings to a Dharma teacher who has broken the precepts also bring merit? The commentary answers: "If they possess the precepts, they are equal. The question is asked:
"Why not offer human treasures [as gifts]? The answer is: "Because they are considered light and unfit for use; therefore, the various treasures of the heavens constitute a single [unit of value]."
He gathered [the assembly] and made offerings to them, thereby manifesting his profound respect for the sutra.
Regarding the statement that "a single verse exhorts reverence," it describes how one should pay homage wherever [the sutra] may be located; the prose portion of the sutra states:

"In whatever direction one goes, one should turn toward it and pay homage with single-minded palms joined. Now, the verse says: "After my parinirvāṇa, in the evil age, [this single verse, etc. and so forth.
Regarding the "offering of a single verse," the prose sūtra states: "For what reason?

Because this person joyfully preaches the Dharma, and upon hearing it for even a brief moment, one immediately attains ultimate Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Now, the verse says: "Superior delicacies and various sweet flavors [are not equal to] a single verse... and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "an envoy of the Buddha in a single verse," the prose of the sutra states:

"If, after my parinirvāṇa, a son of good family or a daughter of good family should secretly preach even a single verse of the Lotus Sūtra for the sake of a single person, you should know that this person is an envoy of the Tathāgata, one dispatched by the Tathāgata, performing the work of the Tathāgata; how much more so when they preach it extensively for the sake of the great assembly."
The present verse states: "If one can [recite] even a single verse in a future life," and so forth.
Regarding the statement that the first two verses compare the magnitude of the offense, the prose commentary of the sutra says:

"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, if there were an evil person who, with an unwholesome mind, stood before a Buddha for an entire kalpa constantly reviling and abusing him, his sin would still be light compared to that of a person..."
To disparage with even a single evil word those, whether lay or ordained, who recite and study the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, is a most grave offense.
As it says in the verse: "If, throughout an entire eon, [one were to recite] two verses... and so forth.

Regarding the statement, "Praising the Buddha is easy," etc.: Question: Why is it that praising the Buddha brings little benefit, whereas praising and encouraging those who uphold the sutra brings great merit?
Answer: The commentary states, "Praising the Buddha is easy," etc. Praising the Buddha is easy because the mind is inclined toward it lightly, and thus the benefit is small.

If one praises those who uphold the sutra, however, because there may be resentment or aversion toward them, the person who is able to offer such praise does so with some difficulty; consequently, the mind is more earnest, and thus the benefit is great.
Regarding the statement that there is "more or less" for oneself and others: when one praises the Buddha, he attains only the merit of self-benefit.
When [the Buddha] is reviled, it does not diminish; when praised, it does not increase. It is simply that the person who praises the Buddha gains merit for themselves.
However, if one praises a person who upholds the sutra, the merit of both self and others is great; the merit within the body of the sutra-holder increases day by day, which is self-benefit.
Furthermore, when bystanders hear the sutra, their merit increases; this is what is meant by "benefiting others.

To speak of comparing the hearing of the Dharma [to other acts], the sutra states that over eighty billion kalpas and so forth, the merit of making offerings with material wealth is inferior to that of hearing this sutra for even a brief moment; the merit of the sutra is itself the offering of the Dharma. Question:
One might ask: "Does praising the upholding of this sutra not increase the affliction of clinging to phenomena? Answer: Clinging that arises based on words is censured by all the teachings.
Using metaphors to express the ultimate meaning is agreed upon by all the Sages. Who could enter [the Dharma] except through the gateway? Thus, the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra* says:
It is like a person entering a dark room; though things are covered and hidden, they are difficult to see. Although many forms and images exist there, one cannot see them without light.
So too, those who possess internal clarity and understanding within, yet do not hear the True Dharma—how could they distinguish between good and evil?

Through extensive learning, one attains comprehension. Through extensive learning, one refrains from committing evil. Through extensive learning, one abandons what is meaningless. Through extensive learning, one attains *nirvāṇa*. Since goodness is thus...
It increases. Having heard it, one is able to increase wisdom; wisdom is able to realize purity.
Regarding the statement that this major section reveals the excellence of the Dharma and so forth, the Sūtra says: "O Bhaiṣajyarāja, I now tell you: of all the sūtras I have spoken..."

Within this collection of scriptures, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the foremost. Because the preceding phrase contained the character "various" (諸), the subsequent phrase was changed to the character "this" (此).

To say "this scripture" (*cijing*) is precisely to point to the scripture itself. Many people have raised objections to the phrasing of this scripture. Questioning the structure of these verses, they ask: "The text seems at first glance to describe the Dharma;
how does the Dharma Master clarify his position as a person who teaches the Dharma? [The Dharma Master] explains the Dharma Master's station. He teaches the Dharma.

Yes. The answer is: It is because of the Dharma that the person who teaches the Dharma (the Dharmācārya) is manifested. Therefore, the commentary (*śāstra*) states: "Because the Dharma is supreme, the person becomes worthy of veneration.
Regarding the statement that "the initial Dharma is difficult to believe and understand," the Sūtra says: "The sūtras spoken by me are extremely difficult to comprehend. This refers to the world...
"Honored One, the sutras I have preached over the past forty years are immeasurable, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis. Regarding those 'already preached,' An-yuan says:
from the time I was born in the Deer Park until after my attainment of enlightenment, prior to the assembly on Vulture Peak, these are collectively termed 'already preached.

Those preached during the assembly on Vulture Peak, such as the *Sutra of Immeasurable Meanings* and the *Lotus Sutra*, were all protected by the World-Honored One throughout the long night of the past."
Since that time, it has never been explicitly taught. It was taught during the time of the sixteen princes, and it was also taught during the time of the twenty thousand buddhas;
however, for the forty years prior to this, it had never been explicitly taught. For those forty years, I have relied on knowing that it was not being taught.
At the assembly on Vulture Peak, there were five thousand people who cleared their seats and departed. This was even during the Buddha’s lifetime; how much more so after his parinirvāṇa?
These words clarify that it is by means of the Dharma that one becomes a person. As the sutra says: "O Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa... and so forth.

The character "wei" (with the departing tone) is glossed as "to bestow. Now that these six kinds of Dharma-preachers have received and upheld [the teaching], they are all true sons of the Tathāgata and only then do they receive the covering of robes;
it is not merely that they are protected by Śākyamuni Buddha alone, but they also receive the protective mindfulness of all other Buddhas currently existing [in the ten directions]. (End of Sūtra).
Regarding the phrase "gentle and patient": having shame and remorse as one's clothing has two meanings. First, it wards off wind and frost;
second, it conceals physical deformity; therefore, it is called "clothing. Because they are gentle, their three karmas are all supple. Outwardly, they are free from coarseness and ferocity;

their fists of anger do not clench, and their smiling faces are not enslaved by adverse conditions. There are two types of patience (*kṣānti*): first, the patience of enduring enmity and harm, which refers to evil matters...

It can contain; it is the patience of enduring suffering, which endures conditions such as cold, heat, and verbal abuse, possessing the sense of warding off and resisting these—thus it is called "clothing" (*vastra*).

Because of the presence of shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*), one feels abashed by transgressions and faults, and this is able to conceal physical ugliness—thus it is called "inner" (*antara*); because of the presence of patience (*kṣānti*).

To shield against the winds and frost of insult and humiliation is what is meant by "external. Question: Since those who uphold this sutra naturally possess gentleness, patience, and a sense of shame, why is it said that the Buddha covers them with his robe?
Answer: Gentleness, patience, shame, and remorse are the merits inherent within the body of a Buddha.

These merits are fully contained within the sutra. When the Buddha teaches sentient beings to uphold the sutra, they attain the merits of a Buddha; thus, it is because of the Buddha [that they receive this protection].
Because it is given, it is also called "giving.

Regarding the phrase "protected by the two Buddhas" and so forth: the question is asked, for what reason does the upholder of the sutra obtain the covering of the Buddha’s robe and also receive the protection and mindfulness of the Buddhas of other directions?
The answer, as stated in the commentary, is that through the three great faiths, the three refuges, and the five precepts, one obtains the fruit of a human body.

By faith in the ten wholesome paths and the eight precepts, one obtains the fruit of rebirth in heaven. By faith in and practice according to the six kinds of Dharma masters who cultivate the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, one obtains the fruit of Buddhahood;
this is also due to the power of one's aspiration. As for the power of aspiration: it is the vow to seek the fruit of Buddhahood, even if one’s body withers and life is extinguished.
One cultivates non-retrogression.

To speak of "possessing roots of goodness" refers to the power of the roots of goodness; these are faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, or alternatively, non-attachment and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "dwelling together with the Buddha" and so forth, Jiaxiang says: The principle of the One Vehicle is the place where the Buddha resides;

those who propagate the sutra also dwell therein, and thus it is said they "dwell together. Furthermore, compassion is called a "shelter" (*śaraṇa*): the mind of compassion is where the Buddha dwells, which is termed "lodging" (*vāsa*).
Those who can uphold the sutra possess compassion and thus dwell together with the Buddha within that compassion; hence, it is called "dwelling together."
"Overnight stay" (*sukha*): Because one who upholds the sutras dwells together with the Tathāgata within the dwelling of the Mahāyāna teachings, it is called "staying overnight. Zhang Jing says:

"The mind of compassion is the dwelling for benefiting others according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; contemplating the supreme truth of emptiness is the dwelling for one's own benefit according to the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*."
Regarding the statement that "the Buddha's teaching covers the mind": the mind of sentient beings is the head, and the teaching is the hand of the Tathāgata.
The teaching covering the mind is like a hand rubbing the head.
Regarding the phrase "that which was prophesied by the Buddha," this follows the interpretation of Vimalakīrti. "Prophecy" (*vyākaraṇa*) is equivalent to "reception" (*parigraha*).
The object of reception is *sumati*; *mati* means "to receive a prophecy. Thus, the meaning of "reception" explains *mati*. The sutra says, "he becomes a Tathāgata.
The character "becomes" (*wei*) is pronounced with a level tone; it is glossed as "attainment."
Regarding the statement that "within the title there are five locations," the Sūtra says, "Wherever the Medicine King [is]," and so forth.

This means that the various places throughout the three periods of time are the ten directions. Whether referring to the place where it was preached, the place where it was read, or even the place where it abides, these are termed "already taught.
From the conclusion of this assembly until the closing of the golden coffin, all are collectively termed "to be taught. As the Golden Cloud states, starting from the sixteen princes...

Regarding the twenty thousand Buddhas from the past until before this present life, their names have already been spoken; these are called "previously taught. Regarding this present life at Deer Park, up until the assembly at Nirvana, their names are being spoken now;
these are called "presently taught. Regarding the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of future lives in which one will again preach this sutra, these are called "to be taught in the future.
Among these two types of three periods, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the most difficult to believe and the most difficult to understand.

Regarding the statement, "Commanding the relinquishing of the provisional for the sake of the equal," one asks: What is the principle in this sutra that makes it uniquely termed "difficult to believe and difficult to understand"?

The answer in the commentary states: "Commanding the relinquishing of the provisional for the sake of the equal. Within the house of the elder, three carts were proclaimed, yet upon exiting the gate, one received only the ox-cart;

thus, while three were preached, three were not obtained, and while three were preached, only one was attained. This refers to the teachings of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna prior to the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

The mind is easily led to faith. After the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the "three as one" has already been realized; yet its meaning is difficult to understand, perhaps more so than this sutra.

At the beginning, it opens the gate of expedient means (*upāya*), and at the end, it reveals the mark of reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). It explains that the former three are made into one, and transforms the old fruits into the present causes.
That dharma is difficult to set aside, and this path is difficult to advance upon; because its principle is difficult to believe and comprehend, it is said to be "difficult to believe."
This is the explanation.

To say that there is "birth" within "non-birth" means that although the various afflictions (*kleśa*) of those in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) among the followers of the Two Vehicles have already ceased and they have attained non-birth—knowing that suffering and its origin are entirely exhausted and thus cannot produce further rebirth or induce karmic results—it is therefore called "non-birth. Now, [the Buddha] causes these followers of the Two Vehicles to abandon their provisional [attainments] and proceed toward...

Truly, those who turn their minds toward the Mahāyāna still undergo another layer of *pariṇāmi-ja-maraṇa* (death through transformation) as they proceed through the births of the three great *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*;
this is called "having birth. For forty years, the World-Honored One has been telling others, "My births are exhausted; I shall not receive further existence.
Who would have known that there is still birth and death? It is like sprouts growing from parched grain, withered branches putting forth new shoots, or flowers blooming on dead wood—how strange!
The ashes warm once more; the crow’s head is tinged with white. Thus, it is difficult to believe and difficult to understand. The principles are profound and mysterious.
The three vehicles revolve as a single assembly. Past fruits serve as present causes; through circuitous convergence, one finally realizes the truth.

After practicing for sixty *kalpas* over three lifetimes, or one hundred *kalpas* over four lifetimes, one finally attains the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*). Furthermore, turning the mind toward the Great [Vehicle], one passes through eighty, sixty, forty, twenty, ten, and so forth [thousand] *kalpas*.
[It takes] a thousand kalpas until the initial stage of the ten faiths; thereafter, one must practice for three great kalpas before finally reaching the fruit of Buddhahood.
Therefore, it is called "difficult to believe and understand. Alternatively, "difficult to believe" refers to the profound and mysterious nature of the teaching and its principles.

"Difficult to understand" refers to the manner of personally attaining the realization of true reality—namely, that it is revealed as being realized only after one great kalpa—and thus it is said to be difficult to understand. This is the understanding.
This refers to "realizing and entering.
Regarding the phrase "do not recklessly proclaim it after hearing it," the World-Honored One told Bhaisajyarāja: "This sutra is the secret and essential treasury of all Buddhas.
"Secret" means hidden, like the private seal of a king; because five thousand people were seated there, he did not speak of it—this is what is called "secret."

The three vehicles are unified under the single vehicle; this is called the "Essential. It encompasses the ultimate truth and subsumes the conventional, containing the real and enshrining the provisional; this is called the "Treasury.
For example, it is like the wondrous jewels of a Wheel-Turning King, which cannot be displayed before ordinary people; thus it is called the "Secret Treasury.
It contains and stores the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and all the myriad virtues of both the conditioned and the unconditioned; hence it is the "Secret Treasury."
Regarding the scriptural statement that it "must not be distributed or taught falsely," this is an admonition to carefully discern the spiritual capacities [of recipients].
One must not preach it to those of dull faculties; it should only be taught to those of sharp faculties who possess wisdom and seek the Buddha-way.
Regarding the Buddha’s statement that "the Buddha always maintains [his own requisites] for himself" and so forth:
it is like a *vinaya*-master who gives his water jar, alms bowl, staff, and other items to a novice or junior disciple, keeping only the three robes (*tricīvara*) which he carries with him.

It does not contradict the teaching that even Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—when they have returned to the state of the sublime Lotus—are all required to erect stupas made of the seven treasures. Once the stupas are completed, [they shall not...]
One must further enshrine the *śarīra*. However, one may simply place them within the scripture scrolls. Why is this? Because within these [scrolls] resides the whole-body *śarīra* of the Tathāgata.
This whole-body *śarīra* is not the same as the fragmented body parts, such as finger joints and the like.
Regarding the phrase "among the ten modes of practice" (*daśadharmacaryā*), it is asked: Why are the ten modes of practice not explained in their entirety, but only four modes of practice mentioned?
The commentary answers: "Among the ten modes of practice," the four [specific] locations are the practices themselves, while the remaining six are the bases for the modes of practice.

Question: Why are there five locations (*sthāna*)? When compared with the ten modes of practice (*daśa dharmaparyāyāḥ*), there are only four locations; why is the location where the scripture scrolls are kept not mentioned?
Answer: The location where the scrolls are kept is not one of the ten modes of practice; among the ten modes of practice, there is no such thing as a location for keeping scripture scrolls.
Regarding the statement "the equality of the wisdom of clarity and principle," this explains the "entire body" (sarira) of the sutras. First, the Dharma-body alone is called "entire.
Second, the Reward-body alone is also called "entire. Now, the simultaneous possession of both the Dharma-body and the Reward-body is called "entire" (the preceding term is the heading).
Regarding the phrase "by this, one reflects back," etc., it serves to clarify the preceding meaning.

Its intent is to clarify that in such instances as the recitation of sutra scrolls and the like, there is already the presence of the *śarīra* (relics) of both the Dharma-body and the Reward-body. Thus, both principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*) are fully encompassed.
Regarding the phrase "Therefore, it is by means of the Buddha’s teachings... and so forth: this refers to a verse from the Buddhist scriptures. Question:

Since the principle (*artha*) that is expressed is the *dharmakāya* relic, I wonder whether the expressive teaching (*śāsana*) itself can also be designated as a relic. Answer: There are two kinds of relics: first, the *dharmakāya* relic;
second, the relic of the dharma-verse (*gāthā-dharma*). In the present case, this verse is cited to testify to the *dharmakāya* relic; therefore, [it is appropriate to bathe it].
Like a cloud of merit. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke for the sake of the Bodhisattva Viśuddhamati: "There are two kinds of relics (*śarīra*). The first is the bodily bone relic;
the second is the dharma-verse relic. He then spoke these verses: "All phenomena arise from conditions" — this is the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).

"The Tathāgata says this is its cause" — this is the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*). "When those causes and conditions cease" — this is the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). This is the Great Śramaṇa...

The Gate explains the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*). Regarding the question: "If one is now to write verses, one should write the verse on the original non-arising and non-ceasing (*anutpādānirodha*);

why instead write the four truths beginning with 'all phenomena arise'? The answer is: the intention is to take the principle of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*) from among the Four Truths as proof for the *dharmakāya* relics.
Regarding the "Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings," these two aforementioned sūtras— the *Bathing the Image* and the *Immeasurable Meanings*— attest that the Dharma-body is named śarīra.
Regarding the statement "in accordance with the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*," the *Suvarṇabhāsottama-sūtra* attests that the Dharma-body is the śarīra, and it designates the Tathāgata’s wisdom as such.
The Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). This refers to the four wisdoms (*catur-jñāna*) of the Bodhi, which are called the Dharma-body. Huìyuǎn explains: "This is a dual realization.
The Tathāgata’s wisdom is the wisdom that realizes, which is the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*). The Tathāgata himself is the Dharma-body."
Regarding the statement that "by this person one becomes a Dharma Master," it means that the person draws near to the supreme Dharma and that the person accomplishes its virtues.
When the Sūtra says, "If a person is able to see this stūpa and so forth," it means that they are directing their mind toward it;
gradually approaching the stūpa, one should know that such a person is gradually drawing near to the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) of a Bodhisattva, which is itself *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Regarding the statement that one sees and hears this sutra, such as its "virtuous practices" and so forth: the Sutra says, "O Bhaiṣajyarāja, if there is anyone, whether a householder or one who has left the home life," and so on.
This refers to those who, having already entered the kalpa, cultivate the bodhisattva path by relying on the practice of hearing, reflection, and cultivation; this is "correct cultivation.

What is cultivated here is preparatory virtue and supramundane virtue. Even if one were to attain virtue without relying on the three types of wisdom (hearing, reflection, and cultivation), it would still be [merely mundane].

The "portion of merit" (puṇyabhāga) refers to the virtuous aspiration for the fruit of Buddhahood and Bodhi; it is not yet correct cultivation. Therefore, it is called "not yet skillfully practicing the Bodhisattva path.

This is the stage of entering the Ten Faiths through hearing the sutras; by practicing according to the three wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, it serves as the direct cause for the fruit of Buddhahood and Bodhi.

Regarding the statement, "Thus we know that the mention of reflection (*cintā*) and so forth refers to the three types of wisdom (*trividya-prajñā*)," these three types of wisdom are what constitute the primary cause.

Among the three, if one takes only the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), it is not yet the primary cause and is therefore not called "virtuous conduct" (*sucarita*). Only when the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) and cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) are included is it termed "virtuous conduct."
Furthermore, it says: "To uphold other sutras is not called 'good practice'; only to uphold this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* Sūtra is truly called 'good practice'.
Regarding the phrase "if they hear these," the Sūtra states: "There are sentient beings who seek the Buddha and attain Bodhi.
Jigu (紀國) comments: "As for 'seeing,' it refers to seeing the golden script; as for 'hearing,' it refers to the ears hearing the resonance of the King [of Dharma]."
"Hearing" refers to the definitive understanding of the teachings. "Understanding" means penetrating the principles; having understood, one is then able to receive and uphold them.
The Sūtra says that one attains proximity to Bodhi; this refers to a Bodhisattva of the first stage (*bhūmi*).

Regarding what is called "this analogy," the Sūtra says: "Bhaiṣajyarāja, it is as if there were a person"—that is, one who seeks the path of the Buddha—who, within saṃsāra, is oppressed by the fires of suffering.
For this reason, the verse says "exhausted"; for this reason, the path is said to be "long. For this reason, he is said to be "weary."
Since he lacked verses, he sought water. Water is the nectar of immortality—the pure nirvana that is Buddha-nature. Regarding the term "high plateau" (*gāoyuán*):
Jiguang says that the teachings of the Two Vehicles constitute the plateau, for they are far removed from this water.

The teachings of the *Lotus Sūtra* are like a low-lying marsh, as they are close to the water. Zhangjing says that the Buddha-dharma is the high plateau, while the teachings of external paths are the plain.

"River. This interpretation relies solely on the high and low elevations of the land; it does not concern itself with the depth of the water. Were it otherwise, a level plain would instead be considered "near water.
The intent of the *Śāstra* is to regard the entire Dharma of the Three Vehicles as the "high plateau," for it transcends the realms of non-Buddhist teachings and birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
Just as in the world one must obtain the necessary tools when digging a well, this sutra is likewise intended [to provide such tools].
To bore through the high plateau of the Dharma of the Three Vehicles, one must take sublime wisdom (*prajñā*) as the primary means and the three types of action (*trikarma*) as the instruments:

the bodily action of making offerings, the verbal action of praising, and the mental action of contemplation. Initially, when boring into dry earth, one is very far from water and there is no sign of water at all;
subsequently, when boring until reaching moist soil, one gradually approaches the water. As the Sūtra says: "If one does not cease applying effort..."
Then one sees moist soil. When those of the Two Vehicles, during their intermediate stage, apply themselves to the Mahāprajñāpāramitā teaching on emptiness, it is called "unceasing exertion.
The Mahāyāna teaching of emptiness contains the principle of emptiness; gradually, there arises the potential for the water of Buddha-nature, just like seeing moist soil.
Later, one digs until reaching mud, and within the mud there is water; the water is obtained from within the mud. This is like hearing the teaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
Within the teachings there is the water of the Buddha-nature; the teaching is like the mud, and the water is like the Buddha-nature.
If one digs a well and reaches the mud, one will certainly find water within it. If one hears the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, one will definitively attain Bodhi. Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Those who, having heard it, believe, understand, accept, and uphold it—know that they are near to Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. (This explains the Sūtra.)
Regarding the statement "the treatise that explains the nature of the analogy," this refers to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-śāstra*.
As for the phrase "bodhi of the first stage" (*prathamabhūmi-bodhi*), it is asked: among the five kinds of bodhi, which bodhi is the Buddha-nature bodhi?
The answer in the commentary states: "It is the bodhi of the first stage."
Regarding the term "high plateau" (*gāoyuán*): water emerges from the high plateau, which is why it is excavated there.

Regarding the term "broad and level plain" (*guǎngpíng yuán*): this is also the name of an island located in Hānpíng County; it is called a "plateau" (*yuán*) because it is elevated yet broad and level.
Regarding the phrase "surpassing all paths": the teachings of non-Buddhists are called "all paths," and because the Buddha-dharma surpasses them, it is called "foremost.
Regarding the phrase "difficult to ascend": this means it is difficult to advance upward; thus it is described as a "high plateau."
Regarding what is called the teaching of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas): it is like a high plateau emerging within a level plain;

that is, establishing the Buddha-dharma within the birth-and-death (saṃsāra) phenomena of the non-Buddhists. Since there is no place for transformation outside the three realms, it is like the plateau itself—it does not exist apart from the level plain.
Regarding the statement, “*záo* (鑿) means *càn* (鏨),” (*càn* and *sān* [蠶] share the same pronunciation). It is also said that *càn* is pronounced as *chàn* (鑱, with the final nasal elided).
If one adopts the pronunciation *càn*, it refers to the tool used for construction—a metal chisel. If one adopts the sense of the object being pierced, then it must be pronounced *sān* (蠶);
the hole or cavity that has been pierced is called *sān*. Here, we take the sense of the object pierced as the primary meaning.
Regarding the phrase "preceded by sublime wisdom" and so forth: Question: If one intends to penetrate and discern [the truth], what dharma should be employed as the precursor?
Answer: The commentary states, "preceded by sublime wisdom," and so forth. Question: If one intends to excavate and investigate [the meaning], what dharma should be employed as the precursor?
Answer: The commentary states, "preceded by sublime wisdom," and so forth. One should perform acts of physical respect and offering, and verbal praise of the Great [Teacher].
The vehicle is the mental action (*manas-karman*) that investigates the meaning of phenomena; these three actions are called the "tools.

To discern and seek out [the truth] is precisely the meaning of "piercing" with sublime wisdom (*prajñā*). Diligence (*vīrya*) is the chisel-blade; if the edge of the blade is as sharp as a copper chisel, one will certainly find water.
When the three karmas possess diligence, all that is practiced will be fully accomplished.
Regarding the statement that "the two benefits do not cease": Question: How can the Two Vehicles possess the practice of the two benefits? Answer: They possess them partially.

Furthermore, upon hearing the Prajñā, they gradually practice the two benefits. The Treatise says: "By receiving and upholding this sutra, one obtains the water of Buddha-nature. This reveals [the state of] dryness.
Earth is the cause of moist earth; moist earth is the cause of mud; mud is the cause of water. The teachings of the Two Vehicles are the cause of the teaching of emptiness;
the teaching of emptiness serves as the cause for the Middle Way Mahāyāna.
Regarding the statement that the teaching of emptiness is "distant": it refers to the Mahāyāna’s principle and wisdom, the fruit of Buddhahood, and Bodhi, which are termed the "New Vehicle.
Since the teachings of emptiness serve as the cause for these, they are termed "distant."
The phrase "this refers to the heading" and so forth constitutes the summary.
When the Sūtra says, "The Bodhisattva is also like this," it refers to those who have obtained [the teaching] but are now in want. "Not having heard" means not having attained it;
"not having understood" means not having contemplated it; "not having been able to practice" means not having cultivated it. Having heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*...
If one hears only the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), such a person remains far removed from the Buddha-way.

Regarding the statement that "this explains the reason for this," it interrogates the intent of the preceding declaration: Why is it that failing to contemplate and practice leads to being far from Bodhi?
Why does contemplating and practicing lead to being near to Bodhi? The answer is: because [the former] lacks the conditions of all bodhisattvas...
The Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi all belongs to this sutra. Whether it be the fruit, the principle, or the phenomena—enlightenment and nirvana are entirely contained therein;

therefore, it is said that they all belong to it. When this sutra speaks of "opening the gate of expedient means," it means that within the path of the One Vehicle, the three vehicles are taught according to what is appropriate;
this is called opening the gate of expedient means. Although it demonstrates the true aspect and although it demonstrates various paths, in reality...
Because it is for the sake of the One Vehicle, it is called "revealing the true mark. This *Dharmapada-sūtra* treasury is that which expresses [the meaning].
"Profound, firm, and remote" means that it has been attained through cultivation over three incalculable eons; thus it is said to be both profound and remote.
Regarding the statement that "no one can reach it," this means that the two vehicles do not know it and bodhisattvas cannot fathom it.
Regarding the phrase "thereby providing an exposition," the character "wei" (為) is read with the departing tone (*qùyīn*) and signifies "to bestow" or "to grant."
Regarding the statement "there are proximate causes, direct causes, and so forth," this explains that the words of the sutra all pertain to this specific sutra. Mǔ says:

Among the four dharmas of teaching, principle, practice, and fruit within the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), teaching, practice, and fruit constitute the "causes" (*hetu*). Of these, the teaching is the distant cause, while [the others] are the proximate causes.

This refers to the Middle Gate within the Great Gate. If those of the human and celestial realms, as well as those of the Two Vehicles, turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna], [their respective teachings, principles, practices, and fruits become the causes].
Turning toward the Great Vehicle constitutes both the distant cause (*dūrahetu*) and the auxiliary cause (*pariṣkārahetu*) for the fruit of Buddhahood and Bodhi.

That is to say, among the main gate and the central gate, if those of the human and celestial realms, as well as the teachings, principles, practices, and fruits of the two vehicles, turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle, they likewise constitute the distant and auxiliary causes for the fruit of Buddhahood and Bodhi;
this is what is meant by the side gate and the small gate. As for the five kinds of wisdom, they refer to the nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
The "object" (viṣaya) refers to the accompanying causes.

Regarding the phrase "because it is obtained through the sūtra," this refers to the teaching and practice of the One Vehicle (ekayāna). Regarding the phrase "because it is subsumed by this sūtra," this refers to the teaching and practice of the Two Vehicles (dvayayāna).
The teaching and practice of the Two Vehicles are merely subsumed within the sūtra; they are not the direct cause for the fruit of Buddhahood.

To speak of "opening the gate of expedient means" (upāya-mukha) refers to encompassing remote causes and collateral causes; it refers to the teaching, principle, practice, and fruit of the two vehicles (dviyāna) taught in the past.
To speak of "revealing the true aspect" (bhūtalakṣaṇa) refers to encompassing proximate causes and primary causes.
Regarding the statement "now explaining the One Vehicle," etc., this encompasses all provisional and ultimate principles without exception.
Regarding the statement "furthermore, profound and firm," etc., it explains the deep and remote meaning of the Sūtra-piṭaka;
it is the secret treasury hidden by the Buddha for all Bodhisattvas—whether of fixed or unfixed nature, and whether of sudden or gradual awakening.
Regarding the statement "like a king’s tooth-seal," the Aśoka-sūtra says: King Aśoka had a crown prince named Dharmavivardhana.

His stepmother, out of jealousy and hatred, slandered him to the king and subsequently banished him to another country. That king took his teeth to serve as a seal for writing and then spoke to his son.
"If one receives my tooth-seal, that is true faith; if there is no tooth-seal, it is not my writing.

The king's messenger entrusted the tooth-seal to the prince and immediately sent him out. After the prince had departed, the stepmother’s heart of hatred remained as it was, a hundredfold more than before.
He then waited for the king to fall asleep, extracted the king’s teeth—both large and small, all of equal size—and made them into a seal.

Once the sealing was complete, he sent him away and gouged out the prince’s eyes, taking them back with him. Upon receiving the command, the prince gouged out his own eyes and entrusted them to the messenger;
this is explained in detail as in the sutra. This "tooth-seal" does not belong to any other person; it now demonstrates that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* belongs exclusively to the Buddha.
Regarding the term "profound and remote" (*yōen*): entering the kalpas to cultivate the causes is called "profound" (*yō*) because it is realized through wondrous wisdom.

Regarding the phrase "those who hear the sutra with alarm and doubt, and those of new learning with pride": the meaning of this section of the text is to take the general reality and distinguish its particulars.
It states that while those of new learning are alarmed and doubtful, the Śrāvakas possess pride.
Regarding the phrase "upon first hearing, they are immediately startled," etc.: both Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas harbor doubts, yet their internal mental processes differ.
When Bodhisattvas hear this, they give rise to doubt through reflection; when Śrāvakas hear it, they give rise to overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Both of these types are still ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Their nature regarding spiritual practice is termed "fear."
Regarding the phrase "not yet having entered the three stages," some say it refers to not yet having entered the stage of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.

Others say it refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*) not yet having entered the three levels of the "Sages" (*sbyor lam*), namely the ten abidings (*vihāra*), the ten practices (*caryā*), and the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*). Still others say it means the afflictions have not yet entered the Mahāyāna.

Each of these refers to the three stages within the Mahāyāna's three levels of the Sages, or the five stabilizing mind-observances (*pañca-citta-sthāpanā*) and the distinct-characteristic [contemplation] of the Hīnayāna; here, the term "three stages" refers to these. The underlying intent is simply that one has not yet entered [the path].

Regarding the stages of the Three Vehicles: those with overweening pride have not yet entered the stage of the Lesser Vehicle; likewise, small bodhisattvas have not yet entered the stage of the Great Vehicle.
All such individuals are ordinary beings prior to the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*). In this sutra, the two characters *jie* (介) function as a particle meaning "also" or "indeed."
Regarding this question: the Sūtra states, "Bhaiṣajyarāja, if there be a virtuous son... up to the words "...how should it be preached?
Here, the World-Honored One consults with the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja: "While I am in the world, you need not worry.
Once I have entered parinirvāṇa, you shall take the Lotus Sūtra and preach it for others. How should you cause them to practice?"
Regarding the initial heading: the Sūtra answers, "These sons and daughters of good family enter the Tathāgata’s chamber," which refers to this sūtra.
Regarding the explanation thereof: furthermore, when Bhaiṣajyarāja asks, "What is called the Tathāgata’s chamber? the Buddha answers Bhaiṣajyarāja.
The King said: "The chamber of the Tathāgata refers to the great mind of compassion for all sentient beings.
The phrase 'constantly dwelling therein' explains the meaning of 'chamber. The Buddha designates the mind of compassion as his chamber;
the Buddha-mind rests and abides within compassion."

Regarding the statement "The Vimalakīrti Sūtra says... and so forth: this is explained in contrast to clarify their similarities and differences. In the *Vimalakīrti*, True Suchness (*tathatā*) is taken as the house because wisdom dwells therein;
it is thus the house for one's own benefit. The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states: "Compassion is the woman. She is born into the father’s house but does not inherit the paternal lineage;
she marries into another clan and gives birth to a son who inherits the ancestral line. The wisdom and compassion of a bodhisattva are likewise: they are born...
[They] leave the family of ignorance and the clan of nescience to marry into the family of the Tathāgata, receiving the Buddha’s protective mindfulness and continuing the lineage of the Tathāgata.
When it is said that "this [text] clarifies matters," this refers precisely to this chapter. It speaks of clarifying matters upon each and every phenomenon;
by covering and sheltering sentient beings to their ultimate benefit, it takes compassion as its dwelling—this is the dwelling for the benefit of others.

Regarding the second fascicle mentioned previously: it distinguishes the similarities and differences between the "Chapter on Entrusting the Dharma" (Fa-shi-pin) and the "Parable of the Poor Son" (Qiong-zi-yu-pin).

From the beginning up to the end of the "Chapter on Resolute Belief and Understanding" (Xin-jie-pin), this constitutes the teaching of the house. The empty teaching of the Mahāyāna is the city, while the Middle Way Mahāyāna is the house;

since the house is within the city and the Middle Way is contained within the empty teaching, they are termed "internal and external aspects. This is because the house is established in contrast to the city.
This chapter teaches that loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the practice of equanimity (*upekṣā*). When sentient beings uphold this sutra, they must first give rise to loving-kindness;

this is called "entering the Tathāgata’s chamber. The commentary states: "Regarding the internal and external as relative forms: since the preceding [practices of] wisdom and compassion are 'external' equanimities, the Middle Way is taken as 'internal' equanimity.
Here, because loving-kindness and compassion benefit others externally, they are termed 'external' in relation to the principle of the Middle Way."
The phrase "the mental formations are disciplined and capable" explains the meaning of "laying aside the robes. "Gentle and mild" refers to the mental formations being disciplined;
"patient" refers to being able to endure toil, resentment, and harm. Because of this patience, one is able to accept the pressure of suffering.

Regarding the statement that "external objects do not provide [support]," this is because when one abides in that patience, external favorable and unfavorable conditions cannot move one; therefore, it is said that they "cannot be obtained.

Regarding the statement "enduring enmity and harm," this is because of gentleness (*sauratya*), which corresponds to enduring enmity and harm, and because of patience (*kṣānti*), which corresponds to abiding in the endurance of suffering.
This is patience (*kṣānti*). Huìdù explains: "Patience in enduring enmity and harm has non-anger as its essence; patience in calmly accepting suffering has diligence as its essence.
Furthermore, patience in enduring enmity and harm relates to the sphere of persons, while patience in calmly accepting suffering relates to general spheres such as cold and heat."

Clothing can ward off cold and heat; likewise, through the gentleness and patience of the three karmas, one is able to withstand the winds and frosts of abuse and defamation, and is therefore metaphorically likened to clothing.

Regarding the phrase "venerating the roots of goodness of the worthy," one asks: in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, it is said that "shame and modesty are one's clothing"; what does this sūtra [mean by] this?
Therefore, it is not taken up. The answer is: that [practice] is the common path for those of the three vehicles;

thus, they take shame and remorse as their clothing, honoring the worthy and good while rejecting unwholesome dharmas. This sutra, however, is the distinct practice of Mahāyāna followers; they take gentleness and patience as their clothing.

Regarding the statement "the body of gentleness and harmony": this refers to shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*). Shame and dread of blame are the essence (*tattva*), while the two forms of gentleness and harmony are the function (*karman*).
First, because one possesses shame and dread of blame, one subsequently gives rise to gentleness and harmony. Later, it is explained that these two dharmas are not distinct.

The phrase "settling the body and mind in the realm of emptiness" explains the meaning of "sitting in equipoise. When the Sūtra speaks of the "Tathāgata’s seat," it refers to the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*).
While practicing the six perfections or while teaching and transforming others through the Dharma, one contemplates that these three factors are entirely non-existent:
one does not perceive oneself as the transformer, one does not perceive the sentient beings to be transformed, and one does not perceive anything in between.
The Dharma that is taught—these three things are all empty; this is called "mǎngrán" (vast and expansive). "Mǎngrán" describes a state of being broad, open, empty, and unobstructed;
it is precisely the principle of the two kinds of emptiness. The pronunciation of "mǎng" is *mō lǎng* (the rhyme of *mō* and *lǎng*); it signifies the aspect of vastness.
Regarding the statement that Vimalakīrti [uses] the four dhyānas and so forth: in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, the four dhyāna-concentrations serve as his couch.

This is in terms of the basis upon which wisdom relies and the locus from which wisdom arises; thus, the four dhyāna-concentrations serve as the couch. In this sutra, however, in terms of the object of wisdom’s focus and the support of wisdom, the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) serves as the couch.
Regarding the statement that "great compassion exists": this concludes the preceding section on taking the mind of compassion as one's dwelling.

Now, in the practice of compassion for the sake of delivering sentient beings, one must first regard sentient beings as existing within the realm of phenomena; only then can one extract them from suffering and bestow upon them happiness.

Regarding the so-called "contemplation of the emptiness of the two—the robe and the seat": the "robe" refers to the soft and gentle garment of patience (*kṣānti*). In practice, one must not perceive the existence of sentient beings;

only by contemplating sentient beings as empty can one truly achieve patience. An-guo states: "The robe represents the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), while the seat represents the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*);
these are the two distinct types. Question: How can the robe and bowl be said to be empty? Answer: If one does not contemplate them as empty, then enmity and intimacy will arise.

[Objection: It cannot stand, because there is no basis for the arising of patience (*kṣānti*). [Response: Now, by practicing the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), the two patiences are accomplished.

[Question: Great compassion (*mahāmaitrī-karuṇā*) involves contemplation; yet if clothing and seats are empty, and all this is empty, how can compassion exist? [Answer: The intent is to reveal the simultaneous application of both existence and emptiness, rather than clinging solely to emptiness.
If one does not contemplate existence, how could one ever deliver others? Furthermore, it is called "emptiness" because of attachment to the minor [extremes]; it is not that dharmas are non-existent.
Because it possesses substance, it is called "existent"; one merely removes the attachment to it.

Regarding the statement "to cause emanated beings and others to hear [it]": the World-Honored One told Bhaiṣajyarāja, "You and I shall circulate this sutra according to the three previously mentioned gates of contemplation.
Do not worry about those who listen. Even if there are none to listen, I will dispatch emanated beings from other lands."
"Let them listen. He also sent the fourfold assembly to listen, and he also sent the eight classes of devas, nāgas, and others to come and listen.
Regarding the statement that this enables one to see [the truth] and is not false: the World-Honored One said to Bhaiṣajyarāja, "Know for certain and listen:
I too have looked upon you repeatedly. First, you have frequently seen my body; second, I have caused you to turn toward the great assembly of devas and humans."
While preaching the Dharma among the assembly, he suddenly forgot some phrases and characters. He called out for them but could not recall them.
I shall instruct you so that they may be restored in their entirety. "Dou" (pronounced *dòu*) means to linger or delay; it also carries the sense of staying or halting. "Dòu" is a surname.

"Yi" (also pronounced "yi") refers to the meaning of "to trace and examine. Regarding the character for "surname" (*xing*), it is said that one traces from the head of the rope to the tail of the rope;
thus, "yi" also means "aperture" (*dou*). The *Qieyun* states: "Yi" means "principle" (*li*). The *Jianyao* says: "Yi" refers to tracing and examining the various principles within the phrases;

therefore, the phrase is called an "aperture" (*dou*). In the sutras, the character "dòu" (逗) is used as the correct form. According to the *Shuowen*, the pronunciation of "dòu" is "you" with the "gu" (句) rhyme.
There is also a commentary which states: "The *Shuowen* says it means a 'phrase' (*ju*).

To say 'this is the beginning' refers to the first verse, which describes that which is difficult to believe and understand. The prose of the sutra says: 'At that time, the Buddha again addressed Bhaisajyarāja:
Of the countless thousands of myriads of koṭis of sūtras I have spoken—those already spoken, those currently being spoken, and those yet to be spoken—'" and so forth.
Among them all, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the most difficult to believe and understand. O Bhaiṣajyarāja, this sūtra is the secret and essential treasury of all Buddhas;
it must not be distributed or recklessly handed over to others. Now, the verse says: "Desiring to abandon all indolence," and so forth.
At first glance, the flow of the text seems to suggest that listening to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the condition for abandoning indolence. This is because of listening to the Dharma.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Only then will one abandon indolence; this is the meaning here. If there is someone who wishes to abandon indolence and go to listen to a sutra, they should certainly not listen to other sutras;
the matter requires that they listen to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Question: Why is this? Answer: To explain the reason:
first, because within this sutra it is taught that diligence and the perception of indolent people correspond [to each other]; second, because this sutra is difficult [to encounter].
To hear [this teaching] is difficult; to believe and accept it is likewise difficult.
Regarding the "one and a half verses as a parable," the prose of the sutra states: "Suppose there is a person who, parched with thirst and needing water, digs for it on a high plateau.
Seeing only dry earth, he knows the water is far off. Yet, without ceasing his exertion, he gradually..."
Upon reaching the mud, his mind becomes certain that water must be near. Now, the verse says: "Like a person thirsty for water," etc., for one and a half lines.
In the verse, the character *zào* (dry) should be added accordingly; the rest of the text is the same.
Regarding these two and a half verses taken together, the prose of the sūtra states: "The Bodhisattva is also like this.

If they have not heard, have not understood, and have not yet been able to practice this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it should be known that such a person is far removed from Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
If they obtain hearing and understanding, contemplate, and practice it, they will certainly know that they are drawing near to Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Now, the verse says:
Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that these two and a half lines are equivalent [to the preceding].
Regarding the statement "this first part has two [sections]": the first one and a half verses provide the formal teaching (*uddāna*). The prose sūtra states:

"These sons and daughters of good family, having entered the Tathāgata’s chamber, donned the Tathāgata’s robe, and sat upon the Tathāgata’s seat, should then [teach] for the sake of the fourfold assembly."
The extensive exposition of this sutra is now summarized in verse: "If a person speaks even one line and a half of this sutra...
To explain this with a single verse, the prose of the sutra states: "The Tathāgata’s chamber is the mind of great compassion toward all sentient beings;
the Tathāgata’s robe is the mind of gentleness and patience; the Tathāgata’s seat is all dharmas..."
This is emptiness. Now the verse says: "Great compassion is the chamber; one practice is [the dwelling].
To say "these are the first two" means that the first verse concerns the practice of patience (*kṣānti*). As the Sūtra says: "When this sūtra is being preached... This is the "one practice.
Next, the three verses clarify that I am in another land, causing the fourfold assembly to make offerings and listen to the Dharma. This is the long [explanation].
The *Caryā-sūtra* states that he also dispatched emanated bhikṣuṇīs and others to listen to his preaching of the Dharma.

The present verse says: "In thousands of millions of lands, I manifest a pure and firm body. These three lines constitute the answer. Question: What is the purpose of dispatching emanated persons to listen to the Dharma and assemble the multitude?
Answer: Briefly, there are three intentions: first, to make offerings to the Dharma Master; second, to attract authentic practitioners; and third, to protect the Dharma.
Master: Regarding "obstruction" (罣礙), the dictionary states it means "entangled obstruction. If pronounced with the sound *guà*, it is an error.

In the "Chapter on the Jeweled Stūpa," the statement that discourse is for the purpose of eliminating the three kinds [of obstacles] refers to the diseases to be treated; these are merely those who are without afflictions, namely the Arhats.

The "body of pride" (*māna-kāya*): because within this body, one gives rise to defiled pride (*kliṣṭa-māna*) toward three kinds of phenomena, they are collectively termed the "three kinds of defiled pride.

Prior to the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, when the mind has not yet been turned [toward enlightenment], it is not called "defiled"; it is of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*). From the point the mind is turned onward, it is called "defiled.
The essence of this defiled pride is the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

Regarding the three types of pride: first, those who believe in various things. They place their faith in the non-extinction of the *parīttābha* (small vehicle) city, believing that the sheep and deer vehicles truly ascend, and that there are distinct skillful means among the three and five vehicles.
They hold that the essential nature of these vehicles actually differs. For this reason, the "Herbs Simile" chapter refutes the attachment to the identity of the vehicles;
however, this does not accord with the fundamental tenet of the sutra. If one were to say that there truly are three distinct vehicles, [it would contradict the teaching].
How is it that the two vehicles—the Śrāvaka and [Pratyekabuddha] vehicles—both receive the prediction of attaining Buddhahood? Therefore, we know that only the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) is taken up;
there are no distinctions between three vehicles or five vehicles.
Regarding the statement that those with dualistic faith [distinguish] between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa: persons of the two vehicles loathe suffering and rejoice in nirvāṇa;
they cling to saṃsāra as clamorous and nirvāṇa as tranquil. By clinging to these two as distinct, they are certainly not equal. The Buddha perceives that saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are fundamentally equal.
If they were not equal, how could the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, having already emerged from saṃsāra, return to it?
Nirvana has already been attained; it is not fitting to return again to birth and death.
Therefore, one knows that apart from the world there is no separate other, and apart from suffering there is no separate world. Since clamor and silence are non-dual, they are called "equality."
Regarding the statement, "The three types of faith concern the equality of this body and that body," it means that this Buddha is not that Buddha, and that Buddha is not this Buddha.

It is for this reason that the equality of the body is taught. This is based on many sutras that provide detailed realization and sutras that provide comprehensive realization, which manifest the equality of the Buddha’s body.
Regarding the statement "the equality of the One Vehicle," the following clarifies the method by which [beings] are saved. As previously stated, this refers back to what was said before;
that is, the bestowal of predictions upon the śrāvakas is collectively termed "what has been explained. This is because there is only the Mahāyāna, and no second vehicle.
Regarding the statement that "the two are for the purpose of removing [attachment to] birth-and-death and so forth," a commentary states:

this refers to the two Buddhas sitting together in the same stūpa—the present Buddha Śākyamuni and the Buddha Prabhūtaratna who has entered nirvāṇa. That these two Buddhas sit together in the same stūpa signifies the equality of death and nirvāṇa;
this interpretation is precisely the equality of body (*kāya-samatā*). If one explains it in terms of the body of Śākyamuni, the equality of birth-and-death and nirvāṇa would then appear as follows:
This would diminish the Buddha-dharma; therefore, the Master of the Commentary (*ṭīkākāra*) points out that the textual passages are distinct.
