One attains freedom from affliction and disturbance.

Regarding the statement "attaining two kinds of good friends": because one previously transformed bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and others, they no longer engage in frivolous discourse or disputes over the Dharma, nor do they contend regarding the Buddha's teachings or mutually criticize one another;
thus, within the present fruits of peace and happiness, one encounters excellent fellow students.

Regarding the statement "obtaining the audience of the multitude through three [attainments]": this is due to the aforementioned three perceptions; thus, within the fruit of peace and happiness, one also obtains the arrival of the great assembly to listen and receive the teaching.

Regarding the statement "the fourth is entering into the Dharma": this is because, for the sake of all sentient beings, one previously preached the Dharma with equanimity, in accordance with the Dharma.
Therefore, it is neither more nor less than this. Now, within the fruit of peace and happiness, those who have heard [the Dharma] enter further into the Dharma;
having heard it, they are able to uphold it; having upheld it, they are able to recite it; having recited it, they are able to explain it; and having explained it, they are able to write it down.
Regarding the statement "first departing from the seven evils": first is envy, second is anger, third is pride, fourth is flattery, fifth is deception, and sixth is a crooked and false mind;
these six are the unwholesome dharmas to be abandoned. Seventh is straightforward conduct; this is the mind capable of abandoning them.
Regarding the statement that verse is free from three faults: first, contempt; second, frivolous proliferation; third, doubt and regret. "篾" (miè) means "to disregard.
It refers to seeing someone who appears similar to oneself.
Regarding the statement "practicing the four dharmas while living," they are: first, gentleness; second, patience; third, compassion; and fourth, not giving rise to a mind of indolence.
Regarding the initial teaching on compassion, the Sūtra says: "To give rise to great loving-kindness (*maitrī*) toward laypeople—this is the Great [Vehicle]."
Regarding the lineage of those who ride [the vehicle]: the leaders of the assembly do not fear birth and death;

they do not give rise to aversion, but rather cultivate compassion to extract suffering from others and bestow the bliss of the fruit of Buddhahood upon them. As the Sūtra says: "Those who are not Bodhisattvas" refers to icchantikas and śrāvakas.
Although they possess the Mahāyāna lineage, prior to the arousal of the bodhicitta, they are called "non-Bodhisattvas. They fear birth...
"Die" means: furthermore, arouse a compassionate mind in order to extract them from suffering.

Regarding the phrase "practicing the compassion conditioned by dharmas (*dharmālambana-maitrī*)": the word "practice" (*xing*) is pronounced with a level tone (*píngyīn*). One contemplates sentient beings according to their individual dispositions, forming the conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) of the dharmas—the five aggregates (*skandha*), twelve bases (*āyatana*), and eighteen elements (*dhātu*)—and bestows the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* upon them so that they may attain happiness; this is called the compassion conditioned by dharmas.

Regarding the statement "those who are not bodhisattvas," Zhang Jing says: These are those who possess the spiritual lineage (*gotra*); they are not those without the lineage, such as the icchantikas or śrāvakas of fixed nature.
Rather, it refers to those who have temporarily severed their roots of goodness or śrāvakas who have not yet resolved upon the Great Vehicle—these are termed "non-bodhisattvas.
As for the icchantikas, one perceives their heavy afflictions and extracts them from the suffering of the three miserable realms.

Regarding those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), [the Buddha] extracts them from the suffering of birth and death. As the Sūtra says: "If a person encounters suffering and loathes old age, sickness, and death, he speaks of *nirvāṇa* for them.

As for the statement that this is "actual compassion" (*bhūtā maitrī*) and so forth: one asks, since it is logically appropriate for a Bodhisattva’s practice to be impartial, why is it only directed toward [Bodhisattvas]?
The *Sā* [text] states that one practices loving-kindness (*maitrī*) toward human beings and compassion (*karuṇā*) toward bodhisattvas. The commentary (*śū*) replies that in reality they are equal.
The intent of the commentary is merely to rely on their predominant aspects; in actual fact, the two practices of loving-kindness and compassion are practiced in tandem.

Regarding the mention of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and other texts: because the sūtra text contains the word "great compassion" (*mahākaruṇā*), the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is cited as having ten kinds of great compassion.
First, regarding "observing those who have no refuge": this refers to observing all sentient beings who lack a place of refuge—those who have no parents, estates, or dwellings—and thus rescuing them.
Second, regarding "those who follow deviant paths": this refers to mindfulness of sentient beings who encounter evil friends.
The teaching follows the wrong path. Third, those who are poor and lack roots of goodness (kuśalamūla) are those who lack the faculties of faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
To speak of practicing unwholesome dharmas means to give rise to the ten non-virtuous actions, such as killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and so forth.
Regarding the "bond of desire": the afflictions of the desire realm that have not yet been subdued or severed are called the bond of desire.
Regarding the "ocean of birth and death": this refers to the two types of birth and death.
What is called "a long-term chronic illness" refers to the disease of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
What is called "the wholesome dharmas of desirelessness" refers to having no delight in the wholesome dharmas of the Three Vehicles.
What is called "this is the beginning" refers to the initial moment of delusion. As the Sūtra says: "One should form this thought regarding such persons as these."
Such a person as this is neither a layperson nor a monastic, and is certainly not a bodhisattva. Question: What is called a "great loss"? Answer: The reason for this will be explained below.
The Tathāgata teaches through skillful means according to what is appropriate; that which is taught according to what is appropriate is the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Such a person does not hear it; since they do not hear it, they do not know it; since they do not know it, they do not realize it.
Neither awakening nor inquiring; even if hearing or being told, one does not believe. Lacking belief, one also lacks outward application. Jiguang said:

"Those who do not hear lose the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*); those who do not know lose the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*); those who do not awaken lose the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*)."
Furthermore, those who do not inquire lose the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*); those who do not believe lose the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*);

and those who do not practice outwardly lose the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). Moreover, those who do not inquire lack the wisdom of hearing; those who do not believe lack the wisdom of reflection;

and those who do not practice outwardly lack the wisdom of cultivation. Regarding the scriptural statement "great loss," Master Lufu says: according to the character for "loss" (*shī*) in the sutra, it belongs to the preceding clause [as a verb].

Regarding the phrase "losing the name" (失名失): it belongs to the section below, where it means "having lost the name. However, since the text below says "not hearing and not knowing," this also constitutes losing the name.
[If one were to place it] outside the commentary (*shū*), it would be redundant. The *Chao* states: "Losing belongs to the section below; this is the general heading.

'Not hearing,' 'not knowing,' and so forth, are the specific details that precede it. This interpretation is also without fault; why labor to criticize the *Shū*? If that is so, why does the verse below [state it differently]?

The Sūtra states, "These [beings] do not hear, do not know," and so forth. According to this, the character *shī* (loss) belongs to the preceding term; it carries the meaning of "fault" (*guòshī*). Answer:
In that verse, because the phenomenon that causes the loss (*néngshī zhī fǎ*) stands above, the character *shī* belongs to the preceding term, thus signifying "fault.
Now, in this prose commentary (*chángxíng*), what is lost (*suǒshī*) belongs to the following term. The sub-commentary (*shū*) relies on this sense of "external" (*wài*) regarding what is lost.

Regarding what is called "transforming and guiding through mindfulness," the Sūtra says: "Even if that person does not inquire about, believe in, or understand this Sūtra, one should still uphold the Sūtra and practice for the sake of the practitioner’s peace and happiness.
One should reflect: 'I am currently inferior as an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and cannot transform others.
When I have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, in whatever state that person may fall, I shall be able to transform them.'"

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "he subsequently dwells in the nine stages (*bhūmi*) and so forth," it may refer to the nine stages consisting of the five realms of rebirth (*gati*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), which are perilous grounds of ruin, together with the eight higher stages—or perhaps seven stages.
Some say these are the seven stages of the four bodhisattva practices; or [it refers to] the seven...

The stations of consciousness (*vijñāna-sthiti*), which may be the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi*), the stage of noble ones (*ārya-bhūmi*), or the stage of whichever region—namely, the four continents (*catur-dvīpa*).
Regarding the statement that there is no fault in this initial general designation, there is no error in the external scriptures; "fault" here refers to the fear of departing from the lotus.
This explains the reason for this interpretation. The Sūtra asks, "Why is this so? (so-wêi-shê-hê) to explain the intent of the preceding statement. What is the source of this?
Upon hearing it, the listeners rejoice. The Sūtra answers: "This Sūtra is [the essence] of all [beings]," and so forth.

Regarding the term "Buddha-protected" (*buddharakṣita*): it is called "Buddha-protected" because its meaning is profound. Because it is Buddha-protected, sentient beings attain [realization]. This "attainment" refers to the attainment of what was previously unattained;
it is the attainment of the supreme fruit.
Regarding the initial mention of its "supreme excellence," the Sūtra states: "Mañjuśrī, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* [is such that] from 'immeasurable' down to 'those who read and recite it'...
Someone asked Master Dushun: "In the human world, people hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* every day;
why then do you say it is 'not to be heard'? He replied: "It is simply that those who hear it within the city of Chang'an are many, whereas in other bordering kingdoms, there are few."
In the midst of the continents, there are many places where the sutras are not heard; how much more so when compared to those dwelling within the six realms of existence?

The phrase "the first analogy" refers to the application of the dharma to the past bestowal; it is an explanation that unites the dharma with its analogy. The character for "application" (合) is pronounced in the entering tone (*rùshēng*).
Regarding the term "powerful": because the untainted (*anāsrava*) breaks through the tainted (*sāsrava*) and triumphantly transcends birth and death, it is called "powerful.

Regarding the phrase "as explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi*," etc.: first, when a Golden Wheel-turning King (*cakravartin*) ascends the throne, all nations of the four continents submit to his influence and transformation;

second, a Silver Wheel-turning King brings them under submission only after dispatching envoys; third, a Copper Wheel-turning King subdues them by arraying his forces and displaying his majesty; fourth...
The Iron-Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) is one who is inevitably victorious in battle. The Dharma-body is likened to the Golden-Wheel-Turning King;

those who submit upon hearing his reputation are like the morning audience before the Sovereign. The Self-Enjoyment Body is like the Silver-Wheel-Turning King, who brings others to submission only by dispatching envoys.
Question: What is meant by "bringing others to submission by dispatching envoys"? Answer: The Other-Enjoyment Body serves as the envoy, like the delivery of a message.

Regarding the person [who is subdued], it is said that they are brought to submission by dispatching an envoy. If one asks how the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*), which is itself a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), can further act as an envoy, the answer is given in the second [section]:
it uses the teaching of the Dharma as its envoy. The Enjoyment Body is likened to a copper-wheel-turning monarch;

such a king’s transformation of beings does not require military conquest, but rather brings them to submission simply by his own arrival. Thus, the Enjoyment Body employs supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) for the purpose of teaching and transforming others.

The Bodhisattva severs delusions through their own power, without relying on the power of the Buddha, just as a copper-wheel-turning king (tāmra-cakra-vartin) subdues others naturally without exerting effort.
The transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) is likened to an iron-wheel-turning king (ayaścakra-vartin), who must enter the fray himself and exert force to achieve victory.

When the transformation body converts those of the two vehicles and ordinary beings, severing delusions through the thirty-four moments of mind, it is like a king fighting a battle with his own strength.
Regarding the phrase "all those who are equal": the severing of afflictions (*kleśa*) and the suppression of afflictions are both termed "subjugation.
Regarding the metaphor of "the various Māras resisting and opposing," the Sūtra says: "And those petty kings who do not obey his commands. Master Lu says:
This is discussed in reference to the time before the Iron-Wheel-Turning King has yet raised his army.

As for the minor kings who resist and oppose the King’s transformation through教化 (teaching/transformation), regarding what are called the "three types of māras," the *Jianyao* (Essential Summary) states: because there are the *pariccheda* (segmented) and *pariṇāma* (transformative) [deaths], there are three categories.

First, as for the three types of the segmented: the five contaminated (*sāsrava*) aggregates (*skandha*) within the segmented body are called the *skandha-māra*. Within the segmented body, at the point of death...
Death and that which has already died is called the *māra* of death (*mṛtyu-māra*). Afflictions are called the *māra* of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*). Regarding the transformation of the three *māras*:

the transformation of the five upper aggregates is called the *māra* of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*); the transformation of the upper cycle of birth and death is called the *māra* of death; and the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is called the *māra* of afflictions.

According to the actual state, there are three *māras* for both the fragmented (*paricchinna*) and the transformative (*pariṇāma*) [existences], totaling six *māras*, including those within the fragmented and transformative states.

Each has its own celestial māra; together with the aforementioned [four], these constitute the eight māras. Now, they are collectively referred to as the affliction-māra (*kleśa-māra*), the aggregate-māra (*skandha-māra*), and the death-māra (*mṛtyu-māra*);
thus, there are two categories. In the present commentary, the afflictions and the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) are combined and termed the "affliction-māra.

The five contaminated aggregates (*pañca-skandhāḥ sāsravāḥ*)—both those subject to transformation (*pariṇāma*) and those subject to fragmentation (*bhedana*)—are collectively termed the "aggregate-māra. The two types of death are combined and termed the "death-māra. Thus, there are two categories.

There are three [types of manifestation]. The *jī* (hairpin) manifests the segmented bodies of the celestial Māras (*deva-māra*) and others; because one destroys the celestial Māras upon these segmented bodies, it is not described as a manifestation, for these are mostly substantially existent.

Having attained Arhatship, one subdues the afflictions (*kleśa*). One does not continue into future existence (*punarbhava*), thereby subduing the two Māras of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*) and death (*mṛtyu-māra*).

The sons of the gods of the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*) and those of the Two Vehicles who have reached the stage of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*) apply effortful cultivation (*prayoga*), though [this] is slight.
It can be subdued partially. However, because it cannot be fully subdued over a long period of time, it is not said that the celestial Māras are subdued.
Regarding the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya), the celestial Māras manifest and thus it is said they exist. As for "breaking," one may break them by means of setting forth the signs of breaking.

Regarding the statement that the Noble Ones subdue and eliminate [the defilements] as an analogy: the Universal Monarch (Cakravartin) thought to himself, "This is like a moth throwing itself into a fire, or a cricket resisting the tracks of a chariot.

As for the scriptural passage mentioning the Universal Monarch and others, the intent of the commentary here is that "war" refers only to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), those in training (*śaikṣa*), and the Noble Ones who are in training—namely, those who have attained the first three fruits.
It does not mention those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), because their task is accomplished and they have already ceased [their striving].

The war has ceased; they await only their reward. Thus, when raising an army to punish [the defilements], those in the two vehicles who are still in training (śaikṣa) receive their reward, whereby many māras have already been eliminated.
When they enter the state of nirvana without remainder (anupadhiśeṣa), there is no further separate severance or separate realization via the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga).
It is only at the stage of total remainderlessness, when body and wisdom are extinguished, that their prior attainment is made manifest. Second, regarding the final existence of an arhat:
On the body composed of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), future existence (*punarbhava*) no longer continues;

even with respect to this very body that is currently suffering, it is also said to be "removed. Regarding the statement "not subduing the celestial Māra": Question: For instance, when Upacūḍaka tied three corpses around the neck of Māra, he was indeed able to subdue him.

Why, then, is the celestial Māra not mentioned here? Answer: The present statement concerns his inability to subdue [the practitioner] through spontaneous occurrence (*svarasataḥ*); it is not made with reference to [other forms of subjugation].

This refers to the preliminary application (*prayoga*). Furthermore, the Master of the Commentary (the *Sūshu*), following the subsequent portion of the sūtra text, combines the statement with the phrase "waging war against the five aggregates-māra, the afflictions-māra, and the death-māra," but does not mention the celestial-māra (*devaputra-māra*);
therefore, he says [the Buddha] did not subdue it. In reality, however, he did subdue it. As the *Jianyao* states:

The *bhavāgra* (segmental) celestial Māras can only be eliminated once one has attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*). Furthermore, the *pariṇāma* (transformational) celestial Māras manifest through illusory display;
therefore, they are not mentioned here. If these three Māras are eliminated, all others are subdued.

Regarding the phrase "and the category of the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)": Mouzi states that this section narrates the chapter on refuting Māra, which corresponds to the sevenfold classification in the *Fayuan*.
First, as for the specific names: 1. The Māra of the category of limited segments (*prādeśika*). 2. The Māra of the category of transformation (*pariṇāmika*).
Since the discriminating Māras obstruct the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), they are explained and refuted within this section. The Sūtra says: "Yet the various Māra kings are unwilling to comply."
"Prostrate" (*fu*) and so forth. Since the obstacle of the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa-māra*) obstructs the Bodhisattva, it is also "destroyed" herein.

Furthermore, some speak of three māras, referring to the subsequent combined passage where one battles the māra of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha-māra*), the māra of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*), and the māra of death (*mṛtyu-māra*). Or, some speak of four māras.

As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi* and the *Buddhabhūmi*, there are four types of māras: first, the afflictions (*kleśa*); second, the aggregates (*skandha*); third, death (*mṛtyu*); and fourth, the Māra of the devas (*devaputra-māra*).

Alternatively, eight māras are taught, as there are four each for both the *pariccheda* (segmented) and *pariṇāma* (transformative) forms of existence. Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* also speaks of eight māras, which follows the same pattern by adding four more to the aforementioned four.
Or, ten māras are taught, as explained in the *Kṣudraka-piṭaka*. The verse says: Desire, sorrow, hunger, thirst, craving, ... [the rest of the verse follows].
Sleep, fear, the poison of doubt, fame and profit, self-exaltation, and contempt for others—your army is thus, yet none can destroy it.
With the arrows of my wisdom and the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), I shall shatter it like a clay jar cast into water. Second, regarding the etymology:
in the Sanskrit language, it is fully called *māra*. Because it obstructs and destroys wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*), it is called *māra*. This is abbreviated as *mā*. It is also said:
Pāpīyas: this is translated as "the Evil One. If one uses the specific name Māra Pāpīyan, "Pāpīyan" is a corruption [of the original term].
If one says "Māra Pāpīyan," both names are cited together. Question: Why are there two names? Answer: The Evil Māra is precisely Māra.
"Cloud" (*yun*) means "to destroy. *Pāpīyan* is the same as *Pāpiman*; this is translated as "the Evil One" (*èzhě*). Therefore, it is said that both names are cited together.

Regarding the "demon of afflictions" (*fánǎomó*): "affliction" (*fán*) means "to disturb," and "affliction" (*nǎo*) means "to disorder. Sentient beings constantly dwell within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), [bound by] the aggregates (*skandha*).
"Māra" refers to an accumulation, which is called an *skandha* (aggregate). The "death-māra" (*mṛtyu-māra*) is so named because it is about to end, is currently ending, or has already ended.

The "heavenly-māra" (*deva-māra*) is called "heaven" (*deva*) because its divine function is luminous and pure. Regarding the "ten māras": that which is delightful is called "desire" (*kāma*); mental distress is called "sorrow" (*daurmanasya*);

the longing for food and drink is called "hunger and thirst" (*jighatsā-pipāsā*); indulgence in desire is called "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*); that which causes the mind to become dull and obscure is called "sleep" (*middha*).

Fear is that which is characterized by dread; doubt is the state of wavering between two alternatives; poison is that which afflicts the body and mind; fame and profit are the longing for reputation and wealth;
pride is the exalting of oneself and the disparaging of others. Regarding the three ways of identifying their essential nature: first, they depend upon conditioned activity (*saṃskāra*).

The four truths are established as follows: for the two vehicles and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), coarse and superficial objects and events are established as the *pariccheda-māra* (the demon of segmented existence).

Second, regarding the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*) and the non-established four truths, for Mahāyāna ordinary beings, subtle objects and events are established as the *pariṇāma-māra* (the demon of transformation).

The former applies to all three vehicles, while the latter applies only to Bodhisattvas. Because they can, according to their respective capacities, obstruct the wholesome matters of the three vehicles, they are called "demons" (*māra*). These are referred to as the three demons.
Regarding the "essence" (tǐ): Mōu says that this refers specifically to the three māras within the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

According to the corresponding text below, these are exclusively those previously destroyed by the followers of the Two Vehicles. All categories of afflictive hindrances pertaining to the paths of seeing and cultivation are called the *kleśamāra*.
The five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) produced by delusion, which arise and abide as obstacles to the Buddha-dharma, are called the *skandhamāra*. Based on the impermanence of these five aggregates...
The state of passing away, the process of dying, and the cessation that has already occurred after death is called the *māra* of death (*maraṇamāra*).

The son of a god from the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations (*paranirmitavaśavartin*) in the desire realm is called the celestial *māra* (*devaputramāra*). As for the essence of the eight *māras*: the root afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), whether manifest or in the form of seeds, are called the *māra* of afflictions (*kleśamāra*).
The contaminated five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) brought about by these very [afflictions] are called the *māra* of the aggregates (*skandhamāra*). It is these same five aggregates...
The exhaustion of retribution leading toward death, the actual moment of death, and the mark of cessation after death is called the *māra* of death (*maraṇamāra*).

The sixth is the *māra* of the body with its parts (*bhavāṅgamāra*), consisting of the sons of the gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*) together with their retinues. Next are the four *māras* of transformation (*pariṇāma*):

the seeds, manifest states, and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are called the *māra* of affliction of transformation (*kleśamāra*). The five aggregates (*skandha*) that are the fruit of transformative birth and death are called the *māra* of the aggregates (*skandhamāra*). Mindfulness...
The subtle falling into cessation is called the Māra of Death. As for the Māra of the Heavens (*devaputra-māra*):

it refers to those manifested by Bodhisattvas of the ten stages as Māras. The Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra states: "Those who act as Māra kings are mostly Bodhisattvas dwelling in the inconceivable liberation.
The Drum-Śrī-rāja-sūtra states: "The father of Amitābha Buddha is named Candrottarā; his mother is named Viśeṣacārumatī; the Māra is named..."
There is no one superior; there is only the dragon-elephant (nāga-hastin). To compete with a dragon-elephant, the strength of a donkey is not sufficient.

Therefore, when a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage is about to attain Buddhahood, how could there be no Māra who dares to act as an adversary? Because the objects of perception can give rise to desire, they are called the "Māra of Desire.
Sorrow is the feeling of grief (*daurmanasya*); hunger and thirst are experienced individually. All forms of craving are the craving for the five sensory objects (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*).

Sleep is the first [of the hindrances] of non-concentration. There are five types of fear: 1. Fear of non-sustenance (*ājīvikā-bhaya*), which arises from the discrimination of a self and the craving for the necessities of life.

2. Fear of ill-repute (*aśloka-bhaya*), which arises from performing unbeneficial acts while harboring expectations. 3. Fear of death (*maraṇa-bhaya*), which arises from the view of a self characterized by the apprehension of its destruction. 4.
Fear of the miserable destinies (*durgati-bhaya*), which arises from evil karma that prevents one from encountering the Buddhas. 5. Fear of the assembly (*parṣac-chāradya-bhaya*).
Fear (*bhaya*) consists of the five types of dread arising from perceiving one’s own realization as inferior to that of others; all of these have ignorance (*moha*) as their essence.
Doubt regarding the Māra has doubt as its essence, which is the very poison of hatred (*dveṣa*). "Poisonous harm" refers to reputation, while "raising up profit" refers to material assets.

Self-exaltation and contempt for others have pride (*māna*) as their essence. Regarding the four abandonments and establishments: there are two obstacles, namely, first, *nirvāṇa*, and second, *bodhi*.

"Ti. Based on the obstruction of the initial stage, the *pariccheda-māra* (segmentation māra) is established; based on the obstruction of the final stage, the *pariṇāma-māra* (transformation māra) is established.

Regarding the three māras, only wisdom (*prajñā*) is mentioned, because the Śrāvakas have ultimately severed them. Thus, the gate of the three māras is taught. That celestial māra entered Ānanda’s ear."
It was not heard that the Buddha entered nirvāṇa; however, when Upagupta was seated in meditative concentration, Māra placed flowers upon his neck.
It was only after he subsequently manifested supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) that he was able to subdue him. Because this was not a definitive conquest, it is omitted from the account.

Regarding the establishment of the four *māras*, one asks: why is karma not said to be included within the *māras*? The answer is: because the root of birth and death is dominated by afflictions (*kleśa*), whereas the aggregates (*skandha*) are collectively [the result of] karma.
[Answer: They are distinct. Because the fruit is superior and the cause is inferior, [the obstacle of] karma is not established. Question:

Why are the three matters of birth, old age, and illness not established as *māras*, while only the *māra* of death is established? Answer: Because the three types, such as birth, are inferior to death, they are not established [as *māras*].

As for the ten *māras*, each is established according to its predominant increase; therefore, they are mentioned specifically, as is clear from the *Māra-parivarta* in the *Dharmasaṃgīti-sūtra*. 5. Discerning that which is obstructed.

Regarding these: among the two types of *māra*, the *māra* of fragmented existence (*pariccheda-māra*) constitutes the obstacle for the three vehicles, while the *māra* of transformational rebirth (*pariṇāma-māra*) constitutes the obstacle for the Bodhisattva.

Among the three *māras* of the Bodhisattva, the *māra* of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*) obstructs *nirvāṇa with remainder*; the *māra* of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*) obstructs *nirvāṇa without remainder*;

and the *māra* of death (*mṛtyu-māra*) obstructs birth and longevity. Among the four *māras*, the first three are as previously explained; the celestial *māra* (*devaputra-māra*) obstructs all wholesome dharmas and obstructs the departure from desire.
Regarding the realms, there are three. As for the eight *māras*, the first four are identical to the latter four births; they respectively obstruct the four virtues of permanence and so forth.

The ten *māras* specifically obstruct the two gates of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). Regarding the six true destroyers, these are the four *māras* of the stage of segmented existence (*pariccheda-bhava*).

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that within the first dwelling of the ten dwellings of a Bodhisattva—the Dwelling of Initial Resolve—one is able to manifest the eight phases of attaining enlightenment (*aṣṭākāra-abhisambodhi*), having already subdued them.

The deva-māra of the fragmented stages has already attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and cannot obstruct [the practitioner]. Within the fourth stage, the "Abiding in Noble Birth," one subdues the various afflictive māras of conceptual discrimination among the obstacles of affliction (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
These are gradually subdued during the path of accumulation (*sambhāramārga*) and suddenly exhausted during the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*).

At the moment of the first bhūmi, the mind correctly severs them so that their conceptual essence is entirely exhausted. As for those that are innate (*sahaja*), they are gradually subdued during the path of preparation.

From the first bhūmi upward, these can be suppressed all at once. Nevertheless, by the power of intentional effort (*abhiprāya-bala*), they still arise up to the seventh bhūmi, yet this does not constitute a fault.
From the eighth bhūmi upward, they no longer function at all; this is the severance of their seeds by means of the vajra-like [samādhi]. Regarding the māra of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*):

according to Vasubandhu’s *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-śāstra*, from the first bhūmi upward, one undergoes transformational birth (*pariṇāmika-jāti*), thereby suppressing both the māras of the aggregates and death. As for that death...

If the Māra relies upon *vijñapti-mātra*, one attains the transformation of support (*parāvṛtti*) only upon reaching the eighth stage; it is only at the completion of the seventh stage that one abandons the two māras of the aggregates (*skandha*) and death (*maraṇa*).

As long as that transformation of support remains incomplete, one is said not to have departed from them. Regarding the object of knowledge consisting of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-jñeya*), this is abandoned during the fourth stage, the "Abiding in Noble Birth" (*janmaja-vihāra*);

the types of non-concomitant ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*) are suppressed during the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*) and can be suddenly eliminated during the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*).

They are subdued and exhausted. The innate cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that are forever severed at the first stage (*bhūmi*)—those existing within the six consciousnesses—are severed stage by stage throughout the ten stages;

from the eighth stage onward, they no longer function at all. Those within the seventh consciousness are severed stage by stage throughout the ten stages, until they are forever severed at the moment of the Diamond-like Mind (*vajropamasamādhi*).
As for the two demons of the death of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the aggregates (*skandha*), they alone...

Regarding the two explanations of consciousness: one says that because they have all already been abandoned when the Vajra Path arises, and because they are abandoned simultaneously with the seeds of the two obstacles, this is not the correct meaning;
rather, it is precisely when the Path of Liberation arises that they are finally discarded.

As for the *parināmika-māra*, since Amitābha Buddha already has a *māra* named Ajita (Unconquerable), what fault would there be in applying this to the aforementioned stages? One must [seek] Great Bodhi...

The Bodhisattva is able to perform the deeds of Māra; because he obstructs the great position, he manifests the appearance of having them, yet he also manifests their destruction. Seventh, regarding the manifestation of the destruction [of Māra]: Śākyamuni manifested the signs of subduing Māra.
With the arousal of the Vajra-mind, he subdued the Māra of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*). By relinquishing one-fifth of his lifespan, he subdued the Māra of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*).
Since the Māra of the aggregates delights in birth-and-death together with its concomitants, he accepted the invitation of the King of Māras and remained in his position for three months.

This demonstrates his mastery over death, thereby subduing the Māra of Death (*mṛtyu-māra*). However, regarding the subduing of the Māra of the Heavens (*deva-pūtra-māra*), there are two different textual accounts.

According to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, before attaining Buddhahood beneath the Bodhi tree, the Bodhisattva entered the samādhi of loving-kindness and arose from the *Rulai* (Tathāgata-lakṣaṇa) or *Raile* (Thunder) Samādhi to defeat the Māra of the Heavens;
this is consistent with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, which states that after the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū had defeated the armies of Māra.
One attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of this vehicle. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* speaks of the accomplishment of the Way through the eight phases (*aṣṭa-lakṣaṇa*).
Having attained *bodhi*, one subsequently destroys the celestial Māras. Since sentient beings differ according to their capacities, there is no need for them to assemble together.

However, what is required now is that the Noble One subdues and eliminates [the afflictions]; this is equivalent to the Two Vehicles’ destruction of the three armies. If one follows the Lesser Vehicle, when the true destruction occurs, it is not different from this.

The same applies here. That school admits the Four Truths; thus, when a Bodhisattva abandons the afflictions of the five stages through cultivation, this occurs prior to the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Their claim that "suppressing" (*vibhava*) the afflictions is equivalent to "abandoning" (*prahāṇa*) in the Mahāyāna is as follows:

if in the Mahāyāna one suppresses them such that they do not arise in the present, this constitutes the abandonment of their seeds. Thus, prior to the Path of Seeing, one suppresses the māra of innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa-māra*), and subsequently...

Upon entering the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one then severs the death-aggregate (*skandha-maraṇa*). At the moment of entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, one severs the celestial [existence]; it is only through preparatory effort (*prayoga*) that [the remaining aggregates] are brought down.
To say that this accords with the Buddha’s mind means that it is identical to the elder in the burning house seeing his children emerge from the fire;
his mind becomes serene, and he leaps for joy, and so forth.
Regarding the statement that there are three grades of rewards, the Sūtra says: "Rewards are bestowed in accordance with merit. This is like the seven stages of preparation (*saptavidha-prayoga*);

according to the degree to which one has subdued the afflictions prior to the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*), one is rewarded in accordance with that merit. The roots of goodness such as *uṣmagata* and so forth necessarily lead to the summit of *nirvāṇa*, and one never severs the roots of goodness.
If one considers the merit of what has been subdued and abandoned by those in training (*śaikṣa*), the fruit of the first stage (*prathama-phala*) and so forth are bestowed. Rā...

The bonds of the Han [era] are exhausted. Regarding the sheep and deer carts, as well as the illusory city (*nirmita-pura*), which are said to be initial metaphors for unconditioned merit (*asaṃskṛta-guṇa*): the Sūtra states that rewards are bestowed according to one's merit, such as fields, houses, villages, or cities;
in this context, it specifically says he was granted the city of Nirvāṇa (as in the third chapter).
Regarding the statement "the internal metaphor of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) and so forth," the Sūtra says: "Or it is like clothing and ornaments for the body" (this is the second [simile]).

Regarding the statement "the subsequent metaphor of the distinguished fruits and virtues and so forth," the Sūtra says: "Or various treasures, gold, silver, up to the people" (the upper heading and the lower explanation correspond to the first [simile]).
Regarding the statement that "the virtue of cessation (nirodha-guṇa) is the dwelling": this explains the first character, *huo* (惑, delusion/affliction). Question:

For what reason is unconditioned merit (*asaṃskṛta-guṇa*) designated as a "field" (*kṣetra*)? Answer: A field is the locus where merit grows and flourishes; it is so called because it can draw forth the wisdom of emptiness regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā-jñāna*).
Furthermore, it is called a "dwelling" (*gṛha*) because it serves as the support for conditioned merit. As for the three preceding fruits, there are nine times nine, which is eighty-one.
The six unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are called the "village" (*grāma*). A village is that which dwells scattered in various places.
Because the nirvāṇa thus attained subdues the marauders of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and establishes the deity of right wisdom, nirvāṇa is called the "city."

It speaks of shame (*hrī*), remorse (*apatrāpya*), patience (*kṣānti*), and so forth, explaining the virtues of conditioned activity (*saṃskāra-guṇa*). The Sūtra states: "One may provide clothing and ornaments for the body;
however, sufficient shame and remorse serve as clothing, while the fivefold Dharma-body and the abiding in the six objects serve as ornaments. "Constantly" (*nityam*) has the meaning of permanence.

Regarding the six objects, they correspond to the six thieves of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*); the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) are thus the six that lack meaning. For the sake of the noble ones (*ārya*), [they are otherwise].
These are called the six objects. When ordinary persons perceive them, if they perceive and become attached to an adverse object, aversion arises; because of aversion, distress arises.
If they perceive and become attached to a favorable object, joy and pleasure arise. If they perceive and become attached to a neutral object, craving arises; because of craving, delusion arises.
The Sage, in accordance with the occasion, dwells in equanimity alone, abiding in right mindfulness and impartiality; because he constantly observes [these], it is called "constant abiding.
For an Arhat, this serves as an outward adornment of the body, differing from the Mahāyāna attainment of the marks and signs of radiance.
The mention of "dhyāna, samādhi, and liberation" serves as a metaphor for the excellence of the various fruits [of practice].

The passage in the sutra from "various precious jewels" to "the people" refers to the various distinctions among conditioned merits (*saṃskṛta-guṇa*). "Dhyāna" refers to the four dhyānas; "samādhi" refers to the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*);
and "liberation" refers to the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*). The six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*) of the two vehicles are likened to the elephant, horse, and chariot.

Regarding the statement that "the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā-jñāna) is a servant," one interpretation says: the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) are the masters, and the wisdom of the emptiness of persons is the servant.

Another interpretation says: the fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna) is the master, and the subsequently attained wisdom (prsthalabdha-jñāna) is the servant. (The first interpretation is adopted here. Now, these mental phenomena arise from four conditions.
Driven by the convergence of various conditions, they are only then spurred into action; that which appears before one is what is currently manifesting.

To say that the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭāv abhibhvāyatanāni*) act as maidservants means that for ordinary persons, the object is superior to the mind, and the mind flows following the object, thus being driven like a servant.
For the minds of noble ones, the mind is superior to the object, and the object follows the mind; thus, the master commands the servant, and the mind is brought under control.
Regarding objects—whether they be more or less numerous, or blue or yellow—the mind is superior to the object; this is called "victory over subduing.
Since all objective forms are the instruments of cognition, they are like female servants.
Regarding the "ten spheres of totality" (*daśa-kṛtsnāyatana*) and so forth: they pervade all places. Just as the common people [pervade] a kingdom, the Buddha-dharma is of vast utility and breadth;
because it completely fills the great trichiliocosm, it is called "totality" (*kṛtsna*). It is so named because it is omnipresent in every location.
Regarding the statement "the parable of the Great Vehicle has not yet been bestowed," the Sūtra says: "The bright pearl within the topknot alone is not given to them.

This refers to the period before the forty years [of his ministry], when he had not yet preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Thus, he long remained silent regarding this essential teaching and did not strive to preach it hastily. Had he preached it during those forty years, it would have been like showing the most precious jewel to a fool;

the fool would have laughed at it. As the Sūtra corroborates: *Just as a man who possesses a priceless jewel, Would show it to a foolish person; The fool, seeing it, would laugh in derision.* This is the scriptural evidence.
Why is this? Why not give it to them? The answer is: if one perceives that the various people have owners for the pearl atop their heads, then giving it to them would not cause surprise.
However, this single pearl is upon the head of the King alone; if it were given away, the King’s retinue would surely be greatly shocked and astonished.
Just as forty years ago, when he preached the Lotus Sūtra and bestowed predictions of enlightenment, the Bodhisattvas were astonished—even though...

The delusion regarding分段生死 (paricchinna-jarāmaraṇa, segmented birth and death) is called "minor merit," as it has not yet shattered 變易生死 (pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa, transformative birth and death); thus, it is not called "great merit.

Regarding the phrase "that which is maintained by the mind's preeminent [faculty]," this takes the two dharmas of mindfulness (smṛti) and wisdom (prajñā) as the maintainers, citing the five mental factors that arise simultaneously.
Therefore, it is said that the mind is primary.

Regarding the statement that this accords with the Dharma-king’s transformative teaching: the preceding metaphor states, "Mañjuśrī, for example, it is like a powerful Wheel-turning Sage King who wishes to subdue various kingdoms through his majestic power. The present application of the sutra says, "Mañjuśrī, it is like..."
The coming is likewise thus. As for "reaching the Dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu*), it is partially attained within the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

Having partially attained the Dharma-realm, at the time of attaining Buddhahood, one realizes the *svābhāvikakāya* (Self-nature Body). The *svābhāvikakāya* abides in the realm of the Dharma-nature; this is called "attaining the Dharma-realm."
Regarding the statement "the king within the three realms," this refers to the basis upon which the various emanations—both great and small—rely; thus, it is called the "king.

Within the three realms, the two lands of the *paranirmita-vashavartin* (enjoyment for others) and the *svasaṃbhoga* (self-enjoyment) are omitted. Just as the analogy above takes the Iron-Wheel-Turning King, so too here, the middle [category] likewise refers only to the land that is the basis for the emanated substance (*nirmāṇakāya-rūpa*), because it does not depart from the *dharmatā-dhātu* (dharma-nature realm).
Regarding the statement "this assembly of Māras collectively resists and opposes": the previous metaphor spoke of various minor kings who did not obey their commands;
this corresponds to what the present sutra says: "the various māra kings are unwilling to submit and comply."

Regarding the phrase "corresponding to the Sage and subduing and eliminating": the preceding allegorical sutra states, "At that time, the Wheel-Turning King raised various armies and went forth to punish [the enemy].
The present corresponding sutra states, "A single word of the Tathāgata’s noble sages.

The previous passage concerning the Wheel-Turning King corresponds to the statement in the sutra, "The various generals fought together with him," which corresponds to the aforementioned raising of various armies to go forth and punish.
Regarding the statement that "this [application] follows the merit to receive the Way": first, it corresponds to "joy.

The preceding metaphor states that when a king sees his soldiers who have performed meritorious service in battle, he is greatly pleased; now, the application of the sutra says that those who possess merit likewise experience joy in their hearts.

Subsequently, regarding the correspondence with "bestowing rewards," the original metaphorical sutra states that rewards are bestowed according to merit, such as granting fields, houses, villages, or cities.

A village. Or he may give garments and articles for adorning the body; or he may give various kinds of rare treasures, such as gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, agate, coral, amber, elephants, horses, carriages, slaves, and subjects. Now, this section here is inverted and does not follow the proper sequence.
The Sūtra says: "He bestows upon him the two phrases of dhyāna-samādhi and vimokṣa. This corresponds to the third [section] of the preceding [passage].

The six items—various precious jewels, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musāragalva, agate, coral, and amber—are abbreviated in the sutra text and do not correspond to the preceding phrase regarding "elephants, horses, and carriages.

The sutra’s two phrases—"the roots and powers free from outflows" and "the wealth of all dharmas"—correspond to the second item in the preceding analogy: "or providing clothing and ornaments for the body."
The scriptural passage states: "Furthermore, he bestows upon them the city of Nirvana," meaning that by attaining extinction (*nirvāṇa*), their minds are guided and they are all made to rejoice.
This combines with the first two lines of the preceding section: "Or [he gives] fields, houses, villages, cities, and towns. Therefore, the commentary states:
"According to the previous metaphor, the corresponding meaning can be understood. This corresponds to the part where [the Buddha] has not yet bestowed this sutra.
This is like the statement in the sutra that the bright jewel from within the topknot alone is not given to them.
Why is this? Because this single jewel exists only upon the king’s head; if it were given to them, the king’s retinue would surely be greatly startled and alarmed.

Now, although they are gathered together, he does not preach this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* for them. The preceding was the parable; here, in the application (*yoga*), there is only the Dharma (the former application concerns the past provisional [teachings]).

Regarding the statement that the true teaching of giving has two aspects: first, the explanation of the luminous pearl belonging to the "pearl of understanding" serves as a metaphor for treating those who have accumulated merit through the sixth [perfection].
Second, the luminous pearl belongs to the explanation of the unsurpassed.

Regarding the first analogy, the Sūtra says: "Mañjuśrī, it is like a wheel-turning monarch who, seeing among his troops those who have performed great service, feels profound joy and bestows rewards upon them; this is the direct antidote."

Regarding the phrase "the various hosts of soldiers," the *Huàdù* (Transformation and Salvation) section is divided into four parts. First is the "Mahāyāna Host of Soldiers," which refers to the manifold Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
The word "various" (*zhū*) carries multiple meanings. An-guo states that the Master [of the Commentary] addresses a potential objection:

someone might ask, "If those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) who have turned their minds toward enlightenment can certainly destroy the four māras of the *pariṇāmika-nirvāṇa*, they must already have heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*."

He obtains the jewel. Since the Bodhisattva has already shattered the four māras of transformation and change (*pariṇāma-vikāra*), why does he not bestow upon him the jewel of preaching the sūtras? The answer is:

because the Bodhisattva has already divided and shattered the four māras of transformation and change, his merit and achievement are great; thus, for him, the preaching of the *Anantārtha-sūtra* (The Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings) is called "untying the jewel.
This is termed the "army of the Mahāyāna. Second, regarding the "army of the Two Vehicles," Lu Fu asked: "According to..."

The Sūtra possesses great merit and simultaneously masters the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) of the Two Vehicles. According to the intent of the treatise’s author, however, this refers to ordinary beings still in training (*śaikṣa*).

Why is there this contradiction? Answer: A person at the stage of no-more-learning attains that state by severing defilements and becoming a sage, having previously been at the stage of one in training.
Judged according to this treatise, it does not contradict the Sūtra. Mou quotes Zizhou as saying: "In explaining the seven similes, all..."
There are two intentions: first, to speak of the past; second, to illustrate by contrast with the present.

Regarding the terms "complete destruction" and "partial destruction": before one has attained the state of *aśaikṣa* (no-more-learning), there is partial destruction, which refers to the destruction of the three māras in segments; once the state of *aśaikṣa* is realized, it is complete destruction.

This completely refutes [the objection]. It is universally granted that those of the Two Vehicles who are still in training (*śaikṣa*) can turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna] and be granted the name of "undergoing transformation" (*pariṇāmika*);

thus, they possess great merit. Question: Bodhisattvas have already shattered the four māras of transformation and possess great merit; they may be granted the bright pearl. However, those of the Two Vehicles have not yet shattered the four māras of transformation;
how can they be given the pearl? Answer: They shall be able to shatter them by turning their minds; it is certain that they will shatter them.
The four māras of transformation and change are likewise given the pearl of the name-teaching of the *Lotus Sūtra*.

Because they were previously śrāvakas but later become bodhisattvas, this causes them to give rise to a mind of certainty. First, the pearl of the name-teaching of the *Lotus Sūtra* is bestowed upon them, and only afterward are the four māras of transformation and change destroyed.
It is said that this is like the generals of worldly armies; citing such examples serves to encourage and inspire. It is not only in the Buddha-dharma that this is so.
For instance, in the world, if a general engages in minor battles, he first exerts his efforts and only afterwards receives his reward.
However, if one whose will is valiant and fierce intends to establish great merit, they are first granted official rank and emoluments, and only thereafter do they engage in battle.

The statement that "this person has not yet entered the ten stages" clarifies the essence [of the jewel] by way of its stage. As for the statement that those of the two vehicles and so forth have "obtained the jewel," this refers to the "teaching-jewel.

It is only from the tenth stage onward, when one truly destroys the four māras of the *pariṇāma* (transformative) nature, that one obtains the actual essence of the jewel. (The preceding section concludes the explanation of the parable.)
Regarding the statement that "this light has already destroyed the *pariccheda* [segmented existence] and so forth," Huàdù says: "This refers to destroying the Māras with respect to persons.

Regarding the statement that "it is not all [beings, etc.]," the question is raised: "If even *śrāvakas* of fixed nature destroy the four *māras* of segmented existence, why is it not said that those of fixed nature who are not 'deluded regarding the Dharma' (i.e., those who will eventually attain Buddhahood) are given the jewel upon hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*? The answer in the commentary states: "It is not so."
"All are equal" means that those of indeterminate nature, having attained the fruit of no-more-learning (aśaikṣaphala), shall give rise to the Great Mind and destroy the four māras of transformation;
this is called "great merit. Even if śrāvakas who incline toward tranquility were to destroy the four māras of the segmented [existence], [they would not attain such greatness].
There is no sense of ever turning back the mind; such a person is not said to possess great merit, nor is a jewel given to them.

However, because a *śaikṣa* who has regressed from their resolve is also granted [the jewel], when a *śaikṣa* turns their mind toward [the Mahāyāna] and shall destroy the *pariṇāmika-vipariṇāma*, they too are granted the jewel.
The above applies generally to both *śaikṣas* and *aśaikṣas*, and is collectively termed "great merit."

Regarding the phrase "or again": the former [category] includes those in training (śaikṣa), whereas this refers exclusively to those beyond training (aśaikṣa). The term "one who regresses from the mind" (*cittavivartaka*) is used to distinguish them from those of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*) who are beyond training.
The statement that “there are two types of the four māras” is a general indication within the analysis of their categories.
The statement that “now, following what is essential, the three māras of the segmented [existence]” is a brief explanation provided in response to specific difficulties. The *Fayuan* states:

“Whether they are seeds or manifest, as well as the dharmas such as the corresponding habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of afflictions and the knowable, these are called the māra of afflictions (*kleśamāra*). This refers to the segmented [existence].

The two kinds of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are called the *skandha-māra*. That which is characterized by the cessation of the state of being about to die, the actual dying, and having already died—namely, the death of the segmented [existence]—is called the *mṛtyu-māra*.
Furthermore, the subtle and continuous cessation of the contaminated (*sāsrava*) five aggregates within the body of transformation is also called the *mṛtyu-māra*.
Regarding the "descent of the rank" and the "time of descent," these refer to the sequence of descending from the remaining three māras. As for the different times of descent:
in some cases, one becomes a Buddha and subsequently subdues the celestial māras; in other cases, one subdues the māras and then attains enlightenment. Regarding the *Līlāvatāra-vyākhyā*, Mou says:
This is the commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* composed by the Master [Kamalaśīla].

Regarding the statement, "Now, relying on the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* and other texts," this refers to the four or fivefold analytical examination. By knowing that the body of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) is truly suffering, one does not give rise to craving and attachment;
thus, one can destroy the māra of the aggregates (*skandhamāra*). By severing the afflictions of the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*), one destroys the māra of afflictions (*kleśamāra*).
By realizing the principle of the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya), one accomplishes the body of liberation and attains the two types of nirvāṇa; thus, one destroys the Māra of Death.
By cultivating the wisdom of the Truth of the Path (mārga-satya) and giving rise to supernormal powers (abhijñā), one is able to subdue the fourth Māra, the Devaputra Māra.

The phrase "next, observing that which is with outflows" (*sāsrava*) refers to the second stage. Since one has already realized that what is with outflows is suffering, one develops a profound sense of revulsion and a lack of delight;
thus, one destroys the *skandha-māra*. By observing that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, one does not give rise to afflictions (*kleśa*), thereby subduing the *kleśa-māra*.

By observing that all phenomena (*dharma*) are without self (*anātman*), one destroys the *mṛtyu-māra*, because the *mṛtyu-māra* gains mastery [over one] through [the perception of a self]. Now, one acts without...

For this reason, in order to counteract the Māra of Death, one contemplates the tranquility of *nirvāṇa* and realizes the principle; thereby, one destroys the Māra of the Deva King (*devaputra-māra*).

Regarding the statement "furthermore, contemplating emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and so forth," this is the third stage. Because one contemplates the emptiness of all phenomena (*dharma*), one destroys the Māra of the Aggregates (*skandha-māra*).

Because one contemplates the signlessness (*animitta*) of all phenomena, one destroys the Māra of Afflictions (*kleśa-māra*). Because one does not seek or desire conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), one destroys the Māra of Death.
Māra. Furthermore, if one turns the mind back toward Buddhahood, one immediately destroys the celestial Māra (*devaputra-māra*).

Regarding the statement "next, contemplate the body, sensations, and so forth," this is the fourth stage. Contemplating the impurity of the body destroys the *skandha-māra*, because knowing the body is impure, one does not delight in dwelling within it.
Contemplating that sensation is suffering destroys the *kleśa-māra*. Contemplating the mind as impermanent... [contemplate] mindfulness.

Mindfulness of arising and ceasing destroys the Māra of Death, because one is single-mindedly weary of death. Contemplating the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya) subdues the Māra of the Heavens, because the realization of the principle of selflessness gives rise to untainted wisdom (anāsrava-jñāna). Thus, one overcomes the celestial Māras.
Regarding the phrase "The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says... and so forth: this is the fifth section of the detailed analysis (the preceding section clarified "joy").
The statement "this clarifies the giving" specifically clarifies the bestowing of the jewel. The Sūtra says: "This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* can cause sentient beings to reach [the goal];
now that it is being preached, it is identical to the main body of the teaching. As for why it was not previously preached: the time for its preaching had not yet arrived.
Therefore, now is precisely the time to definitively expound the Mahāyāna.

As for the statement that there are many who harbor resentment and slander, it is identical to what was previously stated in the sūtra: even while the Tathāgata is currently present, there are still many who feel resentment and hostility toward him.
How much more so after his parinirvāṇa? Before it has even flourished in the forest, the wind will surely destroy it. Master Sengyou said: "The Way is great, yet faith is difficult;
when the fame is high, harmony is rare. When Mount Sumeru is lofty, the gale-wind arises; when the treasure-store is accumulated, the enemy-thief appears.

This sutra stands above all other scriptures because it is the cause for attaining Buddhahood; therefore, there are many who harbor resentment and jealousy. This clearly explains the teaching through the Dharma itself.
Regarding "and the jewel":

the statement concerning the principle (*artha*) expressed by the words and so forth takes the principle expressed as the jewel; the subsequent statement takes the expression that brings it forth as the jewel.
These two statements regarding the teaching and the principle constitute the explanatory synthesis of the analogy of the jewel. The text states: "This belongs to the analogy."
Therefore, it is not a textual redundancy; rather, it is a redundancy of meaning. This is also the second time the *maṇiratna* (wish-fulfilling jewel) is explained.

If a Wheel-turning King possessed two jewels and they were explained in two separate places, that would constitute a redundancy. Since the substance of the Wheel-turning King’s jewel is one, it is simply used in two different locations.
According to the scriptural text, this is the application (*yoga*) of the preceding simile; thus, the text itself is not redundant. If...
According to the reasoning of this teaching, the analogy of the priceless jewel refers to the fact that the sūtra being discussed expounds the supreme meaning; this is the remainder of the sense.
Within the exposition of the supreme, there is both principle and teaching; this proclaims the principle.
Regarding the term "foremost" (ch'ui-siang): Mou says that because the two aspects of teaching and principle (*śāstra*) herein surpass those of other sūtras, it is called "foremost.
"Foremost" carries the meaning of being unsurpassed (*anuttara*). Question: While it was previously stated that one aspect is principle, how is it known that the latter aspect is teaching?
The answer is that the Sūtra itself states: "the secret treasury. Here, "treasury" refers to the teaching. It further says: "and expound it.

Regarding the statement that this corresponds to the first fourteen and a half verses: the first four verses establish the *Anrakugyō* (Peaceful Practices), while the subsequent ten verses praise the excellence of the Sūtra.
To combine these two sections into one place is what is meant by "correspondence" (*gō*).
Regarding the term "initial" (*ādi*): Mouyun states that it refers to the second section that follows; it is collectively termed the "fruit of peace and bliss.
Since it is called "initial," it stands in contrast to the concluding response that follows.
Regarding the statement that "the first verse provides a general outline": this refers to the division within the first four verses of the *Anrakugyō* (Peaceful Conduct).
The first verse provides the general outline, which corresponds to the passage in the sutra beginning with "constantly practicing patience" and ending with "praising the sutra."
Regarding these three separate verses, they specifically describe the practice of peaceful conduct (*sukhavihāra*). The prose of the sutra states:
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, in the future final age when the Dharma is about to perish, there will be those who receive, uphold, and recite the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Among householders and renunciants, they shall give rise to great loving-kindness; and among those who are not bodhisattvas, they shall give rise to great..."
Regarding compassion: within these three verses, the first verse and its single line describe the compassion mentioned in the preceding prose.
As for the statement that "one verse and three lines eulogize the arousal of mindfulness," the prose of the sutra says: "One should form this thought:
'Such a person has suffered a great loss; the Tathāgata’s skillful means in preaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate have not been heard, nor known, nor realized by them.'"

They do not inquire, they do not believe, and they do not understand. Although such persons neither inquire about, believe in, nor understand this sutra, when I attain unexcelled bodhi, wherever they may be, I shall use my supernatural powers to lead them so that they may dwell within this Dharma.
The present verse says: "These do not hear" refers to the three phrases.

Regarding the phrase "the one king," this is a metaphor for the Dharma King’s transformative teaching; it corresponds to the two phrases in the sutra: "For example, like a powerful universal monarch."
Regarding the "two merits," it refers to the passage in the sutra that says:

"Those who have merit in battle. Regarding the "three gifts," it refers to the passage that says: "Bestowing various objects as rewards. Other sutras speak of two verses concerning elephants, horses, and chariots;
these verses follow the prose section of the sutra which states: "When the king sees the troops who have achieved merit in battle, he is greatly delighted."
Rewards were bestowed according to merit: some were given fields, houses, villages, and cities; some were given clothing and ornaments for the body;
some were given various kinds of rare treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, agate, coral, amber, elephants, horses, carriages, and male and female slaves.
This is a metaphor for bestowing the Way according to one's merit. For brevity, the previous account of the various Māras’ resistance and opposition is not related here.

The analogies: the three analogies, such as the *Sūtra on the Bestowal of This Sūtra*, which illustrate how the Noble Ones subdue and eliminate [defilements]. Regarding the first verse, which illustrates the reality:
the prose of the sūtra states, "I shall not give him the bright jewel from within my topknot. Why is this? Because this single jewel exists only upon the king’s crown;
if it were given to him, the king’s retinue would surely be greatly shocked and astonished. Now, the verse says: "As if there were..."
"Valiant and resolute conduct is this.

Regarding the phrase "this is the first," etc., the three and a half verses combined with the former provisional [teachings]. In the prose commentary, the textual alignment consists of only five [sections].
Now, these are briefly restated in verse: "The various Māras oppose and resist; the Noble One subdues and eliminates them," and so forth—this solely accords with the Dharma-king’s bestowal.
The analogy of transformation according to merit and receiving the Way: Regarding the Dharma King’s dispensation of transformation, the prose section of the sutra states:
"Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata is also like this; by the power of meditative concentration and wisdom, he has attained the kingdom of the Dharma and reigns over the triple world.
Now, the verse says: "The Tathāgata is likewise," which consists of one and a half lines.
Regarding the merit of a single verse, the long prose version states: "Those who possess such merit feel joy in their hearts;
among the fourfold assembly, they preach various sutras for them, causing their minds to rejoice. The present verse says: "Seeing all people practice this one path."

Regarding the phrase "bestowing a single verse," the prose sūtra states: "He bestows the wealth of dharmas such as meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), liberation (*vimokṣa*), the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), and the powers (*bala*);
furthermore, he grants the city of *nirvāṇa*. He speaks of attaining extinction (*parinirvāṇa*) and guides their minds, causing them all to rejoice.
The present verse says: "For the sake of these sentient beings, this is the single practice."
Regarding the statement "these various sūtras," it refers to the various sūtras prior to the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
As for the statement "this [sūtra] combined with the present one actually consists of two," the first is the "present" and the second is the "analogy. The prose section of the sūtra says:
"Mañjuśrī, it is like a wheel-turning monarch who, seeing among his troops those who have performed great service, feels profound joy and, because of this..."
This jewel of faith has long resided within my topknot; it was not given away recklessly, yet now I give it to you. Afterward, they shall be joined.
Upon being joined, there is first the joy of union. The Tathāgata is likewise so: he is the Great Dharma King within the triple world, teaching the Dharma to all sentient beings.
He beholds the army of the noble ones as they battle together with the Māra of the five aggregates, the Māra of afflictions, and the Māra of death.
...and so forth. Regarding the subsequent synthesis with the first [section], the prose states: "This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* can cause sentient beings to reach all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
It is full of enmity and difficult to believe in throughout all worlds; that which was not previously taught is now being taught.

Now, the first one and a half verses of the verse section describe this synthesis of the present reality. The Sūtra says: "Having known that sentient beings have already obtained its power... and so on.

One and a half lines of the practice are as follows; the subsequent one and a half lines are to be combined with the *maṇi* (jewel). The Sūtra says: "This sūtra is the most honored, the foremost among all sūtras;
these one and a half verses are it. Thus far there are four [sections]: first, the practice of right physical conduct; second, the practice of right verbal conduct;

third, the practice of self-benefit through the mind’s departure from all evils; fourth, the practice of benefiting others by cultivating all virtues within the mind. These four practices differ, each having both prose and verse.
[The Buddha] spoke. This shall be explained in general as the second section, which clarifies the answer. Above, there were three parts; first was the statement of the answer. The Sūtra says:
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī, “If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, in the future final age, wishes to expound this sūtra, he should abide securely in four dharmas.

Second is the clarification of the answer. The Sūtra states: “First, abiding securely in the bodhisattva’s sphere of practice (*caryā-vihāra*) and the sphere of association (*sevā-vihāra*), he is able to...”

For the sake of sentient beings, he expounds this sutra. This consists of three responses. The sutra states: "After my parinirvāṇa, those who seek the Buddha-way [are as follows]," which comprises one and a half lines.
These three sections are distinct; they are all, in essence, the four lines concerning the shared cause of peace and bliss mentioned in the initial proclamation.

Regarding the statement that the second section clarifies the general aspect of peaceful bliss (*anurakṣaṇā-sukha*): it is because this serves as a general announcement of the characteristics of the fruit-bliss resulting from the preceding [practices].
Mōu says: This is named in contrast to the specific fruits of the four preceding practices; since this differs from the fruits within those four types of peaceful conduct, it is termed "general.
Within the first section on the practice of correct physical conduct, four and a half verses describe the fruit of peaceful bliss. The Sūtra states: "If there is anyone..."
"Kauṇḍinya, after my parinirvāṇa, when one enters this sphere of practice and this sphere of intimacy and preaches this sutra, there shall be no timidity or the like.
Within the section on Right Speech and Conduct, there are five verses concerning the fruit of peace and happiness. The sutra says:

'After my parinirvāṇa, if there should be a bhikṣu who is able to expound this wondrous Lotus Sutra, his mind shall be free from envy, anger, and all afflictive obstructions, nor shall he have any sorrow.'"

Regarding those who grieve or revile [the practitioner]: their minds are detached from all evils, and they abide in the fruit of the practice for one's own benefit, which is peace and happiness. As the Sūtra says:

"Mañjuśrī, when this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, in the future final age when the Dharma is about to perish, has accomplished this third practice for peace and happiness, no one will be able to disturb or confuse him while he is preaching this Dharma; he will obtain good companions with whom he may read together."
Recite this sutra. In the practice of cultivating the mind for the benefit of others, there is the fruit of peace and happiness. The long version states:
"Mañjuśrī, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who accomplish this fourth dharma..."
When this sutra was being preached, there were no faults or such [defects]. However, the commentary below does not describe these fruits.
Regarding the statement that the body of one verse and a half is free from the six evils: first, one who reads this sutra will always be free from sorrow and affliction;
second, they will have no illness or pain; third, their complexion will be bright and pure; fourth, they will not be born into poverty; fifth, they will not be lowly or base; sixth, they will not...
Ugly. Regarding the phrase "beings such as those of a single verse," the Sūtra says "beings who delight in seeing [him]," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "the three external evils of a single verse," they are: first, weapons are not employed against him; second, poisons cannot harm him; third, if a person...

When one utters evil abuse, the mouth becomes as if blocked. Question: Why is it that a Bodhisattva who upholds this sutra does not avoid being struck by sticks and stones, or being subjected to insults and derision?

Does this teaching mean that the power of upholding the sutra prevents weapons and staves from being used against him? Answer: That refers to the Bodhisattva’s skillful means in taming sentient beings;
this refers to the empowerment bestowed by the power of the sutra itself. As for the statement that the mouth is "blocked," this does not refer to the act of upholding the sutra.
Feeling moved by others in this way, he likewise merely seeks to discipline sentient beings and cause them to resolve their minds for enlightenment.

It is as with the following incantation against all poisons and curses: "Those who wish to harm one's person, when they recollect the power of Avalokiteśvara, shall have [the curse] return upon themselves."
Regarding the phrase "fearlessness in a single verse," this refers to the scriptural passage beginning with "wandering" and so forth. To summarize briefly:
the commentary’s statement that it "clarifies the fruit of bliss" refers comprehensively to the fruits of all four types of bliss; it does not refer exclusively to the text of the fourth section.

Regarding the statement that the first one and a half verses concern "seeing the Buddha" and so forth, the *Śāstra* (the *Vivṛti*) summarizes the inquiry as follows: "External objects fundamentally do not exist; on what basis, then, does a dream arise?
The answer, as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, is that there are five causes for dreams: First, when heat is predominant, one dreams of fire; yellow is also generally associated with this.

Second, when cold is predominant, one dreams of water; white is primarily associated with this. Third, when wind-energy (*vāyu*) is predominant, one dreams of flying; black is predominantly associated with this. Fourth, it arises from intense reflection.

Therefore, one sees things in dreams. When the five celestial deities grant a dream, it is intended to make one aware of future events. Furthermore, when the yin element is predominant, one dreams of water;
when the yang element is predominant, one dreams of fire; and when both yin and yang are equally predominant, one dreams of neutral phenomena.
Now, this case—where the power of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the sutras bestows a dream—is similar to the fifth category [of dream causes] and is likewise not contradictory.
From here below, the text explains the "Emergence.
Regarding the phrase "the preceding chapter, etc.," this refers to the "Chapter on Peaceful Practices" (Anrakugyō-hon).
The six chapters that follow emerge from this point, extending up to the "Chapter on Never-Despising" (Fukyō-hon).

Regarding the mention of "life span" and "analysis" (*vibhaṅga*), the "Life Span Chapter" (*Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*) serves to resolve preceding doubts. The "Analysis Chapter" (*Vibhaṅga-parivarta*) is named because it describes their successive arising;
