this is due to the ritual procedures (*vidhi*) of the various Buddhas and Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva mentioned in the preceding text. The "Peaceful Conduct Chapter" (*Śuklavidarśana-parivarta*) concerns the practice to be performed.
The "Emergence Chapter" (*Niraya-parivarta*) refers to those who have long been free from injury and destruction while practicing peaceful conduct. Once the assembly of people...
The assembly was vast and their stages of practice were extensive. Maitreya said, "Among this multitude, I do not recognize even a single person.
Śākyamuni replied, "These are my disciples whom I have constantly taught and transformed. Thereupon, Maitreya posed questions, which caused the entire assembly to give rise to doubt.
He then addressed the Buddha: "World-Honored One, Tathāgata, when you were a prince and departed from the palace of the Śākyas, you went not far from the city of Gayā."
Seated at the site of enlightenment, he attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. From that time until now, only forty years have passed.

World-Honored One, this matter is difficult for the world to believe. It is, for example, like a person with beautiful complexion and black hair, aged twenty—

Regarding the phrase "ascending into the air," some say it refers to descending from the flowers to pay homage;

"When these Bodhisattvas reach their dwelling, they first all remain beneath this Sahā world. Mǔ says: "This already excludes other locations; why then does the Sūtra speak of 'this'?"

Regarding the phrase "by means of equality" (*samatayā*), the Sūtra states: "When these bodhisattvas heard the cessation of Śākyamuni Buddha’s [teaching], they raised their voices for the sake of the bodhisattvas here in this world.
When the bodhisattvas heard it said that within our Sahā world there are already sixty thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, this sound arose from below and reached them.

Regarding the phrase "three *nayuta*," the sutra says: "How much more so for thousands of millions of billions of *nayuta* retinues? How much more so for hundreds of millions of retinues?"
Regarding "the four directions," the sutra says: "How much more so ten million, one million, or even ten thousand.
Regarding "five thousand," the sutra says: "How much more so one thousand."

Regarding the statement "seventy," the sutra says "up to eleven.

In total, they belong to the single unit. Mou said: "This is also not the case. Taking ten as the head, all subsequent numbers are subsumed within the ten.

Regarding the term "eight single [cases]," the Sūtra says: "How much more so for a single individual. A second interpretation states that the eight instances of the word "how much more so" (況復) constitute the eight categories. This interpretation is excellent.

The scriptural passage "such as these" serves as the third conclusion. Question: Since the preceding eight categories each have their own specific number, why does the scripture state that "the number is unknown"?

As for the statement that "the second [group] ascended into the air to offer praise and prostration," it is also said that they descended with flowers to offer praise and prostration; logically, they should have come bearing the flowers.

Furthermore, according to the assembly of Bodhisattvas at the ocean-like gathering, they descend with flowers to prostrate before the Buddha. The Sūtra states: "Each went to the void [and offered] the seven treasures..."
The "Marvelous Stūpa" should be called the "Jeweled Stūpa," which is level with the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings; it is named the "Stūpa Reached by Traveling through Space.

Regarding the passage in the Sūtra that says, "He approached the two World-Honored Ones and prostrated at their feet," there are two interpretations: first, it refers to prostrating at the feet; second, it refers to performing four prostrations with the full count of ritual gestures.

Regarding the passage in the Sūtra stating that even the Buddhas seated upon lion thrones beneath the various jewel trees all perform prostrations: Question:

Regarding the phrase "a single praise over a long period," the Sūtra says: "These bodhisattvas [praise] for half a day. The Sūtra also says:

The Buddha is the object of praise, while the bodhisattvas are the agents of praise. It is called the "Dharma of praise by the bodhisattvas" because it follows the name of the person who praises.
Regarding the Dharma, it refers to the passage beginning with "His countenance was most wondrous and sublime.

Since the Buddha’s virtues are vast and great, they were only completely encompassed through praise lasting fifty intermediate kalpas.

Regarding the statement that "the power of receiving praise is also equal": sitting for fifty intermediate kalpas and receiving such eulogies for that duration is likewise due to the Buddha's supernormal power (*ṛddhi-bala*).
Question: Why is it called "supernormal power" when the Buddha sits for fifty intermediate kalpas? Answer: The Sūtra says:
The fourfold assembly likewise remained silent for fifty intermediate kalpas. The fourfold assembly also remained silent for fifty intermediate kalpas;

they sat for fifty intermediate kalpas, truly through the Buddha’s supernormal power (*ṛddhibala*). That which can praise and receive praise during equal intervals of time is called "receiving praise.
The supernormal power is also equal to the duration of the praise.

Regarding the statement, "By means of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), he transforms his original mind," etc.: at that time, although it was actually fifty minor *kalpas*, through the Buddha’s supernatural power, the *kalpa* was transformed in time.
The members of the assembly were able to perceive it as fifty minor *kalpas*, yet their objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) interpreted it as being half a day;

this is called "transforming the original mind. Question: If it is like this, one may simply say that the mind is transformed. But what is meant by "transforming the duration of light and shadow" (*kāla-pramāṇa*)?

The answer states: The scriptural text mentions only the "abbreviated duration" (cu guang jing), whereas the commentary (*shu*) includes the term "Kātyāyana," referring to the person capable of praising [the Buddha].

Although it is fifty minor *kalpas*, this abbreviates that extended duration; those present at the assembly perceive it as being like half a day, which means they regard that extended duration as an abbreviated duration.
Regarding the statement that sentient beings receive the Dharma and so forth, this is the third interpretation. At that time, the duration was not brief, nor did the minds of people shift;
because sentient beings’ love for the Dharma was so profound, they were untiring even as time passed long, and they did not perceive that fifty minor kalpas had elapsed.
Through the Buddha’s supernatural power and protection, it was as if only half a day had passed.
Regarding the phrase "sustained by the food of Dharma," it is asked: How is it that one does not incur the fault of eating, yet attains a lifespan of fifty small kalpas?

It is answered: Because one is sustained by the food of Dharma, there is no need to eat grain. It is asked: Does passing through fifty small kalpas not result in a reduction of one's life span? It is answered:
Because the Buddha’s spiritual power controls [the practitioner], their years and life do not diminish even after passing many kalpas; "diminish" means to decrease. Cold does not... [text ends].
The lifespan is diminished; when the cold returns, it is according to the original years. This is the time when the power of this Dharma abides. As the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says:
"I have sentient beings who delight in dwelling for a long time," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "seen by all people," the Sūtra states: "At that time, the fourfold assembly, through the Buddha's supernormal power, also ascended into the void.

It is orderly and arranged in single rows according to sequence; thus, it simultaneously pervades and fills immeasurable hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, and billions of lands and spaces.
Ordinary beings and the fourfold assembly see only what is near and do not see what is far; it is only through the Buddha’s spiritual power that they are able to see everywhere.
Furthermore, it is like an army in camp that occupies little ground when silent, yet becomes vast when it marches out;
or like birds gathered on a single tree, which are few, yet fill the entirety of space when they take flight.

Regarding those whose conduct and speech are "superior" (*uttara*): their conduct is superior because they understand superior practice; it is "boundless" (*ananta*) because they understand boundless practice; it is "pure" (*viśuddha*) because they understand pure practice;

and it is "established" (*pratiṣṭhita*) because they understand the practice of advancing toward the good. Furthermore, it is understood that their single practice is superior. Because the four practices for peaceful dwelling are superior, it is called "superior practice.
Because it excels in vastness, it is called "boundless practice. Because it is free from the ten kinds of evil conditions and all evils, it is so named.

Purifying conduct (*śuddhacaryā*). Because it is able to advance toward the wholesome, it is called "established conduct" (*vyavasthānacaryā*). Question: Why are eight or ten persons not established, but only four persons are mentioned? Answer:
These are the first four among the four modes of peaceful conduct (*caturvidha-sukha-caryā*); therefore, they are called the "four persons. First is the "Superior Conduct" (*Uttara-caryā*):

because among the bodily conducts within the three types of *bodhi*, this bodily conduct is the most excellent and superior. Second is the "Right Speech Conduct" (*Samyag-vāk-caryā*): [this refers to] speech regarding *bodhi*.

He expounds hundreds of thousands of teachings, whose principles and meanings are boundless. Because among the three types of action (*trikarma*), the action of speech (*vākkarma*) brings the greatest benefit, it is called "boundless conduct" (*anantacaryā*).
Third, because the mind is free from all evils, it is called "pure conduct" (*viśuddhacaryā*).

Fourth, because the mind cultivates all virtues and the merit of benefiting others increases day by day, it is called "established conduct" (*vyavasthitacaryā*). The practices of a Bodhisattva are immeasurable and boundless; to cite them...
The four practices encompass all other practices. Although the assembly of bodhisattvas is as vast as the sands of the Ganges, these four individuals are cited to represent the rest of the people.
The Sūtra states: "These four bodhisattvas are the foremost leaders among the great assembly. Question:
Previously it was said that each individual bodhisattva is a leader who guides the great assembly; now it is said that these four bodhisattvas are the leaders. Why is this so?

This is contradictory. To answer: regarding the "foremost" mentioned previously, each of the bodhisattvas—numbering as many as the sands of sixty thousand Ganges Rivers—acted as a leader for his own sixty thousand disciples, who were as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
These four bodhisattvas, however, were the foremost among the sixty thousand preceptors (upādhyāyas), who were likewise as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Regarding the "three upright provinces," the Sūtra says: "In the presence of the great assembly, each together joins their palms. Mǔ explains that "each" (zhe) means "together" (tóng).
"Together" carries the sense of similarity; thus, it refers to each individual joining their palms in a similar manner.
The Sūtra says, "with little illness and little affliction. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that, according to worldly convention, there are two kinds of inquiries:

first, inquiring about the mind, which is called "little affliction"; second, inquiring about the body, which is called "little illness. This is merely the etiquette of the inquirer; the Buddha is, in reality, without illness.

The scripture’s statement regarding "peaceful and blissful conduct" (ānanda-caryā)—the first syllable being pronounced with a level tone (*píng*)—refers to the first of the four modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*). Whether standing, sitting, or reclining is immaterial;
alternatively, the mention of the first may be intended to encompass the latter three. If it were pronounced with an ascending tone (*qù*), it would signify the sense of cause;
therefore, it is not a phenomenon belonging to the state of fruition.
Regarding the mention of the *Yùpiān* and other such works, these refer to inquiries made by consulting them. "Permitted" refers to the words of such consultation.
Regarding the phrase "inquiries through formal documents," this refers to making inquiries by means of written correspondence; that is, making inquiries by transmitting messages.
The present inquiry of the Bodhisattva is an inquiry made through speech.

In converting and delivering [beings], there is truly no weariness. A question is raised regarding the verses on the Burning House: "These children were so difficult to raise and nurture; why now do you say they are easy to deliver? The answer is:
that [previous statement] referred to the children when they formerly resided in the house, whereas this [current statement] refers to the present time.

Regarding the statement that "the three provisional assemblies also follow [this path]," the Sūtra says: "Excluding those who previously practiced and studied the Hīnayāna and have reached the Buddha-wisdom"—these are the śrāvakas of indeterminate nature.
Regarding the statement, "Although at first they did not follow, later they also followed": for forty years prior, they had reviled and rejected those who heard [the Dharma], so they did not follow;
yet, "later they also followed" refers to the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

This also includes those from forty years ago who did not follow, with the exception of those who were practicing and studying the Hīnayāna—this refers to those who, although they did not follow, are such that I now cause them to attain [enlightenment].
I have heard that this sutra follows the names of the wisdoms of entry and exit.

Regarding the statement that the first two praise the bodhisattvas and so forth: these refer to the sudden and gradual enlighteners among the lesser bodhisattvas, while the last one speaks of the śrāvakas.

This refers to those who were gradually led to the path by means of the Śrāvakas; it also refers to those who attained gradual awakening through hearing the sutras. Mouzi stated: "The following verses describe, in order, the two types of Bodhisattvas—the sudden and the gradual.
As for the statement that the first two verses refer to those "gradually led," these are individuals such as Śāriputra and others, who throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes...
Having previously received transformation from the Buddha, they subsequently retreat and then again give rise to the Mahāyāna mind; thus, they become bodhisattvas of gradual awakening.
Regarding the statement that "the latter group enters quiescence," it is asked: since they enter quiescence, how can it be said that they enter the Buddha’s wisdom? The answer is:

this refers only to entry through faith and understanding (*adhimukti*), not entry through realized understanding (*adhigama*). This is because, by hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, they are no longer deluded regarding the Dharma, and thus have faith.
There is the Mahāyāna. Lu Fu said: "The character 'remove' (chú) in the sutra is an error; it should be the character 'remainder' (yú). The Hīnayāna is the remainder of the Mahāyāna. Mou said:
"Since the commentary provides two distinct analyses, the sutra contains both implications; one cannot definitively rule out [either reading].
If one follows the first analysis, this refers to those who gradually awaken through circuitous means, which would indeed be the sense of 'remainder. Śrāvakas are [the remainder] of Bodhisattvas..."
It is the remainder. If it belongs to the subsequent category, it pertains to those who have entered the state of tranquility (*śamaikāyana*); this refers to the word "excluded" (*apoddhṛta*).

Since persons of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*) can no longer turn their minds [toward enlightenment], they are not called "those who previously practiced"; these are the śrāvakas of the tranquility-vehicle who are excluded.
Regarding the statement that "the seventh [category] consists of four people who rejoice, etc.": these four people see the World-Honored One and further praise him with a verse, saying:
"O World-Honored One, among all sentient beings, those bodhisattvas of the sudden and gradual vehicles are easily transformed; you are able to question the Buddhas regarding their profound wisdom.
The *Chao* (Excerpts) states: "The phrase 'capable of hearing the Way' connects with the following line, 'having heard it, they believe and practice,' thereby continuing the sequence of practice."
The character "ping" (平) is pronounced as it is read. This refers to the wisdom of hearing the cause and effect during the first cycle. The second [section] says:

"The question 'the characters are inverted'—because the word 'hearing' (wen) appears in the subsequent phrase—the meaning is that the three classes of *śrāvakas* requested the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, which constitutes the wisdom of hearing.

Those of superior faculties requested the Dharma-exposition; those of middling faculties requested the parable-exposition; and those of inferior faculties requested the accounts of past causes and conditions. Thus, they are named "those capable of questioning."
Question: Since the Bodhisattva did not perceive the three faculties [of the listeners], how is it known that he spoke these verses of praise upon being requested by the śrāvakas?
Answer: First, because the sagely mind possesses profound discernment; second, because when preaching the Dharma to śrāvakas according to principle, one must necessarily maintain the formal request.
We rejoice in even a single phrase belonging to the Bodhisattva who is capable of praising. The above constitutes the Bodhisattva’s praise of the Buddha.
Regarding the phrase "this is the first," it refers to single-minded mindfulness.
As for the passage in the sutra stating, "At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva and eight thousand Ganges-sands [of bodhisattvas]... [until] the Tathāgata," Lü says:

The *Qianziwen* (Thousand-Character Classic) is exhausted; now it says "eight Ganges-sands. This refers to the eight Ganges-sands of bodhisattvas at the beginning of this chapter who were invited from other directions to uphold [the Dharma].
Some say they are those who came from Mañjuśrī’s ocean-like assembly, which cannot be fully proclaimed by words. Others say they are his emanated attendants.
If it were not so, their names would not appear in the list of [the thousand] characters, nor would their place of origin be seen. Judging by this, [it must be as stated].

This is logical. Even eight thousand Ganges-sands [of bodhisattvas] would not be an obstacle. When the sutra was first preached, there were few bodhisattvas, but they gradually arrived until their number reached eight thousand Ganges-sands;

what fault is there in this? As explained in the "Vibhaṅga" (Discrimination) chapter below, where it speaks of the atoms of a small chiliocosm, a great trichiliocosm, and so forth—how could one raise such an objection based on a mere name?
Regarding the phrase "this is the first": one verse provides a general summary of its intent.
When the sutra states, "At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva... the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings spoke," it indicates that the Bodhisattva wished to resolve his own doubts.
Question: How can Maitreya have doubts? Answer: Others truly do have doubts; Maitreya merely manifests this appearance.
His benefit is vast and great: wherever there are doubts among the multitude regarding the teaching of the sutra, he immediately comes forth to provide answers, and having done so, he departs.
As in the "Introductory Chapter," doubt is also a manifestation of characteristics.
Regarding the statement that there are three [sections] at the beginning: the first two lines indicate the origin; the next five lines praise the virtues;
and the final line indicates the source.
"Beyond conception" means that it cannot be fully understood or comprehended.
"Firm and solid" means that one's faith harbors no doubt. Regarding the phrase "to follow," the character "wei" (為) is used here as a particle to indicate a verbal action.
Regarding the statement that there are three types of enumeration for what has been presented: within the eight verses of the prose section, it is likewise so;

first is the general summary, next are the seven verses of specific detail, and finally is the one verse of conclusion. Furthermore, within the specific section there are eight parts: first, the initial three verses and one line clarify the *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (sands of the Ganges).
This is divided into two parts. The first two verses clarify sixty thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* [disciples]; the final verse and line clarify fifty thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka*.
Regarding the initial sixty thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* disciples: six times six is thirty-six; thus there are three hundred and sixty thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* disciples.
Including the original teacher, the total count for the sixty thousand teachers and disciples together is four million two hundred thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka*.
He is a person from the Śākya clan. Following him are fifty thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* bodhisattvas, each of whom further leads fifty thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* disciples.
When the Sūtra says they lead "fifty thousand *gaṅgā-saṃkhyeya*" (or *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka*), the number exceeds this; thus, they lead fifty thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka*.
The disciples who come are twice as many as the previous sixty thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* masters; that is, there are one hundred and twenty thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* masters.
With fifty thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* disciples for each master, the total number of disciples amounts to six million *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka*.
When masters and disciples are calculated together, there are seventy-two *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* Bodhisattvas. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Taking fifty thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka*... [and so forth].
The number exceeds this;
the sutra mentions forty thousand, thirty thousand, twenty thousand, down to ten thousand, one thousand, one hundred, and so forth.
This is the full amount of river sands. Regarding "two parts of river sands," the sutra says: "down to even one part of a river sand, or half, or three or four parts."
One part in ten million. These three preceding phrases divide the *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (sands of the Ganges).
Regarding the "three *nayuta*s," the Sūtra says: "Ten million *nayuta*s of disciples, ten thousand billion disciples, even down to fifty million;
their number exceeds the former. Mōu [Mouzi] says: "Even down to fifty million"—one suspects this phrase is redundant, as it is not present in the prose section (*chángxíng*). Long...
Regarding the phrase "a retinue of hundreds of millions," the verse states "ten thousand million disciples. This preceding verse refers to *nayutas*.
Regarding "forty thousand," the sutra says from one million down to ten thousand. Regarding "five thousand," the sutra says one thousand.
Regarding "six hundred," the sutra says as well as one hundred. Regarding "seventy," the sutra says fifty and ten, even down to three.
21. Regarding the "eight single [cases]": the Sūtra speaks of those who are alone and without retinue, and so forth.
Regarding the "concluding verse on the one": the prose (long-śloka) of the Sūtra states that such examples are immeasurable and boundless, beyond what can be known through calculation or analogy.
Now, the verse says: "All these great assemblies, etc."—this constitutes the first line.

Regarding these so-called "transformed practices" (*nirmāṇa-caryā*) and so forth: who preached the Dharma for them, and by whom were they taught and brought to fulfillment? From whom did they first resolve their minds [for enlightenment]?

Which Buddha-dharmas did they extol? Prior to the teachings on the three natures and the six perfections, which sūtras did they uphold and practice—the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Nirvāṇa*, the *Vimalakīrti*, or the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*?
Upon which path of the Buddhas did they cultivate—that of Vipaśyin, Krakucchanda, [Kanakamuni, or Kāśyapa]—and so on?
Regarding the statement "not recognizing this," it indicates a failure to recognize the manifested signs. Question:

When the earth is transformed to extend hospitality and the mountains and rivers are entirely exhausted, how can one see [the guest] emerge from the ground? Answer: He emerges from within the lapis lazuli ground.

Regarding the statement that the third section addresses "the assembly" and so forth: from whom [the Buddha] first resolved to attain enlightenment is called the primary causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*);
his body being entirely golden in color and possessing the thirty-two marks is called the secondary causal condition (*pratyaya*).

Regarding the fourth "incidental response," the Sūtra says: At that time, each of the Buddhas addressed their respective attendants, saying, "As for those who have come here to hear [the Dharma], O sons of good family, do not show expressions of incomprehension or cause the hosts to be weary; allow them to listen and let the hosts decide."
I know only how to listen. Have you not heard that Maitreya Bodhisattva, the attendant of Śākyamuni, has already asked this?
You see him about to answer; listen with careful attention. If I were to explain the matter to you, I would not conceal anything; it all depends on your capacity to receive it.
Regarding the subsequent mention of "Ajita," the *Shangsheng shu* (Commentary on the Birth Above) states that Maitreya’s original clan name was Bhāradvāja,
and his personal name was Ajita, which means "Invincible."

Regarding the phrase "this prose passage," some say this refers to a single recitation of the sūtra text. If it were not the Master [Asaṅga] himself who revealed the *Vibhāṣā*, how could he have elucidated its profound meaning?
It is because he wished to reveal the lifespan of the Tathāgata described below that he briefly indicates the three bodies (*trikāya*) at this point;
these are explained extensively in that chapter, while here they are pointed out in advance. The Great Sage’s subduing power illuminates them through their hidden manifestations.

Regarding the phrase "causing the mind to be courageous and sharp," etc., this explains the "arousing of a firm resolve" mentioned in the sutra; both are synonymous with causing the mind to be valorous.

This is precisely what is meant by donning the armor of diligence (*vīrya-saṃnāha*). Question: For what reason does the Tathāgata cause Maitreya to arouse a mind of diligence and develop a firm resolve? Answer:
It is solely because Maitreya requested that the origins of the Bodhisattvas who emerged from the earth be explained. Furthermore...

I intend to explain the lifespan and merits of the three bodies (*trikāya*); however, because their meaning is profound and far-reaching, I fear that those who hear them for the first time might be startled.

Therefore, I shall first offer a verbal caution. Regarding the statement "this explains the four powers," etc.: the first is the power of wisdom (*prajñā-bala*). It is the power of wisdom by which the Tathāgata now wishes to manifest the wisdom of all Buddhas.
This refers to the nature of wisdom and the marks of wisdom of the two bodies—the secret *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya*—as found in the "Chapter on Lifespan" (*Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*).

Collectively, these are termed "wisdom. Second, regarding the power of supernatural faculties (*abhijñā*): this refers to the power of the sovereign supernatural faculties of all Buddhas, which is the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body).
These two powers above constitute the three bodies (*trikāya*). Third, regarding the power of valorous display (*vikrīḍita*):

this refers to the power of the lion-like valorous display of all Buddhas. "Lion" signifies the meaning of fearlessness; "valorous display" signifies the meaning of suddenness. Just as a lion suddenly [leaps]...

"Ma" (Mao) signifies that which is definitively to be performed. It indicates that the Tathāgata exerts the power of *vikrīḍita* (heroic sport), and that he will certainly expound the lifespan of the three bodies (*trikāya*).
Regarding the "fourth, the power of majesty" (*vibhūti-bala*): it is the power of the great might of all Buddhas; "majesty" (*vibhūti*) has the sense of crushing and destroying.

This is intended to shatter the doubts of Maitreya Bodhisattva; therefore, he manifests the power of great majesty (the former based on the Sūtra’s explanation, the latter based on the Commentary’s exposition).

Regarding the phrase "or by means of wisdom," the Master of the Commentary assigns the two characters *fen-xun* (fierce and swift) to the first [category], thereby subsuming the power of wisdom within the Dharma.
This refers to the nature and characteristics of the wisdom of the two bodies of retribution (*vipākakāya*).

Regarding the phrase "by means of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and so forth," the Master of the Commentary (*śāstrakāra*) assigns the two characters "awe-inspiring" (*weimeng*) to the second [category], the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of supernatural power.
Among the four powers, the first two are functional activities; this is because he feared that people might recognize only wisdom and supernatural power.

Regarding the powers: one does not recognize the latter two—the power of valorous display (*vikrīḍita*) and the power of fierce majesty (*pracaṇḍa*). Therefore, the power of valorous display is correlated with the power of wisdom;
this is the functioning directed toward the Dharma-body and the Reward-body. Consequently, the power of fierce majesty is correlated with the power of supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*);
this is the functioning directed toward the Emanation-body.
Regarding the phrase "or wisdom," this refers to the nature and characteristics of the wisdom of the aforementioned two bodies, the Dharma-body and the Reward-body (the second interpretation).

Regarding the phrase "the three [bodies] below, such as the Nirmāṇakāya of the Buddhas," this refers generally to the three wheels of the Nirmāṇakāya: the power of supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*), the power of heroic valor (*vikrīḍita*), and the power of fierce majesty (*pracaṇḍa*).
The power of mastery (*vaśitā*) is assigned to the supernormal faculties; the subduing of non-Buddhists is called a "wheel" (*cakra*); and it is likened to a lion.
The wheel of the mind (*citta-cakra*) is so named because its resolute actions possess the power of vigor; it is called a wheel because it shatters the web of doubt.

The wheel of instruction (*avavāda-cakra*) corresponds to the majestic power of great might; it is called a wheel because it crushes the evils of sentient beings. The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states: "The power of mastery is the bodily action (*kāya-karman*);
the power of the lion’s vigor is the mental action (*manas-karman*); and the power of majesty is the vocal action (*vāk-karman*)."
Regarding the statement that the first two verses exhort one not to give rise to doubt:

the prose of the sūtra says, "You all should together with one mind don the armor of diligence until you reach the power of great majesty. Now, the verse says, "Always diligent and single-minded," and so forth in the two stanzas.
Regarding the statement that "the final two verses reveal the Buddha’s truthful speech and so forth," Zhangjing says: "The four verses are divided into two parts.
The first two verses recount the preceding donning of the armor of diligence and the generation of a firm resolve; 'firm resolve' refers here to the power of faith.
The latter two verses recount the [remaining] four powers among those previously mentioned: the first verse recounts the power of wisdom, and the subsequent verse recounts the other three."
The sūtra states, "Those who abide in the excellence of patience. This refers to the nature of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) in the wholesome dharmas of patience;
this is the cause of faith. Regarding the statement, "I have transformed them from the very beginning," the Buddha told Maitreya:

"All those who have thus emerged from the earth have been transformed by me. How can you not recognize them as my disciples? He asked, "World-Honored One, where did you go, and at what time did you transform them? He replied:
"I have only been able to transform and guide those within this Sahā world. Question: "Is it not the case that the World-Honored One has been transforming and guiding them since the distant past?
Answer: "It is only after I attained the Way in my present life that I have been able to transform and guide them. This is the point where doubt arises.
Regarding the scriptural passage beginning with "In this Sahā world," etc., this answers the first five questions:
who taught the Dharma for them, who transformed and brought them to maturity, and from whom they initially resolved their minds toward enlightenment. However, the wording here is extremely subtle;
although the Buddha spoke of the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body), his underlying intent was the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body). Maitreya, the one being transformed, relied upon these words.

Chen: He summarizes by posing a hypothetical objection. As for why the Master of the Commentary does not provide a detailed analysis and explanation here, his intention is that [the meaning] will arise later through the wisdom of understanding.

Regarding the statement "two ways of interpreting the sutra," when the sutra says "regarding all the scriptures" and so forth, this answers the question of who receives, maintains, and practices them.
In the *Sūtra Commentary*, the outline of this chapter identifies it as "The Practice of the Peaceful and Blissful Conduct" for those who uphold the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Furthermore, Śākyamuni says, "I myself have so many bodhisattvas who uphold the *Lotus Sūtra*. Now, within this direct answer, why does he say "in all sūtras"?
The answer is that "all sūtras" does not refer to sūtras such as the *Avataṃsaka* or the *Nirvāṇa*. Nor...

It is simply that the teachings, principles, practices, and fruits of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* are collectively designated as "various sūtras. Because these four dharmas are not identical, they are called "various.

The verse below states: "Constantly and diligently seek wisdom," which refers to the opening, revealing, and awakening to the nature of wisdom (*jñāna-svabhāva*) and the characteristics of wisdom (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*).
The "teaching of various sublime dharmas" refers precisely to the teaching, principle, practice, and fruit. However, these terms are manifold;
they are, in fact, the teaching, principle, practice, and fruit of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). All of these are the principles elucidated within the teachings.
Regarding the statement that there are four types, such as those who delight in solitude (*viveka-rata*) and so forth: the Sūtra says, "Ajita and others do not delight in being among the multitude.
This answers the question: "What Buddha-dharma does this praise? Question: Since they do not delight in being among the multitude, how can it be said that they have much to say?

Answer: It is not that they delight in frequenting many places; rather, by doing so, they avoid causing people to become deluded. One should say that they do not delight in being among the multitude, nor do they delight in having much [of worldly things].
This is why he dwells in a quiet place below.

Regarding the scriptural statement, "He also does not dwell depending upon humans or devas," a question is raised: since both *paricchinna-vibhava* (segmented) and *pariṇāmi-vibhava* (transformative) [modes of existence] all depend upon humans and devas for their dwelling, how can it be said that he does not dwell depending upon humans or devas? The answer is: with respect to the land upon which he relies, this refers to the Tathāgata.
That which is transformed by the untainted (*anāsrava*) possesses a wondrous, pure land that transcends the three realms; this is called "non-reliance.

When the Sūtra speaks of "constant bliss for those of profound wisdom," it is because fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is "profound" as it realizes suchness (*tathatā*), while subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) reaches [all phenomena].
Regarding the statement that the final verse concerns diligence: the Sūtra says, "In this way, these sons and others who study my Way and Dharma.
This answers the previous question: "What Buddha-way do they cultivate? The character *kuì* (古內反; meaning mental agitation or confusion) has the same pronunciation as *huì* (乎內反).
Regarding the statement that "the first one and a half verses concern the profound wisdom of the dwelling place," the Sūtra says, "expounding various sublime dharmas.

This answers the previous question of which Buddha-dharma is being extolled; namely, the teachings, principles, practices, and fruits of the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna) are called the "various sublime dharmas."
Regarding the statement, "The formation of the self and its transformations," etc.: within the words spoken by the World-Honored One, he refers to the city of Gayā in the present;
yet within his underlying intention (*abhiprāya*), he refers to the location of the city of Gayā from immeasurable kalpas ago.

Maitreya understood only the literal expression and did not understand the underlying intention, and thus he assumed that the World-Honored One was speaking of the city of Gayā in the present. There is a commentary stating that although the city of Gayā...
It is not correct to say that although the kalpa may perish, the name remains constant, being of the same nature as the Ganges; for this is not so.

Rather, it is simply stated that the location of Gayā City is the true one. It is not necessarily the case that there was a "settlement" (śet) there in the past, nor does its existence necessarily mean it is named Gayā.
This is like saying [the Buddha] always dwells on Vulture Peak; it is not because Vulture Peak exists within the Pure Land, but rather because the Pure Land faces toward that Vulture Peak.
Regarding the phrase "at the mountain": this is why it is said to be at Vulture Peak (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*).

As for the statement that he exhorts them to give rise to faith: since it is said to have occurred over a vast period of time, it was not in this very lifetime; therefore, he exhorts them to give rise to faith.
Regarding the statement that Gayā is the birthplace of the Buddha and so forth:
Lu says that Śrāvastī is a great capital city, while this Gayā is a small capital city; both are under the jurisdiction of this kingdom of Kapilavastu.
According to the *Shu* (Commentary), Magadha is also Central India, distinct from this Kośala. According to the *Xiyu Ji* (Records of the Western Regions), Kapilavastu...
The Kingdom of Tu (堵國) is the former name of Kapilavastu. Within this kingdom, there is only the site where the Bodhisattva descended into his mother’s womb;
it is not said that the city of Gayā is located here, nor is the size of the capital city discussed.

However, in the kingdom of Magadha, four or five *li* to the southwest of the monastery of the Master Śīlabhadra, one crosses the Nairañjanā River and arrives at Gayā, which is a place of great strategic security.

The population is sparse, consisting of only some one thousand Brahmin families; they are descendants of the original seers. Traveling five or six *li* southwest from the city, one reaches Gayā Mountain.
Its valleys and gorges are deep and dark, and its peaks and cliffs are perilous; according to Indian custom, it is called the "Sacred Mountain" (*Ṛṣigiri*).
To the southeast of the mountain is the site where the two Kāśyapa brothers, Nadi-Kāśyapa and Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, formerly practiced fire-worship. From...
To the east of here, crossing a great river, one reaches Mount Pāṇḍava-bodhi—here called Mount Former Perfect Enlightenment.
On the southern face of this mountain, fourteen or fifteen *li* away, stands a *pi-pi-lo* (pipal) tree. In the past, when the Buddha was in the world, it stood several hundred feet high;

though it has been repeatedly cut down, it is now still forty or fifty feet tall. It was beneath this tree that the Buddha sat and attained Equal and Perfect Enlightenment; for this reason, it is named "Wondrous Bodhi."
Regarding the tree: this differs from the commentary (*shu*), and the reason for this is not yet clear.

As for the statement that both are in Central India (*madhyadeśa*): the question is, why are they not far apart? The answer is that the Bodhi tree is located twenty-odd *li* to the southwest of the city of Gayā;
since both are in Central India, one knows they are not far apart. Following the wording of the sutra, this interpretation is correct.
The phrase "in the palace of the Śākyas" refers to the place where the Buddha was born.
Regarding the statement "in this sense, briefly," it refers first to the fact that various sūtras do not provide a definitive account;

some say he left home at nineteen and attained enlightenment at thirty. Furthermore, in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, when the Buddha was on the verge of entering nirvana, he addressed Subhadra, saying:
I left the household life at the age of nineteen. From my attainment of the Way until now, fifty years have passed; thus, the total is sixty-nine.

This interpretation holds that the Buddha entered nirvana before reaching eighty. Changjing said: "The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* follows the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) and does not provide the definitive teaching."

Regarding the mention of the *Benqi yinguo jing* (Sutra on the Original Arising of Cause and Effect) and others: the Master of the Commentary (*Shuzhu*) reconciles the texts of the *Dazhidu lun* (Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom) and other works.
The text of the *Dazhidu lun* contains an error; it omits eleven years, mentioning only the years prior to his renunciation as well as the years after his enlightenment, totaling sixty-nine.
It thus omits the five years between his renunciation and his enlightenment during which he practiced austerities.
[He] practiced asceticism for six years; including [the previous period], this totals eleven years. Adding these to sixty-nine years makes eighty; thus, the Buddha was truly eighty years old.
Regarding the phrase "There is an interpretation that says... and so forth, this is precisely the initial heading within the Master of the Commentary’s reconciliation of the various accounts.

The statement regarding the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Zhìdù lùn) is an explanation. It employs the meaning of nineteen years for his renunciation, along with five years spent practicing the "joyful conduct" under the sages and six years of ascetic practice; these calculated together total thirty years until his attainment of enlightenment.

Now, it is said that since his attainment of enlightenment, slightly more than forty years have passed, which means he is just seventy years old. That is, after the assembly at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, further time has elapsed...

Ten years. This refers to the time up until the *Nirvāṇa* assembly. Taking the year of his enlightenment as the starting point and adding the forty years following his enlightenment, there are a total of forty-one years;
thus it is said to be "over forty years" (the above follows the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*).
Regarding the statement, "As for the 'two,' there are also various schools," this sets forth the correct principle.
Regarding the statement, "The Buddha desired to leave home," etc.: he attained enlightenment after six years, and Rāhula was born at that time.

Calculating back from the date of his renunciation (as noted in Note 29), it is known that he attained enlightenment thirty-five years [prior to his passing]. To say he left home at nineteen is merely a conventional designation. Furthermore, see Note [X].
The six years [of practice] correspond to the twenty-fifth year of his life when he attained enlightenment;

thus, it contradicts the holy teaching to say that he did not speak of "eleven years. To claim that the eleven years refers to his time in the womb would allow one to say that he attained enlightenment at thirty by adding those nineteen years [to the eleven].
Since this is not the case, the claim of nineteen years is incorrect.

Regarding the phrase "within six years," etc., that school asks: "If it is said that he left home at twenty-nine and practiced asceticism for six years, then at what time did the Bodhisattva practice the 'pleasant conduct' (*sukha-caryā*)?
If one adds the period of pleasant conduct, it would no longer be thirty-five years. The commentary answers: "Within six years," etc.
Regarding the mention of Bodhiruci and others, one should consult which sūtras they cite.
Regarding the mention of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* and so forth, the sūtra records that Subhūti, the Wondrous Banner, raised a doubt, saying: "The lifespan of Śākyamuni Tathāgata is too short."
Only eighty years.

Regarding the second illustration and so forth, the Sūtra says: "For example, suppose there is a man with handsome features and black hair," and so on. Question: It would suffice simply to say "this is his son";
why is it necessary that the son must have been in the womb for him to be the father? Answer: If one were to speak directly [of the age], [it would be] twenty-five...
"A person" refers to a hundred-year-old man. To say, "This is my son," is quite easy. But for that person to instead acknowledge, "Truly, this is my father," is what is difficult.
"There is such a person" is a way of speaking about the Buddha. "Beautiful in appearance" means that the Buddha is adorned with the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa* and *anuvyañjana*).
"Black hair" signifies the meaning of not aging.

Regarding the statement "even if one were eighty years old" and so forth: as in the present assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, although [the Buddha] was actually seventy-five years old, he showed no signs of aging;
even had he reached eighty, there would likewise have been no signs of aging in the assembly of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
To say "good at wandering" implies that he constantly possesses few worldly attachments; to say "dwelling in an old place" implies that he does not age.
To say he was twenty-five years old signifies that the Buddha has transcended birth and death, demonstrating that he abides above the twenty-five realms of existence.

Regarding the statement that the seven virtues of a bodhisattva are exceedingly great: [The questioner] asks Maitreya, who previously stated he did not recognize a single person, how he can know that [the others] possess these seven virtues.

[Maitreya] answers: The previous statement was based on manifest signs (*nimitta*), whereas this is based on actual knowledge (*jñāna*). Furthermore, when the Path is fulfilled at the time of rebirth, what need is there for such knowledge?
Alternatively, it may be because Maitreya’s faculties and stage (*bhūmi*) are superior to those of the people of that land.
Regarding the statement "speaking with faith according to what is appropriate," the sutra has three sections and the commentary likewise has three.

However, the second section of the sutra states that the words spoken by the Buddha have never been false; this corresponds to the third and fourth [sections] of the commentary being without error, yet [the commentary] takes those three as two.
Regarding the "four infallibilities," the *Shè* (Compendium) states: The Buddha does not speak falsely regarding four matters; these are called the four infallibilities.
First, the Tathāgata does not falsely speak of the Buddha’s bodhi. Second, he does not falsely speak of the Hīnayāna. Third, he does not falsely speak of the Mahāyāna teachings.
Fourth, he does not falsely speak when bestowing predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) concerning the past, future, or present. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The Tathāgata is the Truth."
Regarding "speech": it is truthful speech, speech that accords with reality, and speech that is not otherwise.
As for the statement that "the first [section] has three parts," the long discourse says: within the raising of the objection by citing an example, there are two parts.

First, the citation of the location and the year of attaining enlightenment; second, the formal presentation of the objection. Within the presentation of the objection, there are first the presentation of the three matters, followed by the conclusion of the difficulty regarding faith. These are the three matters.
First, in a short time, great deeds are accomplished. As the Sūtra says: "World-Honored One, how is it that in this brief period you perform such vast Buddha-work?

Second, the time is brief yet the assembly is vast. "World-Honored One, as for this great assembly of Bodhisattvas, even if someone were to count them for thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas, they could not exhaust them nor reach their limit.
Third, the duration is short yet the virtue is supreme. These [Bodhisattvas] have, since long ago, [cultivated]...
Having planted various roots of goodness in the presence of immeasurable and boundless Buddhas, he accomplished the path of a bodhisattva and constantly cultivated pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).
Now, in this verse, the first stanza commemorates the location where he attained enlightenment. The prose of the sutra states:
He then addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, when the Tathāgata was a prince, having departed from the palace of the Śākyas, he sat not far from the city of Gayā."
At the site of enlightenment, he attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. From that time until now, more than forty years have passed.
The present verse says: "The Buddha formerly [departed] from the Śākya clan," which describes this in a single verse.

Regarding the statement "the three verses on the virtues of the bodhisattvas, etc.": this describes how, among the three aforementioned matters, the number [of bodhisattvas] is vast while the time [spent with them] is brief. As the Sūtra says:

"World-Honored One, as for this great assembly of bodhisattvas, even if someone were to count them for a thousand million *koṭi* of kalpas, they could not exhaustively enumerate them nor reach their limit.
The present verses—beginning with "These sons of the Buddhas," etc.—are the three verses that follow.
Regarding the scriptural statement, "The Bodhisattva is not defiled by worldly dharmas," etc.: worldly dharmas are like water, and the Bodhisattva is like a lotus flower.
Just as water does not cling to a lotus flower, the Bodhisattva cannot be defiled by the world. Alternatively, it is said:

"Just as the root of a lotus remains in the mud while its fragrance is emitted upon the water, the Bodhisattva originally dwells in the lower realms, yet emerges like a blooming flower. This interpretation is incorrect.
This merely takes up the sense of being unstained.

Regarding the statement that this verse is an illustration, the prose of the sutra says: "For example, suppose there were a man with a handsome appearance and black hair, twenty-five years of age, who pointed to a hundred-year-old man and said, 'This is my son. That hundred-year-old man likewise pointed to the youth and said, 'This is my...'"
"Father! He who gave birth to us—this matter is difficult to believe. Regarding this, it is said in the verses: "For example, like a young man," and so forth in two verses.
As for the statement that these [verses] correspond with the prose, the prose of the sūtra merely states that the father’s complexion was fair and his hair black.
The son of Yingqu (影取) also has white hair and wrinkled skin; the verse mentions only that "the son’s hair is white and his face is wrinkled.
The father of Yingqu likewise possesses a beautiful complexion and black hair. This explains the meaning of being eternally youthful and never aging.
"To have wandered through old age" explains the blackening of the hair.
"To have practiced for a long time" explains the whitening of the hair.
"To still be deficient" explains the wrinkling of the face.
Regarding the statement that the three verses praise the bodhisattva for possessing ten virtues: first, firm resolve and freedom from timidity; second, practicing the path for immeasurable eons;
third, skillfulness in answering difficult questions; fourth, a mind free from fear; fifth, patience; sixth, certainty of mind;
seventh, physical excellence and majestic virtue; eighth, being praised by the Buddhas of the ten directions; ninth, being well-able to analyze and explain; tenth, [the tenth virtue].
He constantly dwells in meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). This differs from the previous seven virtues in terms of presence or absence.
Regarding the statement that "the first half-verse contains no doubt," the prose commentary states:

"Although we have faith in the Buddha’s teachings as he has spoken them according to what is appropriate, the words uttered by the Buddha are never false, and all that the Buddha knows he has fully realized. Now, the verse says:
They said: "We have heard this from the Buddha; we have no doubt regarding this matter.
Regarding the subsequent half-verse for which others have confusion, the prose of the sūtra states: "So be it, World-Honored One! We pray that you will explain it for us."
"Please dispel our doubts, so that the sons of good family in future ages, upon hearing this matter, shall likewise not give rise to doubt.
Now, the verse says: "I pray that the Buddha, for the sake of the future, will expound this teaching so that they may attain understanding."
Regarding the phrase "a single verse for those who doubt or lose [the teaching]," the prose section of the sūtra states:

"However, if newly resolved bodhisattvas, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, hear these words and either do not believe or accept them, they will give rise to the causal conditions for the karmic offense of destroying the Dharma.
Now, the verse says: "If there is anyone who [holds] even a single verse of this sūtra... and so forth.
From here below, the "Life Span of the Tathāgata" chapter (*Tathāgatāyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*) is explained.
Regarding the statement "the first [of] seven chapters," etc.: the first chapter concerns the practices to be performed, namely the "Peaceful Practices" chapter (*Anraku-gyō-hon*).

Within the remaining six chapters, which clarify the practitioners who engage in these studies, there are two divisions. First, in the "Emergence from the Earth" chapter (*Jūjū-hon*), the Bodhisattvas harbor doubts. This...

The "Chapter on Lifespan" (Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta) arises because it resolves a preceding doubt; the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merits" (Guṇaparikīrtana-parivarta) subsequently gives rise to this one.
Now, because it is for the purpose of resolving that preceding doubt, the "Chapter on Lifespan" has come forth.

Regarding the statement that "the manifested Buddha has recently attained [enlightenment]," the previous doubt—that the Buddha has recently attained the Way yet manifests a multitude of bodies—refers to the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body).

If one considers the principle of the *dharmakāya* (dharma body), it is fundamentally without arising or ceasing; since the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body) has long been realized, what hindrance is there to manifesting a multitude of bodies?
To dispel the doubts of bodhisattvas regarding the long duration [of the Buddha's life], the "Chapter on Life Span" (Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta) is presented.

Regarding the statement that the nineteen chapters constitute the "Principal Doctrine" (mūla-śāstra): twelve chapters clarify the realm (*dhātu*) of the One Vehicle; two chapters clarify the practice (*caryā*) of the One Vehicle;
and the five chapters below clarify the fruit (*phala*) of the One Vehicle. Within the section on the fruit, it is divided into two parts; the first two chapters clarify...

The first [of the three] chapters explains the fruition that has already been fulfilled; the latter three chapters clarify the fruition that is not yet fulfilled. Attaining the merit of the fruition is called "fruition already fulfilled," while attaining the merit within the causal stage is called "fruition not yet fulfilled.
This Chapter on Life Span (*Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*) specifically clarifies the fruition already fulfilled. Regarding the two subsequent chapters on the analysis of merit:
through hearing of the retribution of the merit of the fruition already fulfilled, eleven stages attain realization and one stage generates the resolve for enlightenment (*cittotpāda*).
The fruits of those who have already reached fulfillment are likewise subsumed within "those who have already reached fulfillment.
Regarding the phrase "the three, such as the treatises," this is the initial heading of the text.
Regarding the phrase "in the first vehicle," etc., this is the sixth commentary of the treatise. As for "in the first," "vehicle" refers to the Mahāyāna.
This is the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. "Accumulation" (*saṃcaya*) means cultivation.

Not cultivating the roots of goodness and thus not attaining the foremost [state] is precisely why such persons give rise to perverted views and overweening pride (*adhimāna*). All commentaries state that because they do not accumulate [merit] during both the present and past times, they do not cultivate the Mahāyāna;
this is termed "not accumulating merit. Such sentient beings— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*
Within their very bodies, there have been from the beginning the seeds of the four wisdoms and the bodhicitta.
Furthermore, in the past, during the time they were the sixteen princes, they heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and once again obtained the seeds of the Mahāyāna bodhicitta.
From that point until their present life, they have never practiced the Mahāyāna in their previous existences; this is called "not having accumulated merit. Such beings are [the ones referred to].
In past lives, when they saw a Buddha appear in the world, they gave rise to arrogance; when they saw a Buddha enter parinirvāṇa, they felt longing and attachment.
Even if the Buddha were in the world, although they encountered him, they were unwilling to practice. As the Sūtra says:
"At that time, the sons within the burning house delighted in play and sport; they were neither aware nor conscious of it, neither startled nor afraid, and they felt no revulsion."
In this burning house of the three realms, [the children] merely run about to the east and west, looking only for their father. Second, regarding the present life:
prior to the turning of the mind at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, because the roots for the Mahāyāna were not yet mature, they turned their minds toward the First Vehicle.
To counteract this, the parable of the physician is taught, followed by the proclamation of his passing into extinction. Question: Now, these seven parables primarily clarify...

Regarding the three faculties of the śrāvakas, you have said, "The path you practice is the bodhisattva path. How can it be claimed that both the present and the past times are entirely non-convergent? Answer:

The treatise makes such a statement with reference to the period prior to the initial engagement in practice. The seven similes, however, pertain to the period after the turning of the mind (*cittavivarta*).
The sūtra relies on the latter explanation, while the treatise relies on the former discussion. Thus, there is no contradiction.
Regarding the phrase "the discourse also says, etc.": those whose faculties are not yet matured refer to those whose Mahāyāna faculties are not yet matured.
"In order to bring them to maturity" means that one teaches the Hīnayāna. All that follows—administering medicine and having it ingested—is entirely the Hīnayāna.

For those of a regressive nature who are given the teaching of the Hīnayāna, it is necessary to first teach the Hīnayāna so that they may subsequently enter the Mahāyāna and be brought to maturity therein.
Because it accords with the faculties [of sentient beings], it manifests the measure of nirvāṇa. Even in relation to the Buddha-body, there is no actual entry into extinction;
yet, since he proclaims his extinction and specifies a limited duration, this is termed the "measure of nirvāṇa."
Regarding the phrase "presently not yet having gathered [the roots]," this is the interpretation of the three commentators.

Those who have not yet resolved their minds toward the Mahāyāna in the present are said to have "not yet gathered the roots of goodness," and are also called those whose "roots are not yet matured. As the Sūtra says: "The sons have drunk poison; some have lost their original minds, while others have not."
Regarding the statement "commanding the gathering of all roots of goodness," it refers to preaching the Dharma of the Two Vehicles while secretly hoping they will instead seek the Supreme Vehicle.
The Supreme Vehicle is precisely the Mahāyāna *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. The Sūtra says: "This is an excellent and wholesome medicine; it is now left here."
"You may take this and consume it; do not worry that you will not recover," and so forth.
As for the statement that the Buddha manifested his entry into *nirvāṇa*, the Sūtra says: "He sent a messenger back to announce, 'Your father has already died,'" and so on.

Regarding the term "limitation" (*pramāṇa*): although the two bodies—the Dharma-body and the Reward-body—are likewise without limit, here we establish limitations based upon the body of the transformation-phase (*nirmāṇakāya*) during a single lifetime.
Regarding the statement "instructing to gather roots of goodness," the Sūtra says: "One then realizes that this medicine has a beautiful color, fragrance, and taste, and immediately takes it;
the illness is entirely eliminated and healed.
Regarding the statement "four" and the treatise's mention of "eight," the fourth [section] takes the ten unsurpassed [qualities] as its underlying intent. As for the "eight," they are as follows:
Among these ten unsurpassed things, the eighth is the unsurpassed: unsurpassed bodhi. This refers to the bodhi of the three Buddhas—the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Transformation-body;

all three of these are unsurpassed. Question: Regarding the Reward-body and the Transformation-body, they possess both wisdom and its object, and thus are designated by the two names [of "wisdom" and "bodhi"].
However, the Dharma-body only manifests its essence and is not wisdom; it is therefore not bodhi. Answer: When one speaks of "wisdom and the locus of wisdom," both are collectively termed [bodhi].
Prajñā, bodhi, and the cessation of bodhi are all termed "bodhi. The cessation of bodhi is also termed "bodhi.
As for the statement that the three bodies (trikāya) are present here, this is the Master of the Commentary’s interpretation and is not from the original treatise.

Regarding the statement that this constitutes a "fragmentary text" (wen-can): the three Buddhas' bodhi appears at the beginning of the chapter, while the parable of the physician appears at the very end.

Since supreme bodhi is the conclusion of the physician's parable, and the sutra states that the textual passages are distinct from one another, among the seven similes only the latter passage concerning the physician is mentioned, whereas the former passage concerning the three Buddhas' bodhi is not. Therefore, it is called a fragmentary text.
Regarding the statement "the fifth," the phrase "the ninth manifests, etc. refers to the fact that this chapter explains the physician twice.

In the first instance, among the seven similes, the physician is mentioned in order to eliminate disease. In the latter instance, among the ten unsurpassed qualities, the ninth—Nirvāṇa Unsurpassed—is described as the physician;
this reveals that Nirvāṇa Unsurpassed currently manifests cessation yet does not cease, which is unlike [other states].
The extinction of the two vehicles is a permanent extinction; therefore, it is called "unsurpassed.
To say that this refers to a remainder of meaning from the seven similes is because it belongs to the section on the simile of the physician in the sūtra.
It speaks only of *nirvāṇa* as a remedy for those whose faculties are not yet mature, thereby causing them to reach maturity; thus, it is like a physician.
The Master has already explained the matters concerning the household; herein, by moving downward [in the text], he reveals a portion of the unsurpassed meaning.
This differs from the "once-extinguished, forever extinguished" state of the two vehicles; therefore, it is said that this meaning is "residual" (or "remaining") as being unsurpassed.
Regarding the explanation of the title: Master Xuanzang stated that the text of this chapter is concise yet rich in meaning, profound in intent, and far-reaching in wisdom.

It is called "The Ability to Understand" (*Nengjie*) because it enables one to comprehend its underlying principles, generate inexhaustible wisdom, increase boundless merit, and extinguish immeasurable heavy transgressions.
Formerly, there were several people traveling by boat who encountered a storm; all their companions perished in the water, and only one man remained, clinging to the mast alone.
Qi. He dreamed at night that it was said: "That you have been able to escape [this calamity] is because in the past you heard the 'Life Span' chapter of the Lotus Sūtra.
The "Analysis" chapter states: "When this 'Life Span' chapter was preached, there were twelve kinds of benefits and eight kinds of auspicious signs.
Among the other sūtras that clarify the attainment of the Way, none has ever produced such a response as this. Let the lecturer pay close attention and seek its ultimate meaning. (The Jin edition)
It says: "The Chapter on the Manifested Lifespan of the Tathāgata" speaks of the three types of Buddha-bodies—the body of teaching, the body of form, and so forth.

Ordinary beings take the functional capacity of the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) and the seeds of bodhi as their essence; Buddhas take the eighth consciousness and the seeds of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) as their essence.
The Dharma-body has no limits; the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*) has a beginning but no end, and thus serves as a limit; the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) has... [limits].
That there is a beginning and an end serves as a fixed limit.

Regarding the statement that the lifespan is "left to the nature of phenomena" (*dharmatā*): Question: While this may be acceptable for the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) and *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body), how can one speak of a lifespan for the *dharmakāya* (dharma body)?
Answer: The lifespan of the *dharmakāya* is left to the nature of phenomena; it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere. Therefore, it is called the Tathāgata.

Regarding the phrase "in accordance with the conditions of his vows": it means that he transforms and exhausts the realm of sentient beings; yet because the realm of sentient beings is inexhaustible, the power of his vows never withers or ceases.

Thus, his lifespan is inexhaustible. As the Sūtra says: "When I originally practiced the path of a bodhisattva, the lifespan I accomplished remains undiminished even now, and is twice as long as previously stated.
Furthermore, the lifespan of his transformation bodies accords with the faculties of sentient beings; wherever there are sentient beings, there are transformation bodies.
Regarding the phrase "the self-substance of receiving," this refers to the three bodies each receiving their own respective substance.

Regarding the phrase "due to the lifespan of the three bodies and so forth," this is because the Bodhisattva previously gave rise to doubt, wondering whether the Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment occurred on a specific day.
Having manifested so many bodhisattvas, in order to answer their doubts, he speaks of the lifespan of the three bodies.

The lifespan of the saṃbhogakāya is infinite in its number of kalpas; the dharmakāya is likewise. Because they hear him say, "I [was] the Buddha Dīpaṃkara," and so forth, and furthermore say that he has entered parinirvāṇa—whether speaking of his own body or another's body, or of coming and going—it is all for the sake of the multitudes.
Because the analogy of the physician is explained only later, the title of this chapter is taken from the former instance rather than the latter.

Regarding the phrase "Furthermore, it is difficult," etc., both instances represent the Master of the Commentary’s (Sū-zhǔ) structural divisions; since he designates the first eight chapters as the "Correct Doctrine" (Zhèngzōng), this [nineteenth] chapter is called the "first" in contrast to them.
Thus, the objection is raised based on the initial division. If one were to adopt the latter division, this chapter would still remain within the Correct Doctrine.

Regarding the thesis: there is no contradiction with the objection. The meaning is as follows: this chapter explains seven parables; why are they not taken up in the same manner as in the "Principal Section" (Mūla)? The Commentary answers:
"First, the lifespan is presented in contrast to the subsequent parable of the physician. This is stated because it is explained first in this "Chapter on Entering" (Praveśa-parivarta).
There are two meanings to "firstly presented": first, it presents the unsurpassed nature of Bodhi; second, it presents the fundamental [nature] that has not yet... [been fully realized].
[The opponent] replies: "It is established. This parable of the physician is cited to raise a difficulty against both [the preceding] passages: why is it not part of the primary doctrine?

It would be better to add the word 'and' (及) below the section on the lifespan (*āyus-pramāṇa*). The intended meaning is that the parable of the physician excludes the seventh of the seven types of pride—the person who does not accumulate merit—so why is it not considered part of the primary doctrine?
Furthermore, since this parable primarily refutes illness, why is it not included within the primary doctrine?"

Regarding the phrase "answering according to the capacity and responding to the occasion," this refers specifically to the śrāvakas of the three faculties, for the One Vehicle is precisely suited to them;
therefore, the eight chapters are designated as the main body of the teaching. This chapter demonstrates the transformation [of beings] after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.

This refers to a certain class of people at the assembly of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* who, upon hearing the discourse on nirvāṇa, attained awakening of mind and so forth. In relation to the present assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, they are termed...

It is subsequent. Furthermore, that which manifests for those whose faculties (*indriya*) have not yet matured is called "maturation of the faculties. Because the subsequent bestowal upon those to be transformed consists of the correct preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it is subsumed under the "True Doctrine" (*saddharma*).
However, for those whose faculties mature after the extinction [of the Buddha], this is not the preaching of the True Doctrine; rather, it is subsumed under "Propagation" (*pravacana*). Question:

Since the "untying of the pearl" is an event within the assembly, why is it not part of the True Doctrine? Answer: It is not so. For it is not merely because of the breaking of a disease that it is [the True Doctrine].

This constitutes the main body of the teaching (*śāstramūla*). If one were to say that it "destroys afflictions" (*bhañjati vyādhi*), then at the point below where the physician is correctly described, there is indeed the destruction of afflictions as well.
However, because the matters used as analogies therein describe *nirvāṇa*, this occurs after the present assembly; therefore, it is not the main body.

Only when the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) is correctly expounded and the three types of faculties (*trividhendriya*) are granted their prophecies (*vyākaraṇa*) does it truly constitute the main body. As for the two sections from the eighth chapter downward, since...
[The text is] missing; therefore, it is not subject to objection.

Regarding the phrase "it is not so," and so forth: since the exposition of the single vehicle and the bestowal of predictions upon bodhisattvas constitutes the primary tenet of this record, one cannot raise an objection against citing this passage to establish the eight chapters as the orthodox teaching (*zhengzong*).

Regarding the phrase "this is the first": it refers to the threefold exhortation of Śākyamuni. The sutra states, "You all should have faith and understanding in the Tathāgata’s truthful reality," and so forth.

"Truthful" (*cheng*) arises from "reality" (*zhen*), and "reality" (*di*) arises from "substance" (*shi*). As for the threefold proclamation, it indicates that he intends to speak below of the merits of the three bodies;
therefore, there are three proclamations.

Regarding the phrase "the wondrous essence of the three bodies," etc.: Question—Why is there not a fourth announcement? Why must there be three announcements? Answer—The commentary states, "the wondrous [essence] of the three bodies.
"Exhaustive" (qiong) means reaching the ultimate limit. Since the matter is about to be fully completed, there are three announcements.
Those referred to as "the superior wise" are Maitreya;
those referred to as "the inferior ignorant" are the ordinary beings of the two vehicles.

Regarding the phrase "fearing them," the master of the commentary (Sūzhǔ) has three intentions in his threefold exhortation. First, he fears that upon first hearing this, their minds will harbor doubts and their mouths [will protest].
"Slander. This refers to the Bodhisattva who harbors doubt in his mind and slanders with his mouth, and the ignorant commoner of inferior capacity who, because of the Dharma, destroys the verses.
Thus, this is the first admonition. The second [admonition] is out of fear that even if one has heard it and does not harbor doubt, the mind may become distracted and unable to remain focused.
This is why he spoke for a second time. Thirdly, he established his mind with focused concentration, fearing that those of dull faculties might fail to comprehend;
this is why he spoke for a third time.
To speak of the "Profound Principle" (Xuanzong) refers to the underlying truth.

To speak of these four requests of Maitreya and so forth refers to the conditions: since the Buddha had previously issued three proclamations, it was not permissible for him to respond with only three requests.
To manifest the depth of his reverence, he increased the requests to four. These four represent that each of the three bodies (trikāya) possesses four virtues, namely:

permanence (*nitya*), bliss (*sukha*), self (*ātman*), and purity (*śubha*). Question: The sutra does not mention four requests; for what reason does the commentary (*shu*) categorize them as four? Answer: Because the text of the sutra is concise.
Having thus made these three declarations, he requested a third time. He spoke again, saying, "I only pray that you will explain," which was his fourth request.
Furthermore, [the Buddha] knew that the Bodhisattvas would not cease their requests after three, and this constituted the fourth request. Then [the Buddha] addressed them, saying:
"You all listen attentively to the Tathāgata’s secrets," and so forth; these also constitute four types of formal addresses, though they are not mentioned in the commentary (*śū*).

Regarding the statement, "The first part of the prose exposition (*gadya*) has two divisions," the text of the commentary is abbreviated. It should properly state: "The prose exposition has two parts:
first, the prose exposition; second, the verse recitation (*śloka*). Since the commentator cannot cite each instance in full detail, he simply says, "the first prose exposition."
From the passage following the section on the dissemination of the teaching onwards, all of this pertains to that momentum.
Regarding the statement "the three requests begin from the outset": within the preceding chant, the intent of the three requests has already been expressed;
within the subsequent chant, there are the actual words "three requests. Since these refer back to what was already explained in the initial chant, it is said to "begin from the outset."
Regarding the term "secret" (*guhya*): it is known only by the Buddha himself, while others do not know it; therefore, it is called "secret.

If one follows the explanation in the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) below, which states that what the Buddha conceals and protects is each [of the three bodies] in secret, then the *svābhāvikakāya* (self-nature body) alone is what is "concealed and protected," because it is realized solely within the *mahāprajñā* (great wisdom).

Regarding the phrase "supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and so forth," the explanation here differs from the previous ones. This refers to the manifestation of transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*), which is precisely what constitutes supernormal power.

Regarding the phrase "that which is protected and guarded by the Buddha" and its profound meaning, it explains the sense of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*. To speak of it as an "object" (*viṣaya*) refers to the self-... [text ends] ...self-nature.
The Reward Body Buddha (saṃbhogakāya) perceives itself; the Body of Enjoyment for Others (parasaṃbhogakāya) is not seen by those on the ninth stage and so forth who perceive the tenth stage.
This is a profound and difficult-to-understand meaning. Because it is not seen, it is said to be difficult to understand.
Regarding the statement "furthermore, according to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and other treatises," the *Jianyao* (Essentials) says:

This means that within the Mahāyāna Vaipulya teachings, all the Buddha’s secrets are understood through the four kinds of secrets based on their respective antidotes (*pratipakṣa*); there is nothing that is not resolved thereby.

Regarding the phrase "the one [teaching] that causes entry into the secret," etc.: before the Tathāgata appeared in the world, non-Buddhists exhorted all sentient beings to cling to the notion of a self (*ātman*).
Once the Buddha had appeared in the world, in order to destroy this notion of a self, he taught the three categories of phenomena (*triskandha-dharma*). Someone asked:

"Why not destroy them all? He replied, "If they were destroyed all at once, I fear it would give rise to terror; therefore, I do not sever them entirely. Question: "What is the meaning of 'esoteric' (guhya) in this context? Answer:
