Now, this is explained according to the majestic power of the method for upholding the sutra; it concerns the general permeability and the combination or separation of the six sense faculties.
Second, if explained according to the ordinary person’s own stage, the nose faculty perceives fragrance and does not perceive sound, thus it is not called "hearing.

However, based on the teaching that the faculties function interchangeably, it may also be called "hearing. Question: Regarding the sutra’s statement concerning "above, below, internal, and external," what does this mean? Answer: It refers to the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).

The upper [realms] are called "above," while the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is called "below. Furthermore, sentient beings are called "internal," and the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) is called "external.
Moreover, among sentient beings, internal virtues within the body are called "internal," while external things such as clothing are called "external."
The phrase "since the distance between above and below is vast," etc., constitutes the Master of the Commentary (*śāstrin*) setting forth an objection.
Regarding the phrase "if the sense faculty knows from afar," it means that if the fragrance is located at that distant place, the sense faculty does not go to that place.

If one could know it from afar, this would mean the sense faculty is impaired while the object is not; "impaired" (*bhaṅga*) here carries the meaning of being disordered or lost. It is not [the case that the object is impaired].
This means "to damage. Master Mo said: "According to the discourse on the characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), the nose-faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*) perceives its object through contact.
If one were to perceive an object at a distance in this manner—as if perceiving an object through separation—it would contradict the principle that the nose-faculty perceives through contact.

Thus, it is the faculty that is damaged, not the nature of the object. The second [master] said: "If the matter requires it, the fragrant object must come to the [faculty] before it can be perceived."
[Question: Is it the case that all fragrances willingly approach the sense organ? [Answer: Not necessarily; it is not the case that every single fragrance comes to the olfactory faculty.
The Master of the Commentary sets forth this double objection to clarify the point.
Regarding the statement, "This is knowledge (*jñāna*), etc.," this cites various treatises to provide a general explanation.

As for the phrase, "Concentration (*samādhi*) and knowledge know from afar," this is the commentary on the *Śāstra* text. This is a mental factor (*caitta*) associated with the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*), specifically the "knowledge" among the five object-specific factors (*viṣayapratiniyatālambana*).
This knowledge, together with the sixth consciousness-king, proceeds toward the nasal faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*) and, relying upon the nasal faculty, takes [the fragrance] as its object.
Regarding odors of the upper realms: Question—Since it is consciousness that, in conjunction with wisdom (*jñāna*), cognizes them, this is itself wisdom.

Why, then, does the Sūtra state that the olfactory faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*) perceives the object of odor? Answer—Wisdom relies upon the olfactory faculty to perceive the object of odor. It is spoken of in terms of its basis (*āśraya*) as "the olfactory faculty smelling.
In reality, the olfactory faculty only perceives objects through contact (*saṃyukta-vijñapti*); it cannot perceive odors of the upper realms.
Fragrances from the upper realms do not come to the nose-faculty; rather, they are perceived by the wisdom associated with the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) from afar.

Therefore, the Commentary states: "It is not that the nose can actually grasp an object while separated from it. Furthermore, since the faculties function interchangeably, if even the nose-faculty—which finds it difficult to grasp its objects—can still succeed in doing so, how much more so would the wisdom detached from the faculties, such as those of the eye and ear, not perceive the fragrances of the great trichiliocosm?

Question: Why is it necessary to explain the meaning of the mutual functioning of the sense faculties? Answer: The Master of the Commentary [uses] the fact that the sense faculties of a lower stage take the fragrance of a higher stage as their object to manifest the meaning of the mutual functioning of the sense faculties.

Regarding the statement that "the various faculties are mutually interchangeable," Master Jin says: "As for the mutual interchangeability of the faculties, when a single faculty gives rise to consciousness, it takes all objects as its condition.

If even the five faculties giving rise to the five consciousnesses can take all objects as their conditions, how much more so the wisdom associated with the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) which arises simultaneously with them—could it not apprehend the realm of fragrances throughout the great trichiliocosm? It is not that the essential nature of the nose-faculty itself [is lacking]."

[The text] takes up [the point]. Question: Since it has already been clarified that the nose-faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*) apprehends its objects within specific limits, why does the commentary immediately state:

"Moreover, relying on this nose, do the mental consciousnesses (*manovijñāna*) of the same time not apprehend the great trichiliocosm? Why, then, does it speak of the "eye, ear, and consciousness"? Answer: This is a mutual illustration (*pratibimba*).

Alternatively, because one wishes to establish the significance of the eye and ear, it concludes by using the case of the nose to illustrate that the mental consciousnesses accompanying it likewise [do not apprehend the entire universe]. It is not... [the case].

"Does it grasp the fragrance of the great trichiliocosm? Question: "If the nose is able to apprehend all objects through the power of the sūtras, does it give rise to its own consciousness to see forms, or does it give rise to the visual consciousness to see forms?
Answer: "It gives rise to its own consciousness. Question: "If that is so, this would merely be a case of mutual functioning among the various consciousnesses.

What, then, is meant by the 'mutual functioning of the faculties' (*indriya*)? Furthermore, how can the faculty and the consciousness be said to share the same object (*sādhāraṇa-viṣaya*)? Answer: "The faculty is identical to the consciousness. And yet...
Because they function reciprocally and because the faculties (*indriya*) are predominant, they alone receive the name "faculty.

If that were so, one might argue that just as one has mastery over the faculties—whereby a single faculty apprehends all six—one could likewise have mastery over consciousness, such that a single consciousness would depend upon all six faculties.

However, it is easier for an object to produce consciousness when a single faculty encounters its corresponding object; this is the primary sense of the term. Therefore, it is that [object] which produces its own consciousness, and not this [consciousness] which depends on a single [faculty].

Regarding the meaning of "the sense bases produce multiple consciousnesses": it means that based on a single sense base, a single consciousness is produced. Furthermore, it is said: "However, the sense bases possess five meanings that are superior to other factors such as visible form;

thus they are said to 'attain' [their objects] and so forth. Question: Since fragrance is an object known through contact (*saṃyukta*), how can it be apprehended through separation (*viprakṛṣṭa*)? Answer: [As stated in the] Commentary...
It is said: "One perceives that which is merely a semblance of fragrance and so forth. Question: Why does one not perceive actual fragrance, but rather perceive a semblance of fragrance? Answer:

If it were admitted that fragrance is perceived as a real entity through sensory contact with external objects (*bahir-viṣaya*), it would undermine the definition of the nature of the objective field; therefore, one perceives only a semblance of fragrance.

This refers to the meaning of the non-disruption of the nature of the object. The *Śāstra-saṃgraha* (Compendium of Questions) asks: "In the various holy teachings, one does not see it stated that fragrance is a designation (*prajñapti*).

Why, then, do you say that the 'attained' [fragrance] is a designation, and that the 'similar-to-fragrance' is a designation? The answer, in section 54, states: "When wind moves through the air, there is no co-nascent fragrance;

there is only a 'similar-to-fragrance' which is a designation. For example, when wind passes over and brushes against the fragrance of tree flowers and the like, it carries that fragrance along with it due to its causal conditions."
Because flowers and the like possess fragrance through the wind, it is called "semblance-fragrance" (jiasi xiang). It does not obtain the intrinsic substance (*svabhāva*) of fundamental fragrance;

thus it is called semblance-fragrance. An-guo says: "It is fragrance separated from its substrate. It is also called "solitary-wandering fragrance. The *Triṃśikā* states: "In reality, fragrance is known when [the object] is present;
that which is apprehended when separated is obtained as semblance-fragrance, not the actual substance of fragrance. If one obtains it when separated..."
Regarding "real fragrance," this refers to the destruction of the nature of the object. The meaning is that if one grasps at real fragrance, the nature of fragrance is destroyed;
it is like a monastic wearing a layman's shirt, which destroys the monastic decorum. Artificial fragrance does not destroy it, just as a lay performer might wear a monastic robe.
The sūtra mentions *sumanā*, also called *manas*, which here means "intention"; it refers to the *sumanā* flower, also known as the "excellent intention" flower.
The sūtra mentions *jāti*, newly termed the "gold coin flower."
The sūtra mentions *mallikā*; this is translated as "garland-flower" (*mànhuā*), so called because it is suitable for making garlands.
The sūtra mentions *campaka*; the correct term is *campaka*, which is translated as "yellow flower. It is small but fragrant;
it grows in thickets in the prefectures of the South Sea.
The Sūtra says that *parāra* means "flower of rebirth.
Regarding the sandalwood incense mentioned in the Sūtra: sandalwood incense produced on Mount Malaya is called "ox-head" (*gośīrṣa*).
If it is applied to the body, fire cannot burn it. Beside Lake Anavatapta, there is aloeswood incense in pellets as small as sesame seeds.
"Son, burn a single pellet; its fragrance will pervade Jambudvīpa, and all sentient beings who smell it shall be freed from all suffering.
As for the "tamaraka" and other fragrances mentioned in the sutra, this is translated as "Stainless Sage" (Wugou Xian) and is also called "Huolei Incense" (Huo Lai Xiang).
Regarding the *tagara* incense mentioned in the sutra, it is also called *tagaru*. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* translates it as "wood-scented tree.

Regarding the *pārijātaka* mentioned in the sutra, this is translated as "the flower of the perfectly formed tree" (*yuan-cheng shu-hua*). It is also called "protecting various scents" (*hu zhongzhong xiang*).
The sūtra speaks of the fragrance of the *kovidāra* tree; this is translated as the "Great Play Tree" (*mahāvikrīḍita*) or the "Round-Born Tree" (*maṇḍalaja*).
The tree is five hundred *yojana*s in height, and its fragrance travels fifty *yojana*s against the wind and one hundred *yojana*s with the wind.
This is the Great Assembly Tree (*mahāsannipāta-vṛkṣa*) of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Regarding the scriptural statement, "situated in the supreme [palace]," it is asked: what is called the "Victorious Palace" (*vijaya-vimāna*)? The answer is:
when Śakra battles with the asuras, the victor ascends this palace. Its majestic power (*tejas*) is like that of the midday sun; no devas or humans are able to gaze upon it for long.
Regarding the scriptural passage concerning "the incense burned by the devas" and so forth: Question: What is meant by "the incense burned by the devas"? Answer:
In the Sudharmā Hall there is an incense named *Vimalavyūha* (Pure Adornment). If a single pellet of this incense is burned, it causes the minds of all the devas to recollect the Buddha.
In the Yāma Heaven there is an incense; if a single pellet is burned, the hosts of devas gather like clouds. In the Tuṣita Heaven...

There is a fragrance; if one burns a single pellet before a Bodhisattva bound to one more birth, it will give rise to a great cloud of incense that covers the entire Dharma-realm and rains down all manner of offerings everywhere.

Regarding the statement in the sutra concerning "the fragrance of the Buddhas' bodies," the aforementioned sutra text says: "A wondrous fragrance issues from their bodies, pervading the lands of the ten directions;
sentient beings who are perfumed by it experience a joy they cannot contain."

Regarding the question of what constitutes the "fragrance" in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*): it is asked, since the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) possesses edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*), one may speak of the existence of fragrance;

however, since the form realm lacks edible food, how can it be said that fragrance exists there? The commentary answers: this refers to the fragrance of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), not the fragrance resulting from karmic fruition.

Regarding the mention of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and other texts: it is asked, since this [present] sūtra states that fragrance exists only in the desire and form realms, why does the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* speak of the fragrance of the palaces in the formless realm?
The answer is: this [statement in the present sūtra] is based on the *Dharmapada-sūtra* (Sūtra of the Dharma Blossom), which concerns phenomena based upon physical forms.
That [text] relies on what resembles the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. Now, regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, "relying on form" (*yixing*) means relying upon the former physical form.
"Form" (*xing*) refers to the physical substance; that is, the actual body within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), which is termed "relying on form. It is based upon this former physical form.
Because those who uphold this sutra can alone hear of such things as the transformation-arising of the realm of fragrance, it is called "fragrance based on form.

Regarding the statement that this refers to the "similar" (pratibimba): according to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, that which is "similar to form" means that in the Formless Realm there is no substantial, real physical body;

rather, through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), new and ever-renewing sensory faculties (*pañcendriya*)—which are the "supporting dust"—arise. Although the bases of these five faculties are fivefold...
The shape of the roots is subordinate; because it serves no [independent] function, it is said to be "resembling" [fragrance].

Although the manifested physical bodies and palaces and so forth all possess fragrance, they are termed "provisionally resembling fragrance. Therefore, according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, that which relies on form and fragrance is superior.
In the *Avataṃsaka*, [fragrance] is treated as being like a visible form; thus, it is inferior.

Regarding the statement "However, the *Yogācārabhūmi* and other texts," the question is: Which sacred teaching states that there are fragrances resembling visible forms in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)? The answer is given in the Commentary:
"However, the *Yogācārabhūmi* and others merely have the characteristics of manifest colors and so forth; they lack a real, substantial essence."

Regarding the statement that those causes such as fragrance are absent, there are two layers below. First, it is because in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is no actual substance of matter and thus no actual fragrance;
although there is a nominal fragrance, its generative causes are twofold. First, the absence of the seeds of fragrance and odor is called the deficiency of the generative cause (*janakahetu*).
Second, the absence of the preparatory mind (*prayogacitta*) that produces fragrance, odor, and tangibility—since this mind is absent, it is called [the deficiency of the generative cause].
Regarding the phrase "and because it would be useless": Question: What is meant by "useless"? Answer: Beings in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) do not consume edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*).
If one were to consume edible food, it would necessarily require the three [objects]—odor, flavor, and tangibility—to provide benefit. Since they do not consume edible food, these are unnecessary.

Because of odors, tastes, and tangibles, they are called "useless" (*anupayoga*). Even if a noble one were to transform them through the mind of applied effort (*prayogika-citta*), there would still be no place for their utility;

thus, they are useless. Jin says: They are called "useless" because they lack functional power. Since odors and tastes do not exist within the objective sphere (*viṣaya*), they cause the perceiving mind (*ālambaka-citta*) to be unable to transform [them] as well;
this is what is meant by "useless. This is explained with reference to the perceiving mind. Second, it is said:
Because odors and tastes lack functional efficacy within the objective sphere (*ālambana*), they cannot induce the arising of the perceiving mind nor manifest as odors and tastes.
This statement regarding their lack of efficacy refers specifically to the objective sphere.
Regarding the statement "relying upon the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and so forth," this serves as a dual explanation of the uselessness of the cause of birth. To explain them separately:

if one relies upon the seeds of form within the form realm as the essential nature (*svabhāva*) to transform and produce the form that is the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*), then there is no odor or fragrance, because those factors do not exist [in the form realm].
If one relies upon the seeds of form within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) as the essential nature to transform and produce the form that is the fruit of meditative concentration, then...
There is fragrance and odor because the dharmas of the earth exist. The separate explanation above is of no further use.

As for the statement that "the preparatory mind is inferior," there are two causes for the arising of the [actual] liberation: first, the seed is called the cause of arising; second, the preparatory mind.
The preparatory mind is called the cause of arising. When the preparatory mind is inferior, it is then designated as the cause of arising.
This is an omission. Because it is superior, there is [transformation]; because it is inferior, there is none. In the Formless Realm, transformation of odor and taste occurs;
because it is inferior, one cannot transform them. (The preceding section on the basis of the stages is thus concluded.)

Regarding the statement that "Bodhisattvas have no equals among the two vehicles," this is a distinction made based on the individuals concerned. Question: If the two vehicles lack [this quality], they should not be considered noble ones (*ārya*).
Answer: Among the two vehicles, it exists in the Śrāvakas of Extensive Wisdom (*vipula-prajña*); it does not exist in other persons. Thus, it is said that the two vehicles lack it.
It does not exist for those who lack extensive wisdom.
Regarding the term "Buddha’s disciples," it exists among the noble ones but not among ordinary beings; within the noble ones, it exists among Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas of extensive wisdom.
There are none other than these. As for what Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess: Bodhisattvas, relying upon the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), are likewise able to transform into fragrance and flavor.

Regarding the statement "as it says in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*," etc., this refers to the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) and so forth; they are all capable of being transformed. This was explained previously regarding the mind-made body (*manomayakāya*).
Like those fragrances and so forth, they are capable of transforming both color and taste.
Regarding the sūtra’s statement that there are various hidden treasures within the earth, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* explains: "Gold and silver have no fragrance; the diamond has no taste.
How then can precious hidden treasures possess fragrance? The answer is: the faculties of the Hīnayāna practitioners are dull; they do not know that this sūtra is a Mahāyāna teaching.

How could this be the same as the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*)? Furthermore, their tenets and systems differ. If it were not so, how could the eight objects collectively constitute [the sensory experience]?
Although the Sūtra states that one who has not yet attained the bodhisattva’s untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas may still produce the nose-consciousness, one might ask:

even if one enters the first stage (*bhūmi*), is the nose-faculty itself untainted? The answer is: because it is originally tainted (*sāsrava*). As the *Jianyao* says: "It is induced from untainted dharmas."

"Arising" (*jāti*) also refers to the arising of untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*). It does not mean that the olfactory faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*) which arises is itself untainted. The prose section of the sutra states:

"One who attains the purified olfactory faculty"—this does not mean that the substance of the olfactory faculty is itself untainted. Rather, with respect to a Bodhisattva at the stage of a Noble One (*ārya*), the functional activity of the olfactory faculty is induced by relying upon untainted phenomena;
this is termed the "arising of untainted phenomena. Here, "arising" (*jāti*) is used in the sense of "inducing" (*utpāda*).

It is not that they are born of one's own parents. [Master] She says: "To allow that the five consciousnesses can attain the untainted (anāsrava) is precisely the same as this passage in the Sūtra, which states:
'One attains twelve hundred merits of the tongue. This refers to their measure."
The Sūtra says, "whether good or ugly, whether beautiful or unattractive. This refers precisely to the upward function of the pure tongue-faculty (śuddha-jihvêndriya);
therefore, it is called the "function of the faculty" (indriya-vṛtti). The pure tongue-faculty takes the tasting of flavors as its primary function.
As for the tongue that is seen by the eye, this is the dust-supporting tongue-faculty (rajo-niśrita-jihvêndriya), which serves as the physical basis for the pure tongue-faculty.

Regarding the question, "Why is it that this [organ] lacks the capacity for its object, etc.?"—these latter two organs differ from the others in that they lack the tongue organ's ability to taste all flavors throughout the three thousandfold world system, both above and below. Question:

Why is it that the tongue organ cannot taste and know the flavors of the three thousandfold world system? Since it cannot know the flavors of the triple world, should it not be incomplete in its twelve hundred faculties?
The Master [De] replies in his commentary, stating that the tongue faculty should likewise be able to perceive [objects], and so forth. Within this commentary there are three points. First:
"How could it also be permitted to taste the flavors of the three realms? This implies that the tongue faculty functions primarily for the purpose of preaching the Dharma;

its utility does not lie in tasting flavors. Both the prose and the verse emphasize the function of preaching the Dharma; fearing that the text would become overly prolix, the mention of tasting has been omitted.
The merit of taste is not mentioned.
As for the statement that fragrance exists apart from its substance, this is the second point: while color and fragrance exist apart from their substances, taste does not.
Since there is no taste that exists apart from its substance, the tasting of the flavors of the three thousandfold world-system is not mentioned.
Regarding the phrase "it is also said in the sūtras," etc., this is the third point: the Buddha possesses [these qualities], whereas others do not.

As for the statement "it is also said in the sūtras," it refers to the sixth fascicle of the *Daśabhūmika-vibhaṅga-sūtra* (Ten Stages Sutra on Severing Bonds), which says: "The Tathāgata’s supernormal power of the eye is inconceivable."

The Tathāgata’s supernormal power of the ear is immeasurable; the Tathāgata’s supernormal power of the nose is even more incalculable; the Tathāgata’s supernormal power of the tongue is vast and boundless.
Therefore, it is said that the Buddha possesses the supernormal powers of the nose and tongue which surpass those of the eye and ear. An-guo says:

"This is explained provisionally according to the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), where the dharmas are established for the eye and ear, while they are not so established for the other four faculties. However, if one relies on the Mahāyāna and the state of Buddhahood..."
Regarding the stage where all five sense organs are established, they are collectively able to apprehend objects by departing from the center.
As for the statement that the tongue "possesses function," this refers to the instrument; the tongue-root (*jihvendriya*) that supports the sensory dust is the instrument for preaching the Dharma.
This distinguishes it as the function of the instrumental organ, rather than the function of the tongue-root itself.
Regarding the statement in the Sūtra that all Buddhas preach the Dharma while facing toward that person: the question is asked, "With what tongue do the Buddhas preach? The answer is:

All Buddhas possess the characteristic of always facing forward and never turning their backs. When this person sees the Buddha, the Buddha is thus constantly facing them and preaches the Dharma for their sake.

Regarding the statement that "two verses [are recited] for many assemblies," the Sūtra says: "If this person who preaches the Dharma wishes to fill the trichiliocosm with a sublime voice, they can do so at will.
This precisely refers to the pervasion of sound throughout the trichiliocosm, which is the full utilization of the faculty of the tongue.
Regarding the phrase "the sages and noble ones" in the single verse, the Sūtra mentions "Brahmā, Māra, and so forth. Zhang Jing asks:
"Why are Brahmā, Māra, and others called 'sages and noble ones'? The answer is: It does not preclude that even Brahmā and others may manifest as sages and noble ones.
Those who act as Māras are mostly inconceivable liberation Bodhisattvas; they too are called "sages and noble ones."
Regarding the scriptural passage on "superior and inferior, beautiful and ugly," etc.: the upper realms are called "superior births"; the lower desire realm is called an "inferior birth.

Humans and devas are called "beautiful births," while the three miserable destinies are called "ugly. Alternatively, those born with upright and handsome physical forms are called "beautiful," while those who are deformed and unsightly are called "ugly."
Regarding the scriptural statement that "all appear therein," the question is asked: Why do pure objects appear within the body of one who upholds the sūtra? The answer is given in the *Mahā-śāstra*:

As stated in the *Guhyagarbha-tantra*, the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya dwells within the bodies of all sentient beings, with its radiance appearing externally, just like a mani-jewel wrapped in clean silk; it is without any obscuring marks, and its color is not obstructed.
It is empty. Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The body of the youth Sudhana manifests throughout the ten directions; emptiness does not obstruct form.
If a single pearl is clear and transparent, all images appear within it; when ten thousand waters have calm waves, they all manifest simultaneously. Question:

Why does the tongue-faculty not speak of distinguishing flavors, and why does the body-faculty not speak of perceiving touch? Answer: The tongue undergoes changes in flavor, and thus the Dharma is taught [through its transformations].
The body possesses the function of being able to perceive objects with a pleasant outlook; this highlights its distinct quality, rather than describing its common function.
The eyes, ears, nose, and mind have no other distinct capacity than to rely upon their fundamental functions.

Regarding the scriptural statement, "Only one understands it for oneself," etc.: the forms and images within the body are seen by the practitioner of the sutra themselves, while others do not see them.
This is also a general description; if it concerns those of a higher stage, what prevents them from seeing those of a lower stage? Question:

When one practices the ten dharma-activities for oneself, one understands them clearly for oneself alone; but when teaching others to practice the ten dharma-activities, should others also know them? Answer: [They should.]
One performs and practices it oneself; one knows this matter within oneself. Even if others follow the instructions, it still results in being known by oneself alone.
Now, in understanding the words of others, one distinguishes them from those of lower stations. If they were to bestow their empowerment, they too would be able to accord with this.
The scriptural statement, "Although one has not yet attained the untainted [state] such as the single practice," is the conclusion.

Its intended meaning is that although the principle of the two emptinesses has not been attained, the *dharmatā-kāya* (dharma-nature body) possesses a pure and eternal essence; this "eternity" does not refer to the name of an unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharma, but rather refers to the continuous and enduring essence throughout a single lifetime.

Regarding "inexhaustible speech": if one asks what is meant by "inexhaustible," the answer is that it refers to being able to explain a single phrase or a single verse of the Dharma to others for a month or four months;
hence it is called inexhaustible. Were it not for the power of upholding the sutra, how could such a thing be achieved?

Regarding the statement that "the divisions of months and seasons are cited," this refers to citing four months by way of implication to encompass even more time, or citing a single day to illustrate even less time.
From the longest periods to the shortest, all are instances of expounding a single phrase or a single verse.
Mou said: "According to the laws of the Western lands, there are three seasons in a year, namely: the hot season, the rainy season, and the cold season.
From the sixteenth day of the first month to the fifteenth day of the fifth month—these four months constitute the hot season.

From the sixteenth day of the fifth month to the fifteenth day of the ninth month is the rainy season. From the sixteenth day of the ninth month to the fifteenth day of the first month [is the cold season]."
This is the season of cold. Four months constitute one season; this is called the "limit of months. Three seasons constitute one year;
this is called the "limit of seasons. From within the limit of months, one month is taken; from within the limit of seasons, one season is taken.
Therefore, it is called the year of the "Raising of the Moon. This means that whether much or little, one is able to expound upon even a single phrase or a single verse.
Here, this is divided into eight periods: from the waxing of the moon until it is full is the bright half (śukla-pakṣa);

from the waning of the moon until it is dark is the dark half (kṛṣṇa-pakṣa). The bright half first and the dark half last together constitute one month; six months combined constitute one course (ayana) as the sun travels.
When [the sun] is within, it moves northward; when it is outside, it moves southward. These two movements together constitute a year.
In the west, black precedes and white follows, differing according to the direction.

Regarding the scriptural passage on "the range of the mind" (*citta-gocara*) and so forth: "mind" refers to the cognizing mind (*ālambaka-citta*). "Range" (*gocara*) refers to the objective sphere (*ālambana-viṣaya*).
When the cognizing mind grasps an objective sphere, it is termed the "range of the mind. Thus, it is said to be the "sphere apprehended by the mind.
As for the "active functioning of the mind," this refers to the modes of activity (*ākāra*) of the three natures: the wholesome nature, the unwholesome nature, and the indeterminate nature.

Regarding the phrase "or body, speech, and mind": the movements of the mind are assigned to bodily action (*kāyakarman*); the mind is that which acts, while bodily action is the object of its activity.
The movements of the mind are assigned to verbal action (*vākkarman*); the mind is that which moves, while verbal action is the object of its movement.

Furthermore, "mental activity" (*manas-karman*) refers to the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) of the mind. Conceptual proliferation is synonymous with verbal discrimination (*abhilāpa-vikalpa*).

With phenomena (*dharma*) as the object of discrimination and the mind as the agent of discrimination, it is said that "the mind discriminates. This phrase refers to all instances of mental engagement.
Alternatively, the mind induces the various consciousnesses, and speech is the play of the mental factors (*caitta*), because the mind is that which plays.

Thus, the Sūtra states: "Even those who have not yet attained untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*)... This refers to the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), where one first attains untainted wisdom, which is able to induce the mental faculty (*manas*).

The phrase "even though" means that although one has not yet attained the wisdom associated with the untainted mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) of the first stage, it is still able to induce [the faculties].
The mind-faculty (*manas*)—the seventh consciousness—is also established as being untainted (*anāsrava*). However, what is taught in the sutras all refers to the sixth consciousness;
it is spoken thus because, when considering the six faculties together with the seventh consciousness, [the nature of the latter] is made manifest.
Regarding the statement in the sutra that "all these were spoken in the sutras of previous Buddhas," the person who upholds the sutra reflects upon the principles of the teaching:
"This is within the scriptural instructions of all Buddhas; it is precisely what was spoken in the sutras of previous Buddhas."

Regarding the statement that the text might become overly verbose: within this very section on the mental faculty (*manas*), there are seven paragraphs in prose, whereas only five are described in verse;
thus, they are called "distinct. Furthermore, if one were to examine the differences between the verses and the prose for all the other faculties, the discrepancies would be numerous.
Fearing that the text would become too extensive, I have not been able to analyze each one individually.

Regarding the statement in the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging" that there are six chapters for those who can learn and practice, divided into four sections: the "Chapter on the Emergence from the Earth" clarifies the persons who propagate the current practice of the *Anrakugyō* (Peaceful Conduct); the "Chapter on the Life Span" and the "Chapter on the Distinction" clarify the causes and conditions; and the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging" clarifies the fruit. As for the "Chapter on the Encouragement of Samantabhadra," it clarifies the entrustment. Furthermore, the "Chapter on the Emergence from the Earth" clarifies the persons who propagate the *Anrakugyō*; the "Chapter on the Life Span" and the "Chapter on the Distinction" clarify the causes and conditions; and the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging" clarifies the fruit. As for the "Chapter on the Encouragement of Samantabhadra," it clarifies the entrustment. Thus, the first section consists of the "Chapter on the Emergence from the Earth," the "Chapter on the Life Span," and the "Chapter on the Distinction. The second section consists of the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging. The third section consists of the "Chapter on the Encouragement of Samantabhadra. The fourth section consists of the "Chapter on the Entrustment. This is the meaning of the statement that there are six chapters for those who can learn and practice, divided into four sections. The preceding doubts have arisen in succession. The "Chapter on Rejoicing" and the "Chapter on the Dharma Master" concern the merits obtained by those who assist, rely upon, and propagate the *Anle-xing* (Peaceful Practices).

This "Chapter on Never-Disparaging" clarifies how the Buddha himself, while formerly abiding in the stage of a causal practitioner, practiced the *Anle-xing* and propagated this sutra to exhort the assembly; hence, this chapter follows.
Regarding the statement that "the three chapters have not yet reached equality," this refers to the Chapter on Rejoicing, the Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master,
and the Chapter on Never-Disparaging.
As for the phrase "I am always Never-Disparaging," the character "wei" (為) is pronounced with a level tone (ping sheng).
Regarding the statement that "although one initially undergoes suffering," the Sūtra says:

"Mahāsthāmaprāpta, at that time, because the fourfold assembly—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—treated me with contempt out of a mind of malice, they did not encounter a Buddha, hear the Dharma, or see the Saṃgha for two hundred billion kalpas. For a thousand kalpas, they underwent great suffering and affliction in the Avīci Hell."
Once these karmic retributions were exhausted, he again encountered the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging, who taught him toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
If even one who harmed those who upheld the sutra was still able to attain the Buddha-way, how much more so for one who personally upholds the sutra—how could such a person not become a Buddha?

Regarding the statement that this exposition possesses the causes and marks of prediction (*vyākaraṇa*): it possesses both the two causes of principle (*li*) and practice (*xing*). Jin [Yiqing] says: "It only states that it possesses the cause of the nature of reality (*li-xing-yin*).
Regarding the explanation of the name: the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* refers to it as the "Chapter on Constantly Being Despised."

Regarding the statement "observing that the fourfold assembly possesses the causes of Buddha-nature," this refers to the Buddha-nature of principle (*li-buddhatva*) and the Buddha-nature of practice (*xing-buddhatva*).

Regarding the statement "exhorting others to practice," the intended meaning is as follows: [the Master] feared that if it were said that all possess Buddha-nature, they might all assume it is already self-evident;

therefore, he offers this exhortation. As the Sūtra says: "You should simply practice the Bodhisattva path, and you shall attain Buddhahood. It continues: "Those who have the nature will become Buddhas; those who do not..."
By nature, one does not become a Buddha.

Regarding the statement that the three karmas are equal at all times, the Sūtra says: "If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī, up to and including [all others], should perform prostrations and offer praises, saying:
'I deeply revere you; I dare not treat you with contempt,' this is the bodily karma of prostration."
Prostration; praising through the vocal karma; and not treating [the teaching] with disrespect through the mental karma.
To say that one wishes to clarify the majestic power (*vīrya*) and so forth of this sutra is to reveal that this sutra possesses sovereign might, and furthermore, to reveal the bodhisattva.

At that time, because he had attained the power of great supernormal faculties (*ṛddhi-bala*), the power of eloquence (*pratibhāna-bala*), and the power of great sublime tranquility (*praśama-bala*), he addressed Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
He said that those who practice in accordance [with the teaching] will attain Buddhahood; this refers to the Bodhisattva Viśeṣacintin, who has now attained perfect enlightenment.
As the sutra states: "If I had not, in past lives, upheld, recited, and studied this sutra, I would not have been able to quickly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Regarding the statement that "even an evil person who violates the sutras can [attain liberation] equally," according to the treatise:
one who strikes or reviles a holder of the sutras will fall into hell for a full kalpa; when that kalpa ends, they are reborn again, continuing in this manner through countless kalpas.

Yet, due to the inconceivable power of the sutra, there comes a time when their suffering ends. Having entered hell for only a thousand kalpas and completed these retributions, they shall again encounter the Buddha.
One should not disparage the Bodhisattva.

Regarding the statement that the answer to the Buddha was given "on account of him," this refers primarily to the Bodhisattva, who exhorts the multitude; however, it is spoken incidentally regarding the Buddha.

This is because that Bodhisattva Never Disparaging lived during the time of the Buddha King of Majestic Sound (Vaiśvānara-rāja), and for that reason, the name of the Buddha is mentioned alongside his.
This is not the essential point. Therefore, the title of the chapter is taken from "Not Disparaging" (*Adhimātra-avajñā*), rather than from "Vimalasvara.
Regarding the phrase "this is the first," etc., it first cites the offenses and merits arising from opposition and compliance with the preceding [teachings] to demonstrate them to the assembly.
The Sūtra states: "If there are those who use harsh speech, revile, or slander [the Dharma], they will receive a retribution for their great sins as previously described;

it refers to the passage in the *Upamāna-parivarta* stating that when such a person’s life ends, they enter the Avīci Hell and remain there for a full kalpa, and upon the exhaustion of that kalpa, they are reborn again.
The Sūtra further states: "The merit they obtain is as previously described"; this refers to the attainment of the six faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) as mentioned in the *Dharmabhāṇaka-guṇa-parivarta*.
...merit. Furthermore, Mo said: "One will receive the retribution of a great sin;
for two hundred billion kalpas after birth, one will never encounter a Buddha, hear the Dharma, or see the Sangha. For a thousand kalpas, one will undergo great suffering in the Avīci Hell.
As for the merit he obtained, it was as follows: when this bhikṣu was on the verge of death, he heard in the midst of the void the full majesty of...
He was able to receive and uphold all twenty thousand million verses of the Lotus Sūtra previously taught by the Buddha Ghoṣarāja,
and immediately attained the aforementioned purity of the faculty of the eye, and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "this refers to the very first," it means that the evil person’s power increases. In the past, there was a Buddha named King of Majestic Sound (Vaiśvānara-svara-rāja) Tathāgata.
After he entered parinirvāṇa, there followed a succession of twenty trillion Buddhas, all bearing the same name.

Now, taking the very first of these Buddhas, after his entry into parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Semblance Dharma (Saddharma-pratirūpaka), there were bhikṣus of overweening pride. There were...

"Of great power. This is why the Commentary says: "Evil persons increase in power. If one were within the Buddha’s True Dharma (*saddharma*), the Buddha’s power would augment [the righteous] and evil persons would be powerless.
Now, this is the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpaka-dharma*) and the Buddha-Dharma is in decline; thus, the power of evil persons increases.
Regarding the phrase "the virtuous person increases their diligence": a bodhisattva is called a "virtuous person," and "increasing diligence" means increasing the path.
Regarding the phrase "the bodhisattva bhikṣu," which clarifies that this refers to a bodhisattva and so forth: the sutra states, "At that time there was a bodhisattva bhikṣu named Sadāparibhūta.
This indicates one who is both a bodhisattva and a bhikṣu, thereby distinguishing him from those who are merely bhikṣus and not [bodhisattvas].
Regarding "bodhisattvas": this may refer to those of fixed lineage among the śrāvakas and the two vehicles who have not yet resolved upon the Great Mind;

such bhikṣus are not called bodhisattvas, as they do not seek the Buddha-work by upholding this sutra, and thus do not engage in this practice. This should be distinguished by means of four propositions.

First, there are those who are bodhisattvas but not bhikṣus; these include lay bodhisattvas. Second, there are those who are bhikṣus but not bodhisattvas; these are those of fixed lineage as śrāvakas.
Third, there are those who are both bhikṣus and bodhisattvas; this refers to Sadāparibhūta. Fourth, there are those who are neither bhikṣus nor bodhisattvas;
these are the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). As the Sūtra says: "Mahāsthāmaprāpta, for what reason is he named Sadāparibhūta?"
"Lightness," etc., is the explanation of the terminology.

Regarding the statement that it is not surprising at first that this is a bodhisattva, etc.: the question is, "How is it that a bodhisattva bhikṣu prostrating to a layperson does not violate the precepts?
The answer in the commentary states, "It is not surprising at first," etc. Zhangjing says: "The bodhisattva is not [merely] a bhikṣu."
The former case refers to one who is a bhikṣu but not a bodhisattva; the latter refers to one who is a bodhisattva but not a bhikṣu.

If it is a bodhisattva who is not a bhikṣu prostrating to a layperson, this is called the "first" case and is not to be considered strange, for he does not violate the precepts. If it is a bhikṣu who is not a bodhisattva prostrating to a layperson...
The name is strange. Because he later violates the precepts, what was not strange at first becomes strange later. "Strange" here means to be startled and alarmed;
it refers to a bhikṣu performing the ritual salutation of a layperson who has violated the precepts.

Regarding the mention of the woman Abhayamati and others: one asks, based on which sacred teaching is it that a bodhisattva bhikṣu prostrating to a layperson does not constitute a violation of the precepts?

The answer in the commentary states: if it causes those sentient beings to give rise to dedication (pariṇāmanā) and further causes the roots of goodness (kuśalamūla) of sentient beings to grow, then prostrating does not constitute a violation. If one is merely a bhikṣu and not a bodhisattva, [it is otherwise].

If one performs prostrations for the purpose of dedicating [merit] toward the growth of roots of goodness, it constitutes an offense; however, not performing prostrations in such a case does not constitute an offense.
As for the statement that "performing these prostrations now" refers to the growth of roots of goodness and the act of dedication, therefore no offense is committed.
Regarding the statement "furthermore, one pays homage to the fourfold assembly," etc.: if one pays homage to only a single individual—whether it be a nun or a laywoman—one commits an offense.
This is because one honors the nature of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya-svabhāva*), and does not pay homage to an ordinary body (*prākṛta-kāya*).
As for the statement that there are those who interpret this as meaning one does not recite, chant, practice emptiness, or perform prostrations— this interpretation is incorrect.
Regarding the phrase "therefore we know he does not honor [the teachings]," it means that this bhikṣu does not single-mindedly recite the sūtras, nor does he single-mindedly practice...
Regarding "verbal assault" (*vāg-danda*): it does not refer exclusively to words directed downward.
As for "one who is able to endure verbal assault," the sutra states that among the fourfold assembly, there are those who are equal.
"Verbal assault" refers to all vocal actions; specifically, verbal abuse is called "verbal assault," while physical striking is called "physical assault."

Regarding the fourth point, that the body which can be harmed is capable of receiving [the blow], the Sūtra says: "When these words were spoken, some among the multitude used sticks and other implements... Question:

Since one runs away when struck by a stick, how can this be called patience (*kṣānti*)? Answer: Even secular texts state that when parents strike their children, if they are struck with light sticks, the child accepts it;
however, if struck with heavy sticks, the child must run away, fearing that in a single moment the parent’s anger might erupt and cause them to die. This would lead to a grave downfall.
It is because of the fault of their parents' unrighteousness. It is the same for the Bodhisattva; men and women are like his own parents, which is why he flees. Question:
Does he flee because he has been struck, or even before being struck? Answer: What is the use of fleeing after having been struck? He flees only while not yet struck. Question:
If the Bodhisattva is struck but does not receive the blow [on his body], how can this be called patience (*kṣānti*)? Answer: It is precisely to teach him to strike that [he flees].
"Being hit is itself patience. If one were not hit, one would still enter hell for a thousand kalpas, let alone being struck.
Fearing that the offense incurred would be heavy, he fled; fearing that [the assembly] would not hear the record, he raised his voice."
Regarding the phrase "the fifth, the name 'Good' (Kalyāṇa)," etc.: this precisely refers to the stage of the forty mental states (*cittotpāda*).
It is from this point that the title "Not Disparaging" (*Adhimātra*) arises. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Because he constantly speaks these words, he reaches the stage of 'Light' (*Laghu*)."
Regarding the statement that the "superior fruit" subsequently arises: before this superior fruit has arisen, one still abides in the stage of the equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*).

By taking as the cause the preaching of the sūtra during the Semblance Dharma period under the Buddha King of Majestic Sound (*Bhīṣmagarjitasvara*), one receives the instruction through a voice from space at the time of death as the fruit.
If one does not cultivate the cause, how could the fruit arise without it? First, there is the instruction through a voice from space consisting of a hundred million verses.

First, the ability to maintain [the teachings]; second, the purification of the six sense faculties; and third, the increase of lifespan while preaching the Dharma. These three are termed "superior fruits" because they are brought to fruition.
This occurs during the stage of the four preparatory practices (*prayoga*).
Regarding the statement that one can uphold the Dharma upon hearing it once, the Sūtra says: "When this bhikṣu is about to pass away, he will be able to receive and uphold everything.
This does not necessarily mean that the sūtras he has personally upheld consist of twenty *koṭi* of verses;
rather, through the Buddha’s empowerment at the time of death, he remembers all twenty *koṭi* of verses. [Question: The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* consists of seven fascicles; how is it now twenty?
"Ten million billion verses—is this not far too much? Answer: "In the land of the Small Transformation, there are only seven fascicles;

however, it does not preclude the fact that the scriptural texts in the land of the Great Transformation are numerous. Furthermore, it says below: "Verses as numerous as the sands of the Ganges," and "six hundred trillion *ya*," which is indeed many.
The Sūtra says: "Having fully heard [the teachings] from Buddha Prabhūtaratna and others. Question: Regarding the Bodhisattva Asaṃkīrṇabhadra...
Since Sadāprarudita first appeared during the Semblance Dharma period of the Buddha Vipaśyin, when it is now said that he "heard [the teaching] in its entirety," from which Buddha did he hear it?

If one says it was from the first Buddha, that first Buddha has already passed away. If one says it was from the subsequent Buddhas, how can it be said that he heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* previously taught?
Answer: At the time of his death, he heard only from the first Buddha, Vipaśyin. If that is so, since the first Buddha has already passed away, [how could he have heard it before?]
Question: This is difficult to reconcile. Answer: The Buddha has not truly passed into extinction; how then can you say he does not exist? Therefore, a previous sutra states:

"Those who read and recite the sutras in empty space shall all behold my body. Furthermore, if one examines the intent of the sutra, it is clear that within empty space, hearing is neither non-existent nor not directed toward the Buddha.
What prevents one from hearing those original sutras of the Buddha, known as the "First Teachings," which are manifested through the instruction of empty sounds?

This is precisely the transformation of corresponding verbal karma. Question: According to what is taught in the sūtras regarding lifespan and so forth, how is it that through preparatory application one sees the *saṃbuddha* (the Buddha of retribution) [appearing as] distinct [from the Buddha of transformation] in a single location?

Regarding the statement on "extending the lifespan through the teaching of the Dharma," the sutra says: "further extending the lifespan by two hundred [years]," and so forth. Question: What was the lifespan of people at that time?
Why is it now said to be two million *koṭi-nayuta*, which seems far too much? Answer: First, it is because they are empowered by the majestic power (*prabhāva*) of the Dharma.
Second, it may be due to the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-bala*), whereby their lifespan is not diminished. It is like a person who [should have] further...

After seven days, his body died and he suddenly entered meditative absorption (*samādhi*). After twenty or thirty years, he emerged from absorption and, after another seven days had passed, he died. Regarding the statement "first performing prostrations and so forth," it is asked: "If this is the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi-bala*), what does it have to do with the power of upholding the sutra? The commentary answers: The commentary states: "The power of the Dharma-realm is inconceivable; it is not merely the power of meditative concentration. It is because one has upheld the sutra that one is able to enter such a state of concentration. This means that although the power of meditative concentration is indeed inconceivable, it is not the case that one can enter such a state of concentration without having upheld the sutra. Therefore, it is known that this is due to the power of upholding the sutra. Furthermore, the *Sutra on the Ten Wheels* says: "If there is a person who, for the sake of the Buddha-dharma, upholds this sutra, even if they have committed the five grave offenses, they will immediately be liberated and attain the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*). This is called the power of upholding the sutra. Moreover, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "If there is a person who upholds the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, even if they have committed the four grave offenses, they will immediately be liberated and attain the stage of non-retrogression. This is called the power of upholding the sutra. Furthermore, the *Sutra on the Prophecy of the Bodhisattva Maitreya* says: "If there is a person who upholds the *Maitreya-vyākaraṇa Sūtra*, even if they have committed the five grave offenses, they will immediately be liberated and attain the stage of non-retrogression. This is called the power of upholding the sutra. Furthermore, the *Sutra on the Prophecy of the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati* says: "If there is a person who upholds the *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa Sūtra*, even if they have committed the five grave offenses, they will immediately be liberated and attain the stage of non-retrogression. This is called the power of upholding the sutra. Furthermore, the *Sutra on the Prophecy of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī* says: "If there is a person who upholds the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā Sūtra*, even if they have committed the five grave offenses, they will immediately be liberated and attain the stage of non-retrogression. This is called the power of upholding the sutra. Furthermore, the *Sutra on the Prophecy of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra* says: "If there is a person who upholds the *Samantabhadra-caryā-praṇidhāna Sūtra*, even if they have committed the five grave offenses, they will immediately be liberated and attain the stage of non-retrogression. This is called the power of upholding the sutra. Furthermore, the *Sutra on the Prophecy of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara* says: "If there is a person who upholds the *Avalokiteśvara-sūtra*, even if they have committed the five grave offenses, they will immediately be liberated and attain the stage of non-retrogression. This is called the power of upholding the sutra. Furthermore, the *Sutra on the Prophecy of the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha* says: "If there is a person who upholds the *Kṣitigarbha-sūtra*, even if they have committed the five grave offenses, they will immediately be liberated and attain the stage of non-retrogression. This is called the power of upholding the sutra. Furthermore, the *Sutra on the Prophecy of the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi* says: "If there is a person who upholds the *Vajrapāṇi-sūtra*, even if they have committed the five grave offenses, they will immediately be liberated and attain the stage of non-retrogression. This is called the power of upholding the sutra. Furthermore, the *Sutra on the Prophecy of the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin* says: "If there is a person who upholds the *Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin-sūtra*, even if they have committed the five grave offenses, they will immediately be liberated and attain the stage of non-retrogression. This is called the power of upholding the sutra. Furthermore, the *Sutra on the Prophecy of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī* says: "If there is a person who upholds the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā Sūtra*, even if they have committed the five grave offenses, they will immediately be liberated and attain the stage of non-retrogression. This is called the power of upholding the sutra. Furthermore, the *Sutra on the Prophecy of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra* says: "If there is a person who upholds the *Samantabhadra-caryā-praṇidhāna Sūtra*, even if they have committed the five grave offenses, they will immediately be liberated and attain the stage of non-retrogression. This is called the power of upholding the sutra. Furthermore, the *Sutra on the Prophecy of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara* says: "If there is a person who upholds the *Avalokiteśvara-sūtra*, even if they have committed the five grave offenses, they will immediately be liberated and attain the stage of non-retrogression. This is called the power of upholding the sutra. Furthermore, the *Sutra on the Prophecy of the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha* says: "If there is a person who upholds the *Kṣitigarbha-sūtra*, even if they have committed the five grave offenses, they will immediately be liberated and attain the stage of non-retrogression. This is called the power of upholding the sutra. Furthermore, the *Sutra on the Prophecy of the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi* says: "If there is a person who upholds the *Vajrapāṇi-sūtra*, even if they have committed the five grave offenses, they will immediately be liberated and attain the stage of non-retrogression. This is called the power of upholding the sutra. Furthermore, the *Sutra on the Prophecy of the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin* says: "If there is a person who upholds the *Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin-sūtra*, even if they have committed the five grave offenses, they will immediately be liberated and attain the stage of non-retrogression. This is called the power of upholding the sutra. Furthermore, the *Sutra on the Prophecy of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī* says: "If there is a person who upholds the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā Sūtra*, even if they have committed the five grave offenses, they will immediately be liberated and attain the stage of non-retrogression. This is called the power of upholding the sutra. Furthermore, the *Sutra on the Prophecy of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra* says: "If there is a person who upholds the *Samantabhadra-caryā-praṇidhāna Sūtra*, even if they have committed the five grave offenses, they will immediately be liberated and attain the stage of non-retrogression. This is called the power of upholding the sutra. Furthermore, the *Sutra on the Prophecy of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara* says: "If there is a person who upholds the *Avalokiteśvara-sūtra*, even if they have committed the five grave offenses, they will immediately be liberated and attain the stage of non-retrogression. This is called the power of upholding the sutra. Furthermore, the *Sutra on the Prophecy of the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha* says: "If there is a person who upholds the *Kṣitigarbha-sūtra*, even if they have committed the five grave offenses, they will immediately be liberated and attain the stage of non-retrogression. This is called the power of upholding the sutra. Furthermore, the *Sutra on the Prophecy of the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi* says: "If there is a person who upholds the *Vajrapāṇi-sūtra*, even if they have committed the five grave offenses, they will immediately be liberated and attain the stage of non-retrogression."

Regarding the forty mental states (*citta*) and so forth mentioned previously: it is said that the life span during the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*) is short, whereas it is extended until the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*), thus implying that one's life is naturally long.
Alternatively, since life spans were generally long at the beginning of a kalpa, this interpretation is not untenable.

Regarding the statement that "a single evil person is transformed," this refers to the increase of lifespan. The Sūtra states that "the power of supernormal knowledges" refers to the augmentation of life span.

The Sūtra states that "the power of eloquence" refers to the upholding of hundreds of millions of verses and joyfully expounding them to others. Taking these hundreds of millions of verses, one delights in teaching them to others.
Therefore, it is called the power of discernment (*pratisaṃvid-bala*). The Sūtra says: "Great, virtuous, and tranquil," which refers to *śamatha* (calm abiding).

Regarding the phrase "gradually [engaging] in the contemplation of the truths" (*satya-vipaśyanā*) and so forth: that which is observed is precisely the established (*vyavasthāpita*) and unestablished (*avyavasthāpita*) truths;

it is not like the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), which observe only the established truths. Question: What are the four roots of merit (*catvāri kuśalamūlāni*)? Answer: The first is the fire of wisdom (*jñānāgni*) of the noble path (*āryamārga*).

Because it resembles the preceding stage, it is established with the name "Heat" (*uṣmagata*). Second, because it is the ultimate point of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), it is further named "Summit" (*mūrdhan*).

Third, because consciousness is empty of its objects, it is named "Patience" (*kṣānti*). Fourth, because among the stages of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) this is the most supreme according to the sūtras, it is named the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*).
Mou says: "Because one gradually contemplates the principle through the aforementioned hearing of the Dharma, one performs the contemplation of *tathatā* (suchness)."
Regarding the statement that "in the eighth stage, the wholesome ground, the path increases": because wholesome matters increase further, it is called the "increase of the path.

Regarding the statement that "these two are within the forty stages of mind of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*)," one asks: "When the four groups previously reviled and struck him, he was already in the forty stages of mind;
why then is the forty stages of mind mentioned again here? The answer is: the previous mention of the forty stages of mind refers specifically to the [first] four...

Regarding the ten stages of mind: what is here called the "forty minds" refers to the stage of application (*prayoga*). Question: If this is the stage of application, how can one see the fourfold assembly? Answer:
Seeing the fourfold assembly occurs at the end of the stage of equipment (*sambhāra*), specifically during the thirtieth mind, which is the dedication to the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-pariṇāmanā*).
The increase in lifespan signifies the intent to enter the stage of application. Furthermore, even if these were actually the fourfold assembly [of śrāvakas], [the same principle would apply].

It is not precluded that Bodhisattvas in the stage of application (prayoga) may also be seen by the fourfold assembly. How could it hinder the fourfold assembly from seeing such noble beings as the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, who had attained the stages of Heat (ūṣmagata), Summits (mūrdhan), and Patience (kṣānti)?

Regarding the phrase "by means of this": it is because of this that one encounters the Buddha preaching the Dharma; it is because of this that one encounters the Buddha and receives and upholds [the teachings].

Regarding the statement "obtaining the constant purity of the six sense faculties": a question is raised that since the purity of the six sense faculties was already obtained previously, why is it mentioned again here?

Question: What is the distinction regarding the purity of the six sense faculties? Answer: The statement in this current sutra that "the eye is eternally pure" reveals that these are the six faculties of the transformation body (*pariṇāma-kāya*).

They are called "eternal" because upon attaining the first stage (*bhūmi*), they are no longer subject to interruption. The aforementioned [faculties] belong to the body of the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*) and are subject to the limitations of the fragmented body (*bhinna-kāya*);
therefore, upon entering the first stage, they are designated as "eternal. Question: The previous chapter stated, "By means of this eternal ear... [and so forth].
One hears the sounds of the three thousandfold world system. Furthermore, it is said: "By means of the pure, eternal essence (*dharmatā*), all things manifest within it.

The Master of the Commentary (*ṭīkākāra*) classifies this as belonging to the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga-avasthā*). To answer the objection that [the term] "eternal" refers to the ordinary sense of constancy, he states: "The 'eternal' spoken of here is not the constancy of routine;
it is the eternal of perpetual continuity, the eternal of permanence."

Regarding the statement, "In principle, a bodhisattva should abide [in saṃsāra]," etc.: the question is, since it is logically appropriate for a bodhisattva to enter birth and death to teach and transform sentient beings, why is it specifically stated that they must encounter a Buddha?
The answer, as the commentary (*śūtra*) states, is that in principle a bodhisattva should abide in birth and death to transform beings.
Therefore, the commentary says: "One who does not encounter the Buddhas is like a leaking boat," and so forth.
Regarding the fear of non-sustenance: ordinary persons cling to the body as having a self; fearing that this self will be severed, they harbor the fear of non-sustenance.
Bodhisattvas do not cling to the body as a self; therefore, they have no fear of non-sustenance.
Regarding what is called the fear of ill repute: the Bodhisattva does not seek wealth, profit, or offerings, nor does he fear ill repute.
Since ill repute is the root of losing one's gains, and because the Bodhisattva even desires to give his money and goods in charity to others, he manifests a lack of greed for profit.
For this reason, he does not fear ill repute; thus, the Bodhisattva manifests having a wife, children, and grandchildren.

Regarding various matters such as these, that which is called "the fear of death" refers to ordinary persons who, clinging to the body as having a self, dread the severance of that self and thus fear death. Bodhisattvas are not like this;
therefore, they have no fear of death.
Regarding the fear of the evil realms: the Bodhisattva reflects, saying, "Upon closing my eyes, I shall be reborn in the pure lands of the ten directions to see the Buddhas and hear the Dharma.
Therefore, there is no fear of the evil realms.
Regarding the fear of the majesty and virtue of the great assembly: ordinary persons feel fear toward all people even regarding their own selves.
Bodhisattvas are not like this; they do not even wish to be equal to all sentient beings, let alone superior to them. Therefore, they have no fear of the majesty and virtue of the great assembly.

Regarding the statement "the Buddha’s fearlessnesses," etc., they are: first, fearlessness regarding perfect enlightenment; second, fearlessness regarding the path leading out of suffering; third, fearlessness regarding obstructing phenomena; and fourth, fearlessness regarding the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava*).

Regarding the "fearlessnesses of a Bodhisattva," they are: first, fearlessness regarding dhāraṇī; second, fearlessness regarding knowledge of the faculties (*indriya*); and third, fearlessness regarding answering difficult questions.

Fearlessness. Fourth is the fearlessness of severing doubts. Among these four, the first is the fearlessness of total retention (*dhāraṇī*), which corresponds to the passage in the Sūtra where it is said that for the sake of sentient beings, the mind has no fear.
The remaining three are distinguished from the latter part of the fearlessness regarding the majesty and virtue of the great assembly;
they consist of knowing the faculties (*indriya*), answering difficult questions, and severing doubts. Question: How does a Bodhisattva preach fearlessness to the great assembly?
Is it because of fear? The answer is that the Bodhisattva does not perceive the existence of many people who pose difficult questions, as they possess only slight characteristics.

Regarding the statement that one is "permanently free from the five aforementioned fears," their cause is affliction (*kleśa*). Since the untainted (*anāsrava*) state manifests in the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), the continuity of afflictions no longer functions;

therefore, it is said that one is permanently free from them. Mǔ (Mokṣala) says: From the eighth stage onward, the untainted state functions constantly, whereas for the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*)...
It is not non-existent; therefore, it is called "not separated. Fear of the evil realms has as its causes the fear of death, the fear of unwholesome karma, and a lack of shame and remorse.
Fear of ill repute has greed as its cause. Fear of being unable to sustain oneself and fear of lacking dignity have the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*) as their cause.

Question: Why are they not separated from the four virtues? Answer: The six perfections and the six corruptions counteract one another, and their numbers are equal. The eight difficulties and the four wheels are like medicine and disease.
It is not equal; it is merely based on principle. Why then do you raise such objections?

Regarding the statement that those who committed evil deeds in the first assembly [of the Buddha] experienced the fruit [of their actions], the Sūtra says: "O Mahāsthāmaprāpta, at that time the fourfold assembly...
until they underwent great suffering. Question: With sticks, clubs, tiles, and stones as the cause, one enters hell for a thousand kalpas as the result. Furthermore—
Having completed his retribution for the offense, he again encountered the teaching of the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging and thereby attained *bodhi*. What was the cause? The answer is:

initially, he saw the Bodhisattva practicing the conduct of "Never-Disparaging. For a single moment of thought, he focused his mind on the conduct practiced by that Bodhisattva, and with a mindful heart, he heard and received the sound of the prophecy of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
Because he had not yet committed acts of disparagement, this single moment of pure mind served as the cause, which perfumed [the continuum] until it was realized.
The seed [of awakening] resides within the eighth consciousness. After a thousand kalpas spent in the hells, because the original seed of faith has matured, one finally emerges from hell.
Later, encountering the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging once more, one attains bodhi.
In the present sutra, the causes for the prediction received in the past are concealed; it speaks only of later encountering the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging and thereby attaining [awakening].

They attain *bodhi*. This reveals the power and merit of those who uphold this sutra: if even one who reviles and insults them attains *bodhi*, how much more so one who makes offerings to such a person?
Regarding the phrase "harmonizing the ancient and the modern," the sutra states that five hundred bhikṣus, including Siṃhacandra and others, constitute a single phrase. This...

The bhikṣus are raised up; they gather the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs. The superior are raised up to gather the inferior. As the Sūtra says: "The bhikṣuṇīs think of the Buddha and the five hundred upāsakas," thereby gathering the upāsikās.
Men are raised up to gather women. Thus, these four assemblies are complete.
Regarding the passage from "Questioning Subhūti the Śrāvaka" to "for the benefit [of others]": Subhūti was about to go out for alms;

as it was necessary to first rely upon the streets and alleys to observe [the people] before departing, he considered that if a person would be pleased by seeing him walking but would become angry if he were sitting, he would then manifest the appearance of walking.

This applies even to all other physical postures. Through such skillful means, he caused them to rejoice and did not incite anger in them. Although those of the two vehicles have realized [the truth],...

Regarding the principle of non-contention (*araṇa*): it is not merely that one cannot cause others to extinguish contention; rather, when a Bodhisattva personally realizes the principle of non-contention, they are simultaneously able to bring about non-contention in others.

The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "There are three kinds of contention: first, the contention of afflictions (*kleśa*), which consists of the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) along with the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*);
second, the contention of the aggregates (*skandha*), namely the five aggregates; and third, the contention of strife (*raṇa*), which refers to sentient beings mutually insulting one another."
This contradicts the literal meaning; thus, these three forms of dispute do not exist, which is what is meant by "non-dispute. Now, the difficulty is raised based on the third sense.

Regarding the statement that "the nineteen and a half verses following [the first] and so forth," this refers only to the final three sections of the prose commentary (*gadya*), and does not refer to the first section.
That first section cites the offenses and merits arising from the aforementioned oppositions and conformities in order to demonstrate them to the assembly.
Regarding the first one and a half verses concerning the Buddhas encountered: in the second section of the prose commentary, there are three parts to the encounter with the Buddhas.
First, the indication of the time period: the Sūtra says, "In the distant past, beyond immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
Second, the Buddhas encountered: the Sūtra says, "There was a Buddha named King of Majestic Voice (*Vaiśvānara-svara-rāja*), a Tathāgata, Arhat, and so forth. Now...
The verse states: "In the past there was a Buddha named King of Majestic Sound," and so forth; this refers to protection. The path proceeds by means of guidance.

Regarding the statement that those who encounter opposition or compliance are divided into five grades, the first three [verses] clarify the characteristics of the persons who can practice in opposition or compliance.

While the prose section contains eight points, the verse text describes five. The first three verses describe how evil people increase in power while virtuous gentlemen increase in diligence. The prose section concerns the evil...

People’s influence increases. The Sūtra says: After the Tathāgata King of Majestic Sound (Vaiśvānara-rāja) has already entered parinirvāṇa, and after the True Dharma (saddharma) has ceased, during the period of the Semblance Dharma (pratirūpaka-dharma), monks of overweening pride (adhimāna) will possess great power. Two virtuous men increase their diligence.
The prose section of the sūtra states: At that time, there was a bodhisattva bhikṣu named Never-Disparaging (Sadāparibhūta) who attained great power. By what cause?
The causal conditions are as follows: the bhikṣu named Constantly Not Disparaging (Sadāparibhūta) and his encounters with all whom he saw, and so forth.
These three verses now combine two sections of the sūtra, stating: "When the Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa... and so on.

Regarding the statement that one who is able to endure verbal abuse and accept physical harm is [described] by a single verse: first, concerning the ability to endure verbal abuse, the prose commentary explains the endurance of verbal abuse. The Sūtra states:
"Among the fourfold assembly, there may be those who give rise to a mind of anger and impurity, using harsh words and insults.
Now, the latter half-verse describes this; the Sūtra says: "When people hear this, they slight, disparage, and insult [the practitioner]. This refers to the two types of [abuse]: verbal and physical.
Regarding "the ability to endure harm," the prose section of the sutra states: "When these words were spoken, some among the crowd struck and pelted him with sticks, clubs, tiles, and stones.
Now, this half-verse describes how the Bodhisattva Viśeṣacintin was able to endure it.
Regarding the statement that "the two subsequent verses describe the attainment of the supreme fruit," the prose of the sūtra says:

"When this bhikṣu was about to pass away, he heard in the void of space the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* previously preached by the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, consisting of twenty quadrillion verses, and was able to receive and uphold them all.
The present verses recounting the sūtra state: "His transgressions being exhausted... (two lines); these correspond to the prose.

The Sūtra states that after one has finished undergoing punishment in hell, one speaks of the fourfold assembly. Now, in this verse, the phrase "having finished those offenses" refers to the Bodhisattva Sadāparibhūta himself bestowing predictions upon others;
those who see him are filled with joy. Because he still possessed residual offenses, he was struck by others with sticks, clubs, tiles, and stones;
these were the results of offenses from previous lives that would have caused him to fall into hell. By maintaining [the practice], [he avoided that fate].
By the power of the sutra, what was heavy is made light.
Regarding the subsequent verse on the conversion of evil people, the prose commentary states: "At that time, the fourfold assembly of those with overweening pride..."
