Bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who had looked down upon this person and given him the name "Not to be Despised" (Avalokiteśvara) now see that he has attained the power of great supernormal faculties, the power of eloquence in joyful exposition, and so forth. The present verse describes it thus:
"All those attached to dharmas have all received [benefit] from the descent of the Bodhisattva."
Regarding the statement that "the latter one and a half verses concern the increase of the path by a virtuous person," the prose of the sūtra says:
"After his death, he encountered two thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas, all of whom were named Candrasūryapradīpa. Within their teachings, they preached this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The present verse, however, says: "Not-Disdainful (Adīnapraśa), after his death, encountered innumerable Buddhas... and so forth.
Regarding the first half-verse, which identifies the body [of the Buddha]: the prose of the sutra says, "Mahāsthāmaprāpta, what do you think?
Was that Bodhisattva Never Disparaging at that time anyone else? It was none other than myself. Regarding the subsequent identification of the fourfold assembly:
the prose of the sutra says, "Mahāsthāmaprāpta, as for those fourfold assemblies—the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and so forth—at that time, what do you think..."
Why is this? Those among the fourfold assembly who at that time constantly disparaged this bodhisattva—could they have been anyone else?
It is stated in three and a half verses of the present hymn: "At that time, 'Not Disparaging' was none other than myself" (and so forth).
Regarding the statement "exhorting the multitude to eliminate transgressions and so forth," the prose section of the sutra says:

"Mahāsthāmaprāpta, you should know that this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* brings great benefit to all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and enables them to reach anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Now, the verse recounts this:
"In previous lives, I exhorted these people in the six practices and so forth"—this refers to the "paying homage to the multitude and exhorting them to diligence."

Regarding the statement that there are three modes of circulation in the "Chapter on the Tathāgata’s Supernatural Powers" (*Tathāgata-ṛddhi-anubhāva-parivarta*), this refers specifically to the third: the circulation through the entrustment by the Tathāgata.

As for the mention of "manifesting signs," "entrusting," and so forth, these refer to the manifestation of signs, the entrustment, and the formal assignment found in the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers," as well as the "Chapter on Bhaiṣajyarāja" (*Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta*) and others.
Because they receive the mandate and carry it out,

the mention of "supernatural power" (ṛddhi) and "entrustment" (parindanā) refers precisely to causing the great bodhisattvas to believe what the Tathāgata has spoken and to cause the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to circulate; this is termed "mandate and practice."

Regarding the phrase "the remaining six categories" and so forth: it refers to the entrustment through supernatural power, the manifestation of signs for the sake of transmission, and the carrying out of the mandate.
Because they receive the command and enter life and death to teach and transform sentient beings, this is called "circulation."

Regarding the statement "this is now the first [entrustment]," it refers to the entrustment of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* to the Bodhisattvas who have previously emerged from the earth, as well as the eighty thousand great beings; this is termed the "entrustment to others."
Regarding the statement, "fearing that faith might not arise," etc.: It is asked, "When addressing the great bodhisattvas and the assembly, did they not already produce faith previously?
Why is it necessary to further manifest supernatural powers? The answer is: "It is necessary to cause them to conceive a sense of wonder and rarity."
Only when one believes that what the Tathāgata has spoken is not false will they be willing to circulate it.

Regarding the phrase "entrusting by means of words," this refers to the entrustment of the body in the *Parīndanā-parivarta* (Chapter on Entrustment), whereas this chapter concerns the entrustment of the words.
Regarding the phrase "the force [of the teaching] is the same as before," it means that it is identical to the third section on the circulation [of the teaching] in the preceding commentary.

Regarding the statement "there are three kinds of dharma-gates": first, the manifestation of the broad and long tongue to cause sentient beings to recollect; second, the clearing of the throat; [and third, the emitting of light].

The purpose of reciting verses is to cause them to hear [the teaching]. The purpose of snapping the fingers three times is to cause them to awaken. Question: What is the difference between this [instance of] "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*) spoken within the Chapter on Bestowing Joy and that [previous instance]?
Answer: Jin says: The former refers to the unsurpassed nature of the *means of expression* (*vācaka*) based on the excellence of the *teaching expressed* (*vācya*);
the latter refers to the fact that the person possessing the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) who can speak is not false. Thus, they differ in terms of the object and the subject.
Regarding the explanation of the title: "Rú-lái shén-zú xíng-pǐn" (The Chapter on the Tathāgata’s Divine Footsteps). "Xíng" (footstep/movement) is a synonym for "power" (*bala*).

The two characters "Rú-lái" (Tathāgata) apply to both Śākyamuni and Prabhūtaratna; as they proceed, they likewise manifest supernatural powers. Their transformations and manifestations are unfathomable, hence they are called "divine" (*shén*).
Because they can subdue those who lack faith, they are termed "powers" (*lì*).

Regarding the phrase "the initial heading," the Sūtra states: "At that time, [bodhisattvas] as numerous as the atoms in a thousand worlds... This refers to what was said in the preceding "Chapter on the Earth Quaking":
"When these bodhisattvas heard the sound of the voice spoken by Śākyamuni Buddha, they emerged from below and came forth."
Each and every bodhisattva is a leader of the great assembly who proclaims the Way. Each leads sixty thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (Ganges-sand) retinues;
how much more so those with fifty thousand, down to those who practice alone in seclusion, reaching a state that cannot be known.

Question: How is it known that there are as many worlds as there are atoms in a thousand worlds? Answer: It is said that this cannot be known through calculation or analogy; it is the true reality of the Tathāgata.
One must know the sequence; if it were otherwise, the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) would not be accomplished.

When the Sūtra says "with a single mind, palms joined," this is the request through the action of body (*kāyakarman*). When it says "he addressed the Buddha," this is the request through the action of speech (*vākkarman*).

As for the passage beginning "For what reason?"—this describes the mind, which is the request through the action of mind (*manaskarman*). Therefore, the commentary explains that it is not merely intended to provide relief.

He [said], "Furthermore, regarding the phrase 'truly' (*zhen*) as meaning 'real' (*zhenshi*), it indicates that this is not a provisional or expedient teaching. As for 'purity' (*jing*), there are three types: the original, the newly acquired, and the untainted (*anāsrava*) are named purity;
by extension, the nature of goodness (*kuśala-dharma*) is also named purity."
Regarding the statement "first, manifesting supernormal powers," the sutra says: "He manifests great supernormal powers before the entire assembly.

Regarding the statement "first, to reveal the supreme virtues of the sutra and so forth," the sutra says: "At that time, the Buddha addressed the great assembly of bodhisattvas, such as Śūraṅgama and others, saying:
'The supernormal powers of all Buddhas are thus immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable.'"

Regarding the statement "it is for the sake of teaching sentient beings and so forth," the Sūtra says: "The Buddhas, the saviors of the world, abiding in great supernormal powers, manifest immeasurable displays of spiritual power in order to gladden sentient beings."
Regarding the phrase "the various bodhisattvas and others," Lu says: This refers to the faith-matured bodhisattvas who appeared after the parinirvāṇa of Śākyamuni Buddha;
they made vows to circulate [the teaching] in accordance with the minds of all Buddhas, and thus manifested their supernatural powers. As the sutra states: "After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa..."
Because they are able to uphold this sutra, all Buddhas rejoice and manifest immeasurable supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). These are Śākyamuni and his manifested Buddhas.
Seeing the bodhisattvas who have previously come with faith, making vows and requesting to uphold the sutra, they act in accordance with the Buddhas' minds;
thus the World-Honored One rejoices and manifests these supernormal powers (the aforementioned "supernatural powers").

Regarding the statement that there are now eight [supernatural powers] added: according to the oral tradition of the ancient masters, there were seven supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). This was not exhaustive when the scripture was categorized;

therefore, they have now added a manifestation to complete the eight supernatural powers. This refers to the one power added in the commentary (*śāstra*), which arises because Śākyamuni emits light such that sentient beings in other directions see Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa from afar.
By means of Śākyamuni’s supernatural power, those in other directions see it from afar and take refuge; thus, it is so named.
This is a manifestation.
Regarding the phrase "among the six supernormal powers" (*ṣaḍabhijñā*): this refers to the supernormal power of the basis of psychic power (*ṛddhividhi-abhijñā*) among those six.
Regarding the phrase "such as manifesting bodies and manifesting speech": within the second category of "those capable of transformation," there are three types. The first is Śākyamuni’s division...
First is the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Second is the transformation speech; as the sutra says:

"Good son, go to Vulture Peak to where Śākyamuni Buddha is, and speak these words on my behalf," as well as the teaching through the voice from the sky and so forth. Third is the transformation environment;
the manifestation of jeweled trees, lion thrones, water birds, trees, and so on—all of which are non-existent and suddenly appear.

Regarding the statement "this refers to the eighteen transformations and so forth," this explains the eighteen transformations as set forth in the commentary on the reasons for manifesting such transformations.

As for the term "blazingly radiant," it is like King Subhūṣaṇa (Wondrous Adornment), whose sons, Viśuddhagarbha (Pure Treasury) and Viśuddhanetra (Pure Eye), emitted water from the upper part of their bodies and fire from the lower part of their bodies.
Regarding "fire":
as for the term "pervading," it refers to the light emitted from the introductory chapter (Nidāna-parivarta) traveling far to illuminate eighteen thousand worlds.

Regarding "manifestation," it refers to the emission of light at three locations mentioned previously: in the introductory chapter, the Chapter on the Jeweled Stūpa (Ratnastūpa-parivarta), and the Chapter on the Wondrous Sound (Gandavyūha-parivarta).
Within the light, one sees the beings of the six realms of existence as well as the affairs of the pure lands.
As for "transformation," this refers to the transformation of the defiled into the pure as described in the "Jeweled Stupa" chapter.
As for "coming and going," it is like Maudgalyāyana traveling to the world of Wild Horses (Aśvamedha), or like the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara coming from the East.
"Listen! As for returning to one's own country and so forth, this is it.
Regarding what is called 'the seven fascicles,' it is like the 'Chapter on Supernatural Powers' where the canopy is joined together; in this fascicle, Mount Sumeru enters a mustard seed."
Regarding the "eight expansions": furthermore, within this chapter, it is said that the tongue extends upward as far as the Brahma-world, and a single hair is spread to fill the entire Dharma-realm.

Regarding the "ninefold entry of all images into the body": in the "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master," it is stated that by upholding [the teachings], one attains eight hundred bodily merits;
like pure lapis lazuli, which is transparent both inside and out, an entire world appears within the body.

Regarding the statement "ten instances of manifesting in the same class": this refers to how the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara and Avalokiteśvara appear everywhere in bodies identical to those of their respective classes.

Regarding the statement "eleven instances of manifestation": this refers to the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna emerging from the earth, the assembly at the Dragon Palace emerging from the sea, and the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara surging forth into the void, and so forth.
Regarding the "twelfth, the hidden": when Gadgadasvara vanished from that land, he concealed his body in the Eastern Sea, as described in the Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā.
Regarding the "thirteenth, mastery over actions": this refers to the passage in the *Stūpasaṃdarśana-parivarta* where he moved various devas and humans and placed them elsewhere.

The Earth. Furthermore, in the "Introductory Chapter," it is said that the heavens rained down four kinds of flowers; within this chapter, there is the clearing of the throat and the snapping of fingers.
These are the sovereign acts performed by the Tathāgata. This is broad, for because his transformations are supreme, he alone attains such mastery.
Regarding the statement "fourteen ways of subduing others," this refers, for example, to the subjugation of Māra.
Regarding the statement "fifteen ways of bestowing eloquence," as the verse in the *Śraddhāparivarta* says: "The Buddha commands us to proclaim the supreme path;
those who practice this shall attain Buddhahood. Furthermore, he bestowed his empowerment upon Subhūti to preach the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*.

The sutra states: "I, following the Buddha's teaching, for the sake of the great bodhisattvas, by means of various causes and conditions, diverse parables, and numerous expressions, speak of the sixteen who are capable of recollection.
This is as the Buddha caused Ānanda to immediately recollect the immeasurable past."
He has unimpeded mastery over the Dharma-treasuries of hundreds of thousands of millions of buddhas. As stated in the "Chapter on the Dharma Master":
"If one reads this sutra and forgets the phrases or pauses, I shall recite it for them once more so that they may attain completeness."
Regarding the statement that "seventeen [qualities] can bestow peace and happiness," it is as stated in the Devadatta Chapter:

"If there are good sons or good daughters who, upon hearing the 'Devadatta Chapter' of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, believe and revere it with a pure mind and do not give rise to doubt or confusion, they shall not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals. If they are born among humans or devas, they will experience supreme and wondrous bliss."

Regarding the statement "emitting eighteen great rays of light," this refers to the emission of light in the Introduction Chapter (*Nidāna-parivarta*) and the City of Illusion Chapter (*Gandavyūha-parivarta*), such as the Great Universal Emission of Light, the Wondrous Sound of the Jewel Stupa, and the emission of light within this present chapter. Question: Regarding the third transformation, the "Pervasive Distribution" (*pravartana*); the fourth, the "Manifestation" (*darśana*);

and the eighteenth, the "Emission of Light" (*raśmipramocana*)—in these three transformations, all are described as emitting light. What is the distinction between them? Answer: They are simply the emission of light.
There is no distinction between them. The emission of light that shines through to the farthest reaches is the eighteenth emission of light.
If it reaches other lands, proceeding from the near to the distant, this is the third dissemination. If, within that light, the things seen are manifested, this is the fourth manifestation.
Regarding the phrase "either this or the fourth": "this" refers to the third [action], clearing the throat, while the "fourth" is snapping the fingers;
these constitute the thirteenth mastery of action (*karmavaśitā*).

Regarding the statement that "the eighth [level] universally constitutes a single Buddha-field": Question: In the preceding Chapter on Stūpas, it was already stated that the world universally constitutes a single Buddha-field.
Why, then, is it stated here again that the world universally constitutes one? Answer: In the preceding Chapter on Stūpas, it was said:

Regarding the statement that "the world is universally one Buddha-land," this refers only to the fact that within four million *nayuta* of lands there are no great oceans, rivers, and so forth; thus it is called "universally one Buddha-land.
As for the phrase "this [power] pervades one Buddha-land" in the *Śakti-varga*, it refers to what lies beyond those four million *nayuta* worlds. Question: How can this be?
"Do you know? He replied in accordance with the subsequent scripture: "Beyond these immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya worlds, there is a land named Sahā.
Therein dwells a Buddha named Śākyamuni. Thus, one knows that it is far away.

Regarding the statement, "Now the Buddha extends his tongue," the *Lun* (Treatise) says: this explains that one should recite the scriptural text so that the Bodhisattvas who uphold the sutra may call to mind the One Vehicle Dharma previously entrusted to them, believing that what the Buddha has spoken is not false; this is termed "calling to mind."
Therefore, he first manifested the mark of the tongue as a reminder that he was circulating the One Vehicle.
As for the statement "like the Buddha entering among the Brahmins," etc., this refers to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, which serves as proof that the Buddha does not speak falsely.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. Having completed the summer retreat, he entered a city of brahmins on his almsround.
The king, being faithless, issued a decree: "Whoever gives food to the Buddha shall be fined five hundred gold coins.
Later, when the Buddha arrived in that country, he took Ānanda with him and entered the city with his bowl to beg for alms; the people of the city all closed their doors.

Dare not offer food; the Buddha departed with an empty bowl. At that time, there was an old man in the house of the elder who took a clay vessel filled with foul-smelling rice-water and went out the door, feeling it strange. There he saw the Buddha, endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.

A divine being such as this ought to partake of celestial food. That he now wanders about begging for alms must surely be out of his compassion and pity for all beings, thinking to provide an offering, yet finding nothing else available. "If the Buddha requires it, let him take this humble food.
Knowing that her faith, trust, and purity were clear, the Buddha extended his hand and received the food in his bowl. At that time, the Buddha smiled, and light issued forth.
Five-colored rays of light shone forth, penetrating through heaven and earth.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda, saying, "Do you see this old woman who, with a faithful heart, has offered food to the Buddha? Ānanda replied, "I see her.

The Buddha said, "Because this old woman has offered food to the Buddha, she shall enjoy happiness and receive blessings among gods and humans for fifteen kalpas. In her final existence, she will be born as a man."
He practiced the Way within his own home and attained the state of a Pratyekabuddha, entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
At that time, there was a brahmin standing nearby who spoke this verse: "You are of the solar lineage, of the Kṣatriya caste, the crown prince of King Śuddhodana."
"Yet for the sake of food, you have committed such great falsehoods. How heavy must the retribution for such stinking food be!

At that time, the Tathāgata extended his tongue until it reached the hairline and said to the brāhmaṇa, "In your teachings, is there anyone who extends their tongue to the hairline and yet is a speaker of falsehood?
The brāhmaṇa replied, "If a person can extend their tongue so as to cover their nose," he said, "then..."
"It is not false; how much less so as it extends to the hairline. The Buddha asked, "Do you see this rare thing, difficult to behold, which occurs in the world?

He replied, "I have already seen it. Once, while traveling on a road with various brāhmaṇas, I saw a nyagrodha tree whose branches spread over five hundred cartloads of merchandise belonging to merchants, yet its shade was still not exhausted. The Buddha said, "This tree was planted..."
The seed is as large as one-third of a mustard seed; the seed is extremely small, yet the trunk of the tree is immense.
This old woman offered with faith to the Buddha and obtained a great reward. Because the cause was small, the retribution is great. Why do you not believe?
At that time, all the people of the city sent five hundred gold coins to the king so that he might go to the Buddha to make offerings.

Regarding the statement that [the tongue] reaches the Brahma-world: Question: For what reason does the emitted light reach as far as the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, yet when the tongue is extended, why does it only reach the Brahma-world?
Answer: When the tongue is extended, it reaches up to the Brahma-world because there is vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*) in the First Dhyāna; therefore, it does not exist above that.
As for the emitted light reaching the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, it is to startle and awaken those with whom one has a karmic connection, thereby destroying the darkness of ignorance.

Regarding the phrase "each and every pore," it signifies the equality of compassion; furthermore, it signifies the vast and complete provision of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). These two meanings are discussed separately.

Regarding the phrase "by means of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna and others," the first [instance] is the stupa as testimony, while the latter is testimony by means of the body. This constitutes testimony for the teaching and testimony for the principle—these two.
Regarding the different categories: the scriptural text mentions only the manifestation of the emanations of Śākyamuni and does not speak of the manifestation of Prabhūtaratna.
This is because he has already realized the sūtra and attained full understanding; therefore, it is not mentioned again.
Regarding the statement that "the foolish have deluded minds," this clarifies the temporal context. The Sūtra says: "After a full hundred thousand years, he then withdraws his tongue.
Jiaxiang asked: "How does he retract the tongue? Does he not also retract the light? The answer is: He withdraws the tongue-mark because the task of preaching the Dharma has been completed;
however, he does not withdraw the light because he wishes to allow the ten directions to be transparently interconnected so that beings may see one another. [This refers to] the foolish.

Their minds were deluded; in reality, they had passed through hundreds of thousands of years. Looking at the minds of sentient beings themselves, there is a difference between delusion and awakening, and a distinction between long and short durations.
Through the Buddha’s spiritual power, their minds were transformed so that they collectively failed to perceive it, and all came to understand it as a short duration.
Regarding what is called "the benefit of the recompense and transformation bodies": this refers to seeing differences based on one's particular perspective.

For instance, at Vulture Peak, Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra see the Recompense Body (saṃbhogakāya) of Śākyamuni Buddha, which truly extends its tongue for hundreds of thousands of years; whereas those of the Two Vehicles and ordinary beings see the Transformation Body (nirmāṇakāya) extending its tongue, which likewise lasts only for a brief moment.
Regarding what is said about the Buddha manifesting supernatural power (*ṛddhi*): the Buddha’s supernatural power actually extends for hundreds of thousands of years;
yet, by means of his supernatural power, he causes sentient beings to awaken, doing so as if it were but a brief moment.

Regarding the statement, "It is indeed brief and not extended": if one asks why it is extended [in some cases], this too is the Buddha’s power; that which causes sentient beings not to perceive it is likewise his spiritual power (*ṛddhi-bala*).

Why, then, is it said that the Buddha’s lifespan is hundreds of thousands of years? The answer in the Commentary states: "It is indeed brief and not extended, for the purpose of discourse," and so forth.

Question: Since it is taught that both the *sambhogakāya* Buddha and the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha preach the same single Dharma, which is this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, with no difference between them, yet those who hear it differ in the length of time they have heard it and in its depth, what does this imply?
It implies that whether in a pure land or a defiled land, the preaching of the sutra is of one and the same nature.

Regarding the commentary on the phrase "coughing and so forth": the two characters of this verse are part of the preceding line, yet because they cause [the sound] to be heard, they are associated with the following line.
Question: Why is it necessary to hear the sound? Answer: The sub-commentary (*shu*) states: "Once the sound has been heard, one practices according to reality. The sub-commentary further states:
"Coughing" does not refer to the actual moment of reciting the verse; rather, it refers to the time when one intends to recite the verse. In such a case, it is necessary to cough. As for example...
When a person wishes to speak, they first clear their throat. The intention is that by clearing the throat first, one awakens the listener’s awareness so that they may hear;

only then does one recite the verse. Question: Why did you not clear your throat when you previously recited the verse? Answer: This entrustment is different from others; therefore, it is not to be treated as a precedent. Question:
When you commanded [the practice] in the subsequent chapter, why did you not clear your throat? Answer: Because there was no verse in the subsequent chapter. Furthermore, because...
Because they touch it with their hands and listen intently for themselves.
Regarding the phrase "joy arises at the mere sight," the Sūtra says: "By the Buddha's supernatural power, all these belong to this Sahā world.
Although the ten directions are distant, through the supernatural power of Śākyamuni, they are all part of the Sahā world.

Regarding the phrase "a loud voice in the air" and so forth: the Sūtra states that at that moment, the various devas—namely, the devas from the ten directions within that land—uttered voices from the midst of the void; these were not sounds from this world-system.

Regarding the statement that "the sixth [element] combines with the canopy to form a pavilion": this means they are joined together like a canopy; that is, the precious pavilion completely covers [it] like a canopy.
"Canopy" (gai) carries the meaning of covering.
Regarding the phrase "scattering flowers," among these scattered flowers there are also incense, necklaces (*mālā*), and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "forming canopies and the like," it means that the canopies cover all sentient beings within this realm. Bian states:

"This refers to jeweled curtains (*ratnapaṭa*) that cover everywhere, which are called 'canopies. Sentient beings from the worlds of the ten directions each take gold, silver, and precious objects from the ten directions..."

They came to the Sahā world. By the Buddha’s spiritual power, they gathered in one place and transformed into a jeweled canopy, covering the emanated bodies of the Buddhas from the ten directions as well as Śākyamuni Buddha above them.
Question: Why was it necessary for this to transform into a jeweled canopy? Answer: It signifies the convergence of the two into one.

As for its covering only this world, it signifies that the Buddha’s intention is specifically directed toward the sentient beings of this world. As stated in the "Chapter on the Stūpa": [text follows].
"Who is able to extensively expound this sutra in this Sahā world-system?

Regarding the statement that "the worlds are unified as one," the sutra says: "At that time, the seventh world was unified as one. This signifies that throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there is only the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).
Regarding the statement that "the wisdom of speech and mind being unimpeded means the pure land is no different":

the unimpeded wisdom of mind is precisely the wisdom that awakens to and understands the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), being free from doubt and obstruction; therefore, the world-systems are universally one.
Regarding the statement that "there is only one vehicle (yāna) and no others": it means there is only the One Vehicle and no other two vehicles; therefore, they are collectively designated as one.

Regarding the statement that "the discourse explains only three": among the eight kinds of supernormal transformations (ṛddhiprātihārya), other sūtras generally include five kinds, but those are not superior [to these three].
It is not that they are not explained; however, these three types do not appear in other sutras, and thus the commentators have focused their explanations on them.
Furthermore, these three types constitute the very core of the entrustment, which is why they are explained with particular emphasis. The latter interpretation is superior.
Regarding the statement that "the others are common and not primary": the other five supernatural powers (abhijñā) are mentioned; the light [emanated] as in the *Ūrdhvaṃjāta* and *Nirvāṇa* sūtras;

the shaking of the earth as in the *Prajñāpāramitā*; the merging of canopies as in the *Vimalakīrti*; and the transformation of the land, also as in the *Vimalakīrti*. These are not the essential points of the entrustment (*parindanā*) within this sūtra, and therefore they are not discussed here.
Question: How does this transformation of the land differ from that in the "Chapter on the Stūpa"? Answer: That [transformation in the "Stūpa Chapter"] was threefold...
It was transformed into four hundred myriads of koṭis of nayutas. Now, these worlds of the ten directions are like a single buddha-field, numbering only four hundred and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "one" which summarizes the aforementioned supernatural power, the sutra says: "At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Superior Practice (Uttara-gāmin) and others. The term "others" refers to those who had emerged from the earth.
"Emergence. "The superior practice" refers to the foremost among the four.
Regarding the statement that "the two are for the purpose of entrustment and so forth," the sutra says: "If I were to exhaust [this] through such supernormal power (ṛddhi).

Question: If it were truly exhausted, this statement would be false; if it were not exhausted, how could the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) be established? Answer: This is with respect to the Buddha-lineage (*buddhagotra*).
Wisdom is such that there is nothing it does not exhaustively explain; however, because sentient beings are unable to receive it all, it is not spoken. It is like the leaves in one's hand.
As for what is called "the single path of provisional and ultimate truth," let me speak of its essentials: it is all the dharmas possessed by the Tathāgata.

1. The provisional and the ultimate teachings; 2. the power of the two types of supernormal knowledges—the Sūtra states that the Tathāgata’s all-encompassing sovereign spiritual powers consist of the transformation of bodies and the transformation of environments;
3. the principle hidden by the Buddhas—the Sūtra states that the Tathāgata’s all-encompassing secret treasury is the Dharma-body;
4. the profound matters of wisdom—the Sūtra states that these are the Tathāgata’s all-encompassing most profound matters.
This refers to the *saṃbhogakāya*. The causes and effects, the principles and phenomena, and the merits of the three bodies are all explained within this sutra.

Regarding the statement that "the four [sections] conclude with the exhortation to bestow [the teaching]," the sutra says: "Therefore, you should, toward the Tathāgata and others, practice according to what has been taught.
As for the practitioner, their practice consists of the two benefits [of self and others].

Regarding the phrase "should be offered worship," the Sūtra states: "Wherever a scroll of this scripture resides, or wherever a person upholds the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, that place is an altar of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) worthy of worship.
Originally, one prepares an altar of enlightenment solely for the sake of enshrining the scripture."
Since this person recites and contemplates the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, they are called a true site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and a true offering.

The place where grain is stored is called a granary; the place where wheat is stored is called a wheat-storehouse. This sutra is the place where the Tathāgata attained enlightenment; it is named the site of enlightenment.

Regarding the statement that "the sublime principle of the dharmakāya is fully present herein": this refers to the pure dharmadhātu and the mental states associated with the four wisdoms (caturjñāna-cittavastu), which together are collectively termed "dharma.

Because each possesses the sense of being a support (āśraya), they are called "kāya" (body); thus, it is named the *dharmakāya*. In contrast to the teachings that express it (the *deśanā*), it is called the "sublime principle."

Because these are complete herein. The word "herein" (*atra*) refers to the teaching. This preceding phrase states in general that the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are called the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
This concludes the general explanation of the site of enlightenment.

That which is called the place where one attains the Way, the place where one realizes *bodhi*, is named the *bodhimaṇḍa*. As the Sūtra says: "In this place, all Buddhas attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
That which is called the place where the Dharma is preached is also named the *bodhimaṇḍa*. As the Sūtra says: "In this place, all Buddhas turn the wheel of the Dharma."
Regarding the statement "the intention behind manifesting nirvāṇa": Question: What is the purpose of manifesting supernatural powers? Answer: The Sūtra says:
"In order to gladden sentient beings, he manifests immeasurable supernatural powers so that they may have faith in the Dharma he teaches."

Regarding the five supernormal powers mentioned in the two subsequent verses: Question: What are the five supernormal powers? Answer: First, the tongue-reach extending to the Brahma-heaven; second, the emission of light from the body;
third, the voice of all Buddhas; fourth, the sound of snapping fingers; and fifth, the earth shaking in six ways.
The prose version consists of eight sections, whereas the verse contains only five; thus, the latter three are omitted.
Regarding the phrase "this is the first": the two verses indicate its inexhaustibility. The prose sūtra states:

"If, by means of this supernatural power, I were to spend immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of asaṃkhyeya kalpas for the sake of entrustment, I would speak of this..."
Even the merits of this sutra cannot be fully exhausted. Now, the verse says: "Because I entrust this sutra to you," which consists of two lines.
Regarding the statement that "one and a half verses refer to seeing the Buddha," the sutra says: "Those who can uphold this sutra have already seen me," which consists of one and a half lines.
This is not present in the prose (long-form) version, but it is found in the verse (gāthā) text.
Regarding the "joy of two verses," the Sūtra says: "Those who can uphold this sūtra shall cause me and my emanations [to rejoice]"; these are the two lines.

Regarding the "attainment of the Dharma through one verse," the Sūtra says: "The secret and essential Dharma attained by all Buddhas when seated at the site of enlightenment"; this is the single line.

This is so. Regarding the statement that "one and a half verses can explain," the Sūtra says: "One who can uphold this sūtra possesses the meaning of all dharmas, which is the analytical knowledge of meaning (artha-pratisaṃvid);

the two characters 'name' (nāman) constitute the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid); and the three characters 'speech' (vyañjana) constitute the analytical knowledge of expression (nirukti-pratisaṃvid)."

Explanation: The first phrase, "inexhaustible eloquence," refers to the analytical knowledge of unimpeded eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*). The following two phrases constitute the conclusion, as the Sūtra says:
"Just as the wind in the sky encounters no obstacles whatsoever. This is the summary.

Regarding the "benefit of two and a half verses," the Sūtra says: "After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, for two and a half [kalpas]... This refers to the *Parīndanā-parivarta* (Chapter on Entrustment).

Regarding the "one chapter on the present time" mentioned in the *Sūtra*, this is the version translated by Kumārajīva; it follows the *Prabhāsa-rddhi-parivarta* (Chapter on Manifesting Spiritual Powers) and instructs...

Having completed the entrustment, this present chapter now clarifies the further entrustment. It is brought forth here because [the Buddha] touches their heads and commands them to practice the entrustment; thus, this chapter follows.
The pronunciation of "practice" (行) is the same as that of "stem" (莖).

Regarding the explanation of the names: some say that the character *lei* (pronounced with the departing tone as *lèi*) is incorrect; rather, *lei* simply carries the meaning of "repetition" or "accumulation.

To place [the Buddha] upon the crown of the Bodhisattva’s head is called *lei* (pronounced with the entering tone). "Entrusting" (*fu*) should actually be written as "belonging to" (*shǔ*). This refers to the act of entrusting or commissioning.

Regarding the statement "with one hand, he strokes [them]," etc.: it is asked, since the number of Bodhisattvas who emerge is like the sands of the Ganges, does he stroke them with one hand all at once, or does he stroke each with a separate hand? The answer is: with one hand, all at once; neither before nor after.
It symbolizes the Buddha’s supernatural power (*ṛddhi*). Second, it is said that each of the bodhisattvas touches with one hand; this symbolizes that the Buddha’s wondrous activity is all-pervasive.

Yet, although each bodhisattva sees [the Buddha] touching only themselves—each seeing the World-Honored One touching their own body and not seeing him touch the other bodhisattvas—the single hand signifies that the hand is like the teaching, intended to make known that there is only the teaching of the Single Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
Regarding the scriptural passage stating, "At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha [rose] from his Dharma seat," etc., this section should properly be placed after the *Samantabhadra* chapter.

It is there that the recitation of the sutra concludes; for that is where he rises from the Dharma seat. If it were placed after the *Rddhibala* (Spiritual Power) chapter, there would be no further mention of his rising or departing.

Regarding the scriptural statement, "I [have practiced] for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads," etc.: A question is raised as to why it is said here that the Buddha’s causal practices did not exceed three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, yet now it is stated they were "immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of billions. The answer is found in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 38, which states:

There are two kinds of *asaṃkhyeya* mahākalpas. First, there are those that are "immeasurable" because they cannot be calculated by means of days, months, seasons, or years. Second, [there are those that are immeasurable]...
Because it reaches the ultimate limit of number, it is called "innumerable. This is mentioned first here.

Regarding the statement that he first uses his right hand and so forth, Master Jiashang says: "With one hand, he simultaneously and universally strokes the crowns of the heads of as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in a thousand worlds;
this is called manifesting great supernormal power (*ṛddhi-bala*). If one does not uphold this sūtra, one does not stroke them."
Furthermore, the two vehicles attaining Buddhahood is called "Auspiciousness. This is the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgata’s bodily action (*kāyakarman*). As the Sūtra says:
"I have [practiced] for immeasurable [aeons], up to the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas"—this is the empowerment of his verbal action (*vākkarman*).

It is like parents who, having gathered their livelihoods, entrust them to their children and grandchildren at the time of their old age, saying: "Throughout my life, I have labored together with you."
"Enjoy yourselves well and secure your livelihoods; as for me, I cannot escape impermanence. You who remain behind must greatly simplify your affairs:
manage your wealth and property, provide for your kin both young and old, pursue your social ties, and ensure that the ancestral sacrifices are never interrupted.
Today, the Tathāgata does likewise; he addresses the bodhisattvas and speaks these words: 'During the three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas...'"

Throughout kalpas, one has cast oneself into fire for a single phrase and sacrificed one’s body for half a verse; or, as the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging, one was struck and pelted with staves, wood, tiles, and stones;
or, as a sovereign of a kingdom, one sought the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and practiced it for a thousand years—such is the difficulty of attaining this Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi (and so forth).
Now that it is entrusted to the great Bodhisattvas, you must likewise [preserve it].
"Give it to me," he said, "without sparing even body or life, for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings.

By referring to him specifically as a "great bodhisattva," he distinguishes him from those of the two vehicles who have recently turned their minds toward enlightenment, for they are not yet called "great.
This designation signifies that this One Vehicle is the most supreme among all three periods of time; therefore, he placed his hand upon the crown of Samantabhadra’s head.

The phrase "the Dharma of the Transmitted Lamp" and so forth explains the meaning of *samaya* within the sutra. Rubbing [the disciple] three times with the hand is the empowerment of the body (*kāyakarma*).
Then, speaking these words is the empowerment of the speech (*vākkarma*).

Regarding the phrase "this is the first": it means that within the empowerment of mental action (*manas-karman*), this is the first [section] clarifying that one's own three unwholesome roots (*akuśala-mūla*) have been exhausted and that one is able to bestow wisdom.
Question: Why is there an empowerment through mental action? What is the reason for this? (This is a rhetorical inquiry.)
Regarding the phrase "because of compassion," etc., it answers the question "Why is that? It is because the Tathāgata possesses great compassion and is thus free from anger;
he is able to extract suffering and bestow happiness.

Regarding the phrase "because of being without stinginess": this explains that the sūtra teaches the absence of all forms of parsimony. It means being without greed and not being stingy regarding the Dharma—that is, not begrudging or withholding the Dharma.
Ordinary persons possess greed, hatred, and delusion, and thus they are stingy and possessive.
Regarding "speech that is also fearless": this is because it is determined by the absence of delusion.

Regarding "speech that can bestow Buddhahood": this means that within the interpretation of the sutras, it can bestow upon sentient beings the Buddha-wisdom; "wisdom" here refers specifically to the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
The phrase "the Tathāgata’s wisdom and so forth" refers to fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
The phrase "these two are spontaneous and so forth" means that these two are attained without a teacher; they are called "spontaneous wisdom" (*svayambhū-prajñā*).

Before they are attained, one must practice; once they are attained, they are acquired spontaneously, and thus they are called spontaneous wisdom. This does not mean sitting upright and doing nothing.
"Cultivation" refers to spontaneity (*anābhoga*).
Regarding the phrase "or the first two," this is the second interpretation. The first two are the conditioned wisdom of the Buddha, the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
The latter one is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and is called "natural. These three constitute the disclosure [of the teaching].
Third, regarding speech.
As for the statement that it reveals the Buddha’s ability to act as a great donor (*mahādānapati*) and so forth: the Sūtra says, "The Tathāgata is the great donor of all sentient beings," and so on.

This is intended to exhort and instruct sentient beings, showing them that they should emulate the Tathāgata and not give rise to stinginess or parsimony; thus, it reveals that the Buddha is [the great donor].

The Great Benefactor: Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are called Equal Benefactors, for they are able to bestow upon sentient beings the fruits of the human and celestial realms through the five precepts, the eight precepts, and the Wheel of Dharma of the Four Truths.
The Tathāgata has eternally exhausted the three unwholesome roots; he is able to bestow the Dharma and thereby evoke the fruit of Buddhahood and Bodhi—thus he is called the Great Benefactor.
The phrase "as stated in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*," etc., refers to the scriptural authority (*āgama*) for the practice.
The phrase "stinginess regarding dwelling places (*āvāsa-mātsarya*)," etc., means desiring to dwell alone in a house or courtyard with complete autonomy.
Regarding what is called "the property of the Sangha given as alms": first, when a donor brings an object and says, "This is my property;

it is what I have bestowed," [the recipient] regards it as a mark of their benevolence. Second, even if it is the donor's property, [the recipient] considers it to have been acquired through their own influence and thus as their own kindness.
Regarding the statement that "this person [is attached] to shared property and so forth": when a donor’s money or goods belong to a collective group, they are called "shared property.
If one still gives rise to stinginess regarding such shared things, how much more so regarding one's own money and goods?

Regarding the phrase "as for the four ways of severing the receipt [of offerings]," this single sentence has two meanings according to the commentary (*shu*). First, it refers to severing the recipient's receipt so that they do not obtain the object;
second, it refers to severing the place of giving so that the donor, though seeking to give, fails to obtain the opportunity to give and does not come forward to offer it.
Furthermore, when a donor who ought to receive a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) is dissuaded from giving, or when a teacher or monk does not obtain the benefit, this is termed "severing."
Regarding the recipient: if one does not interact with others through the distribution [of robes], it is called "not obtaining the gift.

As for the phrase "being born into their family in later lives," this refers to being born among filth, earth, and cesspools, as well as in various evil places—namely, within the hells and among the animals.
To say that one "cannot perform merit" means that it is because one has performed [the act].
To say that one "cannot obtain wealth or profit" means that although the teacher and the monks are entitled to receive such money and goods, one exhorts others not to allow them to do so.
Regarding "slandering virtuous people": fearing that a layperson might give alms, one slanders the virtuous person so as not to allow them to give.
Regarding "the mind is constantly anxious and distressed": furthermore, fearing that a layperson might give in private, one harbors anxiety and distress in the heart.
Regarding the phrase "exalting oneself and deprecating others": it means that one's own mind is attached to self-exaltation while regarding others as inferior.
Regarding the phrase "the arising of much resentment": because one was stingy with the Dharma and failed to teach it during the causal stage, who would be willing to associate with such a person?
Consequently, in the resultant stage, regardless of what body one takes on, wherever one dwells, all will become one's adversaries.

Regarding the statement "to cause others to practice other sutras": if one is unwilling to believe and accept the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, one should preach other Mahāyāna sutras to them, such as the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Prajñāpāramitā*. Question: The "Parable Chapter" states:

"If there is a bhikṣu who, for the sake of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), seeks the Dharma in the four directions, receiving it with palms joined upon his head; yet he only delights in upholding Mahāyāna sūtras and does not accept others..."
One verse [of the sūtra]. What does this mean? Answer: That was spoken in reference to those who uphold this sūtra; now it is spoken in reference to those who lack faith in this sūtra.
Furthermore, it is said because all sūtras gradually transform and turn the minds [of beings]; "all sūtras" refers here to Mahāyāna sūtras. Question:
For what reason does one preach other Mahāyāna sūtras to others? Answer: Within the remaining profound dharmas of the sūtras, these are precisely the Mahāyāna.
This is a sutra. The Two Vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) are coarse and shallow teachings.
"Encountering those of the Two Vehicles" refers to those of fixed lineage belonging to the Two Vehicles, or ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) of indeterminate lineage.
Regarding the formation of the intent of exhortation, the sutra says: "If you all can act in such a manner," and so forth; thus it circulates.
The Lotus Sūtra is that which repays my kindness. The "establishment of various gates" is equivalent to [the teaching] within the other profound dharmas of the Tathāgata.
Regarding the "equality of the first three karmas," the sūtra states: "Having heard the Buddha speak these words, they all rejoiced greatly. This refers to the karma of the mind (*manas-karman*).

The Sūtra says that they bowed their bodies and lowered their heads; this refers to the action of body (*kāyakarman*). The Sūtra says that they spoke aloud together; this refers to the action of speech (*vākkarman*).

The Bodhisattvas respectfully received these three types of actions and vowed to uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, saying: "We pray only that the World-Honored One will no longer harbor any further anxiety."
Thus he spoke three times, saying, "Do not worry any further.
Regarding the fourth major section, which states that "the assembly was filled with joy," there are five distinct types of such joy.

First, in the *Dharmabhāṇaka-parivarta*, the World-Honored One bestowed predictions upon the eight classes of beings, commanding them to uphold this sutra; although he praised both the person and the Dharma...
The Master [Śākyamuni] was already revered by all who heard him, yet their faith remained somewhat slight. Consequently, the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna emerged from his stupa to testify to the sutra.

Furthermore, the World-Honored One had originally summoned the emanations from the ten directions to open the stupa; once the stupa was opened, the teaching was verified and the principle was realized, which is why he rejoiced.
Second, the Bodhisattvas such as Śikhin emerged from below, having originally requested that this sutra be upheld. The world...

First, they were permitted by the World-Honored One to uphold [the teaching] and received his blessing upon their heads; therefore, they rejoiced. Second, within this chapter, the World-Honored One instructed them on the ritual procedures for propagating the sutra:
that if there are those with faith, one should preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for them; if they do not believe or accept it, one should preach other profound teachings for them.
They felt shame before the World-Honored One’s instruction regarding the ritual procedures for our propagation of the sutra, and thus they rejoiced. Third, [they rejoiced because... (text fragment).
Fourth, Śāriputra and the others were filled with joy because they saw that the World-Honored One had entrusted the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* to the various bodhisattvas,
allowing them to have someone to consult as a true and virtuous spiritual friend. Fifth, the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings were filled with joy because,
having heard this single sutra to its conclusion, they were free from calamities and obstacles as the dharma assembly came to an end.

Regarding the phrase "hearing the praise of the supreme Dharma," this refers to the praise found within this chapter, or perhaps the praise found in the preceding section on supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).
Regarding the phrase "pure through a single teaching," it is called "pure" because the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) have been exhausted.
Regarding the statement that "the Dharma taught is pure," it is because the Tathāgata realizes each and every aspect through wisdom; this is why it is pure.
Regarding the statement that "the basis upon which the Dharma is taught" refers to the purity of the fruit attained by those who hear it, or the purity of being free from defilement.

Regarding the statement that the two preceding chapters are "equal" [to the present one]: the entrustment and transmission via supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) have been completed; it is now appropriate to reach the stage of receiving the mandate to propagate [the teaching].

There are six chapters concerning this reception of the mandate, and we shall now first address the power of practicing asceticism (*duṣkaracaryā*) oneself in order to propagate it. Thus [it is said].

This chapter follows; according to the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra*, it clarifies the power of protecting the Dharma. Within this power of protecting the Dharma, since the entrustment has already been presented previously, there is only one remaining aspect of protecting the Dharma.

Although the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja was present in the assembly at that time, he cites his own past practice of asceticism—burning his body and setting his arms on fire—to demonstrate how he upheld the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and benefited those in the assembly. Therefore, this chapter follows.
Regarding the explanation of the title: the Jin translation simply says "The Chapter on the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja," omitting the character for "king" (*rāja*).
Regarding the phrase "healing the eight objects of the senses" (*aṣṭa-viṣaya*), Shè (攝) states: these are the eight kinds—form, odor, taste, touch, earth, water, fire, and wind.
The meaning of "dust" (*rajas*) is, in general, a name for defilement. "Chronic illness" (*ku*)—to explain it precisely—is a long-standing ailment.

This [dust] can give rise to the four objects derived from the four great elements, thereby increasing afflictions; because it has existed since beginningless time, it is called a "chronic illness" (the character *'e* is used interchangeably with *ku*).

Regarding the statement that the seven outflows (*āsrava*) are deep-seated ailments: "outflow" refers to mental afflictions. An-guo cites the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Chengshi lun) and the "Lion Chapter" (*Siṃha-parivarta*) of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, which state:

first, the outflow of views (*dṛṣṭy-āsrava*), referring to the afflictions abandoned through the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*); second, the outflow of cultivation (*bhāvanā-āsrava*), referring to the afflictions abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*);
third, the outflow of the faculties (*indriya-āsrava*), referring to the six faculties such as the eye, because they are capable of generating outflows; fourth, the outflow of evil (*pāpa-āsrava*).

This refers to abusive speech and the like, which can give rise to the outflows (*āsrava*) of affliction; therefore, they are called "evil outflows. Because they can produce outflows, they receive the name "outflow. Huàdù says:

"Alternatively, they are called 'objective-field outflows' (*viṣayāsrava*); that is, the five objective fields such as form and so forth are called 'objective-field outflows' because they can produce outflows.

Regarding the "five proximate outflows," this means that clothing, food, drink, and so forth serve as the causes for the arising of greed; when one becomes attached to them through conditions, outflows arise.

This is called the outflow of intimacy (*upavicāra-āsrava*). Sixth is the outflow of sensation (*vedanā-āsrava*); "sensation" refers to the three unwholesome thoughts. The three unwholesome thoughts are: first, desire; second, hatred; and third, delusion.
Seventh is the outflow of mindfulness (*manasikāra-āsrava*); because it arises from false mindfulness, it is called the outflow of mindfulness.

Among these seven outflows, the first two correctly clarify the essence of the outflows, while the latter five constitute the causes and conditions for the arising of the outflows. Speaking of them collectively by way of their mutual relationship, they are all termed [outflows].
[The term] "outflows" (*āsrava*). Question: What illness does the eighth dust (*rajas*) and the seven outflows represent? Answer:

It represents the Medicine King (*Bhaiṣajyarāja*) as a great medicinal tree, capable of curing the two illnesses of sentient beings—those of body and mind. This signifies the emphasis on the Dharma of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*):

practicing asceticism oneself and exhorting others to propagate it, so that those sentient beings who uphold this sutra may have both illnesses completely exhausted. As the subsequent sutra says: "This Lotus Sutra..."
This is the excellent medicine for the ailments of the people of Jambudvīpa.
Regarding the phrase "the initial inquiry" and so forth: the Sūtra states, "At that time, Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña went to that world," which constitutes the inquiry.
"Wandering" means traveling; [he traveled] within the Sahā world. Next is the request: the Sūtra states, "World-Honored One, this Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja..."
There are several [points]. To explain them briefly: regarding the clarification of the intent behind the request later on, the Sūtra states that the devas, nāgas, and others asked the question.
What was the intent of this request? The answer is: it was so that the devas, nāgas, the eight classes of beings, and all the bodhisattvas who had come might rejoice in their questioning.

Why did the eight classes of beings and the others rejoice? The answer is: because in the preceding "Chapter on Not Disparaging" (*Adhimāna-parivarta*), the Buddha’s own past practices were described.
The practice of not disparaging others. This chapter explains the conduct practiced by Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva; it is for this reason that [the Buddha] rejoices.

Regarding the term "Duke of the Constellations" (Śrīkṣetra): if one asks why he is named Duke of the Constellations, the commentary states: "He has been known as 'Constellation' (宿) since past lives."
Holding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is like a king’s sovereign mastery; thus it is called "King.
Regarding the statement that the *Ratnamegha-sūtra* explains the Bodhisattvas and so forth, this is an interpretation of the name of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja.
Why is he named "Medicine King"? The commentary answers: The *Ratnamegha-sūtra* and other texts refer to roots, stalks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits—these six kinds. Furthermore...
There are those who, upon seeing forms, hearing fragrances, tasting flavors, or experiencing tactile sensations—encountering these ten dharmas—all have their illnesses cured.
As stated in that *Ratnamegha Sūtra*, the Bodhisattva truly manifests as a medicinal tree;

among the suffering of sentient beings, some are healed by eating the roots, some are healed by eating the stems, some are healed by eating the branches, and some are healed by eating the leaves. There are...
Regarding those who recover by eating flowers: there are those who recover after eating fruit; some recover upon seeing the color of the tree;
some recover from smelling the fragrance of the tree; some recover from tasting the flavor of the tree; and some recover from feeling its touch.
Although these ten dharmas are actual manifestations of the Bodhisattva’s true transformations, the Master of the Commentary cites them here to provide a comprehensive synthesis.

The statement that "the Bodhisattva is likewise" constitutes the synthesis [of the analogy]. Because sentient beings possess the disease of afflictions (*kleśa*), the Bodhisattva takes the teachings of the Great Perfections (*mahāpāramitā*) as medicinal trees.
There are those who sustain their life of wisdom by relying on generosity (*dāna*); they are like those whose illness is cured by eating the roots.

There are those who sustain their life of wisdom by relying on ethical discipline (*śīla*); they are like those whose illness is cured by eating the trunk of the tree. There are those who rely on patience (*kṣānti*)...
Those who sustain their life of wisdom by relying on vigor are like those whose illness is cured by eating the branches of a tree.
Those who sustain their life of wisdom by relying on meditative concentration are like those whose illness is cured by eating the flowers of a tree.
Those who sustain their life by relying on wisdom are like those [whose illness is cured] by eating the fruit of a tree.
The illness is cured. Furthermore, there are four dharmas. First, seeing a bodhisattva receiving and upholding the teachings of the six pāramitās, one gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy;
this is like seeing the color of a tree and the illness being cured. Second, hearing the sound of a bodhisattva preaching the six pāramitās, one gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy;
this is like hearing the sound of a tree and the illness being cured. Third, through the dharma of a bodhisattva’s six pāramitās, one attains...

Upon realizing the principle, one gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy; this is like a disease being cured by smelling the fragrance of a tree. There are those who, having realized the six pāramitās, initiate practice;
this is like a disease being cured by tasting the flavor of the tree.
Regarding the statement that there are those who share the same purpose and are equal: there are those who practice the six *pāramitās* together with the Bodhisattva.
It is like touching a medicinal tree to cure a physical illness; if one is nearby, one may see its form, hear its sound, smell its scent, or taste its flavor.
If one is far away and too gravely ill to come, merely touching the roots, trunk, branches, or leaves of the medicinal tree will cause the illness to be cured. This is the medicinal tree.
This serves as a general metaphor for the body of a Bodhisattva; the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) are like the roots, stems, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits.
Regarding the phrase "there are such various [qualities]," the Sūtra says: "World-Honored One, these qualities of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja are so numerous;

please explain them. This question concerns the ascetic practices of Bhaiṣajyarāja during his past causal stages (*hetu-bhūmi*), which the Buddha had not yet described, and which the assembly did not understand.
Śrīkṣema: Why does the Bodhisattva宿王華 (Sudr̥ṣṭarāja) inquire with such difficult practices? He speaks of hundreds of thousands of millions of hard-to-practice asceticisms (*duṣkaracaryā*).

Answer: It is because the Bodhisattva possesses the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*). Question: If that is so, the Bodhisattva only knows [the events of] a hundred kalpas; why not immeasurable kalpas and so forth? Answer:
Because this is a Bodhisattva of a higher stage, not one of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), or perhaps because of the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of a Buddha. Question: What is meant by "name"?

"Several hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of difficult and painful ascetic practices. The commentary answers: "These include such acts as burning the body and setting the arms on fire.
Regarding the statement that there is no evil, the question is raised: How is it that the subsequent sutra says, "At that time, devas, humans, asuras, and others saw him..."?
He was without arms; filled with grief, distress, and sorrow, he spoke these words:
"This Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana was our teacher, yet now his arm has been burned and his body is incomplete. How can you say there is no evil? He replied: "In truth, there is none."
The following passage speaks of the existence [of the assembly] in terms of the manifestation of the retinue’s adornments.

If it were not a manifested transformation (*nirmāṇa*), how could the Reward Land (*vipākakṣetra*) possess a community of śrāvakas as numerous as the sands of seventy-two Ganges Rivers? Question: How do we know it is the Reward Land? Answer:
If it were not the Reward Land, how could the Buddha’s lifespan be forty-two thousand kalpas? Furthermore, it is not a kalpa subject to formation and destruction. How do we know this?

According to the account below, the Bodhisattva Priyadarśana burned his arms and offered his body as an oblation for seventy-two thousand years, yet he was only making offerings to the Buddha Prabhūtaratna.
If one calculates this in terms of years and kalpas, his lifespan was short while the duration of his offerings was long;

thus, we know this is a *vipākakṣetra* (retribution land). If it were a *vipākakṣetra*, how could there be parents? This is because prior to the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), there is still an increase in the power of compassion (*karuṇā*).
Question: If these are bodhisattvas who have increased their compassion, how could their parents possibly be in the Pure Land? Answer: One should say that they appear differently in the same place.
As for the statement regarding the adorned terraces and trees: beneath each and every tree, there are bodhisattvas and śrāvakas seated under them.
Furthermore, beneath each jewel tree there is a jewel terrace. Upon these terraces are ten billion devas performing celestial music.

These terraces are at a distance from the trees equal to the range of an arrow; Jiu says "and Jin says" they are separated by the distance of an arrow, which is like the distance to a shooting target—approximately one hundred and twenty paces, or six hundred chi (this is the correct measure). Jiayuan says two [hundred].
[This is] not [the case].
Regarding what is called "the sūtra-dharma that is taught," the sūtra says: "As for the Bodhisattva Priyadarśana, whether one recites [his name] alone or applies the mind [to him]."
"Xi" (喜) is pronounced with the tone of "qu" (去), meaning "to call.

The phrase "having attained this samādhi, one is able to [manifest] equally" refers to the *Sarvarūpakāyasaṃdarśana-samādhi* (Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Bodies). "Samādhi" means meditative concentration (*samādhi*). It is able to manifest all physical bodies.
It is first attained in the First Ground (*prathamā bhūmi*), mastered in the Eighth Ground, and perfected in equality in the Tenth Ground. It is manifested in the First Ground.
In the first stage, one manifests a hundred types of material bodies; in the second stage, a thousand types; in the third stage, ten thousand types, and so forth. Question:
What is the difference between this and the spontaneously born, unconditioned, mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*)? Answer: That [latter] is a transformation body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*).

This, however, is merely a material body that is the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa-kāya*). Because it arises with meditative concentration as its cause, it is distinct from the transformation body. — An-guo (An Guo)

It is said: Having attained this samādhi, one can manifest [forms] accordingly; this is the body that is the fruit of samādhi. Alternatively, having attained the samādhi, one is able to develop supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and manifest various form-bodies (*rūpakāya*);
these bodies are subsumed under the fruit of supernormal power. Here, supernormal power is the cause, and the arising of the body is the fruit.
The "samādhi of the form-body" (rūpakāya) is a *tatpuruṣa* compound.

Regarding the "ten equalities," these refer to the sixth [manifestation], which is the manifestation in accordance with sentient beings; this is already attained at the first stage (*bhūmi*). Thus, the treatise states:

"When the bodhisattva attains these two paths of seeing (*darśanamārga*), he is born into the family of the Tathāgata, dwells in the Stage of Extreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), and thoroughly masters the Dharma."

Regarding the realms: having realized the equality of truth, he has attained mastery over many hundreds of gateways. These "many hundreds of gateways" refer to the one thousand gates of clear illumination (*vidyā-mukha*).
As stated in [the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*] 37: "First, in a single instant, he can realize a hundred samādhis; second, with the pure divine eye..."
1. He sees a hundred buddha-fields. 2. By means of his supernormal powers, he shakes a hundred buddha-worlds. 3. He is able to emit light that illuminates a hundred buddha-worlds.
4. He manifests five hundred transformed bodies. 5. He brings to maturity a hundred types of sentient beings. 6. He is able to maintain his body and remain for a hundred eons.
7. He knows the events of a hundred past eons. 8. He is well-established in the hundredfold classification of the aggregates, sense bases, and elements.
The Dharma-illumination Gate: The tenth consists of transforming one hundred bodhisattvas of one's own kind to serve as one's retinue.

Regarding the ten kinds of equality: first, equality in the superior feeling of joy; second, equality in the realization of dependent origination; third, equality in the absence of distinct characteristics and non-characteristics.
4. The equality of great compassion that universally delivers and saves; 5. The equality of great compassion that is independent of external conditions; 6.

The equality of manifesting in accordance with what sentient beings delight in; 7. The equality of sentient beings respectfully receiving what is taught; 8. The equality of all worlds being tranquil and of one single flavor;
9. The equality of suffering and pleasure being of one single flavor; 10. The equality of cultivating and planting immeasurable merit to its ultimate fulfillment.
Regarding the phrase "this is the first" at the beginning of the *Jingpingdeng* (Commentary on the *Weishi lun*, fascicle six): it refers to the first [type of] joyful thought of making offerings.
The statement in the sutra, from "attaining this samādhi" up to "the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*," is entirely due to the power of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Regarding the statement "it rained two kinds of *candana*": this refers to taking solid black *candana*, crushing it into fine powder, and raining it down.

Regarding the statement "it rained three kinds of 'this-side-of-the-ocean' [incense]": the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states that there is an incense on this side of the ocean that only the noble ones (*ārya*) can obtain;
now, the Bodhisattva, relying on meditative concentration (*samādhi*), transforms and brings forth this incense.
Regarding the statement in the Sūtra that it is "six *zhū*," the *Jianyao* says: twenty *zhū* constitute one *liǎng*.

Because this [incense] is so precious and noble, it is worth an entire portion of this world-system (*sāhasra-lokadhātu*) for just six *zhū*. Question: Since the sandalwood from the seashore already belongs to this [world-system], why does it further state that it is worth the entire Sahā world?
Answer: According to reason, one should exclude the price of this incense and instead take the value of other various items before [the comparison is made].
At this time, [he offers] six *liù* of incense. It is like a slave holding gold; the value of the gold belongs to his master.

Regarding the statement "anointing the body with fragrant oil, etc.," although he has previously made offerings through supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), his mind is still not satisfied, so he further makes offerings with his own body.
Because the body is impure and subject to decay, he applies various perfumes. The Sūtra says: "Frankincense (*turuṣka*)."
Some say it is simply the fragrance of the breast (nipple). That which is made into bright, clear beads is *turuṣka*. Kumārajīva said: "It comes from the land of the nāgas and devas;
this country does not have it, so it is left untranslated. Others say it is *huamuxiang* (transformed-wood incense), which comes from Guangzhou.
I once questioned a person from there about it, and that person called *turuṣka* "transformed-wood incense. *Pilika* means "to save" or "to spare" (*xingxiu*).
Regarding the phrase "the breath follows the reversal": the various commentaries of An-guo state that the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* says that one type of fragrance can be translated as "touch.
[The text mentions] resinous incense (*jiao-xiang*) and white resinous incense (*bai-jiao-xiang*). Question: If one merely uses fragrant flowers, it constitutes an offering;

why is it necessary to sacrifice one's body? Answer: Among all things valued in the world, none surpasses one’s own body. If one does not sacrifice the body, how can one manifest the depth of one’s sincerity and reverence?
Regarding the statement that "the fifth light shines afar and the sixth is praised by all Buddhas alike," the Sūtra says: "The light shines universally upon eighty billion [worlds]," and so forth.

Question: Since one can immediately attain it through the power of supernatural faculties (*ṛddhibala*) by burning the body, why is it necessary to combine this with the power of vows (*praṇidhānabala*)?
Answer: When fire arises and burns the body, the light shines universally upon eight hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta* worlds.

This is supernormal power (*ṛddhi*). If one were to leave the body to remain for a long time and make offerings for twelve hundred years, it would require the power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-citta*).
Question: Since supernatural powers and the power of aspiration naturally accord with this, why is it said that the inconceivable power of the sūtra is being manifested?

Answer: This refers to the meaning of "supernormal power" as the superior force of the majesty and virtue of the Dharma (*dharma-vaipulya*). Question: According to the Vinaya, burning the body constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense. How can this be reconciled?
"By burning one's arm, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (offense). Does this not mean that the Bodhisattva Xijian has violated the precepts?

The answer is: "Because the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna differ, he does not violate them. Master An said: "If it is according to the Hīnayāna, performing [the act] constitutes a violation, while not performing it constitutes upholding [the precept].

If it is according to the Mahāyāna, performing it constitutes upholding [the precept], while not performing it constitutes a violation. Therefore, the Bodhisattva Precepts state: 'If one does not burn one’s body, arms, or fingers...'"
This constitutes a minor offense (light defilement). However, it does not constitute an offense when done for the sake of transforming and benefiting others;

for example, although the Buddha prohibited bhikṣus from sharing a bed or seat with those who have not received the precepts, on one occasion Śāriputra shared a single elephant with the elder Sudatta without committing an offense.
Regarding the phrase "radiance shining afar": this is brought about by the power of vows, which can extend even a six-foot body; how could such a body possibly shine afar?
Regarding the "praise by comparison with the two," the Sūtra states: "If one were to offer flowers, incense, and necklaces... and so forth, up to "not even reaching [the merit of] it.
The intended meaning is that these do not equal the "inner wealth" (internal offerings).

Regarding the phrase "initial silence," the sutra states: "Having spoken these words, they each remained silent. From this point downward, observing that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not speak is termed "silence.
In reality, however, this refers to the Buddhas of the various directions having finished their praise and then falling silent.
Essential Compendium of the Profound Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra, Scroll Thirty-Four and Scroll Thirty-Five.
Compiled by the Mirror-Water Śramaṇa Xifu.
Regarding the phrase "at a later time," the Sūtra states: "His body burns with fire for twelve hundred years. A question is asked: Why must he remain burning for exactly twelve hundred years?
Saṃghabhadra answers: This indicates the period of the causal stages. Among the thirteen *vihāras*, the first twelve belong to the cause, while the thirteenth *vihāra* belongs to the fruit.
Since the Bodhisattva is in the causal stage, it represents the twelve *vihāras*; therefore, [the duration is] twelve hundred.
Sui Mo said: "The *biao* (manifestation) of this sutra involves the practice of ten dharma-practices, each of which mutually supports the others to form one thousand two hundred merits;
therefore, it endures for one thousand two hundred years. Furthermore, it answers that the lifespan of that Buddha is forty-two thousand kalpas."
The Bodhisattvas were likewise equal in this. The Bodhisattva *Priyadarśana* sought Buddhahood with single-minded devotion for ten thousand two hundred years;
he consumed fragrant oil for another one thousand two hundred years; and the duration for which he burned his body was also one thousand two hundred years.

Calculating these three items together, the total is fifty-six thousand four hundred years. Furthermore, what is the significance of this? *Rou* (糅) says: "This is a manifested body (*nirmāṇakāya*), produced through supernatural power (*ṛddhi*)."

The power of his vows will be fulfilled for twelve hundred years; why then should there be any doubt regarding his longevity? This, too, is not fixed, because he will subsequently be born by transformation (*upapāduka*) into the family of King Śuddhaguṇa.
As for the statement that "this is the first," it refers to his place of birth. The Sūtra says: "All sentient beings, up to those born by transformation. [Question: Why is this so?
Is this [being] one born by transformation (*upapāduka*) among the four modes of birth, or is it one born through transformation from a category of beings born together?
