because the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) is supreme among all vehicles, the white elephant is used as a general metaphor for the One Vehicle (Ekayāna). The *Samantabhadra-dhyāna-sūtra* states: "The six tusks represent the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā);

the four feet represent the four bases of supernormal power (catvāra ṛddhipādāḥ); the seven pillars supporting the ground represent the seven factors of enlightenment (sapta bodhyaṅgāni). For the people of Jambudvīpa, [the three...]"
Because their hindrances were heavy, by the power of wisdom, he manifested a riding elephant. This elephant had six tusks and seven pillars supporting the earth;
beneath each of these seven pillars grew seven lotus flowers. The color of the elephant was a brilliant white, such that crystal or the Snowy Mountains could not be compared to it.
The elephant’s body was four hundred and fifty *yojanas* long and four hundred *yojanas* high. At the tips of its six tusks were six bathing pools.
There is a pond. Within the pond grow four lotuses; within each lotus is a jade maiden who magically produces five *pīpā* lutes from her hands.
She has five hundred musical instruments as her retinue. Upon the trunks of elephants are lotuses, and within these lotuses are manifested Buddhas and manifested Bodhisattvas.
It emits golden light, which illuminates the crown of the elephant’s head (and so forth).
Regarding the phrase “the skillful means of the sound of the Dharma,” the Sūtra states: “The sound of the Dharma” refers to the voice that preaches the Dharma.

“Skillful means” refers to the wisdom of all dharmas arising based on meditative concentration (*samādhi*). This wisdom is called *prayoga-jñāna* (preparatory wisdom). [This] wisdom of concentration and...
Expounding the Dharma is a skillful means.
To speak of the "method" (*naya*) of this single teaching refers to the superior grade of upholding [the sutra] as protection.
When the Sutra speaks of "seeking," it carries the sense of begging; to beg for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is what is meant by "seeking. One must seek the Dharma.

Those who delight in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* are called "those who seek" (*yācanaka*). All types of vows made regarding this sutra and other Mahāyāna teachings that lead upward are collectively termed "seeking. It is because they seek the sutra that they are so named.
Regarding the mention of the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-dhyāna-sūtra* and other texts: this explains the passage in the sūtra concerning "single-minded diligence for twenty-one days.

The *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra* clarifies the method of practice, stating that practitioners who apply themselves from the twenty-one days up to three lifetimes will all attain the vision of the Bodhisattva’s body. (The explanation of the sūtra is concluded.)
Regarding the phrase "the ancient explanation herein": the term "herein" refers to the five types of practices cited previously.
As for the "ancient explanation," this refers to Jiaxiang’s division of the *Puxian Xingfa* (Practices of Samantabhadra) into five chapters, which differs slightly from the wording of the scripture.
Those of superior-grade diligence see the body of Samantabhadra after twenty-one days. Those of middle-superior grade see him after the second seven-day period (fourteen days).
Those of inferior-superior grade see him after forty-nine days. Those of middle-grade diligence see him within one lifetime; those of lower-middle grade see him within two lifetimes;

and those of the lowest-middle grade see him within three lifetimes. This applies up to the fifth grade, where they see him within three lifetimes. However, for those whose diligence is particularly superior, they see him after the first seven days.
It is seen daily. For those of inferior diligence, it is seen after three lifetimes; for those of extreme diligence, it is seen quickly; for those of inferior diligence, it is seen slowly.

As for the statement that "this is also not fixed," the commentary takes this as the primary meaning: within the five stages of the *Samantabhadra-dhyāna-sūtra*, [it may be seen] in one seven-day period.

Those who see it after seven days perceive an inferior body; those who see it after two weeks perceive a slightly superior body; and so on, up to those who see it after three lifetimes, who perceive the most excellent body.
Those who have practiced for a short duration see an inferior body, while those who have practiced for a long duration see a superior body.

The sūtra states "Diyu Aduo" (the character 惰 has the phonetic value *tuò*). Some write it as "Yù" (the character 郁 has the phonetic value *yù*), but this is incorrect. In Sanskrit, the word is *atapa*;
it has been corrupted into "Aduo."

Regarding the third point, "the one who can practice it," the sutra states: "If there is one who receives and upholds [this teaching] until it reaches their head. Here, the "head" refers to the head of the sentient being's mind;

the teaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is called the "hand," and what is spoken from the Buddha’s mouth is called "rubbing. When the teachings of the precepts cover the mind, it is termed "rubbing the head."

Regarding the statement that these are of three grades for the benefit of future times: among the ten dharma-practices, it is taught that by performing the single practice of copying [the scriptures], one may be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
The scriptural text mentions only the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and lacks the word "equal" (等).

The commentator has added the word "equal" to include the Cāturmahārājika Heaven, which was not mentioned in the scripture because the text is concise. These are identical to those who perform the inferior grade of copying. If...
Regarding this, those who perform intermediate-level copying are born in the Yāma Heaven; because the scriptural text is abbreviated, it lacks the word "and so forth" (等).
The Master of the Commentary added the word "and so forth" to include the Paranirmita-vaśavartin and Nirmāṇarati Heavens, as those are likewise for individuals who perform intermediate-level copying.
If one performs superior-level copying, they are born exclusively in Tuṣita Heaven. Therefore, the Commentary states that [those of lower levels] are born in the Four Great Kings' Heaven.

Regarding what is called "the middle grade of upholding": by further adding the practices of upholding, reciting, explaining the meaning, and practicing, it becomes the middle grade, which is superior to the preceding stage.
One is thereby reborn in the Yāma Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, or the Nirmāṇarati Heaven.
Regarding the phrase "because they do not see the Buddha," etc., the *She* (攝) commentary states: One should read "not seeing the Buddha" in conjunction with the "omission of the fruit" in the text.
Thus, it is said that for those of middle capacity, because they do not see the Buddha, the text omits the mention of the fruit of rebirth in heaven.
It asks itself: since those of superior capacity are reborn in heaven and see Maitreya as a Buddha, can one infer that this applies to those of inferior capacity?
Those who practice and are reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven do not see the Buddha; thus, it is said that there is the fruit of rebirth in heaven.

For those of middling capacity, in the case of the Yāma Heaven alone, they do not see the Buddha, yet they attain the fruit of rebirth in the higher heavens. The answer is by way of mutual implication (*anyonyapratibimba*):

since it has been stated that there is a fruit for those of inferior capacity who practice to be reborn in heaven, this implies that there is likewise a fruit for those of middling capacity who practice to be reborn in heaven. Thus, those of middling capacity are reborn in heaven.
They do not see the Buddha. Those born in the lower grade of the shadow realm also do not see the Buddha. "Not seeing the Buddha" and "with Wen [the attendant]" are abbreviated;

there is no fruit [of seeing him], as each is distinct. Read this as two separate sections for interpretation. Both belong to the three middle-grade heavens, where none see the Buddha; they are collectively categorized within the middle grade.
The next two heavens below are likewise the same in not seeing the Buddha. This is why [they are classified under] the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

The Four Heavenly Kings (*Cāturmahārājika*) are subsumed under the lower grade (the commentary on the phrase "not seeing the Buddha" in the upper section). Next, the commentary on the following line states:
"The text is abbreviated and lacks mention of the fruit; it should be read separately. Those of the upper grade are born in Tuṣita Heaven, where the fruit of birth in heaven is taught.

Those of the lower grade, by nature, are born in Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where the fruit of birth in heaven is likewise taught. According to the actual reality, those of the middle grade who uphold [the precepts] are born in Yāma Heaven. Why is this not mentioned?

Regarding the mention of the fruit of rebirth in heaven: the answer is that it was not stated because the scriptural text is abbreviated; thus, it is said that the fruit is absent due to the brevity of the text.
As for the previously mentioned three grades (*triprakāra*) and so forth: in reality, all ten types of Dharma-practice possess these three grades.
If this were not the case, why would the middle grade specify "upholding, reading, reciting, explaining the meaning, and practicing," yet omit these when reaching the superior grade?

This explains the practice. Therefore, we know that this is spoken according to a single characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). If one were to rely on both the single characteristic and the distinct characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), then it would follow that for the middle grade there should be three grades of practice, and for the superior grade as well, there should likewise be three grades of practice explained.
Regarding the statement "the practitioner of the ten dharmas": furthermore, in the *Madhyāntavibhāga*, it is explained that within each of the ten dharma-practices, there are three grades;
this is the first interpretation.

Regarding the statement that "the first eight are [the stage of] hearing and so forth," this is the second interpretation: the first eight constitute the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) as the inferior level; the ninth constitutes the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) as the middling level;
and the tenth constitutes the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) as the superior level.
Regarding the phrase "among the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*)": this distinguishes three grades according to difficulty and ease.

Within the wisdom derived from hearing, copying, making offerings, and giving gifts are considered inferior; listening, reading, and reciting are considered middling; and receiving, upholding, and expounding are considered superior because they are difficult [to accomplish].
(Thus, the three grades are distinguished by difficulty and ease.)
Regarding the statement "furthermore, practicing one, two, or three [perfections] etc.," this refers to the division into three grades based on the quantity [of practice].
Regarding the statement "protecting the name of the three," the Sūtra says: "From long ago until attaining the name of Bodhisattva. Lü states:
Previously, the Buddha spoke of upholding the Sūtra, but did not speak of upholding the name of Samantabhadra; why is it now that he protects it through the power of supernormal faculties?

Regarding those who are able to receive and uphold the name of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva: the answer is that the name "Samantabhadra" is itself the principle realized; for it is not separate from the sūtra.

The underlying meaning is that Samantabhadra is the fruit of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. If one were to interpret it in this way now, it would merely mean that the Buddha himself is protecting the Dharma;
how could it be said that he is empowering bodhisattvas? Therefore, this is simply the Buddha himself protecting those individuals who are dharma-preachers. Samantabhadra...
This refers to the person. One who upholds the name is precisely one who respects the Dharma Master. The Buddha said, "I protect those who respect the Dharma Master and those who practice.
Because it was previously stated that this accords with the conduct of Samantabhadra, protecting the one who upholds the name is equivalent to protecting the person.
Regarding the statement, "To see the Buddha is to realize the principle of consciousness," it is asked: what is meant by "seeing the Buddha"? It is answered:
because one realizes the three bodies (trikāya)—the body of reality (*dharmakāya*), the body of reward (*saṃbhogakāya*), and the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
A person who upholds the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* sees these three bodies of Śākyamuni; all are contained within the teaching of this sutra.

Regarding the phrase "as if hearing the Dharma directly from [the Buddha]," the Sūtra states: "As if hearing it from the Buddha’s own mouth. This means that by merely understanding the meaning of the teaching, one is as if hearing it directly from the Buddha;
it is similar to listening in his presence.

Regarding the statement that "the third is for the sake of making offerings to the Buddha": upholding this sutra constitutes making an offering to the Buddha; this is precisely the offering of the Dharma.

Regarding the statement that "the fourth is for the sake of receiving the Buddha’s praise": because one upholds the sutra, one accords with the Buddha’s mind; since the Buddha rejoices in this, one receives the Buddha’s praise.

Regarding the statement that "the five [factors] are like the Buddha’s hand stroking [the head]," this means the Buddha’s teaching is applied to the mind, just as a hand strokes the crown of the head.

This "strokings of the head" is similar to the bestowing of a prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*); it is also called "receiving" or "entrusting. "Receiving" is precisely the hand of bestowal. As for "marks" (*lakṣaṇa*), it refers to the mutual perception of reflected images.
Regarding the phrase "both mind and field are superior": that which can praise is called the "mind," and that which is praised is the "field.

Because both are universally superior and because it is capable of providing authentic records, the scriptures of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) are not esteemed for their excellence; thus, those who study the teachings of the non-Buddhists do not delight in drawing near to them.

Regarding the statement "to speak of faults": if a patient asks whether there truly are faults, what is wrong with speaking of them? The answer is: if one truly upholds the sutras and there truly are faults, they still must not be spoken of.
One should compensate for faults with merit and compensate for clumsiness with diligence; if one were to speak of them, [it would be improper].
Because he obstructed the upholding of the sutras and the work of conversion, and his body possessed blemishes, his person was consequently afflicted with white leprosy.
As for the ten ailments mentioned in the text: first, disease of the gums; second, disease of the teeth; third, sparse teeth; fourth, missing teeth;
fifth, ugly lips; sixth, a flat nose; seventh, [disease of] the hands; eighth, crooked feet; ninth, squinting eyes; and tenth, a foul-smelling body.
The character for "liǎo" (繚) is pronounced with the *lì* rhyme (the opposite of *xiǎo*, meaning "to encircle").

Regarding the term "inner vision" (內視), "mèi" (昧) means to look. In ancient times, the character for "vision" (*shì*) was used such that "inner vision" was called "lài" (睞). There is also the character "nì" (眤) which has the same meaning.
The pronunciation of "tí" (提) as "zhī" (知) is incorrect.

Regarding the statement that the assembly obtained benefit at that time: it is asked, when the sutra says "having paid homage, they departed," did the three roots, the fourfold assembly, and the eight classes of beings all rise and depart?
Furthermore, as for the entrustment in the following "Chapter on Entrustment" (*Parīndanā-parivarta*), to whom was it entrusted? Answer:

This is because the translators placed the "Chapter on Entrustment" after the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers" (*Ṛddhi-parivarta*). Therefore, at the very end of this chapter, they conclude the entire text of the sutra. Thus [the assembly departed].

To say that one should "pay obeisance and depart" is certainly not the word of the Buddha; why then trouble oneself with such confusion? The preceding section concludes the explanation of the seven fascicles of the sutra, and the main body of the commentary (the *zhengzongfen*) is finished.
Hereafter, the "circulation portion" (*liutongfen*) of the commentary will be elucidated.
Regarding the phrase "Ji et al. (基以等): this is the name of the author of the sub-commentary (*shu*). It is improper for later generations to refer to him by his personal name;
therefore, it is said that he is addressed by his courtesy title. "Tán" (談) means to speak; "yóu" (遊) means to travel or to transform through teaching;

and "tú" (徒) refers to a guest-retinue. A dwelling where guests reside is called a "tú. Thus, the author of the sub-commentary says that at the time of his speaking and traveling, he was residing as a guest.
"Boling" is the name of a commandery; it is the present-day Dingzhou. It was the place where the author of the commentary (*śāstra*) composed his work.

Regarding the terms "monastics and laity": "monastics" refers to the clergy, while "laity" refers to worldly persons. "Encouraged" means to urge one forward. "Vainly" means "without"; this is the author’s own modesty.
At that time, the teachers, monastics, and laypeople requested me—a person of no merit or achievement—to deliver a lecture.

Furthermore, the "Rhapsody on Literature" (Wen fu) says: "To set tasks for the void and demand the presence [of substance], to harmonize with silence and seek sound"—these words regarding the task of the void originated from this [text] and gave rise to the discourse on meaning and language.
Both the monastic and the secular have commanded me to task the void; this is derived from that source. As for "cultivation" (xiu), it refers to cultivating the circular [nature of reality];
as for "following" (cong), it means being able to follow the ancient meanings. [If one cannot do so,] that is precisely what is meant by being unable to follow the various ancient principles.
"Speaking of the 'ancient meanings' refers to the commentaries and interpretations of Jiaxiang, Jiguō, and others. 'Compiled by himself' means compiled from these [sources].

Regarding the phrase 'drafted in the evening and discussed in the morning,' this means that after completing the work at night, he would present it for discussion the following day; 'at the conclusion' means that as soon as the lecture on the sutra was finished, the composition of the commentary was likewise completed."
Regarding the term *liǎn* (褊): it refers to the narrow edges of a garment; it denotes narrow clothing (*biǎnzhǐ yīshāng*). It also means to weave or to be small.
The intended meaning is that when the width and length of a woven bolt (*xiāofú*) are narrow and short, it is called *biān*. People say things such as "the family way is *biān* and short.
*Lǐ* (理) refers to principle or doctrine; *cí* (詞) refers to words or teaching.

Regarding the phrase "the meaning of the sūtra is profound and subtle" (*shenze*): "meaning" (*yi*) refers to the signified sense; "profound" (*shen*) means deep and hidden, because the principle being signified is deep.
Lu says: "To reach for an object with the hand but not grasp it is called 'probing' (*tan*). To probe but not reach it is called 'fishing' (*diao*).
To fish but not reach it is called 'subtlety' (*ze*)."

"To say that 'crude words form a radiant praise' refers to the composition of this commentary (*śāstra*). The repeated use of terms such as 'jing-jing' and 'piao-piao' all describe an appearance of extreme trepidation and awe.
To speak of the 'Mysterious Source' (*xuanzong*) refers to its profound purport."

Regarding the phrase "寧輒" (nìng zhé) and so forth: "援" (yuán) means to cite; "據" (jù) refers to relying upon the teachings. Thus, "專輒援引教據" (zhuān zhé yǎo lín jiào jù) means to exclusively and arbitrarily cite and rely upon the scriptural authorities.
The intended meaning is that whatever evidence or basis is presented must all be supported by authentic textual passages.
To speak of "silence, stillness, and non-action" does not refer to the non-action of True Suchness (*tathatā*); it merely refers to the state of non-doing.
To speak of "employing [the mind] for a while" is the meaning of striving and advancing by the mad; few people advance toward the great task, yet they act with the madness of such striving.

To distinguish "simplicity" (*jian*) from "affairs," I now compose this eulogy for this sutra, titled *Shenkuang* (Expressing Simplicity). "Simplicity" is a term of self-humility. As the *Lunyu* says:
"Come back, come back, you young men of my school! You are wild and simple, yet your compositions are elegant. "Elegant" refers to making progress;
"simplicity" is the Great Way itself.
*Fahua Xuanzan Yaoji*, Scroll Thirty-Five (End). This work consists of thirty-five fascicles.
Over the course of several years, I have exerted my humble efforts to prepare the paper and materials and to encourage calligraphers to complete the transcription.
By virtue of this merit, I pray that I and all others may encounter the Great [Dharma] in every birth and throughout all lifetimes.
My Son, the Sage Emperor: wherever you may establish karmic connections with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, you must enshrine it within the Great Scripture Repository of Hōryū-ji.
It shall not be brought out from the temple gates; it must never be allowed to leave for other places.
The twenty-third day of the seventh month in the first year of Kōjō, the Xin-you year.
